## 732 — a bench row still named "TS only" eight items after native landed, and depth 5 priced at 878x and then taken back out

**ANNOTATION FIX + PRICING. No engine change.** Item 731's table listed depth 5 of the trail closed
form (695) as the one remaining tick-sized optimization, so I went to price it. The pricing worked;
what I found on the way was worse than what I went looking for.

### The depth-4 row was describing the state item 692 left behind

`bench.ts`'s depth-4 quantified row said, in its own comment:

> _"ts 3365.6 -> 17.7ms (190x) while ffi still enumerates at ~82ms … **Native is the open half.**"_

and the row was NAMED `count 4-hop quantified [TRAIL, TS only]`. **Item 693 closed the native half**
— ffi 82.4 → 10.5, 7.8x, with wasm at 12.9 — and the annotation outlived it by eight items. Three
separate assertions (the name, "still enumerates at ~82ms", "native is the open half") all describe
a world that stopped existing one item later.

This is the stale-claim failure `CLOSED.md` exists to prevent, sitting in the place a reader is
MOST likely to trust it: the measurement harness itself, next to the query, where you go precisely
to find out what a shape costs. A reader pricing native trail work would have read "native is the
open half" and gone to build something that exists.

### And its figures were at an N the row does not run

Second defect, subtler and the one I nearly propagated. The quoted figures (ts 3365.6 → 17.7, ffi
82.4) are item 692's table at **20,000 vertices**. `bun run bench` defaults to **200,000**. So a
reader running the row as documented reads ts 264.6 and ffi 122.7 and cannot reconcile either with
the comment — which is how I started, and for a few minutes I was looking at a 15x TS "regression"
that was the fixture size.

Both N are now in the comment, labelled, with the instruction to pass `BENCH_N=20000` to compare.

| 20,000 vertices | depth 3 | depth 4 | recorded                 |
| --------------- | ------: | ------: | ------------------------ |
| ts              |    13.6 |    18.7 | 13.5-14.0 / 18.3 (692) ✓ |
| ffi             |     1.4 |    10.6 | 1.4-1.5 / 10.5 (693) ✓   |

Every recorded figure reproduces. **Both closed forms still fire and neither engine has regressed**
— which is the thing a stale annotation makes impossible to check, because you cannot tell a
regression from a comment that was never true.

The row is renamed to `count 4-hop quantified [TRAIL]`. Renaming on a status change is this row's
own precedent — item 692 renamed it from "unbuilt" to "TS only" — and nothing outside the audit
references the old name.

### Depth 5, priced: 878x on ts, 38x on ffi

Native refuses depth 5 in the `deep_trail` gate and says why (`u4` is four disjoint cases; what
they need from the adjacency is unpriced, item 686's rule). So depth 5's enumeration cost IS the
prize for deriving `u4`. I added a depth-5 row on item 692's precedent — that row was carried as
"unbuilt" before the formula existed, which is what made 692/693 measurable the day it landed:

| 20,000 vertices | depth 4 (closed form) | depth 5 (enumerated) |    ratio |
| --------------- | --------------------: | -------------------: | -------: |
| ts              |               18.6 ms |          16,325.9 ms | **878x** |
| ffi             |               10.6 ms |             402.9 ms |  **38x** |

That is the lever's CEILING and not its value — a depth-5 closed form lands somewhere above depth
4's cost, not at it. But it also prices the shape for anyone who writes `->{5}` today, and 16.3
seconds for a counting query is worth knowing independently of whether `u4` is ever derived.

### Then I took the row back out, because the measurement said to

Item 692's precedent does not transfer, and the reason is the number itself. Unbuilt depth 4 cost
82 ms on ffi. Unbuilt depth 5 costs **16.3 seconds on ts at a tenth of the bench's default N** — so
at `BENCH_N=200000` across five reps it would add something like a quarter-hour to a sweep whose
slowest row today is 13.2 s in total.

**A regression sweep nobody runs because it takes a quarter-hour catches nothing.** The row's job is
to make a regression visible, and a row that makes the sweep unusable is a net loss at that job even
though it measures something real. So the figures live in the bench's comment and in this item, with
the instruction to add the row back temporarily to re-price — which is the operation that is
actually wanted, once, rather than five times per sweep forever.

### 🛑 Two things I nearly shipped wrong, both in the same ten minutes

**I wrote the depth-5 figures into the comment before measuring them.** Placeholders — "ts 1177.9,
ffi 354.4" — extrapolated from depth 4 by the branching factor, formatted exactly like a
measurement. The real ts figure is 16,325.9, off by 14x. One commit earlier (item 731) I recorded
that a synthesis is where a remembered figure looks most authoritative; an invented figure in a
comment block is the same failure with a shorter fuse, and the only reason it did not ship is that
measuring was the next step anyway.

**And I wrote `s * 1103515245` in f64 in the throwaway fixture generator** — item 702's defect,
precisely, the one I added to CLAUDE.md's "before trusting a number" list two days ago, in a script
whose purpose was to price a lever. Caught before running it, and the fix was not to repair the LCG
but to delete the script: `bench.ts` already has the fixture, and writing a second one was the
mistake that made room for the first. **CLAUDE.md says to look before building a bench; the same
applies to its fixture.**

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0. No Rust change, so no cargo gate applies.

## 733 — TS's 40x gap on enumerated var-length counting is NOT allocation: the wrapper objects are 11% of it

**SHIPPED (TypeScript), 1.11x at depth 5 — and the hypothesis it was built to test is REFUTED.**
Item 732 priced depth-5 trail enumeration at ts 16,325.9 ms against ffi 402.9 (20,000 vertices), a
**40.5x** ratio where depth 4 reads 1.77x and depth 3 reads 9.6x. Depth 5 is the first depth
NEITHER engine has a closed form for, so at depth 5 both engines run the same algorithm and the
ratio is a claim about TS's enumeration rather than about a missing formula. Item 573's precedent
says a ratio that size may be algorithmic rather than a layout ceiling, so it was worth diagnosing.

### What the enumeration was paying per hop

`trailEnds`'s flat walk pushed one frame per extending hop, each holding
`expandFilteredArr(...)` — an **array of `{edge, node}` wrapper objects**, built by iterating
`expand`'s generator. At degree 5 and depth 5 that is ~780 frames a source, so at 20,000 sources
~15.6M arrays and **~78M wrapper objects** — and the pair exists only to carry a vertex that a
directed single-label hop can derive from the edge (`fwd ? edge.to : edge.from`, which is precisely
what `expand`'s own fast path computes).

So `flatAdj` returns parallel arrays: `edges` always, `nodes` only when the direction makes the
neighbour underivable (`both`, a label set, an inline predicate). The fast case copies the label
bucket with `Array.from` — no generator, no wrappers. The frame shape stays monomorphic.

### 🛑 The measurement refutes the hypothesis

| 10,000 vertices, depth 5 | before                   | after                    |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------ |
| ts                       | 8537.0 / 8124.7 / 8173.8 | 7346.1 / 7629.9 / 7563.3 |
| ffi (CONTROL)            | 196.9                    | 199.2                    |

**1.11x on mins, three alternated rounds, DISJOINT** — and the ffi column is the control a TS
change cannot reach, flat across it. But 1.11x of a 40x gap means **~90% of that gap is not
allocation at all.** The change is kept for the 11%; it is not the answer to the ratio, and the
entry says so in the code as well as here, because the next reader to see a 40x gap and an
allocation in a loop will form the same hypothesis I did.

On every SHALLOW standing row it is **neutral with overlapping ranges**, three rounds each:

| 20,000 vertices                    | before (min) | after (min) |
| ---------------------------------- | -----------: | ----------: |
| `count var-length 1-2 hops`        |         12.5 |        12.3 |
| `… 1-2 hops + end filter`          |         12.1 |        12.6 |
| `count var-length 1-3 hops [WALK]` |         10.5 |        10.5 |

That is the honest shape of the result: the win needs depth-5 path volume to show at all, and the
rows that DO guard this code path cannot see it. Those three rows are the standing coverage — I had
assumed there was none and was wrong; they exercise `trailEnds` at depths 1-3.

**The named suspect for the remaining 90%** is the generator chain per emitted path — ~31M ends at
depth 5 crossing several `yield*` layers, against `expand`'s own note pricing a resume in this
pipeline at ~40 ns. **Unmeasured. It is a suspect, not a finding**, and the next tick can ablate it.

### Teeth, by mutation: three mutants, three caught

| mutant                                         | gql unit suite | the seven fuzzers |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------: | ----------------: |
| the derived neighbour reversed (`fwd` swapped) |    **47 fail** |                 — |
| the label bucket's order reversed              |    **32 fail** |           13 pass |
| the fast path applied DESPITE an inline pred   |    **31 fail** |           13 pass |

The reversed-order mutant passing the fuzzers is **correct behaviour, not a gap**: row order is
unspecified and they compare multisets, so a reordered enumeration is not a divergence. (The unit
suite catches it because it asserts specific orders.)

### 🛑 But the third mutant survives 60,000 generated queries, and that IS a gap

Dropping an inline edge predicate ADDS rows, so a multiset comparison should see it. It does not —
**13 pass under seeds 11, 2026 and 77731, 20,000 queries each.** The abbreviated arm does generate
the shape (`-[e:E WHERE e.w > 2]->`, and `relHasInlinePred` is `hasPredicate(rel.pred)`, which a
bracket `WHERE` sets), so the shape is drawn and still nothing diverges.

**I verified the gap and did NOT diagnose it.** The leading suspect is that `e.w > 2` is satisfied
by every `E` edge in the fuzz fixture, making the filter vacuous — which is the exact class this
file already documents for its endpoint label (_"a filter that excludes nothing cannot show that
the predicate is applied at all, and `(b:T)` over this fixture is exactly that"_). If so the fix is
a `w` value the predicate excludes, not a generator change. Recorded as the next step rather than
asserted, because a guessed cause in a coverage note is worse than a measured gap with no cause.

Correctness today is not in question: the unit suite catches all three mutants. What is missing is
the CROSS-ENGINE guard on the abbreviated var-length path's edge predicate.

### What I got wrong on the way

I wrote my new doc block **above `expandFilteredArr`'s own doc comment**, orphaning it from its
declaration — the same splice that cost a `#[must_use]` its attribute earlier this session. Caught
by reading the grep output rather than by a gate, since neither lint nor tsc has an opinion about
which declaration a comment belongs to.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0; `packages/gql` 2585 pass 0 fail; the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail.
No Rust change, so no cargo gate applies.

## 734 — two spellings of a per-hop edge predicate take different code, and the fuzzer drew only the one that does not reach `rel.pred`

**FUZZER FIX, teeth verified both ways. No engine change.** Item 733 found that a mutant making
`trailEnds`'s flat walk skip inline-predicate filtering survives **60,000 generated queries across
three seeds**, and recorded the gap as verified but undiagnosed, with a leading suspect. **The
suspect was wrong**, which is the reason it was recorded as a suspect.

### The suspect, and why it was wrong

I guessed the fuzz fixture's `e.w > 2` was satisfied by every `E` edge, making the filter vacuous —
the class the file already documents for its endpoint label. The fixture says otherwise: the `E`
edges carry `w` of **2, 5 and 9**, so `e.w > 2` excludes `e1` and keeps two. Not vacuous.

### What it actually is, measured rather than reasoned

Three spellings on the fixture, against the clean engine and then against the mutant:

| hop spelling             | clean | mutant |
| ------------------------ | ----: | -----: |
| `-[e:E WHERE e.w > 2]->` |     2 |  **2** |
| `-[:E {w: 5}]->`         |     1 |  **4** |
| `-[:E]->` (CONTROL)      |     4 |      4 |

So a **bracket `WHERE` does not populate `rel.pred` at all** — it is applied by a different
mechanism — while the **inline property map is** `rel.pred`, which is what `relHasInlinePred`
(`hasPredicate(rel.pred)`) tests and what `flatAdj` branches on. Two spellings of "filter this hop's
edge", one code path each.

And `genAbbrevQuantified` drew `-[e:E]->`, `-[e:E WHERE e.w > 2]->` and `<-[e:E WHERE e.w >= 0]-` —
**bracket `WHERE`s only, never a property map.** So every predicate that arm has ever generated
missed the branch, and the abbreviated quantified form's `rel.pred` filtering had no cross-engine
guard since the arm was added at item 238.

This is the repo's own named bug class, in the fuzzer rather than the planner: _"the planner
recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned for another that meant exactly the same thing."_
Here the GENERATOR knew one spelling and the code it was meant to guard keyed off the other. A
coverage gap of this shape is invisible by construction — the arm's counters say the shape was
generated and it was, just not the shape that reaches the branch.

### The fix, and its teeth proved in both directions

Two property-map hops added to the existing `pick` — not a band of their own, for item 256's reason
(no boundary moves, the arm's counters keep their meaning).

| the same mutant, three seeds | before this item  | after                 |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
| seeds 11 / 2026 / 77731      | 1 pass, 0 fail ×3 | **0 pass, 1 fail ×3** |

Clean, the widened generator passes all three seeds, so the new shape is NOT a divergence — native
and TS agree on an inline property map over an abbreviated quantified hop. **This is the check that
makes the fix worth anything**: a generator widened without re-running the mutant it was widened for
is a test whose teeth were never verified, which CLAUDE.md calls worse than no test because it is
believed.

### What generalises

Item 733 recorded this gap with a cause it did not verify, and the cause was wrong. The entry said
so explicitly — _"a guessed cause in a coverage note is worse than a measured gap with no cause"_ —
and that framing is what made this item twenty minutes of work instead of a fixture change that
would have fixed nothing. The gap was real and verified; only the explanation was speculation, and
keeping those two apart in the record is what let the speculation be cheaply discarded.

The method that found it: run each spelling against the mutant and watch which COUNT moves. A
spelling that answers identically on both arms does not reach the code under test, however much it
looks like it should.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0; the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail, plus the three seeded differential
runs above. No engine change, so no cargo gate applies.

## 735 — the depth-5 walk is 20% of its own query: ~80% is downstream of the yield, measured by ablation

**DIAGNOSIS. No behaviour change; the only edit is the attribution written at the code.** Item 733
shipped a 1.11x and recorded that ~90% of TS's 40x gap on depth-5 enumeration is NOT allocation,
naming the generator chain as a suspect and marking it **unmeasured**. This measures it.

### Reachability first, positively, because a null means nothing without it

A `throw` at `trailEnds`'s flat-walk entry:

| query   | result                                    |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `->{3}` | answers — closed form, never enters       |
| `->{4}` | answers — closed form, never enters       |
| `->{5}` | **THREW** — this walk IS the depth-5 path |

That is the check items 721-723 cost three ticks to skip: _instrumenting one function tells you it
did not run; it does not tell you what ran instead._ It also confirms from the outside that the
depth-3 and depth-4 closed forms are the ones answering, which is what item 732's row comment
claims from the inside.

### The ablation

Count each end in place of yielding it, so the walk runs in full — stack, marks, `flatAdj`, the
budget check — and nothing above it does. The counter accumulates into a module-scope sink so it
cannot be eliminated.

| 10,000 vertices, depth 5   | rounds                   |        min |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------: |
| full pipeline              | 7477.9 / 7795.1 / 7490.4 |     7477.9 |
| walk only, `yield` ablated | 1462.4 / 1462.2 / 1466.6 | **1462.2** |

**5.11x.** The walk is **~20%** of the query and **~80% is downstream of the yield.** The ablated
arm is also remarkably stable (±0.3% across rounds) which is itself a signal: the walk is doing
regular, predictable work, and the variance in the full arm lives above it.

### What this does and does not attribute

The ablation removes **three things at once** — the `yield*` chain up through `walkSegments`,
`matchNode` per end, and the counting sink. So 80% belongs to that BUNDLE, and which of the three
dominates is still open. The next ablation is the inner `yield* walkSegments` in the quantified
branch, which would split "the chain" from "`matchNode` + the sink".

Saying "the generator chain is 80%" would be exactly the overclaim item 710 warns about — an
ablation is a counterfactual, but only for the thing it actually removes, and this one removes a
bundle.

### The number that reframes the target

**TS's bare walk alone — 1462.2 ms — is still 7.3x native's ENTIRE pipeline (199.2 ms).** So the
~37-40x decomposes into roughly 7x inside the walk and a further ~5x multiplier from the row
pipeline above it. Both halves are real and the larger one is the pipeline, which is the opposite of
where I started looking two items ago (the per-hop allocation, now priced at 11% of the whole).

That also prices the ceiling honestly for anyone tempted by a depth-5 closed form: a formula
removes the walk, which is the 20% — the 80% above it is paid by any shape that emits the same
number of rows, and a `count(*)` fast path that never materializes them is a different lever
entirely.

### Why there is no code change

Nothing here is shippable. The walk is already cheap relative to its consumer, so making it cheaper
again — which is what item 733 did for 11% — cannot reach the 80%. Recording the bound is the
product: it retires a vague suspect, puts a measured number against the real target, and stops the
next pass from re-deriving the allocation hypothesis for a third time.

Gates: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. Comment-only edit; the engine, the
bench and the probe are all back to their committed state (`git status` clean before the comment
was written, and the temp row and probe file are gone).

## 736 — every var-length COUNT takes a shortcut, so item 733's "neutral on the standing rows" was the unreachability null again

**CORRECTION + the missing bench row + the second ablation.** Item 735 split 20/80 between the walk
and everything above its `yield`. This splits the 80, and in checking which rows could see any of it
found that item 733 drew the conclusion items 721-723 exist to prevent — in the entry that cited
them.

### The second ablation: the 80% is not one thing

Keeping `trailEnds`'s yield and `matchNode` but cutting the recursion to the next segment and
everything above it, three rounds, 10,000 vertices, depth 5:

| arm                                 |        min |  share of full |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------: | -------------: |
| walk only (item 735)                |     1462.2 |           ~20% |
| + `trailEnds`'s yield + `matchNode` | **3545.5** |      ~28% more |
| full pipeline                       |     7477.9 | remaining ~53% |

So the largest single component is the recursion plus the consuming pipeline at **~53%**, with the
yield-and-match layer at ~28%. No hot spot: three comparable thirds, which is why no small change
here has moved it.

### 🛑 The correction: those rows cannot reach the code item 733 changed

Item 733 reported itself _"neutral with overlapping ranges"_ on `count var-length 1-2 hops`,
`+ end filter` and `1-3 hops [WALK]`, and said — correcting what it called an earlier wrong
assumption — that these rows _"exercise `trailEnds` at depths 1-3"_. They do not. Throwing at the
flat walk's entry and running each query verbatim:

| query                                        | result                 |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `->{1,2}(b) RETURN count(*)`                 | **answers** — shortcut |
| `->{1,2}(b WHERE b.n > 4) RETURN count(*)`   | **answers** — shortcut |
| `MATCH WALK ->{1,3}(b) RETURN count(*)`      | **answers** — shortcut |
| `MATCH WALK ->{1,5}(b) RETURN count(*)`      | **answers** — shortcut |
| `->{1,2}(b) RETURN b.n`                      | **ENUMERATES**         |
| `->{3}(b) RETURN b.n`, `{4}`, `{5}`, `{1,5}` | **ENUMERATES**         |
| `->{5}(b) RETURN count(*)`, `{1,5}` count    | **ENUMERATES**         |

**A `count(*)` is shortcut up through `{4}`; a ROW-RETURNING var-length query enumerates at EVERY
depth.** All three standing rows are counts, so none of them could move whatever that change did.
The overlapping ranges were guaranteed by construction, not measured evidence of no harm — and the
entry presented them as the latter while quoting 721-723 at the reader. **The same null, one item
later, by the same mechanism: a row that cannot reach the code reports no effect.**

That also means item 733's self-correction was backwards. Its original instinct — that this path had
no standing coverage — was right; the "correction" introduced the error.

### The row that was missing, and what the corpus was blind to

A row-returning var-length query is an entirely ordinary shape and the corpus had **none** — every
var-length row is a count, which is exactly the family that routes around this code. So the ~80%
overhead item 735 measured sits on a common shape with no standing guard at all.

Added: `project var-length 1-3 hops + start filter [ENUMERATES]`, start-filtered to ~N/90 sources
(`age` is `i % 90`) so it is ~344k rows rather than 31M, projecting `y.age`, which is PRESENT on
every node (item 726's trap). **Verified positively that it reaches the walk** — the throw fires on
it and on none of the four counts. It reads **ts 219.3 against ffi 26.9, 8.16x** at the default N.

### Item 733 re-measured on a row it can actually reach: no win

Eight readings an arm, two alternated blocks, ffi flat at 26.2-27.2 throughout:

| arm    | readings                                            | median |   min |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------- | -----: | ----: |
| before | 230.2 224.1 200.7 230.1 231.3 230.1 231.5 **149.1** | ~230.1 | 149.1 |
| after  | 220.2 219.6 221.1 222.7 223.8 221.8 220.6 223.8     | ~221.5 | 219.6 |

**~1.04x at the median, and no win worth claiming.** The before arm is BIMODAL — a 1.55x spread with
sporadic fast readings the after arm never produces — while the after arm is unimodal within 2%.
Comparing mins would read as a 1.35x REGRESSION, and that would be cherry-picking the old arm's best
outlier against the new arm's tight distribution; reporting the median as a win would be the mirror
of it. The disciplined statement is that this row cannot separate the two, and the bimodality itself
is unexplained and recorded with its numbers.

Item 733's 1.11x at depth 5 stands — tight, disjoint, with a flat control. It simply does not
generalise to the shape users write, and nothing in that entry had established that it would.

### 🛑 And the red CI was not mine: a recorded intermittent divergence

Item 735's CI failed on `differential fuzz … 20000 random queries render byte-identically`, which
looked like item 734's widened generator finding a real divergence. It is not.

`CLOSED.md` already records it (items 259, **279**): the boolean-context asymmetry where TS raises
`E_INVALID_VALUE` and native answers NON-EMPTY rows, a direction the divergence registry refuses to
excuse **on purpose**, so the fuzzer fails rather than declaring it — _"intermittently: 12 pass / 1
fail on a random seed, `FUZZ_SEED=3668867883`"_. That seed replays on HEAD today, verbatim:

```
MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE (n.x AND (0.0 IN [1e21, n.s])))
  RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y
    ts:  err E_INVALID_VALUE
```

And the evidence that it is not item 734's shape: **36 random-seed runs clean** (6 + 30), and item
734's CI passed on byte-identical fuzzer code. So a push to this repo is intermittently red by a
deferred conformance decision, and the next person to see it will suspect their own change, as I
did. **The entry that matters is at `CLOSED.md`:120** — read it before debugging a red differential
fuzzer.

This also corrects item 734 on a smaller point: it said three clean seeds showed the new shape "is
NOT a divergence". Three seeds show very little; 36 show more, and the right statement is that the
shape has not diverged in 720,000 generated queries.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0; the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail, plus 36 seeded differential runs.

## 737 — skipping the terminal generator frame: BUILT, measured NEUTRAL, REVERTED — and the full-sweep A/B invented a 1.66x regression

**REFUTED, with the methodology finding worth more than the lever.** Item 736 priced the
recursion-plus-pipeline third of a depth-5 walk at ~53% and added the first bench row that reaches
the enumerating path. This is the obvious lever against that third, and it does not survive.

### The lever

On the final segment, `walkSegments(… index + 1 …)` does exactly one thing: construct a generator,
take the `index >= segments.length` branch, yield one binding, return. A `yield*` delegation plus a
generator **per emitted row**, paid by every pattern — a one-segment `MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b)` as much
as a quantified walk, because the terminal frame is always the last one. So: hoist
`index + 1 >= pattern.segments.length` out of the loop and reproduce the base case inline at both
call sites, `pathAcc` and `pathVar` included so the emitted value and its sequence position are
unchanged.

Correctness held throughout: `packages/gql` 2585 pass 0 fail, the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13
pass 0 fail.

### 🛑 But a full-sweep A/B reported a 1.66x REGRESSION that does not exist

The first design ran the FULL corpus per arm. On its single completed after-arm,
`query: project the element + materialize` read **44.8 against the clean arm's 27.0 and 26.5** — a
1.66x regression on a row the change barely touches, which is exactly the shape
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` warns about (a hot-path edit handing an unrelated query a new slow
mode). I was ready to revert on that basis.

Isolated, that row does not move:

| 3 alternated rounds, isolated       | clean              | after              |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ |
| `project the element + materialize` | 25.2 / 24.9 / 25.5 | 24.7 / 25.0 / 25.7 |
| `project the element [ts lazy]`     | 6.9 / 6.8 / 6.9    | 7.2 / 6.7 / 6.8    |

**The regression was an artifact of the instrument.** A full sweep per arm is the wrong tool for a
per-row question: rows interfere, its own ffi column drifts ~10% between arms on a TS-only change,
and the arms themselves took 5 to 15 minutes each, so the comparison drifts with the machine. The
isolated run answered both questions in eight minutes for all six arms — faster AND tighter, which
is not the usual trade.

### And the lever itself is neutral

| 3 alternated rounds                          | clean                 | after                 | controls |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- | -------- |
| `project var-length 1-3 hops … [ENUMERATES]` | 131.9 / 114.0 / 128.3 | 122.7 / 89.3 / 116.4  | flat     |
| `count var-length 1-2 hops` (UNREACHABLE)    | 177.1 / 177.4 / 174.6 | 177.6 / 175.1 / 175.4 | ✓        |
| `… + end filter` (UNREACHABLE)               | 150.3 / 148.2 / 150.0 | 153.3 / 145.1 / 148.0 | ✓        |
| `… 1-3 hops [WALK]` (UNREACHABLE)            | 198.2 / 142.5 / 142.8 | 144.4 / 143.1 / 144.1 | ✓        |

The after arm wins **3/3 pairs at 1.08x, 1.28x and 1.10x** — suggestive, and under a sign test worth
p = 0.125, which is nothing. The ranges OVERLAP, and that row's own **ffi column swings 1.33x
(24.0-31.9)** across rounds while native did not change, so the row cannot resolve a 10% effect at
three rounds.

By this repo's own precedent that is not a win: item 726 reverted an all-equal short-circuit at
1.05x against controls moving 1.06-1.18x, and item 704 refuted a 1.2M-allocation change at 1.02x
against a 1.02x control. Reverted, and the cost it would have carried is recorded too — the base
case duplicated into two call sites, which is the kind of thing a 10% claim has to earn.

The three unreachable controls are the part that worked. Item 736 established WHICH rows cannot
reach this code, and that knowledge turned three previously-useless rows into real controls: flat in
every round, which is what makes the enumerating row's movement interpretable at all.

### What generalises

- **A per-row question deserves a per-row instrument.** The full sweep did not just cost 50 minutes
  of wall clock; it produced a confident wrong answer (1.66x) that an eight-minute isolated run
  refuted. More measurement is not more evidence when the instrument is coarser than the effect.
- **Two of this session's three "regressions" have now been instrument artifacts** — this one, and
  item 736's bimodal before-arm that would have read as a 1.35x regression on mins. Both looked
  exactly like the real thing.
- **Suspecting your own change is correct; believing the first number that confirms it is not.**
  The closure-size precedent made 44.8 feel explained, which is precisely when a reading needs its
  isolated re-run most.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0. The engine is back to item 736's code plus the refutation marker.

## 738 — the two instrument failures from item 737, promoted into CLAUDE.md's list

**PROCESS. No engine change.** `CLAUDE.md`'s "Before trusting a number" list says each bullet is
there "because a wrong conclusion was drawn and committed first". Item 737 produced two that
qualify and neither was on it, so the next pass would have paid for them again.

**A per-row question needs a per-row instrument.** Running the whole sweep per arm feels more
rigorous and is the opposite: rows interfere, the `ffi` column drifts ~10% between arms on a
TS-only change, and arms taking 5 and 15 minutes get compared across whatever the machine did in
between. It reported a **1.66x regression that does not exist** (44.8 against 27.0 on
`project the element + materialize`), refuted by an isolated A/B at 25.2 against 24.7. The isolated
run was also **6x faster in wall clock** — so this is not a rigour-for-speed trade, which is why the
bullet is worth having: the slower, more thorough-looking instrument was worse on both axes.

**Assert each A/B arm IS the code it claims, before building it.** `cp "$S/matching-$arm.ts"` with
one of the two files never written leaves the previous arm in place, and the "after" reading is then
the "before" code — a null that looks like a result. A `grep -c` of the new symbol against an
expected count per arm makes that a loud failure instead. It is the same shape as asserting a patch
anchor appears exactly once, which this session has leaned on repeatedly; the A/B harness simply
never had the equivalent.

Both are now in the list, next to the LCG bullet item 702 added for the same reason.

### Why this is its own item and not a line in 737

737 records what was measured. This records what changed about how the next measurement gets made.
The audit is searched for "what did we conclude about X"; a process rule buried in a refutation
entry is findable only by someone who already knows to look there, and the whole point of the list
in `CLAUDE.md` is that it is read before measuring rather than after.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. Markdown only.

## 741 — I called packing presence "multi-tick" without counting the call sites; it is five operations and one real rewrite

**SCOPING + a correction of item 740, one item old. No engine change.** Item 740 named 342's
packed-presence ladder the best-priced unbuilt Rust lever and closed with: _"It is a `Column`
representation change, so it is a multi-tick piece of work rather than a tick-sized one, and it is
not started here."_ That sentence is an assumption stated as a fact. I never counted the call sites.

### The census

| what                                         | count |
| -------------------------------------------- | ----: |
| `.present` field accesses OUTSIDE `store.rs` | **0** |
| `present_at(..)` callers outside tests       |    31 |
| `present` mentions INSIDE `store.rs`         |   211 |
| `nulls` mentions inside `store.rs`           |    89 |

The 211 looks like the multi-tick number, and it is why "representation change" felt like the right
label. But the DISTINCT OPERATIONS are what has to be implemented, and there are five:

| operation               | sites | under a bitset                          |
| ----------------------- | ----: | --------------------------------------- |
| `present.push(b)`       |    10 | trivial                                 |
| `present.pop()`         |     6 | trivial                                 |
| `present.len()`         |     1 | trivial                                 |
| `present.get_mut(i)`    |     1 | the ONE real rewrite — see below        |
| `present[i]`            |    33 | mechanical rename to `present.get(i)`   |
| `present:` in a literal |    16 | `vec![false; n]` → `Presence::zeros(n)` |

Plus the same for `nulls` (8 `push`, 5 `pop`).

**The 31 external callers need no change at all**, because they go through `present_at` and its
signature does not move. That is the number that decides whether this is contained, and it is zero
work.

**The single hard site** is a bounds-checked clear:

```rust
if let Some(p) = present.get_mut(eid as usize) {
    *p = false;
}
```

`Index`/`IndexMut` cannot return a `bool` by reference out of a packed word, which is exactly why a
bitset is not literally drop-in — but this is the only place that needs the borrow, and `set(i,
false)` with the same bounds check replaces it in one line.

So the real shape is **a ~60-line `Presence` newtype over `Vec<u64>` with five methods, ~50
mechanical edits, and one rewrite.** One tick to write, one to verify. Not a storage feature.

### 🛑 What IS a real hazard, and it is not the one I named

Item 342 measured the READ side and says so explicitly: the packed variant's bitset was _"built
OUTSIDE the timed closure on purpose, since a per-batch build is O(KxN) and the question is what a
permanently-packed `Column` is worth on the read side."_

Making it permanent moves the cost to the WRITE side: every `push` becomes a bit-set in a word
instead of a byte store, and `pop` a mask. That is unmeasured. The repo already has the harness for
it — `write_cost_by_graph_size` — and it is the control the read-side sweep cannot provide. A read
win of 1.9x at K=200 that costs 10% on every property write is a different trade from a free one,
and which it is has not been established.

**That is the thing worth deferring on, and it is a measurement, not a size.** I deferred on size,
which I had not measured, while the actual open question went unnamed.

### The pattern, now three items deep

739: a price inside the window can be dead. 740: a lever outside the window is invisible. 741: the
COST of a lever can be asserted rather than counted, and a one-line census refutes it. All three are
defects in how the open list describes reality, and all three were cheap to check — this census is
four `grep -c` calls against a sentence that had already been committed.

Next: build the `Presence` newtype, measure the read side against `element_render_cost`'s existing
packed variant (which cross-checks itself against the byte-wise one for 1,000 rows before timing)
and the write side against `write_cost_by_graph_size`, with the fuzzers for byte-identity.

Gates: no code change. Census by `grep` against `crates/lenke-engine/src/`.

## 742 — packing presence IS multi-tick, and item 741's census asked the wrong question to find out

**BUILT the type, STARTED the conversion, REVERTED. No engine change.** Item 741 counted the call
sites and concluded a `Presence` newtype was "five operations and one real rewrite… one tick to
write, one to verify", correcting item 740's unmeasured "multi-tick". **740's verdict was right and
741's reasoning for overturning it was wrong**, which only came out by doing it.

### What the compiler says, which is the census that counts

Switching the 13 field declarations (`present: Vec<bool>` ×7, `nulls` ×6) to `Presence` and building:

| the compiler's enumeration           | count |
| ------------------------------------ | ----: |
| errors                               |   167 |
| distinct lines in `store.rs`         |    55 |
| `present[i]` / `nulls[i]` indexing   |   108 |
| constructor sites (`vec![false; n]`) |    23 |
| `present.as_slice()`                 |     3 |
| `&present` used as an iterator       |     2 |

The first four are mechanical. The last five are not, and they are the whole story.

### 🛑 The census asked "who touches the field" when the question is "what signatures mention the representation"

Item 741's headline was **"`.present` field accesses OUTSIDE `store.rs`: 0"** — and that is true. It
is also materially misleading, because the representation escapes through a **public accessor's
return type**:

```rust
pub fn edge_num_column(&self, key: &str) -> Option<(&[f64], &[bool])>
```

consumed by `exec.rs`'s `fn gather<T>(ids: &[u32], present: &[bool], ..)`. Counting `&[bool]` in
signatures instead of `.present` in expressions finds **16 sites across `exec.rs`,
`exec/aggregation.rs`, `exec/fastpath.rs` and `store.rs`** — the aggregate and numeric-filter FAST
PATHS take presence as a byte slice and index it directly.

So a packed column cannot be contained to `store.rs`. Every one of those fast paths has to learn the
new representation, and they are the hottest code in the crate. **That is why this is multi-tick: not
the 211 mentions at the definition, but five slice-shaped holes in four files.**

A field-access census is the right instrument for "can I rename this" and the wrong one for "can I
change its representation". The second needs the type's name searched through signatures, which is
one different `grep` and would have cost nothing at item 741.

### What survives, and is worth re-using when this is actually done

The type itself is sound and tested, and the next attempt should start from this rather than
redesign it:

- `Presence { words: Vec<u64>, len: usize }`, **`len` stored rather than derived** so it is exact
  and never rounds up to the word.
- Six operations, which is what `store.rs` uses: `with_len`, `len`, `get`, `set`, `push`, `pop`.
  `get` guards `i < self.len`; `set` is a no-op out of range, matching the bounds-checked
  `get_mut(..).map(|p| *p = v)` it replaces; `push` allocates a word only on a 64-boundary and then
  delegates to `set`.
- `Index`/`IndexMut` are impossible by construction — you cannot hand out a `&mut bool` into a
  packed word — so the 108 indexing sites become `.get(i)` and the assignments `.set(i, v)`.

**And it was mutation-tested before being wired to anything**, which is how the next finding came
out. Three mutants against an oracle test that walks 400 pushes, sets and clears on both sides of
every word boundary in range, then pops back across all of them:

| mutant                                   | caught? |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `pop` frees a word on the wrong boundary | **yes** |
| `get` uses `% 63` instead of `% 64`      | **yes** |
| `with_len` stops masking its tail bits   | **NO**  |

The survivor is **EQUIVALENT, not a gap**, and diagnosing it is the point: nothing can observe bits
at or past `len` through those six operations — `get` guards, `pop` clears before decrementing, and
`push` delegates to `set`, which writes its bit in both branches instead of assuming a clean slot.
The masking stays anyway, because "no bit is set at or past `len`" is what any later whole-word
operation would rely on (a `count_ones` popcount, a word-wise AND of two columns), and one branch at
construction is cheaper than that bug. A tally would have called this a test weakness; it is a
deliberate invariant with no current observer.

### The honest state of the lever

342's price still stands (re-measured at item 740: 1.79 ns per store key per row hoisted, 0.70
packed). The work is: the newtype above, ~130 mechanical edits in `store.rs`, **and teaching five
fast-path call sites in three other files a non-slice presence**, with `write_cost_by_graph_size`
useless as its write-side control — it measures ONE op at ~30 ns quantized to 0.030 µs, so a 10%
write change is invisible in it. The right write controls are `storage/write` (bulk SET, **28.33 ms
/ 7.1 Melem/s** at HEAD today) and `ingest/phases` (`nodes x4 props` decode **95.52 ms**, recmat
**85.05**), both captured here as the before-arm for whoever lands it.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0 errors on the reverted tree; `git status` clean. No engine change.

## 743 — the direction enum's third variant had no bench row, and the deliberate refusal of it costs 48.78x

**PRICED, one new bench row. No engine change.** Item 736's method — find the code path no bench row
reaches — applied to an enum rather than a query shape. `Dir` has three variants; the degree fast
path gates on `matches!(dir, Dir::Out | Dir::In)`; and **nothing in the corpus used an undirected
hop at all.** The one pattern that looked undirected to a careless grep is
`query: distinct over a reversed hop`, which is `<-[:KNOWS]-` — a direction, not the absence of one.

### The prediction, and it was wrong

TS has a dedicated `undirectedHopCount` with an O(1) route (per-type bucket sizes minus a self-loop
tally, `2*|E_t| - loops(t)`, which an earlier item took from 1352 ms to 0.0 at this fixture's size),
while native's fast path declines `Dir::Both`. I predicted a reversal — native much slower than TS.

| 200k nodes / 1M edges               |  ts |     ffi |
| ----------------------------------- | --: | ------: |
| `count 1-hop [shortcut]` (directed) | 0.0 |     0.5 |
| `count 1-hop UNDIRECTED`            | 0.0 | **1.5** |

Native pays 3x for the undirected spelling of a 1-hop count and that is all — 1.5 ms, no cliff. So
a 1-hop count has a route that does not care about direction, and **the gate I found is not on the
path I measured.** The first probe landed on the O(1) case, where the gate is irrelevant.

### Where the gate actually bites: the QUANTIFIED spelling

| 20,000 vertices, depth 3    |         ts |      ffi |     ts/ffi |
| --------------------------- | ---------: | -------: | ---------: |
| directed `->{3}` (item 732) |       14.4 |      1.4 |      10.3x |
| **undirected `-{3}`**       | **4828.1** | **99.0** | **48.78x** |

An undirected walk has twice the degree, so depth 3 visits **8x** the paths. Per PATH:

| engine |     directed |       undirected |  penalty |
| ------ | -----------: | ---------------: | -------: |
| ts     |  5.8 ns/path |  **241 ns/path** |  **41x** |
| ffi    | 0.56 ns/path | **4.95 ns/path** | **8.8x** |

So both engines fall off their fast path for `Dir::Both`, and TS falls 4.7x further than native
does.

### The refusal is CORRECT, and that is the point of pricing it

`CLOSED.md` already states the obstacle, and it is a real one rather than an oversight:

> _"`Dir::Both` stays refused and is a DIFFERENT SHAPE, not a third branch: from one node an
> undirected edge is traversable two ways, so one edge-indexed traversal mask cannot represent both,
> and a self-loop sits in both adjacency lists."_

Nothing here argues with that. What was missing is the **cost** of the refusal: a reasoned decision
with no number attached is indistinguishable, to the next reader, from one that is cheap. Now it is
48.78x on the cross-engine ratio and 8.8x per path on native's own terms, which is what tells
someone whether a trail-correct undirected recurrence is worth deriving.

**And the TS side is the larger half (41x per path), with a different cause** — TS has no
edge-indexed traversal mask, so native's stated obstacle is not TS's. That half is unexplained and
unattributed here; it is a separate question from the one `CLOSED.md` answers.

### What was added, and what deliberately was not

`count 1-hop UNDIRECTED` stays: it is 0.0/1.5 ms, so it costs the sweep nothing, and it guards two
real shortcuts that had no watcher — TS's `undirectedHopCount` O(1) route and whatever native uses
for the same shape.

The quantified undirected row does NOT stay. At the default N it would be ~48 seconds on ts, which
is item 732's lesson exactly: a regression sweep nobody runs catches nothing. Its numbers live in
the bench comment and here, with the instruction to add it back temporarily.

### 🛑 And the `.so` trap fired, exactly as CLAUDE.md says it does

The first attempt to measure died with `Symbol "lnk_abi_version" not found`. Item 742's conversion
attempt had run `cargo build --release` without `--features capi`, which overwrites
`liblenke_engine.so` with a copy that has no C ABI. It reads like a broken build and is a missing
feature flag; the rebuild with the flag takes 7 seconds. Worth noting that the trap triggered as a
side effect of an UNRELATED item two ticks earlier — the `.so` stays clobbered until something
notices.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0.
No engine change; one bench row added.

## 744 — the var-length count detector was `out`-only, so the mirror spelling cost 53x and nobody had measured it

**SHIPPED (TypeScript), 53x, disjoint, controls flat.** Item 743 priced the undirected variant and
left TS's per-path penalty unexplained. Chasing that found something larger and simpler one step
away: `detectVarLengthCount`'s shape predicate refused `rel.direction !== 'out'`, so of the
direction enum's three variants **the var-length count shortcut covered exactly one.**

### The repo's named bug class, on a traversal instead of a predicate

`CLAUDE.md` describes it precisely: _"the planner recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned
for another that meant exactly the same thing… Each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct
answer, so no correctness test could catch it."_ Same shape here, one level up — the spelling is the
direction of a hop, and the mirror is the same traversal read backwards.

| 20,000 vertices, depth 3 |        ts |     ffi |
| ------------------------ | --------: | ------: |
| `-[:KNOWS]->{3}`         |      14.4 |     1.4 |
| `<-[:KNOWS]-{3}`         | **682.2** | **1.4** |

Native was **1.4 ms either way** — its gate is `matches!(dir, Dir::Out | Dir::In)`, so it had the
mirror all along. That is the existence proof that the arithmetic works backwards; only TS's
detector declined.

### The fix is the two lines that build the CSR

`walkLevelCount` numbers the vertices once and flattens the adjacency into `{off, nbr}`, and
**everything downstream takes only that** — the level recurrence, and the depth-3/4 trail
correction through `buildTrailMasks(u0, csr)` and `buildTrail4Tables(csr, …)`. So direction is a
property of how the CSR is built and is inherited for free:

- the box: `inward ? v.adjTo : v.adjFrom`
- the neighbour end: `idx.get(inward ? e.from : e.to)`

plus `inward` on `DegreeCountSpec` and its two construction sites, and the shape predicate widened
to accept `in`.

**`mirrorAdmissible(inward, max)` refuses a shallow or unbounded mirror**, because
`takesTheLevelRecurrence` is `max >= 2` and below it `varLengthDegreeCount` falls to arithmetic
whose `edgesOf` reads `v.adjFrom` directly — it would answer the FORWARD count for a backward
query. That is items 692 and 699's mistake exactly (a relaxed bound meeting arithmetic nobody
relaxed with it), and it is a named function rather than three inline clauses because
`detectVarLengthCount` sits ON the complexity gate: inline it read 36 against a maximum of 35,
which is why this file already factors out `depth4Admissible`.

### The measurement, with two controls

Three alternated rounds, per-arm assertion on the `inward` symbol count before each build (the
guard item 738 added after nearly measuring a stale arm):

| row                  | clean                 | after                  |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `rev {3}`            | 682.2 / 708.2 / 692.5 | **12.0 / 13.0 / 13.7** |
| `fwd {3}` — CONTROL  | 16.0 / 13.5           | 15.0 / 13.0 / 14.1     |
| ffi column — CONTROL | 1.4-1.5               | 1.4                    |

**~53x, fully disjoint.** The forward spelling is the control that matters most — the change touches
the shared `walkLevelCount` and the shared detector, so a regression there was the real risk — and
it is flat. ffi is flat because a TS change cannot reach it.

### 🛑 Correctness: a TOTAL count cannot witness a direction bug

The bench row cannot validate this change, and item 586 says why: _"over ALL sources, reversing
every path is a bijection between the forward and backward path sets, so `(a:P)-[:T]->{1,2}(y)` and
its `<-[:T]-` twin return the SAME NUMBER whatever the engine does."_ Every node in the bench
fixture is a `Person`, so the row would read identically with the direction wired backwards.

So the guard is a new case in item 690's brute-force oracle, built on the SELECTIVE source
`makeGraph` already provides (a per-vertex `V{i}` label, kept plain enough for the degree-count
route). For each source and each depth in 1-3 it compares the forward count against enumeration
over `edges` and the mirror against enumeration over **`edges` reversed**, and then asserts that at
least one pair DIFFERS — item 586's finding written as an assertion rather than left as a hope.

### Mutation: 2 of 3, and the survivor is honest

| mutant                                      | outcome    |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| the adjacency box ignores `inward`          | **caught** |
| the neighbour end ignores `inward`          | **caught** |
| `mirrorAdmissible` always admits the mirror | SURVIVED   |

The survivor matters and I did not explain it. With the gate removed, an inward `{1}` should reach
the `max <= 2` arithmetic, which reads `v.adjFrom` and would answer the out-degree where the test
expects the in-degree — and on this fixture vertex 1 has 2 out against 3 in, so the test IS
asymmetric at depth 1 and should have failed. It passed, so **something upstream already refuses a
depth-1 inward spec and the gate is not currently reachable.** `varLengthCount` is first in the
shortcut precedence and the detector's existing bound only refuses `max === null || max < 1`, so
which refusal fires is unestablished.

Kept anyway, for the reason this file already keeps `!spec.isTrail` — a documented unreachable guard
against a future relaxation — and recorded as unexplained rather than given a guessed cause, which
item 734 is the standing lesson for.

### What else to look at

`shortcuts.ts` has one more direction-shaped line worth a look: `out: rel.direction !== 'out'`,
which collapses `in` and `both` into a single flag. Not touched here and not measured; noted so it
is not lost.

`bun run check` 0; `packages/gql` **2586** pass 0 fail (one new test); the seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail.

## 745 — the three threads item 744 left open, all closed by reading rather than measuring

**VERIFICATION. One comment corrected; no behaviour change.** Item 744 shipped a 53x win and left
three loose ends. All three resolve from the source, and one of them corrects 744 itself.

### 1. The surviving mutant, explained

744 recorded that replacing `mirrorAdmissible`'s body with `true` SURVIVES, said it should not have
(the oracle's fixture IS asymmetric at depth 1 — vertex 1 has 2 out-edges against 3 in), and left
the cause unestablished rather than guessing. The cause is that **both clauses of the guard are
redundant today**:

- **`max === 1` cannot reach it.** `dropVacuousQuantifier` removes a `{1,1}` quantifier before the
  detectors run — `vacuousQuantifier` is `q.min === 1 && q.max === 1` plus a plain rel, no variable,
  walk/trail mode, no `hopFrom`/`hopTo`/`nested`/`subpathWhere`. So `<-[:K]-{1}` arrives at
  `degreeCountShape` with `rel.quantifier === undefined` and is refused there.
- **`max === null` is already refused nine lines below**, for both directions, by the depth bound
  `max === null || max < 1 || (max > 4 && mode !== 'walk')`.

So the mutant is **EQUIVALENT**, not a test gap, and the distinction is the one CLAUDE.md asks for:
a survivor may be equivalent, inert, a skip or a gap, and a tally cannot tell them apart. This one
needed two mechanisms found in two different files to classify.

**The guard stays**, for the reason this file already keeps `!spec.isTrail`: below `max >= 2`,
`varLengthDegreeCount` falls to arithmetic whose `edgesOf` reads `v.adjFrom` directly and **cannot
decline once chosen** — it returns a number — so the only place to refuse an inward spec is upstream
in the detector. Item 692 is the record of exactly this kind of guard being needed when the future
arrived. The code now carries the mechanism instead of "unexplained".

### 2. `out: rel.direction !== 'out'` is safe

744 flagged it as worth a look, since `'both' !== 'out'` collapses to `out: true` and would make an
undirected pattern traverse one way. It cannot happen: `keyedCountOf` opens at 4726, **refuses
`rel.direction === 'both'` at 4773**, and computes the flag at 4810 — so by then the value is `out`
or `in` and the inversion comment (_"`(x)-[:T]->(q)` is written out from `x`, so from `q` it is an
IN edge"_) is exactly right. Recorded so it is not re-flagged.

### 3. The direction-coverage audit: 744 fixed the LAST out-only shortcut

Every direction test in `shortcuts.ts`, classified:

| sites                   | what they do                                          |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| 2179 / 2200 / 2202      | handle `both` explicitly (the undirected hop count)   |
| 3034-3039, 3236-3239    | handle `both` explicitly (`aBoth`/`midBoth`/`dBoth`)  |
| 2803 / 2804, 3818, 4773 | refuse `both` outright                                |
| 2830 / 2831, 3865, 4810 | `out` vs `in` as a boolean, with `both` refused above |
| 5544                    | **was** `out`-only — fixed at 744                     |

So after 744 **no shortcut covers `out` without covering `in`**, and `both` is either handled or
refused everywhere — never silently treated as one direction. That is the "grep the pattern
elsewhere" step done to completion rather than on the first hit, and the answer is that 744's bug
was the only instance of its kind left.

### Why this is an item and not three comments

Each thread was one `grep` or one `sed` away, and all three were cheap precisely because 744 wrote
them down instead of leaving them in my head. The one that mattered is the first: a survivor
recorded as "unexplained" is a standing invitation to delete the guard as dead code, and the real
reason it survives is that two OTHER conditions in two other files happen to cover it — which is
exactly the state in which a future edit to either one turns it from redundant into load-bearing.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0.
Comment-only change.

## 746 — I committed a row labelled "Remove before commit", argued twice against keeping it, and benchmarked over it for four commits

**DEFECT FOUND AND GUARDED. One row deleted, one hygiene test added.** The mirror audit from item
745 extended cleanly (below), and then a `grep -c TEMP` on the restored `bench.ts` returned **2**
on a tree I had just confirmed clean.

### What was in HEAD

```
  {
    // TEMPORARY depth-5 row for item 736 ablation. Remove before commit.
    name: 'count 5-hop quantified [TRAIL, TEMP]',
    ...
  },
  // 🛑 THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO DEPTH-5 ROW, and the reason is the measurement itself.
```

Those two blocks are **adjacent**. The file asserted the row did not exist, immediately below the
row. It entered at `069e3707` (item 736's commit) and was present in `fa75ecb8` (737),
`466c8755` (743) and HEAD — verified by `git show <sha>:packages/native/bench.ts | grep -c`.

### The cost, and what it probably explains

`REPS` is 5 and does not adapt. That row measured **16,325.9 ms per rep at 20,000 vertices** (item
732), so it added ~82 s to a sweep that takes **17 s** without it — measured just now. The default
`BENCH_N` is ten times larger.

It was therefore present during **item 737's full-sweep A/B**, whose arms I recorded as taking "5 to
15 minutes each" and attributed to instrument choice. The instrument argument stands on its own, but
the dominant term was almost certainly this row, and I did not consider it because I had forgotten
the row existed. (I have not reconciled the exact arm arithmetic — 5 × the default-N cost exceeds
the observed arm times, so something in that estimate is off, and I am not going to claim a number I
cannot derive.)

This is the rule I wrote twice and then broke: item 732 took a depth-5 row OUT because "a regression
sweep nobody runs because it takes a quarter-hour catches nothing", and item 743 declined a
quantified undirected row for the same reason. Both entries are correct. Both were written while the
row they argue against sat in the file.

### 🛑 The guard, because deleting it fixes only this instance

`bench-corpus-hygiene.test.ts` reads the bench sources as TEXT (importing them builds the
200,000-vertex fixtures at module scope — minutes of work to assert on a string) and fails if:

- any row `name` matches `TEMP` / `TEMPORARY` / `TMP`, or
- any bench file contains the text `remove before commit`.

**Teeth verified against the real defect**, not a synthetic one: reinstating the exact block above
turns the file red — `0 pass, 2 fail` — and removing it green again. The name-extraction assertion
also refuses to pass vacuously (`bench.ts` must yield more than 20 row names), because a regex that
stops matching would otherwise assert nothing, which is the failure mode that makes a hygiene test
worse than none.

The second rule is the sharper one. A marker saying "remove this before committing" is only ever
present in a commit _because it was not removed_, so its presence in a committed file is itself the
defect — no judgement about which rows are legitimate required.

### The mirror audit, completed (the tick's original work)

Extending item 744's finding to every other shape with a mirror, at 20,000 vertices:

| shape                                 | forward |   mirror |
| ------------------------------------- | ------: | -------: |
| fixed-length 3-hop chain count        |    17.0 | **12.1** |
| …same, with a start filter            |     9.4 |  **8.1** |
| var-length `{1,2}` + endpoint `WHERE` |    14.5 | **13.6** |
| 1-hop count                           |     0.0 |      0.0 |

All symmetric — the mirror is never slower, and on the chain it is slightly faster (in- versus
out-adjacency locality). So **744's bug was confined to the var-length count detector**, and the
chain shortcut's `outs = segments.map((s) => s.rel.direction === 'out')` handles direction properly,
as 745's classification predicted.

The endpoint-`WHERE` row is the one that mattered: 744 wired `inward` into **two** spec construction
sites and measured only the vacuous one. This is the carried-predicate arm, and it is symmetric, so
that site works too.

## 747 — item 737's phantom 1.66x was the stray row, so "a full sweep is untrustworthy" was the wrong lesson to draw from it

**DIAGNOSIS. No engine change; one CLAUDE.md bullet refined.** Item 746 removed a temporary depth-5
row that had been committed by accident and sat in the sweep for four commits. Item 737's phantom
regression was measured through that sweep, so it could finally be tested against a corpus without
it.

### The phantom is gone

| `query: project the element + materialize` |            reading |
| ------------------------------------------ | -----------------: |
| item 737, in-sweep, stray row PRESENT      |           **44.8** |
| now, in-sweep, stray row GONE (two sweeps) |    28.6 / **26.7** |
| item 737, isolated                         | 25.2 / 24.9 / 25.5 |

In-sweep now agrees with isolated. The 1.66x that nearly got item 737's change reverted was a
16-second-per-rep row running in the same process against a sweep that otherwise takes 17 s at
`BENCH_N=20000`.

### 🛑 So the lesson I drew at 737 was over-general, and that matters

737 concluded that a full sweep per arm is "the wrong instrument… rows interfere", and item 738
promoted that into `CLAUDE.md`. The **rule is right** but the stated reason was a property of
sweeps in general, when the dominant term was a specific defect in mine. Left as written, it reads
as "do not trust the regression sweep" — which would discourage the one instrument the corpus exists
to provide.

**The rule still holds on its own terms**, because residual in-sweep inflation is real and much
smaller: from the same clean sweep, `count var-length 1-2 hops` reads **250.7 in-sweep against
~177 isolated (1.4x)**, and `traverse 1-hop + filter` 43.4 against 39.7. A per-row question still
wants a per-row instrument. It just does not want the 1.66x figure as its justification, so the
bullet now carries both halves: the phantom had a cause, and the residual is 1.4x rather than 1.66x.

That is worth separating because the two failure modes have different fixes. Interference you cannot
remove is a reason to choose a different instrument; a stray row is a reason to fix the corpus — and
item 746 added the hygiene test that makes the second one impossible to recommit.

### 🛑 Three process errors of mine in this one tick, none of which reached a committed figure

1. **I wrote a log with bare `>`.** `CLAUDE.md`'s first rule for this shell is never to do that, and
   `run_in_background` captures output with no redirection at all — which is what the confirming
   sweep used. The file name was fresh, so nothing stale was consumed, but the rule is not
   conditional on getting lucky.
2. **I started a second sweep while the first was still running.** Two benches contending for CPU
   corrupts both, which is the self-inflicted noise this whole run of ticks keeps finding. The first
   sweep survived only because the second died early (at `decode ndjson`) while the row in question
   runs late in the corpus — and I re-ran it cleanly rather than relying on that.
3. **`pkill -f 'bun bench.ts'` killed my own shell** (exit 144), because the pattern matched the
   invoking command line. `CLAUDE.md` warns about exactly this; the right form is `pgrep` then kill
   by PID.

All three are instrument-handling errors in a tick whose subject was instrument-handling errors.
Recording them because the alternative — fixing them silently — is what makes the same mistake
available next time.

## 748 — a 2-hop chain gated at its FIRST position took the slow arm, because item 306 never measured that case: 4.12x

**SHIPPED (native), 4.12x, disjoint, two controls flat.** The first thing the newly-clean sweep
(items 746/747) was used for, and it paid immediately.

### The ordering that is impossible on its face

Item 699's rule — read a sweep for orderings that cannot be true of the work done — applied to the
filter-position family, ffi column:

| row                          |      ffi |
| ---------------------------- | -------: |
| `count 2-hop + start filter` | **14.7** |
| `count 2-hop + mid filter`   |     17.9 |
| `count 2-hop + end filter`   |      3.4 |
| `count 3-hop + start filter` |  **4.1** |

A 2-hop chain with a start filter, 3.3x SLOWER than the 3-hop with the same filter. Isolated to rule
out the sweep's own interference (13.9 / 15.2 / 3.3 / 4.2), then reproduced in-process with the
answers printed beside the times, which is where the scale of it showed:

| query, 200k vertices |       ms | rows counted |
| -------------------- | -------: | -----------: |
| 2-hop + START filter | **26.3** |    1,950,000 |
| 2-hop + END filter   |      4.9 |    1,954,377 |
| 3-hop + START filter |  **5.7** |    9,750,000 |
| 2-hop, no filter     |      3.9 |    5,000,000 |

**5x the results in a fifth of the time**, and a start filter making the 2-hop 6.7x slower than no
filter at all.

### The cause: a condition written for the case next to it

The optimized plans are structurally IDENTICAL — `Scan → Filter → Expand… → Aggregate → Project`,
differing only by one `Expand` — so the routing is at exec time. `try_nhop_sweep_count`:

```rust
2 => chain.gates[hops].is_some(),              // the LAST position only
3 => chain.gates.iter().any(Option::is_some),   // ANY position
```

Item 306 produced that line, and measured a 2-hop INTERIOR gate at **0.74x** — genuinely slower
than the product arm that already answers it. But its table has rows for UNGATED and for a gate at
the LAST position only; **the FIRST position has no row**, and `gates[hops].is_some()` excludes
start and interior together.

Item 309, nine items later, established the opposite about the start: it REVERSES a chain to turn an
end gate into a start one, because a start gate narrows the seed and the degree tail answers the
end — 0.80ms against 0.29. So the sweep's own best case was the one excluded, and the two items
never met.

### The fix and the measurement

`2 => chain.gates[hops].is_some() || chain.gates[0].is_some()`.

Three alternated rounds on the bench row, with per-arm assertions on the symbol count before each
build:

| row                                | clean              | after               |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- |
| `count 2-hop + start filter`       | 14.6 / 15.7 / 13.6 | **3.3 / 3.3 / 3.3** |
| `count 2-hop + mid filter` CONTROL | 17.2 / 16.9 / 16.5 | 17.0 / 17.0 / 17.1  |
| `count 2-hop + end filter` CONTROL | 3.3 / 3.4 / 3.4    | 3.4 / 3.3 / 3.4     |

**4.12x on mins, fully disjoint**, and the after arm reads 3.3 in all three rounds. The two controls
are the ones that matter: the mid gate is the case still excluded (so 306's measured verdict is
untouched) and the end gate is the case already taken (so nothing was stolen).

**AND IT IS A WIN AT EVERY SIZE**, which is what separates completing 306's verdict from inverting
it. In-process, before → after: 5,000 vertices 0.6 → 0.1; 20,000 1.8 → 0.4; 50,000 6.3 → 1.0;
200,000 26.3 → 4.1 — **4.5-6.4x throughout**, with identical answers at every size. Had this
inverted below some threshold, 306's sub-millisecond figures would have been the reason, and it
does not.

### 🛑 The shape had NO test, because the route never received it

`grep` for a 2-hop chain with a start filter in the engine's tests: **zero**. So the change routes a
shape to arithmetic that had never run on it. Added
`a_two_hop_chain_gated_at_its_first_position_agrees_with_the_general_path`, compared against
`count(c.k)` — a spelling that does NOT take this route. That technique is borrowed from
`three_hop_product_agrees_with_the_general_path_in_every_direction`, which records why: its first
version compared the fast path WITH ITSELF and **all five of its mutants survived**.

The fixture is irregular with cycles (13 → 0, 14 → 2) so a mis-walked hop finds walks instead of a
silent zero, and it asserts `gated < ungated` — because if the seed gate were dropped the two would
coincide and a dropped gate would be invisible.

### Mutation, outcomes labelled in advance

| mutant                                 | predicted | actual                                                                |
| -------------------------------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the sweep's seed gate dropped entirely | caught    | **CAUGHT** — and by the new test ALONE, on its differential assertion |
| the route reverted to end-gate-only    | survive   | **SURVIVED**, 1221 pass                                               |

The second is the point of predicting first: a route choice is answer-equivalent, so no correctness
test can see it and [[perf-gate-needs-its-own-test]] says so. Its guard is the alternated A/B above.
The first ran 16 failures across the suite — the seed gate was already covered at 3+ hops — which is
exactly why it mattered to check that the NEW test fails on its own rather than reading the 16.

## 750 — the `_ => true` arm was never measured either, and this time the code was right: 7.9x

**VERIFICATION. Two new bench rows, no engine change.** Items 748 and 749 found both of item 306's
two-hop exclusions wrong. The obvious next question is whether the arm nobody questioned — four or
more hops, taken UNCONDITIONALLY — is right, and item 749's lesson says to ask it with an
instrument: that arm had none.

### The gap

`try_nhop_sweep_count`'s decision, after 749:

```rust
0 | 1 => false,
2 | 3 => chain.gates.iter().any(Option::is_some),   // ungated stays with the product arms
_     => true,                                       // FOUR or more, gated or not
```

The corpus had **no fixed 4-hop chain row at all**. Its only 4-hop row is
`count 4-hop quantified [TRAIL]`, which is the `->{4}` quantified form over different machinery. So
the one arm that takes a shape unconditionally — including the ungated case that items 301/306 say
belongs to the product arms at shallower depths — was never exercised.

### The answer: at four hops the ownership is the OPPOSITE way, by 7.9x

| fixed 4-chain, 200k vertices | sweep (shipped) | forced to the product arms |
| ---------------------------- | --------------: | -------------------------: |
| ungated                      |      **7.0 ms** |                **55.5 ms** |
| with a start gate            |          4.9 ms |                     5.0 ms |

Routing the ungated 4-chain away from the sweep costs **7.9x**. The gated row is unchanged, as it
must be — it is gated either way, so the probe cannot reach it, which makes it the control.

So `_ => true` is correct and the inversion against two and three hops is real: the product arms win
the ungated SHALLOW chain and lose the ungated DEEP one. That is coherent rather than surprising —
a degree product has one term per hop and the sweep has one pass per level — but it was an
assumption until now, and three items in a row have shown what an unmeasured assumption in this
`match` is worth.

**This is the first of the three where the code was right.** Worth saying plainly: 748 and 749 both
found a real defect, which makes it tempting to keep pulling and expect another. The arm got the
same treatment and defended itself, and recording that is what stops a fourth pass from re-probing
it.

### What was added

`count 4-hop` and `count 4-hop + start filter`, both cheap (6.9 and 4.9 ms at the default N, 0.7 and
0.5 at 20,000), carrying the measurement above in the comment. Together with `count 2-hop` from item
749, every arm of the decision now has a row that would notice if its ownership flipped.

### An incidental figure, correctly NOT a finding

`count 4-hop quantified [TRAIL]` reads **123.9 ms** against the fixed 4-chain's 6.9 in the same
sweep — an 18x gap that looks alarming beside it. It is not a routing defect: a TRAIL forbids
reusing an edge and the fixed chain is a WALK, so they are different questions, and the 123.9
includes the depth-4 trail correction's inclusion-exclusion. Noted because the two rows now sit near
each other in the output and the comparison invites itself.
