## 774 — `bun test` reports to STDERR. Items 767, 772 and 773's mutation diagnostics were reading an empty stream, and all three are corrected

**NO ENGINE CHANGE — a guard repaired.** `bun test` writes `N pass` / `N fail` to **stderr**, never
stdout, for the unit suite and for `bun run fuzz` alike; `cargo test` writes `test result:` to
stdout. Measured: a clean `bun run fuzz --no-build` has rc=0 with NO result line in stdout and one
in stderr; a failing `bun test` has rc=1, likewise.

**THE COMPOUNDING ERROR, four ticks long, from one unexamined assumption:**

1. Items 765/766/767/772 saw an in-loop `fuzz=FAIL(1)` with empty stdout.
2. **Item 767 concluded the runner "never ran a test"** and that the exit code carried no
   information. WRONG — it ran and reported to stderr. Those were REAL non-zero exits whose reason
   was never captured. With 20 consecutive clean standalone runs on the pristine tree, the
   remaining explanation is the rare-seed residual `gremlin-fuzz-families` already records.
3. **Items 772/773 then implemented 767's rule against stdout** and printed `DID-NOT-RUN` for runs
   that passed cleanly. Item 773's claim that _"the in-loop fuzz step currently contributes no
   signal at all"_ is WRONG and is corrected here: the step worked throughout, only the label was
   false.

**THE FIX:** concatenate stdout and stderr, look for a result line there, and only then read the
exit code (124/137/-9 still distinguished as timeout/OOM). Validated by re-running item 773's three
mutants: `split` bypassing `splitScalar` FAIL(1)/fuzz pass, arguments swapped FAIL(1)/fuzz pass,
not specialized pass/pass — all as predicted, with the fuzz column reading `pass` where it said
`DID-NOT-RUN` an hour earlier. `CLAUDE.md`'s rule now NAMES the stream, which the version item 767
wrote did not — and that omission is why my own two implementations of it were wrong.

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE.** Every verdict in items 765-773 stands. The decisive ones came with
NAMED failing tests from a stream being read correctly (`cargo test` on stdout for the Rust
mutants; the unit suite's exit plus test name for the TS ones). What was lost was the fuzz column,
and this tick shows it would have read `pass` — so no mutant was wrongly declared caught by it. The
engine is unaffected: 20 consecutive clean fuzz runs on the pristine tree.

**Newly possible:** the rare-seed residual now has a capture path. An in-loop non-zero exit will
name the fuzzer and seed in the stderr now being read, and `bun run fuzz <name> --seed N` replays
it — which has not been possible at any point in this session.

## 775 — ~~TS: an ANONYMOUS end node costs 4.4x a named one, cause located in `hopEnds`~~ — **FIXED AT ITEM 776** (4.60-4.88x, the two spellings CONVERGE; `hopEnds` synthesizes `ANON_FAR_VAR`, verified in the code). Item 773's "edge projection is 22x" is REFUTED

**NO ENGINE CHANGE. A 4.4x equivalent-spelling gap found, located, and added to the spelling probe.**

**ITEM 773'S CLAIM IS WITHDRAWN.** It closed with "TS edge projection is ~22x node projection per
row", from two bench rows that differ in TWO clauses: `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n` is a 1-slot label
scan, `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN r` a 3-slot traversal. The discriminator: **`RETURN
r.since` costs MORE than `RETURN r`** (84.62 ms against 73.80 over the same 200,000 edges). If the
edge RENDER were the cost, adding a property read could not exceed it — so the lazy render is
nearly free and the ~400 ns/row is the traversal.

**Also: `count(*)` cannot baseline enumeration here.** Both `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN
count(*)` and its `->(b)` twin measure **0.00 ms** (the count shortcut), so "traversal minus
count(*)" is not available as a subtraction.

**THE REAL FINDING, isolated to ONE clause and with row counts asserted:**

| query                                  |    rows |        ms |
| -------------------------------------- | ------: | --------: |
| `MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN r.since`  | 200,000 | **83.51** |
| `MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->(b) RETURN r.since` | 200,000 | **19.03** |

**4.4x, both answers correct**, differing only in whether the end node is anonymous.

**CAUSE LOCATED:** `hopEnds` in `executor/hop-projection.ts` returns `null` when
`node.variable === undefined`, so an anonymous end refuses `detectHopProjection` entirely and the
query falls to the general row pipeline. The machinery for "the projection does not read the far

name rather than on whether the name is USED produces this every time** — that is the pattern to
check for, not the individual gap.

| on the END         |                  8.34 |              14.36 | 1.7x FASTER     |

## 779 — NEGATIVE: the Rust engine has no twin of items 776 or 778. Do not look for one

**CLOSED (no change).** Items 776 and 778 fixed two TypeScript fast-path gaps of one shape: a gate
testing whether an AST field is PRESENT (an end-node variable; a start's inline property map) rather
than whether it is USED. Applying "grep the pattern elsewhere" across engines: the native
`spelling_probe` now carries both pairs on a HOP with a projection, and both report
**`✓ identical optimized plan`** (0.247 vs 0.246 ms; 0.664 vs 0.653 ms), with the whole probe at
`NO PERF CLIFFS`.

**The reason is structural, so this generalizes to the whole family.** TypeScript's fast paths read
the PATTERN, so a predicate's SPELLING decides which rung admits it — that is how items 444, 505,
776 and 777 all happened in one file. This engine canonicalizes before any routing decision, so
there is no position at which a spelling can be refused. **A TS gap in this family is not evidence
of a Rust gap**; check the plan before pricing one.

The two groups stay as GUARDS: a future change that routed on the pattern instead of the plan would
show up as a plan mismatch at the two shapes that already cost two ticks in the other engine.

## 781 — TS: a far-only clause `WHERE` lifts into `farPred`. 1.45x, and the refusal item 780 predicted was the WRONG one

**DONE (TypeScript).** A clause `WHERE` reading nothing but the far variable satisfies
`compilePredicate`'s `ownVar` proof exactly as an inline constraint does, so it compiles to a far
predicate and the per-edge gate disappears. `->(b) WHERE b.k = 5` **21.07 → 14.48 (1.45x)**; with a
second far-local conjunct **22.49 → 14.13 (1.59x)**. Controls: inline 1.03x, a REFUSED mixed clause
1.05x (the change runs on it and must decline — a flat reading there is evidence the refusal fires),
a node scan 1.00x. Min of three order-alternated rounds, arms grepped in the built bundle.

**All three spellings now land together** (13.85 / ~14.1 / 14.48) where before item 780 they spanned
13.83 / 20.55 / 21.07. The group in `spelling-probe.ts` carries it.

**ITEM 780'S PREDICTED REFUSAL WAS NOT THE ONE THAT MATTERS — do not re-derive it.** 780 reasoned
the lift would need a PREFIX refusal, since `satisfies` runs before the gate and moving a fault-free
filter earlier suppresses a throw. Sound reasoning, wrong conclusion: `directEqProps` is
ALL-OR-NOTHING, so there is no partial lift to reorder and the question never arises.

What it actually needs: `mergeFarPreds` carries `props`/`eqProps`/`cmpProps` and NOT `where`
(`satisfies` evaluates `where` last, so nothing can keep a generic inline predicate ahead of a
lifted clause one), so **an inline far constraint that did not lift must block the whole lift**.
Mutating that away gives `->(b WHERE b.k IS NULL) WHERE b.j = 1` the answer `[null, five, absent]`
instead of `[null, absent]` — **with 2600 pass, 0 fail**. Four tests pin it; the fixture gives every
far node `j = 1` on purpose, so only the inline constraint can distinguish them and a selective
clause cannot hide the drop. **Seventh consecutive item whose defect was in a fast path's admission
gate, and the first where the gate was written in the same tick.**

**The free-variable refusal is INERT** (mutating it changed nothing — `directEqProps` declines a
foreign variable and the no-gain refusal catches it) and **stays anyway**, because it does not
depend on that internal. Pinned with the explanation so a later reader does not delete a refusal
because a mutant survived it.

**Still open:** a clause reading the far node AND the start stays on the gate (21.71 against 14.48).
Splitting a conjunction so only the far-local part lifts IS a partial lift, and that is where item
780's fault-ordering reasoning becomes load-bearing for real.

## 782 — TS: a MIXED clause hoists its far-local conjuncts and the residual goes start-only. 1.47-1.66x, and a refusal COPIED one function over was untested

**DONE (TypeScript).** Hoist a mixed clause's far-local conjuncts into `farPred`; what is LEFT is
start-only, so `carriedWhere` reports `startOnly` and the existing start-gated walk — which rejects
a vertex before reading its adjacency, and applies `farPred` itself — takes over. **No walk
changed.**

`WHERE b.age = 5 AND a.age > 1` **22.00 → 14.93 (1.47x)**; start-first **24.18 → 14.61 (1.66x)**.
Four controls at increasing distance (far-only 1.09x, both-far 0.98x, start-only 0.99x, node scan
0.99x). Min of three order-alternated rounds, arms grepped in the bundle.

**Two things the decomposition found that nothing had measured.** A mixed clause was **slower than
the unfiltered hop** (21.66 against 17.72) — the gate runs per edge and rejects few rows. And the
two spellings of one predicate differed **1.13x**, because `filterPredicate` DECLINES when no
conjunct can raise, so written order survives and the spelling decides which conjunct
short-circuits. Both closed: the spread is now 1.02x.

**Safety rests on a key shared with Rust, not on our own caution.** Reordering in FILTER position
cannot change the row set (only whether a row already lost pays for a fault), and `filterPredicate`
ALREADY hoists every `truthCannotRaise` conjunct ahead of every one that can. Restricting the hoist
to that key reorders nothing the engine does not. It also blocks the item-420 hazard:
`freePredicateVars` cannot see a subquery's correlated names, and `truthCannotRaise` refuses a
subquery arm.

**A TEST IS PINNED TO THE CODE PATH IT REACHES, NOT THE RULE IT IS NAMED FOR.** The same refusal
(`mergeFarPreds` carries no `where`, so a non-lifting inline far constraint must block the lift)
exists in item 781's full-lift path and in 782's split. 781's test uses a single far-local conjunct,
so `rest` is empty, the split declines and the test never reaches the split's copy. Mutating that
copy returns six rows where the answer is empty — **2604 pass, 0 fail**. Eighth consecutive
admission-gate defect. The new test reaches the split specifically, by giving the clause a far-local
conjunct AND something else.

Two other refusals are **INERT** (dropping `truthCannotRaise`, and hoisting any conjunct) for item
781's reason: `directEqProps` admits only a `compare` with a plain property against a closed value,
a strict subset of both. They stay because they do not depend on that internal.

**Also:** `bun test packages` is NOT a whole-repo gate — `packages/react` runs on vitest and reports
19 bogus `document is not defined` failures under `bun test`, 22/22 green under `bun run test`.

**Still open:** a conjunct reading BOTH ends cannot hoist (pinned as a test); evaluating one per
edge against the bound start is the items 121-123 correlation question.

**REFUTED (no change).** The trim family (`trim`, `btrim`, `ltrim`, `rtrim`) sits on the general
per-row dispatch while `upper`/`lower` are in `unary_str_fn`, and item 765 measured that exact move
at 2.4x — so it reads like a free repeat. Measured by the new `examples/scalarfn_bench`,
`count(f(a.s))` over the same rows, min of 9 at 200k and 5 at 1M:

|                                |    200k |  1M | output | dispatch       |
| ------------------------------ | ------: | --: | ------ | -------------- |
| `char_length`                  |  6.2 ns | 8.7 | `Num`  | **vectorized** |
| `size`                         |     6.4 | 8.8 | `Num`  | general        |
| `upper`                        |     7.5 | 9.7 | String | **vectorized** |
| `trim`/`btrim`/`ltrim`/`rtrim` | 7.7-7.8 | 9.9 | String | general        |

**`size` is the measurement that settles it** (item 339: a two-way difference needs a third
measurement). It is general-dispatch and returns a `Num` with no output string — `char_length`'s
exact shape on the fast path — and they land **0.2 ns apart, 3%, under the noise floor**. So table
membership is worth ~0.2 ns/row; the 1.5 ns separating the two bands is the OUTPUT STRING
ALLOCATION, which every candidate does and the table cannot avoid.

**Item 765's 2.4x does not transfer because its baseline was 30.33 ns/row.** Items 765/767 removed
the boxing that made the clone dominant and took the headroom with it. (The inverse of item 767,
where a refuted path came back once the denominator shrank — same mechanism, opposite direction.)
`reverse`/`size` were never candidates: the table's doc already excludes them as polymorphic over
lists.

**Where scalar work should go instead:** the OUTPUT column, not the dispatch. `Num`/`Bool` output is
1.5 ns/row cheaper than a string, and `split` (a LIST) is **49 ns at 1M, 5x the next worst** — but
its body is already one `Vec` and one `GStr` a piece with no double scan, so that is allocation
cost, not waste. A win there needs a different output representation.

**The instrument is committed:** `examples/scalarfn_bench`, indexed in `examples/README.md`. Items

## 785 — NATIVE: `round(x, d)` joins `binary_num_fn` — 3.45x, and the refutation above is what found it

**DONE.** With 784 refuting the typed arm, item 759's 3.33x had to be the table ENTRY — so the entry

```text

```

The general dispatch costs **2.7-3.5x** the table for a two-argument numeric call, which confirms
759's attribution. And `round/2`'s 35.0 was the exclusion, not the function — its body is three
arithmetic operations. The stated reason ("its second argument is a digit COUNT with its own
non-finite rule") is a VALUE rule, and a value rule fits in an `fn(f64, f64) -> f64`.

**`count(round(a.n, 2))` 35.0 → 10.1 (3.45x) at 200k, 38.1 → 13.0 (2.92x) at 1M**, landing beside
`mod`. Five controls agree to within 0.3 ns — the tightest this harness has read. Values diffed
across arms over ten inputs × nine digit-count spellings (literal, a COLUMN of counts, 0, -1,
absent, `1e400`, 400, null): **identical**, NaN rule and `-0.0` outputs included. The one-arg
spelling stays in `unary_num_fn`; the tables are arity-separated.

**Mutation:** removing `d.is_finite()` fails `round_with_a_non_finite_digit_count_is_nan` — and the
load-bearing half is the **NaN** count (which saturates to 0 digits and would return `x` unrounded),
not the infinite one (which saturates to `i32::MAX`, giving an infinite factor that divides to NaN
by itself). **First refusal in nine items already covered at the position that mattered** — the
exception to 764/768/769/773/776/778/780/782, recorded so the streak is not read as a law.

**Still open:** `atan2` 16.3 against `mod` 10.1 — a 1.6x spread across three names reached through

## 786 — NATIVE: the two-arg numeric table is worth 18-25 ns/row. `nullif` at 28.4 ns is the one name left, and its arm must take UNFOLDED operands

**~~OPEN TARGET~~ BUILT AT 787 (`nullif` typed arm, 3.26x; the two-arg numeric band is now closed,
and the `-0.0` trap predicted here was real), priced, with its hazard identified (no change).**
Item 785 left a question: the same
`round` body cost 35.0 ns general and 10.1 in the table, while `left` — also two-arg, also general —
cost 8.3. Measured instead of reasoned:

```text
  coalesce(a.n,7)  3.2   its OWN path (item 458)      left(a.s,3)    8.3   general
  mod              10.0  table                        nullif(a.n,7) 28.4   general  <- TARGET
  round/2          10.1  table (785)                  round/2 before 35.0  general
  log              11.6  table      power 13.1 table      atan2 16.3 table
```

So the band is real and not about `round`: **a two-arg numeric name on the general dispatch costs
28-35 ns where a table-claimed one costs 10-16.** The entry is worth 18-25 ns/row, which confirms
item 759's 3.33x a second way. `nullif` is the only name left in the slow band — a **2.6x** target.

**`coalesce` is NOT a target:** item 458 already gave it a column-level path (a non-nullable first
argument makes it the identity, 6.5x there).

**MECHANISM NOT ISOLATED — do not assume one.** `left` 8.3 sits on the same general dispatch as
`nullif` 28.4, so "general dispatch is slow" is too coarse. Ruled out already: the per-row argument
`Vec` (the evaluator reuses one buffer) and the `match name` chain by name LENGTH (`left`'s 4-char
bucket is more crowded than `round`'s 5, and `left` is the fast one).

**THE TRAP any `nullif` arm must avoid.** It needs a `fn(f64, f64) -> Value` shape (precedent:
`unary_str_fn`). The general arm returns `args[0].clone()` — the RAW first argument — while every
existing arm in `scalar.rs` receives operands through `num_of`/`zero_folded`, which folds `-0.0` to
`+0.0`. An arm fed folded operands answers `0.0` where the engine answers `-0.0`. A stored `-0.0`
does reach these paths (item 785's value probe shows `round(a.x)` returning `Num(-0.0)`), **no row
count changes, and nothing in the suite looks at the sign of a zero returned by `nullif`** — a
silent divergence. The comparison itself is safe: `value::equals` on two `Num` is plain f64 `==`, so
NaN equals nothing and `-0.0 == 0.0` either way.

## 787 — NATIVE: `nullif` gets a typed arm — 3.26x. The `-0.0` trap item 786 predicted was real, untested and SILENT. The two-arg numeric band is now closed

**DONE.** `nullif` cannot join `binary_num_fn` (it returns a NULL), so the numeric case gets a named
function `eval_nullif` with a typed arm over two `Col::Num`, general dispatch for every other kind
(it is polymorphic over strings, lists, temporals). **Deliberately not a second table:** a
`fn(f64, f64) -> Value` table would have one entry whose operand convention differs from every other
arm, and the next name added would inherit the convention rather than the exception.

`count(nullif(a.n, 7))` **28.7 → 8.8 (3.26x)** at 200k, **31.6 → 11.8 (2.70x)** at 1M. Six controls
within 1% (mod, round/2, power, atan2, char_length, count(a.s)). Three alternated rounds, arms
grepped. At 8.8 ns it is now the cheapest two-arg numeric — correct, since its body is one compare
where `mod`/`power` call libm.

**THE TRAP, confirmed exactly as item 786 predicted it.** Every other arm takes operands through
`num_of`/`zero_folded` (`-0.0` → `+0.0`); `nullif` must not, because the general dispatch returns
`args[0].clone()` RAW. Mutant: apply the conventional fold to the returned value → `Num(0.0)` where
the engine answers `Num(-0.0)`, **with 1224 pass 0 fail**. The asymmetry is the subtlety: the
COMPARISON needs no care (`value::equals` on two `Num` is plain `f64 ==`, so `-0.0 == 0.0` already
and NaN equals nothing), so folding changes only what the SURVIVING rows carry — no row count moves,
which is why the suite was blind.

One test pins it, teeth verified. Two load-bearing details: **both operands must be STORED columns**
(a broadcast literal may not reach `Col::Num`, so `nullif(a.x, -1)` could pass without touching the
arm), and **the assertion is on the `Debug` rendering** (`-0.0 == 0.0` is true, so an `assert_eq!` on
the float passes under the mutant). Values diffed across arms over twelve spellings: identical.

**THE TWO-ARG NUMERIC BAND IS CLOSED** — every name is table-claimed or has its own arm:

```text
  coalesce 3.2   nullif 8.8   mod 10.1   round/2 10.1   power 13.1   atan2 16.3
```

**Still open (not a dispatch question):** `atan2` 16.3 vs `mod` 10.1 is the libm bodies, per item 785. **Process note:** a first values diff reported six missing lines; the cause was piping the run
through `head -6`, which SIGPIPEs `tee` and truncates its file — same shape as the `tail -8`
truncations at items 764/765.

## 788 — TS: the twins of 785/787 — `nullif` 1.97x, `round` 1.65x (1 arg) and 1.44x (2 args). The cross-engine grep FOUND the gap this time

**DONE (TypeScript).** Item 779 established that a TS fast-path gap is not evidence of a Rust one
(the Rust optimizer canonicalizes). **The converse does not follow and is checked here:** TS's
`BINARY_NUM` holds `power`, `log`, `mod`, `atan2` — exactly the four names native had before item
785 — with `round`/`nullif` in the general `switch`. Same two names, same two tables, both engines.

```text
  round(a.n,2) 40.6   nullif 39.4   round(a.n) 35.4   | general dispatch
  mod 26.9   power 22.7   abs 18.0   | specialized (item 760)      floor 15.6
```

**`round` is in NEITHER table at EITHER arity**, which the pricing surfaced. Not `BINARY_NUM`,
because that applies its closure only after `binaryNumCall` turns either null argument into a null
RESULT — and a null digit count means ZERO digits, so `round(5, null)` is `5` (verified:
`round(a.x, null)` → `[3,-3,3,0,1]`, not nulls). Not `UNARY_NUM`, because the second argument is
optional. `nullif` for a third reason: polymorphic and returns a null.

| `nullif` 40.4 → **20.5 (1.97x)** | `round/1` 35.3 → **21.4 (1.65x)** | `round/2` 38.2 → **26.5 (1.44x)** |

Min of three order-alternated rounds; four controls, three within 3% and the cheapest (the no-call
floor) at 0.91x — inside the noise floor. **Each arm rebuilt into the dist AND grepped there**,
which matters more than natively since `@lenke/*` resolve to `dist`. Less than native's 3.26-3.45x,
as item 769 said to expect: much of the native win was a typed output column and TS has none.

**Verified:** 20 value spellings diffed across arms, identical. Three behaviours confirmed present:
`round(x, null)` is digits-0 not null; `round(null, 'x')` RAISES (the order contract); `nullif` on
lists uses `structuralEq`, not `===`.

**Mutation — three caught, and one prediction WRONG.** Checking `x`'s null before validating the
digit count was predicted "likely a gap" and is in fact pinned by `a named numeric function
validates non-null args even beside a null`, which reaches the new closure as soon as it exists.
Second item running where the property was already covered where the change needed it (785 too) —
against the eight-in-a-row with no coverage at 764/768/769/773/776/778/780/782. **Both directions
recorded so the streak is not read as a law.**

## 791 — TS: an all-BMP trim char set scans UTF-16 units — 4.0-4.4x. The mutant's wrong answer is MOJIBAKE, and ONE fixture row catches it

**DONE (TypeScript).** Item 790 priced this at 265.6 ns/row with its cause located. `multiTrim`
allocated THREE times a row (a `Set` over the char set, an array of the whole subject, then
`slice().join('')`) for a set that is one to three characters in every real call.

**The equivalence, which is the whole item:** trimming only ever STOPS at the first non-member, and
every removed character is a member. So when the set holds NO surrogate code unit, a surrogate half
can never match (the scan cannot enter a pair), every removed character is exactly one UTF-16 unit
(so unit offsets equal code-point offsets), and `s.slice(lo, hi)` is what the code-point path would
build. A set with a surrogate or astral character falls through to the code-point path, which stays
the definition. Membership compares CODE UNITS — `s[i]` would allocate a one-char string per test.

`btrim(a.s, ' ')` **254.0 → 63.3 (4.01x)**; `ltrim(a.s, ' ')` **245.8 → 55.4 (4.44x)**. Min of three
alternated rounds, arms grepped in the dist.

**The three unreachable controls all read 0.92-0.95x — a systematic drift, not noise** (noise would
scatter). The astral control's 6% is the design's own cost (it now pays the surrogate scan before
falling through); the other two are most likely the larger module's JIT effect and are not worth
isolating against a 4x win. Recorded because "every control moved the same way" is item 762's shape.

**MUTANT: MOJIBAKE, AND THE SUITE PASSES IT.** Disabling the surrogate check makes
`btrim('😁x😁', '😀')` answer `"\ude01x😁"` — a **lone low surrogate** — because U+1F601
and U+1F600 share the high surrogate `0xD83D`. **2611 pass, 0 fail.**

**AGREEMENT ACROSS ARMS IS NOT COVERAGE.** The values probe's first version used 😀 against a 😀 set,
where the unit scan happens to agree; 25 queries × 11 subjects matched across both arms and would
have missed this entirely. The distinguishing case needs a DIFFERENT astral character sharing a high
surrogate, added only after reasoning about what the mutant would do. Third form of the items
702/790 lesson. Three tests pin it; teeth verified.

**The family now:** `btrim/1` 33.1, `trim/1` 37.0, `ltrim/2` 55.4, `btrim/2` 63.3, astral 335.9.
Items 790+791 took the 2-arg form 265.6 → 63.3 and the 1-arg form 56.9 → 33.1. The astral path keeps
its cost, which is the right place for it — that spelling genuinely needs code points.

## 792 — TS: the POLYMORPHIC string-or-list family gets a factory — `size` 1.89x, `cardinality` 1.79x, `reverse` 1.50x. THE ANCHOR COUNT CAUGHT A MUTANT THAT NEVER APPLIED

**DONE (TypeScript).** Item 790's survey left `size` as the largest RATIO: **42.0 ns/row against
`char_length`'s 19.9 for the same work.** `size`, `cardinality` and `reverse` are _why_
`SCALAR_NEEDS_ARG_ASSERT` exists — their check is "a string OR a list" (plus a PATH for
`cardinality`), which neither the numeric gate nor `SCALAR_ASSERTS_STR0_ONLY` can admit.

`polyStrListCall` is the third factory of this shape (after 761's `unaryStrCall`, 769's
`binaryStrCall`), folding the check in rather than skipping it — **copied verbatim**, since the
message text is a cross-engine contract.

`size` **42.8 → 22.7 (1.89x)**, `cardinality` **43.3 → 24.2 (1.79x)**, `reverse` **122.0 → 81.3
(1.50x)**, a LIST argument 1.33x. Controls: `char_length` 1.07x, `trim` 0.96x. `size` now lands level
with `char_length` — two functions computing a string's length cost the same, which is the point.

**THE PATH ASYMMETRY is the correctness story.** `cardinality(p)` counts nodes + edges; `size(p)` and
`reverse(p)` must RAISE, so `okPath` is NAME-gated. Dropping the name makes `size(p)` answer **1** and
`reverse(p)` answer **null** instead of raising — **2614 pass, 0 fail**; nothing passed a path to
either. Four tests pin it, teeth verified. Values diffed across arms over 17 queries (strings with an
astral char, lists, the three path cases, a raising number, nulls): identical.

**THE ANCHOR COUNT CAUGHT A MUTANT THAT NEVER APPLIED — first time it has earned itself.** The check
is copied verbatim from `assertScalarArgTypes`, so that line exists TWICE; the patch script printed
`ANCHOR 2` and refused, and the run that followed measured the UNMUTATED tree — path rows raising,
suite green. **Read without the anchor count that is exactly a surviving mutant's output.** Fixed by
scoping the replacement to `polyStrListCall` alone (item 780's technique).

**Two bugs in my own tests, both caught by running them** against correct code: the queries used
`(u:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->` where the fixture is `Person`/`KNOWS` (a path query over absent labels
returns NO rows, so `one()` fails on the row count and looks like a disproof), and
`ErrorCode.E_INVALID_VALUE` does not exist — the member is `ErrorCode.InvalidValue`, and
`hasErrorCode(e, undefined)` is false, so the check failed in the safe-looking direction.

**Remaining on the general dispatch**, each worth ~22 ns (1.3-1.55x, no large win left): `replace`
99.6, `substring` 85.2/64.4, `to_string` 84.8, `left` 78.1, `right` 62.1.

surface is swept** — each of the three carries a snapshot-format or public-API consequence and is a
decision, not a 60-second iteration.

## 798 — ~~⚠️ OPEN~~ **CLOSED BY ITEM 799** (1.73x / 2.11x, and the param now costs what its literal costs): a PARAM-valued predicate cost **1.76x** its literal twin per vertex. Diagnosed to one line; 799 found a THIRD route, tick-sized and sound

**OPEN TARGET, priced and diagnosed (no change).** Item 797 specified "price `satisfies`'s arms
against each other" as its next step. That comparison found something larger than the gap it was run
to explain.

**THE SCAFFOLDING DOMINATES, which answers 797's question.** 200k vertices, one shape per process,
all counting:

```text
  CONTROL none / label-only   0.0 ns   O(1) bucket
  {age: 28} inline  19.7  (props)      age = 28  22.0  (eqProps)     age > 28  25.2  (cmpProps)
  age > $a          45.4  (cmpProps, PARAM)
  a SECOND predicate adds only 2.3-4.0 ns
```

The three arms sit within 5.5 ns and a second predicate is nearly free, so **~18-20 ns is per-VERTEX
scaffolding** (`inlineHolds`'s `Map` write, `satisfies`'s `{ binding, params, graph }` allocation,
the `value(env)` call) and 2-4 ns is the predicate. **The shared `satisfies` implementation is NOT
the cost** — item 797's concern about re-deriving semantics does not apply.

**THE PARAM GAP — 1.76x, ranges DISJOINT over three rounds** (literal 24.0/26.6/27.0 against param
42.2/42.6/46.6). `WHERE k > $a` and `WHERE k > 28` ask the same question and the param is the
INJECTION-SAFE spelling this repo's own notes call "the spelling applications actually write". It is
CLAUDE.md's named defect class (`k = $a OR k = $b` vs `k IN [$a, $b]` is on that list).

**NOT PREVIOUSLY RECORDED** — no entry for param-resolution cost, no literal-vs-param comparison, no
mention of `Object.hasOwn`. Checked before claiming novelty (the discipline that caught six closed
candidates at 789-796).

**DIAGNOSED TO ONE LINE.** `compileExpr`'s `param` arm runs `Object.hasOwn(env.params, name)` plus a
dynamic property read **per row**, to produce a value that cannot change during one execution. The
`hasOwn` exists for a real reason (`$__proto__` must read undefined, matching the Rust engine's
`HashMap`) — but that reason is about WHICH value resolves, not about resolving it repeatedly.

**TWO FIXES; route 2 is the recommendation.** (1) Memoize on the params OBJECT identity — tick-sized,
but it assumes params are never mutated mid-execution, trading cost for a behaviour change nobody has
specified (item 310's memo is the precedent for how such a thing fails review). (2) **Normalize
`params` ONCE at the entry point** so the per-row closure is a plain slot read with `hasOwn`'s
semantics already applied — no identity assumption, no mutation hazard, but an entry-point change
touching every `query`/`exec` caller. **Not started: param resolution reaches every predicate in both
surface languages and wants the differential fuzzers plus its own mutation pass** (item 786's
judgement about `nullif`, which paid off at 787).

**This re-scales item 797:** its 2.24x used a LITERAL. With a param the GQL side is 42-45 ns against
Gremlin's ~10.6, so the cross-surface gap on the spelling applications write is roughly **4x**.

## 799 — TS: the `$param` reader is compile-time gated — **1.73x / 2.11x**, and the param now costs what its literal twin costs

**DONE (TypeScript).** Item 798 priced a param-valued predicate at 1.76x its literal twin and named
two routes: an identity memo (tick-sized, unsound) and entry-point normalization (sound, broad).
**Reading the code found a third that is both tick-sized AND sound.**

**THE PER-ROW `Object.hasOwn` IS REDUNDANT, and the proof is code that already runs:** plan execution
validates every referenced name and throws `MissingParameter` unless present, BEFORE any row. So at
row time the property is own. Even `$__proto__` unbound never reaches a row — it fails that
validation first, which is the hazard the per-row check was written for.

**TWO names stay on the slow closure, decided at COMPILE time so the hot path carries no test:**
`__now` (the one name the validation admits as ABSENT — unsupplied `current_*` reads NULL), and any
name on `Object.prototype` (`toString`, `constructor`, `__proto__`), which must read undefined not
the INHERITED value — **`compileValidator` is exported from the package index and runs with
`params: {}` WITHOUT that validation**, so `$toString` there would resolve to a function.

`WHERE n.age > $a` **43.0 → 24.8 ns/vertex (1.73x)**; `= $a` **43.4 → 20.6 (2.11x)**. Four controls
within 4%. **The param now costs what its literal costs** (24.8 vs 23.4; 20.6 vs 19.8) — equal cost
for equal questions, closing an instance of the defect class CLAUDE.md names. `compileExpr` went over
the complexity gate (37/35), so the arm is extracted as `compileParam` (items 781/792's recipe).

**MUTATION — both exceptions were untested; one INERT, one load-bearing.** Dropping `__now` is
**INERT** (`current_date` still answers null, because `undefined` and `null` are both nullish
downstream) and **stays anyway**, keeping the equivalence LOCAL rather than resting on coercion no
test pins — same call as items 781/782. Dropping the prototype exception is a **WRONG ANSWER that
SURVIVED (2621 pass, 0 fail)**; three tests now pin it and two fail under the mutant.

**⚠️ OPEN ANOMALY, not chased:** `two-param` (`age > $a AND score > $b`) moved only 1.03x, and its
PLAIN reading (30.4) is **LOWER than the single-param shape's 43.0** — a two-param query cheaper than
a one-param one on the arm that charges per param. A reachability probe confirms all three shapes DO
reach `buildNodeCount`'s tally, so it is not off-path. **No explanation; recorded rather than
smoothed**, because an unexplained ordering is what items 748/749 were built from.

**⚠️ ITS SPELLING-PROBE FLAG WAS NOISE, NOT A REGRESSION — and the control proved it.** The run
flagged `SEEK: a param equality AND a second conjunct (item 578)` at **2.49x**, a group that had not
flagged in any of the nine earlier runs this session. Three of its four members got FASTER; the
fourth (`WHERE n.k >= 0 AND n.s = $s`) read 9.22 before and 20.57 after. Investigated rather than
assumed:

- the first reproduction used `s: i % 997` (201 rows, 0.1 ms) and showed nothing — **the probe's
  fixture is `k: i % 50`, `s: i % 7`, so the seek returns 28,572 candidates.** A reproduction that

- with the real fixture, **`lit-second` — which has no param and so the change cannot reach — ranges
  10.03-23.57 over nine reps, 2.35x within ONE arm.** A 2.49x between members is inside that.
- the isolated A/B **reverses the sign**: `param-second` PLAIN 13.94 against GATE **7.73 — 1.80x
  FASTER** — with `lit-second` flat at 1.03x.

**No regression.** Recorded because two wrong conclusions were available (commit assuming noise;

## 800 — BUILT AND REVERTED: a cross-language group cannot live in the TS spelling probe. The GQL side arrives POLLUTED, the Gremlin side clean

**REVERTED (no engine change).** Item 797 recommended adding cross-language groups to the TS probe,
"three lines each". Built, measured, reverted — **both halves of that recommendation are wrong.**

**"Three lines" was wrong structurally:** the TS Gremlin surface has NO text entry point (it is a
composable builder), so a Gremlin member cannot be a query string. It needed a `Member` type
(`string | { label, run }`), a runner dispatch plus `labelOf`, and a `ROWS_MAY_DIFFER` opt-out on the
answer check (the surfaces return `[{"c":N}]` against `[N]`, so without it every such group reports
`ANSWERS DIFFER` forever).

**And the probe is the wrong HOME, because the groups measure the probe.** Isolated against the full
sweep, same binary and fixture:

```text
                     isolated   in-sweep
  GQL  unlabelled      4.51 ms    8.84     1.96x
  GRM  unlabelled      2.64       2.54     1.04x
  GQL  labelled        6.27      14.42     2.30x
  GRM  labelled        4.68       3.37     faster
  GQL  one-hop        23.87      54.67     2.29x
  GRM  one-hop        25.10      21.81     faster
```

**Every Gremlin member is stable; every GQL member roughly doubles.** A fixture or warm-up effect
moves BOTH — only the GQL side moving is GQL-path pollution: ~40 GQL groups run first, so those
dispatch sites are megamorphic by then (**item 762**), while the Gremlin member is the first Gremlin
query in the process. Item 747 recorded this at **1.4x** for GQL rows; at the END of the GQL run it
is 2.0-2.3x. The full-sweep ratios (3.49x / 4.27x / 2.51x) are substantially instrument and flagged
as three new >2x entries — exactly the _flag that means nothing_ the opt-out existed to avoid.

**Three fixes considered:** keep them as "isolation only" (rejected — the summary is where readers
arrive, per the probe's own item-635 comment); run them FIRST (fair pair, but moves ~40 recorded
figures to add 3); **ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS, which is what `probe:scalar` does (item 790) — and that
is where a cross-language comparison belongs.** Its own tick.

**Item 797's finding STANDS, and this is why it was trustworthy:** it was measured one shape per
process, which is the only reason its 2.24x was a comparison rather than a position in a run order.
The gap it named is real; the TS side still cannot catch a cross-language divergence.

## 801 — `probe:surface` (one spelling per PROCESS): item 797's cross-surface gap CONFIRMED, RE-PRICED to ~1.71-1.85x at item 929 (recorded here as ~2.1x), and a SECOND gap found running the other way

**DONE (instrument).** Item 797 named the gap, item 800 built the fix in the wrong place and
specified the right one — **one shape per process**. `packages/native/surface-probe.ts`,

Three runs, median-of-11 per spelling:

```text
  filtered node count, unlabelled   GQL 4.71-5.18ms  GRM 2.30-2.52   GQL ~2.1x SLOWER  (2.06/2.05/2.12)
  filtered node count, labelled     GQL 4.59-4.76    GRM 2.11-2.18   GQL ~2.2x SLOWER  (2.12/2.18/2.25)
  project one property              GQL 6.92-10.41   GRM 18.19-26.41 GQL 1.75-3.82x FASTER
  one-hop count / unfiltered count  0.00 vs 0.01     too fast to compare
```

**~2.1x against item 797's 2.24x and item 800's isolated 1.71x** — three measurements, two fixtures,

different shape** — Gremlin at a filtered scan, GQL at a projection. Direction stable across three

**Item 800 is corrected twice:** its one-hop group claimed "no gap", but on this fixture both

**OPEN:** the ~2.1x itself. Item 798 located it in the ~18-20 ns of per-vertex scaffolding around

## 802 — the `satisfies` scaffolding: BOTH halves REFUTED. A part measured dearer than the whole is an instrument result

**DONE (no engine change).** Item 801 named the remaining per-vertex scaffolding as the open target.
Two changes built, both refuted on real queries, both recorded in doc comments on the code they
would have changed.

**The planned change was item 454**, refuted with numbers in a doc comment on `satisfies` ending
"do not re-derive it". It was re-derived anyway — the extraction was written before the comment
three lines above the signature was read. **The seventh already-closed candidate this session**
(789, 793, 795, 796) and the first whose record lives in the SOURCE rather than here, which is the
half of "check the list before pricing" that gets skipped.

**THE LADDER, which is the result worth keeping.** Hand-written loops, 200,000 vertices, one arm per
process, median of 11:

```text
  loop floor                                 1.4-2.1 ns/vertex
  CONSTANT-key property read + compare       9.6-11.1
  propOf: DYNAMIC keyed load + 2 ?. + ??     9.8-11.1    <- the SAME as the named load
  + inlineHolds's binding.set                12.8-15.8   (+~4)
  + { binding, params, graph } + value(env)  13.2-15.7   (+~0.5 — confirms 454 independently)
  the engine's whole filtered count          21-27
```

So **the property read is ~10 of the ~24 ns a vertex**, not the dispatch around it, and a dynamic
keyed load is free relative to a named one. That re-reads **item 798**: its "~18-20 ns is
scaffolding" came from three predicate arms sitting within 5.5 ns of each other, and agreement
across arms is not a floor (item 791's rule, in a new place).

**THE ARITHMETIC CHECK AN ISOLATED MEASUREMENT MUST PASS.** A sixth arm called the real `satisfies`
with a HAND-BUILT predicate and read 41.4-46.8 ns/vertex against the hand loop's 13-15. That 31 ns
looked like the finding and two changes were built to collect it. **It cannot have been real, and
the number says so unaided: the whole query costs 21-27 ns a vertex and `satisfies` is a part of
it.** The literal `{ props: [], cmpProps: [...] }` is a different hidden class from what
`compilePredicate` emits, so the sites inside `satisfies` saw a shape they never see in production.
**Rule: when a probe prices a PART, check it against the measured WHOLE before believing it; if the
part exceeds the whole, the argument is the instrument.** Same family as "a reproduction that does
not reproduce the ANSWER SIZE is not a reproduction" — and answer size would NOT have caught this
one, every arm answered 156,000.

**REFUTED (1): a two-number ORDERING fast path in `compareTruth`** — byte-identical NaN included
(`isNullish` is null/undefined only; a number is not a temporal; `typeof lv === typeof rv ===
'number'` IS the `orderable` test; `=`/`<>` excluded as `structuralEq`'s call). Five reaching
shapes, three alternated rounds, twice: filtered count 4.70/4.75/4.86 -> 4.74/5.13/4.32, two-bound
6.31/5.97/5.78 -> 5.55/6.17/5.46, 156k-row projection 10.54/11.22/10.30 -> 10.37/10.09/14.11,
general arm 13.24/12.21/11.04 -> 10.30/11.61/11.24, per-edge hop 48.1/48.8/48.9 -> 48.0/48.6/47.8.
All overlapping.

**REFUTED (2): indexed loops for the three `for...of` + destructuring loops** in `satisfies` and in
its pre-filter twin (same three loops; a grep found the second copy the first patch missed). It is a
**TRADE**: `eqProps` count 5.66/5.49/5.36 against 5.77/6.51/6.14, but two-bound `cmpProps` count
6.47/7.42/6.14 against 5.93/6.13/5.66 — slower in all three rounds. Both halves together cancel.

**One reading looked like a win and the second A/B took it back**: a string-equality count read
6.69/6.53/6.33 against 5.68/5.69/5.24 (disjoint, 1.17x) and then 5.93/6.23/6.31 against
6.92/5.79/5.49. **A single disjoint triple inside the ~10% noise floor is not a flag.**

**THE CONTROL WAS WRONG, with item 762's exact symptom.** `WHERE n.s = 's3'` was picked as
unreachable because the fast path excludes `=` and strings — but it reaches the indexed loops, so
when it moved while every target stayed flat it read as "the control moved more than the target"
when it was a target. **A control must be unreachable by EVERY change in the arm, not by the one you
have in mind.** Replaced with a no-predicate projection; it did not move.

## 803 — the per-element binding `Map` write is compile-time gated: **1.11-1.34x** (TS), and "alternated rounds" means alternating the ORDER

**DONE.** Item 802's ladder left one unpriced term in the TS filtered-count path —
`inlineHolds`'s `binding.set(bindVar, element)`, ~4 of the ~24 ns a vertex. It is now omitted
wherever nothing can read it back.

**THE RULE.** The binding is read in exactly one of the places a predicate's values come from: a
surviving general compiled `where` (through `env`). `eqProps`/`cmpProps` are CLOSED by construction
in `directEqProps`; `props` are closed where the caller has proved it. So a predicate that lifts
ENTIRELY — inline `WHERE n.k > 10`, clause `WHERE n.s = 's3'`, inline `{k: 2}`, the common case and
the point of items 224/230/276 — writes a `Map` entry per element that nothing ever reads.

**TEN SITES, ONE HELPER.** `grep -n 'bindVar:'` found ten construction sites, nine of them the same
four lines rewritten. All now go through `predFor(pred, ownVar, closedProps)` and `bindVar:` appears
once in the package. `closedProps` is REQUIRED, not inferred, because it cannot be inferred — a
compiled value is a closure and nothing can ask it what it reads.

**Measured end-to-end, 200,000 vertices, one shape per process, ORDER-ALTERNATED:**

```text
  clause 1bound        PRE 4.68/4.74/4.89 ms   POST 4.11/4.42/4.24   1.14x DISJOINT
  inline {k: 2}            3.39/3.47/4.23           2.85/3.26/6.91   1.19x on min (one outlier)
  clause str-eq            7.10/6.16/5.86           5.13/5.99/4.96   1.18x on min
  inline WHERE             4.54/7.52/4.78           3.89/4.63/4.76   1.17x on min
  CONTROL non-lifting     10.19/11.17/11.18        12.57/10.08/13.99  flat
  CONTROL no-pred         13.74/14.58/10.44        10.42/10.60/ 9.88  flat/noisy
```

An independent A/B of the two-site arm agreed: `clause 1bound` 4.90/4.69/5.26 against
4.24/4.58/4.40 (**1.11x**, disjoint), `inline {k: 2}` 3.57/4.14/3.65 against 2.75/2.67/3.24
(**1.34x**, disjoint).

**Item 802's ladder PREDICTED the magnitude** (~4 of ~24 ns, i.e. ~1.2x), which is why 1.11x is a
result rather than noise: **a number inside the ~10% band needs a prior reason to be the size it
is.** Both controls are unreachable BY CONSTRUCTION — `n.k * 1 > 10` does not lift so `bindVar`
stays, and the no-predicate projection runs no predicate — which is the lesson item 802 paid for.

**⚠️ NEW METHOD RESULT — THE ORDER CONFOUND, which cost two A/Bs.** The first two A/Bs ran **PRE
first in every round**. Under that order the `non-lifting` control appeared to improve
10.19-15.10 -> 10.08-11.03 consistently in the change's favour — a control the change cannot reach
moving more than some targets, which is item 762's signature and sent me hunting a redistribution
effect that was not there. With the order alternated (POST,PRE / PRE,POST / POST,PRE) the control is
flat and the targets stand: the PRE arm had been absorbing each round's cold start. **CLAUDE.md's
"min across three order-alternated rounds" means alternating the ORDER, not repeating three times.
Three rounds in a fixed order are one observation of an order, not three of a change.**

**Teeth: four of four, after the first two survived.** Inverting the `where` test — caught, 147
fail. Never binding — caught, 149 fail. Neutering `!closedProps` and `props.length > 0` — **both
survived the full 2,624-test suite**, structurally, because every current caller passes
`closedProps: true` and that disjunct is unreachable from any query. It is not redundant (it is the
precondition that makes the other nine sites safe), so per item 475 it was given teeth rather than
deleted: `predFor` is exported and `bindvar-gating.test.ts` pins all three inputs directly,
including `closedProps: false` over a `props` entry whose value closure THROWS if called. Both
mutants now caught.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0; `bun test packages/gql` 2634 pass 0 fail; `bun run fuzz`
13 pass 0 fail TWICE; `bun run spelling` 0 answer disagreements and only its two pre-existing >2x
groups. **Rust side NOT checked and not claimed** — whether `exec` pays an analogous per-element
write is its own tick.

## 804 — native `split` is AT THE ALLOCATOR FLOOR. Exact capacity REFUTED, and item 783 was wrong about which allocation

**DONE (no engine change).** `scalarfn_bench` prices 30 scalar functions and `split` is the outlier
by five times — 49.4 ns/row against 9.7-10.3 for every other string function.

**Item 783's reading was a guess.** It said "its body is already a single `Vec` and one `GStr` a
piece, so that cost is the allocation itself" — right that there is one, wrong about which, and
reached by reading the body. **`GStr` is INLINE up to 12 bytes**, and every part of every fixture
row (`naïve`, `7`, `ßé`, `  pad7  `, `plain7`) is under that cap, so **the part strings allocate
nothing**. The only heap allocation is the `Vec`.

**REFUTED: `Vec::with_capacity(s.matches(d).count() + 1)`** in place of `collect`. `str::Split` is
not an `ExactSizeIterator` and its `size_hint` is `(0, None)`, so `collect` starts at zero and
doubles. Three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds at 1M rows: **50.04/49.16/49.40 against 51.54/49.05/49.83**,
with `upper`, `char_length`, `replace/3` and both `count` controls flat.

**THE DISCRIMINATOR, which is the keeper.** One bench row settles the null instead of explaining it:
`split/1part` splits on `zz`, which occurs in no fixture string, so it builds exactly ONE part in
one `Vec` of capacity 1 and growth is impossible by construction. It costs **42.4 ns/row** against
49.6. With `replace/3` and `substring/3` at ~10 ns through the same dispatch:

```text
  ~10 ns   the general two-argument scalar dispatch (every string function pays it)
  ~32 ns   split's OWN per-row list construction + teardown — FLAT in the part count
  ~10 ns   per EXTRA part beyond the first
```

**Exact capacity can only remove growth, and growth was never the term.** The null now has a
measured cause, not a plausible one.

**What would remove it is not a tick:** an inline representation for a short `Value::List`, the way
`GStr` inlines a short string. It changes `Value`'s layout, which the cross-engine byte-identity
contract runs through, and pays only for small lists. Priced, not taken.

**Also: item 801's gap after 803.** First `probe:surface` reading since 803 shipped, three runs —

## 805 — `probe:elemread`: item 802's ladder MIS-ATTRIBUTED its biggest line. The walk is 2 ns, the read is 2 ns, together they are 10

**DONE (instrument), no engine change.** `packages/native/elemread-probe.ts`,
`bun run probe:elemread`.

**Item 802's "property read and compare at 9.6-11.1 ns a vertex" is wrong**, and item 804 repeated
it as the remaining term of item 801's gap. Separating the two halves was all it took.

**REFUTED FIRST: `CONST key` vs `DYN key` cannot diagnose V8 dictionary mode.** Item 802 found them
equal and I read that as a hash lookup on both. They are equal in EVERY arm, including a plain
object literal that is certainly fast-mode (1.1-1.3 ns either way), because a hoisted
`const key = 'k'` is as constant to V8 as the literal. The arms stay as the record of the refuted
reading.

**THE DECOMPOSITION** (200,000 vertices, one arm per process, built OUTSIDE the timed region,
median of 11, three rounds):

```text
  walk map values (NO read)        1.4-2.3 ns/vertex
  walk map + read v.properties.k   9.2-10.0            the engine's own shape
  walk label Set + read            8.8- 9.7
  walk ARRAY + read (same objects) 7.1- 8.2
  property bags in a dense array   1.8- 2.2            the read alone, in order
  plain / frozen object literal    1.1- 1.3            the read's floor
  a Map per element                14.9-15.8
```

**The walk is ~2 ns, the read is ~2 ns, together they are ~10** — so **~6 ns a vertex exists only
in the PAIRING**: the `Map` yields vertices in insertion order and `v.properties` is a dependent
load into a separately-allocated bag, one cold line each, which no prefetcher can anticipate.

- **`Map`-per-element REFUTED as a property layout: 8x worse** (14.9-15.8 against 1.8-2.2).
- **The label `Set` walks slightly cheaper than the id `Map`**, the right direction for
  `probe:surface` showing the labelled pair faster.

**PRICED AND DECLINED — a dense vertex array walked instead of the `Map`:** 7.1-8.2 against
9.2-10.0, **1.2-1.3x of the pair**, ~2 ns of the ~24 a vertex, about 1.08x end to end — under the
noise floor, against a structural `@lenke/core` change and a second collection to keep correct
through deletes.

**⚠️ A correction to my own first reading of that arm.** It read 1.5-1.9x while using
`for (let i = …)` where the `Map` arms use `for...of`, so it carried the ACCESS FORM as well as the
collection; the lint gate flagged the indexed loop and matching both sides roughly halved the gap.
**A difference between two arms is only the thing you changed if nothing else differs.**

**WHAT THIS GIVES ITEM 342** (packed presence / columnar), which had no number on this shape: if a
per-element property read were CONTIGUOUS the pair would cost ~4 ns instead of ~10 — ~6 of the ~24
ns a vertex, **~1.3x on a filtered node count**, and the largest single term left in it.

## 806 — packed presence ATTEMPTED and re-scoped: item 741's census missed **123** sites, and item 342's ladder has a rung that is already built

**NO ENGINE CHANGE** (built, reverted, re-priced with a real count). Item 342's packed presence has
been "the best-priced unbuilt Rust lever" since item 740, which called it multi-tick; **item 741
corrected that to "five operations and one real rewrite"**. Built on 741's scoping. **741 was
wrong, and its METHOD is why.**

**RUNG 1 IS ALREADY BUILT, and the ladder's biggest number is not a clean pair.** The
`element_render_cost` step from baseline to "columns hoisted" looks like 4.08x at K=200 (1785.7 →
437.7 ns/row). It is not a candidate: the baseline arm calls the real `node_result_value` while the
hoisted arm ALSO skips the ext-id, the label list and two `Arc` `Value::Map` allocations. The
apples-to-apples pair is elsewhere in the same harness — `props: one lookup per key` **95.4**
against `columns hoisted` **92.6**, i.e. **3%** — and `render_nodes`, the batch renderer, **already
hoists columns and key `Value`s** (items 390/391). Per-node `node_result_value` cannot: it is called
one node at a time from a `Gen` cell, a path and the JSON sinks.

**THE CLEAN PAIR (hoisted vs packed — both pre-resolve columns, both build the same `Vec`):**

```text
  K=  0 extra store keys    92.2 -> 90.4 ns/row   1.02x
  K= 12                    116.4 -> 105.2         1.11x
  K= 60                    168.0 -> 147.7         1.14x
  K=200                    437.7 -> 246.4         1.78x
```

342's "rung 2 1.67x at K=200" is confirmed. **What was NOT recorded: K=12 and K=60 — much closer to
most graphs — are only 1.11x and 1.14x.** This pays in proportion to store WIDTH.

**THE CENSUS THAT WAS WRONG.** A `Presence` bitmap (`words: Vec<u64>` + `len`, with
`zeros/len/get/set/push/pop`, deliberately not a `Vec<bool>` drop-in) went into all six `Column`
variants and all of `store.rs` almost exactly as 741 predicted — then failed to compile in **seven
other files**.

|                                                          | 741 said    | actually |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | -------- |
| `.present` FIELD accesses outside `store.rs`             | 0           | 0 (true) |
| `present`/`nulls` INDEXING sites outside `store.rs`      | not counted | **123**  |
| pattern-match bindings destructuring a column's presence | not counted | **84**   |
| `&[bool]` parameters that ARE a presence slice           | not counted | **16**   |
| files with code sites outside `store.rs`                 | 0 implied   | **10**   |

**The method is the error.** 741 counted `.present`, a FIELD ACCESS, and the exec layer never writes
one — it writes `Column::Num { data, present, .. }` and then `present[i]`. Two of those are even
renamed on the way in (`present: lp`, `present: rp`), so a grep for `present[` misses them too.
**A census is only a scope if it counts the ways the thing is REACHED, not one syntax for reaching
it.**

**And it is not just more renaming:** 16 helper signatures take `&[bool]`, and the vectorized scan
loops gate per row inside a branch-free pass — the "byte-wide presence gate" `scan_layout_probe`
named, i.e. exactly where the win comes from. Converting those to shift-and-mask is its own piece of
work with its own measurement (a packed gate inside a branch-free loop may lose).

**So item 740 was right and 741's correction of it was wrong**, now by measurement rather than
impression. Lever state: priced by width, scoped for real, **not started**, and its precondition is
explicit — the branch-free gates first, measured on their own.

**My own version of 741's mistake:** I checked 741's claim with a grep piped through `head -15`, got
codec prose and two examples back, and concluded there were no bindings outside `store.rs`. **The
`fastpath.rs` hits started at line 16.** Item 319's rule is about `head` closing a mutation
harness's pipe; the general form is what bit here — **a conclusion from a truncated listing is a
conclusion about the truncation.** `wc -l` first costs nothing.

**CORRECTION to item 805's closing line.** It said its ~6 ns pointer-chase finding gave "item 342
(packed presence / columnar) a number on this shape". Item 342 is a Rust `Column` representation;
805 measured TypeScript property bags, and the TS engine has no columns at all. The finding stands —
a contiguous per-element read would take the walk-plus-read pair from ~10 ns to ~4 — but it belongs
to item 617's family (TS layout), not to 342.

## 807 — `probe:adjlayout`: the widest bench gap finally has a layout number. Flat interned index **3.4-3.7x** on the lookup; the concat half-measure is **2.0-2.5x WORSE**

**DONE (instrument), no engine change.** `packages/native/adjlayout-probe.ts`,
`bun run probe:adjlayout`.

TS multi-hop counts are the widest real gap in the bench (`count 4-hop` **84.58x** native, 3-hop
65.61x, 2-hop 39.19x, one row out). Item 795's sweep traced three components, found two spent, and
left the third — `edgesFromByLabel.get(nodeId)` then `.get(type)` — as the only lever **with no
number**. It has one now.

**200,000 (node, type) lookups, 8 types, one arm per process, built outside the timed region, median
of 11, three rounds:**

```text
  nested   Map<string, Map<string, Set>>   52.1 / 54.8 / 55.8 ns/lookup   what the engine has
  concat   Map<string, Set>, key per call 100.2 /113.7 /137.6             2.0-2.5x WORSE
  numeric  Map<number, Set>, ids interned  15.2 / 14.7 / 16.9             3.4-3.7x FASTER
  CONTROL  inner short-key lookup only      6.3 /  6.5 /  8.4             the floor
```

**The OUTER lookup is almost all of it:** the inner is 6.3-8.4 ns, so ~45 of the ~52-56 belongs to
`get(nodeId)` on a 200,000-entry string-keyed map — a multi-megabyte table probed in random order,
one cache miss each. The same 200,000 entries under SMI keys cost 14.7-16.9 for BOTH levels.

**THE HALF-MEASURE IS REFUTED WITH A NUMBER.** A single `Map<string, Set>` keyed by
`` `${nodeId}\u0000${type}` `` needs no interning and no new structure — and it is **2.0-2.5x worse
than the two lookups it replaces**: the concatenation allocates a fresh string per lookup whose hash
has never been computed, where both nested keys are long-lived strings V8 has already hashed. I
predicted this before running it; **predicting is not measuring**, and the number is what stops it
being re-proposed.

**TWO OTHER LEVERS CLOSED BY READING, this tick:**

- `scan_layout_probe`'s "hoisting the operator out of the loop is an independent, much cheaper win"
  **is items 450/453/459/462, built** (453: two-bound range 1.782 → 0.458 ms with monomorphic arms;
  462: the two `match`es hoisted into `arith_step`/`num_pred`).
- `scan_layout_probe`'s variant **C' (6.3-9.7x) is NOT independent of item 806** — it needs both the
  bitset gate and the mask output, since variant B (memory order, byte gate) "barely beats A". It
  inherits 806's precondition.

**WHAT IT DOES NOT LICENSE.** This prices the LOOKUP, not a query: the hot loop looks up once per
middle EDGE and `side()` does more than the lookup, so the honest claim is "3.4-3.7x on one
component of three, two already spent". And the interning the `numeric` arm assumes IS the work —
node ids are strings in `@lenke/core`, so a flat index means an id→u32 intern table maintained
through inserts and deletes.

**CORRECTION to this file's own open-set summary**, which calls the remaining lever "item **617**'s
CSR for TS multi-hop counts". Item 617 is the GQL point-lookup-by-id fix (`Plan::NodeSeed`, 1258x);
the CSR diagnosis is in item **795**'s sweep, which cites 617 rather than being it.

## 808 — the widest bench gap is CLOSED, not open: interning is worth NOTHING, and the one available layout was refuted at item 200

**DONE (no engine change).** Item 807 shipped `probe:adjlayout` and read it as "a flat INTERNED
index is 3.4-3.7x on the lookup". **Two discriminator arms, added one tick later, retract that
framing and close the target.**

**The arms that were missing.** `numeric` changed TWO things at once — two lookups became one AND
the key became an SMI — and 807 credited the win to the interning. Two new arms separate them:
`prekeyed` (ONE lookup, string key, pre-built so nothing is concatenated per call) and `short keys`
(ONE lookup into a 200,000-entry map, short key, still built per call).

```text
  nested       49.6 / 54.2 / 68.3 ns/lookup   two long-lived-key lookups — the engine
  concat      103.2 /107.5 /106.9             one lookup, key concatenated per call
  short keys   83.5 / 83.9 / 90.7             one lookup, SHORT key, still built per call
  prekeyed     14.2 / 14.9 / 14.9             one lookup, string key ALREADY in hand
  numeric      14.2 / 14.6 / 15.6             one lookup, ids and types INTERNED
  CONTROL       6.5 /  8.1 /  8.3             an 8-entry map — NOT a one-lookup floor
```

**1. INTERNING IS WORTH NOTHING.** `prekeyed` 14.2-14.9 against `numeric` 14.2-15.6 — a long-lived
STRING key costs what an SMI costs. **Item 807's "flat INTERNED index" is the wrong name for the
lever**; there is no case here for an id→u32 intern table, which was the expensive half of what 807
said the change would need.

**2. WHAT COSTS IS BUILDING A KEY PER LOOKUP.** `short keys` does ONE lookup where nested does two
and is still **WORSE** (83.5-90.7 against 49.6-68.3). A fresh string is ~70 ns of allocation plus a
hash never computed; a long-lived string carries V8's cached hash. That is `concat`'s mechanism too,
now isolated rather than asserted.

**3. SO THE LEVER IS 3.3-4.5x AT THE LOOKUP AND NOT AVAILABLE.** Three records between it and a
change:

- **Item 590** measured the one-lookup version at the QUERY level: "per-edge `Map.get` on a memoized
  degree map 42.07 — **only 1.5x**", against the per-edge bucket lookup's 61.80. The lookup-level
  3.3-4.5x does not survive the trip to a query.
- **Item 590** also measured a flattened CSR at **37.65 ms to BUILD** on 200k edges — "so no help at
  all" for a per-query index.
- The one layout that gets a single lookup with keys ALREADY IN HAND is the **type-first inversion**
  (`Map<type, Map<vertexId, Set<Edge>>>`): the type string is long-lived and there are ~8 of them, so
  the outer hit is a tiny cache-resident map and the inner is one long-lived-key lookup. **Refuted at
  item 200 and USER-CONFIRMED CLOSED** — it wins the typed lookup 2.2-4.1x (which is what this probe
  re-derives) and **loses get-by-id 1.4x at three edge types and 4.8x at twenty**, with the
  dual-spine variant costing 2.0-2.4x on `indexEdgeLabel`.

**So item 795's "no tick-sized win remains on the widest row" is stronger than it was stated: there
is no win of any size available on that component without the opt-in index item 200 left as the only
surviving direction — a feature with an API, not an optimization.** The target is closed, not open
with a number.

**A correction to item 807's own reading.** Its `CONTROL inner only` is an 8-entry map, and 807 used
its 6.3-8.4 ns as the floor for "one lookup" to attribute ~45 ns to the outer. The arithmetic holds —
the outer IS most of the nested cost — but 6.5 ns is a tiny-cache-resident-map number and does not
generalize; `prekeyed` at 14.2-14.9 is what one lookup into a 200,000-entry map actually costs. Both
arms stay, the control relabelled.

**Eleventh already-closed candidate caught by reading before building this session** (789, 793, 795,
796, 802's item 454, 805's 784, 806's rungs, 807's 450/453/459/462, and now 590 and 200). The two
that found something new (803, and this probe's own discriminators) both came from measuring a pair
that differed in exactly one thing.

## 809 — `nodes(p)` renders each shared prefix element once per path. A per-column memo is **1.14x** — and the 6x the arithmetic predicted did NOT appear, which reframes the row

**DONE (Rust).** `bench_all`'s standout per-row cost is `anchored + nodes(p)`: **241,750 µs for
47,007 rows = 5,143 ns/row**, against `anchored + path` on the SAME rows at 147 ns/row — 35x. Not
previously recorded as a perf target (the only `nodes(p)` entry in this file is a conformance one).

**THE OBSERVATION.** `path_node_values` called `node_result_value(store, id)` per element per ROW
with no memo. `ANY SHORTEST (x)->*(y)` from one anchored source is a **BFS TREE**, so a node at
depth `d` lies on every path into its subtree and was re-rendered once per such path — 47,007 rows
over ≤50,000 distinct nodes.

**This is the shape item 355's rule says YES to** — "a memo helps a REVISITED element and taxes a
VISITED-ONCE one" — and it is why item 591 refused a memo at five of `side()`'s six call sites while
this one takes it: here an element is revisited once per path through it, by construction.

**It also LOWERS peak memory, which is why there is no size cap.** Without the memo every row's list
owns its own rendered copy of each shared element and all rows are live at once in the `Col`; with
it they share one `Arc`, so entries replace duplicates rather than adding to them.

`render::RenderMemo` + `path_node_values_memo` / `path_edge_values_memo`, one memo per COLUMN (not
per row), wired at all four render sites: `Expr::PathAccess` (`Nodes`, `Relationships`, `Elements`),
`Expr::Path` (the `{vertices, edges, length}` value) and Gremlin's `path_nodes`. The two
un-memoized helpers are gone rather than left as a second definition to drift.

**MEASURED — three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds (POST,PRE / PRE,POST / POST,PRE):**

```text
  anchored + nodes(p)   PRE 235735.6 / 237167.2 / 234442.6 us   POST 212008.2 / 210118.2 / 204911.6
                        min-of-three 1.14x, ranges fully DISJOINT
  CONTROL anchored count       6010.7 /  6002.6 /  5957.6        5980.2 /  5918.6 /  5931.8   flat
  CONTROL anchored + y.name    7137.2 /  6313.1 /  6361.2        6838.5 /  6801.3 /  6816.6   PRE min WINS
  CONTROL anchored + path      6387.8 /  7695.6 /  7105.4        6701.8 /  7274.2 /  7237.4   PRE min WINS
  CONTROL varlen control      16105.6 / 17098.9 / 17078.1       15713.9 / 17095.1 / 16687.9   flat
```

**Two controls move AGAINST the change**, which is the strongest control result available — it rules
out the systematic drift item 803 had to go back and re-measure for. `anchored count` reads a path
length with lineage present, so it allocates the memos and never uses them: flat confirms an empty
`HashMap::new()` costs nothing.

### ⚠️ The arithmetic predicted 3-6x and it did not appear — that is the finding

`element p` costs 392.6 ns/row in the same sweep, and with ~6x fewer renders the row should have
roughly halved. It moved 11%. **So the element RENDER is only ~11% of `nodes(p)`'s 5,143 ns/row**,
and the rest is the per-element `Value` and the per-row `List` construction — an OUTPUT-SIZE cost,
the same family as item 289's carrier finding, not a render cost.

That reframes the row: it is not "the element renderer multiplied by path length", and the remaining
~89% is not reachable by anything that makes rendering cheaper. **Recorded so the next pass does not
price the renderer against this row.** Why the render is so much smaller a share than `element p`
suggests is NOT explained here — the social fixture's nodes are narrower than the `perrow` fixture's,
which would account for some of it, and inventing the rest would be the mistake items 804 and 808
were about.

- the `other => other.clone()` arm → `Value::Null` — **SURVIVED** all 1,963 tests. The arm is
  **unreachable**: a lineage stores node and edge ids as `Value::Num`, so nothing else arrives. It is

## 811 — item 809's memo hits **90.6%**, which CONFIRMS its inference and reconciles the one thing it left unexplained: the render is ~65 ns on this fixture, not 392

**VERIFICATION, no engine change** (a temporary counter, measured, reverted). Item 809 shipped the
`nodes(p)` render memo for 1.14x and concluded from that 1.14x that "the element render is only ~11%
of `nodes(p)`'s 5,143 ns/row". **That inference is only valid if the memo HITS** — a memo that never
fires buys nothing for a completely different reason, and the two are the same null (item 339's
rule). It was recorded as an inference, so it got checked.

### Measured directly

A counter in `path_node_values_memo`, on the bench's own row (`ANY SHORTEST (x:Person)-[:KNOWS]->*(y)
WHERE x.name = 'name1' RETURN nodes(p)`, 50,000 nodes, 47,007 rows):

```text
  memo calls (Value::Num)   498,969
  memo MISSES (a render)     47,007
  non-Num elements                0
  hit rate                     90.6%      elements per row 10.61
```

**The memo works as designed and the miss count is exactly the distinct-element count** — 47,007
misses for 47,007 reachable targets plus the source, i.e. one render per distinct node and not one
more. The eight other shortest-path rows in that table print `calls=0`, confirming they do not reach
this path at all (so they are controls by construction, which is what item 809 measured them as).

**`other` is 0**, which independently confirms item 809's surviving mutant: the
`other => other.clone()` arm is unreachable because a lineage holds every element id as a
`Value::Num`. The mutation survivor and this counter are the same fact from two directions.

### The arithmetic now closes, and it reconciles 809's open question

451,962 renders removed for a measured 30,000 µs saving (235,000 → 205,000) prices the render at
**~65 ns per element on this fixture**. Item 809 recorded that it could not explain why the render
was so much smaller a share than `element p`'s **392.6 ns/row** suggested, and declined to invent a
reason. The reason is fixture WIDTH, and item 806's ladder predicts it precisely:

```text
  element render, 4 props + 0 extra store keys   169.8 ns   (item 806's ladder)
  element render, 4 props + 200 extra keys      1785.7
  `element p` in query/perrow                    392.6      a wider fixture again
  social_store, ONE property per node              ~65      THIS fixture, derived here
```

So **both numbers are right and they are not the same measurement**: `element p` renders a
multi-property node from a store with many distinct keys, and `nodes(p)` here renders a one-property
node. 809's "the render is only ~11%" stands, for a reason it can now state.

### What is still unattributed, stated as such

205,000 µs remain over 498,969 elements = **~411 ns per element** that is NOT the render. The
search and lineage are accounted for separately — `anchored + path` runs the identical query
projecting `path_length(p)` for **6,700 µs**, so the BFS plus lineage is ~3% of the row and cannot be
it. What remains is the per-element `Arc` clone, the per-row `Vec<Value>` and `Value::List`, the
`Col::Gen` entry, and the drop of 498,969 `Arc`s at the end — none of which plausibly costs 411 ns
each, so **the dominant term here is still unidentified and is NOT being guessed at.** It is the
largest unexplained per-element cost in the native corpus and the natural next target; items 804 and
808 are both records of what happens when a mechanism is asserted rather than measured.

**Fourteen already-closed candidates were checked and set aside before this** (789, 793, 795, 796,
454, 784, 806's rungs, 450/453/459/462, 590, 200, 339's `algo/call` ratio, 359/382's `map field`
20x, and the bench's own `size(b)` note on `repeat-group control`). The native sweep's every
remaining outlier has a record; this is the one fresh number in it.
