## 812 — `nodes(p)`'s unexplained cost LOCATED: 159 ns/element to build, **265 ns/element to carry out of `exec`**. Two arm names were lies and the counter caught both

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change** (a temporary counter and a temporary example, both reverted). Item
811 left ~411 ns an element unattributed on the bench's worst per-row shape and said explicitly it
was not being guessed at. This locates it.

### The ladder, one arm per process, each differing in ONE thing

Same query and fixture throughout (`ANY SHORTEST (x:Person)-[:KNOWS]->*(y) WHERE x.name = 'name1'`,
50,000 nodes, 47,007 rows, 498,969 path elements):

```text
  CONTROL y.name (no path value)   10889.2 us      the lineage-free floor
  path_length (search only)         7329.4         the search + lineage, no list
  size(nodes(p)) BUILD and DISCARD 86871.3         +79,542 us =  159 ns/element to BUILD
  nodes(p)[0] one element          38447.5         (NOT the arm it looks like — see below)
  nodes(p) ALL elements           219192.5         +132,321 us = 265 ns/element to CARRY OUT
```

**So the dominant term is carrying the element maps out of `exec`, not building them.** The two
arms that matter differ in exactly one thing — whether the list survives into the output — and the
counter below proves they do the same work up to that point.

### TWO ARM NAMES WERE LIES, and a counter caught both

This is the part worth keeping. Item 811's lesson was "a memo that never fires and a memo that is
free are the same null"; the same applies to an arm that does not do what its name says.

- **`nodes(p)[0]` makes ZERO `path_node_values_memo` calls.** An indexed access into a path
  accessor never materializes the list at all, so the arm priced nothing it was built to price. The
  giveaway was arithmetic — it read BELOW `size(nodes(p))`, and an arm that outputs MORE cannot cost
  less than one that outputs a number. **New fact, not previously recorded.**
- **`size(nodes(p))` DOES build it — 3,991,752 calls** (498,969 elements × 8 reps), identical to
  `nodes(p)`'s count. So that arm is honest, and the pair is one-variable. This mattered: the
  evaluator's own comment says "when the plan reads only sizes the elements are never materialized",
  which made the arm look as suspect as `[0]` until it was counted.

### In-process pollution on a RUST probe: 1.68x, measured

The first version of this ladder ran all five arms in one process, and the arm that ran LAST read
**354,895.8 us** against **210,828.4** one-arm-per-process for the identical query — **1.68x of its
own position in the run order.** Item 762's rule was established on the TypeScript side and the TS
probes all follow it; this is the first time the same effect has been QUANTIFIED on a Rust probe, and
it is the same size. The native probes that run several shapes per process are not all wrong, but
none of them has measured this.

### The mechanism is already documented — and the fix is a DIFFERENT shape from the one refuted twice

`Col::Gen(v) => v[i].clone()` on a `Value::List(Vec<Value>)` **deep-copies the whole list**: a fresh
`Vec`, every element copied, then dropped. The evaluator says so in its own comment, and adds "that
clone is on the path of every function over a boxed column, not just this one". `Value::List` is a
bare `Vec`, unlike `Value::Map`, which is `Arc`-wrapped — so item 809's memo makes the element maps
shared but does nothing for the list holding them.

**Item 640 named this at FOUR sites; 641 refuted the borrow at `Expr::Index` and 645 refuted it at
`Expr::In`** ("the clone COMPACTS", and borrowing measured 2.5x slower in the middle of the length
range). So the borrow is not the answer and is not being re-proposed.

**The row-assembly site is not a borrow, it is a MOVE.** At the point the final rows are built the
`Col` is being consumed, so each `Value` could be taken by value instead of cloned — which is a
different change from borrowing for a per-row scan, and the two refutations do not cover it.
Unmeasured, and therefore recorded as a shape rather than a target: ~265 ns an element on the worst
per-row shape in the corpus, and `Value::List`'s bare `Vec` is why it is not already free.

Gates: `cargo build --release --features capi` 0 on the reverted tree; `git status` clean; the
counter, the `pub` on `exec::render`, the `lib.rs` accessor and the temporary example all removed and
grepped to confirm.

## 813 — item 812's suspect REFUTED by reading, and the cost tracks RETENTION exactly. The arithmetic still does not close, and that is said rather than papered over

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change** (a temporary example, reverted). Item 812 located ~265 ns an element
in "carrying the element maps out of `exec`" and named the row assembly as the remaining suspect,
recording it as a shape rather than a target. **Reading the code kills it before any build.**

### The suspect is already fixed

`try_run` **CONSUMES** the batch. Its own comment says so: _"the final render is the LAST use of
these columns, so a materialized Str/Num/Bool/Gen cell MOVES into its `Value` instead of being
cloned out of a column we then drop."_ And `nodes(p)` is a SINGLE output column, where
`col_into_values` documents the `Gen` case as _"already `Vec<Value>` (returned as-is, zero work)"_.

So the move item 812 proposed is the code that is already there. **Fifteenth candidate closed by
reading first**, and the cheapest one yet — it cost one `sed` of `exec.rs`, against a change that
would have measured flat for a reason no A/B would have explained.

### What the cost DOES track: retention, exactly and linearly

Same query and fixture (47,007 rows, 498,969 path elements), one arm per process, with peak RSS
alongside the time:

```text
  path_length (search only)      7312.1 us    41 MiB peak
  size(nodes(p)) build+DISCARD  86580.0      132
  nodes(p) build+KEEP          214461.7      444
  nodes(p) TWICE (two columns) 427787.4      818
```

**The `twice` arm is 1.995x the time and 1.90x the memory of the single one** — so both scale
linearly in how much output is retained, and a one-off allocator or warm-up effect would have broken
that linearity. This is the first arm in the family that discriminates: `size` and `nodes` make the
**identical** 3,991,752 render-memo calls (item 812), so they differ in retention and nothing else.

### Item 809's sharing claim HOLDS, checked arithmetically

`size_of::<Value>()` is **40 bytes**. Peak RSS spans the 8 reps `best_us` runs, so one rep of
`nodes(p)` retains roughly (444 − 31) / 8 ≈ **52 MiB**, i.e. ~104 bytes per element — consistent
with a 40-byte list slot plus an amortized share of the 47,007 memoized element maps, and NOT with
498,969 separate maps (which would be ~500 bytes each). **So the element maps really are shared, and
item 809's "it also lowers peak memory" stands.**

### ⚠️ The arithmetic does NOT close, and no mechanism is being named

~52 MiB per rep of allocation and writes cannot plausibly cost the 128 ms that separates `nodes`
from `size` — that would be 0.4 GB/s, an order of magnitude under what this machine does. So
**retention correlates perfectly with the cost and still does not explain it.** Candidates not yet
separated: 47,007 distinct `Vec` allocations that must come from the allocator rather than reusing
one freed block per row, page faults on a growing heap, and the bulk free at the end. Each is
testable; none is measured, so none is recorded as the cause.

Items 804 and 808 are both records of what happens when a mechanism is asserted at this point
instead. The next instrument wants to separate allocation from writing — the same number of bytes
written into a pre-reserved buffer against the same bytes in 47,007 fresh `Vec`s — and that is a
probe, not a change.

Gates: `cargo build --release --features capi` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary example removed.

## 814 — the probe item 813 specified REFUTES the hypothesis it was built for: per-row `Vec` retention is **20 ns/element**, not 265

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change** (a temporary standalone example, reverted). Item 813 left three
unseparated candidates for `nodes(p)`'s 265 ns/element — the per-row allocation, page faults on a
growing heap, the bulk free — and specified the instrument: the same bytes into a pre-reserved buffer
against 47,007 fresh `Vec`s. Built, measured, and it does not account for the cost.

### The ladder, standalone, one arm per process

Every arm moves the same 498,969 `Value::Map` clones out of a pool of 47,007 SHARED maps, which is
what item 811's 90.6% hit rate means the engine actually does. The arms differ only in where the
clones land:

```text
  CONTROL the Arc clones alone          1642.0 us    3.2 ns/element
  one buffer, reserved, retained        4075.5       7.9
  47,007 fresh Vecs, DROPPED each row   4304.7       8.3
  47,007 Vec::with_capacity, KEPT      11054.5      21.4
  47,007 fresh Vecs, KEPT              14645.8      28.3
```

**Three things, all measured rather than reasoned:**

- **An `Arc` clone of an element map is 3.2 ns.** 498,969 of them total 1.6 ms, so sharing is as
  cheap as item 809 assumed.
- **Allocating 47,007 `Vec`s and freeing each immediately is nearly FREE** — 8.3 ns against the
  single reserved buffer's 7.9. The allocator hands back the same hot block every row, so "47,007
  distinct allocations" is not a cost by itself.
- **Retaining them costs ~20 ns/element**, of which **growth is 7** (`with_capacity` 21.4 against
  fresh 28.3) and the retained allocation itself is ~13.

### ⚠️ So the hypothesis is refuted: 20 ns is not 265

The engine's own pair — `size(nodes(p))` build-and-discard against `nodes(p)` build-and-keep — is
**265 ns/element apart** (item 812). The standalone reproduction of exactly that shape is **20**. A
13x shortfall is not a calibration difference; **the per-row `Vec` is not where the engine's cost
is**, and item 813's leading candidate is closed.

### What the next suspect is, and the evidence for it

Item 813's own peak-RSS figures already contradict the assumption underneath this whole line:
`size(nodes(p))` peaks at **132 MiB** where `nodes(p)` peaks at **444**. If both arms built the same
`Col::Gen` of 47,007 `Value::List`s and differed only in when it was dropped, their peaks would be
close. They are 3.4x apart, so **the two arms do not retain the same thing**, and every
per-element number derived from their difference — including item 812's 159-to-build and
265-to-carry split — is a comparison between two different quantities of work.

That is the thing to establish next, and it is a reading task before it is a measuring one: what the
`size`/`cardinality` fast path does with a non-`Slot` argument. Its comment says it borrows the
column when the argument is a bare slot and otherwise evaluates it into an owned `Col` — but the
RSS says the owned `Col` it builds is a third the size of the one `nodes(p)` returns, and that
difference is unexplained.

**No mechanism is being named for the 265 ns.** This is the second tick in a row whose specified
probe came back negative, which is the method working rather than failing: items 804 and 808 are the
records of what asserting at this point costs, and three negative results in a row are cheaper than
one wrong change shipped with a story attached.

## 815 — `nodes(p)` is PAGE-FAULT BOUND: 69,995 extra minor faults account for the 129 ms that items 812-814 could not place. The arithmetic closes

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change** (a temporary example, reverted). Four ticks have chased the
~265 ns/element in `nodes(p)` that item 811 isolated. 812 split it build-vs-carry; 813 refuted the
row assembly by reading and found the cost linear in retention; 814 reproduced the retention shape
standalone at 20 ns/element — a 13x shortfall — and named faulting a growing heap as the one
remaining candidate nothing had measured. This measures it.

`perf` is not installed and `perf_event_paranoid` is 2, so the counter is `/proc/self/stat`'s
`minflt`/`majflt`, which is all the question needs.

### Measured, one arm per process

```text
  arm       time        minflt    majflt   minflt/element
  length     7266.6us     5450         0       0.002
  size      87029.4      86315         0       0.025
  nodes    216019.2     156310         0       0.045
```

**`nodes` takes 69,995 more minor faults than `size`, and at ~1.8 µs apiece that is ~126 ms against
a measured 129 ms gap.** The step below it closes the same way: `size` takes 80,865 more faults than
`length`, ~80 ms against its ~80 ms gap. **Two independent steps of the ladder, both accounted for by
the same counter** — which is what makes this an explanation rather than a correlation. (The ~1.8 µs
is IMPLIED by dividing, not independently measured; a minor fault with page zeroing is usually
0.2-1 µs, and these are interleaved with real work.)

One fault per ~22 elements is one 4 KiB page per ~180 bytes of element — the 40-byte list slot plus
an amortized share of the memoized maps. The rate is what the footprint predicts.

### Why item 814's standalone probe could not have found this

It allocated ~40 MiB in total where the engine arm's high-water is 444, and its shared pool was
already resident — so it faulted an order of magnitude less per element and measured the writes
rather than the faulting. **A reproduction that does not reproduce the FOOTPRINT is not a
reproduction**, which is the same family as item 702's answer-size rule and a new member of it.
Item 814's 20 ns/element stands as a correct measurement of a different thing: what retention costs
when the pages are already there.

### What this licenses, and what it does not

**The lever is BYTES TOUCHED, not allocations.** Item 814 refuted the allocation count directly
(47,007 fresh `Vec`s dropped per row cost 8.3 ns/element against a single reserved buffer's 7.9), so
arena-allocating or pre-reserving the lists changes nothing — the pages still have to be first-
touched. What would move it is a more compact retained output: a list of element IDs rendered at the
consumer boundary instead of 47,007 materialized lists of maps.

**That is item 415's family — an output-contract change with a public API consequence — and it is a
decision, not a tick.** It now has a mechanism and a number where before it had neither.

**This line is PARKED here, deliberately and not from exhaustion.** Four ticks in, the cost is
explained, the two cheap levers are refuted with numbers (the move at 813, the allocation at 814),
and the remaining one is a contract change. Continuing would be sunk cost; the bench-level ladder is
exhausted and the next instrument for this shape would be a profiler, which this box does not have.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary example removed.

## 816 — item 680's named fix is ALREADY BUILT AND WIRED. My redundant change was caught by its own PRE arm, not by reading

**NO ENGINE CHANGE** (written, measured, reverted). Item 680 diagnosed that `rebuild_csr` runs at
LOAD only, that every adjacency write clears `csr_fresh`, that **nothing re-arms it**, and that the
penalty is selectivity — up to **24.07x** on a 1-in-50 type. It named the fix ("a GLOBAL per-type
edge list … maintainable incrementally") and left it "not costed yet". I verified the diagnosis
holds — `rebuild_csr()` has exactly five non-test callers, all at load — and built the per-node half
of that fix.

### It is already there, and `exec.rs` says so in a comment

`out_typed_csr`/`in_typed_csr` do return `None` when stale, which is what made this look open. But
**`exec.rs` already falls back to the maintained index at both read sites**, with a comment that
states it outright: _"The CSR overlay is stale (an adjacency write since the last rebuild); the
incrementally-maintained index still answers."_ The opt-in `out_type_idx` survives the write that
killed the overlay — O(1) push on `add_edge`, single-removal on delete, per-node rebuild otherwise —
so the data item 680 asked for is built, correct, and consulted.

### 🛑 THE PRE ARM IS WHAT CAUGHT IT — reading had not

My change made the two accessors consult the index themselves. 50,000 nodes, type E 1 in 50, one
`add_edge`, each arm in its own process:

```text
                     PRE (no change)   POST (accessors consult the index)
  fresh                   140.3 us          148.8      the ceiling
  stale, NO index        2867.9            2632.7      CONTROL — gated off, unreachable
  stale, +index           344.6             369.0      no better; slightly worse
```

**`stale +index` already read 344.6 µs WITHOUT my change.** Had I measured only the POST arm and
compared it against item 680's recorded 24.07x, I would have shipped a redundant accessor with an
8.3x story attached — a story that happens to be TRUE about the engine and FALSE about my change.
Sixteenth already-closed candidate this session, and **the first one that reading did not catch**:
the accessor really does return `None`, and the fallback lives in a different file.

The rule this earns: **an A/B's PRE arm is not a formality, it is the only thing that establishes the
change is new.** Comparing a POST reading against a number recorded by another item measures the
engine's history, not your diff.

### What the measurement DOES establish, which item 680 did not have

```text
  fresh                     140.3 us     1.00x
  stale WITHOUT the index   2867.9      20.4x   confirms 680's 24.07x on a nearby fixture
  stale WITH the index        344.6      2.5x   the index recovers 8.3x of the 20.4x
```

So the opt-in index already closes most of the gap, and **the residual exposure is graphs that have
not opted in** — they still pay 20.4x on a selective typed hop after a single write, permanently.

That sharpens the trade item 680 left open, and both sides now have numbers: the index costs a typed
hop **2x in the shape it does not suit** (recorded as E82 in `exec.rs`'s own comment, which is why it
is opt-in and why `expand_bench` exists), against **20.4x for not having it after any write** on a
many-edge-type graph — which is the realistic people-graph shape item 680 named. Whether it should
default ON is a storage decision with that trade stated, not an optimization.

## 818 — ⚠️ NARROWED by item 925: a native append+delete loop degrades **1.64x over a 12x batch**. Its SECOND hypothesis is refuted too — the indexed seek is FLAT across 1M churn, and the write cost is BOUNDED

**OBSERVATION, no engine change.** Item 817 ran `bench:usage` and left one row unexplained: TS beats
the native engine on `write: append then delete node` (443.8k against 178.8k ops/s), which is the
wrong way round for a write workload. Sweeping the batch BUDGET — the axis that turns a constant
factor into a growth rate — says why it is worth a flag.

### Measured, same binary, same fixture, budget swept

```text
  budget        ts(-)     ts(+)   engine(-)   engine(+)
   250ms       443.8k    434.8k     178.8k      170.4k
  1000ms       384.6k    473.4k     164.4k      137.3k
  3000ms       381.9k    513.4k     167.6k      103.9k
                 flat    RISING        flat    1.64x WORSE
```

**Only `engine(+)` degrades, and it does so monotonically.** `engine(-)` is flat within this bench's
own 1.09x floor; `ts(+)` RISES (JIT warming); `ts(-)` settles after the first budget. So the
degradation is native AND index-specific — one arm out of four, which is what makes it a signal
rather than drift.

A rate that falls as the batch lengthens is accumulating state: the longer the loop runs, the more
each iteration costs. At 3,000 ms × 3 batches this row creates ~1M nodes while only ~20k are ever
live.

### 🛑 The obvious cause is REFUTED by reading, before any build

The recorded note at item 1232's entry says index buckets "may count a few tombstoned ids", so the
first hypothesis was that `INSERT (:Tmp {name: $n})` + `DETACH DELETE` leaves the `name` index entry
behind and the map grows without bound. **It does not.** `index_drop_node` removes the id from its
bucket AND drops the empty key — item 367 made it do exactly that, for exactly the reason that a
surviving empty key made `map.len()` overcount. The label bucket is `retain`ed on delete too.

So the growth is somewhere else, and the candidates are the structures that are NOT compacted: the
`deleted` tombstone vector and every per-node property column grow one slot per INSERT forever,
since node ids are never reused. That would be cache pressure in the same family as item 815's
page-fault finding — but **that is a hypothesis, not a measurement, and it is recorded as one.**

Why the INDEXED arm specifically is the discriminating question: without an index the delete's
`MATCH (t:Tmp) WHERE t.name = $n` scans a `Tmp` bucket that `retain` keeps at ~1, so it is flat by
construction; with one it seeks. Whatever grows, the seek path touches it and the tiny-bucket scan
does not.

### Instrument caveat, the second this session

`bench:usage`'s recorded figures for this row are **budget-dependent**: at the 250 ms default the
native arm reads 170.4k, at 3,000 ms it reads 103.9k. Item 817 recorded the same shape for the
indexed `keyed dedup` rows (a 2.4x spread inside one arm). **For this instrument, a single-budget
reading of a write-heavy row is not a measurement of steady state** — which is also why the row's
own comment ("read this row as the parse+bind+tombstone cost it is") is true at 250 ms and
incomplete past it.

### Why this is a flag and not a target yet

It is the shape the bench is drawn from — the "append-only audit log" and "high-rate write" workloads
named in its header — and unbounded per-iteration growth in a serving loop is a different class of
problem from a constant factor. But the mechanism is unidentified, the first hypothesis is already
refuted, and this session has just parked a four-tick chase (811-815) whose lesson was that the
bench-level ladder runs out. **Recorded with its numbers so the next pass starts from the budget
axis and the un-compacted structures, not from the index.**

Gates: no engine change; `git status` clean. The sweep is one command:
`BENCH_BUDGET_MS=3000 BENCH_ENGINES=ts,engine BENCH_ONLY='append then delete' bun run bench:usage`.

## 820 — a node delete was **O(NODES EVER CREATED)**. Now O(1): flat across the churn axis, **114.9x at 1M** and unbounded in churn

**FIXED (Rust), and it is a COMPLEXITY change, not a constant factor.** `delete_nodes` ended with a
loop over `deleted` — the tombstone vector, one entry per node ever created — clearing each
tombstoned node's forward label entry. Item 724 placed it BEFORE the targeted-path branch for a good
reason (that path returns early), which meant **even a one-node delete paid an O(total) scan.**

It now iterates `ids`.

### Measured: the delete goes FLAT

Live set pinned at 20,000, churn (create-then-delete pairs) the only variable, 20,000 timed
append+delete pairs per point:

```text
  churned    PRE delete    POST delete            append (CONTROL)
        0      14,729 ns       3,877 ns   3.80x    237 / 281 ns
  100,000      50,637          4,093     12.4x     240 / 187
  300,000     129,184          3,868     33.4x     359 / 347
1,000,000     444,558          3,871    114.9x     298 / 214
```

**PRE is linear in churn; POST is flat.** The speedup is therefore unbounded — 114.9x at a million
and growing — and the 3.80x at ZERO churn is the same loop scanning the 40,000 nodes that exist
there. The append half is flat in both arms at 187-359 ns, which is the control the change cannot
reach: it touches no delete path.

### How it was found, and why the budget sweep could not have found it

Item 818 saw this row degrade 1.64x as `bench:usage`'s batch budget lengthened and framed it as
"the INDEXED arm only". **Both halves of that framing were wrong**, and isolating the variable is
what showed it: holding the live set fixed and sweeping only the churn, the indexed and unindexed
arms track within 1-5% at every point (9,478/8,910 … 373,035/378,609). The budget axis conflates
elapsed time with nodes created; only the churn axis separates them, and it turned a 1.64x into a
39x.

Then splitting the pair localized it: append flat at 278-734 ns, delete 14.9 → 377.7 µs. One probe,
two arms, one variable each — the discipline items 808 and 814 were about.

### The equivalence is checkable, not plausible

`deleted[i] = true` is set in **exactly one place** — `delete_node_inner`, whose only caller is
`delete_nodes`. So every tombstoned node's labels were cleared by the very call that tombstoned it,
and the old loop re-cleared every earlier one on every call: a no-op repeated V times. A rollback
(`Undo::RestoreNode`) clears the tombstone AND restores the labels, so a node deleted again
afterwards is cleared by its own later call. `get_mut` bounds-checks, so a stale or duplicate id in
`ids` is a no-op exactly as before.

**This is the same defect item 663 fixed for the bucket sweep twenty lines below** — it measured
"~0.33 ns PER NODE across 1k/10k/50k/200k" and added the targeted path to avoid it — and this loop
reintroduced the shape above the branch at the same constant (~0.38 ns a node here). Worth a grep
the next time a per-node sweep is added near a per-batch one.

### Teeth: three of three

- clear NOTHING (`ids.iter().take(0)`) — **caught**.
- clear only the FIRST id (`take(1)`) — **caught**, so the multi-id batch really is covered.
- off-by-one on the index (`id as usize + 1`) — **caught**.

`the_forward_label_map_agrees_with_the_bucket_sweep` is the test item 724 added when the ORIGINAL
placement was wrong, and it is what catches all three.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` **1225 + 13 + 725 passed, 0
failed** under `systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`; `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed;
`bun run fuzz` (all seven byte-identity fuzzers, random seeds) 13 pass 0 fail, run TWICE;
`bun run fmt` 0.

## 821 — item 820 finished: the pattern does NOT recur, the BATCH path it never measured also improves, and the one shape that could lose is priced at 1.8%

**VERIFICATION, no engine change.** Item 820 shipped an O(V)→O(|ids|) fix to `delete_nodes` and
left two things open: it flagged the shape for a grep ("worth a grep the next time a per-node sweep
is added near a per-batch one") and every arm it measured took the `TARGETED_MAX <= 8` branch, so
the batch path was unmeasured. Both are closed here.

### The grep: 820's shape does not recur

Every full-node sweep in `store.rs`, and what each one is:

| site                    | enclosing                | verdict                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deleted.iter()` count  | `recount_live_nodes`     | **test-only** — its one non-test caller does not exist                                               |
| `0..node_count`         | `create_edge_type_index` | one-time index BUILD, O(V) by nature                                                                 |
| `0..node_count`         | `create_interval_index`  | one-time index BUILD                                                                                 |
| `0..node_count`         | `create_range_index`     | one-time index BUILD                                                                                 |
| `0..node_count`         | `rebuild_interval`       | ROLLBACK only, gated on `interval.is_some() && interval_touched`, with item 677's note already on it |
| `by_label.values_mut()` | the rollback-pop guard   | O(#labels), not O(V), and the scan is a `debug_assert!`                                              |

So the defect was specific to that one loop: a per-node sweep whose placement above a branch made it
unconditional. **Nothing else in the file pays O(V) on a hot write path.**

### The control 820 never measured: a BATCH delete

The loop 820 changed sits ABOVE both branches, so a batch above the threshold takes the other one and
was never in 820's numbers. 200,000 nodes, one `delete_nodes` call:

```text
  shape                            PRE us     POST us
  batch of 9 (sweep branch)         143.2       133.2    1.08x better
  batch of 1,000                    196.8       149.4    1.32x better
  batch of 10,000                   681.4       636.2    1.07x better
  batch of 50,000                  2891.2      2822.1    1.02x better
  500,000 DUPLICATES of one id    15836.8     16118.3    1.8% WORSE
```

**No regression on any realistic batch**, and the improvement shrinks as the batch approaches the
node count, which is what O(V)→O(|ids|) predicts: the two converge when `|ids| ≈ V`.

### The one shape where the new code can lose, measured rather than argued

`|ids|` can exceed the node count only through DUPLICATES, and then PRE's O(V) beats POST's O(|ids|).
Pushed to 500,000 repeats of one id against 200,000 nodes — 2.5x the node count — it costs **1.8%**,
inside this probe's own run-to-run spread. The per-iteration work is a bounds-checked `get_mut` plus
`clear()` on an already-empty `Vec`, against PRE's `deleted[i]` probe; both are trivial beside the
rest of the call. So the exposure is real in principle, bounded in practice, and now has a number
instead of a shrug.

**Recorded because a reviewer will ask it**: a caller that passes a duplicate-heavy `ids` far larger
than the graph pays proportionally. If that ever matters, dedup at the entry point — but 2.5x the
node count buys 1.8%, so it does not matter yet.

Gates: `cargo build --release --features capi` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary example removed.
No engine change in this item — 820's diff is unchanged and already carries the full gate run.

**VERIFICATION, no engine change.** Item 820 fixed an O(nodes-ever-created) loop in `delete_nodes`
and measured it on a standalone probe (flat delete, 114.9x at 1M churn). This is the same row on the

  1000ms   164.4k -> 415.8k      137.3k -> 379.3k
  3000ms   167.6k -> 415.5k      103.9k -> 367.7k
                     2.48x                  3.54x   (at 3000ms)

TS's 388.8k; before, TS won 381.9k against 167.6k. Item 818 opened by calling that ordering "the

**The TS columns moved and the change cannot touch them.** `ts(-)` reads 288.4k / 310.3k / 388.8k

### What the pair of items is worth keeping for

818 measured a 1.64x degradation and framed it as index-specific. 820 isolated the variable, found it

## 823 — the CHURN axis priced across EVERY store operation: no second O(history) defect, item 820 re-confirmed, and `set_prop` grows 3.1x for a reason that is not column length

**SURVEY, no engine change** (a temporary example, reverted). Item 820's defect was found on an axis
no committed bench varies: every fixture is built once and queried, so nothing sweeps how many nodes
have EVER existed. That axis just paid 114.9x, which makes the systematic question "what else is
O(history)" rather than "what else is slow" — and the way to answer it is to price every operation on
it, not to pick another row.

Live set pinned at 20,000 (with one edge per node), churn the only variable, 5,000 ops timed per
cell:

```text
  churned   set_prop     seek     scan   add_edge   del_edge   del_node
        0         25      152        5        109         26       1251
   300000         43      167        5        183         41       1193
  1000000         78      160        4        130         36       1173
```

### Three results

**1. `del_node` is FLAT — item 820 confirmed a third time, on a different fixture.** 1251 / 1193 /
1173 ns, where before the fix it was linear in churn. This fixture carries edges where item 820's did
not, so the flatness is not an artifact of the degenerate zero-degree case.

**2. Nothing else is O(history), and the reads are flat.** An index seek (152/167/160) and a label
bucket read (5/5/4) do not move, which also settles the last of item 818's framing: the seek path it
blamed is flat on the axis that actually mattered. `add_edge` (109/183/130) and `delete_edge`
(26/41/36) have no monotone trend — the middle point is the high one in both, which is noise, not
growth. **So item 820's defect was singular**, consistent with item 821's grep finding no other
unconditional per-node sweep.

**3. ⚠️ `set_prop` grows 3.1x (25 → 43 → 78 ns), and the obvious explanation does not fit.**

It is NOT O(history) in the algorithmic sense — 820's loop went 30x for a 67x churn increase, while
this is 3.1x for an unbounded one, i.e. sublinear. The natural reading is memory pressure: the
property columns are indexed by node id and never compacted, so they grow from 20,000 slots to over a
million and a write walks a colder structure.

**But the writes in this probe all target `i % LIVE` — the FIRST 20,000 slots — which stay hot
however long the column gets.** On a pure cache-pressure story those writes should not care. So
either something in `set_prop` touches more than the addressed slot, or the growth is in a structure
the probe is not thinking about (the undo log, the dirty-set bookkeeping, a presence vector reallocating).
**Recorded as a flag with that reasoning rather than a mechanism**, because the cache story is the
one that sounds right and the probe's own access pattern argues against it — and this session has
three records (804, 808, 814) of what the plausible-sounding mechanism costs.

### Why this axis belongs in the corpus

Nothing in `bench_all`, `bun run bench`, `bench:gremlin` or `bench:usage` varies it: the first three
build a fixture and query it, and `bench:usage` only reaches it incidentally, through elapsed time at
a long budget — which is how item 818 saw a 1.64x where the real figure was 39x. **An engine whose
ids are never reused has a history dimension, and it is unmeasured by construction.** The probe above
is five lines of fixture and one loop; the next pass that wants it should add it to `storage_bench`
rather than rebuild it.

## 824 — item 823's `set_prop` flag RETRACTED: it was my probe, in two different ways. `set_prop` is flat in history; a TYPE DE-OPT is the one thing that is not

**RETRACTION + one real finding, no engine change** (a temporary example, reverted). Item 823
recorded `set_prop` growing 25 → 43 → 78 ns across 0 → 300k → 1M churn, noted that the obvious cache
story did not fit because every write targeted the first 20,000 slots, and recorded it as a flag
rather than a mechanism. Reading `apply_set_prop` found two candidates in my own probe, and both are
it.

```text
  churned    cold key   warm key   existing(Num)   same type
        0          35         24              95          56
   300000          40         22             312          52
  1000000          37         22             729          50
```

**1. The first set for a NEW key allocates the whole column.** `apply_set_prop` runs
`Column::new_absent(&value, node_count)` when the key does not exist — a column sized to the FULL
node count, dead slots included. 823's probe used a fresh `score` key, so that one-time O(V)
allocation was amortized over its 5,000 timed writes. `warm key`, with one `set_prop` outside the
timed region, is **flat at 24/22/22**.

**2. 823's growth did not even reproduce.** `cold key` reads 35/40/37 here against 823's 25/43/78 —
no trend on a second run. The allocation is lazy (zeroed pages on first touch), so whether it costs
anything depends on which pages get touched, which makes it exactly the kind of reading that needs a
second run before it is a flag. **823's 3.1x is withdrawn.**

**3. ⚠️ But a TYPE DE-OPT is genuinely O(nodes ever created).** The `existing(Num)` arm writes a
`Num` into `name`, a STRING column — so `col.accepts(&value)` fails and `*col = col.to_gen()`
rewrites the whole column as boxed `Value`s. That grows **95 → 312 → 729 ns** amortized over 5,000
writes, i.e. a one-time cost of ~3.6 ms at a million dead slots. The same-type control writes a
string into the same column and is **flat at 56/52/50**.

That is not a defect — a de-opt must rewrite the column — but it IS history-dependent, and the
reason is item 820's reason: **ids are never reused, so a column is as long as the node count
INCLUDING every tombstoned slot.** In a churn-heavy store the first heterogeneous write to a
property pays for the whole history, not the live set. Worth knowing before anyone proposes
compaction or id reuse: this is one of the costs it would pay for.

### The methodology residue, which is the part worth keeping

**Two different one-time costs hid inside a per-op average in the same probe**, and both inflated the
arm that looked like a finding: a column creation and a type de-opt. The giveaway in each case was
the same — the growth was sublinear where a real O(V)-per-op defect is linear (item 820's was 30x
for a 67x churn increase).

**So: when timing a write in a loop, the timed region must contain no first-time work.** Pre-create
the column, and write the type the column already holds. Both of 823's arms failed that and item 820
passed it only by accident — its probe wrote nodes, which allocate nothing new per call.

This is the third instrument defect this session after items 801 and 817, and the second where my own
arithmetic was the tell rather than a control.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary example removed.

## 825 — ⚠️ OPEN, NEW: `add_node` is **O(distinct property keys)** at 18.4 ns a key — **29x** from 4 keys to 502. The lever is named and its precondition is item 806's census

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary example, reverted). Item 820's defect was found on the
one dimension nothing swept; items 823/824 finished pricing it. **The other unswept dimension is how
many DISTINCT PROPERTY KEYS the store holds.** Item 806's ladder swept it for RENDERING (1785 ns/row
at K=200 against 169 at K=0) and nothing has swept it for WRITES.

`add_node` ends with `for col in self.props.values_mut() { col.push_absent(); }`, so an insert is
O(K) by construction — even for a node carrying two properties.

Live set 20,000, every measured node carrying the SAME two properties, the extra keys present only
because ONE filler node carries them (item 806's fixture trick, so K moves and the per-node work a
caller asked for does not):

```text
  keys    add_node    set_prop    del_node    add_edge
     4         327          25        1117          80
    52        1181          25        1239          88
   202        3915          22        1450          90
   502        9516          22        2107          90
```

**`add_node` is linear in K — 327 → 9,516 ns, 29x — i.e. 18.4 ns per distinct key per insert.**
`set_prop` (25/25/22/22) and `add_edge` (80/88/90/90) are flat, which is the control pair: neither
touches every column, and their flatness says the fixture's growing width is not itself the cost.

**What it means in practice, with no engine change available today:** the heterogeneous people-graph
shape this repo names repeatedly — 50 to 200 distinct keys, a handful on any one node — pays
**1.2 to 3.9 µs an insert against a narrow store's 327 ns, 3.6-12x.** The mitigation that exists now
is to keep the distinct key count down, which is what the first-class map/record values (GV45) are
for: one `meta` key holding a map costs one column, where fifty flat keys cost fifty.

`del_node` grows 1.9x over a 125x change in K — sublinear, and **not attributed**. It is not the
`push_absent` shape (that is per-insert) and the undo log is off in this probe. Left as an
observation, per the three records this session (804, 808, 814) of what naming an unmeasured
mechanism costs.

### The lever, and why it is not this tick

Columns are pushed to on every insert so that cell `i` is always node `i`. **A RAGGED column** —
shorter than the node count, with absence implied past its end — would make `add_node` O(properties
actually set) instead of O(K), i.e. flat at ~327 ns however wide the store.

**Its precondition is exactly item 806's census.** `present_at` is `present[i] || nulls[i]`: it would
**PANIC** past the end, not return false, so every read site needs a bounds check — and the typed
fast paths (item 759's vectorized scans) iterate `data` as a slice in parallel with node ids, where a
short column would silently mismatch rather than fail. Item 806 counted that blast radius for the
presence bitset: **123 indexing sites, 84 pattern-match bindings, 16 `&[bool]` signatures, across 10
files.** The same sites, for the same reason.

So this is priced on both sides for the first time — **18.4 ns a key per insert against a 123-site
change** — where before it had neither number. It is a storage decision, not a tick, and it is the
third item (with 342 and 415) in that class.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary example removed.

## 826 — ⚠️ A CROSS-ENGINE INVERSION on the key-count axis: pure TS is FLAT, native is linear, and they cross at **~32 distinct keys**. Above it TS wins by up to **13.9x**

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (two temporary probes, reverted). Item 825 priced native
`add_node` at 18.4 ns per distinct property key, because a columnar store pushes an absent slot to
EVERY column to keep cell `i` aligned with node `i`. The TS engine stores properties per ELEMENT and
has no such obligation, so it should be flat — and "should be" is what items 804/808/814 are records
about, so it was measured.

```text
  keys     TS ns/insert     native ns/insert      verdict
     4              701                  327      native 2.1x faster
    52              714                 1181      TS 1.65x faster
   202              660                 3915      TS 5.9x faster
   502              685                 9516      TS 13.9x faster
```

**TS is flat across a 125x change in key count (660-714 ns, no trend); native is linear.** The TS
arm used a fresh graph per rep built OUTSIDE the timed region — item 824's rule, learned there the
hard way twice.

### The crossover is MEASURED, not interpolated

825's slope put it near 24 keys. That is an estimate, and an estimate is what this item's whole claim
rests on, so the narrow end was measured directly:

```text
  keys     4    12    20    24    28    36    52
  native 331   386   614   601   603   785  1060      TS band: 660-714
```

**Native crosses the TS band between 28 and 36 keys — call it ~32.** The interpolation said 24; the
measurement says ~32, and the measured number is the one to quote. (The native curve has a plateau at
20-28 and the 4→52 slope is 15.2 ns a key against 825's 18.4 over 4→502, which is allocator
granularity rather than a different law.)

### Why this matters more than the raw numbers

**The native engine's insert advantage is not a property of the engine, it is a property of the
schema width.** Below ~32 distinct keys native wins by up to 2.1x; above it the pure-TS engine wins,
by 1.65x at 52 keys and **13.9x at 502**. Nothing in the corpus could have shown this: `bun run
bench` compares the engines on fixtures of a handful of keys, which is on the native side of the
crossover, so every recorded ingest ratio is measured where native happens to win.

**And ~32 keys is an ordinary schema.** The heterogeneous people-graph this repo names repeatedly
(50-200 keys, a handful on any one node) sits firmly on the TS side.

Three consequences, none of them an engine change:

- **Item 825's ragged-column lever is worth more than 825 said.** It would not just remove 18.4 ns a
  key; it would restore native's insert advantage on the shape the repo calls realistic. Its
  precondition is still item 806's 123-site census.
- **The mitigation available today is unchanged and now has a target**: keep distinct keys under ~32,
  which is what first-class map values (GV45) are for — one `meta` column against fifty flat ones.
- **Any future ingest comparison must state its key count**, the way item 810 established that a
  ratio needs its absolutes. A cross-engine ingest number without K is not reproducible.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `git status` clean; both
temporary probes removed.

## 827 — the key-count axis inverts the engines on READS too: the element render ties at K=4 and native is **4.0x** slower at K=202. The scalar projection does NOT invert

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (two temporary probes, reverted). Item 826 found the INSERT
inversion (TS flat, native linear, crossing at ~32 keys). Item 806's ladder had already measured the
native element render at 169.8 ns/row with no extra keys against 1785.7 at 200, by calling
`node_result_value` directly. Nothing had compared that against TS, and the reason is that the
comparison has a trap in it.

Same fixture shape and the SAME query text on both engines, in-process on both sides (so no FFI
carrier — item 289's caveat does not apply here), 20,000 rows out:

```text
  keys    native n   TS n LAZY   TS n MATERIALIZED    native n.name   TS n.name
     4       313.2        21.2               314.3              7.5        52.5
    52       838.5        49.5               269.2              7.4        55.1
   202      1180.8        48.2               293.0              7.4        55.6
```

### Two results and one refused comparison

**1. The element render inverts, and almost immediately.** Materialized on both sides, the two
engines TIE at K=4 (313.2 against 314.3) and native is **3.1x slower at K=52 and 4.0x at K=202**,
because `node_result_value` iterates `prop_keys_arc()` — every key in the store — and tests presence
per row, where TS reads the element's own bag. This confirms 806's ladder end-to-end through a whole
query rather than a direct call, and it puts the read crossover at **K≈4**, far below item 826's
insert crossover of ~32.

**2. The scalar projection does NOT invert.** `RETURN n.name` is 7.4-7.5 ns/row native against
52.5-55.6 TS — **native ~7x faster, and both flat in K.** So this is not "native loses on wide
stores"; it is specific to materializing an ELEMENT, which is the one shape that reads the key set.
The flat native scalar is also the control that makes the element row a finding rather than a
fixture effect: same store, same width, one shape cares and the other does not.

**3. ⚠️ The TS LAZY number is NOT comparable and is not used.** `RETURN n` in TS hands back the live
`Vertex` (21-48 ns/row) where native builds a map. `bench.ts` names this in the row itself —
`query: project the element [ts lazy]` — and pairs it with a `+ materialize` variant whose comment
says why: `toJSON()` builds the same map the native engine already built. **A first pass here read
45.3 against 1180.8 and would have reported native as 26x slower**, which is a comparison between
materializing and not. The materialized arm is the one in the table.

### What the 825/826/827 arc adds up to

One mechanism — **columns indexed by node id, with the store's key set iterated per rendered row** —
produces all three findings:

| shape                   | native vs TS                                        | crossover    |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| insert (826)            | native 2.1x faster at K=4, TS 13.9x faster at K=502 | **~32 keys** |
| element render (827)    | tie at K=4, native 4.0x slower at K=202             | **~4 keys**  |
| scalar projection (827) | native ~7x faster, flat                             | never        |

**So on the 50-200-key heterogeneous schema this repo names as the realistic shape, the native
engine loses to pure TypeScript on both inserts and element rendering, and keeps a 7x advantage on
scalar projections.** That is an architectural fact about the columnar layout, not a bug, and it has
never been visible because every committed fixture is narrow.

**And it is one lever, not three.** A per-node key list — item 342's rung 3, or the ragged column of
item 825 — removes the per-row key-set scan AND the per-insert column push. Its precondition remains
item 806's census (123 indexing sites, 84 bindings, 16 signatures, 10 files). It is now priced on
three shapes instead of one.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`git status` clean; both temporary probes removed.

## 828 — the element render goes COLUMN-MAJOR: **1.27-2.82x**, disjoint at four key counts. A loop reorder, not the 123-site representation change every prior item named

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Items 825/826/827 all concluded that the fix for the key-count cost was a
PER-NODE KEY LIST — item 342's rung 3, or a ragged column — gated on item 806's census of 123
indexing sites across 10 files. **The cost is not the data layout. It is the loop order.**

`render_nodes` asked, for each row, "is this row present in column 0? column 1? … column K?" — so a
wide store paid K probes into K SEPARATE presence vectors per row, one cache line each. Walking the
columns OUTSIDE and the rows inside asks the identical questions in the other order: one presence
vector at a time, probed at ascending positions (a label bucket is sorted), streaming one allocation
instead of striding across K.

**BYTE-IDENTICAL BY CONSTRUCTION**, which is why this is a reorder and not a representation change:
`cols` is in `prop_keys_arc()` order, which is sorted, so appending column by column leaves each
row's pairs in exactly the order the row-major build produced. No `Column` change, no new structure,
none of the 123 sites touched.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three

```text
  keys   PRE min   POST min            PRE rounds              POST rounds
     4     325.9      219.6   1.49x    415.0/369.3/325.9      219.6/225.0/226.7
    52     851.2      301.6   2.82x   1048.6/962.0/851.2      326.8/307.3/301.6
   202    1177.3      924.3   1.27x   1301.0/1292.5/1177.3    924.3/981.5/929.6
   502    1920.6      847.9   2.27x   2061.8/2058.2/1920.6    847.9/918.6/1303.5
```

**All four key counts are DISJOINT** — every POST reading beats every PRE reading at the same K.
The control is the scalar projection `RETURN n.name`, which never enters `render_nodes`: **6.8-7.8 ns
across all twenty-four cells**, flat in K and flat between arms.

**K=202 is the weakest point (1.27x) and that is not explained.** POST reads 924/981/929 there
against 847/918/1303 at K=502 — so POST is non-monotone while PRE is monotone, consistently across
rounds. The ratio is still disjoint, so the win is real at every K; the shape of the POST curve is
recorded as unexplained rather than attributed, per items 804/808/814.

### What this does to the 825-827 arc

Item 827 put the native element render at 313 ns/row at K=4 and 1181 at K=202, against TS's flat
~290 — native losing 4.0x on the shape this repo calls realistic. It now reads **220 at K=4 and 924
at K=202**, so the crossover moves out and the loss at K=202 falls from 4.0x to ~3.2x. **The
inversion is narrowed, not closed** — TS is still flat and native still scans the key set, just
cheaply enough that the per-node key list buys less than 825/827 estimated. That item should be
re-priced against these numbers before anyone starts the 123-site change.

### Teeth: three of three

- render null rows too (`if false { continue }`) — **caught**.
- the wrong key name (`key_vals[0]` for every column) — **caught**.
- the wrong row (`props_per_row[r - 1]`) — **caught**.

`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` **1225 + 13 + 725 passed, 0
failed** under `systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`; `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed;

## 829 — item 828's grep: the codec IS K-dependent at **11.2 ns a key an element**, the hoist is REFUTED at 1.00-1.04x, and `render_edges` cannot take the reorder at all

**NO ENGINE CHANGE** (built, measured, reverted; the diff is one rejection record). Item 828 fixed the
element render by walking columns outside and rows inside, and flagged the shape for a grep. The grep
found it in two places and neither one takes the fix.

### `render_edges` has the shape and the precondition does NOT hold

`render_edges` is row-major over the key set exactly as `render_nodes` was. **But 828's win came from
POSITIONAL indexing, not from the loop order**: node props live in a presence vector indexed by node
id, so ascending ids are sequential memory. Edge props are `EdgeMap = HashMap<u32, Value>` — hashed,
so ascending eids give no locality and the reorder buys nothing by construction. Not attempted.

Its own doc already prices the residue: 1.54 ns a key a row with the maps hoisted, against 7.99
without — so the edge path took item 391's hoist and is 3x cheaper per key than the node path was.

**The conditional lever, recorded not taken:** iterate each `EdgeMap`'s OWN entries and filter by
membership in the batch, which is O(|map|) instead of O(rows) probes — a win for a SPARSE edge
property and a loss for a dense one, and it needs a batch-membership set. Priced as conditional
rather than built blind.

### The codec IS K-dependent, and much more than the renderer was

`serialize_csv` builds each row as `node_keys.iter().filter(|k| store.has_prop(id, k)).map(|k|
store.prop(id, k))` — **two string-hash lookups per (element, key)**, which is precisely the
anti-pattern `ndjson::encode_object_cols` exists to avoid and whose doc names it. Measured first,
before changing anything:

```text
  keys   ndjson ns/el   csv ns/el
     4           87.9       260.1
    52          146.1       679.4
   202          495.7      2470.0        csv 9.5x, i.e. 11.2 ns a key an element
```

So the same story as items 825-827 in a third place, invisible for the same reason: the corpus
fixture carries two node keys.

### 🛑 But the hoist is REFUTED

Resolving the columns once — the identical `Vec<(&str, &Column)>` the renderer and the ndjson writer
both build — is worth nothing. Three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three:

```text
            PRE min   POST min
  csv K=4     260.8      259.9   1.00x
  csv K=52    648.6      654.5   0.99x
  csv K=202  2434.6     2338.3   1.04x
  ndjson 202  439.9      437.8   flat — UNTOUCHED, the control
```

**So the 11.2 ns a key is not the hash lookups.** The change was correct (1,963 tests green) and
worthless, so it is reverted with its numbers recorded on `serialize_csv`. What remains in the
per-key path is `value_to_neutral`, the `cols.observe` pass that discovers the column set, and the row
writer — none measured, **and none named here as the cause.**

**Fourth time this session the plausible mechanism was not the one** (804: `split`'s capacity; 808:
interning; 814: the per-row `Vec`; now this). The pattern across all four: the mechanism was read off
the code and sounded sufficient, and the arithmetic or the A/B said otherwise. The one that paid —
828 — was also read off the code, so the lesson is not "stop reading" but that **reading tells you
WHERE to measure, never WHETHER you are right.**

One instrument note: PRE round 2 read 440.0 ns at csv K=4 against 260.8 and 265.5 in the other two
rounds — a 1.7x outlier inside one arm. Min-of-three is what makes the 1.00x readable at all.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1225 + 13 + 725 passed 0 failed under
`systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`; the codec diff asserted to be comments only (zero
added non-comment lines); the temporary example removed.

## 830 — item 829's open question CLOSED: **~2.1 ns a key is the "ask every key" cost in EVERY format**, and csv's extra 5x is the format's own output

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, reverted). Item 829 measured the csv encode at
11.2 ns a key an element, refuted the column hoist (1.00-1.04x), and left three candidates
unmeasured: `value_to_neutral`, the `cols.observe` pass, and the row writer. Pricing every FORMAT on
the key axis discriminates between them with no code change, because the per-row property bag is
shared by all of them where csv's two extra passes are its alone.

```text
  keys         csv     pg-text     pg-json    graphson      ndjson
     4       260.2       108.0        98.3       152.2        86.6
    52       615.8       169.1       160.1       220.9       146.1
   202      2371.7       482.0       479.3       574.2       440.0
  ns/key      10.7        2.19        2.09        2.23        2.08
```

### Result 1: every format pays ~2.1 ns a key, and HOISTING DOES NOT TOUCH IT

**`ndjson` goes through `encode_object_cols`, which already resolves the columns once** — it is the
one arm written the hoisted way — and it pays **2.08 ns a key**, the same as the three unhoisted
formats. So item 829's refutation is confirmed from a second direction: the shared per-key cost is
not the hash lookups, because the arm without hash lookups pays it too.

What it is, then, is the irreducible question itself: for every key in the STORE, does this element
carry it? That is `present_at` per (element, key) and nothing in the encoders can skip it — only a
per-node key list can, which is items 342/825/827's lever, now priced on a fourth shape.

### Result 2: csv's extra 8.6 ns a key is the FORMAT's output, measured not argued

csv's slope is 5x the others', and the obvious reading — a flat format must emit a field for every
column on every row, where the others emit only the keys an element carries — is an argument. The
measurement is the output size:

```text
  keys     csv bytes/element     pg-json bytes/element
     4                    26                        76
    52                    74                        76
   202                   224                        76
```

**csv's output grows linearly with K (26 → 224) while pg-json's is FLAT at 76.** So csv is doing
proportionally more writing because it is asked to produce proportionally more bytes. That is the
format's obligation and not engine waste, and it closes the csv question rather than leaving it as a
target.

### What this leaves

The codec's K-dependence decomposes completely: **~2.1 ns a key of unavoidable presence-asking,
shared by every format and immune to hoisting, plus csv's own output growth.** Nothing here is a
defect, and the reducible half is the lever items 825 and 827 already named.

So the key-count arc (825, 826, 827, 828, 829, 830) ends with: **one real win shipped** (828's
column-major render, 1.27-2.82x), **two refutations with numbers** (829's hoist; the edge reorder,
which cannot apply because `EdgeMap` is hashed rather than positionally indexed), and **one lever
priced on four shapes** — insert, element render, codec encode, and the original render ladder —
still gated on item 806's 123-site census.

Gates: `cargo build --release` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `git status` clean; the
temporary probe removed.

## 832 — ~~⚠️ OPEN~~ **the lever it named SHIPPED at item 835** (1.61x on two columns, 1.26x on one), extended at 838 and refused at 839 for the per-edge sites: the TS scalar projection decomposed — the engine's own machinery was **30.8 of 55.1 ns a row (56%)**, and a hand loop did the same job in 24.3

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, reverted). Item 827 measured
`MATCH (n:User) RETURN n.name AS k` at 52.5-55.6 ns/row in TS against **7.4-7.5 native** — 7x, flat
in the store's key count on both sides, on the most ordinary query shape there is. Item 805 had
priced the per-element pieces at ~2 ns to walk and ~2 ns to read, so most of it was unaccounted and
nothing had said what it was.

Each arm adds one thing, so a difference between neighbours IS that thing. 200,000 rows, one arm per
process, graph built outside the timed region, median of 11:

```text
  walk (iterate the label bucket, touch nothing)      1.3 ns/row
  walk + v.properties.name                           11.6        +10.3  the property read
  walk + read + one { k: value } object per row       24.3        +12.7  the row object
  the engine's own query()                           55.1        +30.8  everything else
```

**So the engine spends 30.8 ns a row — 56% of the total — above what a hand-written loop needs to
produce the identical answer.** The read at 10.3 ns reproduces item 805's finding (the walk-plus-read
pairing, a dependent load into each element's property bag) and the 12.7 ns row object is the output
contract. Neither is the headroom; the 30.8 is.

### Where the 30.8 goes, and the lever it points at

`projectRow` builds `{ binding, params, graph }` per row and calls `item.fn(env)` per item — and for
`n.name` that closure goes BACK THROUGH the binding `Map` to reach the element the caller had just
written into it. So one row costs a `Map` write, a `Map` read, two object allocations, a closure
call, and then the property read.

**The predicate path stopped doing exactly this at items 224/230**, which lift
`<ownVar>.<key> <op> <closed value>` into `eqProps`/`cmpProps` read straight off the element — and
item 803 then dropped the binding write entirely when nothing reads it back. **Projections never got
either.** The analogous lever: when a projection item is `<var>.<key>` and `<var>` IS the walked
element, compile it to read the element directly.

### Its precondition, counted rather than assumed

`projectRow` has **13 call sites** (11 in `hop-projection.ts`, one each in `shortcuts.ts` and
`executor.ts`). A direct read needs ONE element, and a multi-variable projection — `RETURN a.name,
b.age` over a hop — has no single element to read from. So the lever applies only to a
**single-variable projection over the walked element**, which is the node-scan shape this item
measured and not the hop shapes that make up most of those 13 sites.

That makes the contained version a fast path at the node-scan site alone rather than a signature
change across 13 callers — **and the signature change is what a first pass would have reached for.**
Item 806 is the record of what an uncounted blast radius costs; this one is counted before anything
was written.

**Not started.** The win is bounded above by 30.8 ns a row (2.3x on this shape), and the part of that
30.8 which is the binding round-trip rather than the row/env construction is itself unmeasured — so
the next pass should ablate the binding read before changing a planner.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary probe removed.

## 833 — the binding round-trip priced at **11.3 ns a row**, disjoint — and **22 of the engine's 55.1 ns remain unreproduced**, which bounds what the lever can deliver

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, reverted). Item 832 decomposed the TS scalar
projection and said the next pass should ablate the binding round-trip before touching a planner,
because `projectRow` writes the element into a `Map` and then calls a closure that reads it back out.
This is that ablation.

### The ladder, min of three rounds

Each arm adds one piece of the engine's shape, so a difference between neighbours IS that piece.
200,000 rows, one arm per process, graph built outside the timed region:

```text
  read + row object                        17.8 ns/row              17.8 / 27.2 / 28.8
  + binding.set('n', v)                    20.7        +2.9         29.6 / 20.7 / 28.1
  + a fresh { binding, params, graph }     26.3        +5.6         26.3 / 29.8 / 30.2
  + fn(env) reading BACK OUT of the Map    32.7        +6.4         32.7 / 32.8 / 34.2
  DIRECT: fn(element) passed as an arg     21.4       -11.3         27.6 / 27.1 / 21.4
```

**The lever is worth 11.3 ns a row and the ranges are DISJOINT** — every `+closure` reading
(32.7-34.2) is above every `DIRECT` reading (21.4-27.6). That is the binding write, the env
allocation and the read-back-out together, which is exactly what passing the element as an argument
removes.

**The first run of this ladder was not usable and said so**: it read `+env` 25.7 BELOW `+map write`
30.7, though `+env` is a superset — non-monotone, so the noise was ≥5 ns and no decomposition could
be read off it. Min-of-three fixed the ordering (17.8 → 20.7 → 26.3 → 32.7). **A ladder whose arms
are not monotone in their own superset relation is not yet a measurement**, which is a cheap check
this file has not stated before.

### ⚠️ What bounds the lever: 22 ns the ladder does NOT reproduce

The full standalone reproduction is **32.7 ns a row** against the engine's **55.1** (item 832). So
~22 ns of the real query is something this ladder does not contain at all — plan dispatch, the scan
setup, the result wrapper, the `Rows` assembly. **The lever's 11.3 ns is measured against the
reproduction, not against the query**, so its effect on a real `MATCH (n:User) RETURN n.name AS k`
could be smaller, and the honest upper bound is 55.1 → 43.8, i.e. **1.26x** — which would narrow the
7.4x gap against native to 5.9x and leave native still well ahead.

**No mechanism is claimed for the 22 ns.** It is the residue of this decomposition and the next thing
to ablate if the lever is pursued; naming it now is what items 804, 808, 814 and 829 are records
against.

### State of the lever

Priced (11.3 ns standalone, 37% of item 832's 30.8 ns engine overhead, 1.26x as the upper bound on
the query), scoped (item 832: a single-variable projection over the walked element, a fast path at the
node-scan site rather than a signature change across `projectRow`'s 13 callers), and **not started**.
By this session's standards 1.26x is shippable — 803 shipped at 1.11x and 828 at 1.27x — so the
decision is whether the planner change is worth it against the 22 ns that is still unaccounted.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary probe removed.

## 834 — item 833's residue cut from 22 ns to ~10: the COMPUTED-KEY row build is **+12.5 ns a row**, the largest term after the read, and its fix is codegen or a contract change

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, reverted). Item 833 reached 32.7 ns a row
standalone against the engine's 55.1 and recorded the ~22 ns residue as unexplained, refusing to name
it. Reading `detectNodeProjection`'s hot loop found two things the ladder had not modelled:

```ts
binding.set(nodeVar, v);
const row: Row = {};
for (let i = 0; i < width; i++) {
  row[cols[i]] = fns[i]({ binding, params, graph });
}
out.push(row);
```

The row is built with a **COMPUTED key**, where 833 used a literal `{ k: value }` whose shape V8
knows up front; and the closure arrives through an **array index**, where 833 called one closure
directly. Each arm adds exactly one of those. Min of three rounds, 200,000 rows, one arm per process:

```text
  closure + literal row (833's arm)   31.3 ns/row          36.8 / 34.9 / 31.3
  + COMPUTED key                      43.8      +12.5      48.7 / 43.8 / 45.1
  + fns[i] and the width loop          45.1       +1.3      45.1 / 49.3 / 45.4
```

**The computed-key row build costs 12.5 ns a row** — the largest single term in this path after the
property read itself — and **the array indirection is nearly free at 1.3**, which is the other half
of the result: the `fns[i]` call site is not the problem, so nothing is gained by specializing it.

833's arm reproduced at 31.3 here against its own 32.7, so the two runs agree and the ladder is
stable across processes.

### The decomposition is now near-complete

```text
  17.8   read + literal row object      (item 832's hand loop)
 + 2.9   binding.set                    (833)
 + 5.6   a fresh env per row            (833)
 + 6.4   the closure reading BACK OUT of the binding   (833)
 +12.5   the COMPUTED-KEY row build     (here)
 + 1.3   fns[i] and the width loop      (here)
 ------
  45.1   reproduced
  55.1   the engine (item 832)
 ~10     still outside the ladder
```

**The residue is cut from 22 ns to ~10, and that remainder is still not named.** It is `query()`'s
entry, the plan dispatch, the detector's own checks and the result wrapper — unmeasured, so
unattributed, per items 804/808/814/829.

### Why the 12.5 ns is not a tick

`{ k: v }` allocates one object with its final shape. `const row = {}; row[k] = v` allocates with the
empty shape and then does a keyed store; the shape transition is cached after the first row, so what
is left is the store itself against a literal's single allocation. The column names are per QUERY, so
a literal cannot be written in the source.

The ways out are both out of scope: **compile a row factory** (`new Function` with the key baked in —
real codegen, and this repo targets wasm and browser contexts where it may be unavailable), or
**return results columnar** (an array per column rather than an object per row — an output-contract
change, item 415's family). A computed-key literal `{ [col]: v }` is the same keyed store and buys
nothing.

### State of the TS projection line

Two levers priced, neither started: **11.3 ns** for the binding round-trip (item 833, scoped at 832
to a single-variable projection at the node-scan site) and **12.5 ns** for the row build (codegen or
contract). Together they bound the shape at 55.1 → ~31, which would take the gap against native's
7.4 from 7.4x to ~4.2x. The binding one is the tick-sized half.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `git status` clean; the temporary probe removed.

## 835 — the direct-read projection: **1.61x disjoint on two columns, 1.26x on one**, and the ablation PREDICTED the magnitude before the change existed

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Items 832/833/834 decomposed the TS scalar projection and priced this
lever at 11.3 ns a row. This is it.

`compileExpr`'s `prop` arm is exactly `(env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable), key)`, so for the
scan's OWN variable the compiled closure writes the element into a `Map`, builds an `env`, and reads
it straight back out. `detectNodeProjection` now records the key at compile time and calls
`propOf(v, key)` on the vertex the loop already holds — **byte-identical by construction, because it
is the same function on the same element.** When EVERY item is direct, the per-vertex `binding.set`
is dead too, which is item 803's rule applied to the projection.

This is the projection half of what items 224/230 did for predicates.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three

```text
  shape            PRE min   POST min            PRE rounds           POST rounds
  two cols            59.2       36.4   1.61x    61.2/59.2/65.5       36.4/51.1/55.1   DISJOINT
  scalar (1 item)     51.8       41.0   1.26x    58.4/51.8/56.0       41.0/52.2/41.2   overlaps
  CONTROL expr        74.7       74.4   flat     74.7/79.5/83.3       74.4/90.1/89.8
  CONTROL count(*)    1710       1700   flat     1710/1980/1810       1700/1800/2700
```

**The two-column arm is disjoint at 1.61x** — every POST reading beats every PRE reading — and the
win scaling with width is what the change predicts, since two items remove two closure calls and two
envs against one. **The one-item arm is 1.26x on mins but NOT disjoint**: POST reads 41.0/52.2/41.2,
bimodal, and its 52.2 lands inside PRE's range. Stated rather than rounded away.

**What makes the 1.26x believable is that it was predicted.** Item 833's standalone ablation measured
the binding write, the env and the read-back-out at **11.3 ns** before this code existed; the real
query delivers **10.8** (51.8 → 41.0). A magnitude predicted in advance and then hit within 5% is a
different kind of evidence from a ratio found by looking.

**Both controls are unreachable by construction, not by hope.** `RETURN n.score + 1` is not a bare
property, so `directKeys` is `undefined` for it and the closure still runs; `count(*)` takes a
different shortcut. The probe also printed the first row of every arm, so a shape that changed its
ANSWER would have shown rather than merely getting faster — `{"k":"user0"}`, `{"a":"user0","b":0}`
and `{"k":1}` are identical in both arms.

### Teeth: two of three, and the survivor is REDUNDANT

- `allDirect = true` always, skipping the binding write even when a closure needs it — **caught**,
  70 failures.
- the direct read taking the ALIAS instead of the key (`propOf(v, cols[i])`) — **caught**, 115
  failures.
- dropping the `variable === nodeVar` check — **SURVIVED**, 2,634 pass. Structural and verifiable:
  the `freePredicateVars` loop above already returns `null` for an item reading another name, and a
  `prop` expr carries no subquery so that loop always ran. **Redundant, not untested** — item 475's
  rule, and the two have opposite fixes. Kept with the dependency written down, so it fails loudly
  if that check is ever loosened; the same argument the rollback path's `schema_reverted` guard
  carries.

**A note on how the first mutation run was read.** Its output went through `tail -2`, which showed
the `expect()` totals and not the pass/fail line — so M1 was being judged by "13,832 calls against
the usual 16,669" and inferred to have failed. That is the truncation mistake in a new place; the
re-run captured `N pass / N fail` directly. **A mutation verdict needs the verdict, not a proxy for
it.**
