## 836 — the hop projection's per-row `EvalEnv`: **REFUTED structurally**, ceiling 5.6/degree ns a row — and the locality result the probe "found" was already in the walk's own doc comment

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, removed). Item 835 shipped the direct-read
projection at the node-scan site and item 832 scoped it there, because a multi-variable hop
projection has no single element to read from. This item asked the follow-up the grep was for: the
13 `projectRow` call sites in `hop-projection.ts` all pass a `Binding` **allocated once and mutated
in place**, while `projectRow` rebuilds `{ binding, params, graph }` every call — item 833's 5.6 ns
term, apparently paid per row at 13 sites.

### It is not paid per row, and the code says so

`farDrivenHopWalk` — the walk this shape actually takes — calls `projectRow` **once per far
VERTEX**, not once per edge, and clones a key/value template for the vertex's whole bucket (item
167's hoist). So the env allocation is already amortized over the degree and the hoist's ceiling is
**5.6 / degree** ns a row: 1.4 ns against ~70 at four edges a vertex, about 2%. The start-driven
walk at line 790 does allocate one env per edge, but it is chosen only when `needsStart`, a far
predicate or a gate refuses the far-driven one — shapes whose per-row cost is higher for other
reasons. **Refused on the structure, not on a measurement that came out small.**

### What the probe measured on the way

60,000 vertices, one arm per process, 14 reps, drop 3, median of the plateau. `epv` is edges per
vertex; `ctlscan` is the node-scan projection, which after item 835 does not call `projectRow` at
all.

```text
  arm                       ns/row     total ms     rows
  hop        epv=1           288.7         17.3    60000
  hop        epv=2           166.2         19.9   120000
  hop        epv=4            71.9         17.3   240000
  hop        epv=8            83.5         40.1   480000
  ctlscan    epv=1..8      20.2-35.3    1.2-2.1    60000
  gen (pathVar, REFUSED)  2002.2        120.1    60000
```

**The total is flat at ~17-20 ms while the rows go 60k → 240k.** So the per-row figure at `epv=1`
is a per-VERTEX cost divided by one row — exactly the fixture trap this repo's bench notes open
with, and the reason the `epv` sweep is here rather than a single ratio.

The shortcut **is** reached, which the `pathVar` row establishes rather than assumes: a path
variable is refused by the detector's first gate and costs 2002 ns a row, 6.9x the admitted
spelling.

### The hand floor says the remaining cost is not machinery

A hand walk over the same public structures (`verticesByLabel` → `adjFrom.get('E')` →
`e.to.properties.k`):

```text
  epv=1    hand 203.6    hop 261.5     hop is 1.28x the floor
  epv=4    hand 129.6    hop  70.4     hop BEATS the floor 1.84x
```

At four edges a vertex the engine is **faster than a hand loop doing the same job**, because the
template hoist projects once per vertex where the hand loop projects once per edge. A part measured
dearer than the whole is normally an instrument result (item 802); here it is the real relation, and
it is the strongest available statement that this path is near its floor.

### The locality finding was already written down

Making the far endpoints sequential instead of permuted took `hop` from 261.5 to **159.6 ns a row,
1.64x**, while the hand walk stayed flat at 198.5 → 203.6 (its `from`-side adjacency is scattered
either way, so it has no far-locality term to lose). That looked like a finding until
`farDrivenHopWalk`'s doc comment was read to the end:

> LOCALITY — the start-driven walk reads a far vertex per EDGE, in edge order, which is random with
> respect to how vertices sit in memory. Over a 1,000,000-edge fixture that lookup and its pointer
> chase cost ~180ns, which is most of the 266ns a row took.

**266 ns there against 261.5 measured here** — independent agreement on a different fixture, and
the whole reason the far-driven walk exists. This is item 802's failure repeated: the answer was in
a doc comment above the function, and the probe was built before the comment was read to the end.
The eighth closed candidate recorded this session, and the second whose record lived in the SOURCE
rather than in `CLOSED.md`.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0; `git status` clean of any engine
change (docs only), the temporary probe removed.

## 837 — `del_node`'s key-count dependence ATTRIBUTED: it is the `set_absent` loop, worth 1.29x at K=502 — and **rejected**, because one test of 1,225 says "a deleted node has no properties" is an observable

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary example, removed; the rejection is recorded on the
loop itself). Items 823 and 825 both measured `del_node` growing with the distinct property key
count and both left it unattributed — 825 explicitly: _"It is not the `push_absent` shape (that is
per-insert) and the undo log is off in this probe. Left as an observation."_ That is right about
`push_absent` and misses its twin. `delete_node_inner` ends with:

```rust
for col in self.props.values_mut() { col.set_absent(i); }
```

O(K) per deleted node, the same shape one function along.

### The ablation attributes it completely

20,000 nodes deleted one at a time, item 806's fixture trick (every measured node carries the same
two properties; the extra keys exist only because ONE filler node carries them), min of 7, the live
set rebuilt outside the timed region per rep (item 824's rule):

```text
  keys    del_node ns    ABLATED    add_edge ns (CONTROL)
     4           3816       3798                    101
    52           3915       3801                    104
   202           4231       3816                    102
   502           4909       3806                    103
```

**With the loop emptied and nothing else changed, `del_node` goes FLAT across a 125x change in K**
— 3798/3801/3816/3806. So the loop is not _a_ term, it is the _whole_ term: 2.2 ns per distinct key
per delete, 1.11x at K=202 and **1.29x at K=502**. `add_edge` is flat at 101-105 either way, which
is the control the change cannot reach.

### Rejected, and the reason is a test rather than an argument

The ablated build fails exactly one of 1,225 unit tests:
`delete_node_tombstones_and_cleans_up`, at `assert!(st.prop(b, "name").is_null()); // props
cleared`. **"A deleted node has no properties" is a public-API observable**, reached by reading a
property off a tombstoned id — so dropping the clear is a semantic change, not an optimization.

That it is the _only_ test that notices is itself worth recording, because it bounds the exposure.
The surface query paths cannot reach a deleted slot: `all_nodes` filters `!deleted`,
`delete_nodes` sweeps the label buckets before returning, `index_drop_node` prunes the hash indexes,
and dense ids are **never reused**, so a deleted slot never becomes a new node's slot. What remains
is an id held ACROSS the delete — which is precisely what the test exercises.

### The alternative, refused on the asymmetry

Drop the loop and have `prop`/`has_prop` answer null when `deleted[i]` — the semantics are preserved
exactly and the delete becomes O(1) in K. **Refused without measuring, and stated as such:** it
moves a per-DELETE cost onto the per-READ property path, the one items 216/224/230 worked on
_because_ it is the hot path, and reads outnumber deletes by orders of magnitude in every fixture in
this corpus. A branch on every property read to recover 2.2 ns per key per delete is the wrong
direction on its face. Item 806's census (123 indexing sites, 10 files) is the other half of the
bill.

### What this leaves

Item 825's open target stands untouched: `add_node` is still **O(K) at 18.4 ns a key**, 29x from 4
keys to 502, and that one is a real defect rather than a paid-for semantic. This item removes its
companion from the list — `del_node`'s growth is explained, priced, and deliberately not taken.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo build --release --tests` 0;
`cargo test --release` **1,225 passed 0 failed** (1,224/1 under the ablation, which is how the
teeth were established); `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0. The
temporary example and the pristine copy removed.

## 838 — the direct read reaches the `FOR` projection: **1.23x disjoint on two items**, because item 832's "no single element" blocker is false where the walk holds BOTH variables

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 835 lifted `<nodeVar>.<key>` projection items to read the scanned
element directly, and item 832 scoped that lever with a blocker worth quoting:

> A direct read needs ONE element, and a multi-variable projection — `RETURN a.name, b.age` over a
> hop — has no single element to read from.

Item 836 confirmed that for hops. **It is false for `FOR`.** `forProjectionRows` holds the anchor
vertex and the current list element _at the same time_, and `detectForProjection`'s admission
already proves every item's free names are a subset of `{anchor, alias, ordinality}`. So for three
item shapes the value is in hand before the closure is called:

```text
  RETURN t AS t          a `var` naming the alias   -> elems[i]
  RETURN n AS v          a `var` naming the anchor  -> vertex
  RETURN n.k AS k        a `prop` on the anchor     -> propOf(vertex, key)
```

`compileExpr`'s `var` arm is `(env) => env.binding.get(name)` and its `prop` arm is
`(env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable), key)`, so each of these writes a value into a `Map`,
builds an `env`, and reads the same value straight back out. **Byte-identical by construction** —
the same value, and `propOf` is the same function on the same vertex. When every item is direct the
per-vertex and per-element `binding.set` calls are dead too (item 803's rule).

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three

200,000 vertices × 3 tags = 600,000 rows, one shape per process, 14 reps, drop 3, median of the
plateau. Both arms came from ONE build behind a temporary env switch, asserted present in the
built dist before measuring — so each arm provably IS the code it claims.

```text
  shape                 PRE min   POST min            PRE rounds          POST rounds
  mixed (2 items)          51.8       42.0   1.23x    51.8/58.4/54.3      42.0/42.8/43.5  DISJOINT
  bare (1 item)            44.2       38.7   1.14x    45.0/48.0/44.2      38.7/44.9/40.0  overlaps
  CONTROL same walk        45.7       42.9   1.07x    49.6/45.7/52.6      42.9/44.4/48.0
  CONTROL node scan        39.9       43.6   0.92x    115.4/56.3/39.9     49.3/43.6/53.3
```

**The two-item arm is disjoint at 1.23x** — every POST reading beats every PRE reading — and the win
growing with width is what the change predicts, the same shape item 835 saw (1.61x on two columns
against 1.26x on one). **The one-item arm is 1.14x and NOT disjoint**, stated rather than rounded
up.

**The controls move in BOTH directions, which is what says the 1.07x is noise.** The same-walk
control (`RETURN n.s + 1`) has no direct item, so `anyDirect` is false and it takes the old
`projectRow` path unchanged — its per-row code is not merely unreached but identical. It reads
1.07x "in favour" with ranges that overlap heavily (PRE's 45.7 sits inside POST's 42.9-48.0). The
node-scan control reads 1.09x _against_. A floor of roughly ±8% in both directions is the honest
reading, and it is why the 1.14x arm is reported as weak and the 1.23x disjoint one as the result.

### The per-item saving is HALF what item 833 predicted, and that is not glossed

Item 833's standalone ablation priced the binding round-trip at **11.3 ns a row** and item 835
delivered 10.8 at the node-scan site. Here the deltas are **5.5 ns for one item** (44.2 → 38.7) and
**9.8 ns for two** (51.8 → 42.0) — about 4.9 ns an item, less than half. The shape is right (linear
in width) and the magnitude is not. **No cause is claimed**: this walk differs from the node-scan
site in that one scratch binding is already shared across every element of every anchor, so there
was less per-row binding work to remove, but that is a hypothesis and nothing here measured it.
Recorded as a discrepancy, per items 804/808/814/829.

### Teeth: three of three caught

- `allDirect = true` always, skipping the binding writes even when a closure needs them —
  **caught**, 2 failures.
- `elem` and `anchor` swapped, so a row gets the vertex where the element belongs — **caught**, 4
  failures.
- the property read taking the column ALIAS instead of the key (`propOf(vertex, cols[c])`) —
  **caught**, 1 failure across the suite, and **2 in the new test file alone**, which is why that
  file was added rather than resting on the existing coverage.

### The tests are a differential, not an expectation list

`for-projection.test.ts` already asked every case twice — once admitted, once with `FILTER true`
inserted so the clause count takes it to the general path — and compared the two as multisets. Nine
cases were added there for the three direct shapes: the element alone and twice under two aliases,
the anchor vertex, an anchor property whose key differs from its alias in both column orders, a
MIXED projection where one item is direct and one is not (so both arms of the per-cell branch run
on the same row), a key the anchor does not carry, and `WITH ORDINALITY`, where the ordinality
variable is not a direct shape and so the binding must still be written. The anchor-vertex case has
no concise literal form, so it is compared against the general path's own answer **and** checked to
contain `"id":"q"` — two paths agreeing on the wrong thing would still fail.

### What the regression sweep can and cannot say

`bun run bench` completed clean (exit 0, no row anywhere near an order of magnitude off its
recorded value — `traverse 1-hop project` reads ffi 71.1 against the 71.3 recorded before item
724's regression, and `project 3 columns` ts 6.9). **But it has no `FOR` row at all, so it cannot
show this change's effect either way**, and there is no same-session PRE sweep to diff it against,
which is the comparison items 737/747 are about. What actually bounds the regression risk is the
diff: all six hunks are inside `detectForProjection` and `forProjectionRows`, no shared code is
touched, and `anyDirect === false` keeps every shape this lever cannot serve on the identical old
`projectRow` path — which the same-walk control then confirms empirically. The sweep is reported
here as a completed regression pass, not as evidence for the win.

## 839 — the seven per-edge hop sites: the direct read APPLIES there and is **refused at under 5%**, because a width ladder prices a projection item at 5.6 ns against a 295 ns row

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, removed; the rejection is recorded at the
call site). Item 838 shipped the direct read into the `FOR` projection and the census it prompted
found the general case: **seven of this file's eleven `projectRow` calls run once per EDGE with every
name they project already in hand.**

```text
  relBoundFilteredHopWalk     start + far + edge
  relBoundHopWalk             far + edge
  the landing-gate path       start + far
  farDrivenFilteredHopWalk    far + start
  filteredHopWalk             start + far
  the start-driven walk       start + far
  undirectedHopWalk           far
```

So item 832's blocker is false in a third place, and the structural case was good: unlike
`farDrivenHopWalk` — where item 836 found `projectRow` amortized over the degree — these pay it
per row.

**The structural case was the whole case, and it does not survive pricing.** A width ladder on the
start-driven walk, min of three rounds, 60,000 vertices at 4 edges each, 240,000 rows, one shape per
process:

```text
  items                1        2        4      ns/row
  start-driven      295.0    294.9    311.7
  far-driven                          73.6      `RETURN b.k` alone, for scale
```

**A projection item costs ~5.6 ns on this walk** (and nothing at all from one item to two). The
whole addressable term at width 2 — one `env` per row, two binding reads, one `set` — is about
**14 ns of 295, under 5%**, against this corpus's own controls measuring **±8%** one tick earlier at
item 838. A sub-noise win across seven call sites is not a trade, and it is refused before a line of
it was written.

### The first ladder was not a measurement, and saying so is the point

A single round read `two` 304.1 and `three` 301.4 and was briefly taken as "a third item is free,
so removing items is free" — a stronger and more interesting claim than the truth. It was noise
between processes: min-of-three gives a monotone 295.0 / 294.9 / 311.7. **Item 833's rule earned
again** — a ladder not monotone in its own superset relation is not yet a measurement — and this is
the second time this session that the _first_ reading of a ladder pointed somewhere the third did
not.

A correction to this item's own framing, recorded because it was stated out loud before being
priced: the census was called "a materially bigger lever" than `FOR`'s on the strength of
`projectRow` running per edge. Per-edge is a reason the cost is _not amortized_; it is not a reason
the cost is _large_. Those are different claims and only the first was established.

### Where the cost actually is

The start-driven walk is **4.0x the far-driven one** (295 against 73.6) on the same fixture and the
same rows, and the projection is ~2% of its row. The gap is what `farDrivenHopWalk`'s own doc
comment prices at ~180 ns: the far-vertex pointer chase in EDGE order, random with respect to how
vertices sit in memory — plus the loss of its template hoist.

**Neither is reachable from this walk, and the reason is symmetry rather than effort.** With
`needsStart` there is no per-far-vertex template to hoist, because the cells are not a pure
function of the far end. And the far-outer ordering already exists as
`farDrivenFilteredHopWalk`; `hopDrivesFar` declines it when the two labels are the same size,
because the locality it gains on the far end it gives back on the start. So a two-endpoint hop over
one label has no better access pattern available, and the 295 ns is the fixture's memory behaviour
rather than the engine's machinery — the same conclusion item 836 reached for the far-driven walk,
now established for its twin.

**What this closes:** the direct-read lever is now priced at all three of its candidate sites —
shipped at the node scan (835, 1.61x), shipped at `FOR` (838, 1.23x), refused at the hop (here,
<5%). The family is finished, and the remaining TS projection lever is item 834's computed-key row
build at 12.5 ns, which needs codegen or an output-contract change.

0; `bun run check` 0; `bun test packages/gql` **2,635 pass 0 fail**. Comment-only change in the
engine; the temporary probe removed.

## 840 — `count(DISTINCT <date>)` was **36.6x** slower than the same shape over a number, and a mutant that HALVED the answer passed all 1,225 tests

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Pricing an enum's variants, which is what this method opens with. `fastpath.rs`
matches `Column::Num` 19 times, `Dict` 16, `Str` 10, `Bool` 3 — and **`Temporal` and `Gen` zero.**
Several arms say so in as many words:

```rust
(AggFn::Min | AggFn::Max, _) => return None,   // Temporal/Bool/Gen → general path
_ => return None,                              // Temporal/Gen → the general aggregate
```

So a date column falls off every aggregate fast path. That is not a corner: this repo's own domain
is people-data-over-time, where MIN/MAX/DISTINCT over a hire date is an ordinary question.

**CLAUDE.md lists temporal-column cost as DEFERRED** because it "needs host `Temporal`
construction". That blocker is real for the TS harness and false for a Rust example: `Date` is a
public struct with a public `days` field, so `Value::Temporal(Temporal::Date(Date { days }))` is one
expression. **The deferred question is answerable; it was only ever unanswerable from one side.**

### The gap, and which aggregate owns it

200,000 `Person` nodes, each carrying a `score` (`Num`) and a `hired` (`Date`) of the same
cardinality — so each pair is the SAME aggregate over the SAME rows and differs only in the
column's type:

```text
  query                       us        vs its Num twin
  min(p.score)               438
  min(p.hired)              1925        4.4x
  max(p.score)               472
  max(p.hired)              1923        4.1x
  count(p.score)             102
  count(p.hired)             101        flat — this one already had a path
  count(DISTINCT p.score)    442
  count(DISTINCT p.hired)  23211        52.5x
  count(*)                     0        CONTROL, reads no column
```

**`count(DISTINCT)` owns the gap at 52x**, and the N sweep says it is a per-row constant rather
than a complexity defect — 2,955 / 6,043 / 11,647 / 21,730 µs at 25k / 50k / 100k / 200k, linear,
ratio steady at ~50x. The general aggregate byte-keys every row through `group_key`, which for a
temporal is `t.format()`: an allocated ISO `String` per row.

### Why only `Date`, and why not a wider pattern

`group_key`'s own comment defines its equivalence: _"two temporals group together iff they render
identically AND are the same kind"_ — **render** equality. `Temporal` derives **structural**
equality. Those coincide only where `format` is injective, so the arm is written for the one kind
where that is demonstrable: `Date::format` is `civil_from_days(days)` through `fmt_year`, which pads
to four digits but never truncates, so distinct `days` render distinctly and dedup on `days` yields
exactly the general path's classes. The kinds carrying a sub-second or zone part keep the general
path — the cost of being wrong here is a wrong COUNT, not a slow query.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three

Both arms built as **separate binaries** and asserted to be the code they claim (the new pattern
occurs 0 times in PRE, 1 in POST) before a single reading was taken.

```text
  shape                      PRE min   POST min
  count(DISTINCT p.hired)      21351        584   36.6x   DISJOINT
  CONTROL count(DISTINCT p.score)  408        406   flat
  CONTROL min(p.hired)          1787       1754   flat
  CONTROL count(*)                 0          0   —
```

**`min(p.hired)` is the control that carries the result.** It is the _same temporal column_ on the
_same general-aggregate route_, differing only in which aggregate asks — so its flatness says the
win is this arm and not something about temporal columns in general. Every arm answered 1,000.

### The hole this opened: a wrong-answer mutant passed EVERYTHING

Mutation under `timeout 900` + `MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, built uncapped first:

- **M1, dedup on `d.days / 2`** — a key that halves the distinct count — **SURVIVED all 1,225
  tests.** There was no coverage for `count(DISTINCT <date column>)` at all, by either route. The
  fast path was shipped into a gap in the suite, and the only reason that is not how it stayed is
  that the mutation ran.
- So the test was written first and the mutants re-run against it: **M1 caught**, **M2 (presence
  check dropped) caught**, **M3 (the homogeneity bail removed) SURVIVED** — correctly, because a
  `Temporal` column holds exactly one kind by construction and
  `temporal_props_use_a_typed_column_and_promote_on_mixed_kind` is the test that makes that true.
  Defence in depth with a named dependency, per item 475 and the same argument item 835's survivor
  carries.

The fixture is built so a lossy key cannot hide: **four CONSECUTIVE days**, which guarantees an
even/odd adjacent pair that any divide-by-two key collapses, plus a far date and two repeats. It
pins the count, the value SET (so a count right by luck still fails), `count(arg)` without the dedup
(separating "the dedup is wrong" from "presence is wrong"), and the same question through the
general path via `WHERE true` (item 570 records that it is not folded away).

**One storage fact found while building it:** an explicit stored `Value::Null` beside dates promotes
the column to `Gen` — measured, the assertion read discriminant 5 — so the null case can never reach
this arm. It is pinned on its own store rather than left implicit, since a reader would otherwise
reasonably expect the nulls vector in `Column::Temporal` to carry it.

### What stays open

`min`/`max` over a temporal column remain on the general path at **4.1-4.4x**, which this item
measured and deliberately did not take: a MIN over a `Date` column is a scan of `days` and looks

## 842 — the differential fuzzer had **no temporal property at all**, so items 840 and 841 shipped uncovered by the hard invariant; closed, and the first fixture I chose did not have teeth

**TEST COVERAGE, no engine change.** Items 840 and 841 each shipped a Rust aggregate fast path for
`Column::Temporal`, and each found a wrong-answer mutant that passed the whole 1,22x-test suite.
Both were then unit-tested. This item asks the question those two should have provoked
immediately: **are they covered by the invariant that actually matters?**

They were not. `differential-fuzz.test.ts` — random GQL, pure-TS engine against Rust, 20,000
queries a run — **mentioned temporals zero times.** Its fixture's node properties were numbers,
strings and maps; its generators picked keys from explicit lists (`['n','s','x','nan']`,
`['n','x','s','nan','st','zz','m.k']`) that contained no temporal key. So two new code paths that
produce answers which must be byte-identical across engines were cross-engine unverified.

### What was added

- A tagged `d` date on five of the six fixture vertices (`{"@date":"…"}`, the NDJSON form both
  engines already round-trip). Vertex 5 deliberately carries none.
- `'d'` in the `count(<property>)` key list, which reaches item 840's shape directly.
- `temporalShapes`, a named generator of thirteen shapes with its own probability band: `min`,
  `max`, `count(DISTINCT)`, each also under a `WHERE`, a different label, `ORDER BY` ascending and
  descending, `DISTINCT … ORDER BY`, a `GROUP BY` fold, a `DATE '…'` literal comparison across all
  six operators, a cross-slot `a.d <op> b.d` over a hop, and a far-side `max(b.d)`.
- A `temp=<generated>/<non-empty>` coverage counter with floors, because an un-counted arm is one
  nobody notices has stopped being drawn.

### The fuzzer's own coverage guard refused my first attempt, correctly

Adding a band took `genQuery` to complexity 36 against a limit of 35. The first fix was to fold the
thirteen temporal shapes into the existing `count` band instead of taking a new one — and the
fuzzer **failed on its own coverage assertion**: `cntPropGenerated` fell from ~430 to **139**
against a `> 200` floor, because thirteen new shapes in a 2.5% band crowd out the five that were
there.

That is the guard doing exactly its job. **Dodging a complexity cap by diluting an existing arm is
a coverage regression wearing a refactor's clothes**, and the file had a tripwire for it. The cap
was then paid off honestly, by extracting the subquery-item arm into `genSubqueryItem` (its three
ternaries were the cheapest honest thing to move, and the draws stay in the same order so a
recorded seed still means what it meant).

### THE FIRST FIXTURE DID NOT HAVE TEETH, AND ONLY MUTATION SHOWED IT

With coverage in place, both mutants were re-applied to confirm the differential now catches what
the unit suite missed:

```text
  item 841's M1, the min/max comparison INVERTED      CAUGHT (divergence)
  item 840's M1, dedup on `days / 2`                  SURVIVED  ← first fixture
```

The reasoning behind the first fixture was that `2024-01-01` and `2024-01-02` are **consecutive
days**, so halving must collapse them. **It does not.** Those are day numbers 19723 and 19724;
`19723 / 2 = 9861` and `19724 / 2 = 9862` are distinct, because integer halving collides only when
the _smaller_ day number is EVEN. The fixture now uses `2024-01-02` and `2024-01-03` — 19724 and
19725, both mapping to 9862 — and keeps the duplicate on another vertex so a distinct count still
differs from a plain one. The mutant is then caught.

**The argument was right in shape and wrong in arithmetic, which is precisely the class of fixture
error no passing run can reveal.** Item 840's unit test caught this mutant and the cross-engine
check did not, so "it is covered somewhere" would have been a true statement hiding a false one.
The dates now carry their day numbers and the parity requirement in the comment, so the next person
changing them knows what the choice is load-bearing for.

### What this closes

The temporal variant is now checked on all three levels it needed: unit (840, 841), cross-engine
differential (here), and mutation-verified at each. **Three ticks for one variant** — which is the
honest cost of a type that a storage layer de-boxes, a planner has fast paths for, and no test
generator had ever produced.

Floors are set to catch the arm going DEAD rather than to pin its rate: the band is 0.5% of 20,000
so ~100 draws are expected, a floor AT 100 flakes (the first run measured 94/94), and the floors
are `> 50` / `> 40`. Three consecutive runs read `temp=121/119`, `117/112`, `100/99`.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check`
0; `bun run check` 0; `bun run fuzz` (all seven byte-identity fuzzers, random seeds) 13 pass 0
fail, run TWICE; `cargo test --release` 1,227 passed 0 failed; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D
warnings` 0. No engine change in this item — the two mutants were reverted and the tree verified
clean of both.

## 843 — the TS engine had the SAME temporal defect from a different cause: `count(DISTINCT <date>)` **4.17x** faster, and the third wrong-answer mutant in four items to pass a whole suite

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Items 840/841 closed two native aggregate arms for `Column::Temporal`.
The TS engine has no columnar store at all — properties live per element — so the native mechanism
(a byte-keyed `group_key` allocating an ISO string per row) could not be the same here, and "so it
should be flat" is exactly what items 804/808/814 are records about. It was measured instead.

**It was not flat.** 200,000 nodes, each pair the same aggregate over the same rows differing only
in the property's type:

```text
  min(p.hired)              6.51 ms      min(p.score)             4.41    1.48x
  max(p.hired)              5.44         max(p.score)             4.58    1.19x
  count(DISTINCT p.hired)  81.29         count(DISTINCT p.score)  4.17   19.5x
                                         count(DISTINCT p.city)   5.21   15.6x  (a STRING)
  count(*)                  0.00         CONTROL, reads no property
```

The string column is the control that makes the diagnosis: at 5.21 ms it is in line with the
number, so this was never "non-numeric is slower" — it was specific to temporals. And `valueKey`
said why in its own comment:

> Temporal / path — **rarer as a group key**, and neither has a -0 to lose; JSON.stringify + the
> replacer keeps their nested non-finite safe.

A `JSON.stringify` per row, behind an assumption about frequency that a date in a people-graph
refutes — and this repo's domain is people-data-over-time.

### The fix changes no equivalence class, which is what makes it a speedup

`JSON.stringify` of one of these instances serializes exactly its own enumerable fields — `kind`
plus numbers — so a key built from the same fields groups the same values. Each kind takes a
distinct prefix (`t0`…`t5`), because native's rule is "the same kind AND the same rendering", and
`t` collides with no other prefix in this keyer (`n`/`s`/`b`/`N`/`@`/`[`/`{`/`j`).

**A non-finite field falls back to the stringify, deliberately.** `JSON.stringify` renders both
`NaN` and `Infinity` as `null`, so those two `LocalDate`s are ONE group today; a hand-written
template would separate them. That is arguably better and is still not done here, because this item
is a speedup and keeping the pathological case bit-for-bit is cheaper than arguing about it. The
behaviour is pinned by a test that asserts the collapse.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three

One build, both arms behind a temporary env switch asserted present in the built dist first.

```text
  shape                        PRE min   POST min
  count(DISTINCT p.hired)        80.64      19.32   4.17x   DISJOINT (80.6-82.3 vs 19.3-20.5)
  CONTROL count(DISTINCT score)   4.00       4.08   flat
  CONTROL min(p.city)   String     7.95       7.42   flat
  CONTROL count(*)                0.00       0.00   —
```

**The gap closes but not to parity:** 19.32 against the number column's 4.08 is still 4.7x. The
residual is the `isTemporal` test plus the `instanceof` chain and a template with two numbers
against a single `n${v}` — **unmeasured, so unattributed**, per items 804/808/814/829.

### The third wrong-answer mutant in four items to pass a whole suite

- **M3, `LocalDate`'s key reduced to a constant** — collapsing EVERY date into one DISTINCT group
  — **SURVIVED all 2,635 tests.**
- Tests written, then all three mutants re-run: **M3 caught** (2 failures), **M1, `Duration`'s
  `nanos` dropped, caught** (2), **M2, `LocalDateTime` sharing `LocalTime`'s prefix, caught** (1).

**Items 840, 841 and 843 are the same finding three times: a temporal arm shipped into a gap in
the suite.** Item 842 closed the cross-engine half; this closes the TS unit half. Four items for
one type is the real cost of a value family that two storage layers special-case, two planners
have fast paths for, and no test generator had ever produced.

The cases are built against the two ways a hand-written key goes wrong rather than to exercise the
arm: **every field of every multi-field kind is the sole difference in its own pair** (a dropped
field cannot hide behind another field's variation), and **two kinds carrying identical fields must
stay apart** (`LocalTime` vs `LocalDateTime`, `ZonedTime` vs `ZonedDateTime`, and a `Duration`
whose `days` equals a `LocalDate`'s), which is invisible to any single-kind case. Each three-value
case answers 2, so a key that over-merges answers 1 and one that over-splits answers 3 — both
failure directions visible from one number.

`bun run fuzz` (all seven byte-identity fuzzers, random seeds, temporal coverage from item 842)
13 pass 0 fail, run TWICE. The temporary probe and the env switch removed.

## 844 — `stddev` over a scan: **7.0x, disjoint**, landing exactly on `sum`'s cost as predicted — and the `min` CONTROL caught a 1.6x regression my first draft introduced

**SHIPPED (Rust).** An `AggFn` census, the method's opening move applied to a second enum:

```text
  Count 38   Min 36   Max 24   Sum 17   Avg 12        matches in fastpath.rs
  Collect 0  CollectList 0  StddevPop 0  StddevSamp 0  PercentileCont 0  PercentileDisc 0
```

**Six of eleven variants had no scan fast path.** Priced at 200,000 rows against `sum`'s 110 µs on
the same column:

```text
  sum  [fast]              110        the reference
  avg  [fast]              110
  min  [fast]              397
  stddev_pop               777        7.1x
  stddev_samp              790        7.2x
  collect_list           2,999       27x
  percentile_cont        5,588       51x
  percentile_disc        5,816       53x
```

**The stddevs were the ones to take, and the census says why rather than the ranking.** Their own
doc calls them one-pass moments — `sum`'s loop plus one multiply-accumulate — so a 7.1x gap was
paying for the fold and nothing else. The percentiles need a SORT, so most of their 51x is
inherent; `collect_list` must materialize a 200,000-element list. A bigger ratio is not a better
target.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, min of three

Both arms built as separate binaries, each asserted to be the code it claims (`StddevPop` occurs 0
times in PRE's `fastpath.rs`, 4 in POST) before a reading was taken.

```text
  shape                PRE min   POST min
  stddev_pop               777        111   7.0x   DISJOINT
  stddev_samp              779        111   7.0x   DISJOINT
  CONTROL min              398        397   flat
  CONTROL sum              110        110   flat
  CONTROL avg              110        110   flat
```

**POST lands on 111 against `sum`'s 110** — the magnitude the census predicted before the code
existed, which is the same kind of evidence item 835's prediction gave and a different kind from a
ratio found by looking.

### THE CONTROL EARNED ITS KEEP: my first draft regressed `min` by 1.6x

The obvious implementation adds `sum_sq` beside `total` and a third arm to the existing fold. It
worked, the answers were right, both stddevs went 7.3x — and **`min` went 394 µs → 632 µs, 1.6x
the wrong way, disjoint across three alternated rounds** (PRE 438/397/394, POST 731/632/661).

The cause is mine and it is specific: an accumulator declared at that scope **stays live across the
min/max loop that never reads it**, which changes its register allocation. This function's own
comment already records the same hazard one level in — a first draft of min/max shared the sum/avg
loop BODY behind a test and moved the `sum` control 1.09x the wrong way. **A shared live RANGE is
that same tax collected somewhere else.**

The fix is a wholly separate early-return block before the existing fold, so every byte of it is
untouched and the question cannot arise. The control then read flat, which is the only reason this
shipped. **Without a control the change could not reach, this item would have been a 7.3x win that
quietly cost 1.6x on a neighbouring query.**

### Byte-identity by construction

The general fold's moments are exactly `sum += x; sum_sq += x * x; cnt += 1` over the group's rows
with nulls skipped, finishing with `stddev_of` — which this calls rather than repeating its
formula. Float addition is order-dependent, so the ORDER is as load-bearing as the arithmetic: a
bare `Scan`'s group rows arrive in scan order, which is what these loops accumulate in. `stddev_of`
went from private to `pub(super)` for this; nothing else changed in `aggregation.rs`.

### Teeth: three of three, and the third needed a new test

- **M1, the second moment dropped** (`sd_sq += x`) — caught, by `corpus_tests_f`. Worth noting
  _where_: the main 1,227-test suite passed, and the catch came from the corpus binary.
- **M2, the sample flag inverted** — caught, same place.
- **M3, the presence check dropped** from the whole-column loop — **SURVIVED every binary.** No
  test had a scan where some nodes LACK the aggregated property while the column exists, so an
  absent cell contributing 0.0 to both moments and 1 to the count was invisible. The corpus covers
  stddev over a FULLY present column, which cannot distinguish "skips nulls" from "counts them as
  zero". A test was added and M3 is now caught.

The new test asserts the arithmetic and not only the agreement: four present values of 2, 4, 4, 10
give population variance 9 and sample 12, where counting the two absent cells as zero would give a
count of 6 and a mean of 10/3 — **a perfectly plausible-looking wrong number**. It also compares
bit-for-bit against the general fold via `WHERE true`, and pins the count-dependent edges (`pop` is
`0.0` over one row, `samp` NULL below two, both NULL over an empty scan).

**One correction to my own working:** the first version of that test expected `sqrt(8.5)` and
`sqrt(34/3)`. The engine answered 3.0 and the test failed — because _my_ arithmetic was wrong, not
the engine's. 2, 4, 4, 10 has mean 5 and squared deviations summing to 36, so the population
variance is 9. Recorded because a test that fails on its author's arithmetic is the cheap version
of this mistake; the expensive version is a test written to match whatever the code printed.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo build --release --tests` 0;
`cargo test --release` **1,228 passed 0 failed** (1,227 before the new test); `rewrite_fuzz` 10
passed; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run fuzz` (all seven
byte-identity fuzzers) 13 pass 0 fail. The temporary example and all four pristine/ship copies
removed.

**Still open, with numbers:** `collect_list` at 27x and the two percentiles at 51-53x, both named
here and deliberately not taken — the percentile cost is substantially the sort, and a fast path
would have to beat it rather than merely avoid the fold.

## 845 — the TS engine has **NO** aggregate gap: stddev and collect are FASTER than its own `sum` — and the cross-engine table reframes item 844's two open numbers

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary probe, removed). Item 844 found six of eleven native
`AggFn` variants with no scan fast path and closed the stddevs at 7.0x. The obvious next move is
"do the same in TypeScript", and item 843 is the record of why that is a measurement and not an
inference: the two engines had the SAME temporal defect from DIFFERENT causes, so neither "it will
be there too" nor "it cannot be there" is worth acting on.

**It is not there.** 200,000 nodes, one shape per process, 14 reps, drop 3, median of the plateau,
min of three rounds:

```text
  sum              6.65 ms      the reference, which has a shortcut (item 468)
  stddev_pop       5.27         0.79x — FASTER than sum
  stddev_samp      4.90         0.74x — FASTER
  collect_list     5.07         0.76x — FASTER
  min              4.06
  max              3.90
  percentile_cont 15.70         2.4x
  count(*)         0.00         reads no property
```

**The three aggregates item 844 had to add or left open in the native engine are all at or below
`sum` here, and disjointly so** — every `stddev`/`collect_list` reading across three rounds sits
below every `sum` reading. The TS engine folds them through `aggregateOverValues` over a streamed
value sequence, which is the same work `sum` does, so there is no fold-vs-fast-path split to
exploit. `percentile_cont` at 2.4x needs a sort, which is the honest cost of an ordered-set
aggregate.

**Nothing to ship, and that is the result.** Recorded with its numbers so the symmetry argument
("844 shipped 7x natively, therefore TS") is refused by a measurement rather than re-derived.

### The cross-engine table, which changes how 844's open items read

Both from this session, same machine, same fixture shape and size — different harnesses (`Instant`
against `performance.now`), so these are wall-clock comparisons of the same query, not one
instrument:

```text native        TS      native is
  sum                            110 us    6,650      60x faster
  stddev_pop (after item 844)     111      5,270      47x
  min                             397      4,060      10x
  percentile_cont               5,588     15,700       2.8x
  collect_list                  2,999      5,070       1.7x
```

**The native advantage ranges from 60x to 1.7x, and it is SMALLEST exactly on the two aggregates
item 844 named as open.** That reframes those numbers: `collect_list` at "27x `sum`" and
`percentile_cont` at "51x `sum`" are ratios against a reference that happens to be one of the
fastest things the native engine does, not evidence of absolute weakness — native percentile is
still 2.8x the TS engine's, and native `collect_list` only 1.7x.

So the remaining headroom in those two is real but it is **not the fold**. Both have to
materialize something — a 200,000-element list, or a sorted copy — and that cost is paid in both
engines, which is why the ratio between them collapses. A fast path that only avoids the general
fold would be chasing the part that is already cheap. **That is a sharper reason to leave them than
item 844's "mostly inherent", and it took this item's measurement to get it.**

### What is now settled about the aggregate family

Native: `Count`/`Sum`/`Min`/`Max`/`Avg` fast-pathed, the stddevs added at 844, `Collect`/
`CollectList` and both percentiles deliberately on the general fold for the reason above. TS: no
gap on this axis at all.

**And the cross-engine coverage is already there**, which is worth stating because this entry
nearly claimed the opposite. The draft of this item asserted that the differential fuzzer's
generator does not draw the stddevs, the collects or the percentiles — item 842's finding
generalized by analogy — and then the list was read: `AGG` holds `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`,
`max`, `collect_list`, `stddev_pop` and `stddev_samp`, drawn into
`RETURN <agg>(<expr>)`, and the percentiles have their own arm with an out-of-range-fraction case
from item 531. **The whole aggregate family is cross-engine checked, so item 844 shipped covered.**

That is the second time in two ticks that checking a claim before writing it reversed the claim
(item 842's fixture arithmetic was the first), and both were the same mistake in different
clothing: reasoning from a pattern that had just been established elsewhere. The temporal gap was
real, which is exactly what made "the aggregates will have it too" feel like knowledge.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0; `git status` clean of any engine
change (docs only), the temporary probe removed.

## 846 — 🛑 **item 831's "first CLEAN absolutes" are the outlier**: its own code reproduces at 350/315, not 234.1/217.7, and the figures it rejected as contaminated were right

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change.** A `bench_all` regression pass after item 844 read `element p` at
**344.6 ns/row** against item 831's recorded **234.1** — 1.47x, on a row no change since then
touches. That is either a regression I introduced or a bad record, and it is not a thing to wave
through.

### It is not a regression: three source versions, one band

The in-sweep figure first had to be separated from in-sweep inflation (items 737/747), so the
`perrow` group was run alone, three times. Then the same group was run against the engine source
checked out at item 839 (before every native change this session) and at **item 831's own commit**:

```text
  source               element p                element r
  HEAD (846)           350.5 / 342.1 / 342.3    310.1 / 330.0 / 315.7
  item 839 (pre-840)   351.8 / 352.9            318.4 / 311.6
  item 831's own       362.8 / 350.0            314.5 / 315.7
  in-sweep (bench_all) 344.6                    308.5
```

**Seven runs, three source versions, one band: ~342-363 and ~308-330.** Items 840, 841 and 844 did
not touch the render path — the question item 844's own `min` control makes worth asking rather than
assuming — and the bisect says so directly.

### What item 831 concluded, and why it was backwards

831 ran the post-828 sweep, read `element p` 234.1 and `element r` 217.7 against records of 392.6
and 323.9, and reasoned: `element r` is **a control the change cannot reach** (item 829 established
that 828's reorder cannot apply to the edge renderer), it moved 1.49x, therefore per item 762 the
comparison is instrument rather than effect — so **the older figures came from item 809's
contaminated run**, and items 811 and 827 were corrected to cite 234.1.

The logic is sound and the direction is wrong. Set beside today's numbers:

```text
  element r    323.9 "contaminated"   vs ~315 reproducible    2.7% apart
  element p    392.6 "contaminated"   vs ~355 reproducible     10% apart
  element r    217.7 "clean"          vs ~315 reproducible      31% LOW
  element p    234.1 "clean"          vs ~355 reproducible      34% LOW
```

**The run 831 called contaminated reproduces. The run it called clean does not.** Its own
reasoning identified the right pair of suspicious rows for the right reason — `element p` at 47 ms
and `element r` at 218 ms are the only rows long enough for machine state to matter, where every
other row in the sweep is ≤ 11 ms and matched its record to the decimal. It then assumed the
anomaly must be in the older run, because contamination makes things SLOWER. **A quiet, boosting box
makes a long row FASTER by the same mechanism**, and nothing in the evidence distinguished those two
cases. 831 had one run on each side and picked.

### Corrections this forces

- **`element p` is ~350 ns/row and `element r` ~315**, at the sizes those rows use (200,000 and
  1,000,000). These are stated as a band from seven runs rather than as a figure from one, which is
  the whole point.
- **Item 831's correction of items 811 and 827 is REVERTED.** Those two cite `element p` at 392.6,
  831 told them to read 234.1, and 392.6 is within 10% of reproducible. Their own conclusions did
  not rest on the precision — 811 showed a part exceeding a whole, 827 did a fixture-width
  reconciliation anchored elsewhere — and they stand either way, but the number they should carry is
  theirs.
- **Item 828's shipped win is untouched.** Its evidence is its own A/B from saved PRE/POST binaries
  at four key counts, order-alternated and disjoint (1.27-2.82x) — independent of any sweep. What
  this removes is 831's claim that the `perrow` row shows that win as 1.68x. It does not show it at
  all: `element p` reads the same before and after 828 on this fixture, because the social store's
  key count is not where the column-major reorder pays.

### The rule, which item 831 half-stated

810 said a contaminated run's RATIOS must not enter the record; 831 extended that to absolutes and
then did the thing the extended rule forbids — **it replaced two recorded absolutes on the strength
of a single run.** The rule that survives both items is stronger and symmetric:

**A single sweep cannot establish an absolute, however clean it looks, and "this run disagrees with
the record" names a disagreement rather than a culprit.** Deciding which side is wrong needs a third
measurement — here, re-running the older code — and that is cheap compared to what a wrong absolute
costs: 392.6 travelled two items before 831, and 234.1 travelled four items after it.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0; `git status` clean of any engine
change (docs only), the bisected sources restored to HEAD and verified clean.

## 847 — `RETURN DISTINCT <date>`: **9.2x on a scan, 5.4x and 4.6x on a hop**, six controls flat — and a mutant took FOUR fixtures to catch because it lived behind a two-condition gate

**SHIPPED (Rust).** `distinct.rs`'s `ColKeyer::of` built a keyer for `Num`/`Str`/`Bool`/`Dict` and
returned `None` for Temporal/Gen. That is the missing variant items 840/841 found in the _aggregate_
fast paths, sitting in a **different code path**: `count(DISTINCT p.hired)` and `RETURN DISTINCT
p.hired` are answered by different machinery, and the probe carries both so that is demonstrated
rather than assumed — the aggregate form reads 579 µs throughout, untouched.

```text
  200,000 rows, 1,000 distinct values            PRE      POST
  DISTINCT date                     (scan)    21,035     2,291    9.2x   DISJOINT
  DISTINCT date+num                 (scan)    23,428     3,719    6.3x   DISJOINT
  hop DISTINCT date                          23,946     4,443    5.4x   DISJOINT
  hop DISTINCT date+num                      26,566     5,785    4.6x   DISJOINT
  CONTROL DISTINCT num                           409       409    flat
  CONTROL DISTINCT str                         1,261     1,270    flat
  CONTROL DISTINCT num+str                     4,610     4,668    flat
  CONTROL hop DISTINCT num                     2,908     2,925    flat
  CONTROL hop DISTINCT str                     3,101     3,175    flat
  CONTROL count(DISTINCT date)                   579       580    flat
```

Three order-alternated rounds, min of three, both arms as separate binaries. **Six controls flat,
four targets disjoint.** An earlier single-round read showed all three controls up ~10%; alternating
showed that was round-to-round machine state, not the change.

### Two changes, the second found by a control

The first adds a `Date` arm to `ColKeyer` (`of`, `key_into`, `key_part`, `value_at`). Keying on
`days` deviates from `group_key_into`'s bytes, which is the **`Dict` arm's own precedent**: a key is
only compared with keys this keyer built for this column at this offset, so it must be INJECTIVE on
the column's values, not byte-equal to the general path's. Distinct days render as distinct ISO
dates, so the induced equivalence is the general path's. `Date` only, for item 840's reason —
`group_key`'s equality is RENDER equality and a field is structural, and they coincide only where
`format` is injective.

**The old comment's stated blocker was half wrong, and that is recorded**: it said Temporal/Gen "may
carry present-null or need typed compare". `Column::read` returns `Value::Null` for an absent cell
AND a present-null one, so both belong in one group — which is exactly what keying both as tag 0
does, and what the `Num` arm has always done while ignoring its own `nulls` vector.

The second change came from a control. `hop DISTINCT date` was included as a control the first
change could not reach, because `try_distinct_frontier_multi` declines every single non-Dict column
— and it read **flat at 24.2 ms** while its siblings dropped. That decline is reasoned: a single
raw Str/Num is better served by the typed post-pull dedup. **There is no typed post-pull dedup for
a Temporal**, so a lone Date fell to the general path on a premise that does not hold for it.
Admitting `Date` there is a one-condition change worth **5.4x**, and `hop DISTINCT num`/`str` stay
flat as its own controls.

### The mutant that took four fixtures

`key_part` is reached ONLY by `ncol == 2 && any(ColKeyer::Str)` — a two-column frontier key with a
**raw** `Str` side. A constant-key mutant there survived, in order:

1. the full unit suite (1,228 tests),
2. the cross-engine differential fuzzer, _with_ item 842's temporal coverage at `temp=120/120`,
3. a Date+**Num** two-column probe — which takes the byte-key path, so `key_part` never ran,
4. a first version of this item's own test, where the paired `Str` was unique per node, so the
   string alone already separated every row and a dead date part changed nothing.

The fixture that catches it has to satisfy three conditions at once: the `Str` column must stay RAW
(> `dict_max_distinct` = 4,096 distinct), must REPEAT, and the DATE must differ between those
repeats. 10,000 nodes with 5,000 names each appearing twice under two dates: 10,000 distinct pairs,
collapsing to **5,000** when the date part dies. The test asserts both column encodings up front,
because it is worthless if either silently stops holding.

**A mutant surviving is not evidence the code is safe; it is evidence the test did not run the
code.** Three of those four survivals were mine misreading which path a shape takes, and the fourth
was a fixture whose other column did the discriminating. Each looked like "no coverage needed".

### A tooling trap worth recording

Three consecutive M2 verdicts were read from a **stale binary**: `cargo build --example` printed
`Finished` in 0.37 s without a `Compiling` line after a source edit, and the mutant was never
compiled in. The reliable assertion is the **presence of a `Compiling` line**, not a successful
exit — `touch` on the edited file forces it. This is CLAUDE.md's "assert each A/B arm IS the code it
claims" in a form the rule does not name: not the wrong file, the right file unbuilt.

### Teeth, and one honest gap

- **M1b, `key_into`'s Date bytes made constant** — caught by item 840's unit test AND the
  differential fuzzer.
- **M2, `key_part`'s Date made constant** — caught by the new raw-Str frontier test (5,000 against
  10,000).
- **M3, the single-column admission reverted** — answer-equivalent by construction, so **no test
  can catch it and none is claimed.** The evidence is the measured 5.4x with two flat siblings, and
  the condition is documented at the site. This is the hard case the "a perf gate needs its own
  test" rule names: the choice has no answer signature, and the predicate is not separable into a
  pure function worth unit-testing on its own.

**Residual, stated:** `DISTINCT date` at 2,291 is still 5.6x the `Num` control's 409, and
`hop DISTINCT date` at 4,443 is 1.5x `hop DISTINCT num`'s 2,908 — down from 8.2x. Not attributed;
the likely terms are the wider `Temporal` element in `data[]` and the per-row enum match, and
neither was measured.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo build --release --tests` 0;
`cargo test --release` **1,230 passed 0 failed** (1,228 before the two new tests); `rewrite_fuzz`
10 passed; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fuzz` (all seven byte-identity fuzzers) 13 pass 0 fail. The temporary example and all
pristine/ship copies removed.

## 848 — `GROUP BY <date>`: **7.5x / 5.9x / 3.8x**, four controls flat — and the second arm I wrote was DEAD CODE, which only an ablation showed

**SHIPPED (Rust).** The last place the Temporal census showed a hole: a temporal group KEY.
`try_scan_group_agg`'s doc says `None` for a "Temporal/Gen key", and `assign_groups` dispatches on
the materialized `Col` — where a temporal key arrives as `Col::Gen` and falls to the byte-key path
that calls `group_key_into` → `t.format()`, allocating an ISO String **per row**.

```text
  200,000 rows, 1,000 distinct keys       PRE      POST
  GROUP BY date, count(*)              21,607     2,882    7.5x   DISJOINT
  GROUP BY date, sum(p.w)              22,551     3,841    5.9x   DISJOINT
  hop GROUP BY date, count(*)          26,643     7,085    3.8x   DISJOINT
  CONTROL GROUP BY num                  1,127     1,093    flat
  CONTROL GROUP BY str                  1,928     1,955    flat
  CONTROL GROUP BY num, sum             1,917     1,828    flat
  CONTROL hop GROUP BY num              2,911     2,951    flat
```

Three order-alternated rounds, min of three, both arms as separate binaries each asserted to have
actually **compiled** (item 847's trap). A single-round read had all four controls up ~10%;
alternating showed that was round-to-round machine state.

The arm is two passes and no allocation: the first confirms every cell is a `Date` or `Null`, the
second groups on `days`. That replaces n String allocations with 2n reads. The check is not "look
at the first value" **because `Col::Gen` is by definition the mixed column** — the homogeneous case
has to be established, not assumed. `u64::MAX` is the Null group and no date can reach it, since
`d.days as u32` widens to at most `0xFFFF_FFFF`. First-seen order is unchanged. `Date` only, for
item 840's reason.

### The second arm was dead code, and the ablation is what said so

I also added a `Date` arm to `group_frontier_by_prop`, the hop-frontier grouping. It compiled, the
hop row improved 3.8x, and **a constant-key mutant in it survived everything** — the unit suite, the
differential fuzzer, a six-node hop test, and then a purpose-built **50,001-row** test written after
finding that `try_node_prop_grouping` declines any batch under `FRONTIER_FOLD_MIN` (50,000).

Four survivals is a pattern, not bad luck, so the arm itself became the suspect. **Removing it
entirely left the hop row at 7,272 against 7,085 with it, and 26,643 before either** — so the whole
hop win comes from the `assign_groups` arm, which the hop shape also routes through, and the
frontier arm was never reached by any shape I could construct. It is deleted rather than kept as
"defence in depth": unreachable code whose correctness nothing can check is not depth, it is
surface.

**The mutant was the instrument that found this, not an obstacle to shipping.** Had I read its
survival as "no coverage needed here" — the reading I have now made wrong three times in two items
— a dead arm would have shipped with a measured win attributed to it.

### Teeth

- **M1, the group key made constant** — caught by three unit tests AND, after this item extended
  the generator, the differential fuzzer.
- **M3, the homogeneity check made unconditional** — caught by four unit tests. Its own case is the
  MIXED column: a date beside a number promotes the column to `Gen`, and an always-admitting guard
  would key that number as NULL. The test asserts the promotion before relying on it.
- **M2, the frontier arm** — survived four fixtures, and the arm is gone. See above.

### The fuzzer gap this closes

Item 842 added `LET g = n.s … min(n.d) … GROUP BY g` — grouping **by a string** with a date
aggregate, which never puts a date in the KEY position. That is why M1 passed the fuzzer. Three
shapes were added: `GROUP BY <date>` with `count(*)`, with `sum`, and over a hop frontier. M1 is
caught by the fuzzer with them in place and was not without them.

**That is the third time a temporal gap has hidden behind coverage that looked adjacent** (842's
fixture arithmetic, 847's `key_part` gate, this). The common shape: a shape was generated _near_
the untested one and read as covering it.

### Where the Temporal family now stands

Aggregates (840, 841), the DISTINCT keyer (847), and the group key (848) in Rust; `valueKey` in TS
(843); cross-engine coverage for all of them (842, 848). Residual: `GROUP BY date` at 2,882 is
2.6x the `Num` key's 1,093 — not attributed, and the likely terms are the two passes and the wider
`Value` element, neither measured.

`cargo test --release` **1,232 passed 0 failed** (1,230 before the two new tests); `rewrite_fuzz`
10 passed; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0;
