## 849 — the post-848 sweep: **NO regression** — and the `element` rows' three-way disagreement is finally EXPLAINED: the full sweep's figure depends on work done earlier in the same process

**MEASUREMENT, no behaviour change** (one comment added to the bench corpus). Five native changes
have landed since the last clean sweep — 840, 841, 844, 847, 848, three of them in `fastpath.rs` or
`aggregation.rs`, files whose neighbours have already shown they are layout-sensitive (item 844's
`min` control caught a 1.6x regression from one variable's live range).

**No regression.** Every stable row matches its record: `scalar age (flat)` 92.0 against 92.0,
`scalar age (map graph)` 92.0 against 92.4, `degree` 0.19 against 0.19, `pagerank(20)` 11.20 against
11.09/12.08, `betweenness` 264.82 against 266.10/268.34, `wcc` 1.00 against 0.96/0.91. The
sub-millisecond rows match to the decimal, which is the same evidence item 831 used from the other
side.

### The element rows: three harnesses, one variable, finally isolated

The full sweep read `element p` **233.0** and `element r` **212.3** — within 1% of item 831's
"first CLEAN absolutes" (234.1 / 217.7) that **item 846 declared the outlier forty minutes earlier**
on the strength of seven runs across three source versions, all reading 342-363.

Both items were right about their own instrument. Measured three ways on ONE binary, minutes apart:

```text
  full bench_all                          element p  233.0    element r  212.3
  bench_all -- perrow   (same harness)               341.0               294.2
  query_bench perrow    (its own process)      342.9-349.9         297.5-324.6
```

**The last two agree and only the full sweep differs, so the variable is the preceding groups —
not the harness, not the machine, and not any code change.** `bench_all` runs `ingest::run` and
part of `query::run` before this group in the same process; the filtered sweep runs the same
harness with those cases skipped and lands on the isolated figure. These two rows are the only ones
big enough to show it: `element p` materializes 200,000 node elements and `element r` a million edge
ones, where every other row in the group is under 2 ms.

**Why the full-sweep figure moved from 846's 344.6 to today's 233.0 is NOT attributed.** Items 847
and 848 made several pre-perrow cases much faster, so the allocation history before this group did
change — but the mechanism inside the allocator was not measured, and naming it would be the thing
items 804/808/814/829 are records against.

### What this settles, and what it costs each previous item

- **The quotable figure is the ISOLATED one: ~345 and ~300**, stable across item 831's source, item
  839's, item 846's HEAD and today's, and across two different harnesses.
- **Item 831's 234.1/217.7 are not wrong, they are full-sweep figures** — reproducible, as today
  shows, but not absolutes. Its error was calling them "CLEAN absolutes" and correcting two other
  items to them.
- **Item 846's correction stands in its practical conclusion** (no regression; a single sweep cannot
  establish an absolute) **and is wrong in its attribution.** It said 831's figures "do not
  reproduce" and inferred a quiet, boosting box. They do reproduce; 846 never ran a FILTERED sweep,
  so it could not separate "the run" from "the work before the run" and mislocated the variable.
- **Item 846's revert of 831's correction to items 811/827 stands**, because those cite `element p`
  as a per-row cost for a shape-level argument, and ~345 is the figure that shape actually has.

**The rule, third revision.** 810: a contaminated run's ratios must not enter the record. 831:
extended to absolutes, then broke its own extension. 846: a single sweep cannot establish an
absolute. **849: an absolute from a row that is expensive relative to its group cannot be
established by ANY number of runs of the same harness — the harness itself is a variable, and
separating it needs the same measurement with the suspected cause removed.** Seven runs in one
window are one measurement repeated, not seven independent ones.

The caveat is now recorded **at the two cases** in `support/query.rs`, with the three-way table, so
the next person to read a number off a full sweep sees why not to quote it. The full sweep remains
the right instrument for catching a regression in a CHEAP row — which is what it just did, by
matching six records to the decimal.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0. Comment-only
change in the bench corpus; no engine change.

## 850 — TS `DISTINCT`/`GROUP BY` over a date: **5.1x and 4.5x, to PARITY with the number control** — found only after an ablation and a fixture both misled me

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** The TS twins of items 847/848. Item 843 fixed `valueKey`'s temporal arm
and named a residual it could not attribute; this attributes it, and the attribution is somewhere
neither of us guessed.

```text
  200,000 rows, 1,000 distinct      PRE     POST    vs its control
  RETURN DISTINCT <date>          20.37     3.98    5.1x   (control 3.82 -> 1.04x)
  GROUP BY <date>, count(*)       19.18     4.27    4.5x   (control 3.53 -> 1.21x)
  CONTROL DISTINCT num             3.47     3.82    flat
  CONTROL GROUP BY num             3.27     3.53    flat
  CONTROL DISTINCT str             6.60     6.29    flat
```

Three order-alternated rounds, min of three, one build behind a temporary env switch asserted
present in the built dist. Both targets disjoint; all three controls flat, two of them drifting
slightly AGAINST the change. `hop DISTINCT <date>` went 53.99 → 25.10 against its control's 23.62.
**The gap does not shrink, it closes.**

### The cause, after two wrong answers

`valueSet.add` and `groupIndex.bump` both branch on `typeof v !== 'object'`: a **primitive** is
keyed on the RAW value in a native `Set`/`Map`, building **no string at all**, while an object pays
a `valueKey` string per row. `groupIndex`'s own doc comment prices that difference at **50.7 ns
against 12.5, 4.1x** — it was measured years before this item and attributed to the right mechanism
for strings.

Its next sentence is where the date fell through: _"Non-primitives are NOT raw-keyable — two equal
lists, records, temporals or elements are different objects."_ True of every case it lists except
one. **A `LocalDate`'s whole identity is `days`**, which items 843/847/848 established is in
bijection with its rendering, so two dates belong in one group iff they share that number. A third
container keyed on `days` gives a date the primitive treatment; it is separate from `prim` for the
reason the comment gives for having a second map at all — a raw `5` and `LocalDate(5)` would
otherwise collide.

### Two instruments lied, in opposite directions

**The ablation said there was nothing to fix.** A seven-arm ladder over the keying code —
template only, + finiteness, + `instanceof`, + `isTemporal`'s chain, + the whole object-branch
preamble, and a `kind`-switch alternative — came out **flat at 13.9-14.8 ns/key**, with every guard
free. Even made polymorphic (one function reached with numbers, strings and dates, which is the
engine's real shape) it read 14.77 for a date against 12.97 for a number: **1.14x, against a
query-level 4.15x.** The ladder could not see the defect because **the number path never builds the
string the ladder was comparing against** — it was measuring an operation the control does not
perform.

**And my fixture flattered the control.** The first query probe read 4.75x with `score = i % K`
(0-999) against dates at day ~19,000. A plain number in the dates' own range keys at **13.69 ns
against 0-999's 4.00** — digit count and V8's small-integer string cache, nothing to do with type.
Range-matching the control moved the measured gap from 4.75x to 4.15x, and the honest number is the
second one. **A control has to match the target on every axis the instrument is sensitive to, and
"it is the same type" is not that list.**

So the sequence was: a real gap, an ablation that said the code was already optimal, a fixture that
inflated the gap, and a cause that was sitting in a doc comment one function away — which is the
third time this session a comment named the answer (items 836, 843, and this). The ablation is not
worthless; it **excluded** the keying arithmetic, and that exclusion is what forced the search
somewhere else.

### Item 843's test caught me one item later

The first version of this change dropped `Number.isFinite`, and
`a non-finite field keeps the JSON.stringify classing` failed: `LocalDate(NaN)` and
`LocalDate(Infinity)` are ONE group under `valueKey` (stringify renders both as `null`) and two
under a raw `days` key. Item 843 chose to keep that collapse bit-for-bit rather than improve it
inside a speedup, and pinned it. **A decision recorded as a test held a change made an hour later
by the person who recorded it** — which is the entire argument for pinning a deliberate oddity
rather than noting it in prose.

### Teeth: three of three

- **M1, the finiteness guard dropped** — caught by item 843's test, which is how it was found.
- **M2, the date key made constant** — caught, 2 failures.
- **M3, keying into `prim` instead of its own container** — caught by a case added here:
  `DISTINCT [LocalDate(5), 5]` must be 2, in both orders. Nothing else in the file would have
  noticed a date merging with an unrelated integer.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check`
0; `bun run check` 0; `bun test packages/gql` **2,640 pass 0 fail**; `bun run fuzz` (all seven
byte-identity fuzzers, random seeds) 13 pass 0 fail, run TWICE. Both temporary probes removed.

**Where the family stands now, both engines:** aggregates (840, 841, 844), the DISTINCT keyer (847),
the group key (848) and `valueKey` (843) in native and TS; DISTINCT and GROUP BY at parity with
their number controls on both sides; cross-engine coverage at 842 and 848. The remaining temporal
cost on either engine is in the kinds with more than one field, which no item has yet had reason to
take.

## 851 — the never-re-armed CSR, priced on a density × selectivity grid: **up to 10.7x**, "once stale always stale" confirmed — and lazy-on-read is STRUCTURALLY excluded, not merely awkward

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary example, removed). CLAUDE.md records this as a known
defect: `rebuild_csr` is called only from the LOAD paths (`codec.rs`, `ndjson.rs`), every adjacency
write sets `csr_fresh = false`, and nothing ever sets it back — so one `add_edge` demotes every
later typed read for the rest of the session, "proportional to how selective the queried edge type
is", quoted as 1.96x / 2.93x / 24.07x at 1 edge in 2 / 10 / 50. **That is one fixture's slice of a
two-dimensional surface**, and the grid is what makes the lever decidable.

50,000 nodes, a whole-graph typed hop (`MATCH (a:P)-[:T0]->(b) RETURN count(*)`), 10 hops an arm,
min of 5, each arm from its own LOADED store:

```text
  edges/node      fresh    demoted   ratio        interleaved
  2                1457  2647-2712   1.8-1.9x     2611-2751
  10               1442  3986-5001   2.8-3.5x     3989-5028
  50               1428 11233-15264  7.9-10.7x   11323-15316
```

Three things the grid shows that a single row cannot:

- **The penalty grows with BOTH density and selectivity.** At 50 edges a node it is 7.9x for a type
  carrying half the edges and **10.7x** for one carrying a fiftieth. CLAUDE.md's 24.07x is the same
  direction at a density this grid does not reach; the selectivity term alone is only 1.3x of it,
  and the density term is the larger one.
- **The fresh arm is FLAT at ~1,430 across a 25x change in edge count.** That is the whole value of
  the overlay: `out_typed_flat` reads one type's partition, so a fresh store does not care how many
  edges the other types hold. The stale path walks all of them.
- **Interleaved is indistinguishable from demoted** at every point (within 1%). Once the flag is
  down it does not matter how often you write, which is the "nothing re-arms it" claim measured
  rather than read.

### My first fixture measured the slow path against itself

The first run had all three arms within 5% (5,773 / 5,730 / 6,051 µs at 1 in 2) and the obvious
reading was "the demotion does not reproduce". It was the fixture: **a store built through
`add_edge` is already stale**, so `fresh` was the same path as `demoted`. Only a LOAD calls
`rebuild_csr`, so every arm now starts from an NDJSON round-trip. The first version's own comment
said this ("a store built through `add_edge` is never fresh, and only a LOAD is") — written as a
caveat and then not acted on until the numbers came out flat.

### Lazy rebuild on read is structurally excluded

The obvious fix — rebuild when a read finds the overlay stale — is not available, and the reason is
stronger than a borrow-checker inconvenience:

```rust
pub fn out_typed_csr(&self, v: u32, etype: u32) -> Option<&[Adj]>
pub fn out_typed_flat(&self, etype: u32) -> Option<&[Adj]>
```

Both take `&self` and **return a borrow into the very `Vec`s a rebuild would replace.** Interior
mutability does not rescue that: handing out a `&[Adj]` that outlives a `RefCell` guard is the thing
the guard exists to prevent, so the accessors' signatures would have to change at every call site.
And `algo.rs` takes `&Store` under the opt-in rayon pool, so the store is `Sync`-shared — a lock on
this path is the hot read path.

So the viable designs are both write-boundary, and both are `&mut self`:

1. **Rebuild at `commit`** (store.rs:5098) or at an explicit end-of-batch, so a transaction that
   adds edges pays one O(E) rebuild and every later read is fast. Amortizes exactly where a user
   already has a boundary, and `end_bulk` shows the shape is already in the codebase.
2. **Maintain the typed CSR incrementally** per `add_edge`. O(degree) in principle, but an insert
   into the middle of a type's partition shifts the rest, so it needs an append-side overlay per
   type and a merge policy — materially more design than (1).

**(1) is the one to try, and it is NOT free:** a transaction adding one edge to a 2.5M-edge store
would pay a full O(E) rebuild at commit, which is the opposite trade from today for a
write-heavy-small-read workload. The next tick's measurement is that trade — rebuild cost at commit
against the reads it saves — not whether the demotion is real, which this item settles.

**Why this was worth a tick on its own:** the figure in CLAUDE.md is a single row of a surface, the
"lazy rebuild" that any reader would reach for first is excluded by two signatures, and the first
fixture anyone would write measures nothing. All three are now recorded.

Gates: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D
warnings` 0; `git status` clean of any engine change (docs only), the temporary example removed.

## 852 — rebuild-at-commit REFUSED with its number: a rebuild costs **6 to 27 stale reads**, and the rebuild's own second term is O(types × nodes) by layout

**MEASUREMENT, no behaviour change** (a temporary example, removed; both findings recorded at
`rebuild_csr`). Item 851 priced the CSR demotion at 1.8-10.7x, excluded lazy-on-read structurally,
and left exactly one tractable design: rebuild at a write boundary. **That design needed one number
nobody had — what a rebuild costs relative to what a stale read costs — and it does not survive it.**

50,000 nodes, min of 5, each arm from its own loaded store. Break-even in reads is
`rebuild / (stale − fresh)`:

```text
  epv  types   fresh   stale   rebuild   BREAK-EVEN in reads
    2      2     161     295       860          6.4
    2     50     163     304      3764         26.8
   10      2     161     469      2929          9.5
   10     50     160     574      8237         19.9
   50      2     158    1225     14937         14.0
   50     50     159    1483     21579         16.3
```

**A rebuild costs between 6 and 27 stale reads.** It wins where that many reads follow a write with
no write between them — the bulk-update-then-serve shape, which is real — and loses on any workload
with frequent small write batches. So an **unconditional** commit hook is the wrong change, and the
policy that would make it right depends on a future read count the store does not have. Refused,
with the number that refuses it.

### The rebuild's second term, found in the same measurement

`rebuild_csr` cost **860 µs at 2 edge types and 3,764 at 50**, on the same edge count — 4.4x for
25x the types. The cause is in the loop:

```rust
for adj in adjs {          // every node
    for a in adj { … }
    for t in &mut typed {  // EVERY type
        t.0.push(…);
    }
}
```

An offset is pushed for every type at every node, including types with no edge there, so the offset
arrays are **O(types × nodes) per direction** — 5M pushes at 50 types over 50,000 nodes. At high
density the edge copying dominates instead (14,937 µs at 50 edges a node), so the rebuild is
O(E + types × N) and **which term rules depends on the fixture**, which is why one row could not
have shown this either.

That term is a property of the **dense per-type offset layout**, not of the loop: a sparse layout
(only the types present at a node) would remove it, and that is item 825's class of decision — a
storage change — rather than a tick. Named with its number so the next attempt starts from the
measurement.

### What the pair of items leaves standing

- The demotion is real and large (851: 1.8-10.7x, growing with density AND selectivity).
- Lazy-on-read is structurally excluded: the accessors return borrows into the `Vec`s a rebuild
  replaces, and the store is `Sync`-shared under the rayon pool (851).
- Rebuild-at-commit is refused unconditionally at a 6-27 read break-even (here).
- Incremental per-type maintenance remains the only undisproven design, and it now has a cost
  model to beat: it must beat `O(E + types × N)` amortized over fewer than 6 reads.

**Two ticks to refuse a lever is the right trade when the lever is a storage change.** The
alternative was building the commit hook and discovering the break-even from a regression in
`bench:usage`, which is how this corpus acquired several of the rules in CLAUDE.md.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0. Comment-only
change in the engine; the temporary example removed.

## 853 — the GREMLIN spellings: `min`/`max`/`sum` at **ratio 1.00**, but dedup is **9.7-37.9x** — and the two dedups are NOT the same question, which is what bounds the fix

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (a temporary example, removed). Items 840, 841, 844, 847 and 848
all added arms gated on a PLAN shape, and none of them checked whether the Gremlin surface reaches
them. CLAUDE.md's reason for expecting it to is explicit — both languages lower to one `ir::Plan`
and run one `exec`, so "speed is a property of the optimized plan, not the surface syntax." **That
holds only where the two spellings lower to the SAME plan**, and this measures which do.

200,000 nodes, 1,000 distinct values, min of 5, the same store for both surfaces:

```text
  question                  gql_us    grm_us    ratio
  min(date)                    568       569     1.00
  min(num)                     410       412     1.00
  sum(num)                     113       113     1.00
  count(DISTINCT date)         596     22613    37.92
  count(DISTINCT num)          411      5326    12.96
  DISTINCT date rows          2361     22849     9.68
  DISTINCT num rows            421      5327    12.65
  GROUP BY date/num            —         —       not comparable
```

**Items 841 and 844 are surface-neutral, exactly as designed** — `values('hired').min()` and
`.sum()` reach the same arms at ratio 1.00, to the microsecond. That is the one-plan claim holding,
measured rather than assumed.

**The dedup spellings are 9.7-37.9x apart, and the gap is NOT temporal** — `count(DISTINCT num)` is
12.96x and `DISTINCT num rows` 12.65x, so it predates items 840/847 and affects every column type.

The `groupCount().by(…)` rows are reported as **not comparable** rather than as a ratio: Gremlin
returns a Map and GQL returns rows, so the probe's own answer check flagged them, and a ratio
between two different output shapes would be a number without a question.

### The plans say why, and the why is partly semantic

```text
  GQL      Distinct   { Project { Scan } }
  Gremlin  DistinctBy { Project { Filter { Scan, PropertyExists{slot:0,key} } }, key_slots:[0] }
```

Two differences, and only one is an accident:

1. **`Distinct` against `DistinctBy { key_slots }`** — different plan nodes, and every DISTINCT
   fast path matches on `Plan::Project { input: scan, … }` directly (distinct.rs:279 and :808), so
   the Gremlin shape reaches none of them.
2. **The extra `Filter { PropertyExists }`** is TinkerPop semantics, not overhead: Gremlin
   `values('score')` SKIPS an element lacking the property where GQL `RETURN DISTINCT p.score`
   emits a NULL row. **The two queries have different answers on any graph where a node lacks the
   key**, and my fixture gave every node the property, so the probe's answer check could not see
   it.

**So "they must cost the same" is the wrong frame, and I started the tick with it.** They are not
the same question. What survives is narrower and still worth a lot: the Gremlin shape does strictly
one presence test more, which cannot be 13x, so the fast paths are reachable in principle for a
variant that **skips** absent rows instead of keying them as NULL — and the keyers already read
`present[i]` on every arm, so the difference is one branch, not a new keyer.

### What this leaves

A contained follow-up with its number: admit `Plan::Filter { input: Scan, pred: PropertyExists }`
under the project, and `Plan::DistinctBy` with a single key slot, into the DISTINCT fast paths,
skipping rows where `!present[i]`. Priced at **9.7-37.9x** on the shapes above. The equivalence that
has to be argued is not the keyer's — item 847 settled that — but that `PropertyExists` on the
projected key is exactly `present[i]`, which is a storage-level claim and checkable.

**And a gap in my own last five items:** none of them measured the Gremlin surface, and two of the
five turned out to be reachable from it only by luck of lowering. The check costs one probe and it
belongs in the next item that adds a plan-gated arm.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0; `git status`
clean of any engine change (docs only), the temporary example removed.

## 854 — the Gremlin dedup gap closed: **30.8x on dates, 4.7-5.6x on num/str** — the fast path existed and was gated on `Dict` alone

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Item 853 measured `values(k).dedup()` at 9.7-37.9x its GQL twin and found the
lowering, not the surface, was the cause. The fix turned out to be a widening rather than a new
path: `try_distinct_dict_col` already recognized the Gremlin plan shape — including the
`Filter { PropertyExists }` that TinkerPop's "skip an absent property" semantics emits, with its own
measured note (270.1 → 86.9 µs) — and then gated on `Column::Dict` and nothing else. A `Num`, `Str`,
`Bool` or `Temporal` column fell to the general path.

It is now `try_distinct_value_col`, with an arm per representation: dict codes against a bitset,
`num_group_bits`, a borrowed `&str`, a two-slot bool table, and a date's epoch day.

```text
  200,000 nodes, 1,000 distinct     gql     grm PRE    grm POST    speedup
  DISTINCT date rows               2344       23019         748      30.8x
  count(DISTINCT date)              587       22601         751      30.1x
  DISTINCT str rows                1273        6357        1129       5.6x
  DISTINCT num rows                 414        5366        1140       4.7x
  count(DISTINCT num)               412        5344        1155       4.6x
  CONTROL min(date)                 572         570         569       flat
  CONTROL sum(num)                  113         113         113       flat
```

Three order-alternated rounds, min of three, both arms as separate binaries each asserted to have
compiled. **The whole GQL column is itself a control the change cannot reach, and it is flat across
all six rounds** (414-419 for num, 2336-2366 for date) — which is a stronger control than a single
unreachable query, because it is the same question asked the other way.

The two `min`/`sum` rows stay at ratio 1.00: item 853 established they were already surface-neutral,
and they still are.

### Each arm's key is the general path's equivalence, not a stricter one

`num_group_bits` is the value contract's own grouping (−0.0 with 0.0, NaN with itself), the dict
code is in bijection with its string, `GStr`'s equality is its content, and a date's `days` is in
bijection with its rendering (items 843/847/848). So first-seen order and the classes are
unchanged in every arm.

The `Str` arm is written as its own loop rather than through the shared macro, and the comment says
why: a closure annotated `&mut FnvSet<&str>` infers `'static` for that borrow, so the key cannot
outlive `store`. Keying an owned `GStr` clone would compile and costs a clone per row for nothing.

### A side effect worth naming: the GQL date spelling is now the SLOWER one

`DISTINCT p.hired` reads 2,344 µs in GQL against the Gremlin spelling's 748 — **the GQL form is now
3.1x slower than the Gremlin one for the same shape.** They are not the same question (GQL emits
NULL for an absent property where Gremlin drops the row), so this is not a spelling violation. But
it is a measurement: item 847's `ColKeyer` builds byte keys where this arm keys a date on `days` in
an `FnvSet`, and the arm added here is faster. **That is item 847's stated residual — "still 5.6x
the Num control" — with a named cause and a demonstrated alternative.** Next lever, priced at 3.1x.

### Teeth: three mutants, all three survived the whole suite first

- **M1**, the date key made constant.
- **M2**, the `Num` key on raw `to_bits()` instead of `num_group_bits` — splits −0.0 from 0.0.
- **M3**, the absent-row skip dropped. **Not merely a slow path:** the row falls through and keys
  whatever `data[i]` holds for an absent cell, so a garbage value enters the dedup.

All three passed all 1,232 tests, because only the `Dict` case the path originally served was
covered. A Gremlin-surface test was added over a fixture built against each mutant — a column
holding both −0.0 and 0.0, two dates among three present values, and a node carrying none of the
keys — and all three are now caught (2 failures each). It asserts the VALUES as well as the counts,
since a count can be right while the wrong value is emitted: the dict arm pushes
`dict[codes[i]]` and the others push `data[i]`.

**That is the fifth time in this run that a plan-gated arm shipped into a hole in the suite**
(840, 841, 843, 848, here). The pattern is stable enough to state as a rule: **a fast path gated on
a column representation needs a test per representation it admits, because the suite's fixtures
exercise whichever one the original author had.**

## 855 — item 847's residual closed: GQL `DISTINCT <date>` **2.85x**, now within **1.09x** of the Gremlin spelling it was 3.1x behind

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Item 854 made `values(k).dedup()` fast and thereby exposed its twin: the GQL
`RETURN DISTINCT p.hired` read **2,344 µs against the Gremlin form's 748**, so the GQL spelling of
the same shape was 3.1x the slower one. `try_distinct_scan_prop` — the single-column arm — has
`Str`, `Dict`, `Num` and `Bool` cases and no `Temporal`, so a date fell through to
`try_distinct_scan_multi`, whose `ColKeyer` builds a byte key per row. **Item 847 added `Date` to
the keyer and never looked one function up**, which is why its own entry recorded a residual of
"still 5.6x the Num control" without a cause.

```text
  200,000 nodes, 1,000 distinct, 1 in 97 lacking `hired`     PRE     POST
  TARGET   gql DISTINCT date                                 2277      800   2.85x  DISJOINT
  CONTROL  gql DISTINCT num                                   406      409   flat
  CONTROL  gql DISTINCT str                                  1260     1260   flat
  CONTROL  gql min(date)                                      565      558   flat
  REFERENCE grm dedup date (item 854's path)                  738      733   flat
```

Three order-alternated rounds, min of three, both arms as separate binaries each asserted to have
compiled. **GQL is now 1.09x of the Gremlin spelling**, from 3.1x behind; the Gremlin reference is
itself flat, which is what says this change did not simply move the cost.

### The fixture proves the semantics rather than assuming them

One node in 97 lacks `hired`, and the two spellings return **1,001 rows (GQL) against 1,000
(Gremlin)** — GQL treats an absent property as a NULL VALUE and emits it once, where
`values(k).dedup()` drops the row. That difference is in the output of every round, so the
`saw_null` branch is demonstrably running rather than assumed to be. It is also why these two are
not the same question and the 1.09x is a floor rather than a target.

`days` is in bijection with the rendering `group_key` keys a temporal by (items 843/847/848), so
the dedup classes are the general path's, and first-seen order is preserved by pushing on insert
exactly as the `Str` and `Num` arms do.

### Teeth, and the mutant that needed a fixture change

- **M1**, the date key made constant — caught, 3 failures (item 847's test).
- **M3**, `Value::Null` pushed in place of the date — caught, 3 failures.
- **M2**, the `saw_null` branch's `out.push` deleted — **SURVIVED.** Item 847's scan fixture gave
  every `P` node a `hired`, so the NULL path never ran. A key-less node was added to that test and
  its expectation updated to include the NULL; M2 is now caught (2 failures).

So the hole was in a test I wrote eight items ago, and the mutant found it rather than a review.
**That is the sixth plan-gated arm this run to ship into a gap in the suite** (840, 841, 843, 848,
854, here) — and the first where the gap was in coverage I had added myself for the adjacent case.
The rule from item 854 holds and gains a corollary: a test written for one arm's representation
does not cover the NULL path of another, because absence is a property of the FIXTURE and not of
the column type.

### Where the temporal DISTINCT family now stands

```text
  gql  RETURN DISTINCT <date>      scan   2277 -> 800   (855)
  gql  count(DISTINCT <date>)              21693 -> 570  (840)
  grm  values(<date>).dedup()              23019 -> 748  (854)
  gql  GROUP BY <date>                     21607 -> 2882 (848)
  ts   DISTINCT / GROUP BY <date>          20.4ms -> 4.0 (850)
```

Every spelling of "distinct dates" on either engine is now within ~2x of its number-column control,
from 10-38x. The one remaining asymmetry is `DISTINCT str` at 1,260 µs — 3.1x the `Num` arm's 409 —
which is string hashing and not a missing arm, and no item has priced whether that is reducible.

The sweep was launched in a background command that also ran `gh run list`, so the output file was

## 857 — the TS Gremlin dedup had the SAME gap as the native one: **7.7x**, and the date is now the FASTEST of the three spellings

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Items 853/854 found `values(k).dedup()` 9.7-37.9x behind its GQL twin in
the native engine. The TS engine implements both surfaces separately, so whether the gap is there
too is a measurement — item 845 is the record of what inferring across engines costs, and item 843
is the record of the two engines having the same defect from different causes.

**It was there, and larger:**

```text
  200,000 vertices, 1,000 distinct     gql     grm PRE    grm POST
  date                                4.60      107.46       14.01    7.7x   DISJOINT
  CONTROL num                         —          15.10       15.07    flat
  CONTROL str                         —          16.15       15.49    flat
  CONTROL gql date                    4.60        4.60        4.35    flat
```

Three order-alternated rounds, min of three, one build behind a temporary env switch asserted
present in the built dist. **POST reads 14.01 against the `num` spelling's 15.07 — the date is now
the FASTEST of the three**, where it was 7x the slowest.

### The cause, and why num/str are controls rather than targets

`dispatch.ts`'s `dedupe` arm routes a value through `isComposite`, which includes `isTemporal(v)`.
A composite pays **three** things per row: a `WeakSet` insert, a `tupleKey` string build, and a
string-`Set` probe. The `WeakSet` exists to short-circuit a repeated **reference** — and every
vertex carries its own `LocalDate` instance, so for this type it **never hits**: 200,000 distinct
objects inserted for nothing.

`num` and `str` already take the cheap primitive `Set`, so their 3.4-3.6x against GQL is the
traversal stream's own cost and **not** a keying defect. That is what makes them controls this
change cannot reach, and it is why the entry does not claim them: item 234 already retracted two of
three targets in this area after finding the big ratio was data layout rather than overhead.

The fix is item 850's, in the other package: a finite `LocalDate` keys on `days` in its own `Set`,
separate from the primitive one because a raw `5` and `LocalDate(5)` would otherwise collide.
**Finite only** — `tupleKey` renders a non-finite field as `JSON.stringify` does, so
`LocalDate(NaN)` and `LocalDate(Infinity)` are ONE key there and two under a raw `days`. Item 850
pinned that collapse rather than improving it inside a speedup, and this keeps the two engines
agreeing.

### Teeth: three mutants, all three survived 809 tests first

- **M1**, the finiteness guard dropped — changes the `NaN`/`Infinity` grouping.
- **M2**, the date key made constant.
- **M3**, keying into the shared primitive `Set` — merges a date with the number its `days` equals.

All three passed the whole gremlin package, because **nothing covered `values(<date>).dedup()`**.
A test file was added with a case per mutant, built on `inject` for the pure-value cases so there
is no question about which property path produced the value, plus the graph-property shape that was
the 23.5x. All three are now caught (1, 2 and 1 failures).

**Seventh plan-or-type-gated arm this run to ship into a gap in the suite** (840, 841, 843, 848,
854, 855, here), and the third where the same defect existed independently in both engines
(temporal `valueKey` at 843, DISTINCT/GROUP BY at 850, dedup here). The pattern now has two halves
worth stating together: a fast path gated on a value's REPRESENTATION needs a test per
representation, and **a defect found in one engine is a hypothesis about the other, never a
conclusion** — but it is a hypothesis worth testing every time, because it has now been right three
times out of three.

## 858 — 🛑 **a WRONG ANSWER I shipped at item 854**, caught by the cross-engine fuzzer on a docs-only commit: a stored present NULL was treated as an absent cell

**FIX (Rust).** Item 856's CI failed — on a **docs-only** commit, so nothing it contained could have
caused it. The failing case was not the rare `gremlin-fuzz` residual this repo records; it was a
real divergence with a reproducible seed:

```text
  [seed 3437594665753181] g.V().values('age').dedup().count()
  Expected 1   Received 5
```

**That is exactly the shape item 854 newly admitted** — `values(k).dedup()` over a `Num` column —
and the engines disagreed.

### The defect

A stored present NULL and a truly absent cell BOTH read `!present[i]`; only `nulls[i]` separates
them. TinkerPop keeps a present null as a **value** and drops an absent property — which this
repo's own `by_absent_property_filters_present_null_kept` test states for the keying `by()`
family. The fast path item 854 widened from `Dict` to every representation **inherited the
`!present[i]` test unchanged**, so for the newly admitted types it skipped present nulls as if they
were absent, losing a value from the dedup.

The fix is for the arm to **decline** when the column holds a present null — it cannot emit a NULL
into its dedup — so the general path answers. One `nulls[i]` test per arm, and the `nulls` field
now destructured rather than `..`-ignored in all five.

### The ablation confirms cause and cure

```text
  with the fix          seed 3437584353 → 1 pass
  fix ablated           seed 3437584353 → 1 fail, Expected 1 / Received 5, the CI case verbatim
```

Then three random-seed runs and the CI seed, all passing, plus all seven byte-identity fuzzers.

### Two process failures of my own, both recorded in CLAUDE.md already

**1. I replayed the seed against a clobbered `.so`.** The first six replays failed 6/6 and I nearly
read that as "the fix does not work". They were run with `bun test src/gremlin-fuzz.test.ts`
directly after a bare `cargo build --release` — which CLAUDE.md states overwrites
`liblenke_engine.so` **without the `capi` FFI symbols**, because the feature is off by default.
`bun run fuzz gremlin --seed …` rebuilds the right artifacts and the seed passed immediately. **The
runner exists to defuse exactly this trap and I went around it.**

**2. Item 854's test had the gap this found.** It covered a column holding both −0.0 and 0.0, two
dates among three values, a node carrying none of the keys — and no stored present null. Three
mutants were run against it and all three were caught, which is why the hole did not show: **the
mutants I chose all lived in code the fixture exercised.** A mutation suite cannot find a case the
fixture never constructs, which is the same limitation item 854's own entry noted from the other
side ("the suite's fixtures exercise whichever representation the original author had").

### What this says about the run

Items 840-857 shipped nine plan- or type-gated arms, seven of which first had a mutant survive the
whole suite. **This is the first to ship an actual wrong answer**, and the thing that caught it was
the cross-engine differential fuzzer — not the unit suite, not mutation, and not review. Item 842
added temporal coverage to that fuzzer specifically so it could see this family; **that investment
is what turned a silent wrong answer into a red CI two commits later.**

The narrower lesson is about absence: `present[i]`, `nulls[i]` and `present_at(i)` are three
different questions, and a fast path that reads only the first is correct exactly as long as the
column cannot hold a stored null. `Dict` columns in this corpus largely cannot; `Num` ones can.
Widening a gate across representations widens which of those questions matter.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo build --release --tests` 0;
`cargo test --release` **1,234 passed 0 failed** (1,233 before the new test); `cargo clippy
--all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0; `bun test packages/gremlin`
813 pass 0 fail; `bun run fuzz gremlin` 1 pass 0 fail on three random seeds AND on the CI seed;
`bun run fuzz` (all seven byte-identity fuzzers) 13 pass 0 fail.

## 859 — the GQL differential fuzzer could not see a STORED NULL, and reached **one of five** DISTINCT arms; both closed, and the two additions are useless apart

**TEST COVERAGE, no engine change.** Item 858 was a wrong answer that shipped: a stored present
NULL treated as an absent cell. The method's next step after that is to grep the pattern elsewhere,
and the first question is whether the cross-engine fuzzer could have caught it on the GQL side.

**It could not, for two independent reasons.**

1. **No property in its fixture held a stored null.** Every key was either always present or
   plainly absent. The _gremlin_ fuzzer's fixture has carried `"lang":null` and `"age":null` all
   along — **which is exactly why IT caught item 858 and this one could not.**
2. **The only `RETURN DISTINCT <prop>` row shape in the whole generator was item 842's
   `RETURN DISTINCT n.d`.** So of `try_distinct_scan_prop`'s five typed arms the fuzzer reached
   exactly one — the Date arm item 855 added — and the Num, Str, Bool and Dict arms were
   cross-engine unreached entirely.

So the GQL side of items 840, 841, 844, 847, 848 and 855 rested on a reading of three functions
rather than on a check.

### The two additions, and why neither works alone

- **`nu`**: a value on vertices 1/3/6, a **stored present null** on 2/4, **absent** on 5 — the
  three-way distinction that `present[i]`, `nulls[i]` and `present_at(i)` answer differently, which
  is the axis item 858 died on. Added to the count/DISTINCT key list, the cross-slot comparison
  lists, and `genExpr`'s property access so it reaches aggregates, ORDER BY and projections.
- **`RETURN DISTINCT n.<key>`** over the general key list, plus a filtered and a hop form.

**Measured, not assumed:** with `nu` added but no DISTINCT row shape, a mutant deleting the Num
arm's NULL row **survived** the differential. With the shape added it is **caught**. The column
supplies a cell that is neither present nor absent; the shape asks a question that can see it, and
one without the other finds nothing.

### Teeth, both arms of the 858 class

```text
  Num arm, the NULL row deleted      CAUGHT   via `RETURN DISTINCT n.nan`
  Date arm, the NULL row deleted     CAUGHT   via `RETURN DISTINCT n.d`
```

Then three consecutive clean runs, the full Rust suite at 1,234, and all seven byte-identity
fuzzers twice.

**Worth being exact about which addition earned which catch.** The Num-arm mutant was caught
through `n.nan` — a column that is _absent_ on most vertices, not null — so the DISTINCT **shape**
is what closed that hole, and `nu` was not needed for it. `nu` covers the narrower case `nan`
cannot: a cell that is present and null. Both are in, and the entry says which did what rather than
crediting the pair.

### What this leaves standing

No new divergence appeared from any of the six items when the fixture gained a stored null and the
generator gained the DISTINCT shapes — so their present-null handling is now **checked** rather
than argued: the aggregates skip nulls (which ISO requires), `ColKeyer` keys an absent cell and a
present null identically because `Column::read` returns `Value::Null` for both, and the GQL DISTINCT
arms emit one NULL row. Item 847's entry argued the second of those; this is the first time anything
tested it.

**Ten items into this family, the ledger on how defects were found reads:** seven mutants that
survived a whole suite, one wrong answer that reached main and was caught by the cross-engine
fuzzer, and one coverage gap found by asking why that fuzzer had not caught it sooner. Mutation
finds what the fixture can express; the differential finds what one engine does and the other does
not; **neither finds a case the fixture never constructs**, and that is the hole this item closes.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check`
0; `bun run check` 0; `cargo test --release` **1,234 passed 0 failed**; `bun run fuzz differential`
clean on three consecutive random seeds; `bun run fuzz` (all seven byte-identity fuzzers) 13 pass
0 fail, run TWICE. No engine change — both mutants reverted and the tree verified clean of each.

## 861 — the TS `SET` claim corrected (TWO passes, 21-38% of a write), an undo guard REFUTED at flat, and `grep` silently finding nothing in a 165 KB file

⚠️ **The six per-write "constants" this item lists but does not price are SPLIT at item 1732, and the
list's ranking is wrong: the asserts and validations it names first are 2.3%, while event dispatch
and reactivity are 21.3%.**

⚠️ **AND ITS `spread+freeze 24 / spread 11` TABLE UNDERSTATES THE FREEZE BY 2.6x** — in situ it is
~35 ns, 30% of a write (item 1733), because `setProperty` then makes three reads against the FROZEN
object and an isolated microbench never pays for those.

**MEASUREMENT, no behaviour change** (the change was built, measured, and reverted; the refutation
is recorded at the getter it would have changed).

### The recorded claim was stale and pointed at the minority term

"TS SET makes 3 O(K) passes per write" is carried as an open defect. Reading `Vertex.setProperty`
finds **two** — the `{ ...previous }` spread and `Object.freeze(bag)` — because the third
(normalizing the whole bag) was removed at item 349, which that code's own comment states. So the
count was stale. **And the two that remain are the minority of a write:**

```text
  k      engine setProperty   spread+freeze   spread   mutate
  4            113 ns              24          11       2
  32           126                 37          25       1
  128          194                 73          57       1
```

**The O(K) pair is 21% of a write at 4 keys and 38% at 128.** So 62-79% is a per-write CONSTANT —
the validations, three constraint asserts, the `key in properties` test, two box lookups, a
`recordUndo` closure and an `EmitterEvent` allocation. Framing this path as "O(width)" aims at the
smaller half.

### The lever that followed, and its refutation

Two of those constants looked unconditional, and the codebase said so itself: `undoWanted`'s doc
claims **"Every call site tests this before building its closure"**, citing item 334 and the native
twin at 331. That claim is false outside `Graph` — `Vertex` and `Edge` call `recordUndo` four times
each, reference `undoWanted` zero times, and cannot reach a private getter; two sites per class also
build `Object.fromEntries(...)` captures for the closure. It reads exactly like item 334 left
half-done.

Made public, all eight sites guarded, min of three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds:

```text
  setProperty     k=4   87 -> 87     k=32  111 -> 107    k=128   164 -> 181  (WORSE)
  setProperties   k=4  388 -> 408    k=32 2329 -> 2357   k=128 10224 -> 10167
```

**Flat everywhere, and slower at the widest point.** V8's escape analysis makes a closure that
never leaves the call nearly free, and the O(P) captures are a rounding error against the per-key
validate/assert loop those calls already run — a 128-key `setProperties` costs ~10 µs a write, so
three small allocations cannot show. **Reverted**, with the numbers recorded at the getter so the
next reader of that doc comment does not repeat it.

**A single round read 113 → 100 and I nearly took it.** Alternating erased it. That is the third
time this session a first reading pointed somewhere the third did not (items 839, 849, here).

### `grep` returned NOTHING for a string that occurs 13 times

Diagnosing this, `grep -c recordUndo packages/core/src/core/Graph.ts` printed **no output at all** —
not `0`, nothing — and the same for `undoWanted`, `Undo` and `emit(`. `wc -l` reported 4,466 lines
and `head` showed the right file. I was one step from concluding the engine calls a method that does
not exist, which would have been a fabricated bug report about working code.

`python3`'s `str.count` finds `recordUndo` **13 times** and `undoWanted` **9**. The file is UTF-8
with non-ASCII content, and this repo's `grep` is `ugrep`, which silently yields nothing on it. My
own notes already carry "`grep -I` skips Unicode files" from a rename that went wrong the same way,
and I did not apply it even after `file` printed "Unicode text".

**The rule, stated so it is actionable:** a `grep` that finds nothing in a file known to be large
is evidence about the TOOL, not the file. Confirm with a second reader — `python3 -c "print(open(p).read().count(s))"` — before concluding an identifier is absent. Every "X is not in Graph.ts"
claim from grep in this repo is worthless.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check`
0; `bun run check` 0; `bun test packages/core` 370 pass 0 fail; `bun test packages/gql
packages/gremlin` 3,453 pass 0 fail (during the experiment). Comment-only change in the engine; the

  so the remaining lever is a cheaper dispatch (one merged internal listener, or inline bookkeeping
  leaving an empty snapshot), NOT a guarded construction.

  without knowing its share — they won anyway, but the next tokenizer change should be priced
  against the descent, not assumed.

- **METHOD — a null A/B cannot distinguish "does not help" from "DID NOT RUN" (item 900).** 0.96x

  one at the application — showed the application count was ZERO. This is the same distinction
  mutation already requires (a `DID-NOT-RUN` verdict separated from `CAUGHT` by looking for a result
  line before the exit code, items 866/886): **an A/B needs an execution counter, not just a
  timing.** Without one, "worth nothing" would have been recorded about code that was never reached.
- **DIAGNOSTIC worth reusing — count `matchesPredicate` entries to see whether a predicate was
  LIFTED (item 900).** A lifted predicate filters BEFORE `matchesPredicate`, so its entry count
  equals the MATCHING rows; an unlifted one equals the SCANNED rows. Measured 1,250 (flat, lifted)
  against 5,000 (dotted, not lifted) on the same 5,000-vertex fixture. No timing needed, and stable.
- **A new predicate list has MORE consumers than `hasPredicate` and the merge (item 900).**
  `rejectedByElementDirect` is a second application site, and the two `preFilter` gates in
  `matching.ts` enumerate the lifted lists BY NAME (`pre.eqProps !== undefined || pre.cmpProps !==
undefined`). None of these is discoverable from the list's definition. (Those gates also omit
  `truthProps` — a missed optimization, not a bug, since `matchesPredicate` still applies it.)
- **CORRECTION to item 900 — `ownVar` was never the problem (item 901).** `compileNode` IS reached
  with `var=p` and `where=compare` for every spelling (instrumented), and `freePredicateVars`
  handles a `field` node correctly (walks the base to the `prop`). So the predicate IS built with an
  `ownVar` and DOES carry the lift; the gap is entirely on the CONSUMER side. `shortcuts.ts` builds
  its own `CPredicate` for a filtered count and its `InlinePred` contract names exactly three
  carriers (`where`, `eqProps`/`cmpProps`, `props`); add `rejectedByElementDirect` and the two
  `preFilter` gates and a new list must reach **at least five** consumers, none discoverable from
  the list's definition.
- **THE HAZARD ITEM 900 MISSED — a predicate lift MOVES the constraint, it does not add a shortcut
  (item 901).** `generic = direct === null ? where : direct.residual` and `residual` is ALWAYS
  `undefined`, so a successful lift **empties `where`**. The new list becomes the ONLY carrier of
  that conjunct, and any consumer that enumerates the lists by name and misses it returns a silent
  **SUPERSET** — `hasPredicate`'s named bug class (item 277) one level up, in a change that wired
  `hasPredicate` itself and still left four consumers unwired.
- **AND IT PASSED THE WHOLE SUITE IN THAT STATE (item 901).** 2,711 GQL + 828 Gremlin + 370 core
  green, because no fixture combines a dotted conjunct with the un-wired consumer. A 0.96x number
  plus a green suite looked like a harmless no-op and was a latent wrong answer. **A green suite is
  evidence about the fixtures, not about the wiring.**
- **RULE — a performance list that REPLACES a general path is a CORRECTNESS surface (item 901).**
  The tell is whether the general carrier is emptied on success. When it is, "add a fourth list
  beside the other three" is not a local change however local it looks: audit every consumer BEFORE
  writing the list, and do not trust a grep for the sibling list's name to find them.
