- **NEW CROSS-ENGINE DIVERGENCE — the engines disagree on WHICH static fault wins (item 916).** For
  `MATCH (n:L) RETURN nosuchfn(n.k) AS a, missingVar.k AS b` TS raises the SCOPE fault and native
  raises **`E_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION`**; with the two faults written in the other order both raise the
  scope fault. **Native is written-order sensitive, TS is not**: TS raises both from `compile` in a
  fixed order (`checkLinearScope` walks every clause before `compileLinear`, the unknown-function
  check runs after it), native raises both from the PARSER. They agree on a query with ONE fault.
  Neither is obviously wrong — a standard rarely fixes which static error is reported first — but
  which error CODE a caller receives is observable, which is this engine's own invariant. Pinned by
  `fault-precedence.test.ts` (six cases, including TS's order-independence as its own assertion).
- **UNBLOCKS — item 908's fusion no longer has the reason I recorded against it (item 916).** 908
  said fusing `checkLinearScope` into `compileLinear` would change a fault ordering that is "compared
  against native". **It is not compared** — native does not share TS's order-independence. The fusion
  is still a deliberate behaviour change for TS callers (it would move TS towards native's
  written-order behaviour), but that is now a known consequence rather than an unknown.
- **RETRACTED — item 908's "fuse `checkLinearScope` into `compileLinear`" (item 917).** The two
  traversals are not of the CLAUSE LIST: `checkExprScope` fully traverses every expression tree and
  `compileExpr` traverses the same trees again. Merging the two clause loops saves ~nothing (the
  list is 2-4 items). Saving the 15-19% means threading scope validation INTO `compileExpr` — **66
  call sites across three files, a 29-arm switch, and callers (the detectors, `hop-projection`) that
  have no scope in hand** — coupling validation to compilation for a win that only appears on a
  parse+plan cache MISS and is at most ~1.4 us. Not worth it.
- **RETRACTED — item 910's "the rewrite pipeline is ten walks over one clause list" (item 917).**
  Ten walks of a 2-item array is nanoseconds, so its 1.259 us (16%) is what each transformation DOES
  when it inspects the patterns and projections, not the walking. Fusing the walks would save the
  walking, which is not the cost.
- **METHOD — "N walks over a small list" is only a target when N × the list length is LARGE (item
  917).** I described items 908, 909 and 910 as one family with one fix. **Only 909 was actually
  that**, and it is the one that shipped — what it removed was a `Set` COPY whose cost scales with
  SCOPE SIZE (1.48x at 48 clauses). The other two look identical and are not: their cost is per-item
  work inside the walk, and the list is 2 items long. Third target retracted after naming it this
  window (912 was the detectors), all three failing the same way — **a block- or shape-level
  description invited a structural fix, and pricing what the fix would actually REMOVE showed the
  time was elsewhere.**
- **DEPRIORITIZED with FOUR dead ends recorded — the clause-vs-inline PLANNING gap (item 918).**
  Item 905's +1.634 us (inline `WHERE` → clause `WHERE`) is in **none** of the four places I
  measured: `checkLinearScope` **+0.007**, `directEqProps` **+0.080**, the seed-hint block
  (`collectHints`/`attach`/`pinFor`, gated on exactly `clause.where`) **0.000** — it reads 0.027 for
  every spelling including the control, i.e. two `performance.now()` calls and no work — and
  `pushWhereIntoNode` was already refuted at 906 (disabling it is 1.20x WORSE). ~~**~95% of the gap
  is unlocated.**~~ **SUPERSEDED by item 919**, which located 73% of it with a CPU profile on the
  very next tick. The four dead ends above still stand as dead ends; the "unlocated" verdict does
  not.
- **METHOD — targeted timers can only confirm the site you guessed; use a PROFILER when the site is
  unknown (item 918).** Four hypotheses on one gap, four refutations, each a plausible mechanism in
  real code. Across this window: 900-902 were three wrong attributions of one null, and 912/917
  retracted named targets. **Finding _a_ mechanism is easy and finding _the_ one is not** — and hand-
  placed instrumentation cannot tell you about a site you did not suspect. The next attempt on this
  gap should start from a CPU profile, and must not re-walk the four dead ends above.
- **AND THE SIZE ARGUES THE SAME WAY (item 918).** ~1.5 us on a parse+plan cache MISS only; repeated
  query text pays it once. Real (item 883: dynamically-built text misses every time) but narrow, and
  three targets of this size have now been retracted for costing more to chase than they return.
- **SHIPPED — `hasSubquery` was walking every conjunct TWICE, and a CPU profile found it in one run
  (item 919). 1.22x on a one-conjunct clause `WHERE`, 1.31x on two**, measured as the over-control
  delta (end to end: 4.511 -> 4.209 us and 5.821 -> 5.253). Three sites, all the same defect: two
  partitions built with complementary `filter`s (`conjuncts.filter((c) => !hasSubquery(c))` then
  `conjuncts.filter(hasSubquery)`, in `pushWhereIntoNode` and in `gatePredicate`) and one
  `hasSubqueryExpr(where)` computed twice inside `nodeWhereOf`. `hasSubquery` is a GENERIC
  structural walk, so each duplicate walked a whole AST fragment for nothing. Fix is a single-pass
  partition and a hoisted `const` — strictly less work, no new route, no data structure. Two
  conjuncts gaining more than one is the predicted shape, since the saving is one walk per conjunct.
  Both controls flat or moving AGAINST the change.
- **METHOD — "where does the time go" and "does it go HERE" are different questions with different
  instruments (item 919, confirming 918).** The profiler's top frame was in NONE of 918's four
  hypotheses, and no further hand-placed timer could have reached it. 918 called this correctly
  before paying for a fifth guess; the four refutations were the cost of not calling it sooner.
- **METHOD — deprioritizing a TARGET is not deprioritizing the DIAGNOSIS (item 919).** 918 was right
  that the gap is small (~1.5 us, cache MISS only) and right to stop chasing it. But once LOCATED,
  73% of it cost three mechanical edits to remove. Price the diagnosis separately from the fix: a
  cheap diagnosis on a small target can still be worth it.
- **METHOD — an unexpected mutation survivor is a hypothesis about the MUTANT, and diagnosing it
  beats filing it (item 919).** Predicted two of three mutants caught; got one. Both survivors were
  answer-equivalent rather than coverage holes: swapping `pushWhereIntoNode`'s partition passed
  `subquery-conjunct-split.test.ts`, whose oracle (a FAULTING subquery body raises iff it was
  evaluated) is the strongest available — `gatePredicate` re-gates downstream, so that site's
  partition direction is a PERF choice, which is why the same swap IN `gatePredicate` fails 7 tests.
- **CORRECTED A COMMENT that claimed correctness (item 919).** `nodeWhereOf`'s free-variable loop was
  described as "the proof the argument requires". Inverting it survived the suite, and a direct probe
  of the shape it exists to decline (a node projection whose clause `WHERE` reads an OUTER variable,
  across `=`, `>`, `<>`) returned identical rows. Same mechanism item 128 recorded for this guard's
  TWIN: a node predicate evaluates against the INCOMING binding, so an outer reference resolves in
  the pattern as it did in the clause filter. KEPT on 128's rule, but it is a route gate and must not
  be cited as load-bearing for correctness.
- **HARNESS — `>>` FAILS on a path that does not exist yet (item 919).** This shell has `noclobber`
  with `APPEND_CREATE` unset, so CLAUDE.md's "`>>` (append) is fine" holds only for an EXISTING file —
  and it conflicts with the same file's "never reuse a scratch filename", since a unique name is by
  construction a path that does not exist. An A/B loop logged nothing for four arms and still printed
  `--- ALL DONE ---`: the write fails, the next statement runs anyway, and the failure surfaces as an
  empty result. `touch` first, then assert the log is NON-EMPTY before trusting any run that wrote to
  it.
- **SHIPPED — the single `delete_node` threw away a position it had already computed (item 920).
  11.9x at 5,000 nodes to 21.7x at 200,000** (75.03 → 3.45 µs). Closes item 370's open entry, the
  oldest unclaimed perf item in section 5. `delete_nodes`' targeted arm guarded each bucket with
  `ids.iter().any(|id| bucket.binary_search(id).is_ok())` and then `retain`ed the bucket it hit —
  discarding the index the guard had just found and rescanning every entry with a closure call and a
  SCATTERED `deleted[x]` probe, where the removal needs one contiguous memmove. Item 663 earned the
  bucket-SKIPPING; the bucket the victim is in never stopped paying a full scan. **Remedy was already
  in the same file**: item 715 made exactly this `retain` → `position`+`remove` trade on the
  adjacency path. `remove` keeps the sort order, so this is not 715's refuted `swap_remove`.
  Control = sweeps A-D (the batch path, unreachable): all 13 rows 0.967-1.000x.
- **METHOD — `CLOSED.md` before pricing saved three ticks, exactly as advertised (item 920).**
  CLAUDE.md presents the never-re-armed CSR as the headline Rust defect at 24.07x; items 851 and 852
  had already priced it, excluded lazy-on-read STRUCTURALLY and refused rebuild-at-commit at a 6-27
  read break-even. The Gremlin dedup gap (853, up to 37.9x) closed at 854/855/857. Two of the three
  biggest-looking numbers in the docs were already dead.
- **METHOD — a "control" whose own bucket is still rewritten is NOT a control (item 920).** Sweep E's
  small-label arm has the BIG bucket skipped, so it looked independent; its own 200-entry bucket is
  rewritten by the same code, and it moved 0.13 → 0.10 µs. It is a SMALL-BUCKET arm — it pins the cost
  to bucket size and establishes nothing about reachability. Second instance this window of
  mislabelling a reachable arm as a control; the test is what the arm EXECUTES, not what it looks
  like it isolates.
- **METHOD — a wrong mutation prediction is evidence either way, and the exactly-once anchor guard
  earns its keep (item 920).** Predicted the duplicate-id mutant would SURVIVE; it was CAUGHT, so the
  suite has more teeth than modelled and no test was needed. Separately, the `swap_remove` mutant's
  first anchor (`bucket.remove(pos);`) also matched `apply_remove_label`, appeared TWICE, and the
  guard refused to apply it — printing VOID rather than a verdict. Without that guard it would have
  been skipped and read as a survivor of a suite that never saw it. Re-anchored, it fails 7 tests
  including four `rewrite_fuzz` ones.
- **REFUTED and ~~DECLINED~~ — `compareCodePoints`' surrogate guard (item 921).** THE REGEX ARMS
  STAND, and item 1711 reconfirmed them from the other side: in its FLOOR arms a NUMERIC column,
  which reaches no regex at all, moved 1.25x against the string column's 1.23x — so the dispatch
  chain is the cost and the regex is a small part of it. But the ~1.07x CEILING below bounds
  only the shape it was measured on — `sortedpage`, `LIMIT 10`, the HEAP path, which never calls
  `rows.sort`. On a full sort item 1711 measured **1.44-1.46x** by eliminating the whole dispatch
  chain rather than the guard. It scans BOTH WHOLE
  STRINGS with a regex on EVERY comparison (6.9% of a sorted-page profile, with the function another
  8.0%), re-establishing a per-string fact O(log N) times in a sort. Three arms: replacing the regex
  with a manual charCode loop is **1.08x on ASCII and 3.6x WORSE on long shared prefixes** (V8's
  character-class match beats a hand loop — the regex is the right tool); deciding from the first
  differing code UNIT is **wrong**, premise and all; hoisting the guard out of the comparator is
  SOUND but can only remove the regex, **~1.07x** on that shape at best, for an invasive change to a
  value-generic comparator. All three recorded above the function.
- **METHOD — a correctness corpus that does not CONSTRUCT the dangerous case will agree with
  anything (item 921).** The first-differing-unit arm had a narrow bug the corpus caught; after
  fixing it the corpus reported **ALL AGREE over 676 pairs**, and the arm was still unsound. Its real
  defect needs the SAME high surrogate PAIRED in one string and LONE in the other (segmentation
  depends on the FOLLOWING unit, so equal unit prefixes do not imply equal code-point prefixes) — and
  the corpus used 0xD800 for lone surrogates and 0xD83D for its astral char, so the two never met.
  One added string produced 6 mismatches. Same discipline as verifying a fuzzer's teeth by mutation,
  applied to a hand corpus; the stakes were a wrong sort order behind a hard byte-identity invariant.
- **THE TS RUNTIME PATH HAS NO UNPRICED HOT CODE ABOVE 2% — measured, five query shapes (item 921) — BUT NONE OF THE FIVE WAS AN UNLIMITED `ORDER BY`: the only sorted shape, `sortedpage`,
  takes the HEAP path, so the full sort's comparator share went unpriced until item 1711. (item
  921).** New `runtime-profile-probe.mjs` + `runtime-profile-analyze.mjs` profile one shape per
  process and cross-check every frame name against THIS file and the audit. Across `control`,
  `point`, `hopfilter`, `sortedpage` and `grouped`, every hot frame carries mentions (`satisfies`
  127, `propOf` 46, `structuralEq` 36, `inlineHolds` 26, `less` 569, `compareSort` 16). **The next TS
  win is unlikely to come from profiling the runtime path**, which is worth knowing before spending a
  tick there.
- **METHOD — a frame's NAME is not its code, and a screen that confuses the two manufactures targets
  (item 921).** The screen's largest "find" was `variable.variable` at 22.8% of the hop-filter
  profile with ZERO mentions. It is the anonymous closure `(env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable),
key)`: V8 synthesises names for arrows from the binding they were assigned through, so no document
  can ever mention one, and that path is items 216/224/230's territory. Synthetic names, `RegExp:`
  frames and Node loader frames now report `n/a`. **The screen's most confident output was the one to
  distrust.**
- **A lone surrogate is not valid UTF-8 and does not survive a source file (item 921).** A literal
  surrogate pair written into a probe was silently normalised into one real character, quietly
  removing the case it was added to test. Build them with `fromCharCode`.
- **SHIPPED — a `SET` paid for every index in the store, including ones on UNRELATED keys (item
  922). 1.61x at 64 indexes, 1.14x at 16, PARITY below the threshold.** `apply_set_prop` asks
  `index_on_base(key) || is_range_indexed(key)` before every write, and both were linear scans with
  a string compare per entry (~0.32 ns per index: 22.6 ns at 0 indexes rising to 43.1 at 64). Now
  derived `FnvSet`s, read only above `INDEX_SET_MIN = 12`. CONTROL `add_edge` — which never reaches
  `apply_set_prop` — flat at 0.99-1.01x across the sweep; `SET` on an INDEXED key unchanged (its
  cost is bucket maintenance).
- **WHY NOTHING SAW IT, and it is this file's own rule (item 922).** With zero indexes both scans are
  an empty-iterator check and cost nothing, and **no fixture in the corpus varies the index count** —
  `bench:usage` and `bench_all`'s write rows build a store with none or one. `is_range_indexed` and
  `index_on_base` had ZERO mentions in this file and the audit. New `setindexcount_922` varies it.
- **METHOD — a lever refuted in ONE engine for an engine-SPECIFIC reason may be live in the other
  (item 922).** `Graph.ts`'s `deIndexVertexLabel` records collapsing `has`-then-`get` as REFUTED in
  TS and gives the mechanism: "JSC appears to cache the key's hash, making a `get` right after a
  `has` on the same key nearly free." Rust's `HashMap` caches nothing between calls. The note reads
  like a general refutation and is not one; porting the SCAN rather than the CONCLUSION found this.
- **THE FIRST VERSION WAS A REGRESSION AND THE THRESHOLD IS THE FIX (item 922).** Unconditional sets
  measured **0.85x at one index and 0.88x at four** — the common case — against 1.64x at 64, because
  the set is a flat ~27 ns `String` hash and the scan is ~0.32 ns per index, so they cross near
  twelve. An `is_empty()` bail protects the ZERO case only; at one index the hash is paid in full.
  Gated on `INDEX_SET_MIN = 12`, same shape as `TARGETED_MAX` in `delete_nodes`. **Measure the cheap
  end of a sweep, not just the end the change was aimed at.**
- **METHOD — a `debug_assert` is NOT a guard in this repo (item 922).** The project's test command is
  `cargo test --release`, where `debug_assertions` is OFF, so an invariant asserted only that way
  never runs and would be cited as protection it does not give. The invariant needs a real `#[test]`;
  the `debug_assert` is a bonus for debug builds.
- **METHOD — a threshold can hollow out the test that guards it (item 922).** Gating the readers on
  `INDEX_SET_MIN` meant the invariant test, which built four indexes, exercised only the SCAN path —
  a stale set would have been invisible to it while still being read in production above twelve. The
  test now builds 24 indexes and **asserts it crosses the threshold**, so the fixture cannot drift
  back under it. Same question as "verify the planner reaches the shape", asked of a test.
- **⚠️ OPEN, found incidentally at 922 — a transaction-created RANGE index SURVIVES rollback.**
  `SchemaSnapshot` carries `index_paths`, `interval_keys` and `edge_type_index` but **nothing for
  range indexes**, so `restore_schema` reverts a tx-created HASH index and leaves a tx-created RANGE
  index in place. Pre-existing (the field has never existed) and unrecorded in either store. Not
  fixed at 922 — reverting them is a semantics change needing its own decision, not a rider on a perf
  commit. `derived_index_key_sets_agree_with_the_vectors_at_every_mutation_site` PINS the current
  behaviour and names the line to flip.
- **SHIPPED — a single delete searched EVERY label bucket to rediscover what it had just thrown
  away (item 923). 50.25x at 1000 labels, 7.89x at 100, 1.50x at 10, parity at 1.** `delete_nodes`'
  targeted arm looped `self.by_label.values_mut()` doing a `binary_search` per bucket, while
  `node_labels[id]` — the forward map that answers exactly that — is CLEARED one block above the
  branch (item 724 moved the clear there because the targeted path returns early). Item 663 earned
  skipping the REWRITE of unrelated buckets; the loop still VISITED them all. Now the victims' label
  ids are captured before the clear, on the stack, gated on `LABEL_CAPTURE_MIN = 4`. CONTROL
  `add_edge` flat at 0.08 µs across the whole sweep.
- **THE BEFORE CURVE IS NON-MONOTONIC, and a shorter sweep would have missed this entirely (item
  923).** 0.43 / 0.18 / 0.71 / 4.02 µs at 1 / 10 / 100 / 1000 labels: item 920's memmove runs over a
  bucket of N/L and FALLS as labels rise, while the bucket loop runs over L and RISES, so the minimum
  sits near ten. A sweep stopping at 10 labels concludes there is nothing here.
- **THE CHEAP END AGAIN, and the first fix was wrong about the cause (item 923).** The capture is a
  fixed ~10-20 ns, so sweep E — every node carrying the SAME single label, where before and after
  visit the identical bucket — read 0.94-0.98x, consistently slower. Skipping the `sort_unstable` and
  dedup for a single-label victim did NOT move it (0.94-0.99x), so the sort was never the cost; the
  capture loop was. Gated on `LABEL_CAPTURE_MIN = 4` and sweep E is back to 1.00-1.02x. **Third
  instance of this shape in `store.rs`** after `TARGETED_MAX` and `INDEX_SET_MIN`: a guard that pays
  only past a size gets gated on that size, and the end of the sweep the change was NOT aimed at is
  where you find out.
- **🛑 METHOD — ADDING A SIZE GATE CAN HIDE THE CODE IT GUARDS FROM THE SUITE, AND ONLY MUTATION
  FOUND IT (item 923).** Before `LABEL_CAPTURE_MIN`, two wrong-answer mutants on the capture logic
  were caught (2 and 14 failures). After it, **BOTH SURVIVED all 1,247 tests** — every pre-existing
  delete test uses three labels or fewer, so the gate made the capture path unreachable from any test
  while it still ran in production above four labels. Item 922 hit the same hazard one item earlier
  and reasoning caught it there; here it did not. **Re-run the mutants AFTER adding a size gate, not
  before** — the gate changes which code the suite reaches, so an earlier verdict is a verdict about
  different code. Closed by `single_deletes_above_the_label_threshold_keep_every_bucket_exact`, which
  uses six labels, asserts it CROSSES the threshold so the fixture cannot drift back under, and
  derives every expected bucket from the surviving set.
- **And the CONTROL mutant is what licenses the other verdicts (item 923).** Forcing the old full
  sweep is answer-equivalent and SURVIVED; had the new test flagged it, the test would be keying on
  which path ran rather than on correctness. Also recorded: the forced-zero mutant fell from 14
  failures to 4 once the single-label fast path landed, because the line it mutates now sits behind
  `n_lids > 1` — its REACH shrank with the change, so the other mutant carries the general case.
- **NO REGRESSION from 919/920/922/923 anywhere in the Rust corpus (item 924).** `bench_all` BASE vs
  HEAD, order-alternated, 322 row-columns: the largest excess over a row's OWN same-binary variance
  is **1.10x**, in no direction and no cluster. The one row the Rust changes reach,
  `storage/write (bulk SET throughput)`, is **0.99x — parity**, as item 922 predicts on a zero-index
  fixture. The TS arm is clean on the same standard — 57 paired rows, self-variance median 1.074x,
  largest excess 1.08x. BASE was verified byte-identical to `90ed30e7` for all three changed files
  before it was trusted as a baseline.
- **🛑 METHOD — A SWEEP'S OWN TWO-RUN SPREAD IS THE ONLY THRESHOLD WORTH USING, and a hand-picked
  band manufactures findings (item 924).** A ±10% band over ONE round reported `query/perrow element
p` at **1.54x FASTER** and `query/shortest repeat-group unread` at **0.81x slower**. Both are
  noise: that per-row row moves **1.48x between two runs of the same binary**, so its excess is 1.04.
  The claim would have been a 1.5x win on per-row projection from a DELETE-PATH change that cannot
  reach per-row projection. An alternated sweep already contains the null control needed to refute
  this — HEAD, BASE, BASE, HEAD gives two readings per arm per row — so compute `self` before
  reading `cross`. Same family as items 737 and 747.
- **Twelve rows cannot support a perf claim at all, and that is now written down (item 924).**
  Self-variance ≥1.5x with cross ≈ 1.00: `algo/parallel`'s pagerank and betweenness speedup columns
  swing **8x** run to run, `ingest/phases` 4x, `query/gremlin dedup out.out` 2.07x. They are a smoke
  test that the path still runs, not a measurement. Check a row's self-variance before reading any
  movement in it.
- **A BENCHMARK THAT CACHES WHAT YOU CHANGED CANNOT MEASURE YOUR CHANGE — checked, not assumed (item
  924).** `bun run bench`'s query rows call `e.query(g, '<literal text>')` with the SAME text every
  rep, and the engine has both a `parseCache` and a `planCache` (228/229), so only the first rep pays
  compile against hundreds of ms of execution. Item 919 changed the compile MISS path, so the TS
  sweep is blind to it in both directions and is only a coarse "nothing else moved" check. 919's real
  instrument is `compile-spelling-probe.ts`, which plans from FRESH ASTs so no cache can serve them.
  **A clean sweep over a blind instrument reads exactly like evidence and is not.**
- **METHOD — a comparator that matches nothing must FAIL, not report success (item 924).** The sweep
  comparator required a `=== section ===` header before recording a row; the TS bench prints a flat
  table, so it would have compared **zero rows and printed a clean result**. Fixed to default the
  section AND to exit non-zero on zero comparisons. The dangerous form of a broken check is not the
  one that crashes — it is the one that returns the reassuring answer, which is also how the
  `noclobber` append and the stale mutation anchors failed this session.
- **ITEM 818 NARROWED, two of three mechanisms dead (item 925).** Its recorded hypothesis was that
  uncompacted per-node growth makes the SEEK path slower — _"whatever grows, the seek path touches it
  and the tiny-bucket scan does not."_ **REFUTED:** with the live set pinned at 20,000 and only the
  churn varied, the indexed seek is **FLAT across 1,000,000 create-and-delete pairs** (67.2 → 67.2 ns
  round one, 70.2 → 69.7 round two) and the unindexed CONTROL is flat too (4.2-4.4 ns). The index is
  innocent at the store level.
- **And what DOES move is BOUNDED (item 925).** `add_node` and `delete_node` step ~1.4x between
  100,000 and 300,000 churn and then come back DOWN at 1,000,000 — reproducibly, in both rounds. A
  monotonic leak keeps climbing; a peak that recedes is a capacity effect (per-node columns crossing
  a `Vec` doubling). So the write primitives do NOT degrade without bound, which is what 818's "a
  rate that falls as the batch lengthens is accumulating state" would need. What remains of 818 is a
  `bench:usage` reading whose own caveat says a single-budget write-heavy row is not steady state,
  plus item 915's finding that its "best recorded" is not a baseline.
- **`churn_925` is kept, because the corpus had no probe on this axis (item 925).** Every other
  fixture varies graph SIZE; this one varies **ids ever created** with the live set pinned. Item 820
  measured the same axis with a temporary probe, so its finding had to be rediscovered from a source
  comment. Keep its CONTROL column — the unindexed scan is what makes "the index is innocent" a
  measurement rather than an assertion.
- **STALE HEADER FIXED — item 798 was marked ⚠️ OPEN and item 799 had already closed it** (1.73x /
  2.11x, param now costing what its literal costs). Same class as the five item 913 corrected; a
  list that says OPEN about settled work is the failure it exists to prevent.
- **ITEM 798'S DECOMPOSITION RE-PRICED AND IT IS STALE IN BOTH HALVES (item 926).** It recorded
  "~18-20 ns is per-VERTEX scaffolding and 2-4 ns is the predicate". At HEAD the FLOOR (`WHERE true`)
  is **9.16 ns a vertex** — tight at 1.03x over three alternated rounds — and the predicate adds
  **4.2-10.6**. Totals moved with it: inline 19.7 → 13.40, `=` 22.0 → 15.34, `> $a` 45.4 → 19.76.
  Three changes landed after 798 was measured (799's compile-time param gate, 803's dropped binding
  write, 835's direct-read projection), which is why item 261's rule exists. **So item 801's "its own
  tick" lever on the ~2.1x cross-surface gap is about HALF the size the list carries** — price
  against 9.16, not 18-20.
- **Item 799's param parity CONFIRMED at HEAD, and my first comparison was wrong (item 926).** `> $a`
  (19.76) against `= 28` (15.34) looks like a 1.29x param residual; it is not. The arms differed in
  OPERATOR and in SELECTIVITY (135,542 rows against 2,222). The matched pair — same operator, same
  bound, identical answers — reads **0.98x** (literal 18.95, param 18.64, readings interleaved).
  `predicate-scaffold-probe.ts` asserts both arms answer identically before printing a ratio, for
  exactly this reason.
- **And `WHERE true` IS a valid floor, verified not folded (item 926).** The worry is that a
  constant-true predicate gets optimized away, leaving a bare scan. It is not: `WHERE true` reads
  9.16 ns/vertex where `count(*)` with no predicate reads 0.01, and a folded predicate would collapse
  to the same O(1) bucket count. (`alwaysTrue` in `shortcuts.ts` is the unfiltered-HOP
  representation, not a folder for this.) Checked rather than inherited from item 570 — and note
  798's 18-20 and this 9.16 are the same quantity in intent but not the same measurement, so the
  TOTALS are the result and the floor is its decomposition.
- **`count(*)` with no predicate is NOT a floor — it is O(1) (item 926).** Answered from the label

  BIDIRECTIONAL (item 932).** `@lenke/gremlin` and `@lenke/gql` are sibling packages — neither
  depends on the other, there is no shared plan module, and each hand-builds its own fast-path table
  (`countShortcut`'s rungs against `shortcuts.ts`'s `tallyHopCount` family). The native engine lowers
  both surfaces to one `ir::Plan` and `spelling_probe` checks the canonicalized plans agree, which is
  **why every cross-surface item in this audit (797, 801, 929, 930, 932) is TS-only.** The matrix
  shows the drift running both ways: Gremlin wins all nine one-sided cells (up to 3.12x at `node:1`)
  and GQL wins all three `both` cells (up to 1.85x), with the margin narrowing as arity rises on one
  side (`post` 2.09x → 1.18x → 1.19x). **A uniformly worse lowering would lose everywhere** — two
  tables with different coverage is what produces a winner that flips with position and arity. So:
  do not reason about a TS cross-surface gap as "one surface is lowered badly"; find which table is
  missing the rung. Giving TS a shared plan is the structural fix and is effectively re-writing the
  Rust architecture in TypeScript; `bun run probe:arity` is the cheap alternative that PRICES that
  decision, which is why it is generated rather than hand-written like `probe:surface`'s 5 pairs.

  neither the answer (a degree sum) nor which far vertices are evaluated (the `deg === 0` skip keeps

  is WHICH fault escapes first, since the walks reach far vertices in different orders. **This bites
  GQL and not Gremlin, and item 930 is why: Gremlin's `matches` CANNOT throw** (every ordering
  predicate filters an incomparable value out via a `NaN` from `predCmp`), so its rung gets raise

  a coincidental mention of the number, one matched a line that is itself an OPEN bullet. The
  sharpest is item **910**: a later line reads "RETRACTED — item 910's '19 detectors are 25% of
  planning' target", but 910's own bullet claims something else (the rewrite pipeline at 16%), so
  **910 STAYS OPEN** and striking it would have been a worse error than the lag. An item can have
  one claim retracted and another still live.
- **MEASURED — a cold small query is 94-97% PLANNING, and ~25x its warm twin (item 942).** This is
  the denominator the whole planning-cost family (items 887, 905, 908, 910, 912) was priced
  without: those items give shares OF PLANNING, and for the serving shape planning is essentially
  the whole of a cold query. Indexed point lookup, WARM (one text, both caches hit) against COLD
  (textually distinct, identical work and answer, texts pre-built so string construction is outside
  the timed region), 3 alternated rounds: warm **0.79 / 1.39 / 1.28 us**, cold **25.32 / 25.75 /
  22.90**, planning **23.93 / 24.96 / 21.62** = **94.5 / 96.9 / 94.4%**. Execution is ~1 us; getting
  to it costs ~24. The same pair over a 50,000-vertex SCAN: warm ~806 us, cold ~850, planning ~45 us
  = **5.4%**, noise against the scan. **So the question for every item in that family is not "what
  share of planning" but "how many of this workload's queries MISS the cache".**
- **RETRACTED on cost/benefit — item 910's rewrite-pipeline target (item 942).** 1.259 us is **~5%
  of a cold** indexed point lookup, **0% of a warm one** (the plan cache removes it entirely) and
  0.15% of a scan. The fusion must preserve a documented composition order — `inlineAggregateCall`
  runs INSIDE `inlineTrailingLet` so the `LET` it produces is itself inlined, _"which the current
  nesting expresses structurally"_, 910's own words — and trading a structurally-expressed
  invariant for 5% of cold queries is a poor deal whose failure mode is a WRONG plan, not a slow
  one. Same call item 878 made about 877.

  lookup's compile is smaller still, so the bulk of the cold cost sits outside the part items

  costs, so this is a direction to measure and not a finding.
- **METHOD — an impossible number is the cheapest check there is (item 942).** The probe printed
  item 910's share of a cold query as **4972%**: `out.cold` was in milliseconds and 1.259 in
  microseconds, so the ratio was off by 1000 and the real figure is 4.97%. The catch was not rigour
  but implausibility — a share over 100% cannot be right. Worth stating because the numbers that are
  merely WRONG rather than impossible are the ones this session has had to retract four times; where
  a quantity has a natural bound, print it in a form that violates the bound when the arithmetic
  is wrong.
- **MEASURED — a cold small query is parse 27-31%, COMPILE 56-69%, run ~5% (item 943).** One arm
  per process, 3 alternated rounds, indexed point lookup: parse **8.2-9.2 us**, compile **17-21**,
  run **~1.5**, whole **~30**. Sum check (parts against the whole) 1.05x / 0.88x / 0.91x, all inside
  the 0.85-1.15 band, so the split is reportable. **Item 942's own guess — "most of the ~24 us is
  probably PARSE" — is REFUTED**: parse is real but not the bulk, so item 887 is NOT where the
  cold-query cost lives, and items 908/910/912 were aimed at the right phase. Being wrong cost one
  probe because 942 recorded it as a direction to measure rather than a finding.
- **RULE — item 762's "one shape per PROCESS" generalises to any arm-to-arm SHARED STATE, not just
  the JIT (item 943).** The first attempt timed all four phases in one process and its SUM CHECK
  rejected it: parts/whole **1.38x, 0.56x, 1.37x** across three alternated rounds. The cause is
  CACHE POLLUTION — this path carries a parse cache and a plan cache, `query()` fills both with the
  very texts the other arms use, so whichever arm ran first paid the cold cost and warmed the rest.
  Reversing the order flipped the answer (the 0.56x round is the one where `query()` ran first and
  left `execute` nothing to compile). 762 was written about megamorphic dispatch sites; the fix is
  identical for an engine-internal cache — re-exec per arm so every arm starts empty.
- **RULE — a decomposition needs a SUM CHECK, and it must refuse to print when it fails
  (item 943).** "Do the parts add to the whole?" caught the cache pollution above before any number
  was believed. Item 937's invalid split is precisely what happens without one: it compared two
  different walks in two different units and had no way to notice. Cheap to add, and it is the only
  check that tests the decomposition itself rather than its inputs.
- **⚠️ NARROWED AT ITEM 944 (two of three candidates eliminated: not size, not bookkeeping) — item 943's 17-21 us compile against item 912's 7.703 us

  looked close enough to explain away.

  AND A CONFORMANCE CONVERGENCE together (item 945).** `compile` runs
  `checkLinearScope(part.clauses, new Set())` over every part BEFORE `compileLinear`, so TS always
  reports a SCOPE fault where a query has both a scope error and an unknown function, while
  **native reports whichever comes FIRST IN THE TEXT** (item 916, pinned in
  `fault-precedence.test.ts`). Fusing the walks saves **15-19% of planning** AND moves TS toward
  native's written-order behaviour, closing part of that divergence. `fault-precedence.test.ts`
  exists to make the change detectable and its header calls it _"a decision to take deliberately
  rather than discover"_. **Both halves are small** — the perf half is a share of a cost that is
  zero on a warm workload — which is exactly why it should be chosen rather than slipped in as a
  side effect of an optimization.
- **METHOD — a line that keeps generating its own next step needs a CEILING CHECK FROM OUTSIDE IT
  (item 945).** Items 936-944 are nine consecutive items with no engine change. Each ended by
  naming a next step inside the same line, and each next step was individually reasonable; what was
  missing was anyone asking what the line's best possible outcome was worth. The check is cheap —
  "if this entirely succeeded, what would it buy?" — and item 942 could have asked it four items
  earlier. **Nine ticks is too many to spend without shipping**, and that is the lesson rather than
  any of the measurements.

- **⚠️ OPEN, better motivated than item 961 had it (item 962).** Routing a one-column `RETURN
DISTINCT` to `DistinctBy` does not merely sidestep a missing fast path — it lands on a path that
  is **already good** (19 us against 293). Teaching `try_distinct_scan_prop` to see through a
  `Filter` fixes one shape; routing to `DistinctBy` fixes every shape whose fast path declines.
  **NEW precondition**: `Distinct`'s fast path at 164 us fuses scan and dedup, so routing
  UNCONDITIONALLY to `DistinctBy` could lose it where it currently fires. The route must be _when
  the fast path declines_ — which the optimizer cannot know without knowing what exec will do.
  That is the real design question and the reason this stays a diagnosis.

  as a secondary, which the per-type bucket count omits: unusable, not merely unsafe. The fix
  shape is a per-type count maintained over ALL labels (O(1) on insert/delete). **Check first how
  common multi-label edges are in the intended workload — the whole 1200x is zero without them.**

  its first act is a chain of eleven REWRITES, and **a clause a rewrite DROPS takes its scope
  fault with it.** Measured by disabling the pre-pass and checking the rewritten list:
  `unread LET` and `unread LET, grouped` go from faulting to **NO FAULT**, so
  `MATCH (n:P) LET x = nosuchvar.k RETURN n.k` would silently return rows. That is fault LOSS,
  not fault ORDER, and the approval covers the second.

  the rewrites is SOUND and buys NOTHING — it is still two walks, and the second walk is the
  cost. Making each clause-dropping rewrite check what it discards would work but spreads the
  obligation across eleven rewrites, where a twelfth added later reopens the hole silently. **The
  target is not available at acceptable risk**; 908's disposition should read blocked-on-
  correctness.

  fastest as long as it's reproducible" is satisfied by losing an error reproducibly. The

  minutes. Ask what the code does before asking whether you are allowed to change it.

  Denying the count path denies an O(1) partition-length read, so the query falls to a full walk —
  1200x. Denying the per-type structure on a traversal that walks the adjacency anyway costs only
  bucket-seek against filtered-scan: zero at degree 1, growing with degree and type count. **Same
  code shape, completely different prize** — which is the argument for measuring each site rather
  than sweeping the pattern.

  UNINDEXED zero-match arm (5.6-6.1), and that is NOT seeding** — both scan. It is the predicate:
  `e.amount = 99999` tests a property every edge CARRIES where `e.other = 500` tests an ABSENT one,
  and a null comparison settles sooner. Attributing that 1.6x to the index would have been wrong in
  a way no timing alone reveals.

  cause. 1009's "the fix is a hoist" also falls — hoisting a check that changes nothing changes

- **THE 1008-1010 PATTERN.** 1008 narrowed a guard for 24x; 1009 applied the identical narrowing

## 1062 — ✅ SHIPPED: the deferred-projection arm. 2.0-2.6x, and the spelling probe caught the first cut creating a 3.8x gap

Item 1061's extension, built. `detectNodeProjection` refused a window whenever any projected item
could fault (`outputColumnSorts`'s rule) because it projected every row and sliced, which would
raise on a row the query never emits. `deferredSortedNodeWalk` ranks on the sort keys and projects
the full width for the `cap` survivors only — what the general path does after `aliasDefinition`,
and what native does.

200,000 nodes, one shape per process, median of reps 4+, alternated POST/PRE/POST:

```text
  arith            RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10          33.21 → 16.20   2.05x
  arith-expr       … ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10                      33.61 → 15.81   2.13x
  unprojected-key  … ORDER BY n.s LIMIT 10                          37.45 → 15.01   2.50x
  fn               RETURN upper(n.s) AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10        45.10 → 21.26   2.12x
  mixed            RETURN n.k AS c, n.k + 1 AS d ORDER BY c LIMIT 10 31.42 → 12.13   2.59x
  CONTROL plain    RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10               13.09 → 12.95   1.01x
  CONTROL nolimit  … ORDER BY c  (no window)                         34.10 → 34.19   1.00x
  CONTROL limit0 / unsorted                                          0.00-0.06, flat
```

### 🛑 The first cut created a 3.8x equivalent-spelling gap, and `bun run spelling` caught it

It ranked on OUTPUT COLUMNS (a second ask of `outputColumnSorts`), which requires every key to NAME
a column and substitutes only a `prop` alias. So `ORDER BY c` resolved and `ORDER BY n.k + 1` did
not — **11.30 ms against 43.13 on the `ORDER BY alias vs its expression` group**, where both had been
converged at ~34 before the change. This repo's named defect class, created and caught in one tick.

The fix was not a wider alias match but a different thing to rank on: **compile the key expression
and evaluate it into a synthetic column**. There is then no alias to match, so the asymmetry cannot
exist — and it admits a key that is not projected at all (`ORDER BY n.s`, 2.50x) as a side effect.
After the rework the pair reads 10.30 against 12.08 and the group no longer flags.

### The window rules, each load-bearing for a different reason

- **`limit === undefined` declines.** A `SKIP` with no `LIMIT` is not a top-k: with no cap the
  general path sorts and projects EVERY row and then drops the skipped ones, so
  `RETURN <faulting> AS x, n.n AS t ORDER BY t OFFSET 1` raises on both engines even though the
  window discards the faulting row. **`page-fold-fault.test.ts`'s existing CLAUSE-position control
  caught the first cut admitting this** — item 1056's own test, one item later.
- **`limit === 0` declines, as CORRECTNESS here.** `applyProjection` returns `[]` before ranking or
  projecting anything, so evaluating keys to emit nothing would raise where the query does not. In
  `outputColumnSorts` the same guard is only a speed guard.
- **A key whose free name is also an output name declines.** The sort scope overlays output columns
  on the binding, so that name means the COLUMN; `aliasDefinition` declines for the same reason.
- **A SUBQUERY key declines.** `freePredicateVars` returns the empty set for one and `itemLocal`
  admits one, so neither can be what refuses it. **Mutation found this guard untested** and it got
  a correlated-`COUNT` fixture (out-degrees 2/1/0) before the entry was written.

Teeth: nine mutants, nine caught — `limit0-admitted`, `skip-no-limit-admitted`,
`alias-not-resolved`, `shadow-allowed`, `subquery-key-allowed`, `nonlocal-key-allowed`,
`stale-binding`, `window-dropped`, `desc-dropped`. 30 new tests in
`deferred-sorted-projection.test.ts`, every expected value first confirmed against native (34 arms
across three cross-engine probes, all agreeing).

**🛑 And one process lesson: piping the mutation loop into `head` SIGPIPEs it mid-loop**, so the
final restore never runs and the mutant stays in the tree. The next two readings — a suite at
`2908 pass 2 fail` and a spelling run — were taken against the mutant before `grep` on the live
file found it. Restore-before-each-mutant contained the damage; the lesson is that `| head` on that
loop is the thing that breaks it.

### The deferred arm is a SEPARATE walk, not a branch

The plain arm is byte-for-byte unchanged, for item 1033's measured reason: a branch added to a
sibling hot loop cost three unreachable controls ~2x. The `plain` control reading 1.01x is that
rule being honoured.

**The `plain` control read 0.78x in the first in-sweep pass and that was the mode lottery, not a
regression.** An isolated six-round alternated A/B put PRE at 12.49/10.14/12.85 and POST at
9.87/12.70/12.68 — **both arms produce both modes** (~10 and ~12.7), exactly the bimodality
CLAUDE.md warns of for this family. Min-to-min, POST is ahead.

### ➡️ Open: a PRE-EXISTING divergence this item's deep sweep found

Running `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000` **27 times on the PRE arm** failed twice, with a shape item 1062
cannot reach:

```text
  MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE (n.nu AND (n.x IN ['1e3', ''])))
    RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y
      ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
      native: ok [{"x":3,"y":null}, …]
```

`FUZZ_SEED=3728333688` and `FUZZ_SEED=2059721365` both **replay deterministically on both arms**. It
is the inline-pattern-predicate boolean-context family ([[boolean-context-static-check]]) inside an
`OPTIONAL MATCH`, and the declared `static-bool-check-misses-inline-pattern-predicates` entry does
not cover this shape. **This corrects item 1059's "no backlog of latent divergences"**: one 150,000
run was clean; 27 runs of 120,000 were not. Whether to widen the registry entry or fix the check is
left open — extending the static check to inline pattern predicates has been tried twice and was
worse both times.

## 1063 — ✅ SHIPPED: the HOP rung's deferred order. 2.7-8.9x across all five walk variants, no walk changed

Item 1062's twin, on the rung it recorded as untouched. `hopOrderPlan` refused a window whenever any
projected item could fault; `deferredHopOrder` ranks on the keys and projects only the emitted rows.

```text
  SUBJECTS (50,000 edges, one shape per process, median of reps 4+, POST/PRE/POST)
    directed-arith      RETURN b.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10        49.61 →  12.76   3.89x
    directed-expr-key   … ORDER BY b.k + 1 LIMIT 10                    48.06 →  12.45   3.86x
    filtered-arith      WHERE b.k > 10 …                               57.55 →  14.19   4.06x
    undirected-arith    (a)-[:E]-(b) …                                112.37 →  41.89   2.68x
    relbound-arith      RETURN e.w + 1 AS c …                          60.29 →  13.88   4.34x
    seeded-arith        (a:P {k: 7})-… …                                8.94 →   1.00   8.94x
    fn                  RETURN upper(b.s) AS c …                       62.29 →  13.66   4.56x
    both-ends           RETURN a.k AS x, b.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY x …     44.43 →  12.44   3.57x
  CONTROLS  directed/filtered/undirected/relbound plain, nolimit, plain-hop
                                                                       1.01x 1.00x 1.05x 1.03x
                                                                       0.98x 1.15x
```

### 🔑 NO WALK CHANGED, which is the only reason this was affordable

Item 159 measured that adding even a BRANCH to one of these walks costs the hot shape 1.6x. So the
arm hands the walk a **reduced projection** — one item per sort key, plus one bare `binding.get(v)`
per endpoint the real items read — and re-projects the survivors. Same `projectRow` call, a
two-or-three column row instead of N. Five construction sites take `proj: walkProj`, which IS `proj`
on every other path.

It covers all five variants at once deliberately: **a partial build would make a filtered hop and an
unfiltered one take different routes for one question**, which is item 1062's first-cut defect.

`proj.orderNeedsOutput` is the whole key check — the flag the general path already sets, mirroring
the Rust `order_needs_output` — so there is no alias matching and no AST walking, and the shadowing
hazard is subsumed.

### 🛑 The in-process sweep invented a 1.5x regression on an unreachable control — the THIRD this session

`undirected-plain` read 33.83 → 50.99 in the single-process sweep and **39.91 → 37.90 isolated**. Its
route does not change and `walkProj` is `proj` on that path. Same shape as items 1034 and 1038. The
giveaway each time: the arm that "regressed" is one the change cannot execute for.

### Teeth, and two mutants that survived first

Nine mutants, all caught. `order-needs-output-admitted` and `far-driven-allowed` SURVIVED the first
run and both were untested, not redundant (item 475's rule):

- A key reading an OUTPUT column needed a case — `RETURN b.k AS b, b.k + 1 AS d ORDER BY d`, where
  `d` reads `b`, itself an output name.
- `startDriven: true` needed a fixture whose TIES discriminate between the walk orders: three starts
  wired `s0 → f0,f3,f6` etc. with all nine far vertices tying. Start-driven gives `51,54,57,52,…`,
  far-driven `51,52,53,…`, and **native gives the start-driven order** — item 605's rule holding on a
  shape nobody had measured.

33 tests, every value confirmed against native first (24 cross-engine arms).

**🛑 And the fixture caught itself twice**, the fourth and fifth instances of the session's rule: a
`{t: 1}` inline against a string property returned `[]` and printed AGREE, and two faulting vertices
at opposite ends of the key order made every window include one — so every faulting case raised and
none proved deferral.

### The spelling probe gained the pair, and rejected a group that was not one

`hop ORDER BY alias vs its expression, windowed` and its FILTERED twin are now in `bun run spelling`.
A first attempt also grouped the walk VARIANTS together and the probe correctly reported
`ANSWERS DIFFER` — a filtered hop and an unfiltered one are not two spellings of one question. That
comparison lives in `defer-hop-probe.ts`, against each variant's own plain twin.

## 1064 — ✅ SHIPPED: select the top `cap` during the scan. 2.7x, and `boundedTopKeyed` de-boxed for both its callers

### ❌ NOT A RUST TARGET — the native engine has no cliff on this axis (measured, do not re-derive)

```text
  node plain 1.10 ms / arith 1.29 / expr-key 1.27 / fn 2.83 / nolimit 29.27
  hop  plain 0.88    / arith 0.91 / fn 1.43        / relbound 0.95
```

1.17x between the plain and arithmetic spellings, against TS's 3-4x before items 1062/1063. Native
already keeps the top-k over input bindings and projects only survivors.

### The TS win

`detectNodeProjection` served a windowed sort by projecting a `Row` for every surviving vertex and
letting `sortRowsByColumns` select `cap` — 200,000 row objects to emit ten.

```text
  topk-plain      RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10              13.02 →  4.84   2.69x
  stmt-topk       ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 RETURN n.k AS c            12.76 →  4.75   2.69x
  topk-two-keys   RETURN n.s AS d, n.k AS c ORDER BY d, c LIMIT 10 15.56 →  8.61   1.81x
  stmt-two-keys                                                    18.82 → 17.68   1.06x
  CONTROLS big-cap 1.29x faster, stmt-big-cap 1.24x faster (NOT CLAIMED — bimodality),
           arith 1.05x, fn 1.00x, nolimit 0.98x, unsorted flat
```

4.84 ms is within **1.05x of TS's 4.63 ms scan floor** (`min(n.k)` over the same fixture), so what
remains on this shape is the scan. Native's 1.10 is BELOW that floor — the rest of the gap is the
layout question, not this one.

### ❌ TWO HYPOTHESES REFUTED on the way, both cheap and both worth not re-trying

- **Routing the plain case through item 1062's deferred arm: 14.25, SLOWER than 12.9.** That arm
  allocates a key row per candidate — one object traded for another.
- **A flat key array plus a full index sort: 27.60, much slower.** Avoiding the row object is not
  the win; the O(n log n) is.

### 🔑 The real cost was in the SHARED helper, so both callers gained

`boundedTopKeyed` boxed EVERY candidate: `keysOf: (item) => readonly unknown[]` allocated an array
per candidate and the loop allocated a `Kept` per candidate — `n` allocations to keep `cap`.

- `keyAt: (item, i) => unknown` so a LOSER is compared against the root without being boxed:
  **11.97 → 8.82**.
- An INDEXED loop instead of `sorts.entries()` in that per-candidate comparison (it allocates an
  iterator and a tuple per call, and runs `n` times where `cmp` runs O(cap log cap)):
  **8.82 → 5.26**.

The hand-rolled prototype read 6.65, so the shared helper now BEATS the one-off — the argument for
fixing the helper rather than adding a second heap.

### 🛑 MUTATION CAUGHT A FIXTURE THAT COULD NOT REACH THE CODE — and nothing else could have

The first mutation run had **six survivors**. Cause: `heapBeatsSort` admits the selection only while
`cap * 16 <= rows`, so at 30 vertices a `LIMIT 5` took the sort-and-slice branch and **the heap never
ran**. 23 tests passed and all 20 cross-engine arms agreed. Widening to 320 vertices killed five of
the six.

Sixth such fixture this session, and the first where neither an empty result nor a vacuous answer
gave it away. **New corollary: a route guard whose threshold depends on the INPUT SIZE makes every
small fixture a vacuous one, silently.**

`tiebreak-dropped` survived and is genuinely REDUNDANT (item 475's other horn): candidates arrive in
increasing `at` and every kept item was seen earlier, so a candidate's arrival index is always
greater than the root's. Kept as the statement of intent; the tiebreak is load-bearing in `cmp`,
which orders the kept items.

Both route gates are pure functions with their own unit tests (`topKPlan`, `heapBeatsSort`) —
answer-equivalent choices, so `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`. `key-by-position` is why `topKPlan`'s
tests earn their place: resolving `directKeys` positionally instead of by the key's own column is a
wrong ANSWER whenever the sort order differs from the projection order.

## 1065 — ❌ REFUTED: item 1064's lever does NOT apply to hops. ✅ LOCATED: the hop charges ~250 ns per START VERTEX, even for vertices with no edges

### The refutation, which took one measurement

```text
  hop min(b.k)   scan + one property read, NO rows, NO selection   11.87 ms
  hop top-10                                                       11.91
```

The rows and the selection together cost about **zero** on a 50,000-edge hop, so there is nothing for
item 1064's "select during the scan" to remove. **Do not re-attempt it on the hop rung.**

### What the same measurement located

Two sweeps, each holding a different thing fixed:

```text
  |E| FIXED at 50,000, degree varied (three rounds)
    degree  1   50,000 starts   13.54 / 13.47 / 16.07 ms     4.4x more than degree 2
    degree  2   25,000 starts    3.03 /  3.09 /  3.06
    degree 10    5,000 starts    0.97 /  1.07 /  0.93

  SCAN FIXED at 50,000 vertices and 50,000 edges, only the number of vertices holding adjacency:
    sources 50,000   hop-min 15.67   hop-proj 11.73   hop-top10 10.36   node-min 0.92
    sources 10,000           11.88            12.48             18.17            0.69
    sources  1,000           10.42            13.73             16.98            0.95
```

**Flat in the second sweep.** Not the degree, not the adjacency-map count, not the edge count: about
**210-320 ns per START VERTEX of hop-specific overhead, charged even for the 49,000 vertices with no
matching edge** — against 0.92 ms for the NODE scan over those same 50,000 vertices. All three hop
rungs pay it, so it is in the shared walk.

### ➡️ The fix it names, and the ceiling

`hop count(*)` is **0.00 ms** on every arm, because `tallyHopCount` reads the EDGE-TYPE BUCKET
(item 1035) instead of walking vertices. So one rung already avoids the overhead entirely, which is
what makes an **edge-driven walk for a whole-graph typed hop** the lever: iterate the type bucket and
resolve both endpoints off each edge. `relSeekedHopWalk` (item 1038) is already edge-driven, so the
shape exists in the file.

Priced: **projection 11.73 → 2-3 ms (4-5x)** — it must still build a row per result, ~42 ns each —
and **aggregate 15.67 → under 1 ms (10x+)**, which builds none.

Two constraints, both already written in `hop-projection.ts`: it applies only to UNORDERED shapes
(an edge-driven order differs, and tie order is observable between the engines, item 605 — which is
why a sort forces the start-driven walk), and a START LABEL has to be re-checked per edge, which is
what the far-driven walk's `vacuousLabel` guard already handles.

## 1066 — ✅ SHIPPED: a vacuous far label costs a hop 2.8x. 🛑 And item 1065's attribution was WRONG

### 🛑 Correction to item 1065 — read this before citing it

- It called `min(b.k)` a **row-free floor**. It is not: `detectHopAggregate` delegates to the hop
  PROJECTION walks and folds over `row[VALUE_COL]`, so it materializes a row per edge. What survives
  is the narrow fact the refutation rested on — top-10 11.91, `min` 11.87, all-rows 15.47, within
  noise — so **the SELECTION costs nothing and item 1064's lever still has nothing to remove on a
  hop.** That refutation stands; its explanation does not.
- Its **second sweep held the actual cause constant**: it varied the adjacency distribution while
  keeping the FAR POOL 50,000 wide in every arm. The flatness says "the cost does not depend on the
  adjacency distribution", not "the cost is per start vertex". **I varied two things and credited
  the one I was thinking about.**

### The experiment that actually locates it

50,000 vertices scanned, 50,000 edges, 50,000 rows — identical in every arm. Only the number of
DISTINCT far endpoints varies:

```text
  far pool 50,000   min(b.k) 15.88 ms   min(a.k) LABELLED 20.38   min(a.k) BARE  8.14   rows 10.72
  far pool 10,000             4.25                       10.33                  5.09         3.59
  far pool  1,000             1.33                        7.64                  5.30         1.03
  far pool    100             1.06                        5.90                  5.48         1.48
```

**9.3-15x from nothing but where the edges point.** A hop's cost is DEREFERENCING THE FAR VERTEX and
it scales with how scattered the far set is — cache residency, CLAUDE.md's first rule as the answer
rather than the trap. The walk's own primitives (bucket iteration + `adjFrom.get` + every edge)
cost **0.76-1.36 ms** against the engine's 9.93-13.86, so the deref is not the data structure.

### The fixable part

```text
  start-only-labelled   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P) RETURN min(a.k)   18.06 →  6.46   2.80x
  start-proj-labelled   … RETURN a.k AS c                         17.13 →  6.12   2.80x
  CONTROLS  start-only-bare (the spelling twin) 6.43 → 7.59; start-proj-bare 1.03x;
            far-read 1.04x; far-rows 1.03x; selective-far 1.00x; node-min 1.01x
```

`matchesLabel(far, farLabel)` dereferenced the far vertex to test a label every vertex carries.
Hoisted to `const fl = vacuousLabel(graph, farLabel) ? undefined : farLabel` ONCE PER CALL, in the
inline start-driven walk and `filteredHopWalk`'s general loop — replacing a variable, not adding a
branch (item 159's 1.6x). **The same decision already guarded the DEDUP walk's far resolve**
(`planFor`, items 215/217, where the label test alone measured 189 ns a vertex).

**The result is the CONVERGENCE**: 18.06-vs-6.43 became 6.46-vs-7.59, so the labelled and bare
spellings of one question now cost the same. `selective-far` (a label on a tenth of the vertices)
did not move, which is the control that matters.

Teeth: `always-drop` 4 fail, `vacuous-means-nonempty` 6 fail, `vacuous-off-by-one` 6 fail;
`hoist-only-inline` SURVIVED and is answer-equivalent (it loses speed only), guarded by the probe's
convergence rows. 17 tests built as fixture PAIRS differing in ONE vertex, because `vacuousLabel` is
a size comparison and the boundary is one vertex wide.

### ➡️ NEXT: the same class on the START label is 5783x, and the probe has been printing it

```text
  57.83ms   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
   0.00ms   MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
```

Two spellings of one question where every vertex carries `P`: the unlabelled form takes the O(1)
edge-bucket count, the labelled form walks 200,000 vertices. `shortcuts.ts` already drops vacuous
endpoint labels in the UNDIRECTED hop count; the DIRECTED count does not.

### 🛑 Two corrections before the result

### The win

```text
  start-labelled     (a:P)-[:E]->(b)      25.59 → 14.75   1.74x
  far-labelled       (a)-[:E]->(b:P)      25.76 → 15.88   1.62x
  start-labelled-in  (a:P)<-[:E]-(b)      26.98 → 15.92   1.69x
  far-labelled-in    (a)<-[:E]-(b:P)      26.01 → 15.38   1.69x

            · two-types 1.01x · rows 1.00x
  SPELLING  `label on start: redundant vs absent`  5783x → 1521x
```

A ladder over the walk's loop body located it: `adjFrom.get('E').size` is the irreducible 85 ns a
vertex (against ~9 ns at 50,000 — cache residency, as at item 1066), and the rest is per-vertex call
overhead on a shape that has nothing for it to do. `bareDegreeSum` drops the label re-check (the
bucket guarantees it), the `try`/`catch` (raise parity needs a predicate to protect), the predicate
call (`alwaysTrue`) and `degreeOfTypes`'s loop. Asked at the top of BOTH walks so the two directions
cannot diverge.

### 🛑 The `both-ends` control's 1.08x was an OUTLIER, and my explanation for it was wrong

It read 98.85 before against 106.5 after, which looked exactly like item 119's closure growth, so I
moved the dispatch into the module-scope walks. **That changed nothing** (106.6), and a second PRE
round read 105.56. The move is kept because it is the right shape, not because it fixed anything.

### 🛑 Mutation: 7 of 8 survived first, and the fix was INSTRUMENTATION rather than reasoning

19 tests passed while seven mutants lived. I added a counter to the fast path and printed which
shapes reach it — the "verify the planner reaches the shape" step I had skipped. It showed only the
four bare labelled counts arrive; every "decline" test was refused upstream, so its guard was
masked. Three were answer-equivalent fixtures: every edge had `w: 1`, `WHERE true` is item 570's
control and answer-equivalent by design, and the multi-type edge made the alternation's right answer
equal the naive sum.

Discriminators that replaced them: **`WHERE 1 = 0`** (no free variables, so not refused upstream,
and unlike `WHERE true` it changes the answer), **`[:E|F]` on a fixture with no multi-type edge**
(there the caller admits many types and only the fast path refuses), **`-[:E {w: 2}]->` over
alternating `w`**, and **`(a:P&S)`** (a label expression nothing satisfies, where
`candidateVertexSource` returns every vertex).

Final: 4 caught; 4 survive with each one's masking condition named — `ignores-inline` and
`admits-seek` mask each other through the inline branch's seed hint (the pair is still necessary),
`ignores-rel-inline` never arrives because `startWalkFits` requires `inRel === undefined`, and
`wrong-end-label` makes the path DECLINE rather than answer wrongly.

One `Value` per LABEL ID, built once per call and cloned per row (a relaxed `fetch_add`), through two
new crate-private accessors (`label_ids_of`, `label_names_table`).

```text
  12 (boundary)     227.3    226.5       221.3    223.5   ← in-arm control
```

## 1069 — ✅ SHIPPED (RUST): the EDGE-label hoist, 1.11-1.31x. 🛑 And its FIRST CUT measured SLOWER than the code it replaced

Item 1068's named next step. The edge side paid THREE costs per row where the node side paid one: a
`Vec<&str>` allocated per row by `edge_labels_of_refs`, each type id resolved through
`etype_name_ref` (a LINEAR SCAN of `etype_ids`), and then a byte COPY per name.

### 🛑 The first cut was a regression, and the mechanism is what saved the idea

Written with `chain`/`filter_map`/`collect` over an `Option`:

```text
  T=1 len=6  222.9 → 241.6  0.92x SLOWER     T=1 len=20  236.3 → 242.8  0.97x
  T=8 len=6  219.3 → 240.2  0.91x SLOWER     T=8 len=20  235.5 → 240.6  0.98x
  T=64 len=6 222.4 → 238.3  0.93x SLOWER     T=64 len=20 258.0 → 241.3  1.07x  (only win)
```

Both axes went flat — which is what the hoist is for — and the FLOOR rose from ~220 to ~240. On those
numbers the call is to revert. **What stopped me is that the mechanism did not fit**: removing an
allocation, a linear scan and a byte copy cannot be a net loss unless the REPLACEMENT costs more than
all three, and the iterator machinery was the only thing added. Rewritten as the node twin writes it
— `Vec::with_capacity(1 + extra.len())` and two indexed pushes:

```text
  T=1 len=6  218.6 → 196.5  1.11x     T=1 len=20  231.7 → 196.6  1.18x
  T=8 len=6  218.5 → 195.1  1.12x     T=8 len=20  235.5 → 196.5  1.20x
  T=64 len=6 222.4 → 196.4  1.13x     T=64 len=20 258.0 → 196.2  1.31x
  CONTROL scalar 7.5 → 7.4           (no element rendered)
```

Flat at ~196 on every arm and below the PRE floor everywhere. PRE is the min of three rounds, POST of
two, alternated. **The ~45 ns/row the chain cost exceeded everything the hoist removed** — and a
measurement that only says SLOWER cannot tell you which it was. **If removing three costs makes a
loop slower, suspect what you added, not the premise.**

### The corpus CAN see this one, unlike item 1068's

`element r` **304.7 → 287.3 ns/row (1.06x)**: the per-row `Vec` and the resolver scan are paid at T=1
and six characters too, where only the byte copy needed a long name. `element p` 345.3 → 338.4
(untouched), scalar and string controls flat.

Teeth: `edge-wrong-type-index`, `edge-extras-dropped` and `edge-labels-unsorted` all CAUGHT by the
existing 1,264-test suite. `bun run fuzz` 13/0 plus three deep differential runs.

### ➡️ Where the element-render target stands now

Items 338/390: element materialization is 129x a scalar read, ablated as **47% property loop, 37% two
`Value::Map` allocations, 12% labels, ~0 external id**. The labels are now hoisted on both sides

## 1070 — ❌ REFUTED: `Value::Map(Arc<[_]>)` is SLOWER than `Arc<Vec<_>>` — +22.9 ns/row, in BOTH halves

The second attack on item 390's "37% in two `Value::Map` allocations", priced before the cross-crate
refactor it would need. `Map(Arc<Vec<_>>)` is two allocations where `Value::Record` in the same enum
already uses the single-allocation `Arc<[(GStr, Value)]>`, so the floor looked like 2 per map
instead of 4 per row.

```text
  outer 3-pair: Arc::new(vec![..])   (today)    min 26.7 ns/row
  outer 3-pair: Arc::from_iter([..])            min 39.0           +12.3  SLOWER
  props: pushes -> Arc::new(v)       (today)    min 44.6
  props: pushes -> Arc::from_iter(v)            min 55.2           +10.6  SLOWER
  CONTROL props: pushes only, no map            min 30.1
```

**The props half was predicted** — `Arc<[T]>` is one allocation only from an `ExactSizeIterator`, and
`Arc::<[T]>::from(vec)` copies, so an accumulated `Vec` pays `Vec` + `Arc` + memcpy. **The outer half
was not**: three pairs with a known length is the case `from_iter` should win, and it loses by more.
`vec![a,b,c]` is one sized allocation and three moves; `from_iter` goes through the iterator protocol
and a layout computation that costs more at N=3 than the allocation it removes. **Item 1069's lesson
one item earlier, same shape: iterator machinery is not free, and at small N it can exceed what it
saves.**

### What the control priced

`pushes only` 30.1 against `pushes -> Arc::new(v)` 44.6 ⇒ **the props map's `Arc` box is 14.5 ns/row**.
So "37% in two map allocations" reads better as ~15 ns of `Arc` boxing plus ~60 ns of `Vec` + pair
building across both maps, of ~338 ns/row.

**🛑 And the first cut of the probe could not have said that**: its `pair()` used `format!`, so the
control read 107.1 ns/row and the 14.5 was invisible under the fixture's own allocation. **A control
is only useful if the effect is above the fixture's floor.**

### ➡️ Element render, where the shares now stand

- **12% labels — DONE** (1068, 1069).
- **37% map allocations — TWO attacks refuted**: pre-sizing the property vector (392, 1.25x slower)
  and the `Arc<[_]>` representation (this item). Close to its floor while each row's map is
  independently owned.
- **47% property loop — the largest share and unattacked.** That is where the next attempt belongs.

## 1071 — ✅ SHIPPED (RUST): the property loop specialized per COLUMN. 1.08x at K=4, 1.18x at K=64

Item 390's last unattacked share: **47% of an element render is the property loop**. It matched the
column's variant TWICE per present cell (`present_at` then `read`) and read the presence bitmap
three times, where the variant is fixed for the whole inner loop. One match per column, then a
specialized row loop per variant.

Byte-identical by construction: the generic path pushes when `present[i] || nulls[i]` with the datum
if `present[i]` and `Value::Null` otherwise, and each arm is that pair of conditions inlined — a
STORED null still pushes `Value::Null`, an absent cell still pushes nothing. `Gen` keeps the generic
path (no `nulls` bitset).

### 🛑 The corpus could not adjudicate it — and said so

```text
  element p  (the changed row)                  PRE 341.9 → POST 332.3    1.03x
  element r  (render_edges — UNREACHABLE)       PRE 267.2 → POST 277.3    0.95x
  scalar p.age CONTROL                              2.4 → 2.4            flat
```

**Subject 1.03x, unreachable control 1.04x the other way.** Same magnitude ⇒ the instrument cannot
separate the change from drift. CLAUDE.md's "under ~10% needs its own isolated harness" as a verdict.

### The isolated instrument: sweep the axis the change acts on

`propcells_1071` sweeps K (properties per node), every cell present, half numeric half string:

```text
  K=4    231.2 → 214.1   1.08x   ← the corpus's width
  K=16   549.2 → 482.4   NOT CLAIMED: POST spanned 482/635/718 (1.5x) against a stable PRE
  K=64  2667.8 → 2254.1  1.18x
  CONTROL scalar @ K=64    1.4 → 1.3, flat
```

**The ratio GROWS with K — the signature of a per-cell saving.** A change to the fixed per-row cost
would show the opposite shape.

`present-ignored`, `nulls-dropped`, `num-arm-zero`, `str-arm-first` all CAUGHT. **`dict-code-zero`
SURVIVED**: no fixture in 1,264 tests rendered an element off a DICTIONARY-encoded column.

## 1072 — ❌ REFUTED: item 578's 2.4x conjunct-order gap is the HARNESS, not the engine

`bun run spelling` reported `SEEK: a param equality AND a second conjunct` at ~2.4x, with
`WHERE n.k >= 0 AND n.s = $s` at 18.83 ms against 8.74 for the same conjuncts in the other order —
read for several items as "the seek fires only when the seekable conjunct comes FIRST".

### Three checks, all saying the engine is fine

1. **The compiled hints are the same SET** — `["eq:s","range:k"]` against `["range:k","eq:s"]`;
   `collectHints` descends the whole chain.
2. **The chooser takes the best, on honest estimates** — `countEquals('s',$s)` = 28,572 against
   `countRange('k',{gte:0})` = 200,000, and `seedVertices` keeps the minimum.
3. **An ad-hoc in-process probe reproduced 2.85x IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION** — whichever spelling
   ran first was the slow one.

### Isolated, it converges

```text
  one spelling per process:  eq-first 10.14  eq-second 9.17  inline 9.09  inline-where 7.61
                             controls: eq-only 9.35, range-only 9.88
  SPELL_ONLY (the group alone):  4.01 / 3.90 / 4.10 / 3.96      1.05x
```

**The 18.83 arm reads 9.17 — the fastest of the three clause spellings. The target is withdrawn.**

### Why `runGroup`'s existing fix missed it, and the instrument change

`runGroup` times each member in BOTH positions and keeps the better reading (items 180/181), which
removes WITHIN-group bias but not the state the ~40 groups before it left behind.

**A flagged group now prints its own confirmation command.** The header already warned against
reading an UNFLAGGED group's times (item 491 learned that at 1.4x); this item adds that being OVER
the threshold is not sufficient either, so the step belongs next to the flag. The emitted group name
is shell-escaped, or `a product's …` would print a command that does not run.

### ✅ And the step DISCRIMINATES — the other two flagged groups survive it

```text
  label on start: redundant vs absent                   1545.22x alone  — REAL (explained at 1067)
  a product's one-sided predicate: comma vs MATCH MATCH    2.30x alone  — REAL, still open
  SEEK: a param equality AND a second conjunct             1.05x alone  — THE HARNESS
```

`seek-conjunct-probe.ts` is the one-per-process instrument for this family.

### 🛑 The instrument lesson, which is the durable part

Item 285's group **PASSED** item 1072's confirmation (2.30x in one isolated run) and is still noise.
`SPELL_ONLY` removes cross-group contamination, not between-run variance — and the NULL CONTROL
cannot bound that either: it runs one query REPS times in ONE process and keeps the min, reporting
**1.01x at 12.8ms** where the same code across three isolated runs spans **1.64x**.

**A group that clears the null control has cleared a ruler shorter than the thing being measured.**
Both facts are now written where they are needed: the confirmation line says THREE TIMES, and the
null control's comment says what it does and does not bound.

## 1074 — ❌ REFUTED as a TS target: the 68x multi-hop count gap is 3x ALGORITHM × ~20x PER-EDGE COST

The widest TS/native ratios in `bun run bench` are the plain multi-hop counts — `count 4-hop` 92x,
`count 3-hop` 68x, `count 2-hop` 39x. Native answers a 5.4M-walk count in 4.8 ms (0.9 ns a walk,
not enumeration) and `bench.ts` names its mechanism: "the tuned degree-product arms".

**The semantics checks out**: a concatenated chain is a WALK count, the quantified spelling a TRAIL
— on a 2-cycle fixture, depth 3 reads 8 concatenated against 6 quantified and both engines agree.
So multiplicity counting is valid arithmetic for the concatenated form.

### What it is worth in TypeScript (200k vertices, degree 3, 3 hops; three rounds, min)

```text
  ENGINE (enumerates)        266.7 ms      —
  map<Vertex, number>        347.9         0.77x   SLOWER than enumerating
  dense index + Float64      160.8         1.66x
  scratch field (FLOOR)      102.3         2.61x   NOT shippable (mutates user objects)
```

```text
  68x  =  3x   algorithm   (1.8M edge visits instead of 5.4M walks)
       × ~20x  per-edge    (native's dense u32 ids + Vec accumulators vs TS's object-keyed Map —
                            the layout ceiling of items 573 and 1066)
```

**Only the 3x is reachable, and a shippable accumulator captures about half of it.** Even the
unshippable floor leaves TS 21x behind native. The engine arm would be substantial — concatenated
chain only, no rel/path variables, label-only endpoints, per-level filter handling — for 1.66x on
one shape family. **NOT BUILT.**

### 🛑 And the first cut of the probe answered 0 while reading 3-10x FASTER than the engine

`v.adjFrom.get('KNOWS')` holds EDGES, not vertices. All three arms answered 0 against the engine's
5,400,000 and looked like a huge win. **An arm that does not do the work is always fast.** The probe
now takes the engine's answer as its oracle and `check`s every arm before printing its time.

### ➡️ What would change the verdict

A dense vertex index maintained BY the graph — so a frontier accumulator is a `Float64Array` with no
`Map` hop — would move 1.66x toward the 2.61x floor AND apply to every frontier algorithm, not just
counts. That is a core-data-structure question, not a planner arm, and nothing here prices adding or
maintaining it.

## 1077 — ❌ REFUTED as a native target: the undirected count is ALREADY one linear pass; O(1) would cost every edge write

`bun run bench`'s `count 1-hop UNDIRECTED` reads **ts 0.00 / native 1.5 ms** — TS answers from
`2 * |E_t| - loops(t)`, native declines (`typed_hop_count_from_size` refuses `*dir != Dir::Out`).

**The self-loop semantics are the GQL contract and both engines agree**: a loop contributes ONE row,
not two — `MATCH (a)-[:T]-(x)` over one edge plus one loop returns `{1,1}, {1,2}, {2,1}`. Native's
`drop_loop` implements exactly that; `double_loops` is the Gremlin rule where a loop traverses twice.

### Doubling |E| is what settles it

```text
  MATCH ()-[:T]-() RETURN count(*)      600k 1.458   1.2M 2.880   1.97x  ← LINEAR, 2.4 ns/edge
  MATCH (a:P)-[:T]-(x) RETURN count(*)       1.292        2.739   2.12x  ← LINEAR
  MATCH ()-[:T]->() RETURN count(*)          0.004        0.002   0.60x  ← O(1), the partition
  MATCH ()-[]->() RETURN count(*)            0.039        0.074   1.88x  ← linear too
  MATCH (a:P) RETURN count(*)                0.002        0.003          ← O(1)
```

**Native is already doing one near-optimal pass.** `2 * |E_T| - loops(T)` needs a per-type loop
count, and **the Rust store has no self-loop accounting at all** where TS carries `selfLoopsByLabel`.
So the arm needs a counter maintained on every edge insert/delete (multi-label edges and tombstones
included) — priced against the write path — or a one-time partition scan, which is the same order as
the pass it replaces and buys nothing.

**The offer is 1.5 ms → ~0.002 ms on 600,000 edges: a big ratio, a small absolute, a cost on every
write. NOT BUILT.** The bench row is the honest difference between an arithmetic TS can do because it
maintains the counter and a pass native does because it does not.

### ➡️ The other open member is a TS arm and a different question

TS's constrained UNTYPED undirected count still declines (257 ms). `degreeOfTypes(box, undefined)`
sums ALL buckets, so a two-type edge is counted twice. Two routes both beat 257 ms: sum sizes when
`multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`, else iterate each PASSING vertex's boxes counting distinct edges —
survivors' edges only, not every row. Named for its own tick.

## 1078 — ✅ SHIPPED: the UNTYPED and MULTI-TYPE constrained undirected count, 9.8-10.8x; and item 1076's reason for declining them was FALSE

Item 1076 built the arm for ONE relationship type and declined the rest on the grounds that
`multiTypeEdgeCount === 0` "is a RUNTIME property and this closure has no way to hand the query back
once built". **The closure can read it** — the undirected branch returns `(graph, params) => …` and
the branch beside it already reads it there. What a closure cannot do is DECLINE, and it does not
need to: there is an exact correction.

**The arithmetic.** A passing endpoint of an edge carrying `m` of the requested types is counted `m`
times by the bucket sums and belongs once (**`m - 1`**); a SELF-LOOP additionally sits in both boxes
(**`2m - 1`**). At `m = 1` these collapse to 0 and 1 — item 1076's formula is the one-type case of
this one. `edgesOfTypes` dedupes across buckets (`edgesOfManyTypes` carries a `seen` set), which is
the fact the correction rests on and was checked, not assumed.

```text
  SUBJECTS                                              PRE      POST
    untyped     -[]-(x) WHERE a.age > 60              254.07 ->  25.94    9.79x
    two-types   -[:KNOWS|LIKES]-(x) WHERE a.age > 60  331.53 ->  30.58   10.84x
  CONTROLS
    clause      -[:KNOWS]-(x) WHERE a.age > 60         24.49 ->  24.89    0.98x  ← the sound path
    directed    -[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE a.age > 60         7.42 ->   7.78    0.96x
    far-pred    -[:KNOWS]-(x) WHERE x.age > 60        910.25 -> 875.58    1.04x
    bare        no constraint                           0.00 ->   0.00
```

One shape per process, alternated POST/PRE/POST, arms asserted by symbol count before being built,
all four answers identical in every round. `untyped` now costs what the typed spelling costs.

### ➡️ `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` earned again, and it unified SEVEN open-coded copies

`never-sound` (forcing every count through the correction) SURVIVED 20 differential tests at 0
failures — a route choice is answer-equivalent. So the condition is now one pure exported function,
**`bucketSumsAreSound(types, multiTypeEdgeCount)`**, asserted as a decision in
`bucket-sum-soundness.test.ts` (`[]` included: `length === 1` must not be `length <= 1`). It had
been open-coded at **seven sites**. Seven mutants of the extracted gate: all caught.
`gate-always-false` fails 5 tests where `never-sound` survived — at least one of the seven sites
treats "unsound" as a wrong ANSWER, not a slower route.

Also: restoring item 1076's own early return now FAILS 3 tests. With the decline removed it would
have been a wrong answer, not merely a conservative one.
