✅ **The shape worth remembering:** the gap was never between the two ENGINES but between the two
SURFACE LANGUAGES of one engine, with a working implementation one package away. "Grep the pattern
elsewhere" paid twice, and the second time "elsewhere" was not where I expected.

## 1161 — ✅ SHIPPED **3.84x / 4.20x** (`min`/`max` over a numeric column) and ⚠️🔧 **FIXED a cross-engine WRONG ANSWER** in the fold I was about to copy. Plus TWO fuzzer blindnesses, both closed

Priced the AGGREGATE-KIND enum after item 1160 closed label-arity in both engines. At 200k nodes on
one dense numeric column: `count` 121.5us, `sum` 122.0, `avg` 122.0, `stddev_pop` 122.2 — and
**`min` 435.0, `max` 472.7**. `percentile_cont` 3674.5 (30x, but a percentile needs a SORT, so most
of it is inherent and it is NOT a target).

**The `AggFn` mention census CANNOT find this, and item 844 drew the opposite inference from it.**
`Min` has 36 matches in `fastpath.rs` and `Max` 24 — the most of any value-reading variant — and
they were the slow ones. A census counts how often a variant is NAMED, not how well it is SERVED.
Price the variants.

**Cause (diagnosed, not assumed): not the comparator.** The single-agg fold carried
`best: Option<f64>` through the loop, so every row paid a `match` on `None`, and tested the
loop-invariant `want_min` inside the same closure. The `Option` is what stops it auto-vectorizing.

### ⚠️ The fast sibling was WRONG, and a stale doc comment had been licensing it

`scan_fold_minmax` already folded with a plain `x < mn`, justified as _"stored Nums are finite, so
`x < mn` == `cmp_num_total`"_. **Checked instead of believed (item 1142's precedent), and it is
false:**

```text
  three nodes 1.0 / NaN / 5.0        (NaN is GREATEST under cmp_num_total)
  single-agg max      NaN   correct      ORDER BY DESC   NaN   the contract's own order
  multi-agg  min,max  1.0, 5.0  WRONG — the NaN is skipped
  SET n.v = sqrt(0 - 1)  ->  stores Num(NaN), _is_nan true   (reachable from the surface language)
```

TS was right all along (`extremumFold` uses `compareValues`, the total order), so this was a LIVE
TS-vs-native divergence. `cmp_num_total` IS `partial_cmp` for two non-NaN operands (it ties `-0.0`
with `0.0` deliberately), so NaN is the whole of the exception.

**The claim traces to a test whose NAME asserts the opposite of the truth.**
`a_numeric_column_cannot_hold_a_nan` cited `Value::finite_only` — **which does not exist anywhere in
this workspace.** It lived in the retired `lenke-core` and was never ported; the sentence stayed.
The test could not notice: it asserts the column terminal AGREES WITH THE WALK and never that the
value is null, so it passes either way — the item-1158 tautology shape, believed long enough to be
cited as a licence. Renamed `the_column_terminals_agree_with_the_walk_on_a_stored_nan` and kept,
because that agreement is a real guard now that NaN is known reachable.
**`stored_infinity_is_a_value` already made "finite" false for ±∞ before NaN came up.**

### The fix gets BOTH: count the NaNs instead of comparing them

`nan_cnt += u64::from(x != x)` is a compare-and-add that vectorizes with the loop; the finish reads
it (`min` is NaN only when `cnt == nan_cnt`, `max` whenever `nan_cnt > 0`). **The sentinels need no
special case for a stored ±∞ because the sentinel IS the fold's identity.** `MIN` is a const
parameter, not a runtime flag. Early-return block, per item 844's measured reason (a shared live
range cost `min` 1.6x there), so the sum/avg loop is byte-for-byte untouched. Same `nan_cnt` in
`scan_fold_minmax` and `scan_fold_all`.
**Grepped elsewhere: NO other site.** Every other min/max fold (frontier, filtered, varlen, string,
dict) already uses `cmp_num_total`. One bug, two functions.

```text
  A3 min  [394.0,396.7,409.8] -> [102.6,103.2,103.1]   3.84x
  A4 max  [431.0,444.9,432.3] -> [102.6,103.6,104.0]   4.20x
  SIX controls flat: count(a.n) 1.01x, sum 1.00x, avg 1.00x, stddev_pop 1.00x,
                     percentile_cont 0.99x, count(*) 1.00x
```

min/max now BEAT `sum` (103 vs 111) — an extremum is a max-reduce with no dependent accumulator
chain. **The alternation earned itself again:** a plain before/after read the untouched `count(a.n)`
control at 121.5 -> 101.5 and would have needed explaining; alternated it is 1.01x. The machine
drifted between runs and visibly within round 3. The ratio survives, the raw numbers do not.

### ⚠️ Why seven byte-identity fuzzers missed a cross-engine wrong answer — TWO reasons

Revert the fix, run the differential fuzzer: **green.** Both causes are now closed, and the second
is the one worth remembering:

1. **It generated exactly ONE aggregate per query.** The native multi-aggregate folds are reachable
   only with two or more aggregates over one column, so the functions holding the bug were
   **unreachable by construction** for as long as the fuzzer has existed.
2. **Its `nan` column holds ONLY NaNs** — so fixing (1) alone LEFT IT GREEN. Every present value
   being NaN means a `max` that skips them falls back to its `NEG_INFINITY` sentinel, and
   **±INFINITY and NaN both render as `null` at egress**: the wrong answer and the right one are the
   same JSON. Observable only with a NaN AMONG FINITES, where it reads as a number against a null.

Fixed with a multi-aggregate arm (one key so they group onto a single column pass, two keys for the
fan-out, plus `count(*)`) and a new `nanmix` column (one NaN, two finites). Teeth verified by
reverting the engine fix — caught on the first seed tried.

**→ RULE: a fuzzer value needs the SHAPE that reaches the code AND the NEIGHBOURS that make the
difference observable at egress.** The fuzzer's own `genPred` note already says value-plus-shape
("the value and the shape never met"); this adds the third term. The first fix felt like the whole
fix and the suite was still green.

### Mutation: 5 mutants, 5 caught, no survivors

Harness proven to kill first (bomb -> SIGKILL, `while true` -> 124); every mutant under
`timeout 900` + `MemoryMax=16G` + `MemorySwapMax=0`, restored BEFORE the next.

**⚠️ The DID-NOT-RUN check caught a harness bug on the first pass** (third time that rule has paid;
items 767, 772-773 wrote it): all five came back `rc=1, result-lines=0` because **`cargo test` takes
ONE TESTNAME** and rejects a second — four filters passed directly ran NOTHING. Filters go after
`--`. `rc=1` with no result line is indistinguishable from a real failure by exit code alone; only
the execution evidence separates them, and a bare exit code would have read as five confident
CAUGHTs on a harness that never compiled a test.

**⚠️ An oracle also had to be WEAKENED, correctly.** `the_extremum_fold_matches_the_contract_order`
first asserted BITS against `ORDER BY`'s extreme rows, and the `-0.0` case failed against a fold
that was RIGHT: `cmp_num_total` ties `-0.0` with `0.0`, so ORDER BY's tie order is unspecified and
cannot be a bit-exact oracle. Now two instruments: the VALUE against the contract via
`cmp_num_total` (not `==`, which `NaN != NaN` makes vacuous), and the BITS across the three
spellings — the half that was broken, and which holds for ties too, where the contract has no
preference but byte-identity still does.

### ✅ NEGATIVE RESULT: the TS engine has NO aggregate-kind gap

TS at 200k: `count` 3.2 ms, `sum` 6.9, **`min` 4.4, `max` 3.6**, `avg` 9.9, `stddev_pop` 8.2,
`min,max` multi 8.5, `count(*)` 0.0. `min`/`max` are the FASTEST value-reading aggregates — ahead
of `sum` and `avg` — so **nothing to close.** `extremumFold` starts from `undefined` and tests it
per value, the same shape that cost native 3.8x, and it does not matter: the TS fold is not
competing with an auto-vectorized sibling, so that test is not the marginal cost. Item 1156's
pattern — the transferable thing is the QUESTION, not the answer — and the per-row `ts === native`
assertion independently exercised the NaN counting shipped here, from an engine that gets the same
answer by comparing rather than counting.

### Still open from this enum

`percentile_cont` / `percentile_disc` at **30x** (3674us vs 122 on the same column). Mostly
inherent — a percentile needs a sort — but an O(n) selection (quickselect / `select_nth_unstable`)
would answer `percentile_disc` without one. NOT priced against that alternative, so not yet a

`query_bench` both arms, 80 rows above the quantization floor: worst **1.08x**, best 0.85x — a
symmetric band inside the sweep's documented ~10% noise floor, and every top row is in a path the
change cannot reach (shortest-k, distinct node, varlen+path, gremlin dedup). `order(local) then

## 1162 — ✅ SHIPPED **9.5x / 9.3x** on the percentiles, by measuring the FLOOR first — the cost was NOT where item 844's numbers implied. ⚠️ Plus a mutant that exposed a test passing for the wrong reason, and a NEW TS target

The one row item 1161 priced and refused to call a target. `percentile_floor_probe` separated
`percentile_of`'s three costs before anything was built (item 234's precedent: a floor per shape
retracted two of three targets there), and **the carried-in diagnosis was wrong**:

```text
  sum                    122.0 us   the scan+column floor / control
  columnar gather alone  156.6      a boxing-free gather is NEARLY FREE
  gather + select_nth    397.8      the SELECTION costs ~241
  gather + full sort    3602.8      the SORT costs ~3446
  percentile_disc       3717.4      the full sort is 97% of it
  collect_list          1450.8
```

**I had inferred BOXING from item 844's recorded numbers** (`collect_list` 2,999 vs percentile
5,588 reads as "materialization is most of it"). It is the SORT. Building the columnar gather alone
would have shipped ~115us of a 3,595us problem and looked like a win.

**Build:** columnar f64 gather + `select_nth_unstable_by`. `percentile_cont` needs the NEXT
adjacent order statistic and gets it free — `select_nth_unstable_by` leaves everything `>= nth` in
its right partition, so it is that partition's MINIMUM, O(n), no second selection. A SEPARATE
function, not another block in `try_scan_num_agg`, because that function's sum/avg/min/max arms
were measured flat one tick ago and item 844 + 1161 both record what a shared live range costs.

```text
  percentile_disc  3717.4 -> 389.8   9.5x        A5 floor 397.8 — both arms land ON it
  percentile_cont  3718.3 -> 400.4   9.3x
  controls flat: sum 122.0 -> 113.9, columnar gather 156.6 -> 142.2
```

### The one exactness guard, and why it is `-0.0`

`percentile_of` sorts with `partial_cmp` and indexes the result. For finite f64 "equal under
`partial_cmp`" implies IDENTICAL BITS — except `-0.0` vs `0.0`, which tie but differ in bits, and a
stable sort keeps a tied run in input order where an unstable selection may not. So a negative zero
is noted in the gather and the path DECLINES (item 1161's `nan_cnt` shape: observe in the loop,
decide at the finish). NaN/±INFINITY need no guard — `percentile_of` keeps only finite values and
the gather replicates that.

**Oracle: the general grouped fold** (`LET g = 1 … GROUP BY g` — one group, same question, and it
routes to `percentile_of` because the fast path needs a sole aggregate over a bare `Scan`).
Compared as BITS over 12 fixtures x 9 fractions x 2 kinds = **216 cross-path comparisons**,
out-of-range fractions included (item 530's panic). Note for anyone writing one: the fraction must
be a numeric LITERAL, so a negative one is `-1`, not `0 - 1`.

### ⚠️ M1 SURVIVED the first mutation run — the TEST was passing for the wrong reason

The negative-zero guard is the purely-correctness part of this change, and the mutant removing it
passed. Settled by taking the engine out of it — a standalone search over BOTH algorithms with the
SIZE swept:

```text
  checked 5,916,000 (input, index) pairs; 1,454,911 differed in bits
  minimal case:  n=2 idx=1 over [-0.0, 0.0]  ->  stable 0.0, selection -0.0
```

Guard is load-bearing. The test used THREE values and fractions up to 0.5, and
**`select_nth_unstable_by` on a slice that short falls into an INSERTION SORT, which is stable** —
so selection and sort agreed and the assertion held for a reason unrelated to the code under test.
Rebuilt from the search's counterexample (two values at fraction 1, plus 64 values to clear the
regime, both input orders); M1 now caught.

**→ RULE: a size-dependent algorithm needs the SIZE swept, and a fixture small enough to be
convenient can sit entirely inside the branch that cannot fail.** Sibling of items 1136/1142, where
a fixture built the wrong way made the path DECLINE so the mutant survived — there the fixture
missed the code, here it reached the code but only its stable regime. Both look identical from
outside: a green test and a surviving mutant.

### Mutation: 7 mutants, 5 caught, 2 survivors BOTH predicted and explained

M2 (`total_cmp` for `partial_cmp`) survives because the two differ only on `-0.0` vs `0.0`, which
the gate already declines — answer-equivalent, a route choice, and PREDICTED before the run, which
is what separates a documented equivalence from a hole. M6 (`.min(n - 1)` on the disc index)
survives because `frac` is clamped to `<= 1`, so `ceil(frac * n) - 1 <= n - 1` always; **I
mispredicted this one.** M3 (removing the clamp) IS caught, so the clamp is load-bearing and the
`.min` is belt-and-braces — kept, because `percentile_of` has it and the two must not drift, and now
labelled defensive in the code with M6 cited.

Process note: editing `fastpath.rs` to record these findings WHILE the mutation script ran got the
edits wiped — the script's pristine copy is taken at its START, so the tree is not yours until it
finishes.

## 1163 — ✅ SHIPPED **17.9x** on the TS percentile fold / **4.5x** end to end: an INTERPRETED O(n) selection beat V8's NATIVE sort by 5.3x. ⚠️ Plus an **18,000x** property no answer test can see, and 🔶 a cross-engine `-0` divergence found by READING

Item 1162's open TS target. The design transferred from the Rust side; **the algorithm did not
transfer for free**, and assuming it would have been the item-234 mistake in a new language.
`percentile-arm-probe.ts`, 200,000 values, median of 14 dropping three, three order-alternated
rounds, all arms checked to AGREE before any was timed:

```text
  A current      map + filter + sort((a, b) => a - b)   26.8  24.7  25.3 ms
  B typed sort   Float64Array + native .sort()           8.0   8.0   8.0    3.4x
  C quickselect  Float64Array + hand-written select      1.4   1.4   1.5   17.9x   <- ships
  D gather only                                          0.1   0.1   0.1   the floor
```

**The interpreted O(n) selection beats the native C++ O(n log n) typed sort by 5.3x at this size** —
the constant favours the sort and only the exponent favours the selection, so this was genuinely
open before it was measured.

`%TypedArray%.prototype.sort` was also wrong for a SECOND reason: **it orders `-0` before `+0` by
specification**, where `(a, b) => a - b` ties them and V8's stable sort keeps input order — item
1162's hazard exactly. It cannot arise here because `numArg` collapses `-0` first, so **the TS fast
path needs NO negative-zero guard where the native one does.** That asymmetry is a fact about
`numArg`, not a liberty.

```text
                     PRE      POST (3 rounds)
  percentile_disc   31.2  ->  6.9  7.0  6.3    ~4.5x
  percentile_cont   30.2  ->  7.0  7.0  6.3    ~4.3x
  controls flat: count 3.3->3.2, sum 6.8->6.6, collect_list 4.3->4.8, min/max/avg/stddev/count(*)
```

Fold 17.9x but query 4.5x, because ~4.3 ms of the 31 is the group materialization `collect_list`
also pays and this cannot touch. The CONTROLLED measurement is the fold-level alternation; the
end-to-end figure is three POST rounds against same-session PRE, quoted as the weaker of the two
on purpose.

### ⚠️ An 18,000x property INVISIBLE to every answer test

`selectNth` uses a **median-of-three** pivot. A first-element pivot is equally CORRECT, so it
passes everything (mutant M6, predicted to survive, did):

```text
  over 200,000 ALREADY-SORTED values:  median-of-three 0.3 ms, first element 5517.2 ms  (~18,000x)
  control, median-of-three over random input: 1.5 ms
```

**An ascending column is the ORDINARY case for a percentile, not an adversarial one.** Per the
standing rule that a route choice is answer-equivalent and so invisible to differential tests, the
property got its own instrument: sorted AND descending input, 2-second budget against a 0.3 ms
expectation — ~6,000x headroom so no machine reaches it, while the mutant exceeds it by 2.7x. The
one timing assertion this suite permits, justified by the five-orders-of-magnitude gap.

### Mutation: 8 mutants, 7 caught, survivor PROVABLY equivalent

M1 non-finite filter, M2/M3/M4 the `cont` interpolation and its tail-min, M5 the disc index clamp,
M8 `numArg` applied to every element (keeping a FAULT where a fault was — a one-pass rewrite is
exactly where that goes missing silently), M6 only after the timing test above.

**M7 (`return a[lo]` for `return a[k]`) is an IDENTITY, and I mispredicted it as catchable.** The
loop maintains `lo <= k <= hi` (it sets `hi = j` only when `k <= j`, `lo = i` only when `k >= i`)
and exits on `lo >= hi`, so `lo == k == hi` and `a[lo]` IS `a[k]`. A survivor with a proof is
documentation; a survivor without one is a gap.

**Oracle = the code this replaced.** `percentile-select.test.ts` carries the old map/filter/sort as
a REFERENCE, so "agrees" means "answers what it answered before". 6,363 assertions over hand-built
edge cases and randomized inputs with **the SIZE swept** (1/2/3/5/9/17/33/64/129/512/2048, 40
trials each, 7 fractions, both kinds) — the sweep is there because of item 1162's M1, since a small
input never leaves the first partition. Narrow value range so DUPLICATES are common (a selection
and a sort can only disagree on ties). `Object.is` throughout, the only comparison that separates
`-0` from `+0` and makes `NaN` equal itself.

### 🔶 ~~OPEN~~ **RETRACTED AT 1165 — THE DIVERGENCE DOES NOT EXIST** (I had compared TS's RAW values against native's JSON round-trip), found by READING `numArg`'s comment: a cross-engine `-0` divergence predating all of this

After `SET n.v = 0 * (0 - 1)`:

```text
  the stored value itself   ts -0  native +0   DIVERGE
  min(n.v)                  ts -0  native +0   DIVERGE
  ORDER BY n.v [first row]  ts -0  native +0   DIVERGE
  percentile_disc/cont, sum        both +0     agree
```

**Direction is the OPPOSITE of my prediction.** Native collapses on the WRITE path (`num_of`); TS
collapses only in the numeric-FUNCTION path, so a `SET`-computed `-0` survives into TS storage and
out through `min` and `ORDER BY`. By the model's own stated rule ("no negative zero in the numeric
model") **TS is the engine out of conformance.**

**Why no fuzzer caught it: `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`.** The differential fuzzer compares
rendered JSON, so the two are the same string to it; `Object.is` is the only instrument that sees
it, hence `negzero-cross-probe.ts` walks raw row values. NOT fixed here — a write-path numeric-model
question, not an optimization, and the percentile rows are unaffected. Probe kept so the next tick
prices the fix rather than rediscovering the fact.

5,695 TS tests green across every package, isolated; 2,030 Rust tests green (unchanged); 7/7
byte-identity fuzzers green, with the differential fuzzer's percentile band now exercising BOTH
engines' new folds against each other over `0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.0001, 1.5, 2, 100`.

## 1164 — ⚠️ **RETRACTED BY ITEM 1165 — the divergence does not exist.** Kept for the method lesson only.

## (as written) 🔶 PRICED AND DIAGNOSED, not built: the `-0` cross-engine divergence has **FIVE** observable surfaces, and the probe that was meant to locate the fix answered a different question

> **Read item 1165 first.** The five "divergences" below are an artifact of the instrument: the
> native rows cross the FFI boundary as JSON, where `-0` renders as `"0"`, so they compare TS's raw
> values against native's JSON round-trip. Rendered output — the actual invariant — agrees on every
> row. The conclusion "TS is the engine out of conformance" is WITHDRAWN.

Follow-up to item 1163's incidental finding. `negzero-cross-probe.ts`, after `SET n.v = 0 * (0 - 1)`,
comparing with `Object.is` because **`JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`** and every renderer-based
comparison — the differential fuzzer included — is blind to it:

```text
  computed, not stored                   ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  computed via negation                  ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  the stored value itself                ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  min(n.v)                               ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  ORDER BY n.v  [first row]              ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  percentile_disc / percentile_cont      both +0             agree
  sum over the zero alone                both +0             agree
  atan2(0, stored) / atan2(0, computed)  both +0             agree
```

**Settled:** TS keeps the sign bit through a BARE PROJECTION, through `min` and through `ORDER BY`;
it loses it only on entering a numeric FUNCTION. Both engines collapse at that function gate
(`numArg` / `num_of`), which is why the `atan2` rows agree. By the model's own stated rule — native
`num_of`: _"the numeric model has NO negative zero… no operation ever observes a -0"_ — **TS is the
engine out of conformance**, and the divergence is wider than the write path, since a computed `-0`
that is never stored diverges too.

**⚠️ NOT settled, and this is the part worth recording: WHERE native collapses.** An early reading
of `min` returning `+0` was taken as evidence that native collapses on the WRITE path. It is not —
an EGRESS collapse looks identical from every one of these rows. The `atan2` rows were added
specifically to separate the two and **cannot**, because `atan2` collapses its own operand in both
engines: the instrument answers a different question than the one it was built for. (The first
instrument tried, `1 / n.v < 0`, is unavailable at all — division by zero is a data exception here,
not an infinity.) Write-collapse and egress-collapse want the fix in DIFFERENT places, so the next
step is to read native's write path directly rather than infer it from the surface. This is the
items 1102 / 1146 / 1159 failure mode — three edits that landed in unreachable paths — caught this
time BEFORE the edit.

Candidate TS sites, once that is known: `normalizePropertyValue` in `packages/core/src/core/validate.ts`
is the single write chokepoint (and a `typeof value === 'number'` early return there would also
short-circuit four checks — `fromTaggedJson`, `Array.isArray`, `instanceof LenkeRecord` and the
plain-object test — for the most common property type, so the conformance fix and a hot-path
shortcut are the same edit). `packages/core/src/numeric.ts` is the established home for exactly this
kind of "the obvious built-in differs between JS and Rust" helper and already holds `mathSign` for
the signed-zero reason. The computed-but-unstored rows need a second site regardless.

NOT built: a numeric-model change across a write chokepoint and an arithmetic result is not an
optimization, and half-building one at the end of a tick is how the wrong-path edits above happened.

## 1165 — ⚠️ **RETRACTED: item 1164's `-0` divergence does not exist.** The invariant holds at 0 of 10 rows; I had compared TS's RAW values against native's JSON ROUND-TRIP

Item 1164 reported five observable `-0` divergences and concluded "TS is the engine out of
conformance". **That conclusion was wrong, and the cause was the instrument.**

Item 1164 itself recorded that it had NOT settled where native collapses, and said the next step
was to read native's write path rather than infer it. Doing that is what broke the finding open:

- `apply_set_prop` has **no** `-0` collapse. So native does not collapse on write — the value goes
  straight into the column.
- Grepping every collapse site instead found `json_fmt.rs:167`, whose own comment is
  _"also normalizes -0.0 → \"0\" (JS drops the sign)"_. **Native collapses at JSON EGRESS.**
- And the FFI query path crosses the boundary as JSON text and comes back through `JSON.parse`.

So a native `-0` **could not reach the probe even if one were stored**: it is rendered as `"0"` and
parsed back as `+0`. The probe was comparing TS's in-process JS values against native's JSON
round-trip — two different things — and reading the difference as an engine divergence.

**The invariant is defined on RENDERED OUTPUT, and it holds.** `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`, the
same string native emits, so:

```text
  5 of 10 differ in RAW JS VALUES (by Object.is)
  0 of 10 differ in RENDERED OUTPUT (the invariant)        <- the question that matters
```

The probe now measures both and labels which is which, so the next reader cannot repeat the
mistake.

### What is actually left, and it is not a bug

A pure-TS in-process caller can observe a `-0` in a raw returned value where an FFI caller cannot,
because the two engines have different egress layers (direct JS values vs JSON text) — structural,
not a defect, and invisible the moment anything serializes. Native's `num_of` claim ("no operation
ever observes a -0") is about its own internals and remains true of them. **Nothing to fix.**

### The transferable lesson, which is the only reason this item exists

**A cross-engine probe compares two TRANSPORTS as much as two engines, and a normalization anywhere
in the transport is indistinguishable from agreement.** Every `Object.is`-level claim about native
values through the FFI is a claim about JSON's value space, not the engine's: `-0`, `NaN` and `±∞`
all normalize on that path, so none of them can be measured through it. The tell was available and
I missed it for a tick — item 1164's own text says `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"` while treating
`Object.is` as the sharper instrument, without asking whether native's values had already been
through a renderer before I got them. Sharper on the TS side; blind on the other.

Related in shape to item 1162's `-0` guard, which is a REAL requirement — there the two values live
inside one engine's sort and selection, with no renderer between them. The distinction is whether a
serialization boundary sits in the middle.

## 1166 — ❌ REFUTED: widening `rearm_if_warranted` to the `algo` surface. Freshness does not move an algorithm at all, and the rebuild costs ~80% of a whole PageRank. ⚠️ Plus my first instrument invented a 1.2x that a second one dissolved

The last uncovered variant of the FFI ENTRY-POINT enum. Items 1121/1122 built the stale-overlay
re-arm (break-even measured at 1.97-2.23 reads, `REARM_AFTER = 4`) and wired it into `lnk_query`
and the prepared-statement run, with `ffi.rs` naming the gap in as many words:

> NOT widened to the rest of `lnk_command`: the algo commands read adjacency heavily and a re-arm
> would be safe there too (…), but that surface has no measurement behind it.

`algo` is the only adjacency-heavy variant left (`merge` is a write; `last_write_scope`, `epoch`,
`prepare`, `prepared_free` do not touch adjacency). This is that measurement, and it says **do not
build it**.

### ⚠️ A false start that nearly ended the investigation at the wrong answer

Grepping `algo.rs` for the typed accessors — `out_typed_csr`, `in_typed_csr`, `out_typed_flat`,
`for_each_typed_out`, `csr_fresh` — returns **ZERO for every one**, which reads as "the algorithms
never touch the overlay, so a re-arm is pure cost" and would have closed this in one step with a
confident, wrong rationale.

It is wrong. `algo.rs` goes through `store.out()` / `store.inc()`, and **both branch on
`csr_fresh`**: fresh returns a contiguous `&csr_out[a..b]`, stale falls back to `out_adj[node]`, a
Vec-of-Vecs with a pointer chase per node. The dependency is real; the accessor's NAME just does
not contain it. **Absence of a name is not absence of a dependency** — item 1165's lesson in a
different dress, and the second time in two items that a grep-shaped inference was the thing to
distrust.

### ⚠️ And the first instrument invented a 1.2x stale penalty

The first probe built a SEPARATE store per arm, so that one arm's reads could not warm the next.
That also made the arms three different HEAPS, which conflates the overlay's state with each
store's allocation layout. It reported FRESH 32.1 / STALE 34.6 (1.08x) — a plausible-looking stale
penalty, and the only reason it did not become the finding is that **arm C refused to confirm it**:
rebuilding never recovered the gap (C 34.9 against B 34.6), which is the tell that the difference
was not freshness.

Driving ONE store through the states removes the confound, and re-entering stale with a second
write closes the cycle on the same heap:

```text
  A FRESH              30.9  28.4  28.8   1.00x
  B STALE (one write)  34.4  34.4  34.7   1.11-1.21x
  C REBUILT            34.5  34.0  34.2   1.12-1.20x   <- a rebuild does NOT return to A
  D STALE AGAIN        34.5  34.5  34.3   1.12-1.21x
  one rebuild_csr      25.1  23.8  24.1 ms, single shot
  E degree [ctl]       0.99x flat in all three rounds
```

**B == C == D, at ~34.4 in every round.** Fresh and stale are indistinguishable; only A, the very
FIRST measurement on a freshly built store, is faster, and a rebuild does not get back to it. So
the 1.1-1.2x is a first-measurement effect, not staleness — and the C-vs-D pair, which differs in
NOTHING but `csr_fresh`, is the comparison the decision rests on.

**What A's advantage actually is remains unidentified** (plausibly the build leaving pages hot) and
is deliberately not asserted here. It does not need to be: the decision turns on C == D.

### The decision

- Freshness does not move an algorithm: `C == D`, flat across three rounds, control flat at 0.99x.
- A rebuild costs **23.8-25.1 ms** against a whole 10-iteration PageRank at **~30 ms** — roughly
  80% of the run it would precede.
- So widening the re-arm would add ~80% of an algorithm's cost to change nothing measurable.

**REFUTED. The pending task is retired, not deferred.** `ffi.rs`'s comment is updated from "no
measurement behind it" to the measurement, so the next reader finds the answer rather than the
invitation.

### Why the overlay matters so much to a QUERY and not at all to an ALGORITHM

Worth stating, because it is the generalizable part. The cliff `CLAUDE.md` leads with — up to 24x,
proportional to how selective the queried edge type is — is a **typed-partition** effect: fresh,
`out_typed_flat` scans only that type's partition; stale, the hop walks every edge and filters. The
algorithms take `None` for `edge_label` on this fixture and sweep EVERY edge by construction, so
there is no partition for them to lose. All that remains for them is the flat CSR's locality, and
at degree 4 that is worth nothing measurable against PageRank's own arithmetic.

**So "a stale overlay costs up to 24x" is a claim about TYPE-SELECTIVE reads, and reads that are
not type-selective should not be expected to recover anything by re-arming.** That is the rule for
pricing the next consumer of this overlay, and it is what the `algo` surface failed.

## 1167 — ✅ item 1120's "standing 6x" is CLOSED and REFRAMED: it is exactly **4 stale reads per write**, by design, and here is the whole curve. ⚠️ Plus I hid the heal behind a median on my own first pass

Item 1120 priced a FILTERED typed count at **6.0x** after one adjacency write and left it open as
"the half item 1118 did not fix". It has been carried as open ever since — including through item
1166's status pass, which missed it. **Item 1120 predates items 1121/1122**, which measured the
rebuild's break-even (~2 reads) and shipped `rearm_if_warranted` at the query boundary with
`REARM_AFTER = 4`. So the question was never re-asked after the fix landed.

Re-asked now, on the exact shape `reverse.rs` names — 200,000 nodes / 80,000 sparse `F` edges /
`MATCH (a)-[:F]->(b) WHERE b.age >= 77 RETURN count(*)` — **through the FFI**, which is the only
path with the re-arm wired in. (An in-process Rust probe measures the engine WITHOUT it, which is
why item 1120's number reads as permanent: its instrument could not see the fix that did not yet
exist.)

### The PER-READ series, which is where a heal is visible and an aggregate is not

```text
  FRESH baseline    0.3 ms      answer 19172
  cycle 1 reads 1..12:  2.3  1.7  1.7  3.7  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3
  cycle 2 reads 1..12:  3.2  2.3  1.8  3.9  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3  0.3
```

Reads 1-3 pay the stale cost (~6x, reproducing item 1120's 1556.9us against 257.9us almost
exactly). **Read 4 pays the stale cost PLUS the rebuild** — the 3.7/3.9 spike, so the rebuild is
~2 ms here, consistent with item 1121's "a rebuild costs ~2x one stale read". Read 5 onward is back
at the baseline to the decimal, and cycle 2 reproduces the whole step, so the heal re-arms per
write rather than once per session.

### The whole curve, which nobody had measured

```text
  reads/write    mean      x baseline   % of reads at baseline      (baseline 0.28 ms)
       1        1.67 ms       6.0x            0%
       2        1.66          6.0x            0%
       4        2.03          7.3x            0%
       8        1.18          4.3x           50%
      16        0.72          2.6x           75%
      32        0.45          1.6x           88%
      64        0.33          1.2x           94%
```

The baseline is a MEDIAN of nine reads, and that detail earned itself: with a single sample as the
denominator the ratio column wobbled run to run (5.1x against 6.0x for the same mean) while the
`% at baseline` column was bit-identical across rounds — the giveaway that the noise was in the
divisor, not the measurement. Fixing it was cheaper than writing the caveat. Stable across three
rounds afterwards: 1.52/1.54/1.52 ms at ratio 1, 0.64/0.65/0.65 at 16, 0.33/0.33/0.35 at 64.

The `% at baseline` column makes the mechanism legible: **exactly four reads per write are stale**,
so the healed fraction is `(ratio - 4) / ratio` — 50% at 8, 75% at 16, 88% at 32, 94% at 64, which
is what the column reads. The mean follows it down to the baseline.

**So item 1120's 6x is real and is not standing.** It is a fixed four-read transient per write. At
≤4 reads per write the re-arm deliberately never fires and the full ~5x applies; by ~64 reads per
write the shape is at its fresh cost. This is the DESIGNED trade, not a defect: item 1121 measured a
rebuild at ~2x a stale read, so rebuilding to serve one or two reads loses, and `REARM_AFTER = 4`
is that break-even plus margin. Item 1122 stated the same boundary from the other side ("nothing
measurable below five") as a limit on its win; this states it as the cost it is, per ratio.

### ⚠️ I hid the heal behind a median, in the exact way the house rules warn about

The first version of the ratio table reported a MEDIAN and read **5.8-6.1x at every ratio from 1 to
8** — i.e. it said the re-arm does nothing, while the per-read series printed six lines above it
showed the step plainly.

The cause is that each cycle is **bimodal by construction**: four stale reads then `ratio - 4` fast
ones. At a ratio of 8 that is exactly 50/50, so the median sits on the boundary and returns the
SLOW mode. _"Print the per-rep series before trusting any summary of it"_ is in `CLAUDE.md` for
precisely this, and the tell was in the output: **a summary that does not move when the thing it
summarizes does.** 5.8, 5.9, 6.1, 5.8 across a ratio sweep is not a measurement, it is a constant.

Amortized cost per read IS the mean, and it is also the decision-relevant number — what a workload
at that ratio actually pays. The `% at baseline` column was added at the same time so the shape is
legible without trusting any single statistic.

### What is left, and its price is now exact

The four stale reads per write exist because a whole-graph rebuild is `O(E + types x N)` for a
one-edge write. **Incremental per-type CSR maintenance** — item 852's "only undisproven design" —
would make the update cheap enough to apply eagerly and remove the transient entirely. Its prize is
now quantified rather than asserted: **~5x on workloads at ≤4 reads per write, decaying as
`(ratio - 4) / ratio` and worth nothing past ~64.** A design whose benefit is concentrated at low
read-per-write ratios should be priced against a fixture at those ratios, which is what this table
is for.

Note for anyone quoting `CLAUDE.md`'s serving-path figure: "interleaving a write with a traversal
already costs ~2.5x" and the up-to-24x type-selectivity figure are both about the STALE read. This
table is the orthogonal axis — how many reads per write — and the two multiply.

## 1168 — ✅ FIXED a cross-engine divergence CI caught: a DOTTED conjunct was raising here and non-raising in the engine, so only the engine could hoist it past a faulting sibling. ⚠️ Plus a RELATED shape that is still open, found by my own probe

**CI went red on `f54c9045`** — the differential fuzzer, `FUZZ_SEED=1433311152`, reproducible:

```text
  MATCH (n:T) WHERE ((CAST(n.nan AS BOOLEAN) IS UNKNOWN) AND (n.m.k = 3)) RETURN n.n AS x
    ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
    native: ok [{"x":5}]
```

Pre-existing, not caused by item 1161's generator widening — but newly REACHABLE, because adding
`r()` calls shifted the RNG stream into seed space the old generator never visited. That is the
third time this session that the generator change was the thing that exposed a standing bug.

### Diagnosis, which took two wrong turns worth recording

**The cast is NOT the divergence.** Isolating it over 7 values x 4 targets — NaN, ±INFINITY, 0, 1,
2.5, -3 against BOOLEAN/INTEGER/FLOAT/STRING — gave **0 of 28 divergences**: both engines raise on
`CAST(<NaN> AS BOOLEAN)`, both answer `null` for `AS FLOAT`, identically throughout. The fuzzer's
query faults only because the fixture stores NaN on SOME rows, so whether the cast is REACHED
depends on conjunct order.

Confirmed by swapping the conjuncts, which is what named the real question:

```text
  CAST first, m.k second (as generated)   ts err   native ok   DIVERGE
  m.k first,  CAST second (swapped)       both ok
  CAST alone, no conjunct                 both err
  the cast projected, not filtered        both err
```

**The cause is the ORDERING KEY, and it is not shared.** The engine's `can_raise` lists
`Arith | Call | Cast` as raising and recurses through `And`/`Or`/`Not`/`Compare`/`In`, so
`Expr::Field` falls into its `_ => false`: a dotted access is non-raising there, unconditionally
and without recursing into the base. This engine's `valueCannotRaise` whitelist had **no `field`
arm**, so `n.m.k = 3` was classified raising, `filterPredicate` saw no safe conjunct to hoist, and
evaluation reached the cast. The engine hoisted it and never visited a NaN row.

This is the same bill the `compare` arm (41 divergences) and the `isTruth` arm (item 322, one seed
in three) were each handed, in the same function, with the lesson written above both of them: **a
narrower key here is not caution, it is disagreement.** The fix matches the engine exactly —
unconditionally non-raising, no recursion into the base — and is sound on this engine's own terms
as well: a field access on a record, a NUMBER, a STRING, an absent key and three levels deep all
answer `null` in both engines and raise in neither.

**Seed 1433311152 now passes.** 7/7 fuzzers green, 8 further random seeds clean, 4,428 tests green
across `gql`/`core`/`native`, and the shape is pinned in
`and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts` — the file whose whole job is to say the contract is
SHARED.

### ⚠️ Two wrong turns, both the same mistake

1. I checked the dist for the new arm with `str.count("=== 'field'")` and got **0**, and nearly
   concluded the build had not picked it up. The bundler had rewritten it to `=== "field"` —
   double quotes. Item 1151 recorded that the bundler strips comments so a comment marker passes
   vacuously; this is the same hazard on QUOTE STYLE. **Assert on a token the bundler cannot
   rewrite, or read the surrounding line.**
2. I assumed `filterPredicate` governed my hand-written repro shapes and spent three calls
   reasoning about why the fix "had not worked" on them. A `TRACE1168` print settled it in one
   run: **`filterPredicate` is never called for those shapes at all** — they work (where they
   work) through `compileExpr`'s `AND` FALSE short-circuit instead. The fix was already correct
   for the fuzzer's shape, which does reach `filterPredicate`. Items 1102/1146/1159 are three
   edits that landed in unreachable paths; this is the fourth time a trace was the cheap answer to
   "which arm actually owns this?", and I reached for it third rather than first.

### 🔶 ~~STILL OPEN~~ FIXED AT 1169, and my repro probe is what found it

The hand-written shapes are a DIFFERENT divergence, ~~unfixed~~ — **item 1169 identified the route
and fixed it**: `pathProps` was APPENDED after the two buckets that can RAISE, so a dotted conjunct
could not settle a row before a coercing sibling faulted:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.m.k = 99 AND n.s   ts err E_INVALID_VALUE   native ok []
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.s AND n.m.k = 99   ts err E_INVALID_VALUE   native ok []
  MATCH (n:P) FILTER n.m.k = 99 AND n.s  ts err E_INVALID_VALUE   native ok []
```

The plain-prop twins AGREE (`WHERE n.n > 1000000 AND n.s` → `ok []` both engines, both orders), so
it is specific to a dotted conjunct beside a bare property in truth position — and it is NOT the
ordering key, which now matches, but the fact that these shapes never reach `filterPredicate`. The
route that compiles them is the next thing to identify. Note the registry may NOT excuse this:
`divergence-registry.ts`'s standing rule is that an error against a non-empty result cannot be
declared, and the conformance file records that rule being enforced before.

## 1169 — ✅ FIXED the shape item 1168 left open: `pathProps` was APPENDED after the two buckets that can RAISE, so a dotted conjunct could not settle a row before a coercing sibling faulted

Item 1168 shared the ordering KEY (a dotted access is non-raising in both engines) and that fixed
the fuzzer's query. It did NOT fix the three hand-written shapes, and the reason is a different
mechanism entirely:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.m.k = 99 AND n.s    ts ERR E_INVALID_VALUE   native ok []
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.s AND n.m.k = 99    ts ERR                   native ok []
  MATCH (n:P) FILTER n.m.k = 99 AND n.s   ts ERR                   native ok []
```

### A predicate attached to a MATCH never reaches `filterPredicate`

Established with a trace, **asserted into the dist before it was trusted** — the lesson from item
1168's wasted calls, where I checked the bundle for `=== 'field'` and got 0 because the bundler had
rewritten the quotes:

```text
  MATCH (n:T) WHERE n.m.k = 99 AND n.s      no trace       ERR
  MATCH (n:T) FILTER n.m.k = 99 AND n.s     no trace       ERR
  MATCH (n:T) WITH n WHERE <same>           TRACE mix=3    ok []     <- the only one that reaches it
  RETURN ((n.m.k = 99) AND n.s)             n/a            false     <- the AND itself short-circuits fine
```

`compilePredicate` LIFTS each conjunct into a typed bucket, and `dotted-predicate-routes.test.ts`
records the fact that makes this decisive: **`residual` is always `undefined`, so a successful lift
EMPTIES `where`.** The lifted lists are the only carriers, and the order ACROSS buckets is what
decides which conjunct runs first.

### The buckets are ordered NON-RAISING FIRST, and `pathProps` broke that

```text
  props -> eqProps -> cmpProps -> truthProps -> notTruthProps -> pathProps -> generic where
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^
                                  these COERCE and RAISE        this only COMPARES
```

`eqProps`/`cmpProps` read a value and compare it; `truthProps`/`notTruthProps` COERCE one, which
raises on a non-boolean — which is exactly why the existing order puts the comparing buckets first.
Item 900 appended `pathProps` at the END, after the raising pair. So `n.s` coerced a string before
`n.m.k = 99` could drop the row, while the engine — whose `can_raise` treats a `Compare` over a
`Field` and a `Lit` as non-raising — hoisted the dotted conjunct and never faulted.

**The fix is moving the block up, nothing more.** Neither block's own semantics change, and the
invariant is now stated where the block sits so the next lift is inserted rather than appended.

```text
  0 of 10 diverged — both orders, the FILTER spelling, two levels deep (`n.m.deep.z`), the NEGATED
  truth bucket, and an ordering operator (`pathProps` carries any comparison, not just `=`)
```

### The CONTROLS are the half that makes this a fix and not a suppression

A reorder that simply stopped raising would be a wrong answer dressed as a pass, so three cases
assert the raise SURVIVES where it is essential:

```text
  [ctl] dotted MATCHES, so the sibling is essential   ERR E_INVALID_VALUE   both
  [ctl] the raising conjunct alone                    ERR E_INVALID_VALUE   both
  [ctl] dotted + a REAL boolean property              ok [{"x":3}]          both
```

### ⚠️ The fixture had to be widened or the test passed for the wrong reason

`and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts`'s fixture carried no `m` record, so `n.m.k = 99` would have
dropped every row because the key was **absent** — the assertion holding for a reason unrelated to
bucket order. Added `m: {k, deep: {z}}` to all three vertices. This is item 1162's vacuous-pass trap
in a third costume: there a fixture too small to leave the first partition, at 1136/1142 a fixture
built the wrong way so the path declined, here a fixture missing the value the predicate reads.

**Mutation:** moving `pathProps` back to item 900's position — after `notTruthProps` — fails the
suite (`13 pass 1 fail`, rc=1). Restored and green.

### Grep the pattern elsewhere: `satisfies` is the ONLY order-sensitive consumer

`dotted-predicate-routes.test.ts` names five consumers that must know about a lifted bucket, so the
obvious worry is that the same append-after-the-raising-pair mistake sits in the others. Checked,
and it does not — for a reason worth recording, since it is what bounds this fix:

- **`satisfies`** (executor.ts) is the only one that EVALUATES the buckets in sequence, so it is the
  only one where order is observable. Fixed.
- **`rejectedByElementDirect`** carries `eqProps` and `cmpProps` only — both non-raising — which its
  own doc gives as the soundness argument for judging without a binding.
- **`mergeFarPreds`** (hop-projection.ts) MERGES buckets into an object and appends within each; the
  object's key order has no bearing on evaluation, which happens back in `satisfies`.
- **`closedFarPred`**'s use of `lifted.*` is an existence test (did anything lift at all?), not an
  evaluation.
- **the two `preFilter` gates** (matching.ts) and **`shortcuts.ts`' `InlinePred`** touch
  `eqProps`/`cmpProps` only.

So the invariant "non-raising buckets first" has exactly one enforcement site, and the note now sits
on the block that moved rather than on the function, which is where a future lift will be written.

### Verification

4,429 tests green across `gql`/`native`/`core`; 7/7 byte-identity fuzzers; **CI's seed
1433311152 plus nine further random seeds, zero divergences**.

## 1170 — 🔶 item 1111's element-egress target SURVIVES re-measurement and is now the TWO BIGGEST ROWS in the gql group. ⚠️ My own hypothesis about its cause was REFUTED by a trace, and the decomposition points somewhere a tick cannot reach

Re-measured before building, per the standing rule. It survives, larger than recorded:

```text
  hop node, NO distinct   177510 us / 1,000,000 rows = 177.5 ns/row
  hop prop, NO distinct     7382 us / 1,000,000      =   7.4 ns/row    24x
  scan node                63996 us /   200,000      = 320.0 ns/row
  scan prop                  564 us /   200,000      =   2.8 ns/row   113x
  distinct node            96356 us /   198,672      = 485.0 ns/row
```

(Item 1111 recorded scan node 151 and hop node 328 ns/row — the two are REVERSED on today's build
and fixture. The target is unchanged in kind and larger in size, but the per-row figures from that
item should not be quoted.)

### ⚠️ REFUTED: my hypothesis that the hop misses the shared render path

`render_nodes_shared` dedups ids and clones one `Value::Map(Arc<..>)` per repeat, so a `Map` clone
is one refcount bump. From that I computed backwards — 199k maps at the `scan node` rate is ~64 ms,
leaving ~113 ns per remaining row, which is far too slow for an atomic increment — and concluded
the hop must be falling through to the per-row `node_result_value` instead.

**It is not.** A trace, asserted into the BINARY before it was trusted (`strings` on the example,
all four markers present — the item-1168 quote-rewriting lesson applied up front):

```text
  hop node        TRACE1170_RENDER_NODES n=1000000   TRACE1170_SHARED_TOOK n=1000000
  scan node       TRACE1170_RENDER_NODES n=200000    TRACE1170_SHARED_DECLINED n=200000
  distinct node   TRACE1170_RENDER_NODES n=198672    TRACE1170_SHARED_DECLINED n=198672
  per-row path    TRACE1170_PER_ROW count=0          (entered once in the whole group)
```

The hop DOES share; the two all-distinct rows decline, correctly, on the 1-in-8 repeat gate. So the
dedup layer is working as designed and is not the gap. Three deductive steps from a correct premise
produced a wrong conclusion that one trace settled — and the trace cost less than the deduction.

### What it is instead, and what it is NOT

**It is not JSON serialization.** `time_query` calls `try_run` and reads `rows.len()`; nothing
renders. So the cost is producing and dropping the `Rows` themselves.

Decomposed against the two rows that bracket it:

```text
  199k distinct element maps        ~64 ms     (320 ns each — exactly the `scan node` rate)
  the remaining 1M rows            ~115 ms     = 115 ns/row
  the same 1M rows as a NUMBER       7.4 ms    =   7.4 ns/row   <- the floor
```

So ~115 ns a row to turn a shared map into an output `Value` and later drop it, against 7.4 for a
numeric cell. Each rep creates 1M `Value::Map` clones (1M atomic increments), collects them into a
1M-element `Vec<Value>` (~32 MB), and then DROPS all of it inside the timed region — 1M atomic
decrements plus freeing ~199k pair vectors. That accounting is consistent with the gap; it is not
proven term by term, and is labelled as consistent rather than established.

### Why this is recorded and not built

The fix item 1111 already named is the right one and it is architectural: keep the node column
COLUMNAR (`Col::Nodes(Vec<u32>)`) through to egress and expand it per consumer, instead of
`col_into_values` expanding it into a full element map per row. That changes the row type and every
consumer of it. Half-building that at the end of a tick is how items 1102/1146/1159 happened, and
this tick has already spent its budget refuting one hypothesis properly.

**What the next tick has that this one did not:** the target re-measured, the dedup layer cleared of
suspicion by trace, serialization ruled out, a 7.4 ns/row floor from a sibling row in the same
group, and the knowledge that `scan node` and `distinct node` DECLINE sharing by design — so a
columnar egress would help all three rows rather than only the hop.

## 1171 — ✅ MEASURED, and it is the half every prior ablation missed: **52% of element egress is the DROP**, not construction. With the three construction attacks already refuted, the only lever left is not building the cells at all

Item 1170 left the ~115 ns/row residual labelled "consistent with" construction plus teardown and
explicitly not established term by term. `egress_split_probe` establishes the one term that changes
the DESIGN rather than the number, by timing the same query with and without `mem::forget`:

```text
  A node, create + DROP   171.8 ns/row        <- what the corpus row measures
  B node, create + LEAK    83.3 ns/row
  C prop, create + DROP     8.5 ns/row  [ctl]
  D prop, create + LEAK     6.9 ns/row  [ctl]

  the DROP, node: 88.5 ms over 1M rows = 88.5 ns/row  — 52% of the total
  the DROP, prop:  1.6 ms              =  1.6 ns/row  — the leak arm validating itself
```

The control is what makes the leak arm trustworthy: a numeric column has nothing to free, so if
`mem::forget` were measuring something other than teardown, C-vs-D would move too. It does not
(1.6 ns/row), while A-vs-B moves 88.5. One store for all four arms, so no arm gets its own heap
(item 1166's lesson).

**Every previous attack on this cost measured CONSTRUCTION only.** Items 338/390 ablated element
materialization as 47% property loop / 37% two `Value::Map` allocations / 12% labels / ~0 external
id — a decomposition of the BUILD. Items 1068/1069 hoisted the labels; 392 refuted pre-sizing the
property vector (1.25x SLOWER); 1070 refuted `Value::Map(Arc<[_]>)` (+22.9 ns/row, in both halves).
Teardown was never in any of those tables, and it is the larger half.

### ⚠️ I nearly re-derived item 1070, and the rule caught it BEFORE the build

Reading the drop figure, the obvious inference is "freeing is proportional to allocations per map,
so cut the allocations" — `Map(Arc<Vec<_>>)` is two allocations where `Record` in the same enum
already uses the single-allocation `Arc<[_]>`. I counted the sites (109, of which 71 non-test across
25 files including the codec crate), judged it a tick's work, and only then checked `CLOSED.md`,
which has it **refuted at item 1070** with numbers.

That is the standing rule earning itself — and note what made it work this time: the count came
first and the check came before the patch, where the session's earlier misses (items 172/200
re-derived twice) checked after. The cheap ordering is: price it, then check the list, then build.

### What this leaves, stated precisely so the next attempt is not a fourth refutation

Teardown is a function of how many allocations each map holds, and the allocation count is PINNED by
1070 and 392. So the drop cannot be attacked by making the map cheaper — the three local levers are
exhausted. **The only remaining lever is not materializing 1M cells at all**: keep the node column
columnar (`Col::Nodes(Vec<u32>)`) through egress, as item 1111 proposed, which removes construction
AND teardown together. That makes the prize up to ~164 of the 171.8 ns/row (toward the 7-8 the
property column costs), not the construction half alone — a stronger case than item 1170 could make.

**And its blocker, located:** `Flat` is `pub` with PRIVATE fields and a four-method surface (`len`,
`is_empty`, `iter`, `from_rows`) plus `Index<usize>` and `IntoIterator for &Flat` — which looks
bounded, and is not, because `iter` and `Index` hand out **`&[Value]`, a borrow into the flat
`Vec`**. A lazily expanded cell cannot be handed out behind a borrow without materializing it
somewhere, which is the same obstacle item 851 recorded for `out_typed_csr` ("take `&self` and
return borrows into the very `Vec`s a rebuild replaces"). So the change is not "add a columnar
variant"; it is "change `Flat`'s borrow contract to an owned or view-typed row", and every consumer
of `&[Value]` moves with it. That is the scope a future tick should budget for, rather than
discovering it halfway in.

### Kept

`examples/egress_split_probe.rs` — the only instrument in the corpus that separates building a row
from tearing it down, with the numeric column as the control that validates `mem::forget`. Reach for
it before attributing any per-row cost to construction.

## 1172 — ✅ SHIPPED **~3107x**: `min`/`max` over a `Column::Bool`, the one representation the extremum enum did not serve — and the only one that can answer WITHOUT finishing the scan

Item 1161 made the numeric extremum 3.8-4.2x faster, so the next question is whether the fast path
covers the store's SIX column representations or only the one that got attention. Priced with
`count(<key>)` on the SAME column as each representation's floor — it reads only the presence mask,
so it should be flat everywhere, and a representation where `count` is flat but `min` is slow has a
FOLD problem rather than a column problem:

```text
  column   min(us)   count(k)(us)   min/count
  num       111.9       101.5          1.10
  dict      178.9       202.3          0.88
  date      112.0       101.4          1.10
  bool     1016.2       101.4         10.0x    <- the gap
  str      1524.3       101.6         15.0x    (comparing unique strings is real work)
  mixed    3162.5       147.9         21.4x    (`Gen` holds boxed `Value`s; not a target)
```

**`Bool` is the simplest representation in the store** — a `Vec<bool>` beside its masks — and was
the slowest of the three that should be trivial, because it had no arm at all: reading first found
`try_scan_num_agg`, `try_scan_str_agg` and `try_scan_temporal_agg`, and nothing for `Bool`, so it
fell to the general grouped fold, which boxes every cell into a `Value::Bool` and compares through
`cmp_total` (200,000 boxed comparisons at ~5 ns).

### The short circuit, which is why this is not merely "one more arm"

`bool::cmp` gives `false < true` — checked in `value.rs`, not assumed — so over a boolean column
`min` is `false` the moment ANY present `false` is seen, and `max` is `true` on the first present
`true`. Nothing later can beat it, so the walk stops. No other representation permits that.

```text
  bool   PRE [978.6, 932.1, 936.6]   POST [0.3, 0.3, 0.3]   ~3107x
  CONTROLS, all flat: num 1.00x, str 0.99x, dict 1.00x, date 1.01x, mixed 0.99x
```

Three order-alternated rounds, each arm asserted to BE its code before being built. **The
alternation earned itself a third time this session:** a single PRE reading against the POST runs
showed every control ~9% faster, which alternated is 1.00-1.01x — machine drift, not the change.

### ⚠️ Mutation found a branch my fixtures could not REACH

Six mutants, and M5 — making the no-present-cell case answer `false` instead of NULL — SURVIVED.
The arrangement sweep has "all absent" and "all stored null" fixtures, and **neither enters the
arm**: with no node carrying the key `store.column` is `None`, and a stored present-null promotes
the column to `Column::Gen` (item 1142). So the NULL branch was never exercised.

It IS reachable, and the fixture that does it is worth stating: a column that exists as
`Column::Bool` because an OUT-OF-LABEL node carries a value, while every node the label covers
lacks the key — so the walk sees only cells whose `present` bit is false. Added; M5 now caught.
That is the fourth costume of one trap this session — item 1162's fixture too small to leave the
first partition, 1136/1142's built the wrong way so the path declined, 1169's missing the value the
predicate reads, and now one that cannot construct the representation at all.

M6 also reported **ANCHOR COUNT 6** rather than a verdict: its first anchor (the `matches!` gate)
appears six times in the file, so the mutant was never applied and the harness said so instead of
scoring it. Re-anchored on the column destructure, then caught.

Final: **5 caught, 1 survivor, and the survivor is answer-equivalent by construction** — removing
the `return false` that stops the walk reaches the same verdict, only slower. Predicted to survive.

### Correctness oracle

The general grouped fold (`LET g = 1 … GROUP BY g`), over 15 arrangements the short circuit could
get wrong: the sought value first, last, only, absent, interleaved with absent cells and stored
nulls — plus a partial label and a post-delete store, which are the two walks `scan_visit_while`
chooses between (and where a label-blind walk could STOP on a row the query excludes, so the
fixture puts the only `true` on an out-of-label node).

**One case needed the oracle withdrawn, for a GQL reason and not a defect:** over ZERO rows a
scalar aggregate yields one NULL row while `GROUP BY` yields NO GROUPS and no rows at all.
Comparing them would assert that two spellings answer the same question when they do not, so the
empty fixture is checked against the contract directly and the grouped oracle is used for every
fixture that has a row.

### ✅ NEGATIVE RESULT: the TS engine has no such gap

```text
  TS, 200k nodes:  num 4.4 / 4.0   str 8.6 / 3.4   dict 6.6 / 3.5   bool 5.6 / 3.5   date 4.3 / 3.3
                   (min ms / count(k) ms)
```

`bool` is 1.6x its own floor — in the same band as `dict` (1.9x) and BETTER than `str` (2.5x) — so
the gap was specific to a columnar store having a `Bool` representation with no arm. TS keeps
property bags per vertex, so every type goes through one `extremumFold` and there is nothing to
miss. A boolean short circuit there would cap at ~1.6x (the scan floor is 3.5 of the 5.6) and risks
the documented closure-size hazard, so it is **priced and declined**, not deferred. Every row of
the probe asserts `ts === native`, which independently exercises the arm shipped here.

```text
  [seed 2150414400223868] g.V().union(has('name', gt('nope')).out('KNOWS', 'NOPE'), out('NOPE'))
                               .order().skip(1).inE('KNOWS').values('weight')

```

## 1173 — 🔶 REDUCED the gremlin-fuzz residual to `union(...) + order()`, and ⚠️ **CORRECTED its standing description: the seed REPLAYS DETERMINISTICALLY.** The mechanism is STATIC vs PER-ROW rejection

Item 1172 identified the rare `bun run fuzz` failure by name (`differential fuzz: gremlin`, 1 pass
in 6) and ruled it out of that change structurally. This reduces it.

### ⚠️ The note that kept it un-investigated is wrong

`gremlin-fuzz-families` has been carried as _"a rare 1-in-30 residual whose SEED REPLAYS CLEAN"_.
It does not replay clean:

```text
  FUZZ_SEED=2150407949 bun test src/gremlin-fuzz.test.ts     ->  1 fail, 1 fail, 1 fail
```

Three replays, three failures, one divergence each time. **"Replays clean" is exactly the note that
stops anyone looking**, so it is the most useful thing corrected here. (A plausible origin for the
old reading: the failure prints BOTH a per-iteration `[seed <caseSeed>]` and the suite's
`FUZZ_SEED=<n>` reproduce line, and replaying the per-iteration number as `FUZZ_SEED` generates a
different 400 traversals and shows nothing.)

### The reduction — everything but two steps is scaffolding

The fuzzer drives the engines DIFFERENTLY (`toArray(plan, tsGraph)` runs the fluent plan with no
parsing; `nativeRun(text)` parses the rendered text), so the reduction uses the same fluent builder
and replicates the fixture adjustments made after `createTestTinkerGraph()` — two stored nulls, a
two-label vertex, a two-label edge. Getting either wrong compares two different graphs.

```text
  union only                        both ok [marko]                      AGREE
  no order                          both ok []                           AGREE
  no union: V().order().skip(1)..   both ERR E_SYNTAX                    AGREE
  union + order only                ts E_SYNTAX / nat E_INVALID_VALUE    both err -> NOT reported
  FULL (+ skip(1).inE.values)       ts E_SYNTAX / nat ok []              <- THE divergence
```

### The mechanism, and why it surfaced as a freak traversal

**Both engines reject `order()` over a stream they cannot compare — at different TIMES.** TS
rejects the PLAN, so no appended step can rescue it. Native raises PER ROW, so appending
`.skip(1).inE('KNOWS').values('weight')` empties the stream before anything is compared, and the
query answers `[]`.

That is why this looked like a one-in-six oddity rather than the general disagreement it is: the
fuzzer's rule is that **both failing is acceptable**, so the plain `union(...).order()` shape — where
the two engines disagree about the ERROR CODE but agree that it errors — is never reported. Only the
longer traversal, where the per-row engine gets to finish, crosses the threshold. The rarity is a
property of the REPORTING RULE, not of the bug.

This is the same static-vs-dynamic axis the repo has hit twice before, with the roles swapped each
time: item 1162's note records native rejecting an aggregate VALUE subquery at plan time while TS
reached the operand per row, and `boolean-context-static-check` records the TS side's static
checker. Here TS is the eager one.

### NOT fixed, and the reason is a rule rather than a budget

Which engine is right is a Gremlin SEMANTICS question — does `order()` over vertices it cannot
compare fault, and does an EMPTY such stream fault? — and the house rule is to settle those against
a real TinkerPop console rather than by argument (`tinkerpop-ground-truth-harness`; item 574 is the
precedent, where `repeat().times(k)` was settled that way and lenke's reading was the one that
moved). Changing either engine before that measurement is how a conformance guess ships.

**What the next tick has:** a deterministic repro command, a two-step minimal case, the mechanism,
and `packages/native/order-union-static-probe.ts` — which prints all ten rows of the reduction and
agrees/diverges per row, so a TinkerPop answer can be dropped straight against it.

## 1174 — 🔶 TINKERPOP GROUND TRUTH settles item 1173, and the answer is bigger than the divergence: **`order()` over ELEMENTS is unsupported in BOTH engines** while TinkerPop orders them. The fuzzer cannot see it, by construction

Item 1173 reduced the residual to `union(...) + order()` and stopped, because which engine is right
is a Gremlin SEMANTICS question and the house rule is to settle those against a real console rather
than by argument. Run on `gremlin-console:3.7.3`, TinkerFactory modern graph:

```text
  case                                      TinkerPop 3.7.3      lenke TS       lenke native
  V().order()                               [v1..v6]             ERR E_SYNTAX   ERR E_SYNTAX
  V().out('nope').order()                   []                   ERR E_SYNTAX   ERR E_SYNTAX
  union(..).order()                         []                   ERR E_SYNTAX   ERR E_INVALID_VALUE
  FULL (union, order, skip, inE, values)    []                   ERR E_SYNTAX   []            <- native right
  V().order().skip(1).inE.values            [0.5, 1.0]           ERR E_SYNTAX   ERR E_SYNTAX
  V().limit(1).union(identity, values)      [29, v[1]]           -              -
```

**`order()` never faults in TinkerPop for any of these.** It orders vertices (ascending id), orders
an empty stream to empty, and orders a MIXED vertex-and-number stream across types without
complaint — `[29, v[1]]`, number before vertex.

So item 1173's framing — "both engines reject an uncomparable `order()`, at different times" — was
right about the mechanism and wrong about the premise. There is nothing uncomparable here.
**Neither engine supports ordering ELEMENTS at all**, and the TS/native disagreement item 1172's
fuzzer caught is a narrow consequence: on the FULL traversal native's per-row raise never fires
because the stream is already empty, so it answers `[]` (correctly, by accident of evaluation
order) while TS's static rejection stands.

### ⚠️ Why a byte-identity fuzzer cannot find this, and what that means for the method

The two engines AGREE on four of the five shapes — both `E_SYNTAX`. The differential fuzzer's rule
is that **both failing is acceptable** (each rejects the query), so it reports nothing. It surfaced
only the one shape where the agreement breaks.

That is not a gap in the fuzzer's coverage; it is what the fuzzer IS. **It checks AGREEMENT, not
CORRECTNESS** — two engines can be identically wrong forever and it stays green. The only
instrument for the other question is the TinkerPop console, which is why `CLAUDE.md` lists it as a
first-class step rather than a tiebreaker. Worth stating plainly, because the natural reading of
"7/7 fuzzers green" is stronger than what it licenses.

### Not built, and what the next attempt should know

Allowing `order()` without `by()` over any stream is a FEATURE, not a bug fix, and it is bounded by
something already in place: native's `cmp_total` orders same-kind element refs by dense id and
ranks across kinds (`Num < Str < Bool < ...`), which is **the same order TinkerPop produced** in
both the vertex case and the mixed case. So the value contract already agrees; the rejection is at
the Gremlin surface (an `E_SYNTAX`, i.e. planner/parser, not a comparison failure). The work is
admitting the step in both engines and pinning the order — not inventing one.

Deliberately not started at tick end: it is a surface change across two engines with byte-identity
consequences, and this tick's budget went on the console run that made it a known quantity.

`packages/native/order-union-static-probe.ts` now carries all ten reduction rows plus the three
TinkerPop cases with the console's answers in a comment, so the next attempt has the oracle inline.

"Grep the pattern elsewhere", applied to the previous tick's win. Item 1172 found `Bool` missing

```text
  distinct.rs   Num 4  Str 4  Dict 4  Bool 4  Temporal 3    even
  order.rs      Num 2  Str 1  Dict 2  Bool 0  Temporal 2    <- Bool at zero
```

```text
  dict 0.7 us    bool 1741.4    num 2299.6    str 2141.7    date 2128.1    mixed 5231.0
```

`dict` is three orders of magnitude below everything else, and **reading why is what justified the
change rather than the ratio**. The dictionary arm has a RANK-BOUNDED EARLY EXIT: sort the tiny
dictionary for ranks, then stop as soon as `limit` rows at the best rank are in hand. The lift
gate's comment states the qualifier explicitly, while excluding numerics on measured grounds (a
numeric lift was a 1.28x REGRESSION):

> Only the dictionary arm has the rank-bounded early exit that pays for streaming.

**A boolean column has strictly MORE rank structure than a dictionary** — two values, ranks known a
priori (`false < true`, checked in `value.rs`), so no dictionary sort at all. It qualifies by the
gate's own stated criterion, which is why this is one arm and a two-variant gate widening rather
than a new mechanism.

```text
  bool   PRE [1759.5, 1755.2, 1765.6]   POST [0.3, 0.3, 0.3]   ~5851x   (now faster than dict)
  CONTROLS: num 1.00x, dict 1.00x, date 1.00x       mixed 1.23x but visibly noisy
  ⚠️ str 1.13x — 2182.8/2182.7/2184.9 -> 1927.8/1923.2/1938.3
```

**The `str` movement is reported as LAYOUT, not credit.** It is tight and consistent across three
alternated rounds, so it is not noise — but `Str` takes the identical path before and after
(`top_k_liftable` false, `_ => return None`), so the only thing that changed for it is code layout
from a new match arm. This is the mirror of `pull-alignment-is-load-bearing`, where the same effect

### ⚠️ A mutant found a fallback my fixtures could not REACH, and the arithmetic says why

M3 — deleting `nulls_seen = true` — SURVIVED the first sweep, which has three null/absent
fixtures. Reaching that fallback (`nulls_seen && buf.len() < kcap`) needs TWO conditions at once:

- `kcap * 2 < node_count`, or the function bails before the scan — with a 4-node fixture only
  `LIMIT 1` gets past it;
- `buf.len() < kcap`, i.e. FEWER present rows than the window.

A small fixture cannot satisfy both: at `LIMIT 1` the buffer is already long enough. The fixture
that does it is 200 nodes of which three carry a boolean, window of ten. A stored NULL is also
unusable here — it promotes the column to `Column::Gen` (item 1142), so the arm declines for a
different reason — which is why the nulls are ABSENT cells. M3 is now caught.

That is the fifth costume of one trap in this session, and this one is new in kind: not a fixture
too small, built wrongly, or missing a value, but a fixture that **cannot satisfy two gate
conditions simultaneously at any small size**.

M4 and M5 also reported `ANCHOR COUNT 2` rather than a verdict: the early-exit code is textually
IDENTICAL in the dictionary arm, so the anchors matched both. Re-anchored on `best_val`, which only
the new arm has.

Final: **4 caught, 2 survivors, both answer-equivalent by construction and predicted** — the exit
one row late, and no exit at all, reach the same window and only cost time.

### Oracle

The SAME query without `LIMIT`. `try_scan_top_k` needs a limit (`let limit = limit?`), so the
unlimited form cannot take the streaming arm and is the general path; the limited answer must be a
PREFIX of it. That also pins the TIE-BREAK, which is the whole difficulty: a boolean column has two
distinct values, so a `LIMIT 10` over many rows is almost all tied and WHICH rows return is the
question — the buffer's `arrival` counter makes it scan-stable. Swept over nine arrangements x
ASC/DESC x every limit from 1 to n+1, plus SKIP, plus a partial label where the `false` rows are
all out of label (an early exit that ignored the label would answer from excluded rows).


All five types sit in a tight 5.6-8.7 band, so **`bool` is not an outlier and this tick's gap does
not transfer** — TS has no column representations to specialize. But the band itself is the finding:
TS has no rank-bounded early exit for ANY type, where native now answers `dict` and `bool` in under
a microsecond. TS already streams (its top-k is 4-11x its own `order-all`), so the missing piece is
specifically the early exit: once the heap holds `limit` rows all equal to the extreme value,
nothing can displace them. **Not built** — it is a new mechanism in the TS planner rather than a
transfer, and this tick's budget went on the Rust arm, its fallback fixture and the alternation.
Priced here so the next tick starts with numbers: `bool` 6.7 ms against a `count` floor of 3.6.

## 1176 — ❌ RETRACTED: item 1175's TS early-exit target cannot be built soundly. The optimization is STRUCTURALLY native-only, which also explains why the TS band is uniform

Item 1175 shipped the boolean top-K arm natively (~5851x) and left a TS target: "TS has no
rank-bounded early exit for ANY type… once the heap holds `limit` rows all equal to the extreme
value, nothing can displace them", priced at 6.7 ms against a 3.6 ms `count` floor.

**That target is not available, and the reason is worth more than the target was.**

### The early exit needs the key's EXTREMUM, and TS cannot know it

`boundedTopK` is a generic max-heap over an `Iterable<T>` with nothing but a comparator. An early
exit must establish that **no unseen row can enter the window**, and for a bounded-rank key that
means comparing the worst kept entry against the key's BEST POSSIBLE value. A comparator cannot
supply that — it only orders the values it is handed.

So the exit needs the key's domain. Checked rather than assumed: the TS core keeps **no per-key
type index at all** — zero hits across `packages/core/src` for any of `propertyType`, `columnType`,
`typeOfKey`, `keyTypes`, `valueKind`, and nothing of the kind in `Graph.ts`. Properties are stored
as per-vertex bags, so "this key is boolean, therefore its minimum is `false`" is not a fact the
planner can read.

The two ways to get it are both refused:

- **Sampling** the first rows is UNSOUND — a later row can be a different type (the engine's model
  is dynamically typed, and `mixed` in item 1172's own probe is a column with a type per node).
  A false "nothing can displace these" is a wrong answer, which is not a trade worth 6.7 ms.
- **A schema hint** exists (`defineNode`, typed nodes via Standard Schema) but is OPT-IN and absent
  from any of these fixtures, so it cannot be the basis of a general fast path.

### What this explains, which is the useful part

Item 1175 measured the TS top-K band as 5.6-8.7 ms across num/str/dict/bool/date and called the
uniformity "a finding". It is, and this is its cause: **TS is uniform because it cannot
specialize.** The native engine's dictionary and boolean arms both depend on the columnar store
knowing a representation — `Column::Dict` carries its dictionary, `Column::Bool` its two values —
and a property-bag store has no equivalent to consult. The 0.7 us and 0.3 us native answers are not
a cleverness TS is missing; they are a consequence of a storage decision TS made differently.

**So this class of win is native-only by construction**, and the next reader pricing a "port the
dictionary/boolean fast path to TS" idea should stop here. The general rule: a fast path gated on a
COLUMN REPRESENTATION has no TS twin, and pricing it there is wasted effort — unlike the gaps at
items 1140/1141/1163, which were gated on query SHAPE and transferred cleanly.

### Not a reason to keep the TS top-K unexamined

The band is uniform, but ~6-9 ms for a `LIMIT 10` is still ~3.6 ms of `count` floor plus ~3-5 ms of
sort-and-materialize, and nothing here says that remainder is irreducible. What it says is that the
_rank-bounded_ attack is unavailable. A different attack — on the per-row cost the heap pays, or on
the materialization the floor represents — is untouched by this retraction and unpriced.

## 1177 — ✅ corpus rows for items 1172/1175 (the two biggest wins of the session had NONE), and ❌ the spelling probe's top flag is NOT a target — I built two theories before reading the comment beside it

### The rows, which is the shipped part

Items 1172 (`min(<bool>)`, ~3107x) and 1175 (`ORDER BY <bool> LIMIT k`, ~5851x) had **no bench
corpus row**, which is the gap item 1167 found for the percentiles: the ts/ffi/wasm sweep that is
supposed to catch a regression in them could not see them, and a win with no row is a win that
quietly comes undone. Added, measured one case per process (`BENCH_ONLY`), with their non-boolean

```text
  query: min boolean [short-circuits]        ts 4.6   ffi 0.0   wasm 0.0   1595.58x / 100.05x
  query: top-k by boolean [short-circuits]   ts 5.0   ffi 0.0   wasm 0.0   1398.05x / 113.10x
  query: min property [fused-scan]   [twin]  ts 4.7   ffi 0.1   wasm 0.1     44.87x /  32.39x
  query: top-k by property           [twin]  ts 5.1   ffi 1.0   wasm 1.3      5.00x /   3.90x
```

**A DEDICATED fixture (`boolDoc`), not a widening of `nodesDoc`.** That document is shared by a
dozen rows and adding a property to it moves every one of their per-node property counts — "widening
a fixture several benches share is how item 1130's comparisons went bad". `graphDoc` was the
precedent for a fixture of its own. `flag` alternates so both values appear early and the
short-circuit is actually exercised; a single-valued column would enter the arm but could not

Two rows rather than one, because they are different code — an aggregate fold and a streaming
