### Item 1270 — `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` / `NOT (… IS NULL)` lift into `nullProps`: 1.66-1.93x, and all three spellings at once (DONE)

Item 1269 left `directEqProps` admitting a bare prop, a `NOT` prop, a compare, a dotted compare and
a membership. `isNull` is an `Expr` kind of its own and was not among them, so it declined the WHOLE
chain — while the INLINE spelling of the same question, `(n {k: null})`, which this engine reads AS
`IS NULL`, landed in `props` and was already element-direct.

The native engine had the identical omission in its own matcher and paid for it twice: item 1261 for
`IS NOT NULL` and item 1262 for the `NOT (… IS NULL)` spelling that was only noticed after the
first shipped. Both are folded here in one pass for that reason.

200,000 vertices, one process, TS estimator rule (14 reps, first three dropped, median, min over
three order-alternated rounds). The first two rows answer an identical 2000:

```text
  shape                   before    after    ns/vertex          ratio
  nk IS NULL               5.683 ms  2.956    28.4 -> 14.8       1.92x
  nk IS NOT NULL           5.549     3.351    27.7 -> 16.8       1.66x
  NOT (nk IS NULL)         6.438     3.332    32.2 -> 16.7       1.93x
  [CTL] {nk: null} inline  3.317     3.219    16.6 -> 16.1       already lifted
  [CTL] age = 50           3.514     3.453    17.6 -> 17.3       already lifted
  [CTL] age IN [50]        3.876     3.857    19.4 -> 19.3       item 1269's family
  [CTL] bare count(*)      0.001     0.001
```

The spread across the null spellings closes from **1.94x to 1.13x**, and `IS NULL` now reads FASTER
than the inline spelling it was being compared against — the lift is one `isNullish` where the
inline form goes through `structuralEq`.

A by-product worth recording: this fixture tests item 1263's claim directly. `IS NOT NULL` keeps
198,000 rows at 27.7 ns a vertex while `= 50` keeps 2,000 at 17.6 — so a TS filtered COUNT costs per
SCANNED node, not per kept row, which is what makes these rows comparable at all.

### `NOT` is folded by FLIPPING the flag, and the flip is exact

`asNullTest` reads `isNull` as itself and `NOT (… IS NULL)` with `negated` inverted. Exact because a
null test is TWO-VALUED — `null IS NULL` is TRUE, never UNKNOWN — so `NOT` of it is its exact
complement. The NaN hazard that makes `NOT (x >= 2)` unequal to `x < 2` cannot arise: there is no
comparison here to be unordered. (`opt::normalize_pred` canonicalizes the same pair in the Rust
engine for the same reason.)

### Consumers: the same seven as item 1269, same dispositions

`satisfies` and `hasPredicate` patched; `mergeFarPreds` patched and pinned by a test that answers 1
where a dropped list answers 2; `hop-projection`'s lift check patched; `rejectedByElementDirect` and
the two `matching.ts` `preFilter` gates deliberately left alone, because that pre-filter runs before
the binding is built and may only ever say "not decided" (item 644's revert is the precedent).
`shortcuts.ts`' `InlinePred` is covered through `inlineHolds` -> `satisfies`.

The lift runs LAST among the lifted families, beside `memberProps`: a null test cannot raise, so
running it before the families that can would let a FALSE test return early and swallow a sibling's
raise.

### Teeth: 7 mutants, 7 caught — after the ordering mutant exposed a flaw in my own test

```text

  satisfies-skips-nulls               CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  reject-condition-inverted           CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  negated-not-flipped                 CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  has-predicate-omits-nulls           CAUGHT  the ROUTE test's `hasPredicate` assertion
  not-arm-removed                     CAUGHT  the ROUTE test (answer-equivalent otherwise)
  nulls-run-before-raising-families   CAUGHT  the raise-order test — after it was FIXED
```

⚠️ THE ORDERING MUTANT SURVIVED THE FIRST RUN, and the reason is worth keeping. The raise-order test
used `WHERE n.s AND n.k IS NOT NULL`, where ONE vertex passes the null test and then reaches the
raising conjunct — so the query raises whatever the order is, and the test could not see the move.
The discriminating shape needs the null test to reject EVERY vertex: `WHERE n.s AND n.s IS NULL`
matches nothing, so under the wrong order every row is rejected before the raise and the query
answers 0 instead of erroring. Same lesson as item 1267's product case — a guard needs the fixture
that makes it load-bearing, and only mutation says whether it has one.

### Item 1271 — parenthesising a conjunction cost 2.14x, and the note explaining why it was left alone had the right facts and the wrong conclusion (DONE)

`directEqProps` declines its WHOLE chain on the first conjunct it cannot read, and a NESTED `and`
was one of those. The note it carried:

> A nested `and` under an `and` is not flattened here — it declines below as a non-`compare`
> conjunct. The parser produces one flat `items` list for `a AND b AND c`, so the nested shape
> arrives only from parenthesisation, and declining it is a missed optimisation, not a wrong answer.

Both halves are true. The conclusion is wrong twice over: a cost that PARENTHESES alone turn on is
this engine's named bug class, and it was the most expensive decline left in the function. 200,000
vertices, one process, TS estimator rule, all three answering an identical 2000:

```text
  shape                      before    after    ns/vertex        ratio
  a=50 AND b=0 AND c=0        3.558 ms  3.641    17.8 -> 18.2     control, flat already
  (a=50 AND b=0) AND c=0      7.615     3.471    38.1 -> 17.4     2.19x
  a=50 AND (b=0 AND c=0)      6.732     3.740    33.7 -> 18.7     1.80x
  [CTL] a <> 50               3.859     3.839    19.3 -> 19.2
  [CTL] a = 50                3.468     3.655    17.3 -> 18.3
  [CTL] bare count(*)         0.001     0.001
```

The spread across the bracketings closes from **2.14x to 1.08x**.

The flatten is depth-first and left to right, so the conjuncts arrive in WRITTEN order — the same
order the flat spelling produces. That is load-bearing rather than tidy: this loop groups what it
lifts into families, so arrival order is the order a RAISE is reached in, and a flatten that
reordered could change which query errors. A test asserts the order directly (`[a, b, c]` for both
nestings) because no answer can see it, and the mutation run confirms that is the only thing that
can: `flatten-reverses-order` is caught by that assertion alone.

```text
  flatten-removed            CAUGHT  the ROUTE test (answer-equivalent otherwise)
  flatten-keeps-first-only   CAUGHT  existing AND short-circuit tests — a SUPERSET
  flatten-reverses-order     CAUGHT  the ROUTE test's written-order assertion
  flatten-descends-or        CAUGHT  existing seed-hint + Kleene-law tests — a disjunction
                                     treated as conjuncts is a wrong answer
```

### Two of my own test errors, fixed before the run

The "different families" case expected 2 and the answer is 3 — `a = 1 AND c > 2 AND b IS NOT NULL`
keeps three vertices, not two, because only `nulled` and `absent` fail the null test. And the
hand-built unliftable conjunct used `arith` with `left`/`right` where the node is `head`/`tail`,
which crashed `compileExpr` rather than declining. Both were my fixtures being wrong about the
engine, not the engine being wrong.

### Still open from the same pricing run

`NOT (a = 50)` costs 6.467 ms against `a <> 50`'s 3.859 — **1.68x**, same answer (198000). `NOT` of
a compare is neither a bare prop nor a compare, so it declines the chain, while `<>` lifts. The fix
is to invert the operator, and it must be EQUALITY-ONLY: `NOT (x >= 2)` is not `x < 2` when `x` is
NaN (this repo keeps NaN JS-unordered, so the negation is TRUE where the flip is FALSE) — the same
restriction `opt::normalize_pred` carries in the Rust engine, and the reason item 1262's rewrite is
equality-only there. `=`/`<>` are exact under negation for NULL (UNKNOWN both ways) and for NaN
(TRUE both ways). Recorded as the next target rather than folded in here, because it needs that
argument tested rather than asserted.

### Item 1272 — `NOT (k = v)` lifts by flipping the operator, 1.65x, and the NaN hole that keeps it equality-only is now DEMONSTRATED rather than argued (DONE)

Item 1271's pricing run left this open. `NOT` of a compare is neither a bare `prop` nor a `compare`,
so `directEqProps` declined the whole chain on it, while the `<>` spelling of the same question
lifted into `cmpProps`. 200,000 vertices, one process, TS estimator rule:

```text
  shape                      before    after    ns/vertex        answer
  NOT (a = 50)                6.467 ms  3.916    32.3 -> 19.6     198000     1.65x
  NOT (a <> 50)                  —      3.206            16.0     2000
  [CTL] a <> 50               3.859     3.631    19.3 -> 18.2     198000
  [CTL] a = 50                3.468     3.193    17.3 -> 16.0     2000
  [CTL] NOT (a >= 50)         6.467     6.172            30.9     100000     EXCLUDED
  [CTL] a < 50                   —      4.334            21.7     100000
  [CTL] bare count(*)         0.001     0.001
```

Both negated equalities now land on their positive twins (3.916 against 3.631; 3.206 against
3.193), and the EXCLUDED ordering shape did not move — which is the control that proves the
restriction is still in force.

This change adds no new carrier: it reuses `eqProps` and `cmpProps`, so unlike items 1269 and 1270
there is no `hasPredicate`, no `mergeFarPreds` and no consumer audit to get wrong.

### ⚠️ THE EQUALITY-ONLY RESTRICTION IS A WRONG ANSWER, NOT A MISSED OPTIMISATION — and it is reachable

The argument is the one `opt::normalize_pred` carries natively (item 1262): `NOT (x >= 2)` is not
`x < 2`, because every ordering comparison against NaN is FALSE here, so the negation is TRUE where
the flip is FALSE. What was not obvious is whether that is REACHABLE in the TS engine at all — a
stored NaN becomes null on ingest (the numeric model), so there is no NaN cell to trip over.

A NaN **param** is not coerced, and that makes it reachable. Measured, then pinned as a test:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE NOT (n.k >= $x) RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  2
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k < $x        RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  0
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE NOT (n.k = $x)  RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  2
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k <> $x       RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  2
```

So widening the flip table to `>=` would make the first query answer 0 instead of 2, silently, on a
shape a user can write today. Equality has no such hole: `= NaN` is FALSE, its negation TRUE, and
`<>` answers TRUE too.

(2 and not 4 on a four-vertex fixture, because `nulled` and `absent` are UNKNOWN under both
spellings and a filter keeps only TRUE — they drop either way and cannot be what distinguishes them.
That arithmetic was wrong in the first draft of the test and is now written down beside it.)

```text
                                      ROUTE test — verified separately, since a route assertion
                                      alone would not show what the widening COSTS
  flip-is-identity            CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  negated-arm-removed         CAUGHT  the ROUTE test (answer-equivalent otherwise)
  negated-eq-family-swapped   CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
```

### The enum, after five items

`directEqProps` now admits: a bare `prop`, `NOT prop`, a `compare` (equality and ordering), a dotted
compare, a membership (`IN` / `=`-OR-chain, item 1269), a null test (`IS [NOT] NULL` and
`NOT (… IS NULL)`, item 1270), a nested `and` (item 1271), and `NOT` of an equality (this item).
What it still declines, in rough order of how likely a user is to write it: `xor`, `isTruth`
(`x IS TRUE`), `isLabeled`, a function call (`startsWith(n.s, 'x')`), an arithmetic operand
(`n.a + 1 = 2`), a dotted NEGATED compare, and `NOT IN`. None of these has been priced.

### Item 1273 — the string half of item 1267 is REFUTED: the seek is already the better route there (RETRACTED)

Item 1267 recorded it as presumably the same gap: "a `Str`/`Dict` column under an unindexed

stays a `Filter(Scan)`):

```text
  column                      seek    range spelling   answer
  `lo`, 50 values (Dict)     0.136 ms     0.141         4000
  `hi`, 200k values (Str)    0.157        0.549         1
```

The seek is already as fast or 3.5x FASTER. The reason is the one thing item 1267 could not have

### Item 1274 — creating an index made a 10%-selectivity count 9.5x SLOWER, and the fix is a measured cost gate (DONE)

The other thing item 1267 left open, in its own words: "at 1% selectivity the unindexed SWEEP (0.028)
now beats the INDEXED seek count (0.036) ... For a far more selective value the index must win.
Neither end is measured, so the preference stays index-first — but it is now a known unmeasured
assumption rather than an obvious one." Both ends are now measured, and the assumption was wrong over
a whole band.

200,000 nodes, the same query against two stores differing only by the index, min of 9 over three
alternated rounds, answers identical by construction and printed:

```text
  matches     sweep   index seek   before            after
        1     0.029      0.003     index 11.4x       index kept, 11.1x
       20     0.028      0.003     index 10.0x       index kept,  9.9x
      200     0.028      0.005     index  5.3x       index kept,  5.3x
     2000     0.028      0.029     tie               tie
     4000     0.028      0.056     SWEEP  2.0x       0.026  -> 2.0x better
    20000     0.028      0.268     SWEEP  9.5x       0.026  -> 9.2x better
   100000     0.028      0.029     tie               tie
```

So merely CREATING an index cost a 10%-selectivity count 9.5x. The sweep is flat in how many rows
match, because it is O(label) and vectorized; the index path pays a label binary-search and a `Vec`
push per candidate, which is linear in the bucket.

### Why the hole was there, and why the fix is not in the optimizer

The optimizer has a selectivity gate of its own and it DOES decline a seek at 50% — verified by
dumping the plan rather than inferred, which is also what explained the non-monotonic row (20,000
slow, 100,000 fine):

```text
  k = <10% value>  ->  IndexSeek
  k = <50% value>  ->  Filter(..)
  k = <1 row>      ->  IndexSeek
```

So this band was the hole between that gate and the seek's execution. The fix lives in the COUNT arm
deliberately: the optimizer's gate also serves row-PRODUCING queries, where a seek avoids touching
the rows it skips and the trade is different. Nothing about those shapes was measured, so nothing
about them changes.

`index_bucket_len` is O(1) and prices a RANGE index as well as a hash one ("its bucket for one key
IS the equality bucket"), so one call covers both kinds and a range-indexed selective key keeps its
point probe.

### The threshold is derived, not tuned

The sweep reads 0.14 ns a node (0.028 ms over 200,000, flat). The index path grows 0.029 -> 0.268 ms
between 2,000 and 20,000 matches: 13.3 ns a candidate. 13.3/0.14 is ~95, so the two cost the same at
a bucket of label/95 — and the measured tie is at 2,000 of 200,000. The constant is 96 because that
is the ratio, and the unit test pins the boundary at N and N-1 (2,083 keeps the index, 2,084 sweeps).

### ⚠️ `saturating_mul` WAS WRONG IN THE CORNER IT WAS THERE FOR

The first cut was `bucket.saturating_mul(96) > label`, with a comment claiming saturation gives
"sweep" for a pathological bucket. My own overflow assertion rejected it: at
`bucket == label == usize::MAX` both sides saturate to `usize::MAX`, the comparison is FALSE, and it
answers "use the index" for a bucket that is the whole graph. Dividing the label instead cannot
overflow and gets that corner right. The two forms agree everywhere reachable, since a bucket is a
subset of the label.

### Teeth: 6 mutants, 6 caught — two only after the tests were made able to see them

```text
  threshold-inverted           CAUGHT  the pure boundary test + the answer test
  threshold-off-by-a-factor    CAUGHT  the pure boundary test (96 -> 8)
  gate-always-sweeps           CAUGHT  both
  gate-never-sweeps            CAUGHT  both
  no-index-stops-sweeping      CAUGHT  after the `None` mapping was FOLDED INTO the pure function
  label-len-uses-whole-graph   CAUGHT  after the fixture was given a strict-subset label
```

Both late ones are the same lesson as items 1267 and 1270: a guard needs the fixture that makes it
load-bearing.

- `no-index-stops-sweeping` — mapping "no index" to "use the seek" throws away item 1267's 4.75x and
  is ANSWER-EQUIVALENT, and item 1267's route test only asserts that `try_scan_count` CLAIMS the
  shape, which it still does via the slower branch. Moving the `None` arm inside
  `seek_count_sweeps` made it a unit-testable decision.
- `label-len-uses-whole-graph` — the denominator must be the LABEL bucket, since a sweep visits the
  label; pricing against the whole graph over-estimates the sweep and keeps the index past the
  crossover. The assertion could not see it while every node in the fixture carried the same label,
  because the two counts were then the same number. 1,000 `Q` nodes make them differ.

`bun run check` 0.

### Item 1275 — the index-vs-scan hole is COUNT-ONLY: row-producing queries never lose, so item 1274's scoping was right (measurement only)

Item 1274 fixed the count arm and scoped the rest out in writing: "the optimizer's gate also serves
row-PRODUCING queries, where a seek avoids touching the rows it skips and the trade is different.
Nothing about those shapes was measured, so nothing about them changes." That left an open question
with real stakes — if a projection also loses to its unindexed self at some selectivity, the same
hole exists one level up, in the optimizer's own gate, and affects far more shapes than a count.

It does not. 200,000 nodes, the same query against two stores differing only by the index, min of 9
over three alternated rounds, row counts identical and printed:

```text
  RETURN b.p                      RETURN b.k, b.p                 RETURN b.p ORDER BY p
  matches  no index  INDEXED      no index  INDEXED                no index  INDEXED
        1    0.126    0.002  77x     0.126    0.002  66x              0.127    0.002  71x
      200    0.146    0.021  7.0x    0.151    0.027  5.6x             0.152    0.027  5.7x
     2000    0.308    0.212  1.45x   0.396    0.279  1.42x            0.393    0.289  1.36x
     4000    0.509    0.434  1.17x   0.647    0.568  1.14x            0.538    0.458  1.17x
    20000    1.941    2.092  0.93x   2.634    2.756  0.96x            2.890    3.034  0.95x
   100000   10.153   10.293  0.99x  14.129   14.167  1.00x           16.150   16.192  1.00x
```

The index wins or ties everywhere, and the worst case is a consistent **0.93-0.96x at 20,000
matches** across all three shapes — a 5-7% loss, which is below this repo's own "anything under ~10%
needs its own isolated harness" line and three orders of magnitude off the 9.5x the count had.
Recorded as a small consistent negative rather than claimed as a finding.

### The mechanism, which is why the count was the exception rather than the first of many

A row-producing query must touch every surviving row whatever route it took, so the seek's
per-candidate cost (a label binary-search and a `Vec` push) is amortised against work the scan also
does. The count was the one shape where the sweep had NO per-row cost to amortise against — it is
O(label) and vectorized and produces nothing — so the seek's per-candidate cost stood alone and
dominated above ~1% selectivity.

So the hole was specific to the shape item 1274 fixed, the optimizer's general gate is sound for
everything else measured here, and the scoping decision is now evidenced rather than assumed.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

### It is NOT a missing path. TS already uses degree algebra.

The tempting read is that native answers these by degree arithmetic while TS enumerates — 5M paths
for the 2-hop, 25M for the 3-hop. `twoSegmentCount` says otherwise in its own comment ("unfiltered
stays on the degree product: it iterates the MIDDLE once and multiplies two degrees"), and the
measurement agrees. V HELD FIXED at 100,000, degree varied, so paths grow while vertices do not:

```text
  degree   edges    2-hop ms   3-hop ms   4-hop ms   2-hop paths   3-hop paths
       2   200k        25.76      76.68      81.13       400,000       800,000
       4   400k        20.22      97.95      73.60     1,600,000     6,400,000
       8   800k        20.86     151.16      84.73     6,400,000    51,200,000
```

2-hop and 4-hop are FLAT while their path counts grow 16x and 64x; the 3-hop grows 2x for a 64x path
increase. Nothing here is O(paths). So the whole family is already algorithmic, and the gap is a
CONSTANT FACTOR — ~209 ns a middle vertex against native's ~14 for the 2-hop. That is the layout
ceiling this repo has priced twice before (item 234: "the big ratio was data layout, not overhead";
item 573's warning is the converse and does not apply, because the algorithm here is not the
difference).

⚠️ SO THE 341 ms ON `count 4-hop` IS NOT A LEVER, and anyone ranking the field by absolute gap will
land on it first. 209 ns for two cached map lookups and a multiply is still more than it should be,
and it is recorded as not-a-lever rather than attempted.

⚠️ AMENDED, SAME SESSION: this entry first named item 164 (hash order against creation order) as "the
one open suspect". That is WRONG on two counts and the correction matters more than the guess did.
`verticesById` is a JS `Map`, which iterates in INSERTION order, so the product's middle walk is
already in creation order — item 164's finding was about iterating the EDGE index and gathering
vertices from it, a different walk. And the obvious follow-up, giving the product the cached
per-vertex adjacency box (`Vertex.adjFrom`/`adjTo`, items 162/321) in place of `side`'s id hash, is
ALREADY REFUTED at the site: `sideOfVertex` exists for exactly that, and its header records why
`side` itself does not take a Vertex — **item 355 measured it, and the box is a MEMO, so first touch
is 1.21x WORSE** (the same hash plus the memo write) while warm is 1.35x better. The two-hop product
visits each middle exactly ONCE per query, so cold is all it would ever get.

`side`'s own header then attributes what is left: "This is most of the two-hop count family ... The
gap it leaves is still the CSR's (items 300, 348, 350, 352)." Which is the same conclusion this item
reached from the other end, and it means the family is closed at the call-site level and open only
as a STORAGE change that has been declined four times.

The lesson is about where I looked. The pointer was already in reach — `count 4-hop` is recorded as
item 300's declined CSR — and I re-derived it from the sweep instead of reading that first. CLAUDE.md
names this exact failure ("three passes in one session re-derived a closed target ... each pass
searched something first and searched the wrong store"). Reading the code AT the site is what caught
it, which is the right order, but the cheaper order was `CLOSED.md` first.

### ⚠️ A FALSE INVERSION I nearly reported, caught by checking the fixture

The sweep looks like it contains a spelling inversion — adding a predicate making a query FASTER:

```text
  count 2-hop               112.8 ms      count 2-hop + mid filter        46.3
  count 3-hop               323.5         count 3-hop + interior filter  115.1
```

It is not one. `age` is `i % 90` and the filter is `age > 60`, so it keeps 29/90 ≈ 32% of middles,
and 112.8 × 0.32 ≈ 36 is the 46.3 observed. The filtered row is cheaper because it is SELECTIVE,
which is exactly the trap item 1263 retracted a whole target for. Checking the fixture's own
statistics before believing the ratio is the rule that caught it.

### Settled on the way: a fixed-length chain counts WALKS, not trails

Needed because it decides whether a degree product is sound at all, and answered from the engines
rather than assumed. A 2-cycle `a <-> b` separates the two readings — `a->b->a->b` reuses an edge, so
it is a walk of length 3 and not a trail:

```text
  MATCH (p)-[:T]->(q)-[:T]->(r)-[:T]->(s) RETURN count(*)   ->  2     (WALK; a trail answers 0)
```

Both engines answer 2, with or without named edge variables. So edge reuse is permitted on a fixed
chain, the degree product is exact for it, and the `reusedTrailsAt3` correction belongs to the
QUANTIFIED shapes the sweep lists separately.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1277 — item 402's "do not fix this in one line" is right about the trap and wrong about the conclusion: TWO of the four spellings are a sound pure SEED, because the range index carries NaN at the top (measurement only)

`CLOSED.md` §5 carries this as open, priced at 10.7x:

> **OPEN, with the trap named — `NOT (k <= v)` scans where `k > v` seeks, 10.7x (402).** The obvious
> rewrite is WRONG under this engine's NaN rule: with `k = NaN`, `NaN <= v` is false so the `NOT`
> form is TRUE, while `k > v` is FALSE. A range seek would silently drop those rows. A correct
> rewrite is `(k > v) OR isNaN(k)`, which is not a pure seek. Do not "fix" this in one line.

Everything in that is correct except the last inference, and the thing that changes it is a property
of the INDEX rather than of the predicate.

### First: the trap is real, and reachable, and I had the wrong reason for doubting it

The hypothesis worth testing was that a NaN CELL cannot exist — this project's numeric model coerces
`NaN`/`Inf`/`undefined` to null. That is the HOST ingest path, not the native store:

```text
  Builder: node k = NaN  ->  Column::Num  present=[t,t,t]  nulls=[f,f,f]  data=[1.0, 9.0, NaN]
  MATCH (a:P) WHERE NOT (a.k <= 5) RETURN count(*)  ->  2      (the 9.0 AND the NaN)
  MATCH (a:P) WHERE a.k > 5        RETURN count(*)  ->  1      (the 9.0 alone)
```

So a NaN sits in a `Num` column as a PRESENT, non-null cell, and the two spellings genuinely differ.
Item 402's trap stands on its own numbers.

### Then: a SEED only needs a SUPERSET, and the range index's total order supplies one

A range index is a `BTreeMap<OrdVal, _>` ordered by `cmp_total`, where NaN sorts LAST. So an UPWARD
seek already returns the NaN rows. Measured, ids 0=1.0 1=9.0 2=NaN 3=+inf:

```text
  range_lookup(Gt, 5)    -> [1, 3, 2]    the NaN row IS returned
  range_lookup(Ge, 5)    -> [1, 3, 2]
  range_lookup(Lt, 5)    -> [0]          NaN excluded — correct, it sorts after 5
  range_lookup(Le, 5)    -> [0]
  range_lookup(Gt, NaN)  -> []           EMPTY, and this is the case a seed must decline
```

That makes the four spellings split, and the split is the result:

```text
  spelling          match set              seed    sound?
  NOT (k <= v)      {k > v}  ∪ {NaN}       Gt v    YES — and EXACTLY equal, not merely a superset
  NOT (k < v)       {k >= v} ∪ {NaN}       Ge v    YES
  NOT (k >= v)      {k < v}  ∪ {NaN}       Lt v    NO — the seek drops the NaN rows
  NOT (k > v)       {k <= v} ∪ {NaN}       Le v    NO
```

The asymmetry is entirely NaN's position in the total order: the upward seeks sweep the tail that
holds it, the downward ones stop before it. `NOT (k <= v)` — the spelling item 402 names — is one of
the two sound ones.

### What implementing it requires, decided but NOT built here

- Admit `Not(Compare { Le | Lt })` to `range_seek_target`'s family, mapping to `Gt`/`Ge`. REFUSE
  `Not(Compare { Ge | Gt })`: those are the two that drop NaN.
- DECLINE A NaN BOUND. `range_lookup(Gt, NaN)` is empty, so seeding a NaN bound turns "every row
  matches" into "no rows" — the same hazard in the other direction. A literal is checkable at plan
  time; a param is not, which likely means declining the param spelling or resolving per execution.
- ⚠️ KEEP THE CONJUNCT IN THE RESIDUAL. `seed_from_conjuncts` DROPS the picked conjunct
  (`filter(|(i, _)| *i != pick)`) because an ordinary `k > v` seek is exact, and this seed must not
  inherit that. The match sets above are exactly equal for a pure `Num` column, but a range index
  also holds STRINGS, and a cross-type `NOT (k <= 5)` on a string cell is a THROW in this engine
  rather than a match — so dropping the predicate would swallow an error the general path raises.
  Re-validating is cheap (the seed is selective) and it is what makes the change a seed rather than
  a rewrite.

That last point is why item 402's "not a pure seek" verdict is half right: as a REWRITE of the
predicate it is not, and as a SEED with the predicate retained it is — for two of the four spellings.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1278 — item 1277's "two of the four are sound" is REFUTED: the seed was built, measured at 12.7x/16.6x, and the NaN test rejected it. Item 402 is right for a DEEPER reason than it recorded (REVERTED, guard kept)

Item 1277 priced item 402's 10.7x gap and argued a way past its trap: a SEED only needs a SUPERSET,
and the range index is a `BTreeMap` keyed by `cmp_total` where NaN sorts LAST — so an upward seek
sweeps the tail that holds the NaN rows. That was verified at the STORE level and is true:

```text
  range_lookup(Gt, 5)   -> [9.0, +inf, NaN]     the NaN row IS returned
```

The seed was built on that basis, with the predicate kept above the seek (the same shape
`prefix_interval`'s arm uses), and it WORKED as a cost change — 200,000 nodes, a range index on `k`,
min of 9 over three alternated rounds:

```text
  shape                         PRE      POST    answer
  NOT (k <= 199000)   SOUND?   0.293 ms  0.023    999      12.7x
  NOT (k < 199000)    SOUND?   0.381     0.023   1000      16.6x
  [CTL] k > 199000   (exact)   0.017     0.019    999
  [CTL] NOT (k >= 1000) refused 0.281    0.307   1000      unchanged, by design
  [CTL] bare count(*)          0.002     0.002
```

### ⚠️ AND IT IS WRONG. The operator filters the NaN rows back out, ON PURPOSE.

The NaN test caught it immediately: the INDEXED store answered **2** where the UNINDEXED oracle
answers **3**. `range_seek_ids` re-checks every candidate the index hands it, and its own comment
states the rule:

> The index orders by the TOTAL order (cross-type by rank), but the OPERATOR is three-valued
> (cross-type → UNKNOWN → drop). Re-check each candidate with `range_pass` so an indexed seek
> returns exactly the scan-filter rows (the equivalent-spellings invariant).

A NaN cell under `Gt` is UNKNOWN there, so it drops. **No `RangeSeek` can produce a NaN row**, which
means the superset argument is unavailable no matter what the index's order does — and item 402's
"do not fix this in one line" is right for a stronger reason than it gave. It is not that a range
seek _happens_ to miss those rows; it is that the operator is _designed_ to return exactly the
scan-filter set, and the NaN rows are not in it.

That also closes the entry's suggested shape. `(k > v) OR isNaN(k)` cannot be a seek plus a filter:
it needs a UNION of a `RangeSeek` with a separate seek for the NaN bucket, which is a different and
much larger change than the 10.7x justifies.

### What I got wrong, and the layer I skipped

Item 1277 verified `range_lookup` — the STORE API — and inferred the operator from it. The operator
is a layer up and does not inherit that behaviour. This is the same error as items 1260, 1264, 1267
and 1269 in a new place: **verify the layer that actually serves the query, not the one below it.**
The difference this time is that the error was caught by a test written BEFORE the measurement was
trusted, rather than by a reviewer or by CI.

### The guard is kept, and it has teeth

`a_not_range_predicate_is_not_seeded_from_a_range_index` asserts both halves:

- the ANSWERS, with the unindexed store as the oracle — `NOT (k <= 5)` is 3 (9.0, +inf and NaN)
  against the exact twin's 2, which is the whole difference a seed would erase;
- the ROUTE — both sound-looking spellings must stay on a `Filter(Scan)` even with a range index
  present, because re-introducing the seed is ANSWER-EQUIVALENT on any fixture without a NaN.

Verified in both directions: with the seed re-applied the test FAILS at the route assertion; without
it, it passes. Three lines of fixture (a NaN, a `+inf`, a null and an absent cell) is what the next
attempt will run into, and the next attempt is likely — the index's order genuinely does carry NaN,
so the idea looks sound right up to the operator.

Gates: 1348 + 13 + 725 Rust tests green, `clippy -D warnings` 0, `cargo fmt --check` 0,
`bun run check` 0. `rewrite_fuzz` not re-run: `opt.rs`'s net diff is EMPTY (verified with
`git diff --stat`), so there is no rewrite to fuzz — the only change is the test.

### Item 1280 — NO TWIN: the TS count has no index-vs-sweep hole, and the reason unifies both engines into one formula (measurement only)

Item 1274 fixed a hole in the NATIVE count: above ~1% selectivity, merely CREATING an index made it
up to 9.5x slower, because the sweep is O(label) and VECTORIZED while the index path pays a label
binary-search and a `Vec` push per candidate. The method's own next step is to grep that pattern
across engines, and item 1274 did not. This does.

TS has a seek gate (item 409's `seekIsWorthIt`) but it is general, and item 1274's point was that a
COUNT differs from a row-producing query because the sweep has no per-row cost to amortise against.
So the question was live. 200,000 nodes, the same query against two graphs differing only by the
index, 14 reps / drop 3 / median, min over three alternated rounds, answers identical:

```text
  matches     no index    INDEXED   winner
        1       3.132      0.001    INDEX  3820x
      200       3.106      0.005    INDEX   592x
     2000       3.113      0.046    INDEX    67x
     4000       3.102      0.092    INDEX    34x
    20000       3.182      0.463    INDEX   6.87x
   100000       3.439      3.665    tie     0.94x
```

The index wins at every selectivity and only ties at 50%. **No twin — nothing to fix.**

### The reason is ONE FORMULA, and it is the transferable part

The crossover sits where `bucket × (cost per index candidate) = label × (cost per swept node)`, i.e.
at a selectivity of `(cost per swept node) / (cost per candidate)`:

```text
  engine   swept node   index candidate   predicted crossover   measured
  native      0.14 ns        13.3 ns            ~1%             tie at 2,000/200,000
  TS         15.5 ns        23-37 ns           ~42-67%          tie at 100,000/200,000
```

TS's unindexed count is FLAT in selectivity (3.102-3.439 ms across a 100,000x range of match counts)
because it is a per-node loop at ~15.5 ns, which is ~110x native's vectorized 0.14. **That is the
whole reason the hole is native-only**: item 1274's gap exists BECAUSE the sweep is vectorized. The
better a sweep gets, the LOWER the selectivity at which its own index starts losing to it — so this
is a hole to re-check whenever a sweep is made faster, not a one-off.

Recorded as the rule rather than as a TS target, since there is no TS change to make.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1281 — `IN $p` costs 1.34x `IN [literal]`, and both candidate fixes are rejected: the faster one can be silently WRONG (priced, declined)

Item 1269 left this open in its own table and this prices it properly. Both spellings lift into
`memberProps`; the difference is inside `membershipTest`, which hashes an all-LITERAL haystack once
at COMPILE time but a closed non-literal one once per EXECUTION. 200,000 vertices, TS estimator rule,
three alternated rounds, every row answering 2000 or 8000:

```text
  shape                      ms     ns/vertex   vs literal
  IN [50]       literal     3.978     19.9        —
  IN $p         param       5.344     26.7       1.34x
  IN [$a]       list-of-param 4.312   21.6       1.08x
  IN [50..53]   literal     4.290     21.5        —
  IN $p4        param       5.063     25.3       1.18x
  [CTL] age = 50            3.328     16.6        —
  [CTL] age = $a            3.458     17.3       1.04x
```

⚠️ THE `eqProps` CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES THIS A FINDING: a parameter costs the EQUALITY path 1.04x,
i.e. nothing. So the penalty is not "params are slower" — it is specific to the membership path's
per-execution arm, whose per-element closure reads three captured mutables (`epoch`, `hay`,
`hashed`) and branches, where the literal arm reads one captured constant and calls `hashedIn`.

Item 184 is why it is worth pricing at all: "binding the list keeps values out of the query text, so
`IN $names` is the injection-safe form and `IN […]` with inline literals is the rare one." The
faster spelling is the one nobody should write.

### Both fixes rejected, and the second one is the interesting rejection

**(a) Micro-optimise the closure.** There is nothing to remove. The cost IS the epoch test and the
captured reads, and they exist to detect that the parameter changed. Specialising the inner call
after resolution (assigning a monomorphic `test`) keeps the epoch test and adds an indirect call.
Identity-keying the param array instead of the epoch is the same compare in a different type — and
item 269 already refuted identity-keying for the LIST form at 2.9x, because `case 'list'` rebuilds
its array per row.

**(b) Resolve ONCE per scan, via a `prepare(env)` hook on `CPredicate`.** This is the fix that would
work: the per-element closure would then be identical to the literal arm's. It is rejected because
of what it would cost in correctness, not in effort. `execEpoch` is bumped once per plan invocation
and the memo is keyed on it, so the current design **cannot go stale** — a predicate re-used across
executions re-resolves automatically. A `prepare` hook moves that obligation onto every caller that
applies a predicate in a loop, which is the same multi-consumer set items 1269 and 1270 had to audit
(`satisfies`, `inlineHolds`, `mergeFarPreds`, two `preFilter` gates, `rejectedByElementDirect`) — and
a caller that forgets the call reads a haystack from a PREVIOUS execution. That is a silent WRONG
ANSWER on a shape that returns a plausible count, traded for 1.34x on one spelling.

A self-healing memo that is 1.34x slow beats a faster one that can be forgotten. Recorded so the
gap is not re-priced as an oversight.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

```text
  equality count  (2,000 kept)   3.259      2.428     0.75x   Gremlin FASTER
  has(k, gt(-1))  (200,000)      3.846      2.453     0.64x   Gremlin FASTER
  has(k) presence (200,000)      3.406      6.842     2.01x   Gremlin slower
  values(k)       (200,000)      3.409      9.857     2.89x   Gremlin slower
  bare label count               0.001      0.001
```

The first pass compared equality (2,000 survivors) against presence (200,000) — which is the trap

against presence's 6.842**. So at MATCHED selectivity and identical answers, Gremlin's presence path

A second reading falls out: `values(k).count()` is 9.857, SLOWER than `has(k)`'s 6.842 — which
INVERTS item 1139's recorded ordering, where `values` was the fast spelling (104-108 ms against
`has`'s 172-189). Whatever item 1140 changed, the two spellings have swapped places since.

### Located: ONE detector of four got item 1140's conversion

`has('k')` with one argument builds `{kind:'hasKey'}`, not `{kind:'has'}`. Item 1140 taught
`hasChain` to convert a single-key `hasKey` into a synthetic `{kind:'has', pred:{op:'present'}}` —
and that is the ONLY site in `count-shortcut.ts` that mentions `hasKey` at all. Its sibling
detectors each test `step.kind !== 'has'` against RAW steps and decline:

```text
  count-shortcut.ts:392    hasChain            CONVERTS (item 1140)
  count-shortcut.ts:1177   multi-hop vfilters  declines a raw hasKey
  count-shortcut.ts:1806   (same shape)        declines
  count-shortcut.ts:1904   (same shape)        declines
  count-shortcut.ts:1925   (same shape)        declines
```

So item 1140 is itself an instance of the class it cites: it fixed one spelling in one place and the
siblings kept scanning. **The fix is to extract that conversion into one shared reader every
detector calls**, rather than to repeat the `if (step.kind === 'hasKey')` block four times — the
drift is the defect, and four copies would re-create it.

Not built here: four detectors plus a shared helper needs its own mutation pass (each detector is
answer-equivalent, so a route test per rung is what gives it teeth), and the measurement above is
the part worth having first. Recorded with the location so the next tick is implementation.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

the rest is now sound where it previously was not, and that is the next step rather than this one."
`residual` was dead plumbing kept for exactly this.

This subsumes the seven leaf variants item 1272 listed as unpriced (`xor`, `isTruth`, `isLabeled`, a
function call, an arithmetic operand, a dotted negated compare, `NOT IN`) — the cost was never in
the leaf, it was in what the leaf did to its siblings.

marker count before running. The unliftable conjunct is `n.a >= n.a`: true for every present row, so
answers are identical, and it cannot raise.

```text

  target   a=50 AND <unliftable>     9.353 ->  4.053    2.31x
                                     6.966 ->  3.806    1.83x
                                     9.127 ->  3.981    2.29x

                                    11.494 -> 11.227    flat
  [CTL]    <unliftable> alone       14.995 -> 14.819    flat
  [CTL]    a=50 alone (all-lift)     3.049 ->  3.013    flat
```

The claim is the conservative **1.8x** against a typical 2.3x. The spread across the four isolated

### ⚠️ THE PREFIX RULE ALONE IS A WRONG ANSWER, and the cross-engine test found it

The first cut lifted any prefix, on the argument that the lifted families run before the residual so
executed order IS written order. That argument is sound and the conclusion was still wrong, because
the generic route does not evaluate in written order either — it lets FALSE dominate. So a bare
`prop`, whose truth-reading RAISES on a non-boolean, raises once lifted where the whole-chain route
suppressed it. `packages/native/src/and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts` caught it as a TS-vs-native
divergence, which is precisely the guard item 259 left behind:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.s AND false             native ok []   TS ok []  ->  ERR E_INVALID_VALUE
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.s AND n.n IS UNKNOWN    native ok []   TS ok []  ->  ERR E_INVALID_VALUE
```

So with a residual present, only the families that CANNOT raise may lift: `eq` (equality is total —
a cross-type `=` answers no-match), `nulls` (`isNullish` returns a plain boolean) and `member` (built
on equality). `truth`, `notTruth`, `cmp` and `path` are held back, `cmp`/`path` because an ordering
comparison DOES throw on a cross-type pair, so a residual that would have settled the row to FALSE
first is load-bearing there too.

A fully-admitted chain is untouched: it has no residual, every conjunct lifts, and item 259 covers
the ordering among families. The guard is therefore conditioned on `residual !== undefined`, and a
mutant that drops that condition is caught by a control asserting the families still lift when the
chain is complete.

**This is where the 1.8-2.3x actually lives anyway** — the target shape is an `eq` prefix — so the
restriction costs nothing measured. But it is the second time in two items that the instrument was
right and the reasoning was not.

### Only a PREFIX lifts, and a tail that reads another variable still declines

Two further restrictions, each with a test that fails if it is widened:

- **Prefix only.** The lifted families run before the residual, so lifting a prefix cannot make any
  conjunct overtake another — executed order IS written order. Lifting out of the middle would
  reorder, so that is a separate item, not a wider `stop`.
- **The tail must read only `ownVar`.** Callers pass an `ownVar` having PROVED the predicate
  element-local, so a tail reading `m` should not arrive — but the three sites that evaluate a
  residual (`relOnlyHopCount` and the two `startLifted` gates) bind only the element's own variable,
  so such a tail would be evaluated against a binding with no `m`. Keeping the old route there costs
  nothing measured, because the 1.8x is a tail on the element's OWN variable.

The second restriction is why `direct-eq-props-param.test.ts`'s existing guard — "a conjunct on
ANOTHER variable declines the WHOLE chain" — **passes unchanged**. That it kept its teeth without
being rewritten is the evidence the restriction is the right shape; only the `upper(n.s)` test was
superseded, updated the way item 278 updated two of its neighbours.

### ⚠️ THIS ENGINE ALREADY DOES NOT PRESERVE RAISE ORDER, measured on both arms

The ordering test was written expecting `CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) = 1 AND n.a = 999` to throw, since the
raiser is first. It does not — it answers `[]`, identically on both arms:

```text
  CAST(s) = 1 AND a = 999    pre []     post []     an empty seed pre-empts the scan
  a = 999 AND CAST(s) = 1    pre []     post []
  a = 50  AND CAST(s) = 1    pre THROW  post THROW  rows survive, so the cast is reached
  CAST(s) = 1                pre THROW  post THROW
```

`a = 999` matches nothing, the seed is empty, the scan never runs and the cast is never reached. So
the prefix rule is MORE conservative than what already holds, not less, and the test now pins the
four actual behaviours as a cross-arm invariant rather than asserting a guarantee this engine does
not make.

### ⚠️ ONE FUZZ FAILURE, UNREPRODUCED, AND ITS SEED WAS LOST TO THE HARNESS

One `bun run fuzz` reported 12 pass / 1 fail. It has not recurred in **14 subsequent runs** (11 with
`--no-build`, 3 with the rebuild), and the differential fuzzer — the only one of the seven that
exercises the TS GQL executor against Rust, and so the only one this change can reach — passed every
one of them, including a run with 4825 generated predicates.

That is 14 clean runs against 1 failure, which is **counting, not a rule-out**, and this file's own
rule is to rule a suspect out STRUCTURALLY. The structural argument is only half available: of the
seven fuzzers, `gremlin` (a separate package, with a recorded rare 1-in-30 residual whose seed
replays clean), `parity` (wasm against FFI, Rust only), `codec`, `algo` and `write` are not reachable
from `packages/gql/src/executor.ts`. But I cannot name WHICH fuzzer failed, because the invocation
piped its output through `grep` to extract the result line and the seed went with the rest.

**So the lesson is the harness one, not the fuzzer one:** a fuzz run's output goes to a FILE and the
result line is read from the file afterwards. Piping it to `grep` discards exactly the thing a rare
failure exists to give you. Every run after this one in this item redirected to a log first — which
is why I can say the 14 were clean rather than merely that they exited 0.

Recorded as unexplained rather than closed. CI runs the fuzzers again.

### ⚠️ THE FIRST TARGET WAS WRONG, and one test settled it

Item 1285 left `nodeWhereOf`'s own declines as the open target, the larger of which is
`!itemLocal(where)` — it abandons the WHOLE node-count shortcut. `itemLocal` refuses any `Expr`
kind outside `ROW_LOCAL_KINDS`, and the six kinds missing from that allowlist are `graphPred`,
`isLabeled`, `isNull`, `isTruth`, `isTyped` and `letIn`. (`label` is in the allowlist and NOT in the
`Expr` union at all — a stale entry, harmless, recorded.)

`isNull` looked like the prize: `WHERE k IS NULL` is a spelling users write constantly. Measured at
200,000 vertices against `n.marker = true`, a `compare` arranged to keep EXACTLY the same rows so
both answer an identical 20000:

```text
  [BASE] n.marker = true     4.473 ms
  n.k IS NULL                4.616      1.03x — FLAT
  n.flag IS TRUE            10.379      2.32x
```

Both kinds are refused by the same allowlist. One is free and one costs 2.32x, so **the allowlist is
not the cause** — and `rowLocal` was checked directly rather than inferred, to be sure both really
decline:

```text
  rowLocal=false kind=isNull     n.k IS NULL
  rowLocal=false kind=isTruth    n.flag IS TRUE
```

The real route is `pushWhereIntoNode`, which moves a clause `WHERE` into the node pattern so it
compiles through `compilePredicate` — where item 1270 gave `isNull` an arm and `isTruth` had none.
The missing arm was the whole cost, and `itemLocal` is a red herring for this shape. One decisive
measurement replaced a plausible story; the enum was worth pricing, just not for the reason I
expected.

### The lift

```text

  n.flag IS TRUE            9.284 ->  3.567    2.60x
                            7.340 ->  3.435    2.14x
  NOT (n.flag IS FALSE)     8.107 ->  3.559    2.28x / 2.46x
```

### ⚠️ AND IT EXPOSED A LIVE DIVERGENCE IN ITEMS 1269 AND 1270

Making `isTruth` liftable turned a MIXED chain into a fully-lifted one, which bypasses item 1284's
raise guard (that fires only when a residual exists) — and the cross-engine conformance test failed.
Chasing it found a bug older than this item.

`satisfies` applies the lifted families in a fixed block order, and that order is an ordering key
which must agree with the engine's. Item 1169 established "NON-RAISING FIRST" for `eqProps`,
`cmpProps` and `pathProps`. Items 1269 (`memberProps`) and 1270 (`nullProps`) then did the opposite,
with an explicit argument: _"running the non-raising family first would let a FALSE membership
return before a sibling conjunct that the generic path would have raised on, changing WHICH queries
error. Running it last cannot: every family that can raise has already run."_

The premise is right and the conclusion is backwards. The generic route does NOT raise when a
sibling SETTLES the row — FALSE dominates — so running a non-raising family LAST is what produces a
raise the engine never produces. Measured on BOTH arms of this item's diff, so it pre-dates it:

```text
  WHERE n.s AND false              ts ok []  native ok []   AGREE
  WHERE n.s AND n.z IS NOT NULL    ts ERR    native ok []   DIVERGE   nullProps, item 1270
  WHERE n.s AND n.n IN [99]        ts ERR    native ok []   DIVERGE   memberProps, item 1269
  WHERE n.s AND n.n = 99           ts ok []  native ok []   AGREE     eqProps — runs FIRST
  WHERE n.s AND n.n > 99           ts ok []  native ok []   AGREE     cmpProps — runs FIRST
```

The two that agreed are exactly the two already in item 1169's group. The file held two opposite
conventions and the evidence picks 1169's. Both non-raising families move into the hoisted group,
closing two divergences that had been live since those items shipped.

### `IS UNKNOWN` goes into `nullProps`, and that is measured, not reasoned

With the families reordered the failure FLIPPED: native raises on `n.s AND n.n IS TRUE` where TS now
answered `ok []`. So "non-raising ⇒ hoisted" is not the engine's rule either. The engine is the
ground truth, so I asked it — `n.s` is a string, each tail is FALSE for every row unless noted:

```text
  n.n IS TRUE          native ERR     FALSE and STILL raises — NOT hoisted
  n.n IS FALSE         native ERR     likewise
  n.n IS UNKNOWN       native ok []   hoisted
  n.z IS NULL          native ERR     tail is TRUE here — uninformative
  n.z IS NOT NULL      native ok []   hoisted
  n.n IN [99]          native ok []   hoisted
  n.n = 99             native ok []   hoisted
  false                native ok []   hoisted
  n.n IS NOT TRUE      native ERR     tail is TRUE here — uninformative
  n.n IS NOT UNKNOWN   native ERR     tail is TRUE here — uninformative
```

So the `isTruth` AST node has TWO destinations, split on `truth === null`. `IS UNKNOWN` **is**
`IS NULL` — `case 'isTruth'` routes `truth === null` through `isNullish`, the very function
`case 'isNull'` uses — so it folds into `nulls` and is hoisted with it, while `IS TRUE`/`IS FALSE`
get their own list applied after `truthProps`. One node, two lists, decided by that table. TS and
native now agree on **13 of 13** shapes, 0 divergences.

### Two existing guards were rewritten, because they pinned one engine's choice

`member-props-lift.test.ts` and `null-props-lift.test.ts` each carried a test named "a sibling
conjunct that RAISES still raises, which is why the lift runs LAST", asserting a throw. Those throws
were the divergence. They now assert the measured cross-engine behaviour, with the old rationale
quoted and corrected in place:

```text
  WHERE n.s AND n.s IS NULL        ts ok 0  native ok 0   was ts THROW
  WHERE n.s IS NULL AND n.s        ts ok 0  native ok 0   was ts THROW
  WHERE n.s AND n.k IN [999]       ts ok 0  native ok 0   was ts THROW
  WHERE n.k IN [999] AND n.s       ts ok 0  native ok 0   was ts THROW
  WHERE n.s AND n.k IS NOT NULL    ts ERR   native ERR    unchanged — the control
```

The last line still throws and is the control: one vertex PASSES `k IS NOT NULL`, so the raising
sibling is reached for that row whatever the order. The real guard now lives in
`and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts`, which compares against the engine instead of pinning TS.

### Item 1287 — the presence-count sweep vectorizes once its invariant is hoisted: 31.8x; the HOP twin is FLAT and reverted (DONE)

Item 1259 nominated the two presence-count sweeps, item 1260 priced the spelling gap instead (and
item 1261 fixed that at ~4x), leaving the loop-invariant hoist itself open. Both sites are now
measured, and they disagree by a factor of 30.

```text
  row                               pre(min)   post(min)  ratio
  SCAN presence count                 190.9       6.0      31.8x
  HOP  presence count                 311.8     313.4      flat — REVERTED
  [CTL] hop count with a BOUND        768.5     771.3      flat (items 1220/1224's arm)
  [CTL] bare hop count(*)               0.3       0.3      flat (a different function)
  [CTL] both rows, with-nulls fixture 838.1     847.7      flat (a `Gen` column — unreachable)
```

200,000 nodes / 800,000 edges, min of 7 per rep, three order-alternated rounds, each arm asserting
its own marker count before the build.

### Why one is 31.8x and the other is nothing

`present[i]` is read SEQUENTIALLY by the scan, so hoisting `bounds.is_empty()` and `nulls_count` out
of the closure leaves a body of one bool read and a branchless add — which LLVM vectorizes. The
result is bandwidth-bound and the arithmetic says so: 200,000 bools is 200 KB, and 200 KB in 6.0us
is ~33 GB/s, which is memory and not instructions. The branch was not costing a mispredict, it was
costing the vectorization.

The hop sweep reads `present[j]` at edge TARGETS — a random-access gather, latency-bound, with
nothing to vectorize. So the hoist buys nothing there and the invariant test stays. **That is item
1225's finding in a new place** ("this loop is memory-bound", 1.08-1.14x where the same substitution
had paid 5.28x), and it is the second time the same shape has split this way on access pattern. The
flat arm is reverted rather than kept: it measured nothing, and the note above it now says so with
the numbers, so the next reader does not re-derive it.

`Q` node that carries it and must not be counted), and asserts the representation before the counts,
because a `Gen` column would make the assertions pass for the wrong reason.

### The native hoisting question was answered BEFORE implementing, not after

Item 1286 cost most of its time to finding that the engine's hoisting rule is per-spelling and has
to be measured. Applying that forward:

```text
  WHERE n.s AND n.n NOT IN [1, 2]   native ok []   FALSE for every row -> HOISTED
  WHERE n.s AND n.n IN [99]         native ok []   the already-lifted control
  WHERE n IS LABELED Q  (beside n.s) native ok []  FALSE for every row -> HOISTED
  WHERE n.s AND n.n NOT IN [99]     native ERR     TRUE, settles nothing -> uninformative
  WHERE n.s AND n IS LABELED P      native ERR     TRUE -> uninformative
  WHERE n.s AND NOT (n.n = 1)       native ERR     TRUE for one row -> reaches the raiser
```

Every row fits one rule — FALSE settles and is hoisted, TRUE settles nothing — so `NOT IN` belongs
in the non-raising group with `memberProps`, and no ordering change was needed. The cross-engine case
is pinned in `and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts` beside item 1286's, with a TRUE-tailed control
that must still raise. **This also pre-answers the same question for `IS LABELED`**, which is why
that target can be taken later without re-deriving it.

### ⚠️ MY TEST WAS WRONG ABOUT THE EMPTY HAYSTACK, and the engine was right

The first version expected `n.k NOT IN []` to drop the null and absent cells, reasoning that a null
needle makes membership UNKNOWN as it does for a non-empty haystack. It does not: an empty set
contains nothing, so `x IN []` is FALSE for every needle INCLUDING null, `not3(FALSE)` is TRUE, and
those rows are KEPT. It is also the one case where the two spellings are complements over the whole
row set (0 + 5 = 5), because nothing is UNKNOWN. The oracle test had already shown both routes
agreeing, so the disagreement was between the engine and my expectation.

### The pattern hit its structural limit, and `mergeFarPreds` got better for it

Adding the ninth family took THREE functions over the complexity cap at once — `directEqProps`,
`satisfies` and `mergeFarPreds`. That is the signal that the repetition had become load-bearing in
the wrong way.

`mergeFarPreds` spelled out the same three-line ternary nine times ("both undefined -> omit, else
concat"). One `mergeList` helper replaces all nine, each family keeping its own comment — which is
what matters there, since forgetting a family is the silent-SUPERSET failure item 901 named. A tenth
family is now one line instead of three plus a complexity budget.

`directEqProps` and `satisfies` got extractions instead (`liftLabelTest`, `liftMembership`,
`labelTestsHold`), matching `liftNullTest`/`liftTruthTest`. **`satisfies` was deliberately NOT
restructured into a list of appliers**, which is the obvious way to stop paying a branch per family:
it is the hottest function in this file, and a per-family dynamic dispatch per element is exactly
the shape this repo has measured as a regression elsewhere. Recorded as a known structural cost, not
fixed by making the hot path polymorphic.

None of the three has a PREDICATE at all — `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(y) RETURN count(*)` —

### ⚠️ A COHERENT CLUSTER IS NOT INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE, and I argued the opposite

Reading the sweep I reasoned: "six related rows moving together is far stronger evidence than one
outlier." **That is wrong, and it is the lesson of this item.** Those six rows share the `graphDoc`
fixture and run adjacently in the sweep, so whatever perturbs one perturbs the family — GC pressure,
fixture residency, whatever the neighbour left behind. They do not constitute six independent
observations; they constitute one, repeated. Coherence across rows that share a confound is what the
confound LOOKS like, not evidence against it.

The correct reading of a cluster is therefore the same as the correct reading of a single row: it
locates a question and does not answer it. Isolate it.

### The `ffi` column was unreadable this run, and the named control set is what said so

```text
  encode ndjson      24.4 -> 38.8   1.59x   [CONTROL - unreachable]
  encode graphson    63.9 -> 87.1   1.36x   [CONTROL - unreachable]
  encode pg-text     29.9 -> 36.5   1.22x   [CONTROL - unreachable]
```

Three codec rows no change in this run can reach moved 1.22-1.59x, so the whole `ffi` column is
noise at that amplitude and nothing in it is interpretable. The TS control band was tighter but
still wide: **0.81x .. 1.07x** across 15 unreachable rows.

This is why the comparison script TAGS the control set from a regex rather than leaving it to be
noticed at read time, and prints the band with the rule stated: a query row moving no further than
the band is indistinguishable from noise. Without that, `encode ndjson` at 1.59x reads as a finding.

I confirmed flag 1 three times in isolation before reading the comment that says it can never
converge. Three runs of wasted work on a documented regression guard.

that flag 1 had just taught me to read the comment first.

QUESTIONS, and each question's answer is written next to the group that asks it. Reading the flag
without reading the group is how a closed item gets re-derived a third time.

### Item 1294 — the TS per-row constant factor, DECOMPOSED: ~45% pointer chase, and both cheap levers refuted (REFUTED x2 + instrument added)

Items 1292 and 1293 left both spelling probes clean and `bench:usage`'s one suspicious row refuted,
so the remaining TS/Rust gaps are all the per-row constant factor that items 1221 and 1276
ATTRIBUTED and neither decomposed — "TS is FLAT across a 22x selectivity change, so it scales with
NODES: ~19ns per vertex against Rust's ~0.5ns". It is the biggest absolute gap in the corpus, so it
is worth knowing what it is made of before concluding it is immovable.

`bun run row-cost` is that decomposition, at 200,000 vertices:

```text
  1. Map iteration only                  1.50 ns/v
  2. + label test (v.labels.has)        24.29        <- the most expensive single operation
  3. + property read                    11.76
  4. + property read by VARIABLE key    10.68
  5. + matches() on that value          10.98
```

It accounts for the Gremlin row exactly: `V().has(age,gt).count()` is 2.6ms at 200,000 vertices =
13 ns/v = 1.5 iteration + ~10 property read + ~1 predicate.

### The property read is a POINTER CHASE, not a slow object

```text
  plain object literal, array-held             1.60 ns/v
  engine `v.properties`, array-held            7.38
  engine `.properties` HOISTED into an array   1.53   <- the bag is as fast as a literal
```

The bag is as fast as an object literal once you hold it; ~5.8 ns a vertex is reaching it through
`vertex -> box -> bag`, three heap objects per vertex. That indirection is the DELIBERATE box design
(`Graph.elementProperties`, items 162 and 321) — a stable box is what keeps a re-write off the map
and what preserves a detached element's throw — so removing it is a storage-layout decision, not a
micro-fix, and not taken here.

The label test at 24.29 is the same indirection plus a `Set<string>.has` hash probe. Its getter
allocates only on the detached path (`this.#lbox?.set ?? new Set()`), so there is no per-read
allocation to remove. `filterChainCount` already avoids it where it can, by SEEDING from the label
bucket for the first single-label test.

### ⚠️ TWO OBVIOUS LEVERS, BOTH REFUTED WITH NUMBERS

**1. Compile `matches()` into a closure.** Its 20-way switch on `pred.op` runs per value, and this
is precisely the substitution items 1224, 1225, 1227 and 1231 made in the Rust engine for 5.28x,
1.08x, 5.31x and 8.65-17.6x. Measured over 200,000 values:

```text
  matches(pred, v) per value   1.11 ns   (0.50 above the loop floor)
  monomorphic closure          0.83      (0.22 above)
  [CTL] bare loop              0.61
```

It does halve the dispatch — and the dispatch is 1.11 ns of a 13 ns budget, so the whole change
buys about **2%**. Refuted on size, not on mechanism: the Rust twin paid because there the dispatch
WAS the loop body, and here it is 8% of it.

**2. Reorder `get properties` so the cached-box path comes first** — one check and one hop instead
of four checks and two. Mocked both shapes over 200,000 instances, three runs:

```text
  current     6.44 / 9.22 / 6.85
  reordered   6.54 / 8.35 / 6.22
```

FLAT, with the rounds disagreeing on the sign. And `Vertex.ts` already records the same outcome for
the same kind of change — bypassing the `id` getter — with the reason: "JSC inlines a getter whose
whole body is a private-field read." Reading that note first would have predicted this result; I
measured it anyway because `get properties` is not just a field read, and the answer is that its
branches still are not the cost.

### What this leaves

The TS constant factor is roughly **45% indirection, 8% predicate dispatch, and the rest iteration
plus the `Set<string>.has` label probe.** The two cheap levers are spent and recorded, so the next
person does not re-derive them; what remains is the box layout, which is a design decision with
correctness obligations (the detached-element throw) rather than a perf bug.

That is also the honest answer to "why is TS 40-60x Rust on a filtered count": Rust reads a packed
column with a vectorized sweep (item 1287 took one such sweep to 0.2 ns a vertex), and TS chases
three pointers per vertex. The gap is the data layout, which is what item 1276 concluded for the hop
family by a different route.

### ⚠️ A NEW OBSTACLE ITEM 1248 DID NOT NAME — and it is resolved

`detectGroupedHopAggregate` carries this, in its own words: "it iterates
`candidateVertexSource(graph, startLabel)` and expands… **Its visit order is the start side's, which
is the general path's.**" That is a deliberate property. A per-endpoint fold iterates the FAR side,
so the groups come out in a different order — which item 1248's note does not mention at all, and
which would be the first thing to break if grouped row order were observable.

It is not. The differential fuzzer states the invariant explicitly: "Comparison is structural (row
multiset), which is the correct invariant: intra-group row order in a CALL without ORDER BY is
unspecified", and every `ORDER BY` query it generates carries a final total sort key for the same
reason. That matches the repo's settled policy that unordered row order is WON'T-FIX, like SQL
without `ORDER BY`. And item 1249 already gave this rung a real `sortGroupRows` path for the case
where the user DOES ask for an order.

So the per-endpoint fold may change group emission order, and the target is unblocked.

### What building it requires, stated precisely so the next pass starts from here

Extend `detectGroupedHopAggregate` with a per-endpoint fold admitted only when **all** of:

- every accumulator is `min`/`max` (the identity is extremum-specific — `count(*)` needs the
  multiplicity and `sum`/`avg` do too; item 1245 established this);
- every aggregate argument reads only the far variable;
- the GROUP KEY reads only the far variable (`!onStart`), which is what makes each distinct
  endpoint belong to exactly one group;
- the start label is absent or `vacuousLabel` — item 1245's measurement is that the
  per-distinct-endpoint fold WITHOUT this is a 1.07x REGRESSION (C in its A/B/C/D table, re-measured
  here at 185384 against A's 107973, 1.72x worse). The win is the universal-label shortcut, not the
  dedup.

The walk to mirror is `primedEndpointExtremum`'s: iterate `candidateVertexSource(graph, farLabel)`,
prove reachability from a bucket SIZE rather than by touching an edge, bind the far variable, fold.
The only addition is a `Map` from the evaluated key to that group's accumulator array.

Not built in this tick, and the reason is scope rather than doubt — the same reason item 1248 gave,
which is honest but worth saying plainly rather than leaving as an implication.

Gates: no code change. `bun run check` 0.

```text
  n.v IS TYPED INTEGER                      12.976      2.97x
  n.v IS NOT TYPED INTEGER                   6.971      1.60x
  [CTL] bare count                           0.001
```

**2.97x, which is larger than "niche" suggested** and in the same band as the lifts items 1286-1290

### ⚠️ AND THE NEGATED FORM IS 1.86x FASTER THAN THE POSITIVE ONE — RETRACTED BY ITEM 1298

**This did not reproduce.** Item 1298's PRE arm, same fixture and same matched twin, reads
`IS TYPED` 9.128 and `IS NOT TYPED` 8.678 — near-equal, where this item measured 12.976 against
6.971. The difference between the two runs is the import (`@lenke/gql`, a built dist, against a
relative `src` import for the A/B), so the figures below are a dist-vs-src comparison and the

paragraph is kept because the retraction is the point.

`IS TYPED INTEGER` is 12.976 and `IS NOT TYPED INTEGER` is 6.971, on a 50/50 split where both
answer 100000. Two complementary spellings of one question, costing differently — which is this
repo's named defect class, and it is NOT explained by the lift being absent, because the lift is
absent from both. Something routes the negated form differently. Recorded as a second, separate
question; it needs its own diagnosis and may well be the more interesting of the two.

### The hoisting question is answered, and the answer is the non-obvious one

Item 1286 established the engine as the authority on which lifted family may run before
`truthProps`, and items 1288-1290 made that check standing practice BEFORE implementing. `n.s` is a
string, so coercing it is a data exception; a tail FALSE for every row settles it IF hoisted:

```text
  WHERE n.s AND n.n IS TYPED STRING        native ERR   FALSE every row and STILL raises
  WHERE n.s AND n.s IS TYPED INTEGER       native ERR   FALSE every row and STILL raises
  WHERE n.s AND n.n IS NOT TYPED STRING    native ERR   TRUE — uninformative
  WHERE n.s AND n.n IS TYPED INTEGER       native ERR   TRUE — uninformative
```

**The engine hoists NO form of `IS TYPED`**, including the two informative ones. So despite being
total and non-raising — the property that puts `nulls`, `member` and `labelTests` in the hoisted
group — `IS TYPED` belongs in the LATE group with `truthTestProps`, after `truthProps`. That is the
same split item 1286 had to measure for `IS TRUE`/`IS FALSE` against `IS UNKNOWN`, and it is why
"non-raising ⇒ hoisted" is not a rule in this engine.

### The build, fully specified

A ninth-and-tenth family on the pattern items 1286 and 1289 established, and the late-group slot
means it can sit beside `truthTestProps` rather than needing its own ordering argument:

- `CTypedTestProp = { key, ty, notNull, negated }`, mirroring `CTruthTestProp`;
- `asTypedTest` folding `NOT (x IS TYPED T)` by flipping `negated`, as `asNullTest`/`asTruthTest`
  /`asLabelTest` all do — both of this file's two-pass mistakes (items 1261 then 1262) came from
  handling one spelling and noticing the other later;
- `liftTypedTest(conjunct, ownVar, out)` returning whether it claimed the conjunct, because
  `directEqProps` is at its complexity cap and this is the fifth arm to be extracted for that
  reason (items 1284-1290);
- applied in `satisfies` through `valueIsTypedTy` — the SAME function `case 'isTyped'` uses, so the
  lift cannot change what `IS TYPED` means — placed in the LATE group per the table above;

### Item 1299 — item 1298's surviving mutant is PROVEN unreachable, and the reason closes a three-way consistency chain (correction: inference replaced by mechanism)

Item 1298 shipped the `IS TYPED` lift with 6 of 7 mutants caught. The survivor was
`merge-drops-family` — dropping `typedTests` from `mergeFarPreds` — and that item said plainly: "I
did not verify non-reachability directly; the inference is from the mutant's own behaviour." This is
that verification, and the inference was right for a better reason than it knew.

### Two structural facts, either of which alone is decisive

**1. `splitFarConjuncts` requires a conjunct LEFT BEHIND.** It returns `undefined` when
`rest.length === 0`, with its own note: "Nothing to hoist, or nothing left behind — the second is
item 781's whole-clause lift". Item 1298's hop test has exactly ONE clause conjunct, all far-only,
so it takes item 781's path and never enters `mergeFarPreds` at all. That explains the survival but
not whether the line is reachable by some OTHER query.

**2. `truthCannotRaise` does not admit `isTyped`, and must not.** The far bucket is gated on it, and
it admits only `lit` (boolean/null), `property_exists`, `isLabeled`, `isNull` (when its value cannot
raise) and `isTruth` — the last **only** for the `IS [NOT] UNKNOWN` form. There is no `isTyped` arm,
so an `IS TYPED` conjunct can never reach the far bucket, from any query. **The merge line is
unreachable, structurally, and `mergeFarPreds` cannot be given a `typedTests` list today.**

### ⚠️ AND IT MUST STAY THAT WAY — the three facts are one fact

The `isTruth` arm carries the reason, in its own words: it admits only `IS UNKNOWN` "because that is
the only one the engine's key admits — and the ordering key has to be the SAME key, in BOTH
directions. A first version of this arm returned `valueCannotRaise(e.expr)` for all three truth
values and introduced TWO NEW divergences."

So the chain closes:

```text
  item 1297  the ENGINE hoists no form of IS TYPED            (measured against native)
  item 1298  so TS applies it in the LATE group, after truthProps
  item 1299  so `truthCannotRaise` must NOT admit it          (the key is the same key)
             so it never reaches the far bucket
             so `mergeFarPreds`' typedTests line is unreachable
```

Three independent-looking facts in three files are the same fact, and adding `isTyped` to
`truthCannotRaise` to "fix" the surviving mutant would reintroduce precisely the divergence the
`isTruth` arm records paying for once already. **The survivor is correct behaviour, not a gap**, and
the merge line is a correctness precondition for the day the engine's key changes — the same
disposition `mergeFarPreds` records for `truthProps`/`notTruthProps`, which survive their own
mutants for their own reasons.

### What this is worth as method

Item 1298's inference ("the test still answers 1, so the filter arrives another way") was sound and
reached the right conclusion from one observation. The mechanism is better, because it answers a
question the inference could not: whether ANY query reaches the line. An inference from a mutant's
behaviour bounds what that mutant saw; only the gate tells you what the code admits.

Labelling a survivor is cheap and leaving it unlabelled is how a later pass "fixes" it. This one now
carries its reason in the entry and the chain that makes it load-bearing.

Gates: no code change. `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1300 — the six predicate forms this run lifted had never been added to the spelling probe, which CLAUDE.md requires of each one (omission corrected)

`CLAUDE.md` is explicit about the TS spelling probe: "Run it when you touch the TS planner or add a
predicate form, **and add the new form's spellings to it**." Six forms shipped in this run — the
mixed-chain prefix (1284), `IS TRUE`/`IS FALSE` (1286), `NOT IN` (1288), `IS [NOT] LABELED` (1289),
the dotted negated compare (1290) and `IS [NOT] TYPED` (1298) — and **none of them added a group**.
I ran the probe twice in that stretch (items 1292 and here) without noticing that it could not see
any of the work.

Three groups added, each a pair that is LOGICALLY IDENTICAL regardless of null or type, so a
disagreement is a defect rather than a semantics question:

```text
  NOT IN vs NOT (IN)                     13.40 / 12.27 ms   1.09x
  IS LABELED vs the doubly-negated form  47.90 / 47.71      1.00x
  IS TYPED vs the doubly-negated form     8.86 /  8.93      1.01x
```

All three converge, and `0 group(s) disagree on the ANSWER`. The three over-2x flags the run reports
are the pre-existing ones item 1292 triaged (a documented-permanent pair, one harness artifact and
one closed at item 644), not these.

Why these three and not six: each pair had to be identical under EVERY cell state, and that rules
out the tempting ones. `IS TRUE` against `= true` is NOT such a pair — they differ on a null, which
`truth-test-lift.test.ts` pins deliberately — and the mixed-chain prefix needs an unliftable
conjunct whose presence changes nothing, which is a fixture property rather than a spelling. The
dotted form needs a record-valued property the probe's fixture does not carry. Those three are
covered by their unit tests, which assert the ANSWER; what this file adds is the COST, and only for
pairs where cost is the only thing that may differ.

The distinction is worth stating because it is the reason the obligation is easy to skip: a form
whose spellings differ semantically has no group to add, so "add the new form's spellings" is not
mechanical, and six items in a row treated an unclear case as no case.

`IS LABELED` at 47.9 ms against the others' 9-13 is not a spelling defect — both members agree to
1.00x — but it is the slowest pair in the file by 4x and nothing has priced it. Recorded.
