### Item 1302 — a far-end `hasLabel` after a Gremlin vertex hop: 1.90-6.02x, and the cross-surface check found a GQL spelling gap it did not fix (DONE + located)

The start side of a hop has always admitted `hasLabel`; the far side never did.
`collectVertexFilters` takes `hasLabel` for the steps BEFORE the hop, so
`hasLabel(P).out(T).has(k,p)` took a rung — while the two far-side readers (`hasChain`,
`collectHasFilters`) admitted only `has`, so moving the label test ACROSS the hop, the same kind
of test one position later, fell off every rung to the general traversal.

### How it was found, which is the part worth keeping

Not by looking for it. The user asked what could speed up the TS per-row cost without giving up
O(1)-by-id lookup or fast mutations, and two layout levers were priced for that question:

- **A label BITMASK on the `LabelBox`** (intern labels, answer `hasLabel` as `(mask & bit) !==
0`). A micro-arm says 19.6x. **REFUTED ON REACHABILITY**: the engine never runs that loop. Real
  queries at 200,000 vertices — `V().hasLabel(P).count()` **0.05 ns/v** and
  `V().hasLabel(P).hasLabel(E).count()` **0.06** — are answered from `verticesByLabel` without
  visiting a vertex, and adding a label test to a property filter costs nothing measurable (12.26
  -> 12.77, inside the 1.11x round spread). I had predicted the two-label AND could NOT be seeded.
  It is. There is no scan shape where the per-vertex `Set<string>.has` is on the hot path. - **A
  parallel box ARRAY**, one sequential load instead of two dependent ones. Real, modest: the
  middle shape item 1294 never measured reads 4.49 ns/v against the current 10.71 (2.39x), of
  which 1.28 is array-vs-Map iteration — so **the hop itself is ~4.94 ns** and removing one
  removes ~5, which confirms the dependent-load-latency reading over cache misses. End to end on a
  property count that is 12.26 -> ~7.3, about 1.7x, against a 4x ceiling that needs the box gone.

Pricing the mask meant asking where a far-end label test IS paid, and that is what surfaced the
defect. ⚠️ **Both arms of lever 1 were measured on a hand-written loop first and the loop was not
the engine.** Third time this file records that shape (items 591 and 1294 are the others): take
ratios from an A/B of the real thing.

### The gap, measured against a FLOOR rather than against its unfiltered twin

200,000 vertices / 200,000 `T` edges, one shape per process, min of three rounds:

```text
  V().out(T).has(age, gt(44)).count()      95.76 ns/v   served by `filteredHopCount`
  V().out(T).hasLabel(Employee).count()   612.45        declined every rung        6.40x
  hand-written loop, the same work        119.70        the floor                  5.12x off
```

The property arm sits **at** that floor — 0.80x, the rung BEATS the loop, because it is far-driven
and tests each far vertex once instead of once per edge. The label arm was 5.12x above it.

⚠️ **`V().out(T).count()` at 0.05 ns/v is NOT the comparison**, and quoting the ~11,000x against
it would have been dishonest: that is a closed-form degree sum that never visits a far end. A
query that must visit far ends needs a floor that visits them too, and the hand-written loop is
it.

### The fix: one far-side reader, and NOT a widening of the shared one

`farFilters` splits the far chain into label sets (each an OR, ANDed across steps) and `has`
filters, and replaces `hasChain` in `filteredHopCount` and `collectHasFilters` in
`bothFilteredHopCount`. `collectHasFilters` is deleted rather than left beside it — item 1282's
prescription, after that item found item 1140's conversion had reached one detector of five.

⚠️ **`hasChain` is NOT widened, and that distinction is load-bearing.** Its other caller is
`edgeHopSeededCount`, where the frontier is EDGES: after `outE`, a `hasLabel` filters the edge's
own label, not the far vertex's — the same step kind asking a different question. Admitting vertex
labels there would be a wrong answer, so `hasChain` keeps the edge reading and `farFilters` owns
the vertex side. The test that holds this is `V().outE(T).hasLabel(E).has(w, 1).count()` = 0,
where a dropped label test answers 1.

`filteredHopCount`'s far-driven arm tests labels per far VERTEX and adds its whole degree; its
edge-driven arm and `tallyFarEnds` test per EDGE, which is more evaluations and still
fault-equivalent, since neither a label test nor `matches` can fault (item 930).

```text
  q-both-label            1661.55     312.74    5.31x  n=200000

  ctl-label2                 0.06       0.06    1.00x  [CONTROL]

```

```text
  labels-never-filter          caught (11 fail)
  or-becomes-negated           caught (9)
  farfilters-drops-labels      caught (10)
  haschain-widened-to-labels   caught (1)     <- survived TWICE first; see below
  tallyfarends-skips-labels    caught (3)
  far-driven-skips-labels      caught (9)
  edge-driven-drops-labelsets  caught (1)     <- survived first, in another form; see below
  bothsides-drops-labelsets    caught (2)     <- both call sites, declared count 2
  values-last-rule-dropped     caught (2)
  empty-guard-removed          SURVIVED        [expected: answer-equivalent perf guard]
```

Two mutants went stale against the refactor and reported ANCHOR rather than a verdict — the
`passesLabels` rewrite to `for...of` removed `labels[j]`, and the collapsed arm turned a deleted
label test into a dropped argument. A stale anchor is NOT a survivor, and the harness
distinguishes them: it asserts the anchor count before applying and prints the mismatch, so a
mutant that never landed cannot be read as a passing suite. Both were rewritten and both are
caught above.

Two survivors were real test gaps and both needed a fixture that did not exist:

- **`edge-driven-skips-labels`** survived all 948 tests because nothing in the suite had a
  two-type edge. `filteredHopCount`'s edge-driven arm needs `hop.labels.length !== 1 &&
multiTypeEdgeCount !== 0` to pass the far-driven arm, and then `bucketsFor` declines a
  MULTI-type hop whenever a two-type edge exists — so **the only reachable combination is an
  UNTYPED hop on a graph carrying a multi-label edge.** Half of my change was untested until that
  fixture existed. - **`haschain-widened-to-labels`** survived twice. First because `hasChain`
  returns `undefined` on an empty filter list either way, so a single `hasLabel` cannot show it;
  then because `edgeHopSeededCount` declines at `if (!best)` without a seekable filter. Observing
  it needs all three of a non-empty `has` chain, an EDGE index, and an equality predicate a hash
  index can serve.

A fixture comment also had the semantics backwards and the test caught it: `out(T, S)` yields a
two-type edge ONCE, not twice — which is `bucketsFor`'s own stated reason for declining ("summing
across types would visit it twice while the walk yields it once").

### The Rust engine already had this shape, so nothing was ported

Recorded in this file at item 1100's reachability markers: `C2  out().hasLabel('Person').count()
->  try_fused_hop_mask_agg`. The native path claims it. This was a TS-only gap, and the asymmetry
is the opposite of the usual direction.

```text
  MATCH (a)-[:T]->(b) WHERE b IS LABELED Employee  215.89        11.9x, same answer (100000)
```

## 1303 — `WHERE n IS LABELED L` folds into the pattern, and the two spellings become one plan

Item 1302 located a GQL gap and did not take it: a far-end label costs 11.9x more written as a
clause `WHERE b IS LABELED Q` than as a pattern label `(b:Q)`. This takes it, and the scan form
turned out to be the larger half by three orders of magnitude.

### What the gap actually was

Two causes, and only one of them is the one item 1302 named.

`bareDegreeSum` (`executor/shortcuts.ts`) is a closed-form degree sum over a label BUCKET, and it
declines outright when `lifted !== undefined`. The pattern spelling carries no clause `WHERE` at
all, so `pred.fn === alwaysTrue`, nothing is lifted, and it takes that path. The clause spelling
populates `farLifted` and falls to the full `farOnlyHopCount` walk over every vertex. That is the
hop case.

The SCAN case is bigger and was not recorded anywhere: `MATCH (n:Employee) RETURN count(*)` is a
`verticesByLabel` bucket SIZE, and the clause spelling of the same question walks 200,000
vertices.

Measured against hand-written floors, 200,000 vertices, one shape per process, selectivity matched
by construction (`age = i % 90` keeps half, `Employee` on even `i` keeps half), every arm
answering the same 100000:

```text
                                                         ns/vertex   off its floor
  MATCH (n:Employee) RETURN count(*)                          0.01   — bucket size
  MATCH (n) WHERE n IS LABELED Employee RETURN count(*)     119.46   5.31x
  a hand-written `v.labels.has('Employee')` loop             22.51   — THE FLOOR
  MATCH (n) WHERE n.age >= 45 RETURN count(*)                20.07   1.93x
  a hand-written `v.properties.age >= 45` loop               10.39   — its floor
```

So the label spelling sits 5.31x off its own floor where the property twin sits 1.93x off its, and
the pattern spelling never visits a vertex. On a one-hop count the same pair reads 196.12 against
16.61.

**REFUTED on the way, so it is not re-priced:** the `labels` GETTER is not the cost. Hoisting it
out of the floor loop reads 22.20 against 22.51 — inside the noise.

### The fix is a clause rewrite, not a tenth lifted family

`foldLabelTestsIntoPatterns` runs in `compileLinear`'s rewrite chain, before
`dropVacuousQuantifier`, and turns `MATCH (n) WHERE n IS LABELED L` into `MATCH (n:L)`.

The two are the same question BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by an equivalence argument: a pattern
label is tested with `matchesLabel` and `IS LABELED` with `labelsMatch`, and both are one call to
the same `evalLabelExpr` over the same `LabelExpr` and the same label set. `IS LABELED` is TOTAL
on an element — TRUE or FALSE, never UNKNOWN — so there is no three-valued row-drop for the
pattern form to lose, and nothing in it can raise, so raise parity (items 139-145) is untouched.

A rewrite rather than a route because every rung already handles a pattern label — scans, one/two/
three-hop counts, the fused hop projection, the endpoint extremum — so folding reaches all of them
at once where a `labelTests` route would have to be taught to each. It is also cheap to get right
for a reason worth recording: `plainNode` tests `properties` and `where` and NOT `label`, so a
folded label cannot make any rung's `plainNode` guard decline.

The detector is `asLabelTest`, SHARED with `liftLabelTest` rather than rewritten, so the `NOT (n
IS LABELED L)` spelling folds too and the two cannot drift on what a label test is.

Exclusions, each for a stated reason: `OPTIONAL MATCH` (moving a filter in changes which rows are
preserved with nulls, and item 1226's conformance decision is open — an optimization must not be
the thing that settles it); a path SELECTOR; any quantified, nested or multi-element segment; a
variable at more than one node position; and a variable that names a RELATIONSHIP.

A path MODE is deliberately NOT an exclusion, and that distinction is load-bearing. A mode
(`trail`, `acyclic`) is a FILTER on walks, a label is a filter on walks, and filters COMMUTE. A
SELECTOR picks an EXTREMUM of the surviving set and does not commute. **The first cut required
`mode === undefined` and therefore folded NOTHING**, because the parser defaults `mode` to
`'trail'` and `selector` to `'walk'` and never leaves either unset — it typechecked, built, and
measured flat, which is a null that looks exactly like "the lever is not there". It was found by
instrumenting the pass, not by reasoning about why the number had not moved.

### What it bought

A/B against the pre-change file, same fixture, one shape per process:

```text
                                   PRE      POST       note
  scan, clause label            119.46      0.01   now a bucket size
  one-hop, clause far label     196.12     23.25
  one-hop, vacuous start        195.73     19.50
  one-hop, non-vacuous start     82.42     55.64
  scan, clause property          20.07     19.44   CONTROL, flat
  hand-written label floor        22.51     22.59   CONTROL, flat
  scan, PATTERN label              0.01      0.01   CONTROL, flat
```

⚠️ **The one-hop pair bounces ~1.6x run to run** — the PATTERN arm, which this change cannot
touch, read 17.06 and 27.57 in consecutive runs. So the hop numbers are reported as convergence,
not to two significant figures, and one intermediate change here was kept on its mechanism after
an apparent improvement turned out to be inside that bounce.

### Item 1302's fixture-dependence question is STILL OPEN, and both its suspects are exhausted

This is the part of 1302 this item did NOT close, and the earlier claim that it had is withdrawn.

Start-label vacuity is a real variable, measured as a 2x2 on one graph, answers identical per row:

```text
                              pattern   clause    ratio   answer
  vacuous start (:Person)       18.77   195.73    10.4x   100000
  non-vacuous start (:Mgr)      55.91    82.42     1.47x   33333
```

With a start label the planner cannot drop, both spellings fail `bareDegreeSum`'s precondition and
converge. **But that does not explain the spelling probe's 1.34x**, which is the number the open
question was about: that fixture labels EVERY vertex `P`, so its `(a:P)` is vacuous too and it
belongs in the top row.

The other recorded suspect — MULTI-LABEL EDGES, `["E","F"]` on 1 in 11, which is what disables the
analogous Gremlin path through `multiTypeEdgeCount` — is now REFUTED. One variable moved, same
arms, same size, 3 alternated rounds:

```text
                     ml=0     ml=11   ml/single
  hop-label-pattern  22.31    18.74      0.84x
  hop-label-clause  200.66   193.08      0.96x
  hop-prop-clause    81.77    83.97      1.03x   CONTROL, flat
  clause/pattern      8.99x   10.30x            — it did NOT collapse
```

So the cause of that fixture's compression is unfound. No third suspect is named here; the next
tick is to read the group's number out of the probe directly rather than infer it.

None of this affects the fold: afterwards the clause spelling IS the pattern spelling, so they
converge whatever the fixture does.

### Teeth

A ROUTE assertion is too blunt for this, and that is measured. `countShortcut` fires for the
clause spelling as well as the pattern one, so "which detector fired" is identical either way:
with the fold disabled, **five of six route twins still passed** and only the projection twin
failed. So `foldLabelTestsIntoPatterns` is exported for its own assertion — the way
`compileLinear`, `predFor` and `selectiveFirst` already are, and not from `index.ts` — and the
rewrite is asserted AS a rewrite: the label lands on the right node, the `where` KEY is absent
rather than holding `undefined`, and each exclusion is left untouched.

10 mutants, 9 caught, 1 survivor:

```text
  fold-disabled                CAUGHT     negation-ignored         CAUGHT
  quantifier-guard-removed     CAUGHT     existing-label-dropped   CAUGHT
  optional-guard-removed-BOTH  CAUGHT     residual-dropped         CAUGHT
  rel-poison-removed           CAUGHT     where-key-kept           CAUGHT
  repeat-poison-removed        CAUGHT     selector-guard-removed   SURVIVED
```

**The survivor is PROVEN unreachable and the condition is kept anyway.** This engine accepts a
path selector only with a single variable-length segment (`ANY SHORTEST (a)-[:T]->(m)-[:T]->(b)`
is a syntax error), so a non-`walk` selector always implies a quantifier and the quantifier guard
declines it first. It stays because the thing making it unreachable is a parser limitation whose
own error message calls itself temporary, and because the unsoundness it guards is not the
endpoint case: for a filter on an INTERMEDIATE node of a fixed-length selector pattern, the
selector keeps one path per endpoint PAIR, so filtering before it can keep a pair that filtering
after would drop. Same shape as `mergeFarPreds`' `truthProps` — a correctness precondition held
live for when the surface grows.

Three results in the FIRST mutation round were the harness being wrong, not the code, and each is
the kind that reads as a clean result:

- `selector-guard-removed` anchored on a line `vacuousQuantifier` also carries, so it appeared 2x
  and never landed. Reporting ANCHOR rather than a verdict is what kept it from reading as a
  survivor.
- `where-key-kept` anchored at 0x: the ternary written across three lines is one line in the file.
- Both `optional` mutants SURVIVED correctly — the guard lives at two call sites and removing
  either leaves the other enforcing it. A single-site mutant of a duplicated guard tests nothing.

And one that was NOT a harness bug: `rel-poison-removed` survived because the plain edge-variable
case is declined by ABSENCE — a rel variable never reaches the site map — so the poisoning only
matters when the name COLLIDES with a node variable. `MATCH (a)-[a]->(b)` parses here and `a`
binds the RELATIONSHIP: `WHERE a IS LABELED T` answers 1 where `WHERE a IS LABELED P` answers 0,
so folding onto the node would answer the second question. A FIXTURE gap, not dead code. The
fixture also gained a self-loop, so the two-node-positions exclusion is no longer asserted against
an empty answer.

### No regressions, measured rather than argued

The full suite reports 68 failures from the repo root, and they are PRE-EXISTING: HEAD 6250 pass /
68 fail / 7 errors against POST 6250 / 68 / 7, delta 0, and no failing suite in POST that was not
already failing at HEAD. Every package passes ISOLATED (6010 tests, 0 fail). Of the 68, 7 come
from `examples/` and from stale A/B snapshots under `crates/lenke-engine/target/a597` and `p597`
that `bun test` picks up from the root; the rest are the run-many timing flakes
(`sync-test-flake-is-timing`).

### What is open after this

- **Why the spelling probe's fixture compresses the UNFOLDED gap** — both recorded suspects are
  now exhausted (vacuity measured but insufficient, multi-label edges refuted) and no third is
  named. Academic for the clause spelling now that it folds, but it is a live question about that
  fixture.
- **There is NO Gremlin equivalent-spelling probe.** `spelling-probe.ts` is GQL-only — 207 `MATCH`
  queries and zero `g.V()` — so the surface that gets `bun run bench:gremlin` has no check of the
  one property every index-seeding bug in this engine's history violated. CLAUDE.md's "equivalent
  spellings must cost the same" is enforced for one of the two languages.
- ~~**A VACUOUS START LABEL COSTS 1545x on a hop count**~~ — **WITHDRAWN at item 1304, it was a
  misread fixture.** This entry claimed `P` is on every vertex of the spelling probe's fixture. It
  is not: that fixture appends four `s0..s3` nodes labelled `["S","Univ"]`, so `P` covers 200000
  of 200004 vertices and `vacuousLabel` correctly declines to drop it. The two spellings agreed on
  the answer only because those four nodes have no edges, which is a property of this fixture and
  not an equivalence — so the pair was two different questions and the 1545x measured nothing.
  `Univ` IS on all 200004, and anchored there the pair reads 0.822ms against 0.192ms, both
  sub-millisecond, while the real label `P` reads 24.379ms. `vacuousLabel` works, and there is no
  target here. The lesson is the one CLAUDE.md already states and this item failed to apply to
  someone else's fixture: CHECK THE FIXTURE'S OWN STATISTICS — the four extra nodes sit ~1000
  lines from the label template that was read.
- **The box-array lever** (~1.7x on a property count), unchanged by this item: cost is delete
  bookkeeping, because swap-remove reorders and Gremlin observably reproduces TinkerPop's order.

## 1305 — the Gremlin surface had no equivalent-spelling probe; it has one now, and it flags 15 groups

CLAUDE.md's "equivalent spellings must cost the same" section records that every index-seeding bug
the old engine had took ONE shape — the planner recognised one spelling of a predicate and scanned
for another that meant exactly the same thing — that each cost 100-300x, and that each RETURNED
THE CORRECT ANSWER, so no correctness test could catch it. It then says the pure-TS engine needs
its own check "and has one".

It has one for ISO-GQL. `spelling-probe.ts` is 207 `MATCH` queries and ZERO `g.V()`. The Gremlin
surface — a separate implementation with its own executor, steps and shortcut ladder — had a
cross-engine BENCH and no spelling check at all. `bench-gremlin.ts` even carries equivalent pairs
as adjacent rows with comments saying "these two ask the same question and must stay close", which
states the claim and then leaves it to a human to eyeball.

A user picks GQL xor Gremlin, so a surface-only gap costs half of them.

### What it found

`0 group(s) disagree on the ANSWER` across all 21 groups, so every pair below is the same
question. Confirmed in ISOLATION, three runs each, as the probe's own output instructs (item 1073:
one isolated run is still one reading):

```text
  V('v137').count()                    0.008ms   vs  V().hasId('v137').count()      5.79ms   757-930x
  E('e137').count()                    0.008ms   vs  E().hasId('e137').count()     12.0ms  1462-1796x
  V().out('T').count()                 0.009ms   vs  V().outE('T').inV().count()  ~204ms   18936-24433x
```

The first two are the O(1)-BY-ID PROPERTY ITSELF: a seeded `V(id)` is a `verticesById` hit, and
`hasId` — the spelling a user reaches for when the id arrives as a filter rather than as a seed —
scans every element. The third is a closed-form degree sum against 400,000 materialised
traversers.

The full flag list at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`, net of the nearest null control:

```text
  both(T) vs union(out, in)                          228822x
  bothE(T) vs union(outE, inE)                       148043x
  out(T) vs outE(T).inV()                             95600x
  edge id lookup: seeded vs hasId                      4422x
  id lookup: seeded vs hasId                           1264x
  id lookup, projected: seeded vs hasId                 690x
  far-end property after a hop: out() vs outE().inV()     6.53x
  membership: within vs an or-chain of equalities         6.42x
  presence: has(k) vs hasKey(k) vs not(hasNot(k))         5.48x
  far-end label after a hop: out() vs outE().inV()        5.09x
  conjunction: has().has() vs and(has, has)               4.75x
  a filter wrapper: has() vs filter(has())                4.42x
  label + property: hasLabel().has() vs has(l, k, p)      4.17x
  values(k).is(p) vs has(k, p)                            3.85x
  hasLabel(a,b) vs or(hasLabel, hasLabel)                 2.81x
```

Null controls — one traversal against itself — read 1.03x at 3.0ms and 1.05x at 31.1ms, so none of
these is the harness.

### Two things the probe is built to do that a bench does not

**THE ANSWER IS CHECKED FIRST, and it earned itself on the first run.** The first cut included
`has(T.id, x)` and `has(T.label, x)` as arms, because TinkerPop accepts those as synonyms for
`hasId`/`hasLabel`. They answered 0 where `hasLabel('Mgr')` answered 667 — which reads exactly
like a silent wrong answer. It is not one: this surface's `has` is typed `has(key: string, ...)`,
so a `T` token there is a COMPILE error, and `bun run typecheck` says so. A spelling that cannot
compile is not a spelling cliff. The arms are gone and the reason is recorded where they were,
because the next reader will have the same idea. The order that got this right is ANSWERS, then
typecheck, then a verdict — reading the timings first would have produced a conformance bug
report.

**THE FIXTURE'S OWN STATISTICS ARE ASSERTED BY THE FILE**, not assumed by its reader: `Univ` and
`Person` must cover every vertex and `Mgr` must cover some-but-not-all, and the probe exits
non-zero if not. That is item 1304's lesson made mechanical — that item read a label template,
concluded a label was vacuous, and missed four nodes appended a thousand lines further down.

### What is open after this

- ~~**`hasId` does not seed**~~ — **BUILT at item 1306**: a single-id `hasId` now seeds from the
  id map (5.79ms -> 0.018 on vertices, 12.0 -> 0.015 on edges, projected 0.015). The MULTI-id case
  is a deliberate decline worth 6.5-7.1ms against 0.020, blocked on a decision about emission
  order rather than on a mechanism; see 1306.
- ~~**`outE(T).inV()` is not normalised to `out(T)`**~~ — **BUILT at item 1307** for both edge-hop
  pairs (`outE.inV` -> `out`, `inE.outV` -> `in`): 144.175ms -> 0.009 and 160.127 -> 0.009, with
  two far-end groups converging as well. The `union(out, in)` -> `both` half is still OPEN and is
  a different rewrite; see 1307.
- The remaining ten groups at 2.8x-6.9x, each confirmed only by the sweep so far and each needing
  its own isolated three runs before it is a finding.

### Verification

`bun run typecheck` 0, `bun run lint` 0, `bun run fmt` 0 and verified idempotent by hashing `git
diff` across a second run. The probe is a PROBE and not a test — time is the only signal
available, so a threshold in CI would be flaky; it is run when the Gremlin planner or a step
changes, which is what the GQL twin's header says of itself.

## 1306 — `hasId` seeds from the id map, so the one spelling whose cost should not scale with the graph stops doing so

Item 1305's new Gremlin spelling probe flagged this as its largest O(1)-relevant gap. `hasId` was
already in `COMMUTING_FILTERS` — allowed to sit among the leading filters a seed looks through —
but there was no seed CANDIDATE for it, so it was only ever a residual filter over a full scan.

Measured on that probe at 200,000 vertices / 400,000 edges, one group per process, three isolated
runs each, both spellings answering identically throughout:

```text
                                   PRE        POST
  V().hasId('v137').count()      5.79 ms    0.015-0.021 ms
  E().hasId('e137').count()     12.0        0.014-0.018
  V().hasId(x).values('age')   (625-713x)   0.014-0.017
```

Both arms of each pair are now under the probe's own `FLOOR_MS`, so those groups report as
not-compared rather than as findings.

### Two routes were tried and the faster-looking one is WRONG

The obvious fix is a plan rewrite: `V()` followed by `hasId(ids)` becomes the seeded source
`V(ids)`, which reaches every rung at once — the shape item 1303's fold has. It is UNSOUND, twice:

- **`V(ids)` RAISES where `hasId` does not.** `applySource`'s `asStringId` throws for a non-string
  id, deliberately, matching TinkerPop's string id manager. `V().hasId(5)` does not throw:
  `dispatch.ts` filters with `ids.includes(v.id)`, which simply never matches, and the answer is
  EMPTY. The rewrite would convert an empty result into a fault — the raise-parity class of items
  139-145.
- **`V(ids)` does not DEDUPE.** `sourceFromIds` loops the ids and yields per id, so `V('a','a')`
  emits the element twice where `hasId('a','a')` emits it once. Two different multisets.

So the seed lives in `index-seed.ts` as a `Candidate`, beside `labelSeed`, where the selection is
exact. It goes through the RAW id map (`graph.verticesById` / `graph.edgesById`) with a `typeof id
=== 'string'` guard, never through `getVertexById`/`asStringId`, precisely so the asymmetry above
is preserved. `removable: true` holds because the lookup is SameValueZero — the same equality
`ids.includes` uses — so the seeded set IS the filter's output.

### The single-id restriction is about ORDER, and it cost a test to find

The first working version seeded any number of ids and broke `hasId.test.ts`'s "we can filter by
ids out of order", which asserts `hasId('6','2','1','4')` comes back `['1','2','4','6']` — the
SOURCE's order, because `hasId` is a filter over the source. A seed emits in the order the ids
were WRITTEN.

That test is NAMED for the behaviour, so it is a pinned contract rather than an incidental
assertion, and the repo's general "an unordered result's order is WON'T-FIX" policy does not
license an optimization to overturn a case someone wrote down on purpose. With ONE id the question
cannot arise — one element has one position, so the seeded and scanned sequences are identical —
and that is the shape the entire measured win is in.

**The multi-id case is therefore a DELIBERATE DECLINE and is worth taking.** The scan cost does
not depend on how many ids are written, so the gap is the full one:

```text
  1 id   (SEEDED)     0.020 ms
  2 ids  (declined)   6.571
  4 ids  (declined)   7.061
```

Taking it needs a decision about that order, made against TinkerPop ground truth (`podman run -i
docker.io/tinkerpop/gremlin-console:3.7.3`) and not as a side effect of a perf change, with that
test updated in the same commit.

### Teeth

The seed is answer-equivalent where it applies, so the mutant that matters is the one that turns
it off: the suite then answers identically by scanning. Item 1303 measured how blunt a route
assertion can be — there, one that asked only "which detector fired" passed with the whole rewrite
disabled — so `seedFromIndex` is called DIRECTLY and the seed is asserted AS a seed: it returns a
plan, the `hasId` step is REMOVED from the residual, and the stream holds exactly the element.

6 mutants, 4 caught:

```text
  seed-disabled                CAUGHT  3 fail    string-guard-dropped-vertex  SURVIVED
  single-id-guard-removed      CAUGHT  4 fail    dedupe-removed-via-array     SURVIVED
  step-kept-not-removable      CAUGHT  2 fail
  absent-id-seeds-everything   CAUGHT  1 fail
```

Both survivors were PREDICTED and both are genuinely answer-equivalent: `Map.get` with a
non-string key misses anyway, so the `typeof` guard documents the raise-parity argument rather
than changing an answer; and `new Set([el, el])` still holds one element, because the `Set` IS the
dedupe. The second is also now VACUOUS — once the seed was restricted to a single id there is
nothing to dedupe, and the mutant surviving is a fair reflection of that narrowed scope rather
than a gap in the tests.

Two mutants were caught that I had predicted would SURVIVE, both because the route assertion is
sharper than expected: keeping the step is visible in the residual, and declining on a missing id
is visible as a `null` seed.

## 1307 — `outE(T).inV()` fuses to `out(T)`, so the long spelling of a hop reaches every rung the short one has

Item 1305's Gremlin spelling probe flagged this as the largest gap on that surface. The long
spelling is what a user writes when the edge is interesting on the way through, and it had no rung
at all: `out(T).count()` is a closed-form degree sum while `outE(T).inV().count()` materialised
one traverser per edge.

A/B against the pre-change file, same fixture, one shape per process, min of three alternated
rounds, every answer identical:

```text
  arm                   PRE ms    POST ms    speedup
  q-long-hop           144.175      0.009  16199x
  q-long-in            160.127      0.009  16855x
  q-long-farlabel      237.110     45.246      5.24x
  q-long-farprop       200.319     26.986      7.42x
  ctl-short-hop          0.006      0.006      0.94x   CONTROL
  ctl-short-farlabel    42.870     43.913      0.98x   CONTROL
  ctl-scan               2.148      2.043      1.05x   CONTROL
```

Control band 0.94x-1.05x, so the controls held. **That A/B exists because the probe could not
answer the question it raised.** After the fusion the far-end-label group reads ~47ms on BOTH
arms, which is equally consistent with the long arm falling to meet the short one and with the
SHORT arm having risen — and a spelling probe compares spellings inside one run, so it cannot
distinguish them. `ctl-short-farlabel` settles it at 0.98x: the long arm fell 237 to 45, the short
arm did not move. Claiming "no regression" from the probe alone would have been the same
argument-instead-of-a- measurement this session already had to retract once.

Four probe groups converged, not two: the far-end label and far-end property pairs came along
because the long spelling now reaches item 1302's far-label rung and the property rung behind it.

### Equivalence was MEASURED first, because item 1306 is the cautionary tale

There, the analogous-looking rewrite of `V() + hasId(ids)` into `V(ids)` was unsound twice over —
it RAISED where the filter did not, and it did not DEDUPE. So before writing this one, both
spellings were run on a fixture built to break them: PARALLEL `a->b` edges, a MULTI-LABEL
`['T','S']` edge, and a SELF-LOOP `a->a`. They agree on the same multiset AND the same ORDER for
`count()`, for the elements, for `values(k)`, for the untyped `outE()`/`out()` pair, and for the
incoming mirror.

⚠️ **THEY DO NOT AGREE ON `path()`**, and that is the whole guard: the long spelling puts the EDGE
in the traverser's path and `out` does not. `planReadsPath` is the test and it is conservative in
the right direction — it recurses every plan-bearing field, covers `path`, `tree`, `simplePath`,
`cyclicPath`, `otherV` and the closure steps, and returns true when in doubt.

ADJACENCY is the second guard and it does more than it looks: any step between the two —
`as_('e')`, `aggregate`, `sack`, a filter on the edge — stops the match, which is exactly right,
because those are the plans where the edge is observable for a reason other than the path and a
fused hop would have no edge to give them.

`bothE(T).otherV()` is deliberately NOT fused. It looks like the third member of the family, but
`otherV` is itself path-dependent, so the guard already excludes it, and folding it to `both(T)`
needs its own argument rather than this one. A `repeat()` body is left for its own item too: only
the TOP-LEVEL step list is rewritten.

### Teeth

The fusion is answer-equivalent where it applies, so the mutant that matters most cannot change an
answer — it just stops CALLING the rewrite.

**The first cut of the tests could not see that mutant**, and that is worth recording. 22
assertions called `fuseEdgeHop` directly, so unwiring it from the pipeline left every one of them
passing while the suite answered identically by the slow walk — the same hole item 1303 found in
its route assertions. The fix was to extract the rewrite composition as an exported
`effectivePlan(plan, graph, tracksPath)` and assert the WIRING and its GUARD separately: it fuses
when nothing reads the path, and it does not fuse when the path is tracked. That also puts one
guard in one place instead of spelled out at the call site, where it could be remembered for one
rewrite and forgotten for the next.

7 mutants, 7 caught, no survivors:

```text
  fusion-unwired            CAUGHT   1 fail     mirror-pair-confused     CAUGHT   2 fail
  path-guard-removed        CAUGHT   5 fail     adjacency-not-consumed   CAUGHT  16 fail
  wrong-far-end             CAUGHT  13 fail     identity-return-dropped  CAUGHT   1 fail
  labels-dropped            CAUGHT   3 fail
```

`fusion-unwired` is caught only by the wiring assertion added above; before it, that mutant
survived by construction. `identity-return-dropped` was expected to survive and did not — the
`toBe` identity assertion sees it, which is what that assertion is for.

## 1308 — every WRAPPED filter was slower than the flat chain that means the same thing; one rewrite fixes it

Item 1305's probe flagged six small groups at 2.8x-6.9x and they looked like six items. The
per-arm numbers at 200,000 vertices say they are mostly ONE defect in several spellings: a wrapped
filter puts its filters in a SUB-PLAN, the flat rungs (`filterChainCount` and the rest) stop
matching, and the whole query drops to the traverser pipeline.

```text
  has('age', gte(45))              2.904 ms   filter(has('age', gte(45)))   36.675 ms   12.6x
  has('k', gte(2)).hasLabel('Q')   6.364      and(has(…), hasLabel(…))      58.731       9.2x
  has('age')                       2.516      hasKey('age')                  2.551       — same step
                                              not(hasNot('age'))            43.123      17x
  has('k', within(7,8,9))          8.985      or(has, has, has)             35.775       4.0x
  has('age', gte(45))              2.523      values('age').is(gte(45))     23.277       9.2x
  hasLabel('Mgr').has(…)           2.199      has('Mgr','age',gte(45))       8.981       4.1x
```

Reading the group ratios alone would have hidden this: `presence` reported 5.68x as a three-arm
group, where in fact `has(k)` and `hasKey(k)` are the SAME step — `has` with one argument builds
`{kind:'hasKey'}` — and the whole spread came from the double-negation arm. Per-arm numbers are
what turned six targets into one.

### What was built

`flattenFilterWrappers` splices `filter(body)` and `and(bodies)` into the enclosing step list when
every step in the body only keeps-or-drops the element. After it:

```text
  filter(has('age', gte(45)))   36.675 -> 2.558 ms   (the flat twin reads 2.564)   14.3x
  and(has(…), hasLabel(…))      58.731 -> 6.227      (the flat twin reads 6.185)    9.4x
```

Both spellings now land on the same rung, which is the claim — not "faster", but "the same plan".

### Why splicing is sound, and the case that makes the rule

It rests on `PURE_ELEMENT_FILTERS` — `has`, `hasLabel`, `hasLabelAnd`, `hasId`, `hasKey`,
`hasNot`, `hasValue` — deliberately NARROWER than the `PRESERVE_STEPS` set already in the file,
which also admits `where`, `and`, `or`, `not`, barriers and pass-through writes.

`filter(body)` keeps a traverser when `body` yields at least one result. If every step in `body`
only keeps-or-drops, then `body` yields the element itself or nothing, so "keeps when the body
yields" IS "the element passed every filter" — which is what the spliced chain computes, in the
same order. `and(plans)` is the same argument once per branch.

**`filter(out('T'))` is the case that makes the purity check necessary rather than merely
cautious.** It keeps the vertices that HAVE an outgoing `T` edge; splicing `out('T')` would
REPLACE each vertex with its neighbours. Asserted as an answer (`['v0','v2']`), not only as a plan
shape, and its mutant — dropping the purity check — fails 8 tests.

RAISE PARITY was measured rather than carried over, because a splice that short-circuits where the
wrapper did not would turn a fault into a row. On THIS surface a cross-type comparison returns
FALSE rather than raising: `has('s', gte(5))` on a string property answers empty, and the chained,
`and`-wrapped and `filter`-wrapped spellings all agree. That differs from the GQL side's
cross-type policy (`cross-type-comparison-no-error`), which is exactly why it was checked here.

### What is deliberately NOT done

- **`or` is not flattened and cannot be** — a disjunction is not a chain. Its group (`within`
  against an `or`-chain of equalities, 4.0x) needs the disjunction recognised as a MEMBERSHIP,
  which is a different mechanism; the mutant that extends this rewrite to `or` turns a disjunction
  into a conjunction and is caught.
- **`not(hasNot(k))` at 17x** is a double negation; it is real but nobody writes it, so it is
  recorded rather than built.
- **Nesting is not recursive.** `filter(filter(has(…)))` declines, because a `filter` is not a
  pure element filter. One level is what was measured; a recursive version would be its own item
  with its own numbers.
- **`has(label, key, pred)` at 4.1x is NOT a wrapper** — it is a single `hasLabelAnd` step, so
  this rewrite cannot reach it and its group stays open.

### Teeth

7 mutants, 6 caught, every result as predicted:

```text
  flatten-unwired         CAUGHT  1 fail     or-also-flattened        CAUGHT  1 fail
  purity-check-dropped    CAUGHT  8 fail     filter-arm-removed       CAUGHT  2 fail
  and-partial-splice      CAUGHT  1 fail     identity-return-dropped  CAUGHT  1 fail
  empty-body-admitted     SURVIVED
```

`flatten-unwired` is caught only by the `effectivePlan` wiring assertion that item 1307 had to add
for the same reason — asserting the rewrite FUNCTION leaves alive the mutant that stops calling
it.

**The survivor is PROVEN unreachable, and the check is kept.** The `plan.steps.length > 0` guard
in `pureFilterSteps` can only matter for an EMPTY body, and neither route reaches one: `filter()`
with no body faults at run time (`step.fn is not a function`), so it is not a usable plan at all,
and `and()` with no branches is declined by the separate `parts.length > 0` test rather than by
this one. Kept as a precondition for the same reason item 1303 keeps its selector guard — if the
surface ever admits an empty body, splicing nothing would silently DELETE the step.

## 1309 — `has(label, key, pred)` was 4.1x the two steps it exists to fuse

`has('Mgr', 'age', gte(45))` is the shorthand for "this label AND this property". It builds a
single `hasLabelAnd` step, and the rungs that answer a filter CHAIN do not recognise it, so the
shorthand dropped to the traverser pipeline while the longhand was served:

```text
  hasLabel('Mgr').has('age', gte(45))   2.199 ms
  has('Mgr', 'age', gte(45))            8.981        4.1x, both answering 33330
```

After splitting it inside `flattenFilterWrappers`: **8.981 -> 1.589-2.253 ms**, indistinguishable
from the longhand, which reads 2.076-3.304 in the same runs. Both arms are now sub-millisecond, so
this is reported as CONVERGENCE and not to three figures.

Sound by construction: the step's whole meaning is the conjunction of a single-label test and one
property predicate, which is exactly those two steps. Verified at the boundaries as well as the
middle — a label NO element carries, an ABSENT key, and a projection off the end all agree between
the spellings.

Found from item 1305's probe by reading PER-ARM numbers rather than the group ratio, which is the
same move that turned item 1308's six flags into one cause.

### A comment I wrote was FALSE and its own test caught it

The first cut put the split inline in the loop and claimed that a `hasLabelAnd` coming out of an
`and(…)` branch would be split too. It would not have been: the splice pushes branch steps
straight into the list without re-examining them. The test asserting that composition failed, and
the fix was to make the CODE match the claim — every push now routes through `pushSplit` — rather
than to weaken the claim to match the code. That bug is now its own mutant,
`splice-does-not-split`.

### ⚠️ A FALSE RETRACTION, CAUGHT BY MATCHING THE FIXTURE

While looking for the next target this item nearly retired item 1248/1296's grouped hop extremum
as a stale entry. It is NOT stale, and the reason the measurement said otherwise is worth more
than the measurement.

The route check was the honest part: `compileLinear` shows `detectGroupedHopAggregate` claiming
the shape, `ORDER BY` included — which is what item 1296 already established and item 1249 fixed.
The re-pricing was the dishonest part. Measured at 200,000 nodes and **200,000 edges**, the
grouped extremum read 194.5 ms against the ungrouped twin's 93.6 — 2.08x, not the recorded 5.1x —
and it cost about what grouped `count` (181.9) and grouped `sum` (171.6) cost. That looked like
the premise ("min/max lacks the fold the scalar accumulators have") having been quietly closed.

**It was the WRONG FIXTURE for the claim.** Item 1296's is 200,000 nodes / **1,000,000** edges,
and the identity the whole target rests on is that ~200,000 distinct endpoints answer what
1,000,000 edges are asked. At one edge per node there is almost no endpoint duplication to
exploit, so the lever cannot show. On the matched fixture:

```text
  GROUPED hop extremum  [TARGET]              366.9 ms   rows=8     (1296 recorded 345.2)
  [CTL] UNGROUPED hop extremum (has the fold) 106.0      rows=1     (1296 recorded  67.9)
  [CTL] GROUPED node extremum (no hop)         16.9      rows=8
  [CTL] GROUPED hop count(*)                  305.6      rows=8
  [CTL] GROUPED hop sum                       339.5      rows=8
```

**3.46x and live.** Every absolute number here is higher than 1296's, so the 5.1x-to-3.46x
difference reads as machine state rather than as an engine change, and nothing licenses re-pricing
the entry downward from one run on one box.

The code fact 1296 states also checks out, and it is fixture-independent: `primedEndpointExtremum`
is imported ONLY by `hop-projection.ts`, which carries the UNGROUPED rungs, so
`detectGroupedHopAggregate` in `shortcuts.ts` genuinely never got the endpoint-primed fold. That
the extremum costs about what grouped `count` and `sum` cost is CONSISTENT with that — the grouped
hop path lacks the primed fold for all of them — and is not evidence against the target.

So item 1248/1296's heading stands unchanged, and this is recorded as the near-miss it was.
CLAUDE.md already says "match the fixture to the claim — one edge per node is sparse"; the cost of
ignoring it here would have been retiring a correct, priced, live target.

## 1310 — the GROUPED hop extremum folds once per endpoint, 3.42x, built from item 1296's specification

Items 1248 and 1296 priced this and wrote the specification; this is that specification built. The
identity is `primedEndpointExtremum`'s, extended by one step: min/max over a multiset equal
min/max over its distinct SUPPORT, and when the GROUP KEY reads only the far endpoint each
distinct endpoint belongs to exactly ONE group, so folding it once into that group's accumulator
is the same answer. ~200,000 endpoints answer what 1,000,000 edges are asked.

A/B against HEAD, same fixture (200,000 nodes / 1,000,000 edges, 8 cities), one shape per process,
min of three alternated rounds, every answer identical:

```text
  arm                            PRE ms    POST ms   speedup
  q-grouped-extremum             346.85     101.46     3.42x
  q-grouped-minmax               338.32     105.94     3.19x
  q-grouped-extremum-order       352.73     102.41     3.44x
  ctl-ungrouped-extremum         102.46      96.39     1.06x   CONTROL
  ctl-grouped-count              282.56     294.67     0.96x   CONTROL
  ctl-grouped-sum                320.45     323.00     0.99x   CONTROL
  ctl-grouped-node                10.51      10.40     1.01x   CONTROL
  ctl-scan                         8.34       8.32     1.00x   CONTROL
```

Control band 0.96x-1.06x. The target now MATCHES its ungrouped twin (101.46 against 96.39), which
is what the identity predicts.

**THE CONTROLS DECIDED WHERE THE CODE LIVES.** A single run had shown grouped `sum` at 1.08x and
the ungrouped twin at 1.11x, which is exactly the `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` signature —
`hop-endpoint-extremum.ts` exists as its own module because living beside a 4,400-line file cost
an unrelated shape 1.08x with DISJOINT ranges, and this change adds ~160 lines to an 11,000-line
one. Three alternated rounds put both inside the band, so the helper stays in `shortcuts.ts`. The
A/B script printed the fallback instruction itself, so the decision was not available to be
rationalised.

### The admission, and the two guards whose mutants SURVIVE

Item 1296 specified four conditions. Two do the work; two are unreachable and are kept anyway,
with the ROUTE EVIDENCE recorded beside them rather than an argument.

- **The key reads only the far variable** (`!onStart`). A start-keyed group is not
  one-group-per-endpoint, so folding it is a wrong answer. CAUGHT.
- **Every non-key projection item is `min`/`max` with one argument.** `foldFor` admits
  count/min/max, so `count(x)` builds a `fold` acc that only the NAME test refuses. CAUGHT.
- **Every accumulator is a streaming `fold`.** MUTANT SURVIVES. Kept as a precondition.
- **The relationship label is a plain type list.** MUTANT SURVIVES. Kept as a precondition.
- **The start label is absent or vacuous** — tested at RUN time, because vacuity is a property of
  the graph. This one is a measured REGRESSION guard, not a correctness guard: item 1245 priced
  the per-endpoint fold WITHOUT it at 1.07x WORSE than the per-edge walk, because proving "x has a
  qualifying in-edge" then has to resolve `e.from` per in-edge. CAUGHT — by the order instrument
  alone, since it cannot change an answer.

### ⚠️ I GUESSED WRONG TWICE ABOUT THE SURVIVORS BEFORE MEASURING

Worth recording in full, because the measurement is one call and the guesses cost two rounds.

Round 3 left `admission-acckind-dropped` and `compound-label-admitted` alive. First guess: both
redundant with the extremum NAME test. Second guess, after confirming that `min(DISTINCT x.n)` and
`-[:!T]->` both parse and are reachable, and that `relTypeNames` really does return `null` for a
negated label: two more TEST GAPS. Two tests were written. **They did not close the mutants
either.**

`compileLinear` settles it in one call:

```text
  plain :T        -> ["groupedHopAggregate"]
  negated :!T     -> []
  wildcard :%     -> []
  min(DISTINCT x) -> []
```

NO rung fires for those shapes. `detectGroupedHopAggregate` refuses a DISTINCT aggregate and a
non-plain relationship label UPSTREAM of the fold's admission, so neither guard ever decides
anything and neither mutant can be caught. Both are kept — the three-way meaning of `relTypeNames`
is easy to collapse, and the first cut of this item's own refactor did collapse it — with the
`routes()` output written next to each, not the reasoning that was wrong twice.

The two tests stay, with their comments CORRECTED to say they do not test those guards. They
assert that a DISTINCT extremum and a negated label answer correctly through the general path,
which nothing else covered.

### Three self-inflicted bugs, each caught by a different gate

**The first admission admitted NOTHING, and the suite stayed green.** It required every
accumulator to be a `fold`, but `groupedAccs` pushes the key column as a `{kind:'rows'}`
PLACEHOLDER so the column can be written by index — no admissible query can satisfy that. The
target did not move and 3,291 tests passed: the silent decline that looks exactly like the lever
not existing. Found by measuring, then reading `groupedAccs`.

**The complexity cap caught the second.** Inlined, the admission took `detectGroupedHopAggregate`
to 40 against a cap of 35 — the wall item 1249 hit there and the reason `groupedSortApplier` lives
outside it. Extracted as `groupedEndpointFold`.

**The typechecker caught the third, inside that extraction.** `relTypeNames` returns THREE things:
`undefined` for an untyped `-[]->` (every type), `null` for a label it cannot reduce (decline),
and an array. The extraction declined on `null` but passed `types` straight through, leaking
`undefined` into a `readonly string[]`. Collapsing those is a wrong answer in either direction —
refusing untyped hops, or reading the wrong buckets — so the distinction is now explicit, and the
untyped case gained a ROUTE assertion, because a value comparison passes whether or not the fold
fires.

### Row order: the opposite call from item 1306, on purpose

The fold iterates the FAR side where the per-edge walk iterates the start side, so groups emit in
a different order, and ONE test of 3,291 hard-coded `[b, a]`.

Item 1306 faced this and RESTRICTED the optimization rather than touch a test. The difference is
stated rather than assumed: that test was NAMED for the ordering ("we can filter by ids out of
order"), so it pinned a contract deliberately. This one is named "the AGGREGATE answers as it does
without the name" — the order is incidental to its claim, the repo's settled policy and the
differential fuzzer's own multiset invariant both say grouped order without `ORDER BY` is
unspecified, and item 1296 established that BEFORE the fold was built. So only the ordering
assumption was dropped; the value claim and the `count(*)` case beside it are untouched.

That same order is then used as the ROUTE INSTRUMENT: the fixture is built so the start-side and
far-side group orders DISAGREE, which is the only way to see which walk ran for an
answer-equivalent change. The test file says plainly that this is an instrument and not a
contract, and that these assertions are expected to change if either walk's order is deliberately
changed.

## 1311 — `union(out(T), in(T)).count()` fuses to `both(T).count()`, and the tail condition is the whole argument

Item 1305's Gremlin spelling probe measured this pair at 128659x net of its null control — the
largest gap it found. `both(T).count()` is answered from degree sums; the union materialises one
traverser per branch per vertex.

Measured on that probe at 200,000 vertices / 400,000 edges, both arms answering an identical
800000:

```text
                               before        after
  both(T).count()             0.008 ms      0.008-0.011 ms
  union(out(T), in(T)).count()  ~1 s        0.011-0.013
  bothE / union(outE, inE)      ~1 s        0.011-0.013
```

Both groups now report under the probe's own floor rather than as findings.

### WHAT WAS NOT BUILT, AND WHY — this is the item

The obvious change is to normalise `union(out, in)` into `both` everywhere, the way items 1303,
1307 and 1308 normalise their pairs. **That is unsound, and item 1308 measured it rather than
reasoning about it.** The two spellings are multiset-equal but NOT sequence-equal: on one fixture
`both` emits `["b","a","a","c","a","b"]` where the union emits `["b","a","c","a","a","b"]`,
because `both` finishes each vertex before moving on and the union does not. A row-returning
traversal rewritten this way would silently change its output order.

So the fusion is gated on an ORDER-FREE TAIL, and that list is deliberately tiny:

- `count()` reads the MULTISET, which the two spellings share.
- `dedupe()` then `count()` reads the SET, which is coarser still.
- **`sum` and `mean` are excluded even though they look order-free.** This repo records them as
  order-sensitive in the last ulp (`foldFor`'s own note), so a reordering IS observable in
  floating point.
- `min`/`max` would be safe by the same argument the extremum identity uses, but they are not in
  the measured shape, so they are not admitted on a guess.

Both admitted tails were verified on a fixture built to break the equivalence — PARALLEL edges, a
MULTI-LABEL edge and a SELF-LOOP — typed, untyped and multi-type, where the pair agrees at 8 and
at 3 respectively.

The branch conditions refuse real non-equivalences rather than merely unusual spellings:
`union(out(T), in(S))` is not a `both` of anything, `union(out(T), out(T))` doubles one side, a
branch with a second step is a different walk, and a three-branch union would lose its third
branch. Label lists are compared POSITIONALLY, which declines a reordered pair — conservative, and
cheaper than proving set equality.

```text
  tail-condition-dropped    CAUGHT  5 fail    branch-length-dropped      CAUGHT  1 fail
  tail-admits-anything      CAUGHT  2 fail    branch-count-dropped       CAUGHT  1 fail
  label-equality-dropped    CAUGHT  1 fail
```

`tail-condition-dropped` and `tail-admits-anything` are the two that matter: each reintroduces
exactly the unsoundness this item is designed around, and each is caught.

**The most useful assertion in the test file is a NEGATIVE one.** For a row-returning union it
asserts the union KEEPS its own order and does NOT equal `both`. That is the property the tail
condition protects, stated as a test: if it ever starts passing, either the two spellings have
genuinely become sequence-equal — in which case the tail list can be widened ON PURPOSE — or the
rewrite has begun firing where it must not.

A lint fix then hoisted the direction-pairing closure to module scope (it captured nothing), which
invalidated that mutant's anchor, so the three affected mutants were RE-RUN: 3/3 caught. A
refactor that quietly disables a guard shows up as nothing at all.

## 1312 — `or(has(k,a), has(k,b))` folds to `has(k, within(a,b))`, one of the four canonical seeding bugs

⚠️ **THIS IS ONE OF THE FOUR SHAPES CLAUDE.md NAMES BY EXAMPLE.** Its "equivalent spellings must
cost the same" section lists the forms every index-seeding bug the old engine had took, and `k =
$a OR k = $b` vs `k IN [$a, $b]` is one of them. ISO-GQL has folded it since item 1269
(`membershipFromEqChain`). The Gremlin surface never did, and nothing was looking until item 1305
gave that surface a spelling probe.

So this is also the cross-surface asymmetry this repo keeps paying for — a user picks GQL xor
Gremlin, so the gap cost half of them, exactly as items 1035/1038 then 1043/1044 did for their
lever.

Measured on item 1305's probe at 200,000 vertices, both arms answering an identical 12000:

```text
  has('k', within(7, 8, 9))                   8.287-9.089 ms
  or(has('k',7), has('k',8), has('k',9))      35.775  ->  8.610-8.712     4.15x
```

The `or` ran a sub-plan per branch per element; the membership form is one step the filter rungs
already recognise.

### Equivalence first, on the cases that break a value list

Checked before the rewrite was written, because item 1306's lesson is that an "obviously
equivalent" pair can differ twice over. Nine pairs, all agreeing: plain numbers, strings, a MIXED
string/number list, a list containing `null`, **`0` against `true`** (the pair that catches a fold
doing loose comparison), a list containing `NaN`, an explicit `eq()` against a bare value, a
single-value `or`, and the whole thing under `count()`.

The `NaN` case is the interesting one: `within(NaN, 1)` and `or(has(k,NaN), has(k,1))` BOTH keep
only the `1`, so neither spelling matches `NaN` against itself and the fold preserves that.
`has(k, v)` routes a bare value through `eq()` itself, so a step's predicate is always a predicate
object and never a raw value — which is why one equality serves both spellings.

Every branch must be exactly one `has` on the SAME key with an `eq` predicate. Each condition
refuses a real non-equivalence: a branch on another key is a disjunction ACROSS keys, a
`gt`/`within` /regex branch does not reduce to a value, and a two-step branch is a conjunction
inside the disjunction.

### ⚠️ A COMMENT OF MINE WAS FALSE FOR THE THIRD TIME IN THIS RUN, and its test caught it

The fold was added to `flattenFilterWrappers`' loop with a comment claiming that an `or` nested
inside an `and` would therefore fold too. **It would not have.** The `and` arm tested branch
PURITY first, and an `or` is not a `PURE_ELEMENT_FILTERS` member, so such a branch was rejected
before anything folded.

The fix was to make the code match the claim rather than soften the claim: `normalizedBranch`
normalises a branch — folding an `or` to a membership and splitting a `hasLabelAnd` — and THEN
judges whether what came out is filter-only. That also makes `filter(or(…))` fold, which the
purity-first order could not. The bug is now its own mutant (`branch-composition-reverted`), and
the helper's doc says plainly that it exists because a comment was false.

This is the same shape as item 1309's `pushSplit` and item 1307's wiring assertion. Three for
three: every time a comment claimed a composition this run, the composition was not there until a
test asked for it.

The lint gate then found `pureFilterSteps` had become dead — `normalizedBranch` replaced it — so
it is removed, and its empty-body guard migrated with its proven-unreachable note intact.

```text
  key-equality-dropped         CAUGHT  1 fail    branch-composition-reverted  CAUGHT  2 fail
  eq-only-dropped              CAUGHT  2 fail    empty-body-admitted          SURVIVED
  branch-length-dropped        CAUGHT  1 fail
```

The survivor is the migrated empty-body guard, PROVEN unreachable and kept for the reason item
1308 recorded: `filter()` with no body faults at run time so it is not a usable plan, and `and()`
with no branches is declined by the separate `parts.length > 0` test — but if the surface ever
admits an empty body, splicing nothing would silently DELETE the step.

## 1313 — the far-key grouped-count degree walk is REFUTED again, and "no SKIP/LIMIT" is not the narrowing

No speedup shipped. This item built the 3.5x walk, had it refuted by two tests, reverted it, and
spent its value on making a fourth attempt cheaper than this third one.

### The target, and why it looked open

`detectGroupedHopCount` has two walks and the key's end picks them: a START key reads the property
ONCE per start vertex and adds that vertex's whole matching degree, O(V); a FAR key reads each
edge's own endpoint, O(E). Priced on this build at 200,000 nodes / 1,000,000 edges:

```text
  FAR-key grouped count   [TARGET]    304.8 ms   rows=8
  START-key grouped count [degree]     87.3      rows=8   <- the same question, other end
  [CTL] global hop count                0.0
  [CTL] grouped NODE count              7.6
  FAR-key + LIMIT 3                   336.9      rows=3
```

**3.5x, not the 7.4x the audit records.** Item 138 measured 1065 -> 144.8 ms; the far walk has
since been changed to go through `expand` (which costs it 17% and is correct for multi-label
edges), so the old figure is stale as a prize. Quoting it would have oversold this by 2x.

Item 138 rejected the far-key degree walk because "group order is first-seen and observable". The
narrowing that looked available: a WINDOW is what makes group order decide which groups come back,
an `ORDER BY` sorts whatever order arrived (item 1249's `sortGroupRows`), and item 1296
established that a grouped result without `ORDER BY` is compared as a row MULTISET — the same
policy that licensed item 1310's per-endpoint extremum fold. So admit the walk only when `skip ===
undefined && limit === undefined`.

The paging half of that is TRUE and was verified rather than assumed: `LIMIT 1` over the far-key
count returns exactly `unpaged.slice(0, 1)` and `SKIP 1 LIMIT 1` returns `slice(1, 2)`, so a
window really does select by position in first-seen order.

### Why it is still wrong

Built, it failed TWO tests, neither of which has a window:

- `grouped-hop-rel-variable.test.ts` — a case named **"the TALLY answers as it does without the
  name, IN ORDER"**. A test named for the ordering pins it deliberately; that is item 1306's rule,
  applied here against my own change rather than for it.
- `grouped-hop-extremum.test.ts` — item 1310's own route instrument, which uses the grouped
  COUNT's start-side order as the "declined" signal. A far-driven count invalidates that signal.

And `paged-count.test.ts` states the contract directly: first-seen group order is **"the pinned
contract both engines keep"**. So it is a CONTRACT, not a consequence of windowing — which also
means changing TS's order would diverge from the native engine on a property the differential
fuzzer CANNOT SEE, because it compares grouped results as multisets. An undetected divergence is
worse than a caught regression.

### Far-driving preserves that order in NO iteration order — measured, not argued

Item 138's rejection names `edgesToByLabel` as the problem (it keys a far vertex at its first
IN-EDGE, so iterating it is edge-insertion order). That invites the reading that a different
source would be fine. It would not:

```text
  fixture: a -> z inserted before b -> y, with y created before z
  general / current (start-driven)   [KZ, KY]      LIMIT 1 -> KZ
  far-driven via edgesToByLabel      [KZ, KY]      agrees HERE, by coincidence
  far-driven via creation order      [KY, KZ]      <- disagrees
```

So the rejection generalises past its own source, and the first fixture I tried (where creation
order happened to agree) would have hidden that. One fixture is not a check.

### What was kept

The rejection comment at the walk site now carries all of it: that "no SKIP/LIMIT" is NOT a
sufficient narrowing, the two pinning tests BY NAME, the 3.5x so nobody re-prices it, the
three-way order measurement, and the cross-engine argument. It ends "do not re-derive this a
fourth time" — item 138 built and rejected it, item 713 re-derived it, this is the third.

Also removed while there: a `rel.direction !== 'both'` condition written into the first cut. It is
DEAD — `rel.direction` is already narrowed to `'out' | 'in'` at that point, and TypeScript
rejected the comparison as having no overlap. A dead guard reads as a live one, so the proof is
recorded in its place rather than the guard.

## 1314 — `values(k).is(p).count()` folds to `has(k, p).count()`, and the tail rule is the OPPOSITE of item 1311's

The last substantive flag on item 1305's Gremlin probe. `values` materialises one value per
element and `is` filters the value stream; `has` is a filter the count rungs recognise.

```text
  has('age', gte(45)).count()            2.566-2.615 ms
  values('age').is(gte(45)).count()     23.277  ->  2.560-2.646      ~9x
```

Converged, both arms answering an identical 99990.

### The blocker was real and resolved by measuring, not by assuming

This gap was recorded OPEN across items 1309-1312 with the reason: `values` emits one row per
VALUE and `has` one per ELEMENT, so the two agree only while every element has at most one value
for the key — and this surface has a `Cardinality` concept, so single-valuedness had to be
ESTABLISHED.

It is. `values('k')` over four vertices — one holding `5`, one an ARRAY `[1,2,3]`, one with the
key ABSENT, one holding `null` — emits exactly `[5, [1,2,3], null]`. So an array is ONE value, a
null IS a value, and a missing key emits nothing: `values(k).count()` and `has(k).count()` both
read 3.

### ⚠️ THE TAIL RULE IS THE OPPOSITE OF ITEM 1311'S, AND THAT IS THE POINT

Item 1311 admits a `dedupe, count` tail. This item must REFUSE one, and the two look like the same
pattern:

|                          | item 1311 (`union`/`both`)                   | item 1314 (`values`/`has`)                             |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| what each spelling emits | the same ELEMENTS, different order           | DIFFERENT THINGS: values vs elements                   |
| `count` tail             | equal (multiset)                             | equal (how many)                                       |
| `dedupe, count` tail     | **equal** — a set is coarser than a multiset | **NOT equal** — distinct values 1, distinct elements 2 |

So the rule is not "dedupe is safe before a count"; it is "the tail may only observe what both
spellings agree on". There the spellings agree on the ELEMENTS, so any coarser view stays equal.
Here they agree on nothing but the COUNT, so the count is the whole admission.

Measured on a fixture where two elements share a value: `values(k).is(gte 2).dedupe().count()` is
1 and `has(k, gte 2).dedupe().count()` is 2. Both declines are asserted as those NUMBERS rather
than as "the plan was left alone", because a plan-shape assertion would pass for a fold that is
simply disabled.

The other decline is multi-key: `values(k, j)` emits one row PER KEY, so the pair reads 4 against 1.

```text
  multikey-check-dropped    CAUGHT   1 fail    values-check-dropped      CAUGHT 635 fail
  count-not-last-dropped    CAUGHT   1 fail    tail-admits-dedupe        SURVIVED (round 1)
  is-check-dropped          CAUGHT   2 fail    tail-admits-dedupe-REALLY CAUGHT   2 fail
```

**The round-1 `tail-admits-dedupe` survivor was MY HARNESS, not a test gap** — the third time in
this run. It rerouted `tail` past a `dedupe`, but the SEPARATE `i + 3 !== steps.length` check

conditions have to move together; mutated properly it is caught with 2 failures, so the item-1311
contrast IS pinned.

`predicate-dropped` is worth noting as the quiet one: it rewrites to a bare `has(k)` PRESENCE
test, which still returns a plausible number — 3 instead of 1 on the fixture — rather than failing
loudly.

## 1315 — `element_id(n) IN [...]` and the id `=`-chain both seed: 614x and 1276x

**Found by checking the standing O(1)-by-id constraint rather than by a probe.** Both spelling
probes were exhausted (the Gremlin one down to a single group at item 1314, the GQL one reporting
no answer disagreements), so the next question was the one the loop is under instruction to
protect: is point lookup by id still O(1) in every spelling a caller writes? It was not. Item 618
gave the single `=` a seed and scoped itself "`=` only"; the two LIST spellings had no hint at all
and scanned the label bucket.

This is CLAUDE.md's equivalent-spelling class exactly — _"the planner recognized one spelling of a
predicate and scanned for another that meant exactly the same thing"_ — and `k = $a OR k = $b` vs
`k IN [$a, $b]` is one of the four it names. Both list spellings returned the correct rows, so no
correctness test could have found it.

### Measured

A/B against HEAD, both files swapped as one arm, three order-alternated rounds, min of rounds,
200,000 vertices. FOUR controls the change cannot reach: the single `=` (already seeded at 618),
an un-indexed property `=`, an un-indexed property `IN`, and a bare label scan.

```text
  arm                    PRE ms      POST ms     speedup  rows
  q-in-ids              7.54313      0.01228     614.26x  rows=3
  q-or-ids             18.50733      0.01450    1276.37x  rows=3
  ctl-one-id            0.00612      0.00613       1.00x  rows=1        [CONTROL]
  ctl-prop-eq           3.21936      3.24124       0.99x  rows=2222     [CONTROL]
  ctl-prop-in           3.95558      3.76905       1.05x  rows=6669     [CONTROL]
  ctl-label-scan        7.95792      7.98653       1.00x  rows=200000   [CONTROL]

  CONTROL BAND: 0.99x .. 1.05x
```

Row counts identical in both arms on every row. A single pre-A/B run had shown `ctl-prop-eq` at
3.7492 → 4.1888 (1.12x) and that is why the full A/B was run rather than the numbers quoted off
the probe: it was noise, and a control moving more than a target is item 762's signature for a
measurement artifact, so it had to be ruled out rather than explained away.

**Fixing `IN` alone would have been the wrong half.** The `=`-chain was the SLOWEST of the three
spellings before (18.5 ms against `IN`'s 10.9 and the single id's 0.0078), so an `IN`-only fix
leaves the two list spellings 1.6x apart — the gap the `or` arm of that switch exists to close.

### Why a reordering seed is sound here, where Gremlin's is not

Item 1306 declined the multi-id Gremlin `hasId` seed and that decline STANDS; this is not a
reversal of it. The two surfaces differ in what a seed IS:

- A GQL seed hint produces a **superset** which `matchNode` and the residual `WHERE` then
  re-validate, and `seedVertices` is free to ignore it entirely at the `seekIsWorthIt` gate. The
  existing `{kind: 'within'}` property seed already seeds a union of index buckets, so seeding a
  union of id lookups introduces no new freedom.
- A Gremlin `hasId` seed replaces the traversal's source and therefore DEFINES the output order,
  which `hasId.test.ts` pins in a case named "we can filter by ids out of order".

So there is in-engine precedent on this side and an order contract on that one.

### What it is

Four pieces. On the producer side in `executor.ts`: a `{kind: 'idIn'; values}` variant on
`CSeedHint`; an id arm in `collectHints`' `case 'in'` (the property arm tests `kind === 'prop'`
and an `element_id` call is a `func`, which is the whole reason the list form had no hint); and
`uniformIdEqChain` — the id twin of `uniformEqChain`, which matches a property key and so cannot
see this shape — feeding an id arm in `case 'or'`. On the consumer side in `executor/matching.ts`,
an `idIn` arm resolving each string id through `graph.getVertexById`.

A NON-STRING entry is skipped rather than refused, and that is correct and not merely safe:
`element_id` yields a string, so no vertex can equal a number and the scan this replaces would
keep nothing for it either. Skipping keeps the seed a superset.

The candidate is built EAGERLY, unlike the indexed ones: the work is one `Map.get` per id and
`orient` needs the count before it can choose a start, so deferring would hide a cost already
paid. That choice is what cost a mutant below.

### Teeth: 8 mutants, 2 rounds, and both round-1 survivors were MINE

```text
  in-arm-unwired         CAUGHT   9 fail      or-mixed-admitted       CAUGHT   1 fail
  or-arm-unwired         CAUGHT   3 fail      or-cross-variable       CAUGHT   1 fail
  consumer-unwired       CAUGHT  12 fail      nonstring-admitted      CAUGHT   1 fail
  dedup-dropped          SURVIVED (round 1)   dedup-dropped-for-real  CAUGHT   1 fail
  count-mis-estimated    SURVIVED (round 1)   count-mis-estimated     CAUGHT   2 fail (round 2)
  count-zeroed           SURVIVED — reachable but cost-equivalent, see below
```

The three NARROWING mutants are the ones that matter, and all three are caught: a seed is
answer-equivalent, so `in-arm-unwired`, `or-arm-unwired` and `consumer-unwired` each return
perfectly correct rows and are visible ONLY through the `getVertexById` call counts. Without the
count assertions this file would be a rows-only test that every one of them passes.

**`count-mis-estimated` surviving round 1 exposed a flaw in the INSTRUMENT, not a test gap, and
the diagnosis is the item's most transferable result.** Because the ids are resolved eagerly
inside `indexCandidates`, `getVertexById` runs even when `seedVertices` then declines the seek at
`seekIsWorthIt` and scans. So the lookup counter witnesses "the hint was produced and resolved" —
the right signal for every DECLINE case, and the signal that catches the three narrowings — but it
CANNOT distinguish a taken seek from a resolved-then-declined one. Accepting the survivor as
"answer-equivalent, nothing to do" would have left the file claiming a route assertion it does not
make.

`spyFullScan` is the missing half: `candidateVertices` reaches an unlabelled pattern through
`graph.verticesById.values()`, which a taken seek never calls, so counting it IS "was the seek
chosen". It has a null control asserting it DOES fire on a declined shape, without which a spy
that never fires would make both assertions pass while proving nothing. With it, the mutant is
caught by exactly those two tests.

`dedup-dropped` survived round 1 because the mutant was a NO-OP — it swapped the `Set` for an
array and then handed `build` a `new Set(hits)`, re-deduplicating on the way out. The fourth
harness error of this run, and the same shape as item 1314's. Mutated properly it is caught;
note that `bun run build` does not typecheck, so it compiled and the duplicate-id TEST caught it
rather than the `ReadonlySet<Vertex>` return type.

`count-zeroed` is a deliberate survivor, and it is a KNOWN class in this exact file rather than a
loose end. Under-reporting the count keeps the seek (0 passes `seekIsWorthIt` as readily as 3) and
changes only which node `orient` drives in a multi-node pattern — and since the true count is at
most `|ids|`, both values are smaller than any label bucket the gate would accept. It is
reachable in principle (two id-seeded nodes in one pattern) and cost-equivalent in practice.

The `edgeEnd` hint twenty lines above carries the same note from item 621 — _"`count` is an
ESTIMATE, not a guard … Mutation confirms it (`count: 1` unconditionally survives) — recorded so
the zero is not later read as load-bearing"_ — so this is the second instance of one documented
class, not a new gap. `hits.size` is the exact count rather than an estimate, so there is no
arithmetic to extract and unit-test in the sense CLAUDE.md's rule intends.
