## 1316 — the EDGE id list pins the hop: 600x, 676x, and 620x for the labelled spelling

Item 1315's twin one level up, and it is the cheapest item in this run for a reason worth
recording: **the hint was already being collected and then thrown away.** `collectHints` keys
hints by variable with REL variables included, so item 1315's `idIn` hint was produced for
`element_id(r) IN [...]` and then dropped by `pinFor`, which filtered for `kind === 'id'`. Exactly
the shape item 621 itself had to fix — item 621's own comment says a pinned edge id "was collected
and then dropped" before it. The same filter did it again to the list form.

### Measured

Probed BEFORE building, against the single edge id item 621 already pinned — 200,000 vertices,
199,999 edges:

```text
  = one edge id (item 621)    0.02447 ms
  IN three ids               30.17316      1233x the pinned single id
  OR-chain of three          40.23598      1644x
```

Then A/B against HEAD (which already contains 1315), both files swapped as one arm, three
order-alternated rounds, min of rounds:

```text
  arm                        PRE ms      POST ms     speedup  rows
  q-in-ids                 30.97505      0.05163     599.94x  rows=3
  q-or-ids                 39.66943      0.05871     675.68x  rows=3
  q-in-ids-labelled        34.13634      0.05502     620.44x  rows=3
  ctl-one-edge-id           0.03013      0.02762       1.09x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
  ctl-node-in               0.01070      0.01122       0.95x  rows=3  [CONTROL]
  ctl-edge-prop             4.14920      4.05060       1.02x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
  ctl-hop-count             0.00236      0.00215       1.10x  rows=1  [CONTROL]

  CONTROL BAND: 0.95x .. 1.10x
```

`ctl-node-in` is item 1315's node id list, used as a control here specifically to confirm the
previous commit did not shift: 0.95x. The A/B asserts item 1315 is present in BOTH arms, so a
half-reverted tree could not be mistaken for a result.

**`q-in-ids-labelled` is the row that matters.** Item 621 records that pinning only the NEAR end
left `MATCH (a:P)-[r:R]->(b:P)` at 7710 us against the unlabelled spelling's 3.00, because
`orient` starts from the FAR node when both carry a label. A list pin wired to one end only would
have looked correct on the unlabelled rows and left that cliff in place. It inherits both pins
from the same `pinFor` call, and 620.44x is the check.

### What it is

Three lines of real change. `pinFor` stops dropping `idIn` and maps it to a new
`{kind: 'edgeEndIn'; values; sourceEnd}`, and `edgeEndSetFrom` resolves each edge id and collects
the chosen endpoint. Every decline carries over untouched, because the direction check and
`pinnableSegment` refuse `both` and a quantified rel BEFORE either hint kind reaches that map.

Also replaced `filter(...).map(...)` with a `flatMap` and narrowing `if`s, which removed a
`(h as { value: CompiledExpr })` cast. The cast was sound for one hint shape; a cast covering two
is how the second gets read off the wrong field, and this is the filter that has now silently
dropped a hint kind twice.

### The pin has a SELECTIVITY THRESHOLD, and it is 1/8

Five route assertions failed on the first run with perfectly correct rows. Two diagnoses, the
first WRONG and recorded because it was plausible: that the spy counted generator CREATIONS rather
than walks, since `candidateVertices` is a generator and a fast path can create an iterator and
abandon it. Rebuilding the spy to count vertices actually PULLED refuted that — `pulled=12` on a
12-vertex graph was a real full scan.

Bisected instead, counting pulls:

```text
  ids=1   never scans, at any size
  ids=2   scans while n <= 16, clean from n = 17
  ids=3   scans while n <= 24, clean from n = 32
```

So a pin is taken iff `|ids| < |V| / 8` — `SEEK_MAX_FRACTION`, and CORRECT: pinning 2 vertices out
of 12 is not worth a seek. The single-`=` pin clears it at any size because item 621's hint
reports a count of 0 or 1. The 12-vertex fixture was simply BELOW the threshold, which is why the
test fixture is 120 and why the bisection is written into the file rather than the size being
quietly raised until the assertions passed. A test guards that premise directly (`3 < N / 8`).

Worth noting the gate's `SEEK_FLOOR_VERTICES` (4,096) branch does NOT explain it — checked by
calling the exported `seekIsWorthIt` directly, which returns `true` for count 2 at n=12. So the
fraction is applied by a consumer that does not take the floor exemption. Not chased further; the
behaviour is right and the threshold is now documented.

### Teeth: 7 mutants, four rounds, every one caught

```text
  pin-unwired           CAUGHT   7 fail     both-admitted          CAUGHT   2 fail
  consumer-unwired      CAUGHT   7 fail     dedup-dropped          CAUGHT   7 fail
  source-end-ignored    CAUGHT   1 fail     count-mis-estimated    CAUGHT   7 fail
  nonstring-admitted    SURVIVED round 1 -> CAUGHT once asserted relatively
```

**`both-admitted` is the one that had to be caught**, and it is, with 2 failures: it removes the
direction guard so an undirected hop gets pinned to one end, which LOSES the other end's row.
Items 620/621 decline it for that reason and the decline is now enforced rather than decorative.
`source-end-ignored` is its partner — always taking `edge.from` breaks the `in` direction and the
labelled far-end pin.

`nonstring-admitted` survived round 1, and the reason is legitimate rather than a gap of the usual
kind: `getEdgeById(7)` is a plain `Map.get` miss, so admitting a non-string returns IDENTICAL
rows. The `typeof` guard cannot be defended by an answer at all — only by the work it avoids, so
the test asserts the lookup count. Writing that assertion exposed something I had assumed wrong:
one string id costs FOUR lookups, not one, because both ends of the segment are pinned and each
end is resolved twice — once for `orient`'s estimate, once to seed. So it is asserted RELATIVE to
a one-id control. Hard-coding 4 would pin that 2x2 by accident; "the two non-strings cost nothing"
is the actual claim and survives any change to how often a hint is resolved.

Rounds 3 and 4 exist because the `lint` gate rejected a nested ternary AFTER the teeth were
verified, moving three anchors — the same trap item 1315 hit. Re-run against the final text, all
three bite. One of those re-runs reported ANCHOR rather than a verdict, which is the harness
working: the trailing context had changed, so the mutant was never applied and no verdict was
recorded for it until the anchor was corrected.

Fixing that ternary also removed a DEAD null-check: an edge cannot exist without endpoints
(`assertValidEdge` throws on a missing one), so `edge ? (… edge.from …) : null` was guarding
something unreachable. A dead guard reads as a live one.

### One error of mine worth recording: `*1..2` is CYPHER

The quantified-rel decline test was first written `-[r:KNOWS*1..2]->`, which is Cypher syntax and
a parse error here. The ISO form is `-[r:KNOWS]->{1,2}`, confirmed against the corpus and then by
running it: a quantified rel DOES accept a variable, and `element_id(r) IN ['e2']` over one
correctly answers 0, since the variable binds a LIST of edges rather than one edge's id. Precisely
what `CLAUDE.md` warns about — GQL is not Cypher, and the grammar is the contract.

### Verification

`packages/gql` 3359 pass / 0 fail (3339 before, +20 new in `edge-id-list-seed.test.ts`), of which
four are DECLINE cases: an undirected hop, a quantified rel, a negated list, and an `OR` mixing an
edge id with another predicate. Gates as separate commands with exit codes read unpiped: `bun run
typecheck` 0, `bun run lint` 0, `bun run fmt` 0 AND verified idempotent by hashing `git diff`

## 1317 — the multi-id `hasId` seed is reachable UNDER AN ORDER-FREE TAIL: 230x, and item 1306's decline STANDS

Item 1306 seeded a single `hasId` and declined the multi-id case, recording that taking it "needs
a decision about that order — made against TinkerPop ground truth, not as a side effect of a perf
change". That blocker has stood through every item since.

**It is sidestepped rather than overruled.** The blocker is about ORDER, so it does not apply
where order is not observable: under an order-free tail the seeded and scanned paths yield the
same SET and differ only in sequence, and the tail reads neither. `hasId('6','2','1','4').count()`
is 4 either way. So no ground-truth decision is needed, and `hasId.test.ts`'s "we can filter by
ids out of order" keeps its contract untouched — it has no such tail. The BARE multi-id `hasId`
remains declined.

### Measured

A/B against HEAD, two files swapped as one arm, three order-alternated rounds, min of rounds,
200,000 vertices. FIVE controls, three of which are the shapes that must NOT move:

```text
  arm                      PRE ms      POST ms     speedup  rows
  ids-count               3.62988      0.01580     229.74x  rows=1
      pre [3.63, 5.953, 6.062] | post [0.016, 0.024, 0.019]
  ids-dedupe-count        5.95261      0.02572     231.44x  rows=1
  one-id-count            0.01445      0.01447       1.00x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
  ids-out-count           6.03207      5.99484       1.01x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
      pre [6.032, 6.166, 6.055] | post [6.152, 6.03, 5.995]
  ids-plain               6.12970      6.06990       1.01x  rows=3  [CONTROL]
  ctl-label-count         0.00698      0.00707       0.99x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
  ctl-prop-count          2.14477      2.21399       0.97x  rows=1  [CONTROL]

  CONTROL BAND: 0.97x .. 1.01x
```

`ids-plain` is the correctness canary, not just a control: it is the shape item 1306's decline
protects. It stayed at 6.07 ms with rows=3, so the bare multi-id seed did not leak through.

**229x is CONSERVATIVE, and the per-rep series is why it is quoted anyway.** `ids-count` PRE reads
`[3.63, 5.953, 6.062]` — the first round is genuinely faster and `min`-of-rounds picks that 3.63.
Against the typical ~6.0 ms the figure is nearer 380x. The smaller number is the one recorded.

That same series settled a false alarm. Across single probe runs a DECLINED arm, `ids-out-count`,
read 3.70 then 6.04 ms, which looked like an allocation the change had introduced — and removing
the allocation left the number unchanged. In the A/B it is flat at 1.01x with
`pre [6.032, 6.166, 6.055]` against `post [6.152, 6.03, 5.995]`, so it was noise either side of
the floor. Recorded because the wrong explanation was briefly written into a source comment, and
that comment now states the non-allocating form is STRUCTURAL with no performance claim attached.

### One list, two callers, different premises

`ORDER_FREE_TAILS` moved from `index.ts` to `index-seed.ts` (the direction the imports already
run) so that both callers share ONE list — two copies of "which tails are order-free" would drift
and each would look authoritative. The premises are NOT interchangeable and the doc says so:

- `fuseUnionBoth` (item 1311) rewrites to a form that is MULTISET-equal but not sequence-equal.
- `idSeed`'s multi-id arm is SET-equal and merely reordered, which is a STRONGER relation — so
  every tail admissible for the union is admissible here too, but not the reverse.

`tailIsOrderFreeFrom(steps, from)` takes an index rather than a slice because `seedRest` asks the
question once per leading filter of every traversal. Structural, not a measured win.

### ~~`[out, count]` is priced and NOT admitted: 213x~~ — BUILT at item 1318

**All three hop tails were admitted at item 1318** (195x / 197x / 146x), with the evidence this
entry asked for: measured per hop rather than as a family. It also turned up an 8.28x win on the
OTHER caller of the shared list, and found that item 1317 had generalized to the EDGE source
silently. The original note read: "any hop then a count" is a broader claim than either caller has
evidence for, and `ids-out-count` serves as a CONTROL in the A/B above precisely because it is not
admitted.

### Teeth: 6 mutants, and one survivor was a VACUOUS MUTANT, not a gap

```text
  multi-id-unwired        CAUGHT   2 fail     tail-index-off-by-one   CAUGHT   2 fail
  tail-check-dropped      CAUGHT   4 fail     dedup-dropped           CAUGHT   2 fail
  order-free-list-widened see below           missing-id-admitted     CAUGHT   3 fail
```

**`tail-check-dropped` is the one that had to be caught, and it is, with 4 failures.** It admits
the multi-id seed with NO tail condition — item 1306's decline reinstated as a bug — so
`hasId('c','a')` emits in WRITTEN order and the out-of-order case fails. Without that, this
narrowing would be indistinguishable from simply overturning the decline.

**`order-free-list-widened` took THREE attempts and all three failures were mine, from inferring
step-kind names instead of printing the AST once.**

1. `['limit']` — there is no `limit` step kind. Unmatchable, so the mutant changed nothing and
   reported SURVIVED, which looks exactly like a test gap.
2. `['range']` — a real kind, but nothing in either caller's tests has a `range` tail, so also
   unmatchable, and it survived too.
3. One `console.log` of the plan: `limit(1)` lowers to **`take`**. Mutated against `['take']`, it
   is CAUGHT.

Attempt 1 earned a HARNESS FIX worth more than the mutant. `'limit'` is not in `Step['kind']`, so
that mutant was a TYPE ERROR — and the harness builds with `bun run build`, which does NOT
typecheck, so it compiled to something inert and scored as a survivor. **A type-invalid mutant is
indistinguishable from a test gap by exit code alone.** The harness now runs `typecheck` after the
build and reports `TYPE-INVALID` as its own verdict. Attempt 2 confirmed the fix in the negative
direction, correctly reporting `TYPE-INVALID: none` because `range` IS a valid kind.

**And the catch was 1 failure, not 2, which exposed a real gap.** Only item 1317's `limit` test
caught the widened list; nothing in `union-both-fusion.test.ts` windows a union, so the SHARED
list was guarded from one side only — the `rewrite-composition-is-not-free` trap in list form.
A windowed-union decline test was added there in the same commit, so both callers now guard it.

`packages/gremlin` 1069 pass / 0 fail (1063 before: +5 in `executor/id-seed.test.ts` and +1 in

fmt` 0 AND verified idempotent by hashing `git diff` across a second run, `bun run check

**One pre-existing test was edited, and the reasoning matters because the rule normally forbids

## 1318 — a single HOP before the count joins the order-free tails: 195x, 197x, 146x — and 8.28x on the OTHER caller

Item 1317 priced `[out, count]` at 213x and declined it, because "any hop then a count" was a
broader claim than the evidence supported. This is that evidence, measured per hop rather than as
a family.

The argument is one line: applying a hop elementwise sums each element's own neighbours, so the
result multiset is the sum over the input multiset and does not depend on the input's ORDER.
`count` then reads that multiset. This holds on BOTH callers' premises — multiset-equal is enough,
which is why the union caller rides it too.

### Measured

A/B against HEAD, one file, three order-alternated rounds, min of rounds, 200,000 vertices:

```text
  arm                      PRE ms      POST ms     speedup  rows
  ids-out-count           5.93032      0.03046     194.69x  rows=1
  ids-in-count            5.99662      0.03046     196.87x  rows=1
  ids-both-count          5.99768      0.04112     145.86x  rows=1
  union-hop-count       211.15580     25.50156       8.28x  rows=1
  one-id-out-count        0.02845      0.02502       1.14x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
  ids-plain               5.89176      3.57668       1.65x  rows=3  [CONTROL]  <- MOVED
  ids-out-limit           0.46695      0.56878       0.82x  rows=2  [CONTROL]  <- MOVED
  ctl-prop-count          2.07829      2.00873       1.03x  rows=1  [CONTROL]
```

**`union-hop-count` is an UNPLANNED SECOND WIN and was predicted before it was measured.** The
three entries go into the list SHARED with `fuseUnionBoth`, so that caller newly fuses a union
with a hop before a count: 211.16 -> 25.50 ms. It was put in the A/B as its own arm rather than
folded into the headline, because a win on a shape the item was not targeting is a different
claim.

### The two moved controls are NOISE, and `min` is why

Both were re-measured on their own at SIX rounds, one shape per process:

```text
  ids-plain        median 6.090 -> 6.215 = 0.98x    min 6.008 -> 5.921 = 1.01x   ranges overlap
  ids-out-limit    median 0.573 -> 0.581 = 0.99x    min 0.532 -> 0.431 = 1.23x   ranges overlap
```

`ids-out-limit` **flipped sign** between runs — 0.82x then 1.23x — and a real effect does not
change direction. `min`-of-rounds is the culprit: on a sub-millisecond arm it picks the luckiest
rep of six, which is why the min reads 1.23x where the median reads 0.99x. CLAUDE.md's warning
about `min` on the TS path, reproduced from the other side.

There is also a structural reason it had to be noise, and it is worth stating because it was NOT
treated as sufficient on its own: for both arms PRE and POST execute the same code — both decline
— so the only difference is iterating a 5-entry array instead of a 2-entry one, once per query.
That cannot cost 2.3 ms on a 200,000-vertex scan. The reasoning was right this time; it was still
checked, because two plausible explanations died on contact with a measurement earlier in this run
(the generator-creation hypothesis at item 1316 and the allocation hypothesis at item 1317).

### Item 1317 had generalized to the EDGE source, silently

`idSeed` is generic and `seedFromIndex` calls `seedRest<Edge>` for `E()`, so item 1317's order-free
multi-id admission reached edges with no extra code:

```text
  E().hasId('e137').count()                   0.01508 ms   (item 1306)
  E().hasId('e137','e9000','e4242').count()   0.01777      already seeded
  E().hasId('e137','e9000','e4242')           6.61027      correctly still declined
```

That was shipped coverage with no test naming it — found by PROBING the generic path rather than
assuming it worked. Three tests now cover it: the admission, the bare-form decline, and agreement
across a reordered list, a duplicate, a miss and an all-miss.

### Two declines shipped WITH the admission

- `[hop, window]` — declined because a window reads the SEQUENCE. Unsound for both callers, so
  both now guard it.
- ~~`[hop, dedupe, count]` — declined because it is UNMEASURED.~~ — **ADMITTED at item 1327**,
  225x: the measurement arrived and the decline was costing 328x. The rule held exactly as written
  — the list grew on evidence, and the test asserting this decline was flipped there because
  "unmeasured" is a CONDITION rather than a contract.

### Teeth: 5 mutants, 5 caught, and the per-file attribution did real work

```text
  hop-tails-unwired         CAUGHT  2 fail   in: id-seed.test.ts AND union-both-fusion.test.ts
  out-tail-only             CAUGHT  1 fail   in: id-seed.test.ts
  hop-then-window-admitted  CAUGHT  2 fail   in: id-seed.test.ts AND union-both-fusion.test.ts
  hop-then-dedupe-admitted  CAUGHT  1 fail   in: id-seed.test.ts
  wrong-hop-kind            CAUGHT  2 fail   in: id-seed.test.ts AND union-both-fusion.test.ts
```

The harness now reports WHICH test files catch each mutant, because item 1317 found a shared-list
widening guarded from one side only. That reporting immediately earned itself twice.

**First, it justified a route assertion added mid-item.** The union cases were AGREEMENT tests, and
fusion is answer-equivalent — so `hop-tails-unwired` would have left every one of them green and
merely 8.28x slower. The 211 -> 25.50 ms win had no route assertion at all. There is now one per
caller, and this mutant failing in both files is that second assertion catching something.

**Second, it exposed `hop-then-window-admitted` as caught on ONE side only**, because the windowed
union case has tail `[take]` and never exercises a two-step windowed tail like `[out, take]`. A
`union(out,in).out(T).limit(2)` guard was added, and the mutant re-run now fails in both files.

`hop-then-dedupe-admitted` stays one-sided DELIBERATELY, and the distinction is the point:
`[out, take]` is UNSOUND, so every caller must reject it and every caller should assert that.
`[out, dedupe, count]` is SOUND but unmeasured, so the only thing to protect is the evidence rule,
and one test does that. A second would be symmetry for its own sake.

### Verification

`packages/gremlin` 1079 pass / 0 fail (1069 before: +7 in `executor/id-seed.test.ts`, +3 in
`executor/union-both-fusion.test.ts`). All seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass / 0 fail. Gates as
separate commands with exit codes read unpiped: `bun run typecheck` 0, `bun run lint` 0, `bun run
fmt` 0 AND verified idempotent by hashing `git diff` across a second run, `bun run check
--skip-nx-cache` 0.

## 1320 — the inline-vs-clause keyed count: ESTABLISHED at 2.44x, DECOMPOSED, and left unfixed with five levers refuted

No speedup shipped. This item took a gap that item 578's chase abandoned as unmeasurable,
established it with an instrument that resolves it, decomposed it into two diffuse costs, and
refuted five candidate fixes — one of which would have been actively harmful. The deliverable is
the decomposition, so the next attempt starts here rather than where the last chase did.

```text
  MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true RETURN count(*)   clause       0.0917 ms
  MATCH (u:User WHERE u.score = $s) WHERE u.active = true …               inline-WHERE 0.0959  1.05x
  MATCH (u:User {score: $s, active: true}) …                              all-inline   0.1390  1.52x
  MATCH (u:User {score: $s}) WHERE u.active = true …                      inline       0.1740  1.90x
```

### THE INSTRUMENT IS THE REUSABLE PART, and it is not "more reps"

Item 578 recorded eight readings of this question spanning 0.94x-1.40x and concluded "the
instrument was the problem, and raising the reps was never going to fix it". It was right that reps
were not the answer and wrong about why. **The confound is warming asymmetry across ROUNDS INSIDE
ONE PROCESS, and it can invert the SIGN of the comparison.** Measured here, same pair, same day:

```text
  3 rounds in one process, min-of-rounds   clause 0.134  inline 0.048   2.78x CLAUSE slower
  1 round per fresh process, 3 processes   clause 0.084  inline 0.213   2.52x INLINE slower
```

The inline arm warmed 0.231 -> 0.063 -> 0.048 across its rounds while the clause arm did not warm
at all (0.134 -> 0.173 -> 0.168), so `min`-of-rounds picked inline's warmest round and clause's
coldest. That is not noise; it is a systematic inversion, and it is how an eight-reading chase
produces readings on both sides of 1.0x.

What resolves it: **one shape per PROCESS**, 80 reps with the first 40 discarded so the median sits
on the plateau, and the DISTRIBUTION reported rather than a summary. At 14 processes per arm:

```text
  clause  n=14  min 0.0719  med 0.0826  max 0.1055   self-spread 1.47x
  inline  n=14  min 0.1258  med 0.2016  max 0.2519   self-spread 2.00x
  inline draws INSIDE the clause range: 0 of 14      null control: 1.08x
```

**Zero overlap over 28 independent processes** — the fastest inline draw is slower than the slowest
clause draw — against a 1.08x null control (the identical query under two arm names). That is the
control item 578 found afterwards in its own raw output, unread, showing a 2.47x self-ratio larger
than the gap it was serving. Run it, and this gap survives it.

A fixture error of mine on the way, worth recording because it produced an INCOHERENT result rather
than a wrong one: the first cut set `active: true` on every user, making the second conjunct
VACUOUS. The pair then read inline 1.39x FASTER with the conjunct and 1.30x SLOWER without it — a
direction flip that cannot describe one mechanism. Item 578's bench uses `active: i % 3 === 0`, and
matching it made the readings coherent.

### The structural facts, all measured

Routes, seeks and the general-path predicate sites, over the same 1000-match operating point:

```text
  spelling       route            seeks  seededRows  bucketPulls   satisfies/row
  clause         countShortcut        1        1000            0            1.00
  inline         countShortcut        1        1000            0            2.00
  inline-where   countShortcut        1        1000            0            2.00
  clause-bare    countShortcut        1        1000            0            1.00
  inline-bare    countShortcut        1        1000            0            1.00
```

And the SHAPE of each predicate `satisfies` receives, which is what finally localized it:

```text
  clause        1000 x  eqProps[2]+props[0]
  inline        1000 x  props[1]   +  1000 x  eqProps[1]+props[0]
  inline-where  2000 x  eqProps[1]+props[0]
```

### Five levers REFUTED, with what refuted each

1. **A missed seek.** Refuted: every spelling makes exactly ONE index seek returning 1000 rows and
   pulls ZERO vertices from the label bucket. The inline form seeds as well as the clause form.
2. **A route difference.** Refuted: `compileLinear` fires `countShortcut` and nothing else for all
   five spellings.
3. **The general path's double pass** (`rejectedByElementDirect` then `matchNode`'s `satisfies`) —
   the mechanism this file names at the "inline props in a PRODUCT" row. Refuted: counters at both
   seed loops and at `matchNode` read ZERO for every spelling. `countShortcut` bypasses them
   entirely, so a fix there would have changed nothing on this shape.
4. **The call count alone.** Refuted: `inline-where` also makes 2 calls per row and is 1.05x. So
   merging the two calls cannot explain, or recover, the gap.
5. **Call-site polymorphism** from `CPredicate`'s conditionally-spread fields. Refuted by
   `all-inline`: ONE call, ONE object shape, and still 1.52x.

### 🛑 And one lever that would have been HARMFUL

"Lift inline `{k: $p}` into `eqProps` the way both `WHERE` spellings are" is the fix the shape
table points at, and `eqProps`' own doc forbids it: _"Deliberately NOT merged into `props`:
`indexCandidates` reads `props` to decide seeding."_ Moving the constraint off `props` moves it off
the list the seed is built from — trading 2.4x for a LOST INDEX SEEK, which is the 100-300x class
this engine's spelling discipline exists to prevent. Audit item 224 also records that the row-order
consequence cannot be verified against native, because the fuzzers canonicalise unordered rows.

### What the gap actually is, and why it is left

Two diffuse costs, neither with a clean lever:

- **~1.25x** for one extra `satisfies` invocation per row (~80 ns/row). Merging is blocked by the
  design above: `props` must stay on the node for seeding.
- **~1.5x** for `props[2]` costing more than `eqProps[2]` (~23 ns/entry) — despite near-identical
  loop bodies, and despite both lists building their value closure with the SAME `compileExpr`, on
  identical expressions (`$s`, `true`).

So the residue is 20-80 ns per row on a 0.09 ms query, spread across two mechanisms. Recorded
rather than chased further: five refutations deep, the remaining levers are micro-optimizations of
two loops that `satisfies` has ordered deliberately (item 1169 pins that order as load-bearing),
and the measured prize does not justify touching them.

**`keyed-dedup-probe.ts` is committed with this item** so the next attempt inherits the instrument
rather than rebuilding it — including the per-process estimator, the null-control arm, the
`all-inline` discriminator, and a fixture that asserts its own match count.

## 1321 — the filtered-count family's 40-85x against native is the LAYOUT FLOOR, measured linear, and my own "superlinear" reading was the harness

> **⚠️ "No lever" was true of the UNINDEXED path only — item 1322 found a 5.78x one in this very
> family.** The sweep below ran without an index, where the cost genuinely is linear and
> constant-factor. WITH an index on the filtered key, Gremlin took an unselective seek and the
> same shape cost 13.10 ms instead of 2.18 — a pathology, not a ceiling. Read 1322 before quoting
> this entry's conclusion.

No speedup, and no lever. Item 573 records that a big TS/native ratio may be ALGORITHMIC rather
than the layout ceiling, so the largest remaining ratios in `bench:gremlin` were checked instead of
attributed. They are the ceiling.

`bench:gremlin` at 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, `BENCH_ENGINES=ts`, all 23 rows answering
`same` (a clean regression pass over items 1315-1320):

```text
  V().has().has().count()          3.6    0.04    85.2x
  V().has(age,gt).count()          2.7    0.04    61.5x
  V().hasLabel().has().count()     2.3    0.04    58.3x
  V().out().out().out().count()  275.0    4.91    56.0x
  V().out().has().count()         41.9    0.85    49.4x
  V().out()x4.count()            284.3    6.58    43.2x
  V().out() [bare]               186.3  332.43     0.6x   <- TS is FASTER here
```

### Linear, so there is nothing to take

One case and one size PER PROCESS, 9 reps, median:

```text
  case                   ns/vertex at 25k / 100k / 400k      trend 25k->400k
  V().count() [CTL]      0.2   0.1   0.0                     0.0x
  has(age,gt).count()   13.2   4.7  13.7                     1.0x
  hasLabel.has.count()  12.4   5.3  12.6                     1.0x
  has.has.count()       36.2  19.1  43.7                     1.2x
```

Flat per-vertex cost across a 16x size range, so the filtered count is LINEAR in N and the 40-85x
is a constant factor: ~13 ns/vertex for one `has`, ~36-44 for two, against a native column scan
that answers 200,000 vertices in 0.04 ms and so plainly is not scanning per-element at all. Item
573's caution is now CHECKED for this family rather than assumed, and the filed explanation holds.

### 🛑 My first sweep said SUPERLINEAR, and that was the harness

The first cut ran every case and every size in ONE process and reported `hasLabel.has.count()`
rising 3.8 -> 24.8 ns/vertex, a 6.5x per-vertex climb, which I wrote up as a possible algorithmic
lever. It is not real.

**What caught it was an internal contradiction, not a second opinion.** `dropVacuousLabels` fires
for an all-`P` fixture — verified, `effective=["V","has","count"]` at both 25k and 400k — so
`hasLabel.has.count()` and `has(age,gt).count()` are THE SAME PLAN. One cannot scale flat while the
other climbs. Two trends for one plan means at least one is the instrument, and re-run one-per-
process they agree to within noise (12.4/5.3/12.6 against 13.2/4.7/13.7).

This is item 1320's own lesson — one shape per PROCESS, because rounds in a shared process warm
unequally — applied two items later to a sweep I had just built, and missed. It is recorded here
because the failure mode is not "noisy numbers": it is a clean, monotonic, plausible trend that
invites exactly the wrong conclusion.

A second artifact from the same cut, for completeness: comparing the two spellings inside one
process gave `hasLabel+has` 2.28 ms against `has` 0.84 at 25k. Same plan, 2.7x apart, because the
first call of the pair paid the cold cost. No warm-up, no comparison.

### What is left in that table, and why it is not a target

`V().out() [bare]` is the row worth remembering: TS is 0.6x — FASTER than native — because the
traversal returns elements rather than a count, so FFI marshalling dominates. The hop itself is not
where TS loses.

`has.has.count()` costs ~36-44 ns/vertex where one `has` costs ~13, so a second predicate adds more
than the first. That is the same `props`-evaluation family item 1320 established has no clean lever
(five refutations, one of them harmful), so it is not reopened here.

## 1322 — Gremlin gets the seek-vs-scan gate it was the only engine missing: an index made a query 5.78x SLOWER

**Not a missed optimization. A pathology: adding an index made a query slower.** Native has had
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION` throughout, GQL's `seekIsWorthIt` arrived at item 409 as "the missing twin",
and `seedRest` had NO selectivity gate at all — it took any seek that was merely the most selective
CANDIDATE, however unselective in absolute terms.

### Found by the one comparison nothing ran: the SAME question in both TS surfaces

Users pick GQL xor Gremlin, so a surface that is slower for an identical question costs half of
them — and nothing measured that. `bench:usage` runs GQL rows plus two native-only Gremlin rows,
`bench:gremlin` compares Gremlin against native, and both spelling probes compare spellings WITHIN
a surface. A cross-surface probe at 200,000 vertices, answers compared per pair:

```text
  question              GQL ms  Gremlin ms     ratio
  count-all             0.0015      0.0047     3.07x  gremlin slower
  filter-count          3.9513     13.4546     3.41x  gremlin slower   <- this item
  seek-count            0.1621      0.0843     1.92x  gql slower
  hop-count             0.0016      0.0076     4.71x  gremlin slower
  both-count            0.0016      0.0078     5.03x  gremlin slower
  two-hop-count        18.1685      9.8534     1.84x  gql slower       <- OPEN, own item
```

GQL answering the identical question 3.41x faster is what proved Gremlin was not at the layout
floor item 1321 had just established — the same engine already had a faster path.

### Measured

A/B against HEAD, both files as one arm, three order-alternated rounds, one shape per process:

```text
  arm                       PRE ms     POST ms    speedup  answer
  unsel-indexed            13.1042      2.2659      5.78x  SAME
  unsel-e-indexed          18.2914      6.6246      2.76x  SAME
  sel-indexed               0.0529      0.0599      0.88x  SAME  [CONTROL]
  sel-values-indexed        0.2117      0.2107      1.00x  SAME  [CONTROL]
  unsel-plain               2.1621      2.2586      0.96x  SAME  [CONTROL]
  sel-plain                 2.1539      2.0166      1.07x  SAME  [CONTROL]
  ctl-bare-count            0.0042      0.0036      1.19x  SAME  [CONTROL]
```

`sel-indexed` is the control that decides whether this is a fix at all: a ~1.1% selective seek is
STILL taken, at 0.06 ms against its unindexed twin's 2.15. A gate that merely stopped seeding would
"fix" the pathology and be a far worse bug. The `ctl-bare-count` flag is 4.2 us against 3.6 us —
0.6 us on a microsecond arm, with POST the faster side.

Re-verified after the dead-code removal below, three processes a side:

```text
  plain    2.4745 / 2.2175 / 2.2306      indexed  2.3336 / 2.1769 / 2.1833     0.98x
```

So an index on the filtered key now costs nothing, which is the correct answer.

### EITHER HALF ALONE IS WORSE THAN NEITHER

`count-shortcut.ts` declines its own fast path wherever a leading filter is SEEDABLE, assuming the
seed is better. Once the gate can refuse a seek, that assumption breaks: the shortcut bows out, the
seed declines, and the query lands on the GENERAL path.

```text
  no index                      2.179 ms   the count shortcut runs
  indexed, seek ungated        13.104      the seek is materialized
  indexed, seek gated ONLY      5.433      neither fast path runs  <- half the change
  indexed, both halves          2.266
```

So `seedForStep(...) !== null` was the wrong question at five sites, and `seekWorthTaking` is the
right one. `seedForStep` going 9 -> 4 in that file is the arm assertion that exactly five changed.

### How it was localized, and two explanations that died

An index on a key the query does NOT filter costs **1.03x**. That one reading ruled out heap and
cache pressure and pointed at a second index consumer, which is how `count-shortcut.ts` was found.
Also refuted: `countRange` as the cost (0.0072 ms — cheap; it walks DISTINCT VALUES in range, ~44
of 90 here, not the 97,768 matches), and a warming artifact, which separate processes showed was
real but only part of it.

### Teeth: 6 mutants, 5 caught, and the survivor was MY DEAD CODE

```text
  seed-gate-unwired          CAUGHT  3 fail   seek-gate.test.ts
  shortcut-gate-reverted     CAUGHT  1 fail   seek-gate.test.ts   <- answer-equivalent
  fraction-widened           CAUGHT  6 fail   seek-gate.test.ts
  floor-removed              CAUGHT  9 fail   index-seed.test.ts
  denominator-always-source  SURVIVED -> CAUGHT once a targeted test was added
  wider-than-scan-dropped    SURVIVED -> the GUARD WAS DEAD; removed
```

**`shortcut-gate-reverted` is caught only by the `countShortcut` route assertions**, which were
added for it: the mutant returns identical rows and is merely slower, so no answer test can see the
half of this change whose loss is worst. `floor-removed` fails NINE tests, the same count GQL
records for omitting its own floor.

**`wider-than-scan-dropped` survived even after a test was written for it, and the test was not the
problem — my reasoning was.** GQL's twin opens with a `count > scan` refusal (item 176's rule) and
this copy does not need it:

- with an EXACT alternative, `scan` is that candidate's count, so the guard fires only for
  `count > exact.count` — which the later `exact.count < best.count` comparison already resolves
  in the bucket's favour;
- with no exact alternative, `scan` is the whole source, and a seek cannot return more elements
  than exist, so the condition is unreachable.

GQL needs it because `seedVertices` has no second comparison. Removed as dead code with the proof
in its place (item 1313's rule: a dead guard reads as a live one), and the test kept with its
comment corrected to say it pins the OUTCOME rather than the guard.

### Verification

`packages/gremlin` 1100 pass / 0 fail (1079 before, +21 in `executor/seek-gate.test.ts`),
`packages/gql` 3359 / 0 unchanged. All seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass / 0 fail. Gates as
separate commands with exit codes read unpiped: `bun run typecheck` 0, `bun run lint` 0, `bun run
fmt` 0 AND verified idempotent by hashing `git diff` across a second run, `bun run check
--skip-nx-cache` 0.

The boundary pair is the assertion worth keeping if only one could be: `lt(11)` admitted at ~12.2%
and `lt(12)` refused at ~13.3% pins the 1/8 fraction exactly, so a change to `SEEK_MAX_FRACTION`
cannot drift silently.

### The 1/8 is MEASURED for Gremlin, not merely mirrored (added after the fact)

This item set `SEEK_MAX_FRACTION = 1 / 8` by mirroring native and GQL, whose ~18% break-even item
409 measured for GQL's own seek and scan. That is not evidence about Gremlin, so the curve was
measured here afterwards — with the gate TEMPORARILY OPENED (`fraction = 1`) and restored, because
with the gate in place both columns run the same scan above 12.5% and the measurement reads as a
tie that proves nothing:

```text
     keep%    seek ms    scan ms  seek/scan
      0.5%     0.1515     2.2936       0.07   seek wins
      2.0%     0.3016     2.7608       0.11
      5.0%     0.7404     2.2657       0.33
      8.0%     0.7956     2.2988       0.35
     12.5%     2.4334     2.3308       1.04   <- TIE: the gate sits exactly here
     18.0%     3.1955     2.2962       1.39   SCAN wins
     25.0%     4.2343     2.4194       1.75
     40.0%     9.0522     2.2392       4.04
     60.0%    16.2684     2.2617       7.19
```

**Gremlin's break-even is ~12.5%, which is where the gate already is** — so 1/8 is the measured
optimum here and not a conservative margin. **The constant was right and my reason for it was
wrong:** I took 1/8 to be a safe margin below an 18% break-even, when Gremlin's own break-even
simply IS ~12.5%, lower than GQL's. Recorded because "mirrored from the other engine" would have
read as justification and was not one.

The 60% row corroborates item 409 from the other side: it measured GQL's ungated seek at 5.02x
slower there, and Gremlin's is 7.19x.

### Open from the probe that found this

**`two-hop-count` with GQL 1.84x SLOWER than Gremlin** (18.17 ms against 9.85) — the other
direction, unexamined, its own item. The cross-surface probe that found both is worth re-running
whenever either planner changes.

## 1323 — the 2-hop count's "5.2x degree-product floor" DOES NOT EXIST: my floor warmed the memo item 355 warns about

No change. Item 1322's cross-surface probe left `two-hop-count` open with GQL 1.84x SLOWER than
Gremlin (18.33 ms against 10.44), so a degree-product route was priced. The price was wrong twice
over and the recorded answer was already in the file being optimized.

```text
  GQL   2-hop count     18.328 ms   -> 199998
  Grm   2-hop count     10.438      -> 199998
  "FLOOR" degree product 3.512      -> 199998      <- INVALID, see below
```

### The degree product ALREADY EXISTS and already fires

`productCountOf` / `twoHopSide` answer `(a)-[:T1]->(b)-[:T2]->(c)` as `Σ_b (edges reaching a valid
a) × (edges reaching a valid c)`, with a three-segment sibling beside it. The admission is "both
rels anonymous + directed and the node variables distinct", which the measured query satisfies. So
there was no missing rung to add — the question was only why the existing one costs 18 ms.

### 🛑 Why the 3.512 ms floor is not a floor

**It ignored EDGE-TYPE filtering.** `twoHopSide` counts edges "of `types`" whose far endpoint
matches, where the hand-written floor read `adjTo.size × adjFrom.size`. The fixture carries ONE
edge type, so type filtering was free in it and is not free in general — a typed degree needs
either a per-type adjacency count or a scan. "Match the fixture to the claim."

**And it warmed a MEMO, which item 355 documents in this exact function.** That item already
measured the same lookup — passing the `Vertex` so the first read is `v.adjFrom` (item 321's
adjacency box) instead of hashing an id into a 200,000-entry Map — and REJECTED it:

```text
  vertex in hand, today   (v.id -> 200k map)     first 203.4   warm 171.3
  vertex in hand, box     (v.adjFrom)            first 247.0   warm 127.1
```

The box is **1.21x WORSE on first touch** (it pays the same hash AND the memo write) and 1.35x
better warm — and **five of the six sites visit each vertex exactly ONCE per query**, so first
touch is the case that matters. Item 355's own note names the trap: _"the box memoizes, so any
variant that touches it warms the box for every variant measured after it — the first version of
this probe had exactly that defect."_

The floor measured here had that defect: 20 reps on ONE graph, median of the warm half. It measured
the warmed memo, not what a query pays. Corrected, the "floor" is SLOWER than what ships.

**Third time in this run that warming inverted a reading** — item 1320 (rounds in one process
flipped a 2.5x sign), item 1321 (a shared-process sweep produced a clean monotonic "superlinear"
trend), and now a memoizing field. The tell differs each time; the cure does not: one shape per
process, on a FRESH fixture, and read the distribution.

### What stays open

**`two-hop-count`, GQL 1.84x slower than Gremlin** (18.33 against 10.44, same answer). Both
enumerate ~200,000 paths — 92 ns/path against 52 — so this is a per-path constant factor inside
two different implementations of one question, not a missing route. Unexplained, priced, and NOT a
degree-product problem. `surface-parity-probe.ts` watches it.

## 1324 — "an index never makes a query slower" becomes a CHECKED invariant: 17 shapes, and item 1322 fixed the CLASS

Item 1322 found a shape where adding an index made a Gremlin query 5.78x slower, and found it BY
ACCIDENT through a cross-surface comparison. The invariant it violated is checkable directly:

    for any query Q and index I,  time(Q with I) <= time(Q without I) * tolerance

A violation is a planner choosing a route because an index EXISTS rather than because it is
cheaper, and it is invisible to every answer test since both routes return the same rows.
`index-never-hurts-probe.ts` is committed for it.

### The invariant HOLDS on all 17 shapes

Both surfaces, 100,000 vertices, one shape per process on a fresh graph, `plain` against `indexed`:

```text
  sel-count.gql        1.3563 -> 0.1515   0.11x        unsel-count.gql     1.5932 -> 1.6278  1.02x
  sel-count.grm        0.7327 -> 0.0620   0.08x        unsel-count.grm     0.7062 -> 0.8096  1.15x
  sel-values.gql       1.2825 -> 0.1827   0.14x        unsel-values.gql    3.0627 -> 3.1511  1.03x
  sel-values.grm       3.6907 -> 0.2106   0.06x        unsel-values.grm    4.7991 -> 7.2911  1.52x*
  boundary-count.gql   1.8408 -> 1.9086   1.04x        unsel-hop.gql       4.0108 -> 4.0026  1.00x
```

### 🛑 Two harness errors of mine, both of which produced a FALSE PASS

**A vacuous PASS.** The first run printed "NONE — the invariant holds on all shapes" against an
EMPTY table. The probe exits 2 when listing its arms, so `ARMS=$(...) && for ...` short-circuited
and the loop never ran; the summary then reported a pass for zero measurements. CLAUDE.md's rule —
a verdict needs evidence of EXECUTION — now sits in the summary itself, which exits non-zero with
`DID-NOT-RUN` when there are no result rows. That guard caught the very next failure.

**A zsh word-splitting trap.** `for a in $ARMS` iterated ONCE with all 17 names as a single string,
because zsh does NOT word-split unquoted expansions the way bash does. The giveaway was the log
holding 34 lines of ARM NAMES (17 x 2 modes) rather than 34 results. Use `while IFS= read -r`.

**And a defect in the probe itself:** `edge-count.gql` filtered `r.w > 45` while `edge-count.grm`
ran an unfiltered hop — not a pair at all, and it would have read as a cross-surface gap that does
not exist. Corrected to an `E()` source with the same filter, which also exercises item 1322's
EDGE gate rather than the vertex one: 4.65 -> 3.73 ms, 0.80x, answer 48884 both sides.

## 1325 — the LIMIT early-exit invariant HOLDS in both surfaces, and the full projection is LINEAR in both

No change, no lever. Two invariants checked rather than assumed, after items 1322/1324 showed that
turning a bug into a property is the cheapest way to find the next one.

### `LIMIT 1` costs O(1), not O(N)

`eager-tail-cache` records a 473x tail-cache bug and a 3,680x whole-cross-product-under-a-LIMIT bug
in BOTH engines, so the early-exit invariant is worth re-checking rather than trusting. One shape
per process, 50,000 against 200,000 vertices (a 4x size step):

```text
  arm                        50k ms      200k ms  4x scale  rows@200k
  gql-scan-limit1           0.01675      0.01213     0.72x          1
  gql-hop-limit1            0.02278      0.02202     0.97x          1
  grm-scan-limit1           0.01555      0.01510     0.97x          1
  grm-hop-limit1            0.01974      0.02159     1.09x          1
  gql-scan-nolimit          1.16180      8.30975     7.15x     200000
  gql-hop-nolimit           3.65910     33.31888     9.11x     199999
  grm-scan-nolimit          6.08357     26.57951     4.37x     200000
  grm-hop-nolimit           6.98718     28.03739     4.01x     199999
```

Every `LIMIT 1` arm is FLAT across a 4x size increase — 0.72x to 1.09x — for a scan and for a hop,
in both surfaces. The class stays fixed.

### 🛑 The "superlinear GQL projection" in those numbers is a TWO-POINT ARTIFACT

`gql-scan-nolimit` at 7.15x and `gql-hop-nolimit` at 9.11x for a 4x size step read as superlinear
against Gremlin's 4.37x and 4.01x. Swept over five sizes instead of two, both are LINEAR:

```text
  arm            25k        50k       100k       200k       400k
  gql         1.1737     2.2333     3.8938     8.3779    17.0388
  grm         1.5548     2.7824     6.1003    13.1763    29.6049

  ns/row
  gql           46.9       44.7       38.9       41.9       42.6
  grm           62.2       55.6       61.0       65.9       74.0
```

Flat per-row cost across a 16x range. The 50,000 sample simply happened to be fast, and a ratio
between two points inherited all of its luck. **Fourth measurement artifact caught in this run by
adding points or repeats** — after item 1320 (rounds in one process inverted a 2.5x SIGN), item
1321 (a shared-process sweep produced a clean monotonic trend), and item 1323 (a memoizing field
warmed by the probe measuring it). Two points cannot establish a slope.

### What it prices instead

The full projection is **~42 ns/row in GQL against ~62 in Gremlin, a 1.5x constant factor** — GQL
returns `{v: …}` row objects and Gremlin raw values, so the allocation profiles differ. Linear in
both, so there is no asymptotic lever here; recorded so the next pass does not re-derive it.

## 1326 — "O(1) access by id" is now a CHECKED invariant, not a single-size measurement

Keeping good O(1) access to a vertex or edge by id is a standing requirement, and items 1315-1319
optimized those paths — but every one was measured at a SINGLE size, which cannot tell O(1) from
O(log N) or from a cliff. `id-lookup-is-o1-probe.ts` checks the property instead: per-lookup cost
must be FLAT in N.

Eight arms, three sizes, ONE arm and ONE size per process, 2,000 lookups per timing with the target
id moving across the keyspace — a FIXED id measures a single hash bucket and would report O(1) for
anything:

```text
  arm                          25k ns    100k ns    400k ns   16x drift
  core-getVertexById            114.5      108.2      121.5       1.06x
  core-getEdgeById               86.7       98.4      116.0       1.34x
  gql-node-eq                  1467.4     1509.3     1467.7       1.00x
  gql-node-in                  2332.1     2308.3     2396.3       1.03x
  gql-edge-in                  6094.1     7759.9     7895.2       1.30x
  grm-hasId-one                3412.2     3298.3     3167.6       0.93x
  grm-hasId-many-count         3599.4     3325.1     3144.6       0.87x
  grm-E-hasId-count            3782.6     3171.2     3215.6       0.85x
```

**The constraint holds** — including the id-LIST paths added at items 1315/1316 and the multi-id
Gremlin form item 1317 admitted under an order-free tail, none of which existed when the
requirement was last considered. 400,000 sits inside the 200k-1M cache transition this repo warns
about, and the arms are flat across it.

### What the absolute numbers say

Recorded because they are the useful part once the scaling question is settled:

- the engine primitive is **~100-115 ns**; everything above it is query machinery.
- **GQL single-id is ~1.47 us**, about 13x the primitive (parse cache, plan, bind, row build) and
  ~2.3x cheaper than **Gremlin's ~3.3 us** for the same question.
- `gql-edge-in` at ~7.9 us is the most expensive id path measured — though it is a HOP query
  binding two nodes and an edge, so it is not like-for-like against `gql-node-in`'s 2.3 us.

Five properties are now probed rather than assumed, and the pattern paid for itself at item 1322:

## 1327 — `[hop, dedupe, count]` joins the order-free tails: 225x, and it is the evidence item 1318 asked for

Item 1318 added `[hop, count]` to `ORDER_FREE_TAILS` and deliberately left `[hop, dedupe, count]`
out, recording it as "sound but unmeasured — the list only grows on evidence". This is that
evidence. The decline was costing **328x**.

```text
  hasId(3 ids).out(T).count()             0.0210 ms   admitted at item 1318
  hasId(3 ids).out(T).dedupe().count()    6.8937      the decline
  hasId(3 ids).both(T).dedupe().count()   6.8622
  hasId(1 id).out(T).dedupe().count()     0.0260      a single id never needed the tail
```

After admitting `['out'|'in'|'both', 'dedupe', 'count']`, with the controls beside them:

```text
  ids-out-dedupe-count       6.8937 -> 0.0307   225x   answer 3
  ids-both-dedupe-count      6.8622 -> 0.0322   213x   answer 6
  ids-in-dedupe-count                  0.0294          answer 3
  ctl-ids-out-count                    0.0285          item 1318's admission, unchanged
  ctl-ids-out-dedupe-limit             0.2270          still DECLINES (the window)
  ctl-ids-plain                        6.6717          still DECLINES, rows=3
```

`ctl-ids-plain` is the one that matters most: the bare multi-id form is still refused, so item
1306's "we can filter by ids out of order" contract is untouched.

### Why it is sound, finishing where item 1314's rule points

The seeded and scanned frontiers are the same SET; a hop applied elementwise sums each element's
own neighbours and so does not depend on the input's ORDER; `dedupe` reduces that multiset to a
SET; and `count` reads only its size.

`dedupe` keeps the FIRST occurrence, so the surviving elements' ORDER genuinely does differ between
the two spellings — and a `count` tail cannot observe that. "The tail may only observe what both
spellings agree on" is satisfied exactly, not approximately.

### A test of mine was flipped, and the distinction is the point

`id-seed.test.ts` asserted this DECLINE, with the stated reason "sound but unmeasured". That is a
CONDITION, not a contract — unlike `hasId.test.ts`'s "we can filter by ids out of order", which is
named for behaviour someone chose on purpose and which item 1317 refused to touch. The condition
changed, so the test changed; it now carries the 328x and an agreement check that the ids written
in either order give the same count.

### Teeth: 3 mutants, 3 caught, and the per-file attribution did real work AGAIN

```text
  hop-dedupe-tails-unwired   CAUGHT  2 fail   id-seed AND union-both
  out-dedupe-only            CAUGHT  1 fail   id-seed
  dedupe-window-admitted     CAUGHT  2 fail   id-seed AND union-both
```

The first run caught all three in `id-seed.test.ts` ALONE — the one-sided guarding item 1318 warns
about, since `ORDER_FREE_TAILS` is shared with `fuseUnionBoth` and a union with a hop+dedupe+count
tail now fuses too. Two guards were added on that side: an agreement case and a route assertion
(fusion is answer-equivalent, so the agreement case cannot see an unwiring). Re-run,
`hop-dedupe-tails-unwired` fails in both files.

`dedupe-window-admitted` was given a second guard as well, and the reason is item 1318's own
distinction applied consistently: an UNSOUND entry — a window reads the sequence — should be
rejected by every caller AND asserted at each, where a sound-but-unmeasured one needs only the
single test that protects the evidence rule. The existing windowed union case has tail
`[out, take]` and never exercises the dedupe variant.

## 1328 — the order-free tail becomes a RULE instead of a list: 113x/245x/239x on multi-hop counts

Items 1318 and 1327 grew `ORDER_FREE_TAILS` to eight enumerated entries, and the measured family
kept extending past it:

```text
  hasId(3 ids).out(T).count()                   0.0193 ms   admitted
  hasId(3 ids).out(T).out(T).count()            4.3231      224x, declining
  hasId(3 ids).out(T).out(T).out(T).count()     6.8018      352x, declining
  hasId(3 ids).out(T).out(T).dedupe().count()   7.0489      declining
  hasId(1 id).out(T).out(T).count()             0.0223      a single id never needed a tail
```

Enumerating those is combinatorial, so the list is replaced by a RULE: **a tail is order-free when
every step in it is order-insensitive AND it ENDS in `count`.**

```text
  ids-out-out-count          4.3231 -> 0.0383   113x   answer 3
  ids-out3-count             6.8018 -> 0.0278   245x   answer 3
  ids-out-out-dedupe-count   7.0489 -> 0.0295   239x   answer 3
  ids-mixed-count                      0.0329          answer 6  (out, in, both)
  ctl-ids-out-count                    0.0188          unchanged
  ctl-ids-out-out-limit                0.4310          still DECLINES (window)
  ctl-ids-out-values                   6.1867          still DECLINES (values)
  ctl-ids-plain                        6.0206          still DECLINES, rows=3
```

All 1,105 existing tests passed unchanged before any new ones were added, including every decline.

### An ALLOW-LIST, not a deny-list, and that is the whole safety argument

`ORDER_FREE_STEPS` lists `out`/`in`/`both`/`dedupe`; anything else declines by DEFAULT. A deny-list
would admit an unknown or newly added step kind SILENTLY, and the cost of being wrong is a
reordering no answer test can see.

The test that pins it: **`[out, has, count]` is SOUND** — `has` preserves order — **and it still
DECLINES**, because `has` is not listed. A new step kind therefore waits for a measurement instead
of being admitted by omission. Mutation confirms that test is the ONLY thing holding the property:
`allow-list-becomes-deny` is caught by it alone (1 failure), where every other mutant fails 3-14
tests across both callers.

This is the honest resolution of item 1318's caution that "any hop then a count is a broader claim
than either caller has evidence for". It now has evidence at one hop, two, three, mixed kinds and
with dedupe — so the generalization is earned, and the allow-list keeps the blast radius of being
wrong at zero new kinds.

## 1329 — ✅ SHIPPED: an id-pinned START no longer sweeps the whole graph for a 3+-segment `count(*)` — **351x/342x**; and the instrument that said "unobservable" was watching the wrong surface — ⚠️ SEE ALSO 1330: the PROPERTY-pinned twin of this cliff needed the opposite mechanism (seed the sweep, not decline the rung), because a compile-time decline costs the unindexed path 2.9x; this item stands as measured for the id pin

`patternCountOf` sends a long chain to the sweep because the sweep is the only route that can carry
an END constraint (item 306). That is right for an end-gated chain and wrong when the START is
pinned by an id: it walks every vertex to answer a question about one.

Order-alternated A/B at 200,000 vertices, measured against the guard ITSELF with the guard removed
(not against an older build), one shape per process, 14 reps, first 3 dropped, median:

```text
  shape          guarded     unwired      ratio
  pinned3         0.0354     12.4278    351.07x
  pinned5         0.0370     12.6641    342.27x
  endgate3        3.2618      3.2478      1.00x   <- the null control, flat
```

The cliff hit the SINGLE-id seed (item 618) as much as item 1315's id list, so it long predates
both, and it was flat from 3 to 5 segments — which is what a fixed whole-graph pass looks like.

### Two routes reach the sweep, and guarding one is not enough

Three segments reach it via `endGatedChainCount`, four-or-more via `longChainCount`. The first cut
guarded only `segments.length === 3` and left a pinned 5-hop at 12.6682 ms while the 3-hop it had
just fixed read 0.0358. Found by instrumenting WHICH rung fired at each depth rather than assuming
one guard covered the family. `walkLevelCount` was the hypothesis and was REFUTED — its counter
read 0.

### ⚠️ THE INSTRUMENT LESSON, which cost more than the fix: a spy on ONE surface that reads zero has not shown there is nothing to find

The route choice is answer-equivalent by construction, so it needs a route assertion. The first spy
wrapped `verticesById.values()` and read **0 pulls for the pinned shape whether the guard was
present or not** — at 2k, 8k, 50k AND 200k. That looked like proof the route is unobservable, and
the conclusion drawn from it was that the test could only be a pure-predicate unit test with the
benchmark as the sole guard on the wiring.

It was the wrong surface. Wrapping EVERY enumeration surface on both vertex maps — `values`, `keys`,
`entries`, `forEach`, `Symbol.iterator`, and the Sets behind `verticesByLabel.get` — showed it at
once:

```text
  guarded   pinned3   NOTHING ENUMERATED
  unwired   pinned3   byLabel[set].iter=200000
  either    endgate3  byId.values=200000
```

**The two sweeps use DIFFERENT surfaces.** The pinned chain's swept route walks the LABEL set; the
end-gated chain's sweep walks `verticesById.values()`. A spy on either one alone reads 0 for the
other and silently loses half its teeth — the end-gate control in the new test failed exactly that
way until both were counted. That probe is kept as `enumeration-surface-probe.ts`, because the
question "which surface does this route actually enumerate?" recurs.

### A SECOND fixture trap, same shape as item 1316's

The first teeth-check ran at N=2,000 and reported the guard making no difference — because 2,000 is
below `SEEK_FLOOR_VERTICES` (4,096), so NEITHER arm seeds and both legitimately read 0. Checked at
5,000 / 8,000 / 20,000: the binary is clean at every one (guarded enumerates nothing, unwired walks
exactly N), so the test takes the smallest. A fixture under the threshold produces a confident null.

### ⚠️ AN INTERRUPTED MUTATION RUN VOIDED THREE CONCLUSIONS, and this is why the restore rule is per-mutant

The mutation run was killed before its final restore, leaving `predicate-inverted` in the working
tree. Every measurement taken after that point was against inverted code, which is what produced
"the route is unobservable" and "the spy perturbs the route it measures" — both false. Worse, the
copy taken DURING that window as a safety net (`t1329-fix.ts`) captured the MUTANT, so restoring
from it would have re-applied the inversion; only the script-written pristine was clean. It was
caught because the new unit test failed with exactly inverted results.

Two rules earn their keep here: **restore before applying the next mutant, never only after the
loop** (an interrupted loop leaves the mutant in the tree), and **a pristine copy is only pristine
if it was taken before the first mutant** — verify it (`inverted=False`, both guards present) before
restoring from it, rather than trusting its name.

### The lint budget moved the guard, and that MOVED THE MUTANTS TOO

Spelling the guard inline at both rungs took `patternCountOf` to complexity **37** against a budget
of 35 — two call sites, two decision points. The decision therefore lives in
`sweepableSegmentCount`, which returns the real segment count or 0 when the start is pinned, so the
rungs spend none. A guard that cannot be added without breaking the budget is a signal about the
function, not about the guard.

⚠️ THE FIRST VERDICT WAS AGAINST THE SPELLING THAT NO LONGER SHIPS. 4/4 was measured against the
inline form; the refactor deleted those anchors. A mutation verdict against code that was then
rewritten is not a verdict about what ships, so the whole run was redone against the shipped
anchors — and it gained a mutant the inline form could not have, because concentrating both guards
into one helper creates a SINGLE point of unwiring that did not exist before.

### Teeth: 5 mutants, 5 caught, no survivors — and the first run is why the test was rewritten

Against the pure-predicate test, THREE of the four then-current mutants SURVIVED, which is what
proved those route assertions vacuous. Against the surface-correct route assertions, at the shipped
spelling:

```text
  three-guard-unwired     CAUGHT   2 fail    pinned-chain-count
  long-guard-unwired      CAUGHT   4 fail    pinned-chain-count
  helper-returns-length   CAUGHT   6 fail    pinned-chain-count   <- new, and the widest
  hint-kinds-narrowed     CAUGHT   4 fail    pinned-chain-count
  predicate-inverted      CAUGHT  10 fail    pinned-chain-count AND long-chain-count
```

`helper-returns-length` failing the most of the three guard mutants is the refactor's own signature:
it is the one place that unwires BOTH rungs at once.

`hint-kinds-narrowed` is the one that pins item 1315's list form specifically: with the predicate
narrowed to `'id'`, the single id stays fast and only the id LIST regresses. `predicate-inverted`
also ran ~6 minutes against seconds for the other arms — inverting the sense sends NON-pinned chains
down a route with no pin to seed from — so it would have been caught by the 600 s cap even if no
assertion had fired.

The pure-predicate unit test is KEPT alongside the route assertions, per
`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`: the route assertions catch the call sites being unwired, the unit
test catches the predicate admitting or refusing the wrong hint kinds. They fail on different
mutants, which is the argument for both.

## 1330 — ✅ SHIPPED: the way-count SWEEP seeds its START from an index instead of walking the label bucket — **458x**; and the compile-time DECLINE that looked equivalent was a 2.9x regression

Item 1329 stopped an id-pinned start from sweeping, by DECLINING the rung. The same cliff exists
for a property-pinned start, and the depth ladder locates it exactly — 200,000 vertices, `k`
indexed, one shape per process:

```text
  depth   indexed a.k = 7    id pin
    0           0.0049          -
    1           0.0066       0.0090
    2           0.0053       0.0069
    3        >> 5.6254 <<    0.0382
    4        >> 5.7319 <<        -
```

So an indexed start IS seeded at nought, one and two hops and then falls off at three, where the
chain rungs hand the whole label bucket to the sweep and let `startGate` filter it. The index was
being built and then ignored: it bought only 1.08x on that shape (6.14 against 5.69).

### ❌ THE OBVIOUS FIX IS A REGRESSION, and only measuring the OTHER index state says so

The obvious move is to admit `eq` to item 1329's pin and decline. Order-alternated A/B:

```text
  shape        IDX        pre       post      ratio
  prop3          1     5.4341     0.0380    143x FASTER
  prop3          0     5.6257    16.5443    0.34x — a 2.9x REGRESSION
  pinned3        1     0.0404     0.0370    1.09x  flat
  endgate3       1     3.1339     3.3406    0.94x  flat
  bare3          1    77.3533    79.9191    0.97x  flat
```

The indexed column alone would have shipped that. **The decline is a COMPILE-time decision and the
index is a RUN-time fact** — whether `k` is indexed is a property of the GRAPH, and plans are
cached across graphs — so a compile-time decline has to assume, and assuming wrong costs the
unindexed path, which is the common one.

### ✅ What shipped instead: the sweep seeds its own source

`sweepStartSeed` prices the start's index candidates with the SHARED `seekIsWorthIt` and returns a
set, or `undefined` so the caller keeps `candidateVertexSource` byte for byte. Three rounds, order
alternated, medians:

```text
  shape        IDX   pre(med)  post(med)      ratio   pre runs / post runs
  prop3          1     5.5985     0.0122    458.89x   [5.598, 5.052, 5.919] / [0.010, 0.012, 0.013]
  endgate3       1     3.2587     3.2031      1.02x   [3.259, 4.949, 3.053] / [3.203, 3.845, 3.164]
  bare3          1    80.0775    78.5904      1.02x
  prop3          0     6.0878     6.3176      0.96x   [6.232, 5.546, 6.088] / [6.318, 7.686, 5.732]
```

`prop5` 0.0162 and `a.k = $k` 0.0143 on the shipped build, so depth and the parameter spelling both
hold. `seedVertices` is not called despite doing the same choosing, for the reason recorded at the
`seeded` site: it hides WHETHER it seeded, and here that is exactly what the caller needs. The
CEILING is not duplicated — `seekIsWorthIt` is shared, which is what item 407's drift was about.

### ⚠️ A 1.57x "regression" on the control, REFUTED BY THE PRE ARM ITSELF

One reading had `endgate3` at 4.9352 against a shipped 3.1339. It is not an effect: the pre arm's
three runs were 3.259, **4.949**, 3.053 — that shape has a high mode near 4.9 and it appears in
BOTH arms. A single reading cannot distinguish a regression from a bimodal shape, and three rounds
were the difference between shipping this and discarding it. (A later single reading came in at
5.299, outside the range seen so far, which is the same variance and not a new fact.)

### Teeth: 6 mutants, 6 caught — and TWO of them exist because mutation said the tests were vacuous

```text
  seed-unwired               CAUGHT   6 fail
  pricing-dropped            CAUGHT   1 fail
  consumer-ignores-seed      CAUGHT   6 fail
  picks-worst-candidate      CAUGHT   1 fail   <- survived pass 1
  unthreaded-at-long-chain   CAUGHT   2 fail
  unthreaded-at-end-gated    CAUGHT   4 fail
```

`pricing-dropped` is the one the file is built around: a mutant that seeks whenever an index exists
passes every answer test, because the answers are identical. The case that kills it is an indexed
but UNSELECTIVE start — `grp` matches half the graph, where audit item 409 measured a seek at 5.02x
SLOWER. `picks-worst-candidate` survived pass 1 because every query in the fixture offered exactly
ONE indexed candidate, so narrowest and widest coincided; two conjuncts differing by three orders
of magnitude fixed that.

### ⚠️ A TEST WRITTEN FOR A MUTANT WAS ITSELF VACUOUS, and the arithmetic is why

`seeds-flipped-reading-too` survived, so a case was added for it — and it survived AGAIN with that
case green. The ring is `i -> (i * 7 + 1) % 5000`, so three hops from `v7` reach `v2458`, which
carries no `Q` label: the true answer was 0, both graphs returned 0, and the comparison held while
asserting nothing. **A cross-graph comparison is FREE whenever the answer is empty.** Exactly ten
starts have a three-hop endpoint on a Q vertex; `k = 201` reaches `v4000`. The case now asserts
non-emptiness, with the derivation written in so the constant is not "simplified" back.

### ⚠️ AND THE MUTANT WAS NOT A COVERAGE GAP AT ALL — it was DEAD CODE, treated as a gap twice

Even non-vacuous, it survived. `labelMayFlip` requires `allGates[0] === undefined` — no constraint
on the start — while `sweepStartSeed` returns a set only when the start HAS one. So `reversed` is
`undefined` exactly when a seed is possible: a seeded start and a flipped reading CANNOT co-occur,
the `pick === forward` guard was dead, and the mutant is answer-equivalent in every REACHABLE
state, so no test can kill it.

Confirmed before deleting: the impossible state was made to `throw` and the suite run — 3,390 tests
over 207 files, no throw — so the structural argument is corroborated rather than trusted. The
branch is gone and item 1313's rule applies: the proof stands where the code was. The guard's
REASONING is kept, because it becomes live the moment the flip is priced — `pick` compares LABEL
BUCKET sizes and knows nothing about seed selectivity, which is items 172 and 173 one family along,
where `orient` reversed away from a selective start.

The lesson is about diagnosis order: a surviving mutant has three possible causes — a missing test,
a vacuous test, or UNREACHABLE code — and this one was mistaken for the first twice before the
third was checked. Checking reachability is cheaper than writing a test, and should come first.

### Verification

`packages/gql` 3,390 pass / 0 fail (3,375 before; +15 in `seeded-sweep-start.test.ts`).
`packages/gremlin` 1,109 pass / 0 fail. All seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass / 0 fail. Gates as
separate commands, each status read into a variable: `typecheck` 0, `lint` 0, `fmt:check` 0,
`check --skip-nx-cache` 0.

Item 1329's heading is annotated rather than struck in the same commit: its fix stands exactly as
measured for the id pin, and this item does not supersede it — the two use DIFFERENT mechanisms
(decline vs seed) for the same cliff, and the decline remains the right one where the hint is
selective on every graph.

## 1331 — ✅ SHIPPED: `not(hasNot(k))` folds to `hasKey(k)` on an element stream — **16.9x**, and the GREMLIN SPELLING SURFACE IS NOW AT ZERO FLAGGED GROUPS ~~AT `SPELL_N=200000`~~ — ⚠️ CORRECTED BY 1332: raising `SPELL_N` to 1,000,000 flagged a NEW group (2.00x), so "zero flagged" is a claim about the N it was run at; and the "raise `SPELL_N`" advice for the 13 sub-ms groups is wrong — they are O(1) id lookups and need more REPS

The last group `gremlin-spelling-probe` flagged. `not` applies a whole sub-plan PER TRAVERSER
(`!hasAny(applyPlanToStream(step.plan, [t], …))`), so this spelling paid 200,000 sub-plan
applications where its twins read a property bag.

### The sweep UNDERSTATED it by 3.4x, which is the opposite of the usual direction

```text
  in the full sweep                       4.95x
  the group ALONE, three runs   16.96x / 17.21x / 17.05x
```

Isolated, `has(k)` 2.529 / `hasKey(k)` 2.505 / `not(hasNot(k))` **42.5 ms**. The sweep's dispatch
pollution slows the FAST arms, so the ratio compresses — the recorded trap is in-sweep inflation
making things look worse, and this is the same mechanism running the other way. A 4.95x flag was
worth three times what it advertised. After the fold, 2.513 ms and the group converges; two further
runs read 2.733/2.533/2.564 and 2.582/2.530/2.550, and the whole probe reports **0 groups over 2x**.

### ⚠️ THE FOLD IS A WRONG ANSWER OFF AN ELEMENT STREAM, and that is MEASURED, not reasoned

`hasKey` is `keys.some(k => k in bag)` and `hasNot` is `keys.every(k => !(k in bag))`, so "not all
absent" IS "at least one present" — exact duals at ANY key count, so no single-key restriction is
needed (unlike `hasChain`'s, item 1140). But `hasNot` returns FALSE for a non-element, so
`not(hasNot(k))` PASSES what `hasKey(k)` filters:

```text
  stream          hasKey(k)   not(hasNot(k))
  element                 1                1   agree
  properties()            1                3   DIFFER
  values()                0                2   DIFFER
```

`notfold-soundness-check.ts` is that measurement, kept because the gate is only justified by it.
The fold is therefore gated on the stream carrying elements, tracked through an ALLOW-LIST over the
92 `Step` kinds: the two sources, every hop, the element-local filters and the windows. Anything
else ends the element stream BY DEFAULT — item 1328's argument, and here being wrong costs a wrong
answer rather than a slow plan.

Both directions fold (`not(hasKey(k))` → `hasNot(k)` by the same duality) and both are measured: a
new `absence:` probe group reads 13.118/13.047, 12.821/12.782, 12.956/12.755 across three runs. ⚠️
Its FIRST reading was 11.837 against 6.817 — a 1.74x that would have looked like the folded
spelling beating the direct one, in a group where both arms become the SAME step. Repeating the
process refuted it; one reading of a converged group is still one reading.

### A test of mine was changed, and item 1327's distinction is why

`filter-flatten.test.ts` asserted `not(hasNot(k))` was LEFT ALONE, under "or and not are left
alone — a disjunction is not a chain". That recorded a CONDITION of the pass (it did not handle
`not`), not a CONTRACT someone chose, and its stated reason is untouched: the fold does not SPLICE
a wrapper body into the chain, it replaces the whole step with the single filter that means the
same thing. The decline is still asserted, now on bodies that genuinely cannot fold — `not(out(T))`
and a two-step body.

### Teeth: 8 mutants, 8 caught — and the EDGE source was a blind spot the tests shared

```text
  fold-unwired               CAUGHT   2 fail
  gate-removed               CAUGHT   1 fail   the WRONG-ANSWER mutant
  multi-step-body-admitted   CAUGHT   1 fail
  reverse-direction-dropped  CAUGHT   1 fail
  forward-direction-dropped  CAUGHT   3 fail
  allow-list-becomes-deny    CAUGHT   3 fail
  tracker-pinned-true        CAUGHT   1 fail   through the lint-extracted helper
  edge-source-dropped        CAUGHT   1 fail   <- SURVIVED pass 1
```

`edge-source-dropped` removes `'E'` from `ELEMENT_SOURCES` and survived a pass where all six other
mutants died, because every case used a VERTEX source. Edges are elements too — `hasKey` and
`hasNot` both test `isVertex(v) || isEdge(v)` and read the same bag — so the duality holds
identically and the gap was in the tests, not the rule. Covered now via `E()` and via `outE()`.

### ⚠️ THE LINT BUDGET MOVED THE CODE AFTER MUTATION PASSED, for the second time this session

`prefer-destructuring` and `no-nested-ternary` failed AFTER the 7/7, and the fix extracted
`streamStaysElements`. That invalidated the verdict exactly as item 1330's helper did: a mutation
result against a spelling that no longer ships is not a result about what ships. Re-run at the
shipped anchors, 8/8, with `tracker-pinned-true` added because the extracted helper is a NEW way to
reach `gate-removed`'s wrong answer.

The process lesson, now twice: **run `lint` BEFORE mutation, not after.** Both times the gate forced
a refactor that cost a full re-run.
