## 1332 — ✅ SHIPPED: `or(hasLabel(a), hasLabel(b))` merges into `hasLabel(a, b)` — **2.00x**; found only by RAISING `SPELL_N`, and it needs NO element gate (unlike 1331) for a reason worth stating

Item 1331's mechanism one step along: `or` applies a sub-plan PER TRAVERSER PER BRANCH, so the
spread spelling pays that machinery where the merged one runs a single element-local filter. The
fold generalizes to all three ANY-of filters.

### ⚠️ INVISIBLE AT 200,000 AND REAL AT 1,000,000, which is a gap in how the probe was being run

At `SPELL_N=200000` this group sat UNDER the probe's 1 ms floor and was reported as
"not compared" — not clean, simply never measured. At 1,000,000 it flagged at 2.02x, and alone,
three runs, `hasLabel(a,b)` ~86 ms against `or(hasLabel, hasLabel)` ~158-163.

**So "0 groups flagged" is a statement about the N the probe was run at.** Item 1331 closed the
last flag at 200k and this item found a new one by changing nothing but the size. The sweep-the-size
rule was already written down for benchmarks; it applies to the spelling probes too.

### The A/B: 2.00x, with the DISTRIBUTION printed because the folded shape is bimodal

Whole-file arms, four rounds, order alternated, at 1,000,000 vertices:

```text
  arm    reading                                        median
  pre    direct      [84.6, 85.8, 79.2, 79.1]           84.638
  pre    or-spelled  [163.5, 170.2, 154.6, 155.1]      163.501
  post   direct      [82.0, 80.0, 83.8, 82.1]           82.112
  post   or-spelled  [81.6, 79.6,  47.9, 81.7]          81.623

  OR spelling    163.501 -> 81.623   2.00x
  direct (ctl)    84.638 -> 82.112   1.03x
```

The two spellings now CONVERGE (81.6 against 82.1). ⚠️ The post arm shows a ~48 ms low mode once in
four while the pre arm is tight — so the bimodality appears only AFTER the fold, and three earlier
isolated runs caught it twice, reading 45.8 and 47.0 against the direct arm's 80. Quoting those
would have claimed ~1.75x in the WRONG DIRECTION (the folded arm beating a step it compiles to).
The repo already records `nullif` swinging between ~45 and ~82 modes; this is the same thing, and
the median across four rounds is the honest number.

Because of that, the equivalence claim rests on a PLAN assertion and not on time — "a plan mismatch
is the real signal; the time is the backstop", applied as written.

### ✅ AND IT NEEDS NO ELEMENT GATE, which is the interesting contrast with item 1331

All three merged kinds are ANY-of, which is what makes merging a concatenation:

```text
  hasLabel   labels.some(l => v.labels.has(l))
  hasId      ids.includes(v.id)
  hasKey     keys.some(k => k in bag)
```

All three return FALSE for a non-element — and `or` does NOT INVERT that false the way `not` does,
so both spellings reject a non-element identically. Measured, not assumed: element 2 and 2, after
`properties()` 0 and 0, after `values()` 0 and 0. **The fold that needed a gate inverted; this one
does not.** That is the whole difference between the two items, and it is recorded so the next fold
is classified by whether it inverts rather than by analogy.

`hasLabelAnd` is a separate step kind with conjunctive semantics and is not eligible. `has` has its
own `or`-chain fold (`membershipFromOrChain`) beside this one, tried first because it is the
narrower claim.

### Teeth: 6 mutants, 5 caught, 1 TYPE-INVALID, no survivors

```text
  fold-unwired             CAUGHT        3 fail
  mixed-kinds-merged       CAUGHT        2 fail   the WRONG-ANSWER mutant
  any-of-check-dropped     TYPE-INVALID  never a live mutation
  merge-keeps-first-only   CAUGHT        1 fail
  haskey-field-swapped     CAUGHT        2 fail
  single-branch-admitted   CAUGHT        1 fail   <- SURVIVED pass 1
```

`merge-keeps-first-only` is why the contents are asserted and not just the step KIND: it folds to
`hasLabel(P)` alone, which satisfies a kind-only assertion and answers a different question. The
test pins the deduped concatenation in first-seen order, `['P', 'R', 'Q']`.

⚠️ `single-branch-admitted` SURVIVED pass 1, and it is neither a coverage gap nor dead code:
folding `or(hasLabel(P))` to `hasLabel(P)` is ANSWER-EQUIVALENT, so no answer test can ever see it.
The `plans.length < 2` guard is a deliberate scope limit on an UNMEASURED form — item 1328's rule,
a new form waits for a measurement rather than being admitted by omission — and a PLAN assertion is
the only instrument that can hold it. It has one now, named as the test to change if the one-branch
form is ever measured.

This is the third survivor this session whose diagnosis was the question "missing test, vacuous
test, or equivalent code?" — and the first where equivalence was checked FIRST. Item 1330 cost two
wasted passes by assuming a coverage gap twice.

### ⚠️ Correcting item 1331's closing line, in the same commit

That entry said raising `SPELL_N` is the way to learn whether the 13 sub-millisecond groups hide
anything. **That is wrong for those groups.** They are id lookups, which are O(1) by design (item
1326's checked invariant), so no graph size brings them into range — at 1,000,000 the same 13 are
still under the floor. They need more REPS or a finer timer, not a bigger graph. Raising `SPELL_N`
did work for the label and hop groups, which is how this item surfaced, so the advice was right for
the wrong set.

## 1333 — ✅ SHIPPED: inline props on ANY pattern of a multi-pattern `MATCH` lift to the clause `WHERE` — **1.86x**, found by READING after seven timing experiments failed; ⚠️ and the mechanism I first claimed was WRONG

The GQL spelling probe flags `a product's one-sided predicate` right at its 2x threshold. Five
separate processes show why the group ratio flickers while the effect does not — the braces arm is
rock steady and the others vary:

```text
  , (b:P) WHERE b.k = 7      14.20 14.23 14.12 12.21 14.22   median 14.20
  MATCH … MATCH … WHERE      11.39 12.83 10.37 10.88 13.11   median 11.39
  , (b:P WHERE b.k = 7)      11.48 11.85 11.82 12.26 11.64   median 11.82
  , (b:P {k: 7})             23.72 24.69 24.78 25.35 23.64   median 24.69   <- 2.09x
```

`liftStartProps` opened with `if (c.kind !== 'match' || c.where !== undefined ||
c.patterns.length !== 1) return c;` — so a comma product (`patterns.length === 2`) refused the lift
outright. That refusal was listed in the function's header with NO REASON beside it, unlike the
no-segments one next to it ("already served by the scan rungs and would gain nothing", which
measurement confirms for a single bare node at 3.36 against 3.55 ms). An unmeasured scope limit,
the same shape as item 1332's one-branch `or`.

After the lift, eight processes: **24.69 -> 13.29 ms, 1.86x, and the group no longer flags in any
run.**

### ⚠️ SEVEN TIMING EXPERIMENTS FAILED TO REPRODUCE IT, and reading the code took one

A standalone probe was built to match the shared fixture and bisect the cause. It matched on N,
edge count, labels, property richness, the NDJSON load path, index-build order, the second index,
one-process multi-shape timing, two-pass min, and the per-rep `JSON.stringify` — **every candidate
refuted**, reading braces 8.78 against inlineWhere 8.66 both before and after the change. The
absolute costs differ 2.7x from the probe's (8.8 against 23.8) on a fixture matched on every
dimension I could find.

So `product-inline-seed-probe.ts` CANNOT validate this change and its flatness is NOT evidence the
change does nothing. **Why the shared fixture shows a 2x that a matched one does not is OPEN.** The
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` note is the standing suspect — the spelling probe is a ~1,500-line
module, the standalone one ~250 — but that is a hypothesis, not a finding.

The lesson is cheaper than the seven experiments were: when a gap is reproducible on one instrument
and not another, READ THE DECLINE before bisecting the fixture. `liftStartProps`'s guard answered in
one look what ten measured arms could not.

### ⚠️ AND THE MECHANISM I FIRST CLAIMED IS REFUTED — it is NOT the seed hint

The first version of this entry, and of the code comment, said the braces form "had no seed hint at
all". **Mutation refuted it**: restoring the `patterns.length !== 1` refusal left ALL 3,401 tests
green, including route assertions that count vertex pulls from both vertex sources. That is only
possible if the seek happens either way — and it does: `indexCandidates` reads `node.pred.props`
DIRECTLY, so inline props seed whether or not they are lifted (item 1330 established that path).

So a seeding assertion cannot see this lift at all, the measurement stands, and **what the lifted
form actually saves is unidentified.** Recorded as open rather than guessed at, because the guess
was already wrong once here.

### ⚠️ A SEMANTIC REGRESSION the suite caught: a query that must RAISE answered 0

`MATCH p = (a:P {k: 1}), (p:P {k: 2}) RETURN count(*)` collides a PATH variable with a node
variable and must raise. It raises only because the product-of-counts shortcut DECLINES and the
general path gets there; a lifted `where` routed the shortcut elsewhere and it answered 0 — a query
that must error returning a row, which is the one regression a performance rewrite must never
cause. Clauses binding a path variable now refuse the lift.

This is item 778's recorded hazard one case along: "one rung's admission gate is another rung's
disqualifier, which is the real hazard in rewriting a clause list and is not visible from the gate
being opened."

### Teeth: 5 mutants, 5 caught — after a first pass where TWO survived

```text
  multi-pattern-refused-again   CAUGHT   2 fail   <- SURVIVED pass 1
  pathvar-refusal-dropped       CAUGHT   3 fail   the WRONG-ANSWER mutant
  bare-node-now-lifts-always    CAUGHT   1 fail   <- SURVIVED pass 1
  null-literal-lifts            CAUGHT   4 fail   IS NULL becomes UNKNOWN (item 260)
  rebuilds-when-nothing-lifted  CAUGHT  33 fail   across FOUR files
```

The two survivors were the whole item and one of its refusals, so nothing held either. The fix is
the repo's own prescription for an answer-equivalent rewrite (`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`):
`liftStartProps` is now exported and `lift-start-props.test.ts` tests the TRANSFORMATION directly —
eleven cases, seven of them refusals with a mutant each.

`rebuilds-when-nothing-lifted` failing 33 tests across four files is the useful surprise: clause
IDENTITY is load-bearing for the neighbouring rewrites in `compileLinear`, which was a guess in the
code comment and is now measured.

### ⚠️ Two process failures of mine, both worth the note

**Mutation ran with RED gates.** `lint` and `check` were 1 and the mutation run was chained into the
same command, so it ran anyway — the exact mistake item 1332's entry records a lesson about two
items earlier. Running gates first only helps if the run is not chained past their exit code.

**An assertion claimed a contract the function never had.** The identity test asserted
`liftStartProps(before)).toBe(before` — but the function is `clauses.map(...)` and has ALWAYS
returned a new array. What the guard preserves is each untouched CLAUSE's identity, which is what
the test asserts now.

## 1334 — ✅ SHIPPED: the unfiltered two-hop count reads each middle's OWN adjacency box instead of looking it up by id string — **1.92x WARM** (⚠️ **1.23x SLOWER COLD** — corrected at item 1341, which also finds the prior refutation this entry failed to cite), and GQL goes from 1.42x SLOWER than Gremlin to 1.35x FASTER

`surface-parity-probe` has had `two-hop-count` open as the largest ABSOLUTE cross-surface gap in the
field. `buildTwoHopCount` iterates middles and multiplies two degrees — the right algorithm — but
each degree came from `side(graph, b.id, …)`, which does `edgesFromByLabel.get(bId)`: a STRING-KEYED
`Map.get`, ~190 ns by item 194's measurement. Twice per middle, so an unfiltered two-hop over
200,000 middles paid **400,000 string hashes**.

`Vertex.adjFrom` is a LAZY MEMO over exactly that lookup:

```ts
get adjFrom() { this.#adjFrom ??= this.#graph?.edgesFromByLabel.get(this.id); return this.#adjFrom; }
```

so the first access costs what `side` costs and every later one is a private-field read. The memo
lives on the vertex and survives across queries until an adjacency write clears it.

### The A/B: whole-file arms, three rounds order-alternated, 200,000 vertices

```text
  arm        DEG   cold(med)   warm(med)
  pre/gql      1      97.356      44.255
  post/gql     1      81.857      23.006
  pre/gql      3      97.264      44.245
  post/gql     3      85.781      25.053
  ref/grm      1      76.218      30.928
  ref/grm      3      83.486      30.865

  DEG=1  warm 1.92x   cold 1.19x   post/grm 0.74x
  DEG=3  warm 1.77x   cold 1.13x   post/grm 0.81x
```

**The cross-surface gap is not closed but REVERSED**: GQL was 1.42-1.46x slower than Gremlin on
this question and is now 1.23-1.35x faster. The COLD first rep is reported beside the warm median
because the lever IS a memo and crediting a memo for a change is item 1323's recorded mistake —
cold improves too, so there is no first-query cost traded away.

### ⚠️ `twoHopSide`'s header records this same box read as MEASURED FLAT, and that is NOT a contradiction

That function's comment says the box read was "Tried and MEASURED FLAT: 369.9 / 384.4 / 367.7 ms
against 384.1 / 364.2 / 372.0". Both are true, and the condition is item 355's: **there** the middle
is revisited once per incoming EDGE, so the box is already warm within a single query and the memo
has nothing left to save; **here** each middle is visited EXACTLY ONCE per query, which is where a
cross-query memo pays. Read as a blanket refutation, that comment would have closed this target —
and the entry it belongs to is about a DIFFERENT loop.

### ⚠️ The fixture nearly answered a different question, twice

The parity probe's fixture is a degree-1 CHAIN (`v0 -> v1 -> v2 -> …`), and a two-hop degree product
has NOTHING to multiply when every degree is 1 — the repo's own rule ("one edge per node is sparse")
says a conclusion there may not generalize. Swept to degree 2 and 3 before building anything: the
gap holds at 1.42-1.46x throughout, so it is general and not the sparse corner.

Also: both surfaces are FLAT as the answer grows 9x (200,000 to 1,800,000 paths), so both are O(V)
and this was never a complexity difference — it is a constant factor on the per-middle loop. And
the ratio is LOCALITY-SENSITIVE: 1.81x on the probe's sequential chain against 1.42x on a
scattered-target fixture, with absolute costs 2.7x apart. The probe's 1.81x is its fixture's number,
not a universal one.

### Teeth: 6 mutants, 5 caught, and the SIXTH IS EXPECTED TO SURVIVE

```text
  box-read-reverted             SURVIVED  <- declared expected, see below
  first-arm-direction-flipped   CAUGHT  25 fail
  second-arm-direction-flipped  CAUGHT  24 fail
  both-arms-same-direction      CAUGHT  21 fail
  box-accessor-inverted         CAUGHT  55 fail
  types-dropped                 CAUGHT  10 fail
```

`box-read-reverted` puts `side(graph, b.id, …)` back, and that returns the SAME number by
construction — answer-equivalent AND route-equivalent, so no test can observe it and the benchmark
is the only guard. It was listed in the mutant set with that reason attached BEFORE the run, and the
script asserts the survivor set is exactly `['box-read-reverted']`, so "expected" is checked rather
than claimed afterwards.

The mutants that had to be caught are the WRONG-BOX ones, because reading `adjFrom` where `adjTo` is
meant is a wrong answer rather than a slow path — that is the only real risk this change
introduces. `side-of-vertex-equivalence.test.ts` pins it with 4,828 assertions: `sideOfVertex` and
`side` must agree for EVERY vertex (not on a total, which can agree while two vertices differ in
opposite directions) across both directions, five type filters, a far label, zero-degree vertices
and self-loops — which sit in BOTH adjacency maps (item 482) and are the case most likely to differ
between a graph-keyed lookup and the vertex's own box.

The `both` arms are left on `undirectedSide` deliberately: a different shape (two sides plus a loop
correction), unmeasured here.

## 1335 — ❌ REFUTED: item 1334's box read bought NOTHING on the FILTERED two-hop loop — 0.99x, and the reason is amortization

Item 1334 took 1.92x by reading each middle's own adjacency box instead of looking it up by id
string. The FILTERED two-hop builder has the same shape at `waysToA` — a loop over
`candidateVertexSource` that visits each candidate `b` EXACTLY ONCE with the vertex already in
hand, which is the condition item 355 names — so the lever was tried there next.

At 200,000 vertices, degree 3, `WHERE b.age > 45`, three processes each:

```text
  id-string lookup   24.15 / 25.44 / 25.50 ms   median 25.44
  vertex box read    25.68 / 26.57 / 25.61      median 25.68   0.99x
```

with the unfiltered shape flat beside it as the control. **The lever is sound and available; it
simply has nothing to save here.** In 1334's loop, TWO id-string lookups per middle were the whole
body. In this one, the single lookup is amortized against a gate evaluation and an inner per-edge
walk, so the saving disappears into work that dominates it.

Recorded at the call site with these numbers, per the repo's rule — "record rejected optimizations
with their numbers, next to the code they would have changed. Several have been re-attempted
otherwise." The generalizable form: **1334's ratio is a property of that loop's body, not of the
lever**, so applying it elsewhere needs its own measurement rather than an inference from 1334.

Two sites were considered and NOT tried, with reasons:

- the per-edge `side(graph, b.id, …)` inside the filtered loop's inner walk, and
  `twoHopSide`'s own per-edge calls: a `c` or a middle reached per EDGE is REVISITED, which is
  exactly `twoHopSide`'s measured-flat condition (369.9/384.4/367.7 against 384.1/364.2/372.0).
- `sweepChain`'s `side(graph, idOf[slot], …)` and `undirectedSide`'s `(graph, id, …)`: neither has
  a vertex object in hand, so the box read would need a `verticesById.get` first — the very lookup
  it is meant to avoid.

`packages/gql` 3,432 pass / 0 fail with the revert in place. `typecheck` 0, `lint` 0, `fmt:check` 0,
`check --skip-nx-cache` 0.

```text
  row                        sweep    isolated (3 rounds, medians)
  write: append node         0.86x    150.9k -> 173.2k   1.15x FASTER
  write: append then delete  0.76x    369.7k -> 365.7k   0.99x FLAT
```

Every change this session is read-path planner work — nothing touches `addVertex` or delete — so a
24% write regression was implausible, and two signs said noise before the re-measurement: the
UNINDEXED column barely moved on those same rows (0.98x, 0.95x) and `append node [params]` was flat
at 1.00x.

**The noise is visible once the row is isolated**: the baseline's own three readings for
`write: append node` were 132.9k / 150.9k / 174.8k — a **1.32x spread for identical code**. That is

So the rule earns another instance: **a sweep row is a screening instrument, and anything it flags

## 1337 — ✅ item 801's open question ANSWERED by in-situ ablation: the whole filtered-count gap is `inlineHolds` per vertex, and the ceiling is **2.23x** — BELOW Gremlin, not level with it — ✅ HALF TAKEN AT 1338 (1.36x shipped, gap 1.78x -> 1.29x); the rest is `propOf` + `compareTruth`, which that ablation also inlined away

Item 801 priced the TS filtered node count at ~2.1x Gremlin (re-priced ~1.71-1.85x at 929) and
diagnosed it as INSIDE `buildNodeCount`'s tally, at the per-vertex `inlineHolds` -> `satisfies`
call. It then said what to do next: **"Next step is a COMPARISON, not a change."** Item 802 tried
that by micro-benchmarking the scaffolding's parts and **refuted both halves** — recording the
reason in its own title, "a part measured dearer than the whole is an instrument result". Item 803
removed the one term it could isolate (the binding `Map` write, 1.11-1.34x).

This is the comparison 801 asked for, done the way item 1105 prescribes when a micro-benchmark
fails: ABLATE IN SITU. The tally's predicate call was replaced, behind an env flag, with the
hardcoded predicate the bench asks (`v.properties.age > 45`) and the whole query timed.

```text
  through `inlineHolds`        3.78 / 3.89 / 3.84 ms   median 3.84
  hardcoded predicate          1.72 / 1.81 / 1.72      median 1.72   2.23x
  Gremlin's twin (reference)                            median 2.16
```

**The entire gap is in that one call, and the ceiling beats Gremlin rather than matching it**:
1.72 against Gremlin's 2.16 is 1.25x the other way. So the surface is not paying for a worse data
layout or a worse scan — item 1336's decomposition already showed GQL's bare iteration and bucket
read are FASTER — it is paying for how a per-element predicate reaches its own variable.

### Why the micro-benchmarks could not see this

802's parts summed to more than the whole, so the parts could not be trusted individually. An
ablation asks a different question: not "what does this part cost" but "what does the whole cost
WITHOUT it", which is immune to the part being hard to isolate. That distinction is the reusable
result here, and it is why 801's open question survived two items.

### What is NOT yet done, stated plainly

**This item measures; it does not fix.** The fix is the re-derivation the tally's own comment
refuses — "the predicate goes through `satisfies` so the two spellings of a constrained node count
agree by construction rather than by re-deriving inline-pattern semantics here" — and that refusal
is a correctness argument, not an oversight. A shippable version has to keep `satisfies` as the
semantic source while pre-resolving WHICH arm applies at compile time, so the per-vertex call
becomes a bound closure rather than a dispatch. The architecture already has the carriers it would
bind to (`eqProps`, `cmpProps`, and items 1269/1270's `memberProps`/`nullProps`).

It also needs a differential test of the specialized closure against `inlineHolds` over a wide
input set — the shape of `side-of-vertex-equivalence.test.ts` from item 1334, where the risk was
likewise that a faster path answers differently rather than slower. Item 801 said as much: "A
change to a path whose stated reason is cross-spelling agreement deserves its own tick with the
differential fuzzers."

**OPEN, priced at 2.23x with the ceiling measured.** No code changed in this item; the ablation was
reverted and the suite re-run (3,432 pass / 0 fail).

## 1338 — ✅ SHIPPED: the filtered node count's per-element predicate is PRE-RESOLVED — **1.36x**, closing half of item 1337's ceiling; and it caused a WRONG ANSWER on the way — ✅ THE REST TAKEN AT 1339 (1.38x more; GQL now at PARITY with Gremlin on this shape)

Item 1337 ablated `inlineHolds` out of `buildNodeCount`'s tally and put the ceiling at 2.23x
(3.84 -> 1.72 ms), below Gremlin's 2.16 rather than level with it. It also showed the cost is
DISTRIBUTED — the env allocation refuted, the right-hand-side call at the noise floor — so the fix
had to replace the whole per-element path rather than remove a term.

`specializeCmpProp` does that for the one shape a filtered count almost always has: a single
ordering comparison on one property. Everything else gets `satisfies` exactly as before.

Whole-file arms (BOTH changed files swapped and asserted per arm), three rounds order-alternated,

```text

  real          4.0467    2.9840    1.36x   <- TARGET
  twoPred       5.0467    4.9091    1.03x   <- two comparisons: the single-entry guard refuses it

```

So the cross-surface gap goes **1.78x -> 1.29x** against Gremlin's 2.29. `twoPred`'s pre arm threw a
12.75 ms reading against its own 4.84, which is why these are medians.

⚠️ `vacuous` (`age > -1`) is NOT a control for this change — one comparison, therefore
specializable, therefore a second target. Item 802's own correction records what picking a reachable
control costs: it read "the control moved more than the target" when the control WAS a target.

### ⚠️ IT CAUSED A WRONG ANSWER, and the deny-list was why

The first guard listed the carriers to refuse BY HAND. `CPredicate` has **twelve**
(`props`, `where`, `eqProps`, `cmpProps`, `truthProps`, `notTruthProps`, `memberProps`,
`nullProps`, `pathProps`, `labelTests`, `truthTestProps`, `typedTests`) and my extraction found
eight, because the regex assumed two-space indentation. So `WHERE p.meta.city = 'NYC' AND p.n > 2`
specialized to the `p.n > 2` half and answered **5 instead of 2**.
`dotted-predicate-routes.test.ts` caught it.

The repair is structural: the guard now iterates the keys PRESENT on the predicate, so a carrier the
function has never heard of makes it REFUSE where a deny-list made it IGNORE. That is item 1328's
allow-list argument applied to a type's fields — and the cost of being wrong here is a wrong answer,
not a slow plan. A synthetic `someFutureCarrier` test pins it, with a control proving the refusal is
caused by that key and not by the rest of the shape.

### Teeth: 7 mutants, 4 caught, 3 survivors whose unreachability is MEASURED

```text
  unknown-carrier-ignored     CAUGHT   2 fail   re-introduces the exact pathProps wrong answer
  single-entry-guard-dropped  CAUGHT   3 fail   two comparisons collapse to the first
  unknown-settles-as-true     CAUGHT  11 fail   UNKNOWN passes instead of dropping the row (259)
  specializer-unwired         SURVIVED          answer-equivalent: falls back to `satisfies`
  allow-list-becomes-deny     SURVIVED          the NON-ARRAY branch
  bindvar-check-dropped       SURVIVED          the bindVar branch
  both-guards-dropped         SURVIVED          both at once
```

⚠️ `specializer-unwired`'s FIRST spelling was `TYPE-INVALID` — it never compiled, so the survivor I
had declared "expected" was never a live mutation. Re-spelled so it typechecks.

**TWO WRONG EXPLANATIONS BEFORE THE RIGHT ONE, and the third is measured:**

1. _"The guards mask each other"_ — refuted: `both-guards-dropped` also survived.
2. _"A surviving `where` never reaches this tally"_ — refuted: a `throw` on that alone fired in **28
   tests**.
3. **What is true:** the CONJUNCTION those mutants need — one pred, a surviving `where`, AND exactly
   one `cmpProps` — occurs in NONE of the 3,460 tests, including cases written specifically to
   produce it (`n.n > 2 AND n.n * 1 > 2`). A predicate that does not fully lift makes the count
   shortcut decline EARLIER, so `buildNodeCount` never sees that combination. Verified by narrowing
   the throw to exactly that conjunction and running the whole suite clean.

So the allow-list's ARRAY branch is live and tested (two mutants die on it); the non-array and
`bindVar` branches are unreachable FROM THIS CALLER. They stay as defence in depth, because the
invariant is not global: a second `bindVar` construction site (the two-hop middle gate) sets it
unconditionally, so a predicate CAN carry one with every inspected carrier empty. The cost is one
comparison per QUERY.

Without the narrowed probe the choice was between claiming coverage I did not have and deleting
guards whose unreachability I had only assumed. Item 1330 is the precedent for checking.

### The differential test, and a vacuity it caught

`specialized-pred.test.ts` — 28 cases. The closure is compared against `satisfies` PER ELEMENT over
300 vertices rather than on a total, because two vertices can differ in opposite directions and
still sum equal. The fixture carries absences, a stored null, mixed types and a nested map, since
the differential is about what `compareTruth` does with each.

⚠️ One case I wrote was VACUOUS: `n.age > 20 AND n.n * 1 > 2` on a fixture with no `age`, so the
predicate was UNKNOWN everywhere, the count was 0, and the agreement with the row form was FREE. The
non-zero assertion caught it — which is why item 1330 put one there.

### ⚠️ `compareTruth`'s HEADER REFUTES A NEIGHBOURING LEVER, and the difference is the whole item

That header records adding `if (op !== '=' && … typeof lv === 'number' …) return fn(lv, rv)` INSIDE

process, three alternated rounds, twice over — ending **"Do not re-derive it."**

This is not that change. That one short-circuits WITHIN the function and still pays the call; this
one removes the call at the site. Both results stand, and read as a blanket refusal the header would
have closed this target. Same shape as item 1334, where `twoHopSide`'s "measured flat" was true for
its own loop and not for the one next door — **a refutation is scoped to the loop it was measured
in.**

The header also supplies the semantics rather than my re-deriving them: it states the numeric arm is
"byte-identical, NaN included", because `isNullish` is null/undefined only so a NaN is not nullish,
a number is not a temporal, and `typeof lv === typeof rv === 'number'` IS its own `orderable` test.
The closure calls the same `COMPARE[op]` that header passes, so no operator is rewritten, and any
non-number pair falls through to `compareTruth` untouched.

Items 1338/1339 specialized `cmpProps` (ordering). `WHERE n.tag = 't3'` lifts into `eqProps`, so it
was refused and still paid the full `satisfies` dispatch per element. `specializeCmpProp` becomes
`specializeSingleProp` and answers either carrier, one at a time.

Measured UNINDEXED at 200,000 vertices, so the scan is 200,000 rather than a 2,222-row seek:

```text
  shape        before      after    ratio    Gremlin
  eqReal        4.4478     3.8013   1.17x     3.4550
  eqParam       4.4292     3.6713   1.21x     3.5404
  real (ctl)    2.2044     2.2906   0.96x       —      <- 1339's arm, unchanged
```

so the equality gap goes **1.29x -> 1.10x**. The `seek-count` row the parity probe still flags at
2.02x is this same shape INDEXED, where the seek returns 2,222 of 200,000 and the per-element
dispatch has far less to amortize — 0.087 ms absolute, the smallest gap in the field.

### THE NULL REJECTION IS THE WHOLE RISK, and it is replicated rather than inherited

`propOf` returns `null` for an ABSENT key and for a STORED null alike, so `structuralEq` alone gives
the INLINE reading (`{k: null}` matches both) where a clause `=` must give the EXPRESSION one and
match neither — item 210's "route two". `satisfies`'s own `eqProps` loop rejects a null right-hand
side for exactly that reason, and so does this arm.

`null-rejection-dropped` is CAUGHT in 6 tests across three files. The test that pins it passes a
**null parameter**: it must match nothing through `=` while the inline spelling still matches stored
nulls — invisible to any test that never passes one.

### Teeth: 5 mutants, 3 caught, 2 survivors whose unreachability is MEASURED

```text
  null-rejection-dropped    CAUGHT   6 fail
  eq-single-entry-dropped   CAUGHT
  both-carriers-admitted    CAUGHT   2 fail   <- a failure mode this item CREATED
  undefined-not-rejected    SURVIVED
  reference-equality        SURVIVED
```

`both-carriers-admitted` deserves its own note: handling a SECOND carrier created the possibility of
`eqProps` and `cmpProps` both populated collapsing to whichever came last. That mutant did not exist
when only one carrier was specialized, so it could not inherit 1338's coverage.

**The two survivors are explained by a measured input contract, not by guessing.** Making the closure
THROW on an `undefined` right-hand side, and again on a non-scalar one, left all 3,477 tests green —
so only SCALARS reach this arm:

- `undefined`-rejection is unreachable today. Kept at one comparison, because nothing ENFORCES that
  contract and an unbound param arriving here would otherwise compare structurally.
- `structuralEq` versus JS `===` is indistinguishable today: the two agree on every scalar (NaN
  false both ways, ±0 true both ways). `structuralEq` stays because it is the function `satisfies`
  uses, so the day a list DOES lift into `eqProps` this arm is already right rather than silently
  wrong.

Defence in depth over an unenforced contract is a different thing from dead code, which is why
neither was deleted — the distinction item 1330 and item 1338 both turned on.

### ⚠️ AND A TEST OF MINE CLAIMED COVERAGE IT DID NOT HAVE

I added "a LIST value still matches a stored list structurally" believing it covered `structuralEq`
in the fast arm. `reference-equality` SURVIVED with it green, and the non-scalar throw showed why: a
list literal never lifts into `eqProps`, so no list reaches that closure at all. The test exercises
the GENERAL path — worth having, not what its comment implied — and now says so.

That is the third vacuous test of mine mutation has caught this session (items 1329, 1338, 1340).
Each time the fix was to state what the test actually covers rather than to delete it, and each time
the only thing that found it was a mutant.

## 1341 — ⚠️ CORRECTING ITEM 1334: the box read is **1.23x SLOWER on a cold graph**, the prior refutation I never cited was RIGHT, and the trade pays back on the SECOND query

Item 1334 shipped the adjacency-box read at 1.92x and stated "cold improves too (1.13-1.19x), so
there is no first-query cost traded away". **That claim was wrong**, and `CLOSED.md` already held the
refutation I failed to find:

> "giving the product the cached per-vertex adjacency box ... is ALREADY REFUTED at the site:
> `sideOfVertex` exists for exactly that ... **item 355 measured it, and the box is a MEMO, so first
> touch is 1.21x WORSE** (the same hash plus the memo write) while warm is 1.35x better. The two-hop
> product visits each middle exactly ONCE per query, so cold is all it would ever get."

I cited `twoHopSide`'s weaker "measured flat" header instead and reasoned around that. This is the
failure CLAUDE.md names — "searched something first and searched the wrong store" — committed by the
same session that had already been saved from it four times.

### What was wrong, and what was right

**WRONG: item 1334's cold evidence.** It quoted the FIRST OF FOURTEEN REPS (79-97 ms against a 23 ms
steady state) as the cold case. That number is dominated by JIT tiering, not by the memo write, so it
never isolated a cold penalty and could not have refuted one. `cold-box-memo-probe.ts` isolates it
properly: warm the JIT on a throwaway graph, then time ONE query against a FRESH one.

```text
  arm        pre (id hash)    post (box)    ratio
  cold             48.2756       59.5181    0.81x   post SLOWER by 1.23x
  warm             49.7718       27.8883    1.78x   post FASTER
```

**The instrument validates itself**: the PRE arm reads cold 48.28 against warm 49.77 — no
distinction, because an id hash has no memo to be cold. Only POST has a gap, so the gap IS the memo.

**RIGHT: the 1.21x.** Measured 1.23x. Item 355's number was accurate and this entry says so.

**STILL WRONG in the refutation: its premise.** "The two-hop product visits each middle exactly ONCE
per query, so cold is all it would ever get" treats the memo as per-query. It is not:
`Vertex.adjFrom` memoizes on the VERTEX and survives until an adjacency write clears it, so only the
FIRST query on a graph is cold. That is a reading of the code, and the 1.78x warm column is the
measurement of it.

### The trade, stated as a break-even rather than a ratio

Serving n queries against one graph: `48.28n` against `59.52 + 27.89(n - 1)`. They cross at
**n ≈ 1.55**, so the box read LOSES the first query and WINS from the second onward. A graph serving
two queries is already ahead (96.6 against 87.4 ms).

**KEPT, deliberately.** The serving case is repeated queries on a long-lived graph — which is what
`bench:usage` measures and where item 1336 recorded `read: 2-hop recommendation` at 1.25x. A
one-shot query against a freshly loaded graph is now 1.23x slower and that is the cost. Anyone whose
workload is load-then-single-query should know it; the alternative would be populating the boxes at
load time, which is a storage change and not attempted here.

⚠️ **The honest reading of item 1334's 1.92x is "warm", not "unqualified"** — its heading is amended
to say so.

### Verification

No code changed in this item; the arms were swapped for measurement and POST restored (box-read=1).
`cold-box-memo-probe.ts` is kept, with a guard that exits non-zero if the JIT warmup never ran —
without it a "cold" arm that skipped warmup would read as a penalty that is really tiering.

### Item 1345 — the per-endpoint extremum fold gets a DEGREE gate: DONE, 1.32x at degree 1

- **CLOSES item 1344.** `endpointFoldBeatsRowWalk(edgeCount, vertexCount)` is a second run-time
  admission beside the vacuity test, declining the fold below 2 edges per vertex. Crossover measured
  at N=200,000 over degrees 1-5: the fold is FLAT (86.9-89.3 ms, O(candidate endpoints), reads no
  edge) while the walk scales with edges, so they cross at degree 2 — admitted AT 2 because that row
  is a tie. A/B: **deg1 87.49 -> 66.37, 1.32x, ranges disjoint**; deg5 control 0.97x (overlapping,
  flat — the gate is one comparison per QUERY); no-hop null control flat. The 1.32x exceeds 1344's

  used, and EXACT on a single-edge-type one-label graph). Average degree 10 over ten types reads 10
  where the wanted type's is 1 (admits where it loses); a selective far label puts true candidates
  far below `vertexCount` (declines where it would win). Narrowing wants a per-type count.

the work, the next item does the work, and nothing makes that item revisit its predecessor's

correcting for at 1344.

### Why this matters more than the four headings

A reader scanning for work takes the biggest number. Three times in two ticks that number was
already banked, and the only reason no cycle was burnt is that verifying at the SOURCE is cheap —
one `grep` for "item NNNN's target" plus the next heading. Item 1301 measured the same thing at
scale: 40 of 265 lines corrected, 35 advertising done work. **Treat any `PRICED` heading as a claim
to check, not a target to take.**

### Item 1356 — the TS multi-hop field reduces to ONE root cause, and ~~the only lever left is a DESIGN DECISION~~ ~~and the autonomous-local field is exhausted~~ (the exhaustion claim is WRONG — see 1358; the ordinal fork is DECLINED at 1358. ⚠️ AND "the only lever left" is over-broad: item 1614 took **2.99x/3.12x** on the two-hop YIELDING shapes, which this item's field never covered because every multi-hop row in the bench and the profile corpus ends in `count()`)

Items 1354 and 1355 cleared the priced list of stale headings, leaving 1152 as the one genuinely
open TS-side entry. Reading it alongside 1104/1105 shows they are not three targets but one.

**The single root cause: TS has no dense vertex ordinal.** Every multi-hop walk interns the far
vertex through a `Map<Vertex, number>.get` per edge touched.

> ⚠️ **1358 "CORRECTED" THIS AND WAS ITSELF WRONG — see 1359.** The phrasing above is RIGHT for the
> row 1152 and 1356 are about. **There are TWO slot maps, one per engine, and they differ:**
> `packages/gremlin/src/executor/count-shortcut.ts:1741` (`SlotSweep.slotOf`) is `Map<Vertex, number>`
> keyed on the VERTEX OBJECT, and that is `expandSlot`'s `slotOf.get(w)` — the Gremlin 3-hop row,
> which is the 55.9x this entry cites; `packages/gql/src/executor/shortcuts.ts` is
> `Map<string, number>` keyed on the edge's `farId` STRING. Both are per-query dense indexes sized to
> the TOUCHED set. Item 1358 read only the GQL file and generalised across engines.

- **1105** ablated it: the per-edge `Map.get` is **24% of the TS sweep, ~46 ns an edge** (and item
  1104's micro UNDERSTATED it at ~28 ns, the usual direction for a probe whose working set is
  smaller than the engine's).
- **1152** traced the same cost to the 3-hop count's **55.9x**, which is still the largest row in
  `bench:gremlin` (362.9 ms today), and confirmed by ablation that item 1110's memo is load-bearing
  (1.53x / 2.04x) — so the residual is specifically the **COLD** first touch of each slot, which no
  memo can reach.
- Native pays none of it: its vertices ARE dense `u32` ids, so interning is identity.

### Both of item 1105's named levers are resolved, so nothing local remains

1. **~24%, "pass 1 records an `Int32Array` of neighbour slots so passes 2-3 skip the lookup"** —
   **this is item 1110's memo, and it is BUILT.** 1152's ablation is what confirms it carries
   1.53-2.04x. What it cannot do is help a slot's first expansion, which is the residual.
2. **~5.9%, split the loop body per direction** — open, and a **bad trade**: it is below the ~10%
   threshold this repo requires a dedicated harness for, in a walk where items 159, 1033 and 1091
   each measured unrelated shapes paying for changes to it — 1091 at **1.54x on an UNREACHABLE
   control**. `pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` is the same lesson one function over.

Also already refuted, so it is not a third way out: keying the intern on the vertex's `id` STRING
instead. This file records that both string-map shapes "cost the lookup this row cannot afford. A
route that wins has to carry a dense ordinal on the EDGE, which is the CSR by another name."

### What is actually left, stated as the decision it is

Closing this means **giving `Vertex` an internal dense slot/ordinal**, or a CSR-equivalent that
carries one on the edge. That is cross-cutting, touches a USER-VISIBLE object, and bears directly on
the one invariant this project's standing instruction names explicitly — O(1) access to a vertex or
edge by id. 1152 already called it "a design decision not a local optimization", and this item
agrees after checking the alternatives rather than by deferring to it.

~~**So the autonomous-local field is exhausted, and that is a finding rather than a stopping excuse.**~~
**WRONG, retracted at 1358.** What was exhausted is the LIST this item was reading — the priced/open
headings — and that was generalised to the implementation. Item 1358 found the largest frame in three of
five profiled GQL shapes sitting in code with zero or near-zero mentions, and the Gremlin runtime path
had never been screened at all. The sentence should have read "the priced list is exhausted".
The session's own evidence for it: items 1342-1355 took every local lever that measured (1345's
degree gate 1.32x, 1347's null carrier 1.45x, 1349's `within` closure 3.44-3.90x, 1350's membership
carrier 1.32-1.48x, 1352's `NOT (…)` lift 2.8x) and every remaining candidate was either already
built, refuted, or this one design fork.

### Gates

Docs only; no code changed. `oxfmt --check` 0.

### Item 1357 — what a dense vertex ordinal would cost WRITES: 0% on realistic shapes, <=2.4% worst case; DELETES are the real question and are NOT measured

Item 1356 left one lever: giving `Vertex` an internal dense slot. The first thing to know is the
write-side penalty, so it was measured rather than estimated.

### Where writes would pay, structurally

- **`addVertex`** — one counter read-increment, one field write. `Vertex` already carries six
  private fields (`#id`, `#graph`, `#box`, `#lbox`, `#adjFrom`, `#adjTo`), so `#slot` adds nothing
  to the public surface, and the constructor is four assignments. Around it `addVertex` already pays
  `validateElementNames`, an id lookup, three constraint gates, map inserts, label indexing, events
  and undo recording.
- **`addEdge`** — nothing; edges get no ordinal in this design.
- **DELETES** — the real cost, and a DESIGN sub-decision rather than a throughput one: tombstones
  (free delete, ordinal space grows without bound and slot-indexed arrays go sparse), a free list
  (O(1), but an ordinal is recycled onto a different vertex so anything cached by slot needs
  invalidation), or compaction (O(n), unacceptable). **NOT MEASURED HERE.**

### The add-path penalty, measured

Prototype: `public vtxSeq = 0` on `Graph`, `#slot` on `Vertex` assigned in the constructor, plus a
getter so the field cannot be dead-code eliminated. Three order-alternated rounds, 14 reps each
dropping the first 3, median, one shape per process:

| arm                                                | N       | pre ms | post ms | penalty   |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------ | ------- | --------- |
| `bare` — one label, no properties (thinnest write) | 200,000 | 198.66 | 203.46  | **+2.4%** |
| `props` — three properties (real ingest shape)     | 200,000 | 219.46 | 219.30  | **-0.1%** |
| `withEdges` — vertices + 5 edges each              | 50,000  | 531.91 | 541.47  | **+1.8%** |

**All three are at or under this repo's ~10% "needs its own harness" threshold**, and `props` — the
shape ingest actually has — is indistinguishable from zero. The `bare` arm's +2.4% is the worst case
by construction (a per-vertex constant is the largest FRACTION of the thinnest write) and is partly
one outlier rep: its POST series is 256.88 / 200.31 / 203.46 against a PRE of 198.66 / 196.72 /
199.01, so the ranges very nearly overlap.

⚠️ **Do not quote the ns/vertex column.** It reads 24.0 ns for `bare` and **-0.8 ns** for `props` —
a negative cost is the tell that these are differences of noisy totals, not a per-vertex
measurement. A counter increment and a field write cannot cost 24 ns. The PERCENTAGES are the
result; the per-vertex derivation is not.

### ⚠️ `bench:usage` CANNOT answer this question, and that is worth recording

It was the obvious instrument and it is unusable here. Between two builds differing by one integer
field it moved `read: point lookup` **+26%** and `write: 100 updates in one statement` **-34%** —
rows the change cannot reach by anything like that much. Its write rows are ops/sec over 250 ms
batches, best of 3, and that variance swamps a 2% effect. A per-row question needs a per-row
instrument: `packages/native/vertex-ordinal-write-probe.ts`.

### 🛑 TWO harness faults, and the second nearly produced a confidently wrong answer

1. **The `withEdges` arm was OOM-KILLED** (exit -9) at N=200,000 x 14 reps — fourteen 1,000,000-edge
   graphs against the 16G cap. The cap did its job; the probe was too heavy. Fixed with per-arm
   sizing (50,000 x 8), which still carries 250,000 edges — ample for an arm whose only purpose is
   dilution.
2. **The arm assertion REFUSED a pristine-vs-pristine run.** The previous run's `finally` had
   restored pristine, so copying "the current tree" into the POST slot made POST pristine. Without
   the assertion this would have measured identical code twice and reported a **0% write penalty** —
   CLAUDE.md's named trap ("the 'after' reading is then the 'before' code — a null that looks like a
   result"), and the worst possible failure for a question specifically about write cost. The script
   now CONSTRUCTS post from pristine by applying the patch with each anchor asserted unique, so the
   drift is impossible rather than merely detected.

### Status

The prototype is REVERTED; only the probe is kept. The add-path cost is answered; the delete
strategy is not, and that is the half that needs a decision.

### Item 1358 — item 921's UNPRICED-frame screen was laundering "could not check" into "already recorded", and it was hiding the LARGEST frame in three of five shapes

The user challenged item 1356's "the autonomous-local field is exhausted" directly — _"Have you really
exhausted the entire optimization of the typescript implementation? This feels hard to believe."_ The
challenge was correct, and the specific way it was correct is worth more than the targets it turned up.

**First, the honest part: re-running a profile was not a new idea.** Item 919 established that a CPU
profile finds what hand-placed timers cannot, and item 921 generalised that into a target GENERATOR
(`runtime-profile-probe.mjs` + `runtime-profile-analyze.mjs`) and ran it over five GQL shapes, reporting
a **negative**: "not one of the five profiles has an unpriced frame above 2%... the next TS win is
unlikely to come from profiling the runtime path." So "profile first" was already repo practice, and
pitching it as the unexplored method was partly the re-derivation CLAUDE.md warns about.

**What was actually wrong is the screen's verdict logic.** Item 921 found a false-POSITIVE class — V8
synthesises names for anonymous closures (`variable.variable`, `RegExp: <pattern>`), those strings can
never appear in a document, so "ZERO mentions" was meaningless for them and the screen "will manufacture
a target every time it runs". It fixed that by reporting them `n/a`. That was right, and it
**over-corrected into a false NEGATIVE**: `n/a` means _could not check_, and the verdict line then printed
"every hot frame is already recorded". Unknown had been laundered into checked.

The cost of that wording, measured by re-running the unchanged instrument on today's engine:

| shape        | largest frame                  | share     | old screen said |
| ------------ | ------------------------------ | --------- | --------------- |
| `sortedpage` | `(anonymous) @ index.mjs:8648` | **24.8%** | `n/a`           |
| `grouped`    | `(anonymous) @ index.mjs:8843` | **41.9%** | `n/a`           |
| `point`      | `(anonymous) @ index.mjs:8784` | **18.0%** | `n/a`           |

**The largest frame in three of the five shapes was invisible to the screen that declared the field
clean.** And the frames are not obscure: V8 reports such a closure at its ENCLOSING declaration's line,
because the hot code is the `return (graph, params) => {...}` of a compile-time builder. The nearest
`const <name> =` at or above that line names it, and THAT name is a real identifier a document can
mention. So the fix is mechanical: resolve the enclosing declaration, cross-check that, and report what
is still unnameable in its own bucket rather than folding it into the all-clear.

### What the screen reports after the fix

Shape wall-clock first, 2,000 reps each over one 20,000-node / 20,000-edge fixture, one shape per process
(item 762): `control` 8.7 ms, `grouped` 503.9, `hopfilter` 547.5, `point` 817.3, **`sortedpage` 1734.0**.
The `ORDER BY … LIMIT` shape is 2-3x every other shape and nobody had profiled it since 921.

- **`topKNodeWalk` — 463.2 ms, 24.8% of `sortedpage`, ZERO mentions in either store.** The returned
  closure of the `ORDER BY`+`LIMIT` node-scan shortcut. A second frame in the same builder (its `project`
  closure) adds 44.4 ms / 2.4%. Genuinely unpriced.
- **`beatsRoot` — 40.1 ms, 2.2% of `sortedpage`, ZERO mentions.** The bounded-top-k heap's admission
  test. Worth recording that the top-k path is NOT a full sort then slice: `boundedTopKeyed` and
  `heapBeatsSort` are both there and both chosen at run time.
- **`detectGroupedNodeCount`'s closure — 265.0 ms, 41.9% of `grouped`, but SEVEN mentions.** Not
  formally unpriced, and that exposes the screen's second limitation: its signal is binary (ZERO vs
  mentioned), so a frame can be 41.9% of its shape and seven passing references are enough to retire it.
  **"Has mentions" is not "is optimized."** The `GROUP BY` path is 66% of its shape across this closure
  and `bump` (153.8 ms, 24.3%) and has never had a tick of its own.

After the fix the residual NOT-CHECKABLE bucket over 2% is only `(garbage collector)`, `(idle)`, Node's
`compileSourceTextModule` loader, and `RegExp: [\uD800-\uDBFF]` (item 921's own `compareCodePoints`
find) — none of which is engine code. That is the honest floor, and it is a much smaller claim than the
one the screen used to make.

### TWO faults in my own fix, both caught only because the frames it was built for were still printed

1. **The enclosing-declaration pass was a NO-OP on its first run.** Node reports frame URLs as
   `file:///abs/path`; the guard required a leading `/`, so every lookup returned `undefined` and the
   output was byte-identical to before. It was caught only because the three frames the pass exists for
   were still listed as NOT CHECKABLE — i.e. by having an expected occurrence to check against, which is
   the same discipline as asserting an A/B arm IS the code it claims.
2. **The backward scan misattributed accessor frames.** `get properties` is a class member, so the scan
   walked out of the class body and landed on `WIDE_BAG$1`, an unrelated bag of keys, reporting it as an
   unpriced 2-3% frame in FOUR of the five shapes. An accessor frame already carries a checkable
   identifier — the property — so it is now matched directly and never reaches the scan. A screen that
   invents a plausible name is worse than one that admits `n/a`, which is item 921's lesson arriving a
   second time from the opposite direction.

### The third blind spot, NOT fixed here and squarely in scope

**The screen is GQL-only.** `runtime-profile-probe.mjs` imports `@lenke/core` and `@lenke/gql` and
contains zero references to Gremlin, so the Gremlin runtime path has never been through an unpriced-frame
screen at all — despite the standing instruction covering both surfaces and despite `bench:gremlin`'s
3-hop count being the largest row in either suite. Next tick.

### Corrections to earlier entries, per the heading rule

- **Item 1356's "the autonomous-local field is exhausted"** was true of the LIST it was reading — the
  priced/open headings — and was generalised to the implementation, which the evidence above refutes.
  The scope of items 1342-1357 is itself the tell: nearly all of them are predicate evaluation (four
  `CPredicate` carriers, the `NOT (…)` lift, Gremlin `within`) plus hop-shortcut routing. Aggregation,
  `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT`, projection, the cold parse/plan path, the Gremlin step library beyond `has`, path
  and quantifier machinery, property-access floor, and serialization were never instrumented in that
  run. The structural cause: every one of those items started from an audit heading or an existing bench
  row, so **a cost that is not already a row was unreachable by the method**.
- ~~**Item 1356's `Map<Vertex, number>`** (and item 1152's same phrasing) is inaccurate.~~
  **THIS CORRECTION IS ITSELF WRONG — RETRACTED at 1359.** There are TWO slot maps, one per engine:
  Gremlin's `SlotSweep.slotOf` IS `Map<Vertex, number>` keyed on the vertex object
  (`count-shortcut.ts:1741`, `expandSlot`'s `slotOf.get(w)`), and that is the row 1152/1356 cite;
  GQL's `shortcuts.ts` is `Map<string, number>` keyed on `farId`. I read only the GQL file and
  generalised across engines, "correcting" a true statement. Both are per-query dense indexes sized
  to the touched set, so that half of the observation holds for both.
- **The dense-vertex-ordinal fork (1356/1357) is DECLINED**, on the user's reasoning rather than mine: a
  global ordinal buys one field read in exchange for a durable second structure — ordinal space, a free
  list, `vertexBySlot`, |V|-sized buffers — that must stay aligned with `verticesById` across every add,
  remove and reload, forever. I had argued it on memory cost; the alignment burden is the stronger
  objection and it is decisive. Recorded separately: the variant that avoids it entirely is per-Vertex
  query-scoped scratch (`#qgen`/`#qslot` + a per-walk generation counter), which keeps slots per-query
  and dense over the touched set, needs no delete strategy, and leaves summation order unchanged — gated
  on proving no two live walks share a generation counter (nested `CALL`, subqueries,
  `primedEndpointExtremum` folding while a sweep is live). NOT built, NOT measured.

### Item 1358's `Map<Vertex, number>` correction is RETRACTED: there are TWO slot maps

Item 1358 declared items 1152/1356's `Map<Vertex, number>` phrasing inaccurate and "corrected" it to
`Map<string, number>` keyed on `farId`. **That correction is wrong, and it corrected a true
statement.** The two engines use different keys:

| engine  | file                                          | type                  | key                |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------ |
| Gremlin | `gremlin/src/executor/count-shortcut.ts:1741` | `Map<Vertex, number>` | the VERTEX object  |
| GQL     | `gql/src/executor/shortcuts.ts`               | `Map<string, number>` | the edge's `farId` |

Items 1152 and 1356 cite the **55.9x Gremlin 3-hop row**, whose walk is `expandSlot` — so
`Map<Vertex, number>` was correct there all along. I had read only `shortcuts.ts` and generalised
across engines. The half of the observation that does hold for both: the slot space is a **per-query**
dense index assigned lazily, sized to the TOUCHED set, not to |V|.

**The lesson is narrower than "verify before correcting" and worth stating as the rule it is:** a
claim about "the TS engine" can be true of one surface and false of the other, because GQL and
Gremlin are separate implementations that share only `@lenke/core`. 1358 is the second time this
session that a confident correction was the thing needing correcting — and both times the error was
generalising from the one file I had open.

   whose property cannot be searched now reports `n/a`. Same failure as 1358's `get properties`, one
   guard further in.
2. **The mention count was a SUBSTRING search.** `pick` read 202 where only 53 are the identifier
   (the rest are "picked", "picking"). Now word-boundary matched. **Measured before changing it,
   because the obvious generalisation is wrong:** `values` reads 1118 substring / 1070 word-bound /

   re-ranks common-word frames and **overturned none of item 1358's conclusions** — which is why it

Also worth recording as a property of the instrument, not a bug: **writing an item about a frame
retires it from the screen.** `topKNodeWalk` had ZERO mentions when 1358 flagged it and has one now —
1358's own entry. The ZERO signal is one-shot, so a flagged frame must be either taken or explicitly

### Item 1360 — the WRITE path screened for the first time: ~~`drainMutations` is the only unpriced engine frame, its lever PRICED at 3.2% and DECLINED, and O(1)-by-id confirmed at 70.9 ns~~ **BOTH NUMBERS WERE THE INSTRUMENT (corrected at 1396): the probe built its fixture inside the timed call and had no windowing. Re-screened, `drainMutations` does not appear AT ALL, and by-id reads 19 ns — matching item 1395's independent ~18 ns**

Items 1358 and 1359 screened both query surfaces. Neither probe touches the write path, and the GQL
`control` profile was the hint: with `RETURN 1` as the query its hottest engine frames are all ingest
(`indexEdgeLabel`, `commitElementLabels`, `insertEdge`, `pushTokens`), because the fixture build is
most of that process. Built `runtime-profile-write-probe.mjs` — six shapes, one per process, 20,000
elements, under the cgroup cap (item 1357's arm was OOM-killed for exactly this).

```text
  addVertexBare    50 reps    890.8 ms     1.43 us a vertex
  addVertexProps   45 reps    933.7 ms     1.04 us a vertex (1 label + 3 keys)
  addEdgeOnly       7 reps   1589.1 ms    ~2.0  us an edge
  setProps         43 reps    912.2 ms
  removeVertices   38 reps    871.4 ms
  pointLookups     37 reps   1193.1 ms    7,400,000 lookups
```

### O(1)-BY-ID, which the standing instruction names explicitly, confirmed at the FRAME level

`pointLookups` puts `getVertexById` at **42.7%, 524.6 ms over 7,400,000 lookups = 70.9 ns each**, flat
in graph size. Previously this was asserted from `bench:usage`'s `read: point lookup` row (977.8k
ops/sec); this is the first time it has been read off a profile of the function itself. `Graph`'s
`vertexCount`/`edgeCount` remain O(1) `Map.size` getters. Nothing in this session's work touches it.

### THE ONE UNPRICED FRAME, and its lever is a measured TRADE rather than a win

`drainMutations @ Graph.ts:1023` — **ZERO mentions, and hot in three of six shapes**: `addVertexProps`
4.0%, `removeVertices` 3.7%, `setProps` 3.0%. Reading it shows a real inefficiency. `pushTokens`
appends one entry **per token per write with duplicates kept**, so
`addVertex({labels:['P'], properties:{k,s,n}})` x 20,000 puts **80,000 entries in `pendingTokens` of
which 4 are distinct**, and the drain walks all 80,000 doing `Map.get`+`Map.set` on four keys to land
on `{P:20000, k:20000, s:20000, n:20000}`. The array also grows by doubling to 131,072 slots, which
is part of the GC bucket below.

The transform is sound: tally `Map<string, number>` at push time, add each distinct count once. The
epoch numbers are identical (a sum is a sum, and the counters are independent so order is free).
Measured in `token-drain-probe.mjs`, 14 reps, first 3 dropped, median, order alternated, with an
equivalence check on both distributions before timing either:

**FIVE PROCESSES, not one** — and the first single-process reading was an OUTLIER that nearly went
into this entry as the result. It put the array arm at 1.196 ms and reported **2.23x**, where the
stable value is ~0.90 ms. The in-process estimator (14 reps, drop 3, median, order alternated) was
already correct and still could not see it, which is precisely why CLAUDE.md says to repeat the
PROCESS and print the DISTRIBUTION rather than a summary of one.

| distribution               | array (today) | count map | ratio (median of 5) |
| -------------------------- | ------------- | --------- | ------------------- |
| narrow — 4 distinct (real) | ~0.90 ms      | ~0.55 ms  | **1.68x FASTER**    |
| wide — all 80,000 distinct | ~8.3 ms       | ~11.8 ms  | **1.41x SLOWER**    |

```text
  ratio array/map, one per process
  narrow   1.61  1.68  1.71  1.65  1.69
  wide     0.71  0.73  0.68  0.67  0.74
```

**DECLINED.** 0.35 ms saved per 20,000 writes is **17.5 ns a write against a ~1.04 us write — 1.7%**,
about half the 4.0% the profile attributes to the frame, and well under the ~10% this repo requires a
dedicated harness for. Against that it costs **1.41x on wide property bags**, and wide bags are a real
workload here (`ts-set-is-o-width`, and the graph-ML substrate's wide-feature `SET`). A hybrid that
switched structures on the observed duplicate ratio could keep both, and that is complexity for 1.7%.
Same disposition and same reasoning as item 921's surrogate-guard hoist (~1.07x, sound, declined).

Recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it: the inefficiency is REAL and the arithmetic is
`O(writes)` where `O(distinct)` would do — it is the ADVERSARIAL case and the effect size that kill
it, not the premise.

### What the write path is actually made of, which is the portable result

Nothing else is unpriced, and the shape of the cost is consistent across all six:

```text
  w-addEdgeOnly (1635 ms)                    w-addVertexProps
    416.1  25.4%  48 mentions  indexEdgeLabel      GC              18.6%
    206.8  12.6%  16 mentions  getEdgeById         drainMutations   4.0%
    202.5  12.4%  n/a          (garbage collector)
    145.4   8.9%   7 mentions  #commitNormalized
    141.5   8.7%   7 mentions  commitElementLabels
```

**`(garbage collector)` is 12.4-20.7% of EVERY write shape** — the single largest bucket after the top
function, and **structurally invisible to this screen**, because a synthesized frame name can never
appear in a document so it is always `n/a`. That is not a new finding so much as independent
confirmation of `ts-ingest-is-constant-factor`'s conclusion (the 4x native gap is JSON.parse + alloc +
freeze, with `addEdge` ~85% of it, and `addVertex` WITHDRAWN as a target at item 312 at 7.4%). The
useful part is the direction it points: **the write path's remaining headroom is allocation, not
arithmetic**, so the instrument for it is an allocation profile (~~`--heap-prof`~~), not a CPU one. Not run
here; named as the next instrument rather than guessed at.

### An instrument defect this run exposed: the screen was flagging ITS OWN probe

`addEdgeOnly`, `setProps` and `removeVertices` were all reported as top unpriced frames. They are the
probe's fixture builders — genuinely hot, and of course absent from the audit, so they report every
run. Frames from a `*-probe.mjs`/`*-probe.ts` file are now excluded. The GQL probe's `build` escaped
notice for two items only because the word "build" happens to appear 841 times in the documents, which
is luck rather than a guard.

That is the FOURTH defect in this screen found by pointing it at a new surface (1358: `n/a` laundering
and the `file://` no-op; 1359: short accessor properties and substring counting). The pattern is worth
naming: **a cross-checking screen is only as good as the surfaces it has been run against, and each
new surface has found a fresh way for it to lie.** Its negatives are worth proportionately less than
its positives until the next surface has been tried.

### Item 1361 — `--heap-prof` is UNUSABLE for this question (calibrated: 0.7 MiB reported for 128 MiB allocated), item 1360's GC figure is CONFIRMED by a second instrument, and the cost is 93% MINOR scavenge

Item 1360 ended by naming the sampling heap profiler as the instrument for the write path's
12.4-20.7% `(garbage collector)` share, since a CPU profile cannot attribute a synthesized frame with
no source location. **That recommendation was wrong, and this item retracts it.**

### The instrument does not measure what it is for, proved before any number from it was used

The first two runs reported **1.7-1.9 MiB total allocated for a process that creates 200,000 vertices
and 300,000 edges**, dominated by Node's module loader, and dropping the sampling interval 16x
(16384 -> 1024 bytes) did not raise the total at all. One of those two facts had to be the instrument
lying, so it was calibrated against a known quantity in `heap-prof-calibrate.mjs` — 128 MiB allocated
in ~64-byte objects through ONE named function `burn`, in a retained arm and a garbage arm:

```text
  cal-retained.heapprofile   0.7 MiB reported   (128 MiB allocated, `burn` not in the top 18 frames)
  cal-garbage.heapprofile    0.7 MiB reported   (128 MiB allocated, `burn` not in the top 18 frames)
```

**0.5% of the bytes, and the allocating function never named**, identically in both arms — so it is
not a live-versus-garbage artifact either. `node --heap-prof` as invoked here cannot answer "where
does this process allocate". The analyzer built for it (`runtime-heap-analyze.mjs`) is kept, because
the format reading is correct and the defect is upstream of it, but **nothing should be concluded from
it until someone establishes a configuration that passes the calibration.** Same discipline as
proving a mutation harness kills before trusting it with a mutant — and this is the first time in
this session that the discipline caught an instrument that was wholly unfit rather than subtly biased.

### The instrument that DOES work, and it confirms item 1360 rather than refuting it

`PerformanceObserver` on `'gc'` entries measures the quantity directly: GC pauses with duration and
kind. Built as `gc-cost-probe.mjs`. For `addVertexProps` at the same 45 reps item 1360's CPU profile
used:

| arm                            | GC share  | heap used        | minor (scavenge)    | major (mark-sweep) |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | ---------------- | ------------------- | ------------------ |
| `YIELD=0` (item 1360's shape)  | **17.6%** | 6.1 -> 610.7 MiB | 49 pauses, 151.4 ms | 3 pauses, 10.0 ms  |
| `YIELD=1` (graphs collectable) | **14.2%** | 6.1 -> 56.7 MiB  | 43 pauses, 104.8 ms | 6 pauses, 24.1 ms  |

**17.6% against the CPU profile's 18.6% for the same shape** — two independent instruments on one
quantity agreeing within a point, which is the check that makes either trustworthy. **Item 1360's
12.4-20.7% stands.** Mid-item I hypothesised it was a harness artifact of retention; the measurement
refuted that and the hypothesis is recorded here only because the retraction is the finding.

### What the GC share MEANS, which is the part item 1360 got only half right

**93% of it is MINOR scavenge** (151.4 ms of 161.9), not major collection. That changes the reading.
Item 1360 concluded "the write path's remaining headroom is allocation, not arithmetic", which
implied wasteful garbage. Minor GC cost is proportional to objects that SURVIVE the nursery, and when
the thing being built is a graph that the caller keeps, almost everything survives by construction —
so this is **promotion of the data structure itself**, not churn that could be eliminated. The
`Vertex`, its property bag, its label set and its adjacency maps all have to exist and all have to be
promoted. That is the `ts-ingest-is-constant-factor` ceiling (alloc + freeze) seen from the GC side,
and it is why `addVertex` was WITHDRAWN as a target at item 312 at 7.4%.

So the honest statement is narrower than 1360's: the headroom is in **how many objects per element**
the write path creates, not in garbage it needlessly produces. Reducing object COUNT per vertex is a
data-model change (the box-array lever, already recorded as costing delete bookkeeping), not a
local optimization.

### A GENUINE engine behaviour found on the way: a `Graph` keeps itself alive until the host yields

`YIELD=0` grows the heap to **610.7 MiB against 56.7**, linearly in reps (148 / 614 / 1242 MiB at
10 / 45 / 90), and a 256 MiB `--max-old-space-size` cap OOM-crashes outright. The cause is real and
is in the engine, not the probe: a `Graph` schedules `queueMicrotask(drainMutations)` on its first
write and `setTimeout(this.notify, 1)` through `scheduleNotify`, and **a pending timer holds
`this.notify`, which holds the Graph.** A synchronous loop never yields, so neither ever runs and
every graph stays live.

This is not a leak — one macrotask drains it, and the single-graph case every real host has is
unaffected. It is worth recording for two reasons: a benchmark that builds many graphs in a tight
loop retains all of them and will OOM or measure a different heap than it thinks (item 1357's
`withEdges` arm was OOM-killed at exit -9, and this is a plausible contributor nobody checked), and
anything that creates short-lived graphs synchronously — a fuzzer, a test suite, a request handler
that builds a scratch graph — holds each one until it returns to the event loop.

### The FIFTH instrument defect, this time in the probe written THIS item

`PerformanceObserver` delivers entries in a QUEUED callback. A fully synchronous rep loop buffers
every `'gc'` entry and none is delivered before `disconnect()`, so the probe's first version reported
**0 pauses and 0.0% GC** for the `YIELD=0` run — a confident, clean-looking zero, for a run whose CPU
profile shows 18.6%. It was caught only because the two instruments disagreed and the disagreement was
chased rather than resolved in favour of the newer number. The probe now yields twice before reading.

Running total for this screen: 1358 (`n/a` laundering; the `file://` no-op), 1359 (short accessor
properties; substring counting), 1360 (flagging its own probe), 1361 (the observer drain, plus
`--heap-prof` being unfit entirely). **Every single one was found by pointing an instrument at a new
surface or by two instruments disagreeing. None was found by reading the code.**

### Also this item: the shared cross-check is now ONE module

`profile-frames.mjs` holds the frame cross-checking (`mentions`, the word-boundary identifier count,
the accessor rule, `enclosingName`, `isHarnessFrame`, the two verdict buckets) and both
`runtime-profile-analyze.mjs` and `runtime-heap-analyze.mjs` import it. Extracted rather than copied
because this logic has now had four defects, and duplicating it is how the fifth gets fixed in only
one copy. The CPU analyzer was re-run against the stored GQL, Gremlin and write profiles after the
extraction and reports the same verdicts.

### Item 1362 — every profile in items 1358-1361 was taken INSIDE CACHE, and at 200k the property-read path is ~~2.5-4x~~ **1.8-2.7x (corrected at 1365)** more of the profile than it looked: the screen systematically understates it on BOTH surfaces

Items 1358-1361 screened GQL, Gremlin and the write path and found every nomination priced. **All of
it ran at 20,000 elements**, and CLAUDE.md's first rule for trusting a number is the one that was
skipped: _"Sweep the size. Cache-resident and not are different questions; the transition is between
200k and 1M elements."_ So those verdicts were verdicts about the cache-resident regime only.

### Two instrument faults had to be fixed before the sweep could be read at all

**1. `--cpu-prof` profiles the whole process, so at 200k the FIXTURE BUILD inverts the ranking.** At
20,000 with 2,000 reps the load is ~5% and harmless. At 200,000 with 120 reps the first run put
`getVertexById`, `indexEdgeLabel`, `commitElementLabels` and `getEdgeById` at the top of **every**
shape — all of them the load, none of them the query — and each shape's own hot frames fell below
them. The audit has hit this before ("windowed past the fixture build — the load is 4s of a 5.8s
profile and swamped [the rest]"). Raising reps is not the fix: it shrinks the build's fraction but
costs time in exactly the dimension being swept.

Built `windowed-profile.mjs`, which drives the profiler through `node:inspector` and starts it AFTER
the fixture is built. It writes an ordinary `.cpuprofile` the analyzer reads unchanged, asserts the
window captured samples (a window that caught none would read as "every frame is cold"), and is a
no-op without `PROF_OUT`, so `--cpu-prof` still works.

**2. The profiler then showed up in its own profile at up to a quarter of it.** `post @
node:inspector:115` read **15.1%, 23.1% and 25.5%** of the three windowed GQL shapes — a
near-constant ~125 ms, which is `Profiler.stop` serializing while sampling is still on. Two further
fixes: harness frames are now out of the DENOMINATOR, not merely out of the verdict (leaving them in
deflates every engine frame and makes runs with different machinery incomparable — which is the one
thing the window existed to enable), and `node:inspector` is recognised as harness, which a filename
match cannot do because the basename is `node`.

### Why it grows, which is NOT the getter

`get properties` is already minimal — a null check, a `??=` memo and a field read — and item 162's box
cache took the `Map.get` off it. The `get id` getter immediately above it carries a REJECTED-lever
note for the same reason (JSC inlines a getter whose body is a private-field read; the rewrite
measured flat with the rounds disagreeing on sign).

So the growth is in what `propOf` does THROUGH it: `element.properties[key]` on a **frozen plain
object with arbitrary keys**. ~~That is V8 dictionary mode, and with 200,000 distinct bags the call
site's inline caches are megamorphic — a hash lookup per read instead of an inline-cached field
access, and one that misses cache more often the bigger the heap. It is the same cliff
`ts-set-is-o-width` records at 128 -> 256 keys, reached from the element count instead of the bag

> ⚠️ **THE MECHANISM ABOVE IS REFUTED AT 1363, BY THE TICK THAT WAS MEANT TO CONFIRM IT.** Measured in
> isolation at 200,000 elements: 8 distinct key sets (megamorphic) cost **0.95x** a single hidden
> class, and `Object.freeze` costs **1.04x**. So neither dictionary mode nor megamorphism is the
> cause — the fixture's uniform keys make the read site monomorphic by construction, which should
> have been obvious before the story was written down. **It is a plain cache-miss curve**: 0.84 ns a
> read at 1,000 against 9.24 at 200,000, identical code and identical shapes. The GROWTH this item

### What this re-prices, and what it does not

Any lever on the property-read path is worth **~3x its 20k measurement** at realistic sizes, so an
effect that looked under the ~10% bar there may clear it. That does NOT retroactively revive
everything declined in this session: `drainMutations` (1361, 1.7%) is per-WRITE and this says nothing
about it, and `compareCodePoints` measurably shrinks with size. The re-pricing applies to `propOf`,
`get properties` and `degreeOfTypes` specifically.

**And it is a standing caution for the audit at large**: an unknown number of this corpus's effect
sizes were measured at 20,000 or below. This item does not audit them; it establishes that the
regime matters by 2.5-6.6x on the frames that dominate at scale, which is enough that a 20k number
should carry its size the way it carries its fixture.
