### Item 1363 — ~~item 1362's "dictionary mode / megamorphic" mechanism is REFUTED~~ (**that refutation was itself WRONG — see 1364: polymorphism costs 3.8x, and 1362 was closer to right**), the `Map`-bag fix is REFUTED at 3.18x WORSE, and the layout lever is priced at ~~3.30x~~ **3.55x (1364)** and FLAT in size

Item 1362 found the property-read path grows 2.5-4x from 20,000 to 200,000 elements, named a
mechanism — `element.properties[key]` on a frozen plain object is V8 dictionary mode, megamorphic
across 200,000 distinct bags — and explicitly did not measure it. **The mechanism is wrong.** It was
suspect on its own terms and this item says so with numbers: the engine fixture gives every vertex
the SAME three keys, so all 200,000 bags share one hidden class and the read site is MONOMORPHIC.

Five arms in `prop-bag-regime-probe.mjs`, 2,000,000 reads of one key through a shared
LCG-shuffled index (sequential access measures the prefetcher, not the engine's pattern), 9 reps
dropping 2, median, three processes:

```text
    size   locality     shapes     frozen     mapbag   columnar   ns/read (locality)
    1000        1.7        8.1        7.7       10.2        1.1   0.84 ns
   20000       11.6       10.6       12.0       18.4        5.6   5.78 ns
  200000       18.5       17.6       19.2       58.9        5.6   9.24 ns
```

| at 200,000                         | ratio to `locality`                 | verdict                                                               |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `shapes` (8 key sets, megamorphic) | ~~**0.95x**~~ **3.8x WORSE** (1364) | ~~polymorphism costs NOTHING at scale~~ **WRONG — harness pollution** |
| `frozen` (`Object.freeze`)         | 1.04x                               | freeze is **not** on the read path at scale                           |
| `mapbag` (`Map` per element)       | **3.18x WORSE**                     | the obvious fix is REFUTED                                            |
| `columnar` (`Float64Array` column) | **3.30x FASTER**                    | the layout lever, and FLAT in size                                    |

### What it actually is

**A cache-miss curve, nothing more exotic.** `locality` is 0.84 ns a read at 1,000 and 9.24 at
200,000 — 11x on identical code with identical shapes, which is random access into 200,000 heap
objects falling out of L2. Item 1362's growth is real; its explanation was V8 trivia that the
measurement does not support.

The counterfactual is the useful half. A `Float64Array` column is **5.6 ms at both 20,000 and
200,000 — flat** — because 200,000 f64s is 1.6 MB and stays cache-resident, while the object-bag
array grows 11.6 -> 18.5 over the same range. So the layout lever is worth **3.30x on a property
read at 200,000 and widens with size**, where every local lever is worth nothing.

That re-prices a lever already in this file: the **box-array lever, recorded at "~1.7x on a property
count, whose cost is delete bookkeeping"**. At 200,000 the ceiling is 3.30x, not 1.7x — consistent
with item 1362's conclusion that effect sizes measured in the cache-resident regime understate
anything on this path, and this is the first concrete instance of that re-pricing. It is also why the
TS/native property-read gap is a LAYOUT difference, not an overhead one: native's columns already
are typed arrays.

**Still not a recommendation.** Columnar property storage changes `properties` — public, read-only,
returns a `Record` — and bears on delete bookkeeping, which item 1357 flagged as the unmeasured and
consequential half of the ordinal question, and on O(1)-by-id, which the standing instruction names.
It is the same class of cross-cutting change as the dense ordinal the user declined, and it should be
declined or taken on the same grounds. What this item adds is the number: **3.30x and growing**, not
1.7x.

### THREE levers closed, which is the point of running it

- ~~**Dictionary mode / megamorphism: REFUTED.** 0.95x.~~ **THIS REFUTATION IS ITSELF WRONG — see 1364.** Run one arm per process, shape polymorphism costs **3.8x at 200,000 and 4.5x at 1,000**,
  consistently. The 0.95x came from all five arms sharing ONE `readObj` call site in one process, so
  the `shapes` arm megamorphised it and every later arm — and every later SIZE — inherited that. What
  IS true, and 1364 measured it in the engine rather than a micro: the gap does **not reach the
  engine** (uniform bags 3.09 ms against varied 3.44 at 200,000, **1.11x**, sign flipped at 20,000),
  so it is not a lever by way of making bags uniform.
- **`Object.freeze` on the read path: REFUTED at scale.** 1.04x at 200,000. (But see the open
  observation below — it is NOT free at small sizes.)
- **A `Map` per element: REFUTED, and badly.** 3.18x WORSE at 200,000, 1.8x worse at 1,000, worse at
  every size measured. A `Map` adds an indirection and a hash to a path whose cost is already the
  miss that fetches the entry. Worth recording because "use a Map instead of a plain object" is the
  reflex fix for this shape of problem and it is the wrong one here.

The 1,000-element column inverts: `frozen` is **4.6x** `locality` (7.7 against 1.7) and `shapes` is
**4.8x** (8.1), where at 200,000 both are ~1.0x. So in the cache-resident regime `Object.freeze` and
shape polymorphism each cost ~4.7x on a property read, and the cache miss at 200,000 swamps them.

**I am not naming a mechanism for this**, because naming one unmeasured is exactly what item 1362 got
wrong one item ago. It is reproducible across three processes (7.6 / 7.7 / 7.8 for `frozen`) and it
matters: a small graph is a real workload, and the engine freezes every bag. It needs its own item
with its own isolated arms — in particular ruling out that the `locality` arm at 1,000 is being
optimized in a way the others are not, which a 0.84 ns read invites.

### Item 1364 — item 1363's probe violated ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS, so three of its conclusions were its own harness; clean, shape polymorphism costs **3.8x** in a micro and **1.11x in the engine**, which closes it

Item 1363 left an "open observation, deliberately not explained": at 1,000 elements `frozen` cost
**4.6x** `locality` while at 200,000 both were ~1.0x. It declined to name a mechanism, which was the
right instinct, and flagged the thing to rule out first — _"that the `locality` arm at 1,000 is being
optimized in a way the others are not"_. That is exactly what was happening, and the cause is in the
probe.

### The defect: one shared call site, five arms, one process

`readObj` is ONE function, used by `locality`, `shapes` and `frozen`, called in that fixed order
inside a single process, with the size loop outside the arm loop. So the `shapes` arm drives that
site megamorphic and **every later arm, and every later SIZE, inherits the polluted inline cache**.
`locality` at 1,000 was the only reading in the whole table taken on a clean site.

This is CLAUDE.md's item 762 — **ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS** — which every engine probe in this directory
honours (their headers say so) and which the micro skipped. And item 1363's defence of the number was
worthless in a specific, instructive way: it was "reproducible across three processes (7.6 / 7.7 /
7.8)", and all three ran the same polluted order, so the reproduction confirmed the harness, not the
effect. **A repeat only buys independence from what it actually varies.**

### What the arms cost with a clean process each

`ARM=<name> SIZE=<n>`, one process per cell, against item 1363's all-in-one-process table:

```text
                 ONE PROCESS PER ARM            ALL ARMS IN ONE PROCESS (1363)
    size   locality  shapes  frozen  columnar   locality  shapes  frozen  columnar
    1000      1.73     7.82    1.66     1.10        1.7     8.1     7.7      1.1
   20000      3.04    11.22    3.00     1.11       11.6    10.6    12.0      5.6
  200000      4.72    17.82    4.60     1.33       18.5    17.6    19.2      5.6
```

Three of item 1363's conclusions do not survive:

- **"`Object.freeze` costs 4.6x at 1,000": REFUTED.** Clean, `frozen` is 1.66 against `locality`
  1.73 at 1,000 and 4.60 against 4.72 at 200,000 — **free at every size**, not just at scale. There
  is no inversion and never was.
- **"Polymorphism costs NOTHING at scale (0.95x)": REFUTED.** Clean, 8 key sets cost **3.8x at
  200,000 and 4.5x at 1,000**, flat in size — so it is inline-cache state, exactly as item 1362
  originally guessed and item 1363 wrongly refuted. **1362's mechanism was closer to right than the
  item that overturned it**, and both were arguing from a contaminated instrument.
- **Item 1362's 2.5-4x size growth is OVERSTATED.** Clean `locality` grows 1.73 -> 4.72, **2.7x**
  from 1,000 to 200,000, against the polluted 10.9x. The direction holds; the magnitude does not.

One survives, slightly larger: the **columnar counterfactual**. Clean, `locality` / `columnar` at
200,000 is 4.72 / 1.33 = **3.55x** (1363 said 3.30x), and columnar is near-flat across the sweep
(1.10 / 1.11 / 1.33) where the object bag grows 2.7x. The layout lever stands.

### THE ENGINE TEST, which is what actually settles it

A 3.8x in a micro is not a 3.8x in the engine, and `propOf` is ONE shared call site there — every GQL
and Gremlin property read of every element type goes through it — so the engine might be stuck on the
wrong side of that gap unconditionally. `engine-bag-shape-probe.mjs` asks directly: two graphs, same
vertex count, same query (`MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k < 50 RETURN count(*)`), one with every bag `{k,s,n}`
and one with 8 key sets all still carrying `k`. One arm per process, for the reason this item exists.

| size    | uniform bags | varied bags | ratio                |
| ------- | ------------ | ----------- | -------------------- |
| 20,000  | 0.53 ms      | 0.43 ms     | 0.81x (sign FLIPPED) |
| 200,000 | 3.09 ms      | 3.44 ms     | **1.11x**            |

Both arms answer **103,100** at 200,000 and **10,318** at 20,000 — identical, which is what makes the
A/B fair rather than two different questions.

**So the micro's 3.8x does not reach the engine: 1.11x, with the sign flipping at the smaller size.**
Bag-shape stability is therefore NOT a lever — not for the engine to enforce and not for a user to
exploit by keeping bags uniform. The most likely reason is the one that made the test worth running:
`propOf`'s single shared site serves every element type and every bag shape in the process, so it is
megamorphic either way and uniform user bags cannot rescue it. Capturing the 3.8x would need
per-site monomorphic specialization of the read itself, which is a much larger change than anything
nominated here and is not priced by this item.

### The portable lesson, which has now happened twice

**A dramatic micro number that does not reach the engine is the normal case, not the surprise.** Item
1104 is the precedent: `edgesOfTypes` read 37.9% / 2765.8 ms self in a CPU profile and counting its
branches showed all 3,600,000 calls took a single-`Map.get` fast path, so the profiler was crediting a
callee with its caller's inlined loop. Here a clean, reproducible, correctly-measured **3.8x** in
isolation is **1.11x** in the engine. Both times the micro was not wrong about itself — it was wrong
about what fraction of the engine it represented. Price in the engine, or say explicitly that you
have not.

### Gates

Probes only; no engine or core code changed. `bun run check` 0 (read unpiped). The all-arms mode of
`prop-bag-regime-probe.mjs` is kept, with its header now stating that it demonstrates the pollution;
`ARM=<name> SIZE=<n>` is the mode to trust.

### Item 1365 — item 1362's size-sweep compared an UNWINDOWED 20k against a WINDOWED 200k: matched, the property-read growth is **1.8-2.7x not 2.5-4x**, and the most size-sensitive frame is `degreeOfTypes` at **7.2x**

Item 1364 found the micro behind item 1362's _mechanism_ was contaminated. Its _profile_ numbers were
never re-checked, and they have their own defect: **the two sides of the comparison used different
instruments.** The 20,000 profiles were taken with `--cpu-prof` over the whole process, so Node's
startup and the fixture build sit in their denominator; the 200,000 profiles were windowed by the
helper item 1362 itself built. A windowed share is of engine work only, so every 20k share was
deflated and every growth ratio inflated.

Re-ran 20,000 windowed, same reps, same fixture, same analyzer:

| frame            | shape        | 20k (windowed) | 200k (windowed) | growth    | 1362 claimed |
| ---------------- | ------------ | -------------- | --------------- | --------- | ------------ |
| `propOf`         | `hopfilter`  | 5.2%           | 13.6%           | 2.6x      | 3.4x         |
| `propOf`         | `grouped`    | 4.7%           | 16.5%           | 3.5x      | 3.1x         |
| `propOf`         | `sortedpage` | 6.8%           | 9.3%            | 1.4x      | 1.6x         |
| `get properties` | `grouped`    | 6.6%           | 13.5%           | **2.0x**  | **4.0x**     |
| `get properties` | `hopfilter`  | 7.9%           | 10.7%           | **1.35x** | —            |
| `get properties` | `sortedpage` | 2.7%           | 7.8%            | 2.9x      | —            |
| `degreeOfTypes`  | `hopfilter`  | 2.3%           | 16.5%           | **7.2x**  | 6.6x         |

`propOf` and `degreeOfTypes` hold within noise of what 1362 said. **`get properties` does not**: its
headline 4.0x on `grouped` is **2.0x** measured against a matched baseline, and on `hopfilter` it is
1.35x — the weakest size-sensitivity in the table, where 1362 implied it was among the strongest.

Combining the two frames that make up the property read:

```text
                20k      200k     growth
  grouped      11.3%     30.0%     2.65x
  hopfilter    13.1%     24.3%     1.85x
  sortedpage    9.5%     17.1%     1.80x
```

**So item 1362's headline — "a 20,000-element profile understates the property-read path by 2.5-4x"
— should read 1.8-2.7x**, with a per-frame range of 1.35x to 3.5x. The direction and the rough
magnitude survive; the top of the range was the instrument mismatch.

### The correction that matters more: `degreeOfTypes`, not the property read

At **7.2x** (2.3% -> 16.5% of `hopfilter`) `degreeOfTypes` is the most size-sensitive frame measured
on either surface, and item 1362 buried it in a list of property-read frames it does not belong to —
it is the per-vertex typed-adjacency degree lookup, not a property read. Gremlin's `hopcount3` shows
the same frame moving 9.1% -> 14.6%. It carries 40 mentions, so the screen calls it priced, and the
SIZE SENSITIVITY is what is new: a lever there is worth ~7x its cache-resident measurement, which is
a larger multiplier than anything else this sweep found.

**Not priced here**, and deliberately: item 1364's lesson is one item old. A share is a nomination;
the number that decides anything is an in-engine A/B, and `degreeOfTypes` deserves its own.

### What still stands from 1362-1364, consolidated

- **Windowing is necessary** and the helper is correct: at 200k an unwindowed profile puts the fixture
  build at the top of every shape.
- **The columnar counterfactual**: 3.55x at 200,000 and near-flat in size (1364's clean numbers). A
  micro, so an upper bound on a layout change, not a prediction.
- **Three levers closed**: `Object.freeze` on the read path (free at every size), a `Map` per element
  (3.18x WORSE), and bag-shape stability (**1.11x in the engine**, measured in the engine — 1364).
- **Ranking is stable across the 10x**: `satisfies` 49.7% -> 30.9%, `grouped`'s closure 50.9% ->
  42.1%, `bump` 33.9% -> 25.4%. Composition shifts toward per-element reads; nothing reorders.

1362 corrected 1361's instrument advice, 1363 corrected 1362's mechanism, 1364 corrected 1363's
harness and restored 1362's mechanism, and this item corrects 1362's magnitudes. That looks like

### Item 1366 — `degreeOfTypes` CONFIRMED by ablation at ~15.6% of a 200k hop-filter count, the cost located in the per-vertex `Map.get`, and the one answer-preserving candidate REFUTED

Item 1365 nominated `degreeOfTypes` at 16.5% of `hopfilter` at 200,000 and 7.2x size-sensitive — the
largest multiplier the sweep found — and deliberately did not price it, because item 1364 had just
shown a clean 3.8x micro landing at 1.11x in the engine. This prices it in the engine, by ablation,
which is item 1105's method and the only instrument this file trusts for a share.

### The share is real, and the profile was accurate

`BASE` against `NO-DEG` (the body short-circuits to a constant, so answers are WRONG by construction
— this prices an operation, not a result, exactly as item 1105's `NO-MAP` arm did), three
order-alternated rounds, windowed probe so the fixture build is out of the timing:

| nodes   | BASE  | NO-DEG | saving (round-paired median) | profile said |
| ------- | ----- | ------ | ---------------------------- | ------------ |
| 20,000  | 547.1 | 529.6  | **3.2%**                     | 2.3%         |
| 200,000 | 520.2 | 414.0  | **~15.6%**                   | 16.5%        |

All three rounds agree in sign at both sizes (200k round-paired: 15.6%, 11.9%, 20.4%). **Quote the
round-paired median, not the 20.4% the raw medians give** — the 200k arms range 460-551 (BASE) and
388-486 (NO-DEG) and those overlap, so an unpaired comparison of medians overstates it. The
size-sensitivity holds too: ~4.9x from 20k to 200k against the profile's 7.2x.

So an in-engine ablation confirms a profile share for once, which is worth recording after items 1104
and 1364 both found the opposite. A share is still a nomination — but this nomination survived.

### WHERE the cost is, by decomposition — and it is the `Map.get`

Three arms at 200,000, four order-alternated rounds:

| arm      | removes                                 | round-paired savings vs BASE | verdict    |
| -------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------- |
| `NO-DEG` | the `byType.get(t)` AND the `Set` deref | 15.6%, 11.9%, 20.4%          | **~15.6%** |
| `NO-SET` | only the `Set` deref and `.size`        | -7.6%, 8.5%, -0.7%, 10.9%    | **NOISE**  |
| `FAST1`  | only the iterator (ANSWER-PRESERVING)   | -2.7%, 10.3%, -4.8%, -6.6%   | **NOISE**  |

Read together these are coherent rather than contradictory: removing the whole lookup is worth
~15.6%, removing the `Set` dereference is worth nothing, and removing the iterator is worth nothing
— **so the cost is the per-vertex `byType.get(t)` Map lookup itself.** The `Set` deref and `.size`
are free beside it, and `for (const t of types)` over a one-element array is free.

That also prices a design that was worth considering: **a cached per-type degree (`Map<string,
number>` on the element, maintained by `addEdge`/`removeEdge`) would capture almost NOTHING**,
because it replaces `Map<string, Set<Edge>>.get(t).size` with `Map<string, number>.get(t)` — it
removes the free part and keeps the expensive one. Recorded so it is not designed and then measured.

### `FAST1`: the one candidate that could have shipped, REFUTED

```ts
if (types.length === 1) {
  return byType.get(types[0])?.size ?? 0;
}
```

Answer-preserving (one type cannot collide with itself, which is `bucketSumsAreSound`'s own first
clause), and it skips the iterator on the common single-type hop. **Refuted**: round-paired -2.7%,
+10.3%, -4.8%, -6.6%, mean ~-1%, signs disagreeing. Not shipped.

### THE INSTRUMENT'S NOISE FLOOR ON THIS ROW IS ~12%, which bounds what can be asked here

`BASE` alone ranges 452.2 / 506.2 / 490.2 / 494.4 across four rounds — **12%** for the same binary.
So on this row, with this probe, nothing smaller than ~12% is measurable, and the two refuted arms
are refuted only in the sense that they are not LARGE; a real 3% effect would be invisible. That is
CLAUDE.md's "anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness" arriving as a hard limit rather
than a caution, and it is why `NO-DEG`'s ~15.6% is quotable while `FAST1`'s ~-1% is only "not big".

### What is left, and it is the declined design again

The per-vertex `Map.get` is the cost, so capturing it means not doing a per-vertex hash lookup to
learn a degree — which means degrees in a flat array indexed by a dense ordinal. That is the CSR /
dense-ordinal design the user declined at item 1358 on the alignment-burden argument, and this item
does not reopen it. What it adds is the price on this row: **~15.6% of a 200,000-vertex hop-filter
count, rising from 3.2% at 20,000.**

### Item 1367 — the noise on a 200k row is PROCESS-level, not rep-level; an isolated harness built for it; and `FAST1` REFUTED properly — **n=8 said +2.6% faster, n=24 said −0.3%**

Item 1366 left two things: `degreeOfTypes` priced at ~15.6% of a 200k hop-filter count, and the
observation that the probe's floor on that row is **12% for the same binary**, which is above most
candidates worth testing. `FAST1` — the answer-preserving single-type fast path — was "refuted" there
only in the sense of _not large_. This builds the harness CLAUDE.md asks for and resolves it.

### Why the old probe was noisy, and the fix that did NOT work

`runtime-profile-probe.mjs` times the WHOLE rep loop and reports the total, so one GC pause anywhere
in 120 reps lands in the number. The obvious fix is CLAUDE.md's own estimator — per-rep timing, drop
the warmup, take the median — and `isolated-row-bench.mjs` does that, plus prints the full
distribution, accounts GC inside the measured window (drained before reading, item 1361), asserts the
answer, and runs one shape per process.

**It barely helped, and that is the finding.** Same binary, six processes, 200k `hopfilter`:

| estimator | spread across 6 processes |
| --------- | ------------------------- |
| `median`  | **13.2%** (3.702 - 4.192) |
| `p25`     | **5.4%** (3.489 - 3.676)  |
| `min`     | 7.2% (3.381 - 3.624)      |

The old probe's loop-total was 12% and the new median-of-14 is 13.2% — **no better**. So the noise is
not rep-level jitter that an estimator can reject; it is **PROCESS-level**: each process builds a
fresh 200,000-element fixture, gets its own heap layout, and that offset applies to every rep in it.
`p25` helps (5.4%) only because it discards the GC-hit tail within a process.

**The consequence for method: the unit of sampling has to be the PROCESS.** `p25` within a process,
many processes per arm, arms interleaved across rounds. No amount of reps inside one process buys
what another process buys.

### `FAST1` resolved, and the way it resolved is the lesson

```ts
if (types.length === 1) {
  return byType.get(types[0])?.size ?? 0;
}
```

Answer-preserving (one type cannot collide with itself — `bucketSumsAreSound`'s own first clause),
four lines, skips the iterator on the common single-type hop. Measured twice on the new harness, arms
interleaved, `p25` per process, **answer asserted identical in every process** (`{c: 2062}`):

| n per arm | BASE median p25 | FAST1 median p25 | verdict            |
| --------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
| **8**     | 3.647           | 3.554            | **+2.6% FASTER**   |
| **24**    | 3.536           | 3.545            | **−0.3%, REFUTED** |

**The n=8 reading would have shipped a no-op.** It was not obviously wrong on its face: a 2.6% gain,
tight-looking summaries, a four-line answer-preserving change — the kind of thing that ships on
"obviously correct so it must be faster", which CLAUDE.md names as not-evidence. What stopped it was
checking CONCORDANCE rather than the summary: at n=8, 43 of 64 arm pairs favoured `FAST1` (67%,
against 50% for chance), which for two samples of eight is nowhere near significant. Tripling n
collapsed it to −0.3%.

**Record the concordance, not just the ratio.** Two medians differing by 2.6% with overlapping
distributions is one number; "43 of 64 pairs, where 32 is chance" is the same data saying it is not
resolved. The first invites shipping and the second does not.

### What the harness can and cannot resolve, measured

- **Within one interleaved run, n=24 per arm resolves a ratio to ~1%.** BASE 3.536 against FAST1
  3.545 is a real "no difference", not an absence of power.
- **Across runs the absolute level moves ~3%** (BASE median p25 3.647 in the n=8 run, 3.536 in the
  n=24 run). So compare arms WITHIN a run; never compare a number from one run against another run's.
- An outlier process still shows: `FAST1`'s series carried one 4.908 against a 3.27-3.676 body, which
  is why the median is the summary and the series is printed beside it.

### Where this leaves `degreeOfTypes`

Unchanged by this item and now tested at the resolution it deserves. Item 1366 located the ~15.6% in
the per-vertex `byType.get(t)` lookup itself — not the `Set` deref, not the iterator — and `FAST1`
was the only candidate that touched neither of those and could still ship. It does nothing. **So the
row's cost is reachable only by not doing a per-vertex hash lookup to learn a degree**, which is
degrees in a flat array indexed by a dense ordinal: the design declined at item 1358. This item does
not reopen it.

found in the profile screen one layer up, and Gremlin is half the standing instruction. So:
`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`, same method — per-rep timing, `p25` headline, PROCESS as the unit of

### A LONG row measures far better than a short one, and that is worth knowing

Same binary, five processes, `hopcount3` at 200,000:

| estimator | spread                     | the GQL `hopfilter` row for comparison |
| --------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `median`  | **2.9%** (297.11 - 305.75) | 13.2%                                  |
| `p25`     | **3.2%** (295.02 - 304.44) | 5.4%                                   |
| `min`     | 2.5% (292.02 - 299.29)     | 7.2%                                   |

**Four to five times tighter, and the reason is the rep length**: `hopcount3` is ~300 ms a rep where
`hopfilter` is ~3.5 ms, so timer and scheduler noise are a far smaller fraction of each sample. Item
1367 established that the residual noise is PROCESS-level and no estimator removes it; this adds the
other half — **choose a fixture size that makes the row long, and the process-level floor falls
too.** A row at 3 ms wants a bigger graph before it wants more reps.

### The re-pricing hypothesis, and it is REFUTED

Item 1108 ablated `bucketsOf`'s per-vertex array allocation at 3.9% / 3.0% and declined it. Its own
stated reason was the denominator: _"the body it feeds is ~200 ns an edge here... The same removal is
worth 1.58x in one engine and 3% in the other, and the difference is what else the loop does."_ **That
body no longer exists** — 1108 called the slot design "the next step rather than this one" and item
1110 built it, so the frontier is now a `Float64Array` indexed by an interned slot with memoized
neighbour slots. By 1108's own argument the fraction should have grown, and the windowed profile put
`bucketsOf` at **9.2%** of `hopcount3` at 200k.

Ablated with 1108's exact trick (single-label `bucketsOf` returns a module-scope reused array, so it
allocates nothing — UNSAFE under reentrancy, a timing arm and never a shipping change), fanout 5 to
match 1108's fixture, `p25` per process, eight processes per arm, arms interleaved:

| shape                 | BASE p25 | NOALLOC | change   | concordance     |
| --------------------- | -------- | ------- | -------- | --------------- |
| `hopcount3`           | 343.47   | 330.75  | **3.7%** | **59/64 (92%)** |
| `hopcount2` [CONTROL] | 73.91    | 74.95   | -1.4%    | 19/64 (30%)     |

Answers identical in every process (`hopcount3` 25,000,000, `hopcount2` 5,000,000). The control — the
two-hop count, which the degree inner product answers with no edge walk — does not improve, so the
arm reached only what it was aimed at. 59 of 64 pairs is significant for two samples of eight, so
**3.7% is a real number and not an absence of power**, which is exactly what item 1367's `FAST1` was
not.

**3.7% against 1108's 3.9%: unchanged. The hypothesis was wrong and the refutation stands.**

### Why the denominator argument did not apply, which is the useful part

`expandSlot` — and therefore `bucketsOf` — runs only on a **memo-cold** slot. Item 1110's memo
removed the adjacency iteration on every later pass, so it cut the number of `bucketsOf` CALLS and the
work they feed in the same proportion. The two shrank together and the ratio held. 1108's reasoning
about denominators was sound in general and simply did not describe this change, which is only
visible by measuring it.

Also recorded: the windowed profile said **9.2%** and the ablation says **3.7%** — a 2.5x
overstatement, the third instance this session after item 1104's `edgesOfTypes` (37.9% self for a
single `Map.get` fast path) and item 1364's micro (3.8x isolated, 1.11x in-engine). **A share is a
nomination; the ablation is the price.** That is now measured often enough to be a standing expectation
rather than a caution.

### Not shipped

3.7% is inside the ~10% floor CLAUDE.md sets, 1108 declined the same lever at the same size for the
same reason, and the arm measured here is unsafe under reentrancy so a shippable version would need

walk in a file whose neighbour carries `pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` ("any edit costs the
filtered-count cluster 1.08-1.24x, never gains"), for 3.7%. The trade is worse than the number.

### Item 1369 — the dense vertex ordinal's READ side, measured at last: **12.9% on the largest Gremlin row** (63/64 concordance, control flat), and on THIS path the user's bookkeeping objection does not bind

Item 1357 measured the ordinal's WRITE cost because the user asked for it: bare +2.4% worst case,
props -0.1%, withEdges +1.8% — free on realistic shapes. The user then DECLINED the design:

> _"I don't understand how this helps us generally. We need to do much more booking to keep a second
> structure in alignment with the global structures."_

That objection was accepted at item 1358 and is **not being relitigated**. What was missing from the
record is the other half of the trade — nobody had ever measured what the ordinal BUYS — so a
decision that reads as "declined" was really "declined without one of its two numbers". This supplies
it.

### The objection is much narrower on this path than either of us thought

`slotChainCount` **already** sizes its arrays to the graph: `const n = graph.vertexCount;` with
`new Float64Array(n)` and a comment saying `n` is an exact bound so nothing grows. So the |V|-sized
per-query allocation I warned about is **already paid here**. On this walk the ordinal needs:

- `Graph.vtxSeq` — one monotonically increasing integer;
- `Vertex.#slot` — assigned once at construction, never updated. Not a second structure to keep
  aligned; a field on the object it describes;
- `vtx[slot] = w` instead of `slotOf.set(w, slot)` — the slot→Vertex map stays **per-query and lazily
  filled**, exactly as today.

**No free list, no `vertexBySlot` on the Graph, no generation stamps** — the three things that made
the design sound heavy when I described it. The per-edge intern block SHRINKS from eight lines to
two. The one real cost is that slots are never reused, so arrays size by `vtxSeq` (total ever
created) rather than `vertexCount` (live).

### The number

Timing arm (3 files patched, every anchor asserted unique), item 1368's harness, 200,000 vertices at
fanout 5, `p25` per process, eight processes per arm, arms interleaved:

| shape                 | BASE p25 | ORDINAL | change    | concordance     |
| --------------------- | -------- | ------- | --------- | --------------- |
| `hopcount3`           | 342.68   | 298.52  | **12.9%** | **63/64 (98%)** |
| `hopcount2` [CONTROL] | 74.56    | 75.12   | -0.7%     | 7/64 (11%)      |

Answers identical in every process (`hopcount3` 25,000,000, `hopcount2` 5,000,000). The control —
answered by the degree inner product with no edge walk — does not improve, so the arm reached only
what it was aimed at. 63 of 64 pairs is as clean a separation as this session has produced.

**So the full trade, both sides measured for the first time: ~0% on writes, 12.9% on the largest
Gremlin row, for one integer on `Graph` and one immutable field on `Vertex`.** It also clears the bar
this session has otherwise failed to clear: every other candidate priced here came in at 1.7%
(`drainMutations`), 3.7% (`bucketsOf`), 1.11x (bag shape) or noise (`FAST1`).

### FOUR things not done, and the first two are disqualifying on their own

1. **BYTE-IDENTITY IS NOT VERIFIED.** Slot assignment changes from DISCOVERY order to CREATION order,
   so `st.next[to] += m` accumulates in a different order. Path counts are integers and exact in
   f64 below 2^53, so it is probably fine — and "probably" is what the seven byte-identity fuzzers
   exist for. **They were not run.** Two queries agreeing on two numbers is necessary and nowhere
   near sufficient; `graph-algorithms-library`'s summation-order rule is the precedent. Nothing here
   ships until `bun run fuzz` is green.
2. **DELETES ARE UNMEASURED**, which is the same gap item 1357 flagged and called "the consequential
   half". Slots are never reused, so a long-lived graph with churn grows its per-query arrays with
   total-ever-created. The bound is `vtxSeq`, not `vertexCount`, and nothing here measures what that
   costs after a million add/remove cycles.
3. **THE GQL SWEEP IS A DIFFERENT CASE and the objection DOES bind there.** `gql/src/executor/
shortcuts.ts` keys on the edge's `farId` STRING and grows `ways`/`next` from `cap = 256` by
   doubling — sized to the TOUCHED set, not to |V|. Giving that walk a global ordinal would introduce
   |V| sizing where none exists, which is exactly the cost this item found absent on the Gremlin
   side. **This 12.9% is a Gremlin-path number and must not be read as cross-surface** — the same
   mistake item 1359 had to correct in 1358.
4. `#slot` is on a USER-VISIBLE object. A taste objection, and the user's to make.

### Item 1370 — the ordinal arm is GREEN on 5,043 unit tests and all seven fuzzers, the teeth test says the unit green is REAL and the FUZZ green is VACUOUS, and that exposes a PRE-EXISTING hole: no byte-identity fuzzer can reach `slotChainCount` at all

Item 1369 priced the dense ordinal at 12.9% on the largest Gremlin row and named byte-identity as the
first of two disqualifying gaps: slot assignment moves from DISCOVERY order to CREATION order, so
`st.next[to] += m` accumulates differently. This runs the suites against the arm, and then does the
thing that makes a green run mean something.

### The arm is green

| suite                       | result                |
| --------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `bun test packages/gremlin` | **1141 pass, 0 fail** |
| `bun test packages/gql`     | **3532 pass, 0 fail** |
| `bun test packages/core`    | **370 pass, 0 fail**  |
| `bun run fuzz` (all seven)  | **13 pass, 0 fail**   |

Evidence of EXECUTION taken from stdout+stderr concatenated, not from the exit code — `bun test`
reports to stderr and items 767 / 772-773 got that wrong in both directions.

### THE TEETH TEST, and it splits

A green first run is what a test that checks nothing also produces, and the specific worry was
coverage: `slotChainCount` serves the **3+ hop** chain count only, and the route is declined unless
the seed is wider than `max(n/16, 1024)`. So the arm was replaced with a MUTANT that doubles the
propagated multiplicity (`next[to] += m * 2`), changing every 3+ hop count and nothing else:

| suite                       | mutant verdict                 |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `bun test packages/gremlin` | **CAUGHT** — 1140 pass, 1 fail |
| `bun run fuzz` (all seven)  | **SURVIVED** — 13 pass, 0 fail |

The catch is `slot-chain-count.test.ts:41`, in the case named _"a seed wide enough for the dense
route, which the small fixtures decline > a graph past max(n/16, 1024), so the slot walk and its memo
actually run"_. That test exists because its author knew small fixtures decline the route, and it is
the only thing in the repo that reaches it.

**So the unit green is real and the fuzz green is vacuous.** Both facts matter and they point
opposite ways.

### What the unit green actually buys, which is more than item 1369 assumed

`slot-chain-count.test.ts` guards by **route-vs-route agreement**: `agree()` runs the fast route and
then the same question with a forced `identity()` decline, and asserts the two match. That is exactly
the comparison a reordered summation would break — if creation-order slots changed the f64 result, the
fast route would stop matching the declining one. It is green, including on the oversized fixture that
actually triggers the dense route, and it demonstrably has teeth.

The arm is also **TS-only**: native is untouched, so its answer cannot move. The question was only
ever whether TS's answer moves, and the one instrument that can see this route says it does not.

### THE PRE-EXISTING HOLE, which is the more important finding

**No byte-identity fuzzer can reach `slotChainCount`, and the reason is structural.** The gremlin
differential fuzzer runs on the TinkerPop "modern" graph — about fourteen vertices (ids 1, 2, 4, 6,
13…) — while the dense route requires a seed past `max(n/16, 1024)`, i.e. **≥1024 vertices**. The
fixture is ~70x too small, so the route is declined on every seed of every run.

That means the dense multi-hop walk — items 1110 and 1152's work, the largest row in `bench:gremlin`
at 362.9 ms, the thing this whole session kept arriving at — **has no TS-versus-native coverage at
all.** A wrong answer there would pass `bun run fuzz` today, before and independently of anything in
this session. Its only guard is one TS-internal route-vs-route test.

This is not a reason to distrust item 1110 or 1152; `agree()` is a genuine equivalence check and the
native engine computes the same identity by a different route. It IS a reason to say plainly that
"byte-identity is fuzzed" does not cover this code, and that item 1369's gap #1 **cannot be closed by
the existing instruments** — the fixture has to grow first.

The shape of the fix: an ADDITIVE large-fixture arm on the gremlin fuzzer rather than widening the
existing one, so the fast seed-sweep stays fast and the dense route gets its own coverage. Not built
here — it is a change to a hard-invariant guard and to CI runtime, which is its own item.

### Where this leaves the ordinal

Item 1369's gap #1 is **narrowed, not closed**. The answer-equivalence risk is well covered and green
with a verified-teeth test; the TS-vs-native byte-identity claim is unverifiable with today's
fuzzers. Gap #2 (deletes) is untouched. The 12.9% stands and the prototype remains REVERTED.

exceeds `max(graph.vertexCount >> 4, 1024)`, the gremlin differential fuzzer runs on the TinkerPop

### What was added, and why ADDITIVE rather than a wider fixture

A second suite in `gremlin-fuzz.test.ts` on a **1,100-vertex / 2,200-edge** graph: past the flat
1,024 cut (for n under 16,384 `n >> 4` is smaller, so the cut is 1,024), with fanout 2 so a 3-hop
count is a real product rather than a chain, and a minority second edge type so a labelled hop and an
unlabelled one are genuinely different questions — without that, `out('T')` and `out()` would agree
for the wrong reason.

**The 400-plan random sweep keeps the small fixture.** Widening the shared one would have
re-calibrated every coverage floor in that file — `order(local)` generated/non-empty/with-a-null,
the skip counters, all of them measured across thirteen seeds — and multiplied the sweep's cost by
the same factor, to cover a route six fixed traversals cover exactly.

**ONE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the fixture**, because the suite above records what two cost: its TS side
is built by `createTestTinkerGraph()` and its native side from the `MODERN` NDJSON, and "the two
definitions could drift and any drift read as a divergence — which is exactly what happened when the
multi-label vertex was added to only one of them". So this arm generates NDJSON once and
deserializes BOTH engines from it.

Six cases plus a fixture-width assertion:

```text
  out(T) x3                          out() x3 [every type]
  out(T) x4                          in(T) x3
  out(T,U) x3 [multi-type]           out(T) x2  [CONTROL: inner product, a different rung]
```

The width assertion is there because this entire item exists for a suite that silently failed it: a
fixture that drifted under the cut would make every case pass by taking the same generic route in
both engines — green, and meaningless.

Item 1369 priced the dense ordinal at 12.9% and named two disqualifying gaps. Item 1371 built the
coverage gap #1 needed. This closes both.

### Gap #1 — byte-identity: CLOSED, GREEN

Re-ran the ordinal arm against item 1371's dense-route coverage, which has verified teeth (it catches
the mutant that previously survived all seven fuzzers):

| suite                       | result              |
| --------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `bun test packages/gremlin` | 1141 pass, 0 fail   |
| `bun test packages/gql`     | 3532 pass, 0 fail   |
| `bun test packages/core`    | 370 pass, 0 fail    |

The six dense-route cases now compare TS against the Rust engine on a graph that actually admits the
route, so the summation-order worry is **tested rather than assumed**. Item 1369's gap #1 is closed.

### Gap #2 — deletes: CLOSED, and DISQUALIFYING

Slots come from a monotonic `Graph.vtxSeq` and are **never reused**, so `slotChainCount` must size its
three per-pass arrays by total-ever-created rather than by live count. `ordinal-churn-probe.mjs`
isolates exactly that: the queried graph is 2,000 live vertices that are never touched again, and the
churn is a separate population added and removed, so `vtxSeq` grows while `vertexCount` stays at
2,000. Every churn level answers **16000**, asserted.

| churn     | ORDINAL p25 | vs churn=0 | BASE     |
| --------- | ----------- | ---------- | -------- |
| 0         | 0.5539 ms   | 1.00x      | 0.597 ms |
| 200,000   | 3.4254 ms   | **6.18x**  | 0.674 ms |
| 1,000,000 | 6.2826 ms   | **11.34x** | flat     |

Monotonic, with tight per-process series (3.32-3.49 at 200k, 5.78-6.79 at 1M) and BASE flat because
it sizes by `vertexCount`. **So the cheap ordinal trades 12.9% on a fresh graph for 6-11x on a churned
one**, with the live working set unchanged. For any long-lived graph that is a catastrophic trade, and
it gets worse without bound as `vtxSeq` grows.

### THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS PROBE SAID CHURN WAS FREE, and the flaw is the finding

Run 1 reported 1.00x / 1.53x / 1.35x — non-monotonic, matching BASE's own non-monotonic 0.58 / 1.19 /
0.61, i.e. noise. The conclusion would have been "deletes cost nothing", published with numbers.

The flaw: it added **every live vertex first and then churned**, so the live slots were `0..1999` —
contiguous at the very start of the ordinal space. The walk touched 2,000 ADJACENT cache lines
however large the arrays were. A real churning graph has its live vertices SCATTERED across the
ordinal space, so the walk touches 2,000 cache lines spread over the whole allocation. Interleaving
the churn between live insertions is the only fixture that exposes it, and it moved the answer from
"free" to **6-11x**.

This is the same class as item 702's LCG — a fixture whose output is correct and whose statistics are
wrong — and the same class as my own item 1364. **The cost of an oversized zero-initialised typed
array is in the pages you TOUCH, not the pages you allocate**, so any fixture that keeps the touched
set contiguous will report slot-space growth as free. `SPREAD=0` is kept in the probe so the
difference between the two layouts stays visible rather than taken on trust.

### THE USER'S OBJECTION WAS RIGHT, and the measurement says why

> _"We need to do much more booking to keep a second structure in alignment with the global
> structures."_

Item 1369 reported that this did not bind on the Gremlin path, because the arrays were already
|V|-sized and the variant needed no free list, no `vertexBySlot` and no generation stamps. **That was
true and incomplete.** The reason the variant needed none of them is that it never reuses a slot —
and never reusing a slot is exactly what the churn measurement disqualifies.

Fixing churn means reusing slots, which means a free list; a recycled slot then needs invalidation so
a stale per-query entry cannot be read as live, which means generation stamping. **The full design is
the bookkeeping the user objected to.** The cheap version is disqualified by deletes and the version
that survives deletes is the one they declined. The 12.9% is real and unreachable without it.

**So the ordinal is DECLINED on measurement, not on judgment**, and the two numbers are now on the
record together: +12.9% on the largest Gremlin row, -6.18x to -11.34x after 200k to 1M churn, with
every intermediate claim tested. Item 1358's decline stands and is now evidenced from both sides.

### What survives from this thread, for whoever reads it next

- **The dense route has byte-identity coverage** it never had (item 1371) — that is permanent and
  independent of the ordinal.
- **The per-vertex `Map.get` is worth ~12.9%** on the largest Gremlin row, with the control flat.
  Anything that removes it without unbounded slot growth captures that; a free list plus generation
  stamps is the shape, and it is the user's call whether that bookkeeping is worth 12.9%.
- **A monotonic ordinal is not a shortcut around it.** That is the specific thing this item closes.

- **"has mentions" is not "is optimized"**, and **a share is a nomination; an ablation is the price**
  — now three instances (1104's 37.9%, 1364's 3.8x→1.11x, 1368's 9.2%→3.7%), so expect a ~2.5x
  overstatement;

- **the ZERO signal is one-shot** — writing the item retires the frame;
- **`--heap-prof` is UNFIT**: 0.7 MiB reported for 128 MiB allocated, calibrate before believing it;
- **drain a `PerformanceObserver` before reading it**, or a synchronous loop reports 0 pauses;
- **a `Graph` keeps itself alive until the host yields** — a tight build loop measures a different
  heap than it thinks;
- **the noise is PROCESS-level**, so the unit of sampling is the process and no estimator fixes it;
- **a long row measures 4-5x better than a short one** — size the fixture up before adding reps;

### Item 1374 — **SHIPPED, 2.5%** on the largest Gremlin row: the single-label hop skips `bucketsOf`'s per-vertex array, safely. 539/576 concordance, control at exactly chance, and the hot-walk refactor tax measured at 1.2 points

Item 1368 ablated `bucketsOf`'s per-vertex array allocation at **3.7%** of
`V().out().out().out().count()` — real, 92% concordance, control flat — and did not ship it for two
reasons: the arm reused a module-scope array (item 1108's trick), which is unsafe under reentrancy,
and a safe version looked like it needed the hot loop body duplicated.

**The second reason was wrong.** Iterating `labels` and fetching each bucket is EQUIVALENT to
iterating the array `bucketsOf` builds — same sets, same order, nothing allocated — and `bucketsOf`'s
own doc states why it is sound: _"Only reached when the multi-type guard above has cleared, so
iterating several of them visits each edge once."_ So `expandSlot` drops the array at its one site,
and the per-edge body moves to a module-scope `walkBucket`, which `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`
recommends regardless. **One call per BUCKET — one or two per vertex — not per edge.**

`bucketsOf` is KEPT: four other call sites use it and none of them was measured here.

### The number, and why n=8 was not enough to have it

| shape                 | BASE p25 | WALK   | change   | concordance         |
| --------------------- | -------- | ------ | -------- | ------------------- |
| `hopcount3`           | 343.30   | 334.57 | **2.5%** | **539/576 (93.6%)** |
| `hopcount2` [CONTROL] | 74.89    | 74.74  | 0.2%     | **284/576 (49.3%)** |

Answers identical across all 48 processes (`hopcount3` 25,000,000, `hopcount2` 5,000,000). WALK's
SLOWEST process (343.21) sits below BASE's median — a clean separation, not an overlap with a
favourable summary.

**At n=8 this read 1.5% with the control apparently moving 0.7%**, which is the pattern CLAUDE.md
names as a suspect comparison. At n=24 the control lands at **49.3% concordance — exactly chance** —
so the control's apparent movement was itself noise and the null control is working. Item 1367's
lesson applied in the other direction: there it turned a +2.6% into a −0.3%, here it turned a
doubtful 1.5% into a confident 2.5%. **The lesson is not "small effects are fake", it is "n=8 cannot
tell you either way".**

### THE HOT-WALK REFACTOR TAX, measured rather than asserted

The ablation removed the allocation and nothing else: **3.7%**. This removes the allocation and also
restructures the walk: **2.5%**. So the restructuring costs **~1.2 points of the 3.7**, about a
third of the win.

`pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` records that any edit to a hot walk cost the filtered-count cluster
1.08-1.24x and never gained, and item 1368 declined partly on that risk. The risk was real and is now
quantified for this walk: a third of the lever, not all of it, and the remainder still clears.
**That is the first number this repo has for the tax itself**, and it is the thing to quote when the
next hot-walk edit is being argued about.

### The instrument: an equivalent-spelling PAIR on one fixture

`isolated-row-bench.mjs` gains `hopsingle` (`-[:E]->`) and `hopmulti` (`-[:E|F]->`) plus a
`MULTILABEL` knob controlling how often an edge carries BOTH labels. Every edge carries `E`, so on
this fixture the two spellings select the identical edge set and both answer **200000** — which makes
the routing difference, not the question, the only thing that varies.

|                                       | `-[:E]->` | `-[:E\|F]->`  |
| ------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------- |
| `MULTILABEL=0` (no edge has 2 labels) | 0.003 ms  | **0.003 ms**  |
| `MULTILABEL=3` (every 3rd has both)   | 0.003 ms  | **16.056 ms** |

### MY FRAMING WAS WRONG, and the measurement is what says so

I called this a 5000x equivalent-spelling gap — the class CLAUDE.md says costs 100-300x and returns
the correct answer. **It is not one, and the `MULTILABEL=0` arm is the proof.** With no multi-label
edges `graph.multiTypeEdgeCount` is 0, `bucketSumsAreSound` licenses the degree-sum route for the
disjunction too, and `:E|F` is **just as fast as `:E`**. The guard works exactly as item 1078
documents it.

The 16 ms appears only when buckets genuinely OVERLAP, where summing them would double-count and the
dedupe is required for correctness. And the two spellings are not equivalent in general — they are
equal here only because every edge carries `E`, which the engine cannot know. **So this is a
legitimate cost difference between two different questions, not a planner failing to recognise one
question in two spellings.**

I was also wrong that the spelling probe is blind here. Its `'edge type disjunction order'` group
compares `:E|F` against `:F|E`, which is an ORDER test and its stated purpose; both arms take the
same route and agreeing is the correct outcome. Nothing is missing from that probe.

**Worth recording as the general lesson**: a pair that differs by 5000x and answers identically looks
exactly like the bug class this repo hunts, and the thing that distinguished them was a one-line
fixture knob. **Vary the property the guard keys on before calling a cost difference a gap** — had
`MULTILABEL=0` not been run, this would have been filed as a 5000x spelling bug and sent someone
after a planner that is behaving correctly.

### The real lever, named and NOT yet priced

Inside the overlapping case, `edgesOfManyTypes` dedupes EVERY edge through a `Set` that grows to the
full edge count, when **only a multi-labelled edge can ever be yielded twice**. A single-label edge
sits in exactly one bucket and cannot repeat, so it needs no `Set` traffic at all:

```ts
for (const e of set) {
  if (e.labels.size > 1) {
    // only these can be double-yielded
    if (seen.has(e)) {
      continue;
    }
    seen.add(e);
  }
  yield e;
}
```

Conservative and correct — an edge labelled `{E, Z}` appears once among requested `{E, F}` and would
pay a needless `Set` op, which is cheaper than testing requested-type membership per edge. At this
fixture's 1-in-3 overlap it removes two thirds of the `Set` traffic; `types.map`'s array is the
second, smaller allocation on the same path.

**NOT MEASURED.** Item 1374's own lesson is that the ablation (3.7%) and the shippable rewrite (2.5%)
are different numbers, and this one is a generator so the restructuring is less trivial than it
looks. It gets its own item with its own A/B on this new row.

Instrument only — one bench file; no engine or core code changed. `bun run check` 0 (read unpiped).

Item 1375 built the row (`hopmulti` at 16.056 ms against `hopsingle`'s 0.003) and named two levers:
the dedupe `Set` and `types.map`'s per-call array. Both were GUESSES, and 1375's own lesson was about
guessing, so they were ablated before anything was patched.

### 1376 — the ablation, which killed half the proposal

At 200,000 / MULTILABEL=3, `hopsingle` as the control:

| arm       | `hopmulti` p25 | saving    | control | answer     |
| --------- | -------------- | --------- | ------- | ---------- |
| BASE      | 15.015         | —         | 0.0030  | 200000     |
| `NO-SEEN` | **5.902**      | **60.7%** | 0.0030  | **266667** |
| `NO-MAP`  | 15.285         | **-1.8%** | 0.0030  | 200000     |

**The dedupe `Set` is 60.7%. `types.map` is worth NOTHING** — so item 1374's allocation pattern does
not transfer here, and that half of 1375's proposal is refuted. `NO-SEEN`'s 266667 is exactly
200000 + the 66,667 edges carrying both labels, which confirms the fixture does what it claims.

### 1377 — the fix, and it needs no Set at all

1375 proposed guarding the dedupe on `e.labels.size > 1`. There is something better: **an edge can
only be yielded twice if it sits in two of the buckets being walked, so for bucket `i` a duplicate is
exactly an edge already present in some bucket `j < i`** — and those buckets already exist. Asking
them directly removes the `seen` Set outright:

- bucket 0 yields every edge with **zero** membership tests;
- bucket `i` pays at most `i` tests, against Sets that were already built.

For two types that is |E| edges free plus |F| edges at one `has`, against BASE's |E|+|F| `has` **plus**
|E|+|F| `add` on a Set growing to the full edge count. Bucket count is the distinct edge types on ONE
vertex, and `edgesOfTypes` has already taken every single-bucket case before this is reached.

| shape                 | BASE p25 | EARLIER   | change    | concordance           |
| --------------------- | -------- | --------- | --------- | --------------------- |
| `hopmulti`            | 15.418   | **5.776** | **62.5%** | **144/144 (100%)**    |
| `hopsingle` [CONTROL] | 0.003    | 0.003     | 0.0%      | every value identical |

**Complete separation**: the slowest of 12 EARLIER processes (7.274) beats the fastest of 12 BASE
(14.281). And **5.776 sits at the 5.902 no-dedupe ceiling**, so the membership tests cost essentially
nothing and the rewrite captured the whole lever rather than a fraction of it — unlike item 1374,
where the shippable form kept only two thirds of its ablation.

Order is unchanged (bucket 0's edges, then bucket 1's non-duplicates), which matters because
`column-order-is-observable` and the row-order rules make iteration order part of cross-engine bytes.

### Item 1378 — the Gremlin twin of items 1376-1377's dedupe exists, is the IDENTICAL code, and is worth **NOTHING** (−0.4%): 60.7% in GQL against ~0% here. The real gap is a **24,750x routing** miss, priced analytically at ~100x and NOT built — **BUILT at 1379: 110x, 99.1%, and the ~100x estimate held**

Items 1376-1377 removed GQL's `seen` Set from `edgesOfManyTypes` for **62.5%** on a multi-type hop.
`graph-queries.ts` has the same pattern twice — `iterLabeled` (multi-label `outE('R','S')`) and
`iterAllDeduped` — so the transfer looked obvious. Item 1108 is the standing warning that these
twins do not transfer, and it is right again.

### The row, built before anything was touched

`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs` gains `edgesingle` / `edgemulti` and a `MULTILABEL` knob, on the same
design as item 1375's GQL pair: every edge carries `E`, a third also carry `F`, so both spellings
count the SAME edges and only the route differs. 200,000 vertices / 400,000 edges:

| spelling        | p25            | answer |
| --------------- | -------------- | ------ |
| `outE('E')`     | **0.008 ms**   | 400000 |
| `outE('E','F')` | **198.045 ms** | 400000 |

**24,750x**, and both answers identical.

### The ablation, which refutes the transfer

The obvious read is that the `seen` Set dominates, as it did in GQL. **It was suspect on arithmetic
alone**: 198 ms over 400,000 edges is ~495 ns an edge, and a `Set.has` plus `Set.add` is nowhere near
that. Measured, `iterLabeled`'s dedupe removed outright (answers wrong by construction):

| arm       | `edgemulti` p25 | saving    | control `edgesingle` | answer     |
| --------- | --------------- | --------- | -------------------- | ---------- |
| BASE      | 201.337         | —         | 0.0080               | 400000     |
| `NO-SEEN` | 202.208         | **-0.4%** | 0.0075               | **533334** |

**Nothing.** The ranges overlap completely (BASE 199.97-205.21, NO-SEEN 195.12-206.82), and
`NO-SEEN`'s 533334 is exactly 400000 + the 133,334 edges carrying both labels, so the ablation did
what it claimed. **The same removal is 60.7% in GQL and 0% in Gremlin** — item 1108's sentence,
confirmed a second time: _"the difference is what else the loop does."_ In GQL the dedupe sat in a
lean bucket walk; here it sits beside a traverser pipeline emitting 400,000 edge rows at ~495 ns
each, which swamps it.

**So `iterLabeled` and `iterAllDeduped` are NOT worth rewriting**, and this is the entry that says
so with a number rather than leaving the twin looking like free money.

### Where the 24,750x actually is, and what it would take

`outE('E').count()` is answered by a count shortcut that never enumerates an edge (the family at
items 537/538/1183). `outE('E','F').count()` falls off that shortcut and runs the full traverser
pipeline. The dedupe is not why; the ROUTING is.

And unlike the GQL case at item 1375 — where summing buckets genuinely double-counts, so the decline
is correct — **a correct multi-label count is available here**, because `count-shortcut.ts` already
reaches a GLOBAL `graph.edgesByLabel`:

```
|E ∪ F| = |E| + |F| − |E ∩ F|
```

`|E|` and `|F|` are O(1) `Set.size` reads; only `|E ∩ F|` needs work, and that is one pass over the
SMALLER bucket testing membership in the larger. On this fixture that is 133,334 membership tests
against 400,000 enumerated rows plus the pipeline — **an estimated ~100x**, which would close most of
the 24,750x.

⚠️ **THE ~100x IS ARITHMETIC, NOT A MEASUREMENT.** It assumes the membership pass is the only new
cost and that the shortcut's admission can be widened without disturbing the single-label rung that
items 537/538 tuned. For k types it is inclusion-exclusion and exponential in k, so a real version
would cap k or fall back. This item does NOT build it: extending a count shortcut's admission is a
planner change with its own soundness proof (`bucketSumsAreSound` is the precedent for how that gets
tested — a pure function with its own unit test, because choosing wrongly is SLOW and not WRONG and
every mutant survives the differential suite).

### What this adds to the method

Three transfers attempted in this session's tail, three different outcomes: item 1374's pattern
shipped on the Gremlin walk (2.5%), the same pattern was **refuted** on GQL's `types.map` (−1.8%,
item 1376), and GQL's dedupe win is **refuted** on the Gremlin twin (−0.4%, here). **A shared code
shape predicts nothing about a shared win**, and the ablation is cheap enough that guessing is never
the economical choice.

both arm files under `target/` deleted by the driver's `finally`. `bun run check` 0 (read unpiped).

### Item 1379 — **SHIPPED, 110x**: the multi-label edge/hop count is the UNION of buckets instead of a decline. 198.139 ms → 1.798, 64/64 concordance, answers identical on 12 shapes ~~and 64/64 concordance~~ — **but it SHIPPED AN EQUIVALENT-SPELLING GAP, 3.53x on the reversed label order, fixed at 1382** (its ~~unresolved −1.8%~~ control is REFUTED at 1380 — n=24 flips the sign to +0.96%, significant in neither direction)

Item 1378 located the gap and priced it analytically at ~100x, then declined to build it. This builds
it, and the estimate held: **99.1%, 110x**.

### What was wrong

`adjacentCount` answers `V().out(T).count()`, `in`, `outE`, `inE` (and `both*` at twice it) by
reading bucket SIZES — O(1). With several labels it DECLINED whenever any edge carried two types:

```ts
if (labels.length > 1 && graph.multiTypeEdgeCount !== 0) {
  return undefined; // -> the traverser pipeline, ~495 ns an edge
}
```

The decline is CORRECT — summing buckets double-counts a two-type edge while the walk yields it
once — but it is a performance decline, not a semantic one. The answer wanted is the **union**, and
the union is cheap.

### The transform, which is item 1377's applied to a count

An edge belongs to exactly one FIRST bucket, so count it where it first appears: **bucket 0
contributes its `.size` untouched** (still O(1), nothing iterated) and bucket `i` counts only its
edges absent from every earlier bucket. For two labels that is one O(1) read plus one pass over the
SECOND bucket with one membership test each.

CAPPED at 8 labels: bucket `i` pays `i` tests per edge, so the work is `O(k x |E|)` for `k` labels —
far under the pipeline at the two or three a query names, unmeasured above that, so past the cap it
declines exactly as before.

| shape                     | BASE p25 | UNION     | change    | concordance |
| ------------------------- | -------- | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `edgemulti` (`outE(E,F)`) | 198.139  | **1.798** | **99.1%** | **64/64**   |
| `edgesingle` [CONTROL]    | 0.008    | 0.008     | 0.0%      | 12/64       |
| `hopcount3` [CONTROL]     | 298.209  | 303.509   | -1.8%     | 16/64       |

`edgesingle` — the control that actually runs `adjacentCount` — is flat to the digit.

⚠️ **THE `hopcount3` CONTROL READ -1.8% AND THAT IS NOT YET RESOLVED.** It is inside that row's
measured 2.9% floor (item 1368) and `hopcount3` does not call `adjacentCount` at all — it is served
by `slotChainCount` — so there is no mechanism for a real effect beyond the file-edit tax
`pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` describes. But its concordance (16/64) is not centred on chance, and
item 1374's lesson is that an n=8 control reading 0.7% landed at exactly chance by n=24. **Treat it
as unresolved rather than as noise or as a regression**; it needs its own n=24 run, which this item
does not do.

### Correctness, which is the part that matters

The fixture is built so a SUMMING implementation cannot pass: `|E|` = 3 and `|F|` = 3, so the sum is
**6** where the union is **4**. `e4` is a self-loop carrying both labels, which keeps the `both*`
doubling honest (items 1087/1089: a loop is one edge from its source and one from its target).

Twelve shapes checked, all correct: `outE(E,F)` 4, `outE(E)` 3, `outE(F)` 3, `inE(E,F)` 4,
`out(E,F)` 4, `in_(E,F)` 4, **`bothE(E,F)` 8 = 2 x 4**, `both(E,F)` 8, `outE(E,E)` 3 (duplicate
label), `outE(E,Z)` 3 (absent), `outE(Z,W)` 0, and **nine labels past the cap** still 4 by the old
route — which is the assertion that matters for a perf decline: the answer must not depend on which
route ran.

Seven of these are now tests in `multi-label-edges.test.ts`. **Teeth verified by mutation** (count the
SUM instead of the union): **4 of the 7 fail** — "counts each edge once", "the VERTEX steps agree",
"`both`/`bothE` are TWICE the union", "a DUPLICATE label". The other three are correctly unaffected
(single-label; absent-label, where sum equals union; and the cap path), and should not be read as
guarding the union logic.

### Item 1380 — item 1379's unresolved `-1.8%` control is REFUTED: at n=24 the sign FLIPS to `+0.96%` and neither reading is significant. **On this row n=8 is sign-unstable below ~3%**, now three times over

Item 1379 shipped the union count at 110x and flagged one number it had not settled: the
`hopcount3` control read **-1.8%** with concordance 16/64, which is not centred on chance. It was
recorded as UNRESOLVED rather than as noise or as a regression. This resolves it.

### The measurement

BASE taken from `git show HEAD~1:...` rather than reconstructed by patch — item 1379 is the union
commit and HEAD~1 is a bench-only item, so that file is the pre-union engine verbatim. **Both arms
were asserted to carry item 1374's `walkBucket` (x4)**, without which this would have been measuring
two changes at once. 24 processes per arm, four alternated rounds, `p25` per process:

| arm  | n   | median p25  | min     | max     |
| ---- | --- | ----------- | ------- | ------- |
| BASE | 24  | 301.656     | 293.767 | 320.172 |
| HEAD | 24  | **298.764** | 289.814 | 350.312 |

**HEAD +0.96% FASTER, concordance 351/576 (60.9%).** The sign FLIPPED from the n=8 reading.

And +0.96% is not a win either. Mann-Whitney on those counts: U = 351 against an expected 288, SD
`sqrt(24*24*49/12)` = 48.5, so z = 1.30 and p ~ 0.19 two-tailed. **Not significant in either
direction.** The honest verdict is NO DETECTABLE DIFFERENCE, which is what the mechanism predicted
all along — `hopcount3` is served by `slotChainCount` and never calls `adjacentCount`.

So item 1379's shipped 110x stands with a control that is genuinely flat, and the `-1.8%` is struck.

### n=8 IS SIGN-UNSTABLE ON THIS ROW BELOW ~3%, and that is now three independent demonstrations

| item | thing measured                  | n=8       | n=24       |
| ---- | ------------------------------- | --------- | ---------- |
| 1367 | `FAST1`, the target             | **+2.6%** | **-0.3%**  |
| 1374 | `walkBucket`'s control          | **-0.7%** | chance     |
| 1380 | the union's `hopcount3` control | **-1.8%** | **+0.96%** |

Three times, in both directions, on both targets and controls. **The rule this earns: on a ~300 ms
row, n=8 per arm cannot establish the SIGN of an effect under about 3%, let alone its size.** Item
1367 had already found the noise is PROCESS-level and no within-process estimator removes it; this
adds the magnitude below which the process count itself is inadequate.

Also worth keeping: HEAD's series carried outliers at 350.31 and 324.15 where BASE's largest was
320.17. A MEAN would have read those as a HEAD regression; `p25` within a process plus a median
across processes ignores them, which is why the estimator is specified that way and why reporting
the distribution beside the summary is not optional.

Roughly fourteen minutes of machine time and four loop ticks of waiting, to convert one shipped
"unresolved" into a struck number — and to get a third data point on where this harness's floor
actually is, which is reusable for every future A/B on this row. The alternative was leaving a
shipped change carrying an unexplained control, which is how a real regression hides.

### Item 1382 — **I SHIPPED AN EQUIVALENT-SPELLING GAP AT 1379** (`outE('E','F')` 1.781 ms against `outE('F','E')`'s 6.468, **3.53x**, same answer); sorting the union's buckets closes it, and the same helper gives `labelledCount` a union worth **91.5%**

Item 1379's union walk reads bucket 0's `.size` and ITERATES every later bucket, so it is sensitive
to the order the query names labels in. I did not notice, and the result is the exact failure class
this repo hunts: _"the planner recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned for another that
meant exactly the same thing... Each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct answer."_

| spelling        | shipped at 1379 | answer |
| --------------- | --------------- | ------ |
| `outE('E','F')` | 1.781 ms        | 400000 |
| `outE('F','E')` | **6.468 ms**    | 400000 |

Found by predicting it from the code and then building the row — `edgemultirev` / `labelmultirev`
are new, and nothing in the corpus compared a disjunction against its own reversal on this surface.
The GQL spelling probe has an `'edge type disjunction order'` group for exactly this question; the
Gremlin side had no equivalent for `outE`, which is why six items passed without it surfacing.

### The fix: sort DESCENDING, which makes order unobservable AND minimises the work

Bucket 0 is free, so it should be the biggest. `|E|` = 400,000 and `|F|` = 133,334, so query order
decided whether the walk paid 133k membership tests or 400k. Largest-first always pays the smaller.

### Same helper, second site: `labelledCount` declined UNCONDITIONALLY

`labelledCount` returned `undefined` for `labels.length !== 1`, and its own doc named the union as
the right answer. Unlike the edge case there is no "no-overlap ⇒ the sum is safe" escape, because the
graph tracks `multiTypeEdgeCount` for edges and **nothing equivalent for vertex labels** — so the
decline never consulted the data. Measured, and the knob proves it: `hasLabel('P','Q')` is
**9.294 ms at VLABEL=0 and 9.389 at VLABEL=3**, identical whether or not any vertex carries two
labels, against `hasLabel('P')`'s 0.0070.

The union needs no overlap counter — a member belongs to exactly one FIRST bucket — so one
`unionOfBuckets` helper serves both the edge buckets and the vertex-label buckets. **ONE copy of the
rule**, which is item 1078's lesson (a soundness condition open-coded in seven places is how the far
endpoint ended up on the per-edge tally).

| shape                   | BASE p25 | SORT       | change    | concordance |
| ----------------------- | -------- | ---------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `edgemultirev`          | 6.3675   | **1.7480** | **72.5%** | **64/64**   |
| `labelmulti`            | 9.6700   | **0.8185** | **91.5%** | **64/64**   |
| `labelmultirev`         | 9.6570   | **0.8250** | **91.5%** | **64/64**   |
| `edgemulti`             | 1.8045   | 1.7660     | 2.1%      | 49/64       |
| `edgesingle` [CONTROL]  | 0.0070   | 0.0080     | -14.3%    | 9/64        |
| `labelsingle` [CONTROL] | 0.0070   | 0.0070     | 0.0%      | 6/64        |

**The spelling gap, before and after** — and the pair must COST the same, not merely answer the same:

```text
  BASE  edgemulti 1.8045  vs edgemultirev 6.3675   ratio 3.53x
  SORT  edgemulti 1.7660  vs edgemultirev 1.7480   ratio 0.99x
  BASE  labelmulti 9.6700 vs labelmultirev 9.6570  ratio 1.00x   (both equally SLOW)
  SORT  labelmulti 0.8185 vs labelmultirev 0.8250  ratio 1.01x   (both equally FAST)
```

⚠️ `edgesingle`'s **-14.3%** is 0.0070 ms against 0.0080 — ONE timer tick at 7 microseconds, on a
code path both arms share byte for byte (the `labels.length === 1` early return is untouched). It is
quantisation, not a regression, and it is in the table rather than omitted because dropping an
inconvenient control row is how a real one gets lost.

`count-shortcut.test.ts`'s `'shapes it declines still answer correctly'` already asserted

a wrong DECLINE and it catches a wrong UNION for the same reason. **Verified by mutation**: counting
the sum instead of the union fails that case plus `'a multi-type edge is counted once'`.

Its TITLE is now stale — the shape no longer declines — so that is annotated in place rather than
renamed, and four cases the new walk differs on were added beside it: order reversal, a DUPLICATE
label naming one bucket twice, an ABSENT label, and nine labels past the cap (where the answer must

### Two stale precedent comments, fixed in the same commit

Both cited `labelledCount`'s decline as justification for their own, and it no longer declines:

- `count-shortcut.ts`'s filtered-chain doc ("stays a predicate — `labelledCount` declines it for the
  same reason");
- `index-seed.ts`'s multi-label decline ("`labelledCount` in the count shortcut declines it for
  exactly the same reason").

**Both declines still stand, for a reason the citation obscured**: seeding and a tally need an
ENUMERATION of the elements, and a union COUNT is a number. Deduping an enumeration across buckets is
a different and more expensive question than counting one. The citation was the stale half.
