### Item 1383 — two disjunction-ORDER groups added to the Gremlin spelling probe, and the honest part: **they would NOT have caught item 1379's gap**, because that gap is on the EDGE side and this fixture has no multi-label edge

Item 1382 found that I shipped an equivalent-spelling gap at 1379 — `outE('E','F')` 1.781 ms against
`outE('F','E')`'s 6.468, 3.53x, same answer — and that it survived six items because **no group in
this probe compared a disjunction against its own reversal**. This adds that comparison.

### What was added, and why only the ORDER pairs

```text
  label disjunction order: (Person, Mgr) vs (Mgr, Person)
  label disjunction order, wide size gap: (Univ, Mgr) vs (Mgr, Univ)
```

A union is COMMUTATIVE, so these are equivalent **unconditionally**, not merely on this fixture —
which is what makes them a legitimate group. The size disparity in the second is the point: `Univ` is
every vertex and `Mgr` every third, so an unsorted walk pays 3x more one way round.

**Deliberately NOT added: `hasLabel('Person','Mgr')` against `hasLabel('Person')`.** Those also answer
identically here — `Person` is vacuous and `Mgr` is a subset — but only on this DATA, which the
engine cannot know. Item 1375 nearly filed a 5000x bug against a correct planner on exactly that
confusion, so a fixture-conditional pair is a false-flag generator, not a guard.

### They need `SPELL_N=1000000`, and converge there

Under the 200,000 default both groups land beneath the 1 ms floor and report as "not compared" — the
same property the multi-id groups have, and not a defect (a group becomes comparable precisely when
one side regresses). At 1,000,000:

| group                          | arm 1    | arm 2    | ratio |
| ------------------------------ | -------- | -------- | ----- |
| (Person, Mgr) vs (Mgr, Person) | 10.633ms | 9.926ms  | 1.07x |
| (Univ, Mgr) vs (Mgr, Univ)     | 10.493ms | 12.374ms | 1.18x |

Both answering 1000000. Inside the probe's 2x tolerance, so item 1382's sort has made the order
unobservable where it was 3.53x on the edge twin. The 1.18x is noise at ~10 ms over 9 reps — after
sorting, the two arms produce the SAME bucket order and differ only in an input array's order, which
nothing downstream reads.

### THE LIMITATION, which is the point of writing this down

**These groups would not have caught the bug they were built for.** Before item 1382 the vertex-label
path declined UNCONDITIONALLY (`labels.length !== 1`), so both orders were equally slow — item 1382
measured `labelmulti` 9.6700 against `labelmultirev` 9.6570, **1.00x**. The order sensitivity existed
only on the EDGE side, and this fixture gives every edge exactly one label (`T`), so
`multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`, the disjunction takes the order-insensitive SUM path, and no edge group
here can expose it.

So what this buys is a REGRESSION guard: if someone un-sorts `unionOfBuckets`, the vertex groups now
flag at N=1M. What it does NOT buy is coverage of the surface where the gap actually was.

### What the missing group would cost, priced rather than deferred silently

An edge-order group needs a second edge label on a MINORITY of edges, to make `multiTypeEdgeCount`
non-zero and reach the union. That is a fixture change with a KNOWN routing side-effect, not a free
addition: `filteredHopCount`'s far-driven arm admits on `labels.length === 1 || multiTypeEdgeCount
=== 0`, so making the count non-zero flips every UNTYPED hop to the edge-driven walk — and this probe
has an untyped-hop group (`label, VACUOUS, before a hop: hasLabel(Univ).out vs out`). Item 1303
already measured this exact fixture change on the GQL side and found a calibrated ratio moved 8.99x
to 10.30x, so the effect is real and tolerable but it re-calibrates groups.

Not done here. The edge-order regression IS guarded in the meantime by
`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`'s `edgemulti`/`edgemultirev` pair (item 1382), which is where the 3.53x
was measured — but that bench is run deliberately, where `bun run spelling:gremlin` is the routine
check, so the gap in routine coverage is real and named.

### Gates

Probe only; no engine or core code changed. `bun run check` 0 (read unpiped). `bun run
spelling:gremlin` runs clean at the default N (both new groups under the floor) and at
`SPELL_N=1000000` (both compared, both converged).

### Item 1384 — the SAME order gap was on the GQL side too (`-[:E|F]->` 5.227 ms against `-[:F|E]->`'s 8.352): **fixed, 29.3% on the reversed spelling, symmetry 1.42x → 1.04x**. And I never ran the spelling probe at item 1377

Item 1382 found that item 1379's union walk was sensitive to the order a query names labels, and
fixed the Gremlin side. **Item 1377 gave GQL's `edgesOfManyTypes` the same earlier-buckets dedupe, so
it had the same defect**, and I went looking rather than waiting to be told:

| spelling     | as shipped at 1377 | answer |
| ------------ | ------------------ | ------ |
| `-[:E\|F]->` | 5.227 ms           | 200000 |
| `-[:F\|E]->` | **8.352 ms**       | 200000 |

Bucket `i` pays `i` membership tests per edge, so the total is minimised by descending size — and
without that the walk costs whatever order the query happened to name.

### The fix is NOT the same fix, which is why it was A/B'd rather than copied

Gremlin's `unionOfBuckets` runs ONCE per query over GLOBAL label buckets, so sorting is free. GQL's
`edgesOfManyTypes` runs **per vertex** over one vertex's adjacency buckets — the sort is paid 200,000
times and orders degrees, not indexes. It could easily have cost more than the asymmetry it removes.
It does not:

| shape                 | BASE p25 | SORT       | change    | concordance     |
| --------------------- | -------- | ---------- | --------- | --------------- |
| `hopmultirev`         | 8.7720   | **6.1995** | **29.3%** | **64/64**       |
| `hopmulti`            | 6.1655   | 5.9590     | 3.3%      | 26/64 (neutral) |
| `hopsingle` [CONTROL] | 0.0030   | 0.0030     | 0.0%      | 0/64            |
| `hopfilter` [CONTROL] | 3.5595   | 3.5480     | 0.3%      | 35/64           |

```text
  BASE  E|F 6.1655  vs  F|E 8.7720   ratio 1.42x
  SORT  E|F 5.9590  vs  F|E 6.1995   ratio 1.04x
```

`hopmulti` at 26/64 is the n=8 instability item 1380 documented — median up 3.3%, pair count below
chance, so **neutral**: the per-vertex sort is free even on the order it cannot improve. Both controls
flat, `hopfilter` at exactly chance.

### THE PROCESS FAILURE, which is the part worth keeping

CLAUDE.md says to run the spelling probe "when you touch the TS planner or add a predicate form".
**I did not run it at item 1377, and the GQL probe has had an `'edge type disjunction order'` group —
`:E|F` against `:F|E` — the whole time.** Had I run it, the defect was at least a candidate to be
caught six items earlier, and item 1382's Gremlin twin might never have shipped.

Run now, post-fix, that group reads **2.09 ms against 2.08 — 1.00x, converged.**

⚠️ **WHETHER IT WOULD HAVE FLAGGED PRE-FIX IS UNMEASURED, and I am not claiming it would.** The
probe's fixture carries `F` on 1 in 11 edges where the bench row above uses 1 in 3, so on most
vertices `buckets.length === 1` and there is no asymmetry to see at all — the group may well have sat
under its 2x threshold. That is a real question about the instrument's POWER, not a reason to skip
running it, and it is the next tick's measurement rather than a guess here.

### What is now guarded

- **Answer** order-independence: `multi-label-edges.test.ts`'s "bucket ORDER does not change the
  union" (item 1377), still valid.
- **Cost** symmetry: `isolated-row-bench.mjs`'s `hopmulti`/`hopmultirev` (new here) and
  `isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`'s `edgemulti`/`edgemultirev` (item 1382).
- **Routine** coverage: the GQL spelling probe's existing group, whose power at its own fixture is
  the open question above; the Gremlin probe's two groups from item 1383, which need `SPELL_N=1000000`.

`bun test` gql **3537 / 0**, gremlin 1148 / 0, core 370 / 0, serialization 144 / 0. `bun run fuzz`
**20 / 0**. `bun run spelling` — the disjunction-order group converged at 1.00x. `bun run check` 0
(read unpiped).

### Item 1385 — the spelling probe **would NOT have flagged** item 1384's gap: it reads **1.22x** pre-fix against a **2x** threshold. The group is right, reproducible, and under-powered — and no documented tolerance reaches it

Item 1384 recorded a real process failure — I never ran `bun run spelling` at item 1377, where the
GQL probe has had an `'edge type disjunction order'` group (`:E|F` against `:F|E`) all along — and
deliberately did NOT claim the probe would have caught the defect. This measures it, because
guessing is what this session keeps getting wrong.

### The measurement: the probe itself, on its own fixture, pre-fix

Not a model of it. My bench row measured 1.42x at 1-in-3 overlap and degree 1; the probe's fixture is
1-in-11 at degree 3, and both differences move the asymmetry in directions I cannot reason about
reliably. So the pre-sort `executor.ts` came from `git show HEAD~1:…` (item 1384 is the sort commit),
with **both arms asserted to carry item 1377's dedupe** — otherwise this measures that change
instead — and the one group was run twice per arm:

| arm             | `:E\|F`          | `:F\|E`          | spread           |
| --------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| BASE (pre-fix)  | 2.060 / 2.050 ms | 2.520 / 2.520 ms | **1.22x, 1.23x** |
| HEAD (post-fix) | 2.110 / 2.070 ms | 2.120 / 2.110 ms | **1.00x, 1.02x** |

**The probe would NOT have flagged it.** Its threshold is 2x, and the defect produces 1.22x here —
below the default AND below the **1.5x** this file documents for a deliberate hunt. **No tolerance
the probe offers would have fired.**

### What that means, stated carefully

- **The group is CORRECT and the measurement is GOOD.** 1.22 / 1.23 against 1.00 / 1.02 is a clean,
  reproducible separation across four runs. The instrument sees the defect; the FLAG does not.
- **The cause is the fixture, not the group.** `F` sits on 1 in 11 edges, so most vertices hold a
  single bucket and have no asymmetry to expose. The isolated bench reads 1.42x at 1-in-3, and the
  Gremlin twin 3.53x because its buckets are GLOBAL rather than per-vertex.
- **So item 1384's process failure was real but not causal.** Running the probe at 1377 would not
  have caught this. Both halves belong in the record: the rule still says run it, and this says what
  running it would and would not have bought.

### What actually guards the property

`isolated-row-bench.mjs`'s `hopmulti`/`hopmultirev` pair (item 1384) and
`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`'s `edgemulti`/`edgemultirev` (item 1382) — both at 1-in-3 overlap, where
the signal is 1.42x and 3.53x. The probe group is annotated in place with its measured power so a
future reader does not mistake an unflagged run for this property being covered, and is pointed at
the bench pair that does cover it.

**NOT done: thickening the probe's overlap to 1-in-3.** That would raise the signal past 2x and make
the group self-sufficient, and it is the obvious fix — but it re-calibrates every other group on that
fixture, and item 1303 measured exactly this change moving a calibrated ratio from 8.99x to 10.30x.
Item 1383 declined the same change on the Gremlin probe for the same reason, with the additional
side-effect that `multiTypeEdgeCount` becoming non-zero flips untyped-hop routing. Both probes now
carry the same named, priced follow-up rather than a silent gap.

### The general lesson

**A group existing is not the same as a group having power, and the ratio that decides it is a
property of the FIXTURE.** This probe has had the right comparison for the whole life of the defect
and its threshold sat above the signal the whole time. When adding a spelling group, measure what
signal the fixture can actually produce for the failure it is meant to catch — otherwise the group
reports green for a reason that has nothing to do with the engine being correct.

### Item 1386 — GQL's multi-type hop count declined to a deduping walk where the UNION of global buckets answers it: **87.0%** (7.7x) on both orders, 64/64 concordance, both controls flat

`MATCH ()-[:E]->() RETURN count(*)` answers in **0.003 ms** from one global bucket's `.size`.
`MATCH ()-[:E|F]->()` measured **6.44 ms** — two thousand times more — not because the answer is
harder but because `bucketSumsAreSound` correctly refuses to SUM overlapping buckets and the query
then fell through to the deduping walk. The sum is unsound; the **union** is not, and it is cheap.

### The measurement

`isolated-row-bench.mjs`, `NODES=200000`, `MULTILABEL=3` (`['E','F']` on every 3rd edge),
`REPS=14 DROP=3`, p25 within a process and the median across 8 processes per arm, two
order-alternated rounds (BASE/UNION, UNION/BASE). Both arms asserted to be the code they claim
(`globalBucketUnion` x0 vs x2) before each build.

| shape                   | BASE p25 | UNION      | change    | concordance |
| ----------------------- | -------- | ---------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `hopmulti` (`:E\|F`)    | 6.4350   | **0.8385** | **87.0%** | 64/64       |
| `hopmultirev` (`:F\|E`) | 6.1870   | **0.8240** | **86.7%** | 64/64       |
| `hopsingle` [CONTROL]   | 0.0030   | 0.0030     | 0.0%      | 0/64        |
| `hopfilter` [CONTROL]   | 3.6170   | 3.6430     | −0.7%     | 27/64       |

64/64 on both targets; `hopfilter` at 27/64 is the coin-flip this session has learned to expect from
a control, and `hopsingle` cannot move because it never reaches this branch. Answers identical per
shape across every arm and process (the driver fails the run otherwise).

### The third instance of one pattern, and the sort was in from the start

Items 1379 (Gremlin `adjacentCount`, 110x) and 1382 (`labelledCount`, 91.5%) replaced the same
decline with the same union over the same kind of label index. An edge belongs to exactly one FIRST
bucket, so count it where it first appears: bucket 0 contributes `.size` untouched, bucket `i` pays
`i` membership tests. **No overlap counter is needed**, which is the whole point — the engine already
maintains `multiTypeEdgeCount`, and the union needs nothing from it.

**⚠️ LARGEST BUCKET FIRST, and this time before shipping.** Items 1382 and 1384 each shipped this
walk unsorted and each created an equivalent-spelling gap — 3.53x on `outE('F','E')` and 1.42x on
`-[:F|E]->` — that had to be found and fixed afterwards. `globalBucketUnion` sorts descending in its
first version, and `hopmultirev` above is the row that proves it (86.7% against 87.0%, a 1.02x
residual).

### A deliberate third copy, cross-referenced in both engines

This repo's stance is that GQL and Gremlin are parallel implementations sharing only `@lenke/core`'s
data types; `bucketSumsAreSound` is "one copy of the rule" _within_ GQL, not across engines. But the
ORDER defect **did** drift across the two copies and cost two items to fix twice, two items apart
(1382 then 1384). So `globalBucketUnion` and Gremlin's `unionOfBuckets` now each carry a pointer to
the other naming that history, rather than relying on a future reader noticing the parallel.

### Teeth, by two mutants

8 tests added to `packages/gql/src/multi-label-edges.test.ts` on a fixture where the buckets are 4
and 3 and the union is 5 — so a SUM answers 7 and is visibly wrong.

- **Mutant A, sum instead of union:** 3 of the 8 new tests fail. Those three guard the union itself.
- **Mutant B, drop the `a === undefined && b === undefined` admission guard:** my test plus **33
  tests across the gql package** fail. That guard is why a hop with a bound endpoint cannot take
  this route, and the remaining 5 new tests pin the behaviour it protects — far endpoint LABELLED
  answers **1, not 5**, and start endpoint LABELLED answers **0**.

gql 3545/0, gremlin 1148/0, core 370/0, serialization 144/0, `bun run fuzz` 20/0, `bun run check` 0

### Item 1387 — the multi-type hop's YIELD side, which no union can fix: GQL **9.8x** (38.9 ms against 379.6) and Gremlin **1.50x** for the same edges and the same rows. The profile says GQL's is a ROUTING miss, and the Gremlin figure PRICES it at ~~~85%~~ **nothing — that premise is WRONG, see 1388**: Gremlin's 1.50x is its OWN single-label fast arm skipping two generator layers, not a floor. **BUILT at 1388: 80.7%**, and the estimate landing near it was luck. **The 1.50x is now TAKEN at 1389 for 25.1%, and the dedupe PRICED at 1.13x** — so 1387's reference was ~75% delegation. The GQL counterpart of the leftover route gap is 1390

Items 1377, 1379, 1382, 1384 and 1386 all landed on the COUNT path, where the answer is a number and
the union of buckets replaces the walk outright. A projection cannot take that route — every selected
edge must actually be produced — so item 1386's closing line ("the remaining multi-type cost is the
yield path") was a nomination, and this measures it. Three yield rows added to each isolated bench.

### The measurement

`isolated-row-bench.mjs` / `isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`, `NODES=200000`, `MULTILABEL=3`,
`REPS=14 DROP=3`, p25 of one process per row. Every edge carries `E` and a third also carry `F`, so
both spellings select the IDENTICAL edge set.

| surface | single-type | `E\|F`      | `F\|E`  | gap       | order gap |
| ------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------- | --------- | --------- |
| GQL     | **38.881**  | **379.579** | 378.908 | **9.8x**  | 1.00x     |
| Gremlin | **139.257** | **209.525** | 211.043 | **1.50x** | 1.01x     |

**Row counts verified identical before pricing anything:** 20,000 rows for `:E`, `:E|F` and `:F|E`
alike, and 20,000 for both counts, on a 20k-vertex twin of the fixture. A 9.8x that turned out to be
the multi arm emitting duplicate rows would be a correctness bug, not a perf gap, and this session
has mistaken a correct decline for a gap once already (item 1375). GC confirms the shape too: 25
collections on the GQL single arm against **331** on the multi.

Neither surface has an ORDER gap, which is the first time one of these pairs has come up clean
without a fix — items 1382 and 1384 both had to be repaired. The union sort is not involved on this
path.

### The profile says GQL's gap is a ROUTING miss, not a frame

CPU profiles of both GQL arms (`NODES=100000`, `REPS=6`), through `runtime-profile-analyze.mjs`:

| arm              | top frames                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `hopsingleyield` | `(anonymous) in farDrivenHopWalk` **15.5%**, GC 14.7%, `getVertexById` 11.5%                                                 |
| `hopmultiyield`  | `evalLabelExpr` **12.9%**, `edgesMatching` **10.2%**, GC 9.6%, `outSteps` **8.2%**, `walkSegments` 5.1%, `matchPattern` 3.0% |

The two arms do not share a top frame. The single-type arm runs `farDrivenHopWalk`; the multi-type
arm runs the general matcher. **No unpriced frame over 2% in either**, which is the screen working
as designed — there is no hot new function here, the query simply left the specialized route.

The cause, in one line: `hopEnds` (`packages/gql/src/executor/hop-projection.ts:698`) returns `null`
when `types?.length !== 1`, so the ENTIRE hop-projection family — fifteen call sites doing
`v.adjFrom.get(typeName)` — declines any disjunction, exactly as `labelledCount` and `adjacentCount`
declined before items 1382 and 1379.

### What the Gremlin number buys: a price, not just a comparison

Gremlin's `out('E','F')` does **not** fall off a route — it pays two buckets and a dedupe and that
costs **1.50x**. So on the GQL side, 1.50x is the honest estimate of the work a multi-type hop
genuinely owes, and the rest is the routing miss:

> **38.881 x 1.50 ≈ 58 ms against 379.579 — a ~85% / 6.5x target.**

That is an estimate from a parallel implementation, not an ablation, and this session's own rule is
that a share is a nomination while an ablation is the price (expect ~2.5x overstatement on a frame
share — though this is a route comparison, not a frame share, which is a better-founded kind of
estimate). It is recorded as the pricing to beat, not as a result.

### Item 1388 — **SHIPPED, 80.7%**: the multi-type hop PROJECTION takes the plain hop walk instead of the general matcher. 576/576 concordance, the control settled at n=24 — and item 1387's "1.50x is the honest cost" premise is WRONG, which changes what is left

Item 1387 measured `-[:E|F]->(b) RETURN b.n` at **379.6 ms against `-[:E]->`'s 38.9** over the

`hopEnds` now admits up to `HOP_MAX_TYPES` (8) names and reports them, and `declinesDisjunction`
(`MULTI_TYPE_PLAIN_ONLY`) sends a disjunction away from **every route but the two plain walks**. That
guard is the load-bearing part, not the walk: `typeName` is still `types[0]` and fourteen walks read
it as THE edge type, so a disjunction reaching one of them answers for `E` alone — a **wrong answer**,
not a slow one. One guard rather than a check inside each walk, because item 159 measured that a
branch added to those inner loops costs the hot single-type shape 1.6x.

The multi-type walk is its own closure and its only difference from `startDriven` is the edge source:
`edgesOfTypes`, which already carries item 1377's earlier-buckets dedupe and item 1384's
largest-bucket-first sort. Three items of count-path work, reused unchanged.

`isolated-row-bench.mjs`, `NODES=200000`, `MULTILABEL=3`, `REPS=14 DROP=3`, p25 within a process,
median across processes, order-alternated rounds. Two A/Bs: five shapes at n=8, then the control and

| shape                               | n   | BASE p25 | MANY       | change    | concordance |
| ----------------------------------- | --- | -------- | ---------- | --------- | ----------- |

### The control's first reading was −3.6%, and chasing it found a real defect

The n=8 A/B read `hopsingleyield` at **−3.6% with 33/64** — chance, and inside the regime this
session has documented as sign-unstable three times (items 1367, 1374, 1380). Treating it as noise
would have been wrong anyway, because there WAS a mechanism: `startDrivenMany` was constructed per
compile even when `types.length === 1`, a closure the hot single-type path allocated and never
called, which is what `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` is about. Moved inside the
`types.length > 1` branch, the control re-reads **+0.6% at n=24 (332/576)** — the sign flipped and
neither reading is significant, which is the fourth instance of that n=8 lesson.

**The shipped code is not quite the measured arm.** `declinesDisjunction` was extracted after both
A/Bs, because inlining the guard put `detectHopProjection` at complexity 41 against a cap of 35 —
the same reason `projectionIsStreamable` and `hopOrderPlan` are their own functions. That is a
per-compile call, not per-row, and a single-process read of the final build confirms it moved
nothing: 69.27 and 36.21 against the A/B's 71.37 and 37.79, both inside process noise.

### Teeth, by four mutants — after the first run of them was VACUOUS

A route choice is answer-equivalent when it is right, so every test passes either way unless the
mutation makes it WRONG. Four mutants, each caught by a different named test, run against the final
extracted code:

| mutant                              | verdict     | caught by                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| M1 no dedupe in the multi-type walk | CAUGHT 41/3 | the union, the duplicate-type and the far-label tests |
| M2 no `MULTI_TYPE_PLAIN_ONLY` guard | CAUGHT 41/3 | the bound-rel, undirected and start-projection tests  |
| M3 no far-label test                | CAUGHT 43/1 | the `:Q` filter test                                  |
| M4 no multi-type dispatch           | CAUGHT 41/3 | the union, type-order and far-label tests             |

**The first run of this reported all four CAUGHT and every one was vacuous.** The driver did
`io.open(SRC, 'w').write(read(SRC).replace(old, new))` — opening for writing TRUNCATES before
`read(SRC)` is evaluated, so each "mutant" was an EMPTY file and `0 pass / 1 fail` was bun failing to
load it. The giveaway was the arithmetic: 44 tests cannot become 1. The `== base` no-op check could
not see it either, because an empty file is not the base. The driver now reads into a variable first
and asserts the mutated text is at least half the original length.

### ⚠️ Item 1387's pricing premise is WRONG, and it changes what is left here

Item 1387 derived its ~85% estimate from Gremlin's 1.50x multi-label yield gap, calling that "the
work a multi-type hop genuinely owes". **It is not.** `packages/gremlin/src/executor/hop-values.ts`
has its own single-label fast arm (`oneType`, line 128) — a hand walk over
`v.adjFrom.get(labels[0])` that exists to skip two generator-delegation layers per edge — and
multi-label falls to `adjacentEdges`, a generator chain. That arm's own comment prices exactly this
at **375.6 ms through the helpers against 251 for the hand walk, 1.50x**: the same number. So
Gremlin's 1.50x is very likely the SAME class of gap rather than a floor, and the estimate landing
near the realized 80.7% was luck, not sound reasoning.

Two consequences:

- **The remaining 1.94x on the GQL side (69.3 against 36.2) is not established as dedupe cost** — and item 1389 settled it: the dedupe costs **1.13x**, so ~1.7x of this is the route. **That route is BUILT at 1390: 74.2% at fan-in 133** — and it LOSES at fan-in 1, so it ships behind a cost gate. The
  single-type arm runs the FAR-DRIVEN walk, whose own comment prices its `projectRow` hoist at 2.3x,
  and the multi-type arm has no far-driven form. The comparison that would separate route from cost
  is multi-start-driven against single-START-driven, which no row measures.
- **The Gremlin twin is the next item, and it re-prices the reference rather than inheriting it.**

both-labelled out-edge, and **the A/B driver refuses to run if the two spellings ever agree** —

two-type edge'` compares fused against piped, which this change turned from a near-tautology into a

### Item 1390 — **SHIPPED, 74.2%** at fan-in 133, behind a cost gate because the route is **SIGNED**: it LOSES at fan-in 1. ~~(threshold 8)~~ **Its threshold was calibrated at OUT-degree 1 only and was refusing 32-43.5% at degree 3-4 — swept and lowered to 4 at item 1403.** 64/64, answers identical — and the gate's first version chose BACKWARDS with the whole suite green

Item 1389 priced the multi-type dedupe at **1.13x**, which left item 1388's residual **1.94x** unexplained
by any real work: the single-type arm takes the FAR-DRIVEN walk, whose own comment prices its
`projectRow` hoist at 2.3x, and the multi-type arm had no far-driven form. This builds it.

### Why a disjunction is cheap in THIS walk specifically

`farDrivenHopWalk` never reads edges — it takes `bucket.size` and emits that many identical rows. So
a disjunction needs only the per-vertex UNION COUNT, and when `graph.multiTypeEdgeCount === 0` the
union IS the sum, so not one membership test runs.

**⚠️ And uniquely here, BUCKET ORDER IS UNOBSERVABLE.** Every row for a far vertex is identical, so
the sequence depends on far-vertex order alone. Largest-bucket-first is a free win rather than the
equivalent-spelling fix it had to be at items 1382 and 1384, and `-[:F|E]->` cannot differ from
`-[:E|F]->` by construction.

### The effect is SIGNED, which is the whole shape of this item

| FANIN | est. in-degree | route taken                  | `hopmultiyield` |
| ----- | -------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------- |
| 1     | 1.33           | start-driven (gate declines) | 70.8            |
| 0.1   | ~13            | far-driven                   | 29.1            |
| 0.01  | ~133           | far-driven                   | **16.1**        |

Unconditionally far-driven, fan-in 1 measured **86.1 ms against the start-driven 69.3** — the hoist
has one row to amortize and the per-vertex union machinery is pure cost. **The bench had no degree
knob at all**, so `FANIN` was added (default 1 reproduces the original fixture byte-for-byte). This
is CLAUDE.md's "match the fixture to the claim" inverted: a change that only helps HIGH-degree
vertices, judged on a degree-1 fixture, can only lose.

### The gate, and the fact that its first version chose backwards

`farDrivenPaysForMultiType(typeEdgeCount, farEndpoints)` — O(k) per call, nothing iterated.

**The first version used `candidateCount(graph, farLabel)`, which counts LABEL MATCHES.** Every
vertex in the fixture is `:P`, so it read an estimated degree of 1.33 at a real in-degree of 133 and
declined the route exactly where it wins: **55.7 ms measured, against the 17.2 it refused to take.**
The denominator has to be vertices that actually RECEIVE these edges —
`edgesToByLabel`/`edgesFromByLabel` are keyed by vertex id, so `.size` is O(1) and is the quantity
the hoist divides by.

**The entire 3,566-test suite stayed green through that**, because a route choice is
ANSWER-EQUIVALENT. Only the bench caught it. So the gate is a pure exported function with **9 unit
tests of its own** (`hop-projection-route.test.ts`) pinning the backwards case, the threshold, the
divide-by-zero and monotonicity — the pattern `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` records.

### Three instrument defects this item, all mine

1. **The A/B's answer check compared the FIRST ROW**, which a legitimately-reordering route must
   change — `{"n": 3}` on BASE against `{"n": 0}` on FAR. It aborted the run and threw away a
   complete 4-arm timing table. Verified properly against `-[r:E|F]->` (which binds the rel, so
   `MULTI_TYPE_PLAIN_ONLY` declines it to the general matcher as an oracle): 20,000 rows both,
   multiset identical, sequence identical. The bench now reports `rowCount` and an
   ORDER-INDEPENDENT digest, and its comment records why the obvious check is wrong here.
2. **`[...buckets].sort()` allocated once per far vertex** — a defensive copy over an array the
   caller already owns as scratch. Sorted in place.
3. **A unit test's comment asserted the opposite of its own assertion** (`4 >= 1 * 8` declines; the
   comment said "the gate accepts"). Corrected, and the test renamed to what it actually checks.

### The Gremlin twin CANNOT be built, and that is a licence difference not an untried lever

GQL's far-driven walk is sound only because an unordered GQL result's row order is unspecified —
`farDrivenHopWalk`'s header says so, and `hopOrderPlan` forces the start-driven arm under `ORDER BY`
(which this branch inherits through `startDrivenForOrder`, covered by
`ordered-node-projection.test.ts`). **Gremlin has no such licence**: stream order is a TinkerPop
contract and the differential fuzzer compares ORDERED, so hoisting `pick(far)` to once per far vertex
would reorder rows. It would otherwise look like a ~100x-fewer-property-reads lever on Gremlin's
hottest yield row. Recorded so it is not priced again.

**M4 removed the `matchesLabel(far, farLabel)` check from the far-driven multi-type walk and the
whole suite stayed green.** The hole is reachable and specific: `hopEnds` constrains the START label
to a simple one, but the FAR label may be any expression, and `candidateVertexSource` seeds from a
label bucket only for a SIMPLE label — for anything else it yields every vertex and leaves the
filtering to its caller. So on `:A&B` that one check is the only thing doing the work. A fixture with
fan-in 20 (over the gate's threshold, so it genuinely takes this route), one endpoint carrying both
labels and one carrying only `A`, answers **20 where a walk skipping the test answers 40**. Four
tests added; M4 is now caught by two of them.

### ⚠️ I MEASURED HEAD AGAINST ITSELF FOR TWENTY MINUTES, AND NEITHER THE TESTS NOR THE GATES NOTICED

The patch script applied two replacements to a string and wrote once at the end. A doc anchor failed
AFTER the code replacement had already succeeded in memory, so the assertion threw and **nothing
reached disk**. I then ran the bench and read 73.7 / 80.8, repeated it four times, reasoned about a
1.10x spelling asymmetry, and drafted a refutation — from numbers that could not contain the change.
`bun run check` was 0 and 3,570 tests passed throughout, because the tree was simply unmodified.

Two things caught it and neither was attention: a `grep -c` of the new symbol returned 0, and the A/B
DRIVER refused to start — _"working tree is not the HAND arm"_. That is CLAUDE.md's "assert each A/B
arm IS the code it claims" doing its job. The rule was applied to drivers and not to the in-place
edit that precedes them; `PROBES.md` now carries the gap: **write, read the file back, count the
marker, and only then build. A patch script should assert on what it can re-read, not on what it
computed.**

Note what this says about the earlier reading: the 1.10x "asymmetry" and the "refutation" were both
noise on an unchanged binary, and the real answer is a clean 12.8% win. An unverified arm does not
merely waste time — it produces a confident wrong conclusion in whichever direction the noise falls.

| arm              | engine | top frames                                           |
| ---------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |

### A constant ablation is NOT a price, and checking that was right even though the worry was wrong

Replacing the picker with `() => 1` read **49.2%** of `hopyieldsingle` (and 43.8% of the multi arm),
with `hopcount3` — which reads no property at all — at 0.5%. But 49.2% of 155.3 ms over 200,000 rows
is **~382 ns a row**, and `edge.to` caches `#toV` on the Edge while `properties` caches `#box` on the
Vertex, so the warm chain is two private-field reads. An ablation to a CONSTANT also lets the
optimizer collapse work downstream of the picker, so it bounds the lever from above.

**So it was decomposed into four arms, each keeping strictly more work than the last** — `CONST`,
`BAG` (touch the accessor, return 1), `READ` (full read, constant output), `BASE`. The worry about
dead-code elimination turned out to be **wrong on the specifics**: `BASE − READ` is 0.573 ms, so a
varied value flowing into the result costs nothing and the 44% is real. It just is not where it
looked.

### The decomposition, and the knob that settled the mechanism

`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`, `hopyieldsingle`, `NODES=200000`, median of 3 (spread) / 2
(concentrated) processes per arm, order-alternated rounds. `FANIN` added to this bench for the
purpose — the GQL twin got it at item 1390.

| term                          | `FANIN=1` (in-degree 1) | `FANIN=0.01` (in-degree ~100) |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| the `far.properties` ACCESSOR | **42.967 ms**           | **1.990 ms**                  |
| the key index `[k]`           | 17.657 ms               | 2.610 ms                      |
| the varied value              | 0.573 ms                | −1.244 ms                     |
| **total**                     | **61.197 ms = 44.1%**   | **3.356 ms = 4.0%**           |

**The accessor is 21.6x cheaper when the far pool is cache-resident.** And the internal control is
what makes this conclusive rather than suggestive: the no-read `CONST` arm is **77.631 ms spread
against 79.674 concentrated — FLAT**. So the entire fan-in sensitivity of this row (136.8 → 82.8,
1.65x) is the property read, and none of it is the walk.

### What that closes, and what it opens

- **CLOSED: there is no per-row lever in the accessor.** `pick` is already a per-compile closure
  capturing the key (`far.properties[valueKey]`), `get properties` is `#box ??= …` with the
  `Map.get` already removed at item 162, and the cost is memory latency reached through both. Nothing
  about the code path can be rewritten to avoid a cold-object dereference. Do not re-price `pick`,
  `get properties`, or "specialize the property read" on this row.
- **It is the same family item 1066 measured from the other direction**: holding the scan, the edges
  and the row count fixed and varying ONLY how many distinct far vertices the edges reach moved a
  far-end projection **9.3x** (14.16 ms over a 50,000-wide far pool against 1.52 over a 100-wide
  one). This item reaches that conclusion by ablation instead of by fixture shape, on a different
  surface, and the two agree.
- **OPEN, and better justified than before**: the columnar property layout, priced at **3.55x**
  (items 1363-1364). It is the only thing that addresses a cold dereference, because it replaces the
  dereference rather than shortening it. It **changes the public `properties` contract** — the getter
  returns the graph's live frozen bag — so it is a deliberate API decision and not an optimization to
  slip into a loop. The number to beat is now concrete: **44.1% of a yield row at in-degree 1**.

### The one NOT built: `RegExp: [\uD800-\uDBFF]` at 4.9% of `sortedpage`

A regex executing per string comparison looks like free money. `compareCodePoints`' own doc already
records the whole investigation, next to the code, exactly as CLAUDE.md asks:

- a manual charCode loop — **REFUTED**: 1.08x on ASCII, and **3.6x WORSE** on keys with a long
  shared prefix, because V8's character-class match beats a hand-written loop;
- deciding from the first differing code UNIT — **REFUTED ON CORRECTNESS**, premise and all: equal
  unit prefixes do not imply equal code-POINT prefixes;
- hoisting the guard out of the comparator — **SOUND but DECLINED** at "~1.07x at best for an
  invasive change", ending "if you come back to this, the hoist is the only live option".

I came back to it and the note was sufficient: 4.9% is consistent with that 1.07x ceiling. **Nothing

### The one built: `isTemporal`, bounded first

`isTemporal` is six sequential `instanceof` checks, at 3.5% of `sortedpage`, 4.1% of `hopfilter` and
5.1% of `point`. Those are 3-5% shares on rows whose noise floor is ~10%, so the ablation came
first — replace the whole predicate with `false`, answer-identical on these fixtures and wrong in
general, to read the ceiling:

| shape                      | BASE p25 | ablated | BOUND     | concordance        |
| -------------------------- | -------- | ------- | --------- | ------------------ |
| `point`                    | 4.2765   | 3.6900  | **13.7%** | **36/36**          |
| `hopfilter`                | 3.6330   | 3.3895  | 6.7%      | 34/36              |
| `sortedpage`               | 10.2755  | 9.6760  | 5.8%      | 24/36              |
| `hopsingleyield` [CONTROL] | 38.8800  | 36.8965 | 5.1%      | **18/36 — chance** |

The control is what made the three positives trustworthy: `hopsingleyield` at exactly 18/36 confirms
the yield path never calls this, so the readings are not a global drift. Digests agreed across arms,
which checks rather than assumes that the fixtures hold no temporal values.

### What shipped, and what it captured

One `typeof v === 'object' && v !== null` before the six `instanceof`s. The guard looks redundant —
`instanceof` on a primitive already returns false — and the point is that it does so SIX times, each
walking the right-hand side's prototype, for nearly every value the engine compares. Sound because
every Temporal is a class instance, hence always a non-null `object`.

| shape                      | BASE p25 | TYPEOF     | change    | concordance         | of the bound |
| -------------------------- | -------- | ---------- | --------- | ------------------- | ------------ |
| `point`                    | 4.2845   | **3.7520** | **12.4%** | **144/144**         | 90%          |
| `hopfilter`                | 3.6885   | **3.4210** | **7.3%**  | 115/144             | ~100%        |
| `sortedpage`               | 10.2085  | **9.5365** | **6.6%**  | 108/144             | ~100%        |
| `hopsingleyield` [CONTROL] | 35.9325  | 37.5420    | −4.5%     | **69/144 — chance** | —            |

n=12 per arm, 3 order-alternated rounds. **The control read +5.1% in the ablation run and −4.5%
here, both at chance** — both signs appearing across two experiments on the same row is better
evidence of noise than either reading alone, and there is no mechanism for it to be real.

### The tests it did not have, and the comment the mutants refuted

`isTemporal` had **no direct tests** — 370 core tests covered it indirectly. That matters because a
wrong guard fails SILENTLY: a temporal misclassified as non-temporal does not throw, it takes the
other comparison branch, and this repo's cross-type comparison policy (string-vs-temporal `=` is
no-match, `<=` throws) would quietly change. 13 tests added, both directions.

Three mutants, and **one survived and refuted a claim I had written in the test's own comment**:

| mutant                                              | verdict           |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| M1 guard inverted (`=== 'object'` → `!== 'object'`) | CAUGHT 7/6        |
| M2 the `v !== null` half dropped                    | **SURVIVED 13/0** |
| M3 the guard swallows everything                    | CAUGHT 7/6        |

I had written that the guard's two halves are "both load-bearing". **They are not.** Dropping
`v !== null` leaves every test green, because `typeof null === 'object'` lets null through to
`null instanceof LocalDate`, which is false anyway. It stays as a PERFORMANCE guard — this engine
treats null as a stored, present value, so nulls reach comparisons routinely and without that half
each one pays all six checks — and the comment now says that instead of the thing the mutant
disproved.

### Item 1395 — by-id access is **genuinely O(1)**, confirmed at **~5 ns hot / ~18 ns cold** by two experiments with opposite predictions. The standing requirement's own probe reported **105-130 ns with a +22-31% drift indistinguishable from O(log N)**, and ~50 ns of that is the probe CONSTRUCTING ITS OWN KEYS

"Keep good O(1) access to get a vertex or edge by id" is a standing requirement, and
`id-lookup-is-o1-probe.ts` (item 1326) exists to verify it. Re-run on two core arms over a 16x range:

| arm                  | 50,000 | 200,000 | 800,000  | drift      |
| -------------------- | ------ | ------- | -------- | ---------- |
| `core-getVertexById` | 105.7  | 112.6   | 129.5 ns | **+22.5%** |
| `core-getEdgeById`   | 99.9   | 111.9   | 130.5 ns | **+30.6%** |

**That is not flat, and it must not be waved away as cache**: `log2(800000) / log2(50000)` is
**1.26**, so a logarithmic structure predicts +26% — between the two numbers measured. A size sweep
cannot tell the two apart, because N moves the structure and the working set together.

### The discriminator: two experiments whose predictions are OPPOSITE

`id-lookup-hotset-probe.mjs` holds one variable fixed at a time. If the cost is CACHE it tracks the
hot set; if it is COMPLEXITY it tracks N.

| experiment                               | result                                               | verdict |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| hot set FIXED at 1,000 ids, N varied 16x | **5.15 / 4.78 / 4.90 ns — FLAT**, and non-monotonic  | cache   |
| N FIXED at 800,000, hot set varied 800x  | **5.15 → 9.05 → 18.64 → 17.93 ns — RISES, plateaus** | cache   |

Both landed on the cache side, so **complexity is ruled out and the requirement holds**: by-id
access is ~5 ns with the entry cache-resident and ~18 ns once the working set exceeds cache. The
edge arm agrees (5.37 ns at a 1,000-id hot set). The hot ids are spread by stride rather than taken
from the front, because a contiguous prefix is exactly how `ordinal-churn-probe.mjs` made a large
structure look small and measured churn as free.

### Where the other 100 ns went: the probe builds a fresh string per lookup

`id-lookup-is-o1-probe.ts` calls `g.getVertexById(`v${i}`)`. Adding a `CONSTRUCT=1` mode that does
the same, with the hot set fixed:

| mode                                | 50,000 | 200,000 | 800,000      |
| ----------------------------------- | ------ | ------- | ------------ |
| pre-built id string                 | 5.15   | 4.78    | **4.90 ns**  |
| constructs `` `v${i}` `` per lookup | 49.17  | 50.08   | **56.32 ns** |

**Key construction is ~45-56 ns — ten times the lookup itself — and it drifts +14.5% on its own**,
because ids grow from 5 characters to 7 across the sweep. So that probe's 105-130 ns decomposes into
~5 ns of lookup, ~50 ns of building the key, and the rest cache misses from touching all N entries;
and its "size drift" is part key length, part cache, no part complexity.

**Both halves matter and neither is the other's correction.** A caller that builds ids in a loop
really does pay the ~50 ns, so the probe is not wrong — it measures "lookup plus building the key".
But quoting it as the engine's by-id cost overstates that cost by ~20x, which is the reading the
standing requirement invites. Both probes are annotated with the decomposition and with which figure
to quote.

### `getEdgeById` at 16.6% of edge ingest is MISATTRIBUTION, not a target

`addEdge` does one `getEdgeById` per call (a duplicate-id guard), so 180 ms over 600,000 edges is
~300 ns a call — against the 19 ns this same screen just measured for a lookup. The function is
`this.edgesById.get(id) ?? null`, one line. **This is the item 1104 self-time trap**: a small hot
callee credited with its caller's inlined loop, exactly as `edgesOfTypes` read 37.9% self for a
single `Map.get` there, and exactly what was declined for `pick` at item 1392. Not pursued.

One real micro-redundancy found while reading it, and declined: the guard is
`if (params.id && this.getEdgeById(params.id)) { return this.getEdgeById(params.id)!; }` — **two
lookups on the duplicate-id path**. It fires only when an id collides, never during ingest, so it is
one `Map.get` on a rare path. Recorded rather than changed.

⚠️ `grep` found NONE of this: `Graph.ts` is the Unicode file `grep` treats as binary, so
`grep -n getEdgeById packages/core/src/core/Graph.ts` printed nothing while the file contains six
occurrences. Read it with python `str.count`/`re`, per the standing note.

### The sixth arrival has an answer the first five did not

**The prerequisite was built and measured in this session.** A dense integer-keyed adjacency needs a
stable dense integer per vertex — the ordinal — and items 1369-1372 measured exactly that:

| side                    | result                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| reads                   | **+12.9%** on the largest Gremlin row (1369), 63/64 concordance — a real win |
| writes                  | **~0%** (1357)                                                               |
| **deletes under churn** | **6.18x at 200k churn, 11.34x at 1M** (1372)                                 |

Deletes disqualify it, because slots are never reused and the touched slot space grows without
bound. Making it correct under churn needs a free list plus generation stamps — which is precisely
the "much more booking to keep a second structure in alignment" the user objected to when this was
proposed, and item 1372 records that the objection was right on measurement rather than on taste.

So the chain terminates: **`indexEdgeLabel`'s only surviving lever is not parked pending work, it is
declined on numbers.** The five arrivals were right that nothing else was there; what they were
missing was a measurement of the one thing left, and it now exists.

### The cliff is not depth, it is a VACUOUS FAR LABEL

Depth 4 _is_ implemented — item 692 built `trailsAt4From` and `Trail4Tables`, validated by a
brute-force oracle. Isolating my query clause by clause, on 100,000 vertices where **every vertex
carries `P`**, so the label rejects nothing. Every row answers **400,000**:

| query                          | ms        | route                               |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `MATCH ()-[:E]->{1,4}()`       | **43.2**  | closed form                         |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->{1,4}()`    | **32.2**  | closed form — a START label is fine |
| `MATCH ()-[:E]->{1,4}(b:P)`    | **433.7** | **declined**                        |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->{1,4}(b:P)` | 478.9     | **declined**                        |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->{1,3}(b:P)` | 20.8      | depth 3 takes it WITH the far label |

A windowed profile of the declined row confirms the route rather than inferring it from the cost: no
`walkLevelCount`, no `varLengthDegreeCount`, no `trailsAt4From` — `flatAdj` 36.6%, `evalLabelExpr`
15.6%, `trailEnds` 14.6%, `walkSegments` 8.1%. It is the general matcher.

### The code had already written this down, without a number

`depth4Admissible`'s own doc: _"The test has to be STATIC. `passesIsVacuous` is the flag that
actually matters, but it is a QUERY-TIME value — it calls `vacuousLabel(graph, …)` — and
`walkLevelCount` returns a number with no way to decline once chosen. So this refuses on the SYNTAX,
which is stricter than necessary: **a label every node happens to carry would be vacuous at runtime
and is refused here anyway.**"_

So this is a **known, documented conservatism, not an oversight** — and it had never been priced.
11-13x is a large number to sit behind the words "stricter than necessary", and it is now recorded
next to the code.

**NOT TAKEN, and the gate must not be relaxed on its own.** The depth-4 terms are derived for a
trivial endpoint mask; item 692 already shipped that mistake once and it answered the WALK count
(450,000 against the trail's 449,998), caught by printing answers beside times. A correct fix needs a
way to **decline after choosing**, so the closure can test `vacuousLabel` with the graph in hand and
fall back when the label really does filter — ~~an architecture change to how detectors hand back work,
not a predicate tweak. That is its own item and arguably its own design decision.~~ **WRONG, and
corrected at 1399: `fastPath` already returns `undefined` to mean "the general clause loop must
run", so the decline mechanism existed and the fix was FOUR SMALL EDITS. Shipped at 1399 for 9.6x —
and the mutants there showed the gate may be removable for FILTERING labels too, 9.9x, pending the
brute-force oracle.**

### Item 1399 — **SHIPPED, 9.6x** on a depth-4 trail with a vacuous endpoint label (433.7 ms → 45.1), by declining at RUN TIME instead of refusing on syntax. Item 1398 called that an architecture change; **it was four small edits and I was wrong.** And all three mutants SURVIVED, which revealed ~~the bigger finding: the gate may be unnecessary for FILTERING labels too — **44.2 ms, correct, 9.9x**~~ **a FIXTURE ARTEFACT — REFUTED at 1400: the extended oracle answers −3, a NEGATIVE count, with the gate removed. The 9.9x does not exist and the gate is load-bearing**

Item 1398 priced `depth4Admissible`'s conservatism at 11-13x and concluded a fix "needs a way to
decline after choosing… an architecture change to how detectors hand back work". **That was wrong,
and reading the dispatch is what corrected it**: `fastPath`'s own contract is already _"Returns
`undefined` when every detector declined and the general clause loop must run"_. The mechanism
existed; only the rung keyed on whether the closure EXISTS rather than on what it returns.

### What shipped: four edits

1. the ladder rung in `clauses.ts` tolerates a runtime `undefined` and falls through;
2. `varLengthCount`'s type widens to `Row[] | undefined` — uniquely among the nineteen detectors;
3. `depth4Admissible` admits a depth-4 trail with a LABEL (still refusing a PREDICATE, which cannot
   be shown vacuous cheaply);
4. the closure declines when `max === 4 && isTrail && eff !== undefined` — and `eff` was **already
   being computed there** via `vacuousLabel(graph, endLabel)`, so no new work on any path.

| graph                          | query        | before   | after       | answer                 |
| ------------------------------ | ------------ | -------- | ----------- | ---------------------- |
| `:P` on every vertex (vacuous) | `{1,4}(b:P)` | 433.7 ms | **45.1 ms** | 400,000 ✓              |
| `:P` on every vertex           | `{1,4}()`    | 43.2     | 38.1        | 400,000                |
| half `:P`, half `:Q` (filters) | `{1,4}(b:P)` | 435.8    | 435.8       | **200,000** ✓ declines |

The filtering row is the correctness half: it answers the FILTERED count, so the decline really does
reach the general matcher rather than the closed form.

### ⚠️ ALL THREE MUTANTS SURVIVED, and that is the finding

Nine tests, both regimes, the triangle where trail and walk genuinely differ (9 against the walk's
12). Then three mutants — dropping the runtime decline, ignoring TRAIL mode, relaxing the compile
gate to admit a predicate — and **every one survived, 9 pass / 0 fail.**

Not because the tests are weak in the dangerous direction. Applying the "no decline" mutant by hand
and measuring it directly:

| no-decline arm             | ms       | answer        |
| -------------------------- | -------- | ------------- |
| vacuous `{1,4}(b:P)`       | 41.4     | 400,000 ✓     |
| **filtering `{1,4}(b:P)`** | **44.2** | **200,000 ✓** |
| filtering `{1,4}(b:Q)`     | 36.1     | 200,000 ✓     |

**The depth-4 closed form answers a FILTERING endpoint label correctly, at 44.2 ms against the
declined path's 435.8 — 9.9x, on a class ten times wider than the one this item shipped.** So the
`passesIsVacuous` gate is conservative rather than load-bearing, at least on these fixtures, and the
decline I shipped is belt-and-braces over a path that appears already correct.

**That is NOT enough to remove the gate.** "It agrees on two fixtures" is exactly the evidence item
692 had when it shipped the wrong count (450,000 against the trail's 449,998) on this very family,
caught by a brute-force oracle and not by any timing. The oracle exists —
`trail-count-bruteforce.test.ts`, built at item 690, which asserts its generator produced
self-loops, parallel edges and reverse edges because those are what separate a trail from a walk —
and it does not currently vary an endpoint label.

**NEXT: extend that oracle to a filtering endpoint label at depth 4.** If it holds over randomized
graphs with all three hazards, the gate comes out and the 9.9x applies to every filtering label, not
just vacuous ones. That is the item this one opens, and it is a correctness question before it is a
perf one.

### Gates

gql **3579/0** (9 new), gremlin 1157/0, core 383/0, serialization 144/0, `bun run fuzz` 20/0, the
brute-force oracle 3/0, `bun run check` 0 (read unpiped). The hand-applied mutant was restored and
verified (marker present, full suite green) before anything was committed.

Two test defects of my own, both caught by the suite rather than by review: `WALK` is a PREFIX
(`MATCH WALK (…)`), which I first wrote as a suffix and the parser rejected outright; and one
assertion stated a count I had guessed rather than derived — replaced with a RELATION (an always-true
predicate gives the unfiltered count, a selective one strictly less), because a number I cannot
derive is a number the test cannot defend.

### Item 1400 — the oracle extension **REFUTES item 1399's own suggestion**: removing the depth-4 endpoint-mask gate answers **−3**, a NEGATIVE count, on randomized multigraphs. The 9.9x it measured was fixture luck, and the gate is load-bearing

Item 1399 shipped a 9.6x and then reported something larger: its three mutants all survived, and
applying the "no decline" one by hand showed the depth-4 closed form answering a **filtering**
endpoint label correctly at **44.2 ms against the declined path's 435.8 — 9.9x** on a class ten times
wider. It explicitly refused to act on that, because "it agrees on two fixtures" is the evidence item
692 had when it shipped a wrong depth-4 count, and it named the next step: extend the brute-force
oracle to a filtering endpoint label.

**That was the right call, and the oracle says the gate stays.**

### What the oracle did not cover, and now does

`trail-count-bruteforce.test.ts` (item 690) already varies the endpoint with a `WHERE` predicate at
depths 1-4 — but `depth4Admissible` refuses a predicate at depth 4, so those rows take the
enumerating path and say nothing about the closed form. **A LABEL is the only spelling that can reach
the depth-4 terms with a non-trivial mask**, and that spelling was untested.

Added: for each randomized multigraph, every depth range including `{4}`, `{1,4}` and `{2,4}`, a
**vacuous** label (`:P`, every vertex — must equal no label at all) and a **filtering** label
(`:V{j}`, exactly one vertex) for every `j`, each against `brute(…, (v) => v === j)`. 2,478
assertions. The generator's own self-checks carry over — self-loops, parallel edges and reverse
edges, the three structures the trail terms exist for — plus one of its own: **a filtering label that
selected nothing anywhere would make every assertion `0 === 0`**, so `nonZeroFiltered > 100` is
asserted.

### The verdict

| mutant                                 | verdict             | answered |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------- | -------- |
| **M1 the runtime decline dropped**     | **CAUGHT**          | **−3**   |
| M2 the decline ignores TRAIL mode      | SURVIVED, by design | —        |
| M3 the compile gate admits a PREDICATE | **CAUGHT**          | 32       |

**A count of negative three.** With a non-trivial endpoint mask the depth-4 trail correction subtracts
more than the walk count it corrects. Not a slightly wrong number — a structurally impossible one,
which is the clearest possible answer to "is this gate necessary".

So **item 1399's 9.9x does not exist.** The two 100,000-vertex fixtures it measured happened to be
shapes where the terms coincide; they have out-degree 1, one long cycle, no self-loops and no
parallel edges — precisely the structures the trail correction exists for, all absent. This is
CLAUDE.md's "match the fixture to the claim" arriving as a correctness failure rather than a
mis-measurement.

**M2 survives by design**, and the distinction is worth keeping straight: dropping `isTrail` makes a
depth-4 WALK with a filtering label decline unnecessarily — slower, same answer. No test can catch an
answer-equivalent change, exactly as at item 1391's sort mutant; its guard is a bench row.

### What this leaves

- item 1399's shipped decline is **correct and necessary**, and now has oracle-grade teeth where its
  nine hand-written tests had none;
- the depth-4 closed form remains restricted to a trivial endpoint mask, and the comment saying its
  terms "were derived for a TRIVIAL endpoint mask… nothing validates them against a filtered one" is
  **vindicated as a correctness constraint, not conservatism**;
- the real open question is unchanged and is mathematical: derive the depth-4 trail correction for a
  filtered mask, as item 600 did for depth 3. The oracle is now the instrument that would check it.

Item 1400 found that a degenerate fixture can hide a **correctness** difference, not merely a cost
one: removing the depth-4 endpoint-mask gate measured "correct and 9.9x faster" on the isolated bench
and answers **−3** on randomized multigraphs, because the structures the trail correction exists for
— self-loops, parallel edges, reverse edges — were all absent. That makes the fixture itself the thing
to audit, and the audit has a specific gap: **the Gremlin bench has had `FANOUT` since it was written
and the GQL bench never did.** Out-degree was exactly 1, one permutation cycle, for every GQL
measurement in items 1386-1400.

### `FANOUT=1` reproduces the old fixture byte-for-byte

Verified by digest rather than asserted — `hopcount` 200,000, `hopsingleyield` and `hopmultiyield`
200,000 rows and digest 19999900000 at `FANOUT=1`, identical to the pre-knob runs. So the knob costs
nothing to leave alone, which is the only way an added dimension is safe to put under existing rows.

### The audit: the session's own spelling fixes, at degree 4

Items 1382, 1384, 1386 and 1388 each closed an equivalent-spelling gap by sorting buckets
largest-first, and **every one of them was validated at out-degree 1 only** — where a vertex has at
most one bucket per type and the asymmetry the sort removes is at its smallest.

| pair                                 | `FANOUT=1`    | `FANOUT=4`      | symmetry  |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------- | --------------- | --------- |
| `hopmulti` / `hopmultirev` (count)   | 0.42 / 0.42   | 1.81 / 1.79     | **1.01x** |
| `hopmultiyield` / `hopmultiyieldrev` | 26.31 / 26.76 | 139.38 / 136.83 | **1.02x** |

**They hold.** Digests match within each setting and the counts scale exactly (400,000 = 4 x
100,000). This is the first evidence for those four fixes at a degree where the sort has something to
do, and it is a positive result rather than a correction — worth recording for that reason, since the
three fixture surprises before it all went the other way.

### And one asserted caveat becomes a measured fact

Item 1398 compared the quantifier against the explicit chain and wrote that they are "NOT equivalent
in general: a quantified path is a TRAIL and may not repeat an edge, while the chain may, so a
fixture with a 2-cycle would make the answers diverge legitimately". At degree 4 that is no longer
hypothetical:

|                     | `FANOUT=1`      | `FANOUT=4`                 |
| ------------------- | --------------- | -------------------------- |
| `{2,2}` vs `chain2` | 50,000 = 50,000 | **799,996 vs 800,000**     |
| `{3,3}` vs `chain3` | 50,000 = 50,000 | **3,199,944 vs 3,200,000** |

4 two-paths and 56 three-paths revisit an edge, so the trail correction is doing real work. The bench
rows are now bounded to `FANOUT=1` for the spelling comparison and documented as a semantics
demonstration above it — a pair that silently becomes two different questions is exactly the kind of
row that produces a confident wrong conclusion later.

Item 1398's routing finding survives the change of fixture: at degree 4 the chain is **2.98x** faster
at depth 2 and the quantifier **3.01x** faster at depth 3, the same non-monotonic crossover.

### Item 1403 — **SHIPPED, 32.0% and 43.5%** (144/144 both): item 1390's `FAR_DRIVEN_MIN_DEGREE = 8` was calibrated at out-degree 1 and refused a route worth that much at degree 3-4. Lowered to **4** on a sweep, and the control's `−2.8%` FLIPPED SIGN at n=24

### What 8 was, and what was wrong with it

Item 1390 swept fan-in **1.33 / 13 / 133** and picked 8. Every one of those readings was at
out-degree 1 — the knob did not exist — so the sweep had a two-order-of-magnitude gap in the middle
and the threshold landed in it. Sweeping OUT-degree instead, n=12 per cell, three order-alternated
rounds:

| est. degree                      | min=8  | min=4     | change    | concordance     |
| -------------------------------- | ------ | --------- | --------- | --------------- |
| 1.33                             | 27.08  | 27.02     | 0.2%      | 64/144 — chance |
| 2.67                             | 65.86  | 65.34     | 0.8%      | 83/144 — chance |
| **4.00**                         | 107.32 | **72.99** | **32.0%** | **144/144**     |
| **5.33**                         | 145.72 | **82.28** | **43.5%** | **144/144**     |
| `hopsingleyield` @1.33 [CONTROL] | 17.95  | 18.24     | −1.6%     | 64/144          |
| `hopsingleyield` @5.33 [CONTROL] | 26.78  | 25.78     | +3.7%     | 103/144         |

**Lowering it changes nothing below the boundary** — the two sub-threshold rows are flat at chance,
because both arms decline there, which is exactly the shape a threshold change should have.
Cross-arm `rowCount` and digest identical on every cell.

### The control's first reading was −2.8%, and the sign FLIPPED

The 8-vs-4 pilot read `hopsingleyield` at degree 4 as **−2.8% with 16/64** — away from chance, and
with no mechanism, since the single-type path never reads this constant. I refused to ship on it. At
n=24 it reads **+3.7% at 103/144**: the sign flipped, which is the n=8 instability this repo
documents (items 1367, 1374, 1380, 1393) rather than a real effect. **That is the fifth instance**,
and the first where the suspicious reading was resolved by sample size rather than by finding a
mechanism — the previous time (item 1390's −3.7%) there WAS one.

### What is bracketed and what is not

~~**The crossover is in (2.67, 4.00] and is not pinned.** Below 4 both arms take the same route, so the
bench cannot see whether 3 or 2 would capture more without a third arm.~~ **CLOSED at 1404: `min=2` is 7.2% faster at 142/144 and is DECLINED, because the estimate's 2x bias would make it accept at a TRUE degree of 1, where this route loses 1.24x. The fix is the estimate, not the threshold.**

**And the estimate is biased HIGH**, which is the argument against dropping further on a hunch:
`typeEdgeCount` sums the named buckets, so a two-type edge counts twice — the estimate reads 1.33x

### Item 1404 — ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED BY ITEM 1434** (its `min=2` was declined for a bias that item 1407 then removed; the threshold is now 1). the bracket is CLOSED: `min=2` is **7.2% faster at 142/144** and is **DECLINED**, because the estimate's bias would make it accept at a TRUE degree of 1 — where item 1390 measured this route losing **1.24x**. The fix is the estimate, not the threshold ~~(threshold stays 4)~~ **— and its 7.2%-at-true-degree-2 is CONTRADICTED at 1405: disjoint types lose 16.9% at the same degree, so bucket structure matters too. Threshold is 3 since 1406.**

Item 1403 shipped `FAR_DRIVEN_MIN_DEGREE = 4` and left one thing open rather than silently: the
crossover was bracketed in **(2.67, 4.00]**, and below 4 both arms take the same route so the bench
could not see further without a third arm. This is that arm, run now rather than named — because
`CLOSED.md`'s own sweep found 35 entries advertising work already done, and a follow-up deferred is a
follow-up that lingers.

### The measurement

One decisive cell plus three controls, n=12 each, three order-alternated rounds. Cross-arm `rowCount`
and digest identical throughout.

| cell                                        | est. degree | min=4 | min=2     | change   | concordance |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ----- | --------- | -------- | ----------- |
| `hopmultiyield`                             | 2.67        | 63.57 | **59.02** | **7.2%** | **142/144** |
| `hopmultiyield` [CONTROL — both decline]    | 1.33        | 28.52 | 27.20     | 4.6%     | 73/144      |
| `hopmultiyield` [CONTROL — both accept]     | 5.33        | 83.03 | 82.70     | 0.4%     | 71/144      |
| `hopsingleyield` [CONTROL — never reads it] | 2.67        | 23.21 | 23.00     | 0.9%     | 80/144      |

**The win is real** — 142/144 is as close to unanimous as this harness gets — and the three controls
sit at chance, which is exactly the signature of a threshold change that differs from its baseline
only where the two values straddle the data.

### Why it is declined anyway

**The estimate is biased high, and the bias is unbounded in the wrong direction.** `typeEdgeCount`
sums the named buckets, so an edge carrying two of them counts twice: the estimate reads **1.33x**
the true degree at `MULTILABEL=3` and **2x** when every edge carries both types.

So `min=2` accepts at a **true degree of 1** on a densely multi-labelled graph — and that is
precisely where item 1390 measured this route **losing 1.24x** (86.1 ms against the start-driven
69.3). `min=4` cannot reach below true degree 2, which is where the win is actually measured.

Trading a measured 7.2% in a narrow band for a measured 1.24x regression on a shape this engine is
built for is the wrong trade. Recorded with its number next to the constant, per the standing rule
about rejected optimizations, so the next person to sweep this gate finds the 7.2% and the reason
together.

### The real follow-up, priced

**Fix the estimate, not the threshold.** `sumIsExact` already exists for "no edge carries two types"
(`graph.multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`), and a gate consulting it could drop to 2 exactly when the sum is
unbiased — capturing the 7.2% with no exposure at true degree 1. Not taken here because it adds a
second condition to a gate whose whole value is being O(k) and obvious, and because the ceiling is
7.2% rather than the 32-43.5% item 1403 already took. Priced, named, and left for a deliberate
decision instead of a reflex.

### Items 1405-1406 — ~~SHIPPED, 18.0%~~ ⟶ **THE THRESHOLD IT SET (3) IS SUPERSEDED BY ITEM 1434, WHICH MEASURED THE SIGN FLIPPED AND SET 1.** Its 16.9% loss at true degree 2 predates item 1407's row builder. Original heading: SHIPPED, 18.0% (144/144): the bench could not build a DISJOINT-type graph, which is what a real schema has. Built, and it pins the crossover between true degree **2 (−16.9%)** and **3 (+25.1%)** — so the threshold is **3**, not 4. And at the same degree the sign DEPENDS ON BUCKET STRUCTURE, which one scalar cannot express

Every multi-type row in this bench has used OVERLAPPING types — every Nth edge carrying both — which
makes `graph.multiTypeEdgeCount` non-zero and `typeEdgeCount` an over-count: at `MULTILABEL=3` the
degree estimate reads **1.33x** the truth. Two distinct relationship types that never co-occur on one
edge is the ordinary schema, and it reads the estimate **exactly**. `MULTILABEL=-1` builds that
(`-1` rather than `0`, because `0` already means "no `F` at all", the control items 1375 and 1390
rely on).

### Why it mattered: the bias was deciding the route

With the 1.33x over-count, a true degree of 3 reads **4.00** and clears a threshold of 4. On a
disjoint graph the same true degree 3 reads **3.00** and is refused — and item 1403 had measured true
degree 3 winning **32%**. So the bias was accidentally helping the bench's own fixture and penalising
the common case.

### The crossover, pinned to an integer

Disjoint fixture, estimate exact, `min=4` against `min=2`, n=12 per cell, three order-alternated
rounds:

| est. = true degree            | min=4 | min=2     | change     | concordance |
| ----------------------------- | ----- | --------- | ---------- | ----------- |
| 1.00 [CONTROL — both decline] | 17.21 | 16.84     | 2.2%       | 72/144      |
| **2.00**                      | 39.99 | 46.77     | **−16.9%** | 35/144      |
| **3.00**                      | 67.84 | **50.80** | **+25.1%** | **144/144** |
| 4.00 [CONTROL — both accept]  | 53.54 | 53.10     | 0.8%       | 80/144      |

**The far-driven walk loses at true degree 2 and wins at true degree 3.** Both controls flat. That is
the tightest bracket this gate has had.

### ⚠️ And the scalar does not capture the decision

At true degree 2 with OVERLAPPING types the route **wins 7.2%** (item 1404); at true degree 2
DISJOINT it **loses 16.9%**. Same degree, opposite sign. So the **per-vertex bucket structure** is a
second, independent factor — a vertex with one 2-edge bucket and a vertex with two 1-edge buckets
cost the union count differently — and `typeEdgeCount / farEndpoints` cannot express it. The
threshold is a conservative line through a two-dimensional space, not a crossover point, and this
entry is the record of that rather than a claim to have modelled it.

It also retires the reasoning item 1404 shipped with: the bias is not the only thing distorting the
decision.

| 2.00 [CONTROL — still declines] | 40.85 | 40.43     | 1.0%      | 84/144      |
| 1.00 [CONTROL]                  | 18.37 | 17.82     | 3.0%      | 73/144      |
| 4.00 [CONTROL — both accept]    | 52.21 | 52.52     | −0.6%     | 55/144      |

3 takes the degree-3 win and **still declines at the degree-2 cell that regresses**, which 2 would
have accepted. Every cell measured says 3 beats 4; nothing measured says 2 beats 3.

principled fix remains the ESTIMATE rather than the threshold — `multiTypeEdgeCount === 0` already
tells the gate when its sum is exact — and it is still not taken, because it adds a second condition

### Item 1407 — **SHIPPED, 28.1% / 16.7% / 16.1%** (144/144 on all three): the far-driven walks rebuilt every row through COMPUTED-KEY stores. `{ ...template }` clones with the template's own hidden class, and the template becomes the first row instead of a discarded prototype

Item 1406's disjoint fixture had never been profiled. Windowed, it shows the hoist working and hands
over its own replacement cost:

| arm                               | engine | top frames                                                                    |
| --------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| degree 2 — declines, start-driven | 780 ms | `propOf` **31.1%**, `startDrivenMany` 21.5%, GC 21.5%, `get properties` 11.5% |
| degree 3 — accepts, far-driven    | 914 ms | **`rows` 58.7%**, GC 27.4%, `propOf` **2.5%**                                 |

That is the threshold's mechanism in one table: the far-driven hoist collapses the property read from
**42.6% to 2.5%**, and the cost moves into row construction — **86% between cloning and GC**. Per
row, degree 3 is 218 ns against degree 2's 279, which is exactly why 3 wins and 2 does not.

### The change

Both far-driven walks built each row as `{}` and then assigned **computed keys** from a hoisted
`keys`/`vals` pair, which cannot reuse the template's hidden class. Two edits:

- **`{ ...template }`** clones with that hidden class. Column ORDER stays correct because spread
  copies own enumerable keys in insertion order — which is the property the `Object.keys` round trip
  existed to guarantee, so the `keys`/`vals` pair is **gone** rather than reorganized. (Column order
  is BYTES for cross-engine identity.)
- **the template IS the first row.** `projectRow` returns a fresh object per far vertex and nothing
  retains it, so pushing it saves one clone in every `n` — a third of them at degree 3.

| shape                                    | est. degree | BASE  | SPREAD    | change    | concordance |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------- | ----- | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `hopsingleyield`                         | 1.00        | 11.14 | **8.01**  | **28.1%** | **144/144** |
| `hopsingleyield`                         | 3.00        | 24.39 | **20.31** | **16.7%** | **144/144** |

**28.1% is at degree 1**, the default fixture shape and the most ordinary hop there is. The control

### The single-type walk was found by its own control

The multi-type arm was measured first, and `hopsingleyield` sat in it as a control reading 1.1% at
72/144 — because only the multi-type walk had been changed. The single-type walk has the **identical
loop** on the **hotter** row: a plain one-type hop projection takes the far-driven route at any
degree, since its choice has no degree gate. So the control was not noise, it was a pointer, and the
change was applied there too and measured on its own row rather than assumed to inherit the result —
**item 159 measured this specific inner loop as 1.6x-sensitive to an added branch**, which is a
reason to measure it, not to avoid removing work from it.

### An edge case I introduced, found by reading my own diff

Pushing the template unconditionally changes behaviour on an **empty bucket**, where the old
`for (let n = bucket.size; n > 0; …)` produced zero rows and the spread form would produce one. The
single-type walk guarded only `bucket === undefined`.

Checked rather than assumed: **`removeEdge` DELETES the bucket** rather than leaving an empty `Set` —
after removing the only `E` edge, `b.adjTo.get('E')` is `undefined` and the query returns 0 rows. So
the case is unreachable today and **a mutant dropping the new guard SURVIVES**. It stays, documented
as defensive, because the spread form's correctness now depends on an invariant maintained in
`Graph`'s removal paths rather than in this file. The walk at the bottom of the same file already
guarded the same thing for its own reasons, which is what makes this a cheap place to stop depending
on another module.

On a fixture where **every vertex is `:P`**, so the label rejects nothing. Item 1066 priced the far
deref `matchesLabel` forces as the dominant cost of a hop once the far set stops being
cache-resident (9.3x over a 50,000-wide far pool against a 100-wide one) and gave every walk in this
file a vacuity drop — **except this one**, which then paid it **twice per vertex**, once in the
out-pass and once in the in-pass.

### The change

```ts
const fl = vacuousLabel(graph, farLabel) ? undefined : farLabel;
```

One line, computed **per call** — not per compile, because vacuity is a property of the graph, the
same reason the start-driven walk computes it there (items 195, 198, 1066) — and read in both
passes.

| shape                                        | est. degree | BASE   | VACUOUS   | change    | concordance |
| -------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------ | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| **`hopundiryield`**                          | 1.00        | 52.95  | **38.78** | **26.8%** | **144/144** |
| **`hopundiryield`**                          | 3.00        | 166.61 | **96.51** | **42.1%** | **144/144** |
| `hopsingleyield` [CONTROL — far-driven walk] | 1.00        | 9.84   | 9.12      | 7.3%      | 104/144     |
| `hopfiltyield` [CONTROL — filtered walk]     | 1.00        | 6.89   | 6.48      | 6.0%      | 93/144      |

`AB_ML=-1` (disjoint, item 1406), n=12 per cell, three order-alternated rounds. Both controls are
walks this edit **cannot reach** and both sit at 6-7 ms, inside their own floor, at 104/144 and
93/144 — weak, against two 144/144 targets at 27% and 42%. The degree-3 cell is the larger win
because the in-pass scan is per-edge, so the dropped deref scales with degree rather than with
vertices.

### ⚠️ The failure mode is a WRONG ROW SET, not a slow one

`undirected-vacuous-label.test.ts` (8 tests) pins both sides on fixtures that differ **only** in
whether the label is vacuous, because the same query is correct on one graph and wrong on another if
the drop is mis-decided. `b:P` and `b:Q` are each pinned against the other and against the
unlabelled total, so a mis-drop cannot pass by returning a superset. The self-loop case is there
too — the in-pass skips `edge.from === edge.to` because the out-pass already emitted it, and that
skip sits directly beside the lines changed.

Mutation verdicts:

| mutant                               | verdict                  |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------ |
| always drop (`const fl = undefined`) | **CAUGHT 4/4**           |
| never drop (`const fl = farLabel`)   | **SURVIVED — by design** |

"Never drop" is **answer-equivalent**: it is the code as it stood this morning, correct and slow.
No correctness test can catch it, which is exactly the shape of every index-seeding bug in this
repo's history. **Its only guard is the `hopundiryield` bench row** — which is the thing that did
not exist, and is why the row is the deliverable here as much as the one-line change is.
