### A prediction that half-held, and the half that did not is informative

The saving is per-EDGE, so the win should grow with degree. For the unfiltered walk it does —
**55.7% → 79.8%**. For the filtered walk it is **flat** (36.2% → 37.2%), and that is consistent
rather than contradictory: the rel gate `r.w < 100` is also evaluated per edge, so the dropped label
test and the work that remains scale together and the RATIO stays put. The absolute saving still
grows (5.58 ms → 29.85 ms). A win that failed to grow in BOTH walks would have said the mechanism
was misidentified; one that grows where nothing else is per-edge and holds where something else is
says it was not.

### ⚠️ The optional hop can be wrong at a CONSTANT row count

Its far test decides `matched`, and `matched` decides whether a start with no qualifying edge gets a
NULL row. So a wrongly-dropped label there does not add or remove rows — **it changes which starts
are padded**:

| on the filtering fixture | rows                    |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| correct                  | `[null, null, null, 2]` |
| label wrongly dropped    | `[null, null, 2, 5]`    |

**Four rows either way.** A suite that counted rows would pass. `startonly-optional-vacuous-label.test.ts`
(12 tests) therefore asserts values throughout, and the one length assertion compares against the
start count the engine itself reports rather than a literal.

The drop is sound because a vacuous label rejects nothing _by definition_, so every edge that set
`matched` still sets it — and the point of these tests is to make that an observation rather than an
assertion.

### A fixture trap, hit while writing those tests

`MATCH (a:P)` filters the START set by the same label, so moving a vertex off `P` to make the far
label meaningful **also removes it as a start**, and the two fixtures then differ in two ways at
once. My first version put the `Q` on a vertex that was the second edge's source, and five
assertions failed — for that reason and no defect. The rebuilt fixture lands the label difference on
`e`, a **sink**, so `a`..`d` are starts in both graphs and the two differ in exactly the property
under test. The trap is recorded in the test file's header, next to the fixture it shaped.

### Item 1411 — ~~MEASURED, no code change~~ ⟶ **BUILT at item 1412 (53.8% / 49.1%)**: the Gremlin hop pipeline costs **0%** over a hand-written generator with the same body. The entire ~~**2.1x**~~ **1.9-2.2x** gap to an array loop is the GENERATOR PROTOCOL, which is what `limit()` is built on — so the lever is a drain route, not a faster pipeline

> ⚠️ **TWO CORRECTIONS from item 1412, which both built this and re-measured it.**
>
> 1. **The `values`-shape ratio below is quoted as a point and is a RANGE.** Repeated as four
>    independent processes per shape: the bare hop is tight at **2.11-2.21x**, but the values shape
>    runs **1.44-1.99x** because its eager floor swings 29.6-40.8 ms — the far-vertex property read
>    is a cache-order-sensitive pointer chase. The 2.03x recorded below is the top of that range
>    reported as a figure. `engine/genfloor` held at **0.98-1.03x** across all eight processes, so
>    the pipeline-is-free finding is the robust one.
> 2. **The probe was missing an arm and had a defect, both found at 1412.** `floor` drained with
>    `push` and `genfloor` with SPREAD, so the ratio conflated two differences; the added `genpush`
>    arm CONFIRMED rather than refuted it (332 against 334 ns/row). And `floor` carried a
>    `wantsValue ?` branch on the hot path that the engine does not have, which showed up as the
>    engine measuring **0.74x the floor** once it took the eager route — a floor the real code beats
>    is not a floor. Hoisted to a `pick`-shaped closure.

### The nomination

A windowed profile of `V().out('E')` at 100k nodes puts **86.2%** in one frame: `values @
index.mjs:4083`, the single-type hop's `*[Symbol.iterator]()` generator body.
`V().hasLabel('P').out('E').values('k')` puts 59.0% there with `pick` at 23.8%. Three Gremlin rows
profiled and this one frame tops all three.

First check was the obvious one, and it came back negative: `graph.vertices` is **not** a generator.
It is `{ [Symbol.iterator]: () => this.verticesById.values() }` — a re-iterable wrapper allocated
once per ACCESS, handing back the Map iterator directly. So this is not audit item 217's trap (a
`yield*`-delegating generator, measured at 1.6x), and that explanation is closed.

### The floor, because a share is a nomination and a floor is the price

Item 234 built floors for three Gremlin shapes and **two of the three targets did not survive** —
the big ratio was data layout, not step overhead. So `gremlin-hop-floor-probe.mjs` was written
BEFORE anything was built. Three arms, so the gap can be attributed rather than merely observed:

| arm        | what it is                                                  |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `engine`   | the real traversal through `toArray`                        |
| `floor`    | the identical walk as a plain nested `for`, array push      |
| `genfloor` | the identical walk as a **generator**, drained with `[...]` |

`genfloor` is the load-bearing one. `engine`-vs-`floor` mixes the protocol with everything else the
pipeline does; **`genfloor`-vs-`floor` isolates the protocol alone**, and `engine`-vs-`genfloor` is
then what the pipeline costs on top of a generator.

100k nodes, out-degree 1, 100,000 rows, p25 within a process and the median across three
order-alternated rounds:

| shape          | floor                 | genfloor       | engine         | protocol  | pipeline on top |
| -------------- | --------------------- | -------------- | -------------- | --------- | --------------- |
| `V().out('E')` | 16.67 ms (167 ns/row) | 35.73 ms (357) | 35.73 ms (357) | **2.14x** | **1.00x**       |
| `…values('k')` | 29.25 ms (292)        | 59.46 ms (595) | 58.29 ms (583) | **2.03x** | **0.98x**       |

**The pipeline is free.** Every step, the plan dispatch, `pick`, `toArray` — all of it together adds
nothing measurable over a bare generator doing the same work. The whole 2.1x is the protocol: one
`yield` and one `.next()` per row.

That first table's `35.73` against `35.73` was too clean to believe, so it was re-run as three
INDEPENDENT processes rather than reported: engine/genfloor came back 34.02/34.58, 33.91/33.39 and
36.00/34.77 — within 2% each time, with `floor` at 12.82-16.01. The exact coincidence was p25 luck;
the conclusion is not.

### What this does and does not license

It **retires** two explanations at once: the pipeline is not the cost (so there is nothing to shave
off the steps), and `pick` is not the cost either — which independently confirms item 1392's decline
of `pick` on self-time-misattribution grounds, now with a floor instead of an argument.

It **does not** license replacing the generator. The generator is what makes `out('E').limit(10)`
stop after ten edges, and `eager-tail-cache` records **473x** and **3680x** regressions from filling
eagerly under a LIMIT. An eager walk is a bound on what any lazy restructuring could win, never a
candidate implementation.

### The lever it does point at, priced but NOT built

**A drain route.** When a traversal is terminated by `toArray` or `count` and no step downstream can
short-circuit, laziness buys nothing — the stream is drained in full regardless. An eager array walk
on exactly that shape is worth the 2.1x, and it is the same kind of plan-level route choice the
existing `countShortcut` / `groupCountShortcut` / `haskey-count-shortcut` family already makes.

Not built here, and the reason is the gate rather than the walk: it has to refuse **every** step that
can stop early, and `eager-tail-cache`'s 3680x is what being wrong about one of them costs. That is
a allowlist-shaped change needing its own item, its own fuzzer pass and byte-identity confirmation —
not a one-liner to append to a measurement item.

### Gates

`bun run check` 0 (read unpiped). No engine code changed; the probe is the deliverable, indexed in
`PROBES.md`. The three arms are asserted to agree on the ROW COUNT, and deliberately not on row
order — all three walk the same adjacency in the same order, but the engine is free to reorder and
the probe must not pretend otherwise.

### Item 1412 — **SHIPPED, 53.8% / 49.1%** (81/81 both): `toArray` is `[...run(…)]`, so it ALREADY drains the fused hop walk in full — an eager fill there is the same answer by a cheaper route. **And it refutes a number in this repo's own code by 38x**, which is what had kept the lever shut

### The number that was wrong

`hop-values.ts`'s header has said since item 170:

> LAZY on purpose. … One generator for the whole walk costs **10ns/row** over the eager form, which
> is the price of not touching that.

Item 1411's three-arm floor says **1.9-2.2x**, not 4%. The decisive reading is at item 170's own
fixture size — 1,000,000 edges, where the property read is most dominant and the protocol's share
should be smallest if the 10 ns were right:

| arm                                        | 1M edges                            |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `floor` (array loop)                       | 416 ns/row                          |
| `genfloor` (same body, generator)          | 795 ns/row                          |
| `genpush` (generator, same drain as floor) | 811 ns/row                          |
| **`engine`**                               | **783 ns/row** — **0.99x genfloor** |

The protocol does not vanish into scale: **1.91x at 1M**. That header is corrected in this commit,
where it lives — a wrong price in a comment is worse than no price, because it reads as settled.

### The gate I had budgeted an item for does not exist

The other half of item 170's argument is sound and I kept it: `run` returns an `Iterable`, callers
`break` out of it, and `eager-tail-cache` records **473x** and **3680x** from filling eagerly under a
LIMIT. **`run` is untouched and exactly as lazy as it was.**

But the argument is about `run`. `toArray` is _defined_ as `[...run(plan, graph)]` — it already
drains everything — so eagerness there is not a behaviour change. And `drain` is only read when the
shortcut consumed the whole plan (`rest.length === 0`), so there is no downstream step to reason
about: a trailing `limit` lands in `rest` and `run` returns a traverser stream instead, making the
route structurally unreachable. **No step allowlist.** I had priced that allowlist as the whole risk
of this change at item 1411 and it was not needed.

`drain` is therefore an ADDITION to the walk object, never a replacement for its iterator, on both
hand walks — the single-type one and the multi-type one, the latter keeping its earlier-buckets
dedupe and its **label-arg order**, which is a TinkerPop contract the differential fuzzer compares
ORDERED.

| shape                                              | BASE   | DRAIN     | change    | concordance |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| **`hopbare`** (`V().out(E)`)                       | 35.70  | **16.50** | **53.8%** | **81/81**   |
| **`hopyieldsingle`**                               | 58.98  | **30.02** | **49.1%** | **81/81**   |
| `hopyieldmulti`                                    | 73.61  | 63.16     | 14.2%     | 72/81       |
| `hopyieldmultirev`                                 | 71.26  | 62.54     | 12.2%     | 66/81       |
| `hoporder` [CONTROL — residual, route unreachable] | 89.25  | 88.40     | 1.0%      | 40/81       |
| `hopcount3` [CONTROL — count shortcut]             | 109.78 | 105.81    | 3.6%      | 54/81       |
| `hopcount2` [CONTROL — count shortcut]             | 30.01  | 29.66     | 1.1%      | 52/81       |

**The controls are the load-bearing part**, because this edit is inside `toArray` itself — a path
every row in the bench passes through, so a `typeof drain === 'function'` test that cost anything
would show up on all three. `hoporder` reads 40/81 against a chance of 40.5.

**The multi-type walk gains far less (14% against 49%)**, and that is the expected shape rather than
a disappointment: its per-edge earlier-buckets dedupe is work the protocol saving does not touch, so
the protocol is a smaller fraction of a bigger row. Same reason the `values` shape gains less than
the bare one.

### The probe had a defect, and the engine beating its own floor is what exposed it

Once the drain route was in, `engine` measured **0.74x `floor`** on the values shape. A floor the
real code beats is not a floor. Cause: the probe's arms did
`acc.push(wantsValue ? edge.to.properties['k'] : edge.to)` — a branch on the hot path the engine does
not have, since its `pick` is a monomorphic closure chosen once per plan. Hoisted to a `pick`-shaped
closure, so all three arms now differ only in how they are driven. Item 1411's entry is corrected
with this and with the missing-`genpush` arm.

### ⚠️ Three kinds of test, because no one kind is sufficient

`eager-drain-route.test.ts`, 29 tests:

1. **Equivalence** — `toArray` against `[...run]` on ten shapes, compared with `toEqual` on the
   whole array rather than lengths or sorted copies, because row order here is a TinkerPop contract.
   Includes the empty graph, a graph with vertices but no edges, a self-loop, a far vertex missing
   the projected key (the `drops` path), and an edge carrying BOTH labels so the dedupe is exercised
   rather than merely present.
2. **The decision** — `drain` present on the six shapes that take the route and absent on `both` and
   the three residual shapes. An eager route is answer-preserving, so **a mutant that never offers
   `drain` passes every equivalence test in the package**; item 1289 had two such mutants survive
   until the route was asserted directly.
3. **Laziness** — a poisoned `drain` that throws, followed by iterating: if the iterator path ever
   consulted it, the test fails. Plus a `break` after one element, and re-iterability.

| mutant                         | verdict                  | evidence         |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------ | ---------------- |
| M1 `toArray` IGNORES `drain`   | **SURVIVES — by design** | 29/0             |
| M2 both drains return `[]`     | **CAUGHT**               | 20 pass / 9 fail |
| M3 eager drain, no dedupe      | **CAUGHT**               | 28 / 1           |
| M4 eager drain ignores `drops` | **CAUGHT**               | 26 / 3           |
| M5 `toArray` ALWAYS drains     | **CAUGHT**               | 25 / 4           |

M1 surviving is the finding: it is the old code, correct and 2x slower, so no correctness test can
catch it and the bench rows are its only guard.

**The driver caught one of my own errors before any mutant ran.** The dedupe block appears **twice** —
once in the generator and once in its eager twin, which is the copy being faithful — so the
"unique anchor" assertion fired. Mutating the LAZY walk instead would have been caught for entirely
the wrong reason and recorded as a pass. The driver now asserts each anchor's multiplicity and
carries an explicit first/last/all policy rather than assuming uniqueness.

(read unpiped). Answers identical across both arms for all seven cases. The A/B driver restored both

### Item 1413 — **DECLINED with numbers** (−0.5% on the target, **−7.5%** where it cannot help, and **two unreachable controls regressed**): skipping the multi-type dedupe when `multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`. The 60.1% that nominated it was a share of the WHOLE walk, not of the scan

### The nomination, and why it was wrong

Re-profiling after item 1412 put **60.1%** of `V().out(E,F).values(k)` in the multi-type walk,
against 81.6% for the single-type twin whose walk has no inner loop at all — and the multi-type row
had gained only 14.2% from 1412's eager route where the single-type one gained 49.1%. The
earlier-buckets dedupe looked like the difference.

`graph.multiTypeEdgeCount` is maintained on every add and remove and counts edges carrying more than
one label, so **at zero no edge is in two buckets and the scan can never fire** — the same one-sided
test GQL uses for `sumIsExact` (items 1386, 1405). Conservative by construction: the counter is
global, so it says nothing about WHICH labels co-occur.

### The measurement

`MULTILABEL=-1` (disjoint, both buckets non-empty), n=9 per cell, three order-alternated rounds:

| shape                                         | ML  | BASE  | SKIP  | change    | concordance |
| --------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ----------- |
| **`hopyieldmulti`** (target)                  | −1  | 58.72 | 58.99 | **−0.5%** | 35/81       |
| **`hopyieldmultirev`** (target)               | −1  | 58.19 | 58.81 | **−1.1%** | 29/81       |
| `hopyieldmulti` [CONTROL — dedupe still runs] | 3   | 60.77 | 65.34 | **−7.5%** | **6/81**    |
| `hopyieldmulti` [CONTROL — `F` bucket empty]  | 0   | 61.18 | 59.49 | 2.8%      | 42/81       |
| `hopbare` [CONTROL — single-type walk]        | 0   | 16.33 | 16.89 | **−3.5%** | 29/81       |
| `hopyieldsingle` [CONTROL — single-type walk] | 0   | 28.31 | 29.94 | **−5.8%** | **12/81**   |

**Three separate reasons this is a decline, and the third is the one worth keeping:**

1. **No win on the target.** −0.5% at 35/81 against a chance of 40.5.
2. **A real 7.5% regression at 6/81** where the dedupe still runs — the cost of one
   register-resident boolean per edge, which is what the guard buys where it cannot help.
3. **⚠️ Two single-type controls regressed** (−3.5% at 29/81, −5.8% at **12/81**) on a branch this
   edit does not touch. That is the file-perturbation effect already on record for `exec::pull`
   (1.08-1.24x on unrelated clusters, never a gain) and for a walk inlined in a returned closure (4x
   on unrelated queries). **Editing `hop-values.ts` is not free**, and an item whose own target is
   flat cannot pay for it.

So the 60.1% was a share of the whole walk — adjacency iteration, the emit, `pick` — not of the
scan, which is a small part of it. **A share is a nomination; an ablation is the price**, and the
ablation came back at nothing. The engine change is reverted; `hop-values.ts` is byte-identical to
its state after item 1412.

### ⚠️ The first run of this A/B measured NOTHING, and the fixture is why

It reported 5.5% on the target against a control moving 4.8% — this instrument's noise. Cause: at
`MULTILABEL=0` every edge is `['E']`, so the `F` bucket is **empty on every vertex** and the
earlier-buckets scan never executes in EITHER arm. The target cell was structurally incapable of
showing the effect.

I had also mis-compared before that: a single reading of `MULTILABEL=0` (55.5 ms) against
`MULTILABEL=3` (67.2) looked like a 17% win, but those are **two different fixtures**, not one
fixture before and after. That gap is the cost of HAVING multi-label edges, not the cost of the
dedupe.

**This is the same missing fixture shape the GQL bench had until item 1405 — found twice, in two
benches, the second time after it had already cost a reading.** `MULTILABEL=-1` is now in the
Gremlin bench with the GQL twin's spelling (`-1` rather than `0`, because `0` already means "no `F`
at all", which the controls at items 1375 and 1390 rely on): every other edge carries `F` INSTEAD of
`E`, so both buckets are non-empty and no edge is in two of them.

| ML  | `hopyieldmulti` p25 | what it is                                 |
| --- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| −1  | 58.16 ms            | disjoint, both buckets populated — **new** |
| 0   | 57.95 ms            | `F` bucket empty everywhere                |
| 3   | 64.08 ms            | edges in both buckets, dedupe required     |

### What is kept, and why it is worth more than the change would have been

- **The `MULTILABEL=-1` knob.** A bench that cannot build the ordinary schema shape cannot price
  anything that happens in a second bucket.
- **`multitype-dedupe-skip.test.ts`, 11 tests.** The multi-type dedupe had almost no coverage; these
  fixtures differ in exactly one bit — whether one edge carries both labels — so a duplicated or
  lost row shows as a changed MULTISET rather than a count. Reframed as that coverage plus the
  record of the decline, with these numbers in the header **next to the code they would have
  changed**, which is where a re-attempt will look. The per-CALL case is kept too: it is a real
  property of `hopValuesShortcut` being consulted on every `run`, not an artifact of the declined
  change.

**Do not re-attempt without an isolated per-row instrument.** The three readings this went through
(17% across fixtures, 5.5% on a dead cell, −0.5% done properly) are a straight line from a
comparison error to a fixture defect to the answer.

`gql-undirected-floor-probe.mjs`. 99,990 rows from 50,000 `E` edges (the undirected walk emits each

### ⚠️ The nomination was wrong in a specific, useful way

The profile's **36.5%** for the property read (`propOf` + `get properties`) is a share of ENGINE
time. As a fraction of the achievable floor it is **25.2%** — and the single biggest component is
the adjacency walk at **59.8%**, which no change to the projection path touches. So even a perfect
engine could remove at most 40% of this row, and the profile's top non-walk frame was overstated by
~1.4x as a target.

That is the third time this session a profile share has needed an ablation to become a price, and
the three outcomes were all different: the Gremlin generator's 86.2% was **real** (2.1x, shipped at
item 1412), the multi-type dedupe's 60.1% was worth **−0.5%** (declined at 1413), and this one is
**real but smaller than it looked**. A share is a nomination; an ablation is the price — and the
nomination is wrong often enough that the rule has now earned itself three times in one session.

### What IS the target, stated precisely for whoever takes it

**`engine / twoPass`, which is 1.37-1.56x and stable across degree:**

| degree | engine | floor | ratio     | adjacency share of floor | property share of floor |
| ------ | ------ | ----- | --------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| 1      | 50.42  | 36.38 | **1.39x** | 59.8%                    | 25.2%                   |
| 2      | 71.04  | 51.99 | **1.37x** | 44.0%                    | 47.0%                   |
| 4      | 112.17 | 71.86 | **1.56x** | 35.0%                    | 36.6%                   |

So **~27-36% is available on this row** and the mechanism is the difference between what the two
arms do per edge: the engine sets a `binding` entry and calls `projectRow`, which evaluates the
projection through the generic `propOf` path; the floor does `rows.push({ n: e.to.properties['n'] })`
directly. The precedented fix is a SPECIALIZED projection closure for the single-far-property case —
the same `pick`-shaped monomorphic closure the Gremlin hop walk already uses, and the shape the TS
spelling probe measured as flat (16.5-17.1 ms) where the general scalar path plateaus high and emits
a rare fast rep.

**Not taken here**, and the reason is scope rather than doubt: `projectRow` is shared by every walk
in `hop-projection.ts`, so specializing it is not a one-line change to one walk, and item 1413 just
measured that **editing this file costs unrelated rows 3.5-5.8%** even when the target is flat. It
needs its own item with controls on walks it does not mean to reach.

### Gates

`bun run check` 0 (read unpiped). No engine code changed; the probe is the deliverable. The four

### Item 1415 — **DECLINED**, and with item 1413 it establishes a THRESHOLD: in `hop-projection.ts` a change worth less than ~10% on its target is likely NET-NEGATIVE across the file. Hoisting `projectRow`'s per-row `EvalEnv` gained 2.3% at degree 1 and cost two unrelated rows 3.4-5.6%

### The change, and why it looked free

`projectRow` built a fresh `{ binding, params, graph }` on every call, and every per-edge walk in
`hop-projection.ts` calls it once per ROW — so a 100,000-row hop allocated 100,000 three-field
objects whose contents never varied. `binding` is the same `Map`, mutated in place between rows, so
an env hoisted to the call observes exactly what a fresh one would.

Item 1414 had priced the room: the undirected hop runs at **1.39x** a hand-written loop doing
`rows.push({ n: e.to.properties.n })`, and this allocation is part of that gap.

Built as an ADDED entry point (`projectRowIn`) rather than a changed signature, because the hoist is
only sound while nothing retains the env past the call, and converted in **one walk only** — 2 sites
changed, 9 left alone as controls, asserted as a relation in the A/B driver.

### The measurement

| shape                         | degree | BASE   | ENVHOIST | change    | concordance |
| ----------------------------- | ------ | ------ | -------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `hopundiryield` (target)      | 1      | 40.69  | 39.77    | **2.3%**  | 46/81       |
| `hopundiryield` (target)      | 4      | 124.37 | 113.77   | **8.5%**  | 61/81       |
| `hopstartonlyyield` [CONTROL] | 1      | 8.50   | 8.97     | **−5.6%** | 28/81       |
| `hoprelfiltyield` [CONTROL]   | 1      | 11.00  | 11.38    | **−3.4%** | 33/81       |
| `hopsingleyield` [CONTROL]    | 1      | 9.81   | 9.85     | −0.4%     | 35/81       |

**At degree 1 — the default shape — the target is 2.3% at 46/81 against a chance of 40.5, which is
a null**, while two controls on walks whose `projectRow` call is byte-identical between arms got
**5.6% and 3.4% slower**. The degree-4 cell's 8.5% is the only real signal and it is not enough to
pay for that.

The first reading already suggested this (383 ns/row against 386), and the likely reason the
allocation is nearly free is that V8 scalar-replaces an env whose only consumer inlines.

### ⚠️ The finding is the threshold, not the decline

The controls moved **against** the change — slower in the arm, not faster — so this is not a control
flattering the target. It is the file-perturbation effect, now measured twice:

| item               | target            | controls on unreachable walks |
| ------------------ | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
| 1413 (dedupe skip) | −0.5%             | −3.5%, −5.8%                  |
| 1415 (env hoist)   | +2.3% at degree 1 | −5.6%, −3.4%, −0.4%           |

Two independent changes to `hop-projection.ts`, both with flat-to-small targets, both costing
unrelated rows **3.4-5.8%**. That is the same effect already on record for `exec::pull` (1.08-1.24x
on unrelated clusters, never a gain) and for a walk inlined in a returned closure (4x on unrelated
queries) — but those were about one hot function, and this says it about the FILE.

**So the operative rule for target selection in this file: a change must be worth ~10% or more on
its own row to be worth attempting at all**, because the perturbation toll appears to be charged
regardless of what the change does. Every item that succeeded here this session clears that easily —
1408 (26.8/42.1%), 1409 (55.7/79.8%), 1410 (31.2/49.1%) — and both that failed are under it. That is
a cheap filter that would have skipped two items, and it is the most useful thing either of them
produced.

### What remains of item 1414's 1.39x

The env allocation was one candidate for that gap and it is now priced at ~2%. The rest is the
`binding.set` per row plus the generic `propOf` evaluation versus a direct property read. A
specialized `pick`-shaped closure is still the precedented fix — but on the threshold above it has to
be worth ~10% on `hopundiryield` alone, and item 1414's ablation caps the whole per-row machinery at
28% of the row (the floor is 1.39x), with the adjacency walk at 59.8% of the floor untouchable. So
the remaining headroom is real but tight, and anyone taking it should expect the toll.

### Item 1416 — **TWO INSTRUMENT FINDINGS, no code change**: `MULTILABEL=-1` makes every multi-hop chain row answer **ZERO**, so a whole ranking of non-hop rows timed paths that find nothing. And `chain3`'s **72.6% `bucketSize`** is misattribution — all 200,000 calls take the O(1) branch, proven by counting them

### Finding 1: the disjoint fixture zeroes every multi-hop count

Item 1415's threshold sent target selection out of `hop-projection.ts`, so the non-hop rows were
ranked by wall time at `MULTILABEL=-1` — the knob item 1413 had just added, carried over from the
hop work where it is correct. **Every chain and var-length row answered `{"c": 0}`.**

`-1` makes every other edge carry `F` INSTEAD of `E`, which halves the `E` edges — right for a
single-hop type question and fatal for a chain, because a 3-hop chain needs three consecutive `E`
edges and at out-degree 1 there are none. Checked across four fixtures rather than assumed:

| shape    | ML  | FANOUT | answer     | p25      |
| -------- | --- | ------ | ---------- | -------- |
| `chain3` | −1  | 1      | **`c=0`**  | 6.77 ms  |
| `chain3` | 0   | 1      | `c=50000`  | 18.09 ms |
| `chain3` | 0   | 2      | `c=400000` | 29.08 ms |
| `chain3` | −1  | 2      | `c=50000`  | 27.78 ms |

Same for `varlen24` and `quant33`. So the ranking that produced "`chain3` 21.5 ms, `varlen24` 20.7,
`varlen13` 16.2…" was a ranking of **dead paths**, and on a live fixture `chain3` is **47.1 ms at
100k nodes** — more than double, and the heaviest GQL row by wall time.

**The rule, which is the opposite of item 1413's:** sweep `MULTILABEL=-1` for anything that reads a
degree estimate or walks per-type buckets at ONE hop; never use it alone for a multi-hop count. An
answer of zero is the loudest possible version of "an answer invariant to the property you varied
cannot validate the fixture", and it still took a second look to notice.

### Finding 2: `bucketSize`'s 72.6% is its caller's loop

On the live fixture `chain3`'s profile reads `bucketSize` **72.6%** and `side` 16.8% — **89.4%** in
two frames. `bucketSize`'s hot path is one line:

```ts
return byType.get(types[0])?.size ?? 0;
```

A string-keyed `Map.get` plus a `.size`. 72.6% of 685 ms is ~497 ms, which would be absurd — so it
was counted rather than believed. A counter in the function, two runs:

|                                          |             |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| whole query                              | 95.9 ms     |
| `bucketSize` calls                       | **200,000** |
| ns per call if it were 100% of the query | 479         |
| ns per call at the profile's 72.6%       | **~345**    |

200,000 `Map.get`s are single-digit milliseconds, not 69. And the branch counters settle the one
alternative that would have made it real — that it was falling through to
`countEdges(edgesOfTypes(…))`, which WALKS the bucket:

| branch                                   | calls       |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| single named type, `byType.get(t)?.size` | **200,000** |
| whole-graph single bucket                | 0           |
| **the O(edges) walk**                    | **0**       |

**Every call takes the O(1) path.** So the 72.6% is item 1104's self-time misattribution — a small
hot callee credited with the inlined loop of `buildThreeHopCount`, which calls it twice per vertex
(100,000 vertices → 200,000 calls, exactly as counted).

### What that leaves

`chain3` is a degree PRODUCT with a middle-edge walk: two O(1) degree reads per vertex plus one walk
over the middle leg. The two degree reads are already `Map.get`+`.size`, the walk is the answer's own
cost, and the profile's top frame is an artifact. **No lever found, and the 89.4% that looked like
one is accounted for.**

This is the fourth consecutive item where a profile share needed an ablation to become a price, and
the scoreboard now reads: **1411 real (2.1x, shipped at 1412), 1413 refuted (−0.5%), 1414 real but
1.4x overstated, 1416 refuted outright.** Two of four nominations were wrong and a third was
inflated. A share is a nomination; an ablation is the price.

⚠️ **And `mentions` in the analyzer output predicted both refutations.** `bucketSize` showed 12 and
`side` 1288 — the analyzer's own ambiguity measure, which it prints precisely because a frame it
cannot locate uniquely cannot be trusted. Reading that column first would have raised the suspicion
before the profile was taken seriously.

### Item 1418 — **SHIPPED, 25.7%** (81/81): the slot memo's ~100,000 per-slot `Int32Array`s become ONE flat buffer with per-slot offsets. And its growth copy needed a DIRECT unit test, because four black-box attempts could not catch a mutant of it

### Re-profiling after item 1417 showed the GC was NOT fixed

Item 1417 replaced `Int32Array.from` with a hand copy and won 10.1%. But `chain4`'s profile still
read the garbage collector at **14.2%** — up from 11.8%, not down. Item 1417 made the per-slot arrays
cheaper to BUILD; it did not change that there are ~100,000 of them and they are **retained for the
whole query**, so they are promoted rather than collected cheaply. The construction cost was never
the GC cost.

So the memo is now one growable buffer plus per-slot `(offset, length)`:

```ts
type SlotMemo = { flat: Int32Array; used: number; off: number[]; len: number[] };
```

No per-slot object exists at all, and the replay pass — two of three passes on a 4-hop chain — reads
a **contiguous run** instead of chasing a pointer per slot. Item 1417's hand copy survives inside it,
writing into a shared run.

| shape                | fanout | BASE  | FLAT      | change    | concordance |
| -------------------- | ------ | ----- | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| **`chain4`**         | 1      | 69.98 | **52.01** | **25.7%** | **81/81**   |
| **`chain4`**         | 2      | 71.22 | **63.18** | **11.3%** | **81/81**   |
| `chain3` [CONTROL]   | 1      | 47.34 | 47.76     | −0.9%     | 46/81       |
| `varlen24` [CONTROL] | 1      | 30.36 | 30.84     | −1.5%     | 46/81       |
| `quant44` [CONTROL]  | 1      | 28.34 | 28.46     | −0.4%     | 44/81       |

Controls chosen on the CONDITION rather than by eye: the memo needs `passes > 2` (item 1106's
measured threshold), so `chain3` at 2 passes routes around it and the other two use
`walkLevelCount`. All three flat at chance.

### ⚠️ Four black-box attempts could not catch one mutant, and both theories were wrong

Five mutants against the offset arithmetic. Four were caught by the query suite at once. The fifth —
`grown.set(m.flat.subarray(0, m.used))` shortened by one, which silently drops the last entry **on
every doubling** — survived:

| attempt               | why it should have worked                                              | what measurement said                                                        |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 4,096-slot fixture    | "too small to grow the buffer"                                         | a counter in the growth branch: it fires **3 times**, 2 with entries to copy |
| path instead of cycle | "a cycle is symmetric, so misrouted weight leaves the total unchanged" | still survived                                                               |
| counted the reads     | "a path never reads the memo back"                                     | a 4,096-vertex path reads it **8,189 times**                                 |
| out-degree 2          | "runs of length 1 hide an off-by-one within a run"                     | still survived                                                               |

Each theory was plausible and each was refuted by **one counter** rather than by argument — which is
the only reason I know they were wrong. The actual reason is narrower: the dropped entry belongs to
whichever slot was written immediately before a growth, and whether it is ever read depends on
frontier ordering. A query shape that reliably reads it would be a test of the arithmetic wearing a
query costume.

### So the guard is the arithmetic itself

`memoReserve` and `SlotMemo` are exported, and `memo-reserve.test.ts` tests the one invariant
directly: **growth preserves every entry already written.** 5,000 single-entry slots with
recognisable values, runs of length 3 over 1,200 slots, a single reserve larger than the whole
buffer, monotone capacity, and the no-op cases.

That is this repo's own recorded answer for this shape — _a route choice is answer-equivalent, so
every mutant survives the differential tests; extract the arithmetic as a pure fn and unit-test it_ —
arriving from a new direction: not a route choice this time, but a data path whose corruption is
real and whose observability depends on scheduling.

**Re-run: ALL FIVE CAUGHT.** M5 dies by 2 tests.

| mutant                  | verdict                                      |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| M1 `off = base + 1`     | CAUGHT (30 fail)                             |
| M2 `len = n - 1`        | CAUGHT (42 fail)                             |
| M3 `used` not advanced  | CAUGHT (35 fail)                             |
| M4 no reserve           | CAUGHT (42 fail)                             |
| **M5 growth loses one** | **CAUGHT (2 fail)** — by the unit test alone |

The six path-fixture tests in `slot-memo-growth.test.ts` stay: they are real coverage of a growth
path that had none, even though they were not what caught M5. Their header records the cycle-vs-path
reasoning, which is sound in general — item 702's invariance trap — and simply was not the cause
here.

### Item 1419 — **MEASURED, no code change**: items 1417+1418 confirmed from the other side — `chain4`'s GC share fell **14.2% → 1.4%** and the row **73.2 → 50.6 ms**. And the sweep beats naive enumeration by **2.0-4.5x**, so the route choice is right and this row is done

### The mechanism, confirmed rather than assumed

Item 1418's claim was that the ~100,000 per-slot `Int32Array`s were the GC cost, not their
construction. Re-profiling says so directly:

|                                         | GC share  | `chain4` p25 |
| --------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------ |
| before item 1417                        | 11.8%     | 73.18 ms     |
| after 1417 (hand copy, per-slot arrays) | **14.2%** | 66.6         |
| after 1418 (one flat buffer)            | **1.4%**  | **50.60**    |

A **10x reduction** in the collector's share. Item 1417 made the arrays cheaper to build and the GC
share went UP; removing the objects is what moved it. That is the distinction the two items exist to
separate, and it is now measured on both sides rather than argued once.

What is left is the sweep's own arithmetic: `bucketSize` 41.0%, `sweepChain` 22.4%,
`sweepSlotCached` 20.0%. ⚠️ `bucketSize`'s share is **misattributed** — item 1416 counted its calls
and proved every one takes the O(1) branch — so those three frames are one loop, 83% of a row whose
allocations are now gone.

### Is the clever algorithm even the right one? Measured against naive enumeration

The sweep is a degree PRODUCT: O(V × passes) regardless of how many walks exist. Naive enumeration
is O(answer). **At out-degree 1 those are ~400,000 slot visits against 100,000 walks**, so the sparse
end is exactly where the clever route could lose — and nothing in the file had measured it.

| fanout | answer     | engine | naive enumeration | engine / naive |
| ------ | ---------- | ------ | ----------------- | -------------- |
| 1      | 100,000    | 74.85  | 151.74            | **0.49x**      |
| 2      | 1,600,000  | 79.41  | 180.86            | **0.44x**      |
| 4      | 25,600,000 | 98.80  | 444.55            | **0.22x**      |

The sweep wins by **2.0x, 2.3x and 4.5x**. Both arms are asserted to agree on the answer, so this is
one question measured two ways rather than two questions. The route choice is correct at every degree
tested, including the one where it had most to lose.

### So this row is done, and that is the finding

`chain4` went from the heaviest row in the GQL bench (73.2 ms) to 50.6 across two items, its
allocation cost is gone (1.4% GC), and its algorithm is 2-4.5x better than the obvious alternative.
The remaining 83% is three frames of one loop doing work the algorithm requires: an O(1) degree read
per slot per leg and a frontier update per edge.

**Recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it.** The profile still shows a 41% frame, and that
frame is still `bucketSize` — which looks like an open target and is not one. Anyone ranking rows by
profile share will land on it again; items 1416 and 1419 together are why they should not.

### Item 1420 — **NOMINATION REFUTED**: the chain family's 4-5x step at the THIRD hop against 1.1x at the fourth looks like a misrouting and is not one. Item 301's route choice RE-VERIFIED on today's code at **1.34x**, and items 1417-1418 do not change it because the memo is gated on `passes > 2`

### The nomination, which was a step pattern rather than a profile share

After items 1417-1419 took `chain4` from 73.2 to ~51 ms, `chain3` became the #2 row at 44-49 ms.
Held across three sizes:

| nodes   | chain2 | chain3 | chain4 | 2→3       | 3→4       |
| ------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | --------- | --------- |
| 25,000  | 1.08   | 3.89   | 8.14   | 3.61x     | 2.09x     |
| 50,000  | 3.92   | 20.78  | 22.11  | **5.30x** | **1.06x** |
| 100,000 | 11.56  | 46.30  | 52.37  | **4.01x** | **1.13x** |

Adding the THIRD hop costs 4-5x; adding the FOURTH costs 1.1x. A fourth hop is strictly more work
than a third, so that ordering is backwards — and the two take DIFFERENT ROUTES (`chain4` through
`sweepChain`, `chain3` through `buildThreeHopCount`), which made "`chain3` is on the slower route"
the obvious reading.

### Why it is wrong, measured rather than reasoned

`threeSegmentRoute` chooses between the degree PRODUCT and the way-count SWEEP, and the choice is
already backed by a measurement: **item 301 found the product winning the unfiltered shape, 250.1
against 374.9 ms.** ~~An unlabelled chain is exactly that shape, so `chain3` takes the product on
purpose.~~ **⟶ CORRECTED at item 1426: `chain3` IS labelled** — `MATCH (a:P)-…->(b:P)` — so
`labelled` is true and the route is decided by the per-call comparison instead. It takes the product
because `P` is on every vertex, so `candidateCount(P) === vertexCount` and nothing narrows. The
measurement below stands (the route was forced and re-measured); only this sentence's reason was
wrong.

That number is from before items 1417-1418, which made the sweep 10.1% + 25.7% faster — so the
ordering could have flipped. Re-measured by forcing the route (the `!labelled` guard and the
per-call comparison both removed), then restored:

| nodes   | product (shipped) | sweep (forced) | product / sweep |
| ------- | ----------------- | -------------- | --------------- |
| 50,000  | 20.78             | 27.09          | **0.77x**       |
| 100,000 | 46.30             | 62.16          | **0.74x**       |

**The product is still 1.3x faster.** Item 301's conclusion holds, now with fresh numbers on today's
code rather than on trust.

### And the reason my own changes could not have flipped it

The flat memo items 1417-1418 built is gated on **`passes > 2`**. A 3-segment chain is **2 passes**,
so `slotNbrs` is `undefined` and the sweep falls to `sweepOneDirection` — **neither item touched the
path a 3-hop chain would take.** Item 1106 had already measured that boundary from the other side:
with exactly two passes the memo is a small LOSS (162.0 against 165.7), which is why the gate is
there.

So the step pattern has a structural explanation and not a routing one: `chain2` is degree arithmetic
over two positions, while `chain3` adds a **middle-edge walk** — O(edges) work that a 2-chain does
not do at all. `chain4` then reuses that same walk with one more cheap pass, which is why its step is
1.1x. The alarming number is the 2→3 transition doing something genuinely new, not the 3→4 one doing
something cheap.

### Recorded because the pattern will be noticed again

A reader ranking rows and seeing 11.56 / 46.30 / 52.37 will reach for the same explanation. The
answer is three facts: the routes differ **by design**, the product is **measured** better for the
unfiltered shape (0.74x, here), and the memo work of 1417-1418 is **unreachable** at 2 passes. This
is the second row this session to look open on its face and be closed underneath — `chain4`'s
41% `bucketSize` frame was the first.

### Item 1421 — **`sortedpage` DECLINED, and an instrument caveat**: `gcMs` is **2-3x noisier than `p25`** and is a SUM over reps rather than a share. The 18.2 ms that nominated this row was the top of a 5.4-17.7 range, and the row was already a bounded top-K walk

### The nomination and its refutation

Ranking the live GQL rows, `sortedpage` (`MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k < 50 RETURN n.s ORDER BY s LIMIT 10`)
showed **18.2 ms of GC** against a 4.48 ms p25 — which read like ~29% of its wall time on a `LIMIT 10`
query, exactly the shape `eager-tail-cache` records a **473x** and a **3680x** for.

It is not that. The profile shows `topKNodeWalk` 29.1%, `boundedTopKeyed` 9.3%, `satisfies` 20.2% —
a **bounded selection already in place**, which is the fix that family needed and already has. 4.23 ms
to scan 100,000 vertices with a predicate and keep ten is ~42 ns a vertex.

### The caveat, measured

Six processes on one build:

| row          | `gcMs`      | spread   | `p25`         | spread |
| ------------ | ----------- | -------- | ------------- | ------ |
| `sortedpage` | 5.4 - 17.7  | **3.3x** | 4.25 - 5.61   | 1.32x  |
| `varlen14`   | 12.8 - 16.7 | 1.3x     | 28.49 - 32.08 | 1.13x  |

`gcMs` sums over every rep while `p25` is a single rep, so it was never a share — and it is 2-3x
less stable on top of that. The noise is shape-dependent, worst on SHORT rows where one collection
landing inside or outside the window moves the total by a third.

**Used carefully it earned its keep this session**: `chain4` read 11.8-14.2% CONSISTENTLY across
runs, which is what justified items 1417-1418, and the fix drove it to 1.4%. The difference was
repetition. `PROBES.md` now says `gcMs` needs more repeats than `p25`, not fewer.

### Item 1422 — **the zero-answer flag was WRONG TWICE, and verifying its FIRING path is what found it**: version 1 false-positived on four live rows, version 2 then missed a real zero count. Both are arrays; the discriminator is the ROW COUNT plus the value's type

### Version 1 cried wolf

Item 1417 added `VACUOUS_ZERO_ANSWER` to both benches so a dead fixture announces itself. The Gremlin
side tested `answer === 0`. Ranking the Gremlin rows, **four of fourteen came back flagged** —
`hoporder`, `hopyieldsingle`, `hopyieldmulti`, `hopyieldmultirev`.

All four are live. They are `values('k')` projections, and `answer` is the **first element**, which is
the first vertex's `k` — legitimately **0**. A flag that cries wolf is worse than no flag, because it
trains the reader to ignore it.

### Version 2 went silent

Split on `Array.isArray(rows)`: array → flag when empty, scalar → flag when 0. Verified by
temporarily adding `hasLabel('ZZZ').count()`, a shape whose answer is 0 by construction:

|                           | answer | flag        |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ----------- |
| `hasLabel('ZZZ').count()` | 0      | **MISSING** |

**`toArray` returns `[0]` for a count**, so a count IS an array — `Array.isArray` cannot separate a
scalar aggregate from a projection, and version 2 took the array branch, found one row, and said
nothing.

### The discriminator

```js
rowCount === 0 || (rowCount === 1 && typeof answer === 'number' && answer === 0);
```

Row count plus the value's type, with `rowCount` captured beside `answer` rather than derived from
it. Verified in all four directions:

| shape                            | answer | flag          |
| -------------------------------- | ------ | ------------- |
| `hasLabel('ZZZ').count()`        | 0      | **VACUOUS** ✓ |
| `labelsingle`                    | 1000   | — ✓           |
| `hopyieldsingle` (`values('k')`) | **0**  | — ✓           |
| `hopcount3`                      | 1000   | — ✓           |

A projection returning exactly one row whose single value is 0 would still be flagged. That is a rare
shape, and a false alarm there costs a second look where a missed dead fixture costs a whole
measurement — item 1416 lost a ranking to one.

### ⚠️ The lesson is about the order of verification

Item 1417 checked the flag by confirming it FIRED on a known-dead GQL row and stayed silent on a live
one — the right test, on the GQL bench. The Gremlin side got the same code and **no equivalent
check**, because no shape in its list answers 0, so there was nothing to point it at. Verifying the
negative direction alone passed both broken versions.

_A generative or diagnostic check whose teeth were never verified is worse than none, because it is
believed_ — already this repo's rule for fuzzers and mutation harnesses. This is the same rule for a
one-line diagnostic, and the cost of obeying it was adding a deliberately-dead shape for one run.

**the exact line items 1417 and 1418 had just removed from the GQL sweep.** Same per-slot

**`hopcount2` is the sharpest control this session has had.** A k-hop chain runs k-1 passes and the

free. `hopyieldsingle`'s −5.1% is inside its own **1.24x** run-to-run spread (six processes, one
build); `hopcount3`'s spread is 1.03x against a 23.4% win.

### ⚠️ I overwrote `slot-chain-count.test.ts`, and here is what caught it

The mutants were all caught (M1-M4 by **one** failing test each, where the GQL twin's failed 29-42).
One test standing between a 23.4% route and a wrong answer is thin, so I wrote a file to thicken it —
and named it `slot-chain-count.test.ts`, **which already existed**, committed at item 1110, the item
that built this memo. 13 tests: TinkerPop 3.7.3 ground truth, three/four/five hops, the shapes the
dense route must decline, and a seed wide enough that the memo actually runs.

Re-running the mutants after "thickening" is what surfaced it: **`M1 off = base + 1` went from CAUGHT
to SURVIVES.** The test that caught it was the one I had just deleted. The suite total had also gone
**1203 → 1199**, and that four-test drop was there to be noticed and wasn't — I only chased the count
after the mutant verdict changed direction, which is the wrong order.

Restored from `git show HEAD:…` into the file (not `git checkout`), verified byte-identical by an
empty diff, and my additions moved to `slot-chain-oracle.test.ts` — kept because they are what item
1110's file does NOT do: an independent brute-force oracle sharing nothing with the engine but the
graph, a self-loop, and out-degree 2 so memo runs exceed one entry. With both present: **1212 tests

### Still open on this row

`st.next = new Float64Array(n)` is allocated **per pass** — the GQL sweep doubles and reuses instead.
Two passes at 100,000 vertices is 1.6 MB of garbage per query, and it is a different allocation from
the memo, so it gets its own item rather than muddying this one's attribution.

### Item 1424 — **DECLINED, −0.3%**: the per-pass `Float64Array(n)` item 1423 left open is 1.6 MB of garbage per query and **costs nothing**. V8's GC tracks object COUNT and promotion, not bytes — which is why removing 100,000 small arrays moved `gcMs` 10x and removing megabytes moves nothing

### The change, and why it looked obviously right

`slotChainCount` allocates one `n`-wide `Float64Array` **per pass**, so a 3-hop chain over 100,000
vertices discards **1.6 MB per query**. The GQL sweep does not: it keeps two buffers and reuses them.
Item 1423 had explicitly left this as the allocation that remained after the memo.

Replaced with two buffers swapped, cleared by `fill(0)` — a memset over 800 KB, tens of microseconds
against an 86 ms row, where the allocation it replaces costs the same zeroing **plus** a collection.

| shape                 | BASE  | SWAP  | change    | concordance |
| --------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- | ----------- |
| `hopcount3` (target)  | 87.76 | 88.00 | **−0.3%** | 17/36       |
| `hopcount2` [CONTROL] | 29.85 | 29.60 | 0.8%      | 19/36       |

Chance is 18 of 36. Flat in both directions, and `gcMs` did not move either: **14.3 against 14.2**.

### The mechanism, which is the part that generalises

**V8's collector cost tracks object COUNT and promotion, not raw bytes.**

| what was removed                  | bytes      | objects      | `gcMs`         |
| --------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------ | -------------- |
| item 1423: per-slot memo arrays   | ~800 KB    | **~100,000** | **148 → 14.2** |
| item 1424: per-pass weight arrays | **1.6 MB** | 2            | 14.2 → 14.3    |

Twice the bytes, four orders of magnitude fewer objects, and no effect. Large typed arrays go to
large-object space and are cheap to collect; the memo's cost was a hundred thousand small objects
being traced and promoted. **"1.6 MB of garbage per query" is an appealing framing and it is the
wrong unit.**

### A note on the cost of confirming a null

This ran at **2 rounds and 2 rows** rather than three and four, deliberately and recorded in the
driver: the first reading was already flat (87.00 against 86.51, `gcMs` 14.3 against 14.2) and
`hopcount3`'s own spread is 1.03x. The job was to confirm a null at proportionate cost, not to hunt
a small effect — and an under-powered A/B is otherwise indistinguishable from a careless one, so the
reason belongs next to the numbers.

Recorded rather than silently dropped **because the per-pass allocation still looks wasteful on
inspection.** Without a number beside it, the next reader takes it again — and the GQL sweep's
reuse-two-buffers shape sitting right there in the twin makes that more likely, not less. The
asymmetry is not an oversight in the Gremlin code; it simply does not matter.

Item 1425 put three numbers side by side — GQL product 46-49 ms, GQL sweep (forced) 62, Gremlin

Both fixtures give out-degree and in-degree **exactly 1** (each multiplier is coprime with `N`, so
each mapping is a permutation) and both answer `N` for a 3-hop count. They differ in **nothing but

- the cross-engine probe's default: `from = (k * 7919) % N`, `to = (k * 104729) % N`. Both

### ⚠️ My prediction was backwards, and the reason is worth keeping

Item 1428 reasoned that `hopundiryield`'s cost "is dominated by the far-vertex property read —
exactly what random stride makes expensive", so the property read's share should RISE. It falls:
**38.7% → 19.9%**.

The adjacency walk is what random stride makes expensive — 113 → 219 ns/row, from 43.4% of the floor
to 63.4% — and it crowds everything else out. The property read's ABSOLUTE cost even drops (10.11 ms
→ 6.89), which is the part I would not have guessed: by the time the row builder reads
`far.properties`, the walk has already dereferenced that vertex to get `e.to`, so at random stride
the expensive first touch has been paid by the walk and attributed to it.

So "random stride makes property reads expensive" is the wrong summary. **Random stride makes the
WALK expensive, and the walk is what first touches the far vertex.** A shape where the property read
is the first touch would behave differently; a hop is not that shape.

### Item 1430 — **PRICED, NOT BUILT: a single pass over the EDGE index answers the undirected hop ~12x faster than the engine** and ~10x faster than the two-pass floor, with the same rows verified by content digest. The adjacency walk, not the property read, is what an undirected hop spends its time on

### The structure, and why it is cheaper

The engine's `undirectedHopWalk` iterates every VERTEX twice — once for `adjFrom`, once for `adjTo` —
so a 100,000-vertex graph pays 200,000 iterations and 200,000 `Map.get`s to produce two rows per
edge. Item 1429 measured the in-pass alone at 53.9% of that floor.

`graph.edgesByLabel.get(type)` is ONE `Set` holding every edge of that type, in insertion order. One
pass over it, emitting both rows per edge, produces the same row multiset:

|               | `twoPass` (the engine's structure) | `edgePass`       | vs floor | vs engine |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------- | --------- |
| small stride  | 25.55 ms (256 ns/row)              | **2.62 ms (26)** | **9.7x** | **12.6x** |
| random stride | 41.60 ms (416)                     | **4.29 ms (43)** | **9.7x** | **12.5x** |

**~10x the floor and ~12.5x the engine, at both localities.** The edge index is sequential in
allocation order, where adjacency iteration chases a `Map` per vertex and then a `Set` per bucket —
`countOnly` (both passes, no rows at all) costs 116-220 ns/row where `edgePass` does the walk AND
builds the rows in 26-43.

### ⚠️ A 12x deserves an answer check, and only got one on the second pass

The probe compared row COUNTS. At 12x that stops being evidence — a walk emitting the wrong endpoint,
or the same endpoint twice, matches on length and means nothing. It now computes an order-independent
summed **content digest** and asserts `engine`, `twoPass` and `edgePass` agree, with `countOnly`
(builds no rows) and `noProp` (writes a constant) excluded **by name** rather than by silence.

They agree. The 12x is on identical rows.

### What the real implementation must also pay, which this arm does not

**It is a FLOOR, so the number is an upper bound:**

- the START label has to be applied to BOTH endpoints — today it comes free from
  `candidateVertexSource`, because the walk enumerates starts; an edge pass enumerates edges and each
  one yields a row with `from` as start and another with `to` as start.
- a FAR predicate, a carried clause `WHERE` and a start-reading item all need somewhere to go.
- a self-loop must be emitted once (`edgePass` already skips the second row for `from === to`).
- it applies only when the hop is UNDIRECTED and the labels permit iterating the type's edge set at
  all — a narrowing start label probably wants the current walk, which is why this is a route choice
  and not a replacement.

Row ORDER changes, and that is allowed: GQL row order is unspecified, `farDrivenHopWalk` already
reorders deliberately, and `hopOrderPlan` already forces start-driven under `ORDER BY`.

it (2.3% against controls moving 3.4-5.6%, under the file's ~10% toll). **That was optimising the
wrong thing**: the gap to the floor is ~1.5x, and the floor itself is ~10x off a better structure.
`hopundiryield` is the #2 row at random stride (86.84 ms), so the prize is large in absolute terms
too.

### The change

`undirectedHopWalk` iterated every VERTEX twice — `adjFrom` then `adjTo` — paying 2 x `vertexCount`
iterations and 2 x `vertexCount` `Map.get`s to produce two rows per edge. When neither label filters
it now makes one sequential pass over `graph.edgesByLabel.get(type)`, emitting both rows per edge and
skipping the second for a self-loop.

| ------ | ------ | ------ | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| random | 1      | 53.02  | **15.57** | **70.6%** | **36/36**   |
| random | 4      | 104.79 | **54.69** | **47.8%** | **36/36**   |
| small  | 1      | 39.49  | **8.23**  | **79.1%** | **81/81**   |

(items 1413, 1415), so same-file controls are mandatory here and these are them.

### ⚠️ THE GATE, which the bench structurally cannot test

Both labels must be FREE — absent, or carried by every vertex. A filtering label keeps the two-pass
walk: an edge pass enumerates EDGES, so each one yields a row with `from` as start and another with
`to` as start, where the old walk gets its start side free from `candidateVertexSource`. A real start
label would cost a `matchesLabel` per ENDPOINT per edge — the deref item 1066 priced at 9.3x over a
wide far pool — and a narrowing label genuinely shrinks the vertex source, which is what the old walk
is good at.

**`isolated-row-bench.mjs` cannot exercise the decline at all**: its `MULTILABEL` knob varies EDGE
labels and every vertex in it is always `P`, so the route always fires and a broken gate would never
appear in a measurement. `undirected-edge-pass.test.ts` (16 tests) is the only guard — filtering far
label, filtering start label, absent label, self-loops on both routes, parallel edges, a two-type
edge, and the per-CALL decision pinned by one query text against two graphs in both orders.

### Two predictions I got wrong

1. **"Random stride favours the edge route more."** It does not: 70.6% random against 79.1% small at

2. **"The win grows with degree."** It shrinks — 70.6% → 47.8% at random, 79.1% → 71.1% at small. The
   mechanism is clear in hindsight: the per-VERTEX overhead the route eliminates is FIXED, so at
   4x the edges it is amortised over 4x the rows and becomes a smaller fraction.

### ⚠️ Item 1431's edge-index route is UNAVAILABLE, and that is semantics not oversight

Item 1431 took GQL's undirected hop from 53.02 to 15.57 ms by iterating `edgesByLabel` ONCE. That
emits rows in **edge** order. `iterBoth`'s contract is **out-edges then in-edges, per vertex** — its
own comment says "to match TinkerPop's `both`/`bothE` ordering" — and the differential fuzzer
compares Gremlin results ORDERED where GQL row order is unspecified. So the structure worth 3.4x
there cannot be used here, exactly as item 167's vertex-side flip could not.

What IS available is removing the delegation while keeping that order, which is what shipped.

### Item 1433 — **DECLINED, ~1%**: replacing the residual wrapper's `function*` with a hand-rolled iterator. ⚠️ And it corrects how I had been reading item 1411: its **2.1x was a generator against a PLAIN LOOP**, not against another iterator protocol

### The nomination

After item 1432, `hoporder` (`V().out('E').values('k').order()`) is the heaviest Gremlin row at
~88 ms. It takes the RESIDUAL path: the hop shortcut fires but `rest = [order]`, so item 1412's
`drain` is unavailable and `run` must hand `applyStep` a lazy stream. That wrapper was a `function*`,
putting a SECOND generator layer on top of the walk's own — every value paying two `yield`/`next`
round trips.

Its profile supports the framing: `values` 36.7%, `pick` 19.7%, `sortByBys` 14.6% — the walk
dominates, and the wrapper rides on every value it produces.

### The measurement

|                            | readings                                   | median |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------ |
| HEAD (generator wrapper)   | 88.92, 89.66, 87.06                        | ~88.9  |
| ARM (hand-rolled iterator) | 86.88 - 88.39, five runs, spread **1.02x** | 87.82  |

**~1%, inside the overlap.** Declined and reverted; `index.ts` verified back to the `function*` form.

### ⚠️ The correction, which is worth more than the change

I reached for this because item 1411 measured the generator protocol at **2.1x**. But that comparison
was a generator against a **plain `for` loop pushing into an array** — no per-item object at all. A
hand-rolled iterator still allocates `{ done, value }` on every `next()`: **the protocol is intact,
only the frame is gone.** V8 optimises a hot monomorphic generator well enough that the frame alone
is not the cost.

So item 1411's number licenses **removing the protocol** (which is what item 1412's `drain` does, for
53.8%, and what items 1431 and 1432 do by walking directly) and does **not** license swapping one
protocol implementation for another. Every win this session in that family removed iteration
overhead entirely; this one only moved it, and measured accordingly.

### What that leaves on this row

`hoporder`'s ~56% walk-plus-`pick` is already the hand-walked path items 1389 and 1412 built, and its
~15% sort is `sortByBys` doing the work the query asks for. The lever that WOULD apply is extending
`drain` to residual shapes whose steps are **fully buffering** — `order` cannot emit anything until
its input is exhausted, so eager draining is unobservable there. That needs a per-step
"buffers-everything" classification, which is the allowlist item 1412 was glad to avoid, and
`eager-tail-cache`'s 3680x is what being wrong about one step costs. Priced, not taken.

### Item 1434 — **SHIPPED, 50.3% / 49.7%** (36/36 both): `FAR_DRIVEN_MIN_DEGREE` 3 → 1. **The sign flipped** — items 1390, 1404 and 1406 all measured this route LOSING at low degree, and all three predate item 1407's row builder. Found via a **2.6x gap between `:E` and `:E|F` on identical edges**

### The nomination was an equivalent-spelling gap, not a profile share

At `MULTILABEL=0` the bench has **no `F` edges at all**, so `:E|F` and `:E` select the identical
100,000 edges and return the identical 100,000 rows:

| spelling                | rows                 | p25       |
| ----------------------- | -------------------- | --------- |
| `:E` (`hopsingleyield`) | 100000               | **26.70** |
| `:E                     | F` (`hopmultiyield`) | 100000    | **69.54** |

**2.6x for the same answer on the same edges** — the class CLAUDE.md says costs 100-300x and returns
the right answer every time. Not literally two spellings of one predicate, but on this graph they
select one edge set, and the cost differed by a route choice.

### The cause, and why three earlier items had it right at the time

`:E` takes the far-driven walk (item 167's hoist: `projectRow` once per far VERTEX). `:E|F` takes
`startDrivenMany` (`projectRow` per EDGE). The multi-type far-driven route exists but was gated at
degree 3 — because it genuinely lost at low degree:

- **item 1390** measured 1.24x against it at degree 1
- **item 1404** declined `min=2` for the estimate's bias
- **item 1406** measured a **16.9% loss** at true degree 2 on a disjoint fixture

All three are correct readings of the code as it then was. **All three predate item 1407**, which
replaced that walk's per-row computed-key stores with `{ ...template }` and made the template the
first row. Forcing the gate open and comparing against the shipped route, 100,000 vertices,
`STRIDE=random`:

| ML  | FANOUT 1  | FANOUT 2  | FANOUT 4 |
| --- | --------- | --------- | -------- |
| 0   | **1.87x** | **1.99x** | 0.96x    |
| −1  | **2.00x** | **2.09x** | 1.00x    |
| 3   | **1.73x** | **1.53x** | 0.96x    |

`FANOUT=4` is the built-in control: the estimate is already ≥ 3 there, so both arms take the
far-driven route and agree — which is what says this is a ROUTE change rather than a walk change.

| shape                                            | fanout | BASE  | MIN1      | change    | concordance |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------ | ----- | --------- | --------- | ----------- |
| **`hopmultiyield`**                              | 1      | 66.60 | **33.13** | **50.3%** | **36/36**   |
| **`hopmultiyieldrev`**                           | 1      | 67.06 | **33.76** | **49.7%** | **36/36**   |
| `hopmultiyield` [CONTROL — gate already accepts] | 4      | 42.62 | 43.57     | −2.2%     | 9/36        |
| `hopsingleyield` [CONTROL — no degree gate]      | 1      | 18.29 | 18.24     | 0.3%      | 19/36       |

`:E|F` and `:F|E` now converge at 33.13/33.76 — both FAST, where before they converged at 66.60/67.06,
both slow. Equal cost for equal meaning was always true; it is now equal cost at the better price.

### Why 1 and not 0

`farEndpoints` counts vertices with an incident edge of a named type, so
`typeEdgeCount >= farEndpoints` holds whenever such an edge exists. `min=1` is therefore "take it
when there is anything to walk", and `min=0` differs only on the empty graph, which the
`farEndpoints > 0` guard already declines. 1 states the intent; 0 would imply a degree of zero means
something.

### ⚠️ Three tests failed, correctly, and each kept its valuable half

A route choice is answer-equivalent, so only deliberate ROUTE assertions can see this change — item
1289's lesson. All three that broke were encoding item 1390's conclusion:

- **monotonicity** — a real property of the formula, still true. Only where it crosses moved, so the
  declining case became a degree BELOW one.
- **"fan-in 1 takes the start-driven walk"** — route expectation reversed; the **answer assertion is
  unchanged**, which is the point of that block: both routes return the same 60 rows.
- **"a fan-in of 1 declines"** — retargeted to the sub-degree-1 case.

The constant has now moved **four times** (8 → 4 → 3 → 1) and the test pinning it has been edited
every time. That is the cost of a measured constant, and this is the fourth time it has been the
right cost: an unpinned constant would have drifted silently.

| mutant                               | verdict        |

| M2 `min=0`                           | **CAUGHT** (3) |

| M4 `>=` becomes `<=`                 | **CAUGHT** (8) |

All four caught purely by the route assertions, which is the evidence they still have teeth after

### Item 1435 — **item 1106's `passes > 2` memo gate is SOUND and nearly MOOT**: the 2-pass sweep is reachable only via a NARROWING label, and a narrowing label makes the whole query ~1 ms. The bench had no row for that route at all; it does now, behind an opt-in knob

### Why look: item 1434's pattern, applied to another constant

Item 1434 found that items 1390, 1404 and 1406 had all priced one gate against code item 1407 then
changed. The obvious next question is which other measured route constant is stale the same way, and
the strongest candidate was the slot memo's `passes > 2` — item 1106 measured the memo a small LOSS
at exactly two passes (162.0 against 165.7), and items 1417-1418 made that memo substantially
cheaper (hand copy, then one flat buffer; `gcMs` 148 → 14.2).

### The first attempt measured nothing, for a reason worth recording

Forcing the gate to `passes > 1` and running `chain3` moved it 49.07 against ~47-49 — nothing.
**Because `chain3` never enters `sweepChain` at all**: item 1420 established it takes the degree
PRODUCT, so the memo gate is unreachable from that row. Same shape as items 1416 and 1428 — a
reading that barely moves because the code path is not taken.

Settled by counting instead of reasoning. A histogram inside `sweepChain`, keyed by pass count:

| shape                   | answer | `sweepChain` calls |
| ----------------------- | ------ | ------------------ |
| chain3, vacuous labels  | 20000  | **none**           |
| chain3, SELECTIVE start | 400    | `passes=2` × 1     |
| chain3, SELECTIVE end   | 400    | `passes=2` × 1     |
| chain4, vacuous         | 20000  | `passes=3` × 1     |
| chain4, SELECTIVE end   | 400    | `passes=3` × 1     |

**The 2-pass sweep is reached only by a 3-segment chain with a label that NARROWS** — which is
exactly the condition `threeSegmentRoute` uses to prefer the sweep over the product (item 1420).

### And that makes the gate low-stakes

With `SELECTIVE=50` (an `S` label on every 50th vertex), at 100,000 vertices and random stride:

| row                        | p25         | answer |
| -------------------------- | ----------- | ------ |
| `chain3sel` (2-pass sweep) | **0.97 ms** | 2000   |
| `chain4sel` (3-pass sweep) | **0.84 ms** | 2000   |
| `chain3` (product)         | 84.46       | 100000 |

A narrowing label seeds the sweep from a small set, so the whole query is ~1 ms. **The memo gate
governs a path that is never expensive**, in either direction — so item 1106's reading stands, and
re-tuning it could win at most a fraction of a millisecond. Recorded so the next reader does not
repeat this tick: the constant looks exactly as stale as item 1434's did, and is not worth the same
effort.

### Item 1436 — **`hopDrivesFar` is SOUND**: forcing the far-driven FILTERED walk is 64.93 against 60.90-64.41 at degree 1 and 123.06 against 116.87 at degree 4 — no better, slightly worse. Item 1434's flip was specific to the walk item 1407 rebuilt, not general staleness

### The suspicion, and why it was reasonable

Item 1434 moved `FAR_DRIVEN_MIN_DEGREE` 3 → 1 because item 1407's row builder had reversed three
earlier readings. `hopfiltyield` is now the heaviest OPEN GQL row (64.41 ms, **644 ns/row** — the
highest per-row cost in the bench) and it has the identical structural setup: a far-driven route
exists (`farDrivenFilteredHopWalk`) and is gated off.

`hopDrivesFar` is `candidateCount(far) < candidateCount(start)` — **strictly** smaller. With `P` on
every vertex both counts are `vertexCount`, so the gate never fires on this fixture and the
start-driven general closure always serves it.

### The measurement

Forced by relaxing `<` to `<=`, so the vacuous-label case takes the far-driven route:

| row                 | fanout | shipped       | forced far-driven |
| ------------------- | ------ | ------------- | ----------------- |
| `hopfiltyield`      | 1      | 60.90 - 64.41 | **64.93**         |
| `hopfiltyield`      | 4      | 116.87        | **123.06**        |
| `hopstartonlyyield` | 1      | 57.12 - 63.35 | **59.90**         |
| `hopstartonlyyield` | 4      | 102.50        | 101.96            |

**No gain anywhere, and 5% worse at degree 4.** Digests identical in every cell, which is the check
that the forced arm really is the other route and still correct. The gate stands.

### Why this one did NOT flip, which is the useful part

Item 1434's multi-type gate flipped because `startDrivenMany` does **per-vertex bucket bookkeeping**
— two `Map.get`s, an array of buckets, a size sort, and an earlier-buckets test — that the far-driven
walk skips entirely. Item 1407 made the far-driven row builder cheap enough that skipping the
bookkeeping became the dominant term.

The single-type FILTERED start-driven closure has no such bookkeeping: it is already one `Map.get`
and a tight edge loop. **There was no structural overhead for the far-driven route to remove**, so
the cheaper row builder buys nothing and the extra far-end indirection costs a little.

So "item 1407 invalidated the gates" is **too broad a reading of item 1434**. It invalidated the gate
on the walk whose alternative had per-vertex overhead. Two consecutive re-checks (item 1435's
`passes > 2`, this one) found their constants sound — which is the right prior for the rest of them.

### Item 1437 — ✅ SHIPPED, **75.9% / 94.2% / 73.8%** (4/4 each): `WHERE true` declined hop projection entirely and cost **7.46x**. Item 444's SURVIVING MUTANT had already proved the refusal was answer-free; nobody measured it

Item 1436 closed routing as the lever for `hopfiltyield` (644 ns/row, the heaviest open row), so I
decomposed it instead. The profile nominated nothing routable — `get adjFrom` is **1.1%**, which
declines the edge-index trick item 1431 took for the undirected walk by profile rather than by
measurement — leaving one structural observation: the row reads `b.n` twice, once for
`WHERE b.n > 5` and once for `RETURN b.n`, with nothing memoizing it.

**The double read is not the cost, and the arms that proved it found something much larger.** Four
arms at 100k nodes, `FANOUT=1 MULTILABEL=0 STRIDE=random`, p25 of 14 reps dropping 3:

```text
  RETURN b.n              (no WHERE)   26.08 ms   100000 rows   260.8 ns/row
  WHERE true  RETURN b.n              194.63 ms   100000 rows  1946.3 ns/row   7.46x
  WHERE b.n > -1 RETURN b.n            62.98 ms   100000 rows   629.8 ns/row   2.41x
  WHERE b.n > 5  RETURN b.n            58.78 ms    99994 rows   587.8 ns/row   2.25x
  WHERE b.k > -1 RETURN b.n            54.51 ms   100000 rows   545.1 ns/row   2.09x
```

Read the last two first, because they are the question I set out to answer: predicate and projection
on the **same** property is 587.8 ns/row and on **different** properties is 545.1 — different is
_cheaper_. **Nothing shares the read** — and ⚠️ "a CSE has nothing to win" is a SEPARATE claim these two arms do not establish, since BOTH of them read twice. It is true, measured at **2.6%** by item 1444's `floor-tworead` arm, but it was not measured here. (The per-row normalisation is
load-bearing: the two arms return 99,994 and 100,000 rows, so the raw 58.78-against-54.51 is not
comparable until divided.)

Then read the second line. **`WHERE true` means exactly what no `WHERE` means and cost 7.46x** —
3.1x worse than a real far predicate doing actual per-edge work. Spread across six processes was
1.007x, so it is not noise.

### The cause: a refusal whose comment reasons only about the case it was written for

`carriedWhere` ended with

```ts
if (!vars.includes(farVar) && !readsStart && !needsRel) {
  return null;
}
```

A predicate with **no free pattern variables at all** — `WHERE true`, `WHERE 1 = 1`, `WHERE $flag` —
has an empty `vars`, so it reads neither endpoint nor the rel and every test is false. The whole
shape fell off hop projection to the general matcher: `(anonymous) in filteredHopWalk` vanishes from
the profile and `expand` 35.2%, `evalLabelExpr` 13.3%, `walkSegments` 8.0%, `get labels` 7.5%,
`matchPattern` 4.5% replace it. The 20.8% in label frames is the general path re-testing labels per
candidate — work the walk had already dropped (items 1066, 1408-1410).

The comment block above that line is 10 lines about **start-only** predicates and items 176/177/206.
The zero-variable case was never considered, which is why the line read as deliberate.

### ⚠️ ITEM 444 ALREADY KNEW THIS WAS SAFE, AS A SURVIVING MUTANT

Item 444 mutation-tested this exact refusal and recorded:

> "Mutation survived with it removed, and survived again with `carriedWhere`'s neither-endpoint
> refusal removed too: `rowLocal` is what refuses a subquery clause `WHERE` here."

That survivor is the precondition for this change — removing the refusal changes no answer, because
`rowLocal` is the real guard — and it sat in the file for ~1000 items. **A surviving mutant says the
tests cannot see the line; it does not say the line is free.** Item 444 read it as defence-in-depth,
which it is, and stopped there. The missing step was to ask what the refusal COSTS, and it cost
7.46x. Worth generalising: a mutant that survives on a REFUSAL is a perf question, not just a test
gap — the code it guards is unreachable, so the guard's only remaining effect is the route it denies.

### The change, and why START-ONLY rather than a new route

A predicate reading no pattern variable is loop-invariant, so it is classified `startOnly` and rides
the existing start-gated closure — which gates a vertex BEFORE reading its adjacency and already
carries items 139-145' raise parity (the bucket check and `try`/`catch`). Reusing it keeps those five
tests pointed at this case instead of asking a new walk to re-derive them. `needsStart` stays false:
there is nothing to read. `rowLocal` is still required, for item 175's reason — a zero-variable
predicate can still hold a faulting uncorrelated subquery.

### Measured, as an A/B with the decline restored as the PRE arm

Each arm asserted to BE the code it claims (`grep -c` against an expected count per arm) before
being built, per CLAUDE.md. `hopfiltwtrue`, 100k nodes, `MULTILABEL=0`, p25 of 10 reps dropping 3,
two alternated rounds:

```text
  stride  fanout        PRE       POST    change   concordance
  random       1     196.59      47.41     75.9%   4/4
```
