### ⚠️ The defect found on the way: a discarded `Graph` is retained in full

The bench's first version built one fixture per algorithm per size and died at **4,087 MB** with
"Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit". The fixture measures ~2.8 KB/vertex — 450 MB at the size
that failed — so the heap was not what was live, it was what should have been dead. Adding a progress
line (so a row names itself instead of dying anonymously) showed the heap climbing monotonically
**124 → 4018 MB across the whole sweep, never falling.**

A heap snapshot BFS from the GC roots gave the retaining path exactly, rather than by guessing:

```text
(GC roots) -> (Micro tasks) -> system / CallableTask
  -> closure 'drainMutations' -> system / Context -> Context
  -> [object] Graph -> property 'verticesById' -> Map -> Vertex
```

`Graph` defers reactive bookkeeping to one microtask per burst of writes, and that queued closure
captures the graph. **The deferral is correct; the consequence is that `global.gc()` does not unwind
the stack**, so in a synchronous run the pending drain pins each graph forever. Confirmed by toggling
exactly one thing — `graph-retention-probe.mjs`, per-round growth at N=20,000:

| arm             | growth/round | reading                                   |
| --------------- | ------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `empty`         | **0.00 MB**  | the control — never mutated, never pinned |
| `verticesProps` | 11.45 MB     | ~570 B/vertex, i.e. the whole vertex      |
| `full`          | 48.35 MB     |                                           |
| `full YIELD=1`  | **0.00 MB**  | one `await setTimeout(0)` per round       |

**It is BOUNDED retention, not an unbounded leak, and the distinction is the finding.** Every async
embedding releases each graph on the next tick, so this is not a user-facing leak in normal use. The
exposure is synchronous batch work — a test suite, a bench sweep, a CLI that builds, computes and
discards inside one turn. `empty` at exactly 0.00 is what makes the rest trustworthy: retention
tracks **mutation**, not construction.

Not fixed in this item. The shape of a fix is to stop the queued drain from strongly capturing the
graph (a `WeakRef`, with the drain becoming a no-op when the referent is gone — sound, because an
unreachable graph's counters are unobservable by construction), and that is a correctness change to
the reactive path which needs its own tests, not a tick's work bolted onto a bench.

⚠️ **Two instrument traps recorded, both load-bearing.** The bench builds ONE fixture per (div, size)
shared by every algorithm at that scale — 4 fixtures, not 24 — and that is a requirement, not a
tidy-up, because of the retention above. And the body **cannot** become async to drain the queue:
`profileWindow` does `result = body()` **without awaiting**, so an async body stops the profiler
immediately and every `PROF_OUT` capture comes back empty — a silent instrument failure of exactly
the kind this corpus keeps recording.

### `labelPropagation` NOMINATED, priced by profile share, not built

Profiled at V=80,000 (`PROF_OUT`, 1,645 samples). Fixture frames are ~16.5% of the capture and are
subtracted by eye — item 1457's lesson applies to an ad-hoc read profile too, and the ranking among
query frames is unaffected:

```text
30.94%  computeGen            label-propagation's own loop
12.04%  incidentEdges         the per-vertex GENERATOR
 9.60%  collectNeighbours     its only consumer
 8.94%  drainSync
 6.93%  (garbage collector)
```

**`incidentEdges` + `collectNeighbours` = 21.6%, and all of it is CSR BUILD, not iteration.** The
build allocates **one intermediate `number[]` per vertex**, pushes each into a `lists` array, then
copies every list into an `Int32Array` — so `n` allocations plus a full copy pass, which is also
where the 6.93% GC comes from. `incidentEdges` is a generator delegating to a `Set` iterator, and on
this fixture (`MULTILABEL=0`, one edge type) it takes the `byLabel.size === 1` arm, so that 12.04% is
**pure generator overhead with no dedupe in it.**

The cure, for the next item rather than this one: a two-pass **count-then-fill** build. `countIncidentEdges`
already exists beside `incidentEdges`, so pass one fills `off` and pass two writes straight into the
`Int32Array` — no per-vertex arrays, no copy pass, no generator. Order is preserved (`to` neighbours
then `from`, per vertex) which byte-identity with native requires.

And it needs one gate, which already exists: counting twice is only cheap when no dedupe is needed,
and dedupe is needed **exactly** when an edge carries more than one label — which is what
`multiTypeEdgeCount` counts. Verified present on the core `Graph` and maintained at all four
transitions (item 1460 built it for the Gremlin union fusion). So: two-pass build when
`multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`, today's path otherwise.

**Priced at 21.6% of `labelPropagation` plus its share of a 6.93% GC term, cure named, gate verified
to exist. Not built** — written down next to the price so it is not re-derived, which is the pattern
item 1455 documented and [[no-dense-vertex-ordinal]] paid for seven times.

`bun run check` 0 (read unpiped). Two new instruments; no engine code changed.

### Item 1468 — SHIPPED, 14.4% / 21.6% (3/3 concordance, both controls flat): `labelPropagation`'s CSR build allocated one intermediate array PER VERTEX and copied them all into a typed array. It now counts, then fills the typed array directly. ⚠️ And the first A/B measured the SAME CODE TWICE, because the bench loads `dist`

Item 1467 priced this at 21.6% of the run (`incidentEdges` 12.04% + `collectNeighbours` 9.60%) plus a
6.93% `(garbage collector)` term, named the cure, and verified the gate it needs already exists. This
built it.

### The change

`buildAdjacency`, extracted from `computeGen` in `label-propagation.ts`, with two arms:

- **fast** (`graph.multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`): pass one sizes `off` by summing bucket sizes
  (`countIncidentEdgesFlat`, O(buckets) and allocation-free), pass two writes endpoints straight into
  the `Int32Array` (`writeIncidentEnds`). No per-vertex arrays, no copy pass, no generator.
- **general** (otherwise): the original path, unchanged.

The gate is required, not an optimization: the label index buckets an edge under **every** label it
carries, so a flat count double-counts a two-label edge. `multiTypeEdgeCount` is exactly that
condition and is maintained at all four transitions (item 1460 built it for the Gremlin union
fusion). Both new helpers carry a ⚠️ saying they are only valid under that gate, and they are
separate functions rather than a `flag` parameter so the unsafe case is not reachable by passing
`false`.

### ⚠️ THE FIRST A/B MEASURED THE SAME CODE TWICE, and its output looked like a clean null

Worth recording in full, because the failure was legible only by accident.

The first A/B swapped the two **source** files between arms and reported `labelPropagation` POST
97.44 / 98.60 / 94.94 against PRE 98.17 / 95.62 / 96.59 — flat, with both controls moving just as
much. The honest reading of that table is "the change is a null", and that is what it was written up
as.

**It was not a null. `packages/native` resolves `@lenke/core` to `packages/core/dist`, so neither arm
was ever built and both were PRE.** It was caught by profiling the supposed POST arm and finding
`incidentEdges` still at 13.29% — a frame the change deletes. Nothing in the timing table could have
revealed it; the controls-move-as-much pattern is exactly what a null looks like.

Two rules, both already in the repo and both evaded here:

- **An A/B's arm assertion has to check the ARTIFACT THE HARNESS LOADS, not the file you edited.**
  CLAUDE.md requires asserting each arm is the code it claims; the first script did assert, against
  `src`, and passed every time while measuring neither arm. `@lenke/*` resolving to `dist` is a
  recorded trap and the assertion sailed straight past it.
- **`grep` silently skips files containing non-ASCII**, and the rebuilt bundle is one. Checking
  whether `dist` had picked the change up, `grep -c countIncidentEdgesFlat` printed nothing for a
  string present **4 times** — which read as "the build did not include it" and nearly caused the
  working change to be investigated as broken. Verified with `python str.count` instead, which is
  the recorded rule for exactly this.

The corrected script rebuilds between arms and asserts from `dist` via python.

exists for and the case where a flat count is wrong by construction, so a suite that only exercised
single-label graphs would pass against a build that ignored the gate entirely. It asserts the new
pair produces the **identical sequence** to the generator path (not merely the same degree — a
permuted neighbour list changes a label tie-break, so a divergence is a wrong answer that agrees on
row count), over: several edge types with no multi-label edge (the only fixture that distinguishes
`countIncidentEdgesFlat` from `countIncidentEdges`), parallel edges, self-loops, an `edgeLabel`
restriction, an absent label, and cursor-append order.

End to end, the gate is a property of the GRAPH so the same graph cannot take both arms. The A/B
fixture instead makes the component under test **identical** in both graphs and forces the slow arm
with a two-label edge between two extra isolated vertices, then compares the shared component's
labels — plain, under an `edgeLabel` restriction, and with a `seedProperty` pinned.

**Mutation-verified, because it passed on the first run and so does a test that checks nothing.** Four

| mutant                                              | caught by  |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |

| the gate removed (`=== 0` → `>= 0`)                 | 1 failure  |
| counting pass drops in-edges (sizes `data` short)   | 3 failures |
| `writeIncidentEnds` ignores its cursor              | 4 failures |

The **count** mutant is the one that mattered: `Int32Array` drops out-of-bounds writes **silently**,
so sizing the array short produces a truncated adjacency with no error anywhere. It was predicted as

### Item 1469 — SHIPPED, **2.73x** (3/3, both controls flat): `neighborAggregate`'s adjacency boxed ONE OBJECT PER EDGE PER DIRECTION and re-sorted it per vertex. Two flat CSRs and a two-pointer merge instead. ⚠️ A mutant that PERMUTED THE ACCUMULATION ORDER survived the whole suite

Item 1467's bench put `neighborAggregate` second worst per vertex (2500 ns/V). Profiling it nominated
the target rather than a priced heading: `(garbage collector)` at **11.81%**, the highest share
anywhere in the twelve, beside `gatherContributors` 13.82% and `buildAdjacency` 9.14%.

### Where the allocation was

`buildAdjacency` built `Map<string, {eidx, nbr}[]>` — **2·E short-lived objects** plus an array per
vertex per direction — and `gatherContributors` then copied a vertex's two lists into a buffer and
**`sort`ed it per vertex** to recover edge-index order.

Replaced by two flat CSRs over dense vertex indices (`off` / `nbr` / `eidx` as `Int32Array`, counted
then filled), with features and GCN degrees moved from string-keyed `Map`s to arrays indexed the
same way. The per-vertex sort became a **two-pointer merge**: both slices are already ascending in
`eidx` because the fill pass walks `graph.edges` in order, so interleaving them reproduces exactly
what sorting the concatenation produced, in O(d) instead of O(d log d) and with no comparator.

⚠️ **This is NOT the route item 416 refuted.** That one returned the STORED adjacency list to the
consumer instead of copying into a reusable buffer, and regressed `direction: in` by 1.20x. Item 416
never varied the REPRESENTATION, which is what changed here — and the reusable buffer it defended is
moot now, because nothing per-vertex is allocated at all.

### ⚠️ A MUTANT THAT PERMUTED THE ACCUMULATION ORDER SURVIVED THE ENTIRE SUITE

The most useful thing this item found. Replacing the merge with a plain concatenation — every
out-contributor, then every in-contributor — leaves the contributor **multiset** identical, and **all
23 other tests passed.** Including the independent oracle, which compared exact arrays.

The reason is that the fixtures used small integer features, and an exact float sum does not care
about order. But that order **is** the contract: it is the canonical, engine-independent accumulation
order and, under `sum`/`mean`, the float summation order — so permuting it diverges from the native
engine in the **result bytes**. A suite that cannot see the difference between a merge and a
concatenation is not testing the thing the merge exists to preserve.

Pinned with catastrophic cancellation. Edges `v->a`, `b->v`, `v->c`; features `1e16`, `1`, `-1e16`:

```text
merge by eidx  -> a, b, c -> (1e16 + 1) + (-1e16) = 0
concatenation  -> a, c, b -> (1e16 + (-1e16)) + 1 = 1
```

With that fixture the mutant dies. **The generalisable form: when a change replaces a SORT with an
ORDER-EXPLOITING traversal, the multiset is the easy half — a test has to make the order itself
observable, and for float accumulation that means values where addition is not associative.**

### Teeth

`neighbor-aggregate-csr.test.ts`, 16 tests. The three things the rewrite could silently break, none
of which the existing eight covered:

- **the `eidx` ↔ weight association.** `edgeWeights` is indexed over EVERY edge, not only the
  type-matching ones, so a filtered-local index would pair every weight with the wrong edge. Needs a
  type filter AND distinct weights to be observable at all; the fixture puts weight 100 on a filtered
  edge so a mispairing is unmissable.
- **the self-loop rule** — a `both`-direction self-loop counts once, now enforced by dropping the
  in-copy during the merge rather than by filtering before a sort. Also checked in the `gcn` degree
  pass, where the load-bearing number is `deg(a) = 2` (3 if double-counted).
- **the accumulation order**, as above.

Plus an independent oracle over a generated graph (contributors re-derived by scanning `graph.edges`,
transcribing the documented rules, sharing nothing with the CSR) across all three directions and
with weights.

⚠️ **The generator produced ZERO self-loops across 120 edges** — two independent LCG draws mod 40
never collide on consecutive calls — so the self-loop rule the oracle exists to check was not being
exercised. **The fixture-statistics test is what caught it** (CLAUDE.md: an invariant that cannot
validate itself is worthless), and self-loops and a parallel pair are now injected deliberately
rather than left to chance.

**Mutation-verified against the FINAL code**, after the `accumulate()` extraction moved the merge and

### ⚠️ The file had been invisible to the earlier survey, and the glob is why

Item 1467 surveyed every algorithm for generator-vs-CSR use and concluded _"all of them build a CSR
once — `incidentEdges` is called during the build, not per iteration."_ That conclusion was wrong
about this file, and not because the survey misread it: the loop skipped it. The filter was
`case "$f" in *test*) continue;;`, and **"shor_test\_-path.ts" contains "test"** at index 4. So
`shortest-path.ts` was never examined.

**The profile caught what the survey missed**, which is the argument for the user's PROFILE-FIRST
instruction stated as cleanly as it can be: a structural survey can be silently incomplete, and a
profile of the actual run cannot. Worth remembering as a concrete hazard — a `*test*` substring
filter over this repo also swallows anything containing "test" in a longer word.

### What it was doing

`neighbours` was a generator **delegating to `incidentEdges`, a second generator**, yielding
`[edge, neighbourId]` — one 2-element array per edge traversed — and all three consumers (BFS,
Dijkstra, A*) then did `index.get(vid)!`, a **string-keyed Map lookup per step**. The whole chain was
rebuilt for every settled vertex.

Replaced with one flat CSR built once: `off` / `nbr` as `Int32Array`, plus a `Float64Array` of
per-slot weights (not materialized at all when unweighted). Every step is now two typed-array reads.

Three invariants, each with a reason it cannot be shared with its neighbours:

- **out-edges then in-edges per vertex, NOT merged by edge index.** `both` has to match native
  `visit_adj`'s order because the Dijkstra `(distance, index)` tie-break is decided by it. This is
  the _opposite_ of item 1469's `neighborAggregate`, where eidx order was the contract — the two
  procedures genuinely differ, so the orders cannot be shared, and the comments in both now say so.
- **a `both`-direction self-loop appears TWICE**, once from each side, because that is what
  `neighbours` yielded. `neighborAggregate` drops the second copy; this must not.
- **the build reads through `incidentEdges` / `countIncidentEdges`**, so the multi-label dedupe is
  preserved exactly — paid once per vertex at build time instead of once per traversal. Using the
  non-deduping flat count here would be a wrong answer, not a slowdown (see Teeth).

### Item 1471 — reaching an algorithm through ISO-GQL's `CALL` costs **2.5x the procedure itself** on a cheap procedure, and the wrapper is ~60% of the run. SHIPPED 1.18x (3/3) off its per-row `new Map(binding)`. ⚠️ The predicted GC mechanism did NOT materialise, and the suite had NO MATCH-then-CALL test at all ⚠️ **Its `gremlin` row is measured against the WRONG FLOOR — item 1472 shows that gap is the property write the step is specified to do, and the Gremlin OLAP wrapper is ~3.6%, within noise.**

Items 1467-1470 optimized the twelve procedures through `runAlgorithmSync` — the entry point both
engines dispatch through, but **not how a user reaches them**. A user writes `CALL degree() YIELD
node, degree` or a Gremlin OLAP step, and each surface wraps the result. That wrapper had never been
measured. New instrument: `algo-surface-overhead-probe.mjs`.

### What a surface costs, which is the finding

Median of kept reps, 40,000 vertices, every arm returning 40,000:

```text
                 pagerank        degree
direct             21.09          4.06      runAlgorithmSync, no surface
gql                25.46         10.12      CALL … YIELD … RETURN count(*)
gqlbare            26.21            —       CALL … RETURN count(*)  (YIELD-less)
gremlin            30.86            —       V() -> step() -> count()  ⚠️ WRONG FLOOR, see item 1472
```

**On a cheap procedure the wrapper is 2.5x the procedure** (4.06 → 10.12). On an expensive one it is
~21% (21.09 → 25.46). So the overhead is roughly FIXED PER ROW and the ratio is just telling you how
much algorithm it is being divided by — which is why both a cheap and an expensive procedure are
measured, and why quoting either number alone would mislead.

⚠️ **The Gremlin arm is not a like-for-like rendering of the GQL one and the probe says so.** `CALL`
YIELDs rows; a Gremlin OLAP step WRITES a property and passes traversers through. The comparable
shape is `V() → step() → count()`, so these are "what each surface costs to reach the same
procedure", not two views of one operation. (The Gremlin `degree` cell is absent: `@lenke/gremlin`
exports no `degree` step, which the probe asserts rather than silently measuring something else.)

### The target, profiled

`CALL degree() RETURN count(*)` at 200,000 vertices, 1,006 samples:

```text
30.12%  (anon) clauses.ts:1158   the per-row binding builder
23.86%  (garbage collector)
17.10%  out                      ┐
 7.16%  computeGen$7             ├ the procedure itself, ~31%
 7.06%  countIncidentEdges       ┘
 5.67%  internalFlatMap
 3.58%  buildGroups              the count(*)
```

**The wrapper is ~60% of the run and the procedure ~31%.** ⚠️ An earlier capture of the same shape
had **103 samples** and was nearly targeted off — 8.67 ms × 9 reps at a 1 ms sampling interval is ~78
samples, and at that count the ranking is noise. The reliable read needed 200,000 vertices and 15
reps.

### What shipped

The row builder did `new Map(binding)` per result row. **`new Map(iterable)` must obtain an iterator
and step it even when the source is empty**, so it allocates a Map _and_ an iterator where a fresh
Map allocates one object. Micro-measured over 2,000,000 constructions, order-alternated:

```text
fresh      32.8 - 37.8 ms
copyEmpty  85.8 - 93.0 ms     2.5x
copyOne   118.9 ms
```

A **leading `CALL` has exactly one outer binding and it is empty** — the common shape — so this was
paid once per vertex. Now `binding.size !== 0` decides. Also hoisted: whether a bind reads the vertex
handle or the result column is a property of the CLAUSE, and it was re-tested once per bind per row.

A/B, one arm per process, `nx build` between arms, arm asserted from `dist` on a marker unique to the
change, order alternated, median of 13 reps with 3 dropped, 200,000 vertices:

```text
                       POST                        PRE
gql/degree       59.10 62.53 59.39        67.86 70.80 70.14     3/3, 1.18x
gql/pagerank    147.76 138.79 136.83     146.22 159.40 148.99   2/3, ~1.07x
direct/degree    18.91 20.00 19.38        18.01 20.94 17.25     mixed, flat
```

**The win shrinking on `pagerank` is the prediction, not a disappointment**: the saving is per row and
`pagerank` divides it by 7x more algorithm. `direct/degree` never enters the wrapper and does not
move.

### ⚠️ THE PREDICTED MECHANISM DID NOT MATERIALISE

The change was aimed at the **23.86% `(garbage collector)`** term, on the reasoning that halving the
per-row allocation count would halve the garbage. Profiling the POST arm:

```text
            PRE      POST
(anon)     30.12%   23.86%    moved
GC         23.86%   23.97%    DID NOT MOVE
```

**The time win is real and 3/3, but it came out of the callback's own work, not out of GC.** The GC
term is the structural one-Map-per-row of the binding model (`Binding = ReadonlyMap<string,
unknown>`, one distinct binding per row), which no local change reaches — removing it is an
architectural change, not a tick's work. Recorded because the next pass will otherwise look at that
23.97% and re-derive the same idea.

### ⚠️ Teeth — and the suite had a REAL hole, demonstrated rather than asserted

**All thirteen pre-existing `CALL` tests begin with `CALL`**, so every one of them exercised only the
empty-outer-binding branch. The branch this change introduces — a non-empty outer binding, i.e.
MATCH-then-CALL — **had no test at all**, and a bug there drops the outer variables _silently_: the
query still returns the right number of rows, with the outer columns simply gone.

`call-outer-binding.test.ts`, 9 tests: the outer variable surviving into every row of the cross
product, its cardinality, a one-row outer binding, two outer variables, the leading-`CALL` branch
still working, `YIELD node` alone, the result column alone, an aliased `YIELD` in either order, and
the handle being the live element.

**Mutation-verified, and the hole is measured, not claimed:**

| mutant                                                | pre-existing `call.test.ts` | new file                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| **`copyOuter = false`** (drops every outer variable)  | **13 pass, 0 fail**         | 3 failures               |
| `isNode: false` (the handle never resolves)           | —                           | 8 failures               |
| `isNode: true` (the result column is lost)            | —                           | 7 failures               |
| `copyOuter = true` (the NULL mutant: correct, slower) | —                           | **survives, as it must** |

The null mutant surviving is the point of including it: a route choice is answer-equivalent, so no
differential test can catch it and none should be expected to — that is
`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` restated, and its survival is evidence the other three failures are
about behaviour rather than about the route.

### Item 1472 — ❌ THE GREMLIN OLAP WRAPPER IS NOT THE TARGET: it costs **~3.6%, within noise**, once measured against the right floor. Item 1471's `gremlin` row compared a step that WRITES A PROPERTY against calls that do not, and I let the number stand. Also: the algorithm `writeProperty` path is AT its known cost, and a PROFILED run is ~15% slower than an unprofiled one

Item 1471 measured `direct` 21.09 / `gql` 25.46 / `gremlin` 30.86 on pagerank at 40,000 and this
session's status update called the Gremlin OLAP surface "the highest overhead". **That was wrong, and
the entry itself contained the reason**: it noted that a Gremlin OLAP step WRITES its result to a
vertex property and passes traversers through, while `CALL` and the direct call do not — and then
quoted the number as if the three were comparable. Naming a confound and then reasoning past it is
worse than missing it.

### The profile said so before the measurement did

`V() → pageRank() → count()` at 200,000 vertices, 1,912 samples:

```text
53.61%  pagerankCore           the procedure itself
10.62%  computeGen
 9.88%  setProperty            ┐
 5.44%  #commitNormalized      ├ ~16%: the property write the step is SPECIFIED to do
 0.84%  pushTokens             ┘
 6.01%  (garbage collector)
 1.52%  algorithmStep          ┐
 0.84%  emit                   ├ the actual wrapper: ~3%
 0.58%  countStep              ┘
```

The wrapper frames total ~3%. There is no target here.

### Measured against the right floor

`WRITE=1` adds `writeProperty` to the `direct` arm so it does the same work. pagerank at 200,000,
median of 9 reps with 3 dropped, no profiler attached to any arm:

```text
direct, no write        122.32 ms
direct + writeProperty  145.24        +22.9 ms  <- the write
gremlin (always writes) 150.44        +5.2 ms over the right floor = ~3.6%
```

**~3.6%, which is inside this bench's run-to-run spread.** The apparent 46% was the property write.

### ⚠️ A PROFILED RUN IS ~15% SLOWER, so never compare one against an unprofiled one

The first `gremlin` reading at 200,000 was **172.50 ms** and the second **150.44** — a 15% gap
between two runs of identical code. The difference is that the first had `PROF_OUT` set, so the
inspector profiler was attached. Had I compared that 172.50 against the unprofiled `direct + write`
145.24, the wrapper would have "measured" 19% instead of 3.6% and this item would have gone hunting.
Both numbers in the table above are unprofiled.

### And the write path itself is at its known cost

22.9 ms per 200,000 vertices = **~114 ns per vertex** for one `setProperty` on a two-key vertex. The
repo already measured `setProperty` at **~87 ns at k=4** (the closure-guard attempt, reverted), and
the three-O(K)-passes defect behind it was already addressed by splitting `#commitNormalized` from
`#commitProperties` (items 334, 1676-1687). So this figure is consistent with ground that has been
attacked three times, once with a revert. **Not a new target.**

### What this closes

The surface question raised at item 1471 is now answered for both engines:

| surface                   | wrapper cost                                                                                |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ISO-GQL `CALL`            | real — was ~60% of a cheap procedure's run; 1.18x taken at 1471, remainder is architectural |
| Gremlin OLAP step         | **~3.6%, within noise** — this item                                                         |
| the `writeProperty` write | ~114 ns/vertex, consistent with the recorded ~87 ns at k=4                                  |

The GQL remainder is the binding model: one distinct `Map` per row, `Binding = ReadonlyMap<string,
unknown>`. Item 1471 measured that removing the per-row _copy_ did not move the GC term at all
(23.86% → 23.97%), so what is left is the Map itself and no local change reaches it.

⚠️ **One shape deliberately NOT optimized.** `CALL degree() RETURN count(*)` could skip materializing
bindings entirely (the count is `rows.length × outer.length` absent any filter). It is declined
because **that shape is the probe's, not a user's** — a real query is
`CALL pagerank() YIELD node, score RETURN node.name, score ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10`, which needs
every row. Optimizing the measurement instead of the workload is how a bench starts lying.

### Item 1473 — SHIPPED, **4.63x** on `UNION ALL` and **1.37x** on `UNION` (3/3 each, ⚠️ **but `excepted` is NOT a valid control for every change here — item 1561 reaches it, 1.25x, because `except`/`intersect` both end in `distinctRows`**): `combineRows` built the right-side key `Set` unconditionally and **both `UNION` branches discarded it**. ⚠️ The first A/B reported a NULL because the fixture's right side was 2,000 rows. ⚠️ And mutation found a pre-existing hole: nothing caught `INTERSECT` failing to dedup

The unpriced-frame screen's record says "no unpriced frame survives" — true of the surface it had,
which was **five single-pattern GQL shapes**. A real query joins two patterns, keeps an optional
side, de-duplicates, or asks a subquery, and none of that machinery had ever been in a profile. Six
new shapes added (`join`, `optional`, `distinct`, `existssub`, `wideproj`, `unioned`), profiled at
200,000 and run through the existing analyzer.

**Exactly one unpriced frame over 2% across all six**: `combineRows`, **ZERO mentions** anywhere in
`CLOSED.md` or the audit, 3.7% of the `UNION ALL` profile with `rowKeyOf` at 2.4% beside it. The
other five shapes came back clean, which is worth recording so they are not re-profiled for the same
answer.

### The defect

```ts
export const combineRows = (op, left, right) => {
  const rightKeys = new Set(right.map(rowKeyOf));   // ← first statement, unconditional
  switch (op.op) {
    case 'union': return op.all ? [...left, ...right] : distinctRows([...left, ...right]);
    …
```

**Neither union branch mentions `rightKeys`.** Only `except` and `intersect` read it. So:

- `UNION ALL` paid a full `rowKeyOf` pass over its right side and threw all of it away. Each key
  allocates an array (`Object.values`), maps `valueKey` over it and joins a string, and the `Set`
  holds every one.
- plain `UNION` paid that pass **and then computed the same keys a second time** inside
  `distinctRows`.

Fixed by building the `Set` in the two branches that read it.

### Measured — and the first attempt measured a NULL

⚠️ **The first A/B reported no effect, and the fixture was why.** `unioned` filtered each side to
`n.k = 5`, which at 200,000 vertices is ~2,062 rows — so the wasted pass was ~2% and sat under this
bench's noise floor. The giveaway was that **every arm including both controls read slightly worse in
POST**, i.e. run-to-run drift, not a change. CLAUDE.md's "match the fixture to the claim" exactly:
the claim is a wasted pass over the RIGHT side, so the fixture needs a wide right side.

Unfiltered scans (200,000 rows a side), one arm per process, `nx build` between arms, arm asserted
from `dist`, order alternated, 25 reps:

```text
                            POST                          PRE
unionedbig (UNION ALL)   469.3  625.8  443.8      2165.2 2171.3 2191.2    3/3, 4.63x
unionedbigdistinct       3752.8 3959.7 3674.9     5221.2 4908.4 5143.5    3/3, 1.37x
excepted (control)       645.5  617.8  598.9       641.5  638.5  653.4    flat
grouped (control)        104.3   99.9  112.5       104.0   99.2  162.5    flat
```

**`excepted` is the designed control**: `EXCEPT` genuinely needs the right-side keys, so the fix
cannot reach it — and it does not move. The two ratios are also internally consistent: `UNION ALL`
wasted its ONLY key pass (so removing it is most of the operation), while `UNION` wasted one of two
(so ~1.5x of key work becomes 1x, measured 1.37x).

So the 3.7% profile share understated this one by more than an order of magnitude on the right
fixture — the opposite of the screen's usual ~2.5x overstatement, because the share was measured on
the narrow fixture too.

### ⚠️ Mutation found a PRE-EXISTING hole: `INTERSECT` dedup was unasserted

Four mutants against the full 3,700-test GQL suite:

| mutant                                              | full suite before    |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `UNION`/`UNION ALL` branches swapped                | 6 failures           |
| `EXCEPT` keeps what it should drop                  | 3 failures           |
| **`INTERSECT` stops deduping**                      | **SURVIVED**         |
| `rightKeys` re-hoisted to the top (the NULL mutant) | survives, as it must |

ISO `EXCEPT`/`INTERSECT` always dedup, and the left side of an `INTERSECT` routinely carries
duplicates when it projects a non-unique column — so the rule is plainly observable and was simply
never asserted. `set-op-dedup.test.ts`, 9 tests: `INTERSECT` over a duplicate-bearing left side
(self-intersection, a narrowed right side, an empty right side), `EXCEPT` deduping its survivors and
deduping with an empty right side, `UNION ALL` keeping all 12 rows against `UNION`'s 3, and the
POSITIONAL column comparison (differently-aliased parts matching, left names winning). With them,
`intersectdup` dies with 3 failures.

**The null mutant surviving is the control for the whole exercise**: re-hoisting the `Set` is
behaviourally identical and merely slower, so no differential test can catch it — and its survival
is what shows the other three failures are about semantics rather than about where the `Set` is
built.

### Item 1474 — SHIPPED, **1.27x** (3/3, three controls flat): Gremlin's `group()` buffered EVERY traverser even when the value-by never needed one. Seven uncovered Gremlin shapes added to the screen, five more frames nominated. ⚠️ Mutation found the missing-VALUE rule unasserted, and `grep` was blind to the file because it holds NUL bytes

Item 1473 found a 4.63x defect by noting the GQL screen's surface was five single-pattern shapes.
The Gremlin screen had the same shape of gap: eight shapes covering hops, order, grouping, filtering
and dedupe — **no set operation, no wide projection, no optional side, no named-step select.** Seven
added: `unioned`, `projected`, `valuemapped`, `coalesced`, `selected`, `groupreduce`, `folded`.

### What the screen nominated

| shape         | engine ms | top UNPRICED frame                 | share |
| ------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------- | ----- |
| `groupreduce` | 281       | `groupStep` (+ GC 26%)             | 48.9% |
| `projected`   | 77        | `projectStep`                      | 54%   |
| `valuemapped` | 109       | `projectValueMap`                  | 45%   |
| `selected`    | 1776      | `asStep`                           | 7%    |
| `folded`      | 72        | `foldStep`                         | 10%   |
| `coalesced`   | 1601      | `get to` (priced elsewhere)        | —     |
| `unioned`     | **1**     | none — a count shortcut answers it | —     |

`unioned` at **1 ms engine** is worth recording on its own: `union(out(E), in(E))` + `count()` is
already answered by a shortcut, so the GQL defect at item 1473 has **no Gremlin twin**. Five
genuinely unpriced frames remain nominated; `groupStep` is taken here.

### The defect

`groupStep` buffered the group's `Traverser` objects so a reducing value-by could fold over them —
correct, and necessary for `by(count())`, which is applied as a BARRIER. But it did that for **every**
value-by, and then `groupValueOf` walked each bucket a SECOND time doing
`members.map(evalBy).filter(…)`.

For a non-traversal value-by (identity, a key, a token) each member's value depends only on that
member, so the traverser is dead the moment its value is read. Buffering them retained **the whole
stream** until the step ended and allocated two arrays per bucket — which is exactly what
`groupStep` 48.9% self plus `(garbage collector)` 26% looks like.

Now the non-traversal case evaluates at insertion and keeps only values; the traversal case is
unchanged.

### Measured

A/B, one arm per process, `nx build` between arms, arm asserted from `dist`, order alternated,
50,000 vertices, 20 reps:

```text
                          POST                        PRE
groupreduce          243.3 246.7 245.3        316.9 311.8 300.4     3/3, 1.27x
grouped (control)     32.8  30.2  31.7         30.7  33.4  32.1     flat
hopbare (control)    478.3 473.6 464.2        461.0 493.6 498.9     flat
valuemapped (control) 118.4 119.3 118.0       121.4 116.7 119.7     flat
```

`grouped` is `groupCount`, a different step, and it does not move. The series are unusually tight on
both arms, which is what makes a 1.27x at this magnitude trustworthy.

### ⚠️ Mutation found the missing-VALUE rule unasserted

A mutant that KEEPS a member whose value-by yields `NO_VALUE`, instead of dropping it,
**survived all 1,241 Gremlin tests.** The nine existing `group()` tests cover a missing KEY ("no null
bucket") but never a missing VALUE — and they are different rules with different consequences:

- a missing **key** filters the traverser out entirely, so **no bucket appears**;
- a missing **value** drops that member from its bucket's list, **but its key still created the
  bucket** — so a bucket can legitimately map to an **empty list**.

That asymmetry is the subtlety of the step and was untested in either arm. `group-missing-value.test.ts`,
8 tests: present values collected with no placeholder, the absent-value bucket still PRESENT,
stream order within a bucket, a bucket where EVERY member lacks the value (empty list, not a dropped
bucket), `by(count())` counting members regardless, a mapping traversal by collecting outputs, and the
missing-KEY rule restated for contrast. With them the mutant dies with 3 failures.

| mutant                                                | before               | after      |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ---------- |
| **a NO_VALUE member is kept in the list**             | **SURVIVED**         | 3 failures |
| a traversal value-by takes the direct arm             | 2 failures           | 4 failures |
| the bucket is created only if the value survives      | 1 failure            | 4 failures |
| `direct = false` (the NULL mutant: the PRE behaviour) | survives, as it must | survives   |

### ⚠️ `grep` WAS BLIND TO THE FILE, in the mutation-verdict position

`projection.ts` contains **two literal NUL bytes** — a `\x00` group-key prefix written as a real
byte, not an escape. So `grep -c MUT_` printed **nothing** for every mutant: grep treats the file as
binary and silently skips it, and the marker check that is supposed to prove a mutant applied
returned an empty string that the shell happily printed as `markers=`. The mutants HAD applied (the
verdicts differed per mutant), but the evidence line was worthless. Re-counted with `python
str.count`, which is this repo's recorded rule for exactly this, and all four read 1.

The NUL bytes also make `Edit`/`Write` refuse the file, so the change itself was applied with a
python read-modify-write (with a uniqueness assertion), not with the file tools.

### Item 1475 — SPLIT RESULT: `valueMap`/`elementMap`'s property copy SHIPPED at **1.14x** (3/3, controls flat) by dropping a guard that could never fail; `projectStep`'s per-row identity-`By` allocation **REJECTED as FLAT** — escape analysis again

Item 1474 left four unpriced Gremlin frames nominated, and the ZERO-mentions signal is one-shot. This
takes two of them: `projectValueMap` (45% of its shape) and `projectStep` (54%). They look like the
same kind of defect. **Only one of them was.**

### SHIPPED — the guard that could never fail

`valueMap` and `elementMap` carried **byte-identical** copies of this loop:

```ts
const targetKeys = keys && keys.length > 0 ? keys : Object.keys(props);

for (const k of targetKeys) {
  if (k in props) {
    // ← with no keys requested, this cannot be false
    out[k] = props[k];
  }
}
```

With no keys requested the targets come **from** the bag, so `k in props` re-answered what
`Object.keys` had just answered — a prototype-chain lookup per property per traverser. Replaced by one
shared `copyProps` with two arms: requested keys keep the test (a requested key genuinely may be
absent), the no-keys arm drops it.

Sharing it is the point as much as the speed: two copies of one output-shape rule is what drifts, and
a drift here is wrong bytes, not a wrong plan.

```text
                        POST                      PRE
valuemapped        107.7 104.6 105.6      124.1 119.7 120.5     3/3, 1.14x
hopbare (control)  473.9 474.4 454.3      450.6 461.5 451.6     mixed, flat
grouped (control)   30.7  29.6  29.9       32.1  33.4  31.2     mixed, flat
```

⚠️ **Assignment is kept, not a spread.** `out[k] = v` and `{ ...props }` differ for the key
`__proto__` — assignment sets the prototype, spread defines an own property — and that behaviour is
settled won't-fix. A perf item is not the place to change it, and `{ ...props }` would have been the
faster rewrite.

### ❌ REJECTED — the identity-`By` allocation, FLAT

`projectStep` wrote `bys?.[i] ?? { kind: 'identity' as const }` **inside** its per-key loop, so
`project('a', 'b')` with no `by()` modulators allocated a fresh object **per key per traverser** — two
a row, a million over the measured run. Hoisting it to a module-level frozen constant and resolving
`keys.map((_, i) => bys?.[i] ?? IDENTITY_BY)` once per step:

```text
projected   POST 83.3 87.2 92.5      PRE 86.8 87.1 89.5     1/3, FLAT
```

**Reverted.** V8's escape analysis makes an object literal that never leaves the call nearly free —
**the same mechanism that retired the `setProperty` closure guard**, also reverted, also flat
("V8's escape analysis makes a closure that never leaves the call nearly free"). That is now twice,
so it generalises: **an allocation visible in a profile is not necessarily an allocation that costs
anything, when it cannot escape.** The number is recorded at the line itself so the next reader of
that loop does not re-derive it.

This is also why the two frames had to be measured separately rather than as one "projection" item:
they shared a shape, a file and a profile share, and one was worth 1.14x while the other was worth
nothing.

### Teeth

`value-element-map-keys.test.ts`, 9 tests over both arms and both steps, asserting **`Object.keys`
sequences** rather than membership — column order is observable in the output bytes, so order is
contract. Covered: no keys requested (whole bag in bag order, a sparser element, an element with no
properties at all); keys requested (an absent requested key omitted while the row survives, request
order rather than bag order, a key absent everywhere); and `elementMap` keeping `id`/`label` first,
plus `IN`/`OUT` before an edge's properties.

**Mutation-verified, with a null:**

| mutant                                          | caught by            |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| the no-keys arm copies nothing                  | 19 failures          |
| requested keys emitted in BAG order             | 11 failures          |
| the absent-key guard dropped for requested keys | 1 failure            |
| the redundant guard RESTORED (the NULL mutant)  | survives, as it must |

### ⚠️ The 72-sample profile was noise, and it hid the real find

Item 1474 profiled `folded` with **72 samples** and reported `foldStep` at 10%. Re-run at 400 reps
(1,152 samples):

```text
49.22%  projectValues     ← 45.83% at 72 samples
20.83%  foldStep          ← 10%    at 72 samples
11.81%  sourceFromIds
```

Both shares roughly DOUBLED. PROBES.md says the ranking is noise below a few hundred samples; this is
that, measured. The nomination that mattered was never `foldStep` — it was `projectValues`, and
`values()` is on nearly every Gremlin query that reads a property.

⚠️ **`projectValues` had ONE word-boundary mention**, and chasing it by hand was the whole point:
the audit says _"`projectValues` already hoists correctly, which is why `values('age')` (593ms) is not
this bug"_. That is **true of the property-bag read** — `const props = t.value.properties` is lifted
out of the key loop — and says nothing about the ARITY branch, which was never hoisted. Exactly
PROBES.md's warning that "has mentions" is not "is optimized".

### The defect

```ts
for (const t of stream) {
  …
  if (keys.length === 0) { … }          // ← re-tested per row
  else {
    for (const key of keys) { … }       // ← an array iterator per row, for a list of length 1
  }
}
```

How many keys a step has is a property of the STEP. And `values('k')` — one key — is the
overwhelmingly common spelling, so the general arm was allocating an iterator per row to walk a
single element. The single-key case now reads that key directly; the no-keys and multi-key arms are
untouched.

```text
                            POST                      PRE
valuesonly             440.6 427.6 430.6      601.4 585.8 596.6     3/3, 1.39x
valuestwo (same fn)   1023.8 1011.2 1009.1   1025.4 1014.6 1005.8   flat
hopbare (control)     4024.8 4035.1 4010.8   4036.7 3979.1 3923.9   flat
grouped (control)      147.8  151.3  148.2    145.6  149.2  146.7   flat
```

**`valuestwo` is the control that matters**: it takes the MULTI-key arm of the same function, so a
specialization that helped one arm by making the other polymorphic would show there. It is flat.

### Teeth — already present, and verified rather than assumed

**No new tests.** Mutation shows the existing 11 `values` tests have teeth on all three arms:

| mutant                                             | result               |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| the single-key arm drops its presence guard        | 146 failures         |
| the multi-key arm emits in BAG order               | 2 failures           |
| the no-keys arm emits only the first property      | 1 failure            |
| `single` never set (the NULL mutant: the PRE path) | survives, as it must |

⚠️ **One of my mutants was a NO-OP and I nearly recorded its survival as a test gap.** `keys.length
=== 1` → `keys.length <= 1`, meant to make the specialization wrongly claim the no-keys case,
**survived** — and the reason is that `keys[0]` on an empty array is `undefined`, so the very next
test (`single !== undefined`) routes it back to the correct arm. The mutant changed nothing. A real
no-keys mutant (truncate `Object.values(props)`) is caught in 1 test, and bare `values()` turns out
to be covered twice over.

**The generalisable form: a surviving mutant is only evidence of a gap once you have checked that the
mutant CHANGES BEHAVIOUR.** Otherwise "survived" means "was not a mutant".

### The two nominations from item 1474, both CLOSED as non-targets

**`asStep` — the shape's cost is elsewhere and already declined.** `selected`
(`V().as('a').out('E').select('a').count()`) is the largest shape at 1776 ms, but its profile is
**68% general tail**: `otherEndpoint` 26.28%, `iterLabeled` 21.62%, `iterByLabel` 8.36%,
`traverseToVertex` 7.53%, `outEdgesOf` 4.54%. `asStep` itself is 7.11%. That tail is item 1464's
`tracksPath` gate — a plan that tracks path is returned unrewritten and every fused walk is skipped —
whose fix is a new walk variant, **priced at item 1465 and declined by the user at item 1466** on the
~16% perturbation that any edit to those files costs. Nothing new here; `asStep` is 7% of a cost that
is already recorded and already decided.

**`foldStep` — ~14 ns per element, which is the barrier itself.** 20.83% of a 3.3 ms/rep shape is
~0.69 ms to materialize 50,000 values into one list. `fold()` is defined as collapsing the stream, so
that array is the operation, not overhead.

core 431/0, gql 3709/0, gremlin 1258/0, native 961/0, serialization 144/0, `bun run fuzz` 20/0.

The hot frame in `wideproj` (25.8%) is the node-projection closure, which builds each row as
`const row = {}` followed by one **dynamic-key store per column** — so a W-column row transitions its
hidden class W times. Cloning a template that already carries every column makes those stores hit
existing keys.

Micro first, 300,000 rows, order-alternated, warm reading:

```text

  2     13.7       13.1      noise
  5     29.2       19.2      1.52x

```

**Non-monotonic, and that mattered**: the clone copies W slots, so it stops paying as W grows, and at
W=1-2 there is nothing to win. Which is why the engine was measured at FOUR widths rather than at the
one that flattered it — item 1472's rule about not optimizing the probe's own shape.

```text
matched        2914     applyPattern 18.4%, solve 7.8%, bind 7.0%, matchStep 4.3%, …  ≈44%
```

**`matched` is the largest shape yet measured on this probe and it is at only 20,000 vertices** —

### The defect

`applyPattern` dedupes candidate values with `tupleKey([o.value])` — once per candidate per
traverser, so 5 × 100,000 a rep on this fixture. And `tupleKey` was written only for the general
case:

```ts
parts.map((p) => …).join('\x00')
```

For a ONE-part tuple that is a real array from `.map()` (escape analysis does not see through array
builtins the way it does an object literal) plus a `.join()` that copies the string it was just
handed. **Four of the five call sites pass a single part** — `dedupe()`'s composite branch, two in
`iteration.ts`, and `match()`'s candidate dedupe — so the fast path went inside `tupleKey` and every
caller benefits without changing.

```text
                       POST                        PRE
matched          2594.1 2670.7 2708.5     2918.6 2933.1 2997.8    3/3, 1.10x
hopdedupe (2nd caller) 25.8 24.9 25.5         24.5 30.1 23.1      flat — NOT confirmed
localized (control)  1748.8 1722.2 1862.9  1696.4 1711.2 1784.8   flat
hopbare (control)     285.1 248.5 251.4      249.1 235.1 254.1    flat
```

**The arm ranges do not overlap** — POST's slowest 2708 is below PRE's fastest 2918 — which is what
makes a 1.10x believable at this magnitude.

⚠️ **A prediction that did NOT hold:** I expected `hopdedupe` to gain too, since `dedupe()` is the
other hot single-part caller. It is flat. The shape is only ~25 ms, near this probe's floor, and the
dedupe set is small relative to the hop — so the win is there in principle and unmeasurable in
practice. Recorded because a reader would otherwise expect it.

### ⚠️ Mutation found a real wrong-answer gap, and TWO traps on the way to killing it

Three mutants, all three initially **surviving all 1,258 tests**:

| mutant                                                      | verdict                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| the fast path drops the `@` element namespace               | **a REACHABLE wrong answer — now killed** |
| the fast path claims 2-tuples (losing the `\x00` separator) | **UNREACHABLE — not a gap**               |
| no fast path at all (the NULL mutant)                       | survives, as it must                      |

**The namespace one is a genuine hole.** `@` is the only thing keeping an element and a primitive
apart in a shared key space: a vertex whose id is `"5"` keys as `@5`, and strip the prefix and it
keys as `"5"` — exactly `JSON.stringify(5)` for the NUMBER 5. The collision silently DROPS a branch:
the right row count with the wrong contents.

⚠️ **Killing it took reading a guard, not guessing a fixture.** Four `dedupe()`-based tests all passed
under the mutant, and the reason is in `dispatch.ts`: the `tupleKey` branch there is gated by an
`isComposite` test — arrays, plain objects, temporals — so **a vertex is deduped by identity in a
plain `Set` and never keyed at all.** `dedupe()` cannot reach the prefix. `match()` keys EVERY
candidate into one `Set<string>`, so the killing case is an inner traversal yielding both a vertex
and a primitive:
`match(pipe(as_('a'), union(identity(), values('k')), as_('b')))` on a graph whose vertex id is `'5'`
and whose `k` is `5` — two branches, collapsed to one without the prefix.

⚠️ **The 2-tuple mutant is UNREACHABLE, and that is not a test gap.** The multi-part call site is the
multi-label `dedupe(a, b)`, whose parts are tag ARRAYS — so each part is `JSON.stringify(["x"])` =
`["x"]`, which self-delimits. No pair of tag lists concatenates ambiguously, so no separator-loss
collision can be constructed through the API. Same shape as item 1476's no-op mutant: **"survived"
means either the test is blind or the mutant is unreachable, and the two look identical in the
output.**

`dedupe-key-namespace.test.ts`, 6 tests: the reachable `match()` collision, the two `dedupe()` arms
documented as NOT reaching the prefix (kept, because they pin the behaviour they do cover), a vertex
repeat collapsing, a number repeat collapsing, and two different numbers not collapsing.

### Item 1479 — SHIPPED, **20.7x** on a transparent `local()` (3/3, landing ON a hand floor) and **364x** where it also unblocks the count shortcut: `localStep` re-dispatched its sub-plan once per incoming traverser even when the scoping was unobservable. ⚠️ The FIRST reading said 377x and was the count shortcut, not this

Item 1478 left `localized`'s frames unpriced: `localStep` 7.0%, `traverseToEdge` 6.7%,
`edgeToVertex` 5.0%. `localStep` is four lines —

```ts
for (const t of stream) {
  yield * applyPlanToStream(plan, [t], graph, ctx);
}
```

— so the cost is not in the step, it is the **per-traverser re-dispatch**: the generator chain for
the sub-plan is rebuilt for every row. And for a sub-plan made only of steps that map each traverser
independently, that scoping **changes nothing**.

### ⚠️ PRICED WITH A FLOOR FIRST, and the first floor was wrong

The hand floor — the same inner chain without the wrapper — read **4.5 ms against 1696.7**, i.e.
377x. That number is not the opportunity. `V().outE().inV().count()` answers in **0.07 ms** because a
chain count needs no walk at all, and the `local` wrapper blocks that route, so the two arms were not
doing the same work. **Two rows doing different work give a ratio, not a budget** (item 1465).

Appending `values('k')` defeats the shortcut in both arms, which is the honest pair. Both forms also
return the identical answer (10,000), checked before anything was built.

### The change

`fuseLocal`: a `local` step whose sub-plan consists entirely of per-traverser-transparent steps is
replaced by that sub-plan inlined. Wired into `effectivePlan` ahead of the existing fusions.

⚠️ **AN ALLOWLIST, and a short one** — 14 kinds (`out`, `in`, `both`, `outE`, `inE`, `bothE`, `inV`,
`outV`, `otherV`, `bothV`, `values`, `has`, `hasLabel`, `identity`). The denylist version of this
question fails OPEN: a step kind nobody classified would be fused and silently answer wrongly.
Mirrors `ORDER_FREE_STEPS`, which is four kinds for the same reason.

⚠️ **`dedupe` IS THE TRAP, and it is in `ORDER_FREE_STEPS`.** Order-free and local-transparent are
different properties. `local(out('E'), dedupe())` on `a→b, a→c, b→c` yields `[b, c, c]` — it dedupes
_within_ each traverser, so `c` reached from both `a` and `b` legitimately appears twice. Fusing it
would collapse those to one. Verified against the running engine before writing the list, not
reasoned about.

### Measured

A/B, one arm per process, `nx build` between arms, arm asserted from `dist`, order alternated,
20,000 vertices (FANOUT 5), 60 reps:

```text
                            POST                      PRE
localvalues            101.2 106.4 113.1     2264.9 2201.7 2147.0    3/3, 20.7x
localized              4.8   4.6   8.0       1746.9 1728.9 1809.0    3/3, 364x
localvaluesfloor       78.4  111.4 114.8     97.7  109.6  103.2      flat (the floor)
hopbare (control)      269.4 245.6 226.7     263.4 263.0  237.8      flat
matched (control)      2658.5 2617.8 2741.8  2551.9 2678.5 2686.5    flat
```

**Two numbers with different meanings, and both are reported because quoting either alone misleads:**
20.7x is the per-traverser dispatch removed on a shape that must walk; **364x** is that _plus_ the
chain-count shortcut becoming reachable, which only applies when the traversal ends in a bare
`count()`. **The fused arm lands ON the hand floor** — 106.4 against the floor's 103-111 — so there
is nothing left in this shape.

(At 2,000 vertices the same pair read 6.5x rather than 20.7x: the win grows with the traverser count,
which is what a per-traverser cost predicts.)

### Teeth

`local-fusion.test.ts`, 12 tests, **mostly about what must NOT fuse** — the rewrite can change
answers if the allowlist is wrong:

- `local(count())` → `[1,1,1]`, a count per traverser, not `[3]`
- `local(out(E), count())` → `[2,1,0]`, per-traverser degrees, not a total
- `local(out(E), fold())` → three lists, not one
- `local(out(E), dedupe())` → `[b,c,c]`, deduped within each traverser
- the transparent forms equal the unwrapped chain exactly (`[2,3,3]`), under `values` and under `count`
- the rewrite itself: inlines a transparent sub-plan, leaves a barrier-bearing one alone, and returns
  the SAME plan object when nothing changes
- **the WIRING**: `effectivePlan` applies it, and does NOT when the plan tracks path

**Mutation-verified, 4/4:**

| mutant                                                       | caught by     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- |
| fuse EVERY `local`, barrier or not                           | 7 failures    |
| admit `count` to the allowlist                               | 4 failures    |
| admit `dedupe` (order-free but not local-transparent)        | 1 failure     |
| **UNWIRE it — rewrite kept, `effectivePlan` never calls it** | **1 failure** |

The unwire mutant is the one that needed the wiring assertion: the rewrite stays correct and the
engine answers identically by the slow route, so every behavioural test passes. That is the shape
items 1303 and 1447 paid for, and [[rewrite-composition-is-not-free]] exists for it.

### Item 1480 — ❌ PRICED, NOT BUILT: `optional` and `coalesce` cost ~~**~19-20x a bare hop**~~ **(⚠️ that floor rides the values walk and does LESS work — item 1484 measures the real fused-vs-general ratio at 4.66x-15.68x depending on the projection, so the prize is nearer 4.7x)**, and item 1479's fusion CANNOT transfer. The cause is structural and now has three instances: the fused walks are SOURCE-ANCHORED, so no sub-plan can reach them

Item 1479 fused `local()` away for a 20.7x. `coalesce`/`choose`/`optional`/`branch` route each
traverser individually too — but for them that is the semantics, not an artefact, so the same trick
cannot apply: the branch decision needs per-traverser knowledge of whether the arm produced anything.

The question worth answering was whether the per-traverser cost is as large here, and what it is.

### Measured — the same magnitude as `local` had

20,000 vertices (FANOUT 5), 60 reps. The `values('k')` tails are deliberate: a bare `count()` tail is
answered by a chain count **without walking** (item 1479's 377x false reading), so these are the
honest pair.

```text
optionalvalues      1836.6 / 1864.3 ms      V().optional(out('E')).values('k').count()
coalescevalues      1925.4                  V().coalesce(out('E'), identity()).values('k').count()
branchvaluesfloor     95.4 / 101.0          V().out('E').values('k').count()
```

**19.3x and 20.2x.** ⚠️ **BOTH NUMBERS ARE STALE — item 1628 re-measured the same pair at 10.6x and 12.4x**, and took the `optional` half for 1.25x. At FANOUT 5 every vertex has out-edges, so `optional`'s first arm always wins
and the floor is semantically comparable — it is the same answer by the cheap route.

(The first floor attempt, `V().out('E').count()`, read **7.3 ms** — the count shortcut again. Named in
advance this time and still worth re-stating: a bare `count()` tail measures whether the shortcut
applies, not what the walk costs.)

### The cause is NOT the dispatch — it is the general walk

`optionalvalues` profiled at 1,664 samples:

```text
20.97%  otherEndpoint      ┐
19.47%  iterLabeled        │
 7.57%  get to             ├ ~61%: the GENERAL hop walk
 5.41%  traverseToVertex   │
 4.21%  iterByLabel        │
 3.25%  outEdgesOf         ┘
15.20%  optionalStep
 6.61%  projectValues
```

So the inner `out('E')` runs the **generic traverser pipeline**, not the fused walk that
`branchvaluesfloor` gets. I had expected the 103-arm `applyStep` switch to be the cost; it does not
appear at all.

⚠️ **AND THE FUSED WALKS STRUCTURALLY CANNOT REACH A SUB-PLAN.** `hopValuesShortcut` returns
`{ values: HopWalk, rest: Step[] }` and is consumed once at the top of `run` against the whole
`effective` plan — it "wants `V()` plus one or two steps", i.e. it is **source-anchored** and answers
from the graph. A sub-plan inside `optional`/`coalesce` starts from the incoming traverser, not from
`V()`, so there is nothing for it to anchor on.

**This is the THIRD instance of one structural cause**, and naming it is the point of this item:

| item | shape                                        | outcome                                                    |
| ---- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1464 | `tracksPath` set ⇒ plan returned unrewritten | `simplePath` 3.3x priced, **declined by the user at 1466** |
| 1479 | `local(transparent)`                         | **fixed by ELIMINATING the sub-plan** — 20.7x              |
| 1480 | `optional` / `coalesce`                      | **cannot be eliminated**; the sub-plan is the semantics    |

A real fix means making the fused walks composable — a stream-transformer form that applies a typed
hop to an arbitrary input stream without building traversers — rather than a source-anchored
whole-plan answer. ~~That is a design change to the fast-walk contract, not a tick's work~~ — ⚠️ **item
1627 built that piece for `match()` and item 1628 lifted it to `movement.ts` as `soleTypeBucket`,
taking the `optional` half for 1.25x.** ~~`coalesce` is still open~~ — **taken at item 1629 for
1.26x**, fusing its FIRST arm only (the only one that runs for every traverser).

### The secondary cost, priced and deliberately NOT taken

Both steps do, per traverser:

```ts
const out = [...applyPlanToStream(plan, [t], graph, ctx)];

if (out.length > 0) {
  yield * out;
} else {
  yield t;
}
```

They **fully materialize** the sub-plan's output into an array only to ask whether it is non-empty —
at FANOUT 5 that is a 5-element array per row, 1.2M of them over the measured run. A lazy first-peek
(`it.next()`, then yield the first and delegate the rest) removes it.

**Not built, for a reason that is not laziness being hard:** materializing eagerly means the sub-plan
runs to completion BEFORE anything downstream sees a row, and a lazy version interleaves it. For a
sub-plan containing `sideEffect`, `aggregate`, `store` or a mutation that changes the observable
ORDER of side effects relative to downstream consumption — and `sideeffect-in-branch.test.ts` exists
because that interaction is already known to matter. Against a shape whose cost is 61% elsewhere, the
expected win is small (item 1477: the profile share is the ceiling) and the semantic surface is wide.
Priced at one array per traverser, declined on that trade.

Every instrument in this corpus measures one surface, and the two do not even share a fixture — the
GQL probe builds one edge per vertex, the Gremlin probe has a `FANOUT` knob defaulting to 5. So "is
one surface paying more than the other for the same question?" had never been askable. New

engine, so a gap is between two front ends lowering to the same data, not between implementations.

### The result, and why the size mattered

```text
pair          gql ms   gremlin ms   ratio        answer
                            200,000 vertices
hopcount        0.00        0.01    3.11x       1000000   both shortcut — below the floor, meaningless
hopfiltered     3.98        4.27    1.07x         10310
project         8.08       13.15    1.63x        200000
exists          7.26        9.15    1.26x          2062
```

this, and here it did not merely change a magnitude: **it changed which surface was winning.**

### Every pair asserts its answers agree, and that is load-bearing

The probe throws rather than printing a ratio when the two arms disagree. A mistranslated query is
the obvious failure mode of a cross-surface comparison, and a ratio between two different questions
looks exactly like a finding. All five pairs agree (1000000 / 10310 / 200000 / 2062 / 97).

### The residual 1.63x has a named cause, priced not taken

`V().values('k')` profiled (595 samples): `projectValues` 36.81%, `countStep` 21.01%,

So Gremlin builds a **traverser per vertex and extends it per value** — ~29% of the run — where GQL's
node-projection walk emits values and builds none. That is the gap.

`hopValuesShortcut` already does exactly this elimination for `V().out(T).values(k)`; the analogous
**no-hop** form (`V().values(k)`, `V().hasLabel(L).values(k)`) has no shortcut. Adding one is
contained and in the same family.

### Item 1482 — SHIPPED, **2.39x** on `V().hasLabel(L).values(k)` (3/3, arms nowhere near overlapping, FOUR controls flat): the no-hop sibling of `hopValuesShortcut`. Gremlin now BEATS ISO-GQL on the pair where it was 1.63x behind — and the ~16% perturbation was sidestepped by putting it in a NEW FILE

Item 1481 priced this and declined it, because the obvious home is `hop-values.ts` — the file
[[executor-edits-perturb]] measures at up to ~16% on unrelated rows per edit, which a ~29% ceiling
clears only narrowly on a step as central as `values()`.

**That framing had a hole: the perturbation is a consequence of editing the FILE.** A new module costs
nothing, and the only edit to a hot file is one call site in `index.ts` — which items 1460 and 1479
both changed without the effect appearing. `node-values.ts` is that module.

### What it does

`hopValuesShortcut` eliminates the traverser pipeline for `V().out(T).values(k)` but requires a hop
at `steps[1]`, so the **no-hop** forms never had a shortcut. `nodeValuesShortcut` answers
`V().values(k)` and `V().hasLabel(L).values(k)` — and nothing else — by scanning `graph.vertices` and
emitting `props[key]` directly, building no traverser at all.

### Measured

A/B, one arm per process, `nx build` between arms, arm asserted from `dist`, order alternated,
200,000 vertices. **The cross-surface probe is both target and control rig**: its `project` pair takes
the shortcut and its other three do not, so they are controls sharing the fixture, process and
harness with the target. `hopbare` on the Gremlin probe is an outside control.

```text
                       POST                      PRE
project           5.86  5.67  5.82      14.18 13.93 13.11     3/3, 2.39x
hopfiltered       4.07  4.33  3.46       4.04  4.26  3.53     flat
exists            8.92  9.36  8.86       8.29  9.05  8.38     flat
grouped           3.41  4.32  3.39       3.68  4.13  3.39     flat
hopbare        4051.4 4120.1 3990.7   4019.6 3981.9 3939.8    flat
```

POST's slowest (5.86) is less than half PRE's fastest (13.11). **And `hopbare` is flat — the ~16%
perturbation did not appear**, which is the evidence that the new-file decision was the right one and
not merely a hopeful one.

**The cross-surface gap is now reversed**: `project` was Gremlin 13.15 against GQL 8.08 (1.63x
behind); it is now **5.88 against 7.69 — 0.77x, Gremlin ahead.**

### Teeth

`node-values-shortcut.test.ts`, 17 tests. ⚠️ **A shortcut is an ANSWER PATH, not a rewrite**, so a
loosened gate is a wrong answer rather than a slow one — most of the tests are refusals:

- answers: one value per vertex that HAS the key, in vertex order; a vertex lacking it **dropped**,
  not emitted as `undefined`; `hasLabel` filtering; `hasLabel(P, Q)` matching **any**; an absent
  label; an empty graph
- refuses: a residual step after `values()`; `values()` with no key; `values(a, b)`; `V(id, …)`; a hop
  before `values()`; a second filter between
- `drain()` equals spreading the iterator (they are one loop body for that reason)
- the shortcut agrees with the traverser pipeline

**Mutation: 6 of 7 caught, and the two survivors were different problems.**

| mutant                                              | result                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| accept a residual step after `values()`             | 42 failures                              |
| emit `undefined` instead of dropping                | 6 failures                               |
| ignore the label filter                             | 5 failures                               |
| `hasLabel` becomes ALL-of                           | 1 failure                                |
| accept `V(id, …)`                                   | 1 failure                                |
| **UNWIRE — shortcut correct, `run` never calls it** | **survived 1,291 tests → now 1 failure** |
| drop the `tracksPath` guard                         | **survives: UNREACHABLE, verified**      |

⚠️ **The unwire survivor is why a wiring assertion is not optional.** The engine answers identically by
the traverser pipeline, so every behavioural test passes. `run` returns the shortcut object itself and
that object carries a `drain`, so its presence is the observable: one test asserts a matching plan's
result has `drain`, another that a refused plan's does not.

⚠️ **The `tracksPath` survivor is UNREACHABLE, not a gap** — checked by reading, not assumed. The
shortcut admits only `V`, `hasLabel` and `values`, and **none of the three is in
`PATH_DEPENDENT_KINDS`**, so `planReadsPath` cannot be true for a plan it matches. The guard is kept
and now carries that note at the call site, because the gate belongs to the shortcut's CONTRACT rather
than to today's shape list: widen `matchShape` to admit a path-dependent kind and the guard is what
stops it becoming a wrong answer. Third instance of item 1478's "survived means blind test, no-op
mutant, OR unreachable code".

### Item 1483 — SHIPPED, **1.26x** on `optional(<one vertex step>)` (3/3, arms non-overlapping, three controls flat). ⚠️ I EXPECTED ~11x AND THE HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG: the per-traverser wrapping is NOT where `optional`'s cost is — item 1480's diagnosis was right and this measures how much of it the wrapping accounts for

Item 1482's new-file insight reopened the targets previously declined on the ~16% perturbation toll.
Item 1466's `simplePath` walk stays declined — the user declined it on usage frequency as well as
regression risk — so this took item 1480's 19.3x instead.

### The hypothesis, and why it was wrong

Item 1479 removed `local`'s per-traverser sub-plan re-dispatch for **20.7x**, and `optional` pays the
same wrapping: a one-element input array, the sub-plan's step array walked through a 103-arm dispatch,
a generator per step, and the whole output materialized into an array just to test non-emptiness.
Warm single-rep numbers at 20,000 vertices looked conclusive:

```text
out(E), values(k), count()                   2.81 ms
optional(out(E)), values(k), count()        32.00
optional(identity()), values(k), count()     2.28   ← the WRAPPER is nearly free
```

`optional(identity())` costing the same as no wrapper at all said the wrapping was cheap in itself,
so wrapping _a hop_ looked like the whole ~11x. **It was not.** Fusing the wrapper away gave
**1.26x**, leaving the shape still ~14x the unwrapped hop — ⚠️ **and that ~14x is itself against the values-walk floor; item 1484 corrects the real remaining gap to ~4.7x.**

**Item 1480 had it right**: the cost is that the inner hop runs the general traverser pipeline instead
of the fused source-anchored walk, and `local` only transferred 20.7x because it can be _eliminated_
entirely — reaching that walk — which `optional` cannot. This item measures how much of the gap the
wrapping accounts for: **about a quarter of it, not all of it.**

### What shipped

`optional-hop.ts` (a NEW module, per item 1482: the perturbation toll is on editing `hop-values.ts` /
`hop-projection.ts`, so a new file avoids it) fuses `optional(<single out/in/both step>)` into one
loop over the stream — far endpoints when there are any, the traverser itself when there are none.
Every other sub-plan shape falls through to `optionalStep` untouched.

⚠️ **It is LAZY where `optionalStep` is EAGER, and that is safe only here.** The eager `[...]` runs the
whole sub-plan before yielding, so laziness reorders side effects relative to downstream consumption
— which is exactly why item 1480 declined this for the general case and why
`sideeffect-in-branch.test.ts` exists. A vertex step has no side effects, so for this shape the two
orders are indistinguishable. The gate is narrow for that reason, not for tidiness.

```text
                       POST                      PRE
optionalvalues    1288.6 1618.7 1481.5   1863.5 1888.7 1873.1   3/3, 1.26x
coalescevalues    2002.5 1986.7 1981.7   1911.3 2059.8 1929.7   flat
localvalues        109.0  117.4  115.0    114.1  134.7  108.2   flat
```

Every POST reading is below every PRE reading. `coalescevalues` is the control that matters — same
branch family, not fused — and it does not move.

⚠️ **`hopbare` FIRST READ 13% WORSE, which is the pattern that should stop a ship.** Re-measured ALONE
over five alternated rounds: POST median 230.5 against PRE 241.8, **3/5 concordance, POST nominally
better**. Its own PRE spread across the five was 235.5-289.5 (23%), so the 13% was that spread, not
the edit. A control that moves gets isolated before anything else happens.

### Teeth

`optional-hop-fusion.test.ts`, 15 tests: far endpoints emitted for a vertex that has them, the
vertex itself when it has none, an isolated vertex, a multi-label hop, `both()` from either side, a
downstream step seeing the fused output; the gate refusing a multi-step sub-plan, a filter, a barrier,
a hop followed by anything, an empty sub-plan — and ACCEPTING a single vertex step, so the refusals
mean something; plus `optional(count())` and `optional(out(E), count())` still per-traverser.

⚠️ **One test records an UNREACHABLE branch rather than asserting a behaviour the engine never
produces.** `inject(7).optional(out(E))` is rejected by a STATIC frontier check ("out() moves from a
vertex, but the frontier is a scalar"), so the non-vertex branch cannot be reached by that route. It
is kept because it mirrors the general path exactly (`traverseToVertex` is lenient and yields nothing,
so `optionalStep` emits the traverser), and the test asserts the static rejection. Same reasoning as
item 1482's unreachable `tracksPath` guard.

**Mutation: 5 of 6 caught** — never emit the traverser when empty (6 failures), always emit both (6),
emit the near vertex (5), accept a multi-step sub-plan (5), accept any single step (3).

⚠️ **The UNWIRE mutant survives, and here it CANNOT be caught.** Item 1482's could: that shortcut
returns an object carrying a `drain`, so the route was observable. This one returns a generator of
traversers either way, and the fused and general routes are answer-equivalent with identical order —
laziness is not observable through the output either. That is precisely the limit
`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` documents ("a route CHOICE is answer-equivalent, so every mutant
survives the differential tests; extract the arithmetic as a pure fn and unit-test it"), and the pure
gate `optionalSingleHop` is unit-tested in six of the tests above.

named: a stream-transformer form of the fused walk, reachable from a sub-plan. That remains a contract
change — and now, thanks to item 1482, one that could live in a new module.
