### Item 1484 — ⚠️ A CORRECTION TO MY OWN NUMBER IN TWO PRIOR ITEMS, and a new instrument: "the fused walk is ~14x the general pipeline" is **not one number**. It is a RANGE depending on what the projection emits ~~**4.66x-15.68x**~~ **(⚠️ those arms carried a THIRD shortcut — `values(k).count()` is a presence-filter count; item 1485 re-measures without it at 4.2x-11.9x, and the 3.3x between the fused arms REVERSES once it is removed)**, and the two FUSED arms differ **3.3x from each other**

Items 1480 and 1483 both sized the `optional`/`coalesce` opportunity by comparing a sub-plan hop
against `V().out(T).values(k).count()`, and called the ratio the prize — 19.3x at 1480, "still ~14x"
at 1483. **That floor rides `hopValuesShortcut`, which emits bare VALUES and never materializes a
vertex traverser**, so it does strictly less work than the thing being floored. The ratio was an
upper bound, not a size.

This is the third level of the same mistake in four items: item 1479's first floor was answered by a
**chain count** (377x, actually 20.7x), 1480/1483's by the **values walk**. New instrument,
`fused-vs-general-probe.mjs`, measures it directly.

### The trick that makes a fair pair possible

`hopValuesShortcut` accepts exactly three third steps — `values(k)` with one key, `id()`, or nothing —
and **declines anything else**, falling back to the full pipeline. So `label()` after the hop gives
the general route over the **identical hop and identical row count**, where `values(k)` gives the
fused one.

```text
                    200,000 vertices, FANOUT 5, 1,000,000 rows each
fused values(k)        34.83 ms      35 ns/row
fused id()            117.23        117 ns/row
general label()       545.92        546 ns/row

general / fused(values) = 15.68x      general / fused(id) = 4.66x
```

At 50,000 the same three read 19.71x and 5.82x, so the ratio shrinks with size but the ordering holds.

### What this changes

**There is no single "fused vs general" number, and the right one depends on what the arm emits.**
A sub-plan inside `optional` must emit **vertex traversers**, because they flow downstream — so the
`values` arm (35 ns/row, no traverser, no vertex) is the wrong reference for it and the `id` arm
(117 ns/row) is much closer. The honest prize for reaching the fused walk from a sub-plan is
therefore nearer **4.7x than 14x.**

That matters because 14x would justify a contract change to the fast-walk interface and 4.7x makes it
a much narrower decision — exactly the distinction item 1465 drew when it corrected 86x to 3.3x.

⚠️ **AND THE TWO FUSED ARMS DIFFER 3.3x FROM EACH OTHER** (35 against 117 ns/row) on the _same walk_,
differing only in the `pick` closure — `far.properties[key]` against `far.id`. `fuseValuesIsCount`
does **not** explain it (that rewrite needs `values(k), is(…), count()`, and there is no `is` here),
and both arms take the same residual path with `rest = [count]`. **Recorded as an open observation
rather than guessed at** — the property read beating the id read by 3.3x is counter-intuitive and
whatever causes it is worth knowing before anyone prices a `pick`-shaped change.

### Not a perfect pair, and the probe says so

A property read is not a label read (first of a `Set`). It is the closest pair available without a
second engine build, and both are one read per far vertex — so a ~1.5x result would have meant the
`hop-values.ts` comments (375.6 against 251, "1.50x", for generator delegation alone) were the whole
story. **4.66x says they are not**: delegation is part of it, and the traverser construction the fused
walk skips is the rest.

### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. One new instrument; no engine code changed. Items 1480 and 1483 keep
their measured results — 1483's 1.26x was its own A/B and stands — but their framing of the REMAINING
gap is corrected here.

### Item 1485 — the 3.3x anomaly EXPLAINED, and it was a FOURTH shortcut I had not accounted for: `values(k).count()` is a presence-filter count (item 1141), so those values are never materialized. With it removed the ordering REVERSES — `id()` is cheaper than a property read, as it should be — and "fused vs general" is a RANGE of ~~**4.2x-11.9x**~~ **(⚠️ measured on a SEQUENTIAL-adjacency fixture; item 1486 flips the stride and it collapses to ~3.2x, which also makes the property-read target vanish)**, not item 1484's 4.7x

Item 1484 flagged an unexplained **3.3x between two FUSED arms** differing only in their `pick`
closure (`far.properties[key]` beating `far.id`), recorded it as an open observation rather than
guessing, and used the slower of them to correct the `optional` prize to "nearer 4.7x". **Both halves
of that were wrong, and for one reason.**

### The cause, found in the code rather than inferred

`count-shortcut.ts:389`: _"A TRAILING single-key `values(k)` under a count IS a presence filter — item
1141."_ So `V().out(T).values(k).count()` is answered as a **presence count** and the values are never
produced. Item 1484's "fused `values(k)`" arm was not the fused walk emitting values; it was a third
shortcut on top of it.

My own data had already said so and I did not read it: at item 1483 the no-count form measured **7.65
ms against the count form's 2.81** — producing the rows cost MORE than "counting" them. That is the
tell for a skipped materialization, and it was sitting in the transcript two items earlier.

### Measured with the confound removed

The probe now runs two families: `rows` (no count tail, so every arm must actually produce its rows)
and `count` (kept so the confound stays visible).

```text
                    200,000 vertices, FANOUT 5, 1,000,000 rows
                  rows family        count family
values(k)          149 ns/row          36 ns/row
id()                53                122
label() (general)  629                588

ROWS  (honest):      label/values 4.21x   label/id 11.91x   id/values 0.35x
COUNT (confounded):  label/values 16.49x  label/id  4.82x   id/values 3.42x
```

⚠️ **THE ORDERING REVERSES BETWEEN THE FAMILIES.** Without a count tail `id()` is **2.8x cheaper** than
a property read — which is what anyone would predict. With one, `values(k)` becomes **3.4x cheaper**
than `id()`, because only `values(k)` gets the presence-filter shortcut. The anomaly was never about
the `pick`.

### So what IS the fused-vs-general number?

**A range, and the tail decides it as much as the projection**: 4.21x-11.91x in the rows family,
4.82x-16.49x in the count family. Item 1484's "nearer 4.7x" came from `count label/id`, which is the
one cell where the general arm is ALSO nearly unaffected by its tail — accidentally close to the rows
family's `label/values` 4.21x, for unrelated reasons.

**The rule this leaves**: match the TAIL, not just the hop. A sub-plan inside `optional` cannot reach
any of these shortcuts — not the chain count (item 1479), not the values walk (1480/1483), not the
presence count (here) — so every top-level plan that ends in `count()` is a doubly unfair floor for
it. The fair reference is a rows-family arm, and for a sub-plan that must emit vertex traversers that
is `rows id()` at 53 ns/row against `rows label()`'s 629 — i.e. the prize for reaching the fused walk
from a sub-plan is **roughly an order of magnitude**, but only for the walk portion, and the traverser
construction `optional` cannot avoid is not in that number.

### Four shortcuts, four items, one mistake

| item | the floor's hidden shortcut                       | claimed | after             |
| ---- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ----------------- |
| 1479 | chain count (no walk at all)                      | 377x    | 20.7x             |
| 1480 | values walk (no vertex, no traverser)             | 19.3x   | —                 |
| 1483 | same                                              | "~14x"  | —                 |
| 1485 | **presence-filter count** (values never produced) | 4.7x    | a 4.2-11.9x range |

**Every one was a legitimate plan giving the same answer by a cheaper route.** That is what makes a
floor seductive: it is not wrong, it is just not doing the work you are pricing. The generalisable
check is now in `bench-methodology`: before quoting a ratio, ask what the fast arm SKIPS — and if the
fast arm is faster than producing its own rows, it skipped producing them.

### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. The probe gained the two families; no engine code changed. Item 1484's
heading is corrected in place.

### Item 1486 — TWO INSTRUMENTS DISAGREED 3.4x ON ONE NUMBER, and the fixture's EDGE STRIDE was the whole reason. Reproduced on a single instrument by flipping one knob: `label/id` goes **11.57x → 3.17x**, and the property-read target this tick set out to chase **vanishes** (2.2x → 1.1x)

Item 1485 left a concrete target: on the same fused walk, a property read cost **149 ns/row** against
`id()`'s **53** — about 96 ns for one `props[key]`, which is a lot for a memoized getter plus an
index, on a step as common as `values()`. Profiling it put the same two shapes through the Gremlin
probe, which reported **126 and 94 ns/row** — a 1.34x gap where the other instrument said 2.8x, and
`id()` three times more expensive in absolute terms.

**Two instruments disagreeing is the signal PROBES.md says finds defects**, so it got chased before
anything was optimized.

### Not the profiler, not the rep count, not the consumption

- profiler detached: the gap persisted (item 1472's ~15% is real but far too small);
- `REPS` 9 / 40 / 120 on one instrument: `id()` read 25, 26, 31 ns/row — **stable**, so rep count was
  not it;
- both instruments drain their result and count rows.

### It was the EDGE STRIDE, and the fixtures differed by accident

```text
                        this probe (before)              gremlin probe
edge source      vs[e % NODES]  — sequential      vs[(e * 7919) % NODES] — scattered
out-degree       exactly FANOUT for every vertex   varies
properties       { k }                             { k, s, n }
```

A `STRIDE` knob now makes that switchable, and flipping **only** that reproduces the entire
disagreement on one instrument:

```text
                  sequential      scattered        (NODES=200,000, 1,000,000 rows)
rows id()           51 ns/row      133 ns/row
rows values(k)     104             160
rows label()       595             423
label / id       11.57x           3.17x
id / values       0.50x            0.84x
```

At 50,000 the same flip reads 15.13x → 3.33x and 0.46x → 0.89x, so both sizes agree.

### What this closes

**The property-read target does not exist.** On a sequential fixture `id()` is 2.2x cheaper than
`props[key]`; on a scattered one it is **1.1x**. When the adjacency walk is cache-bound — which is
what a real graph does — the extra property read is hidden behind the miss it is already paying for.
There is no ~96 ns read to remove; there was a ~96 ns _difference_ that only exists when the walk is
unrealistically cheap.

**And every ratio in items 1484 and 1485 was stride-dependent.** 1485's "4.2x-11.9x" was measured
sequentially; the realistic figure for fused-vs-general is **~3.2x**. So the prize for reaching the
fused walk from a sub-plan (items 1480/1483) is ~3.2x, not 14x, not 19x, and not 11.9x.

### The pattern, now five items deep

| item      | what inflated the number                              | claimed        | honest    |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | --------- |
| 1479      | chain count — no walk at all                          | 377x           | 20.7x     |
| 1480/1483 | values walk — no vertex, no traverser                 | 19.3x / "~14x" | —         |
| 1485      | presence-filter count — values never produced         | 4.7x           | 4.2-11.9x |
| 1486      | **sequential adjacency — the walk is cache-friendly** | 11.9x          | **3.2x**  |

The first three were the FAST arm skipping work. This one is different and worth separating: **both
arms did the same work, and the FIXTURE made that work unrealistically cheap** — which inflates a
ratio whenever the thing being measured is a per-row cost that cache misses would otherwise swamp.

CLAUDE.md already says "match the fixture to the claim" and the two single-surface probes already
carry **opposite STRIDE defaults on purpose**. What is new is the magnitude: the stride moved a
headline ratio by **3.6x**, and it silently reversed a sub-conclusion.

went into the Gremlin probe; no engine code changed. Item 1485's range is corrected in place.

### Item 1487 — the shipped algorithm wins VERIFIED stride-insensitive (1468, 1469 stand), and the `scattered` fixture turns out to be a DEGENERATE FUNCTIONAL GRAPH: every vertex has exactly ONE distinct out-neighbour and `v0` is a fixed point. The corpus's own Gremlin probe has used it all along

Item 1486 showed the edge stride moves a headline ratio by 3.6x, so the shipped wins measured on a
sequential fixture needed checking. Triage first:

| items                        | fixture                  | stride can matter?                        |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| 1474, 1476, 1478, 1479, 1483 | Gremlin probe            | already **scattered** — stand as measured |
| 1473, 1482                   | set ops / a vertex scan  | **no hops at all** — stride is irrelevant |
| **1468, 1469, 1470**         | `algo-scaling-bench.mjs` | sequential, and adjacency-heavy           |

So only the three algorithm wins were at risk. `algo-scaling-bench.mjs` gained a `STRIDE` knob.

### Verified: the CSR wins are stride-insensitive

```text
row                 sequential   scattered
labelPropagation       85.47       86.99     unchanged
neighborAggregate      26.42       27.08     unchanged
degree                 14.89       21.69     1.46x — stride-SENSITIVE
```

**Mechanism, not luck:** items 1468 and 1469 both replaced a per-vertex allocation pattern with a CSR
built ONCE, after which the work is over typed arrays — so the fixture's access order barely reaches
them. `degree` has no CSR and walks adjacency per vertex, which is why it moves 1.46x; nothing shipped
there. **1468 and 1469 stand as measured.**

### ⚠️ And `shortestPath` could not be compared, because the bench's OWN GUARD fired

```text
⚠️ shortestPath at V=40000 returned n=1 col=distance — expected one row per vertex
```

Item 1467 built that one-row-per-vertex check into the bench, and here it earned itself: under
`scattered`, `shortestPath` from `v0` reaches **one vertex**. My first explanation — "`v0` must be
isolated" — was **wrong**: `v0` has 2 out-edges under both strides and NO vertex lacks one. Measuring
the topology instead of assuming it:

```text
             v0's distinct targets   vertices whose 2 edges hit ONE target   self-loops
sequential   v3, v35764              0 / 40,000                              2
scattered    v0                      40,000 / 40,000                         10
```

**The `scattered` formula is a functional graph.** `from = 7919·e mod N` and `to = 104729·e mod N`
means every edge is `x → c·x mod N` for one constant `c`, so each vertex has out-degree FANOUT but
exactly **one distinct neighbour** (the rest are parallel edges) — and `c·0 = 0`, so **`v0` is a
fixed point**. A single-source traversal seeded there measures nothing at all.

This is item 702's class exactly: _"an answer that is INVARIANT to the property you varied cannot
validate the fixture"_ — a generator that looked fine, returned correct answers, and had a topology
nobody had checked. One line counting distinct endpoints found it, as it did there.

### What this qualifies about item 1486

Item 1486's finding **holds**: flipping the stride moved `label/id` from 11.57x to 3.17x, and the
property-read target really does vanish — access order is what drove that, and it is real.

But calling `scattered` **"realistic"** was too generous and is corrected: it is realistic in ACCESS
ORDER and degenerate in TOPOLOGY. One distinct neighbour per vertex is not a real graph either. The
honest statement is that the two fixtures bracket a range — sequential is cache-friendly and
diverse, scattered is cache-hostile and degree-degenerate — and **a per-row hop cost should be quoted
from the hostile one while anything depending on neighbour diversity should not be measured on it at
all.**

⚠️ **This is the fixture `runtime-profile-gremlin-probe.mjs` has used all along**, so every per-row
cost in this corpus measured there is on a graph where each vertex has one distinct neighbour. That
is sound for per-EDGE cost (which is what those items quote) and unsound for dedupe, multiplicity or
fan-out shapes. Recorded rather than fixed: changing that fixture now would invalidate the recorded
history of every row in it, which is the trade CLAUDE.md's stride note already makes deliberately.

### Item 1488 — the GQL screen had NO fan-out knob and ran at 1:1, which CLAUDE.md already calls sparse. Fixed, plus a shape that actually walks — and the result EXPLAINS item 1477's null: row construction is **1.4%** of a row-materializing hop while the GC those rows cause is **44.8%**

anything but one fixture, so the natural hunt was: does a cache-hostile fixture surface a frame the

### ⚠️ Two false starts, both the same mistake in a new place

**First**, `hopfilter` and `join` measured FLAT across strides, and I nearly wrote that down as "no
stride effect on the GQL side". It is not: `hopfilter` is `WHERE a.k = 5`, which leaves **~2,062
sources out of 200,000**, so its cost is the VERTEX SCAN and the hop is a rounding error — raising
FANOUT from 1 to 5 moved it only 113.5 → 127.6 ms.

**Second**, `hopall` (`MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P) RETURN count(*)`) measured **2-8 ns/edge**, which is not
a traversal: a one-hop count is a **degree sum**. That is the **fourth tail in this corpus that
answers without doing the work** — chain count (1479), values walk (1480/1483), presence count (1485),
and now the hop-count shortcut.

⚠️ **And before either of those, an anchor assertion saved a worse error**: my first patch of this
probe failed on the second anchor (`20_000` against the file's `20000`), so **nothing was written** —
and the "sequential vs scattered" numbers I then collected were two runs of identical code. 175.4
against 239.2 ms, a 36% gap, which is this probe's own spread (item 1477: 27-31%). Without the
assertion that would have been a stride finding.

`hoprows` (`MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P) RETURN b.k AS k`) materializes a row per edge, so nothing can
shortcut it.

### The stride DOES matter here, once a shape actually walks

```text
                          20 reps, NODES=200,000
FANOUT=1 sequential    791.3 ms   4,000,000 rows   198 ns/row
FANOUT=1 scattered    1458.5      4,000,000        365        1.84x
FANOUT=5 sequential   2499.6     20,000,000        125
FANOUT=5 scattered    3131.6     20,000,000        157        1.25x
```

Higher fan-out _reduces_ the stride penalty, because one scattered bucket lookup amortizes over five
edges.

### The screen's verdict, and why it closes item 1477

`hoprows` at FANOUT=5 scattered, 3443 ms of engine time:

```text
51.6%  (anonymous) in farDrivenHopWalk   46 mentions — priced
44.8%  (garbage collector)               no source location — NOT CHECKABLE
 1.4%  get adjTo + propOf + projectRow + detectHopProjection   ← row construction, all of it
```

**No unpriced frame** — a clean negative for the hunt. But the shares say something better than that.

⚠️ **ITEM 1477 TRIED TO OPTIMIZE ROW CONSTRUCTION AND MEASURED A NULL. This is why.** That item built
a pre-shaped row template (1.52x in a 300,000-row micro), measured nothing in the engine, reverted it,
and recorded "row construction is a small share of the per-row cost" as an inference. It is now a
number: **1.4%**. And the thing it is small against is not the walk — it is **44.8% garbage
collection caused by the rows themselves**. A million `{k: …}` objects retained in one result array
survive the nursery and get promoted; no change to how each is _built_ can touch that, which is
exactly why a 1.52x micro vanished.

**So the row-materializing GQL hop is GC-bound, and the GC is the result's own size.** That is the
answer's cost, not the engine's — unless the row contract itself changes (a columnar or streaming
result), which is a contract change and not a loop change. Recorded as a bound, not a target.

### Half two — temporal, measured for the first time

`packages/core/src/temporal.ts` is **1,333 lines**, reached from both engines' comparison paths, and
had **zero mentions** anywhere in the probe corpus. It also matters disproportionately here: this
repo's notes record the domain as a people-graph over TIME, so dates are the modelling primitive
rather than an exotic column. New instrument: `temporal-probe.mjs`.

Each pair stores BOTH a `num` and a `d` encoding the same ordinal, so a numeric and a temporal
predicate select the identical set:

```text
pair       numeric   temporal    ratio   witness (numeric/temporal)
filter        2.59       3.86    1.49x   19950 / 19950
order         5.53      15.14    2.74x   3601 / {"@date":"2029-11-10"}   ← day 3601
project      11.01       9.78    0.89x   temporal slightly FASTER
grouped       4.38       4.85    1.11x
```

**`project` and `grouped` being flat is what makes this a finding rather than a vague "temporals are
slow".** Reading a temporal costs nothing extra (0.89x) and KEYING one costs nothing extra (1.11x) —
`temporalKeyFields`/`temporalKeyAdd` already exist for that. The cost is concentrated in the

⚠️ **MY FIRST GUARD WAS WEAK AND I NEARLY TRUSTED IT.** It compared ROW COUNTS — but `count(*)`

different selectivity would have passed. Strengthened to compare a WITNESS (the first row's first
column): the filter pair now proves both arms select **19,950** rows, and the order pair's witnesses
are the same day by two spellings. Only then are the ratios meaningful.

### The cause is a MISSED FAST PATH, not slow comparison

Profiling each arm separately (`ARM=`, because one window over both attributes their frames
together):

```text
numeric  (214 samples)            temporal (584 samples)
35.98%  (anon):8792               19.52%  matchPattern
19.16%  satisfies                 10.96%  seedVertices
11.21%  propOf                     9.76%  candidateVertices
 5.61%  inlineHolds                7.53%  rejectedByElementDirect
 2.80%  beatsRoot   ← topK         6.16%  withBinding
                                   4.97%  isTemporal
```

**They are different routes.** The numeric arm rides the node-projection walk with `topKNodeWalk`
(`beatsRoot` is `boundedTopKeyed`'s comparator); the temporal arm runs the GENERAL matcher. `isTemporal`
is only 4.97% — the comparison itself is not the problem.

Two candidate gates ruled OUT by reading:

- **`topKPlan` has no type gate** either: it requires only that each sort column be a direct property

So the exclusion is somewhere between those two and `detectNodeProjection`, and finding it precisely
is the next item's work rather than a guess at the end of this one.

**Priced at 2.74-3.50x on `ORDER BY … LIMIT` over a temporal key, cause localized to a missed fast

### Item 1490 — **a stored `Temporal`'s `kind` field was read as an AST expression kind**, so `WHERE n.d > DATE '…'` declined every single-node and hop fast path while `WHERE n.d > $cut` took it. **2.35x on the node shape, 3.72x on the hop, between two spellings of one predicate**

Item 1489 priced this at 2.74-3.50x and named "find the gate" as the next item's work. The gate is
found, the fix is two lines, and **item 1489 got the half wrong** — see the correction on its
heading.

### First: it is not the ORDER BY

Item 1489 located the cost on the ordering path, because that was the pair that moved. Crossing the
two halves over one fixture settles it — the WHERE's value type is everything and the sort key's is
nothing:

```text
WHERE type / SORT KEY type        200,000 vertices, 9 reps
num  / num        4.52 ms
num  / temp       3.84        ← a temporal SORT KEY is FREE (cheaper than the numeric twin)
temp / num       15.60        ← a temporal PREDICATE costs 3.45x
temp / temp      14.35
```

So item 1489's "`project` and `grouped` are flat, therefore the cost is in the ordering path" was a
valid inference from an incomplete set: the pair it never ran was a temporal predicate with a
numeric projection, which is where the whole gap lives.

### The cause: two `kind` discriminants, one structural walk

`rowLocal` / `itemLocal` decide the fast route by walking the expression tree against an allowlist,
and `rowLocalChild` / `itemLocalChild` descend through non-`Expr` wrapper objects to reach it. The
existing note says the descent is "safe because every `Expr` carries a `kind`". That is true, and it
is the wrong direction — the walk relies on the **converse**:

```ts
return typeof rec.kind === 'string' ? rowLocal(child as Expr) : /* descend */;
```

`LocalDate` and its five siblings each carry `readonly kind = 'date'` (etc.) as their `instanceof`
discriminant (`core/src/temporal.ts`). The parser lowers `DATE '2029-11-10'` to
`{ kind: 'lit', value: <LocalDate> }` (`parser.ts:2241`). So the walk descended into the `lit`,
found an object with a string `kind`, called `rowLocal` **on the stored date as though it were an
expression**, missed the allowlist, and declined the whole shape. A `$param` carries no temporal in
the AST, so the param spelling was admitted — which is the entire difference.

Confirmed before building anything, by the one discriminator that separates the two:

```text
numeric lit       4.43 ms      temporal lit     15.90 ms
numeric param     5.16         temporal param    6.59   ← 2.41x between two spellings
```

### ⚠️ This is the equivalent-spelling failure class, exactly as `CLAUDE.md` describes it

> "the planner recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned for another that meant exactly
> the same thing … Each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct answer, so no correctness test
> could catch it."

`WHERE n.d > DATE '…'` and `WHERE n.d > $cut` are one filter. Both answered correctly for as long as
the bug existed. The one instrument built to catch this had no temporal property in its fixture and
therefore no temporal group — so it was blind by construction, not by bad luck.

### The fix

A `lit` is `{ kind: 'lit'; value: unknown }` (`ast.ts:484`) — one field, and that field is DATA. So
stopping there is not an optimization but the structural truth:

```ts
if (e.kind === 'lit') {
  return true;
}
```

in both `rowLocal` (the hop paths) and `itemLocal` (the single-node paths). Both declined, and the
hop's gap was the larger of the two.

**The guard is on the `lit`, not on `isTemporal(value)`.** The temporals are only today's instance:
a stored map with a user key named `kind`, or the next value class to carry one, fails identically,
and a literal has no sub-expression to check in any case.

T node templit     15.07      6.41    2.35x
T node tempproj    15.69      6.75    2.32x
T hop templit      26.60      7.16    3.72x
C node numlit       5.40      4.74    1.14x   ← control: no Temporal ever in the AST
C node tempparam    6.59      5.84    1.13x   ← control: already on the fast path PRE
C hop numlit        6.68      6.18    1.08x

global drift, not the redistribution signature item 762 warns about (there the controls moved MORE

### ⚠️ MY FIRST VERSION OF THE PERMANENT GUARD WAS BLIND, AND I VERIFIED IT RATHER THAN BELIEVING IT

The durable fix is a spelling-probe group, so the probe's fixture gained a `d` date derived from
`k`'s own ordinal (`d` is new, every other key untouched — the `ew` discipline from item 1053), and
two groups went in. Written with `count(*)` like every group above them, they reported the five

```text
3.96 / 4.10 / 4.53 / 4.25 / 3.85 ms      ← count(*) spelling, BROKEN build, no flag
```

A `count(*)` is claimed earlier in the ladder by the count shortcuts, whose gate goes through
`compilePredicate` rather than `itemLocal` — so it never reaches the walk the group exists to watch.
Rewritten as projections (`RETURN n.k AS v ORDER BY v LIMIT 10`, and a hop projection held to ~86,000
rows by a shared conjunct so it does not measure row-construction GC instead — item 1488):

```text
BROKEN build                              FIXED build
43.01  n.d > DATE '…'                      7.55
 7.68  n.d > $cut                          7.62
23.54  DATE '…' < n.d                     10.69

6.07x flagged                             1.46x, under tolerance

64.60  hop, DATE '…'                      22.12
22.45  hop, $cut                          22.40
20.95  hop, n.k > 25                      21.22
3.08x flagged                             1.06x
```

**That is the difference between a guard and the belief in one.** `CLAUDE.md`'s rule — a generative
test whose teeth were never verified is worse than no test, because it is believed — applies to a
probe group just as it does to a fuzzer, and this one would have been committed green and useless.

(The broken build also shows a THIRD gap inside itself: the reversed spelling `DATE '…' < n.d` at
23.54 against the forward's 43.01. Moot now — both land together — and recorded only because it
shows the walk was declining different amounts for spellings nobody had compared.)

### Mutation — four mutants, all caught, and the fourth only after the test was fixed

The change is a pure ROUTE choice, so every query in the suite answers identically on both routes
and the differential tests cannot see a mutant in it (`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`). `itemLocal` is
therefore exported for its own test, as `rowLocal` already was.

```text
pristine        SURVIVED   18 pass  0 fail
null-both       CAUGHT     14 pass  4 fail
null-rowlocal   CAUGHT     14 pass  4 fail
null-itemlocal  CAUGHT     15 pass  3 fail
widen           CAUGHT     17 pass  1 fail
```

⚠️ **`widen` first SURVIVED, and it was a real test gap, not a no-op.** It replaces the stop with
`if (e.kind !== undefined) return true;` — admit anything past the allowlist without descending.
All 17 other tests stayed green because every decline they checked is refused by the allowlist at the
TOP level, before the stop is reached. The walk's whole job is the descent, so the refusal has to sit
UNDERNEATH an admissible node: a nested `exists` under an `and` for `rowLocal`, a nested aggregate
for `itemLocal` (which admits subqueries by design), and one level deeper under the `arith` wrapper
item 207 found the walk mishandling. Item 475's rule read in the other direction — a survivor is as
readily an untested guard as a redundant one, and the two have opposite fixes.

GREMLIN gfilter         1.91      5.20   2.70x   ← has('d', gt(…)), the predicate alone

### ⚠️ And isolating one arm per process UNDERSTATES it too — the opposite of item 762's rule

One arm per process, unprofiled, two rounds each: numeric 1.88 / 1.89, temporal 2.86 / 3.53. Paired
in one process: numeric 1.85, temporal 5.20. **The numeric arm is unaffected by isolation and the
temporal arm is ~1.6x faster alone.** `cmpSameType` is one module-level site, so a process that
compares both types makes it polymorphic, and only the temporal arm pays for that.

Item 762's "one shape per PROCESS" exists because a two-shape process FLATTERS a change that
redistributes call sites. Here the same mechanism works the other way: isolation would have reported
1.5-1.9x for a mixed workload that actually pays 2.70x. **So the rule has a direction — isolate to
measure a CHANGE, pair to measure what a mixed workload costs** — and a bitemporal people-graph
filtering on dates AND on numbers is the paired case.

### The cause: four calls to compare two integers

Profiling each arm separately (`GARM=`, the Gremlin twin of item 1489's `ARM`):

```text
numeric (525 ms engine)              temporal (641 ms engine)
70.2%  propertyCount                 37.6%  propertyCount
10.5%  matches                       14.3%  cmpNum          ← inside temporalRelCmp
 9.9%  get properties                13.2%  isTemporal      ← called TWICE per compare
 4.2%  cmpSameType                   11.7%  get properties
 0.8%  cmpOrd                        10.0%  cmpSameType
                                      7.3%  matches
 ─────                                4.1%  temporalRelCmp
 5.0%  comparison total              41.6%  comparison total
```

Per row, a date/date pair ran: three failed `typeof` tests, then `isTemporal(a)` and `isTemporal(b)`
(each a 6-way `instanceof` chain), then `temporalRelCmp` (another `instanceof` pair), then `cmpNum`.
Four cross-module calls — to compare two integers, because `LocalDate` holds a single `days` field.

### The fix

A date/date short-circuit in `cmpSameType`, placed **after** the three `typeof` tests so the numeric
and string paths pay nothing for it:

```ts
if (a instanceof LocalDate && b instanceof LocalDate) {
  if (a.days < b.days) {
    return -1;
  }

  return a.days > b.days ? 1 : 0;
}
```

DATE is the one kind worth special-casing rather than all six: it is the only temporal whose
comparison is a single scalar (the rest are 2- or 3-tuples `cmpTuple` already handles, each needing
its own branch), and it is the kind a bitemporal graph filters on.

⚠️ **The byte-identity hazard is the NaN behaviour, and the two adjacent branches DISAGREE on it by
design.** `cmpNum` tests `<` then `>` and falls through to 0, so a `NaN` day count compares EQUAL to
everything. The number/number branch six lines above returns `NaN` for a NaN operand deliberately
(unordered, so it matches no ordering predicate). `new LocalDate(NaN)` is constructible — the
constructor validates the ARGUMENT COUNT, not the value — so this is reachable, and the fast path
has to copy `cmpNum`'s version, not its neighbour's.

T  gorder   temporal  order()        15.51   12.28   1.26x
C  gfilter  numeric                   1.91    1.92   1.00x
C  gorder   numeric                   9.27    9.44   1.00x
C  gproject temporal  values('d')     7.97    8.03   1.00x   ← reads dates, never compares

### Mutation — four behavioural mutants caught, and `null` survives BY DESIGN

```text
pristine     SURVIVED   10 pass  0 fail
null         SURVIVED   10 pass  0 fail   ← expected: the route is answer-equivalent
flip         CAUGHT      5 pass  5 fail
diff         CAUGHT      7 pass  3 fail   ← `a.days - b.days` instead of normalized -1/0/1
nan          CAUGHT      9 pass  1 fail   ← copied the NUMBER branch's NaN behaviour
overclaim    CAUGHT      9 pass  1 fail
```

`null` removes the fast path entirely and every test passes — correctly, because the change cannot
alter an answer. The perf instrument is the only thing that sees it, and the test file's value is the
other four.

⚠️ **`overclaim` first SURVIVED because every cross-kind assertion used ONE operand order.** It
widens the guard to `isTemporal(a) && b instanceof LocalDate`; with a date on the LEFT that is false
and the generic branch still runs, so the date-first assertions pass. With the date on the RIGHT it
fires, reads `a.days` off a `LocalTime` (`undefined`), and `undefined < x` and `undefined > x` are
both false — so it returns 0 and **two incomparable temporals silently order EQUAL**. A comparator's
guard has two operands; a test for it needs two. Now asserted in both orders, at the function and
through `has()`.

### Item 1492 — `propertyCount` was already the hand-written tally and still ran at **2.8x a floor doing the same work**. Decomposed it: the cost is `matches`'s own megamorphic dispatch, not the property read. **1.92x on the tally, 1.12x on the general `has` row filter**, three real controls flat

Item 1491's profile put `propertyCount` at 70.2% of its arm. A frame that large is either the work
or the target with nothing between, and this one looked like the work: item 234 built it as the fast
path and measured it against a floor. But that item also left **2.5x between the tally and its own
floor** (11.5 ns a vertex against 4.6 "touching no property"), which is the largest unaccounted gap
in this corpus's own numbers, and nobody had decomposed it.

### New instrument: `tally-floor-probe.mjs`, one thing added per arm

⚠️ **IN ONE PROCESS THE ARMS DISAGREED WITH THEIR OWN ORDERING, AND THAT WAS THE FIRST READING.**
`inline` (a literal key and an inline compare) read **12.35 ns** against `dynkey`'s 7.79 and
`closure`'s 7.68 — impossible, since each adds work to the one before. That is the arms-interfere
signature (item 737's family, and item 762's rule), so every figure below is one arm per process:

```text
scan the id map, nothing else            1.31 ns a vertex
+ the `properties` getter                2.94
+ a DYNAMIC keyed read                   5.17        ← `properties[key]` is NOT the cost
+ an inline comparison                   4.94
+ the comparison behind a CLOSURE        4.38-5.05   ← a closure costs the same as inline code
the engine                              14.20-14.23  ← 2.8x the floor
```

**The `closure` arm is the load-bearing one.** It proves a predicate reached through a closure costs
no more than inline code, so the gap is not "a function call per row" — it is `matches` specifically.
`matches` is called from ~20 sites with every predicate shape the surface has, so its `switch` and
its comparator chain (`matches` → `predCmp` → `cmpSameType` → `cmpOrd`) are megamorphic by
construction and cannot inline. And the `dynkey` arm rules out the suspect I would have guessed
first: a dynamic keyed read is free.

### The fix: `specializePredicate`

A new exported function in `predicates.ts` returns a monomorphic closure for one predicate, or
`undefined` for a shape with no operator form. Hoisted at two sites: `propertyCount`'s tally loop,
and `dispatch.ts`'s general `has` filter — the latter on the row path of every traversal carrying a
`has`.

⚠️ **EVERY SPECIALIZATION HAD TO BE DERIVED, NOT GUESSED.** `matches(gt{value:n}, v)` is
`v != null && predCmp(v, n) > 0`; `cmpSameType` reaches its number/number arm only when
`typeof v === 'number'` and returns `null` (→ `NaN` → false) for every other type, and within that
arm it is `NaN` for a NaN operand and `cmpOrd` otherwise. So the whole thing is exactly
`typeof v === 'number' && v > n`, with the `v != null` guard made redundant by the `typeof`. The
same derivation gives `gte`/`lt`/`lte` and the string operands; `eq`/`neq` reduce to `v === b`
because `valueEq`'s temporal arm needs `isTemporal(b)`.

**A temporal or boolean operand is deliberately NOT specialized** — equality would have to reproduce
`temporalCmpTotal` and ordering `temporalRelCmp`'s kind rules (item 1491's work), neither of which
reduces to an operator. Everything else (`between`, `within`, the string-shape predicates, `not`,
`present`) is already one test or has no operator form.

```text

T numrows    has(k,gt) rows         6.25 6.41    5.63 5.68     1.12x
T streq      has(s,eq).count()      2.86 2.94    2.87 2.75     flat
T hophas     out(E).has(k,gt).cnt  50.90 51.51  51.70 51.45    flat
C hoprows    out(E) rows           44.55 44.36  44.68 44.57    1.00x
C valrows    values(k)              6.33 6.37    6.26 6.49     1.00x
C labelrows  hasLabel(P)            8.38 8.36    8.32 8.29     1.01x
F tempcount  has(d,gt(<date>)).cnt  3.28 3.39    2.61 2.66     1.26x
```

⚠️ **MY FIRST THREE CONTROLS WERE USELESS AND READ 0.00 ms.** `V().count()`,
`V().hasLabel('P').count()` and `V().out('E').count()` are all O(1) bucket or degree-sum shortcuts
(items 1479/1488), so they cannot control anything — a control below the clock is not a control. The
three above have real cost and no reachable `has`, and all three are flat.

`F tempcount` is the FALLBACK path (a temporal operand declines specialization) and it improved
1.26x. That is not a confound: the same hoist replaced a per-vertex `step.key` load with a
destructured `key`, which the fallback shares. Named `F` rather than `C` for that reason.

**Two honest negatives.** `streq` is flat — `eq` is a 2-call chain (`valueEq` + `===`) where `gt` is
4, so there is little to hoist, and the win is concentrated on ORDERING predicates. `hophas` is flat
because the hop is 50 ms and the filter is a rounding error. So this is a win on predicate-bound
shapes and nothing else, which is what the profile said it would be.

Post-fix the engine sits at 5.34-6.61 ns a vertex against the closure floor's 5.06-5.77 — **within
1.21x of a hand-written loop**, where it was 2.8x.

### The test is a DIFFERENTIAL, because the risk is equivalence

58 tests, **1,411 assertions**, every one of the form
`specializePredicate(p)?.(v) === matches(p, v)` over the cross-product of every op, every operand
type, and every value a property read can produce (`undefined`, `null`, `±0`, NaN, ±Infinity,
strings, booleans, three temporal kinds, an array, an object). Hand-written expected booleans would
encode my belief about `matches` instead of `matches`, and the belief is the thing that can be
wrong. The matrix also asserts that every UNSPECIALIZED shape still declines, so a later change that
starts specializing one fails here rather than answering from a derivation nobody did.

### Item 1493 — ⚠️ **a 97.1% PROFILE FRAME WAS AN INLINING ARTIFACT, and the lever it nominated had already been refuted at item 593.** The real lever at that site was one item 593 could not have tried; built it wide, measured it, and **cut it back from four shapes to one: 1.10x**

Item 1492's open line was "~18 more `matches` call sites, same one-line hoist, ceiling 1.92x each".
Doing that mechanically would have been list-first work, so this tick profiled instead — and the
profile was wrong in a way worth recording.

### The artifact

`out('E').has('k', gt(44)).count()`, 200,000 vertices at FANOUT 2 scattered, 400 reps:

```text
hophas (21616 ms engine)              hopbare (17896 ms engine)
97.1%  degreeOfTypes                  73.9%  drain
 1.6%  filteredHopCount               24.6%  get to
 0.5%  matches                         1.3%  (garbage collector)
```

**`degreeOfTypes` cannot be 97.1% of anything.** For a single-type hop its whole body is
`byType.get(t)?.size ?? 0` — one `Map.get`. At 80M calls over the run, 97.1% would make it 262 ns a
call. And the companion reading is just as impossible: `matches` at **0.5%** in a loop that calls it
once per vertex, when item 1492 measured that same call as the dominant cost of a structurally
identical loop.

Both numbers have one explanation: V8 inlined the loop's callees, and the sampler attributes an
inlined callee's samples to its own frame, so `degreeOfTypes` absorbed the loop body and `matches`
lost its own time to it. **A single frame over ~95% is evidence of inlining, not of a hot spot** —
and the giveaway is cheap to check: read the frame's body and ask whether its share is arithmetically
possible.

### ⚠️ And the lever it nominated was already closed, with numbers, in a comment beside the loop

Item 593 hoisted `labels[0]`, inlined the single-type degree as `byType.get(only)?.size ?? 0`, and
destructured `{ key, pred }` above the loop — exactly what a reader of this profile would do. Over
four alternated rounds, one case per process at 200,000 / 1,000,000:

```text
out(K).has(age,gt(44)).count()    41.59 -> 41.17   1.01x
in(K).has(age,gt(44)).count()     39.09 -> 37.76   1.04x
out(K).has(age,gt(500)).count()   41.43 -> 40.89   1.01x
out(K).has(city,'c7').count()     43.67 -> 41.48   1.05x
five CONTROLS                                      1.00-1.01x
```

That comment also records _why_ it is there — item 591 had mispriced the same loop from a micro-probe
and read a 24 ms difference as the cost of these calls. So this is the third time this one loop has
invited the same wrong conclusion, and the thing that stopped it the third time was reading the
comment next to the code, not the profile.

### What item 593 could NOT have tried

Its own closing line is the lever: _"what is left here is constant-factor: a JS property read and a
predicate DISPATCH per vertex"_. The dispatch half became addressable at item 1492.

### Built it wide, measured it, cut it back

The first version specialized widths 1-3 and all specializable ops. A/B at 200,000 / FANOUT 2
scattered, 40 reps, two rounds, medians:

```text
out(E).has(num,gt).count()                      52.95 -> 47.42   1.12x
in(E).has(num,gt).count()                       50.39 -> 46.15   1.09x
out(E).has(num,gt).has(m,gt).count()            48.52 -> 49.38   0.98x
out(E).has(num,gt).has(m,gt).has(s,gt).count()  49.22 -> 55.93   0.88x   ← 1.14x WORSE
out(E).has(s,eq).count()                        54.14 -> 56.50   0.96x
four controls (hop rows, values, label rows, node count)         flat
```

**A closure over a chain has to be ONE closure** — a per-filter branch inside the loop would
reintroduce the dispatch it removes — so at width `w` it pays a wrapper call plus `w` closure calls
against `w` `matches` calls. Only `w = 1` wins. The `eq` row is the same arithmetic from the other
side, and it agrees with item 1492's flat `streq`: `eq` is a 2-call chain (`valueEq` + `===`) where
`gt` is 4, so there is less dispatch to remove than the wrapper costs. **Specializing `eq` here is a
LOSS, not a smaller win.**

Restricted to width 1 and the four ordering ops, then re-measured ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS, three
rounds, because 1.10x is at the noise floor CLAUDE.md warns about:

```text
          PRE                    POST                  ratio
hop1      53.83 53.76 53.38      48.87 49.96 48.46     1.10x
hop2      52.72 53.83 52.36      52.40 53.07 53.70     0.99x   ← now declines
hop3      55.99 52.78 54.54      53.94 52.51 54.06     1.01x   ← now declines
hopstr    55.34 53.17 55.84      56.28 55.14 55.71     0.99x   ← now declines
hoprows   43.52 43.50 43.98      43.73 43.63 43.36     1.00x
```

PRE's `hop1` spread is 0.8% across rounds, so a 10% move is an order of magnitude clear of it.

### The test asserts the BOUNDS, each with its number

30 tests, 371 assertions. The route is answer-equivalent and so invisible to the 1,406 differential
tests, which is why `specializedRowTest` is exported and its decisions asserted directly: it claims
one ordering filter, and DECLINES two filters, three filters, `eq`/`neq`, `between`/`within`, and an
ordering filter whose operand has no operator form. Each decline names the measurement that put it
there, so widening one fails loudly rather than shipping a 1.14x regression.

The claimed closure is then checked as a differential against `matches` over every value a property
read can produce, including an ABSENT key (a bag missing the property, not a stored `undefined`), and
one test pins that it reads the key it was GIVEN rather than the bag's first entry.

> ⚠️ **ITS CLOSING PRICE IS CORRECTED BY ITEM 1495.** ~~Ceiling ~1.6x on this shape~~ — that was
> arithmetic (assume the two structural shares go to zero), and measuring it gave **24x** for a

### New instrument: `hop-rows-floor-probe.mjs`

Nine arms, each adding one thing, every one producing the SAME 400,000-element array the engine
produces — a floor that skips the materialization prices a different question, which is the error
items 1479, 1480/1483, 1485 and 1488 each made. One arm per process (item 1492).

```text
arm         total    MARGINAL over the arm above   what it adds
vonly        0.8 ms  —                             walk verticesById.values()
vbox         1.0     +0.2 ms                       + read the adjacency box getter
vget        11.8    +10.8      54 ns a VERTEX      + the per-vertex type Map.get
reach       28.3    +16.5      41 ns an EDGE       + iterate the edge Sets
rowsedge    29.9     +1.6       4 ns an EDGE       + materialize an array of the EDGES
rowsto      41.3    +11.4      29 ns an EDGE       + read e.to instead of pushing the edge
engine      43.2     +1.9                          the real traversal
```

(`rowstoid`, which pushes `e.toId`, lands with `rowsto` at 42.5 — resolving the vertex costs nothing
over reading the id, because the resolution is memoized.)

**The engine is 43.2 against the floor's 41.2 — 4.6%.** So `V().out(T)` has no recoverable pipeline
overhead at all: `drain` at 73.9% of the profile IS the walk, and the two levers a reader would take
from that profile are both dead. The row's cost, as shares:

```text
 2%  walk the vertices and read the box
25%  the per-vertex type lookup           ← 54 ns a VERTEX for a Map.get
38%  iterating the edge Sets              ← 41 ns an EDGE
 4%  materializing the result array
26%  reading the endpoint and pushing it  ← of which the READ is ~9% (see below)
 4%  the engine over the floor
```

### ⚠️ The endpoint-getter lever is REFUTED, and the refutation is the useful part

`rowstoid` pays 33 ns an edge over `rowsedge`, which looked like the getter. `rowsplain` stashes the
SAME string as a plain own property once, outside the timed loop, so the only difference is
getter-versus-plain-property:

```text
rowsedge    74.66  72.67  75.83 ns/edge
rowstoid   103.43 106.28 107.78
rowsplain  125.95 120.09 128.46   ← 1.19x WORSE than the getter
```

**Making it a plain property is slower, not faster.** Adding an own property to 400,000 `Edge`
objects transitions their hidden class, so every access on every one of them gets dearer — the cost
lands on the whole object, not on the one field. That is a general result worth keeping: _you cannot
buy your way out of a getter by adding a field to a class with many live instances._

⚠️ **And the 33 ns was never the getter.** A `rowstotwice` arm reads `e.to` TWICE per edge and pays
only **~10 ns** more (106.85 → 114.26), so a warm endpoint read is ~10 ns an edge — **9% of the row,
not 30%.** My own mid-tick attribution of 30% to "the endpoint read" bundled the materialization with
it; the read alone is 9%, and what the remaining ~23 ns of the `rowsedge`→`rowstoid` step buys is the
push of a string rather than an already-held object reference. Corrected here rather than carried.

(The first version of `rowstotwice` was written `push(e.to === undefined ? e.to : e.to)`, which
conflated a comparison with the two reads and read 177 ns. Its number is quoted nowhere.)

### ⚠️ A probe-only mutation has to be gated to its own arm

The first version applied the `__probeTo` stash whenever `ARM` was unset — so a full-ladder run
transitioned every Edge's hidden class and taxed **every other arm**, by the very mechanism the arm
exists to demonstrate. Now gated to `ARM=rowsplain`. A probe that mutates the fixture to measure one
arm is a probe that can invalidate all the others.

### What is left, and what it is NOT

The two structural shares — the per-vertex type lookup (25%) and the `Set` iteration (38%) — are the
only remaining levers, and both mean replacing `Map<string, Set<Edge>>` with a flat per-vertex
adjacency (a packed array plus per-type offsets): the lookup becomes an offset read and the iteration
an array walk. Ceiling ~1.6x on this shape.

⚠️ **That is NOT the lever `no-dense-vertex-ordinal` disqualified.** That one was a GLOBAL dense
vertex ordinal, built and rejected at items 1369-1372/1397 because deletes went 6.18x/11.34x under
churn. A per-vertex flat adjacency needs no global ordinal and leaves by-id access untouched. It is
also a storage-layout change with byte-identity, delete-path and `executor-edits-perturb` exposure,
so it wants its own item rather than the tail of this one. **Priced, not built.**

> ⚠️ **REFUTED BY ITEM 1498, which BUILT it: 1.58x SLOWER.** ~~per-vertex ARRAYS get 4.1x~~ — the
> `arrayadj`/`arrayedge` arms below rebuild the rows in one tight loop, so their buckets are

Item 1494 closed with "a flat per-vertex adjacency… ceiling ~1.6x on this shape". That number was
**arithmetic, not measurement** — assume the two structural shares (type lookup 25%, `Set` iteration
38%) go to zero and you get 2.7x, which I then hedged to 1.6x. Both are wrong, and the useful part

Three arms added to `hop-rows-floor-probe.mjs`, each built once outside the timed loop, every one
producing the same 400,000-element array the engine produces.

### What it is actually worth

```text
arm                                            ms      vs engine
flatceiling   global packed CSR (off/nbr)      1.82      24x
arrayadj      per-vertex arrays, endpoints     2.11      20.6x
              pre-resolved
arrayedge     per-vertex Edge[], endpoint      10.50     4.1x
              read live during the walk
engine        today                            43.43     1.00x
flatchurn     global CSR + 1 edge per rep,     63.58     0.68x  ← 1.47x WORSE
              rebuild on the next read
```

Flat-adjacency BUILD cost, measured separately: **93.4 ms** — more than two whole queries' worth.

### ⚠️ The arm that decides the design is `flatchurn`, and it kills the obvious version

A global packed array cannot absorb an insert; it has to be rebuilt. With the naive policy (drop on
any adjacency write, rebuild on the next read) a workload of one write per read measures **63.58 ms
against today's 43.43 — 1.47x worse.** That is item 680's failure mode reproduced on the TS side:
there `rebuild_csr` runs only at LOAD and every adjacency write clears `csr_fresh` with nothing to
re-arm it, so one `add_edge` demotes every later read for the session. The break-even is ~1.5
queries between writes; below that the cache is a regression.

So "build a CSR for the hop path" is the version of this lever that should NOT be built, and the
1.6x estimate could not have told me that — it priced the walk and said nothing about maintenance.

### ⚠️ And the MAINTAINABLE design gets the win anyway

`arrayadj` — nested per-vertex arrays instead of `Map<string, Set<Edge>>` — measured **2.11 ms,
within 16% of the global CSR's 1.82**. Appending to a per-vertex array is O(1) amortized and touches
one vertex, so there is nothing to invalidate and no rebuild: the entire reason `flatchurn` loses
simply does not arise.

**But `arrayadj` is optimistic twice over, and `arrayedge` is the honest number.** `arrayadj` stores
`e.to`, which a real adjacency box cannot do on its own — `outE`, edge properties and edge labels all
need the edge. Holding `Edge[]` and reading `.to` during the walk costs 8.4 ms more (2.11 → 10.50),
which is ~21 ns an edge for the endpoint read, the same order as item 1494's ~10 ns for a warm one.
It is also mildly optimistic about the type lookup, since a real box still has to select the type.

**So: 4.1x for the buildable design, 20.6x if resolved endpoints are cached alongside** — and item
595 already established that an endpoint reference is safe to cache under a live edge, so that second
step is a real option rather than a cheat, just a separate decision.

### What a reader should take to the next item

The change is `Map<string, Set<Edge>>` → `Map<string, Edge[]>` in the adjacency box. Two things make
it more tractable than it looks and one thing makes it risky:

- **Iteration order is unchanged.** A `Set` iterates in insertion order and an appended array is in
  insertion order, so the walk emits the same edges in the same sequence — which is what
  byte-identity between the engines turns on.
- **Insert stays O(1)** (`push`), so none of `flatchurn`'s problem appears.
- ⚠️ **Removal becomes O(degree).** `Set.delete` is O(1); keeping order under removal means `splice`.
  That is the thing to measure before building, and it is the same class of regression that
  disqualified the global dense ordinal (deletes 6.18x/11.34x, items 1369-1372/1397) — though
  bounded by one vertex's degree rather than by the whole graph.

**Priced at 4.1x (20.6x with cached endpoints), design selected, removal cost not yet measured.**

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. No engine code changed — three probe arms and a corrected price.

> ⚠️ **THAT BLOCKER WAS A FALSE POSITIVE, corrected at item 1497.** ~~`.has(member)` on a bucket~~ —
> `unionOfBuckets` operates on `graph.edgesByLabel`, the GLOBAL label index, not the per-vertex
> adjacency rows this change touches, so it is never reached. The scan matched lines containing the
> word `bucket`, which names two different structures in that file. The removal measurements below
> stand; the blast-radius conclusion does not, and item 1497 replaces it with a compiler-driven
> census of 83 sites.
>
> ⚠️ **AND THE GATE IS MOOT — item 1498 built the change and measured it 1.58x SLOWER**, so there is
> no read win to pay the removal cost for. The removal measurements here remain correct, and the two
> probe traps are still worth keeping: a member→position `Map` is the WORST removal design at every
> degree, and swap-remove is cheap but unusable because it reorders.

Item 1495 selected the design (`Map<string, Set<Edge>>` → `Map<string, Edge[]>`, 4.1x on a bare hop)
and left one thing unmeasured: removal. `Set.delete` is O(1); an order-preserving array removal is
`indexOf` + `splice`, both O(degree). That is the axis that disqualified the global dense ordinal
(deletes 6.18x/11.34x, items 1369-1372/1397), so it is a gate, not a detail.

New instrument: `adjacency-removal-probe.mjs`, in two halves — because a micro on `Set.delete`
alone is unbounded, which is this corpus's most-repeated correction (items 1364, 1368, 1477).

### Half one — the structures, by degree

Every arm removes EVERY member of the bucket, one at a time, in a SCATTERED order (so the expected
shift is degree/2 — front-to-back would make `splice` look free and back-to-front maximally dear).
Members are objects, not integers, because the real buckets hold `Edge` references and `indexOf` on
objects is a reference scan.

```text
degree        set     splice       swap    indexed   splice/set
     4      220.0      142.5      137.5      290.0   0.6x   ← splice is FASTER
    16       65.0       65.6       69.4      305.6   1.0x   ← crossover
    64       56.6       80.2       74.1      446.2   1.4x
   256       54.7       89.7       66.0      466.3   1.6x
  1024       36.9      129.0       71.4     1408.9   3.5x
  4096       41.6      266.5      202.0     5874.0   6.4x
```

Two results beyond the headline:

- **`indexed` — an array plus a member→position `Map` kept updated — is the worst arm at every
  degree**, by up to 22x. It removes the `indexOf` search and keeps the `splice` shift, then pays to
  renumber every position after the hole. A plausible-sounding optimisation that is strictly worse
  than the thing it optimises.
- **`swap` (swap-remove) is cheap but must not be used.** It reorders the bucket, and adjacency
  iteration order is observable in row order — which is what byte-identity between the TS and Rust
  engines turns on. It is here as the bound and as the trap.

### Half two — what the share is, which is what makes the micro mean anything

```text
hub degree   ns per engine removeEdge
         4              1530.0   ← unreliable: 4 removals a rep is ~6 us, near clock resolution
        64              1127.3
      1024               716.6
```

A real `removeEdge` does far more than touch one bucket — element bookkeeping, both direction
indexes, the label box, the id maps. **So at degree 1024 the bucket operation is ~37-46 ns of a
529-717 ns removal — about 7% — and `splice` makes it ~128-129, a delta of ~82-92 ns, or +12% to
+17% on the whole removal.** At degree 4096 the delta is ~225 ns, roughly +30-40%. Below degree 16
the change is an improvement.

⚠️ **Quoted as a RANGE because the denominator moved 1.35x between runs** (716.6 then 529.4 ns at
degree 1024, with the bucket micro steady at 36.9/45.5). A second run is what turned a confident
"+12.8%" into an honest "+12-17%", and the engine half is the noisy side — it rebuilds a fresh graph
per rep, since removal is destructive and reusing one would measure a shrinking graph.

**Verdict: the gate passes.** A bounded +12-17% on removal at degree 1024 against 4.1x on reads is a
strongly favourable trade for any realistic degree distribution, and the regression is proportional
to one vertex's degree rather than to the graph — unlike the global dense ordinal, whose delete
regression was unbounded by anything local.

### ⚠️ But the enumeration found a blocker the pricing could not

264 mentions of `edgesFromByLabel` / `edgesToByLabel` / `adjFrom` / `adjTo` across 15 non-test files.
Counting which operations are actually used on a bucket shrinks that a lot — most readers only
ITERATE, which is identical for a `Set` and an array — but it also surfaces the one that is not
mechanical:

```text
50  .size      → .length                      mechanical (and over-counted: some are labels.length)
 5  .delete(   → indexOf + splice             Graph.ts, the measured cost above
 2  .add(      → push                         Graph.ts
 2  new Set()  → []                           Graph.ts
 8  .has(      → ⚠️ O(1) becomes O(n)
```

`unionOfBuckets` (`gremlin/src/executor/count-shortcut.ts`) does `buckets[j].has(member)` **inside a
nested loop** over the buckets, to count a union without a `seen` set — the construction items
1078/1382 built deliberately. On arrays that becomes O(k·|B|²) instead of O(k·|B|), which is a
multi-label hop going quadratic. It has a fix (build a `Set` for the union path alone, or keep a
parallel `Set` only where membership is tested), but it is a semantic change inside a function whose
comment already records two order-related defects, so it is not a find-and-replace.

**And a second risk the pricing did not carry:** the change touches `hop-values.ts` (17 mentions) and
`hop-projection.ts` (48), the two files `executor-edits-perturb` records as costing unrelated rows up
to 16% _for any edit at all_. So the net value cannot be read off the bare-hop row — it needs a WIDE
A/B across the corpus, which is itself a tick's work rather than a verification step at the end of
one.

**Gate passed with its cost measured; scope enumerated; two risks named and neither yet addressed.**

### Item 1497 — attempted the array-adjacency change and **REVERTED it**, because the enumeration method was wrong: ⚠️ **`bun run typecheck` is not authoritative until core's DIST is rebuilt.** It reported 0 errors in both engines; after a rebuild it reports **83**. Also: item 1496's `unionOfBuckets` blocker was a FALSE POSITIVE

Item 1496 passed the gate (removal +12-17% at degree 1024 against 4.1x on reads) and enumerated the
scope by counting mentions. This item tried to build it, using what looked like a better enumerator:
flip the two declarations in `Graph.ts` and let the compiler list every site.

That worked, for core. It is **wrong for everything else**, and the way it fails is silent.

### ⚠️ The typechecker lied, and the reason is the dist

`packages/gremlin` and `packages/gql` resolve `@lenke/core` to its BUILT output
(`packages/core/dist/types/...`), so a `bun run typecheck` run before rebuilding core checks them
against the OLD declarations. With the change in place and core NOT rebuilt:

```text
core:     26 production errors (which I fixed, 6 files, gate green)
gremlin:   0
gql:       0
```

I read that as "the engines only ITERATE buckets, so they need no changes" — a conclusion the
enumeration in item 1496 had already suggested. Then `bun run build` rebuilt everything and the
suites said otherwise:

```text
core 431/0 · gql 3254 pass 473 FAIL · gremlin 1285 pass 121 FAIL · native 911 pass 50 FAIL
```

**644 failures, and the shape of them was the tell**: a four-segment hop count returned `0` where it
should return 24. `bucket?.size ?? 0` on an array is `undefined ?? 0` — zero, silently, with no
error anywhere. Re-running typecheck AFTER the rebuild:

```text
83 errors: shortcuts.ts 34 · count-shortcut.ts 18 · hop-projection.ts 10 · executor.ts 5
           hop-values.ts 4 · graph-queries.ts (both) 6 · hop-endpoint-extremum.ts 2 · 2 probes
```

This is `fuzzers-read-built-dists` in a new place. That rule is written about the FUZZERS reading a
stale `dist`; the same resolution applies to the typechecker, and there it is worse, because a
fuzzer failing is loud while a typecheck passing is silence that reads as permission.

**The method for the next attempt: change core, `bun run build`, THEN typecheck — and treat a clean
cross-package typecheck as meaningless until that rebuild has happened.**

### ⚠️ And item 1496's blocker was a false positive

That item named `unionOfBuckets`' `buckets[j].has(member)` — O(1) on a `Set`, O(n) on an array,
inside a nested loop — as the one non-mechanical site. It is not reached by this change at all:
`unionOfBuckets` operates on `graph.edgesByLabel`, the GLOBAL label index, not the per-vertex
adjacency rows. My blast-radius scan matched lines containing the word `bucket`, and that word names
two different structures in this file.

Also worth correcting, since item 1497 reasoned about it before checking: I argued that rewriting
`unionOfBuckets` to accumulate a `Set` would be a strict improvement (O(total) against O(k·total)).
It would not. **Bucket 0 is FREE today** — sorted largest-first (item 1382) and consumed as a bare
`.size` — so an accumulating version pays O(|B₀|) that the current one does not. At k = 2, the
common case, today's version wins. The complexity argument was right about the exponent and wrong
about the constant that matters.

### What IS now known, so the next attempt is execution

The change itself is small and the compiler can drive it, in this order:

- **`core/Edge.ts`**: an `AdjBucket = readonly Edge[]` type, documented as insertion-ordered (which
  is why the swap is answer-preserving: a `Set` and an appended array iterate identically, and
  adjacency order is observable in row order).
- **`core/Graph.ts`**: two declarations; two `new Set()` → `[]`; two `.add` → `push`; the two
  `delete`-and-drop-if-empty sites behind one `dropFromBucket(bucket, edge)` helper doing
  `indexOf` + `splice` (NOT swap-remove — item 1496 measured that as cheaper and it reorders).
- **`core/algorithms/adjacency.ts`**: the four exported helpers are the hub — widening them to
  `ReadonlyMap<string, AdjBucket>` clears 12 of core's 26 errors at once, because they only ever
  iterate and read a size.
- **`core/Vertex.ts`**: the two cached getters, and the two convenience accessors whose empty
  fallback must stay a FRESH array per call (a shared constant would be mutable into every other
  vertex's answer).
- **then rebuild, then the 83 engine sites**, almost all `.size` → `.length`.

Two risks still unretired: the 14 errors in `hop-projection.ts`/`hop-values.ts`, which
`executor-edits-perturb` records as costing unrelated rows up to 16% for ANY edit — so the net value
needs a wide A/B, not the bare-hop row — and the byte-identity fuzzers, which are the real
correctness gate for a storage change and were never reached this item.

**Reverted to pristine; core 431/0, gql 3727/0, gremlin 1406/0 confirm the tree is back.**

### The change, complete and correct

`Map<string, Set<Edge>>` → `Map<string, Edge[]>` in both adjacency indexes, with an exported
`AdjBucket = readonly Edge[]`, `push` for insert, and a `dropFromBucket` doing `indexOf` + `splice`
for order-preserving removal. 18 files. **Typecheck 0, `bun run check` 0, all five suites green
(431 / 3727 / 1406 / 144 / 961), and `bun run fuzz` 20/0 — byte-identity held.** So the swap is
answer-preserving exactly as item 1495 argued: a `Set` and an appended array both iterate in
insertion order.

Then:

```text
                                     PRE      POST
engine  V().out('E')  400,000 rows   43.33    68.56    0.63x  ← 1.58x WORSE
                                     43.05    68.84
                                     43.41    68.03
```

Three rounds each, one arm per process, arm asserted from the built dist (`dropFromBucket` present
3 times POST, 0 PRE). The profile is the SAME two frames in the same proportions — `drain` 74.1%,

### ⚠️ THE FLOOR ARM WAS NEVER A PREDICTION, and one control proves it

Item 1495 built `arrayadj`/`arrayedge` — nested per-vertex arrays, walked — got 4.1x against the
engine, and read that as what changing the storage type would buy. This item added the control that
should have existed then: **`setedge`, the same nested rows built the same way but as `Set`s.**

```text
setedge    (nested SETS,   built locally)   13.34  14.53  13.01 ms
arrayedge  (nested ARRAYS, built locally)   10.12  13.77  13.60 ms
engine                                      67.46  68.41  67.83 ms
```

**13.3 against 13.6 — the container is irrelevant.** The 4-5x those arms showed against the engine
was never about `Set` versus array; it was that both arms REBUILD the rows in one tight loop, so the
buckets land contiguously and the walk has near-perfect locality. The engine's buckets never have
that: they are allocated interleaved with vertices and edges across 400,000 `addEdge` calls.

So every figure in items 1495-1497 was measuring allocation locality and attributing it to the
container. The mechanism for the change being actively WORSE is the other half of the same fact: an
array built by `push` from empty grows its backing store as it goes, leaving scattered,
differently-sized allocations, where a `Set` of the same two members is allocated once.

**This is CLAUDE.md's own rule — "match the fixture to the claim" — failing in the one place I did
not look: the floor arm, which I trusted because I had built it myself to be honest about what it
skipped.** It was honest about skipping the endpoint read (item 1495 corrected 20.6x to 4.1x for
exactly that) and silent about skipping the allocation history, which turned out to be the whole
number.

- **Item 1494's conclusion stands and is now better supported**: `V().out(T)` is within 4.6% of a
  hand-written loop over the real structure, and the remaining 63% that looked structural is
  LOCALITY, which no container swap reaches.
- **Item 1496's removal gate is moot** (there is nothing to pay for), though its measurements remain
  correct and its two probe traps — the member→position `Map` being the worst arm at every degree,
  and swap-remove being unusable — are still worth keeping.
- **Item 1497's method lesson stands and earned its keep**: build core, THEN typecheck. Without it
  this item would have shipped the 644-failure version again.

Both were only visible because the change was actually made:

### Item 1499 — **`bench:usage` has encoded a 4x since item 662 and nobody priced it: parse+plan is 3.1-6.9x the EXECUTION of a cheap query**, and an application that interpolates literals into query text pays it on every single call. The lever is auto-parameterization, not the parser

> ⚠️ **BUILT AT ITEM 1502: 1.46-2.07x for an interpolating caller**, gated at item 1501 and shipped
> as a TEXT rewrite (`normalizeLiterals`) that leaves the parse and plan caches untouched.
>
> ⚠️ **ONE CLAIM BELOW IS WRONG, corrected at item 1501.** ~~`read: keyed dedup lookup` is 5-11x
> slower than its siblings~~ — it is not slow: `WHERE u.score = $s` with `score = i % 100` over
> 20,000 users matches **200 rows** where `read: point lookup` matches **1**, so per row it is ~17x
> FASTER. Comparing ops/s across rows of different cardinality is the match-the-fixture trap. The
> parse+plan pricing itself stands and item 1501 GATES the lever it names.

Profile-first, on the one regime this session had not opened: the SERVING path, small operations
against a warm graph. Two anomalies in `bench:usage`'s TS columns, and the second is the finding.

```text
write: append node            128.6k ops/s
write: append node [params]   512.8k        ← 4x, in the UNINDEXED column where no seek applies
```

The cause is in the harness and it is not a defect there: `append node` interpolates the loop
counter into the text (`INSERT (:Event {name: 'ev${i}', …})`), so every call is a distinct string and
misses the parse+plan cache (items 228/229); the param row's text is constant and hits it. Item 662's
comment already says to read the delete row against the param row for this reason — **so the 4x has
been sitting in the harness, correctly explained and never priced.**

### New instrument: `parse-plan-probe.mjs`

⚠️ **DEFEATING THE CACHE IS THE WHOLE DESIGN.** Each `fresh` arm mints a UNIQUE text per rep by
appending a line comment carrying the rep number — the lexer discards it, so the string differs while
the parsed AST does not. The probe **asserts that** before printing anything (`JSON.stringify(parse(text))`
against the uniquified parse); without it the fresh arms could be measuring a different query and
every ratio would be void.

```text
shape    chars    parse    +plan   warm q  fresh q   fresh/warm
insert      46     2330     3232     2306     7248   3.1x
point       41     2741     8392     3900    13617   3.5x
hop         39     2737     5335     1110     7684   6.9x
agg         42     2603     5756     3140    10016   3.2x
longer     137     6956    14055    30805    50086   1.6x
```

Three things worth separating:

- **Parse alone is 2.3-2.7 us for a ~40-character query** — about 60 ns a character — and 7.0 us at
  137 characters, so it is roughly linear in text length.
- **Planning adds 1-6 us on top**, more than parsing for every read shape.
- **The cheaper the query, the more it dominates.** `hop` executes in 1.1 us warm and costs 7.7 us
  fresh: for that shape, 86% of an uncached call is parse+plan. The `longer` row's 1.6x is the
  opposite end — real execution swamping a fixed cost.

### The lever is AUTO-PARAMETERIZATION, and it is named rather than built

A cache cannot help interpolated text — the key is new every call by construction. The structural
answer is the one real databases ship (SQL Server's forced parameterization, Postgres' prepared
statements): canonicalize literals out of the text into parameters, so `INSERT (:E {n: 'ev1'})` and
`INSERT (:E {n: 'ev2'})` share a plan.

**Ceiling, measured above: 3.1-6.9x for an interpolating caller on a cheap query**, falling toward
1x as execution grows. That is the largest unclaimed factor this session has found, and it is a
feature with its own correctness surface (literal-to-param extraction has to preserve types, NULL
handling and the plan's seeding decisions), so it wants its own item rather than the tail of this one.

### ⚠️ Two frames checked and NOT taken, both because the comment got there first

- **`tokenize`, the largest non-GC frame at 11.4%** — items 887/888 already own it. 887 measured the
  tokenizer at 28-54% of parse; 888 ran a CEILING ABLATION (push one shared constant token instead
  of a fresh object — "as wrong as code gets, so a hard upper bound") and got **1.07x**, and records
  that the 1.24x lever in that function was the keyword lookup, already taken. Reading that comment
  is what stopped a third re-derivation; item 1493 is the precedent for why that matters.
- **`checkKeyword` at 3.2% with ZERO audit mentions**, which is exactly what an untouched frame looks
  like — and it reads two fields of one token through two separate `peek()` calls:

  ```ts
  const checkKeyword = (kw: string): boolean => peek().type === 'keyword' && peek().value === kw;
  ```

  Hoisting the token into a local measured **FLAT: `agg` parse 2318/2272/2257 ns against
  2185/2284/2239** — a 1.5% median difference with the ranges overlapping, at REPS=5000 ROUNDS=7 with
  the arm asserted from the built dist. V8 inlines the cursor closure, so the second call is not a
  second call. **Reverted, with the numbers recorded next to the code**, because a flat change to the
  hot parser is perturbation risk for nothing.

  ⚠️ **An earlier pass of this measurement said 7% and was the instrument.** At ROUNDS=5 the PRE
  readings were 2533/2536 — remarkably tight, which is what made them convincing — and at ROUNDS=7
  the same build reads 2257-2318. The tightness was within a round, not across configurations. Match
  the rep and round counts on both sides before believing a 7% that two tight numbers seem to prove.

### Item 1500 — the planner has **no hot spot**: an allocation removal in `hasSubquery` ships at 1.03-1.13x, and the frame distribution says the rest of parse+plan is a long tail. ⚠️ Also: **three mutants that break that walk's recursion survive all 3,744 gql tests**, rows and faults alike

Item 1499 priced parse+plan at 3.1-6.9x the execution of a cheap query and named
auto-parameterization as the structural lever. This item asked the prior question: is there a hot
spot in the planner worth taking first? `PROF_ARM=plan` was added to the probe so the profiler sees
