```text
21.1%  tokenize          (19 mentions — owned by items 887/888, ablation 1.07x)
 7.6%  parse
 6.6%  hasSubquery       (18 mentions)
 4.4%  check
 4.4%  checkKeyword      (measured FLAT at item 1499)
 3.3%  flattenConjuncts
 2.6%  peek
 2.4%  collectHints
 2.3%  compilePredicate
 2.1%  walk
 …
```

**That distribution IS the finding.** After the two frames item 1499 closed, the largest remaining
is 6.6% and the tail is 1-3% each. No local change can move an uncached query much, which is the
strongest argument yet for item 1499's conclusion that the lever is to skip parse+plan entirely
rather than to speed it up.

### `hasSubquery`: the memoization is already done, so the win is the allocation

The precedent was item 919, which found `hasSubqueryExpr` walked twice on the same `where` and made
it once. So the first question was redundancy — measured by instrumenting the function:

```text
longer   calls 4   distinct top-level nodes 4   total node visits 34
point    calls 3   distinct top-level nodes 2   total node visits 24
agg      calls 2   distinct top-level nodes 2   total node visits 10
```

**2-4 calls on 2-4 distinct nodes — there is nothing left to memoize.** A WeakMap would add a write
per call to save at most one walk of 10-34 nodes.

What is left is the allocation: the recursive step was `Object.values(rec).some(hasSubquery)`, which
builds an array per visited node to throw away. A `for...in` loop enumerates the same keys (these are
plain object literals from the parser, so there is no prototype chain to widen the set) and allocates
nothing.

A/B on the plan arm, REPS=5000 ROUNDS=7, arm asserted from the built dist:

```text
            PRE              POST             ratio
longer   13528 13730      12991 13187        1.04x
point     7677  7750       6927  6667        1.13x
agg       6365  6391       6265  6138        1.03x
```

Non-overlapping on all three. As a share of an uncached query that is ~1% on `longer` and ~5.5% on
`point`.

### ⚠️ THE WALK'S RECURSION IS NOT OBSERVABLE, AND THAT IS A COVERAGE FINDING

A `for...in` change alters how a walk enumerates keys, and `hasSubquery`'s own comment names the
failure direction: it is generic so that it "cannot miss one", because a walk that misses a subquery
lets the planner push a predicate it must not push. So a test file went in — a subquery in every
nesting position the parser allows — and then three mutants to check it had teeth:

```text
norecurse   stop recursing into object children entirely
noarrays    recurse, but skip array children (where and/in/list/args live)
oneLevel    look exactly one level down instead of all the way
```

**All three survive the new file AND the full 3,744-test gql suite.** Rows identical.

So the next hypothesis was fault ORDER, which is where this engine's pushdown hazards actually live
(`and-chain-seeding-divergence`, item 175's deferral rule): a raise can appear or disappear without
any row changing. Faults ARE observable here —

```text
WHERE CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) > 0                              RAISES
WHERE n.k = 999 AND CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) > 0                0 rows
WHERE EXISTS { … CAST … }                                   RAISES
WHERE n.k = 999 AND EXISTS { … CAST … }                     0 rows
```

— but the nested shapes do not diverge either: `WHERE n.k = 999 AND (COUNT { … CAST … } + 0) = 1`
returns 0 rows without raising, on the pristine build and on every mutant.

**So the recursion's result is unobservable through every shape I could construct**, because other
gates (`itemLocal`'s SUBQUERY_KINDS allowlist, `rowLocal`, `freePredicateVars`) decline these shapes
before it matters. The "cannot miss one" claim describes a failure nothing exercises.

⚠️ **Recorded, not acted on.** Removing a conservative gate on the strength of surviving mutants is
exactly backwards — the mutants show the TEST suite cannot see it, not that the guard is useless.
And the test file is kept with its header rewritten to say precisely what it proves (nested-subquery
ANSWERS) and what it does not (anything about the walk), because a believed-but-empty guard is worse
than no guard at all.

This also makes the `for...in` change safer than the A/B alone would: if missing EVERY nested
subquery changes nothing measurable, missing a key cannot be worse.

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. core 431/0, gql 3744/0, gremlin 1406/0, native 961/0,

### Item 1501 — the GATE on item 1499's auto-parameterization lever, and it is **GREEN with exactly one hard exception**: `LIMIT`/`SKIP` loses the top-K walk at **5.3-6.1x**. Also ⚠️ **three flags that all turned out to be the instrument**, by three different mechanisms

Item 1499 priced auto-parameterization at 3.1-6.9x and item 1500 showed the planner has no hot spot,
so skipping parse+plan is the only large win left. The blocker was never performance: **the planner
reads literal VALUES**, and a literal lifted into a parameter is invisible to it at plan time. This
item is the gate, in item 1496's shape — enumerate the positions a literal can occupy and compare the
literal spelling against the parameter spelling on both axes.

⚠️ **THE ROUTE AXIS IS WHY THIS CANNOT BE A UNIT TEST.** Both spellings answering identically is
necessary and not sufficient: every index-seeding defect in this engine's history returned the correct
answer and cost 100-300x. A position where the param spelling is much slower is a position the
rewrite must leave alone. The fixture is INDEXED by default for the same reason — item 578's lesson
that the spelling probe had no index and so was blind to the whole class.

### The result: 15 positions, NODES=1,000,000, REPS=25

```text
case                        literal     param    ratio  answers
clause =                       4.73      5.86    1.24x  same
clause >                       9.93     12.03    1.21x  same
clause string                  0.71      0.71    1.00x  same
clause bool                   17.46     17.81    1.02x  same
inline                         2.80      1.45     see below
inline string                  0.75      0.75    1.00x  same
inline WHERE                   1.11      1.09    0.99x  same
two conjuncts                  1.59      1.99    1.25x  same
IN list                        7.30      7.76    1.06x  same
hop start                      8.28      3.02     see below
hop far                        3.18      3.18    1.00x  same
projection                     2.72      2.09    0.77x  same
LIMIT                         52.75    322.67    6.12x  same   ← THE exception
inline null                   25.25     29.77    1.18x  same
IS NULL vs = $null            13.74     10.38    0.76x  DIFFER (by design)
```

- **ANSWERS agree everywhere.** The single difference is the row that compares two DIFFERENT
  operators on purpose: `IS NULL` is a null test, while `= $v` with a null param yields UNKNOWN and
  matches nothing. That is a stronger statement than "do not parameterize a null literal" — **`IS
NULL` has no parameterized spelling at all**, so there is nothing to rewrite it into.
- **ROUTES hold within 1.25x everywhere except `LIMIT`**, which is the exception the audit predicted:
  `topKPlan` (item 1064) reads the limit VALUE at plan time, so a param limit loses the bounded top-K
  walk and materializes instead. Measured 5.31x at 200,000 nodes, 6.12x at 1,000,000, and 5.62x on a
  third run — stable across sizes and rep counts, which none of the false flags were.
- `inline null` at 1.18x confirms the other audit exception is a SEMANTIC one only (item 260's
  `{k: null}` means IS NULL for an inline constraint): the route is fine, the meaning is not.

**So auto-parameterization is answer-safe for every position tested and route-safe for all but
`LIMIT`/`SKIP`** — which is a much narrower exclusion list than "the planner reads literals" implied,
and it is now measured rather than reasoned.

### ⚠️ Three flags, three different instrument failures, zero findings

Every one of these looked like an equivalent-spelling defect in the LITERAL direction — a user
writing a constant losing a seed the param spelling gets. None survived.

- **`two conjuncts` 0.54x was THE FLOOR.** At NODES=200,000 it read 0.81 against 0.44 ms; at
  1,000,000 the same case reads 1.25x. Both arms were sub-millisecond, so the ratio was clock
  resolution — item 1461's rule, reproduced exactly. The probe now has a `FLOOR_MS` and reports
  sub-floor flags separately instead of mixing them with results.
- **`hop start` 0.37x was INSTABILITY.** Three isolated rounds: **3.03x, 0.73x, 0.32x** — the param
  arm slower by 3x, then faster by 3x. A measurement whose own spread exceeds the effect returns a
  confident wrong answer, not a weak one (item 1293's phrasing).
- **`inline` 0.52x was BIMODALITY IN THE LITERAL ARM.** At REPS=25 DROP=5 over four rounds the
  literal arm reads **0.95 / 3.42 / 1.21 / 0.98 ms**, so the ratio reads 1.07x / 0.53x / 1.04x /
  1.01x. The 0.52-0.54x readings in the first two sweeps had caught the slow mode twice in a row,
  which is what made them convincing. Three of four rounds say ~1.0x.

**All three are now printed by the probe itself**, with the confirm-alone command per flag, so the
next reader does not re-derive them. The in-sweep run flags four cases including `inline` at
**0.10x** against its isolated ~1.0x — the sweep is simply not an instrument for these sub-5ms rows,
and saying so in the output is cheaper than remembering it.

### ⚠️ And a correction to my own flag from item 1499

That item noted `read: keyed dedup lookup` at 83.9k ops/s against other indexed reads at 456k-965k
and called it "5-11x slower than its siblings". **It is not slow.** `WHERE u.score = $s` with
`score = i % 100` over 20,000 users matches **200 rows**, where `read: point lookup`'s
`WHERE u.name = $n` matches **1**. Per row the dedup lookup is ~17x FASTER than the point lookup.
Comparing ops/s across rows with different cardinalities is the "match the fixture to the claim"
trap, and this one would have cost a whole tick.

### Item 1502 — **AUTO-PARAMETERIZATION SHIPPED: 1.46-2.07x for an interpolating caller.** Literals are lifted out of the query TEXT into parameters, so queries differing only in their constants share one cache entry. Byte-identity holds

Items 1499-1501 built the case: parse+plan is 3.1-6.9x the execution of a cheap query, an
interpolating caller misses the cache by construction, the planner has no hot spot to speed up
instead, and item 1501's gate found the rewrite answer-safe in every position tested and route-safe
in all but `LIMIT`. This item builds it.

### The design is a string, not an AST

`MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 7` becomes `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = $__ap0` with `{ __ap0: 7 }`, and that
rewritten text goes through the ordinary parse and plan caches **unchanged**. No AST surgery, no plan
surgery, nothing to keep in sync with either.

⚠️ **THE ORDER OF THE THREE STEPS IN `query` IS THE DESIGN, and step 1 is why this is free for
callers who already do the right thing.**

1. **Ask the parse cache FIRST.** A caller using parameters sends a repeating text, hits, and never
   pays a byte for anything below. A tokenize is ~865 ns against a cached call of 1-4 us, so paying
   it unconditionally would be a **20-60% regression for correct code** — the sloppy caller must not
   be subsidised by the careful one.
2. **On a miss, try lifting.**
3. **If the rewritten text does not PARSE, fall back to the original.** For the positions the
   allowlist admits, a rewrite can only produce invalid syntax, never different semantics — so a
   parse failure is the safe failure.

⚠️ **The guard is around the PARSE and not around `execute`.** Retrying a failed `execute` would
re-run a statement that may already have written — an INSERT that raised halfway would apply twice.
`execute` runs exactly once.

### The eligibility rule is an ALLOWLIST, which gets item 1501's exception for free

A literal is lifted only when it is adjacent to a comparison operator or follows a `colon`. That
excludes **by construction** every position the gate found unsafe, rather than by enumerating
exclusions a new syntax arm could slip past:

- **`LIMIT 10` / `SKIP 10`** — preceded by a keyword. `topKPlan` reads the value at plan time and
  item 1501 measured a param limit at **5.3-6.1x** (52.75 → 322.67 ms).
- **a path quantifier `-[:E]->{1,3}`** — preceded by `lbrace` and `comma`. Lifting a bound would
  change the pattern the planner compiles, silently.
- **`DATE '2020-01-01'`** — preceded by the temporal keyword; `DATE $p` is a different construct.
- **`null` / `true` / `false`** — keywords, not literal tokens, so unliftable. Critical for null:
  `{k: null}` means IS NULL for an inline constraint (item 260) and `IS NULL` has no parameterized
  spelling at all (item 1501).

**Both sides of a comparison are lifted**, and that is not an afterthought: `5 <= u.n` and
`u.n >= 5` are the same question, and CLAUDE.md names that exact pair as a defect this engine has
shipped before. Lifting only the right-hand side would have created the asymmetry rather than found
it.

### A/B — the arm had to be rebuilt twice before it measured anything

```text
                      PRE          POST (3 rounds)        ratio
insert  interp       6708      4556  4541  4705          1.46x
point   interp      11082      6144  6088  6071          1.82x
agg     interp      13693      6788  6873  6701          2.02x
longer  interp      24225     13306 13199 13222          1.83x
```

⚠️ **MY OWN PROBE DEFEATED THE FEATURE, and then my fixture hid it.** Item 1499's `fresh` arm makes
text unique by appending a line COMMENT — which normalization preserves, so that arm cannot see
auto-parameterization at all. Adding an `interp` arm that varies a LITERAL was the fix, and the first
version of it used `i % 7`, giving **seven distinct texts** that the parse cache holds entirely: PRE
then measured FASTER than POST, because PRE was a warm cache and POST paid normalization on top. Only
`${i}` — unique per rep — models an interpolating application. Third instance this session of
"match the fixture to the claim", and the first where the fixture flattered the status quo.

### The cost, measured rather than waved at

A text that misses the cache for some reason OTHER than a liftable literal pays for the attempt. A
regex pre-filter (`[=<>:]` next to a literal start, either side) removes it where it can:

```text
hop (no literals at all)   PRE 7396 7414   POST 7613 7643 7772   1.04x
```

`IN [...]` and `LIMIT 5` also fail the pre-filter and skip the tokenize entirely. What remains is a
text unique for another reason that ALSO holds a constant in a comparison — an interpolated label
beside a constant predicate, say — which pays **1.15-1.27x**. Reported rather than hidden: that case
was already paying full parse+plan, and now pays ~20% more, against ~2x for the common case.

### ⚠️ Mutation: all six caught, but TWO WIDENINGS WALKED THROUGH 31 PASSING TESTS FIRST

```text
widen-quantifier   admit lbrace/comma — lifts PATH QUANTIFIER bounds
widen-keyword      admit keyword      — lifts LIMIT and DATE '…'
raw-string         carry the SOURCE span instead of the decoded value
bad-span           off-by-one on the span end
one-name           reuse one param name for every literal
null               disable the feature
```

The first version of the refusal tests asserted that a refusable token existed in the **input** and
that the query did not throw — a tautology and a near-tautology. `widen-quantifier` and
`widen-keyword` both left all 31 green. Rewritten to assert on the **rewritten text** (`mustSurvive`:
the refused token must still be there), both are caught.

And `bad-span` survived one round longer than that: `not.toContain('1234')` passes when an off-by-one
leaves a single character behind. **Pinning the EXACT rewritten string** is what made it loud —
including the trailing space the rewriter emits, so that spacing is a pinned decision rather than a
guess.

A third thing a test found rather than foresight: the reversed-comparison rule also caught the last
operand of an arithmetic expression (`n.k + 1 = 8` → `n.k + $__ap0 = $__ap1`). Probably harmless —
item 1501 measured a param inside arithmetic at 0.77x — but "probably" is the wrong standard for
rewriting user query text, and it put the feature outside the positions the gate measured. Literals
adjacent to an arithmetic operator are now excluded, which makes the documented rule true rather
than nearly true.

> CONSTRUCTION rather than cached on the execution path. **1.57-1.72x on a reused plan and FLAT on a
> rebuilt one** — where the memo below was 1.07-1.15x worse on that arm. The three refutations here
> all still stand; what changed is that the design they pointed at works.

~~GQL's per-call overhead was parse+plan, and item 1502 removed most of it.~~ ⚠️ **CORRECTED AT ITEM
1508: parse+plan was not all of it.** A warm, fully cached `RETURN 1 AS v` still cost 530 ns, none
of it parse or plan — `projectedRows` built a generator per call for a laziness `toArray`
immediately discards. Item 1508 took that shape to 164 ns (3.24x). Gremlin has no text to parse, so
the question looked inapplicable. It is not: `toArray` re-runs the whole plan ANALYSIS on
every call — `effectivePlan`'s seven rewrite passes, `checkSteps`, `planReadsPath`,
`streamStaysElements` — with nothing cached between one call and the next.

### New instrument: `gremlin-plan-overhead-probe.mjs`

⚠️ **THE FIXTURE IS DELIBERATELY TINY (200 vertices)**, and that is the opposite of every other probe
here. 200,000 elements is right for measuring a walk and wrong for measuring a per-call constant: at
bench scale the graph work swamps it and the answer rounds to zero. A serving workload lives in this
regime anyway — `bench:usage` is small operations against a warm graph.

```text
shape         floor     work  rebuilt  toArray/floor  rebuild cost
count             2      315      787         130.5x         473ns
filtered        587     1186     1870           2.0x         684ns
hop               5      456     1093          84.0x         637ns
vals              5     9205     9638        1688.8x         433ns
```

`work` reuses one plan object, so it is the graph work plus whatever `toArray` re-does per call;
`rebuilt` constructs the traversal inside the loop, which is what an application does when it builds
the traversal in the request handler. **Two separable costs: ~300-450 ns of per-call analysis on a
trivial shape, and ~450-680 ns to construct the plan at all.**

### ⚠️ Hypothesis 1 — memoise `planReadsPath` on the plan. REJECTED, with numbers

A `WeakMap<Plan, boolean>` (plans are built functionally, so a plan is a value and the memo cannot
go stale):

```text
            work (reused)        rebuilt
count       315 -> 207  1.52x    787 -> 904   1.15x WORSE
hop         456 -> 283  1.61x   1093 -> 1232  1.13x WORSE
filtered   1186 -> 1038 1.14x   1870 -> 1994  1.07x WORSE
```

A freshly built plan never hits the memo and pays the set. **The Gremlin equivalent of GQL's
interpolating caller — an app that constructs its traversal per request — is at least as common as
one that hoists the plan, and it would have paid for a win it never collects.** Rejected on that
asymmetry, not on the size of the win.

### ⚠️ Hypothesis 2 — `subPlansOf`'s allocation. REFUTED: it was an INLINING ARTIFACT

The profile of the reused-plan path put `subPlansOf` at **15.7%**, the largest non-GC frame, with
`planReadsPath` another 10.7% — and `subPlansOf` builds an array per step per call to answer a
boolean that early-exits. An obvious allocation to remove.

Rewriting the walk to test the plan-bearing fields inline, allocating nothing, measured **FLAT**:
count 315 → 296-317, hop 456 → 428-434, filtered 1186 → 1195-1235, rebuilt 787 → 785-787. Removing
the use of a frame credited with 15.7% changed nothing, so the 15.7% was not its own.

**Second instance of this exact trap in one session** — item 1493's `degreeOfTypes` at 97.1% was the
first. The tell there was arithmetic impossibility; here it is cheaper still: delete the use and
measure.

### ⚠️ Hypothesis 3 — `planReadsPath` is called repeatedly, as `hasSubqueryExpr` was. REFUTED by counting

Item 919 found `hasSubqueryExpr` walked twice on the same expression, and item 1500 checked the same
hypothesis for `hasSubquery` before touching it. Instrumented here, `planReadsPath` is called
**exactly once per `toArray`** for every shape tested. There is no redundancy to remove, which also
means the memo's 1.52x cannot be explained by saving repeated walks — one walk of a two-step plan
with no sub-plans is not 108 ns. **That number remains unexplained, and it is recorded as unexplained
rather than banked.**

### What is left, and it has the shape item 1500 found in the GQL planner

The per-call overhead is spread across ~8 analysis passes with no hot spot: `checkStep` + `checkSteps`
12.0% (the latter with ZERO audit mentions), `effectivePlan` and its passes ~11.5%, `planReadsPath`
10.7%, `nextFrontier` 6.8%, `countShortcut` 5.4%, `newContext` 5.0%, `streamStaysElements` 3.6%.
Every one of them is a pure function of the plan, recomputed per call.

So the lever is the same shape as GQL's: not speeding up any one pass, but **doing the analysis once
per plan instead of once per call** — which is exactly what hypothesis 1 tried and what the rebuild
asymmetry defeats. A design that wins both arms has to make plan CONSTRUCTION carry the analysis
(build it into the combinators, so a fresh plan arrives already analysed) rather than bolting a cache
onto the execution path. **Priced at ~300-450 ns a call on cheap shapes; not built.**

### Item 1504 — **`Plan.readsPath` is now carried by CONSTRUCTION, not walked at execution: 1.57-1.72x on a reused plan and FLAT on a rebuilt one** — the design item 1503 named after its `WeakMap` memo won one arm and lost the other

Item 1503 measured the Gremlin per-call plan overhead (315-456 ns on shapes whose graph work is
2-5 ns), tried a `WeakMap<Plan, boolean>` memo on `planReadsPath`, and rejected it: **1.52-1.61x for
a REUSED plan but 1.07-1.15x WORSE for a REBUILT one**, because a freshly built plan never hits the
memo and pays the set. It closed by naming the design that could win both — make plan CONSTRUCTION
carry the analysis, so a fresh plan arrives already analysed. This is that.

### The change

`Plan` gains `readonly readsPath: boolean`, computed at the ONE place a step is appended
(`appendStep` in `ast.ts`) as `plan.readsPath || stepReadsPath(step)`. The recursion disappears: a
nested plan is built BEFORE the step that holds it, so `sub.readsPath` is already settled and the
parent just ORs it. `planReadsPath(plan)` becomes a field read, and `subPlansOf` — whose only caller
it was — is deleted.

`PATH_DEPENDENT_KINDS` moved from the executor to `ast.ts`, because "which step KINDS read the path"
is AST-level knowledge once the flag is computed at construction.

⚠️ **CONSERVATIVE IN THE SAFE DIRECTION.** A plan rewritten by `effectivePlan` keeps the flag through
`{ ...plan, steps }`, and a rewrite can only MERGE or REMOVE steps — never introduce a path-dependent
one that was not already inside the step it replaced. A carried-over `true` may be stale, which
merely declines an optimisation; a stale `false` is unreachable. The one place that must RECOMPUTE is
`match.ts`, which builds an inner plan from a SLICE of a step list: the enclosing plan's flag
describes a different set of steps, so `planOfSteps` runs `stepReadsPath` over the slice.

### Both arms, which is the whole point

```text
                work (reused plan)              rebuilt (built per call)
           PRE    POST            ratio     PRE    POST             ratio
count      315    200 201 201     1.57x     787    769  778  788    1.01x
hop        456    261 267 268     1.72x    1093   1089 1122 1132    1.00x
filtered  1186   1022 1032 1039   1.15x    1870   1858 1865 1882    1.00x
vals      9205   9007 9008 9029   1.02x    9638   9577 9591 9597    1.01x
```

The rebuilt arm is flat rather than faster — construction now does the OR — but it no longer pays
the execution-time walk, so it breaks even instead of regressing 1.07-1.15x. **That is the
difference between this and item 1503's memo.**

Wide controls at 200,000 vertices / FANOUT 2 scattered, where a per-call constant cannot matter and
a mistake would show: `hopbare` 1942.2 → 1966.9 (1.01x), `hopcount3` 8676.6 → 8656.9 (1.00x),
`grouped` 170.1 → 171.0 (1.01x).

### ⚠️ A false flag here is SILENT, so the tests are about the false-negative paths

When `readsPath` is false the run skips path bookkeeping entirely, so a missed path-reading step
yields an **EMPTY path, not an error** — `path()` answers `[]` and `simplePath` filters nothing. The
old walk's comment said exactly this; moving the computation to construction adds a new way to miss
one, namely a nested plan whose flag the parent does not consult.

Mutation, all six caught:

```text
never            readsPath: false always                 CAUGHT   2 pass 14 fail
no-carry         drop `plan.readsPath ||`                CAUGHT  14 pass  2 fail
no-subfields     ignore body/plan/until/…                CAUGHT  10 pass  6 fail
no-plans-array   ignore the `plans` array (union)        CAUGHT  13 pass  3 fail
no-bys           ignore `by(traversal)`                  CAUGHT  15 pass  1 fail
always           readsPath: true always (conservative)   CAUGHT   6 pass 10 fail
```

⚠️ **`no-bys` SURVIVED the new file at first and was caught only by a PRE-EXISTING guard** —
`executor/subPlansOf.test.ts`, which hides a `path()` in every plan-bearing field for precisely this
failure. It earned its keep against a change made 580 items after it was written. The case is now in
the new file too, so that file stands on its own rather than relying on a sibling for one of the
three field shapes.

That guard's comment named `subPlansOf`, which this item deleted; it has been corrected in place to
describe `stepReadsPath` and the construction-time flag, with the filename kept so its history stays
findable.

### Item 1505 — `effectivePlan`'s six rewrite passes were **32.2%** of a reused-plan call, almost all of it looking for steps that were not there. A construction-time kind MASK gates five of them: **1.23-1.24x this item, 1.94-2.14x cumulative since 1503**, and the rebuilt arm gains too

After item 1504 removed the path walk, the profile was re-taken rather than worked down from the
old list — and the ranking had changed. `effectivePlan`'s passes were now the top group:

```text
13.6%  (garbage collector)          5.9%  checkStep
 7.7%  nextFrontier                 5.1%  nextHasEdge        ← ZERO mentions
 6.8%  sameDirFromUnion  ← ZERO     5.1%  flattenFilterWrappers
 6.8%  dropVacuousLabels            5.1%  countShortcut
 6.8%  streamStaysElements          4.2%  newContext
 5.9%  effectivePlan                4.2%  fuseLocal
                                    3.4%  checkSteps · 3.4% fuseUnionSameDir
```

`effectivePlan` and its passes total **32.2%**; the `checkSteps` group another 22.1%. And for a plan
like `V().count()` every fusion pass walks the step list hunting a `local`, a `union`, an edge step
or a `values` that is not present — pure waste, plus the GC from what they allocate.

### The change: item 1504's design, applied again

`Plan` gains `readonly kinds: number`, a bitmask of the six step kinds that GATE a pass
(`local`, `union`, `values`, `outE`, `inE`, `bothE`), OR'd in at `appendStep`. Five passes now return
in one test when their kind is absent: `fuseLocal`, `fuseValuesIsCount`, `fuseEdgeHop`,
`fuseUnionBoth`, `fuseUnionSameDir`.

⚠️ **TOP-LEVEL ONLY, which is the OPPOSITE of `readsPath`'s rule.** Every gated pass iterates
`plan.steps` and never recurses, so a `union` buried in a sub-plan is not something it can fuse —
recording it would make the mask pessimistic and the gate useless. `readsPath` must propagate
inward; `kinds` must not. Two flags on the same object with opposite propagation rules, each correct
for its own consumer.

⚠️ **AND ANY PASS THAT CHANGES THE STEPS MUST RECOMPUTE.** `fuseLocal` runs FIRST and INLINES a
sub-plan's steps into the top level, so it can introduce a `union` or a `values` the original mask
never recorded — and a later pass gated on that mask would skip a fusion it should make. All eight
`{ ...plan, steps }` sites became `rewritten(plan, steps)`, which recomputes via `maskOfSteps`. It
costs one walk of the new list, paid only when a pass actually changed something; a pass that fuses
nothing returns the plan it was given.

(`readsPath` is deliberately NOT recomputed there — a rewrite can merge or remove steps but never
introduce a path-dependent one that was not already inside the step it replaced, so a carried-over
`true` is at worst stale and only declines an optimisation.)

`flattenFilterWrappers` and `dropVacuousLabels` are left ungated: the first can fold a PRESENCE
filter at any element position (item 1141), so its precondition is not a kind set, and the second is
already gated cheaply on `steps[0]` being `V`/`E`.

          1504    1505      this  cumulative   1504    1505    this
count      200     162     1.23x    1.94x       778     729   1.07x
hop        265     213     1.24x    2.14x      1117    1065   1.05x
filtered  1031     966     1.07x    1.23x      1865    1837   1.02x
vals      9011    8918     1.01x    1.03x      9588    9548   1.00x

### ⚠️ A WRONGLY-SKIPPED FUSION IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY ANSWER TEST

The passes are answer-equivalent optimisations — `outE(T).inV()` becomes `out(T)` with identical rows
— so a gate on the wrong bit costs only speed. Item 1307 measured that one fusion at
**18936-24433x**, and all 1,422 tests in this package would stay green through losing it. So the new
file tests the MASK and the FUSIONS FIRING, not the rows, and leans on one property:
`plan.kinds === maskOfSteps(plan.steps)`, asserted both as built and after `effectivePlan`.

Mutation, all five caught:

```text
stale         carry the old mask through a rewrite        CAUGHT  19 pass  2 fail
mask-zero     maskOfSteps always 0 (every gate skips)     CAUGHT  12 pass  9 fail
no-bit        appendStep forgets the bit                  CAUGHT   9 pass 12 fail
out-is-edge   treat `out` as an edge step                 CAUGHT  20 pass  1 fail
wrong-gate    gate fuseLocal on the `union` bit           CAUGHT  20 pass  1 fail
```

⚠️ **`wrong-gate` SURVIVED THE FIRST VERSION, because my hazard test guarded its assertions behind
`if ((fused.kinds & KIND_BITS.local) === 0)`** — so a gate that stopped firing made the `if` never
run and the test pass vacuously. Making the assertion unconditional (an all-transparent `local` MUST
be inlined, so the `local` step MUST be gone) is what caught it, and a companion test now asserts
each other gated pass's own observable effect.

⚠️ **And I got the fusion preconditions wrong TWICE while writing that companion** — a bare `outE`
with no `inV` (nothing to fuse, so `outE` legitimately survives), then `union(out, both)` (the
fusion needs `union(out(L), in(L))` with identical labels). Each wrong guess failed for a reason
unrelated to the gate. **Read the precondition out of the code; the third attempt did and passed.**

### ⚠️ MY FIRST GATE LISTED FOUR KINDS AND THE SUITE CAUGHT IT

Reading the function body, the explicit tests are `step.kind === 'filter'`, `'or'`, `'and'`, plus
`presenceFoldOf` (which needs `not`). Four. I wrote the gate, and **two existing tests failed** —
`has(label, key, pred)` was no longer splitting into `hasLabel` + `has`.

The fifth fold is not an explicit kind test at all: `pushSplit(steps, step)` runs **unconditionally
at the bottom of the loop** and splits `hasLabelAnd` (item 1309). A reading of the branch conditions
misses it entirely.

**So: enumerate from the code, not from the comments or the visible branches** — the same lesson item
1505 learned twice on fusion preconditions, in a new shape. The gate's own comment now lists all five
with what each one folds, so the next reader does not have to re-derive the set.

### Item 1507 — the validation walk was the last big group at **27.5%**, and it is skippable: a plan with no step that CAN raise cannot fault. **count 124 → 77 ns (1.61x), 4.09x cumulative since 1503** — and an early-out found along the way made the REBUILT arm 1.14-1.28x faster too. ⚠️ **The GATE is not the end of it: item 1648 found the walk still costs 74% of a `union(out, in).count()` call for a plan whose `mayFault` is TRUE, and cached the verdict per plan**

Re-profiled again (fourth tick running, and the ranking moved again). At 123 ns a call:

```text
12.9%  countShortcut          7.8%  assertPlanIsSatisfiable  ← ZERO mentions
12.9%  (garbage collector)    7.8%  toArray
12.8%  checkStep              6.9%  nextHasEdge
12.1%  newContext             5.2%  checkSteps · 3.5% effectivePlan · 2.6% assertFrontierTypes
```

Two things, one small and one not.

### The small one: `assertPlanIsSatisfiable`, 7.8% with ZERO mentions

Pure, and every fault it raises needs a `path` step to scan FROM — so a plan without one cannot
fault there, and the loop would otherwise walk every step to discover that. Gated on a `path` bit:
**~1.04x** (124 → 119). Smaller than its share, which is the inlining-artifact pattern again, but
real and free.

### The big one: the validation walk, 27.5%

`checkStep` + `nextHasEdge` + `checkSteps` + `assertFrontierTypes`. Item 1503 looked at this and
ruled out moving it to construction, correctly — it tracks a FRONTIER through the step list and
validates branch arms against the frontier AT THE BRANCH, which a sub-plan cannot know when it is
built, and moving it would shift its errors from `toArray` to `traversal`.

But it does not need to MOVE. **`checkStep` is the only thing that raises, and it raises only for a
bounded set of kinds — so a plan containing none of them cannot fault, and the whole frontier walk
is pure overhead.** `Plan.mayFault` says which.

⚠️ **THE GATE SET IS READ OFF THE SEVEN THROW SITES, NOT OFF THE KIND SETS**, and the difference is
large. The first site tests `PATH_INCOMPATIBLE`, which includes `out`, `has`, `values` and
`hasLabel` — a set so broad that gating on it would pass for nearly every plan. But that site also
requires `f === 'path'`, and **the only way the frontier becomes `path` is a `path` step** — so one
kind covers the whole site. The remaining six each need their own kind present: `ADJ_OR_HOP`,
`PROJECTION`, `{sum,min,max,mean}`, `order`, `{inV,outV,bothV,otherV}`.

A boolean rather than a bit, because that set is 25 kinds and the `kinds` mask is already 13 bits
deep — JS bitwise operators are 32-bit.

⚠️ **AND IT MUST PROPAGATE INTO SUB-PLANS, WHICH I NEARLY GOT WRONG.** The first version computed it
over top-level steps only — the right rule for the `kinds` fusion mask (item 1505) and the WRONG one
here, because `assertFrontierTypes` recurses into union/choose arms. `V().union(inV())` must still be
rejected, and a top-level-only flag would have skipped the check and silently lost the fault. Caught
while writing the gate, not by a test; the `top-level-only` mutant now exists so it cannot come back.

### ⚠️ The regression it caused, and the early-out that paid it back with interest

With the flag added, the REBUILT arm got worse: hop 971 → 1035 ns (1.07x), because `appendStep` now
walked the nine sub-plan fields TWICE per step — once for `readsPath`, once for `mayFault`. Merging
them into one `analyzeStep` pass recovered part of it, and then the real fix:

**most steps have no sub-plan at all.** `out`, `has`, `count`, `values` carry none of those nine
fields, so the walk read nine `undefined`s per append to learn nothing. An early-out on five field
reads skips it entirely — and that was a cost item 1504 had been paying silently since it introduced
the walk:

```text

          1506    1507     this   cumul(1503)    1506    1507    this   cumul(1503)
count      124      77    1.61x      4.09x        672     525   1.28x     1.50x
filtered   903     821    1.10x      1.45x       1748    1514   1.15x     1.24x
hop        162     161    1.01x      2.83x        971     854   1.14x     1.28x
vals      8860    8838    1.00x      1.04x       9479    9337   1.02x     1.03x
```

`hop` barely moves on the reused arm because `out` is in the gate set — it CAN fault off an edge or
scalar frontier, so a hop still pays the walk. That is the honest shape of this win: it is for plans
built from sources and filters, not hops.

⚠️ **THE PREMISE OF THE EARLY-OUT IS CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED.** It holds only if every `Step` variant
declaring a sub-plan field also declares one of `{body, plan, plans, test, bys}`. Scanned the union:
`until`/`emit` appear only on `repeat` (which has `body`), `thenPlan`/`elsePlan` only on `choose`
(which has `test`). A future variant that broke that would lose a nested flag, so the comment says
so at the code.

### ⚠️ A test expectation that was wrong, and how I knew which side to fix

Two cases failed: `local(inV())` and `union(local(inV()))` returned `[]` where I expected a throw.
**The deciding fact is that `mayFault` was TRUE for both** — so the gate let the walk run, the walk
is byte-identical to before, and a non-throw there is the engine's own pre-existing answer (`local`'s
arm starts from an `unknown` frontier, and the engine's documented rule is that an unknown frontier
never faults). My expectation was wrong, not the engine. The cases stay, asserting the flag
propagates and that these two do NOT raise — which is the behaviour, written down.

`parse-plan-probe`'s `hop` row is `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P)` over a 200-vertex graph with **no
edges**. It returns ZERO rows — which is exactly why I read 1091 ns as per-call overhead. It is not:
it iterates 200 vertices looking for outgoing edges and finds none. **200 iterations at ~5 ns each
IS the number**, and a fixed cost of a few tens of ns cannot show in it. Zero rows out does not mean
no work in.

### New instrument: `gql-call-overhead-probe.mjs`

The GQL analogue of item 1503's `gremlin-plan-overhead-probe.mjs`, with the fixture as small as the
language allows and the arms ordered by how much graph they touch, so the fixed cost is read off the
DIFFERENCES:

```text
floor   RETURN 1 AS v                     441.7 ns   ← no graph access at all
param   RETURN $x AS v                    490.1
one     MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(*) AS c   62.6      ← ONE vertex
onerow  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS k       149.6
ten     the same count over TEN vertices   62.7      ← invariant: reads vertexCount
```

⚠️ **`RETURN 1 AS v` costs 7x a whole-graph count.** A query with no MATCH, no graph access and one
constant column was the most expensive shape in the probe. `count(*)` is 62.6 ns and flat in N (the
item 204-209 node-scan family reads `vertexCount` directly, which is why `ten` equals `one`), while
a bare `RETURN` reaches no shortcut at all and falls through to the general projection path.

### The cause: a generator for a laziness nobody observes

`projectedRows` ends in `toArray(map(f, bindings))` on both its branches. `@lenke/fp`'s `map` is a
**generator**; `toArray` is `Array.from`. So every call constructs a generator and every row costs a
resume plus an iterator-result object — to produce an array that is materialized before anything can
observe the laziness. Replaced with `mapToArray`, which drives the same iterable with one `for…of`
and pushes. Four sites: the two projection branches, and `INSERT`/`_MERGE` per binding in
`runLinearClauses`.

Gremlin has no composition of this shape (its own `toArray` is the traversal terminal); all four
sites are GQL's.

### Item 1509 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1508's REFUTATION WAS MEASURED ON THE WRONG FIXTURE, by the very error item 1508 documented.** The parse cache's LRU touch IS the cost: gating it on the cap is **1.15-1.32x across every warm read shape**

Item 1508 profiled `parseCacheHit` at 27.5%, deleted its `delete`+`set` pair, measured **flat**, and
recorded it as an inlining artifact. Then — in the same entry — it worked out that the fixture it
measured on (`parse-plan-probe`'s `hop`, 200 vertices, zero edges) spends its 1091 ns on 200
iterations rather than on per-call cost, and built a smaller instrument because of it.

**It did not go back and re-run the refutation on the new instrument.** On
`gql-call-overhead-probe`'s `floor` arm the same frame is **24.5% of 103.5 ns ≈ 25 ns** — the exact
magnitude the `PARSE_CACHE_CAP` comment had priced the pair at (57.2 ns, halved by the cache holding
5 entries instead of 64). On `hop` that 25 ns is 2.3% and cannot be seen.

**A refutation is only as good as the fixture it was measured on, and a fixture correction
invalidates every number taken before it.** Item 1508's other refutation (the two per-call
allocations) was re-run here and does still stand.

### What the gate is

The `delete`+`set` maintains a recency order that is read by exactly ONE thing: the eviction in
`parseCached`. Below the cap nothing is ever evicted, so the order is never consulted and the pair
is bookkeeping for a decision that will not be taken. Most processes live there permanently — the
cap is 64 and applications send a handful of distinct texts.

```ts
if (parseCache.size >= PARSE_CACHE_CAP) {
  parseCache.delete(text);
  parseCache.set(text, hit);
}
```

⚠️ **TWO GATE SITES, NOT ONE.** `parseCacheHit` serves the plain route; `parseCached` has its own hit
path, reached when `query` parses the AUTO-PARAMETERIZED text (item 1502), which is the hot route
for a caller that interpolates literals rather than binding params. Both are gated.

⚠️ **AND A THIRD SITE THAT MUST NOT BE TOUCHED.** `parseCached` also contains `} else if
(parseCache.size >= PARSE_CACHE_CAP) {` — the EVICTION check. A plain substring anchor matches all
three, which is how the first mutation run failed its anchor assertion (`gate count=3`, expected 2).
Mutating that one breaks the cap, which is a different property. The mutation script anchors on line
start.

### The approximation it accepts, stated precisely

While under the cap no recency is recorded, so at the moment the cache FILLS its order is insertion
order rather than true LRU, and the first eviction may drop a hot entry that full tracking would
have kept. From then on every hit is tracked and the order converges back. It is a choice among 64
cached parses — it can cost a re-parse, never an answer.

**Dropping the pair outright measured the same 1.24x and is strictly worse:** it makes eviction
permanently FIFO, which thrashes for a caller cycling over more than 64 hot texts. The gate keeps
true LRU for exactly the workload that needs it.

⚠️ **The `full` arm needs its OWN PROCESS, and building it taught that twice over.** Saturating the

Item 737's one-shape-per-process rule, arriving as a 55% baseline shift.

The win is a ~15 ns fixed cost, so it is invisible wherever a call does real work: flat on a 4 µs

of, and relatively largest on `count(*)` — 1.32x — because that shape is the smallest total in the

cannot move a 5 ms query, so it was variance; three repeats put it back at 4.86/4.97/4.70. A single

### Mutation — three caught, and ⚠️ one SURVIVOR that is supposed to survive

```text
notouch    remove both touch bodies (permanent FIFO)   CAUGHT   16 pass  2 fail
inverted   `<` instead of `>=` (touch only when NOT full) CAUGHT 16 pass  2 fail
offbyone   `>` instead of `>=` (never true: FIFO)      CAUGHT   16 pass  2 fail
always     `if (true)` — the ungated PRE behaviour     SURVIVES 18 pass  0 fail
```

Each caught mutant fails **both** new tests — one per gate site, which is how the second site is
known to be covered rather than assumed. And `always` surviving is the point of the pair: the tests
assert the eviction POLICY, not the presence of the gate, so the PRE code passes them too. A test
that failed on `always` would be pinning an implementation.

The tests observe eviction without timing anything. `parseCacheStats().seen` is the admission
filter's occupancy: an evicted text's next sighting is a MISS, and a miss on a text absent from the
filter ADDS it, so `seen` moves. Saturate, hammer one text, turn over the other 63, then ask for the
hot one — under FIFO it is gone.

⚠️ **The fixture had to be made LITERAL-FREE.** The first version used `WHERE t.k = 1`, which
auto-parameterization rewrites — so the cache key was the LIFTED text and the test reached
`parseCached`'s gate while its name claimed `parseCacheHit`'s. Caught by reading the route, not by a
failure. A second case now covers the lifted route deliberately.

### Item 1510 — `runLinear` recomputed "does this query write?" on every call, a closure plus a `Set` lookup per clause to re-derive a property of the compiled query: **1.16x on the count shapes, 5.61x cumulative on the `floor` arm since item 1508** — and adding the field broke **five** test files, four of them for the same reason

Re-profiled after item 1509's gate. `parseCacheHit` had fallen from 24.5% to **7.8%**, which is the
check that its share was tracking a real cost rather than an inlining artifact. The clause machinery
was now top:

```text
24.8%  runLinearClauses       9.5%  plan           4.2%  (anonymous) in projectedRows
10.2%  runLinear              9.2%  execute        3.6%  mapToArray
 9.6%  (garbage collector)    7.8%  parseCacheHit  3.3%  fastPath
                              5.7%  projectRow     2.1%  reviveParams
```

`runLinear` opened with:

```ts
const writes = linear.clauses.some((clause) => WRITE_CLAUSES.has(clause.kind));
```

`runLinear` 10.2% plus the 4.5% `(anonymous) in runLinear` — **that anonymous frame IS this
closure** — is 14.7% of an 82 ns call, spent re-deriving something `compileLinear` settles. Same
move as `Plan.readsPath` and `Plan.mayFault` on the Gremlin side (items 1504, 1507): `CLinear.writes`
is now carried by construction.

⚠️ **TOP-LEVEL CLAUSES ONLY, which is the right rule here and the OPPOSITE of `mayFault`'s.** A
nested write — a subquery or a `CALL` body that inserts — is a `CLinear` of its own, and `runLinear`
is what runs it, so it opens its own transaction when it executes. Propagating inward would claim a
read-only outer query writes, and `graph.transaction` nests. Three flags across two engines now,
each with its own propagation rule, each correct for its one consumer.

widefilt   4.86      4.85    flat
aggrows    2.74      2.74    flat

scales with CLAUSE COUNT** — `.some()` over two clauses costs more than over one. That reading is
inferred from the arm shapes, not measured: **an attempt to measure it directly failed and the arms
were removed rather than kept.** `LET a = 1 … RETURN` chains looked like the instrument (no graph
access, one clause per `LET`) but cost **1087 / 2086 / 4425 ns** at one, four and eight clauses —
~450 ns per `LET` of binding machinery, against a ~2.5 ns per-clause saving. They also pushed the
probe past a 120 s timeout and, co-resident with the ns-scale arms, moved `floor` from 85 to 104 ns
(item 737, again). A bad instrument kept "for completeness" is worse than an honest gap.

### ⚠️ Adding ONE boolean field to `CLinear` broke five test files, and the process gap is why I found out late

```text
deferred-hop-order.test.ts         13 fail
deferred-sorted-projection.test.ts  ─┐ same cause
label-test-fold.test.ts             ─┤
routes-fired.test.ts (routes)       ─┘
routes-fired.test.ts (the count)     1 fail, a DIFFERENT cause
```

Four of them share a `routes()` helper that reads **every non-null field of the compiled `CLinear`
except `clauses`** and calls that the set of rungs taken. A scalar `writes: false` is not null, so
it reported as a rung and `['hopProjection']` became `['hopProjection', 'writes']`. Fixed by
filtering on what a rung actually IS — `typeof v === 'function'` — which excludes `clauses` and
`writes` and any future scalar without a growing exclusion list.

The fifth is `routes-fired`'s `covers all nineteen detectors`, and it is a **different** failure with
the same trigger: it enumerates `Object.keys` and asserts the count is 19, so `writes` made it 20.
That one cannot use the function filter — it needs ALL nineteen detectors and most are `null` for any
single query shape — so it gets a named `NON_DETECTORS` set instead. That test is a deliberate guard
("a detector added later without a route case fails HERE") and it did its job.

⚠️ **AND THE PROCESS GAP: I ran the mutation sweep BEFORE the full suite.** The sweep's numbers were
inflated by 13 pre-existing failures I had not yet seen — `alwaysfalse` read "74 fail" when the
honest figure is 10, and ~63 of those were my own broken helper, not the mutant. Mutation verdicts
are only readable against a GREEN baseline. Gates first, then mutate.

### Mutation — all six caught, with honest counts

```text
alwaysfalse  writes always false (lose every transaction)  CAUGHT  3793 pass 10 fail
alwaystrue   writes always true (wrap every read)          CAUGHT  3791 pass 12 fail
dropinsert   drop `insert` from the set                    CAUGHT  3800 pass  3 fail  ← all 3 MINE
dropset      drop `set` from the set                       CAUGHT  3798 pass  5 fail
firstonly    test only clauses[0]                          CAUGHT  3796 pass  7 fail
invertuse    invert the gate in runLinear                   CAUGHT  3797 pass  6 fail
```

⚠️ **`dropinsert` fails exactly three tests and all three are in the new file.** A write kind dropped
from the set has no other coverage in 3,803 tests, which is `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` confirmed
with a number rather than quoted.

### Why the flag needed its OWN test, and both halves of it

`writes` is the single input to the one decision `runLinear` makes: wrap in `graph.transaction` or
not. **A `writes` that is wrongly false writes the same rows** — every answer-comparing test passes.
The difference appears only when a write FAILS PARTWAY: with the transaction the statement rolls
back, without it the rows written before the failure stay. A unique constraint makes that observable
with no timing and no internals:

```text
createUniqueConstraint('T', 'k'); INSERT (:T {k: 1})
INSERT (:T {k: 3}), (:T {k: 1})   → raises, and k=3 must NOT survive
```

So the file asserts the flag per clause kind (which names a missing kind precisely) AND the
consequence as rollback (which catches the flag being right and the wiring wrong — `invertuse` is
caught only by the second half).

```text

13.2%  execute              9.2%  fastPath              4.4%  reviveParams
12.9%  plan                 6.6%  parseCacheHit         4.4%  (anonymous) in projectedRows
                            6.3%  projectRow            4.1%  mapToArray
```

`fastPath` at 9.2% is the natural next target and the natural next instance of the items-1505/1510

a write, any uncovered MATCH shape — all nineteen `!== null` tests run on every call to learn

### It was built, it works, and it does not pay for itself

```text
arm      PRE      POST    ratio
floor   77.8 ns  72.2 ns  1.08x   RETURN 1 AS v        — no rung
param   89.0     81.4     1.09x   RETURN $x AS v       — no rung
one     35.6     36.1     0.99x   RETURN count(*)      — HAS a rung
onerow 106.2    107.4     0.99x   RETURN n.k           — HAS a rung
ten     36.1     36.2     flat
insert 3981     3900      1.02x   a 4 µs call cannot see 6 ns
wide/widefilt/aggrows                flat within the ~15% ms-scale band
```

One arm per process, **median of three runs each**. 7-9% on the bare-RETURN family, ~1% worse on
`count(*)` and the node projection — which pay one extra property load to reach a rung they were
always going to reach. Those are the more central shapes, both margins sit inside the run-to-run
bands, and it would add a **third** scalar field to `CLinear`, each of which has to be registered in
`routes-fired`'s `NON_DETECTORS` (item 1510 learned that by breaking five test files). Declined.

The recipe is recorded at `fastPath` itself as well as here, because the repo's rule is that a
rejected optimization lives next to the code it would have changed.

### ⚠️ The in-sweep A/B said the opposite, and the giveaway was the one item 762 names

Run as one multi-arm process rather than one arm per process:

```text
arm      PRE in-sweep  POST in-sweep   in-sweep ratio   ISOLATED ratio
floor      78.7 ns       72.9 ns          1.08x            1.08x
param      89.0          81.2             1.10x            1.09x
one        40.2          36.5             1.10x            0.99x   ← SIGN FLIP
ten        40.2          38.3             1.05x            flat
```

`one` has a rung and cannot gain from a gate that only skips a ladder it was going to enter — so
reading it 1.10x faster was the signal something was wrong with the instrument, not the change. The
cause is exactly item 762's: **in the PRE arm `fastPath` sees both rung-having and rung-less shapes;
in the POST arm only rung-having ones, so its inline caches are cleaner.** A change that
REDISTRIBUTES call sites flatters itself in a shared process, and the tell is a control moving more
than the target.

⚠️ **AND A SINGLE ISOLATED READING WAS NOT ENOUGH EITHER.** The first isolated POST run of `one` read
**39.7 ns against a PRE of 35.4 — 12% worse**, which would have been reported as a real regression.
Three repeats put PRE at 35.5/35.8/35.6 and POST at 36.1/35.9/36.3: the true figure is 1.4%, and the
39.7 was an outlier. `param` threw a 112.5 against its own 80.8/81.4 in the same sweep. **At this
scale one reading per arm is not a measurement, isolated or not** — which is the same lesson
`ts-spelling-probe` records for the TS per-row path, arriving on the GQL call path.

(5.67x). The construction-time seam is exhausted there, so this tick profiled the regime the arc had

### ⚠️ The shape I assumed was wrong before the first measurement

`gql-projection-reach-probe`'s `wide` arm — `MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k, n.n, n.k + 1` over 200,000
vertices — is NOT on the general projection path. It takes the `nodeProjection` rung. At 60
iterations (the first window, at 3 iterations, gave ~40 samples and was unreadable):

```text
44.5%  (anonymous) in detectNodeProjection   5.4%  variable.variable in compileExpr
18.1%  (garbage collector)                   3.8%  get properties
12.0%  fastPath            ← the INLINED rung call, not the ladder
10.4%  propOf                                3.4%  (anonymous) in compileExpr
```

`fastPath` at 12% is the same inlining artifact as ever: it `return`s the rung's closure call, so
the callee's time lands on it. The rung's per-row loop is therefore ~56%, and GC is 18.1%.

### What the per-row loop does, and the allocation the profile pointed at

```ts
row[cols[i]] = dk === undefined ? fns[i]({ binding, params, graph }) : propOf(v, dk);
```

A fresh `EvalEnv` **per non-direct column per row**, holding three references that are invariant for
the whole walk (`binding` is ONE map mutated in place). Hoisting it is already the established
spelling at ~30 sites across `shortcuts.ts` / `hop-projection.ts` / `clauses.ts` — one comment there
even records removing it from inside a `.map` — so these five were stragglers, not a new idea.

Five sites hoisted: the `nodeProjection` row loop, the `FOR`-projection row loop, and three per-edge
`gate(...)` calls in `hop-projection.ts`.

### ⚠️ A new arm, because `wide` cannot see the effect

A DIRECT column (`n.k AS k`) is served by `propOf` and never allocates. `wide` has two direct columns
and one expression, so it has **one** allocation per row to remove — against a ~15%
process-to-process spread at ms scale (established at item 1509). Unresolvable by construction.

`exprcols` — `RETURN n.k + 1 AS a, n.k + 2 AS b, n.k + 3 AS c, n.k + 4 AS d` — is the same row count
with **four** non-direct columns, so 800,000 allocations per call instead of 200,000: four times the
effect, same shape, same rung.

### It is flat

```text
          runs (5 isolated processes each, each a median of 10 reps)        median
PRE   22.74  23.32  23.84  23.85  26.50                                     23.84 ms
POST  22.80  23.13  23.57  24.80  25.70                                     23.57 ms   1.01x
```

⚠️ **The arm was verified to take the `nodeProjection` rung before the numbers were read** — the
"assert each A/B arm IS the code it claims" rule — so the hoist did reach the executed loop. Flat is
the answer, not a miss.

**This is item 424's corollary arriving in a new place: _"it allocates per row" is not by itself a
cost in this engine._** V8's young-generation bump allocation is near-free, and an 18.1% GC share
does not track allocation COUNT — the remaining GC is the row objects themselves, which the API has
to return. Declined and recorded at the loop as well as here.

Item 1508 refuted two allocation hypotheses on the per-call path for the same reason; this is the
third, now on the per-row path. **Allocation count is not a target in this engine on either path,
and the profile's GC share will keep nominating it.**

### What is left on this path, unpriced

At 23.8 ms for 800,000 expression evaluations, each `n.k + 1` costs ~30 ns: a `binding.get('n')`
string-keyed `Map` lookup, a `propOf` (the `properties` box getter plus an index), and the arith
step. The four columns of one row each repeat the same `binding.get` and the same `.properties`
read — four Map lookups and four getter calls for one vertex. Hoisting THAT (per row rather than per
column) is a different change from this one and is not priced here.

### Item 1513 — priced GREMLIN AT SCALE for the first time in this arc, and ⚠️ **the comparator A/B that came out of it was measuring its own harness: the "1.24x" flipped when the arms were reordered, and `(a, b) => a - b` measured SLOWER than a type-switching comparator.** Isolated properly, a numeric-specialized `order()` comparator is worth exactly **nothing**

Items 1503-1507 did Gremlin per-call and 1508-1512 did GQL. Nothing in the arc had profiled Gremlin
at 200,000 rows, so this tick did, through `isolated-gremlin-bench` (which already has the right
method: per-rep timing, p25, GC accounted, one shape per process).

```text
hopbare   V().out('E')                   38.2 ms / 200k rows    drain 79.6%  ·  get to 19.1%
hoporder  V().out('E').values('k').order() 193.9 ms             values 36.9% · pick 18.3%
                                                                sortByBys 11.6% · get properties 9.1%
```

`get to` is already memoized (`#toV ??=`) and the analyzer flags it NOT CHECKABLE, so it was not
chased. `hoporder`'s `order()` cluster — `sortByBys` 11.6% + its closure 3.6% + `orderStep` 2.8%,
~18% — was the target, with ~3.4M `compareTotal` calls for one 200,000-row sort. `compareTotal`
handles nulls, temporals, strings, lists and maps; a column of numbers needs none of that.

### ⚠️ The in-process A/B said 1.24x. It was measuring the inline cache

Five comparator spellings, timed in one loop driven through a wrapper `(a, b) => cmp(a.key, b.key)`:

```text
compareTotal  19.6 ms      ← ran FIRST
isNaNcall     24.3
selfNeq       26.9
orderFirst    24.1
subtract      24.9         ← `(a, b) => a - b`, SLOWER than the type-switching comparator
```

`(a, b) => a - b` cannot plausibly lose to a comparator that type-switches on five value classes.
That impossibility is what exposed the harness. **V8 keeps feedback per SOURCE POSITION, and the
wrapper arrow is one source position shared by every iteration of the loop** — so the first arm runs
monomorphic and every later arm runs against a polluted call site. Reversing the order:

```text
forward  (compareTotal first)   compareTotal 19.6   subtract 24.9
reversed (subtract first)       subtract     19.3   compareTotal 30.5
```

**Whichever comparator ran FIRST measured ~19-20 ms and whichever ran LAST measured 24-30 ms.** The
ordering was the entire effect; the instrument had no resolving power at all. This is item 762's
redistribution trap reached from the other side — there a CHANGE redistributed call sites, here the
HARNESS did — and the giveaway was the same: an arm moving in a direction it cannot move.

### The honest answer, one comparator per process

`order-comparator-probe.mjs`, alternated across four processes:

```text
compareTotal  23.81   24.08
numeric       23.91   23.85
```

**Identical.** A numeric-specialized total order is worth nothing: V8's inline caches already make
`compareTotal`'s numeric path monomorphic, so the type-switching it does for other value classes
costs a well-predicted branch and no more. ⚠️ **And correctness was never the blocker** — the probe
checks both comparators agree on all 121 pairs of
`{0, -0, 1, -1, NaN, ±Infinity, 1e308, ±5.5, 2^53}` before printing a number, and they do, including
NaN-last and NaN-equal-to-NaN. The lever is refuted on SPEED with a correct specialization in hand.

A by-product worth recording because it is the usual reason to reach for the inline form: `a !== a`
and `Number.isNaN(a)` measure the same (23.7 vs 23.9 ms, one process per spelling). The probe uses
`Number.isNaN`, which is also what `no-self-compare` wants.

### Where this leaves the arc

Three consecutive declines (1511 gate, 1512 allocation hoist, 1513 comparator), each with numbers,
and the common cause is worth stating once: **after items 1504-1510 the remaining profiles are
DIFFUSE.** No frame on either surface's hot path is now both large and reducible — `hoporder`'s
biggest is 36.9% and it is the walk itself; GQL's biggest is 33% and it is the row loop itself. The
levers that remain are each worth a few percent of one shape, which is under the resolving power of
an ms-scale instrument even when the instrument is honest.

The two allocation refutations (1512) and this one also share a cause: **V8 makes the obvious targets
free.** Young-generation allocation is near-free, and inline caches make a type-switch free on a
monomorphic path. Both are now recorded with numbers, on both the per-call and per-row paths.

### ⚠️ And then I re-derived item 1494

`hopbare` at 187.9 ns/row against `project` at ~30 looked like a 6.3x asymmetry worth decomposing,

```text
vonly      18.0 ns/row   iterate the id map
vbox        9.1          + the adjFrom getter
vget       64.3          + ONE string-keyed Map.get('E') per vertex
reach     137.9          + iterate the bucket
rowsedge  143.8          + push the edge
rowstoid  188.0          + read e.toId   (a plain string field)
rowsto    184.7          + read e.to     (the memoized vertex getter)
engine    184.0          V().out('E')
```

**The engine equals the hand-written floor** (184.0 against 184.7), and `rowstoid` ≈ `rowsto` says
reading ANY field off the edge costs the same — so the cost is the edge object's cache miss, not the
getter.

**Item 1494's heading already says this: _"`V().out(T)` is already within 4.6% of a hand-written
loop, so the Gremlin bare hop has no pipeline overhead left"_, and it refuted the endpoint getter
there too.** CLAUDE.md's rule is _"check the list before measuring or flagging"_ and I checked after
— about eight process runs spent confirming a closed result. The one thing that is new is the
FIXTURE: item 1494 measured FANOUT=2, this is FANOUT=1, and the conclusion holds at both. That does
not justify the runs; it is what they bought.

The decomposition is worth keeping for its shape: `hopbare`'s 188 ns/row is **9 + 55 + 74 + 6 + 44**,
where the 55 is one `Map.get` on a per-vertex adjacency map and the 74 is walking the bucket. All of
it is memory-bound, and the layout changes that would fix it are already disqualified — the array
adjacency is **1.58x slower** (item 1498), the global CSR **1.47x worse under churn** (item 1495),
and the dense vertex ordinal was built and disqualified on deletes (6.18x/11.34x, items 1369-1372).

### The O(1) id invariant, verified for the first time since item 1451

This is a standing requirement of the brief rather than a hypothesis, and **nothing in items
1504-1512 re-checked it** — those items changed plan construction, parse caching, clause flags and
the projection loop, none of which should touch id lookup, but "should not" is a reading of the
source and not a measurement. All three modes, 10,000 → 1,000,000 elements:

```text
mode   engine growth   raw Map growth   relative   constant factor at 1M (vertex / edge)
hit        3.30x           2.94x          1.12x            1.20x / 1.22x
miss       2.54x           4.06x          0.63x            1.77x / 1.59x
seq        2.11x           3.42x          0.62x            1.82x / 1.80x
```

**O(1) holds on all three.** The engine's per-lookup growth tracks a raw `Map`'s, so what growth
there is is cache and not complexity, and the constant factor over a raw `Map` is 1.20-1.82x.

```text

count 2-hop + start filter   93.7         count 3-hop + start filter  182.5
count 2-hop + end filter    108.1         count 3-hop + end filter    195.4
count 2-hop + mid filter     34.0         count 3-hop + interior      108.2
```

At THREE segments every filter helps, as a filter should. At TWO, the start and end filters make the
query SLOWER. Re-measured with `BENCH_ONLY` so each row is its own process (the sweep's in-process
inflation is documented), TS only, `BENCH_N=200000` — and isolated the gap is **larger**, not smaller:

```text
count 2-hop                 51.0 ms    the degree product — no edge pass at all
count 2-hop + mid filter    32.0        the product, gated once per middle — FASTER
count 2-hop + start filter  88.5        1.74x the bare product
count 2-hop + end filter   100.0        1.96x the bare product
```

**A strictly more selective query costs up to 1.96x.** That is the equivalent-spelling failure family
this engine is named for, except these are not two spellings of one question — they are a query and a
narrowing of it, and the narrowing is the slow one, which no correctness test can see.

### It is not a routing loss, and the cause is documented in the code

All four spellings take the SAME rung (`countShortcut` — checked, not assumed, via `compileLinear`),
so this is a split INSIDE the rung. `patternCountOf`'s own comments give the design: no constraint or
a MIDDLE one goes to the degree product (which iterates middles, so a middle gate is free); a START or
END constraint does not.

And the END case already had my idea written down, verbatim, as an OPEN item:

> The END is still refused: `Σ_b indeg(b) · |out-edges of b whose target passes p|` is a correct
> formula, but its second factor is a per-EDGE predicate evaluation, which is a different cost class
> from a once-per-middle gate. **Recorded as open rather than guessed at.**

So the lever was known, the formula was derived, and it was left open for want of exactly the
measurement above. The comment now carries it.

### ⚠️ The start case is NOT a defect and must not be chased with the end case

The bare product is O(V) arithmetic over middles and touches no edge. Any start-gated form has to
enumerate a→b, so 51.0 → 88.5 is "an edge pass against no edge pass" and is inherent — there is no
closed form that gates a start without visiting its edges. Treating the two together would turn a
real target into an unachievable one.

**The END is the one with a cost-class gap**, and the sharpest evidence is not against the product but
against the start: the formula above is ONE pass over the edges, and whatever the end spelling reaches
today measures **worse than the start's walk (100.0 against 88.5)** on a predicate of the same
selectivity over the same fixture. Two routes that should both be one-edge-pass-shaped differ by
11.5 ms, so the end spelling is doing more than an edge pass. That is both the reason to build the
formula and the thing to explain first.

### Not built this tick, deliberately

A new count route is 100-300x territory — it needs the byte-identity fuzzers and a mutation pass with
verified teeth, not the tail of a measuring tick. Priced at the code and here.

### Item 1516 — ⚠️ **THE GQL BENCH'S MAIN FIXTURE WAS A FUNCTIONAL GRAPH: every vertex had out-degree 5, in-degree 5, and exactly ONE distinct out-neighbour.** 1,000,000 edges spanned 200,000 distinct pairs. Fixed, self-checked, and it **flips the sign** of item 1515's sub-claim while making its headline bigger — a strictly more selective two-hop count costs **2.75x**, not 1.74x

Item 1515 priced a selectivity inversion on `count 2-hop` and flagged an 11.5 ms gap between the
start- and end-filtered routes as "the thing to explain first". Explaining it led to the fixture.

### What `graphDoc` actually was

```ts
from = (k * 7919) % N;
to = (k * 104729) % N; // k runs 0 .. 5N
```

The five edges leaving one vertex are exactly `k0, k0+N, k0+2N, k0+3N, k0+4N` — and **any linear
`(a·k + b) mod N` is invariant under `k → k+N`**, so all five pointed at the SAME target. Measured
rather than reasoned:

```text
vertices with an out-edge        200,000 of 200,000
out-degree distribution         {5: 200000}
in-degree  distribution         {5: 200000}
DISTINCT out-neighbours/vertex  {1: 200000}     ← the whole finding
1,000,000 edges                 200,000 distinct (from,to) pairs
```

**Every degree statistic was perfect.** The graph was a functional graph (each vertex points at one
other) wearing 5-fold parallel edges, so a k-hop count is `5^k · N` by construction — invariant to
the topology it is meant to measure. That is item 702's trap exactly, and item 702's rule is the one
that catches it: _count the DISTINCT endpoints, not the degrees._ I only looked because items 1426
and 1486 record two instruments disagreeing **1.91x and 3.4x** on identical queries, both from the
fixture's edge stride.

⚠️ **The defect is structural, not bad luck with these primes.** No multiplier fixes it: splitting on
`Math.floor(k / N)` — the repeat index — is what breaks the invariance. `to` is now
`((k % N) * 104729 + floor(k / N) * 977) % N`: out-degree 5, **5 distinct out-neighbours**, in-degree
exactly 5, no isolated vertices, and both terms stay far inside 2^53 so it does not reintroduce item
702's f64 overflow either.

**The fixture now checks its own topology** (`assertGraphDocBranches`), because every degree
statistic was already perfect while the graph was degenerate. It asserts the PROPERTY — every vertex
branches — rather than an exact fan-out, so a deliberate future change to the generator is free to
alter it.

### ⚠️ NUMBERS FROM BEFORE THIS CHANGE ARE NOT COMPARABLE WITH NUMBERS AFTER IT

Every multi-hop, var-length and DISTINCT row in `bench.ts` ran over the degenerate graph. The file
already carries that warning once, for the setup/teardown split; this is the second time. Rows that
walk get slower because they now branch; rows with a closed form do not move at all, which is itself
the diagnostic:

```text
                        degenerate   corrected
count 2-hop                 51.0       51.4    product: O(V), no edge pass — insensitive
count 2-hop + mid filter    32.0       31.6    gated once per middle — also insensitive
count 2-hop + start filter  88.5      141.4    the walk now branches 5 ways
count 2-hop + end filter   100.0      132.4
count 3-hop                332.8*     475.3
count 3-hop + start filter 182.5*     363.8
count 3-hop + end filter   195.4*     369.2
count 3-hop + interior     108.2*     172.8
```

(\* in-sweep; the 2-hop rows are `BENCH_ONLY`, one process each.)

### What this does to item 1515

- **Its headline is CONFIRMED and LARGER.** A strictly more selective two-hop count costs
  **2.75x** (start) and **2.58x** (end) against the bare product, where the degenerate fixture said
  1.74x/1.96x. No correctness test can see it.
- **Its sub-claim is REFUTED, by a sign flip.** Item 1515 read end (100.0) > start (88.5) and
  concluded "the end spelling is doing more than an edge pass… that 11.5 ms gap is the evidence the
  formula is worth building". On a correct fixture **start (141.4) > end (132.4)** — the gap reverses.
  Both routes are the same start-driven walk (an end predicate becomes the start of the reversed
  pattern, via `reversedTwoHop`), so there was never a cost-class difference between them; the 11.5 ms
  was the degenerate topology's forward/reverse asymmetry. Item 1515's heading now says so.
- **And the 2-vs-3 asymmetry SURVIVES**, which is what makes the target real: at two segments a filter
  costs 2.58-2.75x, at three it SAVES 1.3x. The explanation is now verified rather than guessed:
  **the two-segment bare count is the only one with a closed form that touches no edge at all**, so it
  is the only one a gate can make worse. The three-segment product already walks middle edges, so a
  gate there only removes work.

That also makes the formula in `patternCountOf`'s comment MORE attractive, not less: the arm that
does not care about branching is the product, and `Σ_b indeg(b) · |out-edges of b whose target passes
p|` keeps the end-filtered count on a product instead of a walk.

### Item 1517 — ⚠️ **BUILT the end-filtered degree product and it is 2.0x WORSE: 265.5 ms against the reversed walk's 132.4.** `patternCountOf`'s own comment predicted this ("a different cost class") and I read it as an invitation to measure rather than as the answer. The formula is **selectivity-blind and structurally so**. ⚠️ **THIS REFUTATION STANDS AND THE ROW IS STILL TAKEN — by item 1690, which is not a cheaper route to the same degree lookup but an INDEX in place of it: 126.7 -> 6.5 ms. The distinction is items 1335/310's at the three-hop twin, and it is why a refuted formula does not close a row.**

Item 1516 left this as the next build, and the comment in `patternCountOf` had carried the formula as
OPEN for some time: `Σ_b indeg(b) · |out-edges of b whose target passes p|` replaces the reversed walk
for an end-constrained two-segment count.

### It was built properly, which is why the refutation is worth something

- `sideOfVertexGated` — which already existed, module scope, with item 268's closure warning — as the
  second factor, so the end gate costs one pass over a middle's out-edges.
- Both the clause (`WHERE c.age > 60`) and inline (`(c {k: 2})`) spellings routed into the same arm,
  which is the equivalent-spelling discipline; before this they shared a route only by both being
  refused.
- The product's end-plainness guard relaxed to "plain OR handed over as `endPreds`", so a constrained
  end with an empty gate list still declines — ⚠️ dropping an end constraint silently is a wrong
  answer, not a slow one, so the guard tests both halves and not just the pattern.
- `both` on the end leg refused, because `undirectedSide` has no gated twin and routing a constraint
  into it would drop it.
- Answers verified against a brute-force walk on a hand-checkable fixture (3 = 3), gql **3803/0**, and
  `bun run fuzz` **20/0** — a new count route is 100-300x territory, so byte-identity came before any
  timing.

### And it is 2.0x worse

```text
                        before    after
count 2-hop               51.4     50.9    unchanged
count 2-hop + mid filter  31.6     33.1    unchanged
count 2-hop + start       141.4   139.6    unchanged
count 2-hop + end         132.4   265.5    2.0x WORSE
```

Only the row whose arm changed moved, which is also the evidence the new arm is what ran.

### ⚠️ The cause is structural, and the comment had already named it

The refused-formula note said the second factor "is a per-EDGE predicate evaluation, which is a
different cost class from a once-per-middle gate". That is precisely the defect:

- **the formula** evaluates `p` once per EDGE — 1,000,000 endpoint resolves plus 1,000,000 predicate
  calls at this fixture;
- **the reversed walk** evaluates it once per end VERTEX (200,000) and then expands only the ~32%
  that pass.

**The walk is selectivity-aware and the formula cannot be.** There is no way to enumerate "edges whose
target passes `p`" without either visiting every edge or starting from the targets — and starting from
the targets IS the reversed walk. Pre-computing the passing vertices into a set does not rescue it:
that replaces the predicate call and keeps all 1,000,000 endpoint resolves.

**The lesson for reading these comments:** "recorded as open rather than guessed at" meant the cost was
unmeasured, not that the stated objection was weak. Item 1515 read it as the former and treated the
objection as a hypothesis to test; the objection was the answer, and the measurement confirmed it
rather than overturning it. Three ticks (1515 pricing, 1516 fixture, 1517 build) to establish that —
of which 1516 was worth it independently.

### What stands

The **2.58x selectivity inversion is real and now has no known cure on this route** — the formula was
its only candidate. The remaining direction is the product's START factor rather than its end factor,
which is a different shape and unpriced. Recorded at the code as well as here, with the numbers, so
the formula is not re-attempted as an idea.
