### The defect, generalized

```text
to = (a * k + b) % N            is invariant under  k -> k + N
```

and every generator in this corpus runs `for (k = 0; k < NODES * FANOUT; k++)`, so the FANOUT edges
leaving one vertex are exactly `k0, k0+N, k0+2N, …`. Measured at N=50,000:

```text
                                            distinct out-neighbours per vertex
                            FANOUT=1   FANOUT=2   FANOUT=5
to = (k * 104729) % N        {1: …}     {1: …}     {1: …}      ← collapses
to = (… + hop * 2654435761)  {1: …}     {2: …}     {5: …}      ← tracks fanout
```

⚠️ **At FANOUT=1 it is harmless** (degree 1 cannot have more than one distinct neighbour), which is
why it survived so long and why this arc's own readings at FANOUT=1 are unaffected. It bites the
moment anyone raises the fanout — which two probes do **by default**.

### ⚠️ The fix was already in the file, one line above the defect

`isolated-row-bench.mjs` and `isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs` both build their `small` stride as
`(i * 7 + 3 + hop * 2_654_435_761) % pool` and comment it:

> The FANOUT-th edge out of `i` lands elsewhere, **so degree rises without the targets collapsing
> onto one vertex**

…and then the `random` arm immediately below it was `(k * 104_729) % pool`, which is exactly the
collapse that comment describes preventing. The knowledge was present and applied to one arm of two.

### Six instruments fixed

```text
hop-rows-floor-probe.mjs          FANOUT default 2   ← broken at its default
runtime-profile-gremlin-probe.mjs FANOUT default 5   ← broken at its default
isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs        STRIDE default random
isolated-row-bench.mjs            random arm only
gremlin-hop-floor-probe.mjs       random arm
gql-undirected-floor-probe.mjs    random arm
```

### ⚠️ What a degenerate fixture does and does NOT invalidate

This is the distinction that decided the scope, and it is worth having written down:

- **An A/B on ONE fixture survives it.** Both arms see the same graph, so "the engine is within X% of
  a hand-written loop" is still a fair comparison — only its absolute ns/row describes a graph nobody
  has.
- **A claim about branching, selectivity or fan-out does not.** Those are claims about the topology
  the fixture failed to provide.

So item 1494 — _"`V().out(T)` is already within 4.6% of a hand-written loop"_, measured on
`hop-rows-floor-probe` at its degenerate FANOUT=2 default — was predicted to survive, and it does.
Re-run on the branching fixture, 200,000 vertices / 400,000 edges / 2 distinct neighbours each:

```text
reach      71.53 ns/row     rowstoid  108.03
rowsedge   75.78            rowsto    107.95
engine    107.37   ← still at the floor, and still fractionally under it
```

`rowstoid` ≈ `rowsto` again (43.21 ms against 43.18), so item 1494's other finding — reading `e.toId`
costs the same as the memoized `e.to`, because the cost is the edge object's cache miss rather than
the getter — also re-validates.

### Item 1521 — item 1520's unexplained 4.7x was **not comparable per element**, and correcting the instrument found a real one: with the WALK HELD CONSTANT, `RETURN r` costs **246.5 ns/row against `RETURN x`'s 132.2 — 1.86x to bind the edge you already hold rather than the far vertex you must resolve.** Mechanism verified in the code, not inferred

### First, item 1520's observation was an instrument error and is withdrawn

```text
project the element   MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n              — a LABEL BUCKET scan, 200k rows
project the edge      MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN r — a 1-HOP WALK, 1M rows
```

Dividing one by the other prices neither: the 4.7x mixed the element TYPE with the walk that produced
it. That is item 1480's error ("that floor rides the values walk and does LESS work"), and item 1520
was right to flag it as unexplained rather than bank it.

### The experiment that does work: hold the walk constant

New `element-row-probe.mjs`, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges at FANOUT=5 with item 1518's repeat
term, one arm per process:

```text
edge     MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->()  RETURN r      1M rows   246.5 ns/row
farnode  MATCH (:P)-[:E]->(x)  RETURN x      1M rows   132.2 ns/row   ← 1.86x CHEAPER
relprop  MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->()  RETURN r.w    1M rows   334.8 ns/row
bucket   MATCH (n:P)           RETURN n    200k rows    15.8 ns/row   (no walk, for scale)
```

Same walk, same row count, same single column — only what lands in the row differs. **Binding the
edge is 1.86x binding the far vertex, which is backwards**: `r` is already in hand at that point and
`x` has to be resolved through `edge.to`.

### The mechanism, read off the code and confirmed by the profile

The two spellings take DIFFERENT routes — `farnode` the fused `detectHopProjection` closure (62.5%),
`edge` a separate `relBoundHopWalk` (68.1%, plus `get to` at 4.7% in a query whose far node is
ANONYMOUS). And `relBoundHopWalk`'s inner loop explains the 4.7%:

```ts
for (const edge of bucket) {
  const far: Vertex = out ? edge.to : edge.from; // ← ALWAYS resolved
  if (fl !== undefined && !matchesLabel(far, fl)) {
    continue;
  }
  binding.set(farVar, far); // ← ALWAYS written
  binding.set(relVar, edge);
  rows.push(projectRow(proj, binding, params, graph));
}
```

**Both are dead work when the projection never reads the far variable**, and the repo already has the
rule for it — `shortcuts.ts` carries _"When every item is direct the binding is never read, so writing
it is dead work — item 803's rule, and the same deletion item 835 made at the node-scan site"_ —
applied at other sites and not at this one.

⚠️ **And the guard needs no expression analysis in the common case.** `hop-projection.ts:805` is
`const farVar = node.variable ?? ANON_FAR_VAR` — a name no GQL identifier can collide with — so for an
anonymous far node (`->()`) **nothing can read it by construction**. The condition is
`fl === undefined && farVar === ANON_FAR_VAR`.

whether this route does has to be established before the guard goes in, not after. A projection route
is 100-300x territory, so this needs the byte-identity fuzzers and a mutation pass with verified

refute its own build.

`relprop` at 334.8 ns/row is the same route and the larger row, so the same saving should reach it;
that is a second measurement to take, not a claim.

### The hazard, cleared the way this file demands

`relBoundHopWalk` resolves `edge.to` and writes `binding.set(farVar, far)` per edge; for `-[r:E]->()`
the far name is `ANON_FAR_VAR` (`'\u0000anon_far'`), which the parser cannot produce, so nothing can
read it. ⚠️ **But `mapToRow` copies EVERY binding with no NUL filter**, so if `RETURN *` took this
walk, skipping the write would change its OUTPUT — a wrong answer, not a slow one.

I did not settle that by reading the call chain, because **this file records a comment of exactly that
shape being refuted by running it**: the rel-variable guard's claim that "the projection guard rejects
any item that reads a name other than the far variable" is _false for a correlated subquery_, and the
file calls it "the second comment in this file to be refuted by running the thing it described".
Measured instead:

```text
MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN *     780.6 ns/row
MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN r     236.4 ns/row    ← this walk
```

**3.3x says star is on the general path and cannot reach the guard.** Hazard cleared.

### Built, correct, and it does not pay

gql **3803/0** and `bun run fuzz` **20/0** with the guard in — a projection route is 100-300x
territory, so byte-identity came before timing. Then, 1,000,000 edges at FANOUT=5, three processes per
arm, alternated, medians:

```text
             RETURN r          RETURN r.w
PRE        236.4 ns/row      346.2 ns/row
one loop   209.5  (1.13x)    402.0  (−16%)
two loops  228.4  (1.03x)    395.5  (−14%)
```

⚠️ **Both spellings are THIS walk**, so `RETURN r.w` is not an unrelated row — the change made the
same loop's other caller 16% slower. And the second variant is the textbook fix for that: hoist the
test out, select one of two loops once, leave the skipping body branch-free. **It lost most of the win
and kept the loss.**

So the regression is robust to the implementation and the gain is not. `RETURN r.w` is at least as
common a shape as `RETURN r`, so the trade is negative either way. Declined and reverted; recorded at
the code with both variants' numbers, because "try hoisting it into two loops" is the obvious next
idea and it has now been tried.

### Why this loop is that sensitive

`RETURN r.w` is **~65% `propOf` + `get properties`** (44.3% + 20.4% windowed) — a cold-object
dereference through the edge's property box. That is the read **item 1392 already closed** as having
no lever in it, and it is also what makes the loop memory-bound: a memory-bound loop charges more for
an added test than the skipped work returns. Same toll as `pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` (items
1413-1466: "any edit costs the filtered-count cluster 1.08-1.24x, never gains"), in a new place.

### What stands

The 1.86x between `RETURN r` (236.4) and `RETURN x` (129.5) is real and **now has no candidate cure**
— the dead-work guard was the only one, and it is refuted. The two spellings take genuinely different
routes (`relBoundHopWalk` against the fused `detectHopProjection`), so closing the gap would mean
giving the rel-bound shape the fused route rather than trimming the walk it has.

> ⚠️ **ITS 2.57x COMPARED A NULL READ AGAINST A REAL ONE — see item 1526.** `RETURN x.k` read an
> absent key (the probe's fixture carries `age`, not `k`) while `RETURN r.w` read a real edge

Item 1522 refuted trimming the start-driven walk and named the one remaining mechanism: give the
rel-bound shape the FUSED route. This is that, and it took one measurement and one file read.

### The gap is larger than 1.86x once the comparison is like-for-like

Item 1521 compared `RETURN r` against `RETURN x` — an edge reference against a vertex reference. The
sharper pair holds the WORK equal at one property read per row, far-driven against start-driven:

```text
farprop   MATCH (:P)-[:E]->(x) RETURN x.k    132.0 ns/row   (far-driven)
relprop   MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN r.w    339.2 ns/row   (start-driven)
```

**2.57x, alternated across four processes, bands non-overlapping.** Both read exactly one property per
row, so **the ROUTE dominates, not the thing being read.** And the far-driven route makes a property
read nearly free: `RETURN x` is 129.5 and `RETURN x.k` is 132.0 — **2.5 ns** for the whole read.

### Why that 2.5 ns is the answer, and why it closes the line

`farDrivenHopWalk`'s emit loop:

```ts
let n = unionCount(buckets, sumIsExact); // the DEGREE, from bucket SIZES
binding.set(farVar, far);
const template = projectRow(proj, binding, params, graph); // ONCE per far vertex
rows.push(template);
for (n -= 1; n > 0; n -= 1) {
  rows.push({ ...template });
}
```

**It never iterates the edges.** It takes the degree from bucket sizes, projects ONE row per far
vertex, and pushes `n` spread copies. That is the whole 2.3x of item 167 and the whole reason a
far-side property read amortizes to 2.5 ns a row.

⚠️ **A projection reading `r` needs a DISTINCT edge in each of those `n` rows**, so the
template-and-copy collapses and the walk must iterate the bucket — which is exactly the work the
start-driven walk already does. The two routes are not two implementations of one traversal: **the
fast one answers a question that does not mention the edge.** There is nothing to fuse.

### So the 1521-1523 line closes with a mechanism rather than a number

Every figure is now explained by one fact — far-driven amortizes over degree, rel-bound cannot:

```text
RETURN x    129.5 ns/row   one far-vertex visit, n cheap copies
RETURN x.k  132.0          + a property read, amortized over the degree
RETURN r    236.4          must visit every edge
RETURN r.w  339.2          + read each edge's property box
```

And both cures are gone: **trimming** the start-driven walk is refuted on numbers (item 1522 — the
guard works, gives 1.13x, and costs the same loop's other caller 16%), and **fusing** into the
far-driven walk is impossible by construction. Recorded at the code so the next reader does not spend
a tick re-deriving either half.

⚠️ **The method note worth keeping:** item 1522 cost a full tick to build-and-refute; this one cost a
measurement and a file read. The difference is that I read the fast route's BODY before trying to
route anything into it. Item 1517 made the same mistake in the same arc — building the end-filtered
product whose own comment had already said why it would lose.

> class; `{}` plus `row[keys[c]] = …` cannot reuse it.

### Why the nearby refutations do NOT cover this

Items 1444-1450 worked this same row hard, so the risk of re-deriving is real and was checked:

- **item 1446** explains 90.9% of the engine-to-floor gap as megamorphism (104.9 ns/row) plus per-row
  machinery (52.1%) — a decomposition of the cost, not a cure;
- **item 1447** built a specialized ROW BUILDER for the single-far-property case: **−4.8% / +0.7%**,
  reverted, and its own diagnosis was wiring (one dispatch site holding two closures goes polymorphic);
- **item 1450** built a FUSED projection+predicate specialization: **+1.3% / +2.7%**, and its apparent
  32.8% was an impossible floor because the win needed CONSTANT property keys.

None of those is "emit one row per start vertex and spread-copy it `out-degree` times". They
specialize HOW ONE ROW is built; this changes HOW MANY rows are built from scratch. Item 1407 is the
precedent that the distinction matters — it beat the computed-key store by 16-28% where a specialized
builder beat it by ~0%.

### The target, specified

In the start-driven walk, when the projection reads **only** the start (`startOnly`) and nothing
filters the far end (no far label, no far predicate, no rel predicate — anything that could reject an
edge changes the count), take the bucket SIZE, call `projectRow` once, and push the template plus
`n − 1` spread copies. The guard is the same shape as `relBoundHopWalk`'s and the emit loop the same
as `farDrivenHopWalk`'s.

⚠️ **Hazards to settle BEFORE building, which is item 1523's lesson:**

1. **Row ORDER.** GQL row order is unspecified (`order-is-unspecified`) and the differential fuzzer
   compares multisets, but this does not reorder anything — it emits the same rows in the same
   start-vertex order. Confirm rather than assume.
2. **Anything that can reject an edge** must decline, or the count is wrong — a wrong answer, not a
   slow one. That is the same class of mistake `twoSegmentCount`'s end-constraint decline exists to
   prevent, where a mutant "passed every other test in the file".
3. **`RETURN *`** must be excluded as at item 1522, where it measured 3.3x the walk and so could not
   reach it.

When the projection reads the start and nothing else, every row a start vertex produces is
IDENTICAL, so the bucket SIZE is the row count and one `projectRow` serves the whole group. Item 1407

silent fall-through, so "reads the start" could not be distinguished from "reads both ends".

1. **Count exactness.** `farPred` declines outright; a NON-VACUOUS far label is handled per call by a

### Mutation — five of seven caught, and ⚠️ the two survivors are REDUNDANT guards, demonstrated

```text
ignore-readsfar   drop !readsFar from the derivation    CAUGHT   3798 pass 19 fail
allow-farpred     admit a far predicate                 CAUGHT   3798 pass 19 fail
ignore-farlabel   fold even under a real far label      CAUGHT   3807 pass 10 fail
alias-rows        push the template n times, no clone   CAUGHT   3815 pass  2 fail  ← only MY tests
off-by-one        n copies instead of n − 1             CAUGHT   3802 pass 15 fail
ignore-readsrel   drop !readsRel                        SURVIVES 3817 pass  0 fail
allow-star        drop !proj.star                       SURVIVES 3817 pass  0 fail
```

`alias-rows` is why the distinct-object cases exist: **nothing else in 3,815 tests sees aliased rows**,
and `rows.push(template)` followed by `{ ...template }` is a deliberate idiom whose failure mode is a
caller mutating one row and changing its siblings.

And the two survivors were diagnosed rather than left open: `RETURN *` carries ZERO projection items,
so `projectedEndsOnly` reports `readsStart: false` and the shape declines before `star` is consulted
(verified by parsing it — `star=true items=0`); a rel-reading projection is claimed by the rel-bound
walks ABOVE this one, and the surviving mutant IS the evidence, since the fold still did not fire for
`RETURN a.k, r.w`. Both tests stay, **labelled redundant-today rather than load-bearing** — item 444's
lesson, where a guard called "defensive, not load-bearing" turned out to be the only thing refusing a
correlated subquery.

guard working. Same class as item 1507's wrong expectation, and the deciding evidence was the same:
look at what the engine actually returned before changing either side.

### How it surfaced

Added `startpropfilt` (`WHERE a.k > 5 RETURN a.k`) to measure the mirror item 1525 declined, and it
returned **ZERO rows**. `a.k` is absent from the fixture, so the predicate was UNKNOWN for every
row — and the probe printed a null `ns/row` instead of a number, which is what made it visible.

**Without the filtered arm nothing looked wrong.** A projection of an absent key returns `null` per
row: `propOf` runs, the row count is unaffected, and the output is a column of nulls nobody prints.
⚠️ **This is CLAUDE.md's own rule turned on my own instrument** — _"an answer that is INVARIANT to the
property you varied cannot validate the fixture"_ — and a row COUNT is invariant to whether the
projected key exists. Items 1516 and 1518 applied that rule to the repo's fixtures; this is the third
instance and the first in something I wrote.

**Item 1525's 2.15x survives**, re-measured with a real property (`age`) on both arms:

```text

startprop PRE        247.4 / 255.4                249.2
startprop POST       115.7 / 118.4                117.0
                        2.15x                      2.13x
```

The reason it survives is the mechanism: **both arms pay a property read, just at different rates** —
PRE once per ROW, POST once per START VERTEX — and `propOf` returning `null` costs about what
returning a number costs (a getter plus an index either way). So the fold's advantage is in the row
construction, which is what item 1525 claimed. `farprop` likewise moved 123.9 against 129.7, i.e. not
at all, because the far-driven walk also reads once per vertex.

⚠️ **Item 1523's 2.57x is the one to treat with suspicion**, and it is not re-measured here. That

path would have reached the vertex at all. Copying safety-critical code to gain a branch is a bad
trade, and item 159's warning is about the per-EDGE loop, which this leaves untouched. So the fold is
selected **once per call** and branched **once per vertex**, after the gate:

```ts
const fold = projStartOnly && farPred === undefined && fl === undefined;
…
if (fold) { let n = bucket.size; const template = projectRow(…); rows.push(template);
            for (n -= 1; n > 0; n -= 1) { rows.push({ ...template }); } continue; }
```

### Where the gate's call lives, and why

⚠️ **The `gate(env)` call stays inside the per-compile closure.** Item 159 measured a shared
module-scope walk at **1.29x** because its call sites go polymorphic across compiles, and a compiled
gate differs per query — so extracting the gate CALL is the one thing not to do.

What IS extracted is the **fault** path (`undirectedFaultReaches`), and that is safe for exactly the
reason `anyFarMatches`' own comment gives: _"Used ONLY from the fault path… Cold by construction, so
it is shared rather than inlined per compile."_ The decomposition is the file's own, not a new idea.

### ⚠️ And the parity question is DIFFERENT for this walk

The general path produces a row for a vertex when any incident edge — **out OR in** — would have
survived. So a faulting gate must rethrow in both cases, and `undirectedFaultReaches` asks
`anyFarMatches` of `adjFrom` and then of `adjTo`. **Checking only `adjFrom` would swallow a fault the
general path raises** — which is not a slow answer but a missing exception.

Verified by hand across the full matrix before any timing:

```text
no incident edge at all              suppressed   rows [3, 2]
an IN-edge only                      RAISES       ← the case one-bucket logic loses
an IN-edge, far end fails the label  suppressed   rows [3]
an IN-edge, far end passes it        RAISES
```

### The edge-pass arm cannot carry it

Item 1431's edge pass enumerates EDGES, so each yields two rows with DIFFERENT starts — a gate would
be per ROW, which is neither the once-per-vertex contract nor cheaper than the two-pass walk. It falls
back, which is sound because the edge pass only runs when both labels are free and the two-pass arm
handles that anyway.

same fallback item 1531 established, and sound for the same reason.

### Item 1534 — took item 1529's "what does this fast path DECLINE?" screen to the GREMLIN surface and it found the same class: a SELECTIVE start filter declines `hopValuesShortcut` entirely. **FIVE shapes, 2.78–4.30x, and in every one the more selective query is slower in WALL CLOCK while emitting half the rows.** ~~PRICED, NOT BUILT~~ — ✅ **FOUR OF THE FIVE BUILT AT ITEM 1535** (1.65–3.79x; `both` still open)

Items 1529–1533 emptied the GQL hop-projection decline table. This tick asked the same question of a
different file, because the question has generalized better than any of its targets.

#### Why this was not visible from the bench

`hopValuesShortcut`'s guard destructures `const [source, hop, proj] = steps` and refuses unless
`steps[1]` is `out`/`in`/`both`. So any step between the source and the hop declines the whole plan.

That reads like it should make every realistic hop decline — and it does not, for a reason worth
writing down: `effectivePlan` runs `dropVacuousLabels`, so `hasLabel('P')` on a graph where every
vertex carries `P` is **deleted from the plan** before the shortcut sees it. Every yield arm in
`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs` is written `V(), hasLabel('P'), out('E'), values('k')` on an all-`P`
fixture, so all of them reach the fused walk and none of them measure the decline. The arms look
like they cover a filtered start and they cover a dropped one.

With `VLABEL=2` only half the vertices carry `Q`, nothing is dropped, and the decline is reachable.

#### THE FAMILY, per row, at NODES=200000 FANOUT=1 VLABEL=2

Per-row is the honest normalization here: each declined arm visits half the starts and emits half
the rows, and the per-row work on both sides is one far-vertex property (or id) read.

| shape                             | declined                           | admitted control          | ratio     |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------- |
| `hasLabel(Q).out(E)` bare         | 815.6 ns/row                       | `out(E)` 189.9            | **4.30x** |
| `hasLabel(Q).out(E).id()`         | 834.7                              | `out(E).id()` 240.7       | **3.47x** |
| `has(k, gt(48)).out(E).values(k)` | 1123.4                             | `out(E).values(k)` 372.3  | **3.02x** |
| `hasLabel(Q).both(E).values(k)`   | 1069.8                             | `both(E).values(k)` 359.4 | **2.98x** |
| `hasLabel(Q).out(E).values(k)`    | 1033.7 (two runs: 1032.6 / 1034.8) | 372.3 (366.1 / 378.5)     | **2.78x** |

And the wall clock, which is the part that makes this a route loss rather than a slow walk:
`hopyieldq` is **103.5 ms against the control's 73.2** while doing half the work.

Confirmed by profile rather than inferred. The declined arm spends **~41% in the generator
delegation chain the hand walk skips** — `iterLabeled` 24.6%, `outEdgesOf` 9.2%, `iterByLabel`
7.2% — plus `otherEndpoint` 7.4%, `traverseToVertex` 3.7%, `isVertexShaped` 6.7%, `startTraverser`
and `unwrap`. `hop-values.ts`'s own header prices that chain at 375.6 ms against 251, and this is
that cost showing up through the front door.

Same class as items 1437 (`WHERE true` at 7.46x), 1515 and 1530: **adding a selective filter should
REMOVE work.** This is the Gremlin instance of it.

#### Why the spelling probe did not catch it, which is a gap in the probe

`bun run spelling:gremlin` has exactly the right group — `label, VACUOUS, before a hop:
hasLabel(Univ).out vs out` — and it converges, correctly, because that label IS vacuous and IS
dropped. **Every group in that probe ends in `count()`.** The count side admits a start filter
(`collectVertexFilters`, which item 1302 confirms "takes `hasLabel` for the steps BEFORE the hop"),
so the count surface genuinely has no gap here and the probe reports the truth about the surface it
measures. The yield side has no vacuous-label group at all, and no selective-label group on either
side. That is the same shape as item 1383's own recorded limitation: a group that guards a
regression without covering the surface where the gap was.

#### NOT BUILT, and the two blockers are both about where the code goes

1. **`collectVertexFilters` is private to `count-shortcut.ts`.** The machinery this needs already
   exists and is already the right machinery — it declines a `has` the property index could seek
   (`seekWorthTaking`), which is the correct deference to `seedFromIndex`. Exposing it plus its
   applier is a shared-code change across two 2000+ line modules, and getting that extraction right
   is the first thing to do, not the last — the same judgement as items 1528 and 1530, each of which
   the next tick then shipped.
2. **The obvious home is `hop-values.ts`, and that file has a measured toll.** Items 1441/1466
   price an edit to it at up to 16% on unrelated rows, arbitrarily signed, and item 1466 **declined
   a 3.3x win** on exactly that basis. Item 1482 is the precedent for the way out: it took the
   no-hop sibling (`V().hasLabel(L).values(k)`, 2.39x) into a NEW module rather than editing this
   one. A start-filtered variant should follow that, which also means it must not duplicate the four
   hand walks (`oneType`, `manyTypes`, `bothOneType`, the general tail) — so the shape of the work
   is to parameterize the walk by an optional start gate, not to fork it.

The bare-hop arm (4.30x) is the largest and the simplest — `consumed = 2`, no projection at all —
so it is the one to build first.

### Item 1535 — SHIPPED — ~~**1.65–3.79x on four shapes**~~ ⚠️ **NUMBERS WRONG, CORRECTED AT ITEM 1536 TO 1.44–1.86x** (measured against a dist built from the BUCKET-SEEDED version this entry then replaced — the bench reads `dist`, and only `bun run fuzz` rebuilt it; the module, both hazards and the direction of every number stand): `startFilteredHopValues`, a new module, answers the start-filtered hop `hopValuesShortcut` declined. `V().hasLabel(Q).out(E)` 815.6 → 215.2 ns/row, three controls flat. And the version I nearly shipped was WRONG in two ways the whole suite and all seven fuzzers were blind to

Item 1534 priced the family. This builds it.

#### The change

A new module, consulted as a fallback and in this order, so no plan the existing shortcut already
admits can change route:

```ts
-  const projected = ctx.tracksPath ? undefined : hopValuesShortcut(effective, graph);
+  const projected = ctx.tracksPath
+    ? undefined
+    : (hopValuesShortcut(effective, graph) ?? startFilteredHopValues(effective, graph));
```

**A NEW MODULE RATHER THAN A RELAXED GUARD, and that is items 1441/1466's rule, not tidiness.** An
edit to `hop-values.ts` costs unrelated rows up to 16%, arbitrarily signed, and item 1466 declined a
3.3x win on exactly that basis. Item 1482's precedent — the no-hop sibling into its own module — is
the way out, and here it also kept the ~2% control drift below the measurement floor. `hop-values.ts`
is byte-identical.

**Scope is ONE named type on `out`/`in`.** `hopValuesShortcut` has four walks (`oneType`,
`pairTypes`, `manyTypes`, `bothOneType`); forking all four would be the duplication item 1527
refused. `both` and the multi-type spellings keep declining, which simply leaves them where they
were — `hopbothq` measured flat across the change, confirming it.

What is **not** duplicated is the filter admission. `collectVertexFilters` is `count-shortcut.ts`'s,
exported (`const` → `export const`, no behaviour change) rather than reimplemented, because it
carries a judgement this module must not restate: it **declines a `has` whose key the property index
could seek**, deferring to `seedFromIndex`. Re-deriving that is how the two would drift.

#### ⚠️ THE FINDING: the obvious implementation was wrong twice, and nothing in the repo could see it

The one-line way to write this is to seed the walk from `graph.verticesByLabel.get(L)`, which is
exactly what the count-side twin `startFilteredHopCount` does. I wrote that first. It is wrong here
for two reasons, **both invisible to a count and both observable on a yielded stream**:

1. **ORDER.** Gremlin stream order is a TinkerPop contract the differential fuzzer compares
   **ordered** — unlike GQL, where row order is unspecified. The general pipeline reaches this shape
   as `filterStream(stream, v => step.labels.some(l => v.labels.has(l)))` over `graph.vertices`
   (`dispatch.ts`'s `hasLabel` arm), so the admitted route must emit in **global vertex order**. A
   label bucket is normally insertion-ordered and agrees by accident; `addLabelToVertex` after the
   fact breaks that. The test pins a graph whose `Q` bucket is `[n3, n2]` while the answer is
   `[n2, n3]`.
2. **STALENESS.** The raw `labels` **setter** has never maintained `verticesByLabel` — only
   `addLabelToVertex`/`removeLabelFromVertex` index — and `core`'s `label-box.test.ts` pins that as
   deliberate pre-existing behaviour. So after a setter write the bucket is neither a subset nor a
   superset of the truth: it can list a vertex that lost the label and omit one that gained it. The
   test makes the bucket wrong in both directions at once and asserts `[1]` where a seeded walk
   answers `[2]`.

So the walk tests the label per vertex, like the pipeline. **That costs nothing that matters**: the
2.78–4.30x was never the per-vertex scan, it is the per-edge generator chain and traverser
machinery, and the measured numbers below are with the scan in place.

**The teeth were verified by an attacking mutant, not assumed.** Restoring the bucket-seeded version
fails **exactly the two tests written for it and nothing else — 1482 other tests pass, and all seven
fuzzers pass.** That is the whole justification for writing them: the suite, the differential fuzzer
and the Gremlin fuzzer were all blind to a real wrong answer, because reaching it needs a label
mutation after insertion and none of them generate one.

#### ⚠️ FIRST: ITEM 1535's NUMBERS WERE WRONG, AND HOW

`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs` imports `@lenke/gremlin`, which **resolves to `dist`, not `src`**
(`fuzzers-read-built-dists`, already a standing note). Nothing in the item-1535 tick built the dist
deliberately. What built it was `bun run fuzz`, which rebuilds the `@lenke/gremlin` dist as a side
effect — and I ran it **twice at the end of the tick, after the measurements**.

So the sequence was: create the module **seeding from `graph.verticesByLabel`** → fuzz (dist built
WITH seeding) → **measure** → discover seeding is incorrect and replace it with a per-vertex label
test → suites → fuzz again (dist rebuilt, now correct) → commit. The published numbers are the
**seeded** build's. The shipped code is slower.

Confirmed directly rather than inferred — re-applying seeding, rebuilding, and re-measuring
reproduces item 1535's figures almost exactly:

| arm                            | item 1535 published | seeded, re-measured | shipped (correct) |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------- |
| `hasLabel(Q).out(E)` bare      | 215.2               | 215 (206.1 / 223.6) | 439.0             |
| `hasLabel(Q).out(E).values(k)` | 378.8               | 417 (401.7 / 432.9) | 719.7             |

215.2 against 215 is not a coincidence. The correction is real, and item 1535's heading and table
are struck in this commit.

**What item 1535 still got right:** the module, the two correctness hazards it found (order and
`verticesByLabel` staleness), the attacking mutant, and the direction of every number. The engine
is faster than before on all four shapes. Only the magnitudes were overstated.

#### THE INSTRUMENT RULE THIS EARNS

CLAUDE.md already says to assert each A/B arm IS the code it claims. That rule was followed inside
the tick — the PRE reading was taken with the fallback disabled and grep-asserted — and it still
missed this, because **the assertion was made against `src` while the benchmark reads `dist`.**

So: **for any TS measurement, build the dist and assert the arm IN THE BUNDLE, not in the source.**
Both halves are load-bearing:

```bash
bun run build
python3 -I -c "import pathlib; t=pathlib.Path('packages/gremlin/dist/esm/index.mjs').read_text(); print(t.count('<a symbol unique to this arm>'))"
```

And two traps inside that check, both hit today:

- **The bundle is `index.mjs`, not `.js`.** A `rglob('*.js')` over `dist/` returns nothing and reads
  as "the module is not in the build" — which is exactly the wrong conclusion. It cost a detour here.
- **A window around the symbol can be too small.** Searching 4,000 characters after
  `startFilteredHopValues` said the `both` arm was absent; it is ~6,000 characters in. Count over the
  whole file, or widen until the count stops changing.

#### THE `both` ARM — 2.33x

`hop.kind === 'both'` is now admitted, with its own walk mirroring `hop-values.ts`'s `bothOneType`:
the out-bucket then the in-bucket, per surviving vertex, with **no self-loop filter**.

**A self-loop yields TWICE under Gremlin's `both`, which is the opposite of GQL's undirected hop**
(item 1431's edge pass emits it once). `a -E-> a` sits in both `adjFrom` and `adjTo`, so both passes
see it. That asymmetry is pinned by `both-self-loop.test.ts`, whose own header records that skipping
the in-pass copy **survived the whole 1,214-test suite** before that file existed — so this arm got
its own case rather than leaning on one that covers the unfiltered route.

#### COMPILED GATES — 1.85x on the `has` shape, and a hypothesis that was WRONG about the big one

The start filters are now compiled to closures once per plan: a single-label `hasLabel` becomes
`(v) => v.labels.has(L)` with no closure allocation, and a `has` goes through
`specializePredicate` (item 1492's lever, 1.92x there for the same reason) with `matches` as the
fallback.

**It was built to recover the seeding gap and it does not.** `hasLabel(Q).out(E).values(k)` moved
732 → 738 — nothing. It is kept because it is a real win on the predicate shape, where
`has(k, gt(48))` went 701.3 → 606.6, with every control flat.

#### THE SEEDING GAP, PRICED AND NOT AN ALGORITHMIC COST

Seeding is worth 1.22–2.06x and it cannot ship as written (item 1535's two hazards). Two cheap
cures were tested and both failed:

- **compiled gates** — no effect, above;
- **materializing `[...graph.vertices]` once per plan**, on the theory that array iteration beats the
  `verticesById.values()` wrapper: 757.7 / 766.1, slightly **worse**.

Then the profile said why both failed. Over the correct walk: `drain` 40.5%, `pick` 20.5%,
`get properties` 10.1%, `get adjFrom` 3.1% — and **`get labels` 1.0%, `survives` 0.8%.** The
per-vertex scan the seeding skips is **under 2% of the row cost**, so it cannot be worth 1.8x, and
`graph.vertices` is only `{[Symbol.iterator]: () => this.verticesById.values()}` — one object per
iteration, not per vertex.

`pick` appearing as its own 20.5% frame says it is **not inlined**. So the seeded/unseeded gap is an
**inlining decision that flipped with the loop's shape**, not work saved — the class
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` and `executor-edits-perturb` already describe, where a walk inline
in a returned closure gives unrelated shapes a new slow mode. Chasing it means settling inlining
attribution by deleting the use rather than reasoning about it, which is its own item.

### Item 1537 — **bounded item 1536's correction: items 1525–1533's numbers are CONFIRMED, six of six re-measured against a verified bundle.** Then refuted three cures for the residual 1.86x, and a scaling study shows why all three miss — the per-vertex scan is ~40 ns, not the ~330 ns the algebra implied

#### THE RESIDUAL GAP, and the algebra that was wrong about it

`hasLabel(Q).out(E).values(k)` costs 719.7 ns/row against the unfiltered `out(E).values(k)`'s 387.6.
Both do one far-vertex property read per row. The filtered walk visits 200,000 vertices for 100,000
rows and the unfiltered one 200,000 for 200,000, so the obvious decomposition is `2V + R = 719.7`
against `V + R = 387.6`, giving **V ≈ 332 ns per vertex visit** — which would make the scan the whole
story and seeding (which halves the visits) the obvious cure.

**That prediction is falsifiable and it is false.** Holding the vertex count at 200,000 and shrinking
the rows:

| VLABEL | rows    | wall     | ns/row |
| ------ | ------- | -------- | ------ |
| 2      | 100,000 | 73.46 ms | 734.6  |
| 5      | 40,000  | 31.21    | 780.1  |
| 10     | 20,000  | 18.35    | 917.3  |
| 20     | 10,000  | 9.35     | 934.6  |

At V ≈ 332 ns, VLABEL=10 would be ~3,375 ns/row; it is 917. And the same 200,000 visits that take
73 ms at VLABEL=2 take **9.35 ms** at VLABEL=20, so a visit plus its gate is **~40 ns**. Total time
tracks ROWS, not visits. The profile said this already — `get labels` 1.0%, `survives` 0.8% — and the
algebra talked me out of believing it, because it compared two queries that differ in more than the
vertex count.

#### THREE CURES, ALL REFUTED, recorded next to the code

| cure                                                          | result                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| compiled gates (item 1536)                                    | 732 → 738 — nothing on this shape             |
| materialize `[...graph.vertices]` once per plan               | 719.7 → 757.7 / 766.1 — **worse**             |
| a dedicated loop for the single-gate case, no `survives` call | 719.7 → 731, and `both` 458 → 507 — **worse** |

All three target the scan, which the study above shows is ~5% of the row cost. The third is the
sharpest refutation: it removes the only function call in the gate path and changes nothing, while
costing the `both` arm 10% — item 159's branch-in-a-hot-loop toll, arriving on schedule.

`pick` shows as its own 20.5% self-time frame, so the gap is an **inlining decision that differs
between the two walks' loop bodies** for identical per-row work. That is the class
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` names and that item 1466 declined a 3.3x win rather than disturb.
Settling it means attributing inlining by **deleting the use** rather than reasoning about it, on an
instrument that can see a single loop body — not this bench.

#### What this leaves open

The 1.86x is real and unexplained-but-bounded: not the gate, not the iteration source, not the
`survives` call. Seeding would close it and cannot ship (item 1535's two hazards). The next move is
an inlining-attribution probe, not another cure.

### Item 1538 — built the **by-id scaling probe**, the standing O(1) invariant that had NO instrument. The invariant HOLDS (100x the data for 4–6x the cost is the cache curve, not a lost O(1)). But it found a **~458 ns FIXED cost per Gremlin `run()`**, against a 21.9 ns map hit — and refuted the obvious cause before building it — ✅ **~320 ns of the 458 TAKEN at item 1539 (2.42x on `V(id)`); ~140 ns remains**

`getVertexById` / `getEdgeById` are O(1) by construction and **nothing in this repo measured them.**
An invariant nobody checks is one that can regress silently, and both ways it regresses are
invisible to a correctness test: a lookup that becomes a scan returns the right element in O(N), and
a lookup that stays O(1) but gains a constant taxes every query that resolves an id.

`packages/native/by-id-scaling-probe.mjs` closes that. It measures three surfaces — the core map,
Gremlin's `V(id)`, and the edge map — across four graph sizes, and prints ns/lookup **and the ratio
against the smallest size**, so the shape is the signal rather than any single number.

Two design points that are the difference between a measurement and a decoration:

- **The lookup keys are SHUFFLED**, deterministically. Looking ids up in insertion order walks the
  Map's own iteration order — the access pattern a _scan_ is also fast at — so a sequential probe
  cannot distinguish O(1) from a cache-friendly O(N). `KEYS=seq` turns it off and should be faster.
- **The LCG is integer arithmetic** (`Math.imul`), not the f64 form CLAUDE.md records collapsing to
  a ~11k period.

#### THE INVARIANT HOLDS, and the shape says why

| arm             | 10k     | 50k    | 200k      | 1M     | vs 10k    |
| --------------- | ------- | ------ | --------- | ------ | --------- |
| `getVertexById` | 11.2 ns | 16.5   | 17.7      | 47.3   | **4.23x** |
| `getEdgeById`   | 11.7    | 17.0   | 20.3–45.0 | 51.9   | **4.45x** |
| Gremlin `V(id)` | 1315.6  | 1226.7 | 1195.7    | 1137.7 | **0.86x** |

**100x the data for 4–6x the cost is not linear** — it is the cache-residency curve, and the jump
lands exactly where CLAUDE.md says to expect it ("the transition is between 200k and 1M elements").
A map lookup is O(1) in operations with a constant that grows as the table leaves L2/L3. So the
brief's requirement is met, and now it is _checked_ rather than asserted.

The absolute numbers carry ~2x run-to-run variance at some sizes (`getEdgeById` at 200k read 20.3
then 45.0 across two runs). The conclusion rests on the ratio column, not on any cell.

#### ⚠️ THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST NUMBER WAS WRONG, and it is the same class of bug twice in three ticks

The Gremlin arm's call count was computed in **two places** — inside the arm and again in the
reporting loop. Raising only the first reported **52,940 ns/lookup** against a true ~1,038: a 50x
error, in a brand-new instrument, in the direction that would have made this look like a catastrophe.
It is now one `GREMLIN_CALLS` constant. A divisor used twice is a wrong number waiting to happen —
and the tell was the absurdity of the value, which is not a tell I can rely on for a 2x error.

#### THE FINDING: a ~458 ns FIXED COST PER `run()`

`V(id)` is flat in N, so it is not an O(1) problem — it is a constant one, and the constant is large.
Decomposed at 200,000 vertices:

|                                                | ns/call   |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| `getVertexById` alone, incl. key construction  | 105.6     |
| plan construction (`traversal(V(id))`, no run) | 209.8     |
| **execution of a REUSED plan**                 | **498.6** |
| construction + execution per call              | 1231.3    |

Then the fixed/variable split, by widening the id list on one reused plan:

|              | ns/call | ns/row |
| ------------ | ------- | ------ |
| `V(1 id)`    | 504.8   | 504.8  |
| `V(2 ids)`   | 551.1   | 275.5  |
| `V(10 ids)`  | 923.2   | 92.3   |
| `V(100 ids)` | 5681.4  | 56.8   |

Per-row is **~46–52 ns** and the intercept is **~458 ns of fixed per-call cost**, independent of
result size. For a one-row query that _is_ the query. This is the serving workload `bun run
bench:usage` exists for, and it taxes every small Gremlin call, not just id lookups.

#### AND THE OBVIOUS CAUSE IS REFUTED, before building anything

The natural hypothesis is the per-run plan gauntlet: `effectivePlan` runs six rewrite passes and
then six shortcuts are consulted in turn, all of which **decline** for `V(id)` (every one guards on
`source.ids?.length ?? 0) > 0`). The Gremlin side has no plan-analysis cache — zero `WeakMap`, zero
`epoch` use in `executor/index.ts` — where GQL has a parse cache (items 228/229). So: cache the
analysis per plan object, keyed by graph epoch.

**Measured first, and it is not there:**

```text
   full run (reused plan)    506.2 ns/call
   effectivePlan only         11.5 ns/call     <- 2.3% of it
```

A plan cache would buy ~2%. The 458 ns is downstream of plan analysis — the shortcut gauntlet's own
calls, the traverser/stream construction, and `toArray` — and locating it is the next item's job.
Recording this because the hypothesis is compelling, cheap to state, and wrong: it would have been
a day's work for 2%.

#### Also screened: `nodeValuesShortcut`'s declines, and they are thin

Item 1482's no-hop shortcut (`matchShape` requires exactly 2 or 3 steps) takes only `hasLabel`, no
other filter kind, and has **no residual mechanism at all** — the gap item 881 closed for
`hopValuesShortcut`. Priced at `VLABEL=2`, 200,000 vertices:

| shape                                          |               |                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `V().values(n)` — admitted                     | 32.7 ns/row   |                                      |
| `V().hasLabel(Q).values(n)` — admitted         | 76.3          | the control                          |
| `V().has(k, gt(48)).values(n)` — declines      | 115.0         | 1.51x, but only 3.8 ms absolute      |
| `V().hasLabel(Q).values(n).count()` — declines | 5.09 ms total | **FASTER** than the admitted 7.63 ms |

So the 4-step decline is not a cost at all — the count tail avoids materializing 100,000 rows, which
is worth more than the shortcut. And the `has` decline is 1.51x on a shape already at 115 ns/row.
Not worth taking while a 458 ns per-call floor is open.

### Item 1539 — SHIPPED, **2.42x on `V(id)` and 2.77x on `E(id)`**: `applySource` evaluated `graph.vertices` on EVERY id lookup and discarded it. 508 → 210 ns/call, four controls flat. **48.4% of the profile, and answer-equivalent — which is why no test could have found it**

Item 1538 located a ~458 ns fixed cost per `run()` and refuted the plan-cache explanation
(`effectivePlan` is 11.5 ns of it). This finds where the money actually was.

#### The bug, in one argument

```ts
    case 'V':
      return sourceFromIds(
-       graph.vertices,          // <- evaluated per call, used only when `ids` is undefined
+       () => graph.vertices,
        step.ids,
        (id) => graph.getVertexById(asStringId(id)),
        tracksPath,
      );
```

`sourceFromIds` reads its first argument **only** in the `if (!ids)` branch. JavaScript evaluates
arguments eagerly, so every `V(id)` call ran the `graph.vertices` getter — which is
`{ [Symbol.iterator]: () => this.verticesById.values() }`, an object plus a closure — allocated,
handed in, and never touched. Same for `graph.edges` on `E(id)`.

**It was 48.4% of the profile of a one-row `V(id)` query**, the single largest frame, at 172 ms of a
356 ms window over 600,000 calls. Found by profiling a 1,000-vertex graph so the fixture could not
dominate (the cost is flat in N, so a small graph is the right instrument), then walking the call
tree to the parent: `get vertices <- applySource <- run <- toArray`.

#### ⚠️ NO CORRECTNESS TEST COULD HAVE CAUGHT THIS, and the mutation run proves it

Evaluating an argument and discarding it changes no answer. The whole suite passed before and after;
so did all seven fuzzers. This is `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` in its purest form, and the only
way to pin it is to make the access **observable** — `source-laziness.test.ts` replaces
`graph.vertices` with a counting own property shadowing the prototype getter, and asserts `V(id)`
reads it **zero** times.

Two things that test got wrong first, both recorded in it:

- **The positive control was vacuous twice.** "`V()` with no ids DOES read it" was written as
  `V().count()` and then `V().values(k)`, and both read it **zero** times — `countShortcut` and
  `nodeValuesShortcut` answer those without building a source at all. A spy that observes nothing
  makes every assertion beside it pass for free. It now uses a `has` filter, which item 1538
  measured as declining every shortcut.
- **My first two mutants were wrong, not the tests.** `eager-again-V` read `graph.vertices` _inside_
  the thunk, which only runs on the no-ids path — so it never restored eagerness and SURVIVED.
  Rewritten to hoist the read above the call (`const eager = graph.vertices;`), it is caught.

| `V(10 ids)` | 918.8 (917.8 / 918.8 / 937.7) | **596.9** (589.5 / 622.2 / 596.9) | **1.54x** |

`V(10 ids)` gains less in ratio and the same in absolute terms (~320 ns), which is the signature of a

### Item 1540 — **the auto-parameterization lift DEFEATS the parse cache for exactly the queries it exists to help: 3.75x on a small query, every call, forever.** Mechanism confirmed against the cache's own state, not inferred. Sized as a SERVING cost (2.3% once rows are produced). ~~PRICED, NOT BUILT~~ — ✅ **BUILT AT ITEM 1541, 3.98x** (one slot, not the LRU this entry sketched — that cost all-miss 17%)

Item 1539's win was an eagerly-evaluated argument on the Gremlin side. This tick screened GQL for a
per-call floor the same way, and the floor is healthy — `RETURN 1 AS v` is **110.5 ns/call** against
Gremlin's 210 — but one arm is 10x the others.

#### The measurement, on the durable probe (`gql-call-overhead-probe.mjs`)

| arm                                        | ns/call    |                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------- | -------------------------------- |
| `floor` — `RETURN 1 AS v`                  | 110.5      |                                  |
| `param` — `RETURN $x AS v`                 | 138.4      |                                  |
| `letparam` — `LET x = $p RETURN x`         | **270.1**  |                                  |
| `letlit` — `LET x = 5 RETURN x`            | **1013.2** | **3.75x its param twin**         |
| `letlit2` — `LET x = 1 LET y = 2 RETURN y` | 1348.5     | ~+340 per further lifted literal |

Two spellings that produce the **same plan** and the same answer differ by 3.75x — the
equivalent-spelling class CLAUDE.md says costs 100-300x elsewhere and always returns the right
answer. And it is backwards from the intuition: the _literal_ is slower than the _parameter_.

#### THE MECHANISM, confirmed against the cache rather than reasoned about

`query()`'s three steps (item 1502) are: ask the parse cache; on a miss, lift literals into
parameters and parse the LIFTED text; else parse the original. The lifted statement is cached under
the **lifted** text. So for a text with liftable literals:

- call 1: miss, lift, parse, cache under `LET x = $__ap0 RETURN x`;
- call 2: `parseCacheHit('LET x = 5 RETURN x')` — **misses again**, because that key was never
  stored. `normalizeLiterals` re-tokenizes. The comment above it prices a tokenize at ~865 ns, which
  is the gap measured (1013.2 − 270.1 = 743).

Confirmed by querying the lifted text directly after four calls of the literal form:

```text
   after literal LET x4                      cache size 1
   query('LET x = $__ap0 RETURN x', {__ap0:5})  -> [{"x":5}], size STILL 1
```

The size does not grow, so the key the cache holds is the lifted one — the original text can never
hit it.

**And `RETURN 1 AS v` escapes for the opposite reason.** Its literal position is not in
`normalizeLiterals`' allowlist, so no lift happens and the ORIGINAL text is what gets cached, which
then hits forever. The gap is exactly "did a lift happen" — which makes the queries
auto-parameterization was built for (the "sloppy caller" its own comment names) the only ones that
never hit the cache. The careful caller was never subsidising the sloppy one; the sloppy one was
paying a tokenize per call indefinitely.

#### SIZED HONESTLY: a serving cost, not a throughput one

|                                                      | literal   | param   |                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------- | ---------------- |
| `LET x = … RETURN x` (1 row)                         | 1013.2 ns | 270.1   | **3.75x**        |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = … RETURN n.k` (~2,062 rows) | 3.95 ms   | 3.83 ms | **2.3% — noise** |

Once a query produces rows, ~865 ns is nothing. This taxes the small-query workload `bun run
bench:usage` exists for — point lookups, authz checks, single-row reads — where it is 4x.

#### NOT BUILT, and the design has one real trade-off to get right

The fix is to make the lift path cacheable: a second, LRU-capped memo from the original text to
`{ liftedText, params }`, consulted before `normalizeLiterals`, so a repeated identical text skips
the tokenize and goes straight to the lifted plan.

It is **sound**: `normalizeLiterals(text)` is a pure function of the text, so for an identical text
the lifted text and the lifted params are deterministic. It must be keyed by `(text, chain)` like
the existing cache, since `maxOperatorChain` is part of the parse key.

The trade-off is the one auto-parameterization exists to avoid: **one memo entry per distinct
literal value**, which is the cache pollution the lifted key was chosen to prevent. Two things make
it tolerable rather than self-defeating, and both need checking against a measurement rather than
asserted here: the memo holds two strings and a small object rather than a statement, and a churning
interpolated caller degrades to _today's_ cost (a tokenize per call) rather than anything worse,
because the plan still comes from the lifted-key cache. Whether that memo wants its own cap, or a
share of the existing one, is the question to answer with numbers.

Not started at the end of a tick, for the same reason as items 1528 and 1530 — both of which the
next tick then shipped.

#### Instrument notes, so the next tick does not re-derive them

- **The first arm is unreliable at low N.** At `N=2000` the `RETURN 1` arm read **1785 ns** against
  its true ~100; the JIT has not settled and the first arm absorbs it. Measured at `N=20000` it is
  stable at 100.4 / 102.3 across runs.
- **A row-producing arm needs its own call count.** Giving the two `MATCH` arms the same 2,000 calls
  as the scalar arms meant 4M rows per rep and the probe had to be killed. They run at 60.
- **The probe's own "produced no rows" guard earned its place**: my first `WHERE` arm referenced
  `n.n`, which this fixture does not set, and the guard failed the run instead of reporting a fast
  empty arm.

### Item 1541 — SHIPPED, **3.98x**: a ONE-SLOT lift memo, so auto-parameterization stops defeating the parse cache. `LET x = 5 RETURN x` 994 → 250 ns/call, and the literal spelling now COSTS THE SAME as its `$param` twin. The LRU I built first cost the all-miss workload 17% and was thrown away — ⚠️ **and ONE SLOT was itself superseded at item 1542**: it gets nothing at TWO hot literal queries, so the memo is now a ring of four

Item 1540 priced this and named the open question: what cap does the memo want? The answer turned out
to be **one slot and no cap**, and the two rejected designs are the useful part of the entry.

#### What shipped

```ts
+ let liftSlotText: string | undefined;
+ let liftSlotValue: Normalized | undefined;

-  const lifted = normalizeLiterals(text);
+  const memoed = liftSlotText === text ? liftSlotValue : undefined;
+  const lifted = memoed ?? normalizeLiterals(text);
```

The lifted statement is cached under the LIFTED text, so `parseCacheHit(originalText)` missed on
every repeat call and `normalizeLiterals` re-tokenized forever. The slot removes that, and it is
sound because `normalizeLiterals` is a pure function of the text: for an identical text the lifted
text and values are identical. No `chain` is stored — the lift does not consult it, and the
statement still comes from `parseCached(lifted.text, chain)`, which verifies the chain itself.

#### TWO DESIGNS REJECTED WITH NUMBERS, both on the workload item 1502 cares about

The obvious implementation is a `Map` keyed by the original text, capped like the parse cache. It
holds **one entry per distinct literal value** — the pollution the lifted key exists to avoid — and
it cost the ALL-MISS workload (a value interpolated into the text, so every call has a fresh text
and nothing can ever hit) **17%**:

| design                               | `letlit` | `allmiss` (the risk) |
| ------------------------------------ | -------- | -------------------- |
| PRE                                  | 994 ns   | 1367 ns              |
| LRU `Map`, admit on first sighting   | 253      | **1598 — 17% worse** |
| LRU `Map` + admit on SECOND sighting | 250      | **1500 — 10% worse** |
| **ONE SLOT (shipped)**               | **250**  | **1400 — flat**      |

Adding the parse cache's own admission filter recovered only half the regression, because the
all-miss caller still pays a `get`, a `has`, an eviction and an `add` — and still RETAINS 64 fresh
strings, which is item 1502's retention argument verbatim (that item rejected 16% on this same
workload for the same reason).

One slot has no bookkeeping to pay: a miss is two field writes, it retains one string, and it evicts
by overwriting. The caller it serves is the one that matters — a hot query in a loop — and a caller
alternating between several literal texts degrades to _today's_ cost, never below it.

#### MEASURED — median of 3+ runs per arm, arm read from the BUNDLE every run

| arm                                               | PRE                    | POST                            |                                |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `LET x = 5 RETURN x`                              | 994 (1013.0 / 975.4)   | **250** (240.4 / 268.1 / 249.5) | **3.98x**                      |
| `LET x = 1 LET y = 2 RETURN y`                    | 1350 (1381.8 / 1318.9) | **333** (333.1 / 370.7 / 314.6) | **4.05x**                      |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 5 RETURN n.k` (~2k rows) | 34.9 µs                | 33.8                            | 1.03x — as item 1540 predicted |

| control                             | PRE               | POST              |          |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | -------- |
| `LET x = $p RETURN x`               | 234               | 248               | flat     |
| `RETURN 1 AS v`                     | 128               | 134               | flat     |
| **`allmiss` — fresh text per call** | 1367 (6 readings) | 1400 (6 readings) | **flat** |

**The headline is the convergence.** On the durable probe the two spellings now read `letlit` 275.5
against `letparam` 275.1 — identical, which is what two spellings of one plan should cost.

#### ⚠️ THE ROUTE NEEDED ITS OWN OBSERVABILITY, and mutation is what proved it

A memo is answer-equivalent, so the first mutation run had **five survivors of six**. Three were
real gaps and two were my own bad mutants; only one mutant (`no-text-compare`) was caught, and that
one by 2,786 tests.

So `parseCacheStats()` now also reports `liftHits` and `liftStores` — the same move item 1509 made
with `seen`, whose eviction was otherwise untestable. With those, three of the five are caught:

| mutant                                      | first run         | after the counters   |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | -------------------- |
| `no-text-compare` (serve the slot blind)    | CAUGHT, 2786 fail | CAUGHT               |
| `compare-lifted` (compare the wrong string) | SURVIVES          | **CAUGHT**           |
| `never-store`                               | SURVIVES          | **CAUGHT**           |
| `store-before-parse`                        | SURVIVES          | SURVIVES — see below |
| `no-spread`                                 | SURVIVES          | SURVIVES — see below |
| `params-order`                              | SURVIVES          | SURVIVES — see below |

`no-text-compare` is the one that is a wrong ANSWER rather than a slow one: both `LET x = 5` and
`LET x = 6` lift to `LET x = $__ap0 RETURN x`, so neither the lifted text nor the parse cache can
tell them apart and the slot would serve 5 twice. The original-text compare is the only thing
standing between those two queries.

#### The three remaining survivors, each with its reason — none is a missing test I could write

- **`store-before-parse`** — and **I checked this rather than assuming coverage.** The test I wrote
  for it is VACUOUS: the counters say `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = RETURN n.k` never attempts a lift at
  all (`liftStores` delta 0, `liftHits` delta 0), because `MAYBE_LIFTABLE` rejects it. Covering it
  needs a text whose literals the allowlist ADMITS but whose rewritten form fails to parse; `query`'s
  own comment says that is possible-but-rare by construction, and I could not build one. The guard
  stays as defence and the test now says exactly what it does and does not cover.
- **`no-spread`** — surviving is the _answer_ to a question I deliberately bought out rather than
  investigated. `withClock` returns its `params` argument unchanged when the graph has no clock, so a
  memoised object would reach `execute` by reference on every later call; I spread it for ~25 ns
  against the ~740 saved. The mutant surviving shows nothing currently mutates it, so the spread is
  insurance, not a fix — worth saying plainly rather than claiming it closed a live bug.
- **`params-order`** — unfalsifiable by design, and the code already says why: the synthetic
  namespace is `__ap<n>`, so user and lifted names cannot collide. The order exists so a future
  namespace change cannot silently shadow a caller's binding.

serialization 144/0.

`bun run fuzz` read **19/1 once**, then **20/0 five times**. Ruled out structurally rather than by
counting, per `gremlin-fuzz-families`: the slot is keyed on `liftSlotText === text` (exact string
identity) and returns what `normalizeLiterals(text)` would, so it cannot serve another text's lift;
the fuzzer sends mostly distinct texts, so a single slot is almost never consulted there at all; and
the same 19/1-then-clean pattern appeared in item 1535's tick, before this change existed.
