after.

### Item 1542 — the lift memo is now a RING OF FOUR, because one slot lost everything at TWO hot queries (`rot2` 1030 ns against `rot1`'s 250). Calibrated against the all-miss cost. **AND: the intermittent `bun run fuzz` failure I dismissed TWICE as the known gremlin residual is a REAL cross-engine wrong answer — caught, replayed by seed, and minimized**

Two results. The second one matters more, and it is a correction of my own record.

#### THE RING — item 1541's slot was right about all-miss and wrong about serving

Item 1541's entry claimed a caller alternating between several literal texts "degrades to today's
cost". True, and far more damaging than that phrasing suggests: a server with **two** hot literal
queries gets nothing at all. Measured by rotating N distinct liftable texts round-robin:

| design                  | `letlit` | `rot2`  | `rot3`  | `rot4`  | `rot8` | `allmiss` | vs PRE all-miss |
| ----------------------- | -------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------ | --------- | --------------- |
| PRE (no memo)           | 994      | ~1000   | ~1000   | ~1000   | ~1000  | 1367      | —               |
| 1 slot (item 1541)      | 250      | 1030    | 1080    | 1015    | ~1030  | 1390      | +1.7%           |
| ring of 2               | 258      | **262** | 1027    | 1016    | ~1030  | 1396      | +2.1%           |
| **ring of 4 (shipped)** | **245**  | **249** | **226** | **225** | ~1030  | 1437      | **+5.1%**       |

The all-miss cost is K failed string compares per call, so it rises with K. **Accepting ~5% there is
a different judgement from item 1541's rejection of the LRU at 10-17%, and the difference is what
the cost buys**: the LRU's 10% bought nothing a single slot did not already have, while this 5% buys
rot3/rot4 at 4.2x. The 5% also overlaps the measurement spread (PRE ranges 1304-1551 over six
readings), where the LRU's regression did not. `LIFT_SLOTS = 2` is the cheaper point and the table
is in the code so the knob can be re-tuned with numbers rather than argument.

Mutation: 3 of 5 caught. `scan-first-only` and `cursor-never-advances` by the new ring tests,
`wrong-slot-value` by 100 existing tests. `no-break` survives and _should_ — a text can only be
stored on a miss, so it can never occupy two slots, which makes the `break` a perf detail rather
than a correctness one. `text-not-stored` was a no-op mutant of mine (`String(s)` on a string is
identity).

The ring's own tests had a bug worth recording: the first eviction test asserted that the FIFTH
text evicts the first, and it failed — because the ring is module state shared by every test in the
file, so the write cursor is wherever earlier cases left it. Writing a full ring's worth of new
texts is cursor-independent and is what the test does now.

#### ⚠️ THE FUZZER FAILURE WAS REAL, AND I WAS WRONG ABOUT IT TWICE

`bun run fuzz` has read 19/1 three times in recent ticks. Both times I attributed it to
`gremlin-fuzz-families`' documented "rare 1-in-30 residual whose SEED REPLAYS CLEAN" and moved on,
once with an explicit structural argument. **That was wrong on every count:** it is the
**differential** fuzzer (TS GQL vs Rust), not the Gremlin one, and its seed **replays
deterministically**.

What found it was giving up on inference and instrumenting the hunt:

- all seven fuzzers individually — **54 runs, 0 failures**;
- 12 full sweeps with `--no-build` — **0 failures**;
- 8 full sweeps WITH the build — **1 failure**, captured to a log.

```text
FUZZ_SEED=2949348313 bun test src/differential-fuzz.test.ts    # replays every time

MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE
  (([1e400, local_time('08:30:00')]['a'] <= n.s) AND ((n.s || 0.0) IS NOT NULL)))
RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y

  ts:     ok  [{"x":3,"y":null},{"x":7,"y":null}]
  native: err E_INVALID_VALUE: || requires all operands to be strings or all lists
```

The fuzzer's own note said "an evaluation-order difference, but no registry entry covers this shape",
which is exactly right and is the sentence I should have read the first time.

#### MINIMIZED, and the obvious suspect was a red herring

`divergence-1542-min.test.ts` strips it down. The list-indexed-by-a-string (`[…]['a']`) looks like
the culprit and is **not** — every reduction containing it agrees, and `RETURN [1, 2]['a']` is
`null` in both engines. The native error names the real ingredient: `n.s || 0.0`, a string
concatenated with a NUMBER, which native rejects and TS does too **when it evaluates it**.

| case                                                                               | ts             | native  |              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------- | ------------ |
| `RETURN ('a' \|\| 0.0)`                                                            | err            | err     | agree        |
| `RETURN ((null <= 'z') AND (('a' \|\| 0.0) IS NOT NULL))`                          | err            | err     | agree        |
| `RETURN ((1 = 2) AND (…))`                                                         | `false`        | `false` | agree        |
| `OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE ((n.s \|\| 0.0) IS NOT NULL))`                  | err            | err     | agree        |
| `MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE ((n.s \|\| 0.0) IS NOT NULL))`                           | err            | err     | agree        |
| **the original** — UNKNOWN conjunct, THEN the fault, in a pattern's inline `WHERE` | **ok, 2 rows** | **err** | **DIVERGES** |

**So the rule is narrow and now stated:** inside a PATTERN's inline `WHERE`, an `AND` whose left
operand is UNKNOWN causes TS to skip the right operand — so a faulting right operand never raises —
while native evaluates it and raises. In a scalar expression both engines evaluate it and both
raise. Items 258/259 settled that `AND` short-circuits on **FALSE** in both engines in written
order; this is **UNKNOWN**, and a pattern predicate rather than a value position, which is why that
closure did not cover it.

Found incidentally: native rejects a clause `WHERE` inside `OPTIONAL MATCH` outright ("WHERE inside
OPTIONAL MATCH is not supported") where TS evaluates it — a second, separate gap.

**Deliberately NOT added to `divergence-registry.ts`.** Registering it would stop the fuzzer flagging
it, which is the opposite of what a real wrong answer needs. The fuzzer should keep failing ~1 run in
8 until this is fixed. The new test asserts that every _reduction_ agrees (a real regression guard)
and only PRINTS the original.

#### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. core 431/0, gql **3863**/0, gremlin 1494/0, native **963**/0,
serialization 144/0. `bun run fuzz` is expected to fail intermittently until the divergence above is
fixed — that is now a known, seeded, minimized bug rather than an unexplained flake.

### Item 1543 — diagnosed item 1542's divergence to the exact mechanism, and it is **NOT a bug to fix but a DESIGN COLLISION**: TS's filter position deliberately settles on "not cleanly TRUE", which skips a sibling's throw, and that short-circuit is what the 1.94–2.62x conjunct lift rests on. Three candidate resolutions, each with a measured cost. **NEEDS A DECISION, NOT A PATCH**

Item 1542 left this as "fix it next tick". It is not patchable without choosing between two things the
repo has written commitments to.

#### THE MECHANISM, nailed down

Three more reductions moved the diagnosis past item 1542's:

| case                                                | ts         | native |                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `[1, 2]['a'] <= n.s` AND the fault (plain literals) | ok, 2 rows | err    | **DIVERGES** — so `1e400`/`local_time` were irrelevant |
| the fault written FIRST, then `[1, 2]['a'] <= n.s`  | ok, 2 rows | err    | **DIVERGES** — so WRITTEN ORDER is not the explanation |
| the same chain under a REQUIRED `MATCH`             | ok, `[]`   | err    | **DIVERGES** — so `OPTIONAL` is not the factor         |
| `(null <= 'z')` AND the fault — nothing to lift     | err        | err    | **agrees**                                             |

The last two rows together are the finding. A conjunct comparing an **element property** is lifted
into `cmpProps`; `satisfies` evaluates those lifts **before** `pred.where`, whatever order they were
written in; and a lift that yields UNKNOWN `return false`s, so the residual faulting conjunct is
never reached. Replace the liftable conjunct with one that has no element property and the lift
cannot happen — and the engines agree.

#### AND IT IS DELIBERATE, which is why this is a decision

`compilePredicate` says so in its own words:

> FILTER position: `matchesPredicate` reads this as `asTruth(...) === true`, below a `props` and an
> `eqProps` loop that both `return false` outright. **So a conjunct that is not cleanly TRUE settles
> the element and its siblings need not be evaluated.**

That is the measured behaviour, by design, and it is load-bearing. The same file prices the lift it
enables, over 200,000 vertices:

```text
   a=50 alone, lifts                 4.160 ms
   a=50 AND <unliftable>             8.072        1.94x
   a=50 AND b=0 AND <unliftable>    10.686        2.62x
```

Meanwhile `and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts` pins the SHARED contract as "`AND` short-circuits
on FALSE in both engines… the distinction that matters here — **FALSE settles, UNKNOWN does not**",
and asserts `RETURN (null AND (1.0 / 0.0))` raises in both. Scalar position honours that; the filter
position does not. **Both statements are in the repo and they disagree about UNKNOWN.**

ISO almost certainly permits either: the needed result in a filter is "is it TRUE", and once that is
settled an implementation need not evaluate the rest. So this is not a conformance question — it is a
byte-identity policy choice, which makes it the owner's call rather than mine.

#### WHY THERE IS NO CHEAP FIX

The principled repair is "let the lift short-circuit only when the residual cannot raise", which
needs a totality analysis. There is none: no `canRaise`/`mayRaise`/`isTotal` anywhere in
`packages/gql/src`, and the one adjacent thing — the static boolean-context check — is recorded in
`boolean-context-static-check` as **"CLAUSE-level only. READ IT before extending to inline pattern
predicates: tried twice, worse."** So that route is already closed twice over.

#### THE THREE RESOLUTIONS, with what each costs

1. **TS stops settling on UNKNOWN in the filter position.** Matches native and the shared contract.
   Cost: without a totality analysis the residual `where` must be evaluated whenever one exists, so
   the lift's early exit is lost on exactly the chains the 1.94–2.62x was measured on.
2. **Native settles on not-TRUE in the filter position.** Matches TS, and is plausibly a native perf
   WIN. Cost: a Rust change, and it removes errors some queries raise today.
3. **Declare it.** Ruled out by the conformance file itself: "an error against a NON-EMPTY result is
   something `divergence-registry.ts` explicitly may not excuse" — and TS returns two rows here.

#### Also worth knowing: this makes the NATIVE SUITE intermittently red, not just `bun run fuzz`

`differential-fuzz.test.ts` lives in `packages/native`, so `cd packages/native && bun test` runs it
with random seeds. It read **962/1 once and 963/0 three times** this tick. So the blast radius of
leaving this open is wider than item 1542 said: it is not only the fuzz sweep.

#### What shipped

Only the minimization, extended: `divergence-1542-min.test.ts` now carries a `KNOWN_DIVERGENT` set
of the four shapes and **asserts that every other reduction agrees** — a real regression guard that
will fail if the family widens — plus the characterization test that the scalar `AND` cases agree.
Nothing was registered, so the fuzzer keeps flagging it.

#### ✅ DECIDED BY THE OWNER (2026-11-05), and it is none of the three above

> "It should be whatever is faster. The left or right side of the conjunction should have the easiest
> and fastest evaluate. I think ts only goes left to right. Native can pick either based on a cost."

So the policy is **evaluation order is chosen for SPEED**, per engine, and an error raised by one
engine where the other short-circuits past it is an accepted consequence rather than a bug to fix by
slowing either side down. That rules out resolutions 1 and 2 — both buy error parity with
performance — and it reframes the whole item from a correctness question into a perf one.

**It also authorizes a 3.2x this file has been declining.** `compilePredicate`'s own note says:

> ⚠️ THE REVERSE ORDER IS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE. `<unliftable> AND a=50` measured 13.750 and a lift
> would take it to ~4.3 (3.2x), but only by running `a = 50` FIRST — which is observable when the
> unliftable conjunct can RAISE, because short-circuiting on FALSE would then skip a throw that
> happens today.

That observability is now explicitly acceptable, so the reverse-order lift is the next item's target:
~~**13.750 → ~4.3 ms, 3.2x, on a shape the engine currently declines in full.**~~ — ✅ **TAKEN AT ITEM 1544 at 2.51x** (13.952 → 5.568; the ~4.3 estimate was against a baseline items 1283/1287 have since moved, which is why the PRE was re-measured). Four tests pinned the old boundary and were updated, each keeping its "still in the residual" half.

Two consequences to handle rather than assume:

- **The differential fuzzer will keep flagging the AND/UNKNOWN family**, and
  `and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts`'s "FALSE settles, UNKNOWN does not" line is now a
  statement about one engine rather than a shared contract. Reconciling the registry with this policy
  is its own decision — the conformance file currently says an error against a NON-EMPTY result "may
  not be excused", and that rule predates this one.
- **Order-chosen-for-speed and byte-identity are in tension by construction.** Whatever excuses this
  family has to be narrow enough that a genuine wrong ANSWER still fails.

#### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. gql 3863/0, native 963/0 (three runs; one 962/1, which is this very
divergence). No engine change.

### Item 1544 — SHIPPED, **2.51x**: the conjunct lift is no longer a PREFIX, so a liftable conjunct lifts from any position. `<unliftable> AND n.a = 50` 13.952 → 5.568 ms, and the two spellings of that question now cost the SAME. Five controls flat, and the vanish mutant item 1284 found is caught by 20 tests

The owner's decision at item 1543 — evaluation order is chosen for SPEED per engine — authorized the
one thing `executor.ts` had been declining on purpose. This takes it.

#### The change

`directEqProps` scanned the flattened `AND` chain and `break`ed at the first conjunct it could not
read; `stop` was that index and everything from there on became the residual. So a liftable conjunct
after an unreadable one did not lift, and its siblings' lifts were forfeited with it.

```ts
-  let stop = conjuncts.length;
-      stop = i;
-      break;                     // ×5 sites
-  const residual = residualOf(conjuncts.slice(stop), …);
+  const skipped: Expr[] = [];
+      skipped.push(conjunct);
+      continue;                  // ×5 sites
+  const residual = residualOf(skipped, …);
```

**The other guard is untouched and still does its job.** `residualOf` declines the whole lift when a
raise-capable family (`truth`, `notTruth`, `cmp`, `path`) would lift ahead of a residual, so this
widens only `eq`, `nulls` and `member` — the families the file itself notes "cannot raise: equality
is total, `isNullish` returns a plain boolean, and membership is built on equality".

#### MEASURED — p25 of 12 reps, 200,000 vertices, PRE re-measured rather than taken from the comment

The note in the source priced this at "13.750 → ~4.3 (3.2x)". **Re-measuring first was the right
call**: the target reproduces at 13.952, but the baseline it would land on has moved (items
1283/1287 sped up the lifted arms), so the honest figure is **2.51x**, not 3.2x.

| arm                                     | PRE       | POST                      |           |
| --------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------- | --------- |
| `<unliftable> AND n.a = 50`             | 13.952 ms | **5.568** (5.544 / 5.593) | **2.51x** |
| `<unliftable> AND n.a = 50 AND n.b = 0` | 13.985    | **5.586** (5.553 / 5.619) | **2.50x** |

**The headline is the convergence.** `<unliftable> AND n.a = 50` now costs 5.568 against
`n.a = 50 AND <unliftable>`'s 5.594 — the same question, two spellings, the same price. That is the
equivalent-spelling property CLAUDE.md names, restored on a pair that was 2.5x apart and answering
identically the whole time. Before the change the reverse spelling was even slower than the
unliftable conjunct ALONE (13.952 against 8.595), the "more selective query is slower" signature.

| control                     | PRE   | POST (median of 5) |                                           |
| --------------------------- | ----- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `n.a = 50` alone            | 2.427 | 2.465              | flat                                      |
| `n.a = 50 AND n.b = 0`      | 4.702 | 4.813              | flat (+2.4%, inside the 4.60-4.92 spread) |
| `n.a = 50 AND <unliftable>` | 5.741 | 5.594              | flat                                      |
| `<unliftable>` alone        | 8.595 | 8.227              | flat, slightly better                     |
| no `AND` at all             | 3.669 | 3.544              | flat                                      |

#### ⚠️ FOUR TESTS PINNED THE OLD BOUNDARY, and one of them said so in its own words

> THE BOUNDARY: a decliner FIRST lifts nothing at all. **This is the assertion that fails if the
> prefix rule is ever widened to pick liftable conjuncts out of the middle of a chain.**

It was widened, so it failed, exactly as designed. All four were updated to the new rule — and each
kept the half that still has teeth: **the unreadable conjunct is STILL IN THE RESIDUAL.**

That distinction is the whole item. Item 1284's mutation run replaced these same five
`stop = i; break;` sites with a bare `continue;` and found the conjunct **VANISHES** — neither
lifted nor residual — so the predicate answers a SUPERSET, and **all 3217 tests passed**. The
difference between that bug and this change is one line: `skipped.push(conjunct)`.

One of the four stays a full decline for an unrelated reason worth keeping straight: `NOT (m.k = 1)
AND n.k = 1` declines everything because `residualOf` rejects a residual with a free variable other
than `ownVar`, not because of the prefix rule.

#### MUTATION — the vanish mutant is now caught by 20 tests

| mutant                                                          |            |                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `vanish-all-sites` (drop `skipped.push` at all five)            | **CAUGHT** | 3843 pass **20** fail                  |
| `vanish-one-site` (drop it at one nested site)                  | CAUGHT     | 3862 pass 1 fail                       |
| `residual-empty` (back to lifting everything, residual dropped) | CAUGHT     | 3843 pass 20 fail                      |
| `residual-reversed`                                             | SURVIVES   | consistent with the policy — see below |

So the suite now has 20 assertions standing where item 1284's had none. The two that catch it are
the `GQL fuzz: Kleene boolean-algebra laws` and `feature cross-consistency` properties, which is
pleasing: a generative property test caught the superset, not a hand-written case.

`residual-reversed` surviving is **not** a gap. Within the residual the conjuncts are `and`-combined
and the generic evaluator settles on FALSE in written order, so reversing them changes only which
raise happens first — and item 1543's policy makes that free. Pinning it with a test would encode a
constraint the owner has explicitly lifted.

#### Did this widen the known AND/UNKNOWN divergence? NO

Lifting more could in principle make TS short-circuit past more faults. Checked rather than assumed:
`divergence-1542-min.test.ts`'s `KNOWN_DIVERGENT` set is unchanged — every other reduction still
agrees — and `bun run fuzz` read **20/0 three times**.

### Item 1545 — SHIPPED, **1.46x and 2.52x**: ordering comparisons now lift beside a residual, so `cmp` costs what `eq` costs for the same selectivity. ⚠️ **AND THE GUARD'S STATED REASON TURNED OUT TO BE FALSE** — "an ordering comparison throws on a cross-type pair" is not true of this engine, so the trade I warned the owner about does not exist. `truth`/`notTruth` stay held back, and that half IS real

Item 1544 removed the prefix rule. This removes half of the second guard, and the interesting part is
that it cost nothing it was supposed to cost.

#### The change

```ts
-}): boolean =>
-  lists.truth.length > 0 ||
-  lists.notTruth.length > 0 ||
-  lists.cmp.length > 0 ||
-  lists.path.length > 0;
+}): boolean => lists.truth.length > 0 || lists.notTruth.length > 0;
```

`residualOf` declines the whole lift when a raise-capable family would lift ahead of a residual.
`cmp`/`path` are no longer counted as raise-capable; `truth`/`notTruth` still are.

#### ⚠️ I TOLD THE OWNER THIS WOULD CREATE ERRORS. IT DOES NOT, AND THAT IS THE FINDING

The guard's own comment justified holding `cmp`/`path` back because "an ordering comparison throws
on a cross-type pair (an `=` does not — it answers no-match)". I repeated that to the owner when
asking for the decision, framing it as a 1.55-2.66x win paid for with new `E_INVALID_VALUE` errors on
queries that work today. They took the trade.

**Then I tried to write the test that pins the new error, and could not produce one.** Seven operand
pairs, every one answering no-match rather than faulting:

```text
   n.s < 5                     ok   (string vs number)
   n.s <= DATE '2024-01-01'    ok   (string vs temporal)
   n.L < 5                     ok   (list vs number)
   n.L < [1,3]                 ok   (list vs list)
   n.m < 5                     ok   (record vs number)
   n.b < 5                     ok   (boolean vs number)
   n.s > n.m                   ok   (string vs record)
   RETURN 'x' < DATE '…'       null (not a throw, in scalar position either)
```

So in the TS engine an ordering comparison is TOTAL on the pairs reachable here, and the premise the
guard rested on for `cmp`/`path` does not hold. The relaxation is a pure win — no behaviour change
to trade away. The owner's authorization was sought in good faith against a cost that, measured,
is not there; recording that plainly because the next person to read the guard's comment will
believe it, as I did.

**The `truth` half is real, and the two queries that prove it are now a test:**

```text
   WHERE n.s                                   RAISES   — coercing 'x' to a boolean
   WHERE upper(n.s) = 'ZZZ' AND n.s            ok []    — truth held back, residual settles FALSE
```

Relax the guard for `truth` and the second line throws. That is also the exact TS-vs-native

### Item 1546 — a PROFILE-FIRST tick that shipped nothing and is worth having: a **false nomination** caught by checking the caller, the GQL generic-residual path **declined at its floor** with the arithmetic, and `degreeOfTypes`' 25.8% frame **refuted** by a 3-line change that measured null

Items 1544 and 1545 exhausted the conjunct-lift family. This tick went back to profiling for a fresh
target and found three things, none of them a win.

#### 1. A FALSE NOMINATION — `getVertexById` at 8.6%, in a query that never looks up by id

Profiling `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.a >= n.a RETURN count(*)` over 200,000 vertices put `getVertexById`
third by self time. A label scan has no business resolving ids, so that read as a real defect — an
O(1) lookup per row that should not exist.

The call tree says otherwise:

```text
   getVertexById:3075 <- addVertex:2820 <- (anon):1 <- (root):-1
```

It is the FIXTURE BUILD. Together with `#commitNormalized`, `commitElementLabels`,
`indexVertexLabel` and `validateElementNames` the build is ~15% of that profile, and a self-time
ranking cannot tell build from query. **Resolve a nomination to its caller before believing it** —
the same discipline item 1536 needed when a frame's share was an inlining artifact.

#### 2. THE GQL GENERIC RESIDUAL PATH IS AT ITS FLOOR, declined with arithmetic rather than a shrug

With the build frames set aside, the query's own profile has no fat frame: the per-row driver
(`fastPath`'s closure) 11.8%, `inlineHolds` 9.9%, `variable.variable` 7.3%, `propOf` 4.9%,
`get properties` 3.6%, `satisfies` 1.7%, `compareTruth` 1.6%.

`variable.variable` is the compiled `prop` closure, and it is exactly what it looks like:

```js
   case "prop": { const { variable, key } = expr;
     return (env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable), key); }
```

So `n.a >= n.a` does **two `Map.get` per row**, 16M over the measured run. The fix is to let an
element-local residual read the element directly — what `eqProps`/`cmpProps` already do for lifted
conjuncts — by threading `ownVar` into `compileExpr`.

**Priced and declined.** 46.3 ms over 16M lookups is **~2.9 ns each**, so the whole lever is ~6 ns of
a ~41 ns row. `compileExpr` is called everywhere and `EvalEnv` is shared, so threading a parameter
through is exactly the kind of edit `executor-edits-perturb` prices at **up to 16% on unrelated
rows**. A 14% win on one shape against a 16% risk on many is not a trade worth making.

Two things that are NOT the cost, checked rather than assumed: the binding `Map` and the env object
are allocated **once per query**, outside the row loop — so the 9.6% GC is not env churn — and
`specializeSingleProp` already exists for the shapes it can answer (it refuses here, correctly,
because `where` is populated).

#### 3. REFUTED: a single-type fast path in `degreeOfTypes`

`hopcount3` — the largest row in `bench:gremlin` — has the fat profile this tick was looking for:
**86.9% in four functions.** `walkBucket` 26.8%, `degreeOfTypes` 25.8%, `slotChainCount` 17.9%,
`expandSlot` 16.4%.

`degreeOfTypes` loops `for (const t of types)` and `out(T)` names exactly one type, so skipping the
loop looked free — and item 1374 set the precedent on this very path (the single-label case skips
`bucketsOf`'s array). Three lines:

```ts
if (types.length === 1) {
  return byType.get(types[0])?.size ?? 0;
}
```

**Null.** p25 of 10 reps at 200,000 vertices, arm asserted in the bundle both ways:

|      | readings                    | median |
| ---- | --------------------------- | ------ |
| PRE  | 214.59 / 217.90 / 221.13 ms | 217.90 |
| POST | 212.64 / 222.60             | ~217.6 |

So that 25.8% is the `Map.get` plus `.size` themselves — V8 already handles `for...of` over a
one-element array — not the loop around them. Reverted, with the numbers recorded next to the code.

**And the remaining lever there is one already disqualified.** All four hot functions are per-vertex
or per-edge `Map` work; removing it means caching degree per vertex per type, which is index-shaped,
and `no-dense-vertex-ordinal` records that family as BUILT AND DISQUALIFIED (deletes 6.18x/11.34x
under churn, items 1369-1372/1397). Seven items have arrived at that door.

#### What this tick is for

Three negative results, each with the number that makes it negative, so none of them costs a future
tick. The honest summary of the current state: **the two shapes I profiled are at their floor for
this engine's object model**, and the next real win is more likely to come from a shape that still
DECLINES a fast path than from making an existing hot loop faster — which is what items 1529-1545
kept finding.

### Item 1547 — SHIPPED, **908x**: a VACUOUS `hasLabel` with several labels was never recognized as vacuous, so it stayed in the plan and the plan left the closed-form route. `V().hasLabel(P,Q).out(E).count()` 9.075 → 0.010 ms, two controls flat. ⚠️ **The mutation run was KILLED by memory pressure mid-sweep and left a mutant in the tree — recorded because it is the hazard CLAUDE.md names, observed for real** — ✅ **the owed verification is PAID at item 1548: 4 mutants, 4 caught**

Item 1546 concluded that the wins have been coming from shapes that still DECLINE a fast path rather
than from making hot loops faster. This tick took that advice and it paid immediately.

#### The screen, and why it was the right instrument

`count-shortcut.ts` is 2,771 lines with ~50 guard-level declines. Reading fifty guards is the wrong
tool; `packages/native/count-decline-screen.mjs` times fifteen count shapes in one process and looks
for **order-of-magnitude** outliers against structural twins. A closed-form count is sub-millisecond
and a materialised one is tens to hundreds, so the signal is 1000x, not 10% — which is why many arms
in one process is acceptable here where item 762 forbids it for a 10% claim.

It flagged on the first run:

```text
   V().hasLabel(P).out(E).count()      0.005 ms   [200000]
   V().hasLabel(P, Q).out(E).count()   9.268      [200000]    <- same answer, 1850x
   V().hasLabel(P).count()             0.003
   V().hasLabel(P, Q).count()          1.259                  <- same answer, 420x
```

#### The cause, one clause

```ts
-    if (step.kind !== 'hasLabel' || step.labels.length !== 1) {
+    if (step.kind !== 'hasLabel') {
```

`hasLabel` is **ANY-match**, so a disjunction one of whose labels sits on every element removes
nothing. `dropVacuousLabels` tested only the single-label spelling, so `hasLabel(P, Q)` on a graph
where every vertex carries `P` survived into the plan — and a plan carrying that filter takes the
general route where the dropped form is closed-form.

The replacement costs the same: iterate the named labels and return true if any one bucket covers the
total. Same O(k) `Map.get`s the old single test did.

**SUFFICIENT, NOT COMPLETE, deliberately.** Two labels each on half the vertices could union to
everything while neither bucket covers it alone; deciding that needs a real union and this pass runs
on every query. That case is pinned as a test with its answer asserted — the filter is kept and the
answer is right, just slower.

#### MEASURED — one arm per process, arm asserted in the bundle both ways

| arm                                | PRE      | POST      |          |
| ---------------------------------- | -------- | --------- | -------- |
| `V().hasLabel(P,Q).out(E).count()` | 9.075 ms | **0.010** | **908x** |
| `V().hasLabel(P,Q).count()`        | 1.287    | **0.007** | **184x** |

| control                                          | PRE   | POST  |      |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----- | ----- | ---- |
| `V().hasLabel(Q,R).count()` — non-vacuous        | 0.006 | 0.009 | flat |
| `V().hasLabel(Q,R).out(E).count()` — non-vacuous | 8.530 | 8.498 | flat |

In the many-arm screen the POST figures read 0.002 and 0.001; isolated they sit at the measurement
floor with few reps. Either way it is two to three orders of magnitude, and the non-vacuous twins do
not move.

#### ⚠️ THE MUTATION RUN WAS KILLED, AND IT LEFT A MUTANT IN THE TREE

The sweep ran in the background and was stopped by the harness because the machine was low on memory
— not a failure of the command, and the notice says not to restart it unasked, so it has not been
restarted. **It restores the tree only at the end of the loop, so it was killed with a mutant
applied.** `diff` against the saved pristine copy caught it and the file was restored.

CLAUDE.md names this exactly: _"Restore before applying the next mutant, never only after the loop.
An interrupted loop leaves the mutant in the tree, and `git diff` is then the only thing standing
between it and a commit."_ That is now an observed event rather than a warning, and the script in
`scratchpad/` still has the end-of-loop restore it was written with. The next mutation script should
restore **before** each mutant AND verify against pristine after being interrupted.

**So mutation verification is OWED for this item.** What stands in its place, stated precisely rather
than glossed: the first mutant in the list, `single-label-only`, is byte-identical to the PRE code
that was measured at 9.075 ms, and the new tests assert `effectivePlan(...).steps` is `['V','count']`
for `hasLabel(P,Q).count()` — a plan the PRE code cannot produce, because it never drops a
multi-label filter. So that mutant is caught by construction. The three others — `drop-any-multi`
(drop a NON-vacuous disjunction, a wrong answer), `always-vacuous`, and `wrong-index` (use the vertex
index for an edge source) — are **unverified**, and `drop-any-multi` is the one a future tick should
run first.

#### Two stale claims the screen corrected

- **`isolated-gremlin-bench.mjs`'s `hopcount2` comment is wrong.** It says "answered by the degree
  inner product with no edge walk"; it measures **68 ms**. Two-hop counts are a slot sweep in both
  directions (`out.out` 52.8, `both.both` 61.1). The inner product in `bothChainCount` is gated on
  `unfiltered && hops.length === 2` and ~60 ms is what that path costs at 200,000 vertices — which
  matches CLOSED.md's own "both.both 6241 → 82 ms" prize rather than contradicting it.
- **Multi-type edges do not disable the single-type closed form**, which I suspected and tested:
  `out(E).count()` is 0.005 ms whether or not 1-in-7 edges carry two labels. Only the multi-LABEL
  hops change (`out(E,F)` 0.315 → 0.001), which is `bucketsFor`'s documented soundness condition
  working correctly.

#### THREE PROCESS FINDINGS, each of which cost a command

1. **RESTORE BEFORE EACH MUTANT, which is CLAUDE.md's rule and is now load-bearing rather than

### Item 1549 — SHIPPED, **7406x / 9495x / 6949x**: item 1547's bug has a TWIN on the GQL surface, and it is four spellings wide. `vacuousLabel` tested only a single `label`, so `:P|Q`, `:P&P` and `:!Nope` all stayed in the plan. ⚠️ **And the fifth kind, `:%`, looks statically vacuous and is NOT — `return true` there is a wrong answer that 3,871 tests do not see**

Item 1547 fixed `dropVacuousLabels` requiring `labels.length === 1` on the Gremlin side. The obvious
next question is whether GQL has the same hole. It does, and wider.

#### The hole

```ts
export const vacuousLabel = (graph: Graph, expr: LabelExpr | undefined): boolean =>
  expr?.kind === 'label' && (graph.verticesByLabel.get(expr.name)?.size ?? 0) === graph.vertexCount;
```

`LabelExpr` has **five** kinds — `label`, `wildcard`, `not`, `and`, `or` — and only the first was
tested. The function's own comment already prices what elision is worth: _"When every vertex is a
`Person`, `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x)` and `MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS]->(x)` are EQUIVALENT SPELLINGS of
one question — and they cost 586ms against ~0ms."_ Every compound spelling of a universal label was
paying that.

#### MEASURED — 200,000 vertices, every arm answering the identical 200,000

| spelling                            | PRE      | POST      |                                        |
| ----------------------------------- | -------- | --------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(x)`               | 0.003 ms | 0.003     | the yardstick                          |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(x)`             | 0.001    | 0.001     | already elided                         |
| `MATCH (a:P&P)-[:E]->(x)`           | 9.495    | **0.001** | **9495x**                              |
| `MATCH (a:P\|Q)-[:E]->(x)`          | 7.406    | **0.001** | **7406x**                              |
| `MATCH (a:Q\|P)-[:E]->(x)`          | 7.152    | **0.001** | **7152x**                              |
| `MATCH (a:!Nope)-[:E]->(x)`         | 6.949    | **0.001** | **6949x**                              |
| `MATCH (a:%)-[:E]->(x)`             | 5.960    | 5.671     | **deliberately unchanged — see below** |
| `MATCH (a:Q)-[:E]->(x)` — selective | 2.640    | 2.911     | flat, correctly kept                   |

`or` needs only ONE side universal (a disjunction matches whatever either side does); `and` needs
both; `:!X` is universal exactly when `X` matches nothing, and an empty bucket is the cheap way to
know that.

#### ⚠️ THE WILDCARD IS THE FINDING, and I nearly shipped it as a wrong answer

`:%` reads as "any node", so `case 'wildcard': return true` is the obvious line — it needs no graph
lookup at all, which makes it look like the cheapest win of the five. **It is wrong.** Tested before
implementing, on a graph with one `:P` vertex and one UNLABELLED vertex:

```text
   MATCH (a)     count 2        MATCH (a:%)   count 1
```

So `%` means "carries at least one label", and eliding it invents the unlabelled rows. It is vacuous
only when every vertex has a label, and nothing here knows that in O(1) — the label buckets can sum
past `vertexCount` because a vertex may carry several. Left un-elided, with the reason in the code.

`:!Nope` is the other half of the same question and goes the other way: it matched **both** vertices
including the unlabelled one, which is why eliding it when the inner label is absent is sound.

**The mutation run is what makes this worth writing down.** `case 'wildcard': return true` is caught
by **exactly one test — the one written for it — out of 3,871.** The whole suite is blind to it.

#### MUTATION — four mutants, three caught, and the survivor is correct

| mutant                                                   |          |                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `wildcard-is-vacuous` (`return true`) — **wrong answer** | CAUGHT   | 3870 pass 1 fail — the wildcard test ALONE             |
| `and-needs-either` (`&&` → `\|\|`) — **wrong answer**    | CAUGHT   | 3869 pass 2 fail — mine plus a pre-existing sweep test |
| `not-inverted` (`=== 0` → `!== 0`) — **wrong answer**    | CAUGHT   | 3870 pass 1 fail                                       |
| `or-needs-both` (`\|\|` → `&&`)                          | SURVIVES | correct — tightening only DECLINES an elision          |

The survivor is answer-equivalent by construction: a stricter test elides less, which costs time and
changes no row. Its instrument is the probe (7406x), not a test.

#### ⚠️ TWO OF MY OWN GUARDS WERE VACUOUS, and mutation is the only reason I know

`not-inverted` and `and-needs-either` both passed the first time against tests I had written
specifically for them. The cause: I asserted on a **bare** `MATCH (a:!Q) RETURN count(*)`, and that
shape does not consult `vacuousLabel` at all — the elision fires on the HOP shapes, which is where
every number above was measured. Moving both guards onto `-[:E]->(x)` is what gave them teeth.

That is the same trap as item 1545's vacuous positive control and item 1542's vacuous reduction: a
test that exercises the wrong ROUTE passes for a reason unrelated to what it claims. The rule that
keeps catching it: **assert on the shape the measurement used.**

#### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. core 431/0, gql **3871**/0, gremlin 1500/0, native 963/0,
serialization 144/0, `bun run fuzz` 20/0. Mutants run one at a time in the FOREGROUND with the

#### Also measured this tick and DECLINED: `limit(n).count()`

`V().out(E).limit(n).count()` is `min(n, degree_sum)` — a closed form — and `countShortcut` has no
`limit` handling at all, so any plan carrying one declines outright. The cost tracks `n` exactly:

|                 | ms     |                             |
| --------------- | ------ | --------------------------- |
| `limit(10)`     | 0.026  |                             |
| `limit(1000)`   | 0.615  |                             |
| `limit(100000)` | 32.406 |                             |
| `limit(200000)` | 70.510 | vs `out(E).count()`'s 0.005 |

So it is an early-exit walk materialising `min(n, total)` traversers at ~0.35 µs each — correct
behaviour, and the gap only exists for an `n` so large the caller could have written `count()`. Small
`n`, which is the real shape ("are there at least 10?"), is already fast. Declined on value, not on
difficulty; the table is in `count-decline-screen.mjs` so it is not re-derived.

### Item 1550 — SHIPPED, **212,000x**: a REL wildcard `-[:%]->` is "any type" unconditionally, where item 1549 had to leave the NODE wildcard `(a:%)` alone. **The same operator, two opposite answers, and the difference is a `core` invariant rather than an analogy.** Plus the `:!X` complement priced at 202,000x and NOT taken, with the soundness condition worked out — ⚠️ **item 1551 found a SECOND blocker: `compile(stmt)` is plan-CACHED, so the complement cannot be a compile-time substitution at all**

Item 1549 fixed the vertex-label expressions and left `:%` un-elided because an unlabelled vertex is
allowed. The obvious next question is the edge side.

#### What the screen found

`relTypeNames` maps a rel label to the edge types it admits, and bails on three of the five kinds:

```ts
/** `null` = bail (and/not/wildcard); `undefined` = "any type"; `string[]` = exactly those. */
```

At 200,000 edges, 1-in-10 typed `F` and the rest `E`:

| spelling      | PRE         | POST      | equivalent typed spelling |                         |
| ------------- | ----------- | --------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `-[]->`       | 0.003 ms    | 0.003     | —                         | the yardstick           |
| `-[:E]->`     | 0.001       | 0.001     | —                         | already a type list     |
| `-[:E\|F]->`  | 0.001       | 0.001     | —                         | `or` already folds      |
| **`-[:%]->`** | **212.117** | **0.001** | `-[]->`                   | **212,000x**            |
| `-[:!Nope]->` | 213.331     | 205.550   | `-[]->` 0.003             | priced, not taken       |
| `-[:!F]->`    | 202.345     | 198.602   | `-[:E]->` 0.001           | **202,000x**, not taken |
| `-[:!E]->`    | 118.345     | 109.392   | `-[:F]->` 0.001           | **118,000x**, not taken |

#### ⚠️ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it is decided by a core invariant

`(a:%)` and `-[:%]->` are the same ISO operator — "carries at least one label/type" — and they
differ because:

```text
   g.addEdge({ labels: [], … })   ->  THROWS: "Cannot add an edge with no labels: every edge must carry ≥1"
   g.addVertex({ labels: [], … }) ->  fine
```

So a rel wildcard admits every edge that _can exist_ and is pure cost, while a node wildcard is
genuinely selective — item 1549 measured `MATCH (a:%)` at 3 against `MATCH (a)`'s 4 on a graph with
one unlabelled vertex, and recorded `return true` there as a wrong answer that 3,871 tests miss.

**Reasoning by analogy from item 1549 would have got this backwards**, in the direction of leaving
212,000x on the table. The test that pins it asserts the `addEdge` rejection directly, so if that
invariant ever relaxes the wildcard arm becomes a wrong answer loudly rather than silently.

#### THE `:!X` COMPLEMENT: priced at 202,000x, NOT taken, and the condition is written down

`:!F` over a graph whose only types are `{E, F}` is exactly `:E` — a type list, and the typed
spelling is 202,000x faster on the identical 180,000 rows. The naive complement is **unsound**,
which is measured rather than assumed:

```text
   e1 = [E], e2 = [E, F]
   MATCH (a)-[:!F]->(x)   count 1      <- e2 carries F, so it is excluded
   MATCH (a)-[:E]->(x)    count 2      <- e2 carries E, so it is included
```

So the complement needs **`graph.multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`**, and `relTypeNames` is a pure function
of the label with no graph to read it from. Taking it means either threading a graph through or a
graph-aware wrapper at the shortcut detectors — a real change, not a line. The "no untyped edges"
half needs no check at all, per the invariant above.

`and` is in the same position and has a pleasing special case for a future item: with
`multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`, no edge carries two types, so `:A&B` with `A ≠ B` matches **nothing** and
could return `[]`.

#### MUTATION — two mutants, two caught, and one was ALREADY pinned

| mutant                                                |        |                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------- |
| `wildcard-empty-list` (`return []` — matches nothing) | CAUGHT | 3872 pass 2 fail |
| `not-is-any-type` (the unsound reading, deliberately) | CAUGHT | 3872 pass 2 fail |

The second is caught partly by a test that already existed: **"a NEGATED relationship label must
decline — 'every type' is the wrong reading"**, from an earlier mutation pass. So the exact shortcut
I declined above was already tried and rejected once, which is independent confirmation that the
complement needs its condition rather than a blanket reading. Worth knowing before a future tick
reaches for it.

serialization 144/0, `bun run fuzz` 20/0. Mutants one at a time in the foreground, output

### Item 1551 — the `:!X` complement (202,000x) is **DECLINED for a better reason than "it needs a graph": `compile(stmt)` is CACHED in `planCache`, so any graph-derived compile-time substitution is baked in permanently.** And the same question asked of items 1549/1550 — **verified NOT stale**, empirically, across a mutation that changes the vacuity

Item 1550 priced the rel-type complement at 202,000x and left it because `relTypeNames` is a pure
function of the label with no graph to read `multiTypeEdgeCount` from. That reason was true and
shallow. The real one is worse, and it also had to be checked against what items 1549 and 1550
already shipped.

#### WHY THE COMPLEMENT CANNOT BE A COMPILE-TIME SUBSTITUTION

```ts
const hit = planCache.get(stmt);
if (hit !== undefined) return hit(graph, params) as R[];
const plan = compile<Row>(stmt);
planCache.set(stmt, plan);
```

`compile(stmt)` takes **no graph** and runs **once per statement**, with the result cached. So
`relTypeNames`' purity is not an oversight — it is load-bearing for that cache. Baking `:!F → [E]`
at compile time would survive the next `addEdge`, and the very next `F` edge would make every later
execution of that cached plan answer from a stale type list. That is a silent wrong answer across a
mutation, which is strictly worse than the 202,000x it buys.

`relTypeNames`' result also **picks the route**, at compile time: `if (types === null) return null`
declines the whole shortcut. So a working design needs the admission at compile time and the type
list at run time, with a run-time guard that can still fall back when `multiTypeEdgeCount !== 0` —
and a count closure has no general matcher to fall back to. That is the shape of the work, and it is
a good deal larger than item 1550's pricing implied.

#### ⚠️ AND THE SAME QUESTION APPLIES TO WHAT I ALREADY SHIPPED — CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED

`vacuousLabel(graph, expr)` takes a graph, so if it were consulted during `compile` then items 1549
and 1550's elisions would be baked into cached plans too, and a query would answer wrongly the
moment the graph stopped making the label vacuous. That is the same bug class, on code committed two
ticks ago.

**It is sound, and here is the evidence rather than an argument.** Every shape shipped at items 1549
and 1550, run twice against the SAME query text — once while `P` is universal, then after adding a
`:Z` vertex with an edge, which makes `P` non-universal and changes three of the four answers:

| query                                                           | while `P` universal | after the mutation | truth                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| `MATCH (n:P\|Q)-[:E]->(x)`                                      | 1                   | **1**              | 1 — `c` is `:Z`, not `P\|Q`            |
| `MATCH (n:P&P)-[:E]->(x)`                                       | 1                   | **1**              | 1                                      |
| `MATCH (n:!Nope)-[:E]->(x)`                                     | 1                   | **2**              | 2 — every vertex qualifies, both edges |
| `MATCH (n)-[:%]->(x)`                                           | 1                   | **2**              | 2 — both edges are typed               |
| `MATCH (n:P)-[:E]->(x)` (the pre-existing single-label elision) | 1                   | **1**              | 1                                      |

A baked elision would have answered 2 for the first, second and fifth rows. All five are right, so
`vacuousLabel` is consulted inside the closure that receives the graph, per execution — which is why
it could be extended where `relTypeNames` cannot.

**That asymmetry is the durable finding of this tick**, and it is not visible from either function's
signature: both take or lack a graph for reasons that look incidental and are not. A future item
reaching for a graph-derived optimisation in this engine should ask _when_ the decision is taken
before asking whether it is sound.

#### What remains priced

`-[:!F]->` 202.345 ms against `-[:E]->`'s 0.001 on the identical 180,000 rows, and `-[:!E]->` 118.345
against `-[:F]->`'s 0.001. Still worth having; the cost is a run-time-resolved type list with a
fallback, not a compile-time substitution. `:A&B` sits beside it with the same requirement and the
pleasing special case that with `multiTypeEdgeCount === 0` it matches nothing.

### Item 1552 — SHIPPED, **~146,000x and ~118,000x**: a label carried by NO vertex now short-circuits a multi-hop count to 0, where it used to cost the whole sweep to discover nothing. The selective control is untouched. **Found by taking item 1551's "vacuity is per-execution" and asking the opposite question**

Item 1551 established that `vacuousLabel` is resolved per EXECUTION, and `effectiveLabel`'s own
comment names why: _"Decided per EXECUTION and not at compile time, because vacuity is a property of
the GRAPH."_ The companion question is the other end of the same bucket read — not "does this label
match everything?" but **"does it match nothing?"**

#### MEASURED — 200,000 vertices

| shape                                | PRE        | POST            |                          |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------- | --------------- | ------------------------ |
| `MATCH (a:Nope)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)` | 146.126 ms | **0.001–0.003** | **~146,000x**            |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c:Nope)` | 118.157    | **0.001**       | **~118,000x**            |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b:Nope)-[:E]->(c)` | 0.001      | 0.001           | already free — see below |

| control                                                     | PRE     | POST    |                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `MATCH (a:Q)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)` — **genuinely selective** | 148.264 | 147.201 | flat, correctly not short-circuited |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)` — no label                  | 50.792  | 46.202  | flat                                |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)` — vacuous                 | 52.643  | 46.293  | flat                                |

#### WHY THE MIDDLE WAS ALREADY FREE AND THE ENDS WERE NOT

`buildTwoHopCount` drives from the **middle** — a two-hop count is a degree inner product over `b` —
so an empty middle bucket yields an empty driver set and 0 falls out for nothing. The END labels are
applied as per-edge **filters**, so an empty one takes the same route a selective label takes and
discovers nothing at the end of it.

The tell was in the numbers before the code: `:Nope` cost **146.126** against a genuinely selective
`:Q`'s **148.264**. Identical. A label matching nothing was paying exactly what a label matching half
the graph pays.

The guard sits beside the `effectiveLabel` calls the closure already makes once per execution, and
**before the driver set is even built**. Both the two-hop and three-hop builders got it.

#### MUTATION — the condition is load-bearing; the guard itself is answer-equivalent

| mutant                                                   |            |                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------- |
| `always-empty` (`size >= 0`, so every label looks empty) | **CAUGHT** | 3833 pass **46** fail         |
| `guard-never-fires`                                      | SURVIVES   | answer-equivalent — see below |

`always-empty` is the wrong-answer direction and it is caught by 46 tests, most of them
pre-existing: answering 0 for a query with rows breaks everything that counts a labelled chain. So
the _condition_ has teeth.

`guard-never-fires` surviving is honest and expected: removing a short-circuit leaves the slow path
computing the same 0, so no answer changes. **Its instrument is the probe, not a test** — the same
`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` position as item 1549's `or-needs-both`. Noted rather than papered
over: a route assertion here would need the timing, and a timing threshold in the suite would be
flaky.

#### The test that exists because of item 1551

`compile(stmt)` is cached in `planCache`, so a guard decided at compile time would be baked in and
answer 0 forever once it had seen an empty bucket. The test runs the SAME query text three times —
empty, then after `addLabelToVertex` makes the label universal, then after `removeLabelFromVertex`
takes it away — and asserts 0, 4, 0. That assertion exists only because item 1551 went looking for
the staleness trap; without it this change would have had a plausible-looking test suite and a latent
wrong answer.

#### What is left in this family

`MATCH (a:Nope)-[:E]->(x:Nope)` — a ONE-hop with both ends empty — still reads 4.020 ms against the
0.009 of a single empty end. It is a different builder (`buildOneHopCount`), and 4 ms is two orders
of magnitude below the shapes taken here, so it is recorded rather than taken.

### Item 1553 — ⚠️ **A WRONG ANSWER REACHABLE THROUGH PUBLIC API, pre-existing, and my own items 1549/1550/1552 widened the surface exposed to it.** Every label elision trusts `verticesByLabel`; the public `v.labels = […]` setter does not maintain it. Measured in both directions. **And I had already refused this exact trust at item 1535 — then relied on it three items later without re-raising it**

This tick set out to take item 1552's empty-label idea to the Gremlin side. The Gremlin side turned
out to need nothing, and the screen found something more important instead.

#### THE GREMLIN SIDE NEEDS NOTHING — measured, so it is not re-derived

Gremlin's chain counts seed from the start label's bucket, so an empty one is already free at every
depth. At 200,000 vertices with `R` on nobody:

| arm                                            | ms         | control                              |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `V().hasLabel(R).count()`                      | 0.005      | —                                    |
| `V().hasLabel(R).out(E).count()`               | 0.005      | —                                    |
| `V().hasLabel(R).out(E).out(E).count()`        | 0.011      | `hasLabel(Q)` twin **51.326**        |
| `V().hasLabel(R).out(E).out(E).out(E).count()` | 0.005      | —                                    |
| `V().out(E).hasLabel(R).count()`               | **49.125** | the one gap — a FAR-side empty label |

So one Gremlin gap exists (a far-side empty label, ~10,000x) and it was **not** taken, because of
what follows.

#### ⚠️ THE FINDING: EVERY LABEL ELISION TRUSTS A BUCKET THE PUBLIC SETTER DOES NOT MAINTAIN

`Vertex` has a public `set labels(labels: string[] | Set<string>)`, and it is deliberately optimised
to keep "a re-write off the map entirely" — its own comment prices a 200,000-element re-write. It
does not touch `verticesByLabel`. Every label elision reads exactly that index. Both directions
produce a wrong answer, measured:

```text
   OVER-COUNT (the PRE-EXISTING vacuous elision)
     4 vertices, all :P, 4 edges.  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(x) -> 4   correct
     v0.labels = ['Z']             stale P bucket 4, labels.has 3
     same query                                                     -> 4   TRUTH IS 3

   UNDER-COUNT (item 1552's empty guard)
     4 vertices, no :R.            MATCH (a:R)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(x) -> 0   correct
     every v.labels = ['P','R']    stale R bucket 0, labels.has 4
     same query                                                     -> 0   TRUTH IS 4
```

**This is pre-existing, not introduced here** — the first block is `vacuousLabel`, which long
predates this session. But it is also not harmless: items 1549 (`or`/`and`/`not`), 1550 (the rel
wildcard) and 1552 (the empty guard) each added elisions that read the same index, so the set of
queries that can answer wrongly after a setter write is now considerably larger than it was.

#### AND I HAD ALREADY REFUSED THIS TRUST, THREE ITEMS EARLIER

Item 1535 declined to seed a Gremlin walk from `verticesByLabel` **for exactly this reason**, and
said so: _"the raw `labels` SETTER has never maintained `verticesByLabel` … so the bucket is neither
a subset nor a superset of the truth after a setter write."_ Then items 1549–1552 relied on that same
bucket without my re-raising it. The pre-existing `vacuousLabel` gave the reliance cover, which is a
real argument — but I did not **check** that cover when I leaned on it; I checked it only now, a tick
later, and only because the Gremlin screen put the question back in front of me.

Recording that plainly because the lesson is not "the bucket is stale" (which was already written
down) but **that having written a caution down is not the same as applying it** — the note was in a
file I authored, about the same index, and three items walked past it.

#### THE TRADE, which is why this is a decision and not a fix

The setter is fast _because_ it does not reindex. The elisions are fast _because_ they trust the
index. Those two cannot both be right, and each repair costs the other:

1. **Make the setter maintain `verticesByLabel`.** Fixes the whole family at once, including the
   pre-existing case. Costs the setter the optimisation its comment was written to defend.
2. **Make the elisions not trust the bucket.** Costs them the O(1) property they exist for — it
   undoes items 1549/1550/1552 and the pre-existing `vacuousLabel`, i.e. 146,000x, 212,000x and
   9495x go back.
3. **Accept it and document the supported mutators.** The de facto state today:
   `addLabelToVertex`/`removeLabelFromVertex` do index, and `core`'s `label-box.test.ts` already
   pins the stale bucket as deliberate — but nothing warns a caller of `v.labels =` that queries may
   then answer wrongly.

Not taken unilaterally: it is a core semantics choice with a measured cost on either side, and the
Gremlin far-side gap above is left with it because fixing that would widen the same exposure again.

#### ✅ WHY NO TEST CAUGHT IT — the owner's question, answered with evidence

1. **GQL's own write path INDEXES.** `packages/gql/src/executor/clauses.ts` mutates labels through
   `addLabelToVertex`/`removeLabelFromVertex`, so any label change expressed as a QUERY keeps
   `verticesByLabel` correct. A pure-query workload cannot desync — and that is nearly everything
   the suites and the fuzzers do.
2. **The fuzzers cannot reach it.** They ingest NDJSON (through `addVertex`, which indexes) and then
   run generated queries. A raw-setter write is not a query; it is a host API call, so no generator
   emits one.
3. **The tests that DO use the raw setter never run a query.** `core`'s `label-box.test.ts` uses it
   five times and asserts only the INDEX state — it deliberately pins the stale bucket
   (`getVerticesByLabel('P')` still returns the stale entry) as pre-existing behaviour. Nothing
   connects that state to an answer. My own `start-filtered-hop-values.test.ts` uses it for the
   inverse case: asserting a walk is RIGHT because it reads `labels.has` instead of the bucket.
4. **No production code in the repo uses the raw setter at all.** A grep for `.labels =` finds the
   setter's own definition, those two test files, and one false positive (`state.labels` in the CLI
   shell, which is an autocomplete list, not a vertex). So the exposure is entirely a HOST
   application surface: code that does `v.labels = [...]` and then queries.

#### AND WHAT OPTION 1 WOULD COST, measured

The setter's comment defends a bulk re-write. At 200,000 vertices, min-of-5:

| path                                                | ms       |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `v.labels = ['P','R']` — the raw setter, no reindex | **18.1** |
| `graph.addLabelToVertex('R', v)` — indexes          | **92.6** |

So making the setter maintain the index costs roughly **5x on that bulk re-write** — and it is a
path no production code in this repo takes. That reframes the trade: option 1's cost falls on an
API surface nothing internal uses, while the correctness it buys covers every elision at once. The
owner's own account fits — both were once maintained, and this is the one that was optimised away.

`bun run fuzz` 20/0.

### Item 1554 — first measurement of the GQL **WRITE** path this session, and it is **healthy**: a `SET` is 4.61 µs/op and the read floor 0.31 µs once the lookup key is indexed. The 695 µs/op I first measured was an **unindexed scan**, not a write cost — ⚠️ **and my first reading of it was wrong in a way the probe itself invited**

Items 1508-1553 were all reads. The brief is the whole TS engine, so this is the other half:
`INSERT`, `SET`, `REMOVE`, `DELETE`, one operation at a time against a warm graph — the serving
shape, not bulk ingest (which `ts-ingest-is-constant-factor` already closed).

#### ⚠️ THE FIRST READING WAS WRONG, AND IT LOOKED LIKE A FINDING

The probe's first run, with no index on the lookup key:

```text
   SET one prop        695.08 us/op
   DELETE node         673.83
   [floor] MATCH only  368.00
```

I read that as "~327 µs of write cost per property set" — an enormous number, and a plausible-looking
one because it sat consistently above a floor I had also measured. **It was the 20,000-vertex scan
in the `MATCH`, twice over**: once in the floor arm and once inside each write. Adding one index
settles it:

| arm                                               | no index     | **indexed** |           |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ----------- | --------- |
| `MATCH (a) WHERE a.n = $n RETURN a.n` — the floor | 368.00 µs/op | **0.31**    | **1187x** |
| `SET a.k = $v`                                    | 695.08       | **4.61**    | 151x      |
| `SET a.k = $v, a.s = $s`                          | 708.14       | **3.09**    | 229x      |
| `REMOVE a.s`                                      | 701.63       | **2.13**    | 329x      |
| `DETACH DELETE a`                                 | 673.83       | **5.27**    | 128x      |
| `INSERT (:P {k: …, n: …})` — literals             | 5.89         | 4.17        | —         |
| `INSERT (:P {k: $k, n: $n})` — params             | 1.98         | **2.15**    | —         |

**So there is no write-path target here.** A `SET` costs 4.61 µs against a 0.31 µs read floor, and
`REMOVE` 2.13. The lesson is about the instrument: a per-operation write probe whose `MATCH` is
unindexed measures the scan and attributes it to the write. The probe now creates the index by
default and `INDEXED=0` reproduces the mistake.

#### What the numbers do say

- **The single largest lever available to a caller is an index**, at 1187x on a point lookup. That
  is a DX/docs point rather than an engine one — `discoverability-is-the-bottleneck` is the standing
  note that every dogfood wall was something unfound rather than something missing.
- **`INSERT` with literals costs 1.94x its parameterised twin** (4.17 against 2.15). That is the
  all-miss lift cost items 1540/1541 measured: every interpolated `INSERT` carries a unique text, so
  the lift memo cannot hit and each call pays the tokenize. It is **not** waste — the lift is what
  lets all those unique texts share ONE compiled plan, which is strictly better than a parse and a
  plan each. Correct as designed, and "use parameters" is worth ~2 µs/op.
- `SET` of two properties reading faster than `SET` of one (3.09 against 4.61) is arm-ordering
  noise, not a result. Flagged so it is not quoted as one.

### Item 1556 (absorbing 1555, which was the sweep run itself — there is no separate 1555 entry) — ⚠️ **A REGRESSION, found by the repo's own spelling probe: auto-parameterization (item 1502) silently switched OFF item 778's `liftStartProps` rewrite for every inline-literal query.** `MATCH (a:P {k: 5})-[:E]->(b)` 51.44 → 8.63 ms, **5.96x**, converged with its clause twin. The fix is three lines; the lesson is that both features were individually correct

Item 1554's index finding raised the engine-side question — do all SPELLINGS of a filtered lookup
reach the same route? — so this tick ran `bun run spelling`, which I had not used this session.

#### THE PROBE EARNED ITSELF AGAIN

The full sweep at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` flagged three groups over 2x and clear of the null
control. The largest, confirmed alone three times exactly as the probe's own output instructs:

```text
   MATCH (a:P {k: 5})-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.k         25.19 / 26.33 / 24.86 ms
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE a.k = 5 RETURN b.k   6.84 /  6.98 /  6.87
```

**3.65x, identical answers** — and item 778 had already FIXED this exact pair, recording "5.04 →
0.95 ms, 5.31x, converging with its clause twin at 0.95" and "the spelling probe's item 777 group …
is absent from the >2x list after this". It was back.

#### THE MECHANISM — two correct features, composed wrongly

`liftStartProps` rewrites `MATCH (a:L {k: 5})-[:T]->(b)` into `MATCH (a:L)-[:T]->(b) WHERE a.k = 5`,
and its gate refuses a param because "a param could BE null" (item 260). Auto-parameterization
(item 1502) runs **before the parse**:

```text
   normalizeLiterals('MATCH (a:P {k: 5})…')  ->  'MATCH (a:P {k: $__ap0 })…', { __ap0: 5 }
   parse(that).…start.properties[0].value    ->  { kind: 'param', name: '__ap0' }
```

So the gate's `value.kind === 'lit'` test stopped matching, and the rewrite had been off for every
inline-literal query since. **Neither feature is wrong on its own.** Item 778's refusal is sound,
item 1502's lifting is sound, and the composition is a silent 6x.

#### THE FIX, and why admitting a synthetic param is sound

`normalizeLiterals` lifts **only numbers and strings** — `null`, `true` and `false` are refused,
verified rather than assumed:

```text
   {k: null}  NOT LIFTED      {k: 5}  -> {__ap0: 5}
   {k: true}  NOT LIFTED      {k: 0}  -> {__ap0: 0}      <- falsy, still lifted
                              {s:'x'} -> {__ap0: 'x'}
```

So a synthetic `__ap<n>` carries a value already proved non-null, and the gate may admit it where a
caller's `$p` must still refuse. `isSyntheticParam` is exported from `auto-param.ts` as a PREDICATE
rather than as the prefix, so the namespace stays known in one place — that file's own comment warns
the tagged-template form owns `p<n>`, and two files guessing at the split is how they drift.

#### MEASURED — min of 9, 200,000 vertices, arm asserted in the bundle

| spelling                                     | PRE      | POST     |                                 |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ------------------------------- |
| `MATCH (a:P {k: 5})-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.k`    | 51.44 ms | **8.63** | **5.96x**                       |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE a.k = 5`        | 9.47     | 9.52     | flat — the twin it converges on |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE a.k = $p`       | 8.87     | 9.44     | flat                            |
| `MATCH (a:P {k: $p})-[:E]->(b)` — USER param | 50.50    | 52.10    | **unchanged, by design**        |

And the probe agrees: that group now reports **0 over 2x** across two isolated runs (7.61 vs 7.48,
6.93 vs 7.44).

#### ⚠️ AN INLINE _USER_ PARAM IS NOW 6x ITS OWN LITERAL — a DX cliff, recorded not fixed

`{k: $p}` costs 52.10 against `{k: 5}`'s 8.63 and `WHERE a.k = $p`'s 9.44. A caller doing the right
thing — parameterising — falls off a cliff that the literal spelling does not have. It cannot be
fixed the same way: the plan is cached (item 1551), so the engine cannot see the value, and the null
case is a genuine semantic difference, not a rounding one:

```text
   MATCH (x:P {k: $p})     p = null  ->  2 rows   (IS NULL: the stored null AND the absent key)
   MATCH (x:P) WHERE x.k = $p  p = null  ->  0 rows
```

Closing it would need a null-safe lifted predicate (`a.k = $p OR (a.k IS NULL AND $p IS NULL)`),
which is a different and slower comparison. The advice that follows is "inline a literal, or use a
clause `WHERE` with a param — not an inline param", which belongs in the docs.

#### MUTATION — two mutants, two caught, and the second needed an ANSWER test

| mutant                                      |        |                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `revert-synthetic`                          | CAUGHT | 3880 pass 2 fail — the composed test and the synthetic test |
| `admit-any-param` — item 260's wrong answer | CAUGHT | 3879 pass **4** fail, incl. the new row-count assertion     |

Every route test in `lift-start-props.test.ts` feeds the rewrite a freshly PARSED query — which is
not the path a real query takes, and is exactly why none of them saw this. The new test asserts the
**composed** shape (auto-param → parse → lift), which is `rewrite-composition-is-not-free`'s rule
applied: assert the composition, not each rewrite against hand-written input.

#### THE RATIO IS THE FINDING

**One real regression, two artifacts, out of three flags.** That is not a complaint about the probe —
it is the design working: flag broadly in a sweep where groups pollute each other's dispatch, then
confirm narrowly. A tick that treated all three as targets would have spent two thirds of itself
chasing its own harness, and a tick that dismissed the list would have missed a 5.96x regression
that had been live since item 1502.

So the calibration to carry: **expect roughly a third of this probe's in-sweep flags to survive
isolation**, and never skip the three-run confirmation — the cost is three 110-second runs against a
target that may not exist.

### Item 1558 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1557 WAS HALF WRONG AND THIS CORRECTS IT.** The `node count: inline vs clause` flag I dismissed as an in-sweep artifact was a real **1.37-1.56x**, and the refusal behind it had been priced with the very instrument error I used to dismiss it: **all three spellings timed in ONE process**. Taken on the bare node; both twins flat; the index seek survives

Item 1557 confirmed two of the sweep's three flags as harness artifacts and closed them. One of them
was not. The correction matters more than the win, because the same mistake appears **twice** here —
once in 2026's refusal comment and once in my own entry one tick earlier.

#### THE INSTRUMENT ERROR, which is the whole item

`liftStartProps` refused to lift a bare node in a single-pattern clause, and its comment gave a
measured reason: _"the scan rungs already serve it and the lift gains nothing — measured equal at
3.36 against 3.55 ms."_ Item 1557 then dismissed the flag on the same shape and even identified this
exact code, writing _"the convergence is the isolation and not the change."_ Right code, wrong
conclusion, both times.

Both readings came from timing the three spellings of the group **in one process**. That is item
762's redistribution shape, and here it is large enough to invert the verdict:

|                           | inline | clause   | pattern WHERE | reported gap |
| ------------------------- | ------ | -------- | ------------- | ------------ |
| all three in ONE process  | 3.73   | **1.74** | 2.38          | 2.14x        |
| **one shape per process** | 3.79   | **2.56** | 2.59          | **1.48x**    |

The clause arm is measured **second**, through call sites the inline arm has just made polymorphic,
and it reads 1.74 instead of its true 2.56 — 1.47x flattered. So the in-process instrument inflates
the _gap_ while the isolated-group instrument (`SPELL_ONLY`, which also runs all three arms in one
process) **hides it entirely**: the group converges to 1.01-1.05x both before and after the fix, so
item 1557's three confirming runs could not have distinguished them. Neither reading was the honest
one; only one shape per process is.

⚠️ **And I nearly mis-concluded a third time.** My first lifted build, still all-arms-in-one-process,
reported the clause arm 1.39x SLOWER (1.74 → 2.42) and I wrote that off as a ~40% noise floor. It was
neither a regression nor noise — it was the artifact disappearing, because once the lift routes the
inline spelling through the clause's route the clause arm no longer gets the free warm-up. Five
repeats showed both arms stable to ±3%, which is what made it clear the swing was systematic.

#### THE MEASUREMENT, one shape per process, three runs each

| config        | arm              | PRE   | POST     |           |
| ------------- | ---------------- | ----- | -------- | --------- |
| indexed, 200k | inline `{k: 2}`  | 0.26  | **0.19** | **1.37x** |
|               | clause `n.k = 2` | 0.19  | 0.19     | flat      |
|               | pattern `WHERE`  | 0.19  | 0.19     | flat      |
| scan, 200k    | inline           | 3.79  | **2.43** | **1.56x** |
|               | clause           | 2.56  | 2.43     | flat      |
|               | pattern          | 2.59  | 2.52     | flat      |
| scan, 600k    | inline           | 11.81 | **7.93** | **1.49x** |
|               | clause           | 7.38  | 7.47     | flat      |

Consistent across the seek path, the scan path and a 3x size sweep, and **flat on every twin** — the
control that says this is the inline spelling getting faster rather than a redistribution.

**The indexed row is the one that had to be checked before taking it.** Lifting an inline property
into a clause `WHERE` could plausibly have cost the index SEEK, which would have traded 1.56x on a
scan for far more on a seek. It does not: all three spellings converge at 0.19 ms, so the seeder
recognizes the lifted form. (Consistent with item 1333's finding that inline props seed through
`indexCandidates`'s `node.pred.props` path independently of the lift.)

| shape            | engine ms | top unpriced                                          |

#### The cost is real, and three ablations priced it

`match()` is a depth-first join. `bind` built each branch with `new Map(t.tags)` — an O(bindings)
copy at every node of the DFS.

| ablation                                                               | `matched`, 3 runs (ms) | vs 14781  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------- |
| PRE                                                                    | 14496 / 14781 / 15111  | —         |
| `{ ...t, tags }` → explicit `{ value, path, loopCount, tags }` literal | 15858 / 17275 / 15885  | **WORSE** |
| `new Set(done).add(idx)` → one shared mutable set                      | 15386 / 14940 / 15162  | **flat**  |
| **the tags `Map` copy removed** (wrong answers, ceiling only)          | **2604 / 2565 / 2706** | **5.68x** |

So **82% of the shape is that one copy**, the `done` set copy is worth nothing, and hand-writing the
object literal in place of the spread is actively worse. The two nulls are recorded because both
looked like co-equal targets from the code.

#### ⚠️ THE OBVIOUS FIX IS REFUTED, and the arithmetic says it had to be

I built the deferred-copy version: one mutable map down the DFS, each binding undone on the way out,
and a SNAPSHOT at the leaf (`extend` propagates `tags` by reference, so without one every emitted
traverser would share the map the solver keeps rewriting). `applyPattern` returned a descriptor
(`drop` / `keep` / `bind` + candidate values) instead of built traversers. It passes 1500/0.

It is **flat**:

| shape                                    | PRE                   | POST                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- |
| `matched` (1 pattern)                    | 14496 / 14781 / 15111 | 15276 / 15019 / 16318 |
| `matched2` (2 patterns)                  | 8923 / 8690 / 9185    | 8856 / 8868 / 8667    |
| `matchedsel` (2 patterns, `select('c')`) | 9314 / 9569 / 9334    | 9771 / 9697 / 9716    |

**Why, and this is the general result worth keeping.** The old code copied once per BIND; the new
one copies once per SOLUTION. With branching factor `f` and `b` binder patterns, solutions are `f^b`
while binds are `f + f² + … + f^b ≈ f^b · f/(f−1)`. At `f = 5` that is **1.25x fewer copies at
best** — and the leaf snapshot copies the FULL map where a mid-path bind copied a partial one, which
gives the 1.25x straight back. **In a branching search the leaves dominate the node count, so
deferring work to the leaf amortizes nothing.** Depth is not the axis.

⚠️ **And the probe could not have shown otherwise.** `matched` is
`match(pipe(as_('a'), out('E'), as_('b')))` — ONE pattern, so the DFS is depth 1 and `k = 1`. A
change that trades `k` copies along a path for 1 at the leaf is identically a no-op there. Its own
comment says it is "the smallest shape that exercises the matcher", which is the worst case for this
class of change. **Two multi-pattern shapes are now in the probe** (`matched2`, `matchedsel`) so the
next attempt is measurable; `matchedsel` exists because without a downstream reader the leaf
snapshot would be dead code and the easy half of the question.

A three-pattern shape is deliberately absent: 2383 ms a REP at FANOUT=5, so ~8 minutes on a 200-rep
sweep. Item 1478 made the same call about the 3-hop end-filtered question, for the same reason.

#### The reachable lever, not built this tick

The 5.68x needs the leaf snapshot GONE, not moved — and it is only needed when something downstream
reads the tags. `matchStep` cannot see the downstream steps, but **`RunContext` already carries
exactly this kind of answer**: `tracksPath: boolean`, "computed once from the plan via
`planReadsPath`; defaults to `true` so any context built without it … is always correct, just
unoptimized." A `tracksTags` flag is the same shape, the same default-safe direction, and would let
the solver pass the shared map through untouched when no `select`/`where`-by-label follows. That is
the next target, with its ceiling already measured.
