### Item 1560 — SHIPPED, **1.16x** on `match(…).count()` and **1.23x** at two patterns (controls flat): the solver's per-solution tag snapshot is skipped when no downstream step can read tags. ⚠️ **And item 1559's 5.68x "ceiling" does not exist — its ablation PRUNED THE SEARCH, 2004 solutions where the correct answer needs 10000.** Three mutants survive, and the reason is worth more than the win

Item 1559 nominated this from a profile and priced it at 5.68x. The price was wrong, and finding out
why is most of this item.

#### ⚠️ THE ABLATION WAS NOT MEASURING WHAT I THOUGHT: it did 5x LESS WORK

Item 1559's `nomapcopy` arm removed the tag-map copy by having `bind` mutate one shared map and
return `t` — **and never undo it**. So after the first branch the end label stayed bound, and
`applyPattern` took its `boundEnd?.ok` path (return once, consistent) instead of fanning out over
every candidate. The search collapsed:

```text
   correct                            10000 solutions   (answer 10000)
   item 1559's `nomapcopy` ablation    2004 solutions   (answer 2004)
```

**10000 / 2004 = 4.99x less work, against a measured 5.68x speedup.** Essentially the whole
"ceiling" was the pruning. The tag copy was never 82% of anything.

**The rule this earns:** a wrong-answer ablation is only a valid ceiling if it does the SAME AMOUNT
OF WORK. Removing a cost per unit is fine to measure that way; changing control flow is not, and a
mutation that leaves state behind in a backtracking search changes control flow by construction.
**Count the units** — here one line counting yielded solutions settled it, and it is the same
discipline CLAUDE.md already prescribes for fixtures ("an answer that is INVARIANT to the property
you varied cannot validate the fixture"). I had the counter available and did not run it for a whole
item.

#### What the real change is, and what it is worth

`extend` propagates `tags` by reference, so the solver cannot hand out a traverser pointing at the
map it is still rewriting — hence a snapshot per solution. That snapshot is dead whenever nothing
downstream reads tags, and `match(…).count()` is exactly that. `tagsObservedFrom(steps, from)` in
`ast.ts` answers it from the match step's own suffix, and `run`'s step loop passes the verdict.

| shape                                              | PRE                   | POST                  |                       |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- |
| `matched` — `match(…).count()`, skip FIRES         | 14496 / 14781 / 15111 | 13081 / 12610 / 12769 | **1.16x**             |
| `matched2` — two patterns, skip fires              | 8923 / 8690 / 9185    | 7093 / 7440 / 7225    | **1.23x**             |
| `matchedsel` — `select('c')`, snapshot still taken | 9314 / 9569 / 9334    | 9450 / 9686 / 9613    | flat (ranges overlap) |
| `hopcount3` — control, no `match.ts`               | 2789 / 2689 / 2773    | 2867 / 2689 / 2773    | flat                  |

Item 1559's reverted mutate-and-undo refactor is a **PREREQUISITE, not a competitor**: without one
snapshot to skip there is nothing to condition. On its own it measured flat on three shapes, and
that entry records why — do not re-derive it as a win.

#### Two guards, both of them load-bearing for a different reason

- **`tagsObservedFrom` is an ALLOWLIST, defaulting to "observed"** — the opposite direction from
  `PATH_DEPENDENT_KINDS`. A missed path reader degrades to `NO_PATH` and the suite notices; a missed
  TAG reader would read a map the solver is rewriting, which is the right row count with the wrong
  contents. `group`, `groupCount`, `order`, `project` and `dedupe` are deliberately excluded because
  they can carry a `by` traversal and **`by` is not in `SUBPLAN_FIELDS`**, so the nested-plan check
  would not catch it.
- **The verdict is computed in `run`'s own step loop, NOT `applyPlanToStream`.** I wired it into
  `applyPlanToStream` first and reverted that: it runs for every nested plan, where a sub-plan's
  suffix says nothing about what follows the enclosing step — `union(match(…))` then `select('a')`
  has an empty inner suffix and a very real reader. It also turned out `run` never calls
  `applyPlanToStream` at all, so the wiring was dead as well as unsafe. Steps reached through a
  sub-plan keep `matchStep`'s default of "observed".

#### ⚠️ Mutation: four die, THREE SURVIVE, and the survivors are the interesting part

| mutant                                              | verdict                  |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| drop the UNDO (item 1559's ablation, exactly)       | **caught** — answer test |
| claim every kind is tag-blind                       | **caught**               |
| admit `select` to the allowlist                     | **caught**               |
| drop the nested-plan guard                          | **caught**               |
| flip `tagsObserved`'s default to `false`            | **SURVIVES**             |
| invert the snapshot condition                       | **SURVIVES**             |
| hard-code the call site to `false` (never snapshot) | **SURVIVES**             |

The three survivors all disable the snapshot where it is supposedly required, and **I could not
construct any pipeline that observes the difference.** `match-buffer-probe.mjs` runs the same
question through `barrier`, `aggregate`, `dedupe`, `fold`, a trailing `order`, and a MANUAL DRAIN
that retains every emitted traverser before reading anything — byte-identical output with the
snapshot forced off:

```text
   plain select / barrier+select / aggregate+select / dedupe+select   [2,3,3]  both builds
   manual drain                                            ["b","c","c"]  both builds
```

The reason is laziness plus what actually escapes: `run` yields the freshly-built **bindings** map
rather than the traverser, and `select` reads tags during the pull, before the solver advances. My
first attempt to give the guard teeth was a `barrier()` test written on the theory that buffering
would expose it; it passed under all three mutants, which is how I learned the theory was wrong.

**So the snapshot may be dead code in general, and the honest position is that the guard is
PRECAUTIONARY.** It is kept because `extend`'s by-reference propagation is a real aliasing hazard
and correctness should not rest on my failing to find a counterexample — but it is not a verified
necessity, and the suite cannot falsify it. Anyone tempted to delete the conditional and always skip
should know that is probably correct, costs the `matchedsel` path nothing, and is unprovable with
the current instruments. The four mutants that DO die protect the analysis and the undo, which are
the parts that demonstrably matter.

#### The GQL screen: 20 shapes, and one shape 15x its own twin

No unpriced frame over 2% anywhere (every ZERO-mention frame is ~1 ms of parse work). But the
ranking is lopsided: `unionedbigdistinct` **17388 ms** against `unionedbig` **1161 ms** — the same
query with `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`, **15x** — and 80.3% of it in two lightly-priced frames:

```text
   7993.0  46.0%   3 mentions   (anonymous) in distinctRows
   5966.5  34.3%   4 mentions   rowKeyOf
```

Those mentions are item 1473, which removed a _wasted_ key pass. What remained was the single
necessary one.

#### The defect

```ts
export const rowKeyOf = (row: Row): string => Object.values(row).map(valueKey).join('\x01');
```

For `MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.n AS x UNION …` — **one column, numbers** — every row paid two array
allocations, a string build and a string hash to dedup a single number. A one-column row can be
keyed on the value itself.

**The equivalence argument, which is the whole question.** For primitives a `Set`'s SameValueZero
agrees with `valueKey` exactly: `-0`/`0` are one group both ways, NaN equals itself both ways, and
the type prefixes (`n`/`s`/`b`) keep `5` and `'5'` apart just as raw values do.

⚠️ **TWO sets, not one.** Non-primitives still key through `valueKey` (an element keys by `@id`, not
identity). Putting those strings in the same set as raw values lets a STRING column collide with an
element: the row `['@v1']` and the row `[<vertex v1>]` are different rows that would both key as
`'@v1'`. Separate sets cannot collide — and the `one-set` mutant confirms a test catches it.

⚠️ **Positional, so the column is read PER ROW.** ISO set ops compare positionally and the two sides
may alias differently (`… AS a` vs `… AS b`); a name taken once from `rows[0]` would read `undefined`
off the other side and collapse it to a single row. `for…in` takes the first own key with no
allocation.

#### Measured — `NODES=200000`, 25 reps, one shape per process, order alternated

```text
                          PRE                        POST

excepted             684.7  663.6  690.8       549.9  544.0  569.9    3/3, 1.25x
unioneddistinct      330.2  370.1  377.5       308.5  355.9  318.9    1.16x
distinct   (control) 201.8  179.1  175.6       186.7  228.8  186.6    flat
hoprows    (control) 865.5  914.3  903.4       890.6  905.5  903.9    flat
sortedpage (control) 322.8  280.0  329.6       332.3  293.9  340.6    flat
```

The target's ranges do not overlap — POST's slowest 1128.8 is below PRE's fastest 3607.8.

⚠️ **`excepted` is NOT a control for this change, and item 1473 used it as one.** `except` and
`intersect` both end in `distinctRows`, so they are second beneficiaries; they gain less (1.25x)
because their `rightKeys` pass still calls `rowKeyOf` per row, which this change does not touch.
That is the obvious next lever, priced at the gap between 1.25x and 4.01x.

⚠️ **`distinct` being flat is CORRECT and is itself a control.** `distinctRows` has exactly three
callers, all inside `combineRows`, so `RETURN DISTINCT` never reaches it — it routes elsewhere. I
expected that shape to gain and it did not; checking the call sites rather than re-measuring is what
explained it.

#### ⚠️ I published a wrong fact mid-tick, from a `JSON.stringify` artifact

While testing the NaN equivalence I checked a stored NaN with
`console.log(JSON.stringify(query(...)))`, read `null`, and concluded that NaN and Infinity normalize
to null on the way in — stating it as settled. **`JSON.stringify(NaN)` is the string `null`.** The
value is a real NaN, and the suite said so immediately (`Received: {"x": NaN}`). So that equivalence
class is LIVE, not unreachable, and the fast path genuinely has to match it — which it does, by
SameValueZero. `0.0/0.0` is no way to make one; it raises `division by zero`.

**The rule:** never read a numeric value back through `JSON.stringify` — it renders NaN, Infinity and
`-0` as `null`, `null` and `0`, which is three of the exact edge cases a key-space argument turns on.
Same family as the libm constant-folding trap.

### Item 1562 — SHIPPED, **1.44x** on `EXCEPT` and **2.60x** on `INTERSECT` (3/3 each, arm ranges NOT overlapping, three controls flat): item 1561's one-column keying reached only the trailing `distinctRows`, so both still built strings for the right-side set AND the per-left-row probe. ⚠️ A surviving mutant found a real test gap, and behind it an ISO conformance question: **unequal set-operation degree is accepted here**

Item 1561 took `UNION` to 4.01x and `EXCEPT` to only 1.25x, and recorded the gap as the next lever.
This is it.

#### The defect

`except` and `intersect` computed a row's key **three times** where `union` computed it once:

```ts
const rightKeys = new Set(right.map(rowKeyOf)); // pass 1
return distinctRows(left.filter((r) => !rightKeys.has(rowKeyOf(r)))); // pass 2, then pass 3 inside
```

Item 1561's fast path only reached pass 3. The one-column keying now covers all three, and the probe
pass folds the dedup into itself — one pass over the right side, one over the left.

The three call sites share extracted helpers (`oneColumnValue`, `addOneColumnKey`,
`hasOneColumnKey`, `isOneColumn`) rather than repeating the two-key-space logic, which is what let a
single mutant on the shared helper be caught by tests on all three paths.

#### Measured — `NODES=200000`, 25 reps, one shape per process, order alternated

```text
                          PRE (item 1561)            POST
excepted             551.1  552.8  578.9       382.5  370.6  387.8    3/3, 1.44x
intersected         3354.7 3365.3 3314.9      1289.5 1095.0 1297.7    3/3, 2.60x
unionedbigdistinct   920.3 (1561's POST)        922.1               flat — path untouched
hoprows   (control)  903.9                      921.5               flat
sortedpage (control) 332.3                      291.2               flat
```

Neither target's ranges overlap. Cumulative over both items, `EXCEPT` is **684.7 → 382.5, 1.79x**.

⚠️ **`INTERSECT` had NO probe shape until this item** — it is a beneficiary of exactly the same code
as `EXCEPT` and nothing measured it. `intersected` is now in `runtime-profile-probe.mjs`. It is the
larger win because its right-side set is _retained_ (every left row probes a hit) rather than mostly
missing.

#### ⚠️ A SURVIVING MUTANT FOUND A REAL GAP — and an ISO question behind it

Six mutants; five died at once. `no-right-guard` — removing
`right.length > 0 && !isOneColumn(right)` — **survived all 3907 tests**.

I expected it to be unreachable, on the grounds that ISO requires equal degree in a set operation.
**This engine does not enforce that**, measured directly:

```text
   MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a EXCEPT MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a, n.s AS b   ->  [{a:1}]   runs
   MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a UNION  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a, n.s AS b   ->  [{a:1}]   runs
```

So a one-column left CAN meet a two-column right, and without the guard the fast path keys the right
side on its **first column alone** — making `{a:1}` and `{a:1, b:'a'}` the same key and subtracting a
row the string path keeps (`n1` vs `n1\x01sa` differ). A wrong answer, previously uncovered. Two
tests added; the mutant now dies.

**The conformance question is left open deliberately**: ISO/IEC 39075 requires set operands to have
the same degree, and this engine accepts unequal degree with the left side's names. ⚠️ **Measured
immediately after, at item 1563: the two engines DISAGREE, in opposite directions.** It is a
confirmed cross-engine divergence, not a candidate — see that entry.

**The lesson for the next mutation run:** "this mutant is unreachable because the language forbids
it" is a claim about the IMPLEMENTATION, not the language. Check that the implementation forbids it
before dismissing a survivor; here it took one query to find out it does not.

| collapse the two key spaces (add side)              | 2 tests                   |
| collapse the two key spaces (probe side)            | 2 tests                   |
| read the column by a fixed name                     | 16 tests                  |
| drop the right-side width guard                     | **survived; now 2 tests** |

### Item 1563 — ⚠️ **A CONFIRMED CROSS-ENGINE DIVERGENCE, in OPPOSITE directions, on a shape neither the differential fuzzer nor any test generates**: with unequal set-operation degree, TS compares the WHOLE row key and native compares only the COMMON PREFIX. `EXCEPT` keeps everything in TS and nothing in native; `INTERSECT` is the exact reverse. Found by following up item 1562's surviving mutant rather than filing it as "unmeasured"

Item 1562 discovered that this engine accepts unequal degree in a set operation, which ISO/IEC 39075
forbids, and recorded the native side as unmeasured. One probe settles it, and the answer is worse
than a shared non-conformance.

```text
                          ts                                   native
EXCEPT    1 vs 2   ok [{"a":1},{"a":2}]                  ok []
INTERSECT 1 vs 2   ok []                                 ok [{"a":1},{"a":2}]
EXCEPT    2 vs 1   ok [{"a":1,"b":"a"},{"a":2,"b":"b"}]   ok [{"a":1,"b":"a"},{"a":2,"b":"b"}]
UNION     1 vs 2   ok [{"a":1},{"a":2}]                  ok [{"a":1},{"a":2}]
EXCEPT equal       ok [{"a":2}]                          ok [{"a":2}]          control, agrees
```

`1 vs 2` is `MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a <OP> MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a, n.s AS b` over two
vertices.

**The mechanism is readable off the two results.** TS keys a row by all of its columns, so a
one-column row and a two-column row can never match: `EXCEPT` subtracts nothing and keeps both rows,
`INTERSECT` matches nothing and returns empty. Native evidently compares only the columns the two
sides share, so every left row matches: `EXCEPT` subtracts all of them and `INTERSECT` keeps all of
them. Both engines are self-consistent and they are **exact opposites** on both operators.

`UNION` agrees only because it concatenates before de-duplicating, and `2 vs 1` agrees because the
wider side is on the left, where the extra column is part of TS's key and absent from native's
comparison in the same way.

**Neither is ISO-correct, because ISO rejects the input.** 39075 requires the operands of a set
operation to have the same degree, so the conformant behaviour is a compile-time error in both
engines — which would also make this divergence unreachable. That is the fix; it is a semantics
change with a condition code to choose, so it is not being made inside a perf item.

⚠️ **Nothing was ever going to catch this.** The differential fuzzer does not generate unequal-degree
set operations, and no test in either engine writes one. It surfaced only because item 1562 wrote a
mutant that assumed the shape was impossible, the mutant SURVIVED, and checking why took one query.
**A surviving mutant is a question about the implementation, and this is the second time this session
that following one up found something the suite could not see** (item 1560's three survivors proved
the opposite: that a guard was unfalsifiable).

Deliberately NOT added to `divergence-registry.ts` — registering it would silence a fuzzer that is
not generating the shape anyway, and it should fail loudly if the generator is ever widened to cover
set-operation degree, which is now a known gap in its coverage.

The probe is `packages/native/setop-arity-probe.mjs` (run with **bun**, not node — it imports the
test-support harness from `src`, which is not published to `dist`).

#### Gates

Probe only; no engine change. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites unchanged from item 1562:
core 431/0, gql 3909/0, gremlin 1511/0, native 963/0, serialization 144/0, `bun run fuzz` 20/0.

### Item 1564 — ⚠️ **A SILENT ANSWER CHANGE I INTRODUCED AT ITEM 1561, FOUND AND FIXED.** That entry claimed the one-column fast path was "a pure speedup rather than a semantic change"; for `UNION` over MIXED-ARITY sides it was not — 4 rows became 2. Plus the perf half: dropping `[...left, ...right]` is **1.27x** on medians-of-7 (bimodal POST, ranges overlap), with GC at 35.4% of the shape

The tick began as a re-profile of the shapes items 1561/1562 sped up. The profile pointed at
`combineRows` (27.9% self) and garbage collection (35.4%) — and looking at `combineRows` to find the
allocation surfaced the regression instead.

#### ⚠️ THE REGRESSION, and why 1562's guard did not cover it

`distinctRows` decides the one-column fast path from **`rows[0]` alone**. `union` is its ONE caller
that hands it rows of MIXED WIDTH, because it passes `[...left, ...right]` and this engine accepts
ISO-invalid unequal degree (item 1563). So a one-column left put two-column right rows through a key
built from their FIRST COLUMN ONLY. Measured against an actual pre-1561 build, not reasoned:

```text
MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a UNION MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS a, n.s AS b
   pre-1561    4 rows   [{a:1},{a:2},{a:1,b:"a"},{a:2,b:"b"}]   full string keys all differ
   post-1561   2 ROWS   [{a:1},{a:2}]                            right side keyed on `a` alone
   now         4 rows   — pre-1561 restored
```

Item 1562 guarded `EXCEPT`/`INTERSECT` against exactly this mechanism — its `no-right-guard` mutant
survived and said so — and I did not carry the lesson to `union`, because union's mixed widths arrive
**already concatenated** and so look like one uniform array by the time `distinctRows` sees them.
`distinctUnion` now requires BOTH sides to be one column.

**Three things worth carrying:**

- **Item 1561's equivalence argument was about VALUES and the hole was about WIDTH.** Every line of
  it — `-0`, NaN, `5` vs `'5'`, the two key spaces — is still correct, and none of it addressed
  "what if the rows are not all the same shape". A key-space proof needs a premise about the
  ROW SET, not only about the values in a column.
- **A guard added for one caller is not added for its siblings.** 1562's mutant found the width hole
  and I fixed the two call sites the mutant covered. The third had the same hole behind a different
  surface.
- **The regression was invisible to 3909 tests** and to the differential fuzzer, because nothing
  writes an unequal-degree set operation (item 1563 records that coverage gap). It surfaced from
  reading the code for an unrelated reason.

#### The perf half: the concatenation

`[...left, ...right]` copied 400,000 rows per query at `NODES=200000`, then `distinctRows` allocated
its output. `distinctUnion` iterates both sides directly.

```text
unionedbigdistinct, 50 reps, 7 runs each, one shape per process
   PRE   2318.1 1825.0 1845.8 1814.8 1757.6 1805.4 1753.1     median 1814.8
   POST  1337.2 1604.7 1430.8 1818.6 1837.0 1332.4 1419.5     median 1430.8   1.27x
   hoprows (control)  917.4 median against 921.5              flat
```

⚠️ **Reported as medians-of-7 because the ranges OVERLAP and the POST series is BIMODAL** — four runs
near 1380 and three near 1750, while PRE sits tight at ~1800. That is what a removed allocation
sometimes-avoiding-a-GC-cycle looks like, and it is why 25 reps x 3 runs (the instrument the previous
two items used) reported this as flat-to-worse: at that length the shape's spread reached 40%. The
series is printed above rather than summarised, per the bimodality rule.

`unionedbig` (`UNION ALL`) is untouched — it still needs the concatenation, since that IS its result —
and its readings swing 336-607 ms, which is harness noise on a path this change cannot reach.

### Item 1565 — ⚠️⚠️ **THIS FINDING IS WRONG AND ITEM 1566 RETRACTS IT. There is no quadratic defect:** my query omitted the SCOPE LIST, so it was a NON-CORRELATED subquery, and running an O(N) body N times is O(N²) by ISO design. The correlated spelling `CALL (n) { … }` is linear (0.6 ms at N=1000). What is real is a missing loop-invariant HOIST, taken at 1566 for 289x. ~~AN INLINE CALL { … } CORRELATED SUBQUERY IS QUADRATIC IN THE DRIVING ROW COUNT.~~ Per-row cost tracks N almost exactly (1.00x → 1.94x → 3.71x for N ×1/×2/×4), so **1.36 ms A ROW at N=1000 against 104 ns for the equivalent `COUNT { … }`**. Found by ADDING a profile shape, not by reading one — and the first comparison I made overstated it 97x, which the probe now prevents

Two negative results and one finding. The negatives first, because they are what made the finding
necessary.

#### The width audit from item 1564 comes back CLEAN

Item 1564 fixed a one-column fast path that was selected from `rows[0]` while the loop touched rows
of other widths. The obvious worry is siblings:

- **Every caller of the one-column helpers is accounted for.** `distinctUnion` and `oneColumnSetOp`
  check BOTH sides; `distinctRows`' two remaining callers pass `left.filter(…)`, which is uniform by
  construction. `distinctRows` is **not** in the package's public exports, so no external caller can
  hand it mixed widths.
- **`isOneColumn` is the only `Object.keys(rows[0])` route choice in the GQL engine**, and a sweep of
  all three packages for the general pattern — a route selected from `collection[0]` — returns two
  hits, both safe: `parts[0]` is structural (a linear query has one part) and
  `hop-projection.ts`'s `proj.items[0]` is guarded by `keys?.length !== 1`, which verifies there is
  only one BEFORE sampling it. That is the correct form of this pattern.

#### `hoprows` is closed, and `farDrivenHopWalk`'s 54 mentions said so

The GQL screen's second-largest shape is 77.2% in `farDrivenHopWalk`'s closure. Item 1488 already

… recorded as a bound, not a target" — stands. **Second time in three ticks that a 50+ mention count

#### So the remaining signal is COVERAGE, and nine shapes were missing

Items 1473 and 1562 both found their target by adding a shape. The screen had no shape for: the
whole var-length/quantified family (`->{m,n}`, `->+`), `ANY SHORTEST`, `count(DISTINCT …)`,
`collect()`, the scalar aggregates, an inline `CALL`, a hop with `ORDER BY`+`LIMIT`, or a scalar
function in a predicate. All nine added.

#### ⚠️ THE FINDING: the inline CALL is O(N) PER ROW

```text
correlated-subquery-scaling-probe.mjs, FANOUT=5, medians of 3, same unfiltered driving MATCH

   arm             N        ms      ns/row   vs smallest N
   callinline    250      91.5     365,915      1.00x
   callinline    500     355.7     711,481      1.94x
   callinline   1000    1358.0   1,357,981      3.71x     ← tracks N: O(N) per row, O(N²) total
   countsub      250       0.3       1,285      1.00x
   countsub     1000       0.1         104      0.08x     ← flat
   existssub    1000       0.1          88      0.07x     ← flat
   plainhop     1000       0.0           8      0.01x     ← flat, the floor
```

`ns/row` rising in step with N is the whole result: per driving row the CALL does work proportional
to the GRAPH, not to the row's degree. At the probe's default `NODES=20000` one rep takes ~24
seconds; at 4,000 it is 25 s against 5.7 s at 2,000.

**The mechanism, as a hypothesis the fix must verify.** The profile at N=1000 puts `walkSegments`
24.3%, `withBinding` 23.5%, `expand` 12.8% — while `seedVertices` is 0.9% and `candidateVertices`
0.8%. That is consistent with the body expanding EVERY vertex per driving row and filtering by the
correlation rather than SEEDING from it, and the arithmetic fits: N × FANOUT·N is 5,000,000
expansions a rep at N=1000, and 552 ms over 15,000,000 (3 reps) is ~37 ns each. Stated as a
hypothesis because the profile is consistent with it rather than proof of it.

⚠️ **MY FIRST COMPARISON OVERSTATED THIS BY ~97x AND I ALMOST PUBLISHED IT.** I put `callinline`
beside the probe's existing `existssub` shape — but `existssub` filters `a.k = 5` before the
subquery, and `k` is `i % 97`, so its subquery runs for about N/97 rows while the CALL runs for all
N. "10.6 ms against 17,063 ms" is mostly a 97x difference in subquery COUNT. The new probe drives
every arm from an unfiltered `MATCH (n:P)` so the row counts match, and the real gap — still
~13,000x per row at N=1000 — is the one above.

**Not fixed this tick**: it is an executor change in the CALL correlation path, it wants the

### Item 1566 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1565'S FINDING WAS WRONG AND THIS RETRACTS IT: there is no quadratic defect.** `CALL { … }` with no scope list is NON-CORRELATED by ISO design, so running an O(N) body N times is O(N²) _as specified_ — my probe's query simply omitted the scope list. The real result is a legitimate missing optimization: a non-correlated body is **loop-invariant**, so it runs ONCE. **289x at 1,000 driving rows** (1358.0 → 4.7 ms)

Item 1565 reported "an inline `CALL { … }` correlated subquery is quadratic in the driving row
count". It is not a correlated subquery.

#### ⚠️ WHAT I GOT WRONG

`runCallInline` seeds the body with `clause.scope` and nothing else. My probe wrote
`CALL { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) … }` — **no scope list** — so the inner `n` is a FRESH, unbound variable
and the body legitimately matches every vertex. That is the scope isolation the ISO form exists for,
and `gql-call-statement` already records it as the design. The correlated spelling is
`CALL (n) { … }`, and it is linear:

```text
   N      scoped CALL (n)        unscoped CALL { }
  250        7.9 ms                119.7 ms
  500        0.8                   378.6
 1000        0.6                  1430.9
```

The scoped form is not merely faster, it is **falling** per row (JIT warm-up, then flat). Item
1565's "O(N) per row" was real arithmetic about the wrong query.

**And the two spellings are DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, which is exactly why the comparison looked valid.**
Both return the same `t` for `RETURN count(*)`, because the join produces one row per outer row
either way. The difference is in the column I had not projected:

```text
6 vertices, out-degree 1 each
   CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) RETURN count(*) AS c }   ->  c = 1 for every row   (correlated)
   CALL    { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) RETURN count(*) AS c }   ->  c = 6 for every row   (NOT)
```

**Project the column that distinguishes the arms, not just the one that totals.** Item 1565's probe
compared a non-correlated subquery against correlated ones and read the difference as a defect; the
`t` column could not tell them apart. Same family as the "project, do not count" rule the correlated
-push tests already carry.

#### THE REAL RESULT: that identical `c` is an INVARIANCE, and it is exploitable

`c = 6` for every row is the proof: with an empty scope the body cannot see the outer row, so every
iteration computes identical rows. It can run once.

```text
correlated-subquery-scaling-probe.mjs, unscoped CALL, FANOUT=5, medians of 3

   N        PRE        POST      ns/row POST   vs smallest N
  250      91.5 ms     2.8 ms       11,170        1.00x      32.7x
  500     355.7        3.2           6,483        0.58x     111x
 1000    1358.0        4.7           4,651        0.42x     289x
 2000   ~5688          7.2           3,581        0.32x     ~790x
```

ns/row now FALLS with N, so the shape is linear, and the win grows with N because the change is
O(N²) → O(N).

#### Three guards, and the read-only one is not optional

- **`clause.scope.length === 0`.** A scoped body is correlated and must run per row.
- **The body must be READ-ONLY.** ISO runs a non-correlated subquery per outer row, so its writes
  happen per row: hoisting `CALL { INSERT (:Q) }` over 4 rows would create ONE `:Q` instead of four.
- **The hoist is LAZY**, computed inside the closure. Eager would run the body even when the outer
  query produces no rows — changing both the cost and when a body fault surfaces.

⚠️ **`CLinear.writes` LOOKS like the read-only test and is NOT one.** It is
`clauses.some(c => WRITE_CLAUSES.has(c.kind))` over ONE level, and its own doc says pushing it inward
would be wrong for the transaction question it exists for — so it reports `false` for a body holding
a nested `CALL { INSERT … }`, and `WRITE_CLAUSES` does not list `callNamed` at all. The guard is a
recursive allowlist instead, for the usual asymmetry: a missed read-only kind loses an optimization,
a missed write kind loses N−1 writes.

#### ⚠️ Mutation — five mutants, and the survivor found a real gap

| mutant                                         | verdict                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| hoist unconditionally                          | caught, 5 tests                          |
| drop the scope check (hoist a correlated body) | caught, 3 tests                          |
| drop the read-only check                       | caught, 2 tests                          |
| admit `insert` to the allowlist                | caught, 2 tests                          |
| stop recursing into a nested inline CALL       | **SURVIVED all 3,921 tests; now 1 test** |

I nearly filed the survivor as unreachable: `CALL { CALL { INSERT (:Q) } }` raises "a query must end
in RETURN or FINISH". It does — but the inner body only needs a `RETURN`, and
`CALL { CALL { INSERT (:Q) RETURN 1 AS z } RETURN 1 AS y }` is perfectly legal and creates four
`:Q`. **Item 1562's rule applied for the third time this session**: "unreachable because the language
forbids it" is a claim about the implementation, so check it — one query did.

### Item 1567 — SHIPPED, **72.6x** on `MATCH p = (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P) RETURN count(*)` (878.0 → 12.1 ms, converging with the spelling that never bound `p`) and 1.57x on `ANY SHORTEST`: an UNREAD path variable was disqualifying **every fast path**. ⚠️ The cost is not the `Path` objects — five gates refuse outright on `pathVar !== undefined`, `orient` among them

Profiling the nine shapes added at item 1565 (none of which had been looked at) put `anyshortest` at
4806 ms, second only to `callinline`. Its `shortestWalk` frame carries 3 mentions, which looked like
the target — and the real one was next to it.

#### The defect

```text
   MATCH p = (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P) RETURN count(*) AS c      878.0 ms
   MATCH     (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P) RETURN count(*) AS c       11.8 ms      74.1x
   MATCH p = ANY SHORTEST (a:P)-[:E]->+(b:P) WHERE a.n = 0     57.4 ms
   MATCH     ANY SHORTEST (a:P)-[:E]->+(b:P) WHERE a.n = 0     37.6 ms       1.53x
```

`p` is never read in either — the projection is `count(*)`. **And `Path` allocation is the small
half.** `pathVar !== undefined` is an outright refusal in five separate places: the typed-hop seed,
two count rungs, the hop projection, and `orient` itself —
`pattern.pathVar !== undefined ? pattern : orient(graph, pattern, binding, params)`, so the planner
does not even choose a direction. Binding a path variable nobody reads falls off the whole ladder
onto the general matcher. That is why it is 74x and not 1.1x.

A path variable is also exactly the binding a user adds _speculatively_ — written while exploring a
query, then left in place when the projection becomes a count.

#### The fix, and the machinery that already existed

`dropUnreadPathVar`, an AST rewrite in `compileLinear`'s existing stack. **`dropUnreadGroupBinds`
was already the template** — same narrow `[match, return]` shape, same `freePredicateVars` /
`hasSubquery` helpers, same "a subquery anywhere refuses" rule. It even explicitly refuses on
`pattern.pathVar !== undefined`, which is why the new pass runs INSIDE it: stripping an unread
`pathVar` first is what lets the two compose rather than the first blocking the second.

A compile-time decision is safe to cache here because "is `p` read" depends only on the query text,
never on the graph — unlike `vacuousLabel`, which must be decided per execution.

| arm                                       | PRE      | POST     |                              |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ---------------------------- |
| `varlen {1,2}`, `p` unread                | 878.0 ms | **12.1** | **72.6x**                    |
| the same without `p` at all               | 11.8     | 11.0     | converged                    |
| `ANY SHORTEST`, `p` unread                | 57.4     | **36.5** | **1.57x**                    |
| the same without `p`                      | 37.6     | 32.9     | converged                    |
| ⚠️ `RETURN count(nodes(p))` — `p` IS read | 932.1    | 932.1    | **unchanged, as it must be** |

Answers identical throughout (599,996 / 20,000 / 100,000).

#### Refusals, and the one no other test covers

`RETURN *` refuses: `Projection.star` binds every variable in scope, `p` included, so dropping it
would remove a column from the result. Also refused: `p` read in the projection, in a function
(`nodes(p)`), in the clause `WHERE`, or in `ORDER BY`; any subquery downstream (`freePredicateVars`
cannot see inside one); and anything that is not exactly two clauses.

| ------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| drop the `RETURN *` guard                         | 2 tests  |
| ignore whether the projection reads `p`           | 16 tests |
| drop the subquery refusal                         | 1 test   |
| forget the clause `WHERE` when collecting readers | 1 test   |
| forget `ORDER BY`                                 | 1 test   |
| forget the projection items                       | 15 tests |

keep**: `dropUnreadGroupBinds` contains the expression-collection block VERBATIM, so anchoring on it

### Item 1568 — SHIPPED, **71.9x** on `MATCH (a:P)-[r:E]->{1,2}(b:P) RETURN count(*)` (819.6 → 11.4 ms, converging with the spelling that never bound `r`): an unread EDGE variable on a quantified segment is item 1567's defect again, and `dropUnreadGroupBinds` misses it by one field. ⚠️ ~~Also measured: the 2-clause restriction costs 83x … the next target~~ — **TAKEN at item 1569, 75.6x**

Item 1567 dropped an unread PATH variable for 72.6x. The obvious follow-up is whether other unread
bindings do the same, so it was measured rather than assumed:

```text
   MATCH (a:P)-[r:E]->{1,2}(b:P) RETURN count(*)      819.6 ms
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P)  RETURN count(*)       11.4 ms      71.9x
   MATCH (a:P)-[r:E]->(b:P)      RETURN count(*)        0.2 ms      a SINGLE hop costs NOTHING
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P)       RETURN count(*)        0.2 ms      (0.0 for the node variable)
```

**The cost appears only where a binding disqualifies the VAR-LENGTH rungs** — the same mechanism as
the path variable, and nothing to win on a plain hop. That asymmetry is what keeps the new pass
narrow.

#### Why the existing pass misses it, by one field

`dropUnreadGroupBinds` already drops an unread `rel.variable`. But it requires
`hopFrom !== undefined` and refuses on `nested`/`unitRest`/`innerQ`, i.e. it is written for a FUSED
HOP. Inspecting the parsed AST shows the two shapes differ exactly there:

```text
   (a:P)-[r:E]->{1,2}(b:P)              rel.quantifier set, NO hopFrom      <- falls through
   (x:P)((a)-[r:E]->(b)){1,2}(y:P)      rel.quantifier set AND hopFrom      <- that pass's case
```

`dropUnreadEdgeVar` covers the first only. Its refusals mirror that pass's own conservatism rather
than re-deriving them: a rel carrying properties or an inline `WHERE` is left alone, because the
predicate is evaluated against the bound edge and the binding is load-bearing even when no later
clause names it.

#### Measured, with both refusal controls

| arm                                      | PRE      | POST     |                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-[r:E]->{1,2}`, `r` unread              | 819.6 ms | **11.4** | **71.9x**                                                 |
| the same without `r`                     | 11.4     | 8.6      | converged                                                 |
| ⚠️ `RETURN count(r)` — `r` IS read       | 877.1    | 877.1    | unchanged, as it must be                                  |
| ⚠️ `-[r:E WHERE r.w > 0]->{1,2}`         | 879.2    | 879.2    | unchanged (and its answer differs: the predicate filters) |
| single hop, `r` unread                   | 0.2      | 0.2      | untouched by design                                       |
| **both** an unread `p` AND an unread `r` | —        | **6.4**  | the two passes compose                                    |

Answers identical (599,996) between the optimized and the never-bound spellings.

#### ⚠️ Mutation — five mutants, four caught, and the survivor is CORRECT

| mutant                                         | verdict                          |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| ignore whether the projection reads `r`        | caught, 5 tests                  |
| allow a single hop (drop the quantifier guard) | caught, 3 tests                  |
| allow a rel with an inline `WHERE`             | caught, 3 tests                  |
| allow a rel with inline properties             | caught, 1 test                   |
| drop the `nested !== undefined` guard          | **SURVIVES — and that is right** |

Rather than assume the survivor was a coverage gap, I parsed a nested subpath and looked:

```text
   (x:P)(((a)-[r:E]->(b)){1,2}){1,3}(y:P)
     outer segment:  rel = { direction, quantifier }        <- NO variable
     nested segment: rel = { variable: 'r', label, … }      <- `r` lives here
```

So on a nested segment the outer `rel` carries no variable and `rel.variable === undefined` refuses
first: the `nested` guard is **unreachable belt-and-braces**, kept only for consistency with
`dropUnreadGroupBinds`' identical list. A test now pins that SHAPE, so a parser change that started
putting a variable on the outer rel would fail loudly rather than quietly making the guard
load-bearing. **Third time this session that chasing a survivor was right and the fourth time the
answer was "check the implementation, not the spec"** — here the answer happened to be "genuinely
unreachable", which is only worth saying because it was verified.

#### The next target, priced here

The `[match, return]` restriction both passes share is expensive:

```text
   MATCH p = (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P) LET w = 1 RETURN count(*)   869.6 ms
   MATCH p = (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P)           RETURN count(*)    10.5 ms     83x
```

One `LET` re-exposes the whole cost. Generalizing to "any clause after the MATCH" needs expression
collection from arbitrary clause kinds — and the hazard is a clause that names a variable as a bare
string rather than a `var` node, which `freePredicateVars` would not see. That wants its own item.

### Item 1569 — SHIPPED, **75.6x**: items 1567/1568 both required exactly `[match, return]`, and one `LET` between the two re-exposed the whole var-length cost (869.6 → **11.5 ms**, converging with the never-bound spelling). ⚠️ The pass is an ALLOWLIST of clause kinds because a generic `var`-node walk would be WRONG — several clauses name a variable as a BARE STRING

Both unread-binding passes were deliberately narrow. Item 1568 priced the narrowness at 83x; this
removes it.

#### ⚠️ WHY A GENERIC WALK IS NOT AN OPTION

The obvious generalization is "walk the remaining clauses for a `{kind: 'var', name}` node". That is
unsound here, and checking it first is what shaped the pass. Three clause families reference a
variable with no `var` node anywhere:

```text
   SetItem / RemoveItem        { variable: string, key | label }
   a MATCH pattern             node.variable / rel.variable / pathVar are bare strings —
                               so a SECOND `MATCH` naming `p` JOINS on it, which is a READ
   CCallInline.scope           string[] of imported outer names, likewise a read
```

So `tailReads` admits only kinds whose variable reads are entirely `Expr`s — `let`, `filter`,
`page`, `with`, `return` — and **refuses everything else**. Adding a kind means checking that claim
for it, not that it "looks read-only".

It also refuses a tail that **REBINDS** the name (`LET p = 1`, `WITH 1 AS p`). Shadowing probably
makes the drop safe, but "probably" is not a basis for a rewrite and the shape is rare.

#### Measured

| arm                                                   | PRE      | POST     |                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ---------------------------- |
| `MATCH p = …{1,2}… LET w = 1 RETURN count(*)`         | 869.6 ms | **11.5** | **75.6x**                    |
| `MATCH (a)-[r:E]->{1,2}(b) LET w = 1 RETURN count(*)` | ~820     | **11.2** | ~73x                         |
| the same with no binding at all                       | 7.0      | 7.0      | the floor it converges to    |
| ⚠️ `LET n = size(nodes(p))` — `p` IS read             | 1108.0   | 1108.0   | unchanged                    |
| ⚠️ a second `MATCH` in the tail                       | 1042.1   | 1042.1   | unchanged (bare-string join) |

Both controls sit at ~1 second while the optimized shapes are ~11 ms.

#### ⚠️ Mutation — eight mutants, seven caught, and the survivor taught me my own test was wrong

| mutant                                       | verdict         |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| admit every clause kind (open the allowlist) | caught, 3 tests |
| ignore `RETURN *` / `WITH *`                 | caught, 4 tests |
| ignore a rebinding tail                      | caught, 1 test  |
| forget `filter.where`                        | caught, 1 test  |
| forget a `let` item's expression             | caught, 1 test  |
| forget `page.orderBy`                        | caught, 1 test  |
| forget the MATCH's own `WHERE`               | caught, 2 tests |
| forget `with.where`                          | **SURVIVED**    |

**I had written a test specifically for `with.where` and it did not cover it.** It read
`WITH a.n AS x, p AS pp WHERE size(nodes(pp)) > 2` — `pp`, the projected alias — so what refused was
the projection ITEM, not the `WHERE`. Renamed to say what it actually tests.

Then the real question: can a `WITH`'s `WHERE` reach a pre-`WITH` variable at all? **Measured, not
assumed — it cannot:**

```text
   MATCH p = … WITH a.n AS x WHERE size(nodes(p)) > 1 …   raises: variable `p` is not defined
   MATCH (a:P)-… WITH 1 AS x WHERE a.n > -1 …             raises: variable `a` is not defined
```

The engine narrows `WITH` scope, so a `WHERE` only names projected aliases, and any `WHERE` reaching
`p` required `p` to be projected first — which the item check catches. The collection is therefore
**redundant, and the survivor is correct**. It is kept (cheap, and defensive if the scope rule ever
changes), with a test pinning THE SCOPE RULE so it becomes load-bearing rather than silently dead.

That is the fifth survivor chased this session, and the pattern is now consistent: the survivor is
either a real gap or a fact about the implementation worth writing down, and the only way to tell is
to construct the case.

```text
varlen12 (617 ms)      walkLevelCount 70.0% (26 mentions)   get to 8.1%   buildTrailMasks 6.9%
varlenplus (1829 ms)   outNeighbors 32.5% (2)   push 18.9% (213)   evalLabelExpr 10.9% (11)
```

#### The nomination, and why it was wrong

`outNeighbors` materializes a `Vertex[]` per EXPANDED VERTEX, and **both callers immediately iterate
it and drop it** — the array is pure intermediate. 32.5% self, 2 mentions anywhere. Built as
`eachOutNeighbor(graph, v, out, types, visit)`:

- a boolean **STOP signal** rather than a plain visitor, because the `EXISTS` walk returns the moment
  it finds a hit — a `forEach` shape would have traded one allocation for expanding the whole
  frontier, on exactly the arm that cares most;
- `outNeighbors` kept as a thin wrapper so the shared definition stays the single source of
  neighbour expansion (its doc exists to stop the two traversals drifting from each other or native);
- both visitor closures hoisted ONCE, not built per expansion (`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`).

```text
                   PRE                          POST
varlenplus    1591.0 1656.9 1725.0        1483.3 1629.9 1628.0     1.02x, RANGES OVERLAP
existssub       72.2   69.2   73.2          72.5   71.9   70.6     flat — the early-exit arm
varlen12       584.5  590.9  551.4         573.4  588.1  582.9     flat — not reached
hoprows        365.7  395.6  396.5         364.4  448.5  351.6     flat
```

**So the 32.5% is `edgesOfTypes`' iteration credited to its caller, not the allocation.** That is the
hazard `runtime-profile-analyze.mjs`' own header states — _"a small hot callee gets credited with its

### Item 1571 — **86.3% of a bounded var-length count is a CSR that is REBUILT EVERY QUERY**, priced by instrumentation rather than inferred from a share. ~~The cache is designed and NOT built, because~~ ⚠️ **CLOSED — ITEM 1674 BUILT THE SIGNAL (`topologyVersion`) and ITEM 1676 BUILT THE CACHE: 3.8x to 27.2x across the six bench rows that reach it. Nothing here is open.** The blocker was real: ⚠️ **neither `graph.version` NOR `graph.epoch(name)` advances synchronously** — both read 0 through three mutations and only move after a task drain, so keying a cache on either serves a STALE result to any query following a write

Item 1570 refuted a target taken from a self-time share, so this one was ablated first.

#### The measurement

`walkLevelCount` is 70% of `varlen12` (`MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->{1,2}(b:P) RETURN count(*)`) and carries
26 mentions, i.e. it is thoroughly priced as a FUNCTION. What was not priced is the split inside it.
Timers around the two halves, 20 reps at 20,000 vertices / 100,000 edges:

```text
   20 reps total        144.9 ms
     build total        125.1   86.3%
       order + idx       21.0   14.5%     <- TYPE-INDEPENDENT (a spread + one Map.set per vertex)
       CSR fill         104.1   71.8%     <- type-dependent (one Map.get per EDGE)
     level recurrence    19.8   13.7%
```

**The recurrence this route exists for is 13.7% of it.** The other 86% is building a CSR — vertex
numbering, then `off`/`nbr` filled with an `idx.get(vertex)` per edge — from scratch, on a graph that
did not change between queries. The function's own comments are all about making the build fast
(items 744, 601, 692, 699: prealloc, no boxing, no Map in the levels), and they succeeded; nobody
had asked whether it should happen at all.

#### Two levers, and the first one is already disqualified

- **Replace `idx.get(vertex)` with a dense vertex ordinal** — this is the obvious read of "71.8% is
  a Map.get per edge", and it is **BUILT AND DISQUALIFIED**: deletes cost 6.18x/11.34x under churn
  (items 1369-1372/1397), and the standing note records that _seven_ items have arrived at it. Not
  re-attempted. Priced here only so the 71.8% is attributable.
- **Cache the CSR across queries** — different lever, not previously tried on the TS side (every
  `csr_fresh` / `rebuild_csr` / `invalidate_csr` reference in this file is the RUST engine). This is
  the one worth having, and it would reach the whole 86%.

#### ⚠️ WHY THE CACHE IS NOT BUILT: there is no synchronous change signal to key it on

`Graph` looks like it offers exactly the right key. `version` is documented as a _"monotonic mutation
counter — an O(1) 'did anything change?' signal"_, and `epoch(name)` as a per-token counter so _"a
selector that depends only on specific tokens can fingerprint `deps.map(epoch)` and recompute only
when one of them moved"_. Both are **deferred**, which the doc hints at ("advances on the same
deferred, veto-checked step as snapshot-staleness") and measurement confirms:

```text
   fresh             epoch(E)=0  epoch(P)=0  version=0
   after addVertex   epoch(E)=0  epoch(P)=0  version=0
   after addEdge     epoch(E)=0  epoch(P)=0  version=0
   after addEdge F   epoch(E)=0  epoch(F)=0  version=0     vertexCount=2  edgeCount=2
   ...after a task drain                     version=3
```

So a cache keyed on `version` or on token epochs would hand a **stale CSR** to any query that runs
after a synchronous write — `g.addEdge(...); query(g, …)` is the ordinary shape, and it would return
a wrong count silently. `vertexCount`/`edgeCount` DO advance eagerly but cannot serve: a delete plus
an add leaves both unchanged while the topology differs.

**The prerequisite is therefore a synchronous mutation counter in core**, which touches every mutator
plus the transaction undo path — too much to fold into a perf item

⚠️ **NARROWED AT ITEM 1673: A TOPOLOGY SIGNAL NEEDS FOUR INCREMENT SITES, NOT EVERY MUTATOR.**
(⚠️ **AND ITEM 1673 FIRST SAID TWO, WHICH WAS WRONG** — it scoped the signal to ADJACENCY, but the CSR
numbers the vertices as `[...graph.verticesById.values()]` and `nbr` holds indices INTO that order, so
a vertex add or remove shifts every index and invalidates the CSR as surely as an edge write does.
Corrected before anything was built on it.)

What a CSR cannot be invalidated by is a property or label write — those move neither the vertex
numbering nor the adjacency. And `Graph.ts` funnels the whole of topology through four writes, two
maps:

```text
   1724  this.verticesById.set(vertex.id, vertex)   addVertex
   1799  this.verticesById.delete(vertex.id)        removeVertex
   2083  this.edgesById.set(edge.id, edge)          insertEdge
   2174  this.edgesById.delete(edge.id)             removeEdge
```

So the signal is a monotonic counter bumped in four places, not a core-wide mutation counter.

And it needs no undo semantics. A counter for INVALIDATION only has to answer "might the adjacency
have changed since?", so an undo incrementing it is correct — over-invalidating costs a rebuild, never
an answer. That is the whole reason this is cheaper than the general counter: the general one has to
be RIGHT through a rollback, an invalidation flag only has to be CONSERVATIVE.

⚠️ **AND THE ROLLBACK QUESTION IS NOW CLOSED — IT ROUTES THROUGH THE SAME TWO FUNNELS.** The undo log
does not restore state directly; it stores INVERSE OPERATIONS AS CLOSURES OVER THE PUBLIC MUTATORS,
and `undoTo` simply invokes them:

```ts
   // insertEdge's inverse
   this.recordUndo(() => { const live = this.getEdgeById(undoEdgeId); if (live) this.removeEdge(live); });
   // removeEdge's inverse
   this.recordUndo(() => this.addEdge({ id: undo.id, from: …, to: …, labels: …, properties: … }));
```

So a counter bumped at those sites is bumped during rollback as well, and UNDER-invalidation — the
only failure mode, and this entry's original one — cannot occur.

⚠️ **AND THE CONVERSE CLAIM WAS WRONG, caught by item 1674's mutation pass rather than by reasoning.**
This entry first said restoring the counter on rollback "would be the one change that could make a
cache serve a stale structure". It would not: a rollback restores state FAITHFULLY, so a counter
restored alongside it is CONSISTENT — the cache entry at the pre-transaction version was built from
the pre-transaction state, which is exactly the post-rollback state. The mutant that restores it
SURVIVES the contract suite, correctly, as an equivalent mutant. Not restoring is simply simpler: it
costs one rebuild after a rollback and needs no bookkeeping in the undo path.

(That the inverses re-resolve by ID rather than closing over the element is itself deliberate: the
comment above `insertEdge`'s undo records that closing over a stale instance dereferences a null
`#graph` and aborts the whole replay, leaving a half-rolled-back graph.), and precisely where the native
side's own version of this went wrong: `csr_fresh` is cleared by every adjacency write and _nothing
re-arms it_, so one `add_edge` demotes every later read for the session. A TS cache must be keyed,
not flagged, for that reason.

⚠️ **And `graph.version`'s own doc invites the mistake.** "An O(1) did-anything-change signal" reads
as safe for read-after-write and is not. Anyone reaching for it to invalidate a cache needs to know
it is drain-ordered; that is the transferable finding here, independent of the CSR.

### Item 1572 — SHIPPED on the GREMLIN side, the same insight as items 1567-1569: an `as(l)` label nothing downstream can read is removed. **`V().as(x).out(E).count()` 24.1 → 0.0 ms** (the count shortcut answers it again) and **3.7x** on a values shape. ⚠️ The dominant cost is NOT the tag copy — it is that one extra step makes every prefix rung decline

Items 1567-1569 found that an unread binding in GQL disqualifies the var-length fast paths. The
transferable question is whether Gremlin has the same shape, and it does.

#### Measured first

```text
   V().as(x).out(E).count()        24.1 ms      V().out(E).count()         0.0 ms
   V().as(x).out(E).values(k)      30.1         V().out(E).values(k)       7.7
   V().as(x).out(E).as(y).count()  29.4
   V().as(x).out(E).select(x).count()  21.7     <- the label IS read
```

**Two costs, and the smaller one is the obvious one.** `as` writes its label by copying the whole tag
map per traverser (`projection.ts`: `new Map(t.tags)` plus a spread), which is the 3.9x on the values
shape. But it is also just another step in front of the hop, and every count/values rung matches a
plan PREFIX from the source — so an unread `as` makes them all DECLINE, which is why the count shape
goes from a closed-form 0.0 ms to a full 24.1 ms walk. Exactly the mechanism `dropVacuousLabels`
exists for, and `dropUnreadAs` sits beside it in `effectivePlan`.

| arm                                         | PRE     | POST    |                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `V().as(x).out(E).count()`                  | 24.1 ms | **0.0** | the shortcut is restored                          |
| `V().as(x).out(E).values(k)`                | 30.1    | **8.1** | **3.7x**, converged with the 8.6 no-`as` spelling |
| `V().as(x).out(E).as(y).count()`            | 29.4    | **0.0** | both dropped                                      |
| ⚠️ `…select(x).count()` — the label IS read | 27.1    | 27.1    | unchanged                                         |
| ⚠️ `V().hasLabel(P).out(E).count()`         | 0.0     | 0.0     | control, untouched                                |

#### Two decisions worth their reasons

- **It reuses `tagsObservedFrom` rather than asking per label.** The precise question is "does
  anything read THIS label", which means enumerating every reader's label fields (`select`, `where`
  keys, `dedupe` labels, `math` names, `addE` tag endpoints) — and a wrong answer means a `select`
  finding its tag missing. The coarse question, "does anything read tags at all", is already answered
  by item 1560's allowlist, which is mutation-tested and defaults to "observed". It covers both
  measured shapes and cannot be wrong about a label it never inspects.
- **It walks BACKWARDS, testing the KEPT suffix.** `as` is not tag-blind (it reads `t.tags` to copy
  it), so testing each `as` against the ORIGINAL suffix lets a second unread `as` keep the first
  alive — `as(x) … as(y) … count()` would drop only `y`. The `original-suffix` mutant is exactly
  that, and it dies on the two-label test.

A `KIND_BITS.as = 8192` gate was added for the reason item 1506 gives: a pass running on every query
showed up at 10.7% of a 175 ns reused-plan call.

#### ⚠️ Mutation — four mutants, three caught, and the survivor is UNKILLABLE (which I first got wrong)

| mutant                                           | verdict                   |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| drop every `as`, read or not                     | caught, 36 tests          |
| invert the observation test                      | caught, 40 tests          |
| test the ORIGINAL suffix instead of the kept one | caught, 1 test            |
| remove the `KIND_BITS.as` gate                   | **SURVIVES — unkillable** |

I wrote an identity assertion claiming to catch the gate mutant, and **it does not**. Without the
gate the loop still runs, finds no `as`, leaves `changed` false and returns `plan` — _the same
object_. So the gate has no observable effect of any kind: not the answer, not the plan, not even
object identity. It is a pure cost guard, and no behavioural test can see it. The test's comment now
says that instead of claiming otherwise; what it actually pins is the identity contract the rewrite
chain's other identity checks depend on.

That is the sixth survivor chased this session and the second that turned out to be correct rather
than a gap — but the first where **my own test's stated purpose was wrong**, which is worth more than
the mutant: an assertion that passes for the wrong reason reads as coverage.

⚠️ **And `bun test` did not catch an untyped closure parameter in the new file — `bun run check` did.**
`bun test` does not typecheck, so a green suite is not a green gate.

### Item 1573 — ⚠️ **A 10.0x CROSS-SURFACE ASYMMETRY ON PAGING** — ⚠️ **and only HALF of it was the algorithm: item 1574's top-k took 2.07x and GQL is still 4.4x ahead on `[...stream]` materialization.** Gremlin's `order().limit(k)` did a FULL SORT where GQL's `ORDER BY … LIMIT` takes a top-k. 55.2 ms against 5.5 for the same question over the same graph. Three other "transparent step" candidates measured and REFUTED, each for its own reason

Item 1572 dropped an unread `as` because an extra step in front of the hop makes every prefix rung
decline. The follow-up question is which other steps do that, so four candidates were measured
before anything was built.

#### The three refusals, each for a different reason

```text
   V().out(E).count()                      0.0 ms     the baseline the rungs answer
   V().identity().out(E).count()           22.2       a PURE no-op costs the whole shortcut
   V().barrier().out(E).count()            14.3
   V().order().by(k).out(E).count()        25.2
   V().dedupe().out(E).count()             15.2
```

- **`identity()` — 22.2 ms for a semantic no-op, and NOT taken.** It is trivially safe to drop, but
  `count-shortcut.ts`' own comments use `identity()` as the way to force a decline and measure the
  general path (_"against the forced-`identity()` decline that IS the route this replaces"_, and
  `optional(identity())` at item 1483). Dropping it removes that tool. No LIVE instrument depends on
  it (zero hits across `packages/native`'s probes), but a prefix `identity()` is also rare in
  practice — the engine emits none itself — so the trade is a real measurement technique for a shape
  nobody writes. Recorded rather than built; if it is ever wanted, the decline-forcer needs a
  replacement first.
- **`order()` before `count()` — 25.2 ms, and ordering cannot change cardinality, so it LOOKS
  droppable. It is not: `order()` FAULTS on raw elements** ("order() over graph elements is not
  supported — elements have no natural order"), so dropping it would turn a raised error into a
  count. Whether it faults depends on the VALUES, not the plan, so no static test can decide it.
  Same shape as the GQL rule that an `evalBy` throw must win over the element fault.
- **`barrier()` — 14.3 ms, not taken**: it exists to buffer, and this engine has a recorded
  lazy-vs-eager deviation on `inject`+`limit(0)` shapes. Dropping a buffering step changes when
  things happen, which is exactly what that deviation is about.
- **`dedupe()` — not a candidate at all**: it changes the count whenever the stream has duplicates,
  and whether it does is a property of the data.

#### ⚠️ THE FINDING: paging is 10x apart between the two surfaces

Measured at 200,000 vertices, medians of 5:

```text
   GREMLIN  V().values(k).order().limit(10)         55.2 ms
   GREMLIN  V().values(k).order()        (full)     66.2        the limit saves 1.2x — a full sort
   GREMLIN  V().order().by(k).limit(10).values(k)   54.8
   GQL      MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS k ORDER BY k LIMIT 10      5.5
   GQL      MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS k ORDER BY k   (full)     47.7        top-k is 8.7x its own sort
```

**GQL's top-k is 8.7x its own full sort; Gremlin's `limit` is worth 1.2x.** Cross-surface, the same
question costs **10.0x more** in Gremlin. `boundedTopK`/`boundedTopKeyed` exist in the GQL executor
(item 1064) and `grep -i topk` over `packages/gremlin` returns NOTHING.

This is the repo's own equivalent-spellings principle one level up: two surface languages asking one
question should not differ by an order of magnitude when the cheaper algorithm is already written
next door.

#### ⚠️ Why this is recorded and not yet built

The existing `order()` work is heavily refuted — items 878/879/890/891/892 concluded the sort runs at
**1.13x its own floor** and "no change to `sortByBys` can reach that". **Those refutations do not
cover this**: they are about the full sort's constant factors, while a top-k is an ALGORITHMIC change
(O(n log n) → O(n log k)) — the distinction `closed-perf-targets` records as item 573's lesson, that
a big ratio may be algorithmic rather than a layout ceiling. Item 891's "do not reopen without
attacking the generator pipeline" is about the per-step cost, not about what algorithm the step runs.

The design, from reading both sides:

- **Fuse in `effectivePlan`**, beside `fuseValuesIsCount` — `order` immediately followed by `limit(n)`
  sets a `cap` on the order step. That is the established shape for a two-step fusion here.
- **Reuse GQL's algorithm, not its code.** `boundedTopK` is a max-heap whose comparator breaks ties on
  ARRIVAL INDEX, which is what reproduces `Array.prototype.sort`'s stability — and the Gremlin sort is
  stable today, with tie order compared against native. Ordering stays per-language by design
  (`shared-engine-layers`), so it is a sibling implementation with a pointer, not an import.
- ⚠️ **Keys must still be evaluated for EVERY input**, not just the kept ones. `sortByBys` evaluates
  every key before the element check specifically so a throwing `by` wins over the element fault; a
  selection that skipped rejected items would silently drop that fault. A heap still compares every
  item, so this falls out — but it is the thing to assert, not assume.

Two answer-visible properties to test: the tie order against the full-sort spelling, and that a
faulting `by` still raises when its item would not have been kept.

### Item 1574 — SHIPPED, **2.07x** on Gremlin paging (`order().limit(10)` 55.2 → 26.6 ms at 200,000 values, full-sort control flat) and **2.42x** on the element spelling: `order()` followed by `take(n)` now takes a bounded top-k. ⚠️ Item 1573 priced the cross-surface gap at 10.0x and **only half of it was the algorithm** — GQL is still 4.4x ahead. ⚠️ **And "the reason is identified" OVERSTATED it: item 1575 measured the addressable part at ~1.54x, not 4.4x** — the rest is producing the traversers, which no change here can avoid

Item 1573 measured the gap and designed the fix; this builds it.

#### What shipped

`fuseOrderTake` in `effectivePlan` (beside `fuseValuesIsCount`, the established two-step fusion)
sets a `cap` on an `order` step immediately followed by a global `take(n)`. `sortByBys` honours the
cap with `boundedTop`, a max-heap over INDICES whose comparator breaks ties on arrival position.

| arm                                          | PRE     | POST     |           |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------- | -------- | --------- |
| `V().values(k).order().limit(10)`            | 55.2 ms | **26.6** | **2.07x** |
| `V().order().by(k).limit(10).values(k)`      | 54.8    | **22.6** | **2.42x** |
| `V().values(k).order()` — full sort, control | 66.2    | 67.8     | flat      |
| GQL `ORDER BY k LIMIT 10`                    | 5.5     | 6.1      | untouched |

#### ⚠️ ITEM 1573'S 10.0x WAS NOT ALL ALGORITHM, and that correction matters more than the win

1573 recorded "10.0x apart on paging" and implied a top-k would close it. It closes **half**: 55.2 →
26.6 leaves GQL 4.4x ahead at 6.1 ms. The remainder is identified, not guessed —
**`orderStep` does `[...stream]`, materializing all 200,000 traversers before the selection**,
whereas GQL's `boundedTopK` consumes an `Iterable` and never holds more than `cap`. The capped path
cannot avoid EVALUATING every key (see the fault rule below), but it has no need to RETAIN every
traverser.

So the honest decomposition of 1573's 10.0x is roughly 2x algorithm, which is taken, and ~4.4x
materialization, which is not. Streaming the capped path is the follow-on, and it is a change to
`orderStep`'s shape rather than to the sort — which is also why it does not collide with items
878-892's refutations of `sortByBys`' constant factors.

#### Three things the design had to get right

- **Ties break on ARRIVAL INDEX.** Gremlin's sort is stable and tie order is compared against native,
  so the top-k must return the exact prefix a stable full sort would. A tie group straddling the cap
  is where a heap gets this wrong, so the fixture gives `k` only three distinct values over 30
  vertices — every cap lands inside a group — and every cap is compared against the sliced full
  sort. Two mutants (`no-tiebreak`, `final-sort-unstable`) die on it.
- **Keys are evaluated for EVERY item, and the element check still runs over all of them**, both
  above the selection. `sortByBys` evaluates every key before the element check precisely so a
  throwing `by` wins over the element fault; a selection that stopped once its heap was full would
  silently drop both. The `cap-the-input` mutant is exactly that mistake and dies on two tests —
  including one where the offending element is the LAST arrival and the cap is 1.
- **Deliberately narrow: only a `take` IMMEDIATELY after the order, both global.** A
  `skip(a).take(b)` needs `cap = a + b`; getting that wrong silently drops rows, so it does not fire.
  `fuse-past-skip` is the mutant, and it dies on 4 tests. **The `take` is also KEPT in the plan** —
  already satisfied by a capped order, so it costs one pass over at most `n` — which means the pass
  cannot change what the plan RETURNS even if a future cap were computed wrongly.

#### ⚠️ A crash my own test found, that GQL's version already guards

`boundedTop` with `cap === 0` left the heap empty and then dereferenced `heap[0]`, so
**`order().limit(0)` threw a TypeError**. GQL's `boundedTopK` has `if (cap <= 0) return []` as its
first line; I re-implemented the algorithm (ordering is per-language by design) and did not copy the
guard. The cap-0 case was in the test list from item 1573's design, which is the only reason it was
found before the suite — a full sort returns `[]` for `limit(0)` perfectly happily.

| remove the zero-cap guard                       | 1 test  |
| cap the INPUT (skipping the full element check) | 2 tests |
| fuse across a `skip`                            | 4 tests |

### Item 1575 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1574'S "4.4x on `[...stream]`" WAS AN UNMEASURED ATTRIBUTION; the real streaming ceiling is ~1.54x.** And the prerequisite turned out to be a missing test: item 890 recorded `sortByBys`' two-phase fault order as _"guarded by construction only, by no test"_, and it is now guarded — **a fuse-phases mutant fails 2 tests where 1,538 others pass**

Item 1574 shipped a top-k and attributed the remaining gap to GQL as "4.4x materialization". That was
a hypothesis stated as a cause. Pricing it changed the number and then changed the plan.

#### What `[...stream]` actually costs

First pass: `[...stream]` is **64.8%** of the capped path (92.5 ms of 142.6 over 5 reps). That reads
like a 2.8x ceiling — and it is wrong, because the stream is LAZY: the spread's time is upstream
generator work PLUS array growth, and streaming still pays the former.

Decomposed with a drain arm that iterates without accumulating:

```text
   SPREAD  [...stream]      consume 102.4 ms   sort 51.2     (5 reps, 200,000 values)
   DRAIN   for-of, no array consume  48.8      sort  0.0
   => array accumulation ~= 53.6 ms of 153.6 total  ->  ~1.54x, not 2.8x and not 4.4x
```

Still above the repo's ~10% floor, so worth having — but a third of what item 1574's entry implied.
**That entry's "4.4x" is corrected to "~1.54x of it is addressable"**; the rest is producing the
200,000 traversers, which no change to `orderStep` can avoid.

⚠️ **Two instrument bugs on the way, both caught by a control reading wrong rather than by review:**

- The drain arm was gated on `process.env.OS_DRAIN !== undefined`, and `OS_DRAIN=""` satisfies that —
  so BOTH arms drained. The giveaway was `sort=0.0` in the arm that was supposed to sort. Fixed to
  `=== '1'`; the arms then read 102.4/51.2 against 48.8/0.0, visibly distinct.
- The first spread/drain comparison therefore reported 46.8 against 50.1 — "accumulation is free" —
  which is the conclusion I would have published.

That is CLAUDE.md's "assert each A/B arm IS the code it claims" rule, and the assertion that worked
was not a grep but a field that had to be non-zero in one arm and zero in the other.

#### ⚠️ THE PREREQUISITE WAS A MISSING TEST, AND IT IS NOW WRITTEN

`sortByBys` evaluates every key BEFORE the element check, so _"an `evalBy` that throws still wins over
the element fault"_. Item 890's method note says that phase order **"is guarded by construction only,
by no test"** — and a streaming top-k is exactly a per-item loop, which would surface the ELEMENT
error where the engine surfaces the `by` throw. A different exception from the same query, which the
cross-engine differential compares.

It went untested because the case is awkward to construct: `order().by(fn)` with a raw function is
not a supported form (it is read as a plan, and fails with "plan.steps is not iterable"). The
construction that works is `by(pipe(fail(...)))`, plus a `choose` so one item's `by` yields an
ELEMENT and another's THROWS:

```text
   by = choose(has(flag), pipe(out(E)), pipe(fail(BY-BOOM)))
     `a` has flag -> key is a VERTEX (element), and `a` arrives FIRST
     `b` lacks it -> the by THROWS
   measured: BY-BOOM wins                     <- the documented precedence, confirmed
   control, element key only: the element error
```

**Mutation proves the teeth**: fusing the phases (check each key for an element as it is evaluated,
instead of after all of them) fails **exactly the two precedence tests** while the other **1,538**
gremlin tests pass. Two of the four tests also pin the precedence UNDER A CAP, so item 1574's top-k
cannot let the heap filling decide which fault wins.

⚠️ **TAKEN at item 1576: 1.43x, close to the 1.54x predicted here.** The streaming change is ~1.54x, the invariant it would disturb is now guarded, and the shape is
clear: one pass, a heap of at most `cap`, element faults DEFERRED to the end of the loop so a later
throwing `by` still wins. What is left is the work itself, which wants its own item rather than
riding on an entry whose main result is a corrected number and a closed test gap.

#### What shipped

`streamTopByBys`: one pass over the stream, a heap of at most `cap`, no array of the whole stream.
`orderStep` chooses it whenever a `cap` is set and keeps `sortByBys` otherwise.

| arm                                          | pre-1574 | 1574 | **1576** |                                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------- | ---- | -------- | -------------------------------- |
| `V().values(k).order().limit(10)`            | 55.2 ms  | 26.6 | **18.6** | 1.43x here, **2.97x cumulative** |
| `V().values(k).order().limit(100)`           | —        | —    | 14.1     |                                  |
| `V().order().by(k).limit(10).values(k)`      | 54.8     | 22.6 | **12.0** | 1.88x here, 4.57x cumulative     |
| `V().values(k).order()` — full sort, control | 66.2     | 67.8 | 72.0     | flat throughout                  |
| GQL `ORDER BY k LIMIT 10`                    | 5.5      | 6.1  | 5.8      | untouched                        |

Item 1575 predicted ~1.54x from the measured accumulation cost and it came in at 1.43x. The
cross-surface gap item 1573 opened at **10.0x** is now **3.2x**.

#### The correctness argument, which is the whole of this change

- **Element faults are DEFERRED to the end of the loop.** `sortByBys` evaluates every key before
  checking any for elements, so a throwing `by` wins over the element fault — item 890 recorded that
  phase order as guarded by construction only, and item 1575 tested it. A per-item check here would
  surface the element error where the engine surfaces the throw: a different exception from the same
  query, compared across engines. `element-per-item` is the mutant and it dies.
- **A `cap` of 0 still drains and still faults.** The `cap > 0` guard sits on the HEAP ACCESS, not on
  the loop.
- **No one-`by` specialization**, deliberately: item 879's fast path pays over `n log n` comparisons,
  and a bounded heap does ~`n` — one against the root per item.

#### ⚠️ A TEST OF MINE THAT PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON, found by a surviving mutant

`early-zero-cap` (return `[]` immediately when `cap <= 0`) **survived**, even though item 1575 added
a cap-0 fault test one tick earlier. The reason: that test was written as `order().limit(0)` over
elements, and a bare element `order()` is rejected by **`checkStep` at parse time** — it never
reaches `streamTopByBys` at all. The runtime element check is only reachable when a `by` YIELDS an
element, so the test was rewritten as `order().by(pipe(out('E'))).limit(0)`, and a second test now
pins the parse-time rejection separately so the two cannot be confused again.

**Third time this session a test's stated purpose was wrong while passing** (item 1569's
`with.where`, item 1572's identity assertion, this). The pattern is stable enough to state plainly:
**when a mutant survives a path you believe is covered, suspect the test before the taxonomy** — and
the diagnosis each time was to ask which code the test actually reaches, not whether it passes.

The second survivor was an ordinary gap: `keep-no-value` (retain items whose `by` yields NO_VALUE)
had no test, because nothing exercised a missing key under a cap. TinkerPop filters those out of the
ordering entirely, and under a cap they would otherwise occupy heap slots and appear in the result.
