### Item 1577 — SHIPPED, **4.27x** on building `traversal(V(id))` and **4.68x** on a three-step plan, **1.66x** on a whole small `V(id)` call: `appendStep` marked step functions with `Object.defineProperty`, which was **73% of plan construction**. Found by giving the Gremlin WRITE path its first probe, and the write path itself turned out healthy

`grep -c 'addV|addE|property|drop'` over every Gremlin probe in `packages/native` returned **0** — the
32-shape profile probe is reads only. Item 1554 found and closed the same gap on the GQL side, so
this is its twin, and `gremlin-write-probe.mjs` is now the instrument.

#### The write path is healthy, which is the negative result

Per operation at 20,000 vertices, the lookup key indexed (item 1554's lesson: its first run read a
20,000-vertex SCAN as write cost):

```text
   [floor] V(id)         0.98 us/op      the by-id read every write does first
   property on V(id)     1.80            ~0.8 us of actual write
   addV label            2.30
   addV + 2 props        3.55
   drop V(id)            6.53            detach cascades to incident edges
   addE between ids      7.15            but it does TWO V(id) lookups
```

**And the cross-surface comparison came back clean**, which is worth recording so it is not
re-measured: Gremlin `addE(...).from(V(id)).to(V(id))` is **6.89 us/op** against GQL's two-MATCH
`INSERT (a)-[:F]->(b)` at **7.27** — and net of each surface's own floor the Gremlin edge write is
_cheaper_ (2.68 against 4.22). No asymmetry here, unlike paging at items 1573-1576.

#### ⚠️ The finding was in the FLOOR, not the writes

Gremlin's `V(id)` floor is 0.98 us where GQL's indexed seek is 0.31 (item 1554). Decomposing it took
three passes, and the first two were wrong:

```text
   A  build only        (varying id)   0.235 us/op
   B  build + run       (varying id)   0.774
   C  run only          (FIXED plan)   0.214
   D  build + run       (FIXED id)     0.498
```

⚠️ **My first inference — "executing a fresh plan is 2.4x a reused one" — was a CONFLATION.** It came
from comparing B−A against C, but C uses a FIXED id while B varies it. `D − C ≈ A`, so construction
is ~0.235 and the B/D difference is the memory latency of a RANDOM versus repeated lookup in a
20,000-entry map, not plan freshness. The matched four-arm run is what separated them, and the
earlier two runs also differed in `OPS` and fixture — which is why they could not.

So construction is **~30% of a small `V(id)` call**, and Gremlin pays it on EVERY call whose value
varies: the id is baked into the step, so there is no plan to reuse. GQL's `$n` plus its parse/plan
cache serves every id from one compiled plan. ⚠️ **`bind(graph)` is NOT this** — it closes over the
graph only (`query`/`toArray`/`toSet` partially applied) and provides no value binding.

#### The fix, and why it is safe

`appendStep` ended with `Object.defineProperty(fn, STEP_FN, { value: true, enumerable: false })`.
Replacing it with a plain assignment:

| arm                      | PRE         | POST      |           |
| ------------------------ | ----------- | --------- | --------- |
| build `traversal(V(id))` | 0.235 us/op | **0.055** | **4.27x** |
| build a three-step plan  | 0.627       | **0.134** | **4.68x** |
| build + run `V(id)`      | 0.774       | **0.465** | **1.66x** |

So `defineProperty` was **73%** of construction. The same line existed in `steps/pipe.ts`; both are
changed.

**The `enumerable: false` it replaced bought nothing observable**, and that is the whole safety
argument, in two independent halves:

1. `STEP_FN` is a **Symbol**, and symbols are excluded from `Object.keys`, `for…in` and
   `JSON.stringify` regardless of enumerability.
2. An enumerable symbol does travel through `Object.assign`/spread — but only with the step function
   as the SOURCE, and every `Object.assign` in the package passes `fn` as the TARGET (the fluent
   `addE(…).from(…)`, `pageRank(…)`, `repeat(…)` builders).

`step-fn-marker.test.ts` pins both halves, and a third test states the consequence plainly: a future
`{ ...someStepFn }` WOULD carry the marker. Better met as a documented fact than as a surprise.

#### Mutation — and one mutant is deliberately not claimed

`no-marker` (24 tests) and `wrong-value` (22 tests) both die loudly. ⚠️ **Reverting to
`defineProperty` is behaviourally IDENTICAL**, so no test can catch it — it is a pure cost change,
the same category as item 1572's `KIND_BITS` gate. Saying so rather than inventing an assertion for
it.

⚠️ **A fourth mis-aimed test this session, but it FAILED rather than passing**: I asserted
`isSerializable(V())` is false, and `isSerializable` takes a PLAN — it crashed on `plan.steps.length`.
Rewritten as a plan check. A loud failure is the good outcome; items 1569/1572/1576 were the bad one.

### Item 1578 — ⚠️ **THE 32-SHAPE GREMLIN PROBE BUILDS EVERY PLAN ONCE AND REUSES IT, so it has never measured plan construction** — which is why item 1577's 4.27x moved no row in it. Measured properly, construction is a MEDIAN **48.1%** of `V().count()` and **51.5%** of `V(id)` even after 1577, and noise for anything expensive. ⚠️ My first attempt reported a **NEGATIVE 95.9%** build share. ⚠️⚠️ **AND THOSE SHARES DO NOT TRANSFER TO A SERVING CALL — item 1593 measured ~13-17%, not ~50%**: these shapes build and run the SAME traversal repeatedly, so the lookup KEY never varies, and at serving scale the varying key is 67% of the rebuilt-plan gap while construction is 33%

Item 1577 cut plan construction 4.27x, so the obvious next step was re-measuring the Gremlin shapes.
They cannot move, and finding out why is the result.

#### The standing instrument measures execution only

`runtime-profile-gremlin-probe.mjs` defines every `SHAPES` entry at module level —
`control: traversal(V(), count())` — and the timed loop is `toArray(plan, g)` with the SAME plan
object every rep. That is the right isolation for a profile: it keeps construction out of the frames.
But it means a caller whose values vary pays something the probe cannot see, because **Gremlin has no
parameter binding** — the value is baked into the step, so there is no plan to reuse (item 1577).

#### ⚠️ MY FIRST MEASUREMENT OF THE GAP WAS NONSENSE, AND THE SIGN IS WHAT CAUGHT IT

Four shapes in one process reported:

```text
   control   reused 0.142  fresh 0.265   build share  46.6%
   point     reused 1.139  fresh 0.581   build share -95.9%     <- fresh plans FASTER than reused
   hophas    reused 884.4  fresh 884.4                 0.0%
   valuesk   reused 531.0  fresh 515.7                -3.0%
```

A negative build share is impossible, and `point`'s reused arm reading 1.139 against item 1577's
0.214 for the same query was the second tell. **All four arms share one `toArray` call site, which
goes megamorphic** — item 762's dispatch pollution, and the repo's own one-shape-per-process rule,
which I had just violated. `gremlin-build-share-probe.mjs` takes `SHAPE=<name>` for that reason, and
its header records the -95.9% as the worked example.

#### What construction actually costs, one shape per process, three runs each

```text
   shape     build share (3 runs)          median     reused        fresh
   control   48.1%  47.6%  85.8%           48.1%      0.137-0.147   0.262-1.006
   point     51.5%  46.3%  72.7%           51.5%      0.427-0.616   1.145-1.565
   hophas    -0.4%                          noise     870.1         867.0
   valuesk   -0.3%                          noise     513.1         511.5
```

**So construction is roughly HALF of a cheap call and nothing at all for an expensive one.** The
split is clean: a point lookup or an O(1) count is construction-dominated, and anything that walks
the graph is not. That is the useful decision rule — further construction work only pays for the
serving shape, which is exactly where a server lives.

⚠️ **Take the MEDIAN of several runs.** The `reused` arm is steady (0.137-0.147 for `control`) while
the `fresh` arm spikes — 0.262, 0.284, then 1.006 — which is the GC of allocating a plan per call. A
single run can read the share as high as 85.8%, and I nearly recorded 55.9%/59.2% from one run each
into the probe's own header before re-running.

#### What is left, and the structural fix

~0.18 us of construction remains on `V().count()`: one step object, one closure, one plan object, the
`[...plan.steps, step]` spread (O(n) per step, so O(n²) per plan — trivial at 2-4 steps), plus
`analyzeStep` and `maskOfSteps` per step-constructor call. None of it is memoizable while the value
varies.

**The structural fix is Gremlin parameter binding** — one compiled plan serving many values, which is
what GQL's `$n` plus its parse/plan cache already does. TinkerPop has `Bindings` for exactly this, so
it would be conformant rather than invented syntax. ⚠️ And `bind(graph)` is NOT it: it closes over the
graph only. That is a surface-language feature, not a perf tweak, so it is recorded here rather than
attempted.

#### Gates

and does not measure. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites: gremlin 1551/0, native 963/0; the rest
unchanged from item 1577.

### Item 1579 — the GQL probe does **NOT** have item 1578's blind spot, and the brief's O(1) concern extends to indexed seeks: **varying the VALUE is free** (0.692 against 0.759 us for a fixed one). Varying the TEXT is 2.7x, already priced. ⚠️ **TWO in-process measurements this tick returned IMPOSSIBLE answers, and both would have supported a story**

Item 1578 found that the Gremlin probe reuses plan objects and so cannot see construction. The
obvious question is whether the GQL probe has the same gap. It does not, and the reason is
structural: `query(g, text, params)` is keyed on TEXT, so one cached plan serves every value — which
is exactly what a parameterised caller does. The probe's cached-plan path IS the realistic path.

#### ⚠️ BUT THE FIRST TWO MEASUREMENTS WERE CONTAMINATED, AND THE SIGN SAVED BOTH TIMES

Several arms in one process, in order:

```text
   attempt 1   param FIXED text  1.493     interpolated VARY text  2.101     interpolated SAME text  0.312
   attempt 2   param FIXED value 1.444     param VARYING value     0.657
```

Attempt 1 invited "parameterised queries are 4.8x slower than interpolated ones". Attempt 2 says a
**fixed value is slower than a varying one**, which cannot be true — the varying arm does strictly
more work, a random bucket in a 20,000-entry index against the same bucket every time. The pattern is
that whichever arm runs FIRST pays: the shared `query` call site warms up, so POSITION BEATS EFFECT.
That is item 182's recorded finding for the spelling probe, rediscovered by violating the
one-shape-per-process rule twice in one tick.

I was midway through an explanation of a "1.18 us varying index seek" when the second impossible sign
stopped it. **The explanation was ready before the measurement was.**

#### One arm per process, median of the last four of seven rounds

```text
   paramfixed    0.759 us/op    cached plan, cached bucket
   paramvary     0.692          cached plan, RANDOM bucket each call
   interpfixed   0.672          interpolated but constant text — auto-parameterization normalizes it
   interpvary    1.849          a UNIQUE text per call
   byid          0.084          the raw map lookup underneath
```

**Varying the value costs NOTHING** (0.692 against 0.759, the varying arm nominally faster). So the
hash index seek is genuinely O(1) in the sense the brief asks about, not just `getVertexById` — and
the 1.18 us I was chasing does not exist.

**Varying the TEXT costs 2.7x** (1.849 against 0.692), and that is already priced: the comment above
`normalizeLiterals` records a tokenize at **~865 ns**, which plus the params allocation is the gap.
Item 1502 introduced the normalization so a unique interpolated text still lands on ONE compiled
plan, and item 1541 added the four-slot memo for repeated identical text. For genuinely unique texts
it is irreducible — normalizing requires tokenizing — so there is no target here, only a reason to
prefer `$params`, which is a DX point (`discoverability-is-the-bottleneck`) rather than an engine one.

⚠️ **One caveat on the new probe's own numbers**: the round series still descends at round seven
(`6.4, 6.2, 5.5, 2.3, 2.3, 1.9, 1.0` for `paramfixed`), so the steady state is BELOW the median
reported. The figures above are therefore upper bounds, and a comparison between two arms is sounder
than either absolute. Said rather than quietly over-reported.

#### What is left on the point-query floor

A fully cached GQL point query is 0.692 us against a 0.084 us raw map lookup, so ~0.6 us is engine

### Item 1580 — ⚠️ **THE RUST ENGINE'S WRITE-INVALIDATION CLIFF DOES NOT EXIST IN TS, measured both ways.** CLAUDE.md records that one `add_edge` demotes EVERY later Rust read for the session (up to 24.07x); in TS, `afterone` is **0.30 us/read against `reads` 0.30** over 2,000 reads. What TS does pay is **~1.2 us on the NEXT closed-form count per write**, re-armed immediately — and **nothing at all** on the walking path

CLAUDE.md is emphatic about this on the Rust side: `rebuild_csr` runs only at LOAD, every adjacency
write clears `csr_fresh`, **nothing re-arms it**, so one `add_edge` demotes every later read for the
rest of the session — 1.96x at 1 edge in 2, 2.93x at 1 in 10, **24.07x at 1 in 50**. The TS engine
had no counterpart measured either way, and the natural assumption is that the figures carry over.
They do not.

#### The three arms that distinguish the two worlds

```text
   reads        N reads, no writes             the baseline
   interleaved  N x (one write, one read)      the serving pattern
   afterone     ONE write, then N reads        <- the diagnostic
```

`afterone ≈ reads` means caches re-arm; `afterone ≈ interleaved` means one write poisons everything
after it. At `REPS=2000`, one arm per process, over 20,000 vertices / 100,000 edges with 1 edge in 10
carrying the queried type:

```text
   reads         0.30 us/iter     rounds  2.1  0.8  0.7  0.6  0.6
   writes        1.80             rounds  4.5  4.1  3.9  3.8  3.5
   interleaved   3.30             rounds  6.3  5.1  5.0  4.7  6.6
   afterone      0.30             rounds  1.9  0.8  0.6  0.6  0.6    <- identical to `reads`
```

**`afterone` is exactly `reads`**, so after one write all 2,000 subsequent reads run at full speed:
the first read re-arms whatever the write invalidated. That is the Rust bug's absence, and it is the
result worth having — the alternative reading (that CLAUDE.md's 24x applies here too) would have
justified a large piece of work on a problem this engine does not have.

What TS does pay: `interleaved` 3.30 against `reads + writes` 2.10, a gap of **~1.2 us per
iteration**. So a write costs the NEXT closed-form count about 1.2 us of rebuild, once.

#### ⚠️ And the first version of this probe was not measuring a walk at all

`V().out(T).count()` is answered in CLOSED FORM off degree sums, which the rounds gave away
immediately: **200 reads in 0.1 ms**. That tests the count rung and says nothing about the walking
path the Rust CSR penalty actually lives on. A second read that materializes a value per edge and
must walk:

```text
   readswalk        425.0 us/read
   afteronewalk     442.5
   interleavedwalk  447.5
```

All three within 5%, so **no rebuild penalty is visible on the walking path** — interleaving costs
only the writes themselves, which are ~1.8 us against a 425 us read. Both paths now covered, which is
what makes the negative result trustworthy rather than an artefact of picking a shape that shortcuts.

#### The one lever this leaves, priced

In a workload that alternates a write with a closed-form count, the ~1.2 us rebuild is **36% of the
3.30 us iteration**. Maintaining the degree sums INCREMENTALLY on write — rather than invalidating
and rebuilding on next read — would recover it. Not attempted: incremental counter maintenance is
precisely where a wrong answer hides (every `addEdge`/`removeEdge`/label change has to agree), and
the payoff is confined to write-then-count alternation. Recorded with its number so the next person
chooses rather than rediscovers.

#### Gates

No engine change — one new probe (`ts-write-invalidation-probe.mjs`), which takes `ARM=<name>` for

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites unchanged from item 1579.

#### Why a cross-surface probe, and why now

Reviewing what actually paid this session: the wins were STRUCTURAL, and almost all were found by
comparing two spellings or two surfaces rather than by reading a profile share — unread bindings
(1567-1569, 1572), a loop-invariant hoist (1566), one-column keying (1561/1562), a top-k (1574/1576).

`bun run spelling:gremlin`). **Nothing compared the same question ACROSS them**, and that is exactly
where item 1573 found paging 10.0x apart — by hand. `cross-surface-probe.mjs` makes it systematic:
10 questions, each asked in both languages, **every pair's answer asserted equal**, timed in two
passes in opposite order keeping the better reading per surface.

```text
   hop distinct     gql  34.283ms   gremlin  0.655ms   52.37x  GQL slower
   group count      gql  24.433     gremlin  0.789     30.97x  GQL slower
   paging           gql   1.359     gremlin  3.839      2.83x  gremlin slower   (item 1576's residual)
```

```text
   hop distinct   gql  30.75  30.04  29.55 ms    gremlin  0.55  0.54  0.32    56.3x  55.9x  93.6x
   group count    gql  21.19  20.89  21.24       gremlin  0.78  0.78  0.79    27.1x  26.7x  26.9x
```

⚠️ **Quote the GQL absolute, not the ratio.** The GQL side is stable to ~4%; the entire spread lives
on the Gremlin side, which at 0.32-0.55 ms is close enough to `FLOOR_MS` that the third run's

#### ⚠️ The `group count` flag is NOT a cross-language cost difference. It is a spelling defect

`CLOSED.md` has 74 mentions of `count(DISTINCT` and 7 of `detectGroupedNodeAggregate`, so the first
move was the mentions rather than a profile. Item 1249 closed `ORDER BY` on a grouped aggregate; this
shape has no `ORDER BY`. Reading the rung's gate instead of guessing:

```text
   clauses.length !== 2        -> a LET clause in front of the RETURN declines on ARITY ALONE
   proj.items.length < 2       -> a ONE-COLUMN grouped count declines, before anything reads the key
```

So `group-count-spelling-probe.mjs`, one arm per process, 50,000 vertices, 97 groups, identical
answers:

```text
   alias2   MATCH (n) RETURN n.k AS key, count(*) AS c GROUP BY n.k    0.652 ms   <- reaches the tally
   alias1   MATCH (n) RETURN count(*) AS c            GROUP BY n.k    16.051      24.6x
   let2     MATCH (n) LET grp = n.k RETURN count(*) AS c GROUP BY grp 22.421      34.4x
   nokey    MATCH (n) RETURN count(*) AS c                             0.003      (ungrouped control)
```

**Gremlin's `groupCount({by:'k'})` answers the same question in 0.78 ms, which is `alias2`'s cost.**
So the fast rung is the CORRECT price and the other two spellings are the defect — the cross-surface
ratio was reporting a GQL-internal gap, not a language one. This is precisely the failure mode
CLAUDE.md names: _"the planner recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned for another that
meant exactly the same thing… each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct answer."_

⚠️ **And the one-column spelling is the one a user reaches for**, because it asks for strictly LESS:
the group key is not even wanted in the output. The rung declines it for needing a second projection
item it has no use for. Not fixed this tick — a rung-selection change wants its own item, its own
mutation pass and the `one shape per process` instrument item 762 prescribes, since routing some
shapes elsewhere cleans the inline caches of the site left behind.

#### ⚠️ `GROUP BY <output alias>` is a syntax error, which narrows the fast shape further

`MATCH (n) RETURN n.k AS key, count(*) AS c GROUP BY key` raises `variable \`key\` is not defined`.
That is correct — GROUP BY is evaluated before the projection, so it cannot see an alias the
projection introduces — but it means the fast two-column shape must REPEAT the expression, and the
memory note recording "GROUP BY takes a bound name only" is narrower than it reads: `GROUP BY n.k`
is accepted, and it is the spelling the fast rung requires.

#### Two things the cross-surface probe needed, both learned from this session's own mistakes

- ⚠️ **A FLOOR.** Its first run flagged `count label` at 2.06x and `hop count` at 2.87x on readings of

  item 127 for the same reason.
- ⚠️ **TWO PASSES IN OPPOSITE ORDER.** Items 1578 and 1579 each produced an impossible in-process

⚠️ **And the normalizer was wrong in a way that faked ten findings.** `query` yields ROW OBJECTS
(`[{c: 50000}]`); `toArray` yields bare VALUES (`[50000]`). Taking `Object.values(row)[0]` on a number
gives `undefined`, so the first run reported **"ANSWERS DISAGREE" on all ten pairs** with timings
beside them. Had it been wrong in the other direction — silently agreeing — the ratios would have
been published against nothing.

Restructuring the question list from tuples to objects, three multi-line entries did not match because

### Item 1582 — **24.7x on the one-column grouped count**, both spellings, by admitting it to the tally that already answered its two-column twin: 15.33 ms to 0.62, measured against a general-path control on the SAME build. The cross-surface flag item 1581 opened at 30.97x now reads 1.32-1.48x, with GQL the FASTER side. ⚠️ And writing explicit coverage for the shape found a PRE-EXISTING WRONG ANSWER in the Rust engine

Item 1581 priced this and did not take it. The gate was arity, in `groupedProjection`:

```text
   proj.items.length !== 2     declines a grouped count that does not project its key
```

`MATCH (n) RETURN count(*) AS c GROUP BY n.k` asks for strictly LESS than the two-column form —
the group key is not even wanted in the output — and was refused for lacking a second projection
item the tally has no use for. The key for that form comes from `GROUP BY` instead of from a
projection item, which is the whole of the change: `groupedProjection` now returns `keyExpr` and a
`keyCol` that is `undefined` for the one-column form, and one shared `groupedCountRow` emits either
one column or two.

#### The numbers, all 97 groups over 50,000 vertices, three runs each

```text
   ord1     RETURN count(*) AS c GROUP BY n.k ORDER BY c     15.761  13.990  15.329 ms   <- general path
   alias1   RETURN count(*) AS c GROUP BY n.k                 0.608   0.623   0.621      24.7x
   let2     LET grp = n.k RETURN count(*) AS c GROUP BY grp   0.616   0.623   0.611      24.7x
   alias2   RETURN n.k AS key, count(*) AS c GROUP BY n.k     0.624   0.613   0.622      CONTROL, flat
   nokey    RETURN count(*) AS c                              0.001   0.001   0.001      ungrouped control
```

⚠️ **`ord1` is the instrument's point.** `ORDER BY` declines the new rung by design, so that arm asks
the same question over the same scan and still runs the general path — on the SAME BUILD as the fast
arms. That is what makes 24.7x a measurement rather than a comparison of two builds, and it
independently reproduces item 1581's cross-build 16.05 ms. The `alias2` control is flat (0.613-0.624
against 0.652 before the change), which matters because CLAUDE.md's rule is that a control moving
more than the target is the giveaway for a bad instrument.

⚠️ **AND IT DID MOVE, at 9 reps.** The first post-change run read `alias2` at **1.427 ms**, a 2.2x
REGRESSION in the control. The series was `1.5 1.0 1.0 1.4 1.5 1.6 0.7 0.6 0.6` — bimodal, with
warm-up running past the three dropped reps, so the median landed on the wrong mode. At 30 reps it is
0.62 and flat. Nine reps is not enough for this shape, and the control is what said so.

Cross-surface, the flag item 1581 opened:

```text
   group count   BEFORE   gql 24.433ms   gremlin 0.789ms   30.97x GQL slower
                 AFTER    gql  0.589      gremlin 0.812      1.32-1.48x, GQL FASTER
```

#### ⚠️⚠️ A PRE-EXISTING WRONG ANSWER IN THE RUST ENGINE, found by covering the shape

```text
   SELECT count(*) AS c FROM MATCH (n:P) GROUP BY n.k
       ts   [{"c":2},{"c":1},{"c":1}]     3 groups  — correct
       nat  [{"c":4}]                     ONE group — the GROUP BY is DROPPED
```

Native drops the grouping exactly when the form is `SELECT`, the grouping key is **not** in the
select list, and there is **no** `HAVING`. Each conjunct matters and each was checked: the `RETURN`
spelling of the same question agrees, `HAVING count(*) >= 1` makes native correct, and the
two-column `SELECT` agrees. Per ISO a select list holding only an aggregate still yields one row per
group, so TS is right.

⚠️ **That it predates this change is MEASURED, not assumed.** `ORDER BY` declines the new rung, so
`… GROUP BY n.k ORDER BY c` runs the TS GENERAL path — the code that answered this shape before item
1582 — and it diverges identically. `select-group-probe-1582.mjs` prints the five-way comparison.

**NOT registered**, deliberately: `divergence-registry` refuses a `value` axis on purpose ("if the
engines disagree about the answer to a determinate question, that is a bug in one of them, and no
entry may excuse it"). It is encoded as an `test.failing` expected failure, which documents it and
turns red the moment native is fixed, rather than a skip that would go quiet. Fixing it is Rust-side
and out of this item's scope. **This is the 10th open cross-engine divergence.**

#### ⚠️ `bun run fuzz` was GREEN before any of this was written, and said nothing

Every fuzzer's grouped shape is the TWO-column `RETURN k, count(*) AS c GROUP BY k` — `genQuery` in
`backend-parity-fuzz`, and the `simpleGroup` counter in `differential-fuzz`. **No fuzzer generates
the one-column form at all**, so a change to which columns a rung emits sailed through the sweep
that exists to catch exactly that. The shape now has explicit TS-vs-native coverage
(`one-column-grouped-count-parity.test.ts`, 22 queries, compared as row multisets with column order
asserted exactly). This is CLAUDE.md's own warning arriving in a new place: a generative test whose
teeth were never verified is worse than no test, because it is believed.

#### Mutation: 8 of 8 caught, and the first run caught only 5

The three survivors all degraded the rung to DECLINING, which is answer-equivalent, so no
correctness test could see them — `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` exactly. Adding ROUTE assertions
against `detectGroupedNodeCount` / `detectGroupedHopCount` (does this query reach the tally, yes or
no) turned all three red:

```text
   row/keyCol-inverted              CAUGHT  56 fail
   row/count-zeroed                 CAUGHT  19 fail
   gate/admit-three-items           CAUGHT   1 fail
   route/refuse-one-column          CAUGHT   2 fail     <- SURVIVED before the route tests
   gate/no-groupby-required         CAUGHT   9 fail
   gate/admit-multi-key-groupby     CAUGHT   7 fail
   gate/allow-order-by              CAUGHT   2 fail
   key/from-projection-not-groupby  CAUGHT   2 fail     <- SURVIVED before the route tests
```

A ninth mutant, `gate/admit-zero-items`, survived and was NOT a test gap: an empty projection
already declines at `countAt === -1`, since `findIndex` finds no `count(*)` in it. So the
`proj.items.length < 1` half of the guard was dead and went the way of item 475's — a line no test
can fail on, whose redundancy is provable by reading. The mutant was replaced with
`gate/admit-three-items`, which the route tests catch.

The cap was proven before it was trusted, per CLAUDE.md: an allocator bomb died 137 and a bare
infinite loop 124.

#### What the one-column form still declines, and why

`ORDER BY`. Its only resolvable sort target is the count column, and `colSortsOf` is written around a
projected KEY column this form does not have. Declining is answer-equivalent — `ord1` proves the
general path answers it correctly — so this is a missing optimization and not a bug. It is also the
same 15.33 ms, which makes `ORDER BY c` on a grouped count the next rung-level target in this
family.

#### ⚠️ Process: item 1581 shipped markdown the formatter rejects

`bun run check` ran BEFORE that entry was appended to this file, not after, so `fmt:check` never saw
it — and oxfmt normalizes `*` bullets to `-` and `*…*` to `_…_`. The normalization rides along in
this commit. Memory already records that `fmt` exiting 0 is not `fmt:check` passing; the sharper rule
is to run the gate AFTER writing the entry, which is the order this item used.

### Item 1583 — **up to 6.00x on `count(DISTINCT …)` over a hop**, because the dedup-while-walking rung was WRITTEN, CORRECT AND WILLING and a broader rung sat ahead of it in the chain: `hopAggregate` took every such shape and `distinctCount` never ran. The node-only twin reached it and was 10x faster, decided entirely by which detector happened to be listed first

Item 1581's cross-surface probe flagged `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(DISTINCT b)` at **52.37x**
its Gremlin twin. The useful part was not the ratio but what the diagnosis turned out to be.

#### Time could not answer the question; `compileLinear` could

The hop spellings measured 17.9-29.9 ms while the node-only twin measured 2.6 — but a hop walks
150,000 edges where the node scan visits 50,000 vertices, so a slow arm might simply have more work.
**Timing cannot distinguish "declined the rung" from "took the rung and had more to do."**

`compileLinear` runs all nineteen detectors and returns the set, so reading its fields names the
route directly (`hop-distinct-route-probe.mjs`). That gave the answer at once:

```text
   count(DISTINCT b)      hopAggregate, distinctCount      <- BOTH accept
   count(DISTINCT b.k)    hopAggregate, distinctCount
   count(DISTINCT a.n)    hopAggregate, distinctCount
   MATCH (n:P) count(DISTINCT n.n)   distinctCount, nodeAggregate
```

`distinctCount` was non-null for **every** hop spelling — the narrow rung was willing all along. But
`hopAggregate` was non-null too, and it sits at `runLinear`'s line 1562 against `distinctCount`'s
1592, so it answered first every time. For the node-only shape the competing rung is `nodeAggregate`
at line 1608, **below** `distinctCount`, so there the narrow rung won. Same rung, opposite outcome,
decided by nothing but listing order.

#### The fix is a compile-time gate, not a reordered branch

```ts
const distinctCount = detectDistinctCount(fast, clauses);
const hopAggregate = distinctCount === null ? detectHopAggregate(fast, clauses) : null;
```

Moving the `distinctCount` branch above `hopAggregate` in the chain would put a branch ahead of a hot
dispatch, which **item 418 measured costing the shape it does not claim 1.12x**. This decides it once
per query at compile time, so the runtime chain is untouched. And no shape rule is duplicated —
nothing re-derives what `distinctCount` accepts, it just asks, because two copies of one rule is how
the far endpoint ended up on a per-edge tally once before (`detectDistinctCount`'s own note).

The index-seek concern answers itself: `distinctShape` requires `whereReadsOnly(where, keyedVar)`, so
a cross-end `WHERE` — exactly the shape where `hopAggregate`'s EXECUTION-TIME decline can hand the
query to a seek on the end it does not drive — already declines `distinctCount`, and there the gate
does nothing. That is asserted as a route test, not reasoned about and left.

#### The numbers, 50,000 vertices / 150,000 edges, answers unchanged throughout

```text
                                      PRE      POST
   count(DISTINCT b.k)   far, 97       22.418    3.735    6.00x
   count(DISTINCT a.n)   start, uniq   17.870    4.416    4.05x
   count(DISTINCT b.n)   far, uniq     29.230    8.820    3.31x
   count(DISTINCT a)     start, node   20.923   11.545    1.81x
   count(DISTINCT b)     far, node     29.928   16.611    1.80x
```

The spread is the rung's own structure showing through: the start-keyed arms benefit most because
`detectDistinctCount` **breaks out of a vertex's bucket at the first qualifying edge** when the dedup
is keyed on the start, which `hopAggregate` cannot do — it has to fold every row.

⚠️ **Controls, measured as a real A/B rather than argued from construction.** The gate only nulls
`hopAggregate` when `distinctCount` accepts, so a non-DISTINCT hop aggregate executes identical code
and a regression is "impossible by construction" — which is the reasoning this file exists to
distrust. Both arms were built from saved copies, each ASSERTED to be the code it claimed before
either was built:

```text
                PRE      POST
   hopmax       10.715    9.307
   hopmin        8.605    8.480
   hopsum       20.945   18.623
   hopmulti     20.439   18.678
   hopproj      12.060   11.768
   nodeonlyprop  2.614    2.559     (the untouched route)
```

Flat within noise. POST reads marginally faster across the board, which is noise and **not** claimed
as a win.

#### Correctness: the two rungs could have disagreed about NULL, and that is checked

`detectDistinctCount`'s own doc records that it drops nulls before the set, where the ROWS path keeps
a null as a row. If `distinctCountFold` — the fold `hopAggregate` used — did not hold the same rule,
this reroute would have silently changed answers. So the null cases are pinned twice: against NATIVE
as the oracle (unaffected by a TS route change) in `hop-distinct-count-route-parity.test.ts`, and as
LITERAL values, because two engines can agree and both be wrong. `count(DISTINCT b.nope)` over a
property no vertex has is **0, not 1**, and the rows spelling still yields its null row.

⚠️ `bun run fuzz` was green throughout and is not evidence here: `genQuery` generates no
`count(DISTINCT …)` over a hop at all — the same blind spot item 1582 found for the one-column
grouped count, now confirmed to extend to a second rung family.

#### Mutation: 4 of 4 caught, and all four are ANSWER-EQUIVALENT

Reverting the gate, inverting its condition, and nulling either detector all leave every answer
correct and change only the speed. The route tests are the only thing that can see them, which is
item 1582's lesson applied before the fact rather than after:

```text
   gate/reverted                    CAUGHT   6 fail
   gate/condition-inverted          CAUGHT  11 fail
   gate/hopAggregate-always-null    CAUGHT   5 fail
   gate/distinctCount-always-null   CAUGHT   7 fail
```

#### What remains, priced

The cross-surface flag went **52.37x to ~31x** (GQL 34.28 to 17.0 ms on that query) and is still
open, because the flagged spelling dedups on the NODE and that is the arm this change helped least.
The residual has a measured cause rather than a guessed one: `count(DISTINCT b)` at 16.611 against
`count(DISTINCT b.n)` at 8.820 — **same cardinality (50,000), same walk, same rung** — so **1.88x is
attributable purely to keying an ELEMENT instead of a scalar**.

⚠️ ~~An identity-keyed set for the element case is the next target~~ — **TAKEN AT 1584, but NOT that
way, and the mechanism named here was half wrong.** An identity `Set` in front of the key made it
**1.24-1.39x WORSE**; what worked was a container keyed on the id ITSELF rather than on `valueKey`'s
`'@' + id` string (1.92-2.31x, and it did also land on `distinctProjection` as predicted). Gremlin's
`dedupe()` keying on object identity was the wrong model to copy.

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites gql 4008, core 431, gremlin 1551, native 1010, serialization
144 — 0 fail. `bun run fuzz` 20/0 under the 16G cap.

### Item 1584 — **1.92-2.31x on dedup over ELEMENTS**, by giving them a container keyed on the id itself instead of on the `'@' + id` string `valueKey` builds. ⚠️ Two hypotheses were REFUTED first, one of them made it 1.24-1.39x WORSE — and the sweep for more of item 1583's starved-rung defect found NONE, which closes that class

Item 1583 left the cross-surface `hop distinct` flag open at ~31x and priced the residual as
"element-identity dedup, 1.88x". Two of the three attacks on that price were wrong, and the order
they were tried in is the story.

#### First: the sweep for more starved rungs, which found NOTHING

Item 1583's defect — a willing narrow rung starved by a broader one above it in `runLinear`'s lazy
19-branch chain — looked like a CLASS rather than a one-off, so `rung-contention-probe.mjs`
enumerates it: 40 shapes through `compileLinear`, reporting every one that more than one rung will
answer. Of 40 shapes, **4 are contended, and in all four the winner is the narrower, faster rung**:

```text
   distinctCount      WINS over nodeAggregate          MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(DISTINCT n.k)
   distinctCount      WINS over nodeAggregate          MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(DISTINCT n)
   groupCountShortcut WINS over groupedNodeAggregate    … RETURN n.k, count(*) GROUP BY n.k
   groupHopShortcut   WINS over groupedHopAggregate     … RETURN b.k, count(*) GROUP BY b.k
```

So item 1583's was the only instance in this corpus and **the class is closed, not open.** A negative
result, recorded because the alternative is re-running the sweep next time the thought occurs. The
probe stays, since "which rung answers this?" is a question that cost item 1583 a near-mis-pricing.

#### ⚠️ REFUTED, with numbers: an identity `Set` in front of the key

The graph hands out one object per vertex — verified through id lookup, scan, and both ends of an
edge — so a far-end dedup offers 150,000 elements that are only 50,000 objects. An identity `Set`
consulted first should then skip two thirds of the key building, and it is SEMANTICS-PRESERVING
(having seen this exact object, it was already keyed). It made things **worse**:

```text
   count(DISTINCT b)   16.611 -> 20.546 ms    1.24x WORSE
   count(DISTINCT a)   11.545 -> 16.022       1.39x WORSE
```

A `Set<object>` probe costs more than the key it saves. Reverted.

#### ⚠️ ALSO REFUTED: the per-element binding write and closure call

`count(DISTINCT b)` names the bare variable, so `directPropKey` is undefined and the rung takes its
general arm: a `binding.set` and a compiled-expression call PER ELEMENT whose whole job is to read
the binding back out and return the element already in hand. Short-circuiting that to `value = el`
is **flat** — 16.611 to 16.100, 11.545 to 10.842, 7.059 to 6.756, all inside the ~10% noise floor.
Not shipped: a flat change to the executor is not free, because `executor-edits-perturb` records
that a new walk variant costs unrelated rows up to 16%.

#### What actually worked, and why the first attempt could not see it

`valueKey` keys anything id-bearing as `'@' + String(v.id)`. The `'@'` is a CONSTANT within a
container of its own, so a dedicated container keyed on `String(v.id)` is **exactly the same
equivalence** and builds no string at all for a string id — the same "one container per kind" trade
`LocalDate` and the zoned kinds already make, and the same reason they are never shared.

```text
                                                 PRE      POST
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN DISTINCT b        21.958   11.425 ms   1.92x
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(DISTINCT b) 17.895    9.172      1.95x
   MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(DISTINCT n)            7.425    3.210      2.31x
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(DISTINCT a) 11.381    5.126      2.22x
   count(DISTINCT b.n)   scalar control            8.820    8.497      flat
   MATCH (n:P) count(DISTINCT n.n)  control        2.559    2.559      flat
```

Both arms were built from saved copies, each ASSERTED to be the code it claimed before either was
built. **The first attempt was CONFOUNDED**: it removed string builds _and_ added an object `Set`, so
its regression was read as "the string was never the cost" when the string was most of it. One change
at a time is the rule that would have found this two attempts earlier.

`count(DISTINCT b)` is now 9.17 against `count(DISTINCT b.n)`'s 8.50 — the element/scalar gap item
1583 priced at 1.88x is **1.08x**, so the diagnosis is confirmed by the gap closing rather than by
the speedup alone.

#### ⚠️ MUTATION FOUND A REAL GAP, AND THE GAP WAS A PRE-EXISTING TS BUG

The first run caught 2 of 6. Four survived, and chasing them produced the tick's most useful finding
— starting with a tripwire, because `always-new` surviving meant either the branch was not reached
or the tests did not look:

```text
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(DISTINCT b)   ids-branch hits = 20,000   edges = 60,000
```

**The set is offered each element EXACTLY ONCE.** The walk is far-driven — one visit per candidate
vertex, not per edge — so `ids.has` never fires in any shape that reaches this container, and the
var-length and two-hop shapes do not reach it at all (0 hits). Hence the survivors: with the verdict
never consulted twice, breaking the verdict changes nothing.

Except one of them was not that. `ids/no-string-coercion` survived because nothing covered it, and
**a vertex id may be a NUMBER** (`addVertex({id: 5})` stores `5`). Which exposes this:

```text
   two DISTINCT vertices, ids 5 and '5'
       count(*)            ts 2   nat 2
       count(DISTINCT n)   ts 1   nat 2      <- TS conflates them
```

`'@' + String(v.id)` makes a numeric id and its string form one value, so TWO REAL VERTICES collapse
in a dedup. **Native is right and TS is wrong**, and it is PRE-EXISTING — item 1584 preserves it
deliberately, because preserving the equivalence exactly is what makes a perf change a perf change.
It is now pinned as the CURRENT state, with the fix described where the test is: two containers, one
for string ids and one for the rest, which costs nothing since neither needs a tag. **That fix is its
own item**: `valueKey`'s conflation is shared by `groupIndex` and the set-operation dedup, so fixing
one site alone would make DISTINCT and GROUP BY disagree with each other.

Final mutation, after that test: **4 of 6 caught.** `CONTROL/elements-to-structural` is the intended
answer-equivalent control (it reverts to pre-1584 keying and costs only speed), and
`ids/shared-with-structural` is unreachable-equivalent — no structural key can equal a raw id string,
since a string value keys into `prim`.

#### ⚠️ Two more PRE-EXISTING divergences, found by writing the parity coverage

Both proven to predate this change: the probes produce **byte-identical output against a build with
the change and one without**.

- **A WRONG ANSWER in native.** Over five edges with five distinct ids,
  `MATCH ()-[e:E]->() RETURN count(DISTINCT e)` is **ts 5, nat 3** — while `RETURN DISTINCT e` agrees
  at five rows and `count(*)` agrees at 5. So native's dedup finds five distinct edges in the ROWS
  path and counts three in the COUNT path; the two disagree inside native itself, which localizes it
  to `count(DISTINCT <edge>)` and rules out the match. Naming the ends changes nothing. **11th open
  divergence.**
- **A COLUMN NAME divergence.** An UNALIASED list projection is `expr` in TS and `col0` in native;
  `AS x` makes them agree. Column naming is part of the bytes a caller sees. **12th.**

Neither is registered: `divergence-registry` refuses a `value` axis on purpose. Both are `test.failing`
expected failures, which turn red when fixed rather than going quiet like a skip.

#### Also recorded, pre-existing and unrelated

An edge may be created with a vertex's id, and a vertex then renders with the EDGE's labels — found
while probing reachability, byte-identical across both builds, and not pursued.

#### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites gql 4021, core 431, gremlin 1551, native 1031, serialization
144 — 0 fail. `bun run fuzz` 20/0 under the 16G cap. **And the fuzzers are partly informative here
for once**: `differential-fuzz` does generate `count(DISTINCT b)` over a var-length hop. What it does
not generate is the ROWS spelling over a bare element — every distinct-rows arm is a PROPERTY — so

### Item 1585 — **1.89x on `values(k).count()`**, because an existing rewrite's equivalence argument never needed the predicate its GATE required. The two spellings now converge exactly, and the gap went unseen because the Gremlin spelling probe had no values/aggregate group at all. ⚠️ The aggregate family is NOT a target: max/min/sum/mean all cost the same, and the cost is `values()`

The cross-surface probe flagged Gremlin's `max` at 2.46x its GQL twin and `sum` at 1.63x. Profiling
that first is what redirected the tick.

#### The aggregate terminals are FREE, which refutes the obvious target

```text
   gremlin  V().count()                      0.004 ms   <- closed form
   gremlin  V().values('k')                  2.181      <- the floor
   gremlin  V().values('k').count()          2.256
   gremlin  V().values('k').fold()           2.189
   gremlin  V().values('k').max()            2.120
   gremlin  V().values('k').min()            2.526
   gremlin  V().values('k').sum()            2.093
   gremlin  V().values('k').mean()           2.138
   gql      RETURN max(n.k)                  0.851      <- builds no rows
   gql      RETURN n.k AS k                  1.299
```

Every terminal costs what `values('k')` alone costs, so **the reduce is free and the whole 2.1 ms is
producing 50,000 property values.** The 2.46x against GQL is not an aggregate problem; GQL's `max` is
faster than GQL's own row projection because it materialises nothing, where Gremlin's does not.

A CPU profile at 800 reps (the first attempt at 40 was swamped by fixture construction — `addVertex`
and `#commitNormalized` in the top ten is the giveaway) puts 75.8% in three generator frames:
`projectValues` 35.6%, `sourceFromIds` 20.8%, `aggregateComparable` 19.4%, with GC only 2.7%. So it
is the generator plumbing and not allocation, and `projectValues` is already tuned — item 1476
hoisted its arity branch.

#### What the Gremlin spelling probe never asked

`bun run spelling:gremlin` reports **0 answer disagreements and 0 groups over 2x** — the spelling
surface is clean. But it has **no values/aggregate group**, so this pair had never been compared:

```text
   V().values('k').count()               2.43 ms      V().has('k').count()          1.18   1.89x
   V().values('k').is(gt 44).count()     0.235        V().has('k', gt 44).count()   0.235  1.00x
```

`fuseValuesIsCount` rewrites `values(k).is(p).count()` to `has(k, p).count()`, and its equivalence
argument — single-valued properties, so `values(k)` emits one value per element that HAS `k` — **never
needed the predicate**. The gate required an `is` anyway, so the plain spelling kept materialising a
value per element. The predicate pair converging EXACTLY is what distinguishes "the mechanism is
wrong" from "the mechanism's gate is too narrow"; it was the latter.

#### The fix, and the measurement

The `is` is now optional. ⚠️ **Without a predicate the step is `hasKey`, not `has`** — `has` carries a
required `pred`, and `G.has('k')` parses to `{kind: 'hasKey', keys}`, which is checked against what
the builder produces rather than inferred from the surface spelling (emitting a `has` without a
`pred` does not typecheck).

```text
                  PRE                      POST
   count      2.073 2.091 2.166 ms     1.084 1.096 1.132     1.89x
   hascount   1.102 1.112 1.122        1.102 1.113 1.123     the control, FLAT across builds
```

Both arms built from saved copies, each ASSERTED to be the code it claimed before either was built.
The two spellings now read 1.11 against 1.11 — **converged** — and the spelling probe confirms it at
its own scale (2.675 against 2.719, 1.02x).

⚠️ **One arm in that probe is not usable as a control at this precision**: `V().values('k')` with no
terminal ranges **1.466-2.130 across five runs** (1.45x), because it returns 50,000 traversers. Its
earlier 2.181 reading looked like a moved control after the change and was its own spread. The arms
that matter are tight to ~4%.

#### The ceiling, measured first, as a LADDER

`gremlin-agg-ceiling-probe.mjs`, 50,000 vertices, each arm adding one mechanism:

```text
   rawloop    iterate, read props, reduce            ~1.0 ms   (bimodal 0.4-0.6 / 0.9-1.3)
   rawgetter  same, through the `properties` getter    0.96     the getter is FREE
   rawtyped   same, plus the isVertex/isEdge tests     0.98     the guards are FREE
   gentwo     the same work across TWO yields         ~1.5      the BOUNDARIES cost ~0.5
   gremlin    the real traversal                      ~2.18
```

So the property read and the type guards are not the cost — the generator boundaries and the
per-element traverser are, which is what a fusion removes. That is also what disqualified the
cheaper alternative: a numeric fast path in `aggregateComparable` (19.4% of the profile) was priced
at only ~1.18x and on `min`/`max` alone.

⚠️ **The floor is BIMODAL** — `rawloop`'s series alternates between ~0.4-0.6 and ~0.9-1.3 in blocks,
with a 2.0-2.8 GC spike — so it is quoted as a range. A single number there would have been invented.

That loop already carries the precedent for the fix: `match` is dispatched there and not in


That is worse than the 16% `executor-edits-perturb` warns about, and it was very nearly the reason

a moved row in isolation — applied to a REGRESSION rather than a win, which is the direction it is
easier to believe uncritically. No unrelated row moved.

#### Where it is wired, and why not as a plan rewrite

A rewrite would need a new step kind, a `KIND_BITS` entry, a `maskOfSteps` arm and a `Step` union
member — four places a later pass could read the new kind wrongly. `run`'s loop is the only consumer
of the pair, so recognising it there costs one comparison PER STEP PER CALL (not per element) and
leaves the AST, the mask and every rewrite untouched. The recognizer is a pure exported function
(`fusableValuesAggregate`), which is what gives the gate its own test.

Semantics are re-asserted rather than re-derived: `projectValues`'s element-and-presence rule,
`aggregateComparable`'s total order (strings, booleans, NaN greatest, nulls skipped, empty yields ONE
null), and `aggregateNumber`'s `asNumber` that THROWS rather than coercing.

```text
   gen/nulls-not-skipped      CAUGHT  4 fail     gate/multi-key-accepted   CAUGHT  1 fail
   gen/minmax-inverted        CAUGHT  9 fail     gate/any-scope-accepted   CAUGHT  1 fail
   gen/naive-compare          CAUGHT  1 fail     gate/never-fuses          CAUGHT  2 fail
   gen/mean-wrong-divisor     CAUGHT  5 fail
   gen/empty-yields-nothing   CAUGHT  7 fail
   gen/missing-key-included   SURVIVED  — equivalent, and the guard STAYS
   wire/no-skip-terminal      SURVIVED  — equivalent
```

- **`key in props` is currently redundant**: a missing key reads `undefined` and the next test
  (`v == null`) skips it, so for these four terminals "absent" and "present null" are
  indistinguishable. It is kept because it is ONE RELAXATION from a wrong answer — `count` and
  `fold` CAN tell them apart — and that is now written at the line rather than left for someone to
  re-derive with a mutant.
- **Not skipping the consumed terminal is unobservable**: it would run a second time over the
  one-element stream the fusion just produced, and all four reduces are IDEMPOTENT there. So the
  `i += 1` is a cost fix, no test can fail on it, and none pretends to.

### Item 1587 — ⚠️ **A REFUTATION with its numbers, and a redirect worth more than the thing refuted.** GQL's `count(DISTINCT <far end>)` walk is ALREADY the optimal shape, so the 13x against Gremlin is a constant factor — and the micro-ladder that nominated a cause could not survive repetition. What Gremlin actually does differently: **`dedupe` puts element references straight into a `Set`, with no key built at all**

`hop distinct` is the largest remaining cross-surface flag: GQL ~7.0 ms against Gremlin's 0.527 over
50,000 vertices / 150,000 edges, both answering 50,000.

#### The walk is not the problem, which the profile says before any hypothesis

```text
   walkFarSide    50.5%     the far-driven walk
   add            22.5%     the dedup set (item 1584's id container)
   everything else <4% each, mostly fixture construction
```

And `walkFarSide` is already optimal in SHAPE: for each candidate far vertex it does ONE adjacency
lookup and never touches an edge, so it is O(V) where the question looks O(E). There is no
algorithmic gap to close — 1041.6 ms / 200 reps / 50,000 vertices is **~104 ns per vertex** for what
should be a cached getter plus a `Map.get`, so the gap is a constant factor.

#### ⚠️ The micro-ladder nominated a cause, loudly, and it was WRONG

A ladder priced each mechanism separately (`far-driven-ceiling-probe.mjs`):

```text
   iterate     iterate the vertex map, touch nothing        0.9-4.3 ns/vertex
   getter      + read the cached `adjTo`                    5.9-6.9
   bucket      + `.get(type)` and the size test            18.1
   dirbranch   + the `direct.forward ?` ternary            46.7     <- +28 ns?!
   idset       + add the id to a Set<string>              78.2-115.2
   gql         the real query                            143.7-151.4
```

`bucket` 18.1 against `dirbranch` 46.7 is a textbook polymorphic-inline-cache story: the ternary
puts TWO getters at ONE access site. **Four rounds each destroyed it:**

```text
   bucket     36.0  33.3  34.1  36.7
   dirbranch  46.7  52.1  17.2  50.0      <- 17.2
   splitloop  38.4  16.9  20.8  34.9      <- the "fix", also 16.9
```

All three are bimodal across a 3x range, so the original 18-vs-47 was **one mode read against
another**. At tens of nanoseconds per vertex this instrument has no resolution, which is the floor
CLAUDE.md names ("anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness") arriving in a new place.

Eight rounds each, asserted builds:

```text
   PRE   7.551 8.010 6.751 7.328 7.770 8.460 8.002 7.362   median 7.66
   POST  7.105 7.703 6.632 6.755 6.763 6.940 7.684 11.523  median 7.02   1.09x
```

#### ⚠️ THE REDIRECT, and it is the useful half of the tick

The `idset` ladder arm — `walkFarSide`'s work PLUS the id-string dedup, nothing else — reads
**3.9-5.8 ms**, while Gremlin answers the WHOLE question in **0.527**. So Gremlin is not paying
GQL's per-element keying at all, and `dispatch.ts`'s `dedupe` says exactly what it does instead:

> Primitives and stable graph-element references dedupe directly in this Set — value/identity
> equality, **no allocation (the hot path)**. Composite values … upgrade to a structural string key
> in a second, lazily-created Set.

A `Set<unknown>` holding the elements themselves. GQL's `valueSet` builds `String(v.id)` per element
(item 1584 got that down from `valueKey`'s `'@' + id`, 1.92-2.31x) and still pays a string-keyed
`Set` op per element.

⚠️ **This does NOT contradict item 1584's refutation, and the difference matters.** There an identity
`Set` was added **in FRONT of** `valueKey` — paying both — and measured 1.24-1.39x WORSE. Gremlin's
evidence is for identity **as the only container**, which is a different change.

**And it would fix a correctness bug at the same time.** Divergence 13 (item 1584): two distinct
vertices with ids `5` and `'5'` give `count(*)` 2 but `count(DISTINCT n)` **ts 1, nat 2**, because
`String(v.id)` conflates them. Identity keying makes them two, which is what native already answers.
So the next item is a speed fix and a divergence fix with one mechanism, and Gremlin's own executor
is the worked precedent — including its `WeakSet` short-circuit for composites, which is the part
item 1584's attempt lacked.

Open questions it must answer, named now so the measurement is designed rather than improvised: does

so native's answer there has to be checked too), and does the element path keep its 1.9-2.3x from

### Item 1588 — ⚠️⚠️ **SILENT DATA LOSS in core storage, found while designing a perf measurement: `addEdge` with an id equal to an existing VERTEX's id REPLACES that vertex's labels AND properties.** `elementProperties` and `elementLabels` are each ONE map keyed by bare id, shared across two separate id spaces. No fix in this item — a speed tick is the wrong place — but it is reproducible in four lines. ⚠️ It also means item 1584's divergence 13 was mis-described

This tick set out to build identity-only element dedup (item 1587's redirect). Its own design note
said to settle the correctness question FIRST, because a vertex/edge id collision is a reachable
shape where identity and `String(v.id)` disagree, and native's answer there decides whether the
change fixes a divergence or creates one. Asking that question is what found this.

#### The bug, through the public API, in four lines

```js
const a = g.addVertex({ id: 'x', labels: ['P'], properties: { k: 1 } });
const b = g.addVertex({ id: 'y', labels: ['P'], properties: { k: 2 } });
g.addEdge({ id: 'x', from: a, to: b, labels: ['E'] });
```

```text
   vertex x labels before: ["P"]   props: {"k":1}
   vertex x labels after : ["E"]   props: {}
```

The VERTEX is overwritten by the EDGE — both its labels and its whole property bag. It is still the
same object (`verticesById.get('x') === a`), still listed in `verticesByLabel.get('P')`, and
`vertexCount` is still 2. So the damage is invisible to the shapes a reader would check first and
shows up as a wrong answer:

```text
   MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(*) AS c                     2   <- the stale label index is trusted
   MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 1 RETURN count(*) AS c       0   <- was 1; the properties are gone
   MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 1 RETURN count(DISTINCT n)   0   against native's 1
```

**Native keeps both elements and answers correctly**, so this is TS-only. Vertex and edge ids are
separate spaces here (`verticesById` and `edgesById` are distinct maps) and TinkerPop treats them as
separate too, so sharing an id is legal input and not user error.

#### The mechanism, and why the fix does not belong in this item

```text
   Graph.elementProperties: Map<string, PropBox>     ONE map, keyed by BARE id
   Graph.elementLabels:     Map<string, LabelBox>    ONE map, keyed by BARE id
```

Both `Vertex` and `Edge` read and write them by their own `#id`, so an `Edge` with id `x` does
`elementProperties.set('x', box)` over the vertex's box. The field's own doc states the invariant it
is built on — "there is still exactly ONE source of truth per id" — and that is precisely the
assumption that fails when two ELEMENT KINDS with independent id spaces share the map.

#### ⚠️ OWNER DECISION: WON'T FIX — document only

Asked directly, the owner's call is that **a vertex and an edge sharing an id is OUT OF CONTRACT**:
no per-kind storage split, and a guard or a documented limitation instead. So the entry below prices
a fix that is NOT going to be built, and is kept only to explain the mechanism.

⚠️ **A GUARD HAS A COST THE QUESTION DID NOT MENTION, and it needs deciding before one is added:**
native ACCEPTS a colliding id and answers correctly, so a TS `addEdge` that THREW would be a new
cross-engine divergence — TS raises where native returns rows. That trades silent data loss for a
loud byte-identity break. Documenting the limitation has no such cost, which makes it the reading of
"a guard or a documented limitation" that does not create a second problem. Settled this way unless
the owner says otherwise.

A correct fix would be per-kind storage, and the surface is larger than it looks: `elementProperties` has
6 references each in `Vertex.ts` and `Edge.ts`, while `elementLabels` is written at ~10 sites in
`Graph.ts` — several through `commitElementLabels(id, next)`, which takes a BARE id and would need
the kind threaded through. Plus `label-box.test.ts`, `Graph.test.ts` and two probes read the maps
directly. **Fixing properties without labels would be worse than recording it**, since the result
would look fixed while labels still cross over. So this wants its own item, with the fuzzers and a
look at whether any codec or snapshot path depends on the shared keying.

#### ⚠️ And it corrects item 1584's description of divergence 13

⚠️ **Precisely: item 1584's entry in THIS file is right** — it says `addVertex({id: 5})`, the direct
API, and shows `count(*)` 2 on BOTH sides with `count(DISTINCT n)` ts 1 against nat 2. What is wrong
is the claim I wrote in its TEST COMMENT and in the memory note, that the conflation is "reachable
from untyped JS or NDJSON ingest".

Through NDJSON, **`count(*)` ALSO diverges (ts 1, nat 2)**, which means TS's graph holds only ONE
vertex: deserialization coerces a numeric id to a string and the second node overwrites the first —
an INGEST defect, not a dedup one. Both have been corrected.

The divergence as a DEDUP bug is real only through the direct API, where `count(*)` is 2 and
`count(DISTINCT n)` is 1. Two different defects wearing one entry, and the giveaway was there all
along: a dedup bug cannot move `count(*)`.

#### What this means for the perf target, which stays open

Identity-only element dedup (item 1587's redirect, Gremlin's own `dedupe` being the precedent) is
unaffected as a performance idea. But **the shapes meant to validate it cannot do that job**:

- the vertex/edge collision shape is CORRUPT in TS before any dedup runs, so comparing dedup answers
  there measures this bug, not the keying;
- the NDJSON numeric-id shape is an ingest defect, so it cannot validate a dedup change either;
- what is left is the direct-API numeric-id shape, which identity keying would fix — and that one is
  real.

Walking into the measurement without this would have produced a confident wrong conclusion about
either the change or the engine. That is the item's value: a probe designed before the code, which
is the discipline item 1587's refuted micro-ladder earned the hard way.

#### Gates

No engine change — three probes. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites unchanged from item 1587.

### Item 1589 — the id-space limitation is now DOCUMENTED and pinned by a test (owner's call at 1588), and ⚠️ **identity-only element dedup is REFUTED: a 5% REGRESSION on the one arm tight enough to read.** So Gremlin's 12x on hop-distinct is NOT its dedup keying, and three mechanisms are now ruled out

#### The documented limitation, which was the owner's decision

Item 1588 found that `addEdge` with an id equal to an existing VERTEX's id replaces that vertex's
labels and properties, and asked. The call: **out of contract, document only** — no per-kind storage
split. Done in three places:

- `Graph.addEdge`'s doc comment states the contract (ids unique across BOTH kinds, not merely within
  each), shows the four-line reproduction, and says why it is not guarded.
- `Graph.elementProperties`'s doc names the one place its own "exactly ONE source of truth per id"
  invariant does not hold.
- `id-space-contract.test.ts` pins it, for two reasons worth stating: so the documented promise
  cannot drift silently if someone later changes the storage, and so the SHAPE of the loss is pinned
  — `vertexCount`, the vertex object's identity and the label index all SURVIVE it, which is exactly
  what lets a label-index count still answer 2 while a property filter answers 0.

⚠️ **The collision is SYMMETRIC**, which the test pins and the prose would otherwise get wrong: a
VERTEX reusing an edge's id loses in the same way. Whichever element is added second wins the shared
box, so the contract is "unique across both kinds", not "edges must avoid vertex ids".

⚠️ **And it is deliberately NOT guarded.** Native ACCEPTS a colliding id and answers correctly, so a
TS `addEdge` that threw would trade silent data loss for a cross-engine divergence — TS raising where
native returns rows. That is why "documented limitation" is the reading of the owner's instruction
that does not create a second problem.

#### ⚠️ REFUTED, with its numbers: identity-only element dedup

Item 1587's redirect looked strong, and it was wrong. The case for it: Gremlin's `dedupe` keys
elements by identity with no key built ("no allocation (the hot path)"), Gremlin answers hop-distinct
in 0.527 ms against GQL's ~7-9, and identity would ALSO fix divergence 13. It is sound as well — the
graph hands out one object per id, so identity agrees with id equality within a query.

Implemented precisely (`isElement`, not `'id' in v`, so a plain object carrying an `id` keeps its
old key and two structurally equal ones still collapse), then measured as an asserted A/B at 40 reps:

```text
   count(DISTINCT n)   node-only    PRE 2.569-2.610   POST 2.700-2.730   1.05x WORSE
   RETURN DISTINCT b                PRE 10.39-11.39   POST 10.76-13.30   worse
   count(DISTINCT b)   hop          PRE  8.35-10.05   POST  6.63- 8.62   ranges OVERLAP
   count(DISTINCT n.n) control      PRE 1.934-2.006   POST 1.900-1.955   flat
```

⚠️ **The hop arm's apparent 1.26x is noise, and reading it as a win would have shipped a
regression**: its PRE minimum (8.348) sits INSIDE POST's range (6.625-8.623). The node-only arm is
tight on both sides and does not overlap, so the 5% regression is the real reading. Which arm to
trust is decided by the spreads, not by which number is more welcome — the same discipline item 1587
needed in the opposite direction, where a single sweep row claimed a regression that did not exist.

This is item 1584's refutation arriving again by a different route: there an identity `Set` was added
IN FRONT of the key, here it REPLACED the key, and both are slower than `'@' + id`. A `Set<object>`
probe simply costs more than the string it saves.

#### What this rules out, which is the useful residue

Three mechanisms have now been tested against the hop-distinct gap, and only one ever paid:

```text
   valueKey string building        item 1584   1.92-2.31x    TAKEN
   identity keying (in front)      item 1584   1.24-1.39x worse
   identity keying (replacing)     item 1589   1.05x worse
   per-element binding + evalFn    item 1584   flat (1.03-1.06x)
   the polymorphic adjacency read  item 1587   1.09x, at the noise floor
```

So **Gremlin's 12x is not explained by any of them**, and the walk is already the optimal shape
(item 1587: one adjacency lookup per far vertex, no edge touched). ⚠️ **ANSWERED AT 1590, and the
instrument found it in one profile:** Gremlin has a `distinctHopCount` shortcut that keeps NO dedup
set, because a far-driven walk already visits each far vertex once. GQL paid for a set on top of the
same walk — 3.13x, and 14.5x cumulative on that query. The next attempt should stop
guessing at the keying and instrument the two ROUTES side by side — what Gremlin's executor actually
does for `V().out(E).dedupe().count()`, step by step, against what GQL's `detectDistinctCount` does —
because the remaining difference is evidently somewhere neither profile has separated yet. Recorded
next to `valueSet` so the next reader starts from the ruled-out list rather than the top.

### Item 1590 — **3.13x on `count(DISTINCT <far end>)` over a hop** by deleting the dedup set entirely: the far-driven walk visits each far vertex ONCE, so distinctness was already guaranteed and the set only re-derived it. Found by instrumenting the two ROUTES after five guesses at mechanisms had failed — Gremlin's profile named a `distinctHopCount` shortcut that keeps no set at all

Items 1584, 1587 and 1589 each guessed at a mechanism for the hop-distinct gap and four of five guesses
were wrong. Item 1589's conclusion was to stop guessing and instrument the two routes side by side.
That is what this item did, and it took one profile.

#### What the Gremlin profile said

```text
   hasAny            38.6%     "does this vertex have any edge of this type"
   distinctHopCount  10.2%     the shortcut built on it
   everything else   <8% each, mostly fixture construction
```

Gremlin has a dedicated `distinctHopCount` shortcut, and **it keeps no dedup set**. It does not need
one: a far-driven walk visits each far vertex exactly once, so "how many far vertices have a
qualifying edge" IS the distinct count.

GQL's `detectDistinctCount` does the same far-driven walk — item 1587 established it is already the
optimal SHAPE, one adjacency lookup per far vertex with no edge touched — and then pays for a dedup
set on top of it.

⚠️ **Item 1584 half-saw this and wrote down the smaller half.** Its tripwire found that `ids.has`
NEVER fires on this route, and the note recorded the _guard_ as redundant. The whole _set_ is. The
observation was right there; what was missing was asking why the guard never fires.

#### The change, and why it is sound rather than merely faster

`countFarSide` at module scope: iterate `candidateVertexSource`, test the per-type adjacency bucket,
increment. No set, no `take` closure, no per-element value.

It is gated on two conditions, and **the gating is where the correctness lives**:

- **The dedup value must be the keyed ELEMENT** (a bare variable). A PROPERTY key still needs the
  set, because two distinct far ends can SHARE a value — counting visits would say 2 where distinct
  values is 1. Pinned by a test that does exactly that.
- **No clause `WHERE`**, so the fast walk needs no binding and no `satisfies`.
- **Only `walkFarSide` may skip the set**, which is the subtle one. `farDrivenFits` requires
  `!onStart`, so that walk is always far-keyed and visits each candidate once. The other two cannot
  promise it: `walkFarSideResolvingStart` enumerates the far side and resolves STARTS, so one start
  is reachable through several far vertices; and `walkStartSide` breaks after the first qualifying
  edge on its BUCKET path but **not** on its `expand` path. Both keep the dedup.

#### The numbers, an asserted A/B at 40 reps

```text
                                            PRE                      POST
   count(DISTINCT b)   hop, TARGET     6.923 7.721 8.202 8.750   2.209 2.213 2.340 2.448   3.13x
   count(DISTINCT a)   start-keyed     4.342 4.437 5.180 5.513   4.720 4.739 4.992 5.392   flat
   count(DISTINCT b.n) property-keyed  6.195 6.244 6.503 8.753   5.784 7.805 9.333 11.873  flat
   count(DISTINCT n)   node scan       2.542 2.609 2.652 2.653   2.545 2.597 2.604 2.634   flat
```

The node-scan control is tight on both sides and identical, which is the one to read; the other two
controls overlap. Both arms were built from saved copies, each ASSERTED to contain or lack
`countFarSide` before either was built.

Cross-surface, the flag that has driven four items:

```text
   hop distinct   item 1581   gql 34.283ms   gremlin 0.527   52.37x
                  item 1583   gql 17.0                       ~31x     (rung precedence)
                  item 1584   gql  6.577                      12.49x  (id-keyed container)
                  item 1590   gql  2.356-2.480  gremlin 0.530-0.567   4.16-4.50x
```

**14.5x cumulative on that query**, 34.283 to 2.356.

The walk's mutants change an answer; the gate's are answer-equivalent, which is why

### Item 1591 — **1.12x on Gremlin's top-k paging** by extending item 1586's fusion to a CAPPED `order()`, the last big absolute cross-surface gap. ⚠️ A modest win, taken on tight non-overlapping ranges and flat controls — and the gate's first version made its own `desc` parameter DEAD CODE, which only a literal expectation caught

`paging` was the biggest ABSOLUTE gap left in the cross-surface probe: GQL 1.247 ms against
Gremlin's 3.700 for the same top-10, with Gremlin on the slow side after items 1574/1576 had already
taken 2.97x out of it.

#### Item 1590's method again: profile the FAST side first

```text
   GQL (fast)      boundedTopKeyed 5.3%, beatsRoot 4.9%, compareValues 7.2%
                   -> a bounded top-k heap, rejecting most values in O(1) against its root,
                      reading properties in a scan with NO traverser
   Gremlin (slow)  streamTopByBys  23.2%   <- the sort is NOT the problem
                   projectValues   21.6%
                   sourceFromIds   12.8%
                   extend           4.8%   get properties 3.7%   isElement 3.5%
                   startTraverser   2.7%
```

**48.6% is the generator chain feeding the sort**, which is exactly what item 1586 fused for the
reducing terminals. `order()` was left out then because its terminal is not a reduce — but
`fuseOrderTake` (item 1574) folds a following `take(n)` into the order as a `cap`, so a capped order
IS bounded and can be driven the same way.

`streamTopByBys` is generic over its item type, so raw VALUES pass through it with an identity
projection: one generator instead of two, and no traverser per element. Re-deriving the heap to also
shave its per-entry key array was declined — ~100 lines of tie-breaking and bounds logic is where a
top-k goes wrong silently.

#### ⚠️ The win is MODEST, and the judgement is recorded rather than dressed up

```text
                     PRE                             POST
   paging (target)   3.208 3.208 3.211 3.222 3.311   2.854 2.863 2.890 2.892 2.894   1.12x
   max (sibling)     1.117 1.181 1.204               1.107 1.112 1.158              flat
```

12% is near the line, and **item 1587 refused 1.09x**. Three things decide it the other way here:
the ranges are tight (3% and 1.4%) and do NOT overlap, so the gain is real rather than noise; a
broad `bench:gremlin` sweep run TWICE per arm shows every unrelated row flat (`values(age)` 136.0
against 135.0, the UNCAPPED `order()` row 387.4 against 383.5, bare `out()` 120.3 against 120.1); and
the change is a small extension of a mechanism already built and tested at item 1586 rather than a
new walk. Had any of those gone the other way it would have been a reject.

#### ⚠️⚠️ The gate's first version made its own `desc` parameter DEAD CODE

The first gate refused any `bys`, on the reasoning that a `by` projects a sort key off each item and
is therefore a different question. True of every `by` kind except the one that matters:

```text
   order()                   ->  { kind: 'order', cap: 10 }
   order().by(Order.desc)    ->  { kind: 'order', cap: 10, bys: [{kind:'identity',direction:'desc'}] }
```

The natural DESCENDING spelling arrives as a single identity `by` with a direction, **not** as
`desc: true`. So the descending form silently took the unfused path while the fused step's `desc`
parameter was never reached. An identity by with a direction still means "sort by the value itself",
so it is now admitted, with the direction read off it; any other kind, or more than one, still
declines.

⚠️ **AND THE TEST THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT THAT PASSED VACUOUSLY.** The fixtures compared the capped
result against an uncapped-sort-and-slice ORACLE — a genuinely independent path — but both arms were
written `order().by(undefined, 'desc')`, which sorts **ASCENDING** (`[5,1,3]` comes back `[1,3,5]`).
Both sides were wrong identically, so every descending assertion agreed. **Only a LITERAL expectation
caught it**, which is the argument for pairing an oracle with literals rather than trusting it alone:
an oracle written by the same hand can share the same misunderstanding. The correct spelling is
`order().by(Order.desc)` — the comparator-only form, token FIRST.

With the gate fixed, the descending form measures 2.496 ms and answers `[96,…]` correctly.

#### Mutation: 9 of 10 caught

```text
   topk/missing-key-included   CAUGHT  4 fail     gate/admits-uncapped      CAUGHT 30 fail
   topk/cap-ignored            CAUGHT 21 fail     gate/admits-local         CAUGHT  1 fail
   topk/desc-inverted          CAUGHT 25 fail     gate/admits-any-bys       CAUGHT  1 fail
   topk/no-element-guard       SURVIVED (equivalent)  gate/drops-by-direction CAUGHT 20 fail
                                                  gate/never-fuses          CAUGHT  2 fail
                                                  gate/admits-multi-key     CAUGHT  2 fail
```

`gate/drops-by-direction` is the mutant that reproduces the bug above, and it is caught — the gate's
own regression test now exists. `topk/no-element-guard` survives because `assertFrontierTypes`
rejects `values()` on a non-element frontier at PLAN time (`inject(5).values('k')` raises before any
of this runs), so the guard defends against something a static check already prevents. It stays, and
the note at the line says why — including that a test of it would pass because of the frontier check
and not because of the guard, which is how item 1576 shipped a test that covered nothing.
