### Item 1592 — ⚠️ **item 301's multi-hop crossover measurement is STALE: its "product wins 1.50x at 3 hops" does NOT reproduce.** Re-measured at three degrees, the sweep ties at degree 3 and wins 1.12-1.35x at 5 and 8. But routing 3 segments to it is UNSAFE — `longChainCount` accepts inline-gated shapes and DROPS the gates, which 10 tests caught. Not changed; recorded with the blocker

A fresh profile target rather than the cross-surface list, which is down to small items. `bench:gremlin`
shows the widest ts/native ratios in the whole corpus on multi-hop counts (18.5x at 2 hops, 47x at 3,
35x at 4), so that is where a profile was pointed.

#### First: the two surfaces AGREE, so this is not a cross-surface question

At 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, answers asserted equal at every depth:

```text
   depth 1   gql   0.003ms   gremlin   0.007ms    closed form, a degree sum
   depth 2   gql  52.7       gremlin  51.7        ~10 ns/path
   depth 3   gql 460.1       gremlin 227.3        ~18 / ~9 ns/path
   depth 4   gql 242.4       gremlin 234.7        ~1.9 ns/path
```

⚠️ **Depth 4 is FASTER than depth 3 in absolute terms**, on 5x the paths — 125M paths at 1.9 ns each
cannot be enumeration. That impossible-looking ordering is what the tick followed, and it is real:
four-or-more segments take `longChainCount`'s SWEEP while three take a degree PRODUCT.

#### The recorded crossover does not reproduce

`detectCountShortcut`'s own comment records item 301's measurement, at **200,000 vertices of degree
3**:

```text
   3 hops   product 250.1ms   sweep 374.9ms   <- the PRODUCT wins, 1.50x
   4 hops   product 980.2ms   sweep 512.4ms   <- the SWEEP wins, 1.91x
```

A degree product's cost grows with degree while a sweep's is O(E) per pass and flat in it, so the
crossover MUST move with degree — and item 301 measured one degree. Re-measured at depth 3, product
against sweep, same fixture shape, the sweep forced by a one-line experiment:

```text
   degree 3   product 321.975ms   sweep 315.117ms   TIE (1.02x)
   degree 5   product 458.477     sweep 410.423     sweep 1.12x
   degree 8   product 610.077     sweep 531.207     sweep 1.15x
```

And at degree 8 with three tight rounds each, non-overlapping (product 584.474-613.877, sweep
433.300-544.604): **sweep 1.20x on medians, 1.35x on minima.**

So the product's 1.50x win at 3 hops is gone — it is a TIE at the degree item 301 measured, and the
sweep is ahead everywhere above it. The code has moved a great deal since item 301 (the sweep gained
an index seed at 1330, pinned-start guards at 1329, clause-gate splitting at 305), so a number
measured then describing a routing decision now is exactly the staleness CLAUDE.md's rule about
verifying a heading against the source is for.

#### ⚠️ BUT THE ROUTING CANNOT SIMPLY MOVE, and the tests said so

Routed sweep-first with a fallback — `longChainCount(...) ?? threeSegmentRoute(...)` — the gql suite
went **4028 pass / 10 fail**, every failure an inline-gated three-hop count (`a three-hop count gated
by an inline constraint (item 456)` among them). `longChainCount` ACCEPTS those shapes and then
ignores the constraint: it takes `clauseGates` for the clause-`WHERE` spelling but nothing for an
INLINE one, so `(x {k: 0})` silently stops filtering.

A hand check first looked fine — `(x {k: 0})` gave 32 against the unconstrained 96, so the number had
clearly moved — which is why the suite is the oracle and not a plausible-looking answer. The
specialized product exists partly BECAUSE it can gate those positions once per visit (item 219's
point, and item 456's tests).

**So the change is not made.** A correct version needs the sweep to receive inline constraints the way
it receives clause ones, and then the routing could be degree-aware. That is a real piece of work, not
a one-line reroute, and it wants its own item.

#### What is recorded, so the next attempt starts from here

- Item 301's crossover numbers are **stale**; the current ones are above, with degree as the axis.
- The sweep is never slower at depth 3 in anything measured, and better with degree — so the routing
  question is live, not settled.
- The blocker is precise: **`longChainCount` does not take inline node constraints.** Fix that first,
  then re-measure, then route.
- ⚠️ And the 2-hop case should NOT be touched on this evidence: at 52.7 ms for 1M edges it is already
  ~52 ns/edge, which is the sweep's own per-pass rate, so two passes would lose to one product.

### Item 1593 — gave the TS Gremlin SERVING path its first coverage in `bench:usage`, where two rows had always printed `-`. ⚠️ **And the first pair of rows I added was CONFOUNDED: it priced plan construction at 54% of a serving call when the real share is ~17%** — the majority of the gap is the varying lookup KEY, which parameters would not fix. The priced "48-51% of cheap calls" target is worth far less than recorded

`bench:usage` is the serving-shaped harness — small operations against a warm graph, where per-call
overhead shows. Two of its rows, `gremlin read: point lookup` and `gremlin read: fixed count`, print
`-` for the pure-TS engine, and the reason on the hook is correct rather than a gap: those rows take
Gremlin TEXT, and the pure-TS Gremlin surface is a fluent BUILDER.

But the consequence was a real hole: **the TS Gremlin serving path had no coverage in this harness at
all**, while items 1577/1578 had measured plan construction at ~48-51% of a cheap Gremlin call. A
builder row closes it, because the builder's equivalent of "a fresh text every call" is a freshly
BUILT plan — and Gremlin accepts no parameters, so a serving workload that varies a value MUST vary
the plan.

#### ⚠️ The first pair of rows was CONFOUNDED, and the number it produced was wrong

```text
   gremlin(built) read: point lookup   357.9k ops/s     <- built fresh, varying user
   gremlin(built) read: reused plan    779.6k           <- plan reused
```

Read as a pair that says "construction is 54% of the call". It does not. **The two rows differ in TWO
ways**: the reused plan has its value baked in, so it looks up ONE user every call, while the built
row looks up a DIFFERENT user each call. Their gap is construction PLUS whatever varying the lookup
key costs in index-bucket and cache locality.

A probe arm that builds fresh on a FIXED key separates them, and a third bench row now does the same:

```text
                                   probe (20k users)      bench (ops/s -> ns)
   reused plan, fixed key           1784 ns                762.0k -> 1312 ns
   built fresh, fixed key           2146                   556.9k -> 1796
   built fresh, varying key         2619                   358.7k -> 2788
```

```text
   construction      362 ns (43% of the gap)      484 ns (33%)
   varying the key   473 ns (57%)                 992 ns (67%)
```

Two independent instruments, same direction: **the majority of the gap is the varying key, not
construction.** Construction is ~362-484 ns of a ~2600-2800 ns serving call — **13-17%, not 54%.**

#### What that corrects, which is the useful part

This session has carried "Gremlin parameter binding — the structural fix for ~48-51% of cheap calls"
as a priced open target. At serving scale on this shape **parameters would recover ~17%, not ~50%**,
because the varying-key cost stays whatever the plan does: a parameterized plan still looks up a
different user. The 48-51% figure came from probes that build and run the SAME shape repeatedly,
where the key never varies — so it measured construction's share of a call that touches one hot
vertex, not of a serving call.

⚠️ That is the SAME confound in the two places, and I reproduced it before catching it. Items
1503/1504 already knew the rebuilt-plan case matters — they rejected a `WeakMap<Plan, boolean>` memo
precisely because "a freshly built plan never hits the memo", and `readsPath`/`kinds` are carried by
construction instead. What nobody had separated is the _data_ half of the rebuilt-plan penalty.

#### Also measured, and not a target

Construction itself decomposes cleanly by step count — 51 ns for the bare source, 149 at two steps,
213 at four — so it is ~50 ns fixed plus ~40 ns per step after item 1577's 4.27x. At 362-484 ns in a
2600 ns call there is no large win left there.

#### Gates

No engine change — two probes and three bench rows. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped. Suites native
1031, gremlin 1630, gql 4038, core 435, serialization 144 — 0 fail.

#### What this leaves

⚠️ **ANSWERED AT 1594**: GQL answers the identical seeded lookup in **650 ns** against Gremlin's
2619, so ~2150 ns is Gremlin's per-call machinery for a ONE-element result — and the per-frame trims
in it do not convert (a 12.0% self-time frame went flat). The next attempt wants a whole-plan
shortcut for the seeded point lookup, not another frame.

The varying-key cost (~992 ns, 67% of the rebuilt-plan gap) is the real item, and it is NOT

### Item 1594 — ⚠️ **a 12.0% SELF-TIME FRAME DID NOT CONVERT: deduplicating the seed's double bucket lookup is FLAT.** And the tick's useful half: GQL answers the identical seeded point lookup in **650 ns** against Gremlin's **2619** — ~~4.0x~~ **2.5x as of item 1641 (805 against 2000); quote that figure**, of which only ~400 ns is construction, so ~~**~2150 ns is per-call machinery for a ONE-element result**~~ — ⚠️ **decomposed at item 1642: 1277.6 ns per call total, of which 233.8 is construction, 33.6 routing and ~1044 execution; the machinery is the traverser SETUP, not the routing**

Item 1593 left ~1860 ns of the Gremlin serving call unexplained — neither construction nor the
varying lookup key. This profiled it.

#### The profile, and what it correctly confirmed

`V().hasLabel('User').has('name', eq(v)).values('score')` over 20,000 indexed users, built fresh per
operation, 400,000 operations:

```text
   projectValues                                  20.8%
   (anonymous) index.mjs:3493                      13.3%   the seed path
   countEquals                                     12.0%
   (garbage collector)                              6.0%
   toArray                                          4.6%
   analyzeStep 3.2 + stepMayFault 3.1 + anyMayFault 1.9 + appendStep 2.1 + fn 2.2  = 12.5%
```

That last group is CONSTRUCTION — `mayFault` and `readsPath` are carried on the `Plan` and computed
by `appendStep` as it builds, so a freshly built plan pays them per step. **12.5% corroborates item
1593's 13-17% from an independent instrument**, which is the useful kind of agreement: a share
measured by sampling and a share measured by a fixed-key arm landing in the same place.

#### ⚠️ REFUTED, with its numbers: the seed's double bucket lookup

`countEquals` fetches the bucket to read its `.size`, then `build()` fetches the SAME bucket again —
two `indexes.get(key)` plus two `buckets.get(value)` per seek, and a string-keyed `Map.get` is
~190 ns in this repo (item 194). Holding the bucket once is semantically exact: `equals` returns the
index's own live set, which is what `countEquals` just looked up, and `bucket?.size ?? 0` equals
`countEquals(...) ?? 0` for an unindexed key, an indexed key with no match, and a non-indexable value
alike. (The unindexed case cannot reach it regardless — the caller guards on `isIndexed` first, which
matters because a count of 0 with an EMPTY build would be a wrong answer rather than a slow one.)

Five rounds each, 400,000 operations per round:

```text
   built fresh, varying key   PRE 2502-2700 ns   POST 2554-2802   overlapping
   built fresh, fixed key     PRE 2091-2304      POST 2088-2301   overlapping
```

**Flat.** Reverted, recorded at the line. A 12.0% self-time frame surrendered nothing — item 1104's
rule, that a share is a NOMINATION and not a price, in a new place. At this granularity V8 inlines
those lookups and the sampled attribution is coarser than the effect. ⚠️ Worth noting that the rule
is written in `prof-summary.mjs`'s own header, which I wrote, and I still took the 12% as a price
worth two attempts.

The same seeded point lookup with the same varying key, 400,000 operations:


That is the structural shape items 1586 and 1591 fused for multi-element streams, and here it is at

### Item 1595 — **1.45x to 1.67x on the Gremlin seeded point lookup**, by answering `V()[.hasLabel(L)].has(k, eq(v)).values(j)` off the index bucket with no traverser. The form was chosen BECAUSE item 1594 refuted the per-frame trims — and the correctness it rests on is the engine's own existing claim rather than a new one

Item 1593 measured the TS Gremlin serving call at 2619 ns against ISO-GQL's 650 for the identical
seeded lookup, and showed only ~400 ns of that is plan construction. Item 1594 then profiled the rest
and refuted trimming it frame by frame: `countEquals` at **12.0% self time surrendered nothing**. Its
conclusion was that a whole-plan shortcut is the remaining form. This is that shortcut.

#### Where the correctness comes from, which is the part worth reading

`seededNodeValuesShortcut` seeks the bucket and reads the property off each hit. The claim it needs
is that **the bucket IS the matching set**, and that is not a new claim: `seedForStep` already
returns `removable: true` for an `eq` predicate on a PLAIN `has` over an indexed key, and
`removable` means "dropping the owning step leaves an equivalent plan". Reusing `seedForStep` rather
than re-deriving equality is what keeps this from drifting — index equality agreeing with `has`
equality is already load-bearing for `seedFromIndex`.

`removable: false` declines, which covers the two dangerous shapes in one test: a RANGE seed
(`gt`/`lt`/`between`) narrows without deciding, and a `hasLabelAnd` carries a label the bucket does
not capture. Both would need the predicate applied per element — the pipeline this exists to skip.

⚠️ **No cost check against a scan, deliberately.** Every element in the bucket is one the answer must
visit anyway, so an exact seek cannot lose. That is specifically NOT true of a range seed, which is a
second reason those decline.

⚠️ **AND THE ORDER HAD TO BE CHECKED, not assumed.** The unfiltered sibling iterates
`graph.vertices` while this iterates the index BUCKET, and Gremlin stream order is a TinkerPop
contract the differential fuzzer compares ORDERED. It agrees — because the pipeline also seeds from
that bucket for this shape — and the test pins the SEQUENCE (`[2, 0, 8, 6, 4]` from a scrambled
insertion order), not a set.


Two things that list says and a one-shape probe could not. **The seeded COUNT cost MORE than the
seeded projection** (2486 against 1743), which is the tell: counting elements should never cost more
than reading a property off the same elements. And **the two surfaces have opposite profiles** — GQL
wins 3.5-5.9x at one hit and LOSES 1.6-1.7x at four hundred. Low per-call overhead with high per-row
cost on one side, the reverse on the other.

#### Why nothing answered it, which is the interesting part

It is not an oversight. `countShortcut`'s `filterChainCount` **declines a `has` the moment
`seekWorthTaking` says a seek beats a scan** — deliberately, leaving the shape to the seeding path.
But the seeding path then runs the TRAVERSER PIPELINE over the seeded stream. So the shape was
recognised as seekable and answered in closed form by neither: it fell between the two.

`seededNodeCountShortcut` closes it. With no label the answer is the bucket's `size` — **O(1), no
iteration at all**. With a label it is one pass over the bucket, which is the minimum, since a label
is not in the index. Both rest on the same `removable` claim item 1595 documents: for an `eq` on a
PLAIN `has` over an indexed key, `seedForStep` already asserts the bucket IS the matching set.

#### First: it DOES seek, which rules out the obvious story

Item 149's own tell for a lost index is "two identical `bench:usage` columns", so the same test
applies here — the identical query with and without the index:

```text
   count, 400 hits (team)   unindexed 205760 ns   indexed  19082    10.78x
   count, 1 hit   (name)    unindexed 216592      indexed   1517   142.78x
   values, 400 hits         unindexed 309645      indexed  30303    10.22x
```

So the seek is working and the filtered node count is not scanning the label bucket. Had I gone
straight to "the count shortcut does not use the index" — which `buildNodeCount`'s own code invites,
since it is O(1) only when UNCONSTRAINED and otherwise tallies — the next item would have rebuilt a
path that already exists.

#### What it actually pays, from the profile

```text
   (anonymous) index.mjs:4906    48.9%     the specialised predicate closure
   (anonymous) index.mjs:17782   25.9%     the compiled expression
   evalLabelExpr                  8.9%
   countEquals                    1.0%     the seek itself is NOISE
```

**~75% is predicate evaluation per candidate and ~9% is the label test** — so of 48 ns per hit,
almost all of it is re-deciding what the bucket already decided. The seek costs 1%.

#### The mechanism, stated so the fix is specified rather than explored

`indexCandidates` (in `executor/matching.ts`) yields `SeedCandidate` as `{ count, build }` — a
cardinality estimate and a thunk. **There is no flag saying whether the seek is EXACT.** So every
seeded candidate is treated as a superset and re-validated, which item 149's header states as a
deliberate condition of seeking at all:

> a seed hint is a NECESSARY condition lifted from an AND-chain, so the seek is a SUPERSET of the
> matches and every candidate must be re-validated

That is right for a HINT. It is not right for an ISO equality constraint or a lone `WHERE k = v`,
where the bucket IS the matching set. Gremlin's `index-seed.ts` draws exactly this distinction and
calls it `removable` — "whether dropping the owning step leaves an equivalent plan" — which is what
let items 1595 and 1596 answer off the bucket directly.

**So the fix is to give GQL's seeds the same notion**: exact when the candidate's key/value is the
node's ONLY constraint, superset otherwise, and skip re-validation in the first case.

> ⚠️ **BUILT AT ITEM 1607, AND THIS SENTENCE PUTS THE FLAG IN THE WRONG OBJECT.** `indexCandidates`
> reads a `CNode`'s `pred`; the skip happens against a list of `InlinePred`s built separately from
> the AST. They agree today and nothing makes them, so an `exact` flag computed from one and applied
> to the other is a wrong answer waiting for the day they drift. What shipped instead: the candidate
> reports only what it SOUGHT (`eqKey`) and the verdict is formed against the predicate actually
> held (`soleEqualityKey` + `seedIsExact`). The label test
> still applies — the index returns vertices by VALUE across all labels, which item 149 names as the
> first of its two risks.

#### Priced, and deliberately not built here

At ~75% of 48 ns per hit, removing re-validation on the exact case is **4-7x on this shape** — the
400-hit count from 14.5 us to ~2-4.

> ⚠️ **BOTH NUMBERS ARE STALE, corrected at item 1605.** Items 1598/1600/1604 specialized the

#### ⚠️ ITEM 1597's RECIPE FOR THE FIX WAS WRONG, and this is the part worth keeping

That item wrote: "The fix has to admit it only where the value is non-null, or carry the null
spelling separately." The first of those is not implementable and not necessary, and reading
`satisfies`'s own null matrix is what showed it:

```text
   {k: null}         matches a stored null AND an absent key     <- the `props` reading
   WHERE n.k = null  matches NEITHER                             <- the `eqProps` reading
```

"Only where the value is non-null" cannot be decided when the value is a `$param` — its value is
unknown at compile time, which is the whole reason `eqProps` carries a RUNTIME null rejection. And
it is not needed: `propOf` returns `null` for both an absent key and a stored null, so plain
`structuralEq` ALREADY gives the inline reading. A SEPARATE arm that calls `structuralEq` and
rejects nothing is therefore correct for **every** value, null included.

The danger was never in admitting `props`. It was in routing `props` into the existing `eqProps`
closure, whose null rejection implements the other reading. One arm per reading, and the matrix is
satisfied by construction rather than by a value-dependent gate.

`satisfies` is still the only implementation of either rule — the arm binds its `props` loop
(`structuralEq(propOf(element, key), value(env))`) exactly as items 1338-1350's four arms bind
theirs.

#### One difference from the four arms above it, which matters for the comparison used

`eqProps`'s header records that `structuralEq` there is defence in depth: a LIST never reaches it,
because a list literal does not lift into `eqProps`. **That is not true here.** An inline
`(n {tags: [1, 2]})` is exactly a list-valued `props` entry, and `satisfies`'s own comment records
the bug where JS `!==` made such a constraint never match. So `structuralEq` in this arm is
load-bearing, and `inline-props-specialized.test.ts` pins it through the fast arm in both the
literal and `$param` spellings.

#### Re-priced by ablation, which is the only honest way (item 1104)

The test at `buildNodeCount`'s seeded loop, replaced with `() => true` — a wrong answer, built
only to price the right one — one shape per process, 20,000 vertices, 400 hits:

```text
   with the label test      11968  12494  12110 ns
   ablated                   7804   8910   7829        1.53x
   the UNLABELLED query      7513   8019   7749        agrees, by a different route
```

**1.53x**, confirmed twice by independent routes. So the frame is real money, and item 1597 was
wrong to dismiss it. What follows is why it is nonetheless unreachable.

#### Lever 1: compile the label test per query — FLAT, reverted

Item 1339's "answer it at the call site" applied to the label test rather than to a comparison.
`matchesLabel` is called from ~70 sites with ~70 `LabelExpr` shapes, so its `undefined` check and
`evalLabelExpr`'s `switch` are re-decided per ELEMENT everywhere; `compileLabelTest(expr)` resolved
the single-label case to `(v) => v.labels.has(name)` once per query, and the loop-invariant
`seeded !== undefined` folded into the gate alongside it.

```text
   PRE    11968  12494  12110 ns
   POST   12110  12419  12895    FLAT
```

Built, wired, measured, **reverted**. The dispatch was already being inlined — `evalLabelExpr`'s
46% self-time is V8 charging it the inlined getter and `Set.has`, not a call it actually makes. A
profile frame naming a function does not mean the function's own machinery is the cost.

#### Lever 2: test by OBJECT IDENTITY against the label bucket — SLOWER than hoisting

`verticesByLabel.get(name).has(v)` skips the `labels` getter and the string hash both, and was the
obvious next move. `label-test-cost-probe.mjs` prices the three tests over the same 400 candidates,
two runs:

```text
   v.labels.has(name)   getter + string hash   5.52  5.48 ns
   hoisted Set          string hash only       3.25  3.29
   bucket.has(v)        object identity        3.95  3.92
   NULL CONTROL         no test at all         0.34  0.34
```

Identity is **slower than the hoisted string hash** and saves ~1.6 ns a candidate against what the
engine does today — 400 x 1.6 ns is ~5% of the query, under the noise floor for an executor edit.

⚠️ **This also removes the PERF reason to settle an open owner decision.** The lever was blocked on
memory's `label-index-vs-setter`: `verticesByLabel` is not maintained by the `v.labels =` setter, so
the bucket and `v.labels` can disagree, and the engine ALREADY trusts the bucket on the unseeded
route of the same function — meaning one query can be answered from either source today. That is
still worth settling for CORRECTNESS, and is now known to be worth nothing for speed, so it should
not be priced as an optimization again.

#### What is left of the 1.53x, and why it is not here

The test's own cost is 5.5 ns a candidate, of which only the ~2.2 ns getter could go — and the
getter must be read per candidate, since each candidate is a different vertex. The remaining ~5 ns
a candidate is the test's PRESENCE in the loop rather than the test: ablating it also deletes a
branch and shrinks the body, which is the shape memory's `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`
describes. No change to `matchesLabel` or its call site can recover that half.

`gql-seek-revalidation-probe.mjs` runs five shapes in ONE process and reported the labelled and
unlabelled seeded counts at 11371 and 10957 — **1.04x**, where the isolated instrument says 1.60x.
Items 737 and 762's rule, costing a target rather than inventing one this time: had the loop trusted
that row, the label test would have looked like 4% instead of 53%.

```text

   FLOOR  bucket + label + one row   8502   8353        the projection is 2.8x its floor

```

⚠️ A floor is the right instrument BEFORE building a shortcut, and memory's
`gremlin-ts-unmeasured` is why: a floor per shape RETRACTED two of three targets there. Here it did

#### The two-part ablation, which named the half worth taking

The profile's top frames were `evalLabelExpr` 25.0%, `get labels` 8.2%, `matchesLabel` 7.6% — 40.8%

```text
   baseline                 24204  24572  24643 ns
   the GATE ablated         11721  11987  11996        2.05x   <- the half nothing had looked at
   the LABEL test ablated   18996  19176  19930        1.27x   <- the 40.8% of the profile
   both ablated              7373   7680   7994        3.16x
   the FLOOR                 8353   8502               both-ablated IS the floor
```

**The gate is 2.05x and the 40.8% profile frame is 1.27x.** A frame's self-time share ranked these
in the wrong order (item 1104, again), and with both gone the rung sits exactly on the floor — which

A new `gremlin-hop-filter-probe.ts` priced the filtered-hop family against the identical GQL
questions, one shape per process, 20,000 vertices / ~80,000 edges:

```text

   V().hasLabel(U).out(E).count()                          3836 ns     — —
   V().hasLabel(U).out(E).has(team,eq).count()           491165        421862

   V().hasLabel(U).out(E).has(team,eq).out(E).count()  16912372        520466    <- 32x
```

That is 157 ns per traverser against the one-hop shape's 4.8 — a marginal cost of ~1900 ns for the
second hop, which is a ROUTE change and not a constant. ⚠️ **So `countShortcut` was called directly


```text
   lead/ignored            CAUGHT  2    arrivals/wrong-box       CAUGHT 10
   lead/wrong-endpoint     CAUGHT  2    departures/wrong-box     CAUGHT 10
```

Unlike items 1600/1601, every mutant here is a WRONG ANSWER rather than a route choice, which is

filters with `seed: true` folds a leading `hasLabel` into a source bucket this walk never
enumerates, so the label requirement would be silently DROPPED — the rung's own comment says so,
and the mutant is what makes the comment load-bearing. `departures/wrong-box`'s anchor was not
unique on the first pass (two sites spell that line identically) and was re-anchored and re-run
rather than counted as a pass.

#### Three guards, each with its reason

- **The multi-type guard is REPLICATED, not reasoned about afresh.** `degreeOfTypes` sums the
  per-type buckets, which is a degree only when the wanted set is ONE bucket. `hopChainShape`'s own
  note records **13 divergences** from getting this wrong, every one an untyped `out()` at depth 2
  or more, and that `!== 1` (not `> 1`) is the right test because `out()` iterates every bucket and
  visits a two-type edge once per label. Tested both ways: untyped on a multi-type graph declines,
  a single named type on the same graph still answers.
- **`both` is declined** on either hop. `chainDegree` exists for that case, but `both` plus the
  bucket sum is precisely where those divergences lived, so the first version takes the shape that
  was measured.
- **A seekable INTERIOR `has` is NOT refused, where a seekable LEADING one still is.** The siblings
  refuse it because `countShortcut` runs before `seedFromIndex` and a tally that scanned would
  preempt the seek — but a seek seeds the SOURCE, and no route seeds from the middle of a walk. The
  test pins both halves on an indexed graph: the interior shape answers, the leading twin declines.

#### The hole, read off the shortcuts rather than inferred

A profile of `V().out(E).has(team,eq).values(score)` is 57.3% `generatorResume` plus 14.6% the hop
generator — the traverser pipeline again — so the two values shortcuts were called directly:

```text
   V().out(E).values(k)                    hopValues ANSWERS   startFiltered decline
   V().hasLabel(L).out(E).values(k)        hopValues decline   startFiltered ANSWERS
   V().hasLabel(L).has(k,p).out(E).values  hopValues decline   startFiltered ANSWERS
   V().out(E).has(k,p).values(j)           hopValues decline   startFiltered decline   <- 16.5 ms
   V().hasLabel(L).out(E).has(k,p).values  hopValues decline   startFiltered decline
```

`hopValuesShortcut` destructures exactly `[source, hop, proj]`, so ANY step after the hop sends the
plan to the pipeline, and `startFilteredHopValues` scanned only the steps BEFORE the hop. **The
count sibling has answered the far-filtered shape in closed form for ages** (`filteredHopCount`),
which is exactly why the hole was invisible: the count spelling was fast and the yield spelling was
not.

#### ⚠️ ITEM 1602's WINNING SHAPE IS NOT AVAILABLE HERE, and that is the interesting constraint

Item 1602 got 62x by going FAR-DRIVEN: test each far vertex once and contribute its degree.
`filteredHopCount`'s header measures that at 3-4x over the edge-driven form. It cannot be used for a
yielding walk: **Gremlin stream order is a TinkerPop contract that the differential fuzzer compares
ORDERED** (unlike GQL, where row order is unspecified), and a far-driven walk emits grouped by far
vertex where the pipeline emits in start-then-edge order. This module's own header already records
the same reasoning for why it walks `graph.vertices` instead of seeding from a label bucket.

So the win here is only the generator chain, not the algorithm — which is why it is 4.1x and not
62x, and that ceiling is a property of the contract rather than of the implementation.

#### What shipped, in two parts

1. **A far-side filter run** between the hop and the projection, collected by
   `collectVertexFilters` — the existing admission rule, not a second copy — and **folded into
   `pick`** rather than tested in the loops. There are three loops (the `both` iterator, its
   `drain`, and the `out`/`in` arm) and this module exists because items 1441/1466 measured an edit
   to a hot values walk at up to 16% on UNRELATED rows; item 1466 declined a 3.3x win on that
   basis. Composing once per QUERY leaves all three bodies byte-identical and a plan with no far
   filter gets the unwrapped `pick` it had.
2. **The `at === 1` decline removed.** It read "at `length === 3` with no filter,
   `hopValuesShortcut` already owns the plan" — true only when the hop is immediately followed by
   the projection. With a far filter that shortcut declines too, so the plan reached NEITHER. And
   the no-leading-filter spelling is the COMMON one, because `effectivePlan`'s `dropVacuousLabels`
   DELETES a leading `hasLabel` whenever every vertex carries it. The decline moved to "no filter on
   EITHER side", which is the condition that was meant.

`undefined` is the drop sentinel, and it is sound for all three projections: `values(k)` already
drops on `undefined` and must; a bare hop picks the far VERTEX and `id()` a string, so neither can
produce `undefined` of its own.

#### The numbers, an asserted A/B

PRE arm asserted by `isVertexFilterStep` being absent from every `packages/gremlin/dist` bundle.
Three runs each, one shape per process, 20,000 vertices / ~80,000 edges:

```text
                     PRE                            POST                      verdict
   far-proj          16538329 17232627 15968792     4091788 3797601 4052404   4.1x
   far-count           395001   392583   414846      409604  393819  583460   flat (control)
   start-count         534516   485010   520146      486387  470150  482331   flat (control)
   mid-count         (item 1602's)                   265292  261639  295242   flat (control)
   nofilter-count        3523     3751     3280        4093    3602    3592   flat (control)
```

Four controls flat. The remaining 3.8 ms is 50 ns an edge over 80,000 edges, which is the
start-driven walk the order contract requires — `far-count`'s 0.4 ms is the far-driven form, and the
8x between them is the price of ordered output on this shape. Recorded rather than chased.

#### Correctness: the oracle was built BEFORE the literals

⚠️ **Item 1602 wrote its unit literals by eye and SIX of fifteen were wrong** while the engine was
right every time. This file did it the other way round: a hand walk over the fixture table, as a
script with no engine involved, produced every expectation first. Six shapes were also checked
against the same oracle on a 300-vertex graph, comparing the full ARRAY — values AND order — because
order is the contract.

The discriminating row is `e`: `Admin` with NO `score`. `V().out(E).hasLabel(Admin).values(score)`
yields `[3,3,3,3]` while the `id()` form yields six ids — so the filter keeps it and `values` drops
it, which is what proves the sentinel is not conflating "rejected by the filter" with "has no such
property".

#### Mutation: 8 of 8 caught, 0 survived

```text
   far/ignored            CAUGHT 15    far/consumed-stale        CAUGHT 10
   far/inverted           CAUGHT 15    guard/claims-bare-hop     CAUGHT  2
   far/drops-not-forced   CAUGHT  4    far/values-as-filter      CAUGHT 13
   far/boundary-overruns  CAUGHT 13    collect/refuses-nothing   CAUGHT  1
```

`far/values-as-filter` is the one worth naming: `count-shortcut.ts`'s `farFilters` treats a trailing
single-key `values(k)` as a PRESENCE filter (item 1141), so reusing that reader here would consume
the PROJECTION as a filter. The boundary scanner deliberately does not admit `values`, and the
mutant is what makes that comment load-bearing. `collect/refuses-nothing` guards the seek deference
in the shared admission rule.

#### A seekable FAR `has` is not refused, where a seekable LEADING one still is

The same split item 1602 made for its interior run, and `collectVertexFilters` now takes it as a
parameter instead of each caller re-deriving it: a seek seeds the SOURCE (`seedForStep` reads the
source step), nothing seeds from the far side of a hop, so refusing there declines the shape on
every indexed graph and gains nothing. Both halves are pinned with the index present.

#### What the sweep said — ⚠️ AND MY FIRST READING OF IT REPEATED AN ERROR ITEM 1501 HAD ALREADY CORRECTED

`read: keyed dedup lookup` reads 76.4k ops/s against other indexed reads at 468k-1.49M, and my first
framing of this entry called it "the slowest indexed read by 6-20x over its siblings".

⚠️ **THAT COMPARISON IS THE ONE ITEM 1501 STRUCK OUT**, in a block that is still in this file:
"~~`read: keyed dedup lookup` is 5-11x slower than its siblings~~ — it is not slow: `WHERE u.score =
$s` with `score = i % 100` over 20,000 users matches **200 rows** where `read: point lookup` matches
**1**, so per row it is ~17x FASTER. Comparing ops/s across rows of different cardinality is the
match-the-fixture trap." Item 1501 added that it "would have cost a whole tick". It was found here
only by reading this file before committing, which is the discipline's whole point — and it is the
third time this session that `CLOSED.md` has corrected the tick that was about to be written.

**Two things about the row DO survive that correction, and they are what the work rests on:**

- **Same query, two engines, same cardinality:** TS 76.4k against native 162.0k. It is the ONLY
  indexed read row where TS loses, and that comparison has no cardinality confound.
- **Same fixture, same cardinality, one conjunct against two** — which is the measurement that
  actually nominated the change, and which no cross-row reading is involved in. The row's own
  comment asked for exactly this: "use a standalone probe at ~1000 matches a seek to resolve the gap
  itself".

⚠️ **The sweep also says something worth keeping about where TS stands overall**, because it is the
first run of it this session — and these ARE same-query cross-engine comparisons, so the
cardinality trap above does not apply to them: indexed, TS BEATS native on most reads (point lookup
1.49M against 476.6k, permission check 491.0k against 148.4k, 2-hop 596.9k against 243.6k) and is at
parity or better on writes (append node [params] 540.0k against 451.0k). Unindexed it is 10-34x
behind. So the TS engine's weakness is the unindexed scan, and the indexed rows — where it is
already ahead — are where a regression would actually be felt.

#### The cause, read off the planner rather than profiled

```text
   WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true    carriers eqProps(2)           specializes FALSE
   (u:User {score: $s}) WHERE u.active       carriers props(1) eqProps(1)  specializes FALSE
   WHERE u.score = $s                        carriers eqProps(1)           specializes TRUE
```

`specializeSingleProp` takes exactly ONE entry in exactly ONE carrier, so items 1598/1600's work
answers the one-conjunct shape and refuses both spellings of the two-conjunct one. Priced over 1000
seeded candidates, one shape per process:

```text
   one-clause    20708  21140 ns    specialized
   two-clause    54575  56653       NOT          2.7x its one-conjunct twin
   three-clause  76166  81336       NOT
```

The first conjunct costs ~21 ns a candidate and each unspecialized one adds ~34.

⚠️ **The fix is the shape `filteredHopCount` had already paid for**, which is why this is a
half-tick of building rather than a research item. That function's header records a two-filter count
at **54.81 ms against a one-filter 28.49**, an inline indexed loop at 41.79, monomorphic key/pred
arrays at 43.82 ("so the polymorphic `Step` property load was NOT the cost — that hypothesis is
refuted"), and an unrolled straight-line pair over captured locals at **30.25**. Same cliff, same
arity, different file.

#### ⚠️ THE FIRST HALF ALONE WOULD HAVE OPENED A 2.7x SPELLING GAP, and a tripwire is what caught it

`specializeEqPair` moved the clause row 1.27x and left the inline row **FLAT** — and the reason was
invisible in the predicate, because the inline form's carriers (`props(1) eqProps(1)`) are exactly
what the new function admits. A one-line stderr print of `bindVar` and the live carriers at the call
site showed the inline shape **never arriving at all**: the ISO spelling reaches `buildNodeCount` as
TWO `InlinePred`s (`inlineOf(start)` and `nodeWhereOf(where)`), and the gate there read
`preds.length === 1`.

`fastTallyPred` closes that: up to two preds, every one `bindVar`-free, each pre-resolved and
composed in `preds` order (the written order, inline before clause, so an inline filter matching
nothing still short-circuits a faulting clause `WHERE`). Shipping the first half alone would have
put a 2.7x gap between two spellings of the row that nominated the work — the defect class this
engine is named after. Item 1586's `fused-hits=0` lesson, in a new place.

#### The numbers, an asserted A/B

```text

   two-clause    54575 56653    41555 41908 45567                  1.29x
   two-inline    58921 59478    43759 44042 44053                  1.37x
   one-clause    20708 21140    21058 21420 22144                  flat (control)
   one-inline    21515 21759    20916 22054                        flat (control)

```

Four controls flat, and **two of them are deliberately outside the gate** rather than merely


⚠️ **`pair/mixed-lifted-admits-null` survived TWICE before it was caught, and both reasons are worth

the null on the LIFTED side of a hand-built mixed pred.

#### ⚠️ AND THAT FOUND SOMETHING ELSE: the mixed arm is UNREACHABLE from any engine query

Measured, not assumed, by the technique `specializeSingleProp` itself uses — making the arm THROW
and running the suite. It fired 4 times, all of them **this file's own direct tests**. Every real
query carrying both an inline and a clause constraint splits them into two width-1 preds, which
`fastTallyPred` composes from two `specializeSingleProp` results; a single pred holding both
carriers only arrives from a hand-built `compilePredicate(properties, where, ownVar)`.

It stays, for the reason `specializeSingleProp` gives for its own two unreachable guards: nothing
ENFORCES that split, so a caller that ever does combine them must find a correct arm rather than a
decline costing 2.7x. Item 475's rule — a surviving mutant on a new guard means "redundant" as
readily as "untested", and the two have opposite fixes — makes this the redundant kind, with its
semantics pinned by direct unit tests rather than by a route that does not exist.

#### The one survivor, and the generalization

`tally/never-fires` replaces the CALL SITE with `undefined` and survives. The route is
answer-equivalent, so no test of answers can see it, and the decision itself IS extracted and tested
(`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`) — what is unprotected is the WIRING. ⚠️ **That hole is not specific
to this item**: items 1600/1601's equivalent mutants were caught only because they mutated the
FUNCTION. Every fast-arm call site in `shortcuts.ts` has the same unguarded wiring, and nothing short

### Item 1605 — ⚠️ **A WRONG ANSWER: an index made `{k: null}` UNDER-COUNT by exactly the vertices that lack the key.** Found while re-pricing item 1597's target, which is also corrected here — its "4-7x" is now **2.08x**, and the 75% predicate share it rested on is 19.4%. That target is **BUILT at item 1607**, which this item unblocked

This tick went looking at what `isScalar` admits, because the exactness lever item 1597 priced
threads a flag through the same loop. The loop turned out to be already wrong.

#### The bug

`indexCandidates` seeds from `node.pred.props` — the INLINE constraint — and `isScalar` admits
`null`, so a null-valued inline property seeded from the index's null bucket. The two equality
readings differ precisely there:

```text
   {k: null}         matches a stored null AND an ABSENT key   (item 260, and `satisfies`)
   WHERE n.k = null  matches NEITHER
```

A value bucket holds the stored nulls. It **cannot** hold the vertices with no such key, and no
re-validation can add them back — a seed is only ever NARROWED. On a fixture with 10 stored nulls,
10 absent and 20 valued:

```text
   MATCH (u:P {note: null}) RETURN count(*)    unindexed 20    indexed 10
   MATCH (u:P) WHERE u.note IS NULL            unindexed 20    indexed 20
```

**Twenty is right**, and three independent sources say so: the unindexed path, the `IS NULL`
spelling (which canonicalizes TO `{k: null}`), and `satisfies`'s own `props` loop. The indexed path
silently dropped ten rows. This is item 149's one contract — "an index may change the COST and must
never change the COUNT" — and the fix is to decline the seek, because the matching set is not a
value bucket.

⚠️ **NATIVE AGREES WITH THE FIXED BEHAVIOUR**, which is why `inline-null-seek-parity.test.ts`
exists: had native matched the pre-fix TS answer, this would have been a new DIVERGENCE rather than
a repair, and that is worth a test rather than an assumption. 9 of 9 shapes byte-identical.

#### How it hid, which is the part worth keeping

- **Every probe this session used a non-null `$param`.** The one contract that would have caught it
  is asserted by `gql-seek-revalidation-probe.mjs` — on exactly the shapes it measures, none of them
  null-valued.
- **No fuzzer covers it.** `differential-fuzz` does generate inline constraints, but over generated
  property values; a null-valued inline property against an INDEXED key is outside what it builds,
  and the index is what makes the two readings diverge.
- The whole suite was green, and items 1598/1600/1604 all touched this family without tripping it.

#### ⚠️ AND I BRIEFLY BELIEVED SOMETHING FAR WORSE, because of the dist

The first reproduction showed `MATCH (u:P {note: "x"}) RETURN count(*)` returning 3 on a 3-vertex
graph while the ROWS twin returned 1 — every filtered count ignoring its predicate, at every size.
That was **my own ablation still in the built `dist`**: the source had been restored with
`git restore` and never rebuilt. `fuzzers-read-built-dists` is the standing note and this is the
same trap in the DIAGNOSTIC direction — it manufactures a catastrophic-looking bug rather than
hiding a real one. Two minutes, and the tell was that the wrongness did not scale with anything.

#### Item 1597's target, re-priced — and the number was stale in BOTH directions

That item priced "skip re-validation on an exact seed" at **4-7x**, from a profile where predicate
evaluation was ~75%. Items 1598/1600/1604 have since specialized that predicate, so a fresh profile
of the same query reads:

```text
   45.8%  evalLabelExpr          the label test, which item 1599 REFUTED both levers for
   9.9%   structuralEq
   8.2%   get labels
   5.4%   (anonymous) :4988      the specialized predicate closure
   4.1%   propOf
   1.4%   countEquals            the seek itself
```

So the predicate is now **19.4%**, not 75%, and the label test is 55.6%. By share the target looked
dead at ~1.24x. ⚠️ **The ablation says 2.08x** — 12766-13279 ns down to 6324-6354 with the predicate
call removed — which is item 1600's lesson again: a share under-reads a per-element cost by its
effect on the loop's shape. So:

- **item 1597's 4-7x is wrong and corrected to ~2.08x** (its heading is struck);
- **the target is still real**, and unlike item 1599's label test it is fully reachable: for an
  EXACT seed, removing the predicate IS the ablation rather than an approximation of it;
- **this item is a prerequisite for it.** A null-valued seed must not survive into an exactness
  check, which is why the clause-side guard below went in now.

#### Mutation: 4 of 5 caught, and the fifth was MEANT to survive

```text
   null/guard-removed             CAUGHT  6     null/checks-undefined-instead  CAUGHT  6
   null/guard-inverted            CAUGHT 20     null/clause-hint-also-guarded  SURVIVED
   null/never-seeds               CAUGHT 14
```

`null/never-seeds` is the over-reach control: the route assertions in `inline-null-seek.test.ts`
check that a non-null inline value still yields a candidate, so "no wrong answer" cannot be achieved
by never seeking.

⚠️ **`null/clause-hint-also-guarded` was run to find out whether the clause side depends on seeding
a null, and its survival is the answer: 0 failures across 4,094 tests.** So the guard is
answer-neutral there — and that is the evidence on which it then became CODE. It stops pointless
work (a bucket walk that cannot produce a match) and, more importantly, it stops being harmless the
moment a seed may skip re-validation. Closing it next to the `props` fix that had the mirror-image
bug is cheaper than rediscovering it as a wrong answer.

### Item 1606 — ⚠️ **bun auto-upgraded 1.4.0 -> 1.4.4 MID-SESSION and made a zero-length FFI result THROW**, turning three native tests red and `write-fuzz` unreliable with no repo change behind it. One guard fixes it — and the way it was nearly misattributed is the part worth keeping

Found while finishing item 1607: the native suite went from `1040 pass 0 fail` to `1054 pass 2 fail`
with nothing in the tree to explain it.

#### What broke

`takeResult` copies a crate-owned `(ptr, len)` pair with
`new Uint8Array(toArrayBuffer(resPtr, 0, len)).slice()`. Under **bun 1.4.4** that raises

```text
   TypeError: length must be > 0. This usually means a bug in your code.
```

for `len === 0`, where **1.4.0** returned an empty buffer. A zero-length result is not a bug here:
`asByteLength` admits it BY CONTRACT (it rejects only a negative or non-integer length), and an
empty payload is the right answer for serializing an empty graph or dumping an empty schema. Three
tests went red — `differential fuzz: write path`, `dropIndex … dumpSchema round-trip` and `an empty
graph dumps an empty schema` — and the first of those is a byte-identity fuzzer, so the invariant it
guards was simply not being checked.

The fix answers `len === 0` with a shared empty array and never calls `toArrayBuffer`. `lnk_free`
still runs for it, because it always did: under 1.4.0 this path built the buffer and then freed, so
the crate side already expects `lnk_free(ptr, 0)`. Both call sites are fixed — the result path and
the last-error decode, where an empty report now yields `''` and `parseErrorReport` turns that into
the generic code exactly as before.

#### ⚠️ AND IT WAS NEARLY BLAMED ON THE ITEM IN FLIGHT

The obvious reading was that item 1607's exact-seed skip had broken byte-identity — a GQL read
change showing up in a write-path differential is strange but not impossible, and the test was
failing. The first check seemed to confirm it:

```text
   with the change in the tree       1 of 1 runs FAILED
   with the change reverted          1 of 1 runs PASSED
```

⚠️ **Both of those were single runs, and the second was the fluke.** Repeating:

```text
   with the change      1 pass, 2 fail  of 3
   with it reverted     0 pass, 5 fail  of 5
```

So it fails either way and the change is innocent. CLAUDE.md's "match sample counts on both sides,
and prefer min or p25 over the mean" is written for PERFORMANCE arms; this is the same rule applied
to a PASS/FAIL arm, where it matters more — a one-run comparison was about to send the next hour
into reverting correct work. Two further wrong turns came off the same root before the cause was
found: removing the new parity test file made the count WORSE (3 fail, not 2), which ruled out test
pollution, and only then did the version banner in bun's own output — `v1.4.0` in the session's
earlier runs, `v1.4.4` in the later ones — point at the real cause. `~/.bun/bin/bun` is restamped
13:04 today.

#### What this says about the gates

The session had read `bun run fuzz` 20/0 and the native suite green several times before 13:04, so
the regression window is bounded by the upgrade rather than by any commit. ⚠️ **An environmental
change can turn a byte-identity fuzzer red, and a red fuzzer is indistinguishable from a broken
engine until someone checks the toolchain.** Worth knowing the next time a suite goes red with a
clean `git diff`: check `bun --version` and the mtime of the binary before reading the diff again.

3 of 3 where it passed 0 of 5 before.

### Item 1607 — **the exactness lever item 1597 named is BUILT: 1.8-2.1x on the seeded count, 3.9x unlabelled**, by not re-validating what the seek already decided. ⚠️ And `exact` does NOT go on the candidate, which is where item 1597's own sketch put it

Item 1597 named it, priced it at 4-7x, and deliberately deferred it as "a correctness-sensitive
change that gets its own tick". Item 1605 re-priced it at **2.08x** by ablation and cleared its
prerequisite (a null-valued seed, which would have become a wrong answer under exactness). This
builds it.

#### The design, and the one place item 1597's sketch was wrong

That item proposed marking each `SeedCandidate` `exact`. ⚠️ **That puts the judgement in the wrong
object.** `indexCandidates` reads a `CNode`'s `pred`; `buildNodeCount` skips a list of
`InlinePred`s built separately from the AST. They express the same constraints today and nothing
makes them — a flag computed from one and applied to the other is a wrong answer waiting for the day
they drift.

So the candidate reports only a FACT — `eqKey`, "this set is every vertex whose `k` equals the value
I sought" — and the verdict is formed against the predicate actually held:

- `soleEqualityKey(preds)`: the one key this pred list asserts an equality on and NOTHING else —
  one `InlinePred`, no `bindVar`, exactly one entry in `props` or `eqProps`, no residual `where`, no
  second carrier. The loop iterates the keys PRESENT, so a thirteenth carrier added to `CPredicate`
  REFUSES rather than being ignored (`specializeSingleProp`'s structure, for the reason its first
  version shipped a wrong answer by missing four of twelve).
- `seedIsExact(candidate, soleKey)`: the two-line verdict.

**The LABEL is not covered and still runs** — the index returns vertices by VALUE across all labels,
which is the first of item 149's two risks.

#### The numbers, measured on two fixtures

```text
                                        PRE              POST          verdict
   count 400 hits (own probe)      12363 13279 ns    6707 6716 7428    1.8x
   count 400 hits (149's probe)    10568 11371       5139             2.1x
   count 400 hits, NO label        10739 10957       2724             3.9x
   count 400 hits, inline          15559 19045       8724             1.8-2.2x
   count, 1000 candidates clause   21058 22144      13836             1.5x
   count, 1000 candidates inline   20916 22054      13838             1.5x   (spellings converged)
   count, 1 hit                      513   572        513             flat (already closed form)
   values, 400 hits                21752            21752             flat (control: not the tally)
   count, two conjuncts            41271 45567      42946             flat (control: NOT exact)
   count, three conjuncts          76166 81336      79439             flat (control: NOT exact)
```

The **unlabelled row is the full ablation** — no label test to pay either — and at 3.9x it is the
shape where the seek now costs essentially nothing per hit. Four controls flat, two of them
deliberately outside the gate. The index-neutrality contract holds on every row of item 149's own
probe ("answers agree"), which is the assertion that matters more than any of the timings.

#### Correctness: the fixture is built so the LABEL can fail

#### The lever, and that it is already shipped TEN times

`effectiveLabel`/`vacuousLabel` (items 1551/1552) drop a label carried by EVERY vertex. They are
used at **ten** sites in `shortcuts.ts`, all hop builders; `buildNodeCount` is not one, so a
single-label graph pays a per-candidate test that is a tautology by construction. ⚠️ **That also
disposes of item 1599's blocker without reopening it**: that item declined to test a candidate
against the label BUCKET because `verticesByLabel` can disagree with `v.labels`, and left the call
to the owner. `vacuousLabel` reads the bucket's SIZE, and that reading is already shipped.

Built and measured, asserted A/B over 1000 seeded candidates:

```text
   SINGLE label (vacuous: the elision fires)
     one-clause      13877 14255 ns  ->   2463  2516     5.6x
   MULTI label (NOT vacuous: it cannot fire)
     one-clause      13563 14325     ->  14001 14268     flat (CONTROL)
     two-clause      36889 37414     ->  36374 38660     flat (CONTROL)
```

On item 149's own probe the seeded count went 5139 -> **1481** (3.5x, and 161x over unindexed) and
its inline twin 8724 -> 2751. ⚠️ The MULTI control took two attempts: the first used `i % 2` for the
label and `score = i % 20` for the seek key, so **parity correlated with the bucket** — every score
bucket was all-`User` or all-`Other`, making each query all-match or all-reject on the label alone.
`i % 3` decorrelates it (gcd(3, 20) = 1) and each bucket then holds a mix, which is the only fixture
a label test can be measured over.

#### ⚠️ WHY IT IS REVERTED: two spellings of one question, disagreeing — ⚠️ **AND THIS SECTION IS WRONG, see item 1609**

> ⚠️ **The hop comparison below is the one pair that cannot show the problem.** Both a hop count and
> a hop ROWS query take SHORTCUTS, and shortcuts elide; a hop spelling that DECLINES its shortcut
> goes to the general matcher, which does not. Measured at item 1609:
> `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.n ORDER BY a.n` answers 6 where the four shortcut spellings answer 7. So the split shipped with items 1551/1552 and the node family joins an existing class rather
> than inventing one — which is why item 1609 ships the elision uniformly instead.

Ten vertices all labelled `P`, then `v.labels = ['Q']` through the RAW setter, which does not
maintain `verticesByLabel`:

```text
   MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = $v RETURN count(*)    5     <- with the elision
   MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = $v RETURN n.k         4 rows
```

The defect class this engine is named after, as a CORRECTNESS bug. And the ten existing sites do
**not** have it: measured, a hop count and a hop ROWS query both answer 9 after the same setter
write, so they are uniformly elided and agree with each other. The node count would be the first
site whose own two spellings diverge, because the rows path (`detectNodeProjection`) does not elide.

#### What is faster across the board — the measurement, not the preference

The alternative is to fix the raw setter so the index is never stale, which makes the elision sound
everywhere. `label-setter-cost-probe.mjs`, 20,000 vertices:

```text
   v.labels = [different]    the raw setter today       35.2  37.1 ns
   v.addLabel + removeLabel  the MAINTAINED API        390.6 412.9     ~200 ns a call
   v.setProperty             for scale                 121.0 126.6
```

So index maintenance on a label write costs what the maintained API costs — **5.5x the raw setter** —
for read gains IDENTICAL to the elision's. ⚠️ **And it is not a 150 ns patch.** `verticesByLabel`
holds vertex OBJECTS, so the setter would have to find the canonical instance (two `Vertex`es can
share an id, which the box comment states outright); and `addLabelToVertex` participates in the
TX-TOUCHED SET and the UNDO LOG, so a setter mutating buckets without joining that machinery leaves
a rolled-back transaction with a stale index — the same bug in a new place. Done properly, the raw
setter becomes `addLabel`.

**So the elision is the faster answer and the setter fix is the slower one.** The elision's single
requirement is UNIFORMITY: the label-test line appears at **seven** sites in this file and today none
of them elides, so the engine is consistent. Eliding at all seven keeps it consistent; eliding at
fewer is the gap above. That is a seven-site edit to hot walks, which `executor-edits-perturb` prices
at up to 16% on unrelated rows and so wants measured PER SITE — its own item, with its own numbers,
rather than the tail of this one.

> with every control flat. That item also found the per-ELEMENT version of the hoist costs the
> control fixture 1.32x, and that two of the seven sites are unreachable when seeded.

#### ⚠️ ITEM 1608's OBJECTION, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG

It found that eliding at `buildNodeCount` alone made `count(*)` answer 5 where the rows spelling
answered 4 after a raw `v.labels =` write, called that a new equivalent-spelling gap, and reverted.
It also checked the hop family and reported it CONSISTENT — "a hop count and a hop ROWS query both
answer 9".

**Both of those hop spellings take shortcuts.** A hop spelling that DECLINES its shortcut goes to the
general matcher, which does not elide:

```text
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*)            7    <- shortcut, elides
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.n                 7    <- shortcut, elides
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN collect(b.n)        7    <- shortcut, elides
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN DISTINCT b.n        7    <- shortcut, elides
   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.n ORDER BY a.n    6    <- GENERAL, honours the setter
```

So the shortcut-vs-general split shipped with items 1551/1552 and the node family now JOINS an
existing class rather than inventing one. Item 1608 compared the one pair that could not show it —
the same shape of mistake as testing two arms that are both the fast one.

What this item does guarantee is the property 1608 actually wanted: **every shape that takes a NODE
shortcut agrees with every other.** That is what the test pins, and it is what the single-site
version broke.

#### ⚠️ THREE FAILED ATTEMPTS AT THE EDIT, and each failure mode is worth keeping

The change is five near-identical sites, which invites a blanket pass. Three of them went wrong:

1. **A blanket `labelEff`-anchored pass** added a declaration at the two walks that ALREADY had one
   (items 1607 and 1610), and at sites where `soleKey` was not in scope. `Cannot redeclare
block-scoped variable`.
2. **Matching the gate by INDENT** hit three gates in walks that are not single-node scans at all —
   no `seeded`, no `soleKey`, no `eqKey` — so they referenced names that do not exist there.
3. **A regex anchored on `labelEff … label test … gate`** matched SIX walks where five lack the
   skip, because `(?:.|\n)*?` between the parts can span a walk boundary. The assert on the hit
   count is what stopped it writing.

What worked is a bounded backward scan: a gate belongs to a single-node scan iff a label test sits
within the preceding eight lines, and the declaration goes after that walk's own nearest `labelEff`.
⚠️ **The assert-the-count discipline earned itself three times in one item** — every one of those
attempts would have shipped something broken or over-broad without it.

#### And a literal I got wrong for the third time in this family

`MATCH (u:Admin) … RETURN max(u.n)` — I wrote 51; the engine said 56 and was right. `Admin` is not
the complement of `User` in this fixture: `i % 3 === 0` is Admin-only and `i % 3 === 2` is BOTH, so
the Admin set includes the overlap. ⚠️ Worse, **`max` cannot discriminate the label test at all here**
— every label's `t1` set contains 56, so the folding-arm mutant answered correctly by accident and
SURVIVED on `max` alone. `min` differs by label (User 1, Admin 6, both 11, all 1) and catches it. An
overlapping-label fixture is exactly what this file needs and exactly what makes its literals easy to
get wrong by eye.

### Item 1613 — **21.6x on a DISTINCT far count with a filter** (`V().out(E).has(team,eq).dedupe().count()`, 13.31 ms to 616 us), closing a **76.5x** cliff whose no-filter neighbour was already a closed form. OPEN: nothing. Both spellings around the `dedupe` are answered.

#### The cliff

```text
   V().out(E).dedupe().count()                  180212 ns   CLOSED (`distinctHopCount`)
   V().out(E).has(team,eq).dedupe().count()   13309727      THE PIPELINE      76.53x
   ... after this rung                           616026      21.6x, and 3.42x of its neighbour
```

One `has` between the hop and the dedupe. `countShortcut` gates `distinctHopCount` on
`mid.length !== 2`, so any filter between them dropped the whole query to the traverser pipeline —
which then also builds a `Set` of every distinct far vertex, the cost item 1590 deleted from the
unfiltered shape.

`filteredDistinctHopCount` sits BEFORE that arity gate, so the two rungs do not fight over it.

#### What the rung does, and the one thing it does NOT re-derive

`distinctHopCount`'s insight carries over unchanged: the distinct targets of type-`T` edges are
exactly the vertices holding at least one `T` IN-edge, so the question is per-VERTEX and needs no
`Set` and no edge walk. The filter needs the vertex itself, which is the only change.

**⚠️ No multi-type guard, and that is `distinctHopCount`'s own reasoning rather than an omission.**
This counts VERTICES, and "has a non-empty bucket for any of these labels" is a UNION per vertex, so
an edge carrying two named types makes its target qualify once either way. The guard the hop-COUNT
rungs need (`hopChainShape`'s 13 divergences) exists because `degreeOfTypes` SUMS buckets; nothing is
summed here.

**Both spellings around the `dedupe` are admitted**, and must be: `has` then `dedupe` and `dedupe`
then `has` describe the same set of far vertices, and a COUNT makes emission order unobservable
anyway. Two spellings of one question, one rung.

**A LEADING filter is handled rather than declined**, because declining it would leave every
selective-label graph on the pipeline. The far vertex must then be reachable from a SURVIVING start,
which is an early-exiting `any` over its in-edges, not a count — item 1602's `anyStart` split in the
same words.

#### Driving from the VERTICES rather than the reverse index was worth 1.64x

The first version iterated `edgesToByLabel`'s ENTRIES and called `getVertexById(id)` per candidate:
**1009957 ns** against this version's **616026**. Every vertex carries its own adjacency box, cached
on first read, so "does `w` hold a `T` in-edge?" is a FIELD read rather than a string-keyed `Map.get`
into the graph. Items 162/321 priced the three ways over 200,000 vertices — string key **59.7 ns**, a
`Map` keyed on the vertex object 30.5, a `WeakMap` 43.8, a cached reference **16.1**. Driving from
`far.source` also reuses the filter run's own candidate set instead of enumerating twice.

#### ⚠️ The instrument lied first, and the lesson generalizes to every probe in this repo

`gremlin-cliff-finder.ts`'s first version called `countShortcut` on the plan as written. `run` calls
it on `effectivePlan(plan, graph, false)`, which runs `dropVacuousLabels` — so a leading
`hasLabel('User')` on a fixture where every vertex is a `User` is DELETED before any rung sees the
plan, and `mid.length` differs by one. Fixing the probe flipped a verdict from `pipeline` to
`CLOSED`.

That is not a one-off: **most of this repo's fixtures are single-label**, so an instrument asking a
rung about the raw plan invents cliffs wherever a vacuous label is present. The probe now carries the
reason at the call site, and `filtered-distinct-hop-count.test.ts` pins it with a shape where the
verdict actually differs — the UNFILTERED one, because the first attempt at that test used a shape
THIS rung answers on the raw plan too.

#### What the rung is, and what it deliberately is not

A SEPARATE module, not an arm inside `hop-values.ts`: `executor-edits-perturb` prices an edit to that file at up to 16% on unrelated rows in an arbitrary direction (items 1413/1440/1442), and its four existing hand walks are the hottest one-hop paths in the surface. The new rung is one `??` link at the end of `run`'s chain, in item 1535's order, so no plan an earlier rung admits can change route.

- **ORDER IS TINKERPOP'S BY CONSTRUCTION** — `out` flatMaps per traverser, so the row sequence is the depth-first nesting written literally. Gremlin streams are compared ORDERED by the differential fuzzer, so walking the edge index once or hoisting the far side is a cross-engine failure, not an optimization — items 167, 1431 and 1432's limit. This removes DELEGATION only.
- **NO DEDUPLICATION**: two paths to the same far vertex are two rows and a self-loop is a step. `dedupe()` lands in `rest`.
- **NO MULTI-TYPE GUARD NEEDED** — nothing is summed; each hop reads its own single bucket, unlike `degreeOfTypes`.
- **EXACTLY TWO HOPS, SINGLE-TYPE, NON-`both`** — `pairTypes`' stated reason: a general N is a stack of iterators, which is the per-vertex array that branch measured as the whole cost of the general form. `both`'s contract is out-bucket then in-bucket PER VERTEX, so nesting two is four interleaved orders.

**59.12 ms by hand against the pipeline's 381.37 at 1,279,840 rows — 6.45x**, essentially this item's own ratio. The lever is real; it is a second measurement.

A verdict column that is wrong for a whole family is worse than none: the `values` rows looked uniformly unanswered and the ratios beside them could not be read. It now consults every rung `run` consults, in `run`'s own `??` order. Two defects in two consecutive items on an instrument three days old — the cost of a verdict read from the engine is that it has to be read from ALL of it.

#### Correctness: the PIPELINE ITSELF as an ORDERED oracle

The rung declines a `V(id, …)` source, so the same query with every vertex id listed in `graph.vertices` order runs the identical question down the pipeline — `sourceFromIds` neither dedupes nor reorders. The two row sequences must match element for element, which is the strongest check available for a walk whose whole risk is row ORDER. A hand nested walk is the second oracle and derived literals the third; all three agree on the eight-path fixture, including a self-loop, a vertex with no `k` (dropped by `values`, kept by `id`), an isolated vertex, mixed `out`/`in` directions and per-hop type differences.

#### What was reused rather than re-derived

`collectVertexFilters` (admission, including the seek deference), `compileGates`, `survives` and `isVertexFilterStep` are all `count-shortcut.ts`'s and `start-filtered-hop-values.ts`', exported rather than copied. `compileGates` alone is worth 1.93x on the label side and 1.16x on the predicate side (items 1536/1492), and a second copy of a specialization table is precisely the drift this executor keeps paying for.

`lead/ignored` and `mid/ignored` **SURVIVED in the LAZY loop while their EAGER twins died**. The far filter was covered lazily _by accident_, through the `limit` test item 1614 wrote for a different reason.

The fix is a trailing `limit` — it puts a step in `rest`, which routes through the generator — asserted for all three positions, each against the pipeline and each with a DIFFERENT row count (1, 3, 5) so no position can pass another's expectation.

**This generalizes to every `HopWalk` in the executor.** `hop-values.ts` has four such pairs, `start-filtered-hop-values.ts` more; the rule its header states ("written twice as the same loop") protects against drift in the CODE and says nothing about whether the tests reach both. #### The question, and why it is not "is this code tested"

Item 1615 found two mutants SURVIVING in a fused walk's LAZY loop while their EAGER twins died. Every `HopWalk` in the Gremlin executor is written twice — a generator and a `drain()` — and `toArray` with an empty residual reads `drain`, so a suite that only calls `toArray` reaches the eager copy and never the generator. `hop-values.ts`' header states the rule that keeps the two loops from DRIFTING; **nothing stated that the tests reach both.**

So the generalization got screened rather than reasoned about. The mutant is deliberately crude and universal — DUPLICATE one `yield` — because every row through that loop then comes out twice, which no fixture and no unspecified-order liberty can excuse: GQL's row order is unspecified, its row MULTISET is not.

```text
   gremlin   9/13 caught on the first run
     hop-values.ts:454                  the THREE-OR-MORE-TYPES walk (`manyTypes`)
     start-filtered-hop-values.ts:229   the `both(T)` walk, OUT bucket
     start-filtered-hop-values.ts:241   the `both(T)` walk, IN bucket
     optional-hop.ts:83                 `optional`'s non-vertex PASSTHROUGH
   gql      10/11 caught
     executor/matching.ts:1261          `anyWalk`, the bare-`ANY` trail enumerator
```

Reaching a lazy walk takes a RESIDUAL: a trailing `limit` leaves a step in `rest`, so `run` wraps the generator instead of reading `drain`. That is the only spelling that routes there — and it is the same mechanism `eager-tail-cache` says must never read `drain` under a `limit`.

#### The two that are not lazy/eager at all, and are the more interesting finds

**`optional-hop.ts:83` — a branch chosen by a type test.** `optionalHopStep` emits the traverser unchanged when its value is not a vertex. Reaching it took three attempts: the static frontier check rejects `values(k).optional(out(E))`, `inject(…)` and `id()` with _"out() moves from a vertex, but the frontier is a scalar"_. What gets through is a frontier the checker cannot type — a `select` of a tag holding a scalar. So the branch is reachable and was simply untested, not dead. Oracle: the general path, reached by giving `optional` a two-step sub-plan.

**`executor/matching.ts:1261` — `anyWalk`, and the route predicate is why it was invisible.** `pickSeedDriver` sends `ANY` to the O(V+E) BFS driver whenever `bfsReducible` holds (one segment, `min <= 1`, no inline predicate), and **every existing bare-`ANY` test uses `*` (min 0) or `{1,1}`** — including `gql-conformance.test.ts`'s "bare ANY yields one path per endpoint", which has existed since item 614. TS and native agreed on it all along — the path was unpinned, not wrong.

This is the same CLASS as item 1615's finding — a branch chosen by a route predicate where every test happens to take the other side — which is why both items pin the ROUTE and not only the answer.

Depth-first PREORDER by construction: the stack advances the deepest live iterator and descends on each non-leaf edge, which is what the nested loops produce. That claim is checked rather than asserted — every depth-3+ test compares against the pipeline ORDERED via the `V(id, …)` oracle, including mixed directions and per-hop types, and `drain` is compared against the generator element for element.

#### The instrument

`gremlin-cliff-finder.ts` produced four items in a row by asking what no absolute benchmark asks: take shapes that differ by ONE clause, ask the engine which rung answers each, and time them all. The GQL twin can do better than a boolean — `compileLinear` returns a record of ~22 NAMED rungs, so it prints WHICH fire. That matters because of `rung-precedence-decides-speed`: a willing rung can be starved by a broader one above it in `runLinear`'s chain (1.80-6.00x at item 1583), and the fired-rung SET is the only thing that shows it.

The rung reader is `deferred-hop-order.test.ts`' `routes` helper, including its warning — a rung is a FUNCTION, so filtering on `typeof v === 'function'` is what keeps it honest as `CLinear` grows; excluding fields by name let item 1510's `writes: boolean` register as a rung and fail 13 tests.

#### The lever that shipped: the cached box, not a hashed id

`expand`'s directed fast path read `(forward ? graph.edgesFromByLabel : graph.edgesToByLabel).get(v.id)` — one hash of an id STRING per expansion, on the hottest line of the matcher. `Vertex.adjFrom`/`adjTo` memoize the same `Map` object, and `@lenke/core`'s `adjacency-box.test.ts` states the purpose outright: _"every consumer that already holds the vertex object stops hashing (audit items 162, 321)"_. Those items priced the three ways over 200,000 vertices — string key **59.7 ns**, a `Map` keyed on the vertex object 30.5, a `WeakMap` 43.8, a **cached reference 16.1**. The Gremlin engine has read the box for ages; this is the GQL side adopting the same access. `outSteps`, `inSteps` and `hasIncidentEdges` were on the same string-keyed path and move with it.

**O(1) by-id access is untouched**: `getVertexById` is unchanged, and the box is the same object the id-keyed map returns — asserted as IDENTITY in the new test, because a copy would pass a deep comparison and then go stale.

#### ⚠️ THE PATH MODE CHECK WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, and the engine corrected me twice

First I refused `pattern.mode !== undefined` — and `mode` is never `undefined`, it defaults to `'trail'`, so the rung declined EVERY query. `routes-fired.test.ts` caught that on the first run: it asserts each of the twenty detectors fires for its own shape, and the new one fired for nothing.

Then the real question: is TRAIL load-bearing across two SEGMENTS? It forbids a repeated edge, and a self-loop lets a two-segment pattern traverse the same edge twice. It is NOT, and that is **measured rather than reasoned** — on a fixture with a loop at `a` plus `a->b`, the default, `WALK`, `TRAIL` and `ACYCLIC` all answer the same rows, including the one that reuses the loop edge. The restrictors apply per REPETITION of a quantifier, exactly as `detectHopProjection`'s comment states, and a quantifier is declined by `plainRel`. `detectHopProjection` checks neither field for the same reason.

#### ⚠️ An UNREAD path variable is DROPPED before any detector sees the clauses

`MATCH p = … RETURN c.k` fires this rung and SHOULD: there is no `Path` to build. I wrote the test expecting a decline; `drop-unread-path-var` is the rewrite and the clauses the detectors receive are the post-rewrite form. The decline is real the moment `p` is read, and the test now pins both halves.

#### ⚠️ TWELVE eyeballed literals wrong, the engine right every time

The sixth through seventeenth of this session. Two causes, both avoidable: I listed six two-hop paths and then wrote four rows, and I forgot that `d` carries BOTH labels so an `M` start includes it. Every literal in the file is now **derived by a script over the table**, and the file says so.

What actually settles each case is the oracle: the rung declines any clause `WHERE`, so appending `WHERE true` runs the IDENTICAL question down the general matcher — item 570 records `WHERE true` as _the_ control for this engine, and here it is the only way to reach the path this rung replaced. Row order without an `ORDER BY` is unspecified (item 198), so the comparison is a multiset. The literals exist to catch the case where both arms are wrong together, which is the only thing the oracle cannot see.

#### One more wrong intuition, recorded rather than deleted

I wrote `RETURN c.k AS k, size($p) AS n` as a decline, reasoning that it reads a name the pattern does not bind. The engine is right: `$p` is a PARAMETER, `freePredicateVars` does not report it, and `projectRow` is handed `params` anyway. #### The ratio was a nomination; the profile was the price

`gql-cliff-finder.ts` flagged grouped-hop-count, topk-over-a-hop and collect-over-a-hop at 16.9x, 21.4x and 20.3x their non-hop neighbours — all three walking 80,000 edges where the neighbour touches 20,000 vertices, so the ratio alone says nothing. Per EDGE they are 69-91 ns against the one-hop ROW projection's 46, which is the number to beat. The profiles:

```text
   groupedhop   detectGroupedHopCount's closure 23.7%   expand 16.3%   gc 8.1%
   collecthop   startDriven 14.6%   gc 13.5%   projectRow 5.0%   walkRows 4.1%

```

Only `groupedhop` has a frame to attack, and it is not the rung's own closure — it is **`expand`**, the general path's adjacency iterator, which the rung calls per edge. `collecthop` is `startDriven` plus garbage collection, which is `hop-projection.ts`'s own walk doing what it does; `topkhop`'s profile is flat. So two of the three SUSPECTs are honest work, recorded here so nobody prices them again from the ratio.

#### What `expand` costs a caller, and the narrow substitution

`expand` is a GENERATOR that yields a fresh `{ edge, node }` per edge, so a caller pays one resume and one object allocation per edge — 80,000 of each on this fixture, with the garbage collector at 8.1% beside it. For a DIRECTED SINGLE-TYPE hop there is one `Set` to walk and nothing to dedupe.

`directedBucket(v, rel)` returns `{ set, forward }` for exactly that shape and `undefined` for every other, and the refusal is the load-bearing half. `detectGroupedHopCount`'s own comment records what hand-rolling the general case cost: **a `T|S` edge counted TWICE** under `-[:T|S]->`, because the per-type buckets both hold it and only `expand`'s `Set` dedupes across them. So the multi-type, untyped and `both` patterns still go through `expand`.

It also returns a shape for an EMPTY bucket rather than `undefined`: `undefined` means "this pattern needs `expand`", and conflating that with "this vertex has no such edge" would send every zero-degree vertex down the general path.

#### Where the resolution happens is the whole design

`walkSegments` recurses once per matched edge, so resolving inside it would be PER ELEMENT — and item 1609 measured exactly that mistake at **1.32x WORSE** on its control. The mutant that writes it back is CAUGHT with 5 failures, and the test runs one cached plan against two graphs where `Q` is selective in one and universal in the other, in both orders.
