#### `idRank` is one helper in `adjacency.ts`, not two copies

`rank[a] < rank[b]` iff `ids[a] < ids[b]`, because ranks are assigned in id order and vertex ids are UNIQUE — so the tie-break can never itself tie, and the sort uses the same `<`/`>` on strings the loops used rather than a second definition of "lexicographic". Cost: one O(V log V) sort of V string compares per call, against O(rounds × E) in the loop. The extraction was forced by the lint gate (`max-statements` 87 against 80, and `no-nested-ternary` on the comparator) and is better than the inline form anyway — it measured 121.25 against the inline version's 125.41.

#### ⚠️ Mutation 12 of 12, and it took THREE attempts at one fixture

The rank's comparator (inverted, constant), the sort removed, a numeric sort, the permutation inverted, the id read replaced; and at both call sites the tie-break dropped, inverted, and the primary key ignored.

**`lp/count-ignored` and `pp/energy-ignored` survived TWICE before dying**, and both reasons are worth having:

1. First I had no test for them at all — a PRE-EXISTING gap, since item 1625 does not touch `c > bestCount`. My first attempt to fix it guessed a fixture; label propagation on a small graph OSCILLATES (a triangle-plus-tail answered `v10, v9, v10, v10, v9` at iterations 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, and the `v9` readings were the tie-break picking the smallest of three distinct labels, not a majority). I removed it and wrote down that I could not pin it.
2. Then I derived one properly from the round-by-round labels — and it STILL survived, because **the edge order is load-bearing**. The dirty list is built in first-sighting order, so dropping `c > bestCount` only changes the answer when the MAJORITY label is seen SECOND. With `x—p, x—q` inserted first the best is already the majority and the condition is never re-tested. Reordering so the minority neighbour comes first killed both mutants with one failure each.

**A fixture that exercises the line is not the same as a fixture that discriminates on it** — and the thing that decided it here was neither the graph nor the query but the INSERTION ORDER of three edges.

#### The fingerprint earned itself three times, which is the tick's product

Item 1625 added one line to the probe: print the number of DISTINCT values in the result column, so an ablation that changes the answer cannot read as a win. Generalizing the probe to every algorithm then broke it three different ways, and the fingerprint caught all three:

1. **The column map was guessed.** `closeness` and `betweenness` return `centrality`, not `score`, so `r[COL]` was `undefined` on every row and the probe reported **1 distinct answer over 80,000 rows**. The map is now printed off the engine, in the file.
2. **`shortestPathWeighted` IS NOT AN ALGORITHM.** `runAlgorithmSync` returned `undefined` and the probe crashed. `algo-scaling-bench` runs `shortestPath` with a `weightProperty` and LABELS the row `shortestPathWeighted` — so reaching for the name found nothing. `WEIGHTED=1` is the probe's equivalent.

That third one is the whole argument for printing an answer beside a timing: the ratio was RIGHT and the mechanism was wrong, and no amount of repetition or control-matching would have found it.

A fourth, smaller hazard is now documented in the file rather than discovered again: **the centralities hang at the probe's default size.** `betweenness` and `closeness` are O(V·E) and `algo-scaling-bench` runs them at V=1000/4000 while everything else runs at 40,000+ — that is what its `div` column is for. ### Item 1629 — **1.26x on `V().coalesce(out(T), identity()).values(k)`**, the half item 1628 left open: `coalesce` now reads the adjacency bucket for its FIRST arm when that arm is a single vertex step. ⚠️ And the mutation pass found a real hole the whole test file had missed — reading the LAST arm instead of arm 0 was answer-equivalent across every case, because in all of them the last arm is one the fusion refuses

OPEN: nothing in the branch-step family. `optional` (item 1628) and `coalesce` are both fused for the one shape that matters; `choose` routes on a test rather than on emptiness and is a different question.

#### Why only the first arm

`coalesce` emits the output of the first arm that produces anything, so **arm 0 runs for every incoming traverser** and the rest run only for the rows arm 0 missed. On `coalesce(out(T), identity())` — the "hop, or keep what you had" spelling — arm 0 succeeds for every vertex with an out-edge, so fusing it reaches almost every row while fusing the others would reach almost none.

```text
   shape                      PRE                     POST                     verdict
   coalescevalues    362.8 372.5 365.2 ms     277.4 303.3 281.3            1.26x
   branchvaluesfloor  30.7  36.4  29.8 (ctl)   29.4  28.9                  flat
   optionalvalues    (item 1628's arm)        259.7 246.7                  flat (control)
```

Non-overlapping (POST's slowest 303.3 below PRE's fastest 362.8). Item 1480's pair is now 12.4x → **9.8x** of its floor.

#### `from = 1` is the correctness question, and it is the one the comment calls out

When the fast arm's bucket is EMPTY the remaining arms must run — starting at arm **1**, because the general loop would have moved past arm 0 after it produced nothing. Skipping arm 1 drops rows (`from/skips-arm-one` dies with 5 failures); re-running arm 0 is answer-equivalent and merely wasteful (`from/rewinds-to-zero` SURVIVES, as the comment predicted).

**Laziness is safe here for `optional-hop.ts`'s stated reason, which applies verbatim.** The general loop's `[...]` means the whole arm runs before any row is yielded, so a lazy arm reorders side effects relative to downstream consumption — item 1480 declined exactly that for the general case and `sideeffect-in-branch.test.ts` exists because the interaction matters. A single vertex step has no side effects, so for this shape the two orders are indistinguishable.

#### ⚠️ The hole the mutation pass found, and why nine tests missed it

`arm/picks-last` — reading `optionalSingleHop(plans[plans.length - 1])` instead of `plans[0]` — **survived the entire file**. The reason is uniform across every case I had written: the last arm is `identity()`, which `optionalSingleHop` refuses, so the fast arm never engaged and the two readings agreed.

The separating shape has a first arm the fusion REFUSES and a last arm it would accept —
`coalesce(out(E).out(E), out(F))` — where the mutant runs arm 1's hop as if it were arm 0 and the two-hop arm never runs at all. Pinned now, with the oracle spelling asserted beside the literal.

**Nine tests covering four fall-through patterns, three refusals and a self-loop did not touch which ARM the detector reads.** That is the same shape as item 1625's edge-order finding: a fixture that exercises the line is not a fixture that discriminates on it, and what decided it here was which STEP the other arm happened to contain.

#### The twenty-second eyeballed literal, and a new cause

The three-arm case: I derived `[4, 1, 2, 3, 1, 5]` and the engine answered `[4, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. Two errors in one literal — I dropped `a`'s second `E` edge, and I wrote the in-neighbour's `k` where the fall-through row's own `k` belongs. The cause is new and worth naming: **I derived from MEMORY of the fixture rather than from the fixture**, four tests after writing it. The derivation is now in the test with the edge list spelled out.

**The lesson is a correction to how a share is read, and it is the inverse of item 1104's.** 1104
says a share OVERSTATES a realizable change (~2.5-3.5x here). This row shows a share can also
UNDERSTATE one by an order of magnitude, because a share prices ONE FRAME and this change removes a
composite route: the lazy `values` generator, 1M `startTraverser`, `[...stream]`, the wrapper plus
three passes, 1M `unwrap`, and the GC of all of it. Item 1394 enumerated three of those frames at
0.1-5% and concluded correctly about each one. **Enumerating the frames on a route is not pricing the
route.**

#### Priced against a hand floor BEFORE building (item 1465's rule)

`order-values-floor.ts`, 200,000 vertices / 999,996 edges, min of 7:

```text
   arm                               PRE        POST     note
   engine hop+values+ORDER        471.56      170.92     the target
   HAND  walk + sort              146.27      142.80     the FLOOR — 3.22x before
   HAND  walk + WRAPPED sort      195.15      198.21     so the wrapper is 48.9 of the 325 ms gap
   engine hop+values (fused)       96.81         —       the same walk with rest EMPTY
   engine hop+values+order+LIMIT  272.00 for TEN ROWS    the capped spelling, same hole
```

The wrapped-sort floor is what made this worth building: at 195 ms it says the `{item, key}` wrapper
and its passes are 15% of the gap and the traverser round trip is the rest, so the fix is the route
rather than a cheaper sort. Item 1513 had already refuted a numeric-specialized comparator at exactly
nothing, and the floor uses a comparator of `compareTotal`'s SHAPE so as not to flatter itself by the
amount that item refuted.

#### ⚠️ The CAP declines, measured rather than assumed

The first version admitted a capped order and drove `streamTopByBys` from the fusion. It measured
**flat** — `hopordercap` above — and the reason is clean: what this change removes is the
MATERIALIZATION, and a capped order never materialized. So the branch is GONE rather than kept as an
unmeasured route, and the capped spelling keeps item 1591's streaming top-k. The 272 ms it takes to
return ten rows is the walk of a million values through the heap, which no route here avoids.

#### ⚠️⚠️ A test I wrote to pin the one correctness question passed for a different reason

The gate requires the walk to be in VALUE MODE, because `hopValuesShortcut` also serves a bare hop
(`pick` = the far vertex) and `id()`, and `order()` over graph elements throws by contract. I wrote
that up as _the_ correctness question, with `sortByBys`' element pass as what raises — it raises even
for a one-element stream, so a comparator-side check would not be equivalent.

It is not `sortByBys`. **`assertFrontierTypes` raises at PLAN-CHECK time**, before any route is
chosen — `checkStep` / `checkSteps` / `assertFrontierTypes` / `run`. An element walk never reaches a
sort by either path, and `id()` mode sorts strings, which a raw sort gets right too. So the gate is
CONSERVATIVE, not load-bearing, and removing it is answer-equivalent through the public API.

Two things follow, both recorded in the code rather than left implied. The guard stays, for the
reason `fusedValuesTopK`'s own unreachable guard states: the static check is a SEPARATE mechanism
that could narrow. And the mutant is caught anyway — **by the gate's unit test, not by anything
differential** — which is the whole argument for testing a route gate as a pure function.

This is the same trap as item 1576's test that covered a parse-time check while claiming the runtime
path, and it was caught here only because the route assertion (below) failed on an unrelated case.

#### The route is asserted through an observable, and that caught the wiring mutant

A route choice is answer-equivalent, so `wiring/route-never-taken` and an off-by-one on the
last-consumed-step index survive every differential assertion by construction (item 1619 recorded
that for all twenty GQL rungs). The fusion's return value exposes `drain` and the general path's
`unwrap` generator does not, so the route is observable — and both mutants DIE on it.

⚠️ **That same observable is a pre-existing test's subject, and it failed.** `eager-drain-route.test.ts`
pins item 1412's decision "drain is offered exactly where the route applies", and it listed `residual
order` under DECLINES. The case has moved to TAKES — the same way `both('E')` moved there at item
1432, which that file documents as _"it failed the moment that stopped being true, which is the test
doing its job."_ Second time that file has earned itself.

`gate/rest-any-length` needed a residual the oracle spelling does not provide: a trailing
`identity()` after the sort is answer-equivalent, so the separating case is `dedupe()` — DERIVED
[null, 1, 2, 3] against the six values a route consuming the whole residual returns.

Two survivors, both predicted: `element/pass-removed` (the unreachable guard above) and

CAUGHT — `gate/value-mode-dropped`, by the unit test asserting the gate declines an `id`

#### ⚠️ `order('local')` is silently accepted as a config object

The 23rd eyeballed-literal-class slip, with a cause that is not a derivation error. `order()`'s
overloads are `order(symbol)` and `order({key?, desc?})`, so a STRING has neither field and reads as
a bare `order()` — the local-scope test asserted the walk's own order and failed by returning the
correctly-sorted stream. The spelling is `order(Scope.local)`. Recorded because the failure mode is
an API slip that type-checks.

**1. A 1.67x that was eight arms in one process.** The cliff finder nominated

It does not. **Isolated, one shape per process: 86.7 and 88.03 — within 1.5%.** `pick` is called
through a closure VARIABLE inside the walk loops, so several arms in one process make that call site
polymorphic. Item 1558 is the same error on a GQL spelling ("all three spellings timed in ONE
process"), and the floor instrument's own eight-arm design is what produced it.

**2. A 1.30x regression that was a rep count too short.** With `REPS=9, DROP=3` the always-true arm

```text
   POST  160.2 157.9 164.2 | 113.0 115.6 114.9 112.1 113.4 113.8 111.8 111.8 109.7
   PRE   160.6 133.9 128.7 | 124.4 126.3 131.5 133.1 123.7 125.2 127.8 126.5 126.1
```

POST's JIT takes 3-7 reps to settle where PRE's takes 1-3, so a 9-rep window with 3 dropped was

— it would simply have produced no evidence while looking like evidence.

#### The change, and the price that justified it

A FAR filter runs one test per EDGE where a start filter runs one per VERTEX — 1,000,000 against
200,000 at fanout 5 — so the per-call layers add up differently on the two sides. The general
composition is `pick` → `survives` iterating a one-element array → the gate → `specializePredicate`'s
`fast`. For a single `has` whose predicate specializes, that is now `pick` → `fast`, reading the
property directly.

⚠️ `start-filtered-hop-values.ts`' header already refutes three levers nearby — compiled gates
(nothing on its shape), per-plan vertex materialization (worse), a dedicated single-gate LOOP (worse,
719.7 → 731 and `both` 458 → 507). **None is re-attempted here**: all three were measured on the
START side, and this composes `pick` once per QUERY, which that file names as the safe place to
change ("leaves all three loop bodies exactly the code they were").

Priced first (`far-filter-one-shape.ts`, 200,000 vertices / 999,996 edges, median of 12 reps):

```text
   engine far-filtered (selective)   86.7 ms     <- 87 ns/edge
   HAND  walk + inline test          57.44       <- the FLOOR, 1.51x
```

So 30 ns/edge was the entire budget and this recovers ~7 of it, which is what item 1394's own "a
share overstates a realizable change by ~2.5-3.5x" predicts from the profile's 45.5%.

### Item 1632 — ⚠️⚠️ **`bench:gremlin`'s MAIN FIXTURE WAS FUNCTIONAL**: every one of its 200,000 vertices had out-degree 5 and exactly **ONE** distinct out-neighbour, so all 1,000,000 edges were 200,000 pairs with five parallel copies. The documented items-1516/1518 defect, in the primary Gremlin instrument, which those items' own note says they checked everywhere but here. Multi-hop yielding rows were **2.4-6.2x** too fast; **five more generators are degenerate at their default degree**

OPEN: the five other degenerate generators listed below, each needing its own fix AND a
re-measurement of whatever it published — `edge-spelling-probe.ts` (DEG 5),
`hop-multi-agg-floor-probe.ts` (DEG 5), `order-cost-probe.ts` (A_DEG 5),
`fused-vs-general-probe.mjs` (FANOUT 5), ~~`hop-rows-floor-probe.mjs` (FANOUT 2)~~ — ⚠️ WRONG, see item 1633: that one was fixed at item 1518 and documents it; I classified it from a pattern match without reading the expression. And five whose
generator shape could not be classified from the degree knob alone: `gc-cost-probe.mjs`,
`route-cost-probe.ts`, `runtime-profile-write-probe.mjs`, `src/hop-extremum-ab.ts` /
`-price.ts`, `vertex-ordinal-write-probe.ts`.

#### The defect, verbatim in the form CLAUDE.md predicts

```text
   for (let k = 0; k < N * 5; k++)
     from = (k * 7919)   % N
     to   = (k * 104_729) % N        <- INVARIANT under k -> k + N
```

Both terms are invariant under `k -> k + N`, so a vertex's five out-edges are `k0, k0+N, …, k0+4N`
and **all five land on the same target**. Counted numerically: 200,000 vertices with an out-edge,
out-degree min/max 5/5, **distinct out-neighbours min/max 1/1**, 200,000 distinct `(from, to)` pairs
behind 1,000,000 edges.

Out-degree, in-degree and isolated-vertex counts are all perfect, which is the whole trap. CLAUDE.md
records this after items 1516/1518 and says they found it "in the GQL bench's main fixture and in six
probe generators" — **this bench was not among them, and it is the primary Gremlin instrument.**

The fix is the GQL bench's own expression, byte for byte, so the two fixtures are now IDENTICAL —
which is what this file's header has claimed since it was written:

```text
   to = ((k % N) * 104_729 + Math.floor(k / N) * 977) % N     -> distinct out-neighbours 5/5
```

#### ⚠️ What this invalidates, and what it does NOT

**It is LOCALITY, not row count.** A k-hop count over a functional graph is `F^k · N` by
construction, and it is `F^k · N` over the branching one too — the row counts are IDENTICAL and every
`answers` column still reads `same`. What changed is that five parallel edges to ONE far vertex read
the same cache line five times, and at depth two all 25 traversers sat on one vertex. This is item
1392's far-vertex locality (which it measured at 36% of `hoporder`) compounded per hop:

```text
   row                                   functional   branching   factor
   V().out().values(age)                      137.7       173.8    1.26x
   V().out().id()                             178.8       205.1    1.15x
   V().out().values(age).order()              260.9       384.3    1.47x
   V().out().out().count()   [closed form]     51.5        52.1    flat
   V().out().out().out().count()              220.9       243.1    1.10x
   V().out().out().values(age)                 381.5      993.1    2.60x
   V().out().out().id()                        354.8      906.3    2.55x
   V().out().out().has().values(age)           478.3     1146.5    2.40x
   V().out().has().out().values(age)           369.0      976.9    2.65x
   V().out()x3.values(age)                    1108.7     6868.6    6.20x
```

So:

- **Every A/B ever run on this bench SURVIVES** — both arms saw the same graph, which is exactly the
  distinction CLAUDE.md draws ("an A/B on ONE fixture survives it… any claim about branching,
  selectivity or fan-out does not"). Items 1630 and 1631's sweeps are unaffected as A/Bs.
- **Every ABSOLUTE magnitude and every `ts/nat` ratio quoted from this bench for a multi-hop yielding
  row predates the fix and is too fast on the TS side**, by the factors above. `V().out()x3.values(age)`
  sat at `ts/nat` ≈ 1.0 — the row that said TS matches native on a deep yield — and now reads **5.5x**.
  `V().out().out().values(age)` went 1.7x to 4.5x.
- The closed-form count rows are unmoved, correctly: they never walk.

#### The fixture now checks its own topology

`assertBranches()` runs once at startup and asserts the PROPERTY (every vertex branches) rather than
a count, so a deliberate fan-out change does not trip it. Same shape as `bench.ts`'s
`assertGraphDocBranches`, which this bench should have had when that one was written.

⚠️ **Proven to fire rather than assumed**: re-introducing `to = (k * 104_729) % N` in both the
generator and the assertion's own recomputation throws from `assertBranches` before any row runs.

#### ⚠️ And item 1631's own new row was degenerate in a second way

Item 1631 added `V().out().has(eq).values(age)` — filtering `age == 30` and projecting `age`, so
**every emitted value is `30` by construction**. The answers column is
`JSON.stringify(rows).slice(0, 48)`, which compares about FIFTEEN of them: a differing row count was
invisible to it, and so was a different subset of the same size. That is the fixture-invariance rule
quoted in item 1631's own entry, broken one item later. It now projects `id()`, whose values are
distinct and ordered, and `V().out().id()` above is its unfiltered twin.

Its 62.5x is also restated: on the branching fixture the row reads **TS 156.2 ms against native 2.70
— 57.8x**, still the largest ratio of any yielding row in the sweep.

### Item 1633 — ⚠️⚠️ **THE SAME DEGENERATE FIXTURE IN SIXTEEN MORE GENERATORS**, including a SECOND one in the GQL bench that item 1516 left when it fixed the first. OPEN: nothing on the fixture class — the corpus is clean and guarded. What is open is RE-MEASUREMENT:

#### The defect, once more, and why a comment did not stop it

```text
   to = (a * k + b) % N      is INVARIANT under  k -> k + N
```

Every generator loops `for (k = 0; k < N * FANOUT; k++)`, so one vertex's FANOUT edges are exactly
`k0, k0+N, k0+2N, …` and all of them land on the SAME target: full out-degree, **one** distinct
out-neighbour, every degree statistic perfect. Items 702/1516/1518 found it, item 1632 found it in
`bench:gremlin`'s main fixture, and this item found the remaining sixteen.

**`hop-rows-floor-probe.mjs` has carried a nine-line warning naming this exact trap since item 1518.** Nine other files kept the defect anyway. That is why this is now a TEST
(`src/fixture-branching.test.ts`) and not another comment.

#### Fixed (verified: distinct out-neighbours 5/5 at each probe's own default N)

```text
   edge-spelling-probe.ts            order-cost-probe.ts  (TWO sites)
   hop-multi-agg-floor-probe.ts      route-cost-probe.ts  (TWO sites, now one shared `toBase`)
   gc-cost-probe.mjs                 runtime-profile-write-probe.mjs
   src/hop-extremum-ab.ts            src/hop-extremum-price.ts
   vertex-ordinal-write-probe.ts     addedge-cost-probe.ts
   bench.ts — `hopPairDoc`           fused-vs-general-probe.mjs      (`scattered` arm)
   gql-filtered-hop-floor-probe.mjs  gremlin-multitype-floor-probe.mjs  (`random` arms)
   runtime-profile-probe.mjs         (`scattered` arm)
```

⚠️ **`bench.ts` is the GQL bench, and item 1516 fixed `graphDoc` while leaving `hopPairDoc` — also
five edges per node — degenerate in the same file.** So the GQL bench's edge-pair rows have the same
correction coming that item 1632 measured for the Gremlin one.

⚠️ **`order-cost-probe.ts`'s second site is not a graph at all**: `raw.push(((k * 104_729) % N) % 90)`
builds the VALUE sequence its sort arms consume, and the invariance made that 200,000 distinct values
repeated five times — a materially different sort from `N * DEG` draws.

#### The test found what my pattern screen could not

I screened for `k < N * FANOUT` plus a `% N` target and got five files. The text test got **nineteen
hits across fifteen files**, including:

- `bench.ts` — the GQL bench, which my screen cleared because it had already been fixed ONCE;
- second sites in `order-cost-probe.ts` and `route-cost-probe.ts`, two files my own patch had just
  touched — my `count(old) == 1` anchors matched the first occurrence and asserted nothing about the
  rest;
- `direction-spelling-probe.ts`, `present-spelling-probe.ts`, `literal-param-gate-probe.mjs`,
  `label-arity-probe.ts`, `addedge-cost-probe.ts`, which my screen never considered because their
  loop bound is not of the form it matched.

**A `count == 1` assertion proves the anchor is unique; it says nothing about whether the DEFECT is.**
That is the lesson, and it is the second time this session an anchor assertion passed while leaving
work undone.

#### The allowlist is reasoned, keyed on source text, and self-validating

Six hits are genuinely harmless and each carries its reason rather than being silently excluded —
four are ONE edge per vertex (degree 1 cannot branch), one has `FANOUT` defaulting to 1, and
`label-arity-probe.ts` nests `d < DEG` inside the vertex loop, so a vertex's edges get CONSECUTIVE
`k` and `k -> k + N` never relates two of them.

Two design points, both learned by the test failing:

- **Keyed on the LINE TEXT, not its number.** The first version keyed on `file:line`, and editing
  `bench.ts` above `hopSparseDoc` shifted it from 201 to 206 immediately. Text changes exactly when
  the code does, which is when the entry should be re-reviewed.
- **Every allowlist entry must still match something.** Otherwise an entry whose code was fixed sits
  there excusing a line that now means something else — which is how an allowlist becomes the hiding
  place it is meant not to be. That check is what caught the line-number shift, and then caught two
  keys I had guessed wrong rather than read.

`assertBranching` (`src/fixture-branching.ts`) is the behavioural half, for a probe to call on its own
numbers; its own test proves it REJECTS the degenerate form rather than only accepting the fixed one.

#### The nomination, and why it is not a price

A windowed profile of a three-hop count at NODES=100000 FANOUT=5:

```text
   bucketSize                        76.7%   887.8 ms
   side                              11.1%
   (anonymous) in buildThreeHopCount  5.6%
   get toId                           2.3%
```

`bucketSize` is `byType.get(types[0])?.size ?? 0` for a single named type. At 76.7% it nominates an
obvious lever: a three-hop count is a degree product, so if each vertex's degree were re-read once
per incident edge, memoizing it per query would turn O(|E|) lookups into O(|V|).

**It is not re-read.** Instrumenting the function and counting:

```text
   20,000 vertices, 99,992 edges  ->  119,992 calls, 119,992 on the fast branch
                                      = |V| + |E| exactly: one per vertex, one per edge
```

No vertex's degree is read twice, so the memo has nothing to save. At the profiled fixture that is
~600,000 calls for 111 ms a rep — **~185 ns for a `Map.get(…)?.size`** — which is not credible on its
face. The time is the CALLER's per-edge loop credited to a small hot callee, which is what item 1634
measured in the strongest form yet recorded (`pick` at 19.0% of a Gremlin row, priced at +0.4%).

⚠️ **Item 1416 had already found this for `chain3`** (72.6%, "all 200,000 calls take the O(1) branch,
proven by counting them"). Reading `CLOSED.md` before building is what turned a multi-tick memo
attempt into a counter and a comment. The verification was still worth doing separately: `chain3` and
`count3` are different shapes on different fixtures, so 1416's count does not transfer — and the
cheap instrument (a counter, not a build) is what makes re-verifying affordable.

The finding is now recorded **on `bucketSize` itself**, where the next profile will send someone.

Engine per-row: trailing 603.1, mid 353.6, lead 328.7 — for the SAME 2,680,230 rows. That looks like

```text
   LEAD filter      tests    200,000 start vertices
   MID filter       tests  1,000,000 first-hop far ends
   TRAILING filter  tests  5,000,000 second-hop far ends
```

Five times the predicate work for the same output. Confirmed by profile rather than inferred: the
gate closure is **30.4%** of the trailing row against **8.7%** of the mid one — 1381.6 ms against
192.5, a 7.2x difference in absolute terms, which is the 5x plus its own overhead. Filtering later is
more work; the floors move by the same factor (305.4 trailing against 185.9 mid per row).

and measured **1.06-1.077x** against a 1.51x floor gap. That recovered ~12% of its gap; the same
proportion here is ~1.08x.

measured at **1.6x on this very family**, or a fifth and sixth copy of the literal two-hop walk (it is

### Item 1639 — ⚠️ **THE CLOSURE-ENVIRONMENT HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED, and it was the one candidate three items pointed at.** A walk capturing **14 locals costs 0.4% against one capturing 3**, and reading a context local per EDGE costs nothing either — so the persistent 1.2-2.0x engine-vs-floor gap is not the environment, and the engine's per-edge `hops[d]` / `runs[d+1]` / `drops` reads are not it either

OPEN: the **1.2-2.0x engine-vs-hand-floor gap** on three unrelated shapes (items 1634, 1636, 1638)
is now short of candidates. Per-frame ablation accounted for a minority each time (0 for 3), and the
structural explanation those items converged on is dead. What has NOT been tested is whether the
remaining difference is the instruments rather than the engine — see the caution below, which is the
honest next step and cheaper than another lever hunt.

#### The hypothesis, and why it was worth one experiment

Items 1634, 1636 and 1638 each found an engine walk 1.2-2.0x a hand floor doing the same work, with
per-frame ablations explaining a minority:

```text
   item 1634  Gremlin depth-3 stacked walk     1.23x   ~60% across four causes; `pick` priced at 0%
   item 1636  GQL filtered hop (after 1.19x)   ~2.0x   a 41.5% probe arm realized ~19-30%
   item 1638  Gremlin two-hop + any filter     ~1.9x   the gate collapse is ~1.08x of it
```

The one candidate common to all three was the thing a hand floor structurally cannot reproduce: the
engine's walks are closures returned per compile capturing **eight to fourteen** locals
(`stackedWalk` captures graph, hops, runs, pick, drops, depth, leadGates, anyLead, t0, fwd0;
`filteredHopWalk` more) where a floor captures two or three. `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`
records the EFFECT as real — a walk inline in a returned closure gave unrelated queries a new 4x slow
mode — but nothing had measured the cost of the environment itself.

#### The measurement: three byte-identical walks, one arm per process

`closure-env-probe.ts`, 200,000 vertices / 999,990 edges, 12 reps, median of the last 9:

```text
   arm                                      run 1 median   run 2 median   run 1 min  run 2 min
   lean     3 captured locals                     144.78         142.60      144.27     137.41
   fat      14 captured, cold-referenced          145.31         142.82      144.36     140.65
   fatread  14 captured, ONE read per edge        144.85         145.18      144.34     144.29
```

**0.4% across all three in run 1 and 1.8% in run 2**, with run 1's series tight to ±1 ms. Two runs
are reported because the first was tighter than the second and quoting only it would overstate the
instrument: `fatread` is the slowest arm in both, by 0.1% and then 1.8%, which is as close to no
effect as this corpus measures anything. A real null, not an unresolvable one.

Two things die at once:

- **the environment itself is free.** Fourteen captured locals cost nothing against three.
- **reading through it is free too.** `fatread` does one context read per edge — the engine's actual
  pattern (`hops[d]`, `runs[d + 1]`, `drops`, `pick` are all context reads inside the loop) — and is
  indistinguishable from `lean`. That independently corroborates item 1634's bookkeeping ablation
  coming out small, by a different route.

#### ⚠️ The cold reference is load-bearing, and without it this arm would have BEEN `lean`

A captured local referenced nowhere is dropped from the context entirely, so `fat` would have been
`lean` and the arms would have differed by nothing — a null result that looks like a result, which is
the exact failure this corpus keeps producing (items 1626, 1631, 1632). Each extra local is
referenced in a branch guarded by a condition the fixture never satisfies, and the probe counts the
branch's firings and THROWS if the count is not zero. It is zero.

#### ⚠️ A caution this item raises about its own neighbours

`closure-env-probe`'s `lean` arm walks 1M edges, reads a property and counts, in **144.78 ms**.
`two-hop-values-floor.ts` reports its 1-hop engine arm doing comparable work in **99.63 ms**. Two
hand-written walks of the same shape in different instruments differ by 1.45x — which is the same
order as the 1.47x run-to-run swing item 1638 measured on one arm of one file.

So the cross-item 1.2-2.0x gaps may be partly instrument, not engine. The ratios in items 1634/1636/
1638 are all same-run engine-vs-floor pairs, which is the right construction and is why they stand —
but the NEXT step on that family is to put the engine and its floor in one process with one arm per
measurement, not to hunt a fifth lever. **Do not compare a number from this probe with a number from
another file.**

#### The experiment item 1639 asked for

Item 1639 refuted the closure-environment hypothesis and noticed something sharper: two
HAND-WRITTEN walks of the same shape, in two different instruments, differ by **1.45x**. So the
untested variable was never the engine — it was the harness. `closure-env-probe.ts` already had the
right shape (one `ARM` per process, one fixture builder, one timing loop), so the engine and its floor
went in there as two more arms.

```text
   pair                              run 1                run 2             ratio
   one hop, fused
     engine1  V().out(E).values(k)   181.10               169.22
     floor1   hand walk + push       153.41               149.58            1.13-1.18x
   two hops + trailing filter
     engine2f out.out.has.values    1153.22              1112.01
     floor2f  hand walk + inline     888.05               892.36            1.25-1.30x
```

Both pairs return identical row counts (999,990 and 2,680,204). The floors PUSH rather than count,
because `toArray` materialises an array and a counting floor is not doing the same work — the
`lean`/`fat`/`fatread` arms above it do count, which is exactly why item 1639 forbade comparing
across them.

#### What this corrects

```text
   shape                        as measured            one arm per process   inflation
   two-hop + trailing filter    1.97x  (item 1638)     1.25-1.30x            ~1.55x
   two-hop unfiltered           1.08x  (item 1638)     —                     (already small)
   one-hop fused                —                      1.13-1.18x            —
```

Item 1638's own header already warned that its engine arm swings **1.47x** run-to-run and that only
same-run pairs mean anything. Its ratios WERE same-run pairs, which is why they were defensible — and
they were still wrong by 1.55x, because interference moves the engine arm and the floor arm by
different amounts within a single run. **Same-run pairing is necessary and not sufficient; the
process must contain one measurement.**

#### Why four items found so little

Items 1634, 1636, 1638 and 1639 each tried to attribute a 1.2-2.0x gap and each accounted for a
minority — `pick` priced at 0% against a 19.0% share, a 41.5% arm realising ~19-30%, a gate collapse
worth ~1.08x of 1.9x, and the closure environment refuted outright at 0.4%. That reads as four
failures of attribution. It is better read as four correct measurements of a gap that was ~1.55x
smaller than the instrument said: there was less to find than the denominator implied, and the
ablations that came back small were right.

#### The rule

**An engine-vs-floor ratio comes from a one-measurement-per-process instrument, or it does not
count.** The multi-arm floor files (`two-hop-values-floor.ts`, `hop-chain-depth-floor.ts`,
`gql-filtered-hop-floor-probe.mjs`) are useful for ranking shapes against each other and for the
ablation DIFFERENCES within one arm's family, but their absolute engine-vs-floor ratios overstate.
`closure-env-probe.ts` is the pattern to copy: `ARM` selects one thing, the process does nothing
else.

### Item 1642 — the Gremlin seeded POINT LOOKUP decomposed for the first time: **1277.6 ns per call = 233.8 construction (18%) + ~1044 execution, with routing at 33.6 ns (2.6%)**. ⚠️ **The profile's ~15% plan-analysis tail prices at 2.6% — the FIFTH share this session that did not survive an ablation.** And `effectivePlan` genuinely runs per call with no cache, which is correct and not worth changing

OPEN: **~840 ns to execute a ONE-ELEMENT seeded lookup** with the plan reused. ⚠️ **Item 1643 took 1.44-1.60x of the `hasId` spelling of it** by rewriting to the seeded source; what remains is the ~330 ns the ALREADY-seeded spelling costs, still 35x a 9.3 ns hand floor. That is item 1594's
finding re-measured in a single-purpose instrument, and it is the largest per-call cost left on a
cheap Gremlin query. Construction and routing are both small; the traverser setup is the bulk.

#### What was asked and what the profile said

Item 1594 attributed "~2150 ns per-call machinery for a ONE-element result" and item 1641 re-measured
the pair at 2000 ns, leaving ~1200 ns unexplained. A windowed profile of a seeded point lookup
nominated a long tail of PLAN-ANALYSIS frames — `effectivePlan` 1.8%, `hopValuesShortcut` 2.7%,
`startFilteredHopValues` 1.8%, `fuseOrderTake` 1.8%, `seededShape` 1.8%, plus `matchShape`,
`seededCountShape`, `fusableValuesTopK`, `fuseValuesIsCount`, `dropVacuousLabels`, `isHop` — about
**15%** of the row, on a query returning one element. And `run` really does call
`effectivePlan(sliced, graph, ctx.tracksPath)` per call, with no cache anywhere in the file, so the
rewrite passes and the whole rung chain are re-consulted on every invocation.

#### The ablation says 2.6%

One single-purpose instrument, 60,000 reps, min of 5, plan reused except where stated:

```text
   build plan only                       233.8 ns/call    18% of the realistic cost
   full run (toArray, reused plan)       843.5
   build + run (per-call id, REALISTIC) 1277.6
   effectivePlan alone                    33.6            2.6% of 1277.6
```

**33.6 ns, not ~15%.** The fifth time this session a profile share has failed to convert — after
`pick` at 19.0% priced at +0.4% (item 1634), `propOf`'s share (item 1444, corrected at 1446),
`bucketSize` at 76.7% proven misattribution by counting (item 1637), and the closure environment at
0.4% (item 1639). The tail is small frames hit once per call being credited with their caller's
setup.

So the per-call `effectivePlan` is **correct as it stands**. A cache would also have to be keyed on
the GRAPH — `dropVacuousLabels` reads the graph's label counts — and invalidated on mutation, which
is the `csr_fresh` staleness trap CLAUDE.md records going wrong on the native side. 2.6% does not buy
that risk.

#### The decomposition, and where the cost actually is

```text
   construction   233.8 ns   18%     item 1577 already cut this 4.27x
   routing         33.6 ns    2.6%
   execution     ~1044 ns    ~82%    of which ~840 with a warm plan object
```

The 200 ns between reused-plan execution (843.5) and fresh-plan execution (1277.6 − 233.8 = 1043.8)
is the inline-cache cost of handing the engine a NEW plan object every call — not construction
itself, which is counted separately.

⚠️ **This also re-frames item 1578.** It measured construction at a MEDIAN of 48.1% of `V().count()`;
here it is 18% of a point lookup. Both are right — `V().count()` is answered from a bucket size in
O(1), so construction is a bigger share of a cheaper query. Neither figure transfers to the other
shape.

#### What would actually move it

The bulk is the traverser pipeline's per-call setup for a one-element answer (`projectValues`,
`seedRest`, `newContext`, `unwrap`, `toArray` in the profile). Two structural options, neither a
tick's work:

- **a closed-form route for "seeded by id + one projection"** that never builds a traverser, in the
  spirit of the fused walks items 1613-1636 built for multi-row shapes. `seededShape` and
  `seedFromIndex` already exist, so the seeding half is there; what remains is the emit half.
  ⚠️ **ITEM 1649 BUILT THE `count()` HALF OF THIS** — `V(ids).count()` and `V(ids).<one hop>.count()`
  now answer from the graph's indexes (5.19x on the hop) — and ⚠️ **ITEM 1650 BUILT THE PROJECTION
  HALF**: `V(ids)[.hasLabel(L)].values(k)` at **1.36x** (286.0 → 211.2 ns). Both halves of this
  bullet are now done; what is left is `run`'s own per-call floor, ~195 ns of the 211.
- **parameter binding for Gremlin**, which it does not have (item 1577): a caller whose id varies
  cannot reuse a plan, so it pays construction AND the fresh-object inline-cache cost on every call —
  together ~434 of the 1277.6 ns, 34%. That is a feature, not an optimization, and it is the larger
  of the two.

same question, measured in a single-purpose instrument at 200,000 vertices, plan reused, 60,000 reps,
min of 5:

```text
   spelling              values     count
   V().hasId(id)         821.8      646.7   ns/call
   V(id)   (seeded)      348.5      228.6
                         2.36x      2.83x
   hand floor              9.3        9.3
```

⚠️ **`gremlin-spelling-probe.ts` HAS a group for this pair** — "id lookup: seeded V(id) vs hasId" —
and reports it among the "19 group(s) under 1ms, not compared (raise SPELL_N)". The instrument built
to catch exactly this class could not see it at its default size. That is the third instrument hole
this arc has found after items 1631 and 1634, and the first where the right group already existed.

#### What it is NOT

`hasId` already seeds: item 1306 built `seedFromIndex` so it reads the id map instead of scanning,
and `id-seed.test.ts` documents the three semantics that make that sound. So this is not seek-vs-scan
— it is one seeded route being cheaper than another, and the rewrite routes to the cheaper one.

```text
   hasId.values   821.8 -> 514.4 / 571.5     1.44-1.60x
   hasId.count    646.7 -> 328.6 / 341.8     1.89-1.97x
   V(id).values   [CONTROL, unreachable]     329.5 / 373.2
   V(id).count    [CONTROL, unreachable]     263.7 / 186.8
```

#### ⚠️⚠️ EXACTLY ONE ID, and a pre-existing test caught the case I missed

The spellings diverge above one id, measured BEFORE the rewrite was written:

```text
   V().hasId(v3, v1).id()  ->  ["v1", "v3"]   GRAPH order, filtered
   V(v3, v1).id()          ->  ["v3", "v1"]   the order the IDS were given
   V().hasId(v1, v1).id()  ->  ["v1"]         a filter matches a vertex once
   V(v1, v1).id()          ->  ["v1", "v1"]   a seed emits once per id
```

Order is a TinkerPop contract the differential fuzzer compares ORDERED; the multiplicity difference is
a wrong answer outright. The single-id gate excludes both.

**And a fourth case I did not anticipate.** `id-seed.test.ts` (item 1306) pins "a non-string id must
not raise" — `V().hasId(5)` answers EMPTY because a number cannot match a string id, while `V(5)`
RAISES "a vertex/edge id must be a string". The first version of this rewrite converted the first
spelling into the second, **turning an empty answer into a throw**, and that pre-existing test failed
on it. A `typeof === 'string'` guard fixes it, and the boundary is now pinned in this rewrite's own
tests as well, so it does not depend on a file three directories away.

That is the suite doing the job no measurement could: the rewrite was answer-equivalent on every case
I thought to write.

#### Mutation 7 of 8

The single survivor is `gate/bit-dropped` — removing the `KIND_BITS.hasId` fast-path gate. It is
unobservable by construction: the bit is DERIVED from the steps, so a plan whose bit is clear also
fails the structural check one line later and the pass returns the same object either way. The gate
is a speed fast-path (item 1505's reason) and has no answer to change.

`mask/not-recomputed` is caught, which matters: `rewritten()` recomputes `kinds` and `mayFault`, and
this pass REMOVES a `hasId` step — a later pass reading the stale mask would be reasoning about a
step that is gone.

inE)` 2.27x, `multi-id lookup, dedupe tail` 2.03x.

#### The blind spot, and what it hid

`timeOf` wrapped ONE `toArray` in a `performance.now()` pair. For a sub-microsecond query that
measures the clock as much as the work, so the probe skipped any group whose max was under 1 ms — 19
of them, listed every run under "not compared (raise SPELL_N)". Raising `SPELL_N` cannot help: it
grows the GRAPH, and a point lookup stays sub-millisecond at any size.

Item 1643 is what exposed the cost. One of those 19 groups — "id lookup: seeded V(id) vs hasId" — was
hiding **2.36x on `values` and 2.83x on `count`**, on a point lookup, the commonest query there is.
The instrument built to catch equivalent-spelling gaps could not see the fast half of its corpus, and
the group was right there in the list.

#### The fix

Each group now calibrates an inner count until one sample takes `SPELL_SAMPLE_MS` (default 2 ms) and
reports the PER-CALL median. A slow group calibrates to `inner = 1` and behaves exactly as before;
the spread between two spellings is a ratio, so nothing about the flagging logic changes. `FLOOR_MS`
drops from 1 ms to 500 ns — it no longer guards timing resolution, only the regime where allocation
noise swamps a difference.

**And sub-millisecond times now print in ns.** `toFixed(3)` rendered every fast group as `0.000ms` or
`0.001ms`, so a CONFIRMED 2.79x was unreadable and nothing said which arm was slow. That is a second,
smaller instance of the same failure: the number was there and the instrument would not show it.

```text
   before   19 groups "under 1ms, not compared"
   after    10 under 500 ns/call, 7 FLAGGED, and the rest judged clean
```

#### The seven flags, and why three readings matter

```text
   multi-id lookup: V(ids) vs hasId(ids)                        5.93x
   label, two of them: hasLabel(a,b) vs or(hasLabel, hasLabel)  3.06x
   edge-type union vs an explicit union                         2.75x
   multi-id EDGE lookup: E(ids) vs hasId(ids)                   2.50x
   hop, both directions: both(T) vs union(out, in)              2.40x
   hop, both as edges: bothE(T) vs union(outE, inE)             2.27x
   multi-id lookup, dedupe tail: V(ids) vs hasId(ids)           2.03x
```

The probe's own instruction is to re-run each ALONE three times before treating a flag as a finding,
and that instruction earned itself immediately:

- **`multi-id lookup` 5.93x — REFUTED.** Isolated, both arms read 0.001 ms, equal. The largest flag
  in the list was dispatch pollution from earlier groups.
- **`label, two of them` 3.06x — REFUTED.** Two isolated runs, 0 groups over 2x.
- **`hop, both directions` — CONFIRMED four times** (2.79x, 4.47x, 2.15x, 2.92x), and with the ns
  display the slow arm is unambiguous: `both(T)` 236.7 / 193.6 ns against `union(out, in)` 509.0 /
  564.3.

So of three flags checked, two were the harness and one is real. The four unchecked ones are recorded
as flagged, not as findings.

#### Gates

No engine code changed — the probe only. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped.

### Item 1645 — ⚠️⚠️ **A SPELLING THAT NEEDS A REWRITE TO BECOME THE FAST ONE CAN NEVER MATCH THE ONE THAT DID NOT, because the rewrite runs PER CALL** (⚠️ **the per-call part is FIXED across items 1647-1648 — the rewrite AND the static-check walk are both cached, and the two spellings now cost the same; the conceptual point stands, and the lesson is that it was NOT only the rewrite**)**.** `union(out(T), in(T)).count()` is 2.41x `both(T).count()` even though `fuseUnionBoth` collapses the first into the second — and **52% of the gap is `effectivePlan` doing that collapse** (117.5 of 225.2 ns). A conceptual correction to this repo's central invariant, not a lever

~~OPEN: the 2.41x itself~~ — ⚠️ **CLOSED ACROSS ITEMS 1647 AND 1648.** 1647 cached the rewrite
(395.0 → 274.7 ns, gap 1.58x); 1648 cached the static-check verdict the rewrite's residual turned out
to be (274.7 → 73.0 ns, **gap 1.02x**). The union and `both` spellings now cost the SAME, and all
three union groups this item flagged have dropped off the Gremlin spelling probe's comparison list
entirely — they fell below its 500 ns floor. ⚠️ **And this item's guess that the three were ONE
finding was right**: one fix removed all three. ~~**A `WeakMap<Plan, Plan>` memo on `effectivePlan`**~~ — ⚠️ **ANSWERED AT ITEM 1646 (a WeakMap is 1.25x worse rebuilt; a field on the plan is not) AND BUILT AT ITEM 1647 — though not with that item's key, which is a wrong answer: `graph.version` is asynchronous.** **Removing
`fuseUnionBoth`'s two per-call allocations** — `plan.steps.slice(i + 1)` handed to `tailIsOrderFree`,
and the `[...plan.steps]` spread — is worth maybe 8% of the row, below the bar for a file whose edits
perturb.

#### The measurement

`both(T).count()` and `union(out(T), in(T)).count()` over 200,000 vertices / ~400,000 edges, plans
reused, 60,000 reps, min of 5, one purpose per process:

```text
   both(T).count                  159.6 ns/call
   union(out,in).count            384.8            the gap is 225.2 ns — 2.41x
   fuseUnionBoth alone (union)     94.5            it FIRES, and costs this
   fuseUnionBoth alone (both)       4.6            the gate declines, as designed
   effectivePlan (union)          131.7
   effectivePlan (both)            14.2            → 117.5 ns of the 225.2 is the rewrite
```

Both answer `[799984]`. So the rewrite works, fires, and produces the identical plan — and accounts
for **52%** of the gap it exists to remove. The remaining ~108 ns is the cold-inline-cache cost of
executing a freshly-allocated plan object, which item 1643 priced at ~200 ns on a point lookup and
which scales with how little else the query does.

#### ⚠️ Why this matters beyond one pair

CLAUDE.md's invariant is that equivalent spellings must cost the same, and the stated reason it holds
here is that "this engine lowers BOTH GQL and Gremlin to one `ir::Plan` and runs one `exec`, so speed
is a property of the optimized plan, not the surface syntax — two spellings that optimize to the same
plan cannot differ."

**That is exactly right for the Rust engine and not quite right for the TS one.** In Rust the plan is
optimized once and executed; in TS `run` calls `effectivePlan` on every invocation, so the spelling
that needs normalising pays for the normalisation every time. Two spellings that optimize to the same
plan therefore CAN differ, by the cost of the optimization — and on a sub-microsecond query that cost
is the whole gap.

This is the same mechanism as item 1643's residual: after rewriting `V().hasId(x)` to `V(x)`, the two
spellings were still 1.44x apart. I recorded the cause there as per-call reallocation; it is more
precisely this, and it is general.

So three of the probe's confirmed-or-flagged union/multi-spelling groups (`union(out, in)`,
`union(outE, inE)`, `out(T,U) vs union(out(T), out(U))`) are likely the same finding rather than three
separate ones. **Not verified for the other two** — flagged for whoever takes them, so they are not
re-derived as novel.

#### What would actually close it

Only caching the rewrite. The allocation trims are real but small, and the memo is a trade item 1503
already measured and refused for a cheaper pass. What has changed since is that this item puts a
number on the other side of that trade for the whole rewrite chain rather than one boolean: **117.5
ns per call for a reused plan.** Whether that beats a 1.07-1.15x penalty on rebuilt plans is a
measurement nobody has made, and it needs both arms — reused AND rebuilt — in one instrument before
anyone builds it.

⚠️ And it is not obviously the right shape even then: `effectivePlan` takes the GRAPH, because
`dropVacuousLabels` reads its label counts. A memo keyed on the plan alone would go stale when the
graph's labels change, which is the `csr_fresh` trap CLAUDE.md records going wrong natively. A sound
key is (plan, graph, mutation-epoch) and the graph has no epoch today.

#### Gates

No code changed — measurement only. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped.

### Item 1646 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1503'S REFUSAL DOES NOT APPLY TO THE RIGHT DESIGN.** A plan-cached `effectivePlan` makes a REUSED plan **33x cheaper (155.0 → 4.7 ns)** and a REBUILT one **FLAT** — no trade at all — where the `WeakMap` form it refused is 1.25x WORSE rebuilt. Three designs priced in one instrument, and the first two of mine were wrong: an object-per-miss and a key without the graph's identity. ~~**And the key `Graph` already has is enough**~~ — ⚠️⚠️ **IT IS NOT, AND THIS DESIGN IS A WRONG ANSWER: `graph.version` IS ASYNCHRONOUS. BUILT AT ITEM 1647 AS A PREFIX CACHE INSTEAD (6.9x on the chain, 1.44-1.58x on the call).**

~~OPEN: **build it.**~~ **CLOSED AT ITEM 1647 — but not this design.** `version` and `epoch(name)` are
REACTIVE counters that advance on a microtask DRAIN, so `addVertex(); graph.version` reads the OLD
value and a whole-chain cache keyed on it serves a stale rewrite to every read in the same
synchronous block as a write. For `dropVacuousLabels` that is a dropped filter against a graph where
it is no longer vacuous. Item 1647 caches only the GRAPH-FREE PREFIX of the chain, which needs no key
at all, and measures **167 → 24 ns** on the chain rather than this entry's 4.7. The three designs
priced below are still the right pricing of the SHAPE, and the symbol-key question the build raised
is answered there.

#### The trade, priced for the whole rewrite chain

`plan-memo-trade-probe.ts`, one arm per process, 20,000 inner calls per sample, 12 reps, median of 9,
three rounds. The plan is the UNION spelling, because that is the one `effectivePlan` does work on
(`fuseUnionBoth` fires); the `both` spelling measures the gate declining, which item 1645 priced at
14.2 ns and is not the question.

```text
   design                        REUSED plan        REBUILT plan (fresh every call)
   no cache                      155.0 ns           495-509 ns
   WeakMap<Plan, Plan>             3.8              639.9      1.25x WORSE
   on-plan {version, plan}         4.8              502-592    1.01-1.15x worse
   on-plan 3 scalar fields         4.7              490-570    FLAT (ranges overlap)
```

**33x on a reused plan and flat on a rebuilt one.** Item 1503 measured the same trade for the much
cheaper `readsPath` boolean and refused it — **1.52-1.61x reused but 1.07-1.15x WORSE rebuilt** — and
that refusal was right for a `WeakMap`. It is not right for a field on the plan.

#### ⚠️ My first two designs were both wrong, and the probe caught one while reading caught the other

- **`{ version, plan }` on the plan allocates an object on every MISS**, which put the rebuilt arm at
  +7 to +77 ns across three rounds and left break-even at ~30% reuse — no better than the `WeakMap`.
  Three SCALAR fields allocate nothing and the penalty disappears.
- **keying on `graph.version` alone is a WRONG ANSWER**, caught by reading rather than measuring:
  `effectivePlan(plan, graphA)` then `effectivePlan(plan, graphB)` HITS WRONGLY whenever both graphs
  share a version, and two freshly built graphs both start at the same one. `dropVacuousLabels` reads
  the graph's label counts, so the cached plan would be the other graph's answer. The key is
  (graph identity, graph version), and the sound version costs the same — 4.7 against 4.8 ns.

⚠️ And the prerequisite item 1645 thought was missing is already there: **`Graph` carries `version`
(a mutation counter) and per-token `epoch(name)`**. No core change is needed, and `epoch(label)` is
available later as a tighter key than the whole-graph version.

#### Three build concerns, none a blocker

- **`Plan` is `readonly`.** The cache needs a deliberate mutable field on the type, not a cast at the
  use site.
- **HIDDEN CLASS STABILITY is the real risk.** Adding fields to a `Plan` on first use mutates its
  shape, and this corpus has measured that class of effect repeatedly (item 159's 1.29x from
  polymorphic call sites, `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`'s 4x slow mode). The fields should be
  initialised wherever a `Plan` is constructed so every plan has one shape from birth — which is also
  why this is not a two-line change.
- **`tracksPath` belongs in the key, or only the `false` case gets cached.** `effectivePlan` returns
  the plan unchanged when `tracksPath` is true, so that case needs no cache at all.

#### Gates

No engine code changed — one new probe. `bun run check` 0 read unpiped.

### Item 1647 — ⚠️⚠️ **`Graph.version` IS NOT A SYNCHRONOUS MUTATION COUNTER, so item 1646's whole-chain plan cache was a WRONG ANSWER** — caught by a test, not by reading. Shipped the sound half instead: a keyless cache of the rewrite chain's GRAPH-FREE PREFIX, **6.9x on the chain (167 → 24 ns)** and **1.44-1.58x on the whole `union(out, in).count()` call** against a flat control, at a measured cost of ~5% on a plan rebuilt every call

CLOSED. It also corrects two things about its own instruments: the premise item 1646 recorded as
already satisfied, and a null A/B the Gremlin spelling probe cannot avoid giving a `src`-only change.

#### The wrong answer, and how it surfaced

Item 1646 priced a cache of the WHOLE chain keyed on `(graph identity, graph.version)` and recorded
that "the prerequisite item 1645 thought was missing is already there". It is not there:

```text
   g.addVertex(...)             g.version  g.epoch('P')  g.vertexCount
   immediately after the write      0            0             1
   after one microtask drain         1            1             1
```

`version` and `epoch(name)` are REACTIVE counters that advance when the mutation queue DRAINS. So
every read in the same synchronous block as a write sees the old value, and a cache keyed on it
serves the pre-write rewrite. `dropVacuousLabels` reads the graph's label counts, so the specific
failure is **a filter dropped as vacuous and still dropped after the write that made it selective** —
a wrong answer, not a stale optimisation. The whole-chain version was built, and the test
`a write immediately before the read is seen — no drain in between` failed on it. `vertexCount` and
`edgeCount` ARE synchronous and are not sufficient alone, because a label's distribution can change
at a constant vertex count.

⚠️ **This is the second time in two items that a premise recorded as settled was false.** Item 1646's
own entry says reading caught one hole in its design (a key without the graph's identity) that
measuring missed; this one measuring did not catch either — a test did, and only because the test was
written to exercise a write between two reads.

#### What shipped: the prefix, which needs no key

Six of the chain's ten passes read only the plan (`fuseLocal`, `seedSingleHasId`, `fuseValuesIsCount`,
`flattenFilterWrappers`, `fuseEdgeHop`, `fuseUnionBoth`); two take the `graph` (`fuseUnionSameDir`,
`dropVacuousLabels`). A plan is immutable, so an entry for the graph-free prefix **can never be
stale** — the cache has no key, nothing to invalidate, and no `Graph` reference to pin. The two
graph-dependent passes run per call, gated as they already were. And the expensive pass is inside the
prefix: item 1645 priced `fuseUnionBoth` alone at 94.5 ns of the chain's 131.7.

#### The numbers, one arm per process, order-alternated, 12 reps / median of 9

```text
   plan-memo-trade-probe.ts        PRE                POST
   the chain, plan REUSED          167.0 / 181.9 ns   24.3 / 25.4 / 27.7    6.9x
   the chain, plan REBUILT         480.0 / 487.0      504.9 / 510.7 / 570   1.05x WORSE
   plan construction alone         284.0 / 286.4      283.1 / 299.3        FLAT

   union-both-call-floor.ts (new)  PRE                POST
   toArray(union(out,in).count())  395.0 / 438.2      274.7 / 359.7        1.44x (mins 1.58x)
   toArray(both(T).count())  CTL   174.5 / 177.8      174.2 / 172.9        FLAT
```

**Break-even is 16% plan reuse**, from the per-call figures: `0.16·24 + 0.84·180 = 155`. Gremlin has
no parameter binding (item 1577), so a caller whose id varies rebuilds every call and pays the 5% —
item 1503's refusal was right to protect that case, and at 6.9x against 1.05x the asymmetry now
settles it the other way.

#### ⚠️ The residual is NOT the rewrite ~~and that is the new target~~ — **CLOSED AT ITEM 1648: it is the static-check walk, and caching its verdict is another 3.5x on this call**

`union-both-call-floor.ts` decomposes the POST call, and the cached rewrite is a small part of what
is left:

```text
   full  toArray(union plan)                 285.3 ns
   rest  toArray(the ALREADY-rewritten plan)  167.1
   eff   effectivePlan alone (cache hit)       27.0
   both  toArray(both(T)) — the same answer   166.0
```

`full − rest` is 118 ns but `eff` is only 27, so **~91 ns is `run`'s PRE-REWRITE validation**:
`assertPlanIsSatisfiable`, `assertFrontierTypes` and `planReadsPath` all walk the UN-normalised plan,
and the union spelling makes them walk two nested sub-plans the `both` spelling does not have.
~~OPEN: validate the EFFECTIVE plan rather than the written one, or cache the validation verdict the
way the rewrite is now cached.~~ ⚠️ **TAKEN AT ITEM 1648 by the second of those** — the verdict is
cached, and the ablation that priced it put the walk at **74% of this call**, far more than the
`full − rest` subtraction above suggested. That is the rest of item 1645's gap, and it is gone.

#### Why the slot is symbol-keyed, which the measurement did not ask

`serialize.ts` does `JSON.stringify(plan)` as a public API and `traversal.test.ts` round-trips a plan
through JSON. A plain field would change that output — and could not survive it: the common case
(no pass fires) caches the plan AS ITSELF, which is a CYCLE, so `JSON.stringify` would throw. A
symbol key is invisible to `JSON.stringify`, `Object.keys` and `for…in`, the same argument `ast.ts`
already records for `STEP_FN`. Priced before building: **4.8-5.0 ns against a string field's
4.7-4.8 — no cost.** A `WeakMap<Graph, number>` graph token was also built and measured (0.4-0.6 ns,
to avoid pinning a graph a cached plan outlives); the prefix design needs no graph in the key at all,
so it is not in the shipped code.

#### ⚠️ The Gremlin spelling probe CANNOT A/B a `src`-only change, and silently returned a null

Three isolated runs per arm of `hop, both directions` showed **no movement** — POST 524-547 ns
against PRE 505-601 — while the `src`-level instrument on the same query showed 1.44x with a flat
control. The probe imports `toArray` from `@lenke/gremlin`, which resolves to the BUILT DIST, and the
arm switcher swapped only `src`: **both of its arms ran the same unbuilt code.** This is the
`fuzzers-read-built-dists` trap, and it reads as a refutation rather than an error. After rebuilding
both arms the group reads 503.4/185.7 → 251.6/163.8 ns, so the union arm is 2.0x and the gap is
1.54x — but the `both` arm moved too, which the controlled instrument reads as flat, so the
`src`-level A/B is the one to quote. **Rebuild before any probe that imports from `@lenke/*`, or
measure through `src`.**

#### Teeth

Five mutants, each under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p
MemorySwapMax=0`, restored before each, stdout and stderr both read for a result line:

```text

   cache-graph-pass         dropVacuousLabels INSIDE the      CAUGHT (3 fail)
                            cached prefix — item 1646's
                            design, i.e. THE wrong answer

   inherit-slot             `rewritten` keeps the slot        SURVIVED, then CAUGHT

```

⚠️ **`inherit-slot` surviving was a real gap in my tests and the reason for one more.** Deleting
`rewritten`'s reset left the whole suite green, because every `rewritten` call the chain makes today
happens BEFORE the slot is written — the inherited value is `undefined` either way, so the reset is
defensive rather than load-bearing. The test that kills it reaches the hazard through the exported
`fuseLocal`, called on a plan that is already cached. ⚠️ **`no-init-appendstep` is an EXPECTED
survivor**: initialising the slot at the four construction sites buys one hidden class per plan, which
is a perf property no answer test can see (and which measured FLAT in `rebuilt-build-only`, so it is
not costing anything either).

#### What shipped

Both checks are pure functions of the plan, and a plan is immutable, so a PASS can be remembered on
it — the same soundness argument as item 1647's prefix cache, and the same symbol-keyed slot
(`EFF_CHECKED`), initialised at all four construction sites and reset in `rewritten`.

⚠️ **ONLY A PASS IS EVER RECORDED.** The flag is written AFTER both checks return, so an invalid plan
is never marked and raises again on every call. ⚠️ **AND THE RESET IN `rewritten` MATTERS MORE HERE
THAN FOR THE PREFIX**: a rewrite can INTRODUCE a faulting kind (`fuseLocal` inlines a sub-plan's
steps into the top level, which is why `mayFault` is recomputed there), so an inherited pass would
skip a check that should raise.


**So the correctness property costs nothing**, and the 41% share is the generator PROTOCOL rather than
a choice between lazy and eager. Worth knowing for any future tick tempted to trade item 169's
one-derivation rule for speed here: there is no speed in it.

#### Refutation 3 — lifting the rung up `run`'s chain is a WASH, which is the shape of trap item 762 names

The rung sits after `countShortcut`, `groupCountShortcut` and `nodeValuesShortcut`, all of which
DECLINE its shape (they need a count tail or an id-less source), so moving it first changes no route —
asserted by the suite and by the shapes being disjoint. Measured with the ORDER itself as the arm
assertion (the first attempt asserted a line number that both arms shared, which made three rounds
worthless):

```text
                            lifted                   original               verdict
   V(id).values(k)           125.0 / 123.5 / 122.9    128.1 / 126.9 / 126.6  1.03x BETTER
   V(id).out(T).count()      122.6 / 123.4 / 121.1    117.5 / 119.6 / 118.7  1.03x WORSE
   V(64 ids).count()         756.7 / 767.3 / 740.8    747.1 / 752.0 / 731.1  1.01x WORSE
   V(id).values(k, kk)  CTL  296.0 / 299.7 / 296.8    307.6 / 296.9 / 300.5  FLAT
```

Unanimous in both directions — 3/3 rounds each way — and it nets to nothing: the `values` shape gains
exactly what every `count` shape loses, because a count query now runs `matchSeededShape` before
reaching its own rung. **A reordering that moves cost between shapes is not an optimisation unless
there is a reason to prefer one shape**, and there is none here. (`conjunct-order-chosen-for-speed` is
the case where there IS such a reason and the owner stated it; this is not that.)

#### The floor, stated so the next tick does not re-derive it

At ~126 ns against a 15.4 ns hand floor (8.2x), the remainder is `run`'s prologue, the shape match,
the rung chain, `getVertexById` (which is the O(1)-by-id invariant and must stay), and the generator
protocol — each a few nanoseconds, none removable without trading a measured property. **The one
unbuilt lever with a real ceiling is a per-plan ROUTE token** — caching WHICH rung answers a plan, the
way items 1647/1648 cache the rewrite and the static-check verdict — which would remove the whole
declining chain rather than reordering it. Its ceiling is the chain's own cost, which refutation 3
puts at **~3-4 ns**, so it is not worth the design either. Priced, not built, and said here so it is
not re-priced.

#### The screen: ten GQL shapes nothing had profiled, and one outlier

```text
   join 0.40ms/call   optional 0.19   existssub 0.37   unioned 0.70   varlenplus 5.35
   anyshortest 2.00   groupedhop 1.07  collecthop 0.95  scalaraggs 2.23
```

#### ⚠️⚠️ FIRST: `CALL { … }` IS NOT CYPHER'S, AND THE PROBE CAUGHT ME ASSUMING IT WAS

I wrote `MATCH (n:P) CALL { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) … }` expecting the body's `n` to be the outer `n`.
It is not: **ISO-GQL imports outer names through an explicit scope list, `CALL (n) { … }`**, and
without one the body's `n` is a FRESH variable. The probe asserts its two spellings agree before
reporting a time, and that assertion fired:

```text
   CALL { … }      sum(c) = 799,800,000   = 39,990 edges x 20,000 outer rows
   CALL (n) { … }  sum(c) =      39,990   = the edges, once
```

CLAUDE.md says GQL's CALL correlation "has been gotten wrong many times". It is right, and an
assertion in the instrument is what stops it becoming a number in this file.

#### The measurement, 20,000 vertices / 39,990 edges, median of 5

```text
   arm                                                   ms      ns/outer row   answer
   outer      MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(*)              0.003         0.1        20000
   inline     MATCH (n:P)-[:E]->(x) RETURN count(*)    0.002         0.1        39990
   bodyonce   the uncorrelated body, alone             0.001         0.0        39990
   correlated CALL (n) { … count(*) } RETURN sum(c)    1.486        74.3        39990
   calltrivial       CALL { RETURN 1 }                10.770       538.5        20000
   calltrivialscoped CALL (n) { RETURN 1 }            14.657       732.8        20000
   uncorrelated      CALL { … count(*) }              35.643      1782.1        20000
```

#### Finding 1 — the clause path is ~538-733 ns/row and a RECOGNISED body skips it

`correlated` does a real hop per row for **74.3 ns**; `calltrivialscoped` does NOTHING for **732.8**
— same form, same scope, 10x apart. So the 74.3 is not the CALL clause at all: a body of the shape
`MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) RETURN count(*)` is taken by a degree rung (`degreeCountSubquery` /
`landingPredDegreeCount` are the candidates) and the clause machinery is bypassed. **Every body the
rungs do not recognise pays 538-733 ns per outer row**, which is the open target.

⚠️ **AND THE SCOPE-LESS FORM IS NOT THE SLOW ONE** — my first hypothesis, refuted by its own arm:
538.5 scope-less against 732.8 scoped for an identical body. Whatever the 538-733 is, it is not
scope handling.

#### Finding 2 — item 1566's uncorrelated hoist WORKS, and the residue is the replay

`uncorrelated` at 1782 ns/row looked like a body re-run per outer row — the thing item 1566 built the
hoist to stop. It is not. Scaling says so:

```text
   N        uncorrelated   calltrivial   calltrivialscoped   correlated
   5,000        8.06 ms       2.81            3.57              0.65
   10,000      16.38          5.27            6.70              0.65
   20,000      34.01         10.78           14.82              1.21
```

**Exactly linear** (2.03x, 2.08x) where a re-run body over an O(N) fixture would be quadratic. So the
body runs once, as designed, and the 1782 ns/row is the per-row REPLAY of the hoisted rows plus the
outer aggregate — of which `calltrivial`'s 538 is the floor. Checking the list before building saved
this item from re-implementing a working optimisation: **`runCallInline` already carries the hoist,
its read-only allowlist and the lazy-computation rule**, each with the reasoning I was re-deriving
from scratch.

shows the ceiling: a body answered without the clause machinery costs 74 ns/row, so there is ~7-10x
in it for every body that is not a bare `count(*)`. ~~`runCallInline`'s per-row work is visible and

materialise 20,000 bindings** — which is `rung-precedence-decides-speed`'s shape exactly: a willing
fast rung declined because of a clause further down the chain.

### Item 1655 — ⚠️⚠️ **A 237x "EQUIVALENT-SPELLING GAP" THAT IS A WRONG ANSWER.** `match()` counts distinct variable BINDINGS; a hop chain counts PATHS. The flattening rewrite was built, verified against a fixture that confirmed it, and REVERTED when a fixture with ONE parallel edge separated the two spellings

REFUTED, no engine change. One guard test added (`match-binding-semantics.test.ts`).

#### The screen found it, and the ratio looked like the session's biggest lever

Ten unscreened Gremlin shapes through `runtime-profile-gremlin-probe.mjs`, 300 reps:

```text
   shape                                                        ms/call
   V().hasLabel(P).out(E).out(E).count()        hopcount2          1.40
   V().out(E).out(E).id()                       hop2idrows        26.10
   V().match(as(a).out(E).as(b)).count()        matched           58.47
   V().match(2 patterns).count()                matched2         332.40    237x hopcount2
   V().match(2 patterns).select('c').count()    matchedsel       438.81    313x
```

The profile is the solver: `solve` 32.6%, `applyPattern` 17.2%, `next` 16.2%, `bucketEnds` 7.0% —
a two-pattern DFS enumerating what `hopChainCount` answers in closed form.

#### It verified, twice, and both verifications were worthless

On a generated 200-vertex fixture all three spellings answered **1750**, and the `select('c')` rows
were **ORDERED-equal** (310 of them, first twelve identical). On that evidence the rewrite is sound
for counts AND for rows. It was built: a `fuseMatchChain` pass in its own module, gated on a new
`match` KIND bit, wired into item 1647's cached graph-free prefix, dropping the `as` steps because a
`count()` tail cannot observe a tag.

⚠️ **The fixture had no PARALLEL edges, and that is the only property that separates the spellings.**
CLAUDE.md's own rule — "an answer that is INVARIANT to the property you varied cannot validate the
fixture" — and I varied the pattern count, the direction and the labels, never the multiplicity.

#### What a differential against the SOLVER said

The new test's fixture carries a parallel edge, a self-loop and a second edge type, and its oracle is
the solver itself (a `select(tag)` tail, which the rewrite declines, so that plan runs the DFS).
**8 of 9 taken shapes failed**, and the minimal case is three vertices:

```text
   a -T-> b -T-> c                 match 1   chain 1    agree
   a =T=> b -T-> c  (a->b twice)   match 1   chain 2    DIVERGE
   the same on ONE hop             match 2   chain 3
```

`match` enumerates distinct `(a, b, c)` BINDINGS; the chain enumerates PATHS. A second `a -T-> b`
edge is a second path and the same binding. **So the two spellings answer different questions**, and
the 237x is not a defect to close.

⚠️ **AND IT CANNOT BE GATED.** "No parallel edges of the matching types" is a property of the DATA,
not of the plan, so no plan-time test decides it. `Graph` maintains `multiTypeEdgeCount` but nothing
counts parallel edges, so the gate does not exist today either. A `graph.parallelEdgeCount === 0`
gate would work and would have to live with `dropVacuousLabels` rather than in the cached prefix
(it reads the graph) — that is a core change for a rewrite whose benefit vanishes on exactly the
graphs that motivate a graph database. Not taken.

#### The second trap, found while writing the pass

A `match` step's output VALUE is a tag map, not the chain's end element:

```text
   V().match(…)                            -> [{}, {}, {}]
   V().as(a).out(E).as(b).out(E).as(c)     -> the c vertices
   V().match(…).id()                       -> [null, null, null]
   V().as(a)….id()                         -> ['v2', 'v5', 'v3']
```

`count()` and `select(tag)` both hide that, which is why the count-tail-only gate looked safe. Even
where the counts agree the spellings are not interchangeable mid-plan, and the guard test pins this
too.

#### What is left on `match()`

The 237x is real as a COST — the solver is genuinely 237x the closed form for the question it
answers — but it is the price of a different, stricter aggregate. The honest open question is whether
the SOLVER can be made cheaper (its own DFS, `solve`/`applyPattern`/`next` at 66% of the profile),
not whether it can be replaced by a chain. ~~Nothing here prices that.~~ ⚠️ **ITEM 1656 PRICES IT,
and the answer is not a constant factor: the solver has no SELECTIVITY-driven entry choice, so its
cost is independent of the answer size — 37-89x a hand route the engine already has the index for,
GROWING as the selective pattern gets rarer.**

### Item 1656 — ⚠️ **`match()` HAS NO SELECTIVITY-DRIVEN ENTRY CHOICE, and the cost is ALGORITHMIC rather than constant: it pays ~11 ms whether the answer is 60 solutions or 30,000.** 37-89x a hand route the engine already has the index for, and **the ratio GROWS as the selective pattern gets rarer** — the signature four constant-factor items could not have found

MEASURED, no engine change. New instrument: `gremlin-match-selectivity-floor.ts`.

#### Why this is a different question from the four items before it

The solver has been optimised four times — item 1478 (`tupleKey`, 1.10x), items 1559/1560 (the tag
snapshot, 1.16-1.23x), item 1627 (the adjacency read, 1.08-1.11x) — every one a CONSTANT FACTOR, and
item 1559's 5.68x "ceiling" was a pruned search. None of them could ask whether the solver's WORK is
asymptotically right.

#### Two cheap refutations first, so the target is not mis-aimed

- **Written pattern ORDER does not matter.** `match(p1, p2)` and `match(p2, p1)` for a chain answer
  the same (11,910) and cost the same (7.2-9.0 ms either way, both orders twice). So the solver is
  not naively following the written order, and "reorder the patterns" is not the lever.
- **The 237x of item 1655 is not available** — that was a different aggregate (bindings vs paths),
  refuted the same session.

#### The measurement: the gap GROWS as the answer shrinks

`match(as(a).out(T).as(b), as(b).out(S).as(c))` over 3,000 vertices, every vertex carrying 10 `T`
edges and one vertex in `rarity` carrying a single `S` edge. The floor is the route the solver could
take — for each `S` edge its source is a satisfying `b`, and the `a`s are that b's incoming `T`
neighbours — and **every row asserts the two answers agree before it is timed**:

```text
   rarity   S edges   solutions   solver     hand      ratio
        1      3000       29990   31.43 ms   0.524 ms   59.9x
        5       600        5998   18.57      0.402      46.2x
       25       120        1200   12.09      0.322      37.5x
      100        30         300   11.29      0.135      83.7x
      500         6          60   11.07      0.125      88.8x
```

⚠️ **READ THE SOLVER COLUMN, NOT THE RATIO.** It is 11.07 ms for SIX `S` edges and 31.43 for three
thousand — so the solver's cost is **driven by |V| x deg(T)**, the candidates it enumerates and
discards, and is nearly INDEPENDENT of how many solutions exist. The hand route scales with the
answer (0.125 → 0.524). That is why the ratio grows without bound as the selective pattern gets
rarer, and it is the one shape of finding a constant-factor sweep cannot produce.

#### The route exists; the choice does not

Driving from `S` needs `edgesByLabel.get('S')` — the same index `adjacentCount` already uses for a
global edge count — plus one `in(T)` per hit. So this is not a missing structure. What is missing is
an entry choice: the solver always enters from the incoming stream and tests each pattern forward,
where a selective pattern should be entered from its own bucket and traversed BACKWARDS to bind the
earlier tags.

OPEN, with that number. **Not built**: an entry/join-order choice in the solver is a planner feature,
not a tick, and it needs a cost model (the engine has `cost.rs` on the native side, nothing
equivalent in the TS solver). ⚠️ **AND ITEM 1657 RE-PRICES WHAT "NOT BUILT" MEANS HERE: it is not a
cost model, it is a JOIN OPERATOR, and it conflicts with Gremlin's per-traverser emission.** What this item fixes is the PRICE — the next attempt starts from
"37-89x and growing", not from the four constant-factor items' 1.1x.
