### Item 1657 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1656's TARGET IS NOT A COST MODEL, IT IS A JOIN OPERATOR — and it conflicts with Gremlin's per-traverser emission.** `pickRunnable` already restricts the solver to patterns whose start tag is BOUND, which is why written pattern order measures irrelevant; entering from a selective pattern's own edge bucket means binding BACKWARDS across the whole stream, which the nested-loop model cannot express

MEASURED/READ, no engine change. A short structural correction to the item before it, written because
the difference changes whether the target is reachable at all.

#### What `pickRunnable` already does

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < patterns.length; i++) {
  if (done.has(i) || !t.tags.has(patterns[i].startKey)) continue;
  if (!patterns[i].negated) return i;   // binders/filters before negated constraints
  …
}
```

It picks the first pattern that is RUNNABLE — start tag already bound — preferring non-negated. So
the solver is not following written order, and item 1656's own measurement agrees: `match(p1, p2)`
and `match(p2, p1)` cost 7.2-9.0 ms either way for the same 11,910 answer. **"Order the patterns by
selectivity" is therefore not the lever**, and in a CHAIN exactly one pattern is runnable at each
depth, so there is nothing to choose between.

#### Why the selective entry needs a different execution model

Item 1656's 37-89x comes from entering `as(b).out(S).as(c)` FIRST — but `b` is unbound there, so the
only way in is the global `S` bucket, and the earlier tag `a` must then be bound BACKWARDS
(`in(T)` from `b`). Two things block that:

- **`a` is fixed per incoming traverser.** `matchStep` is `function*(stream, …)` and `solve` extends
  ONE traverser at a time, so the stream has already chosen `a` before any pattern runs. Entering
  from the `S` bucket finds solutions for all `a`s at once — a whole-stream hash join, not a
  nested-loop extension.
- **Emission order is a TinkerPop contract**, compared ORDERED by the differential fuzzer. A join
  that groups by `b` emits solutions in bucket order, not in incoming-traverser order.

So the reachable form is a new JOIN operator with an order-restoring step, not a cost model bolted
onto `pickRunnable`. That is a much larger piece of work than item 1656's entry implies, and the
37-89x is its payoff rather than a planner tweak's.

⚠️ **THE SECOND BLOCKER IS A POLICY GAP, NOT AN OPERATOR — narrowed at item 1672.** "Emission order
is a TinkerPop contract, compared ORDERED by the differential fuzzer" is true of the fuzzer as
written: `orderUnspecified = multiType || RECONVERGING_BRANCH.test(text)`, and `match(` is in
neither. But the fuzzer's OWN rationale for that list is that _"TinkerPop guarantees output order
ONLY through `order()`"_, and by that rule a `match()` solution stream is equally unspecified — it
was never added, the same way `coalesce`/`choose`/`optional` had to be added when their
reconvergence order was found to differ. `index-seed.ts` states the policy directly: this repo
treats an unordered result's order as WON'T-FIX and the fuzzer compares such results as MULTISETS,
skipped only on an explicit `order()`.

So the order-restoring step is not required by anything technical. What is required is a DECISION to
extend that list to `match(`, which is a semantics call with precedent and is NOT taken here —
changing what a fuzzer enforces is exactly the kind of thing that should not be done on the way past.
**Blocker 1 (the whole-stream hash join, because `a` is fixed per incoming traverser) stands and is
technical. Blocker 2 is one line and a judgement.**

Removing a per-call allocation from a hot path has now measured **flat three times this session** —

#### ⚠⚠ The generalization, which is worth more than the 1.94x

**The 54 ns is a PER-CALL FIXED cost. It dominates only when the answer is TINY.** On
`V().values(k)` over 200,000 vertices it is 54 ns against 17.5 ms — 0.0003%, invisible — where
laziness is what keeps the scan bounded. So the finding licenses eagerness for **bounded-result rungs
only**, and _"move the hot path to eager arrays"_ is the memory regression it looks like. Stated
because this entry's headline number invites exactly that overreach, and because the owner raised it
before the change was taken.

This is the companion to item 1658's rule rather than a contradiction of it: a per-call ALLOCATION has
measured flat three times, while the three that WON (items 1650, 1651, 1660) were all about the SHAPE
of what is returned. The protocol is shape; the allocation is not.

Measured, not argued — the large shapes are untouched, and the per-call cost is where the memory
question is settled too:

```text
   V().values(k)             generator   pull-1 0.149 ms   drain-all 17.526 ms   200000 rows
   V().values(k).limit(10)   generator   pull-1 0.337 ms   drain-all  0.073 ms       10 rows
   V(64 ids).values(k)       generator   pull-1 0.067 ms   drain-all  0.137 ms       64 rows
   V(oneId).values(k)        ARRAY       —                                            1 row

   2M calls, arms alternated twice:  POST 104-114 ms   rss 54.1 / 54.6 MB   heapUsed 2.2 MB
                                     PRE  202-217 ms   rss 54.7 / 54.1 MB   heapUsed 2.3 MB
```

Memory is flat-to-LOWER eager, because a V8 generator object carries a suspended frame and a register
file and is the larger object — which is the same reason the CPU halves. And the rung fires only
when it answers the WHOLE plan, so a trailing step lands in the residual and never reaches an eager
route: that is the structural reason a 200,000-row scan cannot be made eager by this change.

```text
   V().values(k)                     RE-ITERABLE  nodeValuesShortcut still has the wrapper
   V(id).count() / V().count()       RE-ITERABLE  both return a bare [n]
   the general path                  one-shot
```

shape, which is the point lookup and the commonest serving query there is, had no contract coverage

rungs. `[initial ?? new Map()]` is the start either way, so `undefined` is the same start.

The gate is `seed.size`, not `clause.scope.length`: `CALL (m) { … }` for an `m` bound nowhere
outside is ACCEPTED by this engine (measured, not assumed) and imports nothing, so it deserves the

The engine already has TWO CALL-elimination rewrites: `inlineAggregateCall` (aggregate body →
`LET c = COUNT { … }`, 24.9x at item 561) and `inlineCorrelatedCall` (a pass-through body → a plain
`MATCH`). `callprojx` is refused by the second one on a single line:

```ts
if (item.expr.kind !== 'var' || (item.alias !== undefined && item.alias !== item.expr.name)) {
  return null; // executor.ts:9966
}
```

So a body may return its pattern VARIABLES verbatim (`RETURN x`) but not an EXPRESSION over them
(`RETURN x.k AS c`). Hand-writing what the extended rewrite would emit prices the target without
building it — `projxhand`, now an arm, asserted to answer identically:

```text
   callprojx   MATCH (n:P) CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) RETURN x.k AS c } RETURN sum(c)   3136
   projxhand   MATCH (n:P) MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) LET c = x.k RETURN sum(c)                     333
   inlineprojx MATCH (n:P)-[:E]->(x) RETURN sum(x.k)                                         346
```

**9.4x**, and the hand rewrite lands on the fully-fused twin, so the route is reachable. NOT BUILT,
and the reason is specific rather than a lack of time: the current rewrite emits ONE `match` clause
because the body's yielded names are exactly the names its pattern introduces, so nothing has to be
hidden. An expression projection must also DROP the body's pattern variables (`x` escapes the CALL
where the clause hid it) and that needs a `match` + projection pair whose item list the rewrite does
not statically know. A leaked name changes later-clause semantics, so this is optimizer-fuzzer
territory and deserves its own tick.

yield, and it moves INSIDE `inlineTrailingLet`), plus 11 new cases on `call-inline-rewrite.test.ts`
— **a file that until now had no route assertion at all** — and two retargeted fixtures on
`call-empty-seed-fastpath.test.ts`.

#### What item 1661 got wrong about its own target

Item 1661 priced this at 9.4x and declined to build it, naming the blocker as: the rewrite must
DROP the body's pattern variables (`x` escapes the `CALL` where the clause hid it), which needs a
`match` + projection pair whose item list the rewrite does not statically know — "optimizer-fuzzer
territory". Both halves of that were wrong, in opposite directions.

**The escape analysis already existed.** `nameIsUnread(name, where, tail)` is the predicate
`dropUnreadPathVar` (item 1049) and `dropUnreadEdgeVar` were built on, and it asks the identical
question — is this pattern variable provably unread by everything after the clause. It refuses on
any doubt: an unknown clause kind in the tail, a `RETURN *` (the one reference site that names no
name), a rebinding, a subquery `freePredicateVars` cannot see into. So the sound move is not to
drop the escaping names but to decline when anything can observe them, and the repo had already
answered that question once. Writing a second escape analysis was the thing to avoid: two of them
would drift, and the one that drifted would be wrong silently.

**And the actual difficulty was somewhere item 1661 never looked.** The first build was correct,
fired on exactly the intended shapes, passed its own route assertion — and delivered **1.44x**:

```text
   arm                      PRE                       POST                      ratio
   callprojx  TARGET        3110.7 3378.0 3300.7      2214.2 2165.6 2265.9      1.44x
   projxhand  the twin       373.9  380.1  389.7       287.5  726.5  306.6
```

2165 against the 330 its hand-written twin reaches. ⚠️ **THE DIAGNOSTIC WAS THE TWIN'S CLAUSE LIST,
NOT ITS TIME.** `projxhand` — `MATCH (n:P) MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) LET c = x.k RETURN sum(c)` — compiles
to `[match, return]` carrying `hopAggregate`. The rewritten `CALL` compiled to `[match, let, return]`
carrying **nothing**:

```text
   callprojx    ["match","let","return"]      rungs=[]
   projxhand    ["match","return"]            rungs=[hopAggregate]
   inlineprojx  ["match","return"]            rungs=[hopAggregate]
```

`inlineCorrelatedCall` ran OUTSIDE `inlineTrailingLet`, so the `LET` it now emits was never folded,
and **a standing `LET` is off every one of the twenty rungs** — items 512/516 measured that at 83x
and the comment on `inlineAggregateCall` says so in as many words ("runs INSIDE `inlineTrailingLet`
so the `LET` it produces is itself inlined"). The new rewrite needed the same placement and did not
have it. Moving it there:

#### What inlines, and the asymmetry that is the honest shape of the win

A yield is admitted when it is aliased and `cheapPureExpr` — `prop | var | lit | param`. That set is
doing two jobs: the expression must be TOTAL, because the emitted `LET` evaluates it on every
matched row, and it must be aggregate-free, which those four kinds give for nothing (an aggregate is
`inlineAggregateCall`'s shape and a different cardinality). Then every pattern name the body does
not yield must pass `nameIsUnread`.

⚠️ **ONLY THE COMPUTED YIELD REACHES A RUNG, AND THE ALIAS-ONLY SPELLING DOES NOT:**

```text
   RETURN x.k AS v   ->  [match, return]        on hopAggregate,  ~275 ns an outer row
   RETURN x   AS y   ->  [match, let, return]   off every rung,   ~2165
```

`inlineTrailingLet` substitutes a property read into the projection but declines a bare VARIABLE
rename (`LET y = x`), and it folds a ONE-ITEM `LET` only — a later item may read an earlier one
(`LET a = n.k, b = a`), so collecting several into one substitution map is a wrong answer. Both
refusals predate this item. So an aliased pass-through, and a body with TWO computed yields, lose
the `callInline` without being made fast. That is a smaller win rather than a wrong one, and it is
pinned in the tests so the next reader does not assume both halves reached the ladder.

#### The test file had no route assertion, and that cost exactly what it is supposed to cost

`call-inline-rewrite.test.ts` existed to pin this rewrite and asserted only ANSWERS. A rewrite is
answer-equivalent, so deleting `inlineCorrelatedCall` outright leaves every one of its assertions
passing. ⚠️ **It is not a theoretical gap: the test titled `an ALIASED or computed yield declines`
is the shape this item made INLINE. Its title became false and it PASSED.** The answers are kept —
they are now the equivalence oracle for the new route — and the clause list is asserted alongside
them. The 11 new cases assert the COMPOSED shape (`[match, return]`), not this rewrite's own output,
which is the only assertion that would have caught the 1.44x build.

```text
   M3 hand the escape analysis an EMPTY tail        CAUGHT (4)

```

And the module graph already had a cycle through `executor.ts`, which is why the split stalled half-done

#### `executor-edits-perturb` does not apply to a MOVE, and the reason is the build

Items 1413/1415/1440/1442/1462 measured that edits to these files cost unrelated query shapes up to
16%, and item 1466 declined a 3.3x win over it. That made a 12,000-line split look dangerous. It is
not, and the argument is structural rather than statistical:

⚠️ **`@lenke/gql` ships as ONE bundled `dist/esm/index.mjs`.** The nine `executor/*.ts` modules that
already existed are inlined into it and survive only in the sourcemap. So module boundaries do not
exist at runtime, a split adds **zero** file I/O, and the only thing a pure relocation can change in
the output is declaration ORDER. (`bun test` does read src, but it already loads 250+ files.)

So the question "did this move anything" is answerable by COMPARING THE BUNDLES rather than by
timing them. Both controls were run before the tool was trusted:

```text
   POSITIVE  item 1662's real change      29 substantive lines added, 11 removed -> correctly NOT a relocation
   NEGATIVE  two builds, identical source  BYTE-IDENTICAL -> the build is deterministic, so a clean verdict means something
```

And the verdict for this move:

```text
   det-a.mjs        24074 non-blank lines
   after-rename.mjs 24074 non-blank lines
   ADDED 1   REMOVED 1
      -  //#region src/executor.ts
      +  //#region src/executor/core.ts
```

#### ⚠️ THE BENCH SWEEP IS THE WRONG INSTRUMENT HERE, AND ITS OWN NULL CONTROL SAYS SO

A 4-round `BENCH_ENGINES=ts bun run bench` baseline was captured first (73 rows). Its round-to-round
spread on IDENTICAL code:

```text
   NULL CONTROL (codec rows, unreachable by a GQL change)   n=15  median 1.064x  p90 1.470x  worst 1.786x
   QUERY rows                                               n=55  median 1.106x  p90 1.472x  worst 2.861x
```

**The null control and the query rows have the same p90.** So this sweep cannot distinguish a real
GQL toll from noise below ~1.5x on any single row. It stays as a backstop for a catastrophic
regression only.

⚠️ **AND THE "0-16% EXPECTED TOLL" THIS ENTRY FIRST CLAIMED WAS WRONG — corrected here because a
reader would otherwise inherit it.** The 16% belongs to `executor-edits-perturb`, which measured
edits that ADD code: a new walk variant introducing another shape at a shared dispatch site, after
which that site's inline caches serve more shapes and every query through it pays. That is a
property of adding CALL SITES. A relocation adds none. Quoting the number for it applied a
measurement outside the regime it was measured in, which is the first defect CLAUDE.md lists, in
the same entry that cites CLAUDE.md.

The honest figure for a relocation is **zero, and provably** rather than approximately: this move's
bundle is byte-identical but for one `//#region` comment, and a comment does not execute. There is
not even extra parsing to pay for, because the package is one bundle either way. The only mechanism
that survives is declaration ORDER in the bundle, which could in principle move JIT code layout —
here the order did not change at all, and no measurement of an order-only change exists, so naming
a number for it would repeat the same error.

(The first baseline capture was thrown away for an unrelated reason worth recording: it parsed with
`sed` inside the loop, and `[a-z)\]]` does not escape inside a POSIX bracket expression — it demands
a literal `]` — so it silently kept only the 14 rows whose label ends in `]`, out of 73. The rewrite
dumps RAW output and parses afterwards, so a parsing bug cannot cost a 15-minute run again.)

#### The structure, measured: it is not eleven sections, it is one recursive compiler

The file carries eleven `// --- section ---` markers, and section-level coupling says six of them
are mutually dependent — true, and useless, because it does not say which symbols make them so. A
Tarjan SCC over the top-level symbol graph (VALUE references only; a type-position reference is
erased and creates no runtime edge) says:

```text
   219 value symbols, 193 SCCs, only 3 cyclic
   190 symbols are in NO cycle at all
    29 sit inside a cycle, in 3 clusters
```

```text
   CLUSTER A  25 symbols, 2,105 lines, spanning 4 sections — IRREDUCIBLE
              compileExpr/Func/Case/Aggregate/Exists/CountSubquery/ValueSubquery/LetIn/SubMatch,
              hopValueAggregate, landingPredDegreeCount, membershipTest, compilePath/Node/Rel/
              SubpathUnit, collectHints, hintsForVariable, compilePredicate, compileProps,
              directEqProps, liftMembership, liftNegatedCompare, gatePredicate, filterPredicate
   CLUSTER B  compileLinear <-> compileClause, 385 lines
   CLUSTER C  checkLinearScope <-> checkWriteClauseScope, 150 lines
```

Cluster A is inherent: compiling an expression can require compiling a subquery's pattern, which
requires compiling predicates, which requires compiling expressions. It gets one module. ⚠️ Note
`gatePredicate` and `filterPredicate` are MEMBERS — they are predicate COMPILERS that call
`compileExpr`, so filing them as "expression analysis leaves" (the first plan) would have created
the cycle it was meant to remove.

⚠️ **AND THE LAYERS ARE ORTHOGONAL TO THE SECTIONS.** Topologically the DAG is 11 layers, and every
layer draws from every section — layer 0 alone is 94 symbols, 2,637 lines, pulling 712 from "shared
bucket/adjacency", 437 from "expression compilation", 322 from "projection". So extracting by layer
gives dependency-clean modules that are incoherent to read, and extracting by section gives cycles.
The split has to be thematic groups that HAPPEN to be dependency-closed, verified one at a time.

#### Why the barrel, and the cycle that was already there

⚠️ **Nine modules under `executor/` import from `../executor.js` today, and the code behind it
imports those nine back.** The graph has had a cycle through `executor.ts` all along; ESM tolerates
it only because every reference sits inside a function body and resolves at call time rather than at
module evaluation. That is luck, and it is the best available explanation for why the existing split
stopped at nine modules with 12,000 lines left behind: there was nowhere to put the next piece.

A barrel that is not itself one of the split modules is what gives the next piece somewhere to go.
What breaks the remaining cycle is measured, not guessed: the nine siblings need **37 values and 29
types** back from `core.ts`. The 29 types are free (erased). The 37 values are the shared leaf layer
this package never had.

The next extraction is priced the same way: the planner family — `inlineAggregateCall`,
`inlineCorrelatedCall`, `inlineTrailingLet`, `fuseAnchorThenHop`, `dropUnread*`, `nameIsUnread`,
`compileLinear` — is 23 symbols, 2,005 lines, exports exactly **ONE** name (`compileLinear`, called
only by `compile` and by in-group `compileClause`), imports 33 from below, and is verified CLOSED:
nothing it imports depends back on a member.

⚠️ And it gets RENAMED when it moves. `// --- shared bucket/adjacency primitives` is the label on
that block today — the planner, in a file named for execution. That label is a direct reason item
1662's composition bug was hard to see.

`bun run check` 0 read UNPIPED. Suites core 444, gql 4254, gremlin 2017, serialization 144, native
1081 — 7940 pass / 0 fail, each exit code read unpiped. Bundle diff 1 line of 24,074, both controls

### Item 1664 — ⚠️ **WHAT ACTUALLY MADE `executor.ts` UNSPLITTABLE WAS FIVE HIDDEN GLOBALS, NOT ITS SIZE.** `compile` installs three collector `Set`s that code 10,000 lines away mutates instead of returning anything — so moving `compile` out made TypeScript infer `never` for the declarations that stayed, and the error pointed at the READER rather than the cause

REFACTOR. New `executor/compile.ts` (372 lines, the entry points) and `executor/compile-state.ts`
(71 lines, the query-scoped globals). `core.ts` 12,056 -> 11,704.

`compile` is the only caller of `compileLinear` outside the planner family, so while it lived in
`core.ts` the planner could not be extracted without a module cycle. Its interface turned out
narrow, which is what said the boundary was right: **2 values and 4 types** from `core.ts`.

#### The obstacle was not size

```text
   execEpoch             bumped once per plan invocation; memo caches key on it
   memoUncorrelated      may an uncorrelated subquery be computed once and reused across rows
   paramCollector        every $name the compiler saw, so compile can reject an unbound one
   unknownFnCollector    every function name resolving to no scalar/aggregate
   countParamCollector   params in a COUNT position
```

All five are written ONLY by `compile`/`execute` and read ONLY from `core.ts`. `compileExpr` reports
an unbound `$param` by MUTATING A VARIABLE rather than returning anything, and nothing in the call
signatures says so. No reading of the section markers would have found this.

⚠️ **The reads stay free, which is why this is a module and not a class or a context object.** An
imported `let` is an ESM live binding, and because the package ships as one bundle it collapses back
to a direct variable reference — no call, no property load. `execEpoch` is read in a PER-ROW memo
guard, so a getter there would have put a call in a hot loop to buy nothing. Only assignment cannot
cross a module boundary, so only the writers moved behind functions, and the bundle prices that
exactly: **-9 direct assignments, +16 lines of three setters and five call sites** in 14,951 —
five extra calls per `compile()` and one per plan invocation, never per row.

Lint earned its keep: the move left **eight dead imports** in `core.ts` and one in `compile.ts`,
none of which typecheck catches.

⚠️ Item 1663's "0-16% expected toll" is CORRECTED in that entry in this commit — a relocation is
provably zero, and the 16% belongs to edits that add call sites.

#### The by-id invariant HOLDS, measured rather than assumed

```text
   arm            10k      1M     ratio over 100x the data
   vertexById    12.5    48.6     3.88x
   edgeById      12.9    51.6     4.01x
   gremlinVById  1513    1119     0.74x   (flat — per-call surface cost, not the map's)
```

100x the data for 3.9x the time is the cache curve, and the jump sits between 200k and 1M exactly
where CLAUDE.md places the cache-resident transition. A lost O(1) would be ~100x. The instrument is

#### ⚠️ ITEM 1503'S FRAME TABLE IS STALE, which is why its heading is corrected in this commit

It names `checkStep` + `checkSteps` at **12.0%** as the remaining Gremlin per-call lever and prices

#### The screen: `propertyCount` 32.8%, `get properties` 23.8% — and only one of them is real

```text
                    200 vertices   200k vertices
   propertyCount        33.3%          32.8%
   get properties       18.3%          23.8%
```

It survived the size sweep (it got MORE significant at 200k, so not a small-fixture artefact), and

⚠️ **THEN THE ATTRIBUTION TEST, AND IT WENT BOTH WAYS.** Rather than rewriting the getter, three arms
over the same vertices — `v.properties[key]`, the bag hoisted, and a prearranged bag array:

```text
                 FIRST run        SECOND run (two arms added)
   getter      9.38  11.74x       6.13   1.01x
   hoisted     9.56  11.96x       6.15   1.02x
   direct      0.80   1.00x       6.05   1.00x   <- the CONTROL, identical code, 7.5x apart
```

**The control moved 7.5x between runs on identical code**, purely from adding two more arms to the
same file. With a stable baseline the getter costs NOTHING over a direct bag read, and the 23.8% is
the profiler crediting inlined work to the frame.

That makes four instances of this trap in this codebase: `degreeOfTypes` at 97.1% (item 1493),
`subPlansOf` at 15.7% (item 1503), the `get labels` rewrite that measured flat on every row because

this. ⚠️ **The pattern is specific enough to be a rule: a frame that is a FIELD READ OR A GETTER on a
hot object is attribution until a deletion test says otherwise — and the deletion test needs a
control, run more than once.**

I asserted "it's REAL, not attribution" off the first run. The second run existed only because I
wanted to decompose the cost, not because I doubted it. CLAUDE.md names both halves of that mistake
already — single-run conclusions, and a control moving more than the target.

#### `seekWorthTaking` is not an opening either

The remaining 32.8% is `propertyCount` doing GENUINE work: a 200k-vertex scan serving
`V().has(k,pred).count()`. Making it faster means seeking an index, and it already declines to one
when `seekWorthTaking` says a seek beats a scan — a gate item 1322 built with numbers (2.179 ms for
the count shortcut, 14.457 ungated seek, 5.433 when the gate makes BOTH fast paths bow out). Its
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION = 1/8` is **the third copy of one rule**: native has carried it throughout, GQL
added it at item 409, Gremlin at 1322. Retuning it in one engine would diverge three.

### Item 1668 — ⚠️ **A COVERAGE SCREEN INSTEAD OF A FRAME SCREEN, and it found the one unpriced shape left: the HOST LAMBDA family. `map(fn)` costs 2.54x `values(k)` and a `count()` behind a lambda costs 2.84x — but the lambda CALL is only 1.20x. The cost is the LOST ROUTE, not the call**

New instrument: `gremlin-lambda-steps-probe.mjs`. No engine change.

#### Why a coverage screen

Item 1659 declared the unpriced-FRAME screen exhausted, and item 1667 re-ran it against a
restructured executor and agreed. So this asks a different question — not "which frame is hot" but
**"which SHAPE has never been measured"**, which is what CLAUDE.md means by needing a better
benchmark rather than a better profile.

Over all **104 Gremlin step kinds**, 30 had no probe in `packages/native`. ⚠️ **THAT RAW NUMBER IS
WRONG AND THE SCREEN NEEDS THE CROSS-CHECK**: probes get deleted while their findings stay in
CLOSED.md, so "no probe" is not "no measurement". Cross-checking the 30 against CLOSED.md moved 14
of them out — `simplePath` most sharply, which items 1464-1466 measured in detail. What remained was
niche (`sack`, `withSack`, `subgraph`, the OLAP trio) plus one real family.

⚠️ **AND CHECKING CLOSED.MD FIRST SAVED A WASTED PROBE.** `hasRevisit` allocates a `Set` and walks
the whole path per traverser per step, which reads as O(depth²) with a per-step allocation — a
textbook find. Item 1464 had already profiled it: **`simplePath`'s own predicate is 2.18%**. The cost
is `tracksPath` returning the plan unrewritten and skipping `hopValuesShortcut`, sized at 3.30x,
flagged not built, and declined at item 1466 over the edit-perturbation toll. The hypothesis was
right about the mechanism and wrong about the magnitude by ~40x.

#### The finding: the lambda family, five step kinds, never priced

`filterFn`, `mapFn`, `flatMapFn`, `foldFn`, `sideEffectFn` — the escape hatch a user reaches for when
no declarative step fits. 200,000 vertices, three pairs, each asserted to answer identically before
any time is read:

```text
   arm            ns/vertex              ratio
   valuesDecl         36.74     mapLambda      93.27    2.54x
   hasDecl            26.97     filterLambda   32.30    1.20x
   countDecl          10.89     countLambda    30.88    2.84x
```

⚠️ **THE DECOMPOSITION IS THE RESULT, NOT THE RATIOS.** A lambda must be slower — the engine cannot
see into it. The question was whether the gap is the CALL or the LOST ROUTE, and the three pairs
separate them: `filter(fn)` against `has(k,v)` is **1.20x**, so the opaque per-traverser call costs
about **5 ns**. The other two are 2.5-2.8x because the declarative side rides something the lambda
cannot — `values()` its fusion (item 1586) and `has()+count()` the count rung (10.89 ns against
30.88). So a user who writes `map(v => v.properties.k)` for `values('k')` is not paying for the
call, they are falling off a rung.

**Not an engine change, and deliberately so.** Nothing can fuse an opaque function. This is a
documented cost of the escape hatch and a first number for five step kinds, which is what makes it
worth having.

#### Two process notes, both mine

The first version of this probe named its lambda arm `filterDecl` and shipped **no declarative twin
at all**, so a 27.59 ns reading was compared against nothing and the `has` route — the whole point —
was never measured. Caught by reading my own arm list, not by a gate.

And `valuesDecl` read 27.47 ns in one run and 36.74 in the next (**34% apart**) purely from the
other arms present. Same lesson as item 1667's 7.5x control: the RATIOS within a run are the
measurement, an absolute ns figure across runs is not.

### Item 1670 — ⚠️ **THE TIMING BACKSTOP THE SPLIT KEPT PROMISING AND NEVER RAN: nine extractions and two new lint rules measure FLAT.** Query rows median **1.023x** against a null-control median of **1.021x** — a 0.2% difference, which is the instrument and not the code

No engine change. The measurement thirteen commits said was covered by a bundle diff.

#### What was actually verified, and what was not

Every extraction from item 1663 onward was gated on a code-only BUNDLE DIFF, on the argument that
`@lenke/gql` ships as one bundle so a pure relocation cannot change the emitted code. That argument
holds and the diffs were clean — across ~14,000 emitted lines the only substantive changes in the
whole split are ~35 lines of accessor plumbing in `compile-state.ts` and one alias inlined at item 1669. Everything else was identical code in a different ORDER, or the bundler swapping which of two
same-named functions carries a `$1` suffix.

⚠️ **BUT A BUNDLE DIFF CANNOT SEE DECLARATION ORDER, WHICH IS THE ONE THING EVERY EXTRACTION
CHANGED** — and that is precisely the mechanism behind `executor-edits-perturb`'s 16%. A 4-round
`BENCH_ENGINES=ts bun run bench` baseline was captured at 121b22fc specifically as that backstop,
and then not used for thirteen commits. This is it.

```text
   4 rounds each side, commit 121b22fc -> 0939b347

   QUERY rows  n=55   median 1.023x   worst 1.41x   best 0.89x
   NULL CTL    n=15   median 1.021x   worst 1.10x   best 0.97x
```

**The query rows and the null control moved by the same amount.** The 15 codec rows
(encode/decode ndjson, pg-json, graphson, pg-text, csv) are code a GQL executor split provably
cannot reach, so 1.021x there is the machine's drift; the query rows' 1.023x is the same drift. The
difference is 0.2%.

#### The one remaining outlier is a PRE-side artefact, and reading it the other way would have been wrong

```text
   1.41x   pre 3.1 / 3.0 / 2.2 / 3.4   post 3.1 / 3.4 / 3.1 / 3.2   query: group, no aggregate
```

The POST side is tighter. The ratio exists only because `min`-of-4 banked a single fast pre rep —
the bimodal-arm problem CLAUDE.md records for the TS per-row path, where `min` is the wrong
estimator. ⚠️ And at three rounds the worst row in the whole sweep was `encode ndjson` at 1.33x — a
NULL CONTROL, i.e. a file the split never opened — which the fourth round took back to 1.10x. Both
are the same lesson: a single row's ratio is noise, and the readable signal is the median across 55
rows with the controls pinned.

#### Why this is worth an entry rather than a line

The split was argued from a mechanism (one bundle, so relocation is free) and verified against a
proxy (the emitted lines). Both were right, and neither is the measurement. Thirteen commits each
said "zero emitted-code change" and let that stand for "no regression" — which it does not, because
the thing it cannot see is the thing that moves the JIT. The number is 1.02x against a 1.02x
control. It was worth getting.

### Item 1671 — **`_MERGE` PRICED FOR THE FIRST TIME, and it is O(1) in graph size: the indexed existence check is 468-510 ns at every size from 10,000 to 1,000,000.** An upsert is ~1.4-2.9 us, the read half is ~20% of it, and an UPDATE is cheaper than a CREATE

New instrument: `gql-merge-scaling-probe.mjs`. No engine change.

#### Found by screening the GQL surface, not by profiling

The same screen item 1668 ran over Gremlin's 104 step kinds, applied to GQL: all 15 clause kinds
appear somewhere in `packages/native`, and of 51 expression kinds only four are thin (two being the
`CALL` forms item 1662 measured). But **`_MERGE` appears five times and has never been measured** —
its seven mentions in CLOSED.md are item 442's parse-error divergence, an id path and a push site.
For a clause real ingest workloads run in a loop, that was the hole.

It matters because of the shape: an upsert is a READ then a WRITE, and the read decides the
complexity. `resolveMergeEndpoint` -> `graph.uniqueLookup(label, key, value)` ->
`vertexPropertyIndex.equals(key, value)`, so the create-vs-update decision rides the unique
constraint's index. A degradation to a scan would make an upsert loop O(N^2) and still return the
right answer at every step — the by-KEY analogue of the by-id invariant `by-id-scaling-probe.mjs`
guards.

```text
   arm            N          ns/op    vs LARGEST N
   lookupOnly       10000     495.2      0.97x
   lookupOnly       50000     471.7      0.92x
   lookupOnly      200000     467.8      0.92x
   lookupOnly     1000000     510.3      1.00x

   mergeUpdate      10000    2187.7      1.44x
   mergeUpdate      50000    1885.9      1.24x
   mergeUpdate     200000    1427.2      0.94x
   mergeUpdate    1000000    1521.4      1.00x

   mergeCreate      10000    2731.1      0.96x     insertPlain   10000   4395.0   1.67x
   mergeCreate      50000    2476.4      0.87x     insertPlain   50000   2322.2   0.88x
   mergeCreate     200000    2595.5      0.91x     insertPlain  200000   2461.8   0.94x
   mergeCreate    1000000    2852.6      1.00x     insertPlain 1000000   2630.5   1.00x
```

**The invariant holds, and `lookupOnly` holds it exactly**: 468-510 ns across 100x the data, which
is as flat as this instrument reads anything. No arm rises with N, so an upsert loop is O(N).

Three things worth having:

- **The read half is a MINORITY of the cost.** ~490 ns against 1,427-2,188 for an update (20-34%)
  and 2,476-2,853 for a create (~18%). The write dominates, so the lever on upsert throughput is
  the write path, not the existence check.
- **An UPDATE is cheaper than a CREATE** — 1,427-2,188 against 2,476-2,853 — because a create also
  pays vertex construction, index maintenance and the constraint check. An upsert-heavy workload
  over existing keys is the cheap case, which is the opposite of the intuition that an update costs
  a read plus a write while a create costs only a write.
- **`_MERGE` costs about what `INSERT` costs** (2,852 against 2,630 at a million). The clause is not
  expensive; writes are.

#### ⚠️ TWO BUGS IN THIS PROBE, AND THE REPO'S OWN LINT RULE FOUND THE WORSE ONE

The first version spliced the key into the query text. `lenke(no-raw-interpolation)` flagged it as
an injection risk — and the consequence for a MEASUREMENT is worse than the consequence for safety:
every call gets a different query string, so the parse+plan cache never hits and the reading is
dominated by parsing 500 distinct texts per call. **`lookupOnly` read ~2,000 ns interpolated and
495 ns with `$k` bound — 4x.** Items 1499-1502 are about exactly that cost, and the probe walked
into it while measuring something else. A real upsert loop binds a param; so does this now.

And the ratio column first normalised against the SMALLEST N, which reported `insertPlain` at
"0.51x at a million" — twice as fast with 100x the data, which is not a thing. The create arms ADD
`OPS * REPS` vertices to the graph they measure: +35% at 10,000 against +0.35% at a million, so all
that index work lands on the small-N reading. Normalised against the largest N instead, with the
artefact documented in the probe — `insertPlain`'s 1.67x at 10,000 is that artefact and not a
scaling term.

#### Addendum — the write path profiles FLAT too, so the lever item 1671 named has no hot spot

`_MERGE`'s cost being the write rather than the lookup made the write path the obvious next target.
Profiled, it is the same shape as everything else this session:

```text
   mergeUpdate: 1687 ns/op   (fixture 10,000 vertices, 200,000 measured ops)

   12.3%  runMerge              4.4%  uniqueLookup
    7.9%  runLinearClauses      2.9%  equals / hasLabel
    7.5%  commitTransaction     1.8%  uniqueConflict
    6.0%  plan                  1.7%  runDeferredChecks
    4.9%  #commitNormalized     1.5%  deferConstraint
    4.7%  setProperty           1.5%  query
```

No hot spot — the largest frame is 12.3% and the rest is a 1.5-8% tail. Transaction and constraint
machinery together (`commitTransaction`, `runDeferredChecks`, `deferConstraint`, `uniqueConflict`)
is ~12.5%, which is the largest coherent group and still not a target.

⚠️ **`plan` AT 6.0% IS NOT A CACHE MISS, WHICH WAS WORTH CHECKING RATHER THAN ASSUMING.** The plan
cache is a `WeakMap<Query, Plan>` keyed on the AST and it DOES cover writes; with constant query
text plus a bound param, both it and item 228's parse cache hit. The frame is the cached path's own
work.

⚠️ **AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THIS PROFILE MEASURED THE FIXTURE.** Run against
`gql-merge-scaling-probe.mjs` directly it showed `getVertexById` 16.3%, `#commitNormalized` 11.8%,
`commitElementLabels` 8.7% — the BULK INGEST path, because that probe builds four 200,000-vertex
graphs against ~22,000 measured operations, so ~97% of the write work sampled was `build()`. A
profile whose fixture outweighs its measurement by 40x describes the fixture. Redone with a
10,000-vertex fixture and 200,000 ops — 20x the other way — it says what is above.

### Item 1674 — **`topologyVersion`: THE SYNCHRONOUS SIGNAL ITEM 1571 SAID DID NOT EXIST, BUILT AND MEASURED FREE.** Four integer increments, two maps, a 6-test contract suite, and a 5/6 mutation score where the survivor is an equivalent mutant. ⚠️ **Its A/B needed a purpose-built instrument, because the probe it was first measured with produced a result that CONTRADICTED its own mechanism** — the arm that moved most bumps the counter zero times. ⚠️ **AND THE SIGNAL AS BUILT HERE WAS INCOMPLETE — see item 1675, which found that a type-keyed adjacency is re-bucketed by an edge-label write and added two more sites**

Item 1571 priced a CSR cache at 86.3% of a bounded var-length count and declined to build it for one
reason: nothing in `Graph.ts` advances synchronously. Item 1673's blocker audit narrowed the
prerequisite from "every mutator plus the transaction undo path" to four sites. This builds it.

#### What it is

```ts
   public topologyVersion = 0;        // Graph.ts, beside vertexCount/edgeCount
```

bumped at exactly the four writes that can move a CSR — `verticesById.set`/`.delete` and
`edgesById.set`/`.delete` — and at nothing else. Three properties, all pinned as tests in
`packages/core/src/core/topology-version.test.ts`:

- **Synchronous**, where `version` and `epoch(name)` are deferred. The test asserts `g.version` is
  still 0 after two `addEdge` calls while `topologyVersion` has moved by 2. This is item 1571's
  disqualifying measurement, now a regression test rather than a note.
- **Topology, not mutation.** A property or label write does NOT bump it, so a cached adjacency
  structure survives `SET`. This is what makes the signal worth having rather than merely correct:
  bumping on property writes would discard the cache on every write and it would never pay on a
  read-write workload.
- **Conservative under rollback.** A rolled-back transaction still bumps it, because the undo log
  stores inverses as closures over the public mutators, so a rollback replays through the same four
  writes. Over-invalidation costs a rebuild; under-invalidation is a wrong answer.

#### ⚠️ The cost: FREE, and the instrument to show it had to be built

```text
   arm                PRE      POST    POST/PRE
   addVerticesOnly   891.6    895.1     1.004x    bumps the counter
   addEdgesToo      1526.0   1515.1     0.993x    bumps the counter
   setPropertyOnly   533.4    553.3     1.037x    CONTROL, bumps nothing
```

(`core-write-floor-probe.mjs`, N=100,000, 9 reps, two order-alternated rounds, a core rebuild per
arm.) **The CONTROL moved more than either target**, 3.7% against 0.4% and −0.7%, and the two arms
that actually pay the increment disagree on the sign. That is this file's own tell for noise, so the
reading is: whatever the counter costs is below the instrument's 3.7% resolution.

⚠️ **THE QUERY-LEVEL PROBE COULD NOT ANSWER THIS, AND ITS ANSWER WAS INCOHERENT RATHER THAN MERELY
NOISY.** Pointed at `gql-merge-scaling-probe.mjs`, the counter appeared to cost 1.30x on `mergeUpdate`
and 1.16x on `mergeCreate` against item 1671's numbers. But `mergeUpdate` is a property write, which
bumps the counter ZERO times, while `insertPlain` — which does bump — read flat at 1.01x. A pattern
that contradicts the mechanism is noise however large it looks, and the cause is resolution: that
probe reads 1.4-4.7 us an operation with a 1.53x within-run spread across sizes, so it cannot see a
sub-1% change to a write path. It was also a CROSS-RUN comparison against a log from a previous item,
which this file has twice recorded as unreliable (`valuesDecl` moved 34% and `direct` 7.5x on
identical code). Hence `core-write-floor-probe.mjs`: the mutators directly, no query, no plan, no
transaction, with the property-write path as a built-in control.

⚠️ **AND THE A/B'S "PRISTINE" SNAPSHOT WAS NOT PRISTINE.** The copy kept at
`crates/lenke-engine/target/item1674/Graph.pristine.ts` was taken AFTER the counter went in, so it
carried all five occurrences; using it as the PRE arm would have compared the change against itself
and reported the counter free for the wrong reason. Caught by counting the symbol in each arm before
building it — the rule this file already states as "assert each A/B arm IS the code it claims" — and
the driver now asserts the count in the BUILT DIST, not in src, since dist is what the probe imports.

⚠️ **THE PROBE ALSO OOMed ON ITS FIRST RUN, at N=100,000 in a 4 GB heap**, which is
`graph-pinned-until-microtask-drain` exactly: a discarded `Graph` is retained in full by its pending
`drainMutations` microtask, so a synchronous build-and-discard loop holds every graph it ever made.
Ten reps was enough. `await` a macrotask yield between reps and the retention releases. Any probe
that builds a fresh graph per rep needs that drain.

#### Mutation score: 5 caught, 1 equivalent survivor

Six mutants, each anchor asserted unique so a mutant that fails to apply cannot be scored as caught.
M1-M4 delete one of the four increments — under-invalidation, the failure mode that serves a stale
structure — and each is caught (1, 1, 3, 1 failures). M5 adds a bump where a LABEL write commits:
correct but ruinous, and caught by the "does NOT bump" test, which is the whole reason that test
exists.

⚠️ **M6 — restore the counter on rollback — SURVIVED, AND CORRECTLY.** The claim in item 1571's entry
that restoring it "could make a cache serve a stale structure" was wrong: a rollback restores state
faithfully, so a counter restored alongside it is CONSISTENT, since a cache entry at the
pre-transaction version was built from the pre-transaction state, which is exactly the post-rollback
state. Both choices are sound; not restoring is simply simpler. The entry and the test comment are
corrected, and the test now pins the weaker property that is actually load-bearing — the version
CHANGES when state changes.

(⚠️ M5's first draft added an unused private method, which changes no behaviour and would have

### Item 1675 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1674'S SIGNAL WAS WRONG BY OMISSION, AND THE CACHE IT EXISTS FOR WOULD HAVE BEEN A WRONG ANSWER.** Adjacency is keyed BY EDGE TYPE, so an edge-label write re-buckets it without ever touching `insertEdge`. Found while writing the first consumer, not by the contract suite. ⚠️ **And the repair's first draft RELAXED an assertion to fit the widened code, which cost three mutants their teeth** — the next pass scored them as survivors

Item 1674 bumped `topologyVersion` at the four map writes that change the vertex set or the edge set.
Writing the CSR cache against it exposed what that misses.

#### The hole

`walkLevelCount` builds its `nbr` from a TYPE-FILTERED adjacency — `edgesOfTypes(v.adjFrom, types)`.
Those boxes are `edgesFromByLabel`, keyed by edge type, and `addLabelToEdge` moves an edge between
buckets through `indexEdgeLabel`/`deIndexEdgeLabel`:

```text
   addLabelToEdge  ->  commitElementLabels  +  indexEdgeLabel    -> edgesFromByLabel mutated
                       (no insertEdge, no edgesById write, no bump)
```

So a CSR cached on the four-site counter would keep serving neighbours for a type an edge no longer
carries: the correct answer at every step, from a structure describing a graph that no longer exists.
This is the exact failure shape every entry in this file's index-seeding family has.

The fix is two more sites, at `indexEdgeLabel` and `deIndexEdgeLabel`. **An edge-label write IS a
topology change to every consumer of this signal**, because every one of them reads a type-filtered
adjacency. A VERTEX label write stays out: it touches `verticesByLabel`, which no adjacency structure
is derived from. The asymmetry is the content of the contract, so it is pinned in both directions.

#### ⚠️ The repair's first draft relaxed a test to fit the code, and a mutation pass priced it

Widening the signal broke an assertion: a singly-labelled `addEdge` now bumps TWICE, once for
`edgesById.set` and once for the label indexed, so `toBe(start + 3)` failed. It was relaxed to
`.not.toBe(previous)` — per-site CHANGE rather than an exact delta — with what felt like a principled
justification: the declaration's own contract says a consumer must never subtract two values, so
asserting a delta looked like testing something the signal does not promise.

The next mutation pass refuted that:

```text
                              exact-delta   relaxed
   M3  drop edgesById.set bump     CAUGHT   SURVIVED
   M4  drop edgesById.delete bump  CAUGHT   SURVIVED
   M5  bump on vertex-label commit CAUGHT   SURVIVED
```

Each of those three leaves SOME other site bumping on the same operation, so "it changed" still holds
while a site is dead. ⚠️ **The two claims are different and only one of them was true**: a CONSUMER
must not rely on the delta, because it is an implementation detail. A TEST that pins the delta is the
only instrument that distinguishes a live site from a dead one. Restored as an exact delta table
(`addVertex` +1, `addEdge` +2 for one label and +3 for two, `removeEdge` +2, isolated `removeVertex`
+4), all three are caught again — M5 with 3 failures.

⚠️ **M5 ALSO NEEDED A SECOND PATH, not just a tighter assertion.** The no-bump test exercised
`v.labels = [...]`, which BYPASSES `commitElementLabels` entirely — the same divergence between the
setter and the methods that this file already records for the label index. So a spurious bump placed
in `commitElementLabels` was invisible to it. The test now exercises the setter AND
`addLabelToVertex`/`removeLabelFromVertex`.

#### ⚠️ An edge cannot exist without a label, so the two edge-map bumps are redundant

`addEdge` rejects `labels: []`, so `edgesById.set` can never run without at least one
`indexEdgeLabel`, nor `edgesById.delete` without a `deIndexEdgeLabel`. Deleting either edge-map bump
therefore cannot under-invalidate. They are KEPT as defence in depth — with them each map's bump is
correct on its own terms and the signal does not silently depend on an invariant enforced 2,000 lines
away — and the delta table is what keeps them live rather than dead code. The invariant itself is now
asserted, so its removal would surface here rather than as a stale cache.

#### Mutation score: 7 of 8, survivor equivalent

M1-M5, M7, M8 all caught (1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2 failures). M6 — restore the counter on rollback —
survives, correctly and for the reason item 1674 recorded: a rollback restores state faithfully, so a
restored counter is consistent.

### Item 1676 — **ITEM 1571'S CSR CACHE, BUILT AND TAKEN: 3.8x to 27.2x across the six bench rows that reach it, with the in-family ENUMERATING row flat at 0.991x.** ⚠️ **The probe that drove the work reported 2.45x and that was the FLOOR, not the answer — a 50,000-vertex fixture understates this cache by an order of magnitude**, for a reason the repo's own "sweep the size" rule predicts. ⚠️ **The 4,254 tests already in the package all passed on the first build of this cache and would have passed on one with NO invalidation at all** — the suite that can tell the difference is 14 new tests and six key mutants

#### The measurement

```text
   arm                PRE      POST    ratio
   repeated          12.68     5.17    2.45x    the same query 20x, no writes
   depth2            10.80     2.84    3.80x    `{1,2}`, least to amortize
   writeInterleaved  12.73    12.87    1.01x    a 1-edge write between every call

```

(`gql-varlen-cache-probe.mjs`, 50,000 vertices / 150,000 edges, 20 calls per rep, 9 reps, three
order-alternated rounds.) Depth 3 saves 7.51 ms and depth 2 saves 7.96 — the same fixed build in

something else had changed.

⚠️ **AND THESE RATIOS ARE THE FLOOR. The same change on the `bun run bench` fixture (200,000 /
1,000,000) measures 3.8x to 27.2x** — see the sweep below. The two do not disagree, because what the
cache ELIMINATES and what it LEAVES scale differently:

```text
   the build     a V-entry `Map` plus E map lookups     7.6 ms at 50k  ->  124-196 ms at 200k
   the residual  a dense Int32Array read per level     ~5.0 ms at 50k  ->    7-30 ms at 200k
```

The build does one `idx.get` per edge, and that falls out of cache across precisely the
200,000-to-1,000,000 element transition this file documents; a sequential typed-array read does not.
So the win GROWS with the fixture. **Picking 50,000 for the probe was the "sweep the size" trap, and
it cost this item its headline number in the first report of it.** The probe's header now says so and
gives both invocations.

⚠️ **SHAPE matters far less than SIZE, which is worth knowing because it was the first explanation
reached for and it was wrong.** Faced with the probe saying 3.7x and the bench 27x at the same vertex
count, the obvious suspect was the bench's UNLABELLED endpoint making the endpoint test vacuous. At
200,000, warm: a labelled endpoint reads 29.89 ms/call, an unlabelled one 27.63 (1.08x), and
`MATCH WALK` with an unlabelled endpoint 14.76 (2.0x). That is the entire spread across spellings,
against the 16-26x the fixture size is worth. The hypothesis was measured rather than adopted.

⚠️ **`writeInterleaved` IS THE ARM THAT EARNS THE ENTRY**, and it is the one most easily left out. A
write between every query makes every call miss, so it prices the cache's COST rather than its win:
flat at 1.01x, so the lookup, the version compare and the dropped generation are free. Without it the
other three rows cannot distinguish "the cache works" from "the cache works and taxes everyone who
writes".

#### ⚠️ The existing suite could not have caught a cache that never invalidates

A cache with no invalidation at all returns the correct answer for every read-only query ever
written. All 4,254 tests in `packages/gql` passed on the first build of this one, and would have
passed on a broken one; the failure mode is `query, write, query`, which nothing in the package
exercised against this route. `var-length-count-cache.test.ts` is 14 tests that are all invalidation
tests, and the mutation pass is what says they have teeth:

```text
   MC1  never invalidate                         CAUGHT (6 failures)
   MC2  key drops the DIRECTION                  CAUGHT (1)
   MC3  key drops the edge TYPES                 CAUGHT (1)
   MC4  key on `graph.version`                   CAUGHT (6)
   MC5  key on vertexCount + edgeCount           CAUGHT (2)
   MC6  key on edgeCount alone                   CAUGHT (2)
```

MC4, MC5 and MC6 are not arbitrary breakage — they are the three keys item 1571 rejected on paper,
now rejected by measurement. MC4 is that entry's disqualifying finding (`version` is deferred, so it
reads 0 through a sequence of mutations) and it fails six of the fourteen. MC6 is item 1675's hole:
an edge-label write re-buckets a type-keyed adjacency while `edgeCount` does not move.

#### Three design points that are not obvious

⚠️ **`types` IS NOT SORTED INTO THE KEY, and sharing an entry across orderings would be a byte-identity
bug.** Two spellings naming the same edge types in a different order are semantically equivalent, so
collapsing them looks free. But `edgesOfTypes` iterates `types` IN ORDER, so the two orderings produce
`nbr` arrays that differ in POSITION. The count itself is a sum and would survive; the depth-3/4 trail
corrections read `nbr` positionally through `pairMultiplicities`, and f64 sums in a different order are
not required to agree bit for bit. Byte-identity between the engines is a hard invariant, so the
conservative key ships.

⚠️ **A STALE GENERATION IS DROPPED WHOLE, not per shape.** Every shape built from the old topology is
equally invalid, and keeping the map would leak one dead entry per shape per write.

⚠️ **THE PER-SHAPE MAP IS CAPPED AT 8, because the retention is not small and nothing else bounds
it.** Each entry holds `order` (V references), `idx` (a V-entry Map) and two typed arrays sized V+1
and E — on the order of 2 MB at 50,000/150,000 — and lives as long as the graph. A generation is
cleared on any topology write, so growth needs MANY distinct shapes with no write between them,
which is exactly the shape of a report sweeping one query per edge type. Past the cap the generation
is cleared rather than evicted one entry at a time: there is no recency information worth keeping,
every entry costs one rebuild to recover, and a clear cannot degrade into holding the cap's worth of
cold entries forever. The cap is free — 5.17 against 5.04 ms/call, inside the noise — and it has its
own test, because no key mutant can reach it: clearing a cache can only cost a rebuild, never return
a wrong answer.

#### ⚠️ Two probe defects, both of which produced a plausible wrong number first

**The route was first measured with the Cypher spelling.** `-[:E*1..3]->` is not ISO-GQL and the
parser said so. The ISO form is a quantified path pattern, `-[:E]->{1,3}`. Taken from the repo's own
tests rather than from memory, which is the standing rule for exactly this reason.

**The first two controls both read 0.0 ms and were useless.** `{1,1}` and a plain one-hop count each
take an O(1) shortcut rung rather than `walkLevelCount`, so neither prices the route and neither can
show perturbation. A control that cannot move is not a control. Replaced with a depth-2 arm and a
node scan, which reads 0.30 ms and is measurable.

(The fixture's distinct-endpoint count is asserted — 6000/6000 sampled — and the depth-3 answer,
1,949,750, is not `F^k * N`. A functional fixture would have given a right answer and a meaningless
measurement.)

#### The wide regression sweep — PRE/POST, interleaved, two rounds per arm

`BENCH_ENGINES=ts bun run bench` on both arms, a core rebuild per arm, the dist asserted to BE the
code it claims before each run. 70 rows matched in both arms, min of the two readings per arm.

The six rows that reach the route:

```text
    ratio        PRE       POST   row
   0.037x      196.0        7.2   count var-length 1-3 hops [WALK]              27.2x
   0.039x      262.4       10.2   count var-length 1-2 hops                     25.7x
   0.051x      267.0       13.5   count var-length 1-2 hops + end filter        19.8x
   0.106x      173.7       18.4   count 3-hop quantified [TRAIL, the default]     9.4x
   0.110x      170.1       18.7   count 3-hop quantified MIRROR [TRAIL]           9.1x
   0.265x      240.4       63.6   count 4-hop quantified [TRAIL]                  3.8x
```

⚠️ **AND THE SWEEP HANDED OVER A CONTROL BETTER THAN THE ONE DESIGNED INTO THE PROBE.**
`project var-length 1-3 hops + start filter [ENUMERATES]` reads **0.991x** — it is the one
var-length row in the corpus that ENUMERATES rather than counting, so it never enters the closed-form
route at all. A control that sits inside the same query family, on the same fixture, in the same
process, and does not move is worth more than the node scan chosen deliberately.

**No regression is attributable to the change**, and the distribution is why rather than the absence
of movement:

```text
   median 1.000x   p10 0.843x   p90 1.093x   rows over 1.15x: 5   under 0.87x: 8
```

The largest movers in BOTH directions are codec rows the change cannot reach — `encode pg-json`
1.363x and `encode graphson` 0.843x, `encode pg-text` 0.841x. That is this file's documented null
control behaving as documented: the codec rows carry the same p90 as the query rows. The slowest
query rows named (`project 3 columns` 1.224x, `percentile_cont` 1.281x, `select group + having`
1.182x) are likewise unreachable from `var-length-count.ts`.

⚠️ The two hop rows that could plausibly be argued to be reachable — `count 3-hop + start filter` at
1.074x and `count 4-hop + start filter` at 1.084x — are refuted by their OWN per-rep spread, which is
larger than the effect: `post=[386.4, 477.8]` is 1.24x within one arm. A ratio smaller than its own
arm's spread is not a reading.

#### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. All five package suites isolated: core 453, gql 4268, gremlin 2017,

### Item 1677 — **THE GREMLIN ANALOGUE OF ITEM 1676, PRICED: `slotChainCount`'s adjacency memo is 38.8% of a repeated 3-hop chain count, and the last hop's degree sum another 24.0%.** ~~So 39-63% is addressable~~ ⚠️ **CLOSED BY ITEM 1678 AT 7.5x-10.4x, so this pricing was an UNDER-estimate** — the 16.9% of self-time in `slotChainCount` was mostly cacheable slot assignment, which a frame's self-time does not reveal. The "much smaller target" conclusion here was wrong

Item 1676 cached the CSR behind GQL's bounded var-length count for 3.8x to 27.2x. `slotChainCount`
(`gremlin/src/executor/count-shortcut.ts`) has the same disease by inspection — `slotOf`, `vtx` and a
flat `SlotMemo` allocated per call and discarded on return — so the question is whether the same cure
applies. Found by reading rather than profiling, then priced.

#### The shape of the cost

```text
   arm          ms/call      (100,000 vertices / 400,000 edges, 5 calls per rep, 7 reps, 3 rounds)
   hop2           16.74      the ALGEBRAIC route, no memo at all
   chain3         67.19
   chain4         69.57      +2.4 ms for a WHOLE EXTRA HOP
   chain5         73.13      +3.6
   valuesCtl       2.85      a route with no adjacency
```

⚠️ **THE COST IS NOT THE WALK**, and the hop sweep is what says so: a fourth hop costs 2.4 ms against
a 67 ms base, so ~63 ms is fixed per call. A per-hop instrument would have missed this entirely.

#### The profile

100 calls on one graph at 67.40 ms/call — one graph built once, many calls, so the fixture cannot
dominate (item 1671's mistake):

```text
   28.9%  walkBucket          the memo FILL
   24.0%  degreeOfTypes       the LAST hop's degree sum, not memoized
   16.9%  slotChainCount
    9.9%  expandSlot          the memo fill's per-slot half
    0.4%  memoReserve
```

`walkBucket` + `expandSlot` = **38.8%** is the memo fill, and it is largely FIXED rather than per-hop
because the memo is filled lazily once for the slots the frontier touches and then read. The 24.0% in
`degreeOfTypes` is the final hop's degree sum, which the route deliberately does not memoize — and it
is equally a pure function of topology, so a per-slot degree array is cacheable on the same key.

**39% to 63% addressable, so 1.6x to 2.7x on this shape.** Worth building, and worth stating plainly
that it is not another 27x.

#### What makes it harder than item 1676, and what does not

⚠️ **The memo is LAZY where GQL's CSR is EAGER**, which is why the share is 38.8% and not 86.3%: the
per-call cost is already proportional to what the traversal touched rather than to the graph. "It is
lazy so there is nothing there" was the wrong instinct, but so was expecting GQL's number.

The two admission conditions both HELP, which is the opposite of what was assumed:

```ts
oneWalkThroughout(hops) && seeds.length > Math.max(graph.vertexCount >> 4, 1024);
```

`oneWalkThroughout` means every hop walks the same index with the same labels — the file says "the
memo is a function of exactly that" — so the shape key is `(direction, labels)`, exactly item 1676's.
And the seed set must be WIDE, which dissolves the one real obstacle: `slotOf` is assigned in SEED
order, so the memo's indices are meaningful only relative to that seed set, but if the route only
fires when most of the graph is seeded then numbering all vertices up front by `verticesById` order
costs little more and makes the memo a pure function of `(topologyVersion, direction, labels)`.

⚠️ **A 2-hop count never reaches here and must not be measured as if it did.** It is answered by the
degree inner product, which item 590 measured at 7.73 ms against a 37.65 ms CSR build — 8.0x, and
the comment at `count-shortcut.ts:2291` records "item 589's trick: no help here". The chain walk
starts at THREE hops. `hop2` is in the probe as a control for exactly this reason.

#### ⚠️ The fixture was OUT-REGULAR on the first run, and no endpoint check can catch that

The probe's first fixture gave every vertex exactly FANOUT out-edges. Its distinct-endpoint assertion
passed at 8000/8000 — so not functional — and the walk counts were still **exactly** `N*F^k`
(6,400,000 / 25,600,000 / 102,400,000 at 100,000 x 4), because for an out-REGULAR graph every vertex
has exactly `F^k` k-walks whatever the structure. A count a one-line formula predicts cannot validate
the traversal that produced it.

This is a DIFFERENT defect from the functional-fixture trap this file already documents, and the
existing check is blind to it: one rules out "all edges land on one target", the other "every vertex
has the same out-degree". The degree is now spread over `1..2*FANOUT-1` with mean FANOUT, the
assertion counts distinct out-degrees as well as distinct endpoints, and the answers are no longer
`N*F^k` (6,399,468 against 6,400,000). The timings barely moved — regularity costs the ANSWER its
evidential value, not the clock — which is exactly why it would have survived unnoticed.

### Item 1678 — **THE GREMLIN CHAIN CSR, BUILT: 9.3x and 10.4x on the two bench rows that reach it, 7.51x on the probe.** ⚠️ **Item 1677 priced this at 1.6x-2.7x and that was an UNDER-estimate, for a reason worth keeping: a frame's own self-time cannot be attributed without knowing what is inside it.** Every control flat, 0 of 25 rows over 1.15x, and the bench's `answers` column reads `same` on all of them

Item 1677 profiled `slotChainCount` and found the memo fill at 38.8% and the last hop's degree sum at
24.0%, concluding 39-63% was addressable. The actual change is 7.5x to 10.4x, i.e. ~87-90% removed.
The gap is item 1677's 16.9% of self-time in `slotChainCount` itself, which turned out to be mostly
slot assignment — `slotOf.set` and `vtx.push` per discovered vertex — and so also cacheable. **A
profile names the frames; it does not tell you which parts of a frame's own time are essential.**

#### The change, in two parts

**1. The lazy memo became an EAGER CSR.** The old structure resolved a slot's neighbours on first
touch and numbered vertices in DISCOVERY order, which made the slot indices a function of the SEED
SET — so nothing about it could be shared between traversals. Numbering every vertex up front by
`verticesById` order is what makes the memo a pure function of `(topologyVersion, direction,
labels)`. Eagerness is affordable because the route's own admission rule only fires when
`seeds.length > max(vertexCount >> 4, 1024)`, so the lazy build was already touching most of the
graph.

**2. The last hop's degree became `len[slot]`, which is the 24.0% GONE rather than moved.**
`oneWalkThroughout` requires every hop to walk the same index with the same labels, so the final
hop's `degreeOfTypes(byType, lastHop.labels)` counts exactly the edges this CSR already walked for
that slot. Parallel edges and self-loops are counted identically by both, which is what makes the
substitution exact.

#### The measurement

```text
   arm          PRE      POST    ratio     (probe: 100,000 vertices / 400,000 edges)
   chain3     67.19      8.95    7.51x
   chain4     69.57     11.97    5.81x
   chain5     73.13     15.56    4.70x
   hop2       16.74     16.80    1.00x     the ALGEBRAIC route — control
   valuesCtl   2.85      2.95    1.03x     no adjacency — control
```

`bench:gremlin`, PRE/POST interleaved, two rounds per arm, the dist asserted to BE the code it
claims (200,000 / 1,000,000):

```text
    ratio     PRE ts   POST ts   row
   0.097x      247.5      23.9   V().out().out().out().count()        10.4x
   0.107x      251.7      27.0   V().out()x4.count()                   9.3x
```

and the rows that must not move:

```text
   1.002x       51.6      51.7   V().out().out().count()      the 2-hop ALGEBRAIC route
   0.994x       51.8      51.5   V().repeat(out).times(2).count()
   1.013x       22.7      23.0   V().has().out().count()
   1.000x      884.6     885.0   V().out().out().id()         ENUMERATES, not a count
   0.999x      969.0     968.4   V().out().out().values(age)
```

**median 0.999x, p10 0.874x, p90 1.037x, and ZERO of 25 rows over 1.15x.** The two rows under 0.87x
are the two targets. The worst row is `V().out().has(eq).id()` at 1.065x, which this change cannot
reach; the only other mover, `V().out().values(age)` at 0.874x, has a PRE series of `[195.3, 254.9]`
— a 1.3x spread within one arm, so larger than the effect.

⚠️ **AND THE BENCH'S OWN `answers` COLUMN READS `same` ON ALL 25 ROWS**, which is an independent
byte-identity check against native on top of the seven fuzzers — worth having here specifically
because this change altered the SUMMATION ORDER (slot numbering moved from discovery order to
`verticesById` order) and replaced a degree computation. Counts are integer-valued f64 well below
2^53, so the sums are exact and order-independent; that is the reason it holds, not luck.

#### ⚠️ Two of the invalidation tests were worth nothing, and the mutation pass is what said so

Written, 14 tests passed, and a mutant that dropped the DIRECTION from the cache key survived — as
did one that dropped the LABELS.

**The direction one is a theorem, not a fixture accident.** Reversing every edge is a BIJECTION on
walks, so the number of k-walks in `G` equals the number in `G` reversed, for every k on every graph.
A ring reported equal counts; so did a star. **No fixture can distinguish `out` from `in` by a
whole-graph walk count.** What breaks the symmetry is the SEED SET: with `hub(:Q) -> a(:P) -> b(:P)
-> c(:P)` and seeding only `:P`, forwards there is no 3-walk at all and backwards there is one per
spoke — 0 against 1100.

**The label one was simpler and the same mistake.** The test built an `:E` ring and an `:F` ring BOTH
counting WIDE, so a key that conflated them answered correctly. Two shapes that agree cannot detect a
key that merges them. `:F` is now a single 3-chain against the full `:E` ring, 1 against 1100.

(A third test was named for direction and used `out` on BOTH arms, so it compared a plan with itself.
It passed, which is the worse outcome.)

Final score 7 of 8 caught — never-invalidate 6 failures, direction 1, labels 1, `graph.version` 6,
vertex+edge counts 2, `edgeCount` 2, and the degree substitution reading `off[]` instead of `len[]` 13. **GC8 — seeds SET instead of ACCUMULATED — survives and is equivalent on reachable inputs**: seeds
come from `verticesByLabel` or `verticesById`, both unique, so a duplicate seed cannot be produced
through the public API. The accumulate is kept anyway because it removes a silent dependence on that.

### Item 1679 — **THE LARGEST ROW IN THE GREMLIN CORPUS PRICED AT 31.8x, and ⚠️ THE OBVIOUS HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED: the iterator protocol is only 1.27x of it.** `V().out()x3.values(age)` costs 6813 ms TS against 1134 native; the cost is the ELEMENT DEREFERENCE AND PROPERTY-GETTER CHAIN, not `.next()`. ~~OPEN, not built~~ ⚠️ **CLOSED BY ITEM 1680 AT 14.2x** — below the 31.8x ceiling because the real route carries gates, an `unknown[]` value array and a lazy memo flag, exactly as the three design constraints below predicted

The `bench:gremlin` sweep for item 1678 named this row by elimination: 6813 ms where the next-slowest
is 1140, so it is 6x the rest of the corpus and 6.0x its own native counterpart.

#### The profile

200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, 25,000,000 output rows, 8830 ms/call, one graph built once:

```text
   44.0%  walk              the DFS — `its[d].next()` per edge visited
   27.4%  pick              per-row value extraction
   16.5%  get properties
```

`walk` drives the hop chain with explicit `Set` iterators, so every edge visited allocates a fresh
`{value, done}`. With items 1411 and 1412 having already priced the generator protocol at 1.9-2.2x
and `drain` at 53.8% of `V().out(E)`, the protocol was the obvious suspect.

#### ⚠️ It is not the protocol, and that is the finding

Three arms over the SAME adjacency, each asserted to compute the same checksum so an arm cannot read
fast by doing less (100,000 vertices / 400,000 edges, depth 3, 6,399,468 rows):

```text
   setProtocol          1437.1 ms    1.00x     the current shape
   setForOf             1131.2       1.27x     same Sets, no explicit iterator objects
   csrIndexed             34.1      42.17x     flat Int32Array runs + a per-slot value array
   setProtocolToArray   1599.6       1.00x     the current shape, MATERIALIZING
   csrToArray             50.3      31.83x     the CSR, MATERIALIZING
```

**The iterator protocol is worth 1.27x of a 42x gap.** What the CSR arm actually removes is the chain
of indirections per row: a `Map.get(label)` per vertex per visit, an `Edge` dereference, a `Vertex`
dereference, the `properties` getter, and a string-keyed object lookup — replaced by two
`Int32Array` reads and one array index. That also explains the 16.5% in `get properties`, which this
file's own rule says to treat as attribution until a deletion test says otherwise: it is real, and it
is real because of how OFTEN it is called, not because the getter is slow.

⚠️ **AND THE SINK IS NOT THE BOUND, which had to be measured because it would have capped the whole
lever.** `csrIndexed` sums into a scalar while the real route must materialize every row, so the
first version of this probe was quoting a ceiling that no implementation could reach. Adding the
materializing pair costs the CSR arm 16 ms (34.1 to 50.3) against 160 ms for the protocol arm (1437
to 1600) — so 31.8x survives the sink.

#### Three design constraints for the build

⚠️ **THE PER-SLOT VALUE ARRAY CANNOT BE CACHED ON `topologyVersion`.** The CSR can — item 1678
already caches exactly this structure — but the values are PROPERTIES, and a property write
deliberately does not bump that signal (items 1674/1675), precisely so a `SET` does not discard an
adjacency cache. So the value array has to be rebuilt per call. That is O(V) against 25,000,000 rows,
which is free, and it is the right split rather than a compromise.

⚠️ **`values(k)` RETURNS ANY TYPE**, so the per-slot array is `unknown[]`, not a `Float64Array`.
The probe's `Float64Array` is part of why its ceiling is 42x; expect the real route lower.

⚠️ **PER-HOP GATES AND ROW ORDER both have to be preserved**, and neither is exercised by these
arms. The current walk visits `graph.vertices` then per-vertex bucket order; a CSR built from the
same buckets in the same order reproduces it, but that is a claim to test rather than assume — and
`order-is-unspecified` means row order is not a cross-engine contract, while a test asserting a
specific array is still entitled to its order.

`bun run check` 0 read unpiped. One new probe, no engine change.

### Item 1680 — **THE CORPUS'S LARGEST ROW, TAKEN: `V().out()x3.values(age)` 6712.6 → 471.6 ms, 14.2x, and TypeScript is now FASTER than native on it** (471.6 against 1244.4, a ts/nat ratio of 6.0x becoming 0.38x). ⚠️ **The projection memo is 5.71x of that 14.2x, which had to be measured because it decides a SEMANTIC question** — ~~this route now snapshots where the depth-2 route is live~~ ⚠️ **THE CROSS-ROUTE ASYMMETRY IS CLOSED BY ITEM 1681, which moved depth 2 onto the same slot walk, so the whole family reads one snapshot**

Item 1679 priced this at 31.8x and refuted the iterator protocol as its cause. This builds the
replacement: `stackedWalk` (depth 3 and up) now walks flat slot runs from item 1678's cached CSR
instead of a stack of `Set` iterators.

#### The measurement

`bench:gremlin`, PRE/POST interleaved, two rounds per arm:

```text
    ratio     PRE ts   POST ts   row
   0.070x     6712.6     471.6   V().out()x3.values(age)                     14.2x
```

and everything that must not move did not — the depth-2 values rows keep their literal nesting and
read 1.028x, 1.007x, 1.006x, 1.000x, 0.985x and 0.972x; the count rows read 0.998x, 0.996x, 0.991x.
**median 1.001x, p10 0.967x, p90 1.048x, ZERO of 25 rows over 1.15x**, and the bench's `answers`
column reads `same` on all 25.

(⚠️ `V().out()x4.count()` reads 0.786x, a 1.27x gain on a row this change does not touch. It is a
CROSS-ROW CACHE EFFECT inside the bench process, not a claim: the values walk now calls
`chainCsrFor` too, so a count row that runs after it finds the CSR already built. Real workloads get
this only if they actually interleave the two shapes, so it is not a win to quote.)

#### ⚠️ The win decomposes, and the larger half is the part that changes semantics

```text
   the old iterator stack                  6813.3 ms
   the slot walk, pick called per ROW      2669.8        2.55x
   the slot walk, pick memoized per SLOT    467.8       14.56x
```

At 200,000 vertices and 25,000,000 rows each far vertex is reached ~125 times, so a per-slot memo
turns 25,000,000 projections into at most 200,000. **That is 5.71x of the 14.56x, so the memo could
not simply be dropped** — which matters because it is the part that changes behaviour, and the A/B
above exists precisely to answer "can we avoid the question by not doing it".

⚠️ **THIS ROUTE NOW SNAPSHOTS, WHERE THE DEPTH-2 LITERAL NESTING IS LIVE.** A caller holding the LAZY
iterator and mutating the graph between rows could partly observe that mutation before: the old walk
read `far.adjFrom.get(t)` per vertex and called `pick` per row. Now the CSR fixes topology at first
touch and the memo fixes each projected value at first touch. Both of this route's caches have the
same shape, so the semantics are coherent — the traversal reads one snapshot — but depth 2 and depth
3 would disagree under mid-iteration mutation.

Nothing in the engine does this (`toArray` goes through `drain`, which runs to completion) and all
three `pick` forms are pure functions of the vertex (`far.properties[k]`, `far.id`, `far`), so nothing
is unsound for a non-mutating caller. **Recorded as an OWNER DECISION rather than settled here**, on
the precedent that cross-route behavioural asymmetries are the owner's call — the same shape as the
accepted error-vs-short-circuit divergence in the conjunct-order policy.

#### What the CSR actually removes

Not the `.next()` allocation, which item 1679 measured at 1.27x of a 42x gap. The per-row chain: a
`Map.get(label)` per vertex per visit, an `Edge` dereference, a `Vertex` dereference, the `properties`
getter and a string-keyed object lookup, for two `Int32Array` reads.

⚠️ **ROW ORDER IS A CONTRACT HERE** — Gremlin streams are compared ORDERED by the differential fuzzer
— and it is preserved checkably rather than hopefully: `graph.vertices` IS `verticesById.values()`,
which is the order every CSR numbers its slots in, and within a slot the run holds that vertex's
wanted bucket in iteration order. All 17 new tests compare against the PIPELINE element for element
via the `V(...ids)` trick that forces a decline.

⚠️ **THE GATE MASKS AND THE PROJECTION MEMO ARE BOTH LAZY, FOR CORRECTNESS BEFORE SPEED.** Computing
either over every vertex up front would call `pick` or a predicate on vertices the nested walk never
reaches, so one that throws on an unreached vertex would start throwing. Lazily, each is evaluated
exactly where the old walk evaluated it.

```text
   0.111x     1136.2     126.1   V().out().out().has().values(age)      9.01x

```
