25 rows over 1.15x**, and the `answers` column reads `same` on all 25.

#### ⚠️ The first attempt cost the depth-3 row 1.26x, and the cause was not what it looked like

Routing depth 2 through the EXISTING generic walk gave the four wins above and regressed
`V().out()x3.values(age)` from 468.7 to 591.8 — **1.26x, with both rounds agreeing** (pre 468.7/484.1,
post 615.8/591.8), on a row the change does not touch.

The obvious suspect was item 1680's shape cap: more routes sharing the CSR cache, so a generation
gets cleared and the depth-3 row rebuilds. **Measured and refuted** — `MAX_CHAIN_SHAPES` at 8 and at
32 both left the row at ~618. The cap is not involved.

It is POLYMORPHISM. One function serving depths 2, 3, 4 and 5 has worse inline caches for each than a
function serving one depth. Giving depth 2 its own copy (`pairSlotWalk`) recovers the row to 445.1 —
**better than the 468.7 it read before depth 2 moved at all** — while keeping the depth-2 gains.

⚠️ **AND THE DUPLICATION HAS TO BE LITERAL.** V8's inline caches live on the FUNCTION, not the call
site, so two call sites of one function share them: a factory, a wrapper or a parameterised shim
would all have tested nothing and fixed nothing. Only a second function object with its own body
gives depth 2 its own caches. This is the same reason this file already writes its lazy and eager
halves twice rather than sharing a sink closure, and the same reason a literal depth-2 nesting sat
beside the generic iterator stack before item 1680 — the old split was right for a reason that
survived the implementation changing underneath it.

#### What was retired, and what replaced the threshold

The `walkKindFor(...) === 'stacked'` branch is now always taken, so **130 lines of literal `Set`
nesting are unreachable and deleted**. `walkKindFor` now decides `'pair' | 'stacked'` rather than
`'literal' | 'stacked'`.

⚠️ **ITS TEST IS THE ONLY REASON THE 1.26x WAS NOTICED RATHER THAN SHIPPED**, which is
`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` earning itself again: a route choice is answer-equivalent, so the
2,046 other tests passed on the regressing arm and exactly one failed — the threshold assertion. It
is updated with the numbers above rather than flipped, and it stays a pure function with its own test
for the reason item 1617 recorded. (Inlining `at.length === 2` back into the caller would survive a
mutant and must: it is the same predicate, equivalent in answer and speed. What dies is a changed
THRESHOLD, and only because the function has a test of its own.)

#### ⚠️ This closes item 1680's open decision

Item 1680 recorded an OWNER DECISION: the depth-3 route snapshots (CSR fixes topology at first touch,
memo fixes each projected value at first touch) where the depth-2 literal nesting was live, so the
two depths would disagree under mid-iteration mutation. **Both depths now run the same slot walk, so
the asymmetry is gone** and the whole family reads one snapshot. The remaining semantic question is
no longer cross-route but whole-route, and it is the narrow one: a caller holding the LAZY iterator
and mutating between rows sees the snapshot rather than the mutation. Nothing in the engine does that
(`toArray` goes through `drain`, which runs to completion) and all three `pick` forms are pure
functions of the vertex.

#### What shipped, and why it is sound

The last position was calling `hopSide(graph, idOf[slot], …)` — `edgesFromByLabel.get(id)`, an id
STRING through a Map — once per frontier slot, to re-ask a degree the memo already holds as
`len[slot]`, an `Int32Array` read.

Sound because of what the memo's existing eligibility already guarantees: `uniform` means every leg
shares a direction and none is `both`, and the memo additionally requires every leg to carry the same
types with no gate and no effective label. **So the last leg IS the leg the memo was built from.**
`lastFar` is `undefined` and `last.both` is `false` whenever the memo exists, which is why neither is
consulted on that path. `len[slot] === undefined` means "never walked as a SOURCE" — a slot first
reached in the final pass has no run — so the fallback is the original call.

Item 1683 left two questions: which route answers `count 3-hop`, and whether item 1682's pricing
holds. Both are answered, and both answers correct something.

#### The route, by counting call sites

Each `hopSide(` call site in `shortcuts.ts` was wrapped with a per-site counter:

```text
   count 2-hop              (no hopSide)
   count 3-hop              L3111 = 99,999 = |E|     L3148 = 20,000 = |V|
   count 3-hop + interior   L3111 = 55,278           L3148 = 10,878
   count 4-hop              (no hopSide)
```

So `count 3-hop` is the **three-hop degree product**: for each `b`, `waysToA = hopSide(b.id, …)` once
per VERTEX (L3148), then for each middle edge `b->c`, `dSide(c) = hopSide(c.id, …)` once per EDGE
(L3111). `count = sum over b of indeg(b) * sum over (b->c) of outdeg(c)`, at |V| + |E| string-keyed
`edgesFromByLabel.get(id)` lookups — which is where item 1637's |V| + |E| count came from.

⚠️ **TWO ADJACENT LEVERS ARE ALREADY REFUTED AT THAT EXACT SITE, with numbers in the code.** Item
1335 replaced the id-string lookup with `b`'s own box read and measured **0.99x** (25.44 against
25.68 ms, three processes), noting the lever is worth 1.92x on the UNFILTERED twin and nothing here
because a gate and an inner walk amortize it away. Item 310 memoized the d-side degree per `c` and
rejected it after alternated rounds despite a 1.063x first reading with disjoint ranges. Neither is
the lever below: both keep a hash lookup per unit, where a CSR replaces it with an index.

#### ⚠️ The fixture trap, which cost item 1682 its number

The probe's generator used `to = (i * 7919 + r * 104729 + 13) % N`. That is LINEAR in `i`, hence a
BIJECTION per layer, so **every vertex had in-degree exactly 3** while out-degree varied 1..5.
Verified against brute-force enumeration: the 3-walk count was exactly `N * F^3` — 2,700,000 at
100,000 x 3.

It passes both checks this file already records:

```text
   item 1516/1518  distinct ENDPOINTS      passes — not functional
   item 1677       distinct OUT-DEGREES    passes — five of them
   the count       still exactly N*F^3
```

**Because a 3-walk count collapses on the IN-degree distribution, not the out-degree.** A check on
out-degrees cannot see it, and item 1677's check was written to catch out-regularity specifically.
The generator is now nonlinear in `i` (14-34 distinct in-degrees across the sweep, 0-4.9% of vertices
with no in-edge), the probe asserts the IN-degree spread, and the counts are no longer `N * F^k`. A
quadratic form was tried first and rejected the other way: it left 46% of vertices unreachable.

`csrLevels` counts PATHS, which is O(E * F), where the engine's degree product is O(V + E). So its

```text

      3       119.3        5.4    22.24x
      8       216.3       17.5    12.37x
     15       350.2       46.6     7.52x
```

The same arithmetic as the engine, over flat arrays, holds instead:

```text
   FANOUT    engine   csrDegreeProduct  warm     +build   cold
      3       119.3         0.5        242.94x    25.1   4.76x
      8       216.3         0.7        297.93x    49.4   4.38x
     15       350.2         1.3        278.24x    93.2   3.76x
```

`count = sum over b of indeg[b] * sum over (b->c) of len[nbr[i]]` — one `Int32Array` read where the
engine pays a string-keyed `Map.get`, same complexity, and the ratio holds across a 5x fanout range

#### The change

The route computes `count = sum over b of indeg(b) * sum over (b->c) of outdeg(c)` and pays a
string-keyed `edgesFromByLabel.get(id)` for each degree — one per VERTEX for the `a` side and one per
EDGE for the `d` side. Three `topologyVersion`-keyed CSRs replace both with `off[s + 1] - off[s]`, at
the same complexity. The legs may differ in direction and type, and the CSRs are keyed independently
on `(direction, types)`; they share one slot numbering because every CSR numbers by `verticesById`
order.

```text
   count 3-hop   463.9 -> 5.7 ms   81.4x   (interleaved, both rounds: pre 518.9/463.9, post 7.7/5.7)
```

On the probe's own fixtures the engine reads 3.3 / 3.7 / 4.9 ms against 119.3 / 216.3 / 350.2 at
fanout 3 / 8 / 15 — **36x / 58x / 71x**, rising with fanout because the complexity matches. The
residual gap to the raw arm (6.7x down to 3.9x) is parse, plan, dispatch and the per-vertex
`candidateVertexSource`/`matchesLabel`, which the probe's arm does not pay.

Every other row is unchanged: only this shape takes the arm. median 1.000x across 70 rows.

#### Three structural constraints, each enforced by a limit rather than by judgement

- `buildThreeHopCount` hit **complexity 47 against a cap of 35** with the arm inlined, and 42 with
  only the loop extracted. So the walk and the eligibility predicate are each their own function.
- `shortcuts.ts` then crossed the **3,000-line cap**, which is what moved the new code into
  `three-hop-degree-product.ts`. The limit that fired is the one that says "this belongs elsewhere".
- The cache could not simply be exported from `var-length-count.ts`, because that file imports
  `shortcuts.ts` — importing it back is the CYCLE `import/no-cycle` forbids. Hence `csr-cache.ts`, a
  leaf module both can use.

#### The guards, and why they are narrow

`csrDegreeProductApplies` is a pure function with its own test. ⚠️ Unlike the route thresholds this
file also carries, a wrongly RELAXED clause here returns a WRONG COUNT, so the differential tests
catch it; what they cannot catch is a clause wrongly TIGHTENED, which silently abandons the arm. That
is the direction the unit test covers.

Each clause excludes something a degree array cannot express: an undirected leg is `undirectedSide`'s
two buckets minus the self-loops counted twice (item 1097 fixed a half-answer bug there); a
label-filtered degree counts only edges whose far endpoint carries the label; a gate is a predicate
over a vertex the array has reduced to a number. ⚠️ A VACUOUS label is already `undefined`, so
`(a:Person)` on an all-`Person` graph still qualifies while `(a:Q)` declines — the two are
indistinguishable from the pattern text, and the test pins both.

#### The design, and the hazards

Seeds and the accept set are **per-query** and must stay so: the predicate reads properties, which
deliberately do not bump `topologyVersion` (items 1674/1675), so an accept mask cached on that signal
would go stale with no signal to catch it. That is the same split item 1680 recorded for its
projection memo. The mask is O(V) against a walk over E per pass, so it is free.

⚠️ The real obstacle is `sweepChain`'s slot numbering: `slotOf`/`idOf` are grown LAZILY in seed
discovery order, so its slot indices are a function of the seed set and nothing about them can be
shared between queries. The fix is the one Gremlin's item 1678 used — number every vertex eagerly by
`verticesById` order — and the knock-ons are real: `ways`/`next` are sized by a growing `cap`, and
the `cache`/`cached` arrays are indexed by slot too.

⚠️ Two levers are already REFUTED inside this function and must not be re-attempted: the failed-gate
memo (sign not consistent — 0.87x at a gated last position, 1.27x at an interior) and an indexed loop
in place of `for...of` (did not reproduce; the whole side had moved). Item 1681's 1.26x polymorphism

### Item 1688 — **THE FILTERED THREE-HOP COUNTS, TAKEN: 33.9x and 28.8x, and `count 4-hop` 32.2x**, by making every position's constraint a per-slot mask over `topologyVersion`-keyed CSRs. ⚠️ **A mutant SURVIVED because the code it mutated was UNREACHABLE — a dead branch behind a live exclusion, which reads as a tested path.** ⚠️ **And my own fixture correlated the LABEL with the DEGREE, so two cases counted zero with both routes agreeing**

Item 1687 priced this at 92.27x / 66.87x warm and ~3.6x with the CSR build inside the timed region.
Built, the arm lands between those bounds, interleaved over two order-alternated rounds with one row
per process and each arm asserted in the BUILT dist (min across rounds):

```text
   count 3-hop + start filter    336.0 ->   9.9    33.9x
   count 3-hop + end filter      343.1 ->  11.9    28.8x
   count 4-hop                   261.1 ->   8.1    32.2x
   count 4-hop + start filter    316.0 ->   9.9    31.9x
   count 3-hop + interior filter 176.7 -> 168.6     1.05x   does not reach the arm
   count 3-hop (control)           5.9 ->   5.6     1.05x   item 1685's degree product
   count 2-hop + start filter      129.8 -> 136.9   0.95x   two legs, a different builder
```

The mechanism: `count = sum over starts of surviving walks`, accumulated level by level over flat
`off`/`nbr` arrays, with a `Uint8Array` accept mask per constrained position. That is what lets ONE
arm serve a start, an interior and an end filter — the filter is no longer a position the walk has to
reach, it is a multiply. An unconstrained last position is still answered by a weighted DEGREE sum
and needs no pass, which is why `count 4-hop` (four legs, no filter) gains as much as the filtered
three-hop rows.

A mask is only sound because `inlinePredOf` refuses a correlated predicate, and that was CHECKED
rather than assumed: it returns `null` when an inline property's value has free variables, and for
an inline `WHERE` it refuses every free name but the node's own. So an `InlinePred` is a pure
function of its own vertex. A clause `WHERE` cannot make that claim — `inline-gate.ts` says so
directly — which is why the arm takes its gates from the compiled legs and asks nothing about where
they came from.

#### Two exclusions, one of which a TEST found and reasoning had missed

`both`: an undirected leg walks two adjacency indexes and must count a self-loop ONCE, which item
1097 fixed a half-answer bug over. A single CSR run cannot express it.

⚠️ `seeded`: an index seed makes this arm a REGRESSION, and `seeded-sweep-start.test.ts` is what
said so. `sweepStartSeed` returns a set when an index seek beat the label bucket (item 1330), so the
query is already sub-linear; the arm's masks are O(V) per constrained position, which throws that
away. That test asserts the 5,000-element label bucket is walked ZERO times for a selective
`a.k = 7`, and with the arm taking the query it walked 5,000. **The ANSWER was right — the count
assertion passed — and only the WORK was wrong**, which is precisely the thing a timing-based check
cannot see and that test exists to observe.

#### ⚠️ A MUTANT SURVIVED BECAUSE ITS CODE WAS UNREACHABLE

The arm shipped with a seed-set branch, narrowing `ways` to `sweepStartSeed`'s vertices. A mutation
pass replaced its condition with `false` and SURVIVED — 72 pass, 0 fail. Not a test gap: the
`seeded` exclusion above means `startSource` is ALWAYS undefined here, so the branch could never
execute and no test could ever distinguish it. Dead code behind a live exclusion is worse than no
code, because it reads as a tested path. It is removed, with a note saying it comes back WITH the
test that reaches it if the exclusion is ever lifted.

Thirteen real mutants, all caught, across two valid passes — relaxing either exclusion, tightening
the predicate to never apply, both directions of the last-pass count, dropping the degree weight,
ignoring the start / interior / end mask, flipping the leg direction, ignoring the leg edge types,
starting every slot dead, and dropping either half of the mask. One mutant SURVIVES by design: an
all-ones mask where the code returns `undefined` is ANSWER-EQUIVALENT and costs only an extra pass,
which is exactly why the eligibility predicate carries its own unit test. A wrongly RELAXED clause
is a wrong count and the differentials catch it; a wrongly TIGHTENED one silently abandons the arm
and every answer stays right.

A profile of a process running four query shapes put **39.20% of self time in

This repo already requires one shape per PROCESS for an A/B, because a two-shape process flatters
any change that redistributes call sites (item 762). The same rule governs PROFILING, and it was not
written down: a multi-shape process can hand a hot frame a name belonging to another shape's work,
and the name is the whole output of a profile. **A call counter costs one line and converts an
attribution into a fact.**

The corrected single-shape profile, 12 calls at 200,000 v / 1,000,000 e, with ~19% fixture-build

#### The mechanism, and what the code already said about it

The closure is b-driven: `count = sum over b of ways(b) * sum over (b->c) of outdeg(c)`. Its
`needsC` branch resolves the `c` VERTEX and tests its label and gate **once per middle edge**, with
a comment calling that "the honest cost of this position: the walk meets `c` as an edge endpoint,
not as something it enumerates". That is an accurate description of the walk and not a law about the
question. The arm stops meeting `c` that way: `weight(c) = accept(c) ? outdeg(c) : 0`, memoized per
slot, so the inner loop is one `Float64Array` read per middle edge.

```text
   count 3-hop + interior filter   155.1 ->  10.5    14.8x
   count 3-hop (control)             7.56 ->  7.63    1.01x
   count 3-hop + start filter         9.8 ->   9.8    flat   item 1688's arm
   count 4-hop                        8.5 ->   8.6    flat
   count 2-hop + end filter         132.8 -> 124.1    1.07x  a different builder
```

On the route probe's own fixture (200,000 v / 1,000,000 e, `c.age > 60`) the same change reads
**523.2 -> 70.1 ms (7.5x)** for the clause spelling and **448.1 -> 63.3 (7.1x)** for the inline one.
The residual 70 ms is ~200,000 single gate evaluations, which is the floor for a per-vertex
predicate — so this arm is now gate-bound rather than walk-bound.

#### ⚠️ THE MEMO IS LAZY FOR CORRECTNESS, NOT SPEED

An eager mask over all V vertices was written first and is wrong: **a gate can THROW** — a
string-vs-temporal `<=` does, which is settled policy here — so gating every vertex raises errors on
vertices the walk never visits, for data the walk accepts today. Resolving on first arrival keeps the
EVALUATED SET exactly the walk's: every `c` reached by a middle edge and no other. What changes is
only how OFTEN each is evaluated, which is the whole lever. (`state` is a separate byte array
because a weight of zero — a rejected `c`, or an accepted one with no out-edges — must not read as
"not yet asked".)

#### Three of five exclusions lift, and the split is not cosmetic

A constraint on `b` or `c` says which VERTICES are accepted; a label at `a` or `d` says which edges
a DEGREE may count. The first is a mask over the shared slot numbering at O(V) once; the second
needs a label-filtered degree, a different array this arm does not have. So `cEff`, `cGate` and
`bGate` lift, while `aEff`, `dEff` and every undirected leg still decline. `bGate` gets no mask at
all: the loop already visits each `b` once, so a mask would add a pass over V to save nothing.

A LITERAL SIBLING of the unfiltered arm rather than a flag on it, for item 1681's 1.26x: V8's inline
caches live on the FUNCTION, so a branch inside the unfiltered arm would hand `count 3-hop` — 5.7 ms
after item 1685 — a second shape to dispatch over, and a factory would not help because one closure
body still shares the caches.

#### ⚠️ WHAT THE ROUTE COUNTER CORRECTED, AND WHY READING THE CODE WAS NOT ENOUGH

Item 1689 found a four-shape PROFILE attributing 39.2% to a function the row never enters. This item
is the same lesson at the level of a function's doc comment. A counter at each candidate builder's
entry AND at its successful return — an entry counter cannot tell "answered" from "declined" — said:

```text
   row                  answered by
   bare 2-hop           buildTwoHopCount
   2-hop start filter   buildFilteredTwoHopCount
   2-hop mid filter     buildTwoHopCount
   2-hop END filter     buildFilteredTwoHopCount      <- not the general pipeline
   2-hop end inline     buildFilteredTwoHopCount
```

1. **The END-filtered row reaches the START-filtered builder**, because the pattern is ORIENTED so
   the predicate-carrying node becomes the start. `buildTwoHopCount`'s comment says a constraint on
   the end "has no once-per-element place to go", which is true of that builder and not of the
   query; I had read it as "the end filter falls to the row pipeline".
2. **`longChainCount` is never entered for two legs**, so item 1688's arm could not be reached by
   relaxing a leg count — which was my first plan, and is the shape of mistake item 1683 made by
   relaxing a gate on an assumption.
3. **`HopPred` can carry `farVar` and `relVar`.** The walk binds only `startVar`, so in practice the
   caller passes a start-only predicate — but the eligibility clause REFUSES the others rather than
   trusting that, because such a predicate has no per-vertex form at all.

#### The mechanism

`count = sum over b of (accepted a's reaching b) * outdeg(b)`: one pass over the first leg to
accumulate arrivals, then a weighted DEGREE SUM for the second, with no second pass because nothing
constrains the end (`cEff` declines). The walk's own per-edge cost was already O(1) — `side` with no
far label is `bucketSize`, and items 1416/1637 settled that there is no repeated-lookup lever there
— but O(1) through a `Map.get` plus an `edgesOfTypes` generator frame is not O(1) through an
`Int32Array`.

⚠️ **THE ACCEPT TEST ORDER IS THE WALK'S, AND THAT IS CORRECTNESS, NOT STYLE.** The walk
enumerates the label bucket and only then applies the predicates. A predicate can THROW (a
string-vs-temporal `<=` does, settled policy here), so testing the LABEL first keeps the evaluated
set exactly the walk's: a vertex outside the bucket never reaches the predicate, as it never does
today. Item 1689 learned this with an eager mask and fixed it with a lazy one; here the ordering is
enough.

Exclusions: both `both` legs (an undirected leg must yield a self-loop ONCE — items 1092/1093 — and
one CSR run cannot express it), an END label (it filters which edges the final DEGREE may count,
where the CSR counts them all: the boundary item 1689 drew), an index SEED (`hopSeek` makes the
query sub-linear and an O(V) mask throws that away — item 1688 learned this from a test rather than
from reasoning), and a predicate that can read the far node or the edge. A MIDDLE label is on the
other side of that boundary and is taken: the middle is a slot.

#### ⚠️ AN ASSERT THAT PREDICTED A COUNT DISCARDED TWO WRITES WHILE REPORTING SUCCESS

The route counters first read `{}` for every row — the builders run at PLAN time and the plan is
cached, so resetting before the warm run measured the wrong run. Then they read `{}` again, and the
reason is worse: a python patch script replaced two anchors, printed "instrumented" for each, and
then raised on a THIRD assert — before the single write at the end. The file was unchanged while the
log said otherwise. **The dist-marker check is what surfaced it** (`__r.filteredTwoHop` present 0
times in `dist/esm/index.mjs` while two other counters were present 2 times each).

And the assert itself was wrong twice in a row, the same way: each counter bump NAMES its counter
twice, so the post-count is 2 and I predicted 1. The same slip appeared once more in this item's
mutation driver, where the mutated text `if (w !== 0) {` also matches a branch already in the file.
**So: count the occurrences in the mutated file; do not predict them.** A patch script that writes
nothing looks exactly like one that worked.

### Item 1691 — **THE WIDEST GREMLIN RATIO PRICED AT 33-42x, AND THE HEADING THAT CALLED IT "SMALL HEADROOM" WAS WRONG ON BOTH HALVES.** ⚠️ **My own probe then produced a 91x that does not exist — a mask hoisted OUT of the timed region — and a SEVEN-ARM process whose same arm read 31.9, 44.2 and 65.6 ms.** ~~Not built; the route and the shippable form are identified~~ ⚠️ **BUILT AT ITEM 1692 at 38.08x and 29.91x — and the form it identified as shippable was WRONG: the mark pass it prescribed was justified by GQL's throw rule, which Gremlin does not share.**

`V().out().has(age, eq(30)).id()` is the widest TS-vs-native ratio of any yielding row in
`bun run bench:gremlin`: TS 159.7 ms against native 2.69. Item 1631's heading recorded it as OPEN but
with "small" TS-side headroom, on two grounds that are both wrong.

**"Native seeks; TS scans every edge."** There is no `createIndex` anywhere in `bench-gremlin.ts`, so
native has no index to seek. What native has is columnar properties, which let it test the predicate
once per VERTEX and then test a bit per edge. The ratio is not a seek-versus-scan difference.

**"1.51x its hand floor."** That floor was a hand arm that still resolves the far VERTEX OBJECT and
reads `.properties` per edge — this item reproduced it at 1.31-1.52x, which is what validates the
instrument. A floor that keeps the engine's own data access is a floor on TUNING, not on the
question.

One arm per process, 14 reps, median of the warm ones:

```text
   arm                    median ms   vs engine   what it changes
   engine                   143.5       1.00x
   perEdge                  109.4       1.31x     the audit's hand floor
   perVertex                 76.4       1.88x     predicate once per vertex, Map lookup per edge
   perEdgeCsr                67.7       2.12x     flat CSR, predicate still per edge
   lazyMaskCsr               21.7       6.47x     CSR + resolve on FIRST ARRIVAL, in the hot loop
   markThenMask               3.4      ~42x       CSR + mark / resolve / emit  <- the shippable form
   perVertexCsrPlusMask       2.9      ~46x       CSR + EAGER mask over all V
```

The engine arm itself spans 112.7-143.5 across processes, so the headline is **33-42x**.

#### The form that ships, and why it is not the obvious one

An EAGER mask over all V is fastest and is wrong for the reason item 1689 recorded: a predicate can
THROW (a string-vs-temporal `<=` does, settled policy here), so gating every vertex raises errors on
vertices the walk never reaches. Resolving on FIRST ARRIVAL keeps the evaluated set exactly the
walk's — and measured **21.7 against the eager form's 2.9**, because it puts a branch and a property
read inside a 1,000,000-iteration loop.

Three passes fix both: mark which slots an edge reaches (1M typed-array reads), resolve the predicate
for MARKED slots only (the walk's own set), then emit. **3.4 ms**, within 17% of the eager form, with
no change to which vertices are tested. Two passes over `nbr` instead of one is the trade, and array
reads are cheap where the property read is not.

The infrastructure exists: `chainCsrFor` (item 1678) is `topologyVersion`-keyed, numbers slots by
`graph.verticesById` order, and already backs `hop-chain-values.ts`'s two-hop walks. **Order is
preserved by construction**, which this route requires absolutely — Gremlin streams are compared
ORDERED by the differential fuzzer (unlike GQL rows), and `start-filtered-hop-values.ts` says so in
terms: "any cleverer structure — walking the edge index once, hoisting the far side — is a
cross-engine failure and not an optimization". A CSR built per vertex in bucket order, walked in slot
order, emits the identical sequence.

**A 91x that does not exist.** The eager arm reused a mask built once at module scope, so it excluded
all 200,000 property reads and reported 80-105x. Building the mask inside the timed region puts it at
2.9. Same class as timing a warm cache against a cold one, and it nominated a size of win that was
never available.

**A seven-arm process.** The same arm read 31.9, 44.2 and 65.6 ms across three runs and the engine arm
108.1-145.4 — a 2x spread on identical code, wider than several differences being compared.
`start-filtered-hop-values.ts` records exactly this about the PREVIOUS probe for this shape ("`pick`
is called through a closure VARIABLE … several arms in one process make that call site
polymorphic"), and item 1689 hit the same thing when a four-shape PROFILE named a function the row
never enters. The probe now takes `ARM=<name>` and the driver runs each in its own process.

single-gate LOOP measured WORSE there (719.7 -> 731, and `both` 458 -> 507), and items 1441/1466

QUERY is the sanctioned place to change: all three loop bodies stay byte for byte the code they

an eager-only arm would break `limit(1)`, which is the 473x/3680x failure the eager-tail-cache entry

### Item 1692 — **THE WIDEST GREMLIN ROW, TAKEN: 38.08x and 29.91x**, by resolving the far filter once per vertex into a mask and emitting from flat slot runs. ⚠️ **ITEM 1691 PRESCRIBED A THREE-PASS FORM TO AVOID A THROW — AND GREMLIN'S PREDICATES DO NOT THROW: I imported the OTHER ENGINE's rule.** ⚠️ **And a mutant proved the eligibility predicate could not decline, because its call site passed two literal constants**

Item 1691 priced this at 33-42x and corrected both halves of the heading that called its headroom
small. Built, interleaved over three order-alternated rounds, one SHAPE per process, 14 reps, median
of the warm ones, min across rounds, each arm asserted in the BUILT bundle:

```text
   shape                                      PRE      POST    ratio
   target        V().out(E).has(k,eq).id()   120.34     3.16   38.08x
   targetValues  … .values(n)                113.66     3.80   29.91x
   limited       … .id().limit(50)             0.26     0.26    1.00x   early exit intact
   noFilter      V().out(E).values(n)        122.66   121.29    1.01x   declines
   bothHop       V().both(E).has(k,eq).id()  335.19   324.29    1.03x   declines
   startOnly     V().hasLabel(A).out(E)…      61.34    63.44    0.97x   declines
```

Every declining shape is within 3%, which is the attribution this win needed, and `limited` is
EXACTLY flat — 0.26 ms for 50 rows against the arm's 3.16 for all 11,118, so the lazy path still
short-circuits.

#### ⚠️ THE THREE-PASS FORM ITEM 1691 PRESCRIBED WAS THE OTHER ENGINE'S RULE

Item 1691 specified mark / resolve / emit: mark which slots an edge reaches, resolve the predicate
for marked slots ONLY, then emit — so that the evaluated set stays exactly the walk's, because "a
predicate can THROW (a string-vs-temporal `<=` does, which is settled policy here)".

**That policy is GQL's, and Gremlin's is the opposite.** `predicates.ts` states it: for ordering
predicates "a cross-type pair is `NaN`, so every comparison against it is false and the predicate
FILTERS the value out rather than throwing — `g.V().has('name', gte(0))` returns nothing, exactly as
TinkerPop (verified on createModern())". And this arm runs only when `specializePredicate` returned a
closure, every branch of which is a total `typeof v === … && …` test. So the predicate is TOTAL on
this route and gating a vertex the walk never reaches is UNOBSERVABLE.

Which makes the mark pass pure cost — it measured **3.4 ms against the eager form's 2.9** — and a
mutation replacing it with the eager form SURVIVED, correctly, because the two are answer-equivalent.
The shipped arm is two passes.

`CLAUDE.md` warns against reasoning about GQL from Cypher. The same applies between lenke's own two
engines, whose comparison policies differ ON PURPOSE (`cross-type-comparison-no-error` records the
GQL side as settled and not to be re-raised). A constraint carried across them looks like diligence
and buys a 1.17x regression.

#### ⚠️ A PREDICATE THAT COULD NOT DECLINE, AND THE MUTANT THAT FOUND IT

The arm shipped with `farMaskDrainApplies({ both, fastKey })` and its own unit test. A mutant making
it ALWAYS APPLY survived — because the call site passed two literal constants: `both: false` (this
arm lives in the `out`/`in` branch, which the `both` hop returns before reaching) and `fastKey: true`
(implied by the mask state existing at all). **A predicate that cannot decline is decoration, and a
unit test for it passes vacuously while reading like coverage.** Same shape as the dead seed branch
item 1688 removed after a mutant survived it; both were found the same way, and neither by reading.

The predicate is gone, the guard is the real condition, and the two exclusions are recorded where
they actually happen.

#### Why it serves `drain` only

A pass over V+E before the first row would destroy early exit — the 473x/3680x failure the
eager-tail-cache entry records for both engines. `drain` is already eager and is read only by
`toArray` when `rest` is empty (item 1412), so a plan carrying `limit` puts a step in `rest`, takes
the lazy iterator, and never reaches the arm. Both lazy loop bodies stay byte for byte the code they
were, which `start-filtered-hop-values.ts` requires: a dedicated single-gate LOOP measured WORSE
there (719.7 -> 731, `both` 458 -> 507) and items 1441/1466 measured an edit to a hot values walk at
up to 16% on unrelated rows.

ORDER is preserved by construction, which this route requires absolutely: Gremlin streams are
compared ORDERED by the differential fuzzer (unlike GQL rows), and `chainCsrFor` numbers slots by
`graph.verticesById` order and fills each run from that vertex's own bucket in set order. The tests
compare SEQUENCES, with a guard that the output is not merely sorted — a multiset comparison would
pass for an arm that emits the right rows in the wrong order, which is the cross-engine failure
`start-filtered-hop-values.ts` warns a "cleverer structure" would cause.

A LEAF MODULE, because importing `survives`/`Gate` from the file that imports it is a cycle and
`import/no-cycle` is an error here — the same shape `csr-cache.ts` has on the GQL side. The gate loop
is four lines; a shared four-line loop is not worth a cycle.

fuzzers 20 pass, 0 fail. **Eight mutants, all CAUGHT** — the accept test inverted, the emit pass
ignoring the mask, the start-filter survival ignored in either pass, the drop sentinel ignored, the

### Item 1694 — ⚠️ **THE GREMLIN BENCH'S FIXTURE IS CACHE-HOSTILE, AND IT IS WORTH 2.26x ON THE SAME GRAPH.** Edge INSERTION ORDER alone: 61.59 ms grouped against 139.18 scattered, identical vertices, edges and per-vertex bucket order. ⚠️ **This WITHDRAWS item 1693's refutation — the lever it priced at 1.58x is 6.00x on the bench's layout** — and it means every adjacency-walking TS row in that bench is inflated relative to a grouped build, while standalone probes that group UNDERSTATE it

Item 1693 flagged that `V().out().id()` reads **207.6 ms in `bench:gremlin` and 61.06 in a
standalone probe** — the same traversal, 3.4x apart — and said it mattered because the bench's
ranking nominates every target. It does, and the cause is worse than a quirk.

#### The decomposition

```text
   61.06 ms   standalone probe: own fixture, one shape per process
   61.59      bench's EDGE SET, inserted GROUPED BY SOURCE, one shape per process
  139.18      bench's fixture as built (scattered), one shape per process
  207.6       bench's fixture, 31 shapes in one process          <- as the bench reports it
```

So the 3.4x is **2.26x of fixture locality and 1.39x of multi-shape polymorphism**, and the two are
independent.

The loader and the edge properties were ruled out one at a time, which is why the locality claim is
attributable rather than inferred: the bench's own NDJSON deserialization reads 147.6, the same
values built through `addVertex`/`addEdge` read 140.7, and the same NDJSON with the edge property
`w` removed reads 144.9 — all within noise of each other. The only remaining difference was
INSERTION ORDER: the bench's `from = (k * 7919) % N` scatters each vertex's five edges ~200,000
insertions apart, so its `Edge` objects land far apart in allocation order and walking one vertex's
adjacency chases pointers across the heap. Re-inserting the identical edge set grouped by source —
same graph, same bucket order, same emitted sequence, only the layout changed — gives **61.59**.

#### ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES TO ITEM 1693, AND WHY IT IS THE LESSON

Item 1693 refuted a CSR drain for the unfiltered hop at **1.58x warm and 0.76x cold**, measured on
the standalone probe's grouped fixture. On the bench's scattered layout, the same arms:

```text
   engine id            139.18 ms    1.00x
   handGen               95.78       1.45x
   handCsr               23.21       6.00x   ⚠️ against 1.58x on the grouped fixture
   handCsrPlusBuild     167.00       0.83x   the first query only; the CSR is cached
```

**A grouped-insertion fixture is the best case for a pointer-chasing walk and therefore the worst
case for the lever that replaces it.** CLAUDE.md's rule is "match the fixture to the claim", and the
claim here was about a DATA LAYOUT — so the one fixture property that could not be allowed to vary
was the one I varied. The refutation understated the win by ~4x and would have steered the next
reader away from it; its heading is struck and the note on `hopValuesShortcut` is corrected in the
same commit.

The cold figure still holds in shape: the build costs more than one query saves (167.00 against
139.18, a 1.20x regression on the FIRST query), and it is slower to build here than on the grouped
fixture (~144 ms against ~89) for the same pointer-chasing reason. The CSR is keyed on
`topologyVersion`, so a write-heavy workload pays that build repeatedly — which is the real
remaining question for the build, not the warm number. ⚠️ **ANSWERED AT ITEM 1695, and the answer is
reassuring for the shipped arms but not automatic: the arm is safe under writes exactly when the WALK
it replaces costs more than the REBUILD. The far-filtered hop passes (192 against 182) and is a win
even at one write per read; the UNFILTERED hop does not (139 against 182).**

#### What to do with the bench

Nothing, yet — and deliberately. A scattered insertion order is not unrealistic (a real graph is
rarely built source-by-source), so the bench is not WRONG; it measures a harder case than a grouped
probe does. Two consequences to carry instead:

- **A standalone probe that groups its inserts understates the bench's adjacency rows by ~2.3x.**
  Every probe in this corpus that builds a graph with a `for (i) { for (r) { addEdge } }` loop is
  grouped. That is most of them, including the ones used in items 1691-1693.
- **The bench's TS/native ratios partly reflect layout, not just engine work.** Native stores
  adjacency flat, so it is immune to the insertion order that costs TS 2.26x here. A ratio on an
  adjacency-walking row is therefore an upper bound on the engine-work gap.

### Item 1695 — **THE CSR CACHE'S INVALIDATION, MEASURED: item 1692's shipped arm is 56.7x warm and STILL 1.19x BETTER at one topology write before EVERY read.** ⚠️ **Six arms shipped on this cache and every one of their A/Bs measured consecutive reads with no writes — so this was unmeasured until now.** And the criterion it yields is shape-specific: **safe iff the walk costs more than the rebuild**, which the unfiltered hop FAILS

Items 1676, 1685, 1688, 1689, 1690 and 1692 all ship arms over the `topologyVersion`-keyed CSR, and
the cache is dropped WHOLE on any topology write (`csrFor` and `chainCsrFor` both discard the
generation when the counter moves). Every one of those A/Bs timed 14 consecutive reads with no write
in between, so the serving case — write, read, write, read — had never been measured. Item 1694
named it "the real remaining question".

Item 1692's arm, on a SCATTERED fixture (item 1694's lesson: a grouped build understates both the
walk and the rebuild), per read:

```text
   write rate              PRE (no arm)    POST (arm)    ratio
   warm, no writes             192.37          3.39      56.7x
   1 write per 20 reads             —         14.35
   1 write per 10 reads             —         21.37
   1 write per read            221.62        185.77       1.19x
```

**The arm is never a regression on this shape**, because the rebuild (~182 ms on 1,000,000 scattered
edges) is still cheaper than the walk it replaces (~192 ms). The walk is expensive enough that a
full CSR rebuild per query beats it.

#### ⚠️ THE CRITERION, AND THE SHAPE THAT FAILS IT

A CSR arm is safe under arbitrary writes **iff the walk it replaces costs more than the rebuild**.
That is not a property of the cache; it is a property of the shape:

- **far-filtered hop** — walk 192.37, rebuild ~182. Passes. 56.7x warm, 1.19x at the worst write
  rate, and monotone in between.
- **unfiltered hop** (items 1693/1694's target) — walk 139.18, rebuild ~182. **FAILS.** Warm it is
  6.00x; at one write per read it would be a ~1.2x regression. So that build needs either a write-rate
  argument or an incremental update, and "item 1692 shipped it" is not that argument.

The GQL arms (1685, 1688, 1689, 1690) replace walks measured at 120-460 ms against the same rebuild
order, so they sit on the safe side of the line — but each is a separate instance of the criterion,
not an inheritance, and none has been measured under writes.

#### Why the rebuild is ~182 ms here and ~89 elsewhere

The same reason item 1694 found for the walk: building the CSR iterates every vertex's adjacency, so
on a scattered insertion order it chases the same pointers the walk does. A grouped fixture builds it
in ~89 ms. Both figures are real; the scattered one is what a bench-like graph pays.

```text
   count 3-hop (1685)           438.08        9.12   48.0x    427.71     354.84   1.21x  ✓
   + start filter (1688)        261.64        9.01   29.0x    275.75     160.19   1.72x  ✓
   + interior filter (1689)     549.76       89.82    6.1x    545.74     415.10   1.31x  ✓
   count 2-hop + start (1690)   101.08       10.75    9.4x    102.72     157.36   0.65x  ✗
```

`wr1` is one `addEdge` before EVERY read — the worst case, since one topology write drops the whole
cached generation. The PRE walks are flat across write rates, as they must be: they cache nothing.

#### ⚠️ THE ONE THAT FAILS, AND WHAT IT COSTS

`count 2-hop + start filter` is **9.4x faster warm and 1.53x SLOWER when a write precedes every
read** (157.36 against the walk's 102.72). The criterion predicts it exactly: the two-hop walk is
101 ms and its rebuild is ~147, so there is nothing for the rebuild to amortize against.

This is a real property of shipped code, recorded rather than fixed, because the fix is a policy
trade and not mine to make silently: the alternatives are to keep 9.4x on read-mostly traffic with a
1.53x pathological worst case, or to gate the arm on a cache HIT — which would mean the first query
after every write takes the walk, and the CSR would then never be built at all unless something else
builds it. A per-shape "reads since the last write" counter would decide it properly and is more
state than this question has earned. **The 13.4x and 19.5x in item 1690's heading are correct for a
read-mostly workload and that heading now says so.**

#### The rebuild scales with DISTINCT CSR SHAPES, not with legs

`count 3-hop` pays ~345 ms of rebuild and `count 2-hop` ~147, and the ratio is not 3:2. The key in
`csrFor` is `(direction, types)`, so legs sharing a shape share one build:

- `(a)-[:K]->(b)-[:K]->(c)-[:K]->(d)` needs `aSide = csrFor(inward=true)` and
  `mid = dSide = csrFor(inward=false)` — **two** distinct shapes, ~2 x 172 ms.
- `(a)-[:K]->(b)-[:K]->(c)` needs `csrFor(inward=false)` for both legs — **one**, ~147 ms.

So a query whose legs alternate direction pays more rebuild than one that does not, independently of
its depth. Worth knowing before adding an arm to a mixed-direction shape.

of the six: 220x warm and still 23.1x at one write per read.** Its fixture shape (a quantified path)

### Item 1698 — **THE INTERIOR-FILTER ARM'S GATE IS 83% OF THE ROW (an ablation: 89.82 -> 14.77 ms), AND THE DISPATCH IS ONLY 1.11x OF IT.** ⚠️ **A clause `WHERE` and an inline `WHERE` take DIFFERENT gate routes — confirmed by a counter, `bindVar: 'c'` refuses `specializedConjunct` — and that route difference is worth 1.11x, not the 6.08x the ablation promised.** So the prize is the per-vertex PROPERTY READ, which is a TS data-layout question, not a dispatch one

On a scattered fixture (item 1694), `count 3-hop + interior filter` is the slowest of the GQL CSR
arms by an order of magnitude: 89.82 ms against `count 3-hop`'s 9.12 and `+ start filter`'s 9.01
(item 1696's table). This item asks why and answers it with two measurements that disagree about the
cause until both are in.

**The ablation sizes the prize.** Replacing the arm's `cGate(...)` with `true` — a deliberate wrong
answer, item 1600's method, and the count changes to 25,000,000 to prove it — takes the row from
**89.82 to 14.77 ms**. So the gate is 83% of the arm and up to 6.08x is available. At ~200,000
evaluations that is **~375 ns per gate call**, where item 1600 priced a specialized gate at ~31 ns.

**The route is genuinely split by spelling, and a counter proves it.** Instrumenting
`composeInlineGate`'s `specializedConjunct` call for the three spellings of the same question:

```text
   WHERE c.age > 60        fast 0  slow 1   bindVar "c"    <- the general `inlineHolds` path
   (c WHERE c.age > 60)    fast 1  slow 0                  <- specialized
   (c {age: 61})           fast 1  slow 0                  <- specialized
```

The clause form must BIND `c`, and `specializedConjunct` refuses a conjunct with a `bindVar` for a
documented correctness reason ("`inlineHolds` WRITES the binding for a correlated conjunct before
testing it, and the specialized closure never writes one"). That is this repo's opening defect class
— equivalent spellings on different routes — so it looked like the whole 6.08x.

**It is not. The two spellings are 1.11x apart:**

```text
   h3interior        (clause WHERE)   69.73 ms
   h3interiorInline  (inline WHERE)   62.97       1.11x
   h3interiorProp    (inline prop)    68.65       (a different count, same cost)
```

⚠️ **So the dispatch is ~7 ms of the gate's ~75.** The remaining ~68 is the per-vertex work the
ablation also removed: reading `c.properties[key]` for every reached slot. On a scattered adjacency
those vertex objects are spread across the heap, so each read is a cache miss — the same mechanism
item 1694 measured at 2.26x for the walk itself.

#### What that leaves

- **The specialization lever is REFUTED for this row at 1.11x.** Extending
  `specializedConjunct` to the `bindVar !== undefined` case (by writing the binding inside the
  specialized closure) would be a general improvement across its thirteen call sites, and it is
  worth ~7 ms here, not 75. Not re-attempted on this row's strength.
- ~~**The real prize is a property READ, which TS stores per-vertex as an object.** … A columnar
  property store for the TS core is an architecture change, not an arm~~ ⚠️ **TOO PESSIMISTIC, and item 1699 corrected it one item later: the read's ORDER was an arm.** Resolving the gate in
  SLOT order instead of arrival order took the row 69.73 -> 18.51 (3.77x) with no change to
  storage. A columnar store would close the rest; the scattered-access half did not need it.
- The row's own variance is wide on this fixture: the same build read 89.82 and 69.73 across
  processes (1.29x), so neither figure should be quoted without the other.

### Item 1699 — **THE INTERIOR-FILTER ROW, TAKEN: 69.73 -> 18.51 ms (3.77x)**, by resolving the gate in SLOT order instead of arrival order — same reads, same set, sequential instead of scattered. ⚠️ **AND THE "A GATE CAN THROW" RULE I USED TO JUSTIFY THE LAZY FORM AT ITEM 1689, REPEATED AT 1692, AND REPEATED AGAIN IN THIS ITEM'S FIRST DRAFT IS WRONG ON THIS PATH: eighteen cross-type comparisons were tried and every one returns a clean no-match**

Item 1698 sized the gate at 83% of this row and found the dispatch worth only 1.11x of it, then
concluded the remainder was a property read and "an architecture change, not an arm". That was too
pessimistic by a factor of 3.77.

The arm already read each reached vertex's property exactly ONCE — but in ARRIVAL order, which is
whatever order `mid.nbr` happens to hold. Resolving in SLOT order instead walks `order[]` in
`verticesById` order, which is the order those objects were ALLOCATED in. Same reads, same evaluated
set, sequential instead of scattered:

```text
   h3interior        (clause WHERE)   69.73 -> 18.51    3.77x
   h3interiorInline  (inline WHERE)   62.97 -> 16.84    3.74x
   h3  (control, the unfiltered arm)   9.12 ->  7.19    flat/better
```

This is item 1691's mark / resolve / emit shape, which that item measured on the Gremlin side at
**3.4 ms against the lazy form's 21.7** — the mechanism transferred, and the ablated floor of 14.77
is now 1.25x away.

#### ⚠️ THE THROW RULE WAS NEVER TESTED, AND IT IS WRONG HERE

Item 1689 justified the lazy memo with "a gate can THROW — a string-vs-temporal `<=` does, which is
settled policy here". Item 1692 cited the same rule to explain why Gremlin DOESN'T need it. This
item's first draft repeated it again. A mutation making the resolve pass eager then SURVIVED the
whole suite, which named the claim as untested — so it was tested: eighteen combinations, the six
ordering operators against string-vs-number, string-vs-date and number-vs-date.

**Every one returns a clean no-match.** `<>` correctly returns 1. Nothing throws. The policy
`cross-type-comparison-no-error` records is real but lives in ORDER BY / min / max, where
`compareValues` throws — not on the predicate path these arms use. Item 1692's reasoning happened to
reach the right conclusion for Gremlin by the wrong route: it contrasted the two engines' policies
when in fact neither throws here.

**So a test cannot catch that mutant, and one should not be written to pretend otherwise.** The
earlier draft of this item added a "lonely vertex with an incomparable value" test which passed
whether the pass was lazy or eager — a test with no teeth that read like coverage. It is gone.

#### What the mark pass is actually for

A WORK BOUND, not correctness. Measured both ways on this dense fixture, where nearly every slot is
reached, the EAGER form is **1.08x faster** (17.65 against 19.30) — so on this row the mark pass
costs a little. It ships anyway because the two have different WORST cases: the mark pass's downside
is bounded at ~1.08x, while an eager resolve gates all |V| vertices even for a query whose middle is
selective enough to touch a handful. **A bounded loss is preferred to an unbounded one**, and that is
the justification now written on the function — replacing the one that was never true.

### Item 1700 — ⚠️ **A 1411x EQUIVALENT-SPELLING GAP, FOUND: a clause `WHERE b.age = 7 AND c.age > 60` costs 1411.1 ms where the same question spelled inline costs 1.0 — same count, 9,275.** The machinery to answer it already exists and only the CLAUSE READER refuses. ~~Diagnosed and priced; the fix is its own item~~ ⚠️ **FIXED AT ITEM 1701: 1411.1 -> 2.0 ms, and the two spellings now converge.**

Item 1699 left this as "slow and unexplained" after a 200,000-vertex run did not finish in 600
seconds. At 20,000 vertices / 100,000 edges, warm, median of 5:

```text
   WHERE b.age = 7                           1.0 ms   count    27,875
   WHERE c.age > 60                          2.2      count   804,750
   WHERE b.age = 7 AND c.age > 60         1411.1      count     9,275   <- the gap
   (b {age: 7}) + (c WHERE c.age > 60)       1.0      count     9,275   <- same answer
   WHERE a.age = 7 AND c.age > 60            2.2      count     9,290
   WHERE b.age = 7 AND d.age > 60            1.3      count     9,290
```

**This is the failure family the repo's spelling discipline exists for**, in its textbook form: "the
planner recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned for another that meant exactly the same
thing … each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct answer, so no correctness test could catch
it". This one is 1411x, and the two spellings' counts are asserted equal in the probe so the
comparison cannot be of two different questions.

#### Only the b+c pair collapses, and a route counter says why

```text
   b only      neither counter      -> the gated degree product (item 1689)
   b AND c     threeSegDecline      -> declines, and NO sweep route exists at 3 segments
   a AND c     longChain            -> the sweep
   b AND d     longChain            -> the sweep
```

`interiorPredOf`'s `readsOnly(name)` requires EVERY free variable of the clause to be that one name:

```ts
const onB = readsOnly(bName);

if (free.size === 0 || !(onB || readsOnly(cName))) {
  return null;
}
```

For `b.age = 7 AND c.age > 60` the free set is `{b, c}`, so both tests fail and it returns `null`.
`patternCountOf` then declines, and the three-segment path has no second route — the sweep is
entered at `>= 4` segments, or through `endGatedChainCount` when the END is constrained, which is
exactly why `a AND c` and `b AND d` are fast and `b AND c` is not. The query falls to the general row
pipeline.

#### ⚠️ THE MACHINERY TO ANSWER IT IS ALREADY THERE

`threeSegmentCount` carries `interior: { b: readonly InlinePred[]; c: readonly InlinePred[] }` — two
independent gate LISTS — and the closure composes `bGate` and `cGate` from them. The INLINE spelling
fills both, which is why it answers in 1.0 ms. Only the clause reader refuses to produce two. And
the splitting logic exists as well: `chainGatesOf` already buckets a clause `WHERE` by the variable
each conjunct reads (item 305), for the sweep.

So the fix is to make the clause reader produce what the inline reader already produces, not to add
a route. Deliberately NOT done in this item: it changes a signature threaded through
`patternCountOf`, `threeSegmentCount` and the closure, and this session has twice shipped a
regression by making a change in the same tick it was diagnosed.

### Item 1701 — **THE 1411x SPELLING GAP, CLOSED: `WHERE b.k = 7 AND c.k > 60` goes 1411.1 -> 2.0 ms and now converges with its inline twin.** The clause reader was widened to bucket conjuncts per interior position, which is what the inline reader already did. ⚠️ **THREE MUTANTS SURVIVED THE WHOLE SUITE because every one made the reader NARROWER — the shape then declines, the general pipeline answers, and no count moves**

Item 1700 diagnosed this: `interiorPredOf`'s `readsOnly(name)` required EVERY free variable of the
clause to be one name, so a conjunction over both interior positions returned `null` and the
three-segment path had no second route. The machinery to answer it was already there —
`buildThreeHopCount` takes `{ b, c }` as two independent gate LISTS, which the inline spelling fills.

The fix is the reader: split the clause with `flattenConjuncts`, require each conjunct to read
exactly one interior variable, and bucket it. 20,000 vertices / 100,000 edges, warm, median of 5:

```text
   row                                     before      after
   WHERE b.k = 7 AND c.k > 60             1411.1        2.0     706x
   (b {k: 7}) + (c WHERE c.k > 60)            1.0        0.9     the twin it now matches
   WHERE b.k = 7                              1.0        4.0     flat (see the variance note)
   WHERE c.k > 60                             2.2        2.0     flat
   WHERE a.k = 7 AND c.k > 60                 2.2        1.8     flat — still the sweep
   WHERE b.k = 7 AND d.k > 60                 1.3        1.2     flat — still the sweep
```

An earlier run of the same build read the fixed row at **0.9**, so the honest range is **706x-1568x**.
At these magnitudes the rows carry real run-to-run spread — `WHERE b.k = 7` alone read 1.0 and 4.0
across two runs of identical code — so the residual clause-vs-inline difference (2.0 against 0.9) is
inside that spread rather than a remaining gap.

#### ⚠️ THREE MUTANTS SURVIVED, AND ALL THREE FAILED THE SAME WAY

A mutation pass on the new reader caught five and lost three:

```text
   bucketing a `b` conjunct under `c`        SURVIVED
   never filling the `c` bucket              SURVIVED
   not splitting the clause at all           SURVIVED
```

Each makes the reader NARROWER, so the conjunct falls to the `return null`, the shape declines, and
the general row pipeline returns the identical count. `interior-and-gates.test.ts`'s decline cases
assert ANSWERS — which is right for them, since the route is not observable from a count — so they
cannot see this. **A route choice is answer-equivalent when tightened**, which is
`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`'s rule and the reason `csrDegreeProductApplies` and
`gate-conjunct-route.test.ts` exist in this shape.

So `interiorPredOf` is now EXPORTED and its bucketing asserted directly: which bucket each conjunct
lands in, that three conjuncts become three gates, that each carries its own `bindVar`, and that the
five declining shapes return `null`. The inputs are PARSED rather than hand-built, so the test feeds
the reader exactly what the engine feeds it. All three mutants are then CAUGHT.

One mutant remains SURVIVED and is unreachable rather than untested: admitting an empty gate set
(`b.length === 0 && c.length === 0`) cannot happen, because `flattenConjuncts` never returns an empty
list.

#### What still declines, and why it should

A conjunct on the START or the END, one spanning two variables, a constant, and an `OR` all still
decline. The product reaches `a` and `d` only as DEGREES, so a conjunct there has no once-per-element
place to go — `chainGatesOf`'s rule (item 305) at the two positions this shape visits — and those
shapes already have the sweep, which is why `a AND c` and `b AND d` were never slow.

#### ⚠️ MY GATE READING WAS BROKEN, AND IT SHIPPED A LINT ERROR

Several recent items report `check exit 0` from

```sh

```

`$?` there is **`tail`'s** status, which is always 0. That is the exact trap `CLAUDE.md` documents
for piping clippy into `grep -c`, and it means those readings said nothing. Item 1701 was committed
with a `prefer-optional-chain` error in its own new test file as a result; it and one in this item's
replica probe are fixed here, and the gate is read through `${pipestatus[1]}`.

Items 1693 and 1694 shipped lint-failing probes for a DIFFERENT reason — gating before a later edit —
so this is the second distinct way the same gate has been defeated in one session. The rule that
covers both: **run the gate as its own command, read `${pipestatus[1]}` or no pipe at all, and make
it the last thing before `git add`.**

The inline spellings do not move; both clause spellings collapse; every count is identical. So this
is not the equality/index question item 1702 ruled out — an ORDERING clause is hit hardest.

#### ⚠️ WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE RATIO

**A graph with exactly one vertex label is the unrealistic case.** Four extra vertices out of 200,004
— 0.002% of the graph, carrying no edges and matching no pattern here — flip the route. So the 35x-44x
is what a real multi-label graph pays, and the fast numbers in items 1689, 1699 and 1701 were taken
on accidentally single-label fixtures. **Item 1701's "1411.1 -> 2.0 ms" is a single-label figure**;
its fix to the AND bucketing is real and independent of this, but the absolute numbers there do not
describe a multi-label graph.

The mechanism is almost certainly label VACUITY: with only `P` vertices, `(a:P)` matches everything,
`effectiveLabel` returns `undefined`, and `csrDegreeProductApplies` — which requires
`aEff === undefined`, because "a label-filtered degree counts only edges whose far endpoint carries
the label, where the CSR counts them all" — admits the arm. Four non-`P` vertices make the label
real and the arm declines. ~~What is NOT yet explained is why the INLINE spellings stay fast under the
same condition~~ ⚠️ **EXPLAINED AT ITEM 1704, and it is one line: `threeSegmentRoute` skips the sweep
whenever `interiorPred !== undefined`, which a clause `WHERE` always sets and an inline constraint on
`c` never does.**

### Item 1704 — **THE 35x-44x IS ONE LINE: `threeSegmentRoute` skips the sweep whenever `interiorPred !== undefined`**, which a clause `WHERE` always sets and an inline constraint on `c` never does. ⚠️ **And the guard is there for a REASON that is itself the fix: the sweep is called WITHOUT `clauseGates`, so sweeping would silently drop the predicate — but that signature has accepted them since item 305.** ~~Diagnosed and located; the fix is its own item~~ ⚠️ **FIXED AT ITEM 1705: 64.6x and 77.7x on a multi-label graph, 40.8x on the probe's fixture, and the spelling probe no longer flags the group.**

Item 1703 found that four edgeless vertices under another label cost a clause-filtered three-hop
count 35x-44x while the inline twins stayed fast, and left the asymmetry unexplained. A route counter
at each candidate rung, 20,000 vertices, with and without those four nodes:

```text
   spelling        single-label                        + other label
   clause eq       csrDispatch -> armGated   46.3ms    csrDispatch -> csrDeclined   66.9ms
   clause ord      csrDispatch -> armGated    9.4      csrDispatch -> csrDeclined   57.1
   inline where    longChain + armGated       3.6      longChain ONLY               20.6
   inline prop     longChain + armGated       2.5      longChain ONLY                3.4
   unfiltered      longChain + armUnfiltered  1.4      longChain ONLY                1.4
```

So with a non-vacuous start label the CSR arms decline for EVERY spelling — correctly, since `aEff`
is real and "a label-filtered degree counts only edges whose far endpoint carries the label, where
the CSR counts them all". The inline spellings then fall through to the SWEEP. **The clause spellings
never reach it**, and land in the general row pipeline.

#### The line, and why it is written that way

```ts
if (product === null || interiorPred !== undefined || !labelled) {
  return product;
}

const swept = longChainCount(start, segments, rowOf);
```

`interiorPred !== undefined` is true for every clause `WHERE` that produced interior gates and false
for an inline constraint on `c` (`inlineInteriorGate` only sets it for an inline `b`). So the clause
spelling returns `product` — which is `null` once the arms decline — and `patternCountOf`'s
three-segment branch returns unconditionally, so nothing downstream tries the sweep.

⚠️ **The guard is not an oversight, and its own comment says so**: "dropping the `interiorPred` guard
above loses a clause `WHERE` on the way to the sweep and fails". That is true of the call AS WRITTEN —
`longChainCount(start, segments, rowOf)` passes no gates, so the sweep would count every path and
silently ignore the predicate. **But `longChainCount` has taken `clauseGates` since item 305**, which
is how the four-or-more-segment branch sweeps a clause `WHERE` correctly. The three-segment route
simply never passes them.

So the fix is to give the sweep what it already accepts: build `chainGatesOf(where, start, segments)`
for three segments as well, pass it, and narrow the skip to the case where those gates cannot be
built. Expected: the clause spellings join the inline ones at 3.4-20.6 ms, which on the replica
fixture is 467 -> ~12.

#### Deliberately not built in this item

The same discipline as item 1700, which paid: this changes a signature and a route guard whose own
comment records that **no test can police the choice** ("always-sweep, always-product and an INVERTED
comparison all leave every test green"). What the tests DO catch is the predicate plumbing — so the
fix needs the clause gates asserted on the way to the sweep, and a mutation pass that checks a
dropped gate fails. That is a build, not a tail.

### Item 1705 — **THE CLAUSE SPELLING NOW SWEEPS: 781.5 -> 12.1 ms (64.6x) and 979.6 -> 12.6 (77.7x) on a multi-label graph, 467.68 -> 11.45 (40.8x) on the spelling probe's own fixture, and `bun run spelling` no longer flags the group.** The fix is to give the three-segment sweep the `clauseGates` it has accepted since item 305. ⚠️ **Two surviving mutants turned out to be unreachable and answer-equivalent rather than untested — and my first explanation of WHY was wrong**

Item 1704 located the 35x-44x to one guard: `threeSegmentRoute` skipped the sweep whenever
`interiorPred !== undefined`, because the call below it passed no gates and sweeping would have
dropped the predicate. `longChainCount` has taken `clauseGates` since item 305. So:

```ts
const gates = where === undefined ? undefined : chainGatesOf(where, start, segments);
const swept =
  labelled && gates !== null ? longChainCount(start, segments, rowOf, gates, cstart) : null;

// The product declining is no longer the end of the road: the sweep may still answer.
if (product === null) {
  return swept;
}
```

Measured, median of 7, one query per process:

```text
   fixture / row                              before     after
   multi-label, WHERE c.k = 2                  781.5      12.1    64.6x
   multi-label, WHERE c.k > 9                  979.6      12.6    77.7x
   multi-label, inline twins                11.0-15.1   11.4-12.2  flat
   SINGLE-label, WHERE c.k = 2                  22.1      22.1    unchanged
   the replica (the probe's fixture)          467.68     11.45    40.8x
   the replica, inline twin                    12.07     11.54    flat
```

Counts identical throughout, the two spellings converge (11.45 against 11.54), and the single-label
case is untouched — `candidateCount` equals `vertexCount` when the label is vacuous, so the runtime
comparison still picks the product there.

**`bun run spelling` no longer flags the group.** The one group it flags afterwards — `SEEK: a param
equality AND a second conjunct` at 2.10x — is dispatch pollution, not a regression: isolated three
times it reads 3.59-4.37 ms across all four spellings with zero flags, which is the contamination the
probe's own header describes.

#### ⚠️ A SURVIVING MUTANT IS NOT ALWAYS A MISSING TEST, AND I GOT THIS WRONG FIRST

The mutation pass caught the one that matters — passing NO gates to the sweep, the pre-fix call, fails
6 tests — and lost two:

```text
   M1 the sweep is given NO gates            CAUGHT (6 fail)
   M2 a NON-sweepable clause is swept        SURVIVED
   M3 gates built from the wrong positions   SURVIVED
   M5 always sweep (route choice)            SURVIVED — expected, see below
```

My first explanation was that the test fixture labels every vertex `P`, so `P` is vacuous, the
product always applies and the sweep is never exercised. That was worth fixing on its own — nothing
in the suite reached the sweep path — so a non-vacuous fixture and eight cases were added. **M2 and
M3 still survived**, so the explanation was wrong.

What is actually true: `patternCountOf` returns `null` at `interiorPred === null` BEFORE calling
`threeSegmentRoute`, and `interiorPredOf` declines any conjunct that is not a per-vertex test on `b`
or `c` — a stricter rule than `chainGatesOf`'s. So inside that function `where !== undefined` implies
`gates !== null`: **M2 is unreachable**, and M3 only turns a `b`-clause into a decline, which is
answer-equivalent. M5 is the route choice the function's own comment already says no test can police.

So the `gates !== null` check is dead today. It is KEPT with that stated on it, as the honest
statement of what the sweep requires — unlike item 1688's dead seed BRANCH, which was removed
because it contained logic that read as a tested path. A one-term guard documented as unreachable is
not the same hazard.

The new multi-label tests stay regardless: they are the only ones that reach the sweep for an answer,
and item 1703's measurement says that is the common case rather than the exotic one.

#### ⚠️ TWO FAILED A/B RUNS, AND BOTH WERE THE GUARD WORKING

The arm-identity guard aborted all four arms twice, which is the only reason a wrong number was not
reported:

- A trailing `// A/B: … forced` comment marker: **the bundler strips comments**, so the dist carried
  no marker.
- `const narrow = graph.vertexCount;`: **the bundler INLINES a single-use local**, so that vanished
  too.

Both times the driver refused to time a build it could not identify. Without the guard it would have
timed the pristine bundle twice and reported "no difference" — the null that looks like a result.
**The guard is now a HASH**: assert the marker in the SOURCE that was patched, and assert the built
bundle differs from a pristine bundle hashed once at the start. Three distinct hashes appeared
(pristine `f032f4c3`, product `ee746c8c`, sweep `51243ca6`), each stable across both rounds. That is
immune to stripping, inlining and renaming.

### Item 1711 — **THE ORDER BY COMPARATOR'S DEAD BRANCHES, ELIMINATED UNDER A CHECKED PRECONDITION: a 1,000,000-row string sort 896.9/765.6 -> 525.3/528.0 ms (1.71x / 1.45x), with the no-sort control drifting up to 16% AGAINST the change.** ⚠️ **CONFIRMED ON THE SWEEP AT ITEM 1716, 1.30x-1.46x — but only after fixing the sweep row, which projected an ABSENT property and was sorting a million NULLS; it read 1.01x-1.03x until then.** ⚠️ **Two CLOSED entries already priced this exact chain and neither bound this row — item 423 measured it on a SINGLE-PASS aggregate (one comparison per row, a sort does ~20) and item 921's ~1.07x ceiling was computed on `sortedpage`, which is `LIMIT 10` and takes the HEAP path.** ⚠️ **A numeric arm was built, measured six times (0.93x-1.18x, straddling 1.0) and DROPPED.** Plus the 15th cross-engine divergence, found on the way out

The profile nominated it: `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN x.name AS n ORDER BY n` is the
largest live row in the re-ranked field, and one shape per process put the comparator chain across
`compareCodePoints` 8.04%, `compareSort` 7.57%, `typeRank` 5.43%, `compareValues` 1.67% and the
surrogate regex 4.13%, under a comparator closure at 16.81%.

**THE FIRST THING THAT HAPPENED WAS THE FUNCTION'S OWN NOTE STOPPING A REPEAT BUILD.** `values.ts`
carries item 921's three refuted arms and the line "If you come back to this, the hoist is the only
live option and the ceiling above is what it has to beat" — which is exactly what I was about to
build. Third time this session a function-level note has done that (1684, 1686, this).

**WHY THE CLOSED ENTRIES DID NOT BIND, which is the reusable part.** Both priced the same chain and
both were right about what they measured:

- Item 423: "`compareValues` ... for a string pair runs ten statically-false type checks before
  `compareCodePoints`", refuted at **12%, 11 ns/row**, "under the repo's own 10% rule, refuted
  before any code". It measured a `max` AGGREGATE — **one comparison per row**. A sort does
  ~n log n ≈ **20 per row**, and the chain's cost scales with COMPARISONS, not rows.
- Item 921: the surrogate guard, declined at **~1.07x**. Measured against a `sortedpage` profile —
  `LIMIT 10`, so `(skip+limit)*16 <= rows.length` sends it to `boundedTopRows` and `rows.sort` is
  never called.

So a refutation carries its INSTRUMENT with it. "Refuted at 12%" is a claim about the shape it ran
on; re-ask it when the per-row comparison COUNT changes by an order of magnitude. Both headings are
corrected in this commit, plus item 424's (its `compareSort` suspect is confirmed for the full sort
and deliberately left on the heap path).

**AND THE PROFILE CORPUS IS WHY IT SAT FOR ~790 ITEMS.** Item 921's "THE TS RUNTIME PATH HAS NO
UNPRICED HOT CODE ABOVE 2% — measured, five query shapes" is sound for its five, and NONE of them is
an unlimited `ORDER BY`: the only sorted shape is `sortedpage`, on the heap path. A corpus with no
full sort in it cannot price a full sort's comparator. `isolated-row-bench.mjs` now carries
`hopsortstr`, and that gap is closed.

**THE CHANGE.** `sort-column-specialize.ts` scans a sort column once; if every value is a non-null,
surrogate-free string it sorts with `x < y ? -1 : x > y ? 1 : 0`, else `compareSort` runs untouched.
⚠️ **It is branch ELIMINATION WITH A PROOF, not the "second derivation of which row sorts first"
that `sortRowsByColumns`' own note forbids**: under that precondition `compareSort` takes neither
null branch, both `typeRank`s are 1, the temporal/array/record arms and the `ra === 4` arm are dead,
and `compareCodePoints`' own fast path — reached when neither string holds a high surrogate — IS that
expression, by inspection. `HAS_SURROGATE` is exported and SHARED rather than copied, so there is one
definition of "can code-unit order disagree with code-point order".

**THE NUMERIC ARM, BUILT AND DROPPED, with its numbers next to the code.** Numbers reduce equally
exactly (`compareValues` also ends in that expression once NaN is excluded). Six readings over four
runs: **0.93x, 1.05x, 1.06x, 1.11x, 1.14x, 1.18x** — it STRADDLES 1.0, and on the quiet machine the
adverse round read 0.93x while the control moved 0.84x. Its best evidence was POST against a
string-only build (1.053x, 1.112x, matched controls), which does not buy a second code path, a second

string arm nets 1.45x is the part worth keeping: a FLOOR arm (reduced comparator, NO scan) measured
1.25x on the numeric row, so the reduction IS worth ~25% there and the O(n) scan eats it.** The
string comparator saves far more per comparison, so the same scan is cheap against the saving. **The
open question is a CHEAPER CLASSIFICATION, not this arm** — rebuilding it as written will measure
~1.0x again.

**A WARM-UP EXPLANATION THAT LOOKED TRUE AND WAS REFUTED.** A three-arm run put POST ahead of a
NO-SCAN floor build in both rounds, which is impossible if the floor is the floor, and the tempting
mechanism was that the scan pre-touches every `row[col]` so the comparator's ~20M property reads

read **0.92x and 0.95x** — slower than PRE by the scan's own cost. So the scan buys nothing beyond
classifying, the floor anomaly was drift, and the whole win is the comparator.

**The crux test is a column holding both `''` and an astral char**, where code-point and
code-unit order genuinely disagree, with the oracle derived independently (`Array.from` iterates code
points) rather than by calling the engine's comparator. The differential fuzzer already builds this
case — `STR_CHARS` carries `` and 20% of strings splice an astral char — and compares ORDER BY
shapes IN ORDER, not as multisets.

#### The 15th cross-engine divergence, found while checking whether this transfers to Gremlin

⚠️ **TS GREMLIN ORDERS STRINGS BY CODE UNIT WHERE RUST AND TS GQL USE CODE POINT.** One process, same
data:

```text
    gremlin TS   a  z  U+1F600  U+E000      code UNIT  (high surrogate D83D < E000)
    gql     TS   a  z  U+E000   U+1F600     code POINT (57344 < 128512)
```

`cmpSameType` sends a string pair to `cmpOrd`, a plain `x < y ? -1 : x > y ? 1 : 0` with **no
code-point comparison and no surrogate guard at all**. The Rust side cannot differ by language:
`exec/order.rs` compares `Col::Str` with `v[a].cmp(&v[b])` (Rust `str::cmp`, byte-wise UTF-8 = code
point) and `ir.rs`'s `SortKey` doc states both languages order non-nulls by `cmp_total`, with only
null PLACEMENT differing (GQL last, Gremlin first). ~~Recorded as the 15th open value divergence;
`test.failing` registration and the native-engine leg are the next item.~~ ⚠️ **ITS CI GAP IS CLOSED AT ITEM 1728** (a dedicated parity test with its own corpus; 2 of 3 fail on revert). ⚠️ **CONFIRMED AGAINST
NATIVE AND FIXED AT ITEM 1712** — the native leg ran (the engine agrees with GQL), so no
`test.failing` was needed; `compareCodePoints` now lives in `@lenke/core` and both engines share
it. **No fuzzer could find it:
`gremlin-fuzz.test.ts` calls `order(` 59 times and generates ZERO astral and ZERO U+E000..U+FFFF
characters** — item 921's "a corpus that does not CONSTRUCT the dangerous case will agree with
anything", firing in the other engine.
