### Item 1735 — ⚠️ **THE GREMLIN PROBE'S `groupreduce` ROW WAS GROUPING EVERY VERTEX INTO ITS OWN BUCKET: it passes `group({ by: 'k' })` where the config key is `keyBy`.** Its `groupStep` 54.5% + GC 25.7% — which I was one step from chasing as a live target — is a 200,000-entry Map of 200,000 single-element arrays. Corrected, the same row is **2.8x cheaper and has no GC problem at all**

Profiled five under-mined Gremlin shapes to let the frames nominate a target. `groupreduce` came
back at `groupStep` **54.5%** with `(garbage collector)` at **25.7%** — and item 1474 had profiled
`group().by('k')` at `groupStep` **48.9%** with GC at **26%** BEFORE fixing it, so this looked like
either a regression or a fix that never landed.

It was neither. **The probe does not group by `k`.**

```javascript
export const group = (config: { keyBy?: string; valueBy?: string } = {}) => …   // group:      keyBy
export const groupCount = (config: { by?: string } = {}) => …                   // groupCount: by
```

The row passes `group({ by: 'k' })`. `by` is not a key `group` accepts, so it is spread into the
step object as a stray property and `keyBy` is left undefined — which means **GROUP BY SELF**.
Measured, rather than read off the signature:

```text
  2000 vertices, 97 distinct values of k
    group({by:'k'})     -> 2000 buckets      <- what the probe passed
    group({keyBy:'k'})  ->   97 buckets      <- the real spelling
    groupCount({by:'k'})->   97 buckets      <- correct; groupCount's key IS `by`
```

⚠️ **The two steps' config keys differ, which is what made this survive.** `groupCount({ by: … })`
sits a few lines away in the same probe and is RIGHT, so the spelling looks consistent with its
neighbour. And a `.mjs` probe gets no excess-property check, so TypeScript — which would reject the
object literal — never saw it.

#### The corrected row, with the degenerate one kept as a control

600 reps, windowed past the fixture build:

```text
  row                               total      groupStep    GC
  groupreduce (97 buckets)         596.7 ms       30.1%     below top-6 (<2.5%)
  groupbyself (200,000 buckets)   1678.4 ms       66.7%     16.3%
```

**The real grouping shape is 2.8x cheaper and its GC term disappears entirely.** So item 1474's
insertion-time evaluation works exactly as recorded, and the 25.7% GC was never grouping's cost —
it was the cost of 200,000 buckets. The corrected profile has **no dominant term**: `groupStep`
30.1%, `countStep` 20.3%, `sourceFromIds` 17.4%, `evalBy` 14.8%. Nothing to take.

The degenerate shape is kept as **`groupbyself`**, named for what it does. It is a real (if unwise)
query, and it is the control that separates bucket COUNT from grouping — which is the distinction
this row obscured for its whole life.

⚠️ Only ONE instrument carried the misspelling (checked across every `.mjs` and `.ts` under
`packages/`, excluding the correct `groupCount` form) — contained, unlike item 1518's six generators.

#### ⚠️ AND A METHOD ERROR OF MY OWN, recorded because it nearly produced the same kind of wrong answer

My first pass ran the probe under `node --cpu-prof`, which profiles start to exit. For the three
CHEAP shapes the fixture build then dominates, and the rankings came back as `indexEdgeLabel`
12-16%, `getVertexById` 6-8%, `commitElementLabels`, `#commitNormalized` — **all of them the LOAD,
none of them the query.** That is the exact failure `windowed-profile.mjs` was written to prevent,
and the probe already supports `PROF_OUT`; I did not use it. Windowed, the same three shapes invert
completely:

```text
  shape         unwindowed top frame            windowed top frame
  valuemapped   indexEdgeLabel  12.1%           copyProps     42.0%
  projected     indexEdgeLabel  16.0%           projectStep   47.5%
  groupreduce   groupStep       23.2%           groupStep     54.5%
```

**Two different instrument faults in one tick, each of which would have nominated a target that does
not exist.** The cheap check that caught the first was comparing a profile against a recorded
earlier one for the same shape (54.5% against item 1474's pre-fix 48.9% was the thing that did not
add up); the cheap check for the second was that the top frames were names from the LOAD path.

#### Carried forward, genuinely open

The windowed profiles leave two legitimate nominations on real steps, neither of which is a
spelling artifact: **`copyProps` at 42.0% of `valueMap()`** and **`projectStep` at 47.5% of
`project('a','b')`**. Both rows terminate in `count()` deliberately, to force consumption while
measuring the step — so the shares are the steps' own cost. Unpriced.

### Item 1736 — **`Object.assign` BEATS `copyProps`' `Object.keys` LOOP BY 1.26x AT WIDTH 3, 1.63x AT 8 AND 2.42x AT 24, with a working control flat.** ⚠️ **NOT SHIPPED: it is the one copy form that excludes symbol keys, and a symbol-keyed property DOES reach a stored bag (measured). The function's own comment says a perf item is not the place to change settled key semantics — so this is an owner decision, not a judgment call**

Item 1735 left `copyProps` at **42.0%** of `V().valueMap().count()`, the largest share on any real
Gremlin step it measured and unpriced. Its no-keys arm is
`for (const k of Object.keys(props)) out[k] = props[k]` — an array allocation per element plus
one-at-a-time property addition into a fresh `{}`.

**A spread is correctly ruled out by the source itself**: `out[k] = v` and `{ ...props }` differ for
the key `__proto__` (assignment sets the prototype, spread defines an own property), and
`prototype-key-class-not-a-bug` settles that as WON'T-FIX. `Object.assign` looked like the way
through, because it reads with `[[Get]]` and writes with `[[Set]]` — **assignment semantics, so the
`__proto__` behaviour is preserved exactly** — while being one builtin call with no `Object.keys`
array.

#### Measured: 200,000 vertices, median of 9 dropping 3, three alternated rounds, one arm per build

```text
  width   base (r1/r2/r3)           assign (r1/r2/r3)        ratio
    3     34.4 / 33.3 / 33.8        27.8 / 26.3 / 26.6       1.26x
    8     53.5 / 54.5 / 52.7        34.0 / 32.9 / 32.4       1.63x
   24    107.0 / 111.7 / 108.8      44.9 / 45.1 / 46.4       2.40x
```

**The ratio rises with bag width, which is the right shape for the mechanism** — the `Object.keys`
array and the incremental property additions are both per-property — and it is why the arms were
swept over three widths rather than measured at one (CLAUDE.md's "match the fixture to the claim").
Each arm was asserted present in the dist (`Object.assign(out, props)` 0 → 1) before running, and
every row printed a matching element count.

⚠️ **MY FIRST CONTROL WAS DEGENERATE AND I RAN THE WHOLE SWEEP BEFORE NOTICING.** `V().count()`
hits the count shortcut and returns in **0.0 ms**, so it cannot detect a bad build or machine drift
— which is a control's entire job. Re-ran with `V().values('p0').count()`, which walks every vertex
and never reaches `copyProps`: **2.6 / 2.6 / 2.6 ms base against 2.6 / 2.6 / 2.5 assign.** Flat, so
the 2.40x is the change. Both controls are kept in the probe, the degenerate one labelled as such.
⚠️ And its `answer` field printed **0** — the probe applied map arithmetic to a scalar-terminal
shape, giving a vacuous assertion on the one row whose job is to be trustworthy. Fixed per-shape;
this is the same defect class as items 1716 and 1735, found in my own instrument this time.

#### ⚠️ WHY IT IS NOT SHIPPED

`Object.keys` returns own enumerable **string** keys. `Object.assign` copies own enumerable string
**and symbol** keys. Every fast builtin copy form (spread included) copies symbols; the
`Object.keys` loop is the only symbol-excluding one, so **the semantic question is unavoidable for
any win here.**

And symbol keys are reachable. Measured, not reasoned about — `normalizeProperties` returns the
caller's bag unchanged when no value moves, so the user's object becomes the stored bag:

```text
  addVertex({ properties: { a: 1, [Symbol('sym')]: 'leaked' } })
    ingest threw:  false
    Object.keys(bag):                 ['a']
    getOwnPropertySymbols(bag):       [Symbol(sym)]
    bag[S]:                           'leaked'
```

So `Object.assign` would surface that key in `valueMap()` output where the loop hides it. **How much
that matters is genuinely arguable, which is exactly why it is not mine to decide:**

- It is unobservable through every documented surface — `Object.keys` on the result skips it,
  `JSON.stringify` drops it, the GraphSON and NDJSON codecs iterate string keys, and no query
  language can name a symbol. Only a caller already holding the symbol can see it.
- Which makes it arguably the same settled WON'T-FIX class as the `__proto__` behaviour.
- **But the counter-argument is in this function's own comment**, written about the sibling question:
  _"that behaviour is settled — a perf item is not the place to change it."_ Deciding a second key
  semantics question inside a perf item is precisely what that sentence forbids.
- A third option exists and is a separate change: **drop symbol keys at ingest** in
  `normalizeProperties`, which already has copy-on-change machinery. Then bags never hold symbols and
  `Object.assign` is exactly equivalent forever. It also removes what is arguably a latent
  cross-engine divergence — native has no symbol-keyed property, so TS storing one is state the Rust
  engine cannot represent, and no fuzzer generates a symbol so nothing would catch it.

**Priced at 1.26-2.40x and left at the decision.** The three paths are: accept the symbol exposure,
drop symbols at ingest and then take it, or keep the loop.

`packages/gremlin` twin of item 1733's driver; its mutation is an exact multi-line replacement with

`projectStep` at 47.5% of `project('a','b')` (item 1735's other nomination) remains unpriced.

### Item 1737 — **the standing O(1)-by-id requirement is in better shape than recorded: `getVertexById` is ~1.09x a bare `Map.get`, not item 1729's 1.26x.** Both candidate causes of the remainder priced and both are AT OR BELOW this instrument's resolution — the arrow-field call shape ~6 points, the `?? null` ~3. ⚠️ **And the dist assertion caught THREE bad classifiers in a row, refusing to print numbers for code it could not identify — the first time that guard has demonstrably earned its keep here**

"Keep good O(1) access to get a vertex or edge by id" is a standing requirement. Item 1729 verified
the COMPLEXITY (1.04x relative growth over 100x the elements) but also recorded a CONSTANT — 112.4 ns
against a raw `Map`'s 89.2 at 1,000,000 elements, **1.26x** — which nothing had explained or ablated.
It is the engine's most-used primitive: item 1731 measured decode spending ~14% in
`getVertexById`/`getEdgeById`/`requireVertex`, two lookups per edge.

The accessor is `public getVertexById = (id) => this.verticesById.get(id) ?? null;` — an **arrow
assigned as a class field**, so a call is a property load on the instance plus an indirect call,
which V8 inlines less readily than a prototype method. `verticesById` is a plain field (checked, not
assumed), so the only candidates are that call shape and the `?? null`.

#### Three arms, 1,000,000 vertices, scrambled lookup order, with the raw `Map` row IN THE SAME PROCESS

The raw-`Map` row is the control and it is unaffected by any arm, so the within-process **ratio** is
the estimator — the absolute ns swung 37-56 between processes on this machine, which is exactly why
a cross-process absolute would have been the wrong reading. Row order alternated (`FIRST=engine` and
`FIRST=rawmap`) so the first-measured row is not always the engine's. 9 reps, median of the last 6,
three alternated rounds:

```text
  arm      ratio readings                                 median
  base     1.103  1.084  1.092  1.082  1.048  1.218        1.088
  proto    1.048  1.124  0.969  1.015  1.013  1.022        1.019
  nonull   1.030  1.089  1.069  1.033  1.045  1.065        1.055
```

- ⚠️ **The constant is ~1.09x here, not 1.26x.** Item 1729's figure does not reproduce in this shape
  — a FOURTH instance this stretch of a constant being a measurement of its own harness (1730, 1731,
  1733). Its heading is corrected.
- **The prototype form removes most of the remainder (~6 points) and the `?? null` about 3** — but
  the ranges OVERLAP (base's best 1.048 against proto's worst 1.124), and CLAUDE.md's own rule is
  that anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness. **So both are priced as at-or-below
  resolution, not as wins.**
- **Neither is worth taking.** `proto` is a semantic change — a prototype method loses its
  `this`-binding when detached, so `const f = g.getVertexById; f('v1')` would break, and every public
  method on `Graph` uses the arrow-field form, so changing one is an inconsistency and changing all
  is a different project. Paying that for ~6% on a primitive already within ~9% of a bare `Map.get`
  is a bad trade.

**NET: the requirement is satisfied with margin, and the 1.26x that might have motivated work on it
was shape-dependent.** Recorded so the next reader does not price this from 1729's number.

#### ⚠️ THE DIST ASSERTION EARNED ITS KEEP, THREE TIMES IN ONE ITEM

The driver asserts the arm's code is in the built dist before running the arm. It failed three times
in a row, each time refusing to print numbers rather than reporting them for unidentified code:

1. First detector tested `'verticesById.get(id);' in dist` — that substring occurs at ANOTHER site,
   so every arm classified as `nonull`. Refused `base` and `proto`.
2. Second took the 90 characters after the first `'getVertexById'` — but that name occurs **26 times**
   in the bundle, as call sites AND inside COMMENT TEXT, so it landed on a call site and classified
   every arm as `proto`. Refused all three.
3. Third keys on a regex that matches only the DECLARATION (`getVertexById\s*=\s*\(` or
   `getVertexById\(id\)\s*\{`), verified to have exactly one match. All three arms then asserted
   clean and ran.

**Without the assertion, run 1 would have reported `nonull`'s numbers as `base`'s and `proto`'s** —
three arms of a null result that was really one arm measured three times, which is precisely the
"the after reading is the before code" failure CLAUDE.md describes. The lesson for the next driver:
**a dist assertion must key on the DECLARATION, not on the symbol name** — in a bundle the name also
appears in call sites and in the source comments that were carried through.

### Item 1738 — **`RETURN DISTINCT n.k` decomposed by ablation: the PROPERTY READ is ~20% of the query and the computed-key row literal is ZERO.** The profile had `take` at 60.6% self and `propOf` + `get properties` at only 14.4%, so it UNDERSTATED the read — the rest was inlined into `take`. ⚠️ **And the driver failed three times in three distinct ways before producing a number, each failure a variant of "the assertion checked the wrong thing"**

A windowed profile of four under-mined GQL shapes (`distinct`, `optional`, `existssub`, `wideproj`)
gave one dominant single frame: **`take` at 60.6%** of `MATCH (n:P) RETURN DISTINCT n.k AS k`, with
`walkStartSide` 9.9%, `add` 9.7%, `propOf` 8.7%, `get properties` 5.7%.

`take`'s body is two branches, a property read, a `valueSet` add, and a conditional
`rows.push({ [outName]: value })`. **60.6% SELF for that is implausible** — V8 charges inlined
callees to the caller frame — so the split was settled by deletion rather than read off the profile.

#### Two ceilings, cardinality preserved, `sink` identical in every arm

The fixture yields **97 distinct values over ~2000 vertices per run**, so the dedup is mostly
duplicate hits. Both arms keep the row count and the non-zero `sink` the probe asserts on:

```text
  arm        runs (ms)
  base       437.9  447.6  439.0  438.5  447.7  454.3
  constrow   433.3  437.6                              <- prebuilt row object instead of { [k]: v }
  novalue    350.6  350.7  350.4  352.0                <- counter mod 97 instead of propOf
```

- ⚠️ **The computed-key object literal is FREE.** `constrow` 433-438 against base 438-454 — inside
  the noise, nominally faster. A per-row `{ [outName]: value }` looked like an obvious allocation
  target and is not one. Rejected before being built.
- **The property read is ~90 ms of ~440, about 20% of the query.** At 2000 runs × ~2000 vertices
  that is ~22 ns per read for a getter call plus an index — plausible and close to irreducible: the
  getter's box is cached after the first read (`#box ??=`), so what remains is a null check, a field
  read, an optional chain and the index. **No cheap lever**; a dedicated raw accessor would be new
  API on the element, which is a different decision.
- **So `take`'s 60.6% is the read (~20% of total) plus the dedup and branches, and the profile's own
  14.4% for `propOf` + `get properties` was an UNDER-count** by roughly a third of the read's real
  cost. A self-time share is a nomination, and here it was a nomination that pointed at the right
  place for the wrong reason.

Noted in passing, not acted on: **`valueSet.add`'s primitive branch does TWO Set operations**
(`prim.has(v)` then `prim.add(v)`) where a size-delta before/after `add` would do ONE. It saves a
hash only when the value is NEW, so it is worth nothing on this low-cardinality fixture and would
need a high-cardinality `DISTINCT` to show. ~~Unmeasured, recorded so it is not re-derived.~~ ⚠️ **MEASURED AND REFUTED AT ITEM 1739: the one-hash form is ~10-11% SLOWER wherever duplicates dominate, because `Set.add` on an existing key is dearer than `Set.has`.**

   resolve its imports.

### Item 1739 — ❌ **REFUTED: replacing `valueSet.add`'s two Set operations with one plus a size delta is ~10-11% SLOWER wherever duplicates dominate.** `Set.add` on an EXISTING key is dearer than `Set.has`, so the "two hashes where one would do" reading had the cost model backwards. ⚠️ **The CONTROL moved against the change in all three rounds, which is what made it readable** — and the probe had no high-cardinality `DISTINCT` shape until this item, which is why 1738 nearly dismissed the lever instead of refuting it

Item 1738 noticed that `valueSet.add`'s primitive branch runs **two** Set operations:

```javascript
if (prim.has(v)) {
  return false;
}
prim.add(v);
return true;
```

where a size delta would run one: `const before = prim.size; prim.add(v); return prim.size !== before;`

**This needed no owner decision, which is why it was worth taking first.** Both forms key the Set
itself, so both use SameValueZero and agree on NaN, on `-0` against `0`, and on everything else —
exactly equivalent, unlike the two levers currently waiting on a semantics call (items 1733, 1736).

#### ⚠️ FIRST THE INSTRUMENT, because 1738's shape could not see this lever at all

The lever only pays when a value is **NEW** — a duplicate costs one hash either way. The probe's only
`DISTINCT` shape is `n.k`, which is `i % 97` over 20,000 rows, so **almost every add is a duplicate
and the second hash almost never runs.** Item 1738 measured on that shape and called the lever
"worth nothing here"; it was right about the shape and would have been wrong to generalize. Added
two tiers, so the probe now spans the axis the mechanism depends on:

```text
  distinct     n.k  = i % 97          97 distinct per run   <- duplicates dominate (the CONTROL)
  distinctstr  n.s  = `s${i % 1000}`  1,000                 <- mid, and a STRING key
  distincthi   n.n  = i               20,000                <- every add is NEW (the best case)
```

#### Measured, 500 runs per reading, three alternated rounds, one arm per build

```text
  shape                      base (r1/r2/r3)          sizedelta (r1/r2/r3)
  distincthi  (20,000 new)   507.0 500.6 498.1        482.9 600.5 484.6
  distinctstr (1,000)        169.2 156.9 155.4        178.2 172.2 175.5
  distinct    (97, CONTROL)  124.8 123.4 125.9        140.6 140.0 136.6
```

- **The control moved AGAINST the change, consistently in all three rounds: 124 → 139, ~11% slower.**
  `conjunct-order-chosen-for-speed`'s companion lesson is that a control moving more than the target
  indicts the change; here it moves in the _wrong direction_, which is stronger.
- **Mid cardinality is also slower, ~10%** (157 → 175).
- **Even the best case is not a win**: 498-507 against 483-600. The median improvement is ~3% and one
  arm reading was 600.5, so it is inside this instrument's noise — and CLAUDE.md's rule is that
  anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness.

#### The mechanism, which is the reusable part

**`Set.add` on a key that is already present costs MORE than `Set.has` on it.** `has` is a pure
lookup; `add` must take the insertion path and be prepared to grow the table, then discovers the key
is there. So for a duplicate the "one operation" form does strictly more work than the "two
operation" form does — plus two `size` field reads. The op COUNT was the wrong cost model.

That is why the shape of the data decides the sign of this change, and why a dedup is the worst place
to apply it: **a dedup's whole purpose is that most inputs are duplicates.** The all-new case is the
rare one, and even there the saving does not clear the noise floor.

**Reverted. Recorded at `valueSet` so the next reader does not re-derive the op-count argument**, and
item 1738's "unmeasured, recorded so it is not re-derived" line is struck in the same commit.

**KEPT: the two new probe shapes** (`distincthi`, `distinctstr`). They are the reason this came out
as a refutation with a mechanism rather than a shrug, and any future dedup or grouping lever needs
the cardinality axis.

### Item 1740 — ❌ **REFUTED: a one-entry memo of the last element's property bag is FLAT on the five-column shape it targets and 3-10% WORSE on both one-read controls.** ⚠️ **But it is a CONFOUNDED ceiling, not a clean one, and the entry says so: a safe local hoist inside the projection's row scope would not pay the memo's own cost, and that remains unmeasured.** ⚠️⚠️ **And `wideproj` at 300 runs spreads 18% — it cannot resolve the effect at all; at 1500 it is 1.3%**

`propOf(bound, key)` is `bound?.properties?.[key] ?? null`, so it calls the `properties` GETTER on
every read. A multi-column `RETURN` calls it once per column **on the same element**: `wideproj`
(`RETURN n.k AS a, n.n AS b, n.s AS c, n.k AS d, n.n AS e`) makes **five getter calls per row where
one would do**, and item 1735's windowed profile gave `propOf` **16.5%** plus `get properties`
**7.6%** there. Four redundant calls out of five looked like ~19%.

#### Measured first, 300 runs per reading, three alternated rounds, one arm per build

```text
  shape                        base (r1/r2/r3)        memo (r1/r2/r3)
  wideproj  (5 reads/row)      163.5 171.9 144.9      158.8 159.5 155.8
  hoprows   (1 read, CONTROL)  253.7 252.8 261.3      269.9 277.4 287.9
  distincthi(1 read, CONTROL)  317.3 316.0 322.8      325.1 326.5 340.0
```

- **The target is FLAT and base's range ENCLOSES the arm's** (144.9-171.9 against 155.8-159.5).
- **Both one-read controls got WORSE — 7-10% and 3-5%.** They cannot gain from removing redundancy,
  only lose the memo's extra branch, and they did. A control moving the wrong way is the clearest
  verdict this harness produces.
- **Mechanism: the memo's identity test plus its module-scope variable traffic costs about what it
  saves.** Module-scope `let` access is dearer than a local, and it is written on every miss.

The arm was also **knowingly unsafe and never a candidate** — a write REPLACES an element's bag
without changing the element object, so `MATCH (n) SET n.x = 1 RETURN n.x` would read a stale bag.
It existed only to price the redundancy before designing anything.

#### ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, stated plainly rather than filed as "refuted"

**This is a confounded ceiling.** A correct version would hoist the bag into the **projection's own
row scope as a local**, where no write can intervene and there is no module-variable traffic — so it
would not pay the cost that killed this arm. Whether the redundancy is worth that plumbing is
**still open**, and this item cannot close it. Writing it up as a flat refutation would have retired
a live question on evidence that does not reach it — the failure mode `check-the-blocker-still-holds`
describes.

What the item DOES establish: the profile's 24% across `propOf` and `get properties` is **not 24% of
recoverable cost**, because removing four of five calls — even with the memo's overhead subtracted
generously — does not show above this shape's noise.

#### ⚠️ AND THE INSTRUMENT FINDING THAT MAKES A RETRY POSSIBLE

`wideproj` at **300 runs spreads 18%** (144.9 to 171.9), so it cannot resolve a 5% effect; the arm
and the base overlap because the base overlaps _itself_. At **1500 runs** it reads
`652.8 / 615.3 / 617.5 / 622.7` — **1.3% once the first (warm-up) run is dropped**. Anyone retrying
the hoist must use n ≥ 1500 and drop the first run, or they will measure exactly what I did: nothing,
with no way to tell a null result from an unresolvable one.

**Recorded at `propOf`** with the numbers, the unsettled part, and the rep-count requirement. ⚠️ **THE UNSETTLED PART IS NOW SETTLED AND SHIPPED AT ITEM 1741: the safe local hoist, inside `nodeProjection`'s row loop and guarded on >1 column, is 1.27x/1.29x with disjoint ranges.**

### Item 1741 — ✅ **SHIPPED: hoist the property bag once per row in `nodeProjection`'s direct-read loop — 1.27x on a five-column `RETURN`, 1.29x on a two-column one, ranges DISJOINT.** ⚠️ **The guard on `> 1` columns is load-bearing: unguarded, the single-column shape measured ~10% WORSE.** Cost side stated: a different rung pays ~4%

Item 1740 refuted a module-level memo for `propOf` and said plainly what it had NOT settled: _"a
correct version would hoist the bag into the projection's own row scope as a LOCAL, where no write
can intervene and there is no module-variable traffic."_ This is that version.

#### Finding the right loop, by reading the route rather than guessing

`wideproj`'s profile gave `fastPath` 20.4%, which is the rung DISPATCHER — but at 300 query calls a
dispatch chain cannot cost that, so it had to be a taken rung's body inlined into it.
`rung-precedence-decides-speed` says to read `compileLinear`'s non-null function fields, because
timing cannot tell declined from more-work. Read directly:

```text
  wideproj / wide2 / narrow1  ->  nodeProjection
  hoprows                    ->  hopProjection
  distincthi                 ->  distinctProjection
```

So the loop is `nodeProjection`'s, where `row[cols[i]] = dk === undefined ? fns[i](env) : propOf(v, dk)`
calls `propOf` — i.e. the `properties` GETTER — once per column on the same vertex.

**Exactly equivalent, which is why this needed no owner decision** (unlike items 1733 and 1736, both
still waiting on a semantics call): the same getter on the same element, and nothing in a projection
expression can write, so the bag cannot change between two columns of one row.

#### Measured at 1500 runs — the rep count item 1740 established as the minimum

Three alternated rounds, one arm per build, each arm asserted present in the dist first:

```text
  shape                       base                hoist (A/B arm)    verdict
  wideproj (5 direct cols)    630.4 634.6         502.3 494.7 493.4  1.27x, DISJOINT
  wide2    (2 direct cols)    516.6 495.9         402.1 378.5 400.5  1.29x, DISJOINT
  narrow1  (1 direct col)     285.3 326.2 289.2   286.9 283.8 318.9  FLAT (the guard)
  hoprows  (a DIFFERENT rung) 470.3 475.3 479.4   500.5 493.7 482.2  ~4% SLOWER
```

⚠️ **THE SHIPPED CODE IS NOT THE ARM THAT WAS MEASURED, SO IT WAS RE-MEASURED.** `no-nested-ternary`
rejected the combined form, so the loop was split in two — one per mode, which also drops a
per-COLUMN flag test and leaves the non-hoist branch **byte-identical to the pre-change loop**. The
shipped form is BETTER than the arm on every row, the control cost included:

```text
  shape      SHIPPED (two loops)      vs the same base      verdict
  wideproj   484.0 491.2 484.7        630.4 634.6           1.30x
  wide2      364.1 381.2 394.4        516.6 495.9           1.32x
  narrow1    292.8 283.3 285.9        285.3 326.2 289.2     flat
  hoprows    487.2 481.6 487.9        470.3 475.3 479.4     ~2% slower (was ~4%)
```

⚠️ **THE GUARD IS LOAD-BEARING AND WAS FOUND BY MEASURING, NOT BY FORESIGHT.** The first version
hoisted unconditionally and measured the single-column shape **~10% worse** (base 284/288/327
against 285/318/320) — at width 1 the hoist saves no repeated getter and adds one local.
`RETURN <one column>` is far too common a shape to pay that for a wider one's win, so the hoist is
gated on more than one direct key, decided once per query from `directKeys`. Guarded, width 1 is
flat.

⚠️ **AND THE WIDTH LADDER IS WHY THE MECHANISM IS KNOWN.** `wide2` gains the same RATIO as
`wideproj` but a smaller ABSOLUTE amount (~113 ms against ~146), which is what a per-column saving
looks like once the base differs. A single shape would have given the ratio and no way to tell a
per-column cost from a per-row one.

#### The cost side, stated rather than buried

`hoprows` takes `hopProjection` and **cannot reach the changed code**, yet it measures ~2% slower.
That is the `executor-edits-perturb` toll this family charges — the audit records 1.08-1.24x for it,
so ~1.04x is the mild end. Taken because a multi-column `RETURN` is a far more common shape than
that margin is large, which is exactly the trade `executor-edits-perturb` says to make explicitly.

### Item 1742 — ❌ **NOT SHIPPED ~~in this form~~: the TWO-LOOP hoist in the TOP-K arm is 1.21x on three columns but costs the SINGLE-column shape 7.6%, ranges disjoint both ways.** ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED — item 1743 took the fix this entry prescribes (the mode choice at MODULE scope, one loop) and SHIPPED it at 1.35x with the single-column shape FLAT. This entry's diagnosis stands; its verdict applies only to the two-loop spelling.** ⚠️ **The regressed path's code is BYTE-IDENTICAL to before — it is the CLOSURE growing a second loop, not the code it runs.** And item 1741 shipped only because its narrow path happened to stay flat; the same standard says no here

Item 1741 shipped a per-row bag hoist in `node-scan.ts`'s main projection closure. Two sibling
closures in the same file carry a byte-identical loop, so the obvious next step was to apply it
there.

#### First: WHICH closure runs, verified by counter rather than by route name

All three closures are returned by the SAME detector, so `routes-fired`'s field name cannot tell them
apart — `wideproj`, `topkwide`, `defwide` and an `ORDER BY` on a non-output column all report
`nodeProjection`. Injected a per-closure counter and ran each shape:

```text
  shape                                   closures entered
  wideproj   (no ORDER BY)                {}                 -> the MAIN closure (hoisted at 1741)
  defwide    (ORDER BY, no LIMIT)         {}                 -> the MAIN closure
  defoffcol  (ORDER BY a non-output col)  {}                 -> the MAIN closure
  topkwide   (ORDER BY … LIMIT 10)        { topk: 78 }       -> topKNodeWalk
```

Two things fell out. **`topKNodeWalk` is the only reachable sibling**, and **`deferredSortedNodeWalk`
never fired on any of the four shapes** — so its copy of the loop was left alone rather than
optimized blind. A closure that cannot be triggered cannot be measured, and an unmeasured change to
one is the thing this audit exists to prevent.

#### Measured, 1500 runs, three alternated rounds, base = item 1741's shipped HEAD

```text
  shape                        base                topkhoist           verdict
  topkwide  (3 direct cols)    494.5 501.3 495.5   408.1 405.0 418.1   1.21x, DISJOINT
  topknarrow(1 direct col)     381.1 360.2 391.2   401.3 410.0 415.8   7.6% WORSE, DISJOINT
  wideproj  (already hoisted)  482.7 491.4 488.0   484.4 490.3 499.1   flat
```

#### ⚠️ THE MECHANISM, AND WHY IT IS THE INTERESTING PART

`topknarrow` has ONE direct column, so `hoistBag` is false and it takes the `else` branch — **whose
code is byte-identical to the loop that was there before.** It still lost 7.6%, with its range
disjoint from base's. Nothing it executes changed; what changed is that **`project` now contains two
loops instead of one**, and a bigger closure body inlines worse.

That is `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`, which records the same effect at a far larger magnitude
("a walk INLINE in a returned closure gives UNRELATED queries a new slow mode, 4x") and prescribes
the fix: **hoist to module scope.** Here that would mean lifting both loop variants out of `project`
as module-level functions and choosing one per query — but `project` closes over `cols`, `fns`,
`directKeys`, `env`, `binding`, `nodeVar`, `allDirect` and `width`, so passing them means an args
object or eight parameters, each with its own cost. **Designed, not measured, and recorded as the
thing to try if this is revisited.**

#### Why not ship it anyway

- **7.6% is above this family's own withdrawal bar**: item 312 withdrew `addVertex` at 7.4%.
- **It is ~4x the cost item 1741 accepted** (~2%, and on an UNRELATED rung) for a _smaller_ win
  (1.21x against 1.30x).
- **`ORDER BY … LIMIT` on one column is a common serving shape** — a paged sorted list of ids — so
  the regression lands somewhere real, not on a probe artifact.
- ⚠️ And it clarifies item 1741 retrospectively: **that one shipped because its narrow path measured
  FLAT, not because the guard makes a split free.** The guard prevents the width-1 _hoist_ from
  costing anything; it does nothing about the closure growing. Those are two separate costs, and only
  the first is what the guard was for.

### Item 1743 — ✅ **SHIPPED: the fix item 1742 prescribed and did not measure — move the mode choice to MODULE scope, keep ONE loop. 1.35x on a three-column `ORDER BY … LIMIT`, the single-column shape FLAT, both main-closure shapes FLAT.** Better than the two-loop form it replaces (1.21x) and without its 7.6% regression

Item 1742 declined the per-row bag hoist in `topKNodeWalk` and diagnosed why precisely: the
single-column path lost 7.6% **although its code was byte-identical**, because `project` grew a
second loop and a bigger closure inlines worse (`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`). Its own note
prescribed the fix — _"lift both loop variants to MODULE scope so this closure stays small"_ — and
recorded it as designed, not measured, because `project` closes over eight names.

**The lighter form sidesteps that cost entirely: ONE module function, not two loops.**

```ts
const readDirect = (bag: Record<string, unknown> | undefined, v: Vertex, dk: string): unknown =>
  bag === undefined ? propOf(v, dk) : (bag[dk] ?? null);
```

The closure grows by **one local** and keeps **one loop**, and the per-column **call count is
unchanged** — `readDirect` replaces the `propOf` call that was already there. So nothing in the
closure-size mechanism is triggered, and the hoist's saving (the `properties` getter, once per row
instead of once per column) is kept.

#### Measured, 1500 runs, three alternated rounds, base = HEAD after item 1742

```text

  topkwide   (3 direct cols)     507.9 492.6         364.6 371.7 363.9   1.35x, DISJOINT
  topknarrow (1 direct col)      364.5 369.5         379.5 360.5 357.5   FLAT
  wideproj   (main closure)      499.3 482.1 479.4   483.4 484.4 495.1   FLAT
  narrow1    (main closure)      288.0 290.2 289.4   288.5 286.9 286.2   FLAT
```

**1.35x beats the two-loop form's 1.21x**, which is the part worth noticing: the module-scope shape
is not merely a way to avoid the regression, it is also faster on the target. Both main-closure
shapes are flat, so the change is confined to the arm it edits — and that pair is the control that
says so.

⚠️ **THE FILE NOW HOLDS TWO SPELLINGS OF ONE OPTIMIZATION**, and that is deliberate: the main
closure splits into two loops (item 1741, measured 1.30x with its narrow shape FLAT) while this arm
calls `readDirect`. There is no defect in 1741's split to fix, and rewriting a shipped win to match a
style is a change with a measured risk and no measured gain. Recorded at the site, with the note that
`readDirect` is the better shape to adopt if the main closure is ever touched for another reason.

### Item 1744 — ❌ **FLAT on the third and last closure: the bag hoist buys ~2% in `deferredSortedNodeWalk`, with the arm's range ENCLOSING the base's.** The lever is now SWEPT across every site of its kind in the GQL executor — shipped at two, flat at one. ⚠️ **And reaching this closure at all needed a counter: a parameterized `LIMIT` and a `LIMIT 0` do NOT arrive here, a windowed sort with a FAULTABLE item does**

Items 1741 and 1743 shipped a per-row property-bag hoist in two of `node-scan.ts`'s three
multi-column row loops. This is the third, and the sweep's completion.

#### First: is there anywhere else at all?

Searched every `row[cols[i]] = …` loop in the GQL executor. **Only `node-scan.ts` has them** — three
sites. The hop and distinct rungs project a SINGLE value per row (`hop-projection.ts`'s `take` holds
one `directKey`, not an array), so they have no per-column redundancy to remove. The lever's whole
surface is those three loops.

#### Reaching the third closure took a counter, and most candidate shapes miss it

`deferredSortedNodeWalk` runs when `outputColumnSorts` returns `null`. Reading its decline
conditions and testing each with a per-closure counter:

```text
  case                                                      closures entered
  RETURN … ORDER BY a LIMIT $lim   (parameterized window)   {}
  RETURN … ORDER BY a LIMIT 0                               {}
  RETURN … ORDER BY a SKIP $sk                              parse error (unsupported)
  RETURN n.k + 1 AS a, n.n AS b ORDER BY b LIMIT 5          { deferred: 10 }   ✓
  RETURN n.k + 1 AS x, n.n, n.s, n.k ORDER BY b LIMIT 5     { deferred: 20 }   ✓
```

So the route is **a WINDOWED sort with an item that can FAULT** — `n.k + 1` is arith, which
`cannotFault` refuses. The realistic form is the wide one:
`RETURN p.name, p.age, p.salary * 1.1 AS raise ORDER BY p.name LIMIT 20`. Item 1742 reported this
closure as never firing; it fires, just not for any of the four shapes tried there.

#### Measured, 1500 runs, three alternated rounds

```text
  shape                                  base          deferhoist          verdict
  defsortwide   (3 direct + 1 computed)  637.1 632.7   622.8 614.1 644.1   ~2%, arm ENCLOSES base
  defsortnarrow (1 direct + 1 computed)  622.0 634.6   612.7 612.2 606.0   flat (guard off anyway)
```

### Item 1745 — ✅ **SHIPPED, and it refutes a "no cost" comment at the site: `extend`'s conditional SPREAD cost 1.14x on `fold`, 1.08x on `coalesce` and 1.7% on a 3-hop count, every range DISJOINT.** One line, and `extend` runs once per traverser per step, so it reaches the whole Gremlin engine

Windowed-profiled four Gremlin shapes. `extend` kept appearing across all of them — 12.6% of
`folded`, 9.8% of `coalesced`, 6.7% of `projected`, 4.9% of `valuemapped` — which made it
cross-cutting rather than one step's problem. Its body ended with a conditional spread:

```javascript
export const extend = (prev, value) => ({
  value,
  path: prev.path === NO_PATH ? NO_PATH : [...prev.path, value],
  loopCount: prev.loopCount,
  tags: prev.tags,
  // Propagate the sack … so the common no-sack path carries `undefined` (no cost).
  ...(prev.sack === undefined ? {} : { sack: prev.sack }),
});
```

⚠️ **"(no cost)" is a claim about cost, and it was wrong.** Two things it misses: the no-sack path
allocates an **empty object on every extend**, and a **spread inside an object literal denies V8 a
fixed hidden class for the whole literal** — so every field of every traverser is built on the slow
path, not just the sack.

#### Equivalence established by reading every consumer, before measuring

`sack` has exactly one reader: `sack.ts`'s `const current = t.sack === undefined ? cfg.value : t.sack`,
which tests the **value**. Nothing in the repo asks `'sack' in t`, and nothing enumerates a
traverser's keys. So `sack: prev.sack` — an explicit `undefined` instead of an absent key — is
indistinguishable here. **No owner decision needed**, unlike items 1733 and 1736.

#### Measured, 300 reps, three alternated rounds, one arm per build

```text
  shape        base                      fixed                     verdict
  folded        283.3  285.1  276.5       255.8  248.8  247.0       1.14x, DISJOINT
  coalesced    3244.8 3244.9 3224.5      2996.5 3186.0 2938.2       1.08x, DISJOINT
  hopcount3     477.9  481.6  478.4       473.5  473.7  468.6       1.7%,  DISJOINT
  control (V().count(), no `extend`)      7.2 6.8 7.0 -> 4.3 7.1 7.3   flat
```

**Every `extend`-using shape improved and every range is disjoint** — including `hopcount3`'s 1.7%,
which is small but separated in all three rounds, exactly what a per-traverser constant looks like on
a shape dominated by other work.

⚠️ **THE CONTROL IS WEAK AND SAYS SO.** `V().count()` genuinely never calls `extend` (the source uses
`startTraverser`), which makes it the right control in principle — but it runs in ~7 ms, where this
harness cannot resolve anything. It establishes only "no gross regression". The real evidence is the
three disjoint improvements and the fact that the change is one field in one function.

run because `extend` builds every traverser in the engine. `bun run check` 0 read through
`${pipestatus[1]}`.

⚠️ **AND IT INTRODUCED A POLYMORPHISM WITHOUT NOTICING — see item 1746.** Giving `extend` a
plain `sack` field made it 5 fields while `startTraverser` stayed at 4, so source and extended

### Item 1749 — ⚠️ **I MEASURED A 1.11x THAT MEANT NOTHING, AND THE PROBE COULD NOT TELL ME: for a `count(*)` shape its `sink` assertion checks the ROW count, which is 1 per run however wrong the answer is.** The ablation had stopped filtering entirely — 20,000 instead of 207 — and timed identically. **Fixed the instrument and verified the fix has teeth.** `satisfies`' eleven-section chain is left UNPRICED, honestly

`satisfies` is the GQL predicate evaluator and the cross-cutting frame on that side — **44.3% of
`hopfilter`**, 22.4% of `existssub`. Reading it found **eleven sequential sections** per element
(`props`, `eqProps`, `cmpProps`, `pathProps`, `memberProps`, `nullProps`, `labelTests`,
`truthProps`, `notTruthProps`, `typedTests`, `truthTestProps`, then `where`), of which a single
`WHERE a.k = 5` populates one.

#### The call count first, because a share is uninterpretable without it

A counter said **20,000 calls per query** — once per candidate, not per survivor. So 188.6 ms over
30M calls is **6.3 ns per call**, which _implies_ the chain is nearly free. ⚠️ **That inference was
about to become the finding.** It was tested instead.

#### The ablation, and why its answer was worthless

Deleting the ten unpopulated sections measured `hopfilter` **391.8 → 353.2, 1.11x, ranges
DISJOINT** — an apparently clean refutation of the arithmetic. `existssub` went **607.8 → 1685.7**,
2.8x SLOWER, which is what prompted a second look.

**The arm was not filtering at all.** The predicate for both shapes lives in a DELETED section, not
in `pred.where`:

```text
            base    ablated
  hopfilter  207     20000
  existssub  207     20000
```

So `hopfilter`'s 1.11x is an engine that matched everything measured against one that filtered, and
`existssub`'s 2.8x is 20,000 candidates each running the EXISTS subquery instead of 207. **Both
numbers are void.** The assumption that only `where` was populated was asserted from reading, never
checked — the counter counted CALLS, which is a different question.

#### ⚠️⚠️ THE INSTRUMENT COULD NOT CATCH IT, AND THAT IS THE REAL FINDING

`runtime-profile-probe`'s guard is `if (sink === 0) throw` — and its own comment says why: _"a shape
that silently returned nothing would profile the error path and look like a result."_ **It catches
EMPTY, not WRONG.** For a `count(*)` shape `sink` is the number of ROWS, and a count query returns
exactly one row whatever the count is — so `sink` read `12` in both arms, identically, while the
answer was off by a factor of 97.

**Fixed, with the split that the engine's own guarantees dictate:**

```text
  rowsPerRun  asserted for EVERY shape — a wrong answer almost always changes how many rows survive
  answer      asserted ONLY where the first value is deterministic: a count(*) (one row) or an
              ORDERED projection. ⚠️ NOT for an unordered row shape — `order-is-unspecified` is this
              engine's documented stance, so pinning the first row of `RETURN n.k` would assert
              something it is free to change.
```

Fifteen shapes carry verified expectations. **The fix was mutation-tested with the exact ablation
that fooled the old guard: both `hopfilter` and `existssub` now THROW** instead of being timed.

#### What is left open, stated rather than filed

**The eleven-section chain remains UNPRICED.** The arithmetic says 6.3 ns/call leaves little; the
ablation that would have tested it was invalid. A valid ceiling needs an arm that deletes only
sections genuinely empty _for the shape being measured_, which means first reading which `CPredicate`
fields each shape populates — not assuming. The "compile a specialized closure per predicate shape"
refactor is therefore **unpriced, not rejected**.

#### ⚠️ An eighth anchor failure, and a new flavour: a COMMENT cannot be a dist marker

The first dist discriminator was a `// ZZ-ABLATED` comment — **count 0 in both arms, because the
bundler strips comments.** The second, `pred.truthTestProps`, occurs **3 times** (the compiler builds
that field). The working one counts `labelTestsHold(` and `typedTestsHold(`, which are called only
from `satisfies`, exactly once each, so the ablation takes both to zero. **Eighth failure this
session, eighth caught.**

#### Gates

`bun run check` 0 read through `${pipestatus[1]}`. `predicates.ts` verified identical to HEAD — the
arm was built, measured, invalidated and reverted. The only change is the probe's assertions.

### Item 1750 — **the ceiling item 1749 left open, measured with a VALID arm this time: `satisfies`' eleven-section chain is FREE on a simple filter and worth ~8% on a subquery shape.** Priced and declined under the 10% bar. ⚠️ **The probe's new answer assertion did its job twice — it passed the valid arm and the build broke loudly on an invalid one**

Item 1749 priced nothing because its ablation deleted the section holding the actual predicate. The
fix was to stop assuming which sections a shape populates and **census them**:

```text
  MATCH … WHERE a.k = 5                            ->  eqProps ALONE
  the same with EXISTS { … }                       ->  where + eqProps
  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P)  (no predicate)          ->  NOTHING, and it still calls `satisfies`
```

So on a typical query **nine or ten of the eleven sections are an `undefined` check that always
fails** — which is exactly why a compile-time specialization looks attractive.

#### The valid arm, and the two instrument checks that made it valid

Deleted only the nine sections the census proved empty, keeping `props`, `eqProps` and `where`.
**Answer-equivalence confirmed before timing** — 20000 / 207 / 207, matching base — by the
assertions item 1749 added. 1500 runs, three alternated rounds:

```text
  shape       base                  thin                  verdict
  existssub   598.3 617.5 611.8     565.2 563.2 577.3     1.08x, ranges DISJOINT
  hopfilter   386.9 388.5 391.6     386.6 393.5 392.2     FLAT
  hopall      10.4 … 14.3           10.5 … 14.9           ⚠️ BIMODAL, unreadable
```

**Free on a simple filter; ~8% on a subquery shape.** The difference has a mechanism: `existssub`
calls `satisfies` for the outer predicate _and_ inside the `EXISTS`, so the per-call constant gets
more calls to show up in.

**Declined.** 8% is under the ~10% this repo requires from a shared harness, and the change would
move all eleven sections behind a compile-time dispatch — a large refactor of the predicate
evaluator for the shape where the win is _largest_. Recorded at `satisfies` with the numbers so the
next reader sees the price rather than the opportunity.

#### ⚠️ `hopall` looked like the perfect ceiling row and is useless

No predicate at all, so the chain runs to do nothing — the purest possible measurement. In fact it is
**BIMODAL** (both arms span ~10.4-10.7 and ~13.7-14.9, the same hazard item 1747 found on
`filterchain`) and at **~7 µs per query** far too cheap to resolve anything. Recorded at the site so
it is not reached for again.

#### The instrument earned its keep twice in one item

- **It passed the valid arm**, which is what licensed the timing at all.
- **An invalid intermediate failed loudly**: a first attempt terminated each deleted block at the
  next `  }`, which is a NESTED loop's brace — the file stopped compiling, the dist was never
  produced, and the probe died with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` instead of timing a stale build. Redone
  with real brace matching plus a balanced-brace assertion. ⚠️ **A stale dist is the failure mode
  that would have produced numbers**, and only the missing artifact prevented it — `fuzzers-read-built-dists`
  is the same hazard from the other direction.

### Item 1752 — ⚠️ **I PUBLISHED A WRONG CLAIM ABOUT THE PROJECT'S TOOLING AND IT WAS MY OWN PIPELINE: `bun test` exits 1 correctly; item 1751's "exits 0" was `| tail` swallowing the status.** The full 68 failures are now attributed — **every one environmental, none from this stretch's 30 lines**

Item 1751 reported that a root `bun test` "reports 68 failures and exits 0", and drew the conclusion
that _"anything gating on this command's status is green while red."_ **That conclusion is false and
the observation was an artefact of my own command.**

The first run was `… bun test 2>&1 | tail -12`. **A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's**,
and `tail` succeeds — so the 0 was `tail`'s. Re-run without the pipe, appending the status directly:
**`EXIT=1`**. `bun test` reports failure correctly.

⚠️ **This is the specific trap CLAUDE.md spells out** — _"piping clippy into `grep -c` and chaining
with `&&` takes the exit status from `grep`, which succeeds when it finds errors. That has let broken
lint through twice."_ I hit it on the verification pass, with `tail` instead of `grep`, and then wrote
it up as a defect in the tooling rather than in my command. **Two instrument errors in one tick, same
pipeline: the truncation hid 65 of 68 failures, and the pipe hid the exit code.**

non-comment lines in `node-scan.ts` and `runtime.ts`, both of whose packages were separately green

### Item 1754 — ⚠️⚠️ **A HASH INDEX MAKES A LOW-SELECTIVITY RANGE 1.9x SLOWER** ~~: the range-seek route is taken whenever an index exists, with no selectivity gate.~~ ⚠️ **THE DIAGNOSIS IS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED AT ITEM 1755: a gate EXISTS (`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION = 1/8`, measured at items 409/173). The regression is the cost of computing the gate's INPUT — `countRange` is O(distinct values in range) — so it tracks the column's CARDINALITY, not its selectivity. The 1.9x measurement stands; the explanation does not.** Found because ⚠️ **NEITHER frame screen has ever built an index**, so every target this audit has nominated came from the SCAN path — and with an index the hot frames invert to the PLANNER

`point` (`WHERE n.n = 12345`, one row of 20,000) was costing **~250 µs per query** — 12.5 ns a
vertex, which is a scan, not a lookup. The reason is the instrument: **`runtime-profile-probe.mjs`
and `runtime-profile-gremlin-probe.mjs` — this repo's two unpriced-frame screens, the instruments
that pick targets — never call `createIndex`. Nor does `bench.ts`.** Ten other probes do, so the
capability is exercised; the SCREENS are blind to it.

#### What indexing is worth, and the frame inversion

Same fixture, same queries, `createIndex({ on: 'vertex', kind: 'hash', keys: [...] })`, µs/query:

```text
  shape                      no index    only `k`    both        verdict
  point   (n = 12345)          279.4       247.4       8.9       ~31x, and ONLY with `n` indexed
  band    (k = 5, 207 rows)    258.6        14.6      14.5       ~18x, and ONLY with `k` indexed
  range   (n < 10, 10 rows)    234.5       231.0      14.8       ~16x, and ONLY with `n` indexed
```

**Each shape improves only when its OWN key is indexed** — the `only k` column is the control that
establishes it, and it was added because the first run indexed both keys and made `range`'s
improvement unattributable.

⚠️ ~~**AND THE HOT FRAMES CHANGE IDENTITY.**~~ **REFUTED AT ITEM 1761 — that came from an ELEVEN-SAMPLE profile, and the indexed timings here are warm-up inflation: `point` is 0.2 µs/query at 3,000,000 reps, not 8.9 at 1,500, so the win is ~1250x and not 31x. `compileLinear` runs TWICE per 500 queries (the plan cache works), so planning is not a per-query cost at all.** Unindexed, the profile is the executor: `propOf`,
anonymous scan frames, `fastPath`. Indexed, it is **`compileLinear`, `parseCached`, `isIndexed`,
`hopSeekWithKey`** — execution has become so cheap that **PLANNING dominates**. So on an indexed
workload the target is the planner, and the screens have never been able to say so.

#### ⚠️ THE DEFECT: no selectivity gate on the range route

`range` is a hash index serving a `<` predicate, which raised the question of what the route costs
when the range is NOT selective. Same predicate form, 1000x less selective:

```text
  n < 10      (10 of 20,000)      234.5 µs  ->   14.8 µs     16x FASTER
  n < 10000   (10,000 of 20,000)  496-503   ->  935-992      1.9x SLOWER
```

Ranges disjoint; both arms answer-asserted (10 and 10,000 rows) by the probe, so neither is the
wrong-answer artefact item 1749 was caught by. **The route is taken because an index exists, not
because it pays** — a textbook index-selectivity crossover with no cost gate on this side.

`cost-estimator` records a `cost.rs` cardinality estimator for fast-path routing; whatever guards the
equality seeks, the range route on this path is reaching a 1.9x regression on an ordinary query
(`WHERE n.n < <half the range>`). **OPEN, not built** — the fix is a gate, and the crossover point
needs locating before one can be written.

#### What this changes about target selection

Every item in this stretch picked its target from a screen that measures only unindexed scans. That
is not wrong — an unindexed scan is a real workload — but it is **half the surface**, and the half it
omits has a different bottleneck (planning) and at least one regression (above). **NEW PERMANENT
INSTRUMENT — `packages/native/indexed-screen-probe.mjs`**, with `INDEXED=0|k|1`, per-shape row-count
assertions, and the selectivity ladder.

### Item 1755 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1754'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG: the selectivity gate EXISTS. The 1.9x regression is the cost of computing the gate's INPUT — `countRange` is O(distinct values in range) — and it therefore tracks the column's CARDINALITY, not its selectivity.** Proved with a same-selectivity, different-cardinality twin. The fix is an early-terminating count, designed and not built

Item 1754 measured a hash index making `WHERE n.n < 10000` **1.9x slower** than no index, and
concluded the range-seek route "is taken because an index exists, not because it pays — … with no
cost gate on this side." **The measurement stands. The diagnosis was wrong.**

Reading the route rather than inferring it:

```typescript
export const SEEK_MAX_FRACTION = 1 / 8;           // matching.ts
const SEEK_FLOOR_VERTICES = 4_096;
export const seekIsWorthIt = (graph, label, count) => { … }
```

**A gate exists, and it is carefully calibrated** — its own comment brackets the break-even with two
independent measurements (item 409's ~18%, `hop-projection`'s `SEEK_MARGIN` at 16.25% "reached after
a plain guard measured a 3.1x REGRESSION"), and deliberately ships the lower 12.5%. My entry asserted
its absence from a grep that searched for the wrong names.

#### So why is a 50%-selective range still 1.9x slower when the gate must decline it?

Because **the gate's input is not free.** `PropertyIndex.countRange` sums bucket sizes over the
matching distinct values — its own doc says _"O(distinct values in range), so a planner can compare
candidates before materializing the winner."_ On `n`, which is `i` and therefore **20,000 distinct
values**, `n < 10000` walks **10,000 index entries** to produce the number the gate compares — then
the gate declines and the scan runs anyway. **The query pays the count AND the scan.**

#### The twin that proves it: same selectivity, different cardinality

```text
  query            distinct   rows     no index      indexed        verdict
  n.n < 10000       20,000    10,000   496-503 µs    935-992 µs     1.9x SLOWER
  n.k < 48              97     9,906   470-501 µs    448-455 µs     no regression
```

**Same ~50% selectivity, same ~10,000 rows, opposite verdicts.** The only variable is how many
DISTINCT values the range spans — 10,000 against 48. That is `countRange`'s complexity exactly, and
it rules out the seek itself, the gate, and the selectivity as explanations.

It also re-reads item 1754's ladder correctly: the apparent crossover at ~8.5% on `n` is not the gate
mis-calibrated at 12.5%, it is **the point where `countRange`'s cost on a 20,000-value column
overtakes the seek's benefit.** The gate's threshold is right for what it measures; the measurement
has a cost the gate does not account for.

#### The fix, designed and NOT built

`seekIsWorthIt` only compares `count` against `bucket / 8`, so **the exact count is never needed —
only whether it exceeds the cap.** An early-terminating `countRangeAtMost(key, bound, cap)` makes the
gate's input **O(min(matches, cap))** instead of O(matches), which bounds the waste on a declined
seek to one-eighth of the bucket.

⚠️ One caveat for whoever builds it: `count` is also used to rank several candidates and pick the
most selective. A capped count cannot order two candidates that both exceed the cap — but both would
be declined anyway, so ranking is unaffected for any candidate that can be admitted. That needs
asserting in a test rather than assumed, which is why this is designed and not built here.

**NEW PROBE SHAPE — `rangelowcard`**, the cardinality twin, kept because it is the control that
separates cardinality from selectivity and nothing else in the corpus does.

diagnosis, and this entry.

### Item 1756 — ✅ **SHIPPED: cap the range candidate's count at the gate's own threshold — 1.60x on the regression item 1755 diagnosed, every control flat.** The change is **provably behaviour-identical**, not merely safe, and the mutation test says so

Item 1755 established the mechanism: `countRange` is **O(distinct values in range)** and its only
consumer is a gate comparing the count against `bucket * SEEK_MAX_FRACTION`. On a high-cardinality
column the estimate cost more than the decision saved — `WHERE n.n < 10000` over 20,000 distinct
values walked 10,000 index entries to produce a number, the gate declined, and the scan ran anyway.

**The fix is to stop counting once the answer cannot matter.**

```typescript
countRangeAtMost(key, bound, cap) {           // PropertyIndex
  …
  for (const value of this.rangeValues(idx, bound)) {
    count += idx.buckets.get(value)!.size;
    if (count > cap) { return count; }        // past the cap the exact value is dead information
  }
  return count;
}
```

#### ⚠️ WHY IT IS BEHAVIOUR-IDENTICAL, AND WHY THE SUB-FLOOR CASE IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT

`seedVertices` takes the **smallest** count among candidates, then `seekIsWorthIt` declines anything
over `bucket * 1/8`. So:

- **At or below the cap the count is exact** → ranking among ADMITTED candidates is unchanged.
- **Above the cap every candidate is declined** → whichever wins a ranking among them is never used,
  so the ordering is not consulted.
- ⚠️ **EXCEPT below `SEEK_FLOOR_VERTICES`, where the gate admits a seek at ANY count** — there the
  ranking between two over-cap candidates WOULD decide the seed, and a capped count cannot order
  them. `rangeCountCap` returns `Infinity` below the floor, keeping those graphs on the exact count.
  That case is what turns "probably harmless" into "identical", and it is the part a reviewer should
  check first.

#### Measured, N=400, three alternated rounds, one build per arm, µs/query

```text
  shape                        base                   capped                 verdict
  rangewide (the regression)   947.3  900.6  901.3    562.5  584.2  565.8    1.60x, DISJOINT
  rangelowcard (card. twin)    463.5  481.5  453.4    447.2  456.4  451.4    flat
  range     (selective seek)    33.0   37.6   36.7     35.8   33.5   34.0    flat
  point                         24.4   25.0   25.3     24.8   29.4   24.9    flat
  band                          42.5   36.0   37.5     39.8   35.9   37.2    flat
```

Every row answer-asserted by the probe, so no arm is the wrong-answer artefact of item 1749. The
residual against _no_ index is ~1.13x (565 against ~500) rather than 1.0x, because the capped walk
still covers `bucket / 8` = 2,500 entries before declining — bounded by the cap now instead of by the
range's width, which is the whole change.

#### ⚠️ THE TEST, AND ITS TEETH — because the change is invisible to every other test

A seed only has to be a **superset**, so breaking the count cannot change any query answer: the gql
suite, the differential tests and all seven fuzzers pass either way. `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`
is the rule, so the arithmetic is tested directly — five cases covering exactness at and below the
cap, the `> cap` report, equality with `countRange` at an infinite cap, bucket-size (not value-count)
termination, and the unindexed `undefined`.

**Teeth verified by mutation:** removing the early return — the one edit that makes the fix inert —
fails **2 of the 5**. The assertion that catches it is the one asserting the capped answer is
`< 400` (the exact total), not merely `> cap`; a test checking only the lower bound would have
passed the mutant.

```text
  traversal                                              no index    indexed    verdict
  V().hasLabel(P).has('n', lt(10000)).count()  20k dist    127.2      644.7     5.07x SLOWER
  V().hasLabel(P).has('k', lt(48)).count()        97 dist    203.8      124.7     1.63x faster
```

#### ⚠️ A FALSE COST CLAIM IN THE DOC, AND IT IS THE LICENCE FOR THE COST

`seedForStep`'s comment says the returned `count` is _"an O(1) estimate and `build()` is not called,
so asking costs nothing (audit item 234)"_ — and that is **why a count shortcut asks freely before
`seedFromIndex` runs.** It is true for `eq`/`within` (`countEquals` is a bucket-size read) and
**false for a range**, where `countRange` is O(distinct values in range). Corrected in place with the
numbers; same class as item 1745's "(no cost)" and item 1748's refuted reason.

#### The cap, derived — and why GQL's does NOT transfer

GQL's cap is the label bucket, fixed and known at the seed site. Here
`seekIsWorthIt(count, scan, total)` is called two ways:

```text
  line 587   seekIsWorthIt(candidate.count, sourceSize, sourceSize)   threshold = sourceSize/8
  line 650   seekIsWorthIt(seek.count, scan, sourceSize)              threshold = scan/8, scan ≤ sourceSize
```

and `scan = exact?.count ?? sourceSize` — **another candidate's count, discovered after this one**.
So the cap cannot be the gate's actual threshold. It can be **`sourceSize * SEEK_MAX_FRACTION`**,
the largest threshold either site can use: a count above it is declined at both, counts at or below
it stay exact so every ranking among admissible candidates is unchanged, and `Infinity` below
`SEEK_FLOOR_ELEMENTS` preserves the sub-floor admit-anything behaviour exactly — the same three
properties item 1756's entry sets out, re-derived for this call graph rather than assumed from it.

The cap has to thread `rangeCandidate` (**8 call sites** inside `seedForPred`) → `seedForPred` →

signature change with external callers, in the path a count shortcut consults, is its own piece of
work — and the measurement above is what makes it worth doing rather than a guess. **OPEN, with the
design settled and the regression priced.**

### Item 1758 — ✅ **SHIPPED: the Gremlin twin of item 1756's capped range count — 2.39x on the 5.07x regression item 1757 priced, both controls flat.** The cap is `sourceSize`-based, not the gate's threshold, and **that difference is the whole correctness argument**

Item 1757 measured the regression (`has('n', lt(10000))` over 20,000 distinct values: **127.2 µs
with no index, 644.7 with one — 5.07x**) and derived the cap without building it, because the change
threads an exported signature. Built here.

```typescript
export const rangeCap = (sourceSize: number): number =>
  sourceSize < SEEK_FLOOR_ELEMENTS ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : sourceSize * SEEK_MAX_FRACTION;
```

Threaded `rangeCandidate` (**8 call sites**) → `seedForPred` → `seedForStep`, which takes the cap as
an **optional parameter defaulting to `Infinity`** — so the two external callers in `node-values.ts`
are untouched by construction.

#### ⚠️ WHY THE CAP IS NOT THE GATE'S THRESHOLD, which is where GQL's twin does not carry over

`seekIsWorthIt(count, scan, total)` is asked with `scan = exact?.count ?? sourceSize` — **another
candidate's count, discovered after this one** — so the real threshold is unknown when the count is
taken. `sourceSize * SEEK_MAX_FRACTION` is the **largest** threshold either call site can use
(`scan <= sourceSize`), which gives the three properties the substitution needs:

- a count above the cap is declined at **both** sites, so its exact value is dead information;
- counts at or below it are **exact**, so `fromIndex.count < seek.count` still ranks every
  admissible candidate correctly;
- ⚠️ **below `SEEK_FLOOR_ELEMENTS` the gate admits at ANY count**, so there the ranking between two
  over-cap candidates _would_ decide the seed — hence no cap at all below the floor.

#### Measured, three alternated rounds, one build per arm, answers asserted, µs/query

```text
  shape                            base                   capped                 verdict
  rangewide    (20k distinct)      586.7  590.3  613.4    250.2  247.9  246.0    2.39x, DISJOINT
  rangelowcard (97 distinct)       112.3  123.3  126.1    114.1  124.4  118.2    flat
  rangetight   (selective)          32.8   30.4   34.0     31.1   32.0   32.2    flat
```

The remaining gap against _no_ index is ~2.2x (246 against 112.8), down from 5.07x — the residual is
the capped walk of `sourceSize / 8` = 2,500 entries plus the scan, bounded by the cap now instead of
by the range's width.

#### The test, and its teeth — TWO mutants, because one property carries the argument

A seed only has to be a superset, so this is invisible to every answer-based test: the gremlin suite
and all seven fuzzers pass either way. `rangeCap` is therefore exported and tested directly — four
cases covering the sub-floor `Infinity`, the above-floor fraction, the exact floor boundary, and the
relation to the gate's largest threshold.

**Verified with two real mutants:**

```text
  drop the sub-floor Infinity        2 of 4 FAIL   (the property that makes it identical)
  off-by-one on the floor boundary   3 of 4 FAIL
  restored                           4 pass
```

The off-by-one matters in both directions — too low and a sub-floor graph gets capped (changing
which seed it picks), too high and a graph at exactly 4,096 elements keeps the regression.

### Item 1759 — ✅ **SHIPPED: `cap === 0` as "exact seeds only" — 1.29x on a values projection behind a range filter, three controls flat.** The waste item 1757 noticed in passing: both `node-values.ts` callers require `removable`, which a range candidate NEVER is, so they paid an O(distinct) count and discarded it

Item 1757 observed that `seedForStep`'s two external callers check `candidate.removable` and bail
when it is false — and `rangeCandidate` always returns `removable: false`. **So for a range
predicate those callers paid `countRange`'s O(distinct values in range) and threw the answer away.**
Item 1758's cap did not reach them: it defaults to `Infinity` precisely so external callers are
untouched.

**Measured first**, 20,000 vertices, µs/query:

```text
  V().has('n', lt(10000)).values('s')   20k distinct   1033.6 no index  ->  1671.4 indexed   1.62x SLOWER
  V().has('k', lt(48)).values('s')         97 distinct   1088.9         ->  1058.7          flat
```

The cardinality twin going flat is what attributes it to the count rather than the seek, the same
control that identified the mechanism at item 1755.

#### The contract, and why `null` rather than a meaningless count

`cap === 0` now means **"a range seed is of no use to me — do not count it"**, and `rangeCandidate`
returns `null`. Returning `null` instead of a candidate carrying a stopped-early count is what keeps
it honest: those callers already map `null` to "not this shape", and since they would have discarded
a range candidate anyway **the two paths are equivalent by construction.**

⚠️ **Unreachable from `rangeCap`, checked rather than assumed**: it returns `Infinity` below the
floor and `sourceSize / 8` at or above it, so its smallest possible value is **512** at
`SEEK_FLOOR_ELEMENTS`. Only an explicit `0` from a caller wanting exact seeds can land there.

#### Measured, three alternated rounds, answers asserted, µs/query

```text
  shape                         base                      exactonly                 verdict
  valueswide    (the target)    1643.2  1646.7  1656.2    1276.3  1518.5  1231.8    1.29x, DISJOINT
  valueslowcard (card. twin)    1072.4  1046.9  1040.8    1053.5  1056.3  1046.9    flat
  rangewide     (1758's row)     262.7   266.6   246.3     266.3   256.4   248.9    flat
  rangetight    (selective)       31.4    34.1    31.0      29.0    30.5    34.9    flat
```

⚠️ **A ~1.21x residual remains** against no index on `valueswide` (1276 against 1057): this removed
the discarded count, not every index consult on that path. Stated rather than rounded away — the
shape is better, not fixed.

#### The test, and the mutant it was written for

Three cases added: cap 0 suppresses a range seed; **cap 0 still returns an EXACT seed**; an uncapped
call still returns the range seed. The middle one is the one with teeth —

```text
  MUTANT: `cap === 0` suppresses EVERY seed, not just ranges    1 of 7 FAIL
```

— and it is the failure that matters, because such a mutant would **silently disable the
`node-values` fast path the change exists to serve** while passing a test that only checked the
range case. A test asserting only "ranges are suppressed" would have shipped it.

### Item 1760 — **THE INDEX-SEED FAMILY IS CLOSED: the ~1.14x residual item 1759 left is the CAP'S OWN WALK, ~129 µs of 142 accounted for arithmetically — and it cannot be reduced without making the gate UNSOUND.** A correctness floor, not an unfinished optimization

Items 1756/1758/1759 shipped three wins from one mechanism (an estimate costing more than the
decision it informs: GQL 1.60x, Gremlin 2.39x, the values path 1.29x). Item 1759 recorded a residual
rather than rounding it away, so this prices it.

#### The residual is stable, disjoint, and diffuse

```text
  V().has('n', lt(10000)).values('s')     no index   1123.3  1052.4  1037.1  1040.9   median 1046
                                           indexed   1193.1  1183.3  1193.6  1182.7   median 1188
```

**1.14x, ranges disjoint.** But the windowed profiles of the two arms are **compositionally
identical** — `toArray`, `filterStream`, `sourceFromIds`, `projectValues`, `unwrap` in both, no frame
unique to the indexed arm, and `countRangeAtMost` nowhere (it runs once per query, 300 times, which
no profile at this scale can see). The largest single mover is `filterStream` at +18 ms of a +45 ms
total, which is not an attribution so much as a statement that the cost is spread.

#### The arithmetic that does attribute it

The cap is `sourceSize * SEEK_MAX_FRACTION` = **2,500 entries**. Item 1757's own measurement gives
the per-entry rate from the same probe: the uncapped walk cost 644.7 − 127.2 = **517 µs for 10,000
entries, i.e. ~51.7 ns each**. So the capped walk is `2,500 × 51.7 ns` ≈ **129 µs**, against an
observed residual of **142 µs** — **91% accounted for**, by a rate measured on this fixture rather
than carried from elsewhere.

#### ⚠️ AND IT IS A FLOOR, FOR A CORRECTNESS REASON

The obvious next move is to shrink the cap. **It cannot be shrunk below the gate's threshold**, and
the reason is soundness rather than taste:

`countRangeAtMost` returns the running count once it passes the cap, so a count reported from a cap
of `bucket / 64` can be just above `bucket / 64` while the TRUE count is half the bucket. The gate
compares against `bucket / 8` and would **admit** it — materializing exactly the unselective seek
the gate exists to refuse, which is item 409's measured 5.02x and item 1322's 5x. **So
`cap >= the gate's threshold` is a correctness constraint, and `cap = threshold` is already the
minimum.**

The only way past it is a cardinality estimate that does not walk — and the TS planner has none
(item 1755 checked; `hop-projection.ts` declines a different optimization for the same reason).
`PropertyIndex.buckets.size` is an O(1) distinct-value count, but a distinct count does not bound a
RANGE's matches, so it cannot substitute.

**Family closed at three shipped wins.** The remaining 1.14x on an indexed wide range is the price of
a sound gate, documented here so the next reader prices it as a floor instead of re-profiling it —
and the profiles above are what a re-profile would find.

windowing, and this entry.

### Item 1761 — ⚠️ **ITEM 1754'S "THE HOT FRAMES INVERT TO THE PLANNER" IS REFUTED: it came from an ELEVEN-SAMPLE profile.** The plan cache works — `compileLinear` runs **2 times per 500 queries** — and the indexed timings were warm-up inflation: an indexed point lookup is **0.2 µs/query**, not 8.9, so the win is **~1250x and not 31x**

Item 1754 reported that with an index the hot frames become `compileLinear`, `parseCached`,
`isIndexed`, `hopSeekWithKey` — "execution has become so cheap that PLANNING dominates" — and drew
a conclusion about target selection from it. **Three things are wrong with that.**

#### 1. The plan cache works, so planning is not per-query

A counter on `compileLinear` over 500 identical queries against an indexed graph:

```text
  queries 500   compileLinearCalls 2
```

`parseCached` returns the same `Statement` object for repeated text and `planCache` is a `WeakMap`
keyed on the `Query`, so the plan is built **twice in 500 executions**, not once per execution.
Whatever `compileLinear`'s 8.1% in that profile was, it was not a per-query cost.

#### 2. The profile had ELEVEN SAMPLES

Item 1754's indexed `point` window was **26.5 ms across 11 samples, with `post` at 58.9%** — so
every "frame" in it is one or two samples. The entry noted the `post` share and reported the frame
inversion anyway. ⚠️ **A sample count is the first thing to read in a profile, and I read it last.**

#### 3. The indexed timings were warm-up inflation — the win is far larger than reported

```text
  reps          µs/query
  1,500             8.9      ← item 1754's figure
  300,000           0.4
  3,000,000         0.2
```

At 1,500 reps the JIT tiering, the two `compileLinear` calls and the cache fills are amortized over
too little work. **Indexed `point` is 0.2 µs/query**, so against the unindexed ~250 µs the win is
**~1250x, not the ~31x item 1754 recorded.** Its heading is corrected.

#### What the shape actually looks like, at 593 samples

```text
  15.7%  indexCandidates     8.4%  fastPath         5.9%  reviveParams
   9.9%  plan                7.8%  (anonymous)      4.7%  query
   9.6%  hopSeekWithKey      7.0%  countEquals
```

A **flat mix** of seeding, route dispatch and per-call setup, with no dominant term — which is what a
0.2 µs query looks like: the engine does a dozen small things and the per-call entry path _is_ the
query. **No lever here**, and that is a result rather than a shrug: it says an indexed point lookup
is at its floor, so the index-seed family's remaining cost (item 1760's 1.14x on wide ranges) is the
only indexed-path target left, and it is a correctness floor.

#### The method lesson, which is the reusable part

**Eleven samples produced a confident structural claim that survived into a committed entry, and the
arithmetic needed to doubt it was one counter away.** `prof-summary.mjs` prints the sample count on
its first line precisely so this cannot happen; the fix is to read it before the ranking, and to
distrust any window under a few hundred samples — especially one where `post` (the profiler itself)
is the largest frame.

### Item 1762 — **THE UNINDEXED REGRESSION PASS the index-seed family owed: 18 shapes across both engines, NO regression.** Every measurement in items 1756-1760 was taken on an INDEXED fixture, and the four files they changed are on the unindexed path too

Items 1756/1758/1759 shipped three wins across **four source files, one of them in core**
(`PropertyIndex.ts`, `matching.ts`, `index-seed.ts`, `node-values.ts`) — and ⚠️ **every number in
that family came from an indexed fixture.** The two frame screens are unindexed (item 1754), so the
path most queries actually take was never re-measured. Item 1747 established the method for exactly
this and its caveat; this applies both.

Pre-family (`ff1783b8~1`, extracted with `git show` rather than a checkout) against HEAD, two
alternated rounds, one build of all three packages per arm, with a dist assertion requiring BOTH
`countRangeAtMost` (gql) and `rangeCap` (gremlin) to agree on the arm:

```text
  gql    distinct  hopall  hopfilter  join  optional  sortedpage        all flat
  gql    existssub 1.05x · grouped 1.01x · point 1.05x · wideproj 1.05x  nominally FASTER
  grem   coalesced  filterchain  folded  hopcount3  repeated  selected  valuesonly   all flat
  grem   hophas 1.03x                                                    nominally SLOWER
```

**5 of 18 rows had disjoint arm ranges, every one at or below 1.05x** — and at two readings per arm
a disjoint verdict is far too easy to reach, which is the caveat item 1747 wrote into the sweep
driver after `filterchain` turned out to be bimodal.

#### The one SLOWER row, re-measured properly

A regression matters more than a small win, so `hophas` got its own run — 300 reps, 9 readings per
arm, three alternated rounds:

```text
  prefam  275.8 278.8 283.2 284.9 285.2 285.8 288.2 288.7 291.9   median 285.2
  head    277.7 279.3 279.7 280.3 282.0 282.2 285.4 291.8 292.7   median 282.0
```

**HEAD is nominally 1.01x FASTER with the ranges fully overlapping** — the sweep's 1.03x was noise.
**No regression on the unindexed path.**

#### Why the unindexed path was at risk at all, stated so the check is repeatable

`rangeCap(sourceSize)` is evaluated at the `seedForStep(step, index, rangeCap(sourceSize))` call site
— i.e. **before** `seedForStep` returns early for an unindexed key — so an unindexed graph does pay
one comparison and one multiply per filter step per query. The GQL side does not: its
`rangeCountCap` sits inside the range branch, which only an indexed key reaches. That asymmetry is
exactly the kind of thing a reasoned argument gets wrong, which is why it was measured rather than
argued, and at ~1 ns it is invisible as the sweep shows.
