### Item 1763 — **FIRST MEASUREMENT OF THE GQL WRITE PATH, a surface no screen covers** — and ⚠️ **two instrument defects found in my own new probe before any number could be trusted.** Headline result: **not parameterising a write costs 1.44-1.60x**, and ~97% of a parameterised write is query machinery rather than the write

`runtime-profile-probe.mjs` has fifty-odd shapes and **every one is a READ**. Items 1732-1734
profiled the core write (`Vertex.setProperty`, ~121 ns), but a write issued as a QUERY goes through
parse, plan, the clause runner and the write executor first, and none of that had been measured.

#### ⚠️ DEFECT ONE: the first version was 99% SCAN, not write

```text
  shape        unindexed MATCH    indexed MATCH
  insert             5.93 µs          5.50      (no MATCH — unaffected, the control)
  set               74.67             5.82      12.8x
  insertedge       150.80            10.92      13.8x
```

A probe named "write" whose `set` row is 93% a 2,000-vertex scan would have produced a confident
target in the scan path. **This is item 1754's defect — the screens never index — reproduced in a
brand-new probe one tick after writing that item up.**

#### ⚠️ DEFECT TWO: a literal template is a parse-cache MISS per rep

With the MATCH fixed, the profile of a pure `INSERT` read: **`tokenize` 10.7%, `normalizeLiterals`
5.1%, `digits` 4.0%, `parseCached` 3.0% — ~23% PARSING.** The cause was the probe:
`INSERT (:P {n: 2001, k: 4})` is a **different string every rep**, and `parseCached` keys on text, so
every rep missed. A real application parameterises.

#### Both fixed, and the gap between them is the user-facing result

```text
  shape         literal text    parameterised    gap
  insert            5.62 µs          3.91       1.44x
  set               5.92             4.09       1.45x
  insertedge       10.50             6.56       1.60x
```

**Not parameterising a write costs 1.44-1.60x** — worth saying in the docs, and the kind of thing
only a probe that gets both halves right can state.

#### What the parameterised path leaves

`INSERT (:P {n: $n, k: $k})` has **no MATCH at all** and costs **3.91 µs**, against `RETURN 1 AS one`
at **103 ns** (item 1762) and the core write at **~121 ns** (item 1733). So ⚠️ ~~~97% of a parameterised GQL write is neither the parse nor the write~~ **WRONG, CORRECTED AT ITEM 1764** — it is the write executor, the clause runner and
index maintenance. That is the largest unexplained per-operation gap this stretch has found, and it
is OPEN: the cost is spread (as item 1761's flat mix was), so it needs an ablation ladder rather than
a profile to attribute.

**NEW PERMANENT INSTRUMENT — `packages/native/gql-write-probe.mjs`**: six shapes (three literal,
three parameterised), `INDEXED=0|1`, a per-round element-count assertion so a write that silently
did nothing cannot be the fastest arm, and a fixture rebuilt per batch because **a write probe cannot
reuse its fixture** — every rep mutates, which no read probe has to handle.

### Item 1764 — ⚠️ **TWO CORRECTIONS, AND ONE RE-PRICES A PENDING OWNER DECISION DOWNWARD: `#commitNormalized`'s 17.9% of an INSERT is NOT the freeze** (ablating it is FLAT), **and item 1733's "freeze = 30% of a write" does not reach a GQL write — it is ~1.07x of a `SET` and ~0% of an `INSERT`**

Item 1763 measured the GQL write path and concluded "~97% of a parameterised GQL write is neither
the parse nor the write". Profiled properly — 393 samples, 3.26 µs/write — that is wrong:

```text
  17.9%  #commitNormalized      5.6%  commitElementLabels    2.3%  normalizeProperties
  10.2%  (garbage collector)    4.6%  addEntry (prop index)  2.1%  plan
   7.1%  addVertex              3.8%  runInsert              2.1%  commitTransaction
```

**`plan` is 2.1%.** Element construction and indexing is ~42%, with GC's 10.2% being its
allocations. The error was comparing an INSERT's 3.91 µs against item 1733's **121 ns for
`setProperty`** — but an insert also builds a `Vertex`, commits labels, indexes the label, indexes
the property and commits a transaction. **An insert is not a property update**, and 1763's heading
is struck.

#### ⚠️ AND `#commitNormalized`'s 17.9% IS NOT THE FREEZE

The obvious reading — item 1733 priced `Object.freeze` at 30% of a property write, and here is
`#commitNormalized` at 17.9% of an insert — is wrong. Ablated, three alternated rounds, µs/write:

```text
  shape     base                 nofreeze             verdict
  insertp   2.35  2.40  2.45     2.47  2.33  2.42     FLAT
  setp      2.10  2.14  2.11     2.02  2.02  1.86     ~1.07x, DISJOINT
```

**Removing the freeze changes nothing on an INSERT.** The mechanism is visible once the branch is
read: on an insert the property box does not exist yet, so `#commitNormalized` takes its
`box === undefined` arm — allocating `{ bag }` and doing an **`elementProperties.set(id, box)`** per
insert. That Map insert, not the freeze, is what the frame holds. **A shared frame between two
shapes does not mean a shared cost**, which is `frame-attribution-trap` in a new form: the trap here
was not a getter but a function whose _body differs by path_.

#### WHAT THIS DOES TO THE LAZY-FREEZE DECISION, which is the part that matters

Item 1733 priced `Object.freeze` at **~30% of a property write** and left the lazy-freeze refactor to
the owner, and I have been restating that figure every tick since. **It does not survive contact with
a real query:**

```text
  raw `setProperty` microbench (item 1733)    ~30%
  a GQL `SET` through the query path          ~7%     (2.11 -> 2.02, disjoint)
  a GQL `INSERT`                               ~0%     (flat)
```

The 30% was measured against a 112 ns operation; a GQL `SET` carries ~2 µs of parse-cache lookup,
planning, clause running and index maintenance around it, so the same absolute saving is a seventh of
the share. **The lazy-freeze lever is worth ~7% of a user-visible write, not ~30%** — and it costs an
internal raw accessor at 12 `.bag` sites plus a changed immutability-enforcement contract. On these
numbers I would decline it, and the earlier framing overstated the case.

### Item 1765 — ⚠️ **MEMORY RETENTION, NOT SPEED: `elementProperties` and `elementLabels` are never deleted from, so every removed element's box survives — ~478 bytes per removed vertex, growing linearly with churn.** An empty graph holds **33.7 MB** after three 20k add/remove cycles. **Reported, not fixed: the removal site's comment makes the box's survival part of a correctness proof**

Found while pricing `#commitNormalized` on the insert path (item 1764). Across `Graph.ts`,
`Vertex.ts` and `Edge.ts` those two maps are only ever `new Map()`, `.get()` and `.set()` — **there
is no `.delete()` anywhere.**

#### Measured, forced GC, 20,000 vertices per round

```text
  state                    vertices   elementProperties   elementLabels   heapMb
  empty                           0                   0               0      5.0
  after add round 0          20,000              20,000          20,000     17.9
  after REMOVE round 0            0              20,000          20,000     15.6
  after add round 1          20,000              40,000          40,000     28.4
  after REMOVE round 1            0              40,000          40,000     25.3
  after add round 2          20,000              60,000          60,000     36.7
  after REMOVE round 2            0              60,000          60,000     33.7
```

**Both maps grow with elements EVER created, not with live ones.** An empty graph — `vertexCount`
and `edgeCount` both zero — holds **33.7 MB against 5.0 MB fresh**, i.e. **~28.7 MB retained for
nothing, ~478 bytes per removed vertex.** A long-running process that churns a million vertices
retains roughly half a gigabyte of boxes for elements that no longer exist.

#### ⚠️ IT IS NOT A WRONG ANSWER, and that is why nothing caught it

Checked before reporting: `#commitNormalized` always **REPLACES** `box.bag`, so an id that is
removed and re-added overwrites the stale bag rather than inheriting it. Every answer stays correct,
so no correctness test can see this — and it is memory rather than time, so no probe in the corpus
looks at it either. **It sits in the gap between the two kinds of test this repo has.**

#### ⚠️ AND IT IS KNOWN AT THE REMOVAL SITE, which is why this is reported rather than fixed

`removeVertex` says it outright: _"`evict` does not touch `#box` either, so the bag outlives the
vertex."_ That sentence is the **third of three facts in a correctness proof** — the transactional
undo captures `vertex.properties` **by reference** (item 335, to take the O(width) cost off a
transactional removal), and the bag's survival is what makes the reference a stable snapshot.

My reading is that `elementProperties.delete(id)` would not break it, because the undo closure holds
the **bag**, not the box, and a deleted map entry cannot invalidate a reference some closure already
owns. **But that is a reading, in an area where `label-index-vs-setter` records a WRONG ANSWER
reached through the public API**, and the repo's own rule is that a perf item is not the place to
change a settled invariant. So:

- **the retention is measured and documented here**, with the per-element cost;
- **the fix is a two-line `.delete()` in `removeVertex`/`removeEdge`** plus a test that a
  rollback after a removal still restores properties — the one case the proof above is about;
- **it is the owner's call**, because the downside if my reading is wrong is a silently wrong
  rollback, not a slow one.

**NEW PERMANENT INSTRUMENT — `packages/native/box-retention-probe.mjs`**, reporting counts _and_
heap, with `--expose-gc` detection so a reading that includes uncollected garbage says so instead of
overstating retention.

### Item 1766 — **THE GQL WRITE STATEMENT DECOMPOSED against the direct-API floor: `g.addVertex` is 1.99 µs and a GQL `INSERT` 2.67 (1.34x).** ⚠️ **Two misreadings caught on the way: `toArray` at 16.5% is NOT `Array.from` — it is the generator chain it PULLS — and the "5.3x" on a `SET` compares two different lookups**

Item 1764 left the write path's composition known but not bounded: how much of a GQL write is the
engine's own write, and how much is the statement around it? The only way to bound it is the direct
API, so the probe gained two direct arms.

```text
  operation                                              µs/write
  insertp        GQL INSERT, parameterised, indexed          2.67
  insertdirect   g.addVertex({ labels, properties })         1.99      ← the floor
  setp           GQL MATCH … SET, parameterised, indexed      2.17
  setdirect      getVertexById + setProperty                  0.41
```

**A GQL `INSERT` is 1.34x the direct call** — so 75% of it is the engine's own element construction,
which item 312 closed as a constant factor. **`g.addVertex` at 1.99 µs is itself ~18x a property
write** (item 1733's 112 ns), which is the Vertex construction, the label commit, the label index,
the property index, the box and the validation.

#### ⚠️ THE "5.3x" ON A SET IS NOT A FAIR COMPARISON, and saying so is the point

`setp` against `setdirect` is 2.17 against 0.41 — but those are **different lookups**:
`MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.n = $n` is a property **index seek plus a label check plus a pattern bind**,
while `getVertexById` is a **primary-key `Map.get`**. The honest statement is not "GQL adds 5.3x to a
write" but "expressing a lookup as a pattern over a non-id property costs ~1.76 µs more than an id
lookup", which is a different and much less alarming claim. **A floor has to do the same work to be
a floor.**

#### ⚠️ AND `toArray` AT 16.5% IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE

The largest frame in the `setp` profile is `(anonymous) toArray.mjs:4` — 16.5% — on a statement that
returns no rows, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks like a free win. Two reads settle it:

- `packages/fp`'s `toArray` is `boundary((iterable) => Array.from(iterable))`, and **`boundary` is a
  TYPE-ONLY brand**: its own doc says _"at runtime the value is unchanged"_ and the body is
  `fn as Boundary<F>`. So the wrapper costs nothing.
- `Array.from(iterable)` **drives the generator chain**, so the whole match pipeline's work is
  attributed to the frame that pulls it — `gremlin-values-is-the-floor`'s lesson ("the reduce is
  free; the cost is the generator chain") on the GQL side.

**So it is a puller, not a cost.** Read with that correction, a GQL `MATCH … SET` with a
single-row indexed match is:

```text
  ~37%  the MATCH        toArray 16.5 (as puller) + matchPattern 7.2 + hoistedMatch 7.2 + seedVertices 6.1
   ~7%  the WRITE        setProperty 4.1 + #commitNormalized 3.3
  ~13%  the STATEMENT    commitTransaction 3.6 + withBinding 3.3 + plan 3.1 + runLinearClauses 3.0
```

**The match dominates a single-row write by five to one.** That is the shape of the cost, and it is
not a defect — it is what pattern matching costs when the pattern selects one row.

### Item 1767 — **the EDGE insert gets its floor: a parameterised GQL edge `INSERT` is 5.83 µs against `g.addEdge`'s 2.47 (2.36x, the widest of the three write shapes).** ⚠️ **And `countEquals` at 7.1% of it is REFUTED as a lever — collapsing the gate's count into the seed's fetch measured ~3% with overlapping ranges and a control that moved as much**

```text
  operation                                                       µs/write

  insertedgedirect   getVertexById ×2 + g.addEdge                      2.47   ← the floor
```

**2.36x**, against 1.34x for the vertex insert — and the same caveat item 1766 insisted on applies
here and is larger: `insertedgep` seeks **both** endpoints by a property while the floor resolves
both by id, so the gap prices "two pattern-matched endpoints" and not "GQL overhead". Consistent
with item 1766's single-seek `SET` arithmetic (one seek plus statement ≈ 1.76 µs), two seeks plus
the statement ≈ 3.36 µs is close to twice it, which is what a per-endpoint seek cost predicts.

#### The profile, and the lever it nominated

340 samples at BATCH=60000:

```text
   8.5%  (garbage collector)      7.1%  countEquals          5.3%  propOf
   8.2%  indexEdgeLabel           6.2%  commitElementLabels  4.7%  seedVertices
   5.9%  visitRemaining           4.1%  get properties       4.1%  matchPattern
```

`countEquals` at 7.1% looked like a free win with a mechanism already in hand: `eqCandidate` builds
`count: idx.countEquals(key, v)` for the gate and `build: () => idx.equals(key, v)` for the seed, so
a **taken** exact seed does both for the same `(key, value)` — four `Map.get`s where two would do,
twice over on a two-endpoint pattern. The collapse is exactly answer-equivalent (`equals` returns
`undefined` in precisely the cases where `countEquals` returns `undefined` or `0`, and both arms
`?? 0`), so it is the kind of change that is easy to believe without measuring.

#### ⚠️ IT IS NOT THERE. Three alternated rounds, dist asserted per arm by count:

```text
  shape                      pre (3 rounds)        post (3 rounds)
  insertedgep   TARGET ×2    5.99  6.19  6.36      5.77  6.03  5.97
  setp          TARGET ×1    2.68  2.65  2.81      2.61  2.69  2.81
  insertp       CONTROL      2.72  2.64  2.70      2.59  2.84  2.57
```

Best case ~3% on the nominating shape, **ranges that overlap** (post's 6.03 is above pre's 5.99),
`setp` flat, and — the decisive reading — **the CONTROL moves as much as the target**, on a shape
that cannot reach `eqCandidate` at all. That is `frame-attribution-trap`'s signature, and the
deletion test is the strong form of it: one of the two lookups was removed **entirely** and nothing
moved, so the 7.1% is the frame absorbing its callers' work rather than the cost of the duplicate.
`countEquals` really is two `Map.get`s and a type check; a profile saying otherwise was saying
something else.

**So the surviving nomination from this profile is not the seed path but edge-write index
maintenance** — `indexEdgeLabel` 8.2% plus `commitElementLabels` 6.2%, ~15% between them, which is
on the direct-API side of the floor and therefore reachable without touching GQL at all.

### Item 1768 — **omitting an edge id costs 1.21x of a direct edge insert, and the key's LENGTH is free.** `rando` is `crypto.randomUUID()` at 181 ns, an equal-entropy base-36 is 1.38x faster and hand-rolled hex **5.0x worse** — so **NOT TAKEN: the id format is a collision-safety contract, for ~2% of a write.** ⚠️ **And my own micro's uniqueness assertion, inside the timed loop, compressed that 1.38x to 1.06x**

Item 1767's surviving nomination was edge-write index maintenance on the direct-API side. Profiling
the floor arm with no GQL in the picture (201 samples, BATCH=80000):

```text
  17.9%  indexEdgeLabel        10.4%  #commitNormalized      4.5%  insertEdge
  16.4%  getVertexById          9.0%  (garbage collector)    4.0%  set labels
  14.4%  commitElementLabels    5.0%  direct (the probe)     2.5%  rando
```

**`indexEdgeLabel` + `commitElementLabels` + `set labels` ≈ 36% is label handling** for a
single-label `['E']` — and it is already priced THREE times: item 140 collapsed its twelve lookups
to six and stopped resolving `edge.from.id`, item 312 priced the whole function at 810 ns across
seven hash operations, and **item 323 rejected threading the endpoint vertices in** (four alternated
rounds, 2621.0-2756.6 ms against 2670.2-2707.7, overlapping with the min slightly worse). Its own
doc-comment says what dominates is the inner per-label `Map`/`Set` work. I did not re-derive it a
fourth time; this item took the one frame nobody had priced instead.

#### Omitting an edge id costs 1.21x — and the obvious reading of that is wrong

`addEdge` without an `id` mints one. Three arms, each differing from its neighbour in exactly one
thing, with the explicit ids pre-generated outside the window:

```text
  arm                                             µs/write (3 rounds)
  insertedgedirect        mint + 36-char key      2.79  2.55  2.51
  insertedgedirectlongid  no mint + 36-char key   2.08  2.31  2.28   ← isolates the MINTING
  insertedgedirectid      no mint + 6-char key    2.27  2.06  2.31   ← isolates the KEY LENGTH
```

⚠️ **The two-arm version of this experiment is a trap, and I walked into it first.** Comparing a
minted UUID against `e${i}` gives 1.20x, but that arm changes TWO things — the minting and a key
that is 6 characters instead of 36, hashed into `edgesById` and both endpoint maps. The third arm
separates them: **36 characters against 6 is 2.08 against 2.06, i.e. FREE**, so the whole gap is the
minting, 2.51 against 2.08 with disjoint ranges — **~0.43 µs per edge.**

#### What `rando` is, and what it could be

`packages/utils`'s `rando` is `crypto.randomUUID()`, and it mints the default id for `Vertex`,
`Edge`, `VertexProperty` and `TreeNode`. Its own doc calls it "a not-cryptographically-secure random
string", which the implementation is not — but that mismatch is the doc's, not a licence to weaken
it: these ids reach snapshots and cross **sync peers**, so two clients minting independently must not
collide. Every arm below therefore holds ~122+ bits.

```text
  randomUUID   181.0 ns/id   len 36    the baseline
  base36       131.3 ns/id   len 25    1.38x faster, same entropy, bulk getRandomValues
  hex          899.3 ns/id   len 32    5.0x WORSE — hand-rolled formatting is not the win
```

**NOT TAKEN, and the reason is the payoff rather than the risk alone.** 50 ns off a 181 ns mint is
~2% of a 2.5 µs edge insert, against changing the id FORMAT — observable in snapshots, in the wire
format, in `id-space-contract.test.ts` and to every embedder that has stored an id. That is an
owner's call on a wire contract, and it is not worth asking for 2%. The useful half of the result is
the other direction: **hand-rolled formatting is 5.0x worse, so `crypto.randomUUID()` is already
near the floor** and nobody should try to beat it again. The real lever stays where callers already
control it — **pass an id** (1.21x), which is also what CLAUDE.md's bench rule asks for.

#### ⚠️ AND THE MICRO'S FIRST VERSION WAS CONFOUNDED BY ITS OWN CORRECTNESS CHECK

The uniqueness assertion — there because a minting function that returned a constant would win every
round — interned each id into a 300,000-entry `Set` **inside the timed loop**. That added ~330 ns of
string hashing to every arm:

```text
                 with the Set in the loop      assertion moved out
  randomUUID            439.6 ns                     181.0 ns
  base36                413.2 ns  (1.06x)             131.3 ns  (1.38x)
```

A cost common to all arms does not cancel — **it compresses ratios toward 1x**, and the reported
conclusion would have been "no alternative wins" when one wins by 1.38x. The fix is to run the
assertion as a separate unmeasured pass and leave a one-char sink in the loop. Same family as item
1766's puller and the frame-attribution trap: **the instrument was measuring itself.**

first, which is why it is run unpiped. No engine source changed: the probe gained two arms and
`packages/native/rando-micro.mjs` is kept.

### Item 1769 — ⚠️ **THE GREMLIN BENCH'S `V().out().id()` ROW IS NOT A MISSING FUSION: isolated, the one-hop is 40.2-45.7 ms against the two-hop's 147.2-163.6, i.e. 3.5x FASTER, where the sweep reports 208.4 against 132.1.** And the row next to it, `V().out().values(age)`, is **BIMODAL ACROSS PROCESSES (77.9-138.0 ms, 1.77x)** — so no claim under ~1.8x can rest on it

`bun run bench:gremlin` showed a two-hop beating its own prefix: `V().out().id()` at 208.4 ms and
`V().out().out().id()` at 132.1, on a fixture where the second hop multiplies the rows five-fold.
That is a strong shape of evidence for a missing fusion, and items 877-882 make it plausible — they
record that `V().out()` and `V().out().id()` once had no fused walk while `values(k)` did, which
made ADDING a step 1.9x faster (item 880).

**It is not that.** Both fusions claim `id`: `hop-values.ts:187` for the one-hop and
`hop-chain-values.ts:711` for the chain item 1614 built. So the reading was tested rather than
explained, with a new instrument — **one shape per process** (item 1640's lesson, which found
"1.9-2.0x engine-vs-floor gaps" to be substantially the instrument), **row counts asserted**, and
the fixture's **distinct out-targets per vertex** checked rather than its out-degree:

```text
  shape                     rows        min ms (separate processes)
  V().out(T).id()           1,000,000   45.7  42.6  42.3  43.1  40.2     tight, 1.14x spread
  V().out(T).out(T).id()    5,000,000   163.6 159.9 147.2                tight
```

**The one-hop is 3.5x FASTER, disjoint and tight — the inversion does not reproduce at all.** Note
what that means for the sweep's numbers: its two-hop figure (132.1) is in the right neighbourhood of
the isolated 147-164, while its one-hop figure (208.4) is **~4.5x** the isolated 40-46. My fixture is
generated in-process where the bench's is deserialized from NDJSON, so I am NOT claiming to have
fully explained the 4.5x — only that the ORDERING the sweep reports is an artefact, and that is
enough to retire the target.

#### ⚠️ The neighbouring row is bimodal across PROCESSES, which is new

Five processes, identical configuration, same binary:

```text
  V().out(T).values(age)   79.6  77.9  138.0  93.5  80.9      ← 1.77x, and it is a MODE
  V().out(T).id()          45.7  42.6   42.3  43.1  40.2      ← 1.14x
```

The outlier is not a blip inside one run: process 3's **whole series** is shifted (138-198 ms against
77-154 for its neighbours), so the process picks a mode and keeps it. `id()` on the same fixture does
not do this. CLAUDE.md already records bimodality for `nullif` and `filterchain` WITHIN a process;
this is the same hazard one level up, and min-of-N inside a single process cannot see it.

**So the practical rule: `V().out(T).values(k)` needs min-across-PROCESSES, and the Gremlin bench —
one process — can land in either mode.** A 1.5x reading on that row is inside its own spread.

#### What was NOT concluded, and why

The isolated numbers invite a per-row comparison — 1-hop `values` at 80.4 ns/row against 2-hop at
34.5 — and at equal row counts it looks like 7.2x. **Both readings are confounded and neither is
reported as a result.** Rows are `N·Fᵏ`, so holding the row count equal while varying the hop count
forces the graph to shrink (the 2-hop arm then runs on a 5x smaller, fully cache-resident graph), and
holding the graph equal forces the row counts apart. A size sweep settles the one thing it can:
per-row cost **RISES** with scale (42.9 → 52.9 → 55.5 → 80.4 ns/row from 125k to 1M rows), so there
is **no large fixed cost** to amortize — the rise is the cache transition CLAUDE.md puts between 200k
and 1M. Add the 1.77x process mode on top and this comparison cannot carry a 2x claim, let alone 7x.

### Item 1770 — ⚠️ **A 4.0x CEILING ON THE BIGGEST TS GREMLIN ROW, AND THE CAUSE OF ITEM 1769'S PROCESS BIMODALITY: `far.properties[valueKey]` is 60 of the 80 ns/row of `V().out(T).values(k)`, and ablating it collapses the 1.77x mode lottery to a 1.11x spread.** ⚠️ **FIVE candidate mechanisms REFUTED — not the freeze, not the variable key, not locality, not a stale box, not deopts or GC. The mechanism is OPEN; do not build against a guess**

Item 1769 found `V().out(T).values(age)` bimodal across processes (77.9-138.0 ms, ~27% of runs slow:
6 of 22). A 1.77x slow mode is a 1.77x regression for whoever lands in it, so it is a target, and
diffing eight profiles by mode says exactly where it lives. Converting percentages to absolute (the
slow run is 1.7x longer) is the step that makes the diff readable:

```text
  frame                      fast      slow     absolute ratio
  pick                       47.1 ms   83.2 ms  1.77x  — tracks the total, i.e. neutral
  get properties             15.3 ms   43.8 ms  2.90x  — the only frame that BLOWS UP
  drain                      13.9 ms    6.6 ms  0.47x  — CHEAPER, i.e. attribution moved into pick
```

#### The ablation, which is the whole result

`hop-values.ts:181` is `pick = (far) => far.properties[valueKey]`. Replacing it with
`(far) => (far === undefined ? undefined : 1770)` keeps the row count, the `drops` filter and the
`acc.push` identical and removes only the property read — and because `pick(edge.to)` evaluates its
argument at the call site, it does NOT remove the `edge.to` resolution. Eight processes each:

```text
  real      79.7  93.4  83.8  139.0  80.4  80.5  81.0  93.5     ← 1.75x spread, bimodal
  ablated   19.7  19.5  20.6   21.0  20.5  21.1  19.3  21.4     ← 1.11x spread, NO modes
```

**So the property read is 60 of the ~80 ns/row in the fast mode — 4.0x — and 7.0x of the slow one.
And the mode lottery is CAUSED by it: remove the read and the bimodality is gone entirely.** That is
the largest single ceiling measured in this family, on the row that is already the biggest absolute
TS/native gap in the Gremlin bench.

#### ⚠️ FIVE MECHANISMS REFUTED, each with its number

A 4.0x with an obvious-looking cause is exactly where this audit has gone wrong before, so each
candidate was measured rather than argued:

1. **Deopts** — `--trace-deopt`, six processes: 12-13 deopts in BOTH modes, 1-2 mentioning
   `properties`. Identical. The slow mode is not a deoptimization.
2. **GC** — `--trace-gc`, six processes: 73-76 collections and exactly 3 major in every run,
   regardless of mode.
3. **The freeze.** `Vertex.properties` returns the graph's live bag, frozen, and item 1734 refuted
   "the freeze costs the later reads" for CONSTANT keys. Re-tested for this load shape:
   **frozen 1.45 ns/read against plain 1.47** — free.
4. **The variable key.** Item 1450 found "the whole win came from CONSTANT property keys", and a
   closure-captured `valueKey` cannot use a constant-key IC. Measured: **variable 1.45 ns against
   constant 1.44** — free. (Which is just as well: specializing on a literal key needs runtime
   codegen, and `no-runtime-codegen` forbids that outright, so that win is UNREACHABLE, not pending.)
5. **A stale box.** The getter caches per INSTANCE (`this.#box ??= …elementProperties.get(this.#id)`),
   so fresh `Vertex` objects per row would mean a 200k-entry `Map.get` every row — the right order of
   magnitude. Measured instead: the walk yields **CANONICAL instances, 10,000 of 10,000, 2,000
   distinct objects for 2,000 distinct ids.** The box is cached; amortized that is ~10 ns/row, not 60.
6. **Locality.** 200,000 bags read in a fixed random permutation — the walk's adjacency-order shape —
   measures **3.5 ns/read** against 1.45 sequential. Real, and still **17x short of 60 ns.**

#### What is left, stated as a HYPOTHESIS and not a finding

The arithmetic points at **dependent-load depth**: the micro chases one pointer (`bags[idx]` → key)
where the walk chases four (`edge` → `to` getter → `Vertex` → `#box` → `bag` → key), and four
dependent misses at ~15 ns is the right size. **That is untested.** It predicts a layout change
(reaching the bag in fewer hops) rather than anything about freezing, keys or ICs — and item 1733's
lesson is that a mechanism asserted without an ablation gets refuted by the next one. So: **the 4.0x
is measured and real, the mechanism is OPEN, and the next item owes an experiment that varies chase
depth with everything else held constant.** Do not build the layout change against this paragraph.
